en: Salutations to Śambhu, whose nature is eternal bliss, knowledge, and sovereignty; he who brings to fruition the intentions of all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
I bow to Bhavānī, whose tresses are adorned by the crescent moon,
and who is a river of nectar that extinguishes the fever of worldly existence.
Homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas, whose feet are inlaid with the rays of the crest-jewels of gods and asuras, and who is the sun to the darkness of obstacles.
Victorious are the words of the sage Akṣapāda, purified by the shouts of "Well said! bestowed by the Conqueror of Cities, and serving as the source of the jewels of logic.
Let the virtuous plunge into this flowing stream of eloquence, which is eager to savor the exploration of the ocean of Akṣapāda’s thought.
May the intellect of the wise, though weary from tasting the flavors of various virtues,
favor this labor of ours with even a mere glance.
This supreme essence has been extracted from the forests of the medicinal herbs of logic;
it is like butter drawn from the milk of investigative inquiry.
Or, we are not capable of conceiving of any entirely new subject matter here;
let only the diversity of the arrangement of words be considered.
Having previously fashioned their crests many times with those very same flowers, they still feel a sense of curiosity toward a garland of unprecedented design.
Or rather, virtuous people rejoice even in a request that yields no material gain,
for they are untrained in the practice of rejecting the pleas of those who seek their favor.
Therefore, let this *Nyāyamañjarī* be placed for a long time upon the ears of the discerning, who are intent on sporting in the garden of the realm of speech.
For the vast tree of Nyāya, composed by Akṣapāda,
is replete with a profusion of fruits dripping with the thick essence of nectar.
We, with our feeble movements, are as if paralyzed by the act of ascending it; we are not even capable of beholding the full extent of its splendor.
This labor of exposition has been undertaken as but a mere fraction of a single part of that [work];
may the virtuous, who are affectionate toward those who have sought refuge in them, favor it.
They rejoice even at countless [calamities]; wonderful is their conduct!
The virtuous rejoice because of virtues; wonderful is their conduct!
Fortunate are those who, while revealing their own compositions, behold the faces of the virtuous, their cheeks marked by horripilation arising from the contemplation of the ultimate truth.

In this world, persons acting with foresight, desiring the attainment of human goals and believing that such attainment is impossible without knowing the means to achieve them, first seek to understand those very means.
The path to human goals is twofold, distinguished as the seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).

Regarding the seen object—such as eating, where the status of a means is understood through positive and negative concomitance established by the long-standing linguistic usage of elders—activity occurs without any dependence on scripture.
For a scripture is not required for such things as "one who is dirty should bathe" or "one who is hungry should eat.
However, regarding the invisible realms of heaven and liberation alone, for people whose vision is lost in the blinding darkness of innate delusion, scripture itself is the light.
It alone is the divine eye for people like us to perceive all correct means; it is not the case that there are other means, such as the knowledge born of yogic concentration, as there are for yogins.
Therefore, a person such as ourselves must certainly master the treatise itself.
And that is of fourteen kinds, which the learned call the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Among those, there are four Vedas:
the first is the Atharvaveda, the second the Ṛgveda, the third the Yajurveda, and the fourth the Sāmaveda.

These four Vedas have as their very nature the instruction on the means for accomplishing the goals of human life, according to such scriptural passages as "One who desires heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice" and "The Self is to be known."

The Smṛti scriptures, too, as codified by Manu and others, are seen to teach only the means for achieving human goals (puruṣārtha), such as the Aṣṭakā rites, the tonsure ceremony (śikhā-karma), and the construction of water-stalls (prapā).

Furthermore, it will be explained in the examination of the function of injunctions that even those actions whose results are not explicitly heard possess results; for every purpose of the scripture culminates in a human goal and does not rest in its own form alone.
Even through the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, by means of descriptions such as narratives and the like, the Vedic meaning itself is for the most part elaborated;
as it has been said: "One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas."

"The Veda fears one of little learning [thinking], 'He will deceive me. Thus, because the Vedas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras possess by their very nature the instruction of the means for achieving the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), they constitute branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). The auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*)—grammar, ritual manuals (*kalpa*), astronomy (*jyotiṣa*), phonetics (*śikṣā*), prosody (*chandas*), and etymology (*nirukta*)—attain the status of branches of knowledge by means of explaining words and other elements useful for understanding the meaning of the Veda.
Their designation as "auxiliaries" itself reveals their subordination to it.

Since the meaning of Vedic sentences cannot be determined without critical inquiry (*vicāra*), Mīmāṃsā—which consists of the investigation of the meaning of Vedic sentences—attains the status of a branch of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) by functioning as the procedural method (*itikartavyatā*) for the Veda itself. Thus says Bhaṭṭa [or Bhāṭṭa]: "When Dharma is being cognized through the Veda acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*), Mīmāṃsā shall fulfill the requirement of the procedural part (*itikartavyatābhāga*)."

For this very reason, Mīmāṃsā is not counted as a seventh limb [of the Veda], because it is closely related to the Veda and constitutes a single part of it. For it is only when verbal testimony is assisted by investigation that it is capable of awakening an understanding that is free from expectancy regarding its own meaning.

The *Nyāyavistara*, however, serves as the foundational pillar for all branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), because it is the cause for protecting the authority of the Vedas. For if the authority of the Vedas were undermined by the fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*) devised by wicked logicians, virtuous people, their confidence weakened, would they ever take interest in the performance of Vedic rites—which require great expenditure of wealth, effort, and so forth?
Or, if the Master [the Veda] were to fade away, what purpose would there be for his retinue, the branches of knowledge such as Mīmāṃsā and the rest?

Therefore, this treatise called *Nyāyavistara*, taught by the one whose feet are Akṣapāda, is the foremost among the branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), for it is the foundation upon which all sciences are established; it is capable of providing instruction in reasoning that instills a firm conviction in the authority of the Veda by means of crushing all wicked logicians without exception.

The status of being a *vidyāsthāna* (field of knowledge) for the fourteen sciences is said to consist precisely in their being the means for attaining the knowledge that accomplishes the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to the act of knowing; and this is not the knowledge of jars and such things, but rather the knowledge of the means for accomplishing the goals of human life. A "place" (*sthāna*) for knowledge means its support or its means.

And this status of being a means for the thorough comprehension of the means for accomplishing the goals of human life belongs to some [sciences] directly and to others through the mediation of further means.
These are called the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*),

as it has been said: "The Vedas, together with the Purāṇas, Logic (*tarka*), Hermeneutics (*mīmāṃsā*), the Treatises on Law (*dharmaśāstra*), and the Auxiliary Sciences (*aṅga*), are the fourteen branches of knowledge and of Dharma" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.3).
It is also stated elsewhere: "The four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, Nyāyavistara, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra—these indeed are the fourteen sciences (vidyās)."
That which was designated by the word *tarka* (reasoning) in the former [passage] and by the word *nyāyavistara* (the expansion of logic) in the latter is this very treatise.
Logic (*nyāya*), which is reasoning (*tarka*) or inference (*anumāna*), is precisely what is expounded in this treatise.

For what kind of skill in the instruction of inference do the Sāṅkhyas and the Arhats—that is, the Kṣapaṇakas—possess? To what extent can the authority of the Veda be protected by their logic? Thus, they are not worthy of being counted here.

To what extent does their logic uphold the authority of the Veda? For although the Buddhists carry their necks high, exulting in their proficiency in plunging into the path of inference, nevertheless, since their reasoning is not in contradiction with the Veda, how could it be included among the branches of knowledge such as the Vedas?
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate at every step just what kind of skill in inference the Śākyas actually possess.
As for the wretched Cārvākas, they are simply to be rejected; what occasion is there here to take account of their trivial logic?

Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas are indeed our own followers. Thus, even though this "Sixfold Logic" (ṣaṭtarkī) is well known among the people, it is this very [work] that is designated by the terms "Logic" (tarka), "Systematic Reasoning" (nyāya), and "Exposition" (vistara).

This very *ānvīkṣikī* is counted as the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*) among the four branches of knowledge, according to the verse: "The science of inquiry (*ānvīkṣikī*), the triple Veda (*trayī*), commerce (*vārtā*), and the eternal science of government (*daṇḍanīti*)."

Anvīkṣā means the subsequent investigation (anvīkṣaṇa) of that which has been perceived through perception and scripture; its meaning is inference (anumāna). The science (śāstra) that elucidates this is Anvīkṣikī.

Now, if there are only four branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), how is it that fourteen are shown? This is not a contradiction; for since *vārttā* (economics) and *daṇḍanīti* (statecraft) have only visible purposes, they are unworthy of being counted among the group of sciences that teach all human goals (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, because the *trayī* (the three Vedas) and *anvīkṣikī* (logic/philosophy) are specified therein, there are indeed only fourteen branches of knowledge.

Now, if the purpose of the extensive exposition of logic (*nyāyavistara*) is indeed the determination of the authority of the Vedas, then this is redundant; for that [authority] is already established through Mīmāṃsā alone. Indeed, in that [Mīmāṃsā], just as there is an investigation into the meaning [of the Veda], an investigation into its authority has also been performed. True, but that [investigation into authority] is incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*); in that context, the primary focus is indeed the investigation into the meaning.
For these sciences have distinct methodologies;

this [science of grammar] is a science of the meaning of sentences, not a science of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsakas are not skilled in discerning the path capable of properly safeguarding the authority of the Veda.
We shall indeed say that they have wandered onto the deceptive appearance of a path whose movement is obstructed by a thicket of thorns consisting of fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*).

For even perception and the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not attain the status of being valid without the firmness provided by corroboration from another means of valid cognition; how much less so this word, whose operation is dependent upon them? For the capacity of a word to convey meaning, when aided by convention (*samaya*), is independent; however, regarding the definitive determination of whether the object is as it is or otherwise, its dependence on the person [who utters it] is unavoidable.
Therefore, it is precisely because it is spoken by a reliable person that verbal testimony becomes a means of valid cognition, and not otherwise; this will be demonstrated in this very treatise.

Now, one might ask: before Akṣapāda, how was the authority of the Veda ascertained? This is a very small matter to raise: before Jaimini, by whom was the meaning of the Vedas explained? Before Pāṇini, by whom were words derived? Before Piṅgala, by whom were the meters composed? These sciences have been in existence since the beginning of creation, just like the Vedas.

However, with the intention of speaking both concisely and in detail, various authors are mentioned here and there. [Objection: But surely the authority of the Veda is established beyond doubt, and the virtuous accept this; so what is the use of effort in investigating it? [Reply: No, because it is for the purpose of removing doubt and error.
For the commencement of the treatise is directed toward one whose mind is either doubtful or mistaken regarding the authority of the Veda.
Indeed, the Mīmāṃsā is not presented for one who already knows the meaning of the Vedas.

As it has been said: "The composition of the Sūtras and their commentary is not desired from anyone other than those who know the Vedas. Furthermore, there are four types of persons: the ignorant, the doubtful, the mistaken, and the one of certain mind.

Among these, this Sage—who possesses a certain mind—produces knowledge for the ignorant through this treatise, destroys the doubt of the doubtful, and dispels the error of the mistaken; thus, the undertaking of the treatise is appropriate for them.

But from what did this Sage’s state of having a settled mind arise? It is said: he is indeed one whose mind is settled, whether that be due to the power of asceticism, the propitiation of deities, or the study of other treatises.

What does this matter? One might then argue: "From those very same other treatises, the realization of reality will also come about for people like us; so what is the use of the treatise composed by Akṣapāda? This has already been answered: the composition of a treatise is fruitful because of the intention to present [the subject] both concisely and in detail.
It has been stated that men possess diverse mental dispositions;
therefore, the Teacher composed this work so that it might bear fruit for those whose ignorance, doubt, and error are dispelled by this very [treatise].

In this regard, the first aphorism is as follows: “From the knowledge of the truth concerning the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), established tenets (*siddhānta*), the members of a syllogism (*avayava*), reasoning (*tarka*), ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), discussion (*vāda*), disputation (*jalpa*), cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) [occurs]. (NS 1.1.1) Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of commencing this initial statement? What is the point of this question? If the treatise (*śāstra*) is indeed to be commenced, then since speech proceeds sequentially, the composition of the second and subsequent statements would be justified; thus, the very act of composing the work would be impossible [if there were no initial statement].
He said: "Indeed, it is not that I do not know this; rather, let only that which stands as the subject to be explained in the treatise be explained.

Why, at the outset, is there the mention of its subject matter and purpose? It is replied: "The opening statement regarding the subject matter and purpose must be employed for the sake of achieving enthusiasm in the stream of listeners."
Wise men, whose efforts have ceased due to the absence of knowledge regarding the subject matter and its fruit, would not take care to listen even to a small work.

For what wise person indeed would engage in an action that concerns an unknown subject matter and serves no purpose? As Bhaṭṭa has said: "For of every treatise or even of any action whatsoever, as long as the purpose has not been stated, by whom would it be undertaken? Now, one must consider: how is the initial understanding of the purpose for listeners obtained—is it from this very sentence, or through reasoning? First, how can a sentence whose authority is not yet established be capable of determining the purpose?
Or, if activity were to proceed from doubt, it would be the same regarding the meaning of the Veda; thus, the scripture would not need to be commenced.

The understanding of the purpose [of a treatise] through reasoning is possible only when the entire treatise has been studied, and not otherwise; thus, if one's engagement [with the treatise] were preceded by that understanding, there would be a circularity: the thorough knowledge of the purpose would result from the mastery of the treatise, and the mastery of the treatise would result from the thorough knowledge of the purpose. Furthermore, engagement in listening occurs due to doubt regarding the meaning. For in the case of the Veda, whose authority is not yet established, it is not reasonable to proceed with its performance amidst great hardships if there is a suspicion that it might be purposeless.

It is appropriate to set out upon a path that is easy to traverse— requiring little expense of wealth, little exertion, and no separation from loved ones— and which yields noble fruits with minimal effort.
The wise, merely by hearing it for a few days,
will know whether this scripture is fruitful or of little practical use.
If, however, a subtle scrutiny is applied here at the very first attempt,
it leads to the total destruction of all that ought to be done.
For a person who, being afflicted, consults a physician and then fails to follow what was prescribed,
and who remains full of doubt regarding that treatment, will only suffer an increase in his disease.
Therefore, having understood from the opening statement both the subject matter and the purpose,
one should cultivate a respectful interest in listening to that treatise through the conviction in their possibility.
By those who explain the opening statement as follows: "A sentence whose word-meanings are not syntactically connected is not to be accepted, like the sentence 'Ten pomegranates' (*daśadāḍima*).
Even a sentence whose word-meanings are connected is not to be accepted if it lacks a purpose, like the sentence deliberating on whether the teeth of a crow are white or black.

Therefore, since no purpose—which is the pervader of acceptability—is perceived here, it is to be disregarded. Thus, the opponent, objecting by means of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), has stated that the meaning of the opening statement is the expression of such a purpose and so forth.
By the very demonstration of that, the doubt is dispelled, since the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) has thereby been refuted.

As for what some maintain—that the first sentence produces a doubt regarding the purpose (arthasaṃśaya), which is another name for reasoning (tarka) or appropriateness (aucitya), as the cause for engaging [with the work]—that too occurs only by way of stating the purpose.

For it is either a doubt or a cognition of probability concerning the purpose that serves as a factor for engagement, and thus it must be produced; therefore, the function of the opening sentence in producing that [doubt] is precisely the statement of the purpose.
As for the doubt itself, it arises from the actual state of things, given the observation of the twofold nature of human statements.
However, because of his purity, good conduct, integrity, and so forth, people also develop a conviction regarding him as being trustworthy;
therefore, it is well said that the opening statement is intended solely to demonstrate the purpose [of the treatise].
And that which is a factor for the listener's engagement should be stated first;
moreover, there is nothing that incites engagement other than the knowledge of the purpose.
The statement of the subject matter must indeed be made for the purpose of establishing the goal to be accomplished by it and for the sake of focusing the attention of the listeners.
The relationship, however, which is implied by the sense, pertains to the result, the treatise, and the subject matter;
since it is established by the mention of those [three], it is not stated explicitly.

The relationship between the subject matter and the treatise is characterized by that of the signified and the signifier; the relationship between the purpose of the treatise and the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) is characterized by that of the means and the end to be accomplished; both are established simply through the mention of their substratum.

The subjects to be explained, however, are the sixteen categories beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and ending with the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), which were indicated in the first aphorism; their essential nature will be described further below.
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception and the rest, are those which accomplish the determination of objects.
That which is to be determined by them—the self and so forth—is the object of cognition (*prameya*). Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is the deliberation upon various possible meanings.
The purpose (*prayojana*) is the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful, as well as the means for achieving those ends.
An example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the determination of the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) of the logical reason (*hetu*).
A tenet (*siddhānta*) is an object possessing both general and particular characteristics that is accepted on the basis of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The members (*avayava*) are the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, which constitute parts of the statement of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). Reasoning (*tarka*) is the cognition of probability regarding a doubtful matter, arising from the observation of a cause favorable to one of the two possible sides. Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is the realization of reality born from the apprehension of the means of proof (*sādhana*).
Discourse whose fruit is the determination of the subject matter regarding one free from passion is *vāda* (debate);
whereas discourse whose fruit is the examination of a person's skill is *jalpa* (wrangling);
a specific form of that is *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).
Fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are those which, though lacking the nature of a reason, appear as if they were reasons.
Sophistry (*chala*) is the refutation of a statement through a misinterpretation of its meaning.
Futile rejoinders (*jāti*) are counter-arguments that consist primarily of mere reflections upon the reason.
The appearance of a real object as it is not, and the appearance of something contrary [to reality], constitute points of defeat.
In this regard, following the indications of the sūtras whose definitions will be stated hereafter, some words are to be analyzed with singular endings and some with plural endings.

The analysis of the *pramāṇas*, *avayavas*, and *hetvābhāsas* should be shown with plural endings, while for the remaining items it should be with singular endings, because they are indicated as such in the definition-sūtras.
In this way, the identity of subject matter between the enumeration (*uddeśa*) and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is most clearly demonstrated.
The compound *dvandva* is used in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).
In the phrase "the reality (*tattva*) of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth," the genitive case is used in the sense of a mere relation.

In the phrases "knowledge of reality" (*tattvasya jñānam*) and "attainment of the supreme good" (*niḥśreyasasyādhigamaḥ*), the two genitives are used in the sense of the object (*karman*), because reality is the object insofar as it is being known, and the supreme good is the object insofar as it is being attained.

But if it is explained in this way, since the word *tattva* (reality) would be dependent on words such as *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition), it would lack semantic independence (*asamartha*), and thus a compound would not be possible;
for they say that "that which is dependent is semantically independent.

Nor is this [the word *tattva*] the principal member (*pradhāna*) upon which the dependence rests—such that a compound could occur even when the principal member is dependent, as in the case of *rājapuruṣaḥ śobhanaḥ* ("a beautiful king's man")—because a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the final member as its principal element.

In this context, knowledge alone is the primary reality (tattva) and the other factors are secondary; therefore, as in the expression "the king's man" when the king is prosperous, a non-compound (asamāsa) is more appropriate.

[Objection: But surely knowledge (*jñāna*) also necessarily depends upon means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, since it has those as its objects; [Response: No, because by the word "reality" (*tattva*), this [knowledge] is rendered free of expectancy, as in the expression "knowledge of reality" (*tattvasya jñānam*). Now, it is reality itself that remains dependent, [the question being] "of what is this reality?
Therefore, since reality—being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*)—is dependent, there can be no compound at all.

Suspecting this, some have explained *tattva* and *jñāna* as a *karmadhāraya* compound [meaning "knowledge that is itself reality"]. However, that is incorrect, because knowledge does not possess an internal distinction between being real or unreal;
rather, whether cognitions are such or otherwise is determined by their objects.
Thus, this knowledge has reality as its object, but it does not possess reality as its own inherent nature.

Furthermore, what is this so-called "reality" (tattva)? It is said to be that which serves as the basis for the application of a word—the nature of an existent or non-existent entity as definitively established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Its state of being is "reality," and that is determined by knowledge.
That knowledge which discerns that [object] is called "knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñāna*).
Furthermore, the nature of that knowledge itself must likewise be discerned by another cognition.
Since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth have their reality determined, the use of the negative particle (*vyatireka*) in the expression is indeed appropriate.
Nor is it appropriate to provide a different explanation merely because of the contingency of non-compounding;
for such compounds are frequently observed without any loss of semantic capacity, as in the case of "Devadatta’s teacher’s family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*).
Whether a word is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) or not is no cause for [preventing] compounding.
A compound occurs when there is identity of meaning with the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), and that [identity] certainly exists here;
even grammarians indeed form such compounds, as in: "Now, this is the instruction on words—of which words? Of both worldly and Vedic words."
Therefore, the explanation of the three genitive cases exactly as stated [in the Bhāṣya] alone is faultless.

Now, it must be explained how the knowledge of the reality of the sixteen categories (*ṣoḍaśapadārtha*) serves as the cause for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Furthermore, since this treatise is intended for the purpose of establishing the authority of the Veda, why should one merely teach that much, rather than composing a voluminous manual on the sixteen categories? It is said in reply: we shall demonstrate that the knowledge of the twelve kinds of objects of cognition (*prameya*), beginning with the self (*ātman*) and ending with liberation (*apavarga*), is indeed the direct means for achieving liberation, even though it is not useful for the knowledge of other things.
Since the world-process, which is rooted in that [ignorance], ceases when false knowledge is dispelled by the knowledge of reality, the object of valid cognition (prameya) must certainly be accepted.
However, the comprehension that the self and other objects of cognition are the means for attaining liberation is based solely upon scripture.
The determination of its validity is based upon inference;
and its mark, which is invariably concomitant with it, is observed to be the fact of being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*).
Perception is employed for the apprehension of that [invariable] relation;
what other means is there for crossing the great ocean of infinite regress?
Since it is determined that the word spoken by a reliable person is a means of valid cognition, because one perceives the result directly in statements such as those of Āyurveda.
Since comparison (upamāna) is sometimes useful with respect to an object of action, all four types of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), like their objects of cognition (prameya), must be taught.

However, categories such as doubt and the rest, although they are included within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) as the case may allow, are taught separately because they serve as the causes for the operation of logic (*nyāya*).
And it has been shown that logic attains its utility for human goals by way of establishing the authority of the Veda.
In that regard, reasoning does not operate upon an object that is neither unperceived nor already determined;
rather, it operates upon what is doubted. Therefore, doubt is a constituent part of reasoning.
People do not employ a logical argument without having a purpose in mind;
furthermore, the example serves as the basis for grasping the relationship [between the reason and the probandum] in that context.
The established conclusion (siddhānta) also, by bringing about the dharma [to be proven], removes the fallacy of the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhatā) and sets the reasoning (nyāya) in motion.

Now, one might object: "By using the term 'doubt' (saṃśaya), which denotes the subject (dharmin) that is the object of the formal argument (nyāya) as being doubtful, the fallacy of the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi) has already been excluded. This is true; however, since it will be shown that in some cases the formal argument proceeds even without doubt regarding the subject, there is no rule restricting the formal argument to a single subject that is doubted. Therefore, the established tenet (siddhānta) must also be stated.
The members [of an argument] are useful for another person when the reasoning is being stated;
therefore, proponents of logic call that "inference for the sake of others" (parārthānumāna).

[Objection: But surely, by means of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the example (*udāharaṇa*), their respective referents—the tenet (*siddhānta*) and the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*)—are already understood; what is the point of mentioning them separately? [Response: If that were so, then since the referent of the member called the "reason" (*hetu*) is established by that very member, inference (*anumāna*) too should not be stated separately. [Objection: Let it be so; what is lost? [Response: Not so. When the principle (*nyāya*) as the referent is to be defined, there is an occasion for the members (*avayava*) which are its designators; therefore, those members deserve to be explained separately. Otherwise, the treatise would be concluded with the mere instruction on the members alone.

Reasoning (*tarka*) is taught separately because, by producing a weakening of one side among two equally plausible sides that have been made objects of a doubtful cognition, it favors the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) directed toward the other side; thus, by effecting the removal of the opposing position with ease, it brings about the purification of the path.
And this [reasoning] will be employed in debate in order to demonstrate the purity of one's intention (*āśaya*).

Since a logical inquiry (nyāya) does not reach its conclusion without a determination regarding one of the two opposing positions, determination is the motivator of that inquiry by virtue of being the cause for its cessation;
otherwise, who indeed would undertake a logical inquiry that lacks a finality and fails to attain its fruit?
Is it not the case that since this is already covered by the term "knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñāna*), the "ascertainment" (*nirṇaya*) need not be mentioned separately?

For ascertainment is indeed just knowledge of reality; this is true, however, the knowledge of the reality of the sixteen categories can also be produced by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It does not, in itself, serve as the cause for the cessation of inquiry (*nyāya*).
This determination, however, which arises from the refinement of the path of proof and refutation, cannot be obtained without separately including it as the cause for the cessation of that debate.
[Objection: But surely this desired determination will be obtained from the word "inference" itself;

for inference is the cognition of the probandum (liṅgin) from the probans (liṅga) which is [logically] connected, and that very [cognition] is the determination. [Response: That is incorrect; determination is the fruit of inference, not the inference itself.
Since the cause is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), if the determination were not taken as the result, that inference would be fruitless and incomplete.

In that case, this *nirṇaya* (ascertainment) will be implied by both the terms "knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñāna*) and "inference" (*anumāna*), because inference culminates in the knowledge of reality; for its culmination in that state cannot be established without the inclusion of *nirṇaya*, since there is the possibility of a semblance of knowledge of reality arising from a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*).

[Objection: Since inference is preceded by doubt, it follows by implication that it must necessarily culminate in a definitive conclusion (nirṇaya); thus, the term "definitive conclusion" is already covered by the terms "doubt," "inference," and "knowledge of reality. [Reply: Not so; for even though inference is preceded by doubt, there is the possibility of a fallacious definitive conclusion being produced by a fallacious semblance of inference.

It is not an absolute rule that inference must be preceded by doubt; therefore, the word "ascertainment" (nirṇaya) should be included so as to ensure that inference results in a specific ascertainment. Enough of this digression.

However, when reason is investigated through debate, it effects the purification of reality by producing a certain understanding through the cutting away of doubt, as well as the acceptance of what has been determined; therefore, debate should be employed together with dispassionate disciples and fellow celibates.

We shall explain that *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), however, are occasionally useful even for one free from passion (*vītarāga*), in order to protect the knowledge of reality residing in the heart of the simple-minded who are being terrified by the ostentatious displays of fallacious refutations fabricated by wicked logicians, through providing them with great reassurance.
Pseudo-reasons (hetvābhāsas) are useful by way of assisting in the discernment of correct reasoning;
for when the nature of pseudo-reasons has been ascertained, valid reasons are easily understood by virtue of their being distinct from them.

Is it not the case that here a reversal is observed, since when a valid reason (*hetu*) is understood, there is the establishment of its opposite as a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*)? Even if this is so, both must nevertheless be known: reasons are to be employed, and fallacious reasons are to be avoided.
Thus, reasons are applied and fallacious reasons are rejected.

And as for the fact that fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsas), although already enumerated among the points of defeat (nigrahasthāna), are mentioned again, it is with the intention that they shall be subject to censure during formal debate (vāda).
The *chalas*, *jātis*, and *nigrahasthānas* are the instruments of *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*.

Once their essential natures have been ascertained, it is possible to perform such tasks as avoiding them in one's own speech, employing them on certain occasions, and refuting those employed by an opponent;
therefore, since they are also limbs of *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*, they too must be known, and thus they are taught separately.
How else can those whose faces are set in motion by fragments of ill-taught, fallacious reasoning— those who are "scholars" only in the display of caviling— be defeated?
The world follows what it has already entered and is thus deceived onto a wrong path;
thinking "let it not go [there]," the compassionate Sage spoke of fallacies and the like.
Thus, categories such as doubt and the rest must be taught in this manner,
for the purpose of establishing the authority of the Vedas as determined by the logic rooted therein.
Therefore, by virtue of being a means of valid knowledge through scripture, this science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), which bestows all fruits, is counted among the branches of learning.

And the author of the Bhāṣya said: "The lamp of all sciences, the means for all actions, the foundation of all dharmas—this has been examined in the exposition of knowledge. Thus, by means of this compendium of sixteen categories, the Sage has pointed out the path to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
Other groups of categories, though they exist, have not been taught here because they lack utility for the path to liberation (apavarga).
The operation of this treatise is threefold: enumeration (uddeśa), definition (lakṇa), and critical examination (parīkṣā).
Enumeration is the naming of categories by means of their designations.
Definition is the property that establishes the true nature of what has been enumerated.
Investigation (*parīkṣā*) is the deliberation as to whether that definition applies to the object characterized by it or not.

But is it not the case that there is indeed a fourth activity characterized by classification (*vibhāga*), since such usage occurs in regard to differentiated categories such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), established tenets (*siddhānta*), and quibbling (*chala*)? True; classification certainly occurs regarding a differentiated category mentioned in the first aphorism. However, because its nature as a mere enumeration (*uddeśa*) is not lost, it remains an enumeration itself.
Enumeration is the mention by way of a general name, whereas classification is the mention by way of names for specific types.

And thus, the commentator (bhāṣyakāra) employs the term "enunciation" (uddeśa) in various places precisely in that sense; for instance, when raising the objection, "The enunciation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not in accordance with reality," he states the resolution: "Therefore, the enunciation of the means of valid cognition is indeed in accordance with reality. Consequently, activity is of only three kinds.
In that regard, the enunciation (uddeśa) must necessarily be performed first,
because the definition and investigation of that which has not been enunciated are impossible.
Furthermore, there is indeed a fixed order of precedence between the general and specific definitions.
Since there is no opportunity for the definition of particulars when the universal has not been perceived,
investigation— which occurs subsequent to the definition— is understood to follow precisely from the determination of its essential nature.
However, regarding the classification and the general definition, there is no fixed rule of priority or sequence.

Either the general characteristic is stated first and then the classification, or the classification is stated first and then the general characteristic. Thus, the enumeration has been explained here; however, we shall explain only the sūtras concerning the characteristics.

However, the subject matter indicated by the aphorisms of examination (*parīkṣāsūtra*) will be demonstrated according to my understanding precisely at the occasion of describing their useful characteristics; I shall not undertake the labor of a separate commentary on those aphorisms of examination.

For this very reason, the second aphorism beginning with "suffering, birth," etc., which follows immediately after the first aphorism, has not been explained here because it is subordinate to the [subsequent] definitions.
Since it constitutes a supplement to the examination of liberation (*apavarga*), it will be determined at its proper occasion.

The aphorism concerning the general definition and classification of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is now being explained, as its turn has arrived: "Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition" (NS 1.1.3). First, it must be investigated here: what is called a "means of valid cognition," what is its essential nature, and what is its defining characteristic? Only thereafter will the aphorism be applied.

Thus it is said: the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) whose nature consists of both consciousness and non-consciousness, which brings about the apprehension of an object that is non-erroneous and free from doubt.
For the nature of that [means of cognition] is the causal complex whose essence is both conscious and unconscious;
its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), however, is the state of being the instrument for the apprehension of an object characterized by non-erroneousness and so forth.

But is it not the case that the word *pramāṇa* is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), according to the rule "that by which something is correctly cognized is a means of valid cognition" (*pramīyate yena tat pramāṇam*)?
And an instrument is that which is most effective (*sādhakatama*). Furthermore, the meaning of the suffix *-tama* is excellence (*atiśaya*).
And that [superiority] is relative;
for when another means of accomplishment is possible, something is called "the most effective" (sādhakatama) because it possesses a degree of excellence in relation to that other.
However, since the causal complex (sāmagrī) is a single unity and no other means of accomplishment distinct from it is perceived, in relation to what do we speak of its excellence?

Moreover, in what object does the totality (sāmagrī) possess the status of a means of valid cognition? For the object being cognized, as the objective factor (karman), would—by virtue of being included within the totality—become the totality itself, and thus attain the status of the instrument (karaṇa).

Consequently, all cognitions would now be without an objective support (nirālambana), since the objective factor (ālambana-kāraka), like the eye and other [faculties], is included within the means of valid cognition.
And who is it that cognizes the object of cognition by means of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)? Even the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is dissolved within that very complex.

And thus, the statement that "reality is fully encompassed within these four categories—the cognizer, the instrument of cognition (*pramāṇa*), the object of cognition (*prameya*), and the resulting cognition (*pramiti*)"—is contradicted.
Furthermore, even common worldly usage does not accept the status of the causal complex as an instrument, since people do not employ the instrumental case-ending for it.

For worldly people do not speak in this way, saying, "We see by means of a causal complex" (sāmagrī); rather, they say, "We see by means of a lamp" or "we observe with the eye. Therefore, the causal complex is not the cause; and because it is not the cause, it is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Thus, this [definition] is not a correct nature of a means of valid cognition.

To this it is replied: since the word *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition) is derived from the sense of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) as that which is the most effective factor (*sādhakatama*), for that very reason it is logical that the totality of factors (*sāmagrī*) constitutes the means of valid cognition. This is because, apart from that totality, it is impossible for any other individual causal factor (*kāraka*) to ever possess the contact with the meaning of that [term] "most effective. When an effect is being accomplished through the presence of multiple causal factors, and it fails when any one of them is absent, to whom could one attribute a specific excellence (*atiśaya*)? No such excellence can be determined for any single factor in the production of the effect, since all of them are equally operative therein.

If it is argued that "excellence" (*atiśaya*) consists in being a non-concurrent producer (*asannipatyajanakatva*), we say no; for even those factors that provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*) do not lose their status as causal factors (*kāraka*).

Furthermore, regarding the cognition that is produced, what is the non-concurrent producer? It is all [factors]—the sense organ, the mind, the object, and so forth—since cognition is brought about when they are in mutual contact with one another.

Now, the sudden production of an effect is an "excellence" (*atiśaya*); this can be predicated not only of the instrument (*karaṇa*) but also of the object (*karman*) in a certain state. For example, in the middle of a thick night, when a mass of darkness is bound by a continuous stream from dense clouds, the flash of a lightning bolt suddenly produces the cognition of a beloved woman; yet, even though that cognition occurs, it would not be accomplished in the absence of the woman. As soon as she has arrived, it comes to pass. Therefore, that object-factor (*karmakāraka*) too would be an instrument (*karaṇa*) because of its possession of excellence.

Therefore, the "excellence" (atiśaya) is the very nature of necessarily producing an effect, which consists in the inseparable connection with the arising of the result. And this excellence cannot be predicated of any single causal factor (*kāraka*) included within the totality (*sāmagrī*); however, that excellence is easily expressed as belonging to the totality itself.
If the causal complex is present, the fruit is indeed accomplished; therefore, that very complex possesses the excellence [of efficacy].

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that even for the primary cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and the primary object of cognition (*prameya*), there exists the excellence of being invariably concomitant with the act of cognition (*pramiti*), since they lack that status without a connection to cognition? For one becomes a 'cognizer' by cognizing, and something becomes an 'object of cognition' by being cognized. This is true; however, the attainment of the primary nature of the cognizer and the object of cognition occurs through a connection with cognition obtained by the grace of the totality [of causal conditions]. When the totality is deficient, cognition is absent, and thus the cognizer and the object of cognition become merely secondary (*gauṇa*).

And thus, if valid cognition were possible without completeness (*sākalya*), there would be deviation; however, it is not observed to be so. Therefore, because valid cognition is non-deviant, completeness alone is preeminent; and since it possesses that [non-deviant] efficacy, it alone is the instrument (*karaṇa*).

As for the question of what the causal agency (*karaṇatva*) of the totality (*sāmagrī*) depends upon, we reply that it depends upon the factors (*kāraka*) contained within it. The totality is a property of the factors; it does not lead to the loss of their own essential nature, because even in the state of completeness, those essential natures are recognized.

Now, if it is argued that the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is distinct from its constituent factors, how is it that it is not perceived separately? But if there is no distinction, then all causal factors—including the instrument (*karaṇa*)—would be nothing but the totality itself, which would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of abolishing the conventional usage of agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*). This is not so, because the property called "the presence of the totality" is directly perceived.

For when items such as a pot, water, fire, and rice grains remain separate, there is no cognition of "completeness" (samagratā), but it arises when they are brought together. Therefore, just as in the case of a cloth or similar object composed of a collection of threads, even though there is no distinct substance produced by the assembly of causal factors, the "assemblage" (sāmagrī) consisting of that collection certainly exists; thus, with respect to its constituent members, it attains the status of an instrument (karaṇatā). Consequently, this objection—that "in what action is the assemblage the instrument?"—is not to be raised.

Since the individual members of a causal complex do not lose their own essential nature even while in the state of being a complex, the complex itself functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the specific action of the members.
For this very reason, valid cognition (*pramiti*) is not without a basis (*nirālambana*).
By this, the cognizer and so forth have been shown separately; thus, the fourfold classification is also fully established.
As for what was asserted—that the instrumental case-ending is not seen used for the "assemblage" (sāmagrī)—to that it is replied: the assemblage is indeed a collection.
Since it does not enter the path of linguistic usage apart from the members being collected, there is no such designation as "I see by means of the assemblage."

As for the third designation of the lamp and the sense faculties, it is based on the superimposition of a form identical to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), which is defined as having a nature that is invariably concomitant with the production of the result.
Furthermore, even in other cases, we observe the designation "the pot cooks" through such a superimposition of that form.
Therefore, the causal complex is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when it has acquired the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) in relation to the factors contained within it.

Others, however, assert that "sāmagrī" (the causal complex) refers to the factors of action (*kārakas*) assembled together. Their claim that these possess two forms—that those very same factors, when situated separately, assume the status of objects (*karman*) and so forth, yet those very same ones, when assembled, become the instrument (*karaṇa*)—is unconvincing. What kind of logic is this? Therefore, the *kāraka* that produces a cognition of an object characterized by non-deviation and other such qualities, being distinct from the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), is called the instrument (*karaṇa*).

They designate that very same [cognition] by means of the instrumental case: "I see with a lamp," "I perceive with my eyes," "I understand through a sign," "I know through a word," or "I ascertain with the mind."

Now, one might object: "In this view, there would be only three factors (kārakas) in the act of cognition, exactly as you have stated. While that may be so for acts such as cooking, where the designation of other factors like the locus (adhikaraṇa) occurs upon considering the distinct auxiliary functions such as supporting the substratum of the action;
however, in the case of valid cognition (pramiti), no distinction is perceived among the mind, the lamp, the eye, and so forth. Therefore, all of these are agreed to be instruments (karaṇa)."

If it is asked, "What is the meaning of the superlative suffix (*tamap*) in reference to them?"—there is indeed something: namely, that this world never designates the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*) as an instrument (*karaṇa*), even by mistake—as in "I know by means of myself" (*ahaṃ mayā jānāmi*) or "I know the pot by means of the pot" (*ghaṭena ghaṭaṃ jānāmi*); yet, it does designate the eye, the mind, the lamp, the word, and the logical mark (*liṅga*) in such a way. Thus, one perceives the distinction between the agent and the object on the part of the eye and the other [instruments].

And that very distinction is their excellence (*atiśaya*). Therefore, the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) here is fully encompassed within this fourfold set: the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the knower (*pramātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the resulting cognition (*pramiti*).

Therefore, it is logical that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), which is distinct from the agent and the object, which brings about the comprehension of an object free from doubt and error, and whose nature consists of both consciousness and non-consciousness.
Those who assert that cognition itself is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are not subtle observers;
for cognition is indeed the fruit of the means of valid knowledge, not the means of valid knowledge itself.
Indeed, the word *pramāṇa* denotes the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), for it is defined as "that by which something is correctly cognized" (*pramīyate anena*).
What is the meaning of "it is cognized" (*pramīyate*)? It means that valid cognition (*pramā*) is produced.
When ordinary people say, "We understand from the means of valid cognition," they acknowledge the status of being a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) as belonging exclusively to the instrument.

However, when the word *pramāṇa* is used in the sense that "the valid cognition itself is the means of valid cognition," it should be understood as referring to the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).

And likewise, even a cognition whose nature is doubt or error—which is the fruit of non-valid knowledge—attains the status of valid knowledge because it produces a specific valid cognition in the inference of the self or the mind, or in the determination of the object that qualifies them. Conversely, even a cognition endowed with qualifiers such as non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) is indeed non-valid if it fails to produce a fruit.
We shall explain in the definition of perception that the fruit, which is essentially valid cognition itself, is distinct from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, if it is argued that even that which produces a distinct result is called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only because its nature is consciousness (*bodha*), that is incorrect; for it would entail the undesirable consequence of excluding words, logical marks, lamps, sense organs, and so forth, whose natures are known to the entire world to be other than consciousness.

Therefore, consciousness, as it enters into the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), attains the status of a means of valid cognition—just as the knowledge of a qualifier does in certain cases of perception, just as the knowledge of a logical mark does in the cognition of the possessor of that mark, just as the observation of similarity does in comparison (*upamāna*), and just as the hearing of a word does in the cognition of its meaning.
For this very reason, it has been stated that the causal complex, consisting of both consciousness and non-consciousness, is the means of valid cognition.

Others, however, asserting that the relationship of apprehended object and apprehending subject exists between cognition and its object—both of which depend upon the same causal complex—have accepted that cognition itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since all things are subject to momentary destruction, they sustain the course of worldly life by producing a continuous series of subsequent moments, depending upon both auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) and material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). In the production of cognition, cognition is the material cause and the object is the auxiliary cause; in the production of the object, the object is the material cause and cognition is the auxiliary cause. Thus, since cognition is produced from both cognition and the object, and the object is produced from both the object and cognition, they depend upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*). Therefore, because cognition does not deviate from that object, it possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*) with respect to it.
This is untenable, because it has already been stated that what does not produce a result cannot be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, knowledge is accepted as a means of valid cognition with respect to its object, as it has been said: "[Knowledge] appears as if possessing an operation through its operation upon its own object."

Furthermore, this momentary object, being simultaneous with the cognition and produced by the preceding pair consisting of the cognition and the object, may be considered the object of that [preceding] cognition; it cannot, however, be the object of the momentary cognition produced at the same time as itself.

But surely, since their non-deviation from one another is established by their dependence on the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and their simultaneity, what need is there for "object-ness" (*karmatva*)? Alas, in that case, it must be explained what determines the restriction of subject and object between two things that arise together and share the same causal complex. If you say that cognition is the subject because its nature is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), while the object is the object because its nature is insentient (*jaḍa*), then from where does this distinction come for two things existing at the same time? If you say it is due to a difference in their material cause (*upādāna*) and auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), we say no, because that [theory of distinct causes] will be refuted in the section on the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

Furthermore, those who—perceiving that for a formless consciousness whose nature is pure awareness, there would be an over-extension [of the definition of an object] because it is common to multiple objects such as blue and yellow, and because the status of being a producer exists in the eyes and other sense organs as well—therefore maintain that the restriction of knowledge to its specific object is established solely by the possession of that object's form, and thus assert that "knowledge with a form (sākāra) is the means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa)—they too, while speaking thus with the desire to establish the non-duality of consciousness (vijñānādvaita), will be refuted in the very context of refuting that [non-duality].
For it will be stated later that a single consciousness with a form cannot logically be both the apprehended (grāhya) and the apprehender (grāhaka).
However, for the proponent of cognition with form (sākārajñānavādin), the object does not exist at all.
For that [object] would have to be either inferable or perceptible; it cannot be inferable because there is no apprehension of a [necessary] relation.
For when the object exists, cognition has a form; in its absence, it is formless.
Where has the proponent of the doctrine that external objects are always inferable ever seen cognition?
Nor is the object directly perceived, because two forms (ākāra) are not apprehended;
and if such were admitted, it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress.

For the form of the object is not accessible to a cognition devoid of form, and thus it is grasped by a cognition possessing a form. Now, this very form of the cognition, being itself an object of apprehension, must be grasped by another cognition possessing a form, and that too by yet another, and so on.

Alternatively, since an object cannot be apprehended by a cognition that lacks a form, it must surrender its own nature to the cognition that apprehends it; thus, this very object becomes nothing but a cognition possessing a form. Furthermore, if one were to postulate another distinct object, that too—because it is an object of apprehension—would dissolve into that very [cognition] in order to establish the possession of form for its own apprehender, leaving only cognition with a form as the remainder. And if yet another object were postulated, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

However, the determination of specific objects according to their respective functions will be based on their capacity to produce [cognitions], because the intrinsic nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*) is not subject to questioning.
Even in the case of the theory of cognition with aspects (sākārapakṣa), the same objection applies; all of this will be explained in detail further below.
Furthermore, even in the theory of cognition with aspects, no result distinct from the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has been demonstrated; thus, this is merely an untenable position.

The Śābaras, however, say: "Those who maintain that cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and assert that the result is non-different from that cognition are indeed to be refuted. We, on the other hand, accept that the result called 'perception' (*dṛṣṭa*) is indeed different from cognition.

By that very [result] is that [cognition] inferred; for what is called 'knowledge' is of the nature of an action (*kriyā*), and an action is to be inferred from its result, since results do not come into being without the operation of a knower."

Even the conjunction of the factors of action (kārakas) must have action as its core; for if that were not admitted, with reference to what would the factors be conjoined? And they do not bear fruit when they are not conjoined.
Furthermore, a factor becomes a "kāraka" (agentive factor) through its entry into activity;
otherwise, it would be merely the essential nature of the thing itself and not a kāraka.
Consequently, it would not be employed by those seeking a result, which would lead to the collapse of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Therefore, just as the causal factors—the rice, water, fire, pot, and so forth—which possess established natures, come together by taking up a single effect to be accomplished characterized as cooking, and having combined, produce the action; in the same way, when there is contact between the self, the sense organs, the mind, and the object, the operation called "cognition" arises.

And that [cognition] is not perceptible, because it is the object itself—connected with an external location—that is apprehended, and because there is no appearance of two forms (the form of the object and the form of the cognition). Furthermore, even though it is unapprehended, it serves as a means [of knowing], like the eye and other sense organs; thus, although it is beyond perception (*parokṣa*), it is inferred from its result, which is characterized by the illumination of the object.

As the author of the *Bhāṣya* said: "For when an object is unknown, no one perceives cognition; but when it is known, one understands [its existence] through inference. And the author of the *Vārttika* also stated: "Otherwise, the existence of the object, being perceived, would not be possible."
If it is argued that knowledge does not [arise], then a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is subsequently postulated for this reason.
Thus, this activity of the knower, which is to be inferred from its result and denoted by such terms as "cognition" (*jñāna*), is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As for the sense organs and so forth, because they produce that [activity], one metaphorically applies the term "cognition" to the operation of the sense organs, but not directly.

To this, the following reply is given: Oh, alas! From what are these Vedic scholars so afraid that they have fallen into such extreme despondency? Indeed, knowledge cannot possibly be eternally beyond perception, for we observe in some cases the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of an object as qualified by that [knowledge], in the form "the object is known. For if the qualifier were not apprehended, a cognition of the qualified object could not arise, just as there is no cognition of "this cloth is white" when the whiteness is not perceived.

And what is this great terror? The Śākyas, who deny external objects on the mere ground that consciousness does not grasp them when the saliva of objective apprehension is present, can be easily quelled.
As for the claim that it is imperceptible because its nature is that of an action, that is incorrect; for knowledge does not have the nature of an action, but rather has the nature of a result.

Moreover, for the Bhāṭṭas, even action residing in a perceptible substance is indeed perceptible, and the self is also perceptible; so what wrong has been committed by this [self] that its action is said to be imperceptible?
Furthermore, apart from the activity consisting of motion—which is divided into types such as upward throwing—there is no such thing as a "subtle" action even in external causal factors.
For if that [action] were held to be eternal like a universal (*jāti*), or if it were held to be non-eternal like color (*rūpa*), it would have to be accepted as a property of the real entity.

In that regard, if [the action] were eternal, then because the entity would always be conjoined with action, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the result being produced at all times. Alternatively, if the action is something to be brought about by the causal factors (kāraka), then since that too is an effect, it would itself require causal factors engaged in activity; thus, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā). If, however, the action were an effect produced by causal factors devoid of activity, then—just like the action—the result itself would be produced by causal factors that are themselves inactive; so what would be the use of an action? For indeed, a "causal factor" (kāraka) is defined as that which "acts" (karoti).

It is true that the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is untenable without the entry of an action (*kriyā-āveśa*). When you say "he truly acts," this very [act] is what constitutes the action. In the statement "Caitra makes a mat," since the meaning of "making"—whether it pertains to Caitra or the mat—cannot be denied, it is precisely because of that [act] that Caitra and the others are called *kārakas*. The status of being a *kāraka* is not based on a connection with a supersensible (*atīndriya*) action; for if the status of being a *kāraka* were produced by a connection with an action that is supersensible, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the collapse of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), since such an action cannot be apprehended due to its supersensible nature.
For how could those who do not understand that the status of being an agent is produced by the penetration of activity [into the self] take up that [activity] when they desire a result?
In my view, the state of being a causal factor (*kārakatva*) is not at all supersensible;
rather, the state of being a causal factor consists in the essential nature [of the entity] together with the proximity of auxiliary conditions and so forth.
Having determined it to be exactly so, it is acquired by those who seek it;
and by acquiring that very thing, the fruit is also attained.
What utility do auxiliary factors have for an entity that is devoid of activity? And what utility do auxiliary factors have for an entity that possesses activity?
Now, if this very activity is accomplished by all acting together, what has the fruit done wrong to you? Let that [fruit] be accomplished together as well.
As for what was said—that the meaning of "to act" (karoti) cannot be denied—it is replied here: the meaning of "to act" is simply a physical operation consisting of motion.
For we do not deny the visible operation whose nature is motion, since we perceive various operations such as flaming and so forth directly in every causal factor (kāraka).
However, we maintain that there is no operation that is beyond the senses (atīndriya).

Now, it has been argued that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) called "cooking" must necessarily be sought as something distinct from the visible operations such as flaming and so forth, because without it, the production of the result would be impossible; and furthermore, if that [meaning] were absent, with reference to what would the factors of action (*kāraka*) be combined? That is incorrect. For that single meaning of the verbal root which you conceive as the object to be accomplished—is it to be produced by the totality of all the factors of action together, or is it to be brought about by each factor individually? Regarding the first alternative, each individual factor of action would be devoid of activity. And if each one is individually inactive, how could there be activity even when they are complete?

In the latter case, since the act of cooking would be connected to each [factor] individually, there would be the undesirable consequence that the result could be produced from a single factor independently of other factors;
yet such a conjunction of factors does not occur in the absence of a verbal root capable of expressing that action.
For those who maintain that the connection [between word and meaning] is caused by action, there are two possible courses:
either the connection exists when the action is present, or the action exists when the connection is present.
What is the use of a conjunction in an action that was already established prior to that conjunction? Moreover, the result is produced even by causal factors that are separate from one another.
But if the accomplishment of the action were due to their conjunction, then each one would again be inactive;
that being the case, pieces of wood would not burn without a hearth.

[Objection: "But surely, without a pot, the pieces of wood burn but do not cook. [Reply: Not so; for even when the pot is present, the pieces of wood are seen to burn indeed, but they are not seen to perform any other action.
Therefore, since there is no other action, the factors of action (kārakas) are combined by taking the result itself as the primary object.

Now, if the result (*phala*) is also already established (*siddha*), what connection could there be among all these factors whose natures are already established? To say "the result is established" and "the causal factors (*kāraka*) are established" implies an absence of connection. If, on the other hand, the result is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then that itself would be the action (*kriyā*), distinct from mere motion (*parispanda*). Do not speak thus, for it is untenable for a result to be an action.
For rice (*odana*) is the result, not the action; however, we do not dispute regarding that which is being performed and is designated by the name "action."

Now, what indeed is "cooking" at this moment? Nor is it logical that the root *pac* (to cook) should be devoid of any denotable meaning. It is said in reply: the collective movement (*parispanda*) of the entire assemblage of causal factors (*kāraka*), such as Devadatta and others, when delimited by a specific result, is called "cooking. For that alone is the meaning of the root *pac*. Those very actions of the fuel, the pot, and so forth—which are of the nature of flaming, supporting, and so on—appear individually in their respective forms; yet, when combined, they manifest and are designated under a different form, such as "cooking," due to being delimited by a distinct result.
And likewise, just as one says "Devadatta cooks," one observes such designations as "the firewood cooks" or "the pot cooks.
Even for Devadatta, the activity perceived there is merely the stirring of the ladle and so forth; there is no other, more subtle activity besides that.
Now, it might be argued that the physical activity of Devadatta and others must be preceded by an activity of the self; but this is not so, for there is no such thing as an activity of the self.
It is only through the power of effort preceded by desire and aversion that the self becomes the cause of physical activity.
Therefore, the result is produced by the moving assemblage of causal factors;
furthermore, no activity other than this movement is perceived.
Devadatta and others move, and immediately thereafter the rice [is cooked];
only this much is perceived here, but no other action whatsoever exists.

By this, that which has been accepted—the view that the meaning of the verb "to do" (karoti) called "cultivation" (bhāvanā), or the activity of the person (puruṣavyāpāra), is the sentence-meaning—should also be understood as refuted.
For no such thing as a "person's activity" is perceived;
his agency consists solely in the inherence of specific qualities.
Furthermore, qualities such as knowledge and the like cannot be designated by the term "activity," because their nature is already established.
But surely, since a verbal root (*dhātu*) is defined as that which expresses action, then for the root *jñā* (to know) as well, only an action must be the expressed meaning.

And that action would be a human activity whose essence is cognition. This is not a fixed rule that a verbal root must express an action, for we also see such instances as [the root *gaḍi*] in the sense of "a part of the face."
Furthermore, in the cognition "I know the jar," what appears to you? First, "the jar" is the object; "I" is the self; but as for "I know," one must consider what it is that is manifested here.
It cannot be an activity, because that is imperceptible.
If it is the fruit that is manifested here, then that alone must be accepted as what is expressed by the verbal root;
therefore, cognition does not consist of an action.

Furthermore, if cognition were of the nature of an action (*kriyā*), the Commentator would not have described it as distinct from action; yet he does describe it, stating: "For even cognition and action are recognized [as persisting]; they too would consequently be eternal. Therefore, cognition is one thing and action is another; thus, cognition is not eternal because it has the nature of an action, nor is it imperceptible.
Moreover, if the activity of the knower (*jñātṛvyāpāra*) were eternally imperceptible, then it could not even be inferred because its necessary connection (*pratibandha*) cannot be apprehended;
for the doctrine that establishes external factors as qualified by action has already been refuted.

If it is asked, "What then is the status regarding the inference of the self and so forth? we shall reply that it is not so, because in that case the apprehension of a universal pervasion is possible;
however, in this context, it has been stated that even with respect to external causal factors, an effect is not observed to be preceded by such [an apprehension].

Nor does presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) suffice to postulate an operation of the knower, since the fact of having perceived an object is accounted for solely by the force of the contact between the sense organ and the object.

And what is this so-called "visibility" (*dṛṣṭatā*) of the object? Is it the state of being the object of seeing, or is it the nature of luminosity? In that regard, since seeing is something that is itself perceived, how could the visibility of the object be grasped as its objective state? For when the qualifier is not grasped, there can be no cognition of the qualified. Furthermore, if it were the luminosity of the object, then because that is indistinguishable for everyone, everyone would be omniscient.

If it is argued that [cognitions] would not exist because they arise as related [to an object], this is no reason; for the excellence of the object itself is its luminosity, just like that of a lamp and so forth, and it does not remain restricted by a particular person.
Nor is there a similarity with [objects such as] duality and so forth, because a fixed rule is observed in that case;
however, in the case of illumination, such as that of a lamp, there is no fixed rule regarding its connection [to objects] anywhere.
Duality arises through the cognition of dependence; its apprehension belongs to that very [cognition]. Among the wise, of what, then, is this consciousness said to be an excellence?
If there is another operation between the knower and [the object], what benefit does that provide? Indeed, an agent devoid of activity cannot bring about the accomplishment of a result.
It has been said in this regard: "Let it be accepted that this is indeed an activity according to its appearance;
we recognize that 'knowledge' (jñāna) and 'cognition' (saṃvedana) are synonymous terms."
We do not consider self-awareness to be the fruit of cognition;
furthermore, if one holds the view that the excellence belongs to the object, then everyone would again be omniscient.
Furthermore, no distinction from the position of the Bhaṭṭas would have been stated;
nor does this represent a superiority over both [positions], because both faults would still occur.
And by what could that self-awareness, which makes cognition inferable, itself be apprehended?
For if it were apprehended by another awareness, there would be an infinite regress.
Furthermore, self-cognition will be refuted later on;
and according to the theory of the loss of memory, [the cognition] consists in the recollection of silver.
How will your cognition of the result be self-luminous?
For it appears neither in the form of memory nor in the nature of direct experience.
There is no third possibility; how then could that [consciousness] be manifest?
Furthermore, a cognition devoid of any form is never experienced anywhere.

For there is no cognition of a distinction such that "this is consciousness" and "this is the object"; rather, if consciousness were to manifest as colored by the form of the object, [then they would not be distinct].
In that case, you have denied external objects just like the Buddhists;
however, in the theory of self-luminosity, it is not logical for the result to be of the nature of consciousness.
Therefore, an operation that is to be inferred from its result does not possess the status of a means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, as for the qualification of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is asserted by others—namely, "the grasping of an object not previously apprehended"—that too is incorrect, because there is no difference in the validity of a means of valid cognition whether it operates upon an object already grasped or upon one other than that.
