If it is asked: "What would a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do if it operates upon an object already apprehended? And what would it do if the object is not yet apprehended?"—then [we reply]: even in the case of the apprehended, let it produce that very same [cognition].
If it is argued that this is impossible because one cannot perform what has already been done, we say no, because it produces another cognition (*pramā*).
If it is asked: "What is the fruit of producing another cognition?", the production of another cognition itself is the fruit; and one need not seek a further fruit for a fruit.
Furthermore, a means of valid cognition does not conform to a purpose.
To whom, then, does this objection apply? Not to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is insentient.

As for the person (*pums*), since cognitions arise when an object and the instrument [of perception] are present, why should he be questioned: "Why do you not remain with your eyes closed? Why do you look at an object that has already been seen? However, we see no sublation whatsoever of the means of valid cognition by which we could establish it as invalid.

Nor is there total futility; for when objects to be avoided—such as snakes, thorns, wolves, crocodiles, or venomous serpents—are encountered again and again, there arises from mental distress an immediate activity directed toward their removal. Likewise, even regarding objects to be accepted—such as sandalwood, camphor, necklaces, or beautiful women—when they are perceived, an excess of joy is indeed self-evident.

And as for this which is said: "Even where there may be a determination by subsequent means of valid cognition, surely in that case too, that object was not determined in such a way by the preceding one."
Thus, that too is not convincing,
because there is certainly no further determination by subsequent means of valid cognition;
what additional object is revealed in successive cognitions?

For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operating upon an object that is within its own grasp would never cease; indeed, we find no limit whatsoever for its cessation. Furthermore, the production of a [new] cognition has already been bypassed by this [process]. It is said that cessation will occur either through contact with another object, through fatigue, or through the exhaustion of the means.
Furthermore, this infinite regress does not strike at the root [of the argument],
for the arising of the first cognition is not obstructed without the production of each subsequent cognition.
For they say that an infinite regress (anavasthā) is a defect because it destroys the root;
however, once the root is established, the infinite regress is not averted even by one who has no desire for it.
And if it is accepted that a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) apprehends an object not previously perceived,
then this [position] clearly amounts to a total repudiation of recognition (pratyabhijñā).
And whoever, out of a desire to claim an additional object of cognition— namely, present non-existence—
asserts that those two [perception and inference] are the means of valid cognition, he too seems to deceive us.
Because of the existence of a non-destroyer, its existence is clearly perceived by the preceding cognition; thus it is said that "it is apprehended as enduring for a long time."

Therefore, let the insistence on [perception] grasping an object not previously apprehended be abandoned. [Objection: But if this [requirement] is relinquished, would not even memory possess the status of valid cognition?
The lack of validity in memory is not caused by its grasping what has already been grasped;
rather, its lack of validity is caused by the fact that it is not produced by an object.
[Objection: But how can memory be produced from something that is not a real object (*anarthaja*), since the thing mounted upon it does not exist at that time?

[Response: In that case, how is the inference of past rain not produced from something that is not a real object? For in that case, the subject (*dharmin*) is the object of inference, and that [subject], which generates the cognition, exists there. It is not the subject called "the beginning" alone that is inferred as possessing rain; rather, it is inferred as possessing that [property] by means of the property characterized by its connection with an upper region containing rain, because of its being joined with a specific flood of water.
And since that subject (*dharmin*) which is to be apprehended by inference does indeed exist, inference is not produced from a non-existent object.

How then is intuitive cognition (*pratibha*)—which grasps a future object, such as "my brother will come tomorrow"—accepted by you as being produced from an object (*arthaja*) and thus a form of perception? In that case, there is indeed the grasping of the brother, who exists in another location, precisely as he is characterized by his coming tomorrow; and since he, while being grasped in that very form, is the producer of the knowledge, intuitive cognition is indeed produced from an object.

However, it is observed that recollection arises even without regard for an object—such as when one's father or others have been cremated; therefore, in the case of recollecting an object located in another place, the actual existence of that object is certainly not a cause.
Therefore, since the validity of memory is excluded by its being produced from what is not a [real] object,
"the capacity to reach an unapprehended object" is not a defining characteristic of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Jaimini has also stated that the authority of the word (śabda) pertains to an object not [otherwise] perceived;
how then can you describe it as having all means of valid cognition as its domain?

Others, however, declare that non-contradiction (*avisaṃvādakatva*) is the general definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus it has been said: "A means of valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge."

Non-contradiction (*avisaṃvādakatva*) is said to be the quality of being a means of attainment (*prāpakatva*). A cognition’s status as a means of attainment consists precisely in its indicating the cause for purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), which is the basis for either acquiring or avoiding objects capable of producing pleasure or pain. For when activity occurs toward an object indicated by a cognition, attainment follows; thus, with respect to attainment, the function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is solely that of indication.
By indicating it, that object is effectively attained by the cognition, just as for kings, the act of issuing an order regarding someone to be executed constitutes their very act of execution.

Thus it has been said: "The capacity to lead [to the object] is validity. Furthermore, even in common worldly usage, that which causes one to obtain the indicated object is treated as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And since this quality of being a means of attainment (prāpakatva) exists in both perception and inference, it constitutes the general definition of a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa).

In this regard, since perception has the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object as its domain, and since that [particular] cannot be reached due to its momentariness, its status as a "means of attainment" consists solely in generating a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the continuum (*santāna*), because it is through the attainment of that continuum [that the object is reached].

As for inference, although its domain is a superimposed object, it is a means of attainment by way of attaining that [original object], because it originates from a lineage of the unique particulars of the fundamental object, like the cognition of a jewel arising from the luster of a jewel.

This validity, which consists in the capacity to lead to the attainment of what has been determined, is established even when the object determined is not a real entity, because it results in the attainment of the real thing that is its basis; for it is held that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which leads to the attainment of what has been determined.

Consequently, in the case of cognitions apprehending a yellow conch-shell and the like, even though there is the attainment of the mere conch-shell, there is no validity, because that which was determined is not attained.
For a yellow conch-shell was indeed perceived, yet what is attained is a white one.
Therefore, validity consists in non-contradiction, which is the capacity to bring about the attainment of the object as it has been cognized.

This is untenable; first, you yourself must explain this: does a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) lead to the attainment of what is shown, or to the attainment of what is determined? In that regard, in the case of inference, there is not even a showing [of the object], so what talk can there be of attaining it? As for perception, certainly there is a showing, but what is shown is not attained, because it has already passed away due to its momentariness.
Furthermore, the capacity to bring about what has been determined is also difficult to establish;
for according to your own view, determination lacks a real entity as its object, and it is impossible to attain that which is not a real entity.
As it has been stated by you: "Because it is not in accordance with reality as it is determined, and because it is not a determination in accordance with reality."
The attainment of the fundamental reality, however, is like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence;
it is not something that can be touched by any of the other means of valid cognition, nor is it something that is reached by going there.

Nor is it tenable to say that the attainment of that [result] occurs through the attainment of a continuum (*santāna*), because a continuum is untenable under the alternatives of being either distinct or non-distinct [from its constituent moments]. This will be examined in detail in the section on the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga*).

But surely, even if the continuum (*saṃtāna*) is merely conceptual, this definition of valid cognition will be explained conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), as it has been said: "This is the definition of valid cognition from the perspective of conventional practice; but in reality, this is nothing but mere cognition (*jñānamātra*), in which the manifold diversity (*prapañca*) of the grasped and the grasper and so forth is superimposed by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*). What is there to be attained, or who is there to attain it?"

Thus, this is presented as if it were a mode of flight: what indeed is this so-called "conventional reality" (saṃvṛti)? Even when it is analyzed as being either existent or non-existent, it cannot serve as a basis for conventional discourse.
Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that the conventional usage of difference is not produced by the latent impressions of ignorance, but is indeed ultimately real.

Or, if one maintains that the continuum is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), why are things such as "birth" and the "composite whole" (*avayavin*) not also accepted as conventional? If you argue that this is because they are undermined by refutations such as the dilemma regarding their subsistence (*vṛttivikalpa*), then that same path applies to the continuum as well; thus, this is a mere resort to a desperate hope.
Therefore, since the capacity to lead to what has been shown is impossible, this is not a valid definition.
Furthermore, this definition is too narrow (*avyāpaka*),

because it fails to include even those cognitions of objects that are to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*) which have attained the status of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through their connection with qualifiers such as non-erroneousness (*avyabhicāra*).

Now, one might object: "What indeed is this so-called 'object to be disregarded' (*upekṣaṇīya*)? If it is not taken up precisely because it is to be disregarded, then it must be something to be abandoned (*heya*), since it is not to be accepted. This is not correct, because the existence of an object to be disregarded is self-evident and thus cannot be denied.
That which is to be abandoned and that which is to be adopted serve as the causes for suffering and pleasure;
it is on account of these that embodied beings exert effort toward their rejection and acquisition.
We maintain that there exists a reality distinct from those two, which is self-cognized.
When an object worthy of being accepted is seen, attachment arises;
toward the other, however, aversion arises; but in that [state of equanimity], both are difficult to find.
As for the claim that [the object] must be abandoned precisely because it is not to be accepted, that is irrelevant;
for it does not follow that "this which is a neuter is a male because it is not female," or "it is a female because it is not a male.
A neuter is something entirely distinct from both female and male, since it is perceived as such.
In this way, even an object that is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*) is a distinct entity from both the rejectable (*heya*) and the acceptable (*upādeya*), because it is perceived as such.
When grass, leaves, and so forth appear on the path to one who is walking,
the cognition [of them] is not like that of an umbrella or the like, nor is it like that of a snake or the like.

Therefore, since validity is observed even in the case of a cognition regarding something to be disregarded—which does not lead to its attainment—leading to attainment is not its defining characteristic.
Now, is it not the case that whatever function a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has with respect to attainment,
that same function is accomplished by it even in the case of an object to be disregarded?

For it has been said that for kings, the very act of commanding constitutes the act of killing, and for knowledge, the very act of pointing out constitutes the act of bringing about [an object]. This is not so; such "pointing out" would merely be its definition, and that is seen even in the cognition of water in the shimmering rays of the sun.
But is it not the case that there is invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) in that instance because it does not produce a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) contrary [to reality]?
For perception has as its object only the specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the mirage; it becomes invalid only when it produces a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of water.

Thus, a single perception is described in three ways—namely, as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*), and as neither valid nor invalid—based on the distinction between the production or non-production of corresponding or contrary conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

For the cognition of blue is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the blue object, because it generates a conforming conceptual construction (*anukūlavikalpa*) such as "this is blue.
Momentariness, which is non-different from the blue, is indeed grasped by that same cognition;
however, it does not constitute a valid means of knowledge with respect to that [momentariness], because neither a conforming nor a contrary conceptual construction arises regarding it.
But in the case of stability, that [cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge, because it is defiled by a contrary determination.

If this is so, then in this context, this definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is all the more difficult to maintain, for you have described that "the determination of a continuum (*santāna-adhyavasāya*) is the operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) toward attainment.

Consequently, just as the perception of the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a mirage is invalid because it generates a determination of water, so too the perception of a [real] unique particular would become invalid because it generates a determination of a continuum contrary to it.
And when a conceptualized continuum has been determined, why does one act directed toward the perceived object? Does one act by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object?
Or would attainment occur due to non-discrimination? In that case, valid cognition would be far removed from it.
Therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition that brings about attainment.
Moreover, attainment and non-attainment have as their cause merely the desire of the person;
therefore, it is determined that the very cognition of the meaning is the effect of the means of valid cognition.
Therefore, those who state the definition of cognition must also state its qualification.
However, the Sāṅkhyas maintain that the modification of the intellect (*buddhi*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It is the intellect itself—following the modification of the sense organs and other faculties which have transformed into the form of the object—that, by coloring the *puruṣa*, constitutes the means of valid cognition.
For it is by being colored by that [buddhi] that the Puruṣa becomes the perceiver of specific objects.
This is unconvincing: for he who knows, perceives, and determines does not possess that result, which is the vision of the object, because the Great Principle (mahat) is insentient;

and he in whom the vision of the object exists neither knows, nor perceives, nor determines. Thus, there is a difference of locus between the means of knowledge and its result. The possession of attributes such as cognition constitutes the means of knowledge, yet this is not found in the person (puruṣa); and the result, the vision of the object, does not exist in the intellect (buddhi).
Then, due to the transparency of the person who conforms to the modification of the intellect,
it appears as if there is a contact with the form of consciousness belonging to the intellect.
This being the case, falsity would be stated by one's own words:
for the property of consciousness is false in the intellect, and the property of the intellect is false in consciousness.

And because of the doctrine of cognition with forms (sākārajñānavāda), this [position] is not significantly different from your own view; therefore, by refuting that [doctrine], there is a refutation of this one as well.
Furthermore, this entire elaborate system of the sage Kapila’s methodology will be refuted;
therefore, not even a single means of valid cognition can be established within that school of thought.
Therefore, we do not consider the nature of valid cognition as propounded by other schools to be free from exceptions;
for that reason, they maintain that only the unimpaired completeness of the sense organs and so forth constitutes a flawless means of valid cognition.
That means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is fourfold.
Regarding this, the author of the Sūtra says: "Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition."

For here, regarding that which possesses distinctions and was introduced in the first sutra, three things must be stated: its general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), its classification (*vibhāga*), and its specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
Among these, there will be four sutras—beginning with "arisen from the contact of the sense-faculty and the object"—that establish the specific definition.
However, in this [present] instance, the classification and the general definition are being established.
By means of this single sūtra, the Great Sage has stated two things:
the fourfold enumeration of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as well as their general definition (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).

When the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is uttered in proximity to perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony, it demonstrates that there are exactly four means of valid cognition.
Now, one might object: neither is a word expressing the number "four" heard, nor is there an explicit restrictive statement such as "only perception and so forth.
To this we reply: the understanding of this restriction regarding their number arises from the very nature of the expressive power of the word.
In the commands "Feed the Gargas" and "Bring Yajñadatta and Devadatta," even without a word for number, the understanding of a restriction to singularity and duality respectively occurs.

Likewise here as well, when it is stated that "perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition," the exclusion of fewer or more numbers is determined by implication; thus, first of all, there is the understanding of the division.
The general definition, however, is understood from the very term "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) itself, by virtue of its etymological derivation combined with its conventional designation.

From the word *pramāṇa*, which expresses the sense of an instrument—as in "that by which something is correctly cognized (*pramīyate*) is a means of valid cognition"—it is understood that a means of valid cognition is an instrument for valid cognition (*pramākaraṇa*);
and this has already been demonstrated previously.

Furthermore, by employing the inclusion of the terms "the probandum" (*sādhya*) and "the means of proof" (*sādhana*) in the middle of the aphorism—"[Comparison is] the means of proving the probandum through well-known similarity"—the author of the Sūtras defines this as the form common to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): namely, that the status of being a *pramāṇa* belongs to that which is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the production of valid knowledge (*pramā*) regarding the probandum and the means of proof.

However, since it would follow that validity (prāmāṇya) would also apply to that which produces an impure cognition, the three terms "arisen from an object" (arthotpanna), "non-erroneous" (avyabhicārī), and "of the nature of a definitive judgment" (vyavasāyātmakam)—which are drawn from the definition of perception (pratyakṣa-sūtra)—are brought forward to exclude [the causes of] memory, doubt, and error; for those three terms are common to all four means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

By the term "arisen from an object," which qualifies the result, that which produces memory is excluded; by the term "non-erroneous," that which brings about error is excluded; and by the term "of the nature of a definitive judgment," that which generates doubt is excluded from being a means of valid cognition.

And thus, this is what is stated: that by which a cognition is produced which has an object as its domain, is free from doubt, and is non-erroneous—that is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In this way, both the general definition and the classification are understood from this single sūtra alone.
[Objection: But surely, since a single sūtra would have the nature of both a specific division and a general definition, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*);

for it is said that a single sentence is appropriate only when there is a unity of meaning. [Reply: This is not so; in the case of sūtras that indicate multiple entities by means of both direct statement (*śruti*) and implied meaning (*artha*), the prescription of multiple meanings does not constitute a fault of syntactical split.
Regarding an object of knowledge that is untouched by other means of cognition and is accessible solely through verbal testimony,
objections such as "splitting the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) are indeed considered valid objections;
for it is not logical for a single [sentence] to enjoin two distinct matters therein.

In the view that this is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), namely "One desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the Vājapeya," the sacrifice would have to be enjoined with respect to self-sovereignty, and the accessory of the Vājapeya would have to be enjoined with respect to the sacrifice; thus, because a single sentence would result in mutually contradictory forms such as injunction and restatement, enjoining two distinct meanings is extremely difficult to maintain.

Furthermore, in these sūtras—which are of great value due to their skill in indicating meanings already ascertained by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—the presentation of multiple meanings constitutes an ornament, not a fault;
indeed, it is precisely because they indicate manifold meanings that they are called "sūtras.
This alone is the supreme skill of the authors of sūtras: that by means of a single sentence and with only a few syllables, they present numerous subjects.
There is no fault in this, for this sūtra will convey that meaning either by ellipsis (adhyāhāra), by repetition (tantra), or by recurrence (āvṛtti).

Regarding the formulation of both the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and the classification (*vibhāga*), there is no fixed rule of precedence as there is for the specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*); thus, their simultaneous presentation through a single [concise] method (*tantra*) is not contradictory. This restriction—that the specific definition must not be stated unless the general definition has already been stated—applies only to that [latter case]. However, regarding the general definition and the classification, they may be presented according to one’s preference: either the classification first and then the general definition, or the general definition first and then the classification.

Just as in the case of the *siddhāntacchela*, both [meanings] may be presented simultaneously; thus, there is no fault whatsoever in establishing them either through the method of *tantra* (abbreviation) or *āvṛtti* (repetition).
Let this consideration of whether [the number] is in the Sūtra, in the Tantra, or through repetition stand aside for now;
surely the number four among the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) is not accepted by others.
For it would be difficult to establish that there are exactly four means of valid cognition by way of negating a lesser or greater number;
for instance, the Cārvākas maintain that perception alone is the single means of valid cognition, while the Buddhists hold that there are only two: perception and inference.

The Sāṅkhyas maintain that there are three means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): perception, inference, and authoritative testimony. Regarding the restrictive rule that there are no more than these, we shall first refute the Bārhaspatya position—which claims there are even more—later on. Furthermore, the distinction between verbal testimony and inference will be explained precisely during the definition of the latter; thus, the path of the Śākyas is also not tenable.
Indeed, O monks, this is not accepted; for they, because of the twofold nature of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), have declared that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are twofold.
There is no other cause for the division of the means of valid cognition than the division of their respective objects.

Furthermore, the object of cognition is of only two kinds, either distinguished as direct (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect (*parokṣa*), or distinguished as the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*); for among entities whose natures are established through mutual exclusion, there is no possibility of inclusion in a third category.
If it is asked, "From where does this very determination of the non-existence of the third object arise? we reply: "Precisely from the power of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It is indeed beyond dispute that perception, when operating upon blue, determines the blue as being blue;
and that same perception also excludes what is not-blue, because that [non-blue] does not appear in the cognition of blue.
For that which appears in the cognition of blue is indeed blue; therefore, everything other than that is necessarily non-blue.
For this very reason, he rejects a third category as well.
For that category also must either appear in the cognition of blue or not appear; if it appears, it would be blue itself and not a different kind of thing.
If it does not appear, it would likewise be non-blue, for it could not be a different kind of thing.
For this indeed is the defining characteristic of the blue and the non-blue: namely, being manifested or not manifested by the cognition of blue.

And thus, perception, having operated upon its own object, establishes that object as being perceptible; therein, it establishes what does not appear as being imperceptible, and likewise rejects a third possibility as before.
In this way, even when negating an object distinct from both the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and the universal (sāmānya), this very same method is to be followed;
for in this manner, the object of perception becomes definitively ascertained by direct perception itself.
As it has been said: "It determines that [object], excludes others, and indicates the absence of a third possibility—this is the operation of a single means of valid cognition."
Otherwise, since the very nature of the object itself would remain undetermined,
where could those seeking purposeful action perform their acceptance or rejection?
Thus it has been said: "Even seeing fire as something other than fire, one would neither remain nor stand firm."

Although non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) has its function restricted solely to the mere presentation of the specific particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object situated before one and is indeed devoid of deliberation, nevertheless, it must be understood that the conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) arising in its wake possess the proficiency for a function extending up to the final stage of establishing the exclusion of other objects and the absence of a third alternative within the domain of what was perceived; otherwise, there would be no linguistic or practical activity (*vyavahāra*).

And thus, because the objects of perception and its opposite possess a nature established through mutual exclusion, and because their contradiction is understood through the power of perception which excludes [other possibilities], inference is also able to proceed once the non-existence of a third object is ascertained. At the time of determining one of two contradictories, the negation of the second necessarily appears precisely because of that contradiction, as in the case of cold and heat.
A third object is likewise contradictory to them, since it does not appear when they are present.
But surely you have never apprehended a third object as you have a second; for if it were apprehended, its existence would necessarily follow just as with the two objects.
And how can you determine the contradiction or non-contradiction of that which has not been apprehended?
O good sir, a separate apprehension is not required here, because their opposition is established merely by the non-appearance of one to the cognition of the other.
For that is called "opposed" which, when one is being apprehended, is not apprehended.
Thus, this very non-apprehension constitutes the nature of opposition; therefore, a separate apprehension need not be sought.
Thus, since there is no third category for objects established through mutual exclusion, the twofold nature of objects is proven in every respect.
In the same way, the exclusion of other possibilities—such as existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence, succession and simultaneity, and so forth—is to be understood.

In that regard, perception operates upon its object which consists of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), whereas inference operates upon the remote object which has the form of a universal (*sāmānyākāra*). Since the two means of valid cognition are thus established as cognizing these two distinct objects, tell me: for the sake of what should a third means of cognition be desired?

Nor is it reasonable to claim that, regarding this very object which is imperceptible and consists of a universal nature, another means of valid cognition such as verbal testimony functions just like inference; for it is impossible for multiple means of valid cognition to operate upon a single object due to contradiction and futility.

If that entity were determined again by a subsequent means of valid cognition merely because it possesses the form already apprehended by a prior means of valid cognition, that subsequent means of valid cognition would be entirely fruitless.
For they say: "A means of valid cognition that makes known an object already known would be like grinding what has already been ground."
However, its apprehension as having another form is impossible for a subsequent means of valid cognition, because it would contradict the initial means of valid cognition.
For this very reason, those who know the principles of logic do not accept *saṃplava* (the convergence of means of knowledge).
*Saṃplava* is the operation of multiple means of knowledge upon a single object;
and that [convergence] is refuted precisely by the rejection of such an object.

Furthermore, perception and inference do not overlap with one another, because inference does not operate upon the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and perception does not operate upon the universal (sāmānya).
How can inference, which depends upon the apprehension of a relation, apply to a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes?
How can even perception— which is restricted by its contact with an existing entity— be a grasper of a universal whose form is superimposed by conceptual construction?
And as for those other means of valid cognition, such as verbal testimony and analogy, which are asserted—
given this being so, upon what basis could they possibly find their standing?
First, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an entity is sealed by perception alone;
anything other than that is known through inference, which functions in dependence upon a relationship.
There is no real object that can be apprehended by various means of valid cognition;
therefore, the claims that such an object is either a "whole" (avayavin) or a "universal" (jāti) are merely the chatter of fools.

And if it is maintained that verbal testimony and inference also function with respect to an object of perception, then they too should produce a cognition identical to perceptual awareness; yet this is not the case.
As they say: "When the object is the same, a similar cognition arises;
however, the cognition derived from words or inference does not attain equality with perceptual cognition."
The splendor in the stars, the moon, and the like is one thing entirely;
the majesty of the sun is another, which has opened wide the treasury of the world.
And it has been said: "That which is grasped by the senses is one thing, while the range of the word is another;
one understands through the word that which is distinct from what is seen by the eye, for it is not perceived directly."
Moreover, a person who has been burned perceives the burning from contact with fire in one way,
whereas the meaning of "burning" is understood through the word "burning" in quite another way.
Therefore, since the twofold nature of objects is determined by the path already described, there is no third means of valid cognition, nor is there a convergence of multiple means of knowledge.
To this it is replied:
as for what was stated—that the capacity to exclude other aggregates belongs to perception alone—that is not tenable.
How can this burden be carried by one who is devoid of the capacity for connecting the preceding with the succeeding, and who is free from conceptual construction?

Furthermore, conceptual constructions have their functional capacity exhausted merely in imaginative projection; so, in your view, what talk can there be of establishing the reality of things based upon them?
Alternatively, let it be granted that the exclusion of other categories occurs in the manner described regarding blue and so forth;
however, this method cannot be applied to the determination of the state of being perceptible or imperceptible.
For perception, when engaged with an object, determines only the essential nature of that object, and not its status as being perceptible.

For this is experienced as "this is blue," but not as "this is perceptible. To explain: what is this so-called perceptibility of the object? Is it being an object of the sense-faculties (*akṣa*), or is it being an object of knowledge born from the sense-faculties (*akṣaja-jñāna*)? In that regard, being an object of the sense-faculties is understood only through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); it is not understood through perception itself. Thus says Bhaṭṭa: "Indeed, what is called 'audibility' (*śrāvaṇatā*) is not apprehended by perception."
This is known through positive and negative concomitance among those who are deaf and so forth.

Furthermore, even the status of being the object of a cognition produced by the senses (akṣaja-jñāna-karmatva) as "perceptibility" (pratyakṣatva) cannot be determined at that very moment; for at the time the object appears, that [status] does not appear, and it is impossible to apprehend its status as an object without first apprehending the object itself.

But how is it that at the time of grasping an object, there is no appearance of its [the cognition's] own appearance? It is simply because two forms do not appear simultaneously—namely, "this is the cognition" and "this is the object"—since their distinction is not apprehended.
Furthermore, as will be explained later, this single form that appears must belong only to the grasped (grāhya), not to the grasper (grāhaka).
But surely, knowledge that has not been apprehended is not capable of illuminating an object.
As they say: "For one who does not perceive the means of apprehension, the seeing of the object is not established.
That is incorrect.
The perception of an object is established only for one whose apprehension is not itself perceived;
however, for one whose apprehension is perceived, there is no perception of the object.

Since apprehension itself is what is perceived, and because a second form does not appear, how could there be a perception of an object? Furthermore, if cognition, once grasped, were to manifest the object, it would not transcend two possible courses.
For that cognition must either be apprehended by another cognition or be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).

If it were apprehended by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) which destroys the very foundation [of knowledge], and thus the world would become blind and mute for one who maintains that the perception of an object is preceded by the perception of its apprehension.
Nor is cognition self-luminous, because it is an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*), like blue, yellow, and so forth.
However, we shall refute in detail the self-luminous nature of consciousness when we refute the Vijñānavādins.

Furthermore, since there is no distinction between the arising and non-arising of cognition if it were not itself perceptible, one should not suspect either ignorance or omniscience [of the self]. For the status of being a knower is established for the knower by the mere arising of consciousness; since cognition arises with the very nature of illuminating its object, how could that which has arisen not differ from that which has not arisen? And just as this [self] possesses the status of a knower through the arising of cognition whose objects are blue and so forth, so too does it possess the status of an enjoyer through the arising of cognition whose objects are pleasure and so forth; thus, there is no over-extension of the argument in that case either.

Therefore, at the time of the cognition of an object, because that [cognition] itself is not apprehended, perceptibility as being the object of that [cognition] does not manifest; and when that does not manifest, there is neither the exclusion of the remote (parokṣa) nor the indication of the non-existence of a third category. Thus, how can perception be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the duality of objects? As for the inference that was also stated for the sake of establishing the two objects, it is based on the contradiction with that [object] as determined by perception.
The capacity of perception to cognize contradiction has been refuted;
and if that [perception] is not apprehended, inference, which is rooted in it, cannot be established.
And thus, since it is impossible to establish a duality of objects,
let this desire for a duality of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) caused by that [duality] be abandoned.

Alternatively, even if there is a twofoldness of objects, how can the distinction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—which arises from the difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) and the difference in results (*phala*)—be set aside? For indeed, the causal complexes and results of perception and inference are one thing, while the causal complexes and results of verbal testimony and analogy are quite another.
Thus we shall explain;
therefore, since the distinction between the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is established even from that [distinction], there are not only two means of valid cognition.

By this, the number "three" asserted by the Sāṃkhyas as the number of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is also refuted, because comparison (upamāna) will be established as a fourth means of valid cognition through the distinction between the causal complex (sāmagrī) and its result.

Furthermore, that refutation of the convergence of means of knowledge (*saṃplava*) which was carried out by the Buddhist—seeking to exclude the application of multiple means of valid cognition toward a single object—is merely a manifestation of intellectual delusion; for if such convergence did not exist, it would be impossible to establish the validity of inference.
For a logical mark whose relationship [to the probandum] is unknown is not accepted as a means of cognition;
and the cognition of that relationship is preceded by the apprehension of both relata.
And if the apprehension of the relatum, which consists of the universal, were desired to occur through inference from that very [universal],
then it is evident that there would be mutual dependence.
The comprehension of a relation, which is preceded by the apprehension of its relata and dependent upon another inference,
would not be possible even in hundreds of Manvantaras.

Therefore, even with respect to what is distant, perception must be admitted as the grasper of the relationship between the mark and the possessor of the mark; and this being the case, there is a convergence [of the means of knowledge].
In this regard, it might be argued that this objection applies only to those who are ignorant of the Buddhist tenets (*saugatakṛtānta*).
For they maintain that the operation of both verbal testimony and inference occurs within the domain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

And since the establishment of the relationship [between word and object] is derived from these [constructions], there is neither an infinite regress nor a confusion of means of knowledge (*saṃplava*).

For indeed, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), whose bodies are colored by the shadow of perception (*darśana*) acquired immediately upon its arising, appear as if they were direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*). This operation of inference (*anumāna-vyavahāra*), which is established upon the universal form (*sāmānyākāra*)—the nature of which consists in the exclusion of both that [object] and its other, as delineated by those [constructions]—is rooted in that [perception] through a traditional lineage, like the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel; thus, it is capable of leading to the attainment of that [object]. However, it does not touch the reality (*vastu*) that is accessible solely through direct perception. Therefore, how could there be a convergence (*saṃplava*) [of means of knowledge], or how could there be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)? All this is merely a deception.

For that which is accepted as the essential connection (*pratibandha*) consisting of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)—is it a property of a real entity (*vastu-dharma*), or is it a property of a form superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpāropitākāra-dharma*)? In this regard, it cannot be a superimposed property;
for a real entity is produced by a real entity, and a real entity must possess the nature of a real entity.
Therefore, the connection is a property of a real entity.
It is indeed remarkable that while the object is not touched by conceptual constructions, the connection with it is nevertheless ascertained!

And this well-spoken [verse] states: "The relation between two things consists of identity (*tādātmya*) and so forth; and the status of being the signified and the signifier belongs to two exclusions (*apoha*) superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Thus, the relation is in one place, the means of grasping it is in another, the cognition is in another, and the activity and attainment are in yet another—everything is deceptive.
Furthermore, for conceptual constructions whose nature is devoid of contact with the perceptible, no shadow of perception whatsoever is possible.

Even qualities such as the apprehension of "this-ness" (*idantā*) or clarity, being devoid of contact with a real entity, are ineffective, since they do not escape the status of being non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Furthermore, since the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not truly determined as being limited by [the evidence],
the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) is therefore false.
If this [relation] is indeed accepted because it is described as being mounted upon the intellect,
then alas, what is the use of this obsession with proving a real (tāttvika) relation?

Just as the apprehension of a relation is impossible without accepting perception regarding a universal object—and thus inference itself is undermined—likewise, for one who has not grasped the relation, the observation of the second mark (liṅga) is also difficult to establish; therefore, for those who deny the convergence [of means of knowledge], inference would perish even from that point.
For it is not possible for the unique particular (asādhāraṇāṃśa) to function as a logical mark (liṅga),
nor can the universal (sāmānya) be apprehended without inference.
That very same infinite regress occurs there as well, and that same mutual dependence persists; and that indeed is the process for quelling the power of conceptual constructions.

Therefore, how can the doctrine of the convergence [of means of knowledge] be denied without first refuting inference, which is preceded by the apprehension of a mark and the cognition of its relationship?

Moreover, even if the twofold nature of objects were established, perception and inference alone would overlap with one another; for, through differences in place, time, and so forth, an object is apprehended as being both remote and perceptible, and as being both perceptible and remote.

We shall refute momentary destruction; and as for the continuum (saṃtāna) that has been postulated, it is of the same nature even when there is a convergence [of moments], as was shown in the demonstration of the proof of attainment and so forth.

Furthermore, as for the attempt to refute the theory of the convergence [of means of knowledge] through the desire to deny objects such as universals (jāti), the very defense of universals and so forth will serve as the rebuttal. Your collection of refutations merely serves to remove the turbidity [from our position].
The claim that "the possessor of those [parts] is the universal" is indeed a most excellent statement!

As for the claim that there is no coalescence (saṃplava) due to contradiction and futility, therein, futility has already been countered by the very exclusion of the qualification "cognizing an object not previously apprehended.
Nor is there contradiction, because a subsequent cognition does not arise by way of subverting the preceding cognition—as is the case with the thought "this is not silver."

Since a substratum (*dharmin*) is characterized by a manifold expansion of diverse properties (*dharma*), what contradiction is there in the fact that at some time, a certain specific property is determined by someone? Furthermore, regarding the objection raised that if perception, verbal testimony, and inferential signs have the same object, they must produce a similar cognition—on this point, some explain that even when the object is identical, a difference in cognition certainly occurs due to the difference in the means (*upāya*), just as in the case of the cognition of objects situated at distant or near locations.
Others, however, think that the difference in cognition does not arise from a difference in the means (*upāya*), but rather solely from a difference in the object (*viṣaya*).
Even when perceiving what is near or distant, the objects themselves differ:

from a distance, there is the apprehension of the subject (*dharmin*) as qualified by its mere general properties (*sāmānyadharma*); but from nearby, there is the direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of all its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*).
Thus, these means of valid cognition—perception, inference, and verbal testimony—are distinguished by the distinction among their respective objects of knowledge.
Visual cognition perceives the object as connected with its specific properties;
however, inferential cognition perceives only that which possesses those properties, in accordance with the understanding of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
From a word, a cognition arises regarding the object as delimited by this or that [quality];
for a cognition of the word-meaning does not occur devoid of the permeation of the word.

How, then, is there a convergence (*saṃplava*) of these [means of knowledge] everywhere? Since a difference in objects has been demonstrated, it is true that convergence is spoken of with reference to the substratum (*dharmin*). These two positions, however, will be examined in detail under the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In any case, it is established that there is indeed a convergence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The author of the Bhāṣya has provided an illustration of this: "Fire is cognized through the instruction of a reliable person; it is inferred by one who approaches it upon seeing smoke; and it is perceived by one who is even closer," and so forth.

In some cases, however, a fixed rule is observed: for example, regarding the injunction "one desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," the knowledge [of its nature] comes from scripture alone (*āgama*), and not from perception or inference;
from hearing the sound of thunder, the thorough knowledge of its cause comes from inference alone, and not from perception or scripture;
and regarding one's own hand and so forth, cognition arises from perception alone, and not from verbal testimony or inference.

Therefore, it is established that, for the most part, the means of valid cognition converge upon the object of cognition, but in some cases they may also remain restricted to a single object of cognition.
Thus, having removed the fear of the onset of the entire multitude of faults raised by others, the convergence [of the two means of valid cognition] alone is established here;
and all those long-rooted desires of the Sugata’s followers for the establishment of a dual object of the means of valid cognition have been shattered.
Thus, the deficiency of number has first been examined; now its excess is being examined.
In this regard, Prabhākara maintains that there are five means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), namely perception and the others, together with presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
The Bhāṭṭa maintains that there are six [means of knowledge] together with non-existence (abhāva).
Some say there are eight [categories] by means of probability and tradition.
"The restriction of the number of means of valid cognition is indeed impossible," say the well-trained Cārvākas.
In this regard, the Bhāṭṭas explain presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as follows: "Presumptive testimony is the postulation of another fact because a fact seen or heard is otherwise inexplicable.

"Seen" means understood through the five means of valid cognition beginning with perception; "heard" means understood from some source, whether worldly or Vedic speech. Thus, the postulation of another fact that is otherwise inexplicable is presumptive testimony. In this way, it becomes sixfold, according to its origin from the six means of valid cognition.

Although the meaning is already conveyed by the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), which signifies that which has been perceived, *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard) is mentioned separately because it concerns a portion of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is thus distinct from the five types of presumption (*arthāpatti*) whose objects are the things to be known (*prameya*).

Among these, presumption based on perception (*pratyakṣapūrvikā arthāpatti*) is the postulation of the burning power of fire, because the effect known as burning—which arises from contact with fire as perceived through direct perception—would otherwise be inexplicable.

Inference preceded by perception (anumānapūrvikā) consists in the postulation of the sun’s power of motion based on its reaching another location—a fact inferred from the mark (liṅga)—since such movement would otherwise be inexplicable.

Inference based on analogy (*upamānapūrvikā*) is the postulation of a capacity for that [object] to be grasped by that cognition, through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), regarding the object of knowledge such as a *gavaya* which is qualified by its similarity to a cow or similar entity as understood through analogical cognition (*upamānajñāna*).
Therefore, these presumptive arguments (*arthāpatti*) are indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because they have as their object a power that transcends the senses;

for it is impossible for power to be determined through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and since it is impossible for it to be the object of inference (*anumāna*) due to the absence of a comprehension of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) dependent upon that [perception].
For positive and negative concomitance follow the form of the substance;
however, the power residing therein is subtle and is not apprehended by those two.
Since there is no possibility at all for verbal testimony or comparison here, this is the domain of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) alone.

That which is preceded by presumption (*arthāpatti*) is as follows: having understood the expressive power of a word through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of an object produced by that word, one then postulates its eternity through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for that [expressive power]. This will be discussed in the "Examination of Sound" (*Śabdanirūpaṇa*).

However, the author of the Bhāṣya has cited that which is preceded by non-existence: having ascertained the absence of the living Caitra from his house, one postulates his existence outside because that [absence] would otherwise be inexplicable.

[Objection: But surely, since the unperceived is established by means of the perceived, this would be nothing other than inference (*anumāna*). [Reply: It is not inference, because the necessary conditions (*sāmagrī*) are absent.
For logicians maintain that inference is the knowledge produced by the complete set of conditions, such as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*);
and that [set] does not exist here.
Whether the object of inference is Caitra as qualified by his being outside, or his being outside as qualified by Caitra, one must consider what serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*).

Is it Caitra as qualified by his absence from the house, or the house as qualified by Caitra’s absence, or the absence of Caitra in the house, or the non-perception of Caitra there? Not even one of these possesses the property of being a "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*).

For neither the house, nor Caitra, nor his absence, nor the non-perception of him is a property of Caitra or of his being outside; thus, because none of them possesses the property of the subject, not even one of them can function as a logical mark.
Moreover, this is not inference because it would entail the consequence that the object of cognition (prameya) enters into the means of cognition itself.

For instance, Caitra’s existence outside is postulated on the basis of his absence from the house, while his life has been understood through scripture; otherwise, the reason would be inconclusive due to the possibility of him being dead.
Furthermore, non-existence, like smoke, makes known external existence only when it has been apprehended, not when it has not been apprehended.
Furthermore, the apprehension of non-existence is preceded by the complete cessation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend an existent;
however, in this case, there certainly exists a means of valid cognition that apprehends existence, namely, that which grasps [the person] as living.
For "living" is said to be existence in some particular place.

But while the means of valid cognition that apprehends existence has not yet ceased, how could non-existence function? Indeed, as it functions, it presents the means of valid cognition apprehending existence as having a distinct object, such that "his existence is outside and his non-existence is in the house.

Therefore, since the apprehension of non-existence in the house is only possible by first establishing the existence [of the person] outside while he is alive, there is an intrusion into the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
In inference, however, at the time of perceiving the mark such as smoke, there is not even the slightest touch of the entry of that fire, which is the object to be inferred, into the cognition.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that even in presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the inclusion of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) within the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is a fault? We reply: it is not a fault. Presumptive testimony proceeds for the purpose of establishing an absence whose object is a single entity presented by two means of knowledge; it necessarily refers to both objects of knowledge, for otherwise their coordination would be impossible.

Consequently, that very cognition which previously arose from scripture as the awareness that [the person] exists somewhere because his location was not specified, has now become the cognition that he exists outside, once his absence from the house has been apprehended.
Therefore, due to this difference, presumptive testimony is not inference.

And thus, because there is no apprehension of a relationship in this way, existence and non-existence— situated respectively inside and outside the house— cannot be cognized as being connected simultaneously by a single [cognition], just as fire and smoke [are not].
And since the cognition of the necessary connection first occurs through the impossibility of otherwise [accounting for the evidence],
if its status as inference is asserted later, let it be asserted as such.
Surely, the apprehension of a relation exists for one standing at the door of a house;
but how will this [apprehension] occur when establishing non-existence through existence?

In a case where, having understood Caitra’s presence in a certain house, his non-existence in other places is understood through the impossibility of that [presence] otherwise, the necessary connection (pratibandha) is difficult to apprehend there, because of the infinity of those places.

If it is asked, "What is the status of smoke once the absence of non-fire has been ascertained? it is replied: in that case, since the apprehension of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between smoke and fire is possible, they would not rely on the apprehension of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

For those whose minds are satisfied by the attainment of the probandum (*sādhya*) through the knowledge of the rule easily obtained from repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), what is the use of ascertaining the absence of non-fire? In this present case, however, at the very moment of determining the positive concomitance, the difficulty of perceiving the property to be known (*gamyadharma*) has been stated, because it exists in infinite locations.

If it is argued that its absence is ascertained through non-perception, we say no; for if you argue, "I shall ascertain its absence by means of a non-perception restricted to a specific location," do not speak thus: "Even after going to all those places, I do not know its non-existence there, because of the suspicion that it might have entered Kauśāmbī once you had departed."
Therefore, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone, it is certain that this [domain] is not the sphere of those who lack omniscience.

[Objection: "But surely we shall ascertain this matter through inference: 'The other places are devoid of Caitra, because they are distinct from the place occupied by Caitra, like a place near him. [Reply: No, because it is subverted by a counter-inference: 'The other places are not distinct from Caitra, because they are distinct from the place near him, like the place occupied by Caitra.

Therefore, it is established that the determination of his non-existence in all other places follows solely from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the body of a person of limited dimensions being perceived in a specific location."

Upon hearing the statement "Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," which is an expression that requires completion, the resulting cognition of one part [of the meaning]— namely, that he eats at night— is called presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*).

In this case, when such a sentence containing an expectancy is heard, the cognition of eating at night that arises must be produced by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because perception and the other [means] are not present.
Perception is incapable of producing the cognition of eating at night, because its object is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*).
Nor is it inference, because the cognition occurs even for one who has not apprehended a [logical] relation (*sambandha*).
But as for analogy and the other means of knowledge, not even a suspicion arises [that they could produce such a cognition];
therefore, verbal testimony alone is the source of the cognition of eating at night.
Furthermore, the word being heard is not capable of expressing this meaning, because a single sentence lacks the capacity to support two meanings—one affirmative and one negative.

Moreover, since words such as "night" are not heard here, it is impossible for something that is not a word-meaning (apadārtha) to be the meaning of a sentence. Nor is the meaning characterized by eating at night a modification (bheda) or a combination (saṃsarga) of the word-meanings of the sentence concerning the day, such that it could be understood even though it is not a word-meaning.
Therefore, the cognition that "he eats at night" is produced by an imagined scripture;
and regarding the imagination of such a sentence, let the means of valid cognition be carefully considered.
It is not perceived by direct perception, for that [perception] lacks the power to grasp unmanifest sound;
nor is it established by inference, because [the object] is ascertained even without apprehending a pervading mark (liṅga).
In some cases, because [the object] is eternally beyond perception, even the cognition of pervasion (vyāpti) is difficult to achieve;
where the injunctive scripture (viniyoktrī śruti) must be inferred through context (prakaraṇa) and other such means.

For it is accepted by those learned in the science of sentences that it is *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) alone that possesses the power of application (*viniyoktrī*) in all cases, including *prakaraṇa* (context) and so forth;
as it has been said: "Indeed, *śruti* is acknowledged as the applicator in all of these.
And because that [direct statement] is eternally imperceptible, the connection of the *liṅga* (indicative mark) therein is difficult to ascertain.

Moreover, it is not even possible to infer the existence of the word "night" (*niśāpada*), because if such a thing existed, the reason (*hetu*)—being characterized by presence, absence, or both—would be either unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and thus would not function as a valid reason.
Furthermore, no property (*dharma*) is perceived here by means of which the subject could be inferred as possessing that [word], like a mountain possessing fire.

Neither the statement regarding the day nor its meaning can serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the inference of the statement regarding the night; for if the statement regarding the night has not been heard, how can there be a grasp of that property (*taddharmatā*)?
But if it has been heard, what is the purpose of grasping that property?

Let alone the status of the word-meanings in the daytime sentence as inferential marks (*liṅga*); even by way of their being logically untenable (*anupapatti*), they cannot be understood as indicators of the nighttime sentence.
For since word-meanings consist of universals (*sāmānya*), their unaccountability would exist only in the absence of a particular (*viśeṣa*), not in the absence of another sentence.

Therefore, it is the very sentence that is being heard, which—failing to reach the point of fulfilling its own function of producing a cognition free from expectancy in the absence of one of its parts—implies that missing part. This is *śrutārthāpatti*, which has as its object a single part of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Now, how can one thing be inferred from another merely by the force of the facts? For "corpulence," being perceived as an effect of eating, should establish its own cause—eating—just as smoke establishes fire.

And since that [eating] is prohibited by the statement at a specific time, it will refer to other specific times; so what is the use of inferring the statement? Furthermore, even a statement does not have an unseen purpose, but rather exists solely for the sake of conveying a fact.
What fault is there in postulating that very object itself directly, such that you resort to this mediation? It is said: "O child, you are ignorant of this path of verbal authority;
for this [word] does not even possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) since it produces a cognition that is still expectant [of further information]."

Just as perception and other means of knowledge are valid by virtue of the satisfaction derived from seeing and attaining a portion of an object situated before one, verbal cognition is not held to be so.
For when the meaning of a sentence is well-established through the completion of all its constituent parts,
the operation of the intellect does not reach its conclusion until it has formed a cognition of that meaning.
Having imparted that much understanding, the word attains validity;
and because it denotes that object, that speech is accepted as a sentence.
Therefore, upon hearing a single part of the word, the completion of that constituent part must be postulated first; for otherwise, how could there be a comprehension of the meaning?
Generally, the Veda is completed in its practical application through the presumption based on what has been heard;
however, the meaning being so postulated there would not itself be Vedic.

That which is postulated by means of mantras possessing the eight indicative marks (liṅgas) and their specific applications, as well as that scriptural statement (śruti) which is postulated through indicative marks and so forth to serve as an applicatory injunction— know that [all such things] are [to be understood in this manner].
In the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is an injunction regarding entitlement because of the scriptural statement that the sacrifice must be performed;
whereas in the case of the Saurya and other such rites, it is an originative injunction because of the scriptural statement regarding the injunction of entitlement.
In the modifications (vikāra) such as those dedicated to Indra and Agni, because only the specific task is taught,
the "being like the archetype" (prakṛtivadbhāva), which constitutes the ritual procedure (vidhyanta), is established.
Thus, because the apprehension of a relationship is impossible at the outset,
this presumption based on what is heard (śrutārthāpatti) unfolds without rival.
By means of that [perception], a portion of the Veda is postulated everywhere;
however, if one adopts the position of postulating the meaning [directly], then the Veda would not be the sole means of knowledge for it.
Thus has this presumption (arthāpatti), arising from the six means of valid cognition, been described;
yet when it is examined, it is not distinct from inference (anumāna).
Without a necessary connection, one thing does not cause the cognition of another thing;
for upon seeing some object, not just anything is apprehended.
Even a causal relation does not become a cause for cognition if it is unknown;
otherwise, cognitions would arise even in newborn infants and the like.
Even in cases where the cognition of a relation is not possible by way of a specific individuality,
there is indeed the apprehension of it by way of its universal form.
Furthermore, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is the conceptualization that "without this, [the other] is not possible.
And the statement "without this, it is not possible" is an expression of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Since negative concomitance is understood, it implies positive concomitance (*anvaya*), namely: "when that [cause] exists, [the effect] is possible."

Since positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are properties of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that makes [the object] known, how could presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) not be inference? We shall explain that even a purely negative reason (*kevalavyatirekin*) is a means of cognition only when it is rooted in positive concomitance.

Furthermore, those presumptive arguments (*arthāpatti*) cited as being preceded by perception and other means of knowledge regarding the postulation of power (*śakti*) are entirely without an object, because an imperceptible power does not exist.
An effect arises from its own nature when augmented by auxiliary factors;
indeed, it is not possible to postulate another power that is beyond the reach of the senses.
Surely, without power (*śakti*), a causal factor (*kāraka*) would not even be a causal factor.
Just as an axe is raised by one intending to cut down a tree, so too might sandals or other such objects be raised.
For if power were not admitted, then because there would be no distinction in the essential nature of the substance, it would follow that every effect would arise from everything at all times.

For instance, when the power of poison and fire to kill and burn is restrained by a mantra, even though their own nature is recognized and they remain indifferent toward their own effects, what is the reasoning here? Certainly not this: that the presence of the essential nature and its auxiliary factors is obstructed by the mantra, because that [nature] is still recognized.
Rather, it is the power (*śakti*) that is obstructed; thus, it is logical that there is no production of the effect despite the existence of the essential nature and the auxiliaries.

Furthermore, since a diversity of results is observed even when service, study, and so forth are equal, you yourselves have necessarily postulated some supersensible cause, such as *dharma* and the like.
Therefore, let it be accepted that power (*śakti*) is likewise supersensible.

This [objection] is untenable. As for what was said regarding "the restriction of the material cause," we reply: we are certainly not able today to establish some new causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) among entities; rather, we conduct ourselves by following the way things have always functioned.
For it is not by our own will that water quenches cold or fire quenches thirst.

In that regard, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) or through the linguistic usage of elders, we determine that the axe and such alone are the cause of cutting and so forth; therefore, one who desires that result takes up precisely that [axe], and not sandals or other such things.

Furthermore, even when the axe and other such instruments are present in their own essential form (*svarūpa*), the effect does not arise at all times, because they must depend upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) just like their own nature; thus, the presence of these auxiliaries cannot be established at all times. Moreover, merit (*dharma*) and so forth also fall within the category of auxiliaries; since the production of the effect depends on them, how could it possibly occur at all times? Furthermore, the postulation of merit and demerit (*adharma*) is unavoidable due to the force of the observed diversity of the world as an effect.

And it is not because of being a "power" (*śakti*) that these two are beyond the senses, but rather by virtue of their very nature (*svarūpa-mahiman*), just like the mind (*manas*) or atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Even that case where the effect [of poison or fire] is not observed despite the presence of the poison or fire due to the application of a mantra is not based on the obstruction of power, but rather has its cause in the introduction of another causal complex (*sāmagryantara*).
Now, one might object: "What was done by the mantra as it entered? Nothing at all was done; rather, another causal complex (*sāmagrī*) was brought about.
For a particular causal complex is the cause of a particular effect."

If it is argued that its own nature remains exactly as it was, then why would poison not kill even when not consumed? If you say that in that case there is a requirement for contact with the mouth and so forth, then let the absence of a mantra also be considered a requirement.
Just as merit (dharma) is present at the time of a divine ordeal, a mantra also, when not employed, obstructs the effect.

Even on the view that there is a potency (*śakti*), what is the function of the mantra? For does the mantra effect the destruction of the potency or its obstruction? It cannot be destruction, because when the mantra has ceased, its effect is seen once again.
But let the restriction belong to the very nature [of the entity] itself, just as it does to its power.
If it is asked, "What has happened to the essential nature, and what has happened to the power, such that there is indifference toward the effect? then that is equally true in the other case as well.

If it is argued that the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) certainly exists because it is being perceived, then power (śakti) also certainly exists, since it is inferred through the subsequent observation of its effect.

Furthermore, if power (*śakti*) is admitted, it must be admitted as either eternal, like the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the entity, or as produced. If it were eternal, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the effect arising at all times. If, however, dependence on auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) is required, let that dependence belong to the intrinsic nature itself; what is the use of postulating a "power"? If, on the other hand, power is produced, does it have the mere intrinsic nature of the entity as its cause, or does it have the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*), such as auxiliary factors, as its cause? If it has the mere intrinsic nature as its cause, then again there is the consequence of the effect being produced at all times, because the power would be produced at all times.

If, however, the effect is the product of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then let the effect itself be the product of that complex; what is the use of an intermediate power? If it is argued that the effect is not produced from an incapable causal factor, [we reply: even power is an effect, and if another power must be postulated for its production as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

He said: "Indeed, the unperceived (adṛṣṭa) is postulated for the sake of establishing what is perceived (dṛṣṭa), not for the sake of subverting what is perceived. If one were to postulate a further power [for that power], the causal factors (kāraka) would be exhausted merely in the production of a series of powers, and thus there would be a failure of the effect; therefore, only a single power is postulated. So how could there be an infinite regress? To this it is replied: If the perceived cannot be established without the unperceived, then let the unperceived be postulated as much as you wish. However, if its production occurs otherwise, what is the use of postulating it? Furthermore, the possibility of its occurrence otherwise has already been demonstrated.
Even if it were to be postulated, let that which is unperceived be postulated—
provided it does not lead to an infinite regress, as in the case of the dharmas and so forth.

Moreover, you maintain that even the operation (vyāpāra) is beyond the senses, like the potency (śakti); since the effect is established by the postulation of either one alone, what is the point of the cumbersome postulation of both?

If it is argued that a factor which is capable but not currently active is not a causal factor (*kāraka*), then how do we know that it is "capable"? If you say, "I shall know it from the observation of the effect," then the effect will be accomplished through the activity itself.

If it is argued that even when a sandal or similar object is active, the cutting of the foot is not observed [to occur], then that activity must be perceptible and not beyond the senses, since Your Honor has already recognized its state of being active prior to the observation of the effect.
For an activity that is to be inferred from an effect would simply not be known in the absence of that effect.
Furthermore, since the effect can be accomplished by either one [of the two causes] alone, it is not capable of establishing both; so, enough with this digression.
Let us return to the subject at hand.
Therefore, since there is no such thing as a supersensible power (*śakti*), those instances of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) cited above are devoid of an object.
Alternatively, power (*śakti*), which is beyond the senses, is the very object of inference;

for, since the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs through the fact that an effect is preceded by a cause, and since the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone cannot account for causality, something additional must be inferred, and that is power.
As for the presumption (arthāpatti) that was cited in order to establish the eternity of sound,
its resolution will be stated in the "Examination of Sound" (Śabdaparīkṣā).
Presumption based on non-existence (*abhāvapūrvikā arthāpatti*) is also nothing but inference.
