This is because the existence outside [the house] is understood through the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the absence from the house of one who is alive.

Here, Caitra’s absence from the house is the subject (*dharmin*), and "possessing that [absence]" by virtue of being outside is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*). This is because it is an absence from the house of a living person, just like the previously observed absence from the house of such a person.
Just as smoke is the subject (dharmin) in the proof that "it possesses fire" as the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma), because it is smoke, like previously perceived smoke.
Therefore, the suspicion that houses and the like constitute [valid] indicative marks (liṅga), as well as its refutation, are merely empty verbiage.
Furthermore, as for the objection raised regarding the entry into the object of cognition, that too is not correct.

What is intended here as the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for you—is it mere existence, or is it existence qualified by an external location? Mere existence, first of all, is already understood from scripture alone; thus, it does not depend on being an object of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Existence qualified by an external location, however, is indeed the object of knowledge. But how can there be an entry of that [external existence] into the cognition at that time? For the means of knowledge that apprehends absence in the house merely removes the scope for a means of knowledge that perceives presence in the house itself; it does not initiate an inquiry into the non-existence of the person outside.
Whether one who is dead stands far away, or one who is alive stands even in the courtyard,
there is no difference whatsoever in the determination of the absence from home.
However, when this [breath] is apprehended as qualified by life, it assumes the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) because its deviation has been eliminated.
Furthermore, the apprehension of the qualifier itself is not the apprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya*);
for life is one thing, and the object of cognition called "interiority" (*gahirbhāva*) is another.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the very cognition of the absence from the house qualified by life is itself the cognition of being outside?

[Reply: This is not so; for the cognition of being outside does not arise from the cognition of the absence from the house qualified by life, nor is that cognition itself the cognition of being outside. Indeed, the cognition of smoke in a locus containing fire is not itself the cognition of fire.
Is it not the case that fire is indeed something other than smoke, and here too, external presence is indeed something other than the absence from the house and the presence in the forest?

Since the mountain and fire have already been established, only the possessive sense (*mattvartha*) therein remains to be inferred as something new (*apūrva*); likewise here too, only the connection with an external location remains to be inferred as something new.

If, however, that additional object of cognition (*prameya*) is not accepted here, then, since the absence from the house and the [person's] being alive are ascertained by their own respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), presumption (*arthāpatti*) would be redundant.

Therefore, because there exists another object of cognition and because it does not enter into [the scope of those other means] at that time, the fault of "non-inclusion of the object of cognition" (*prameyānupraveśa*) does not apply.

Moreover, this same fault applies equally to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because there too one accepts the postulation of another object on the basis of an existing object, as established by the textual formulation: "An object seen or heard is not otherwise possible; thus, there is the postulation of an object. Wherever there is the conventional usage that "the cognition of B arises from A," the entry of A into that cognition of B is necessarily a fault.

For, as in the case of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), that [probandum] is established through the establishment of the cognition of it; thus, other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be redundant.
The Prabhākaras, however, describe the distinction from inference by means of another method:

in inference, the qualifier of the prover (*gamaka*) is "otherwise impossible" (*anyathānupapanna*), for smoke is indeed not possible without fire; here, however, it is the reverse: the thing to be proven (*gamya*) is "not possible without the prover," as in the case of one who has gone out of the house and is alive, [the fact that] he exists outside [is not possible without his being outside].
They also interpret the commentary in this way: "An object seen or heard" means that the postulation of an object (*arthakalpanā*) postulates another object.
The meaning is that since that postulation is mediated by the object of cognition (*prameya*), it would otherwise be inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*).

Thus, because there is a reversal of the inexplicability between the understood (*gamya*) and the signifier (*gamaka*), this presumption (*arthāpatti*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) from inference; for instance, [in the case of] "external existence," it is not otherwise explicable, and that [existence] is the object to be understood.
This too is merely an attempt to resolve an inconsistency in the text, rather than a presentation of a new, original insight.

For as long as the object to be inferred (the *gamya*) is not apprehended, how could its inherent incongruity (*anupapadyamānatva*) be determined? But once the object to be inferred is apprehended, what is the use of apprehending its incongruity, since the probandum has already been established?
If you argue that previously the impossibility of that [conclusion] being otherwise had been grasped, oh, what a great distinction this is from inference!
For this would have to be called the prior apprehension of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Furthermore, when it is stated that the existence of a person outside [the house] is untenable without his absence from the house, it must be explained how that [existence] is established when that [absence] exists.
Is this [establishment] an origination (*utpatti*) or a cognition (*jñapti*)? If it is cognition, that too exists in the case of inference.
The path is the same: the object of comprehension (*gamya*) does not exist without the means of comprehension (*gamaka*), yet it exists when that [means] exists.
But the arising [of the cognition] is difficult to explain, because the absence from the house is not established;
for if the absence from the house were already established, then its production would occur in a subsequent moment.
For a cause that is already established is capable of producing an effect;
therefore, living at that very moment, he would be neither in the house nor outside.
Therefore, this is of no consequence whatsoever.

And thus, that which some have imagined as a distinction here—namely, that while fire is merely inferred by smoke, the external presence [of Devadatta] is actually produced by his absence from the house—that too is refuted.

As for what was said—that [the inference is invalid] because of the absence of the apprehension of a relation—that too is not sound, since that [relation] arises for one standing at the door of the temple.
Having anticipated this objection themselves, they did not provide a rebuttal;
instead, they presented another example by way of inversion.
Regarding the claim that "the postulation of non-existence outside [is made] by means of the state of being inside," this very point must be stated:
this presumption (*arthāpatti*) is not at all preceded by non-existence (*abhāva*).

Having asserted six types of presumption and then having spoken of this one which is preceded by non-existence, to now abandon it—as if abandoning a doe in this thicket who is terrified by the side-glances of the lion that is the Naiyāyika—is an action utterly unworthy of your honors and characteristic of the vulgar.
As you depart, abandoning this young girl who has you as her sole refuge,
how will other women even look upon your face?
The conceptualization of non-existence based on existence is indeed an *arthāpatti* (presumption) preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, its relationship is not difficult to comprehend;
for when a substance that is not all-pervading exists in a restricted location, one can effortlessly determine its non-existence in other locations.
And if there were a certainty of smoke being distinct from fire, what would be your recourse? Whatever the position is in that case, that same one shall be ours here as well.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to say: "It is only for one whose absence of another entity is to be known through mere positive concomitance (anvaya) understood via repeated observation that the fault applies; but for me, co-occurring factors are indicators by mere non-perception.
We shall demonstrate that this is so because there can be no certainty regarding the probandum (sādhya) for one whose negative concomitance (vyatireka) is uncertain.

Just as the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also not a member of inference if it is not apprehended.

And regarding the proof of external existence, the very formulation of inference that was shown by you is merely a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) because it contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition; so, enough with this digression.

Even the wretched *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard) does not differ from inference (*anumāna*), because there is no justification for postulating a partial statement, and because the object [of the presumption] is something that can be known through the mark of an effect (*kāryaliṅga*).

Just as you, upon observing smoke situated on the slope of a mountain, infer its cause, fire; so too, having ascertained from scripture the effect called "corpulence," one should likewise infer its cause, which is eating.
What is the distinction here?
It is because [the relationship] is established through repeated observation by virtue of its being the effect of that [cause].
As for the logical mark (*liṅga*), however, it is apprehended sometimes through direct perception and sometimes through verbal testimony; thus, this is not a great difference.

Is it not the case that a statement which is incomplete is incapable of producing even the appropriate cognition? Does the cognition of Devadatta’s corpulence not arise from the sentence "The fat Devadatta does not eat during the day"? It is not that it does not arise; rather, it arises as one that is expectant (sākāṅkṣā).
And since a statement that produces an expectant cognition lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇya), it is precisely for that reason proper to complete it.

That being so, what here possesses expectancy? Is it the word, or its meaning, or perhaps the cognition thereof? First of all, a word independent of its meaning has no expectancy whatsoever, just like an unmanifested sound.

But since it is the meaning that remains expectant, let it supply another meaning; what occasion is there for the postulation of words? Furthermore, it is the cognition itself—having the meaning as its object—that is expectant, not the auditory cognition which has the word as its object.
Therefore, for the sake of fulfilling the expectancy of the cognition, the postulation of that very meaning is logical.

Even the postulation of a portion of a statement is solely for the sake of understanding the meaning; therefore, let that [statement] alone be postulated—what is the use of an intermediate step? As for the objection that the meaning being postulated would result in being non-Vedic, under the view of postulating a statement, that meaning would be even more decidedly non-Vedic, because the statement being postulated is something other than the Veda.

If it is argued that what is heard and what is inferred are both of two kinds and that both constitute the Veda itself—namely, that the meaning of the revealed word (*śrauta-artha*) and the meaning of the revealed word as inferred (*śrautārthānumita*) are both simply the meaning of the Veda—then what is the point of postulating an additional ladder of verbal statements? For its status as the meaning of the Veda will be established simply by virtue of being obtainable through the force of the meaning conveyed by the Vedic statement that is actually being heard. In every respect, the theory of presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*) regarding a portion of a statement is not superior;
this is because it is rejected by the position that avoids the postulation of a partial Vedic text.

As for what was said—that the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] is impossible because [the meaning] is beyond the senses—that too has been refuted; for it is easily established that the apprehension of the relationship can indeed occur through the general form (*sāmānya*) of the object, since in various instances, the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) and others is seen to be connected with other meanings such as the qualification (*adhikāra*) and so forth.

The Prabhākaras, however, explaining the *bhāṣya* passage "seen or heard" as "this is merely a conventional synonym for the word 'perceived'," reject the doctrine of presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*).
They maintain that the expressive power of the very word being heard extends to that much of the meaning, and thus they assert that such a meaning is indeed verbal (*śābda*).

In the cognition of the sentence-meaning—which consists of an action colored by a multitude of factors such as qualities, defects, and various agents situated far or near—the operation of the sentence is like that of an arrow, reaching out over a very long distance.
And that cognition arises when the operation of the word is uninterrupted, but it does not arise when its operation ceases,
because of the absence of the causal factors that produce it. Furthermore,

people learning the usage of words through the linguistic practice of elders, seeing those elders employing such sentences, determine that the capacity for such a sentence-meaning resides in the sentence itself.
But the words that follow it become the causes for that effectual [state].

By considering the suitability of the indicative marks (*naimittika*), even those [words] not explicitly heard in certain cases may function as indicators, just as the words "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) and so forth do in the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and similar rites.

In some cases, even those [words] that are heard are discarded because they are not favorable to that [context], as in the case of [the rule]: "If both sacrificial offerings of someone should meet with ruin... and so forth.

In some cases, things that exist otherwise are established in a different way in accordance with that [context], as in the case of [the rule]: "One sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings."

Therefore, since the status of words—whether they are actually present or absent—as causes [of cognition] is established in accordance with the meaning of the sentence perceived initially as a single, compact whole, it is possible to understand that meaning even from a sentence where such a constituent part is not heard; what then is the use of *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard)? For this very reason, the verbal nature of that meaning is not mediated by a series of steps, because it is established directly.

[Objection: But if the causes (*nimitta*) are not being heard, from where do we understand their meaning? And not understanding it, what kind of effect (*naimittika*) can we conceive? [Reply: It is said that even when those [causes] are heard, their status as causes is not conceived by virtue of their own power, but rather through the mediation of following the effect;
this will be the same for those [causes] that are not heard.

We do not hear the instrumental case-ending in the word *yajña*, nor the accusative case-ending in *svarga*; we do not find the *kvip* suffix in words such as *agnicit*, nor the base form in words such as those beginning with *adhuna*; nor do we find the appropriate case-endings in compounds or secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and yet we certainly comprehend their meaning.

In the same way, even in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, we shall understand the meaning of terms such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) precisely through the force of the occasional injunction (*naimittika*), namely, "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).

Furthermore, because the application (*viniyoga*) is inherently pregnant with the mandate (*niyoga*), the indicative marks (*liṅga*) and other means of proof will—without even the postulation of a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)—assume the operation of the mandate and thereby establish their power to apply the constituent elements to the ritual act.
But if this were the case, since the operation of the word would be possible everywhere,
even the primary sense would be equal to the secondary, metaphorical, and indicative senses.
Furthermore, how will that which is described— the superiority of each preceding means among the authorities such as direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth— come to be?
It is said: even though the operation of words is present everywhere, this is not a fault because the distinction between their modes of functioning is possible.
For the cognition of the signified object does not arise by completely abandoning the status of the words as its causes;
and since that status is not abandoned, the diversity of their own forms necessarily persists.
Otherwise, the cognition produced by the word "lion" regarding the son of a lioness is one thing,
while the understanding generated regarding Devadatta and others is quite another.

Just as the word "Ganges" functions as the instrumental cause in the expression "he bathes in the Ganges," it does not function in that same way with respect to a dwelling place such as a cowherd settlement.

Since there is indeed a distinction among direct assertion, indicative mark, syntactic unity, context, position, and name based on the proximity or remoteness of their connection with the purpose, there is likewise no equality in their application.
Even for one who would postulate an applicatory power (*viniyojikā*) by means of direct statement, indicative mark, and so forth—
for such a person as well, since that [postulated power] is equal [to the others], how could there be a relationship of sublation and sublated?
Furthermore, if one were to imagine that [the atoms] possess the states of being distant or near, then since that very principle resides in the object itself, what is the use of such an imagination?

In modified rituals (*vaikṛta*) such as those dedicated to Indra and Agni, there is no inference of the archetypal procedural rules (*prākṛtavidhyanta*); rather, their acquisition occurs through the operation of the *codaka*.
The requirement of the modified injunction (*vaikṛtavidhi*) for certain elements is what is termed the *codaka*.

Now, if there is no distinction in the comprehension of that [obligation] in both cases, what is the difference between an original injunction (*upadeśa*) and an extended application (*atideśa*)? There is no distinction whatsoever in the comprehension of the *niyoga* (the mandate); rather, the difference between these two is this: in an original injunction, one must act according to the instruction, whereas in an extended application, the instruction follows the requirements of the action.

Now, one might object: "In an injunction according to the specific purpose, there would be no application at all for acts such as the threshing of *kṛṣṇala* gold grains—which are useless for that purpose—so what is the point of sublation (*bādha*)? [The answer is: It is because of the application of the entire section on the archetypal procedure (*vidhyanta*).

For the extended injunction (*codaka*) does not operate by partial application; enough, then, with this introduction to a detailed discourse containing the internal arguments of other treatises, which has arisen through this incidental digression."
Thus, the view of the masters of sentences has been explained briefly by way of digression;
but as for the discernment of what is logical and illogical therein, who are we?
The presumption based on what is heard (śrutārthāpatti) stands as something to be refuted by us;
and its refutation may proceed either by the previously mentioned method or by this present path.
By the power of this very capacity of words, that [doctrine] has also been refuted,
which another who considers himself a scholar has resorted to as some kind of "suggestion" (*dhvani*).
The understanding of a prohibition arises from an injunction, and the cognition of an injunction arises from a prohibition; for example:
"O pious man, remain confident," and "O traveler, do not enter the house."
It is the very capacity of words that teach the nature of objects cognizable through other means of knowledge which functions in such and such a manner in each respective case.
Alternatively, such a discussion with poets does not shine;
for even the learned are bewildered on the path that is deep within the meaning of sentences.
Therefore, enough with this discussion appropriate for learned men; this system is exceedingly profound and is not the domain of those who possess only logical knowledge.

We shall now speak of the subject at hand: it is established that even the slightest distinction between inference (*anumāna*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) does not appear [to exist] for the wise.

He said: "In that case, let non-existence (abhāva) be a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara) which determines what exists, where no [other] means of valid cognition operates. That which is the means for the cognition of its absence is called the 'absence of a means of valid cognition' (pramāṇābhāva)."

In this case, the statement "there is no jar here" means that there is no operation of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) capable of apprehending a jar; thus, this absence of a means of valid cognition determines the non-existence of the jar.

And in that case, the non-arising of the cognitive activity of the knower with respect to the object, the jar, is precisely what is expressed by the term "non-perception of the perceptible"; this is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), while the resulting cognition "it does not exist" is the fruit (phala).

Alternatively, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) will be the nature of the cognition "it does not exist," which consists of the activity of the cognizer apprehending the absence of a jar and is produced by the non-existence of a means of valid cognition that would otherwise perceive it; the result (*phala*), however, will be the knowledge of avoidance and so forth.

As it has been said: "The non-arising of perception and the other [means of knowledge] is called the absence of a means of valid cognition; it is either the non-modification of the self or a consciousness directed toward another object."
By the term "other entity," the very absence of the jar is expressed.
In that regard, first of all, the cognition "this is not here" is not produced by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because there is no contact between the sense organ and its object.

For contact consists essentially of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), or it is a specific variety arising from them, such as "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), and none of these exist here.
Nor is the relation of being a qualifier of the conjoined (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇabhāva*) possible, because the absence of a jar does not serve as a qualifier of the location on the ground.

For nothing that is neither conjoined (*saṃyukta*) nor inherent (*samaveta*) can function as a qualifier; this is because we observe such a status [of being a qualifier] only in the case of things like a staff, which is conjoined, or the quality of whiteness, which is inherent. Furthermore, non-existence (*abhāva*) is not conjoined with anything, because it is not a substance (*adravyabhāva*).
It does not inhere anywhere, because of its distinctness from qualities and so forth.

And if the eye, assisted by the contact consisting in the state of being a qualifier of that which is conjoined, perceives absence, then, since there is no difference in this regard, it would also perceive taste and other qualities residing in the substance conjoined with it.

If it is argued that [the sense organ] does not apprehend [absence] because of its incapacity (*ayogyatva*), then it should likewise not apprehend the non-existence of that [object], since there is no difference in the nature of its incapacity.

Or, if one maintains a rule regarding apprehension and non-apprehension based on capacity and incapacity, then let capacity itself be the "contact" (*saṃnikarṣa*); what is the use of the talk of the sixfold contact? Therefore, the cognition of the absence of a jar is not visual.

Now, when the eyes are wide open, we perceive both the locus of the ground and the absence of the jar; but when they are closed, we do not perceive either of them. Since the occurrence of their cognition is equally dependent upon the presence of those eyes, how do we understand the distinction that the cognition of the locus of the ground is visual while the cognition of the absence is not? We certainly understand it: precisely because of the lack of sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*).
For the eye, when not in contact with its object, is not capable of producing a cognition.

However, this "being manifested by the existence of that" (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*) is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*), just like the cognition of heat associated with fire—which is dense with a series of thick flames situated at a great distance—following upon the perception of its brilliant color. In that case, just as the conformity to the presence and absence of the eye (*nayanānvayavyatirekānuvidhāna*) is established otherwise for the sensation of touch when the touch is inferred from the color, so too here, since the apprehension of the absence of the jar is inseparable from the perception of the spot of ground, the conformity to the presence and absence of the sense organ is established otherwise; thus, the manifestation of the absence of the jar is not visual.
Thus it has been said: "Having apprehended the existence of the object and having remembered the counter-correlate, a mental cognition of non-existence arises independently of the senses."
And for this very reason, there is sometimes the apprehension of even that which is not present.

For example, one who has perceived Gauramūlaka in its mere essential nature (svarūpamātra) and subsequently travels to another region, being asked by someone there whether Garga exists or does not exist, apprehends only the essential nature [of Garga].
Then, for one who is recollecting Gauramūlaka, at that very moment, knowledge of Garga's existence arises, even though he is not in contact with him.
In that case, since there is not even a mention of the sense faculties (*indriya*), it cannot be a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Nor can this absence (*abhāva*) be known through inference (*anumāna*), because it is impossible for either the location of the ground or the non-perception of the jar situated there to serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*).

The location of the ground cannot be the mark, because the absence is cognized even by one who has not grasped a relationship [between the two], because it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*), and because it is impossible to grasp a relationship due to the infinity of absences that have that location as their substratum.
Nor is the non-perception of a jar a logical mark (*liṅga*), because it lacks the property of being a feature of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).
The non-perception of a jar is a property of the jar, not of its absence.

If it is argued that it possesses the status of being a property [of the absence] because it functions toward the cognition of the jar's absence, we say no, for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
[The opponent argues: "Its being a property of that [subject] consists in its producing the cognition of the mark; and its being a property of that occurs when the cognition has already arisen.
[We reply: But if the cognition of the absence of the jar is not yet established, it is impossible to know that non-perception is a property of that subject.
On the other hand, if it is already established, what is the use of knowing its status as a property of the subject, since the cognition of the probandum is already accomplished?

Moreover, how could this mark called "non-perception" (adarśana), whose pervasion (vyāpti) is unknown, serve as an inferential indicator for non-existence? And the apprehension of pervasion, as in the case of smoke and fire, must be preceded by the apprehension of both relata (the subject and the property). Therefore, it must be considered: at the very moment of apprehending the pervasion, from where could there be the apprehension of the subject known as "non-existence"?
If it is argued that [the object] is known from that very inference, then there is mutual dependence;
if its apprehension is based on another inference, however, there is an infinite regress.
The mark (liṅga) called "non-perception" also has the nature of the absence of perception; thus, even when considering the determination of its own essential form, this very same path applies.

Therefore, even if one were to go as far as to postulate another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) skilled in determining non-existence for the sake of establishing that [absence], since its establishment is achieved through that [non-perception] itself, it cannot be an object of inference (anumeya).

Furthermore, it is not even reasonable to suspect that this cognition—"there is no jar here"—is caused by any one of the means of knowledge such as verbal testimony, comparison, or presumptive testimony; therefore, since it transcends the means of knowledge that apprehend existent things, it is logical that non-existence (abhāva) is the very domain of non-existence.

Moreover, it is appropriate that an object of cognition (*prameya*) be cognized by a corresponding means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for when the object of cognition is of the nature of an existent (*bhāva*), non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot be the means of valid cognition.
And when the object of cognition is non-existence, existence cannot be the means of valid cognition.
You have not denied the object of cognition called non-existence, as the Buddhists have;
therefore, this means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must also be admitted to be of the nature of non-existence.

To this it is replied: It is true that non-existence (*abhāva*) is accepted as an object of cognition (*prameya*), because its nature is determined by perception and the other [means of knowledge]; however, it does not seek a separate means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its own determination. For that which exists in a place not far removed from one's location is determined by the eye, while that which is remote is determined in some cases by other means of cognition as well.

And likewise, the cognition "there is no jar here" is indeed a single cognition that has both as its object, just like the cognition "there is curd in this bowl," for one whose visual activity has not ceased. In that case, how can this distinction be made—that the cognition regarding the mere patch of ground is produced by the eye, while the other is produced by another means of knowledge? For the appearance "fire is here" is rightly considered non-sensory (*anakṣaja*), since it occurs after the perception of smoke and is possible only through the intervention of other cognitions, such as the recollection of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
But here, it is not at all like that.
For the cognition of the non-existence of a jar, which is as immediate as the [cognition of] a patch of ground, is experienced without interruption.

Nor does non-existence become an object of perception in the same way that a fire on a distant mountain is not, because the cognition of that [non-existence] conforms to the presence and absence of the operation of those [senses].

For in that case (the perception of fire), even one whose eyes are fully engaged is not able to perceive the fire residing on the mountain; but here (in the case of non-existence), one perceives the absence of a jar while the visual operation of the eyes is still unrelaxed. Thus, the cognition of non-existence is visual, because it conforms to the presence and absence of that [visual operation].

Nor is this relation of "occurrence upon the existence of that" (tadbhāvabhāvitva) otherwise established [as accidental], like the inference of touch preceded by the sight of the form of a fire situated at a distance;
for in that case, it has been repeatedly ascertained that the eye lacks the capacity to perceive touch, and another cause—the tactile organ (tvagindriya)—is known to be the determiner of touch.

Furthermore, since the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitā*) between such color and touch has been perceived, it is logical that this touch is indeed to be inferred; thus, in that case, the operation of the eye is established as being otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddhatva*).
In the present case, however, such a mode does not exist.
Nor can it be assumed that because something is invariably concomitant with another in one instance, it is established as such everywhere;
for if it were so, even visible form would have to abandon its status as being perceived by the eye.

Now, how can it be asserted that absence (*abhāva*), being formless and unconnected, is visible (*cākṣuṣa*)? For visibility consists in being the object of a cognition produced by the eye, not in possessing color-form (*rūpa*); for even atoms, though possessing color-form, are not visible, and color-form itself, though formless, is visible.

Not everything that is connected is visible to the eye, because even though space is connected [to the eye], it lacks that quality [of visibility]. However, it is not the case that if something unconnected were perceived by the eye, it would follow that even distant or obstructed things like Vibhīṣaṇa would become visible. It is said in reply: this rule indeed applies to positive entities—that what is unconnected is not perceived by the eye; but a non-entity (abhāva), even though unconnected, will be perceived by the eye.
The description of the sixfold contact is also intended to convey the existence [of the object]; for whatever is perceived is perceived through one or another of the six types of contact.
The claim that the sense organs function by reaching their objects is stated only with reference to real entities.
Therefore, since non-existence is not a real entity, there is no fault in the fact that the eye produces a cognition of it even without attaining contact with it.

Nor should it be suspected that there is a perception of the non-existence of everything in other locations and so forth, simply because there is no difference in their lack of connection [to the senses]; for the cognition of non-existence depends upon the perception of its locus, and a locus is perceptible only when it is in close proximity.
Alternatively, the eye, assisted by the sense-object contact known as "the state of being qualified by what is conjoined" (saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇabhāva), will apprehend absence,
just as it does "inherence" (samavāya) in the view of those who maintain that inherence is perceptible.

Now, one might object: "This [inherence] is unestablished; how can that which is unestablished be used as an example? Do not say so, for even by you, some mode of subsistence between substance and quality must necessarily be admitted.

Since we never observe a substance and a quality to be unrelated when their difference is established through the cognition of distinction, some form of subsistence must certainly be accepted; therefore, enough with this consideration of other matters.

As for the claim that "because conjunction (saṃyoga) and inherence (samavāya) do not exist, non-existence cannot be a qualifier of a location on the earth," that too is incorrect; for we shall demonstrate immediately, by the force of perception, that there exists a relation called the "qualifier-qualified relationship" (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva) which is indeed distinct from both conjunction and inherence.

As for the objection raised regarding the over-extension [of the definition] to taste and other qualities when the sense-object contact consists in the state of being a qualifier of that which is conjoined, this same fault applies equally even to the visual contact with color known as "inherence in the conjoined" (saṃyuktasamavāya).

In that case, let conjunction-inherence (saṃyuktasamavāya) also not be a sense-object contact; what is lost to us? Let the eye then grasp color even though it is entirely unconnected. For there is no relation between the eye and color other than conjunction-inherence.

Is it not the case that the very operation consisting in the apprehension of an object is the contact (*sannikarṣa*) of the eye, or its capacity (*yogyatā*); and that it is precisely by virtue of this that the eye is accepted as the grasper of color, and not through [other relations] such as inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*)? If so, why would that operation or that capacity not also apply to non-existence (*abhāva*)?
Furthermore, it is contradictory to maintain that the sense organs act by reaching their objects because they are causal factors (*kāraka*), while at the same time denying the existence of contact.

Therefore, one must state that there is a sixfold capacity (yogyatā) which follows upon the various types of contact (sannikarṣa), and one should not rest content with mere capacity alone. For those who accept that wherever there is capacity, contact is also present, but that where there is contact, capacity is not necessarily present, the objection regarding the over-extension [of perception] to taste and so forth does not disturb their minds. Even though contact exists in the case of taste and so on, they are not perceived because of the absence of capacity.
Even according to the theory that [non-existence] is merely a capacity, non-existence does not lack capacity;
for what property of a real entity do you not admit it to possess?
Because it is devoid of all designations, let it be said that "it simply does not exist," or else let non-existence itself be accepted as the object of visual cognition.

As for the statement: "Even after seeing only the intrinsic nature [of an object], even while subsequently remembering something, when asked about the non-existence of another thing therein, one understands it at that very moment," that too is not tenable. For at the very time of grasping the intrinsic nature of the white root-stone as distinct from other objects, the apprehension of the absence of all objects not present there is established by a variegated cognition (*mecakabuddhi*). Therefore, the current recollection of Garga's absence residing therein is not an experience of that which was previously beyond perception.

For instance, having remembered that "Garga was not there at that time," this speaker of truth says so; yet he indeed remains in doubt regarding Garga's current existence or non-existence, because it is possible for Garga to have arrived there from somewhere at this present moment.

If it is argued that he did not previously experience the apprehension of the absence of everything at the foot of the *gauramūlaka* tree, we reply: even though it was not experienced, that [absence] is necessarily postulated for him, just like the recollection of an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) regarding a familiar object.
For instance, when questioned about this or that [object], he recalls the absence of each respective thing and provides an answer to everyone.

[Objection: But surely, if the absence of everything were grasped by a "dark-blue" (mecaka) cognition, the memory of the absence of everything would arise all at once. [Reply: Not so. Only that for which he has a cause of recollection—such as a question or the like—does he remember; he does not remember everything, as there is no cause for remembering what is not present.

Furthermore, even in the case of phonemes perceived sequentially, there is a simultaneous recollection immediately following the experience of the final phoneme; however, in other cases, even when things are perceived simultaneously, recollection will occur sequentially. Thus, this fault does not apply to the "dark-blue" cognition.

Furthermore, by you who claim that "only the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) is perceived," the cognition of a variegated color (*mecakajñāna*) is indeed admitted; for by the use of the term "only" (*mātra*), the apprehension of the absence of anything other than that is established.
For you yourself have stated: "This very determination which occurs regarding an entity—that 'it is this'—does not exist without the concomitant perception of the absence of other things."

Therefore, since at the very time of perceiving Gauramūlaka one apprehends the absence of Garga and others who are not present there, it should not be accepted that the apprehension of absent objects occurring at this later time is caused by non-existence (abhāva); rather, this absence is accessible through perception alone.
Furthermore, as for the statement that non-existence is not inferable—that it has as its object the absence under discussion, namely "there is no jar here"—that is precisely what we accept.

However, some absences, occurring in places beyond sensory range, are indeed inferable; for example, when rain falls upon a crop drenched by a stream of water in the darkness, the absence of contact with dense wind is inferred. Or, as illustrated in the context of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the absence of Caitra outside is postulated based on his absence from the house.
The ascertainment of non-existence also occurs in some cases through scripture,
such as the knowledge of the absence of thieves and so forth for travelers from a reliable authority.

Furthermore, the argument that "the object of cognition is cognized by a corresponding means of cognition because it is an object of cognition, like an object of cognition consisting of a positive entity" is also an unproving reason (*aprayojaka-sādhana*).
The absence of cataracts and other such defects is apprehended by direct perception,
and the absence of the mark's occurrence in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) serves as a cooperative factor for the inference.
The absence of defects in the statements of a person is also required;
from that absence, which is included within the causal complex, there arises the cognition of existence.
And non-existence is sometimes accepted as a mark for the cognition of existence;
even the absence of rain is an inferential indicator of the conjunction of wind and clouds.
Therefore, it is logical that the cognition of a non-existence occurs only through a non-existence;
for a spirit is not called by the same name as the offering made to it.

On this point, the Raktapaṭas say: "When an object of cognition exists, the application of a means of valid cognition is indeed appropriate; however, that very [object] is extremely difficult to find."

That which is called non-existence (abhāva), when it is cognized, is not experienced as independent in the manner of the positive essence of things such as a jar; rather, it is experienced as qualified by place, time, and counter-correlate (pratiyogin). For such is the cognition: "This is not here, now. If non-existence, even while being understood in this way, were indeed connected with those [qualifiers], who would hate it?
But it is not connected with that [space].
For there is no connection whatsoever between this [absence] and space, time, or its counter-positive, because connections such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) are untenable.
And a qualifier cannot exist without a connection.

Now, one might object: "Is not the very relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) itself the relation? What need is there for another relation? Do not say so; for that [relation of qualifier and qualified] is understood as being rooted in another relation.
A thing becomes a qualifier only when it is either conjoined (*saṃyukta*) or inheres (*samaveta*), as in "Devadatta has a staff" (*daṇḍī devadattaḥ*) or "the lotus is blue" (*nīlam utpalam*).
Therefore, the relation of qualifier and qualified is not a real, independent relation in its own right.
We observe that even this [relation] is reversed according to human will;
for a qualifier becomes the qualified, and the qualified also becomes the qualifier—thus, this relation is purely conceptual and not an inherent property of the thing itself.
There can be no relationship whatsoever between an absence and its counter-positive, because they do not exist at the same time;
for when the jar exists, its absence does not, and when its absence exists, the jar does not.

If it is argued that there will be a relationship called "contradiction" (*virodha*), what is the meaning of contradiction? For if the pre-established absence of a jar were to come and contradict the jar, then it might indeed be its opposite, like a jar and a mallet; but this is not the case, because those two do not exist at the same time. Or, if such a thing were admitted, one would experience the coexistence of the jar and its absence as being like a killer and his victim, like a jar and a mallet. What could the absence of the jar do to contradict the jar? If something that does nothing were considered a contradiction, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasakti*) of the term.
But if one were to posit another non-existence [to account for the destruction], there would be an infinite regress.
Hammers and the like cannot be the causes of the non-existence of a jar, because a thing, being perishable by its very nature, does not depend on a cause for its destruction.
If an entity has a perishable nature, then what is the use of causes for its destruction? If it has an imperishable nature, then what is the use of causes for its destruction?

Therefore, the operation of causal factors such as a hammer consists precisely in the production of a series of heterogeneous shards and so forth; when another set of conditions enters [the process], there is the arising of a different series, but it is not that a non-entity (*abhāva*) is produced from that.
For if that [non-entity] were a distinct entity from the jar, what would have occurred such that it is no longer perceived as before?
If you argue that this is due to its being incompatible [with perception], this has already been refuted.
If, however, [the jar] were not a different entity [from its destruction], then the jar itself would be the effect of the mallet.
Now, one might argue: "The very shards produced by the mallet are themselves the absence of the jar.
Alas, in that case, when the shards are shattered, since the absence of the jar would have perished, it would follow that the jar must reappear!
Furthermore, if it is asserted that shards are the non-existence of a jar because they do nothing toward it, then the same could be said for cloth as well.
Their status as performing some function must be rejected, just as before.

Furthermore, this non-existence must either possess the nature of coming into being or not possess the nature of coming into being. If it possesses the nature of coming into being, then it would be an existent thing, like a jar or other such objects. However, if it does not possess the nature of coming into being, then if that non-existence exists, it would necessarily be eternal.

Furthermore, this non-existence (abhāva) must either be related to a single entity or related to all entities. In the case of its being related to a single entity, we do not perceive it as being eternally without a cause.

However, if it were related to all entities, then because non-existence—which is opposed to every object—would be eternal and eternally present, there would follow the absurd consequence that the three worlds would be destroyed all at once.
Therefore, there is no such thing as non-existence, whether it be eternal or non-eternal.
But surely, if non-existence is not admitted, there would result a collapse of all worldly transactions due to the mutual confusion of entities;
as it has been said: "In this way, curd would exist in milk, and milk in curd; a cloth in a jar; a horn on a hare; and consciousness in earth and the other elements, and corporeality in the self."

If, however, one accepts the non-existence of entities on the grounds of their mutual non-existence, then their non-confusion will be established; yet this is incorrect, because entities possess a non-confused nature by their very own essence.

But in the explanation intended to avoid the confusion [of categories] caused by the reason being non-existent, there is all the more a collapse: "An entity must certainly be accepted as unmixed even with the portion that is non-existent, just as it is [unmixed] with another entity; how then will that [entity] come to be?"
If even non-entities possess mutual distinctness by their own nature, what wrong have entities done to you? If [that distinctness] is extrinsic, from where indeed does it arise?
If it were to be derived from existing entities, there would be mutual dependence;
if it were produced from another non-existence, there would be an insurmountable infinite regress.

Furthermore, since the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvatā*) is indistinguishable for all things, any differentiation among them must be based solely on the objects of negation (*pratiṣedhya*).

Since the entities to be negated are themselves differentiated from one another, they in turn differentiate that [non-existence]; thus, it is more appropriate to say that the non-confusion of non-entities depends upon entities, rather than the reverse.
Therefore, even out of fear that the established order of all categories would fall into disorder, the acceptance of non-existence as a real entity is not tenable.
Now, if negation is rejected, what could possibly be the denotation of the negative particle?
Let it be said: the status of a denotation is not accepted as being established merely by following the word.
We Buddhists indeed possess fame renowned throughout the entire world;
we are experts in conceptualizing word-meanings as being nothing more than mere mental constructs.

In some cases, a negative particle (*nañ*) that functions by attaining the status of a nominal stem (*nāmapada*) produces a cognition that delineates an object other than that which is excluded by the negation.
In some cases, however, having entered into a connection with a verb,
it merely provides a description of the commencement and cessation of the action denoted by that verb.
But if non-existence is refuted by this path,
where then shall these eleven types of non-apprehension go?
Non-perception of the intrinsic nature is, for example: "There is no jar here, because it is not perceived."
Non-perception of the cause is, for example: "There is no smoke here, because fire is not perceived."
Non-perception of the pervader is, for example: "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here, because no tree is perceived."
Non-perception of the effect is, for example: "There are no unimpeded causes of smoke here, because smoke is not perceived."
Perception of what is incompatible with the essential nature [of a thing], as for example: "There is no sensation of cold here, because fire is perceived."
Perception of an effect that is incompatible with the essential nature [of a thing], as for example: "There is no sensation of cold here, because smoke is perceived."

The perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory [of the probandum] is, for example: "The destruction of even an existing entity is not necessarily certain, because it depends upon other causes."
Perception of what is incompatible with the effect is, for example: "There is no cause of cold here whose capacity is unimpeded, because fire is perceived."
Perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi) is, for example: "There is no sensation of cold here, because fire is seen."
Perception of what is incompatible with the cause is, for example: "He does not possess specific symptoms such as horripilation or chattering teeth, because of the presence of a particular fire."

Perception of the effect of that which is incompatible with the cause is, for example: "This place is not occupied by a person who has begun playing a lute with his teeth and so forth, because it contains smoke."
It is true that eleven kinds of non-apprehension are accepted here;
however, it is the cause for the conventional usage of "non-existent," not for the cognition of absence itself.

Now, it has been stated that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is included within the essential nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), and in the case of an essential nature reason, it is maintained that there is no distinction between the probandum and the probans. Furthermore, since the conventional usage of "non-existent" consists of cognition and verbal designation, it is distinct from that [non-apprehension] itself; how then could it fall within its scope? True, this is so; however, it is not the conventional usage of "non-existent" that is established by that [non-apprehension], but rather the fitness (*yogyatā*) for such usage. And since this fitness is not a different entity from that [non-apprehension], there is no loss of its status as an essential nature reason.

[Objection: But surely, capacity (*yogyatā*) is of the nature of existence (*bhāva*), whereas non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) has non-existence (*abhāva*) as its essence; how then can they be non-different? [Reply: This is not so, for those who understand non-apprehension do not say that non-apprehension—which is of the nature of the negation of apprehension—has non-existence as its essence; rather, they say it is precisely the apprehension of another object excluded by the negation that has the nature of the absence of the [target] object.

For this very reason, the following objection is also not to be raised: "Since non-apprehension is of the nature of absence, it must be determined by another apprehension, leading to an infinite regress. This is because non-apprehension, which consists in the apprehension of another thing, is indeed self-cognized.

Now, one might object: "If the conventional usage of 'non-existent' were established through non-apprehension alone, then even that which is invisible would be established as such. [We reply: No, because the qualification "perceptibility" is employed; it is the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) that establishes the conventional usage of "non-existent," not the non-apprehension of just anything. In this regard, since the perceptibility of a jar or similar object previously seen is firmly determined, its conventional usage as non-existent is indeed established through non-apprehension.
In the case of things such as sky-flowers, which are never perceived at any time,
there is a definitive determination of their non-existence because they lack the fitness for being perceived.
However, because a ghost or similar being cannot be definitively ascertained as visible,
it is not possible to establish its non-existence through non-perception.
Even in those cases such as "This Caitra is not a Piśāca," where there is a negation of identity, perceptibility is of no use.
For Caitra, who is indeed of a nature other than that of a *piśāca*, is the object of direct perception;
if his nature as such is already ascertained, what purpose would there be for that qualification?
Thus, since the conventional usage of "non-existent" is established through non-apprehension,
an object of knowledge called "non-existence" is not conceivable in the same way that existence is.
To this it is replied: First of all, two types of cognition are observed arising as witnessed by all living beings, namely, "The jar exists here" and "It does not exist here.

Regarding these, whatever is asserted—such as that the cognition consisting of mere conceptual construction is without an objective support (*anālambana*) or has as its support only a portion of itself—that applies equally to the cognition of existence as it does to the cognition of non-existence.
Therefore, let both be valid, or let neither be valid.

As for the claim that the cognition "it exists" is valid while the other is invalid, that is merely a matter of preference; moreover, since the cognition "it does not exist" shares the same logical status as the cognition "it exists," its object must be investigated.

Now, it was argued that the non-apprehension of a jar consists in the apprehension of the ground as distinct from the jar; however, that is incorrect. What is this "distinctness from the jar"? Is it non-different from the patch of ground or different? If it were non-different, then because there would be no distinction from the patch of ground itself, the cognition "the jar does not exist" would arise even when the jar is present.
If, on the other hand, it were different, the dispute would merely be over a name.
And its distinctness even from a jar must be considered in terms of both difference and non-difference;
for if there were no difference, it would be the jar itself, and if there were difference, it would be a mere non-entity.

In this case, regarding the cognition "there is no jar here," which has as its objective support a ground devoid of a jar, there is no dispute that in the "here" portion of this cognition, space is indeed the objective support; for even at the time of the positive perception "there is a jar here," one must admit the manifestation of that same space therein.

However, in the case of "there is no jar," that which manifests is not merely the ground itself, because—as in the case of the positive perception—a manifestation distinct from that [ground] necessarily occurs.
But as for that which appears as distinct from it, let it be called either "the exclusion of the jar" or "the absence of the jar"; there is no difference in the actual entity itself.

Is it not the case that "the jar does not exist" is merely a conceptual construction (vikalpa), since—as occurring immediately after perception—it is equivalent to an affirmative conceptual construction?
It is said that conceptual constructions (kalpanā) arise in accordance with experience;
however, a negative conceptual construction is not suited to the experience of an affirmation.
Surely we do not assert that conceptual constructions are valid cognitions; let it be that even conceptual constructions of injunctions lack the status of being valid means of knowledge.
If you hold that the validity of perceptions follows from their being non-conceptual,
then here too, theirs [the yogis'] validity exists precisely because they follow what is non-conceptual.

If it is argued that the conventional usage of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for positive conceptualizations occurs through the attainment of a real entity (*vastu*), then here too, let the conventional usage of validity for negative conceptualizations occur precisely through that same attainment.
If it is asked, "What real entity is attained here?", [we reply: what is attained there either? If you say "blue," this very thing is indeed the attainment of an absence as well;
for when blue is attained, it is attained in a form excluded from yellow and other colors that are invariably concomitant with its absence.
And this attainment of blue as such is also the attainment of the absence of others; for otherwise, there would not even be the attainment of blue.
And this has been accepted by you yourselves when you spoke of contradiction in terms of essential characteristics (*lākṣaṇika-virodha*).
The arising of pleasure and pain occurs only when enemies and friends exist;
having observed the absence of thorns, one places one's foot upon the path.
Having understood the non-existence of a jar prior to its production, one applies effort toward its cause;
having determined the absence of disease, one desists from taking medicine.
Seeing here this continuous succession of conventional usage established upon non-existence, what conscious person indeed would deny non-existence?
Now, surely that which is not a cause cannot be the objective support (*ālambana*) of cognition;
for non-existence (*abhāva*), being by nature devoid of all description, is not capable of producing cognition.
Therefore, how can it be called an objective support? For the Buddhists, at least, no entity whatsoever appears as a producer [of cognition].
Because it would entail the consequence of persisting for two or three moments, which would result in the destruction of the vow of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*);
for there is no simultaneity among these actions—namely, that [the object] arises, produces the cognition of the object, and is apprehended by that cognition once it has arisen.
Therefore, an entity appears as being entirely devoid of causal agency.
And we shall refute the position that [the object] deposits its form [into consciousness];
thus, like an existent entity, a non-existent entity too should appear as something that does not produce [cognition].
We, however, maintain that non-existence (*abhāva*), like existence (*bhāva*), is capable of producing cognition.
For the definition of non-existence is not the total absence of all causal capacity; rather, it is that which is apprehended by the cognition "it does not exist.
Indeed, existence is held to be that which is apprehended by the cognition of "being," whereas non-existence is that which is apprehended by the cognition of "non-being."
Thus, this has been stated: "Reality is both existent and non-existent."

"Is it not the case that this non-existence, being a producer of cognition just like existence, does not differ from existence? Ah, how clever the "Beloved of the Gods" (the fool) appears! There is a difference in cognition, yet you say that the cognized existence and non-existence do not differ—how can this be so? Furthermore, O fool, if form and taste are distinguished despite the lack of difference in their status as producers of cognition, [you might ask] "Is it not because of a difference in cognition? [We reply: Then existence and non-existence should also be distinguished solely by a difference in cognition, even though they share the common property of being producers.
For you yourself have admitted that there can be no difference in appearance without a difference in the objects appearing;

as it has been said: "The two [cognitions] possess validity regarding real entities, yet they declare a difference in their objects because the appearance is variegated, which would be impossible in a single [unitary] entity."
Thus [it is said].
Therefore, just as the cognition "it exists" has existence as its ground, let it be accepted that the cognition "it does not exist" has non-existence as its ground.
Alternatively, let the Vijñānavāda itself be clearly adhered to; however, an intermediate state is not tenable.
Furthermore, its capacity for causal efficiency has already been demonstrated.
The power of action known as self-cognition belonging to this [entity] is undeniable;
however, causal efficiency produced by another is not produced even by an existent thing.
And this being the case, that theory of potency which was previously described here results only in parching one's throat, because it contradicts direct perception.

Regarding what was stated—that there is likewise an absence of a relation—therein, first, the relation between non-existence and location is that of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*). However, this rule applies to positive entities (*bhāva*), as that relation is rooted in another relation; it does not apply to non-existence (*abhāva*).
Alternatively, even in the case of an existent entity, this rule does not hold;
for it is not the case that whatever is related is necessarily a qualifier,
since the cognition "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍin*) does not arise when a staff is merely being held against the foot or the head.
Nor is it the case that whatever is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) must necessarily be a relation; for even though inherence (*samavāya*) functions as a qualifier, it lacks any other underlying relation.

Therefore, although devoid of any further relation, the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is determined to be an independent relation in its own right—just like logical necessity (*pratibandha*) or the signifier-signified relationship (*vācyavācakabhāva*)—because it is perceived as such.

Since both [the locus and the absence] possess a dual nature, and because they may sometimes appear in such a way to someone, there is no fault even if a reversed cognition occurs by following human intention;
therefore, the relation of the absence with the location, such as the ground, is indeed the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
In the same way, that very [relation] should be understood as existing even with respect to time;

for even in the absence of conjunction or other relations, whether with an action—such as going—which resides in the agent, or with an action—such as breaking—which resides in the object, there is indeed a relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*). Just so, it will also exist for non-existence (*abhāva*).
Its relation with the counter-positive (pratiyogin), however, is opposition (virodha).
And this alone is the meaning of opposition: that the two do not coexist in the same locus.
Consequently, upon the destruction of one, there is not the destruction of all, because the absence of a jar has only that specific jar as its counter-positive.

As for the conceptual distinction made between that which has the nature of coming into being (*bhavanadharma*) and that which does not have the nature of coming into being (*abhavanadharma*), it is accepted therein that non-existence (*abhāva*) indeed possesses the nature of coming into being.

Furthermore, even though it has the nature of coming into being, non-existence is not distinct from existence, because a difference in appearance has already been demonstrated in the case of form, taste, and so forth.
And its possession of the nature of coming into being occurs because it follows the presence and absence of causes (*hetu*).
For just as a jar follows causes such as the lump of clay and the staff during its production, it likewise follows causes such as the mallet during its destruction.
Even on the view that a dissimilar continuum is produced, the absence of the capacity to produce a similar continuum is indeed established.
Otherwise, even upon the impact of a mallet or other such instruments, a similar continuum would be produced just as a dissimilar one is.

If it is argued that the jar possesses the capacity to produce both a similar and a dissimilar continuum, then either the production of a continuum of shards would be observed even before contact with the mallet and so forth, or else the production of a continuum of jars would be observed even when such contact occurs; thus, there would be no fixed rule.
Furthermore, if a jar has the inherent nature of producing a moment of a different kind, then the mallet and other such instruments would be entirely useless.
For if its nature were to arise from that [cause], nothing would be effected by the hammer and so forth;
and even if it does not arise from that, nothing would be effected by the hammer and so forth.
And when another moment has arisen due to the falling of the hammer,
what has happened to the moment of the jar such that it does not appear as before?
Surely its non-existence has occurred; that very same meaning is expressed here.
What offense have you committed against the suffix *ghañ*, or what service has been rendered by the suffix *lyuṭ*?
But was it not said that "nothing happens to him; he simply does not exist"? That is incorrect, for his very non-existence is precisely what constitutes his absence.

"Is it not the case that 'he is not' [refers to the person], and not to his non-existence? Do not say so; for there is a difference in the objects of the words 'he' and 'not,' as well as of their corresponding cognitions.

The object of the cognition 'he' is a jar or the like being remembered, whereas the object of the cognition 'not' is non-existence. Enough, therefore, with this crushing of fruitless and crooked speech composed by those who are falsely clever."
Therefore, since the status of non-existence as an object of cognition has been established in this manner,
non-apprehensions are indeed capable of serving as the basis for the conventional usage of "non-existent."

Nor is it possible for inference of intrinsic nature (svabhāvānumāna) to include that [inference of non-existence], since it has been established that the object of cognition (meyam) called "non-existence" is distinct from these [other types of inference].
Granted that [non-apprehension] of a cause and so forth may indeed be inference;
however, it has been established that the non-apprehension of an essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi) is perception.

And this "perception of the pervaded by the contradictory" (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), which was cited as an example within the inner harem of the eleven types of non-perception—namely, "the destruction of even an existing entity is not certain to occur, because it depends upon other causes"—has just now been effectively refuted; however, its detailed refutation will be undertaken under the section on the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
But we too are ashamed today because of that error of those excellent Mīmāṃsakas who do not accept non-existence.

By those who say, "Indeed, the jar is not perceived, but its absence is not perceived," it would be asserted that the existence and non-existence of things consist merely in their being seen and not being seen.
This, however, is incorrect; for while existence and non-existence are determined by seeing and not seeing, seeing and not seeing themselves are not existence and non-existence.
Nor can linguistic conventions based on the non-existence of something be established merely by its non-perception,
as in the case of water hidden beneath the earth.
Indeed, no distinction appears to us between a sky-flower, a piśāca, and water hidden by earth, insofar as they are all unperceived.
For non-perception at all times, when it produces the certainty of non-existence,
is distinguished from the non-perception of water existing within the ground.
Furthermore, based on scripture and reasoning, one arrives at the conviction that a sentient being exists;
thus, even though it is never perceived, a *piśāca* is not like a flower in the sky.

Therefore, as for what is said—that "the non-apprehension of a non-apprehension is itself a non-apprehension"—that is mere verbiage. In the case of things such as a sky-flower, however, its very absence is determined by a non-apprehension that includes a specific qualification; it is not merely its non-apprehension [that is established].
Furthermore, if the non-existence of entities were not admitted as their counter-correlate, it would follow that these are eternal; for, according to you, they are not momentary.
If it is asked what the function of the hammer and so forth is [if they merely produce a collection of potsherds],
then why does the jar, since it has not yet perished, not perform its own function?

If it is argued that [the object] is not seen, then what has happened to this very same stable object which was seen at that very moment? Why is there non-perception even when the entire collection of causes, such as the sense faculties, is present?
Therefore, its non-perception at that time is caused solely by its absence.
In your view, the cognition "it does not exist" is self-luminous;
yet this [cognition] is not without an object, just like the cognition "it exists."
Words have conceptual constructions as their objects, just as they are used in the house of Śauddhodani;
"it is not so" is what is sung by you—let that which is expressed by the negative particle (nañ) be stated.
Common consensus has been abandoned, yet non-existence has not been refuted;
and the meaning of the Bhāṣya has been disregarded—oh, what skill in reasoning!
Enough with much speaking; conflict here is not fitting. For even the lapse of great souls must be forgiven by those such as I.
Therefore, it is established that non-existence is that which is apprehended through the cognition "it does not exist."
And that [non-existence] is of two kinds: antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).
Others say it is of four kinds, adding mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), making those two as well.
Still others say it is of six types, adding relative non-existence (*apekṣābhāva*) and functional non-existence (*sāmarthyābhāva*), making those four as well.
And in that regard, non-existence prior to the acquisition of its own nature is designated as "prior non-existence" (prāgabhāva);
whereas the loss of the nature of what has arisen is called "subsequent destruction" (pradhvaṃsa).
But other types of non-existence do not differ from prior non-existence in the ultimate sense;
for that which is called mutual non-existence is merely a limiting adjunct consisting of another entity.
Because it is devoid of limits, that very [entity] has reached a state of absolute non-existence;
its state of being relative is dependent upon spatial adjuncts.
If its capacity is already established prior to destruction, then there is the cognition of its absence [only] upon that destruction;
if it is not so established, then its distinction from antecedent non-existence is difficult to find.
The destruction of what has arisen, or rather its non-arising, is non-existence in reality; other distinctions, however, are considered to be merely adventitious.
Therefore, this object of cognition called non-existence and its apprehension by means of a sense faculty are established.
For this reason, the Sage Akṣapāda rightly declared that the number of these means of valid cognition is four.
But surely their number as four has not yet been established, because *saṃbhava* and *aitihya* constitute two additional means of valid cognition.
"Occurrence" (saṃbhava) means the comprehension of the whole through its parts, as in: "A *droṇa* occurs in a *khārī*; a hundred occurs in a thousand."

Tradition (*aitihya*) is a succession of rumors whose original speaker has not been specified, such as "A yakṣa dwells in this banyan tree"; nor is this a valid scripture (*āgama*), because there is no certainty regarding a trustworthy teacher.

This [argument] is untenable; for this occurrence is distinct, as it was not stated that a *droṇa* necessarily exists within a *khārī*. Indeed, this cognition is inferential (*laiṅgikī*) because of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Tradition (*aitihya*), however, is not true here; for who knows whether there is a *yakṣa* in this fig tree or not, when, where, by whom, or what the body of the *yakṣa* is like?
Furthermore, tradition (*aitihya*) is not distinct from scripture (*āgama*), because it consists of instruction (*upadeśa*).
We shall explain later that the mention of "reliable persons" (*āpta*) in the aphorism is not intended as a definition.

The rogue Cārvāka, however, having made the promise, "Now, therefore, we shall explain reality," explained that reality is precisely the impossibility of establishing the number and definitions of the means and objects of knowledge.

And in order to prove this impossibility regarding the number and definition of the means of knowledge, he pointed out such instances as those not produced by perception or other means of knowledge due to the variety of cognitions: "This hand has curved fingers" or "this hand has widely spaced fingers"—such a cognition occurs to one whose eyes are closed in the dark.
This [cognition] is not produced by the sense-faculty of touch, for that [faculty], being located in the hand, produces its own cognition only in that very place.

At night, seeing the flame of a lamp from afar, one directs the mind toward the rays of light spreading across the surrounding area; and one perceives the fragrance in a cluster of lotuses shaken by the wind, even when that scent has traveled far downwind.
Being thus skilled in such conjectures based on mere consciousness,
that wretched man does not truly know form through either direct perception or inference.
From direct perception, there is the cognition of the fingers being spread apart; because of its pervasiveness, the sense faculty is not unskilled in that regard.
However, by people drinking the cold water up to their navels, its extremely cool touch is experienced within.
And just as the cognition of conjunction arises from that [conjunction], so too does the cognition of its absence arise from it;
and because of the perception of a specific action, there is therefore the comprehension of the fingers being contracted.

Furthermore, since the cognition of the light of a distant lamp through the fragrance of a lotus is inferential (laiṅgikī) and produced by the knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti), what kind of cognition indeed could depend upon another means of valid knowledge?

There is no fixed rule regarding the number of means of valid knowledge; therefore, this was merely a false clamor uttered by the nihilists (nāstika), whose minds are devoid of the discernment of its functional capacity.

Among our means of valid cognition (*māna*), there exists a fixed limit that is non-distinct; likewise, the object of cognition (*prameya*) will be stated as being endowed with a fixed rule regarding its definition and so forth.
However, by asserting the impossibility of such a task, one would be declaring before the presence of the wise that one's own intellect is dull-witted.

Thus ends the first chapter in the *Nyāyamañjarī* composed by Jayanta Bhaṭṭa. The Second Chapter: Examination of Perception (*Pratyakṣaparīkṣā*). Now that the general definition and the classification of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been determined, the occasion for describing their specific definitions has arrived.
