Since perception is the foundation of all means of valid cognition and was mentioned first, it is treated as the eldest; therefore, to set forth its definition first, he says: "Perception is knowledge produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature. (*indriyārthasannikarṣotpannaṃ jñānam avyapadeśyam avyabhicāri vyavasāyātmakaṃ pratyakṣam*)
[1.1.4] "Perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is the designation of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*); the rest is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
The purpose of a definition is the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of things belonging to the same class and things belonging to different classes.

By this aphorism, the definition of perception—which is distinguished from what belongs to the same class, namely inference and the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and from what belongs to a different class, namely the objects of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth—is established.

Regarding this, they raise an objection: by means of qualifiers such as "produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object," is it the essential nature (*svarūpa*) that is qualified, or the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or the result (*phala*)? Among these, if one takes the position that the essential nature is qualified—such that "knowledge having such an essential nature is perception"—then because the essential nature alone is specified and no qualifier for the result is provided, the definition would be afflicted by the fallacies of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

First, there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*): validity would not be predicated even of that cognition whose nature is not of such a kind, nor of the sense organs and so forth, despite their having attained the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by producing a flawless result.

Furthermore, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*): validity would accrue even to a cognition whose nature is of such a kind [as defined], yet which is non-productive, or which produces a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), or which generates memory, or which instills doubt, or which produces error, because the result has not been specified.

Furthermore, if one were to state its specific qualification, there would be the consequence of having to supply another unmentioned sūtra, and the fault of under-extension (avyāpti) would remain as before; thus, the position that it is a qualification of the essential nature (svarūpa) is not tenable.

Nor is the position that takes "sāmagrī" (the causal complex) as the qualifier tenable; for in that case, the phrase "produced from the contact of the sense-organ and the object" (*indriyārthasannikarṣotpannam*) would have to be explained as "the causal complex produced from the contact of the sense-organ and the object.

Furthermore, since cognition is described as being "inexpressible," "non-erroneous," and "of a determinate nature," the entirety of the causal complex would have to be described metaphorically as such because it produces that cognition—this is an overly strained interpretation.

The position that [the word *pratyakṣa*] qualifies the result (*phala*) is also untenable, because it would entail the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), which respectively denote the result and the instrument (*karaṇa*).
This is so because we are currently discussing the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
wherein perception is said to be the means of valid cognition.
And that has been described as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

But since knowledge produced by it is the result (*phala*), how can there be a common locus (*aikādhikaraṇya*)? Therefore, because all three positions are untenable and no other position is possible, the Sūtra is incorrect.

To this it is replied: first of all, the two positions regarding the qualification of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) are not accepted, as they are afflicted by the aforementioned defects.
We accept only the position regarding the qualification of the result (*phala*).
As for the objection raised there concerning a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*), we shall resolve it by supplying the word "from" (*yataḥ*).
The meaning of the sūtra is that perception is that from which there arises a fruit called knowledge characterized by such specific qualifications.
In this way, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) nor any over-extension (ativyāpti), nor is there any strained interpretation;
for it is possible to establish the consistency of the words of the sūtra through a description of a faultless definition by means of merely supplying the appropriate words.

Objection: Why are the two terms "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) not explained as being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*)? Answer: Because it has been stated here that the instrument is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas knowledge is its result (*phala*); and since the difference in nature between a result and its instrument is established, [the terms cannot be in apposition]. Furthermore, [it would require] the superimposition of a word [to make them co-referential].
Therefore, in this context, with respect to the status of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), that cognition is held to be the result;
but when it itself has the status of a means of valid cognition, the results are the cognitions of avoidance and so forth.

But surely, since there is the possibility of an intervention by numerous cognitions such as memory and so forth, how could the non-discriminative perception (*ālocanājñāna*) produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object have "rejection" and so on as its result? To explain: having perceived an object belonging to the class of *kapittha* fruits through the causal complex of the contact of the sense-organ and so forth, one remembers that it is a means to pleasure, thinking, "Previously, pleasure was produced in me by something of this kind.
Then, immediately after that memory, a reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*) arises in him: "This is that very thing belonging to the class of *kapittha* fruits."

From that, the cognition of its desirability arises [in the form]: "Since this object, belonging to the class of wood-apples (*kapittha*) and so forth, is a means to pleasure, it is therefore desirable.

In the interim, even the name of the first cognition—the mere perception (*ālocana*) of the wood-apple produced by sensory contact—no longer remains; how, then, can this [subsequent cognition] be its fruit?
On this point, the teachers first say: "Well said!
It is true that such indeed is the sequence of cognitions.

However, we do not claim that the initial sensory perception (*ālocanājñāna*) possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatā*) with respect to the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth."

For instance, the initial non-conceptual awareness (*ālocanājñāna*) produced by the contact of the sense faculty with its object is merely the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, perception—which consists in the causal complex of the contact of the sense faculty with the object and so forth; it does not itself attain the status of a means of valid cognition, because it generates memory.

Immediately after that, there arises the recollection of its being a means to pleasure; thus, although this recollection is not itself a result of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it becomes a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it operates together with the sensory contact (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*) when the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the object of the senses arises—[namely], "This belongs to the class of wood-apples (*kapittha*) and so forth."

Furthermore, that ascertainment, being produced by perception, is called a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) through inference—just like the cognition of smoke—because from it there is an understanding of the capacity of the means to happiness, which is as imperceptible as fire.

Although no such thing as a supersensible power (*atīndriya-śakti*) exists in our view, nevertheless, capacity (*sāmarthya*), which consists in the inherent nature of the proximity of a collection of causes—both visible and invisible, such as the essential form and auxiliary factors—is indeed supersensible.

Therefore, this cognition—“this object belonging to the class of *kapittha* and so forth is a means to pleasure”—is inferential, having as its logical mark (*liṅga*) the fact of belonging to that same class, just like the cognition of a mountain possessing fire.

This very cognition, which consists in the ascertainment of being a means to pleasure and is the fruit of inference, becomes a means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) when it produces, along with the sense-object contact, a cognition of something to be acquired (*upādeya-jñāna*) regarding the *kapittha* and other objects within the range of the senses.

Having established that very point in his heart, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "When cognition is the mental modification (vṛtti), then the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference constitute valid knowledge (pramiti)."

The commentators, however, say: "This sequence of cognitions is not as [described]. It is true that the initial sensory perception (ālocanājñāna) produces a recollection of its being a means to pleasure; and by means of that recollection, the [perception] reaches the state of perishing. While in that state of perishing, it brings about the ascertainment of the object—such as a wood-apple (kapittha)—as a means to pleasure. This very cognition of being a means to pleasure is called the 'cognition of desirability' (upādeyatājñāna), and nothing else.
No intermediate reflective cognition (parāmarśa) is experienced at all. Thus, that very [result] has been shown to be the goal."

Since it is possible for [cognition] to be produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object and to have the knowledge of desirability as its result, what is the use of postulating a mass of cognitions that are not themselves experienced?
But surely the *parāmarśa* (reflective judgment) is indeed experienced and not merely postulated?
Immediately after the cognition of smoke, one recollects the invariable concomitance—namely, "wherever there is smoke, there is fire"—and then reflects: "And this is such smoke.

For if the *parāmarśa* were absent, the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) would not attain the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the object possessing the mark (*liṅgin*), since that [cognition of the mark] would merely be a generator of memory.
Furthermore, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not accepted as that which produces memory;

and since the cognition of the logical mark (liṅga) occurs immediately after remembrance, it would not be possible for it to arise as a restatement of what has already been perceived, such as "this [mountain] possesses fire."

Furthermore, regarding the statement "and likewise, sound is produced" (*tathā ca kṛtakaḥ śabdaḥ*), which is recited among the members of the syllogism—what would be its referent for those who deny the existence of *parāmarśa* (reflective consideration)?
We shall explain that just as one's own comprehension is produced by the members of the syllogism, so too is the comprehension of another;
therefore, *parāmarśa* cannot be rejected.
Regarding this, they say: "No intermediate reflective awareness is experienced at all, either prior to the cognition of the object to be inferred or subsequent to the recollection of the rule."
Therefore, having perceived the object, worldly people indeed determine its apprehension and so forth without even a slight delay.

Furthermore, the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*), while in a state of perishing yet still functioning toward the apprehension of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), will attain the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is by that very [cognition] that the awareness of the mark will occur as a restatement of what has already been perceived.

Therefore, it is proper to say that the perception of objects such as the wood-apple (*kapittha*) bears the fruit of the knowledge of what is to be acquired (*upādeya*), even without ascending the ladder of reflective consideration (*parāmarśa*).

Moreover, in the case of the inferable object such as fire, you certainly do not possess the cognition of its desirability (*upādeyatājñāna*) produced by the recollection of it being a means to pleasure.

Consequently, even in that instance, you must necessarily admit a subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) in the form: "And this belongs to the class of blazing fire. Furthermore, it must be investigated what the instrumental cause of that reflection is.
First of all, it does not arise through the door of the sense faculties, because fire is beyond the reach of perception.
Nor is it even reasonable to suspect that it arises from verbal testimony or comparison;

for if it is argued that it arises solely from the mark (liṅga) called smoke, we say no, because it is not admitted that a mark which has not been made the object of a reflective awareness (parāmarśa) possesses the capacity to produce inferential knowledge.

Because at that time the consideration of smoke (*dhūmāvamarśa*) has already passed away. To explain: first there is the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*); then the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*); then the consideration of smoke; then the cognition of fire; by that [cognition], the consideration of smoke reaches its state of perishing; then follows the recollection of fire as a means to pleasure. And at that moment, the consideration of smoke has indeed perished; once it has perished, the mere smoke is not capable of producing a consideration of fire at that time.
If it is argued that after the recollection of fire as a means to pleasure, the cognition of smoke arises again from the sense organ—this is not so, because such a sequence is never experienced.

Or, even if the cognition of smoke were to occur, there would necessarily follow a further recollection of the pervasion (vyāpti) and a subsequent reflective awareness (parāmarśa) of the smoke; in this interval, the recollection of fire as a means to pleasure would have already passed away, and thus the production of a certainty regarding its being a means to pleasure—which is generated by a reflective awareness aided by that recollection—would be impossible.
For it is observed that this object of perception is produced by a memory of the means to pleasure that is in a state of perishing.

Now, if you think that at that time a chain of cognitions—consisting of the cognition of smoke, the recollection of pervasion, the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*), and so forth—is not admitted, but rather that the very same previous consideration of smoke will be remembered immediately after the recollection of fire as a means to pleasure, and that this consideration of smoke, existing as the object of memory, will generate a consideration of the blazing fire in the form "this is of the same class as fire," this too is incorrect; for it would entail the simultaneous arising of two recollections immediately after the cognition of fire: namely, the recollection of its being a means to pleasure at that very moment, and the recollection of the consideration of smoke at that very same moment.
For there is no reason whatsoever for their arising sequentially,
and the simultaneity of cognitions is prohibited in the treatise.

Or, let it be granted that there is a sequential arising; even so, the subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of fire, which arises immediately after two acts of recollection, does not arise by way of restating what was previously perceived. Furthermore, even under the theory of succession, first there would have to be the recollection of its being a means to pleasure following the cognition of fire; then follows the recollection of the reflective awareness of smoke. By that [recollection], the former [awareness] reaches the state of perishing; then follows the reflective awareness of its belonging to the same class as that [fire] with respect to the fire. By that, the recollection of its being a means to pleasure is destroyed. Thus, having been destroyed once again, it could not function toward the production of the certainty that it is a means to pleasure.

Furthermore, it is not reasonable for the recollection of smoke to occur immediately after the cognition of fire inferred from the mark of smoke; for when people perceive fire, they recollect its status as a means to pleasure inherent in that fire, not the smoke.
Therefore, the "consideration" (parāmarśa) regarding the object of inference is extremely difficult to establish.
If this is so even in the case of perceptual objects, what is the use of this crowning crest (śikhaṇḍin)?

Furthermore, as for the objection raised that the statement of application (*upanaya*) would result in being devoid of meaning and thus useless, we shall examine that very point under the discussion of the "whole" (*avayavin*).

Therefore, since there is no intervening cognition of reflection (*parāmarśajñāna*), the initial perceptual cognition (*ālocanājñāna*) itself will, according to the method already described, bear the fruit of the cognition of what is to be avoided and so forth.

But surely, it is the fruit of perception that is to be examined here; and since this [cognition] arises from the mark (liṅga) of being a means to pleasure, it is inferential and does not rely upon the fruit of perception. True, this is so; however, at the time of grasping the relation, there exists a determination of being a means to pleasure produced by perception, from which inference proceeds, just as in the case of observing smoke and fire in a kitchen and the like.

Therefore, having established in the mind the certainty that [the object] is a means to pleasure—which occurs at the time of grasping the relationship—the author of the Bhāṣya described perceptual knowledge as having that [certainty] as its result.

Now, one might object: since even at the time of grasping the relationship, the capacity to be a means of pleasure is supersensible (atīndriya), how can it be accessible through perception? If you maintain that it is grasped even then by means of an inferential mark (liṅga) based on its belonging to the same class, then there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) because one would have to grasp the relationship again from that [mark].

If it is argued that the understanding of that [word] occurs precisely from the effect, which is pleasure (*sukha*), even then, that which has not had its relation [to the word] known is incapable of producing understanding. Therefore, at the very time of grasping that relation, since perception is incapable of grasping the capacity (*śakti*), there would be a requirement for another inference, leading to the same state of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Indeed, we do not accept that capacity is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), such that it would be impossible to know the relation of the effect with it.
Power (*śakti*) is simply the presence of the essential nature together with its auxiliary causes, and that is indeed easily understood.
[Objection: But surely the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is also included among the auxiliary causes;

and since dharma is beyond the senses, it cannot be apprehended by perception, so that power (śakti) is not easily understood either. [Reply: This is not so. Dharma and the like are not beyond the senses because they are powers, but rather they are innate.
We shall explain the inference of that [innate power] on the basis of the diversity of the world.

Thus, since it is possible for a capacity consisting in the presence of its own nature along with other auxiliary factors to be apprehended by perception, the grasping of the relationship [of the mark] through the reason of belonging to that same class is established.

Now, it might be objected: since pleasure, which is the effect of the wood-apple (*kapittha*) and so forth, is not currently grasped by the eye, how can the relationship [between them] be apprehended through visual cognition, given that there is no prior apprehension of that relationship? It is not the case that the relationship is apprehended by the eye; rather, it is apprehended by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
Having cognized pleasure and the like with the mind, and the wood-apple and the like with the eye, the fact that the former is the cause of the latter is understood by the mind alone.

Now, if it is admitted that the mind grasps the fact that the wood-apple (*kapittha*) and such things are means to pleasure, then in the cognitions of external objects, the mind alone would become the unrestrained instrument; thus, the eyes and other sense organs would be rendered useless.

Consequently, no one would be blind or deaf. This is not a fault, because we admit that an external object is graspable by the mind only after its form has been made the object of a cognition produced by an external sense organ functioning in conjunction with the mind (*manas*). Since that [prior sensory cognition] itself acts as the regulator, the internal organ does not operate upon an external object without restraint.

Now, one might object: "If at the time of grasping the relationship [between a word and its meaning] the determination that something is a means to pleasure occurs through mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), then at the time of practical activity (*vyavahāra*)—just as at that time—the certainty regarding its being a means to pleasure should likewise be a matter of mental perception alone; what need is there for dependence on a logical mark (*liṅga*) such as 'belonging to that same class'? Do not say so. For when the operation of words, logical marks, and the sense organs has ceased, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone is postulated as the instrument, since it is impossible to deny the cognition that is actually being observed.

However, if other means such as inferential signs (*liṅga*) and so forth are possible, yet the mind alone is asserted to be the cause, then mental cognition (*mānasa*) would be the only single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and there would not be four means of valid cognition; but enough of this digression.

Therefore, what was in the mind of the author of the Bhāṣya was this: at the time of grasping the relationship, that sensory cognition (akṣaja-jñāna) which has the wood-apple (kapittha) and so forth as its object has as its fruit the cognition of [the object] as something to be acquired (upādeya) and so on;
for it has been stated that the very cognition of being a means to pleasure (*sukhasādhanatva*) is the cognition of [the object] as something to be acquired and so on.

He asks: "For what purpose is such a hardship undertaken? Let the result be non-different from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself. That very perception of objects such as the wood-apple (*kapittha*), produced by the eye and other senses, appears as if functioning through the illumination of the object; let this be called the instrument (*karaṇa*). And since it has the nature of the experience of the object, let it be called the result (*phala*).
In this way, the means of valid cognition and the result will not have different loci—where the means is one thing and the result another.
As it has been said: 'Because it is perceived as possessing an operation, the result itself is the means of valid cognition.'"
This is untenable, because it would entail the loss of the very nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For a means of valid cognition is called an instrument (*karaṇa*), since by it something is correctly cognized (*pramīyate*);
and an action itself can never be an instrument.
When an action is to be accomplished, any instrument that serves as its cause is called a *karaṇa* (instrument).

In this regard, just as in the case of "Caitra cuts a stalk of rice with a sickle," where the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the instrument (*karaṇa*) are perceived as distinct from the action itself, so too here in the case of "he sees a jar with his eye," it is logical that these [the eye, etc. exist as separate from the act of seeing; it is not the case that the instrument is the very act of seeing itself.

As for the expression "valid cognition (*pramā*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*"), it is merely a statement of the grammatical correctness of the word *pramāṇa* when applied to the result, similar to the expression "action (*kṛti*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*)."

As for the claim that "the means of valid cognition and its fruit will not thus have different loci," this is an unprecedented mode of expression. What is intended here by the term "locus"? If it refers to the object, then there is indeed a single object;
for whatever is the object of the visual perception is precisely the same object of the instrument, such as the eye.
The statement that "the substratum (āśraya) is the locus (adhikaraṇa)" is, for its part, a non-significant text within the Buddhist school;
for, due to the momentariness of all effects, they are devoid of any substratum.
In our position, however, the relationship of effect and instrument is observed even between things with distinct substrata, as in the case of cooking and firewood;
likewise, it will also exist between the eye and visual cognition.

Furthermore, in some cases, even when two cognitions exist as effect and instrument despite having different bases—such as the cognitions of the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), or the cognitions of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*)—they possess a commonality of being based on a single identity.
But there is no purpose served by this [requirement of] having a common substratum, since it cannot be established in the case of the eye and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that there must be a common locus for the operation in the production of a single result, let that be so for other causal factors; however, in the case of cognition, which is itself of the nature of the result, an operation toward the production of that result is not possible.
As for the argument that [the means of knowledge] possesses activity because it is perceived as such, this too indicates only the distinctness between the means of knowledge and its result;
for possession of activity is not possible in the mere production of its own nature, but rather only in the accomplishment of a separate result.
[Objection: "But in reality, cognition is indeed the result; moreover, while being a result, it is active with respect to the experience of the object.

[Reply: O you of deluded intellect! It is the experience of the object itself that is called cognition, and it is not the case that the experience of the object becomes active with respect to the experience of the object.

Now, you claim that the conceit of having attained an object arises when that [object] exists. What is this so-called "conceit"? Is it distinct from the experience of the object, or non-distinct? If it is non-distinct, the statement "it arises when that exists" is an incoherent argument.
If, however, it is distinct, then you have entered into our own position.

Furthermore, when considering whether cognition produces the conceit of having apprehended an object because it is "active" (*vyāpṛta*) toward that apprehension, or rather simply because its very nature is the apprehension of the object—since no activity distinct from the apprehension of the object is perceived therein—it is determined that cognition has the apprehension of the object as its very nature.
And since the conceit is produced by that [apprehension], cognition is logically established as the result (*phala*) alone, not as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
For indeed, one is never seen to designate [cognition] by saying, "I know by means of knowledge," but rather says, "I see with the eye" or "I know by means of a sign."

[Objection: But surely, even when the eyes and other [senses] are present, the world does not designate them as instruments (*karaṇa*) if they do not produce the cognition of an object, whereas it does so when they do produce it. Thus, in common usage, their designation as instruments is due solely to their producing an instrument, not because they are instruments in themselves. [Reply: That is incorrect; the eyes and so forth are themselves the instruments, and no other instrument is produced by them.
If you ask, "What indeed is that other instrument?"—if you say "cognition" (*jñāna*), then this must be examined: in what action is that [cognition] an instrument?
For indeed, no instrument whatsoever can be an instrument with respect to itself.
As for the fact that people do not designate the eye and so forth as instruments when they produce cognition, that is indeed appropriate;
for something that is not actively engaged in the production of an action cannot be an instrument or a causal factor (*kāraka*).

Therefore, since the eye and so forth produce the action of cognition, they possess the status of an instrument, whereas cognition itself possesses the status of a result; thus, such a designation is logical.

Therefore, for those who accept that a means of valid cognition possesses the status of being a means of valid cognition, a distinct result must be admitted; for if they were one and the same, that [distinction] would be impossible.

However, as for that most foolish person who endeavors to carry out the entire practical operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the result (*phala*) within the single nature of cognition itself—claiming: "That which appears is the object; the means and the result are, moreover, the form of the grasper and the self-awareness; therefore, these three are not made separate"—we shall censure that ill-behaved one in the chapter on Liberation (*apavargāhnika*) during the discussion on the refutation of the non-duality of cognition (*jñānādvaita*). Enough with this prolixity. Therefore, it was well said: "When cognition is the means of knowledge, then the cognitions of avoidance and so forth are the result."

Thus, according to the view that the result is the defining characteristic, the sūtra is expressive by supplying the word "from which" (*yataḥ*); that from which there arises a result called cognition, qualified by such attributes as being produced from the contact of the sense organ with its object, is perception (*pratyakṣa*).

In this context, the phrase "arising from the contact of a sense-faculty with its object" is intended to exclude memory and other cognitions that arise independently of an object, as well as inferential and other types of cognition that, although produced by an object, have an imperceptible (parokṣa) object. Therefore, it does not follow that the producer of such [inferential] cognition would itself be perception.
[Objection: But is there not also the inference of the movement of a sense-organ produced by the contact between the sense-organ and its object?

For that [inference] is generated by the contact between the sense-organ and its object acting as a logical mark (*liṅga*), just as the inference of the sun’s motion is [generated] by its arrival at another location. How, then, is inference excluded by this term [“produced by the contact between the sense-organ and its object”]? [Reply: This is not so. We say here that what is “produced by the contact between the sense-organ and its object” is that cognition which arises precisely where the sense-organ is in contact with its own object.
And the inference of the movement of a sense-organ is not of such a nature.
If it is asked, "From where is the attainment of this distinction? we reply: "Because of the mention of what has arisen.
For by the mention of what has arisen, the status of contact as a causal factor (*kāraka*) is made known;
and that [status] is fulfilled when contact produces cognition regarding an object within the range of the sense faculty.
However, regarding the inference of the movement of the sense faculties, they do not say that sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) is a causal factor (*kāraka*), but rather an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
For this very reason, it functions in that inference while depending upon the apprehension of itself, and not independently as it does in the cognition of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
The sense organs—the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and ears—are said to have as their material cause (*prakṛti*) the five elements, beginning with earth.

The objects (*artha*), however, are smell, form, taste, touch, and sound, as delimited by their own respective universals such as "smell-ness" (*gandhatva*). Their substrates are the substances—earth, water, and fire—and the qualities residing therein, such as number and so forth; the actions, such as upward throwing and so forth; and the generalities (*sāmānya*) inherent in them, which are apprehended by touch and sight according to the system of Kaṇāda.
Non-existence (*abhāva*), mentioned previously, is also indeed an object, because it is understood through investigation.
The contact between the sense organs and their objects is of six kinds.

Among these, a substance is perceived by the eye or by the tactile organ through conjunction (*saṃyoga*). A quality such as color residing in that substance is perceived through inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*).
The universals such as "color-ness" (rūpatva) are apprehended through inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-what-is-conjoined (saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya):
the substance is conjoined with the eye, color inheres in that [substance], and color-ness inheres in the color.
Sound is apprehended through inherence (samavāya).
The auditory organ is the substance space (*ākāśa*); sound is inherent (*samaveta*) therein.

The universal "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) is apprehended through inherence-in-what-is-inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), for it is inherent in that sound which is itself inherent in the space of the auditory organ.
The apprehension of non-existence (*abhāva*) has been explained as occurring through the state of being a qualifier of what is conjoined (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇabhāva*).
In the case of "there is no jar here," the portion of ground conjoined with the eye is the substratum, and its qualification is the absence [of the jar].
Now, what is the means of valid cognition for the apprehension of contact? We reply: it is the non-perception of that which is obstructed.

For if the sense organs, such as the eye, were to grasp an object even when not in contact, then an object situated behind a barrier would also be perceived; yet it is not so perceived. Therefore, contact exists.

[Objection: Let there simply be non-intervention; what is the use of "contact" (saṃnikarṣa)? [Reply: Not so, because the sense organs, being causal agents (kāraka), act by reaching their objects (prāpyakāritva). And since a causal agent is capable of producing an effect only when it is in contact [with its object], such contact must be postulated. This will be determined with precision in the *Indriyaparīkṣā* (Examination of the Sense Organs), and thus it is not analyzed here.

Furthermore, since the fact that the senses of taste and touch function by reaching their objects is clearly perceived, it should be inferred for the other sense organs as well, on the basis of this commonality.

But if this is so, since proximity is already implied by the very fact of being a causal factor (*kāraka*), why is it stated explicitly? It has been said that this is for the purpose of making known its sixfold nature.
By the inclusion of the term "arisen" (*utpanna*), he demonstrates that both the sense faculty and the object are generators of cognition;
therein, the sense faculty is the generator by way of being the instrument (*karaṇa*), while the object is so by way of being the objective (*karman*).

Now, how is it known that an object produces cognition? Precisely from the arising of a cognition having that as its object; for the view that cognition possesses an aspect intrinsically has been refuted, and no other way of establishing the determination of objects according to each specific action is established.

[Objection: "Surely this is the purpose; you have been asked about the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so tell us that. [Reply: It is said: This very thing is the means of valid cognition. Just as the causality of other causal factors such as *vīraṇa* grass in the production of an effect such as a mat is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) established by perception and non-perception, so too is it for the object (*artha*) in the production of cognition.

For instance, suppose someone seeking Devadatta goes to his house and does not see him there because he is absent; yet at another moment, he sees him arriving. There, having determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the arising and non-arising of cognition follow the presence and absence of Devadatta, he understands—by means of mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*)—that Devadatta is the cause of that [cognition], just as sandalwood is the cause of pleasure.

[Objection: "Surely this principle is appropriate in the case of the *vīraṇa* grass and the mat, because they are perceived separately; however, since an object is never perceived apart from cognition, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are difficult to establish there. [Reply: It is said that this very thing is "separate perception": namely, that when an object is not present, a non-sublated cognition having that object does not arise. Enough of this for now; we shall address the objection embedded within the doctrine of idealism (*jñānavāda*) at its proper time.

Just as the status of the sense organs—the instruments—as causes of cognition is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), so too is it established for the object—the action; this is what is indicated by the term "already arisen" (utpanna).

Now, one might object: "Is not perception whose object is pleasure and so forth excluded by the phrase 'produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object'? No, it is not excluded; for the mind (*manas*) is a sense-organ, and pleasure and so forth are objects grasped by it.
However, because the mind differs in its properties from material sense-organs such as the nose, it was not included in that specific category.
And this perception proceeds from the contact of four, three, or two [factors].

Among these, with respect to external objects such as form (*rūpa*), knowledge arises from the contact of four: the self (*ātman*) is conjoined with the mind (*manas*), the mind with the sense organ (*indriya*), and the sense organ with the object (*artha*).
However, with respect to pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, knowledge arises from the contact of three, because in those cases there is no operation of the eyes or other [external] senses.

In the case of the self, however, for the yogin, knowledge arises solely from the conjunction of two—the self and the mind—because a third element, whether an object of cognition (*grāhya*) or a cognizer (*grāhaka*), is absent there.
Therefore, since it includes the cognition of pleasure and so forth, it is rightly stated [in the Sūtra] that [perception] "arises from the contact of the sense-organ with the object.

Although the self and the mind do indeed possess the capacity to generate knowledge, this is not explicitly formulated here in the Sūtra because it is common to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The mention of "knowledge" (jñāna) is for the purpose of specifying the substantive;
for it is that [knowledge] which possesses qualifiers such as "being produced by the contact of the sense-organ with the object.
If the substantive did not exist, of what would these be the qualifiers?
Alternatively, the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is included for the purpose of excluding pleasure and the like.
For pleasure is also produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object;

in that case, the entire collection of causal factors (*kārakacakra*) that produces it should not be considered a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The inclusion of the term "knowledge" is so that only that which produces knowledge shall be the means of valid cognition.

On this point, the Śākyas object: it is neither proper nor possible to exclude pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth by the term "cognition" (*jñāna*), because pleasure and the rest are also of the nature of cognition.
These—pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort—are merely distinctions of cognition itself.
For the distinction between entities must indeed depend upon their causes.

Furthermore, if a distinction were asserted even among things that possess identical causes, then the fixed nature of entities would not be produced by their causes; this would entail the consequence of their being accidental (*ākasmikatva*). As it has been said: "Entities possessing such-and-such a form or its opposite are born from causes possessing such-and-such a form or its opposite.
Therefore, why is pleasure and so forth not cognition, since they are born from causes non-different from those of cognition?
Thus, pleasure and so forth are of the nature of cognition because they are born from causes non-different from it.
This is untenable because the reason contradicts direct perception.

Pleasure and the like are experienced as being perceived, while cognition is experienced as having the nature of the apprehension of objects; since their difference is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can an inference for non-difference proceed? For this very reason, it should not be said: "We see that this single form of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*) undergoes various transformations (*vivarta*) such as joy and despair; let names be applied to these as one pleases. This is because consciousness appears precisely as having the nature of the apprehension of objects, whereas pleasure and the like do not appear as having that nature pervasively.
It is cognition alone, in the form of grasping an object, that manifests, not pleasure or pain.

As for the appearance of "knowledge of pleasure" or "knowledge of pain," that is produced solely by a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the knowledge itself—just as in the cases of "doubtful knowledge" or "erroneous knowledge. It has been stated here that in doubt, error, and so forth, the nature of experiencing an object (*viṣayānubhavasvabhāvatva*) appears as a continuous thread. For doubt is experienced as having the essence of grasping an object, yet it grasps an object that is not certain.
Error, too, has precisely the essence of grasping an object, though it grasps an object that is either distorted or non-existent.

However, pleasure and pain are not experienced as having the nature of grasping an object; therefore, this internal phenomenon such as pleasure or pain is something entirely different, having the sole nature of being an object of apprehension. Thus, like the cognition of a jar, it differentiates cognition solely by way of its object, and not through a difference in its own intrinsic nature, as is the case with a cognition of doubt.

In this regard, it might be argued that because pleasure and the like are self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), they do not possess the nature of being solely the object (*grāhya*); and therefore, since they possess the dual nature of both the object and its apprehension (*grahaṇa*), they are nothing other than cognition itself. Do not speak thus; for self-luminosity has already been rejected with respect to cognition and will be rejected here as well.
So how could it exist in pleasure and the like?
For no one experiences pleasure as having the nature of grasping, in the same way that they experience cognition.

Now, one might object: "If its luminosity is not admitted, then since there would be no distinction between the arising and non-arising of pleasure and so forth, one would either be happy at all times or never at all. This is not so; for pleasure is grasped by cognition immediately upon its very arising—how then is it not distinguished from that which has not arisen? On the contrary, this fault belongs to those who maintain that pleasure is self-luminous: because of the arising of self-luminous pleasure, even one in whom pleasure has not arisen would become happy by that very same self-luminous pleasure.

Furthermore, is it maintained that cognition is a single entity adorned with all aspects such as pleasure, pain, and so forth without exception, or is some [cognition] of the nature of pleasure and some of the nature of pain? In the first case, because a cognition inlaid with all aspects arises, there would follow the undesirable consequence of experiencing a continuous stream of mutually contradictory properties such as pleasure and pain at one and the same moment.

In the subsequent [state], however, there must necessarily be admitted some cognition that is neither pleasure nor pain, which consists in the experience of objects and is interspersed with both pleasure and pain.

And that [cognition] is not transparent; rather, it is colored by some object such as a jar. Furthermore, through positive and negative concomitance, it is perceived as persisting in its nature as consciousness even when the production or disappearance of the jar and other objects occurs.

Therefore, it is understood that even pleasure-cognition, when being experienced now, is colored by the pleasure which serves as its object—just as a jar or similar object [colors cognition]—and not as having pleasure as its own nature by virtue of its own form; for cognition, which is of the nature of pure awareness and possesses a form distinct from pleasure, has been observed at other times [to be devoid of pleasure].
Consequently, pleasure and the like are not of the nature of awareness.

Furthermore, this reason—"because they are produced from non-different causes"—is unestablished (asiddha); for although the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), which is the self (ātman), and the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), which is the contact between the self and the mind (ātmamanasaṃyoga), are non-different, the instrumental causes (nimittakāraṇa)—such as the quality of pleasure (sukhatva) and the quality of cognition (jñānatva)—are indeed different.

Now, one might object: prior to the arising of pleasure, how could the universal *sukhatva* (pleasurability) exist there without a substratum, and what kind of connection could it have with the causal factors that produce pleasure? Or, if it were unconnected, how could it be a causal factor? To this it is replied: since we shall establish that universals are omnipresent (*sarvagata*), the universals such as *sukhatva* and so forth do indeed exist even there.
Furthermore, their connection with the causal factors that produce pleasure is characterized by mere "fitness" (*yogyatā*), just like merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
For merit and demerit are the causes of all effects—such as rice and the like—that arise as the source of pleasure or pain for all living beings.
Furthermore, the "conjunction" between those two and their causes—such as the seed, soil, water, and so forth—is simply their mutual fitness (*yogyatā*).
The same would apply to pleasure-ness (*sukhatva*) and the like.
Therefore, because of the difference in their instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*), the effects—cognition, pleasure, and so forth—are distinct.
Even the difference in efficient causes serves to differentiate the effect;
for indeed, qualities produced by baking are observed to be distinct in jars and other such objects.
Moreover, not all [schools] maintain that pleasure, pain, and so forth are preceded by cognition; rather, they hold that all such things are preceded by the cognition of their respective objects.
Even in cases where pleasure and the like do not arise directly from the experience of an object,
the recollection of that object is the cause for their production.
In some cases, however, even a mere mental resolve (saṅkalpa) functions as the cause of pleasure;
therefore, everything such as pleasure is preceded by cognition alone.
If it is argued that knowledge (*jñāna*) also must necessarily be preceded by [another] knowledge, we say no, because this will be refuted later on.
For we shall explain that knowledge arising in the womb or immediately after states such as intoxication or fainting is not preceded by another instance of knowledge.
Therefore, since the distinct nature of knowledge, pleasure, and so forth is established, the inclusion of the term "knowledge" is purposeful for the sake of excluding pleasure and the like.

But even so, there is no need for the inclusion of the word "cognition" (*jñāna*), because the exclusion of pleasure and the like is already established by the term "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicāri*) alone.
For error and non-error are properties of cognition, not of pleasure and the like.
Therefore, by the inclusion of that [term], cognition—which possesses those properties—is indeed obtained.
"What is the use of including the term 'knowledge' [in the definition]? It is not so, because pleasure is also seen to be subject to deviation.
But what kind of pleasure is seen to be deviant? That pleasure which arises from the practice of prohibited acts, such as violating another's wife—that is deviant."

Now, what kind of deviation does pleasure have? And what kind of deviation does cognition have? It is the appearance of something as being thus when it is not so; and for pleasure, too, it is precisely the appearance of it as being thus when it is not so.

Is the pleasure arising from the embrace of another's wife not pleasure? Is the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell not a cognition? It is indeed a cognition, but it is false; this pleasure also exists, but it is false.

But is it not the case that pleasure is not false? For even that has the very nature of bliss (*ānanda*). If this were so, then even the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell would not be false, for that too has the very nature of experiencing an object.

Now, one might object: even though that cognition has the nature of experiencing an object, it nonetheless deviates from its object; likewise, this pleasure, although having the nature of bliss, certainly deviates from its own cause, which is the object.

Is the cognition produced by that [unpleasant thing] not itself produced by a means of ignorance? Indeed, knowledge is produced by a means of knowledge; yet pleasure is also produced by a means of pleasure, even when that [means], such as another's wife, is unreal—being sublated by direct perception or sublated by scripture.

Is it that another's wife and so forth are not real? Even in that case, that which generates cognition is not real; it is unreal because it is sublated by direct perception. Furthermore, another's wife and so forth, though a means to pleasure, are unreal because they are sublated by the scriptures.

Now, what is sublated here by the scripture? Even in the case of direct perception, what is sublated? By the scripture, it is made known that the object is false; likewise, it is made known that the cause of pleasure is false.

Is that object not a cause of pleasure? Just as this [present] object is a cause of turbid cognition, so too is that [past] one a cause of pleasure that is turbid and has a bitter ripening; thus, even such pleasure is indeed deceptive. Enough of this excessive play with words.

Therefore, because the same logical principle applies, there is deviation (vyabhicāritā) with respect to pleasure; thus, "knowledge" (jñāna) is not obtained from the term "non-deviating" (avyabhicāri).

Another says: "What is the use of this childish quarrel? Even if there is no acquisition of knowledge from the term *avyabhicāri* (non-erroneous), nevertheless, knowledge is indeed obtained from the term *vyavasāyātmaka* (of the nature of ascertainment).
For pleasure, pain, and the like are not of the nature of ascertainment; rather, it is knowledge alone that is of such a nature."

If it is argued that the word "that" (tat) is for the purpose of excluding doubt, this is true; however, it is also quite capable of excluding pleasure and the like, because the nature of being determinate (vyavasāyātmakatva) is impossible in the case of pleasure and so forth.

Thus, even though the exclusion of pleasure and so forth is established, the inclusion of the term "cognition" (*jñāna*) must indeed be made, because its purpose is to specify the substantive (*viśeṣya*). For all these qualifiers have been employed for that [substantive]; if it were not included, they would be without a support. Furthermore, the listener's intellect would not be properly focused. Therefore, although it is understood by implication, the inclusion of "cognition" must indeed be made; for if that which is implied by the sense were not stated, only "perception, perception" would be expressed, while everything else would simply be obtained through the force of the meaning.
Therefore, the word "knowledge" is appropriate for the purpose of indicating the subject (dharmin).

Since it will be established—by means of refuting the Śākya position—that words possess contact with objects, a cognition that is expressible by virtue of the entry of words would otherwise be possible; therefore, the term "inexpressible" (avyapadeśya) is included for the purpose of excluding such [cognition].
Regarding this, the elder Naiyāyikas first explain: that which is "designated" (*vyapadeśya*) refers to cognition that has become the object of verbal expression;

namely, that cognition which, having arisen from the contact of a sense organ with its object, is designated by the name of the object, such as "cognition of color" or "cognition of taste. [They argue] that the inclusion of the term "non-designated" (*avyapadeśya*) is intended so that such designated cognition, being the fruit of perception, should not itself be considered perception. However, this is untenable, for being designated by a name is certainly not a cause for invalidity.

For if that cognition of color and that cognition of taste were non-deviant from their objects and free from doubt, how could they be called the result of invalid cognition (*apramāṇaphala*)? Or, if they were associated with defects such as deviation, they would be excluded by another word [in the definition]; so what is the use of the term "non-verbal" (*avyapadeśya*)? Furthermore, if that cognition is the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), from what source of valid cognition (*pramāṇaprabhava*) would it now arise? It cannot be the result of perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is excluded by this very term.
Nor can it be produced by inference (*anumāna*) and the like, because it differs in character from them.
There is no fifth means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
To claim that this object of definition (*lakṣya*) is not subsumed under the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is a lack of wisdom (*prajñāpramāda*). Therefore, this is a false explanation.
The teachers have described another object to be excluded by the term *avyapadeśya* (non-verbal).

A person learning [the meaning] of words through the linguistic usage of elders understands, at the time of apprehending an object of doubt, that a certain object standing before him—possessing branches and so forth—is denotable by the word "panasa" (jackfruit tree), based on a sentence uttered by an elder who provides the instruction of the name, such as "this is called a panasa.

This cognition of his, although born of the senses, cannot properly be considered to have the sense-faculties alone as its instrument, because it does not arise in the absence of the word that provides the instruction of the name.
Because this cognition is produced by the combination of both [the sense organ and the mental faculty], it is "born of both"; since it arises from verbal designation, it is called "designatable.
That [cognition] is excluded by the term "indesignatable" (*avyapadeśya*).

Nor does this fall under a fifth means of valid cognition; rather, people accept it as if it were verbal testimony (*śābda*). Thus, when asked, "How do you know again that this is a jackfruit tree? one replies, "It was told to me by Devadatta that this is a jackfruit tree. One does not say, even out of forgetfulness, "I perceived with my eye that this is called a jackfruit tree.
Therefore, even though there is conformity with the presence and absence of the sense organ, the instrument (*karaṇa*) here is indeed the word.

For this very reason, when the author of the Sūtras was describing the definition of verbal testimony (śabda), he did not formulate any qualification to exclude its inclusion among the sense organs; he stated only this much as the definition: "Verbal testimony is instruction" (*upadeśaḥ śabdaḥ*).
Consequently, the author of the Sūtras considers this [instruction] to possess the nature of verbal testimony even when it involves the operation of the sense organs.
Furthermore, in this context, because the inclusion of the qualifying term "inexpressible" (avyapadeśya) serves to exclude the intrusion of verbal expression, this cognition is not perception.
Therefore, the term "inexpressible" is used for the purpose of excluding such a cognizable knowledge that is associated with verbal designation.

The commentators do not accept this [explanation]. If knowledge arising from both [senses and words] is excluded by the term "avyapadeśya" (non-verbal), then one must consider: since it is not invalid because it transcends the definition of invalidity, if it is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), into which category does it fall? [Objection: But surely this knowledge is verbal (*śābda*), because it conforms to the presence of that [word]. [Reply:
Let it be sense-born (*akṣaja*) as well, because it conforms to the presence of that [sense-organ].
To say that [cognition] is both verbal and born of both [perception and inference] is a contradiction;
thus, it would simply be another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), just like the previous case.
But was it not said that the world designates this [tree] as being verbal in nature, based on such common usage as "This *panasa* tree was named by Devadatta"? Ah!
What a compassionate, faithful, and noble person you are! Indeed, the actual status of things does not depend solely upon the designations of the world;
for the world designates things according to its own whims.

Have you not heard that the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) known as Nandikuṇḍa is common to various classes of sages? Alas! Therefore, following the intention of the author of the Sūtras, we understand this knowledge to be verbal (śābda). For this author of the Sūtras provides this qualification in order to exclude perception from having verbal elements enter into it, but he does not employ any qualification in the case of verbal cognition to exclude the sense organs. He perceives that even when other causes enter into it, this knowledge remains verbal. It is said in reply: like Manu, the author of the Sūtras is also not merely an instructor of dharma.
In accordance with which we might declare its status as being verbal (śābdatva).

However, when examined according to the actual state of things, this cognition—because it conforms to the presence and absence of the sense faculties—does not transcend the status of being the result of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Consequently, if it were excluded [from that category], it would touch upon the status of being a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) altogether.
Therefore, since it is untenable to exclude knowledge produced from both [the senses and the mind],
this explanation of the term is formulated by means of another method.

The term "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*) is included for the purpose of excluding the fault of impossibility. For an opponent might think: "It is appropriate to describe a definition only when there is a subject to be defined;
however, in this case, there is no such thing as 'perception' produced by the contact of sense-organ and object that could serve as the subject of definition."
This is because cognitions such as "this is white" (gaur) are verbal in nature, since they have as their object a denotable thing delimited by a word;
for in this context, it is difficult to establish any distinction among cognitions apart from their objects, since the nature of awareness is indistinguishable with respect to all [objects].

In this regard, just as the cognition "one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) or "white" (*śukla*) attains excellence by having as its object a qualificandum delimited by a qualifier, so too the cognition "cow" (*gaur*) and others likewise partake of excellence because they have as their object a signified entity delimited by its signifier. Furthermore, this cognition is verbal (*śābda*) because it has as its object a signified entity delimited by a word, and because it is untenable for it to be produced by any instrument other than that [word].
For this cognition cannot possibly have the sense organs as its instrument, because the eye has the qualifier as its object, while the ear lacks the capacity to apprehend the qualified object;
nor is a single cognition ever observed to arise simultaneously through the medium of two different sense organs.
In this regard, it might be argued that this cognition is mental (mānasa), like the perception of the fragrance of a bandhūka flower.

To this it has been replied: when the operation of other instruments such as sound or logical marks (liṅga) has ceased, the effect that arises is postulated to have the mind alone as its instrument; this is not the case even when those [other instruments] are present.
For if that were so, there would be only one means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), namely the mental one.
Moreover, in this case, the word itself is the instrument;
for like the thousand-rayed sun, it illuminates both itself and its object.
Therefore, it is determined that even when a cognition such as "cow" arises with respect to a sensory object, it is indeed verbal in nature.
[Objection: But surely, at the time of learning the convention, a word such as "cow" was heard;

since that has now passed away, how can this cognition be produced by it? [Reply: It is said: because the word, though not being heard at that moment, serves as the cause of that cognition when it has ascended to the mind through memory.
Even upon hearing that [word], are all its constituent phonemes within the range of direct perception?
And what specific distinction is there [to be known] by means of the final phoneme, whether it is being perceived or already remembered?
Thus, it must be admitted that this cognition is produced by a word that has been made the object of memory.

Just as a word, even when uttered regarding something imperceptible, reveals both itself and its meaning, so too, when that very same word is being remembered with respect to a perceptible object, it reveals both itself and the object. Furthermore, in such cognitions, there must certainly be an appearance of the denoted object as delimited by the denoter (the word).
As Bhaṭṭa said: "The state of being the designator (*saṃjñitva*) is merely [the highest]."
The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) produced from a word ending in a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*), such as *saṃjñitva* ("the state of being a name-bearer"), expresses a relationship.

This is because the relationship between a name and its bearer is what is meant by "the state of being a name-bearer" (*saṃjñitva*), according to the traditional rule of the learned: "In the case of primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*), the expression of a relationship occurs through an abstract suffix."
And the name is a word;
thus, this is said to be the appearance of an object as qualified by a word.

Furthermore, no cognition is ever observed to be devoid of the association with words; for even in cognitions where no specific word is explicitly articulated, there is ultimately the emergence of a general term, since a manifestation consisting of luminosity cannot arise apart from the delineation of such a word.
Thus Bhartṛhari said: "There is no cognition in the world that is without the accompaniment of words;
every knowledge is perceived as if permeated by speech."

Therefore, suspecting the fault of impossibility—namely, that since there is no such thing as perception to be defined, for what has this definition been undertaken—the author of the Sūtras says: "inexpressible" (avyapadeśyam).

That cognition which arises for one who has not yet understood the relationship between words and their referents, or even for one who has understood that relationship, at the very moment of the first contact with the sense organ—a cognition that does not delineate a word but serves as the cause for the recollection of a word—is perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is devoid of words, has an object not delimited by words, is inexpressible, is produced solely through the contact of the sense organ and its object, and is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*).
Furthermore, the luminous nature of cognitions is not produced by words; it belongs to them inherently, because they possess such a nature by themselves.
Furthermore, at the time of non-conceptual [perception], no one experiences any verbal expression such as "this is something" or similar general terms.

Therefore, even though cognitions such as "this is a cow" are verbal in nature, since there exists such a cognition as the object to be defined, the definition is not useless; thus, the term "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*) is included in order to exclude this possible defect.
The teachers do not accept this.
It is not proper to say that a cognition such as "this is a cow," even though it arises from the contact of a sense organ with its object, is verbal (śābda).
Furthermore, in this case, an object delimited by a word does not manifest, because there is no cause for the apprehension of such an object.
In the cognition of the object to be qualified (*viśeṣya*), the word is indeed the instrument (*karaṇa*).
But let it be examined: what is the instrument for the apprehension of the word itself, which has become a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)?
It is not the auditory organ (*śrotra*), because no separate operation [of it] is perceived.

Furthermore, it is not even reasonable to suspect that the auditory organ is the instrument for the cognition "cow" and so forth, which arises through the association with a remembered word after the relationship [between word and object] has been grasped.

Nor can the mind be such an instrument, for it is not capable of producing cognition regarding external objects independently of external organs, as this would entail the absurd consequence that there would be no blindness or similar sensory deficiencies.

[Objection: But has it not been stated that the word itself is the instrument (*karaṇa*)? Why then entertain the suspicion of another instrument? [Reply: Not so; for it is impossible for a single factor (*kāraka*) to simultaneously possess the status of both object (*karman*) and instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the very same action.
[Objection: It is like the light of the sun. [Reply: No, because of the difference in actions.
In one case where it is the instrument, it is not there as the object; or where it is the object, it is not there as the instrument.

The light of the sun is indeed the instrument (karaṇa) for the production of valid cognition regarding objects such as a jar; it is not the object (karman). However, at the time of its own apprehension, it is the object alone and not the instrument.
If it is asked, "What then is the instrument (karaṇa) in that case? we reply: it is the eye alone.
If it is asked, "How can this be so, since the eye requires another light for the perception of illumination?"—the power of things (vastu-śakti) is indeed not subject to questioning.
We may ask why the eye depends on light for the perception of jars and the like, but not for the perception of that very light itself.

Thus, it is logical that this solar light, first apprehended by the visual faculty without depending on any other light, persists for a long time and serves as an instrument (karaṇa) while its very object—namely, that which is perceivable by that same faculty—is being perceived.

Sound, however, is momentary and is apprehended by the auditory faculty; having served as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the act of cognizing an object that is otherwise determinable, how could it possibly become the object (*karman*) of that very same act?
For sound, like smoke and the like, is merely a means (*upāya*) and not the goal (*upeya*).
While it may indeed be grasped first because it is a means, it does not deserve to be grasped again at the time of grasping the goal, just like smoke.

Even in the case where a word, though being remembered, is the cause for the cognition of its meaning, there too first occurs the remembrance of the word, and from that follows the comprehension of the word's meaning.
Therefore, at the time of the cognition of the meaning, the apprehension of the word is not possible;
hence, there is no manifestation of the signified object as qualified by the signifier.
Furthermore, since the cognition "this is a cow" and so forth follows the positive and negative concomitance of the sense-organ and its object, how can it be forcibly called verbal?
If that very cognition which arises from a sense faculty dependent upon the recollection of a word is for you "verbal" (śābda), oh, how truly a Naiyāyika you are!
[Objection: But was it not said that neither of the two organs—the eye nor the ear—is capable of apprehending an object delimited by a word?

[Reply: O good sir, why do you not say that the eye itself will apprehend this [object]? [Objection: Indeed, it is not proper for a sense organ to operate upon what is not its own object-domain (*aviṣaya*).
Therefore, I do not claim that the cognition of an object qualified by a word is produced by a sense organ.
How can your cognition of water in mirages be produced by the sense faculties? For even in that case, there is no contact of the eye with water.
But is it not the case that water present in memory is what is apprehended there?
In this case as well, why is the word not apprehended as it has ascended into memory?
Now, is it not true that sound is never within the range of the eye? Or does water ever become an object [of the eye] even when it is not present?

Would it not follow that there is a doctrine of a single sense-faculty, since sound would be perceived by the eye? Furthermore, in this case too, there would be cognition of everything, even that which is not present.

Now, one might object: since the cognition of water in a mirage is erroneous, how can it be used here as an example? In what sense is it erroneous—is it because it is not produced by the senses (*anindriyaja*), or because it is deviant (*vyabhicārin*)? If it were due to its not being produced by the senses, then its exclusion from the category of error would already have been accomplished by the very phrase "produced from the contact of a sense-organ with an object" (*indriyārthasannikarṣotpanna*); thus, the term "non-deviant" (*avyabhicārin*) would be superfluous. Since that term is indeed employed, its erroneous nature must be due to its deviance; therefore, one must certainly admit that this cognition of non-proximate water is produced by the senses.
Just as visual cognition arises with respect to that water which is not its [proper] object,
why is it not likewise accepted [that cognition arises] with respect to the denoted object when it is touched by the denoter?
And just as time and so forth, though formless, are visible to the eye according to you,
why then is an object, even when colored by a word, not visible?
In this way, indeed, the conformity to the distinction of the sense faculties will not be contradicted here.
But surely, as long as I live, I cannot venture to assert that sound is visible;
therefore, abandon this difficult-to-grasp notion that the object of expression is understood through a designator endowed with [the property of] being expressive.

Moreover, if that [knowledge] were verbal, how could there be a grasping of the relationship [between word and meaning]? For a word does not become expressive when its relationship [to its meaning] has not been grasped.
Furthermore, there is no apprehension of that [object] within the domain of non-conceptual cognition;
however, you have relegated conceptualization to the category of verbal [cognition].
The relation cannot be understood without another means of knowledge;
if it were understood through verbal cognition itself, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence.

Furthermore, people do not perceive a relationship with respect to an object that is already colored by a word; for if there were such a perception, it would take the form: "The word 'cow' is the denotatum of the word 'cow'."

For since the referent, such as a cow, is designated by the word "cow" when it is qualified by that word, the word "cow" itself assumes the status of being the referent, just like the object that is the referent.
And if the cognition of the signified were to arise from the signifier through its own internal connection,
then there would also be a cognition of the probandum from the logical mark (liṅga) by means of its own delimitation.
If fire were not understood through its association with smoke,
then here too, cows and the like would certainly not be understood through their connection with words.
Furthermore, there is no property whatsoever called "denotability" belonging to a real entity;
for if it existed, it would appear even in non-conceptual cognition, just like color-form.
The wicked follower of the Sugata, who speaks words that do not touch upon actual objects, ought to be pierced by the weapon of direct perception; how then can he be slain by you?
How can words have an operation upon an object of direct perception? For whatever is the object of their operation, that has indeed been rendered verbal by you.

Moreover, out of the vain hope that a difference in appearance arises from a difference in objects, you perceive the object of conceptual cognition (*savikalpa*) as something additional to the object of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpa*), namely as an object qualified by words; yet, by entering along this very path, you do not see the ultimate superimposition of words—what kind of delusion is this? You have become one who must be told: "O fool, you see the honey, but you do not see the precipice!"
Therefore, let it be determined that the cognition "this is a cow" is perception,
produced by the visual faculty even while depending upon the recollection of a word.
If its being mental is not accepted, that is indeed correct;
because it conforms to the existence of those [external objects], it is produced solely by the external sense faculties.

On this point, however, the Pravaras say: "If, in cognitions such as 'this is a cow,' the appearance of the denoted object as delimited by the denotative word is rejected in every respect, how could these [cognitions] differ from the non-conceptual awareness whose existence was established at the moment of the first contact with the sense-organ?
For an excellence in appearance cannot occur without an excellence in the object;
for instance, in the case of 'the man with a staff,' a man qualified by a staff appears, otherwise this cognition would not be distinguished from the cognition of a mere man."
Even when both appear [in cognition], there is no cognition of "the staff and the man," because the relation of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) serves as the restrictive factor.
Even in the cognitions of priority, posteriority, duration, and brevity,
and so forth, an object qualified by space, time, and the like manifests, due to the apprehension of a specific excellence.
Is that time and so forth directly perceived? Ask your own cognition: "What is grasped by me? It is a marvel that you say it is an object qualified by that [time], yet it is not.
By this, the perceptibility of inherence (samavāya) is also demonstrated,
because we observe the cognition "here" with respect to a cloth connected to its threads.
Because of the cognition "this is a cloth," this cognition "the cloth is here in these threads" is distinct [from the former].
If the qualifying relation between the threads and the cloth were not perceptible, it would not be distinguished from the mere cognition of the cloth.

Now, if it is thought that a difference in cognition arises from a difference in the means—just like the cognition of objects such as a post situated at a distant or near location, or like the cognition of an object through the instrument of the sense organ when it is either refined or unrefined—that is incorrect, because even when there is a difference in the means, a difference in that [cognition] is not established. The means produces an excellence in the cognition, not in the object.
The Naiyāyikas maintain that at the time of the cognition of an object, the cognition itself does not appear.

Thus, there is this dilemma: that substratum in which the excellence (atiśaya) resides—namely, the cognition—does not manifest, yet that object which appears at that time possesses no such excellence, and yet the experience of that excellence is observed; this is a difficult path.
Furthermore, the cognition of an object situated at a distance or nearby does not differ because of a difference in the means [of perception].
For that [cognition] also differs solely on account of the difference in its objects.
For from a distance, the commonality of an object is perceived as characterized merely by its general properties; but from nearby, it is determined with its specific particulars clearly manifest.

As described by Māgha: "First he was perceived as 'a mass of light'; then, his form having become manifest, he was recognized as 'an embodied being'; then, as his limbs were distinguished, he was known as 'a man'; and finally, in due order, he was understood to be 'Nārada'."
While whatever cause there may be for the diversity of other actions,
the distinction in the action of cognition, however, is based upon the distinction of its objects.
Regarding this, the teachers respond: it is not only due to a difference in objects that there is a difference in appearance; rather, such a difference indeed arises from a difference in means.

As for the objection raised—that because the appearance of the object is not itself apparent at the time of its manifestation, the path of speaking of such a distinction is a narrow one—that is an objection only from one who does not understand the Nyāya system.
