Our view is that the very production of cognition constitutes the apprehension of the object; it is not the apprehension of the cognition itself.

In this regard, just as when the cognition "man" arises as a mere production of unsurpassed knowledge, there is direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) of that much alone, and the knowledge itself does not shine forth—wherein the object alone appears even while the knowledge is not grasped—so too, in the case of "the man with a staff" or "the one in white clothes," when a cognition with a specific qualification is produced by means of the cognition of the qualifier, that very same object shines forth even when that [qualifier] is not grasped. How narrow a path this is! And thus, the cognition "the man with a staff" is indeed directed toward the person.

Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "Which man is the one with a staff? and "Who is the man with a staff?", it is the person alone who appears without doubt.
Likewise, in cases such as "Feed the one with a staff" or "Give to the one with a staff," the connection with actions like eating is observed in the person alone, and not in the staff.

But surely, in common worldly usage as well as in the Veda, we observe that the stick (daṇḍa) is also connected with the action—for instance, in the statement "the man with the stick (daṇḍī) climbs the mountain," and in the Vedic injunction "the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, possessing the stick, recites the directions" (*daṇḍī maitrāvaruṇaḥ praiṣānanvāha*), since the recitation of the directions is already established by another text, this sentence serves to enjoin the stick.

Just as in the case of [the injunction] "The priests, wearing red turbans, perform the rites," this is merely a prescription of the red turbans for the priests who are already established in the sacrifice by virtue of the principle of extension from the archetype (*prakṛti*), such as the Śyena; it is said: let it be so, but a person ascends a mountain by leaning on a staff, not the insentient staff itself. Even in the Veda, it is a person holding a staff who recites the directions (*praiṣa*), not the staff; nor do red turbans perform the rites, but rather the priests themselves, who have become the primary referents of the compound. Thus, in every instance, the cognition is directed toward the substantive (*viśeṣya*).
If, however, both were being expressed, it would have to be "the staff and the man," and not "the man with the staff."

If it is argued that the relationship between qualifier and qualified acts as the regulator [of the cognition], then this very cognition is already described as being inclined toward the qualified (viśeṣya), because the qualifier, by virtue of being a qualifier, is merely subordinate.
In the expression "the man has a staff," it is the man alone who is expressed, not both the staff and the man.
Thus, cognitions such as "prior" and "posterior," cognitions such as "slow" and "quick," and cognitions such as "the cloth is here in these threads" apprehend space, time, and inherence.

These [space, time, and inherence], being included within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), produce a specific excellence in cognition; they do not themselves become the objects of those cognitions, unlike substances such as cloth.

Thus, cognitions such as "the stone is heavy," which are produced by specific causes like gravity that are themselves to be inferred from effects such as falling, take as their object a substantive qualified by an imperceptible attribute; enough of this elaboration.
Therefore, the cognition "this is a cow" and so forth does not have as its object a denoted thing delimited by a denoter;
consequently, it is not verbal (śābda) in nature,
but is rather clearly nothing other than perception (pratyakṣa).

And since, when that object of definition exists, there is no possibility of raising the objection regarding the uselessness of the definition, the term "avyapadeśya" (indesignable) is not for the purpose of refuting the fault of impossibility.
For what purpose, then, was this stated by the teachers: "In order to exclude knowledge born from both"?
But has it not been stated that even this [cognition] is indeed perception and thus not to be excluded?
In this case, perception has its capacity exhausted by the mere apprehension of the essential nature of an object such as a cow standing before one;
however, regarding the fact that it is denotable by the word "cow," the word itself, which teaches the application of the name, is the means of valid cognition.

Although other means of determining the relationship between a word and its meaning are possible, nevertheless, in cases where elders instruct by pointing out the named object and teaching the name—saying, for example, "this is what is denoted by the word *go* (cow)," or "this is what is denoted by the word *panasa* (jackfruit)"—in the determination of that denotative capacity, that [instruction] alone is the instrument.
For this very reason, the world as well considers [the Veda] here to be verbal in nature,
being satisfied by the extraordinary knowledge of the unprecedented (*apūrva*) constructed by words.
The cognition that something is denotable by that word does not occur without words that provide the instruction of its name;
therefore, in this case, that very [name] possesses excellence even though the sense organ is present.
Therefore, even the author of the Sūtra, perceiving here a superiority in sound, formulated that exclusion; he did not do so as a teacher of Dharma.
Therefore, this term is intended solely for the purpose of excluding knowledge produced from both [senses and mental factors].

Others, however, think as follows: if this word is described as excluding the "dual-born" cognition—which arises at the time of grasping the convention from the words of the instructor of the name that will occur in the future—then how is it that that [cognition] which also arises at the time of linguistic usage, namely the cognition "this is a cow" preceded by the recollection of the words of the instructor of the name (such as Devadatta) uttered at the time of grasping the convention, is not also excluded by it, since that too is indeed dual-born?
But surely, in that case, it is the recollection of the word that is the cause, not the word itself;
for even at the time of the convention, it is precisely the recollection of the word that is the cause. Indeed, phonemes occurring in a temporal sequence cannot be experienced simultaneously.

But when the final phoneme is being perceived or remembered, is the operation of the word (śabda) any different? Is it not the case that at the time of linguistic usage, only the denotative word—such as "cow" and so on—is remembered and, together with the sense organ, functions toward the arising of a determinate cognition (*savikalpapratyaya*)?

If you argue that at the time of the convention (*saṅketa*), however, it is the statement of an elder who teaches the name that [functions], we say: do not say so. For even at the time of usage, it is precisely the statement of an elder teaching the name that is remembered; because if that were not remembered, the fact of being denotable by that word would not be understood.

Having recollected, "The name 'cow' was taught to him by Devadatta," one engages in linguistic usage precisely through the fact that the word 'cow' is its designator; therefore, this cognition is born solely from the recollection of that sentence. Consequently, for this person as well, that sentence which teaches the application of the name functions as the cause; thus, this too should be accepted as verbal (śābda) cognition.
If it is said, "Let it be so," then alas!
for the ascetic Naiyāyikas, conceptual perception has arisen.
Wherever the knowledge of a convention is possible even through another means,
there too, by this same principle, its status as verbal cognition is not negated.
Furthermore, for the Naiyāyikas, conceptual perception (*savikalpapratyakṣa*) constitutes their very lifeblood.
Therefore, it cannot be said that knowledge arising from both [perception and word] has the nature of verbal cognition (*śābdatva*).
The comprehension of the relationship, however, is based on multiple means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that regard, each respective means of valid cognition operates within its own specific domain.
As Bhaṭṭa has said: "The relationship is established by three means of valid cognition."
Therefore, the burden of [defining] a single word should not be imposed [upon it].

Since perception, even at the time of grasping the convention, grasps its own object, the position that excludes knowledge produced by both [perception and inference] is not faultless. Consequently, it is better to adopt the very position stated by the Elder Naiyāyika: the exclusion of knowledge that has become the object of a word. Let that alone be accepted.
In that regard, when the action has been performed and the duty fulfilled, the term "to be designated" (vyapadeśya) becomes more consistent with its actual meaning.
Now, it might be objected: "Was it not stated there that such knowledge is neither invalid nor a fifth means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? True; however, this is their intended meaning:
that sense-born knowledge directed toward the apprehension of objects such as form is called either the means of valid cognition or its fruit.

But when that very same [cognition] is expressed by a word as "the cognition of color" or "the cognition of taste," then, having abandoned its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatā) which is obtained through the operation of grasping the objects of the cognitions of color and so forth, it assumes only the status of an object of cognition (prameyatā) produced by becoming the object of a word; therefore, in that state, it is not a means of valid cognition—so how could there be the consequence of a fifth means of valid cognition?

Another says: having raised the same objection as before—that perceptual cognition which is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), involves the synthesis of words, and arises in dependence upon the association with words might be considered verbal (*śābda*)—the author of the Sūtras shows that very cognition to be non-verbal by means of the term "non-designatable" (*avyapadeśya*).
The meaning is that this cognition is indeed perceptual because it conforms to the presence and absence of the sense organs; it is "non-designatable," that is, non-verbal.
Because it is clear, because there is no [other] denoter, because it conforms to the sense faculties, and because it is so accepted by the world, this is held to be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Even though it arises from the recollection of words, such knowledge is not verbal;
the recollection of words serves as an auxiliary to the sense organ, like a lamp.
Now, if conceptual perception has been established in this way as being direct perception,
would non-conceptual perception not then be excluded from the category of direct perception?
If even a perceptual cognition is admitted to be permeated by words,
then what need is there for deliberation regarding the fact that it remains such [i.e., perceptual] even when devoid of contact with them?
Therefore, just like non-conceptual [perception], conceptual perception is also direct perception;
and the author of the Sūtras has included this by means of this word.
Thus have the views of the teachers been presented here according to tradition;
O learned ones, let that which appears as the truth among them be relied upon.
The inclusion of the term "non-deviating" (*avyabhicārin*) is for the purpose of excluding deviating cognition.

For example, when the sun blazes in summer, scorching the forehead, a cognition of water arises regarding the shimmering rays of that sun which, having struck a parched wasteland, surge upward and assume the form of waves; because it is a grasping of something as what it is not, it is deviating.
That [cognition] is excluded by this term, such that it is not considered perception.

In this regard, even the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) arising from the first contact of the eye with its object produces a conceptual cognition of water; it apprehends water exactly as it is, and thus the Tathāgatas declare that a non-conceptual cognition whose object is a mirage is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it generates the conceptualization of water. This is because, while one is not yet investigating during the state of non-conceptuality, there is an immediate appearance of water to one whose eyes have just been opened.
Alternatively, it has been demonstrated that even cognitions preceded by the mention of a denotative word do not forfeit their status as being produced from sense-faculties and objects.
Therefore, whether determinate or indeterminate, any cognition that arises as "that" with respect to what is "not-that" is erroneous; and such [erroneous cognition] is what must be excluded here.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the cognition of water in mirages is produced without the contact of sense-organ and object, because it manifests as water that does not exist?

Therefore, since its exclusion is already accomplished by the phrase "produced from the contact of sense-organ and object," what is the purpose of the term "non-deviant"? [Reply: This is not so; for its production from the sense-organ and the object is established by the fact that it exists when they exist.
Indeed, one whose eyes are closed does not have the perception of water in the desert.
The object also exists as its producer; there is no manifestation of what is non-existent. However, the teachers have formulated a threefold reflection regarding its objective support.
By some, the objective support for that [cognition] has been stated to be the rays of the sun,
which conceal their own form and assume the appearance of water.

In that case, when there is the apprehension of common properties such as waves and the like, the specific features of both [a post and a person] do not enter the path of recollection as they do in the case of a post and a person;
nor do the specific features of the nearby rays of light enter the path of recollection.
Rather, it is the specific features belonging to water, which is contrary to what was previously perceived, that enter the path of recollection.
And because their own specific qualities are obscured by the recollection of that [water], the rays of light, being unable to manifest their true nature, appear in the form of water.
Others, however, have stated that the object of perception is water brought to mind by a memory arising from the sight of similarity in a subject situated before one.

In a cognition, that form which appears as an illusion is said to be its objective support (*ālambana*), not something merely present nearby; for otherwise, it would follow that the ground and the atoms composing it would also be its objective supports.
And this consciousness manifests as water;
therefore, that [water] alone is its objective support.

And that [water] is not present here; nor is the manifestation of something absolutely non-existent, such as a sky-flower, possible. Therefore, it is water existing in another place or the like that becomes the objective support here, having been mounted upon a memory produced by impressions awakened by the perception of a similar object.
Some maintain that the objective support (ālambana) is one thing while what appears is another; the Dīghitiyas hold that the objective support is water and it is water that appears.

The objective support (ālambana) is said to be that which generates cognition and is distinct from the agent and the instrument; thus, there is no application [of this definition] to atoms and the like.
These three positions will be examined more precisely below.

Thus, since it is impossible to exclude by means of the phrase "arisen from the contact of the sense-organ with its object" those errors that follow the presence and absence of external sensory objects, the inclusion of the term "non-deviating" (avyabhicārin) is appropriate.

However, as for those mental errors (*vibhramāḥ*) that arise independently of the external sense organs, their exclusion is indeed intended by the term "contact between sense organ and object" (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*); therefore, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārin*) is not for their sake.
For example: "Those whose vision is agitated by intense passion ignited by separation see their beloved standing nearby, even though she is far away."
Now, one might ask: in such objectless delusions, from where does the form appear? It is said in reply: in a delusion, a form generally flashes forth as it has ascended into memory;
however, the cause of that memory occurs somewhere, at some time, and in some way.
In some cases there is a cognition of similarity; in some cases, desire, grief, and so forth;
in some cases, the habitual practice of seeing; and in some cases, an optical disorder such as cataracts.
In some cases there is sleep, in others anxiety, and in others a disorder of the bodily humors;
when no such cause is perceived, the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) is remembered as the cause.
Who knows whether a child’s cognition of two moons exists or not?
Even if it does exist, they consider its cause to be unperceived memory.
Surely the appearance of the progenitor is for the sake of establishing a restrictive rule;
moreover, that which is absolutely non-existent is never observed to possess the capacity to produce cognition.
And no object such as a woman or the like is present there;
therefore, they consider that this appears because it has ascended to memory.
Therein, by the first word, these delusions arising within one's own internal organ— which arise devoid of contact with the senses and so forth— are excluded.
Furthermore, regarding those cognitions such as that of a yellow conch or water in a mirage which arise from the senses— for the sake of excluding them, this word was placed in the Sūtra.

When a person perceives from a distance a common property—such as height and girth—which is shared by both a post (*sthāṇu*) and a man, and yet does not perceive the specific features belonging to either one, such as crooks and hollows, or hands and feet; and when, due to the awakening of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) by that common property, he recollects the specific features residing in both, there arises with respect to the object situated before him a doubtful cognition (*saṃśayajñāna*) in the form, "Is it a post or a man?
Although this [cognition] possesses qualifications such as being produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object, it is nonetheless not the result of perception (*pratyakṣaphala*).
Therefore, the inclusion of the term "determinate" (vyavasāyātmaka) is for the purpose of excluding that [indefinite cognition].

[Objection: But surely, since doubt (*saṃśaya*) is mental, its exclusion is already established by the inclusion of the phrase "produced from the contact of a sense-organ with an object" (*indriyārthasannikarṣotpanna*); what is the point of another word? Moreover, the Commentator will say: "[Memory, inference, verbal testimony, doubt, intuition (*pratibhā*), dream-cognition, recognition, pleasure and so forth, and perception—desire and the rest—are the marks of the mind (*manas*).
[Response: Not so; for doubt regarding a post (*sthāṇu*) and the like follows the positive and negative concomitance of the external sense-organs.

For indeed, there exists a certain mental doubt, such as that of an astrologer or calculator who, having given an incorrect prediction once and another time, experiences doubt when predicting for a third time: "Will this prediction of mine correspond with reality, or will it fail?
This [doubt] resides in the mind of the author of the Bhāṣya as something produced by the internal organ alone.

As for the doubt that arises when one with wide-open eyes thinks, "Is this a post or a person? and so forth—who indeed would call that not born from the contact of a sense-organ with its object? Now, has it not been explained that a cognition of "that" in what is "not-that" is erroneous (*vyabhicārin*)? Furthermore, doubt—such as "Is this a post or a person?"—touches upon an object standing before one in a single form by way of multiple forms.

Since this very [doubt] consists in apprehending something as being thus when it is not, it is simply a case of error (*viparyaya*); because it has already been excluded by the preceding term, it does not deserve to be excluded by a subsequent term.
This is not so, because of the difference in their intrinsic natures and the difference in their causes.
A misconception (*viparyaya*) arises when one delineates a single, contradictory form, such as "a person" in regard to a post, or "a post" in regard to a person.
Doubt (*saṃśaya*), however, consists in the delineation of two indefinite forms, such as "it might be a post or it might be a person."
Thus, this distinction of intrinsic nature is to be personally realized by each individual.

Furthermore, error arises from the recollection of specific features of a contrary object; when mother-of-pearl is present, there occurs the error of one who recalls the specific features of silver, and when shimmering rays of light are present, there occurs the error of one who recalls the specific features of water. However, doubt—which is born from the recollection of the specific features of both—is to be excluded by a separate term [in the definition]. Thus, this [error] is indeed to be excluded by another word.
But surely, since non-conceptual doubt and error are also impossible, their exclusion would be established by the term "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*) alone in the view of the Proponent [Prabhākara].
For the mere perception of a substrate such as a post standing before one is non-conceptual and born from the operation of the sense organs;
however, immediately thereafter, doubt and error arise—associated with verbal expressions—being produced by the recollection of the specific qualities belonging to both alternatives.
In that case, since the penetration by words is already implied by the very recollection of the specific [object],
neither of the two terms need be employed for the purpose of excluding it.
In this regard, first of all, only this must be said:
the position of the Pravaras has already been refuted, since it has been established that even that which arises from the interpenetration of words is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*).
[Objection: "Granted that the position of the Pravaras has been refuted;

however, when the operation of the eye has culminated in the perception of similarity, the doubt and error that subsequently arise after the recollection of particulars cannot be produced by the sense organ (*aindriyaka*), and thus they are already excluded by the very first word [of the definition]. [Reply: This is incorrect, because it has already been stated that the operation of the sense organ continues even after recollection;
and this is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), since such [doubt and error] do not arise in one whose eyes are closed.
At that time, there is no verbal articulation even in the form of internal conceptualization (*antaḥsaṅkalpa*).
However, once doubt or error has arisen, the recollection of the denotative word will occur; thus, like correct cognition, both doubt and error are experienced as being devoid of verbal articulation.
As for the recollection of particulars, since its object is the particular itself, let it project those very particulars.
What function does the word have? It is the recollection of the expressive word that presents the word [to consciousness], and that recollection has not yet arisen.

Therefore, like [cognitions] possessing correct conditions, doubt and error— which arise from the operation of the sense faculties— are not present when they are devoid of the verbal expression of a denoter.
Since such as these two cannot be excluded by the first term alone,
it is therefore appropriate to employ both terms in order to eliminate them.
Such are the words denoting the definition (*lakṣaṇapada*).

However, the word denoting the definiendum (*lakṣyapada*), namely "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), functions by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) alone with respect to a specific type of cognition, because its etymological application (*yoga*) is subject to deviation.
The literal meaning of the term is "that which has reached the sense-organ" (*pratigatam akṣam pratyakṣam*).
And since this [term] can also apply to pleasure and so forth, its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) alone is more appropriate.

Alternatively, since the term *jñāna* is specified in the Sūtra, let there also be the aspect of yoga; for it is not proper to deny what is clearly perceived. Moreover, the so-called "conventional-technical" (*yogarūḍhi*) meaning is certainly not accepted by the learned.
For even where a pair is perceived, it is precisely that which serves as the motivator for the application of a word.

Furthermore, how is it maintained that cognition is "dependent upon the sense organ" (*akṣam pratigatam*)? It cannot be by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because that would entail the consequence that collyrium and the like are also perceived.
Nor can it be by way of inherence (*samavāya*), because that would entail the consequence that color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities residing in the sense organ would likewise be so [perceived].
Nor can it be by way of being a producer (*janakatva*), because that would entail the consequence that even the atoms (*paramāṇu*) which constitute the sense organ would possess that same status.
Therefore, it should be explained that knowledge has reached the sense organ precisely by virtue of being produced [by it].

However, an explanation [of the term] as an *avyayībhāva* compound is not tenable, because we observe such usage as "the person is perceptible" (*pratyakṣaḥ puruṣaḥ*) and "the woman is perceptible" (*pratyakṣā strī*); therefore, enough of this over-elaboration.

Therefore, it is established that perception is that cognition which arises from [the contact of] the sense-faculties with their objects and is endowed with a collection of qualifiers such as being produced by them.
Thus the wise Akṣapāda established this definition for it, free from all blemish;
for definitions composed by others do not enter the minds of those with subtle vision even for a moment.

Thus ends the section on the commentary on the Sūtra on Direct Perception (pratyakṣa). As for that definition of direct perception which the Bhikṣu [Dignāga] proclaimed—namely, "that which is free from conceptual construction (kalpanā) and non-erroneous (abhrānta)"—that is utterly improper.
Conceptual construction (kalpanā), it is said, is the cognition of an object capable of being associated with a word; by what defect, then, is its status as a valid means of knowledge not tolerated?

Now, one might object: "By stating that [the object] has an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression, what other fault are you seeking? This very point—that it has a non-existent thing as its object—has already been stated, because there is no real referent for a word.

For a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), whose nature consists in its exclusion from both similar and dissimilar things, cannot be made an object by a word whose operation depends upon the apprehension of a relationship;
moreover, no entity distinct from that [particular characteristic] is perceived."

Furthermore, conceptual cognition (kalpanā) does not follow the positive and negative concomitance of the contact between sense-faculties and their objects, because it occurs even in the absence of that contact, and because—even when that contact is present—it does not arise without the association of a previously experienced expressive word.
If the contact between sense-faculty and object were its producer, it would produce such a cognition at the very first moment; yet it does not.
Therefore, we conclude that this [contact] is not its producer even after the recollection of words.

As it has been said: "That which was previously not a producer of cognition because there was no difference in its utility would likewise remain so later; thus, even when the object has disappeared, there would be visual cognition [of that non-existent object]."
Moreover, even when there is contact between the sense organ and the object, if there were a dependence upon memory, that object would be separated by that very [memory].
And it has been said: "If sensory cognition, even when the object is present, were to depend upon the application of a word through memory, then that object would be separated."

If it is argued that the sense faculty (*akṣa*), depending upon the cooperation of the recollection of conventions, produces such a cognition, we say no; for the status of a "cooperator" has been refuted by the dilemmas regarding whether the assistance is distinct or non-distinct from the faculty.
Furthermore, conceptual cognitions such as "the man with a staff" do not arise at the very moment of sensory contact, but rather depend upon many intermediate processes.
As it is said: "The qualifier, the qualified, the relation, and the worldly convention..."
Having grasped all of this, one understands it exactly as it is and not otherwise.

Nor is this entire process capable of being sustained by the non-conceptual cognition produced at the very first incidence of the sense-organ; thus he says: "How could that [process], which has the recollection of conventions as its means and consists of the synthesis of what is seen, exist in visual perception, which is devoid of reflection upon the preceding and the succeeding?"

In this regard, it might be argued: conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are of two kinds—those fabricated by the whims of students, such as "this-ness" (*idantā*), and those that grasp at "this-ness," such as "this is blue.
Among these, let the former not be valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*);

for who would insist on their validity when they arise independently of an object? But how can those that grasp at "this-ness" lack validity, since they are invariably concomitant with the object? To this it is replied: from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), all these conceptual constructions fail to touch the object at all.
For that [object] is indeed determined in its entirety by non-conceptual [cognition] alone.

As it has been said: "When the single nature of an object is itself directly perceived, what other unperceived part could there be that would need to be examined by means of further instruments of knowledge?"* (*Pramāṇavārttika 3.459) *Note: The original Sanskrit provided in the prompt contains a minor error; the standard reading for the second line is *ko 'nyo na dṛṣṭo bhāgaḥ syād yaḥ pramāṇair vicāryate*. I have translated based on this corrected version.*

As for the fact that certain conceptual constructions possess a nature such as grasping "this-ness" (idantā) or clarity, this is produced by contact with the reflection acquired from occurring immediately after a non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-darśana*) which is invariably concomitant with the object; it is not, however, any kind of direct touch with the object itself, because the very essence of the object is sealed by non-conceptual perception alone.
Therefore, conceptual constructions, preceded by the delineation of unreal forms, never arise in accordance with reality.

And these five are conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*): the construction of genus (*jāti*), the construction of quality (*guṇa*), the construction of action (*kriyā*), the construction of name (*nāman*), and the construction of substance (*dravya*).

They are called "conceptual constructions" because in some cases they construct a distinction even where there is no distinction, and in other cases they construct a non-distinction even where there is a distinction.
In ultimate reality, there is no distinction whatsoever between the universal and that which possesses the universal;
rather, the conceptualization of a universal arises in the form of a superimposition of difference.
For no one perceives any difference in the sense that "this is the cowness of this cow";
therefore, since there is no difference, it is merely a conceptual construction of difference.
The conceptualization of qualities should be understood through this same logic;
even there, a distinction is postulated between the quality and its possessor, though they are non-different.
And so they have said: "It is a marvel that this possessor of qualities does not show itself as a distinct entity from color and the other [sensory objects], yet you desire its separation from them."
The conceptualization of action, like that of qualities, consists precisely in the superimposition of difference;
for there is no such thing as "action" apart from its own essential nature.
In the expression "Devadatta goes," it is Devadatta alone who appears, neither less nor more.
However, the conceptual construction of a name proceeds by way of non-difference between two distinct things;
for instance, the determination "this is Caitra" is one of non-difference between the name and the named.
"Caitra" is this word; "this" is the object. Of what nature is the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between these two?
In this way, the conceptualization of a substance, such as "this person is to be punished," should be understood [as a construction],
because those two distinct things are apprehended through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).

Now, if conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) proceed by superimposing difference upon identity and identity upon difference, why does no subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) arise in their case, as it does in the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl? It is said in reply: A subverting cognition occurs where one thing appears in the form of another thing, as in the cognition of water in mirages.
But here, there is no other entity such as a "universal" (*jāti*) and so forth, through which this [individual] could be grasped as being another thing.
These conceptual constructions of universals and the like have only the individual (*vyakti*) as their object.
Therefore, since these [cognitions] do not manifest as other real entities, no subverting cognition arises;
consequently, conceptual constructions are not of the nature of error.
And these [mental constructions] are not valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), because the universals (*jāti*) and so forth that are delineated by them lack ultimate reality (*apāramārthikatva*).
For this very reason, they declare that this is a distinct kind of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is neither valid cognition nor error (*viparyaya*); enough with this elaboration.
Thus do these five types of conceptualization proceed, constructed solely from latent predispositions; they are the manifold elaborations of imagined distinctions such as "unreal" and so forth.
And seeing thus the dullness of the fragrance of the authority of those [scriptures],
the monk composed in the *Lakṣaṇagrantha* a verse that removes it.

To this, it is replied: by your lamenting so excessively and in such a confused manner, you have made it clear that you have not definitively identified any specific reason for the invalidity of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, let it be stated: is the intended cause of its invalidity (1) the denotation of non-existent objects, which is implied by the appearance of word-meanings; or (2) the state of not being produced by sense-object contact, which arises from dependence on the recollection of linguistic convention; or (3) the state of being accomplished through great effort, resulting from dependence on the apprehension of particulars and so forth; or (4) the state of being investigative, as conveyed by the verbal expression of its distinction from visual perception, which lacks prior and subsequent reflection; or (5) the state of apprehending what has already been apprehended, based on its grasping an object previously determined by indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*); or (6) the apprehension of "that" in what is not that, as described by the superimposition of identity and difference; or (7) the state of being sublated, as indicated by the apprehension of universals that are refuted by arguments concerning their subsistence (*vṛtti*) and so forth?

In this regard, it is not appropriate to state that the cause of their invalidity is the apprehension of unreal objects by way of grasping objects capable of being associated with words; for the reality of the referent of words will be established [later].
If it is asked, "What, then, is this? [the answer is: it is precisely that which appears in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*).
Does the universal and so forth appear in non-conceptual [cognition]? We shall say: "Certainly it appears."

For this very reason, it should not be asserted that sublation (*bādhyatva*) is also a cause for the loss of validity (*prāmāṇya*) in these cases, because the sublaters—such as the dilemma regarding their occurrence (*vṛtti-vikalpa*) and so forth—will be refuted later; and furthermore, you yourself do not accept another kind of sublation in the form of the cognition "this is not [it]," as in the case of the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl.

Nor can it be said that [the cognition] is not produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object, because this [cognition] depends upon the recollection of the word experienced at the time of grasping the convention; for even when there is dependence on an auxiliary factor, the operation of the sense-organ does not cease.
That which was previously not a producer of cognition, once it has obtained an auxiliary cause,
who can prevent it from producing that cognition at a later time?
As for the alternatives regarding whether assistance is rendered as distinct or non-distinct, these will be refuted in the section on the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga*).
Furthermore, since the eye depends upon a lamp or other factors for the apprehension of form, those logical dilemmas (vikalpas) are difficult to avoid;
for you yourselves also recite that "nothing whatsoever is a single producer," so these [dilemmas] apply equally to your own position as well.
If a fault applies to both sides, one side should not be singled out for criticism on that account.
Therefore, the reason "because there is no difference in their utility" is unestablished (*asiddha*).

This very thing is the difference in utility: namely, that the recollection of the denotative word, like the sense organ, light, attention, and the object, also functions as another causal complex (*sāmagrī*) in the production of this cognition. Thus, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not invalid simply because it is produced by the recollection of a denotative word and is therefore of the nature of memory (*smārta*). For otherwise, it would follow that even non-conceptual visual cognition—which is produced by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) known as the memory of form—would likewise be invalid.
As for what is said—that "the object would be obstructed"—we do not understand what kind of obstruction there could be for the object;
for an object is never obstructed by a lamp or by the mind, which are causes of cognition.

And since the recollection of the expressive word, like the mind, functions toward the apprehension of that object while being included within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), how could it possibly obstruct the object?

If it is argued that the word, having become an object of memory, acts as an obstruction to that object [the meaning], we say no; for since the word is an illuminator of that [meaning], like a cognition or a lamp, it lacks any obstructive quality.
Nor is "obstruction" the concealment of the operation of the sense organ, because that operation continues even now.
Just as the initial consciousness is produced from the sense organ because it arises when that [organ] exists,
so too the subsequent cognition is produced from the sense organ because it arises when that [organ] exists.
For one does not, after recollecting the expressive word, close one's eyes and then conceptualize, "This is a cloth."

Now, the claim that by the time the expressive cognition (*vācakavijñāna*) enters the path of the heart, the object has already passed away due to its momentariness and is thus said to be "obstructed," is merely a vain hope;
for the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) will be refuted later on.

Moreover, just as in the case of the conventional usage of "attainment" (*prāpti*) and so forth that has been demonstrated, the apprehension of that [object] here too will occur by way of the continuum (*santāna*); thus, there is no obstruction whatsoever.

Thus, even though conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*) depends upon the recollection of conventions (*samaya*), it does not transcend the state of being produced from the contact of the sense-faculty with its object; so how could it be non-perceptual? Furthermore, as for the claim that its dependence on a complex of conditions—such as the apprehension of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*)—and its being accomplished through great effort constitutes a cause for invalidity, that is a most ill-spoken argument. For being accomplished through much hardship does not indeed undermine validity. And it has been said: "For that which is grasped after having climbed a mountain peak is not thereby non-perceptual."

Furthermore, in comparison with the cognition of taste and so forth, the cognition of form and so forth would lack validity, since it is accomplished through the exertion of bringing forth light such as that of a lamp.

Furthermore, as for the claim that conceptual cognitions (*vikalpajñāna*) lack validity because they are investigative in nature— contrary to visual perception which is devoid of reflection on what precedes and follows— that too is not correct;
for it is impossible for cognition itself to be investigative in every case,
since it is the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) who is investigative.
For we shall explain that he indeed sees, remembers, synthesizes, deliberates, desires, hates, exerts himself, grasps, abandons, and experiences pleasure.
Furthermore, how could there be invalidity for a cognition that touches upon its object even while it is deliberating?

Now, if you think that because this [subsequent cognition] has already been touched by the [initial] cognition in its entirety through non-conceptualization alone, it is like grinding what is already ground and thus improper, and that it is therefore not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it grasps an object already apprehended by conceptualization—that too is not correct, as it has already been refuted previously.

For it has been stated that being a cognizer of what is already cognized does not constitute invalidity; even when grasping what has already been grasped, a means of knowledge does not lose its status as a valid means of knowledge.

As for what was asserted—that conceptual constructions which imagine non-difference among things that are different, or difference among things that are non-different, lose their status as valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) because they grasp something as what it is not—that is correct; for grasping something as what it is not is indeed the cause of invalidity. However, that [cause] does not exist here. For the determination of that [invalidity] occurs through the occurrence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), and there is no such subverting cognition whatsoever regarding the five types of conceptual constructions you have described, such as those concerning universals (*jāti*) and so forth. Therefore, these conceptual constructions do not grasp something as what it is not.
The universal is distinct from that which possesses the universal, and the possessor of qualities is separate from the collection of qualities;
likewise, because they are perceived as such, conceptual expressions are uncontradicted.
And this will be determined further below.
Let there be for the substance and its name, which are distinct, a cognition precisely as distinct; there is no conceptualization of non-difference.
For the referent of that [name] is not cognized in such a way as "this is the word Devadatta."

If it is argued that the conventional usage of non-difference between the name and the named—such as "This is Devadatta"—is indeed observed, we say no; this is an apprehension of the object as qualified by the word, but the word does not appear as having ascended onto the object within this cognition.
Nor does the object manifest in the form of a transformation (*vivarta*) of the word.
What then? It arises from the excellence of the causal capacity of the complex of conditions known as the recollection of the word.
That this is a specific excellence of the causal conditions has already been established previously.

The conceptualization of non-difference between the substance [the person] and the attribute [the staff], such as "this one is a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍy ayam*), has been propounded only by those of dull intellect.
For there is no cognition regarding Devadatta of the form "this is a staff" (*daṇḍo 'yam*); rather, it is "he is a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍī*).
And in that case, the base and the suffix are perceived as entirely distinct, as in "one who possesses a staff is a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍo 'syāsti daṇḍīti*).
Therefore, in this case, since the determination of the object is exactly as the object itself is, there is no superimposition of non-difference.

But regarding the object of action, neither of these two exists: there is no conceptualization of difference in what is not different, nor is there conceptualization of non-difference in what is different.
For action is distinct from that which possesses it and is perceived as such,
because its own nature appears [as distinct] in cognitions such as "it moves."
Therefore, by indicating an object colored by action, quality, substance, name, and genus, the conceptual cognition "not this" does not lack validity.
We accept that one has "crossed over" by way of the reversal [of error];
however, we do not tolerate a conceptual construction that lies outside the means of valid cognition.
If its lack of validity in some cases is due to the presence of a subverting factor,
then that same [lack of validity] applies equally to non-conceptual [cognition] as well when it manifests a double moon and so forth.
Let there be, at will, an immeasurability of conceptual constructions regarding mental desires;
however, such [immeasurability] does not apply to those [cognitions] produced by the senses, which proceed in accordance with the actual state of things.

Nor is this form of theirs produced by being subsequent to a non-conceptual [cognition], because it is impossible for cognitions—which are inherently transparent by nature—to possess such a form without contact with an object; what, then, will being subsequent to a non-conceptual [cognition] achieve? For even memory, which occurs immediately after that, is indeed observed in some cases, yet it does not possess the reflection of that [object]; thus, this [claim] is merely a vain hope.

Now, it might be argued that the entire reality of a single object's nature is grasped by non-conceptual [perception] alone; however, this has already been refuted, because its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not lost even when it apprehends what has already been grasped.
Furthermore, we do not even know what it is that is apprehended by non-conceptual cognition.
Sirs, you declare that the object of non-conceptual [cognition] is the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), which is excluded from both similar and dissimilar things.

Others, however, understand that "Great Universal" (mahāsāmānya) to be existence (sattā), and they consider its object to be reality; others still regard the nature of speech (vāgrūpa) as the ultimate reality and hold it to be the object of cognition.

Some maintain that the object of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is a variegated entity (*śabala-vastu*) characterized by distinctions such as qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), substances (*dravya*), and universals (*jāti*).
It is remarkable that there are such conflicting disagreements even regarding objects of direct perception;

for while doubt concerning an imperceptible object is stilled by direct perception, by what can doubt that has arisen regarding a perceptible object be stilled? This is so in cases where there are conflicting cognitions as to whether "this appears" or "this does not appear."
In persuading others, men have recourse to oaths and declarations.
But we do not remain idle, taking refuge solely in oaths;
we determine that object of knowledge even by means of another path.
Since conceptual cognition arises in accordance with non-conceptual cognition, we consider the object of apprehension to be that which conforms to the non-conceptual.
In this regard, first of all, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is excluded from everything of its own class, is not the object of perception.
When the particular characteristic has indeed been grasped by non-conceptual [cognition] and [all other objects] have been excluded,
how could a conceptualization of a universal suddenly arise?

For conceptual constructions can only arise in accordance with non-conceptual [perception]. Moreover, if conceptualization has as its object that which is excluded from what is of a different class, then alas, the universal in the form of exclusion must be grasped by direct perceptions!
Indeed, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no exclusion other than that which is excluded;
by the very apprehension of the excluded, the apprehension of that [exclusion] occurs all the more clearly.
Even when there is the apprehension of a universal, because its operation is not conceptualized in that way,
it does not remain restricted solely to the determination of the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
Nor is it logical that the object of non-conceptual [cognition] is that which is called "existence" (sattā), as accepted by the proponents of the non-duality of existence.

Even on the view that existence (*sattā*) is what is apprehended, from where does the cognition of particularity arise? If it appears as touched by difference, then the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*) is established.
Furthermore, existence cannot even be apprehended without difference;
nor will it be established that this [world] is merely ignorance alone.
The appearance of the essence of speech is also refuted by this same line of reasoning;
furthermore, how could the essence of speech appear in visual cognition?
But if the relationship has not been grasped, or even if it has been grasped but forgotten,
or if the latent impression (saṃskāra) has not been awakened— how can there be an understanding of the denoter?
If it is maintained that the manifoldness of the substratum is due to its inherence in distinct properties such as genus and the like, then let it be so.
But identity with that [nature] cannot belong to a single entity, because its essential nature would not be consistently maintained;
however, in the view that parts are extracted, a distinction between properties necessarily arises.
To say that whenever and wherever there is manifestation and the desire to perceive, the phenomena (dharmas) possess that very nature, is incoherent.
Furthermore, we do not accept a spatial distinction among properties; for the substratum is their locus, but it is not identical in nature with them.
Therefore, that very nature of the object which is the domain of conceptual cognition is itself the domain of non-conceptual cognition, devoid of the verbal articulation [of thought].
If it is asked what its nature is, one should question the actual objects and the cognitions of those objects as they appear at that time, rather than the proponent.
In some cases it is a genus, in some a substance, in some an action, and in some a quality;
whatever is grasped by conceptual cognition is precisely what is grasped by this [perception].

In this system, all cognition that grasps objects such as universals (jāti) and the like— whether it is devoid of the association with words or accompanied by them— is accepted as perception (pratyakṣa).
Therefore, regarding that term "free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha) which was recited by the Bhikṣu in the definition of perception, there exists nothing to be excluded by it.
Even in that system, we do not perceive anything that must be excluded by the term "unmistaken."

Now, it has been stated by others that the perception of two moons, a whirling firebrand, or moving trees—which arises from errors induced by cataracts, rapid spinning, or the agitation of a boat—is to be excluded [from the definition of direct perception]. This is true as stated, but it is incorrect; for such cases are already excluded by the very term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*).

Even in those instances, the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) has as its object only the single moon and so forth, while the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) grasp a contrary form, just as the conceptual construction that determines water occurs in relation to a non-conceptual cognition that grasps a mirage.

Now, one might argue that because the eye is split in two by cataracts (timira), it is unable to apprehend the moon as a single entity; thus, even non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) would take the form of a double moon and so forth. If this were the case, then since the circle of rays in a mirage (*marīcicakra*), colored by its similarity to shimmering waves and the like, cannot be discerned by the eye, why is it not accepted that there too a non-conceptual cognition apprehending water arises? Or, if such an admission were made, the conventional distinction between valid and invalid cognition—based on the production of conceptual constructions regarding what exists and what does not exist—would cease to function.
Moreover, the erroneous nature of cognitions cannot be conceived without the occurrence of a sublater;
and in the view of those who maintain momentariness, the relationship of the sublated and the sublater between cognitions is not tenable—so enough with this further scrutiny.
Thus, desiring to state the definition with most skillful intellect, he composed even these two verses that are beyond reproach.
Let this be the achievement of the great mind of the wise Dharmakīrti, which is steadfast enough to overcome the world.
The definition of perception as "the functioning of the ear and other senses, which is non-conceptual according to others" has also been refuted;
for that principle is equivalent [to our own], and it was established previously that the self cannot be a seer by means of a mental modification (buddhivṛtti).

The sūtra—"When there is contact with the six, the arising of cognition for a person through the sense organs is perception; it is not a means [for knowing Dharma], because it is the apprehension of what is already present"—has not been explained by the followers of Jaimini as being intended primarily to define perception itself. This is because it lacks connection with the thesis under discussion, namely, "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*).

Rather, it has been applied to the definition of perception by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*), in the sense that perception is not a means regarding Dharma precisely because it possesses such a character (i.e., the apprehension of what is present).
As it has been said: "This being the case, it is possible for even a definition to function as a restatement."
Therefore, this application of the Sūtra in the description of the definition is incorrect, because it does not avoid the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
For the meaning of the Sūtra is: "Perception is the cognition arising for a person when there is contact with the sense organs.
And thus, there is over-extension, because doubt and erroneous cognition would also result in being perception, since they too are born from contact with the sense organs.

Now, if "contact with the existent" (*satsaṃprayoga*) is explained as "contact with that which exists," even so, only those delusions that are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*)—which arise independently of an object—would be excluded, but not doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*), which do have an objective basis (*sālambana*).
Now, the position that "contact" (*saṃprayoga*) is expressed in the locative case (*sati*) is not abandoned; furthermore, the prefix *sam-* is explained as that which eliminates doubt and error.
As it has been said: "The word *sam* signifies 'correctly' and serves to exclude faulty application;
therefore, contact with mother-of-pearl, being defective, should be excluded from what is produced by the senses."

Nevertheless, since the correctness of the application (*prayoga-samyaktva*) is beyond the senses and thus not apprehended through perception, its comprehension must be stated to be derived from its effect (*kārya*).
And that effect is knowledge (*jñāna*).
Yet, that [knowledge], if left unspecified, does not itself make known the correctness of the application.
Furthermore, we do not perceive in this sūtra even a single word, syllable, or phoneme intended as a qualification for that [object].
Moreover, the phrase "contact with the six" (*ṣaṭsu samprayogaḥ*) has been explained as being for the purpose of precluding the notion of cognition without an object (*nirālambana-jñāna*).
As for the word "when" (*sati*), it is redundant because its meaning is already conveyed by the locative absolute construction itself (*satisaptamī*).

If it is argued that we shall understand the correctness of the application from common worldly practice itself because the specific nature of the effect is understood from the world alone, [we reply]: since perception is established from the world itself, what is the point of the laborious effort to apply the power of the aphorism to its definition?
Regarding this, the venerable author of the *Vṛtti* has said: "That which is perception does not err; that which errs is not perception. What then is perception?
It is the arising of cognition in a person when there is contact [of the sense organs]. That is true perception.
When there is contact of the sense organs with that very object regarding which the cognition arises, the arising of cognition in a person is true perception."

The claim that "a cognition which has one object as its content, when it occurs during contact with another, is not perception" is likewise a mere futile wandering, because it does not escape the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) due to doubtful cognition (saṃśayajñāna).
For in that case, there is indeed contact of the sense organs with that very object which constitutes the content of the cognition.

[Objection: But surely the cognition has both as its objects, yet the sense organ is not in contact with both. [Reply: Not so; for in the cognition of doubt, both do not appear simultaneously like two distinct trees, such as a *dhava* and a *khadira*.

Rather, a doubt arises which reflects upon the reality of one or the other object without determining it—thinking "Is it a post or a man?"—and certainly, the sense organ must be in contact with one of those two.
Since both [conditions] would indeed exist, the fault of over-extension (ativyāpti) has not been avoided.
Now, they might say: "What is the use of this trouble? We do not intend to describe the definition [of perception], because that would fall under the category of mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

Rather, by restating what is already well-known through worldly perception, it is only established that perception is not a means of knowing *dharma*—that is, perception is not a valid authority regarding *dharma* because it perceives only what is currently present; the meaning is that it grasps only existing objects.

And *dharma* is not something present, because it is understood from such verbal expressions as 'one should sacrifice,' 'one should give,' and 'one should offer oblations,' which are not restricted to the three periods of time."

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the purpose of the text [perception is the arising of cognition when there is contact of a person's sense organs with something existent]," the answer is: no, because its purpose is to establish that perception apprehends only what is currently existing.

If an opponent were to say that the property of apprehending only what is currently existing is unestablished, he should be told: "Perception apprehends only what is currently existing, because it arises from contact with something existent."

The inclusion of the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is also solely for the purpose of stating the reason (*hetu*). One who asserts that there is no established proof for "contact with the existent" (*satsaṃprayoga*) is refuted by this very point: "That which is born from contact with the existent is perception, because it is perception. As it has been said: "Perceptuality is not the reason here; the remainder [of the definition] is for the sake of establishing the reason.
Furthermore, perceptuality must be stated independently in order to negate its capacity to apprehend *dharma*.
This is not because of the intended meaning of the Sūtra; for here there is no occasion for defects such as over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

This too is not consistent with the mind of one who relies on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For which perception is it being established that it is not a cause (*animitta*) regarding *dharma*—is it the perception of people like us, or the perception of a yogi? In that regard, if it concerns the perception of people like us, there is no dispute at all; so what is the point of such great effort? As for the perception of a yogi, since it is unestablished (*asiddha*) for you, for whose sake would there be the establishment of its being non-causal regarding *dharma*? Thus, due to the absence of the subject (*dharmin*), it would touch upon the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).
The proof [of the non-existence of external objects] consists in [the reasons] such as "being perceived only when present" (vidyamānopalaṃbhatva) and "being direct perception" (pratyakṣatva). //117//

If it is argued that its establishment is by means of what is well-known to others (*paraprasiddhi*), what is this so-called "well-knownness"? Is it rooted in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or the opposite? In the first case, since valid cognition is impartial, let there be establishment for you just as there is for the other. But if it is not rooted in valid cognition, then this "well-knownness" belongs to no one at all.
If you merely restate the knowledge of yogis that is established for others, then a contradiction between your very two thesis-terms follows for you. (118)
For others indeed accept that the cognition of a yogin is a grasper of phenomena (*dharmagrāhin*);
therefore, in restating that [position], it would be as if saying that what grasps phenomena is not a grasper of phenomena.
Furthermore, an inference whose basis is established by another is not tenable;
this very point was stated by you yourselves in the critique of the "objectless" [cognition].

Just as the establishment of the probandum does not occur by means of a reason established for another, so too the establishment of the locus (*dharmin*) is not tenable through what is established for another. //120//
In this regard, it might be argued that this is a *prasaṅgasādhana* (a reductio ad absurdum).
And what is called a *prasaṅga* is said to be the production of an undesirable consequence for an opponent by means of what is already established for them.
Furthermore, for the opponent, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is established as the apprehension of an existing object and as being produced from contact with an existent thing.

"Therefore, by that very reason, its quality of being signless (*animitta*) is established; what fault is there? This is not so, for in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no such thing as a "reductio ad absurdum" (*prasaṅgasādhana*).
For that [reductio] is perceived like a painting on a wall in the absence of a wall. (121)
For it is not appropriate to deliberate upon the fragrance or lack of fragrance of a sky-flower.
Furthermore, what is the point of this? Let it be a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum);
nevertheless, even that is based upon pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Furthermore, the cognition of pervasion is not possible here for those like me; and who knows that the perception of all people does not grasp [the] property? (122)

"You do not know that my own perception is incapable of grasping dharma; nor do I know that your perception likewise does not grasp dharma. That the perception of another is exactly like this—both of us simply do not know."
If you have indeed perceived such things directly before everyone, then you alone are a yogi; why do you needlessly harbor hatred toward other yogis? (123)
Therefore, O learned Vedic scholar, understand the established position of the means of valid cognition in this way;
do not further voice objections against matters beyond the senses that are based on the words of others.

Refutation is powerless against that which is established by valid cognition; it is likewise futile against that which is devoid of valid cognition. Therefore, having cast aside this obsession with caviling, let us instead seek the means of proof regarding supersensible realities. (125)
If, when questioned, he is able to state a proof, one should accept it by saying "So be it"; if not, he simply possesses no such proof.
He replied: "We have been trained in the conduct of authoritative persons;

we do not offer a refutation. Rather, we question you: let it be told now, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the direct perception of yogins who are skilled in the realization of the Dharma? To this it is said: "The excellence of vision itself is the means of valid cognition."

For instance, someone like us, who requires light, perceives a multitude of objects situated nearby; however, the enemies of mice (owls) perceive even those fallen in places smeared by thick layers of pitch-black darkness. Furthermore, it is heard in the Rāmāyaṇa that Saṃpāti, the king of vultures, saw the beautiful wife of the son of Daśaratha, even though she was separated from him by a distance of a hundred yojanas.

Thus, this excellence of vision, like the excellence of qualities such as whiteness, is endowed with degrees of intensity; this leads one to understand that there is also a supreme, unsurpassed excellence.
And therefore, those in whom this reaches its ultimate limit are celebrated as *yogins*.
Furthermore, the supreme excellence of vision consists in having as its objects things that are subtle, concealed, remote, past, future, and so forth.
But surely, let that assumption of excellence occur without overstepping its own object;
however, color (dharma) is not even an object of the eye.
As it has been said: "Even where an excellence is observed, it does so without transgressing its own proper object."
In the perception of distant or subtle objects and so forth, there would be no functioning of the auditory faculty with respect to visible form.
Moreover: "Even those superiorities seen among men—such as wisdom, intelligence, and strength—are due to small incremental differences, and not from the perception of objects beyond the senses."
Thus [it is argued].

This is incorrect because, although *dharma* is not within the range of the eyes of people like us, it will nonetheless be accessible to the senses of the masters of yoga (*yogīndra*). For instance, while an object separated by a hundred *yojanas* or hidden by darkness does not come within the range of the vision of people like us, it certainly becomes an object for the sight of Sampāti and the cat.
But if it were so, would not the eye of yogins, operating upon what is not its proper object, also perceive odors, tastes, and so forth?
As it has been said: "If one imagines that the omniscient one is [known] by means of a single instrument of knowledge, surely he must perceive all tastes and so forth with his eye."

This is not so; for even though the sense-faculties of yogins perceive taste and other objects, they possess excellence just like the eye, and thus the operation of the eye is not postulated with respect to taste and the rest.

If it is argued that, in that case, such an operation should not be postulated with respect to *dharma* either, we say no, because *dharma*, unlike taste and the rest, is not excluded from being its object.

Furthermore, how have you understood that dharma is not an object of the senses of a yogin? That it is not an object is understood from the fact that it is not apprehended even when those senses exist, just as the fact that sound is not an object of the eye is determined because sound is not heard even when the eye is present. However, you cannot understand that dharma is not apprehended despite the existence of the yogic eye, because both of these [the yogic eye and the non-apprehension of dharma] are beyond your perception; therefore, it is not proper for you to say that "it is not an object" of him.

Is it not indeed an act of extreme audacity to claim that Dharma, which consists of the nature of what ought to be done and is untouched by the three divisions of time, falls within the range of visual perception? (127)
This is indeed a rash act for you or for me, who possess only the eye of flesh;
yet this path is not difficult to traverse for yogins who see all things. 128.

Furthermore, as for the claim that Dharma—understood solely through words such as "one should perform" (*yojayet*) which are connected with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, and which is not delimited by the three periods of time—could be determined by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that too is merely a formal argument.

For what indeed is the purpose of [discussing] contact with or non-contact with the three times? Just as we know that actions such as going have the attainment of another location as their purpose, so too will yogis know that actions such as the *agnihotra* have heaven and the like as their fruits; what rashness is there in this? If there is resentment toward the external senses—that no excellence is tolerated in them—then enough of this persistence.
Knowledge produced by the mind, arising from the practice of contemplation, occurs for those who meditate upon the Dharma, just as it does for lovers regarding their beloveds and the like. //129//
For the mind has all things as its object; there is nothing that is not its object.
By the power of practice, it is observed that even with regard to objects beyond the senses, perfectly clear appearances arise.
As they say: "Those afflicted by desire, grief, disease, madness, thieves, dreams, and so forth..."

[They see even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them. Now, one might object that because these [cognitions] are false knowledges, it is not appropriate for them to serve as examples for the cognition of a yogin; [we reply: this is not so, because their status as examples is established by the mere fact of their appearing with vivid clarity. For even in the case of a word and a jar, there is no equality in every respect. Among those [cognitions], those arising from the repeated cultivation of passion, grief, and so forth, will lack validity due to the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), but not the others, because such an absence does not exist in their case.
However, the quality of having a vivid appearance is equal in both cases.
[Objection: But surely even practice, when performed, does not bring about an absolutely unprecedented excellence, just like the practice of jumping.

For even one who practices jumping every day, performing no other task, can leap over a ground measured by only a few paces, but not over a mountain or an ocean. [Reply: It is said that jumping is a property of the body and is subject to impediments such as phlegm-induced sluggishness;
however, what obstacle could there be to its reaching excellence in the case of knowledge? (131)
However, in the case of fasting and similar practices, no specific excellence acquired through effort on the preceding day remains in the body on the following day. (132)
In that regard, once the phlegm and fat have been exhausted through practice alone, and having attained lightness of the body, they perform the fasting regimen as prescribed. //133//
In this case, however, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by cognition remains stable;
gradually accumulating, it becomes the cause of a supreme excellence. (134)

Just as, in the learning of a section of the Veda, the latent impression (saṃskāra) produced through repeated practice becomes stable and brings about proficiency in recitation, memory, and so forth. (135)
Or just as gold being purified by the process of smelting gradually attains a supreme state of excellence, shining like pure, unalloyed gold. //136//
In the same way, through the practice of cultivation, the mental cognition of yogis also becomes capable of directly perceiving all objects of knowledge. //137//
And the mind of those such as ourselves, dusty with the veils of impurities like passion and the rest, does not attain the supreme state of the excellence of knowledge. (138)
For yogis whose minds are purified by the daily practice of meditation, destroying all impurities—what object is there that their mind does not perceive? (139)
And how their abandonment of passion and the other defilements is logically possible will be explained in detail in the investigation of liberation. //140//
Thus, for those yogins whose defects have been exhausted and whose minds are absorbed in meditative concentration, there arises a stainless knowledge that encompasses all objects. (141)
Moreover, even for people like us, there is sometimes valid intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) regarding the future, such as the perception: "My brother will arrive tomorrow. (142)
Let this be accepted as valid cognition (pramāṇa): that which is not produced by a non-existent object, not doubtful, not sublated, and not caused by a defective source. //143//
If there is sublation in some cases, let that [cognition] be non-authoritative; but what can be said regarding that which is erroneously perceived on another day? (144)

If it is argued that [the object] is "like the crow and the palm fruit" (accidental), we say no; for a real entity demonstrated by a means of valid cognition cannot be suspected of being accidental. //145//
[Objection: But surely this cognition is produced from a non-existent object, because at that time its producer—the brother—is non-existent.
[Reply: This would indeed be so if one were to apprehend the brother as being existent at that very moment;
however, one apprehends him as being future.
And since its cultivation exists at that time as well, how could that cognition not be produced from a real object?
But surely, apprehension by means of "having been produced" (bhāvitayā) is untenable;
for what is called "having been produced" is indeed prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) delimited [by a subsequent moment].

And what connection can there be between non-existence and existence, its "brother," due to the contradiction between a real entity (vastu) and a non-entity (avastu)? This is incorrect; for the prior non-existence resides there in relation to that specific location, but not in relation to the substratum (dharmin).

For that [object] indeed exists, having been previously apprehended; and having ascended to the path of memory due to some cause such as a longing for food, it appears as qualified by its future arrival tomorrow. Thus, that very object is the producer of the intuitive cognition (*prātibha*). Therefore, because it is not born from a non-existent object, intuitive cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And valid cognition, being indeed perception alone, is not another means of knowledge, because it does not depend on causes such as words, logical marks, or similarity.

[Objection: But surely even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) should not exist, because it would not depend on the sense faculties. [Reply: Not so; for in that case, the mind itself serves as the sense faculty.
It has been stated that the mind is the grasper of an external object qualified by a previously arisen visual consciousness; thus, there is no absence of blind persons and the like.
Furthermore, when other means such as sound and so forth cease, the faultless cognition that arises is mental direct perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*).
It has also been stated that the cognition "the ketaka flower is fragrant" or "sugar is sweet" is like [the cognition of] knowledge;
for this very reason, it should not be said that knowledge is *pratibhā* (intuition) when its cause is indeterminate,
because its cause is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Nor is there such a thing as knowledge called "ṛṣi-knowledge" (ārṣa-jñāna), for there exists no cognition named "ṛṣi" that is distinct from perception or inference;
indeed, they say, "Even the knowledge of the ṛṣis is preceded by scripture (āgama). And the mention of "scripture" is for the sake of illustration.
Because for them, there is no knowledge that is devoid of skillful means.
Furthermore, intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) is not a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it exists even for people like us;
therefore, intuitive insight is nothing other than perception (*pratyakṣa*).
But is it not the case that even this is not perception? For perception has only the present as its object, as it has been said:
"That which is connected and present is grasped by the eye and other senses," and likewise:
"And this is the very nature of perception, namely, that its object is only the present."
Do not say so, for it has been stated by [the author] himself in another section that perception apprehends what is present, not what is future.
Furthermore, you yourself have stated that "silver, when being perceived, is perceived as something enduring.
Therefore, it is established that perception can apprehend the future, as in the case of the thought: "My brother will arrive tomorrow."
And thus, just as it is for people like us, there will be a direct perception of the Dharma by yogins regarding a future brother;

therefore, that which is stated for the purpose of negating an omniscient being— namely, "Whatever kind of perception of objects of whatever kind occurs for people now through means of valid cognition, such was also the case at other times"— [is refuted].
Thus, that [objection] is refuted.
