In this regard, it might be argued: "Is the omniscience of yogins achieved by means of a single cognition or by many? It cannot be by a single one, for mutually contradictory objects—such as cold and heat—do not appear within a single cognition."

Nor can those [objects] be known by many [cognitions], for they would have to occur either successively or simultaneously; yet simultaneous cognitions do not arise, because [the senses] depend upon the subtle internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

But since it is difficult to accomplish even the three types of objects in their entirety through cognitions that occur successively, how can yogins be called "omniscient"? It is said that yogins will perceive all objects everywhere simultaneously with a single cognition.
As for the argument that this is contradictory, it is irrelevant, because even contradictory things such as blue and yellow appear together in a single variegated perception (*citrapratyaya*).
Furthermore, it has already been shown that in a single instance of the cognition of "black," there is the apprehension of the non-existence of all things other than the objects present.

Moreover, even in the case of cold and heat, there is sometimes a simultaneous perception; for example, in the summer when the young heat is scorching with rays resembling a mass of sparks from a blazing fire, a person whose body is submerged up to the neck in a lake of water as cool as a fragment of ice simultaneously experiences the sensations of cold and heat residing respectively in the lake-water and the solar heat.

Now, one might object: how could yogins—who perceive all objects, whether past or future, even those beyond the senses—be distinguished from the Lord, the teacher of the entire world, who perceives the history of the whole threefold universe?
There is indeed a distinction: such knowledge belongs to the Lord eternally, whereas for yogins it arises through the practice of yogic meditation.
But surely, no cultivation of a mental impression can arise with respect to an object never before perceived?
But when the Dharma has been definitively determined through scripture, what is the use of cultivation?

The meaning of the restrictive proposition that "injunction alone is the means of valid cognition regarding Dharma" is stated as follows: even though there may be yogis who have understood the nature of Dharma through scripture, this [principle] does not fail. This mode indeed exists among yogis;
however, once direct perception (pratyakṣa) which apprehends Dharma subsequently arises, the restriction that "injunction alone" is the means becomes truly relaxed.
Furthermore, we shall explain that the innate knowledge of God, which has Dharma as its object and serves as the cause of the Veda, is likewise established.
Since that [inference] exists, the establishment of the restrictive sense of "only" in the phrase "not only verbal testimony" is achieved.
Therefore, such proofs as "[the yogic perception does not apprehend dharmas because it perceives only what is present, and because it arises from contact with what exists]" are inconclusive.
A word that teaches an object of cognition already known through other means of valid cognition is [authoritative], because it is a word, just like the word "pot. (149)
"Dharma is perceptible to someone, because it is an object of cognition, like a jar and so forth"—such counter-reasons (pratihetu) are indeed easily available. //148//
Why do you vainly utter this deceptive mass of fallacious reasons, as if to mock the yogic wisdom established by irrefutable logic, which perceives all objects?
Thus, even in this way, the Jaiminīya sūtra has an inconsistent meaning;
moreover, its status as a definition has already been refuted.

Furthermore, as for the definition of perception stated by some—namely, "that cognition which arises from the contact of the self, the sense-faculties, the mind, and the object is perception, distinct from inference and the rest"—this too must be disregarded, as it fails to encompass cognitions such as pleasure or the nature of the self that arise from the contact of only three or two factors, and it over-extends to include erroneous cognitions and the like.
Īśvarakṛṣṇa stated the definition of perception as "the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of each respective object.
However, even that is unsatisfactory because it over-extends (*ativyāpti*) to include inferential and other types of cognition, since these too possess the nature of determining their objects.

As for what the King has explained—that *prati* occurs in the sense of "facing toward," and thus perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the determination of an object by way of such facing toward—it is indeed present in inference and other means of knowledge as well;
for just as in the case of "this is a jar," there is a cognition of "the mountain possesses fire" precisely by way of facing toward it.
Clarity, however, exists in all cognitions with respect to their own respective objects.
Now, if you think that because a general rule is set aside by a specific one, the exclusion of inference and the other means of knowledge will be established—

[namely,] that the determination [of an object] which was generally prescribed is here qualified by the terms "sign" (liṅga) and "word" (śabda), so that the determination other than that will remain as perception—
if this is so, then the definition of perception need not be formulated at all now.
Since the apprehension of words and logical marks has already been described, perception will be known simply by its distinction from those;

therefore, without the inclusion of the phrase "contact between sense-organ and object," the exclusion of inference and the other means of knowledge is not established. Thus, this definition of perception is also not faultless.
Enough with this excessive elaboration; for there is no definition proclaimed by other schools that is free from blemish regarding sensory cognition.
Therefore, let this definition composed by the Sage Akṣapāda alone captivate the minds of those of noble intellect.
And inference, which is preceded by that [perception], is threefold: pūrvavat, śeṣavat, and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa. //5//
Consequently, there would also be an absence of both the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), since their very nature depends upon that [subject].

Thus, by superimposing the status of a "dissimilar instance" onto this existing subject and thereby raising an objection regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*), even the inference of fire would be undermined.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the subject (*dharmin*), such as a mountain, is not ascertained there to be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) called "fire," whereas the composite whole (*avayavin*) consisting of light is ascertained through perception by the very opposite of "non-heat"? Therefore, is the mountain now ascertained as possessing fire? Or, if this were accepted, what would be the use of inference? [Reply: Indeed, the mountain is neither ascertained as possessing fire nor as being its opposite.
Rather, it remains simply doubtful. [Objection:
If this is so, then smoke and the like, even if they exist in a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) that is merely doubtful, would be non-reasons (*ahetu*).

Since even a reason whose presence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful would be non-reasoning (*ahetu*), just like one whose presence in the dissimilar class is certain, all inference would perish.
Therefore, it is improper to charge this [reason] with deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the subject (*pakṣa*); thus, this reason possesses negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that this [reason] lacks the property of occurring in a subject that is not refuted—that is true; we ourselves indeed accept that this subject is sublated by perception.
However, that sublation does not terminate merely in the subject, but rather touches upon the reason as well.
There is no such thing as a "proposition" (pakṣa) that is independent of a reason; for it is only that which one intends to establish by means of a reason that is called a proposition. (159)
When the counter-positive is directly perceived, that [probandum] cannot be established;
by way of the removal of the probandum, the reason becomes sublated. //160//
Therefore, its definition is simply "being inferable without being sublated.
This reason is not unestablished, because its occurrence in fire is possible. (161)
But as for the claim that it is impossible to know whether [the object] is uncontradicted—O Illustrious One, how will you establish that even for the subject (pakṣa) itself? (162)
Even when an effort is made [to establish it], if no sublation is observed, it must be understood as simply not existing; for practical activity does not proceed otherwise. //163//
Therefore, since sublation is possible even when a reason possesses the three characteristics, the property of being unsublated must be stated as an additional characteristic.
And thus, as for what is said—that there is a contradiction between sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—that is in some respects correct and in some respects incorrect.

It is correct in this sense: that where invariable concomitance is fully established in a reason possessing the five characteristics (*pañcalakṣaṇaka*), there can be no sublation whatsoever. However, with reference to a reason possessing only three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇaka*), it is incorrect.
In this way, a reason should also be understood as being contradicted by scripture (*āgama*), such as:
"Wine may be drunk by a Brahmin because it is not harmful, like milk."

One might ask: "Why is an inference that contradicts another inference not cited as an example, just like those that contradict perception or scripture? We reply: because it is impossible; for an inference that contradicts another inference is not logically tenable. For the relationship of sublated and sublator occurs only between two inferences that are either of equal strength or unequal strength. In that case, if they are of equal strength, there can be no relationship of sublated and sublator precisely because they are of equal strength.

For if their strength is equal, what could be the sublater or the sublated? Even in the case where their strengths are unequal, since the invalidity of one is established by that very fact which caused its weakness, what is the use of a sublation by inference? Therefore, we do not consider an inference to be contradicted by another inference.

For this very reason, the Commentator, not seeing an inference that contradicts another inference, stated: "Furthermore, an inference that is contradicted by perception or scripture is a fallacy of reasoning (nyāyābhāsa)."
However, where two inferences of equal strength fall upon one another, that is the domain of the "counter-balanced" (satpratipakṣa) [reason].
Thus, the fifth characteristic of a valid logical mark (liṅga) is taught as being "not having a counter-balanced opponent" (asatpratipakṣatva).
But surely, since entities do not possess two forms, how could there be the occurrence of two probative reasons—each implying two mutually contradictory properties—within a single locus?
For this very reason, that which is called "the non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is not accepted here as a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

It is true that it is extremely difficult for a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*) to exist, so as to what could this fifth characteristic of a reason be taught in order to exclude it? Nevertheless, when the non-perception of specific features—which is a seed of doubt—is employed through delusion for the sake of determining one or the other, it becomes a counter-balanced reason, as in: "This is a post because the qualities of a person are not perceived," and "This is a person because the qualities of a post are not perceived."

This very non-apprehension of either one of the two objects, when employed as a reason through the delusion that the presence of the property in the subject (pakṣadharma), positive concomitance (anvaya), and negative concomitance (vyatireka) are established, becomes a "counter-balanced" (sat-pratyakṣa) pseudo-reason; this will be explained in detail during the investigation of the *prakaraṇasama* pseudo-reason. Furthermore, it will be stated in that same context that the dual nature of an object arises from the error of human intellect.
Therefore, another definition must necessarily be stated to avoid manifold defects;
for this reason, those who know the path of inference have accepted a mark (liṅga) characterized by five features. //163//

It has been explained [above] that [the inference arises] "from the mark (liṅga) after five lakhs [of moments]. Even though the nature of the mark was already apprehended at the time of grasping the pervasion (vyāpti), if its form is not subsequently ascertained in a particular locus (dharmin), it cannot serve as a means for definitive cognition (adhyavasāya); therefore, a second observation of the mark must be required. Thus it is said, "from what has been grasped. For a mark is an indicator (jñāpaka), not a causal agent (kāraka) like the eye and other sense organs.
Furthermore, this is the nature of a signifier (*jñāpaka*): that it makes known what has already been known.

If it is argued that the mark (*liṅga*), being remembered as possessing pervasion (*vyāpti*) exactly as it was grasped at the time of apprehending that pervasion, will cause one to understand the object to be proven (*liṅgin*), we say no; for without the initial apprehension, there can be no memory of the pervasion either. Enough of this digression.

Regarding the phrase "from the recollection of the rule" (niyamasmṛteḥ), let it be explained: what is this so-called "rule"? It means pervasion (vyāpti), inseparable connection (avinābhāva), or constant concomitance (nityasāhacarya).
He said: It is not appropriate to stop at this much alone;
for logicians must investigate the underlying reason why that [reason] is invariably concomitant with it.
And the monks have observed that this [logical connection] consists of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*).
For how can an entity that has a certain nature abandon that nature? Indeed, a *śiṃśapā* tree has the very nature of a tree; therefore, it leads one to infer its "tree-ness.
This is called a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), as in: "This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*."
In that case, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) consists in identity (*tādātmya*).

An effect, by its very nature, acquires its existence only in dependence upon a cause and not independently of it; therefore, when that effect is perceived, it leads to the inference of its cause, as in the case of the "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*): "There is fire here because there is smoke. In this context, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*).

Thus, to describe merely the rule of coexistence (*sāhacarya-niyama*) without stating these two types of necessary connection—which are the basis for the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the object to be inferred—is nothing but a "stretching out of the legs" (i.e., a lazy or superficial argument).

It is said that it is far better for those of coarse vision to resort to the very "stretching out of the feet" (pādaprasārikā) than for those of subtle vision to imagine logical connections such as identity (tādātmya).

First, regarding identity (*tādātmya*), since the probans (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*)—the two factors of the indicator—are non-distinct, the very relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) is difficult to establish.
Indeed, a logical mark (*liṅga*) that has not been apprehended is not capable of producing the cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).

In that regard, does the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) appear in the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*), or not? If it does not appear, then since it is not apprehended by that cognition, how could it have that [mark] as its nature? If, however, it does appear, then that object is simply perceived just like the mark; what, then, is the use of inference? If you argue that inference is for the purpose of excluding a contrary superimposition (*viparīta-samāropa*), we reply: when its own nature is apprehended, there is no opportunity for a contrary superimposition to arise.

Indeed, when the specific features such as the head and hands are seen, the superimposition of a post (*sthāṇu*) does not occur. In that case, [the exclusion of the contrary] might be possible because of the difference between them.

For it may well be that even when the head, hands, and so forth are perceived, there could still be the superimposition of "non-person" upon them, since the person is not identical to those very parts.

But here, because "tree-ness" and "śiṃśapā-ness" are non-different, what possibility is there for the superimposition of something other than a tree once "śiṃśapā-ness" has been perceived? Furthermore, while the perception of "tree-ness"—due to the perception of a general property and the lack of ascertainment of the specific—might occasionally lead to the superimposition of "non-śiṃśapā," the superimposition of "non-tree" once "śiṃśapā-ness" has been perceived is not logical.

For it is not at all contrary to common worldly experience that for a cognizer to whom the state of being a *śiṃśapā* (a specific kind of tree) is within the range of perception, the state of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*) remains beyond perception. (164)

Furthermore, because there is no distinction between the probandum and the probans, just as "tree-ness" is inferred from "śiṃśapā-ness," so too would "śiṃśapā-ness" be inferred from "tree-ness," since there is no difference in their identity (*tādātmya*).
Likewise, just as impermanence is established by means of "being produced immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), it would likewise be established by means of "impermanence" itself.

Consequently, the distinction that was stated between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "being produced immediately after effort"—namely, that the former pervades the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) while the latter does not—would be lost.
But surely, relation (*sambandha*) is one thing and necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is another?
A relation resides in both [terms], whereas necessary connection is characterized by dependence on the other.
In that case, being a *śiṃśapā* is necessarily connected to being a tree, but being a tree is not necessarily connected to being a *śiṃśapā*.
The state of being produced immediately after an effort is necessarily concomitant with impermanence, but impermanence is not necessarily concomitant with it.
Likewise, there is an invariable connection of smoke with fire, but not of fire with smoke.
This is true; however, if this were asserted, it would be an admission of mere invariable concomitance (niyama), and not identity (tādātmya).

For if there were identity (*tādātmya*), just as a *śiṃśapā* tree is not seen apart from being a *śiṃśapā*, so too "tree-ness" would not be seen devoid of being a *śiṃśapā*. Yet, in the case of the *khadira* tree and others, "tree-ness" is observed even when devoid of being a *śiṃśapā*, and in the case of lightning and such, "impermanence" is perceived even when devoid of being produced immediately after an effort. How, then, can there be non-difference? For this property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) exists even without the proving property (*sādhanadharma*);
to claim it is identical to that [proving property] despite being seen apart from it is mere deception. (165)

Now, if it is argued that the impermanence of a jar and so forth is indeed different from the impermanence of lightning and so forth—since the former is said to be non-distinct from being immediately subsequent to volitional effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*)—then, given that properties differ according to the difference of their substrata (*dharmī*), the apprehension of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) would be impossible, and all inference would collapse.

In the case of smoke and fire, however, because they are distinct as effect and cause, it is appropriate to say that the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of smoke lies in fire, but not that of fire in smoke. Here, however, since there is no distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), it cannot be stated in that manner.
Or, if it is designated in that way, there is no non-difference [between the two].

Either identity must be abandoned altogether, or else *śiṃśapā-ness* and *being produced immediately after effort* must be inferred from *tree-ness* and *impermanence* respectively; it is not possible for them to exist in between.
Regarding this example cited as a "reason based on essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*): "Sound is impermanent because it is produced"—how is this a reason based on essential nature? Consider this:
what is meant by "impermanence," and what is meant by "being produced"?
In this context, impermanence is the connection with destruction, and being produced is the connection with origination.

Furthermore, the destruction of an entity that has arisen is distinct from its arising itself; how then can there be no difference between the probandum and the proof? On this point, they raise an objection: if impermanence consists in the connection with destruction, then the cognition would be "sound is destructible," not "sound is impermanent. Moreover, that cognition would be false, because it is impossible to perceive sound as being qualified by destruction in the same way a mountain peak is qualified by fire.
For how could a subject possess a property that is non-existent, since at the time of apprehending the non-existence, the subject itself is not perceived? //166//
Furthermore, how could the abstract suffix in the term *anityatva* (impermanence) apply to a non-entity, given their contradiction?
Therefore, let it be said that impermanence is the existence of a real entity delimited by both temporal ends.
Likewise, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is also simply existence itself, which, having been brought forth by causes, is designated as such while persisting like a stream.
And thus, since both the probandum and the probans are nothing but existence itself, the status of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is established.
This is untenable, because the probandum and the probans do not appear as such [i.e., as identical].
For if it were stated in this way, it would be understood as: "Sound possesses existence, because it possesses existence."
But it is not observed in that way;
rather, [the inference is stated as]: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced."

Now, if it is argued that existence (*sattā*)—delimited by both ends, produced by causes, and inherent in its substratum—is the probandum (*sādhya*) while [the aforementioned properties] are the probans (*sādhana*), this is untenable; for at that time, the end consisting of destruction does not exist, and thus it lacks the capacity to delimit existence.
Or rather, let its determination be accepted by that Buddhist as being the very determination of the sound itself through such a destruction. (167)

Even though a dharma is simultaneous [with the cognition], it is made an object by the intellect alone and thus attains the status of its qualifier; likewise, that which is yet to be (bhāvya) will also attain it.
Thus, since the relationship between qualifier and qualified is established in the statement "sound is perishable," what is the use of postulating existence as something to be proven?

Furthermore, as for the objection raised—that suffixes such as *tva* and *tal*, which denote abstract states (*bhāvapratyaya*), would not apply to a non-existence (*abhāva*)—this is the criticism of one who is utterly ignorant.

For in that case, the ground for the application of the word (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*) is expressed by the abstract suffix; indeed, it is because of the presence of that quality (*guṇa*) that a word is applied to a substance (*dravya*).
This is seen even in the case of non-existence, where we have the expression "the state of being non-existent" (*abhāvatvam*).
Therefore, impermanence is simply the connection with destruction as it exists within the intellect.
Even "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is merely the connection with origination, not existence itself;
for if its delimitation by a locus produced by causes is desired, let that delimitation belong to the subject (dharmin) itself—what is the use of an intermediate step?
Now, it might be argued that the two properties known as arising and perishing do not persist [through different things];
for what exists in a jar does not exist in a sound, and what exists in a sound does not exist in a jar. (139)
Now, if it were maintained that there is only one single property connected to all things, then it would follow that when one thing arises, everything arises;
and at the time of the dissolution of one thing, there would be the dissolution of the whole. //170//
Therefore, the position that [the universal] exists is indeed better.
This is not so, because even when the substrata (dharmin) differ, the properties (dharma) appear as having an identical form.
For it is not conceivable that the very nature of the jar and so forth is destruction, such that there would be the fault of non-continuity based on their difference. (171)
Even unity does not exist for a property (dharma) across all its substrates (dharmin), such that at the time of the destruction of one, there would be the confusion of the destruction of all. (172)
Furthermore, even though phenomena are distinct, because they appear as having a similar form, there is no contradiction in functions such as the apprehension of a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

For this very reason, since conventional usage regarding positive concomitance and so forth is possible based on common properties even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), the author of the Sūtras did not employ the term "universal" (*sāmānya*);

rather, he adopted the term "similarity" (*sādharmya*), as in: "The reason (*hetu*) is that which establishes the probandum through similarity with the example," and "The example (*udāharaṇa*) is an instance where, due to similarity with the probandum, it possesses the property of the subject."

Therefore, because there is a relationship of probandum and probans between the properties of destruction and arising, and because those two are distinct, it is established that "sound is impermanent because it is produced" is not a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
The causal relation based on the effect (*kāryahetu*) is also possible.

For according to your position, the relation of cause and effect must exist either between two moments or between two continua; we shall explain later, in the refutation of momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), that it does not exist between two moments.
Even if it were possible, it would be difficult to perceive because of the subtlety of those two. (173)
However, because the continuity of smoke and fire is merely conventional and not real, there is no relationship of cause and effect [between them].
To be a real entity (vastu) is precisely to possess causal efficacy (arthakriyākāritva).

If smoke were to lead to the inference of fire by virtue of being its effect, it would also have to be an indicator of that fire by means of its qualities such as being pungent, dirty, or moving through the sky.
Furthermore, it is not possible for smoke to be both an effect of that [fire] in some respect and not its effect in some other respect;
for that which possesses the nature of everything must have its origin following the positive and negative concomitance of those very things.
Now, even if it were an effect of that [fire] in every respect, you must admit that it is merely the nature of smoke (*dhūmatva*) that is concomitant with fire.
Let there be mere concomitance; talk of "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) is useless. (174)
But surely you yourselves have also accepted inference from effect (*kāryānumāna*), as will be explained in the passage beginning with "possessing a field" (*kṣetrasvat*).

As Kaṇāda said: "The inferential mark (*liṅga*) consists of the effect, the cause, the conjoined, the inherent, and the contradictory"—this is not so, because that statement is intended to indicate concomitance (*sāhacarya*).

The capacity to indicate [the presence of another] in the case of smoke and fire, or the swelling of a river and [upstream] rain, does not arise from a causal relationship according to the logic already stated; rather, it arises solely from the necessity of their constant concomitance (*nityasāhacarya*).

If it is asked how there can be concomitance (*sāhacarya*) between two contradictory things, [the answer is: because of the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) between existence and non-existence, the absence of one of two contradictories is inferred from the perception of the other.
And such concomitance certainly exists between existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, the mention of "effect" (*kārya*) and so forth in the *Kaṇāda-sūtra* is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Since many other causes are observed in the world, the rising of the stars is inferred by observing the setting of the sun. (175)
The increase of the ocean is understood from the rising of the full moon; by its rising, the rivers are inferred to have risen as well, just as by the appearance of Agastya. (176)
Along the edges of their drying banks rested rows of birds,
while the recent rains were inferred by the activity of ants carrying their eggs.
Other travelers also become intent on constructing leaf-huts, freed from the two obstacles proclaimed by the Sugata. (178)

Alas, how few indeed are the reasons known to the world that are accepted as establishing the probandum, since they disregard the principles of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*)! //179//
The justification of that [effect] by means of one's own intellect is like the talk of a child;
therefore, such claims as "it has that nature" or "it is its effect" are merely a source of affliction. (180)

Moreover, how can this be consistent: that there is the relationship of sign and signified between two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), and that there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between two real entities (*vastu*), while their apprehension occurs through conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)? (181)
This has already been established in the very first chapter; therefore, enough of this digression.
Thus, it is proven that the relation which is the cause of inference is concomitance (*sāhacarya*);
however, neither of these two [definitions] is that imagined by the disciples of Śauddhodani.
As for what was stated by others—that "what has he studied?"—and that their concomitance [is the answer], in that case, the injunction is the authority.
Furthermore, this same challenge applies equally to them regarding identity and causality; so why these fruitless prattlings? (182)

The rule (niyama) has been explained. What is the meaning of "from memory" (smṛteḥ)? It is said: For the rule, once grasped, is a constituent factor with respect to the valid cognition of the inferable [object].
One who dwells on the Coconut Island does not perceive fire from smoke. (183)
At the time of the inferential cognition of the probandum, there is no grasping of the rule;
and at the time of grasping the rule, the probandum is not inferred. (184)
Having been previously apprehended, it is now within the range of memory;
thus, the restriction is a factor for comprehension, as is seen from the resulting understanding. (185)
For even when there is the perception of a second indicative mark, the cognition of the probandum does not arise in the absence of the recollection of the rule of concomitance.
Even in a case where memory is not consciously perceived regarding an object that has been repeatedly practiced, it is nonetheless forcibly postulated there by this same principle. //183//
For this very reason, some have stated that memory itself—produced by a presently existing cause—is inference.

And the presently occurring cause is the observation of a mark (liṅga) concomitant with another property in some subject; thus it is said that [inference] concerns an imperceptible possessor of the mark (liṅgin).

In this regard, the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) is first explained: the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by a property (*dharma*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), and that alone is the possessor of the mark.
It is not the mere subject that is the probandum, because subjects such as mountains and the like are already established; nor is it the mere property.
Since fire is already established in various places,
and since neither of two independent [factors] can be the probandum— because both are likewise already established—
it is not possible for either one or both to be the object of inference independently; therefore, one must necessarily state that one of them is the probandum as qualified by the other.

In that case as well, it is logical that the subject qualified by the property (*dharmin-viśiṣṭa-dharma*) is what is to be proven (*sādhya*), and not the property qualified by the subject (*dharmin-viśiṣṭa-dharma*).
For if fire qualified by a location were the object of proof, sixteen alternative possibilities (*vikalpa*) would arise.

Either (1) every fire (*agni*) as qualified by all locations—whether qualified by an unspecified location, qualified by a previously experienced location such as a kitchen, or qualified by a currently perceived location such as a mountain—is the object of inference; or (2) some fire, unspecified in its particularity, as qualified by all locations, qualified by an unspecified location, qualified by a previously experienced location, or qualified by a presently observed location, is the object of inference; or (3) a previously experienced fire, as qualified by all locations, qualified by an unspecified location, qualified by a previously seen location, or qualified by a presently perceived location, is the object of inference; or likewise, (4) the fire intended to be proven, as qualified by all locations or [unspecified], is the object of inference. Thus it would be.
In this regard, these fifteen positions are indeed to be disregarded, as they are afflicted by defects such as contradiction with direct perception and proving what is already established.

As for the sixteenth position—that "this fire is qualified by this particular place"—even there, it is simply impossible to apprehend "fire" without first delimiting it by a specific location; therefore, the location itself is understood first.

Since that [location] has already been previously established, and since it is now fit to be inferred as qualified by the fire which was not yet cognized, it is logical that the location itself is the probandum (*sādhya*).

Moreover, if fire were already established, how could smoke—having not yet perceived its property (taddharma)—be an inferential mark? Yet, while fire is unperceived, smoke cannot be grasped as being a property of it.
On the other hand, if fire is already perceived, the grasping of smoke as its property is indeed fruitless, because the object of inference (the fire) no longer exists at that time.

Therefore, it is precisely the observed location, as qualified by fire, that is the object to be proven (*sādhya*). Although that location is perceptible in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), it is to be inferred as being qualified by a property (*dharma*) that is beyond perception. Thus, due to its connection with the property of smoke, that very same [location] is inferred as possessing the property of fire.
That is called the "subject" (*liṅgin*), which is the object of inference.
And this inclusion of the term "imperceptible" has precisely this intended meaning.

However, in some cases, immediately after the recollection of the pervasion (vyāpti), because the cognizer is in close proximity, fire suddenly flashes forth and becomes directly perceived; thus, it is not possible for the locus (dharmin) to be non-manifest (parokṣa) even as qualified by that [fire]. To exclude such instances, the term "non-manifest" (parokṣa) is included.
Furthermore, we shall explain later that even eternally non-manifest things, such as God, unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), and the sense organs, are objects of inference.

Therefore, it is established that inference is the cognition of the aforementioned probandum (liṅgin) based on the aforementioned mark (liṅga) and the recollection of the aforementioned rule [of pervasion]. //187//
Now, if the validity of inference were established, then an investigation into its definition should be undertaken; however, its validity itself is not tenable. (188)
And so they have said: because validity is not secondary (*agauṇatvāt*), the ascertainment of an object through inference is difficult to obtain.

For the character of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth must be shown of the logical mark (*liṅga*) by force of a secondary application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*). For when the property (*dharma*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason does not possess the state of being a property of the subject, since smoke is a property of fire [and not of the subject].

If the subject (*dharmī*) itself is the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) lacks positive concomitance (*ananvayitva*); for there is no positive concomitance such as "wherever there is smoke, there is a mountain.
But if both [the subject and the property] are the probandum, neither [concomitance] exists;
for smoke is not a property (*dharma*) of both fire and the mountain.
Nor is the positive concomitance (anvaya) formulated as "wherever there is smoke, there is fire on the mountain";
for when the subject (dharmin) qualified by a property is the probandum, both [the presence of the reason in the subject and its presence wherever the probandum occurs] would be impossible.
Nor can smoke be perceived at first as having the property of being located on a mountain distinguished by fire.
Nor is there such a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) as "wherever there is smoke, there is fire on the mountain.

Therefore, in order to establish the conventional usage of positive concomitance based on the property-possessor being the locus of the property (*pakṣadharmatva*), the word *pakṣa* must be understood as conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property; yet, if it were applied in that same way to only a part of that [subject], it would be a highly figurative definition (*atigauṇalakṣaṇatva*). Because it lacks the status of a non-figurative definition—just like [the definitions of perception] such as "being produced by the contact of sense-faculties with their objects"—inference (*anumāna*) would not be a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).

Moreover, because there is no positive concomitance (anugama) with respect to a particular, and because proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) occurs with respect to a universal, and because that which possesses [the property] is untenable, how can there be any talk of inference? //189//
To place confidence in a relationship based on mere concomitance is ignorance, because even if that [concomitance] is observed a hundred times, the possibility of deviation remains. (190)
In objects whose natures are diverse due to the distinctions of ten times and ten states, it is impossible to state a rule of invariable concomitance; and so he said: [191]
Since the powers of entities differ according to variations in state, place, time, and so forth, their establishment through inference is extremely difficult to achieve. (192)
Even if there were an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva), it could not be ascertained without an observation of all objects existing throughout the three worlds. (193)
As long as all individual instances of smoke and fire have not been directly perceived, it may still be suspected that this particular smoke might belong to something other than fire. (194)
But for those like you who perceive the universe through direct perception, what need is there for inference for those possessing divine vision? (195)
Nor is there a determination of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) even by means of a universal (sāmānya), for no such thing as a real universal exists at all. //196//
Even a pervasion that is understood through repeated observation is not tenable;
for even when it has been observed a thousand times, one may ascertain a deviation. (197)
Even though the nature of an object has been repeatedly ascertained as being thus, it is nevertheless perceived otherwise due to differences in place, time, and other factors. (198)
Furthermore, through repeated observation, let it be understood that smoke is concomitant with fire;
however, the fact that smoke does not exist when fire is absent is not known through repeated observation. (199)
Nor are co-occurring factors indicative merely by being observed together;
for their necessity in that very context is preceded by the absence of anything other than them. (200)
And the rule (niyama), which is a constituent of inference, is apprehended once it has been grasped; and its grasping does not occur without a certainty that it does not exist elsewhere. (201)

If the apprehension of a rule [of concomitance] occurs through observation and non-observation, that too is incorrect; for indeed, the non-observation of smoke in the absence of fire is required. (202)
And how much fire is there in the entire world devoid of flames?
Therein, those who are not yogis do not perceive the non-existence of smoke at all. (203)
Thus, because there is no such restriction, or because even if it existed, its communication would be impossible, let the vain hope for inference as a valid means of knowledge be abandoned. (204)
If even a contradiction with inference were to invalidate one's intended [conclusion], then a "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) reason would be easily found everywhere. (205)
Therefore, seeing no validity in inferential cognitions, the wise have said this for the purpose of prohibiting reliance upon them: [206]
For a blind man running on an uneven path by means of hand-touching and the like, relying primarily upon inference, a fall is not difficult to encounter. //207//
Moreover, even an object that has been inferred with great effort by skilled inferents may be established in a completely different way by others who are more proficient. (208)
To this it is replied: is this merely a refutation of the nature of inference itself, or is it a refutation of those specific definitions characterized by various logicians?
In this regard, the very nature of inference is indeed impossible to deny, as it is well-established among all people in the world.
Even women, cowherds, laborers, and farmers undoubtedly understand one meaning from a fixed meaning. //209//

If inference were denied, however, even the worldly course of life would become as difficult to obtain as direct perception; people would remain motionless, as if they were painted in a picture. (210)

Even regarding a class of objects perceived directly, worldly people, having ascertained through the operation of a mark consisting in belonging to that same class that it is a means to pleasure or otherwise, either adopt it or abandon it.

Now, [the opponent might argue: "The reality is simply that which is not deliberated upon; a restriction by means of a definition cannot be established for it. This is called the "rejection of the definition," but that too is incorrect. For: "Upon perceiving any object whatsoever, it is not the case that anything at all is understood;
rather, the established rule is that a particular object implies only a specific [corresponding] object. (211)
In this regard, the extension of the foot [as an example] is for the purpose of showing that "this is the nature of the enema";
for indeed, a cognition of one thing arises from another thing with which it is inseparably connected. (212)
Therefore, we consider that there exists some relationship between those two objects, from the perception of which a cognition arises regarding the other. //213//

Those who know [the truth] do not believe in identity (*tadātmatā*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*); rather, that the relationship is mere concomitance (*sāhacaryam*) does not satisfy our hearts. (214)
Only when that [cause] exists is there the manifestation; without it, there is no manifestation.
This very [relationship] is non-separation (avinābhāva), necessity, and concomitance. //215//
If it is asked, "What determines this [causality] in this [effect]?", the answer is as follows.
Even under the view that [the self] is identical with that [body], this question is not resolved. //216//
Smoke arises from fire, not from water—what is the logical ground for this?
If you say it is simply because it is so, then that same logic applies even to the case of mere association (sāhacarya). //217//

To whatever extent there is an object for reasoning, it is determined within that limit; however, regarding the specific distinctions in the intrinsic nature of things, reasoning possesses no power. //218//

And this is the domain of reasoning: as it has been stated, "Without a necessary rule (niyama), there can be no cognition of one object from another object; therefore, that [rule] is postulated. (219)
Furthermore, as for the question "By what is this restriction (niyama) established?", no logical argument prevails;
for neither identity (tādātmya) nor causality (tadutpatti) is tenable here.
Therefore, the very notion of restriction must be abandoned.

Nor is it reasonable to say that inferential valid cognition (*ānumānikī pramiti*) is mere intuition (*pratibhāmātra*), because it has been stated that cognition is observed only from some specific, restricted [mark] regarding an object; and if this restriction were a factor for cognition even when ungrasped, then even the inhabitants of the Coconut Island (*nārikeladvīpa*) would infer fire upon seeing smoke.
Since this is not the case, the grasping of the restriction must be required.

Regarding the claim that the apprehension of that [invariable concomitance] is impossible through conceptualization, some maintain that mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) is the grasper of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Having perceived smoke—through both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*)—as being accompanied by fire and as being excluded from what is not fire, one realizes mentally that "this smoke is invariably connected to fire."
And by whom would it not be accepted that the mind has all things as its object, since it is capable of apprehending an object even when it is not present? (220)

Furthermore, the direct perception of the entire collection of manifest smoke and fire filling the expanse of the three worlds is not required, because the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) occurs by means of the precedence of generalities such as "fire-ness" (jvalanatva).
As for the statement that a real universal does not exist, that will be addressed in the context of the investigation into the referent of words.
Others, however, have indeed maintained that there is a form of perception akin to the perception of yogis—a rational perception that grasps the relationship [of pervasion].

They argue that while the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between the pervaded and the pervader may be grasped by way of the universals of "smokeness" and "fireness," the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), namely the absence of smoke from non-fires, must be grasped;
yet non-fires are exceedingly vast in number.
Furthermore, there exists no such universal as "non-fireness" among those things;

therefore, apart from a perception that grasps the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) residing in all fires and non-fires included within the three worlds, the necessary connection (pratibandha) would not be ascertained. And that which is not ascertained cannot be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

And since there is valid cognition, by the force of reasoning it is stated as a logical conclusion that this perception—which grasps the necessary connection in a single moment and has all individual instances as its object—is postulated, even though it is not actually experienced.

Others, however, for fear of such a conceptualization, have accepted that the inferential mark (*liṅga*) which makes [the object] known is simply the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) preceded by the universal determined through repeated observation, without requiring the ascertainment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). As it has been said: "But for me, the concomitants are indicators merely by being seen."
This is the intention: first, through repeated observation, such a cognition arises—namely, that "this [thing] is invariably connected with that"—which is witnessed by all living beings. (221)
By that much, the general capacity to convey meaning is established.
For the Mīmāṃsakas, however, the observation [of smoke] in the counter-example (vipakṣa) would be a subverting cognition;
yet such does not exist, for up to this day smoke has never been observed where there is no fire.

They have stated that even when no sublation has arisen, such a suspicion is improper, as it is said: "But as long as the cognition of a defect has not arisen, the lack of validity should not be suspected."
But this is not correct,
because it has already been stated that the apprehension of an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is impossible without the ascertainment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
For, being a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*), the rule (*niyama*) depends upon its own apprehension.
And this restriction (niyama) is stated as follows: that when X exists, Y comes to be, and without X, Y does not come to be.

Furthermore, through repeated observation, because one only determines the positive concomitance (anvaya)—namely, that "when X exists, Y comes to be"—the restriction would be only half-grasped, since the meaning of "without X, Y does not come to be" has not been determined.

Others, however, without even postulating the perception of yogins and without relying on the generality of "non-fire-ness," state that positive and negative concomitance is accessible through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
For when the generalities of smoke and fire are perceived as co-occurring, their respective absences are likewise perceived as co-occurring;
this is because the generality of "smoke-ness" is never observed in non-fire, such as water.
It will be explained that even though universals are omnipresent, the specific mode of their occurrence (vṛttibheda) is the determining factor.

Even though there is no such thing as a universal "non-fire-ness" and so forth, nevertheless, the apprehension of the concomitance of that absence is established precisely through the establishment of the concomitance of the universal "fire-ness," which is the object of negation.
In the ascertainment of pervasion, the cognition of every individual instance is not a necessary factor;
just as it is with two positive universals, so it is with their respective absences.
The coexistence of two positive entities is called positive concomitance (anvaya); however, they consider the coexistence of the absences of those two to be negative concomitance (vyatireka). //223//

But where there is a relationship of probandum and probans between two absences, there the positive concomitance (anvaya) belongs to those very two absences, while the negative concomitance (vyatireka) belongs to their respective positives. //224//
Thus, just like the positive concomitance of non-existence, the negative concomitance of existence is indeed accessible through direct perception.

This alone is the distinction between two positive entities: whatever relationship of pervaded and pervader exists between them, that same relationship, when reversed, exists between their respective absences. (225)
But when there is a relationship of the signified and the signifier between two absences, one should observe the reversal of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that exists between two presences.

And thus, since the cognition of the concomitance of the two general absences is established by being preceded by the observation of the object to be negated, even in the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), yogic perception is not required; for the necessary knowledge is accomplished by the mind having ascertained the coexistence of presence and absence. Enough of this insistence.
Therefore, it is established that there exists a means of apprehending that [object] which is likewise governed by a restrictive rule.

Once the rule [of concomitance] has been grasped, until the apprehension of the mark (liṅga), such as smoke, occurs again in some locus (dharmin), there is no cognition of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin). Therefore, in relation to the time of grasping the relationship, that second observation of the mark must be required. This very thing is called "being a property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatā). Even when there is certainty regarding the presence in the subject (anvaya) and the absence in its contrary (vyatireka), if there is a contradiction with perception or scripture, or if a counter-argument (pratipakṣa) arises, it does not possess the capacity to produce cognition; thus, two further characteristics are taught: "having an uncontradicted object" (abādhitaviṣayatva) and "having no counter-argument" (asatpratipakṣatva).
Thus, since it is established by experience, its definition as propounded by the experts in the treatises must likewise be accepted, just like the nature of inference itself.
Moreover, if the definition composed by the Tantrikas is indeed non-expressive, let it be declared as such itself without fault;
however, it is not proper to conceal inference—the object to be defined—on account of that defect.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not secondary (*agauṇatva*), it is difficult to ascertain an object through inference—that we do not understand. For we do not perceive any secondary character whatsoever in the means of valid cognition here.

Even if the terms "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth were used by commentators in a secondary sense, how could the means of valid cognition itself become secondary on that account?
Indeed, if its definition is stated using different words, there is no lapse such as being secondary.

As for what was also stated—that "because there is no positive concomitance with respect to a particular, and because it would be proving what is already established with respect to a universal"—that too is incorrect, since the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) as the probandum has been demonstrated.

As for what was stated—that [the inference is unreliable] due to differences in state, place, and time—that too does not cause fear, because once the pervasion (vyāpti) has been correctly ascertained, there is no possibility of subversion;
in that case, the fault lies solely with the cognizer, not with the inference itself.

As for the claim that "contradiction" (*vyāhāri*) [is a fault] because contradictory inferences (*viruddhānumāna*) and contradictions (*virodha*) are possible everywhere, and because "the non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) and "that which thwarts the desired" (*iṣṭavighātakṛt*) are easily found in some cases—that too is a mere web of nonsense, since such [faults] find no occasion when a probative reason (*prayojakahetu*) has been properly employed.
However, arguments involving a second [term] are not effective;
we shall explain that because they are rooted merely in imagination, they are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
There is neither a contradiction of a specific property nor a sublation of what is desired; for when the reason is well-established, these [fallacies] do not exist as mere sophistries. //227//
And for such a person who attains knowledge of an object through inference, there is no equality with a blind man who follows a path inferred by the touch of his hand. (228)
An object that has been inferred with effort by skilled inferents cannot be established otherwise, even by a hundred attempts.
Those who are more thoroughly trained say that inference is of two kinds: some produce a cognition that has already arisen, while others produce a cognition that is yet to arise;
however, the inference of a creator god (īśvara) and the like is of the latter kind, producing a cognition that is yet to arise.
In that regard, by whom is the validity of inference from smoke and so forth not accepted? For it is through this that even those who are not [mere] logicians understand the probandum. (230)
However, regarding that inference whose object is the self, the Lord, the omniscient one, the next world, and so forth, its validity is not accepted by those who do not perceive such things. (231)
Therefore, the cognition of the inferable does not arise for those who are upright as long as their minds have not been made crooked by wicked logicians. (232)
By speaking in this manner, they were merely proclaiming their own extreme nihilism or their own dull-wittedness, not the invalidity of inference as a means of valid cognition. (233)
Indeed, it cannot be that [the cognition] lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge merely because of the diversity of the means for grasping the relationship.
Whether the relationship is apprehended through scripture, inference, the cultivation of reasoning, or direct perception, it does not differ [in its ontological status]. //234//
We shall discuss the logical arguments for [the existence of] God and so forth, along with their strength, in detail in that context; therefore, enough with excessive talk. //235//
Therefore, let inference be accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for its power remains unimpaired by the refutations you have thus far uttered.
On the other hand, if it were not accepted, living beings would become like senseless stones, devoid of all activity; this has indeed been explained previously. (236)
Now, let us follow the Sūtra:
"That which is preceded by that," and so forth.
"Inference" (*anumāna*) is the designation of the definiendum (*lakṣya*).
"Preceded by that" is the definition.
By the pronoun "that," the previously introduced perception is referred to.
That which has that as its preceding cause is "preceded by that."

If this much were stated, the undesirable consequence that [the definition] would apply to identification (*nirṇaya*), analogy (*upamāna*), and so forth—which are preceded by perception—would not be averted; therefore, to exclude those, the analysis must be shown using a dual ending: "that which has these two perceptions as its antecedent. That one perception which was explained as being invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) and that second perception, which is the observation of the mark (*liṅga*), these two perceptions are the cause of inference alone, and not of analogy or the like.
Among them, the perception that grasps the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is its cause by way of recollection, whereas the observation of the mark is its cause by itself.

Now, an objection is raised: since it is perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone that is under discussion, and since a pronoun refers back to what has been previously mentioned, how is this specific meaning obtained? It is said in reply: it will be stated that "the reason (*hetu*) is that which establishes the probandum through similarity with the example. Furthermore, inference (*anumāna*), which is indicated here as the object of definition, is nothing other than the reason itself.

And since similarity to the example (*udāharaṇasādharmya*) or dissimilarity to it (*tadvaidharmya*) cannot establish the probandum if it is not apprehended, a means for its apprehension must be required.

Furthermore, it has been stated more than once that the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā) applies to the postulation of means for cognizing that [object] other than perception; therefore, perception alone is the means for that [cognition].

Consequently, even when proceeding with "mere perception" in reference to the perception that serves as the cause of inference, the specific instances are implied by the pronoun: namely, the perception that grasps the necessary connection (pratibandha) and the second perception which is the observation of the logical mark (liṅga).

[Objection: But surely, even in fallacious inferences—such as those that are inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*), contradictory (*viruddha*), and so forth—it is possible for them to be preceded by two specific types of perception; thus, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*). [Reply: Not so. For this is rejected by the inclusion of the terms "probandum" (*sādhya*) and "probans" (*sādhana*) in the definition of a reason (*hetu*).
Indeed, the nature of the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) will be explained precisely in that very context, whereas here only the means of apprehending it is stated.

And when perception, which grasps the invariable concomitance, functions correctly, there is no failure of pervasion (*vyāpti*); therefore, there is no contingency of these being fallacious inferences.

Furthermore, when the specific definition is being described by way of restating the general definition, the exclusion of pseudo-means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) is already established from that very [general definition]; therefore, what remains to be stated now is merely the exclusion of those belonging to the same class, such as comparison (*upamāna*), and it is this [exclusion] alone that is conveyed by the phrase "preceded by that" (*tatpūrvaka*).
This is because the qualifiers of the result—[namely,] "arisen from an object," "non-erroneous," and "of a determinate nature"—apply to all means of knowledge.
Furthermore, the operation of both word and logical mark is never simultaneous;
therefore, the qualification "not being expressible" (avyapadeśyatva) does not serve to exclude anything [as a valid means of knowledge]. //237//

Furthermore, since both the word and the logical mark function as indicators, they depend upon the apprehension of their own forms; and because cognition cannot occur simultaneously, it is impossible for them to be apprehended at once.

Surely, in this way, over-extension (*ativyāpti*) may be excluded; but how will under-extension (*avyāpti*) be excluded, since inferences preceded by scripture (*āgama*) and so forth would not be included?
Regarding these as well, some say that perception alone is the fundamental cause;
as it has been stated: "Even where there may be a comprehension of the probandum from an inferred mark, even there the primary mark is known only through perception."

Alternatively, since the statement that [inference] is preceded by perception is made with the intention of highlighting its predominance rather than as a restrictive rule, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti).
Alternatively, for the sake of understanding, the analysis should be performed as follows:
"that which has those [means], namely perception and so forth, as its antecedent.
Although it is perception alone that was introduced as the subject to be defined.
Nevertheless, because they are also to be excluded, the status of inference and the other means of knowledge as being under discussion is not precluded.
Regarding this, they raise the following objection:
The word *tat* (that) must refer either to the instrument (*karaṇa*) or to the result (*phala*).

If it refers to the instrument, then knowledge preceded by instruments such as the sense organs would be the result, and inference would be preceded by that; in this case, the word "preceded" (*pūrva*) would have to be read twice.

Furthermore, that [result] would have to be postulated as something not previously heard. However, if one considers the result, the result of inference would be preceded by the result of perception; it would not be the case that the result of inference is itself the instrument of inference. Thus, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the word "tatpūrvaka" (preceded by that), which denotes the result, and the word "anumāna," which denotes the instrument, in the expression "inference is that which is preceded by that.

For, by means of the observation of the mark (liṅgadarśana)—which is the result of perception—the cognition of an imperceptible object is produced; and while this is the result of inference, it is not called "inference" [itself]. In either case, however, there is no fault.

First, regarding the consideration of the instrument (*karaṇa*): that very perception of the mark (*liṅgadarśana*), which is preceded by the instruments such as the sense organs and results from them, is the instrument for the cognition of an imperceptible object; thus, it is inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, the word "preceded" (*pūrvaka*) need not be read twice [in the definition].

Even when considering the result (*phala*), that recollection of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva-smaraṇa*) which is preceded by the perception of the mark—the result of direct perception—is itself the instrument, because the cognition of the imperceptible object arises from that.
As for the statement that memory produced by a present cause is inference, in that case the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is quite clear.
Alternatively, we shall describe the word "inference" (anumāna) as referring to the result: inference is the act of inferring (anumiti).

Alternatively, we may supply the word "since" [to the definition]: inference is that from which there arises a result consisting of the comprehension of an imperceptible object, preceded by a perceptible result.

For in this process, first there is the observation of the mark (*liṅga*), then the recollection of the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), then—according to some—the reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*), then the comprehension of the object to be proven (*sādhyārtha*), and finally, through the sequence described in the section on the definition of perception, the knowledge of what is to be abandoned and so forth. Since the causal relationship must be stated within this entire complex of cognitions as they arise, the venerable teachers have declared that the phrase "preceded by that" (*tatpūrvaka*) alone is sufficient for the definition of inference.

Others, however, have explained the inclusion of the term "threefold" as being for the purpose of excluding over-extension to comparison (upamāna) and other means of knowledge; for if it were stated simply that "inference is preceded by that," there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its application to comparison and so forth. Thus, the term "threefold" is employed.

The logical mark (*liṅga*) is said to be threefold either because of the distinctions in its effects and so forth to be described later, or because it possesses the three forms consisting of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so on; thus it is called "threefold" as having three aspects.
Since the logical mark is threefold, the cognition that takes it as its object is also designated as "threefold" by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*).
Therefore, when it is stated that inference is "cognition based on perception which has a threefold logical mark as its object," there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition].
[Objection: "Surely we shall understand the description of the distinctions such as *kārya* (the effect) by means of the terms *pūrvavat* and so forth;

however, how is the threefold nature [of the reason], consisting of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the rest, established by these words? [Response: To this they say: In all three types of discourse, such as debate (*vāda*), the subject (*pakṣa*) is called "the prior" (*pūrva*) because it is what is presented first. Since that [subject] exists for this [reason] as its locus, it is "that which has the prior" (*pūrvavat*). Thus, by this term, the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is expressed.
When the subject (pakṣa) has been employed, what remains becomes the similar instance (sapakṣa).
That [reason] exists for this [subject] by virtue of its being a basis; thus it is "śeṣavat.
In this way, the occurrence [of the reason] in the similar instance (sapakṣe vṛttiḥ) is stated by this term.

By the term *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*, the logical mark (*liṅga*) that is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is expressed. How so? Through the elision of the vowel *a* [in the compound], it means "not seen even in a general way" (*sāmānyataḥ adṛṣṭam*). Let alone its specific features, it is not seen even in a general sense.

Since its presence in the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) has already been stated, it follows by elimination that it is not observed even in a general sense in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
Thus, the three-fold characteristic of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is expressed by these words;
the cognition based upon that is inference (*anumāna*).
Thus, someone might apply the entire sūtra to this definition;
however, in that case, the skill of the author of the sūtra would not be made manifest. (238)

Furthermore, since five characteristics are accepted here in this treatise, when that [reason] possessing three forms is described, it does not exclude the cases of the "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) and the "inconclusive due to the context" (prakaraṇasama).
Therefore, the phrase "preceded by that" (tatpūrvaka) alone is faultless for the purpose of establishing the definition.
The mention of "threefold" serves to demonstrate its classification;
the three divisions have been stated in the passage beginning with "the distinctions are as before," and so forth. (239)
Characterized by pure logic set forth through words preceded by that [tradition], they have no regard for anything else other than the brevity of the words of the author of the Sūtras. (240)
The threefold nature [of fallacies] is established by its own statement through the mention of divisions;
likewise, it is established for words, doctrines, and quibbles (chala) from such [statements]. //241//
"As before" means:
where the effect is inferred from the cause, as for example, "there will be rain because of the rising of the clouds."

Here, an objection is raised: since the cause is mentioned first, it is proper to say that "it possesses a prior [cause]," and thus the effect should be described as "prior-like" (pūrvavat). Therefore, one should have cited here an inference of the cause from the effect, not an inference of the effect from the cause.
Nor can it even be possible for a cause to be [the subject] by means of a cause.
First of all, it is illogical for the effect to be the subject (*pakṣa*), because the dilemma of its being established or unestablished persists:
if the effect is already established, what else remains to be inferred? If it is unestablished, it cannot be the subject, like a sky-flower.

Moreover, the argument "the effect exists because the cause exists" is a reason based on a different locus (vyadhikaraṇa), like [the fallacious argument]: "sound is impermanent because a crow is black."

Furthermore, when existence (*sattā*) is the probandum, how can it be established? For a reason that is a property of an existent entity (*bhāvadharma*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); a property of a non-existent entity (*abhāvadharma*) is contradictory (*viruddha*); and a property common to both is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). As it has been said: "A property of an existent does not exist in what is unestablished; a property based on both is deviant; and a property of a non-existent is contradictory. How, then, can that existence be proven?"* *This verse is cited from Śāntarakṣita’s *Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 1687.*

Furthermore, it is not logical for mere causality to constitute the status of a reason (*hetu*), because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is possible even in the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and the like.
Moreover, no specific cause can be ascertained even by a wise man;
for we observe the cessation of clouds—whether moving or stationary, vast in form, and possessing a luster dark as a lotus petal—even when they have not yet released their water.

If, however, the cause existing in its final stage is intended to be the logical mark (liṅga), then at the time of recollecting the pervasion (vyāpti), there would be the direct perception of the effect. (242)

But surely even the Buddhists have accepted inference of the effect from the cause, as it is said: "When the production of an effect is inferred by means of a complete causal complex, that is described as its own nature (svabhāva), because it does not depend on any other factor."
The "Beloved of the Gods" (the King), who knows the highest [truth], explains that "origination" (*utpāda*) refers to the capacity (*yogyatā*) from which something arises;

and since this [capacity] is here to be inferred, it is accepted as an inference of essential nature (*svabhāvānumāna*), because it is not distinct from the thing itself—as it has been described: "that is its essential nature."

To this they reply: all this is an objection raised by one of dull intellect who has not understood the sequence of the application of inference. It is not the mere effect that is made the subject (*pakṣa*), nor is existence what is being proved.
A reason with a different locus (vyadhikaraṇa) is not employed;

rather, it is the clouds themselves that are established as possessing rain occurring at a proximate time, by virtue of their connection with properties such as a specific form of elevation. Thus, there is no occasion for the fault mentioned previously.

Just as smoke, because it possesses properties such as being thick and pale, leads to the inference that "this is possessed of fire, like the smoke observed in a kitchen," and thus it is the smoke itself that is inferred as being characterized by fire;

so too, these clouds which have just produced rain are inferred to be "possessed of future rain, because they possess properties such as extraordinary loftiness, like a cloud previously perceived during a monsoon," and thus it is the clouds themselves that are inferred as being characterized by future rain. As Bhaṭṭa said: "Therefore, the object of knowledge must be the locus (dharmin) as qualified by its property (dharma)."
It is conceived by others as being associated with fire in a particular location and with smoke.
As for the claim that "the cause is mentioned first," that is true.

Because it "possesses what is prior" (*pūrvavat*), the collection of properties such as "elevatedness" residing in the cause is what is called [the reason]; thus, there is no fault whatsoever in the text. Nor do we assert that the mere cause constitutes the logical reason (*hetu*), which would result in its deviation (*vyabhicāra*) caused by the occurrence of adverse conditions (*vidhurapratyaya*) and so forth.
Moreover, only a specific cause is a *hetu* (probans).

Nor is the distinction of the cause difficult to discern: "The clouds, which have burst open the mountain caves with the onset of their deep thundering, possess a luster as dark as bees, buffalo-horns, serpents, and *tamāla* trees."
Clouds such as these, whose lofty forms are turned tawny by contact with the high-creeper-like lightning, never fail to bring rain in this world.
And if one does not accept this [principle], the very life of inference would cease to exist, because it would be impossible to cognize even specific types of smoke. (245)

As for the suspicion that [the effect] is directly perceived, that too is incorrect; for at the very moment of inferring rain, water droplets released by the cloud are not seen falling upon one's head.

Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the qualification "the cognition of the imperceptible indicator" (*parokṣe liṅgini jñānam*), that which serves as the illustration will be a case where the rain is not directly perceived at that very moment.

Moreover, when the production of a cloth is inferred from the action occurring in the final thread—where destruction is not suspected because no action has yet arisen in its parts—the cloth is not perceived at that time, since an interval of time is possible.

For instance, on one side, there are three or four moments: first, the perception of the action in the final thread; second, the recollection of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); third, the reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*); and fourth, the cognition of the object to be inferred.

On the other hand, from the action comes disjunction; from disjunction, the cessation of the prior conjunction; from that, the production of the subsequent conjunction; and from that, the production of the cloth.

When the cloth has been produced, the qualities such as color (rūpa) and so forth begin in a subsequent moment; since the cloth is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) for the arising of color and the rest, a cause must necessarily exist prior in time to its effect. Therefore, even though it is produced, the cloth remains indeed devoid of color for one moment and thus is not perceived at that very time. Then, in the subsequent moment, because color arises, the substance possessing color will become perceptible through sense-contact. Thus, these moments are exceedingly numerous; consequently, there is no perception of the effect [at the moment of its production].
Nor does the non-production of the effect result from adverse conditions and the like,
because by employing the qualification "the absence of action in the parts having been produced," there is no room for the suspicion of its destruction;
and because, due to that action, the subsequent effects necessarily come to be.

Furthermore, that inference of capacity which was explained by the passage beginning with "by a complete cause," etc., is also incorrect, because inference based on essential nature (*svabhāva*) has already been refuted;
moreover, in the world, one infers only the effect from a complete cause, not its capacity—so enough of this digression.
The *śeṣavat* [inference] is that wherein the cause is inferred from the effect, as when rain in the upper region is inferred from the swelling of a river downstream.
Here too, a property of the river—characterized by its connection with the upstream region possessing rain—is inferred by means of that very property, namely a specific fullness and so forth.

This river is connected with an upstream region where it has rained, because it possesses a swelling characterized by froth, turbidity, and so on, just like a river previously observed to be of such a kind.
