This region, or rather this specific location, is inferred to be conjoined with another region characterized by rain, on account of its possessing a particular river-flood; thus, the entire cycle of objections concerning heterogeneity (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) and so forth that was raised previously has no scope here either.

From a conventional standpoint, this formulation of speech is that "the cause is inferred from the effect" and "the effect is inferred from the cause"; however, from the perspective of valid cognition (*pramā*), the established rule is that "the subject (*dharmin*) is inferred as possessing a property (*dharmavattva*) by means of that which possesses the property.

As Bhaṭṭa said: "This very same entity, being of a dual nature, is both the object to be known (*gamya*) and the means of knowing (*gamaka*); it is the object to be known through its unestablished part, and the indicator through its established part."

As for the objection that a river's flood can also be produced by the breaking of a dam or the melting of snow and so forth, it is said in response: "Possessing vast, turbid waters characterized by the whirling of eddies, and adorned with masses of foam flashing from the violent impact of formidable waves. (246)
Even a specific flood of a river, though crowded with thickets of moss and patches of young grass being carried along,
could not fail to be recognized.
This is the fault of the cognizer who does not perceive the distinction;
there is no defect in inference itself, for it is non-deviant with respect to its object of cognition. //248//
Therefore, it is improper to claim that inference is not a valid means of knowledge on the grounds of its similarity to the obstruction [of smoke by dust] or its deviation [from fire]. (249)
And rain is the indirect cause of the river's flood, through the gradual process of the flowing mass of falling drops of water. (250)

Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), however, is the inference of a similar probandum from a mark that is neither its effect nor its cause; for example, the inference of taste from color in a wood-apple (*kapittha*) and the like.
For color and taste, the single substance such as the wood-apple is their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), but there is no mutual relationship of cause and effect between those two.
Even according to the Śākya view, the relationship of mutual cause and effect between two moments occurring simultaneously is simply not possible.

Furthermore, since the possession of taste can be inferred from the possession of color by the subject (*dharmin*), there is no room for objections such as "unestablished" (*asiddha*) as before; this must be stated. As for the example cited by the Commentator—inferring the motion of the sun from its arrival at another location—that is incorrect, because arrival at another location is the effect of motion; thus, inferring the cause from the effect would be nothing other than *śeṣavat* inference.
Furthermore, reaching another location is conjunction with another location;
however, conjunction of the sun (the possessor of a thousand rays) with another location such as a mountain is not possible.

Even if such a conjunction were to occur with space (*nabhas*), it would be difficult to perceive, because it occurs in a substrate other than the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), like the conjunction of wind with a tree or the conjunction of a mother’s womb [with the fetus].

Now, if it is argued that seeing the sun in another location is the cause [of its motion], even for that, the state of being an effect of motion exists through a traditional sequence: from motion comes arrival, and from arrival comes the sight of it there.

Now, taking the observation of the sun in another location as the subject (*pakṣa*), its being preceded by motion is inferred—either by virtue of its being an "observation" (*darśanatva*) or by virtue of its being denotable by the word "observation" (*darśanaśabdavācyatva*)—according to the following reasoning: "The observation of the sun in another location is preceded by motion, because it is an observation in another location, or because it is denotable by that [same] word, like the observation of Devadatta in another location. Even so, its being an effect of motion through a mediated succession (*pāramparyeṇa*) is certainly not avoided.

For "observation-ness" (*darśanatva*) is not a universal (*sāmānya*) like "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like; rather, by means of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), what is expressed here is the capacity (*śakti*) that produces the observation.

And that [power] is not something supersensible or eternal; rather, it consists of the very nature of the essential form and its auxiliary conditions. Thus, even the visible essential form falls within the category of power. Furthermore, since the visible form consists in reaching another location, it constitutes the effect of motion.
The same must be said regarding the fact that [the term] "visibility" (*darśana*) is expressed by the word [itself], even though it is caused by the [act of] going.

Movement produces the reaching of another location; by that [reaching], there is visibility therein, and because of that, the application of the word [“visible”] occurs. This very [application] is what is called “being expressible” (*vācyatva*), as indicated by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).
Therefore, since the fact of being an effect of movement is in no way lost, this is indeed an inference *śeṣavat* (based on the remainder).
This example provided by the author of the Bhāṣya is of such a kind;
therefore, the inference of taste from form has been cited as the appropriate illustration. //251//
And we have demonstrated at length in our debate with the Venerable [Vasumitra] the abundance of reasons that fail to establish either a cause or an effect. (252)
Thus far, the threefold nature of inference has been described by way of explaining the suffix *matup*. However, this is considered by some to be as trivial as the trunk of a *phalgu* tree;

for it has been stated that the capacity of a mark (*liṅga*) to produce cognition arises solely from the force of a relationship characterized by necessity (*niyama*), and not by virtue of its being an effect (*kārya*) or any other such essential nature.
Therefore, as to why such a threefold classification has been shown, they explain it otherwise by resorting to the suffix *vat*.

"Like the previous" (*pūrvavat*) means as follows: at the time of grasping the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*), having ascertained their essential natures through direct perception, one subsequently cognizes that very same bearer of the mark by means of that very same mark; because it functions similarly to what preceded it, it is called "inference like the previous" (*pūrvavad anumāna*).
For example, having seen smoke and fire coexisting in a kitchen, one subsequently infers fire from smoke.

Now, it may be objected: since inferential cognition is not equal to perceptual cognition—which is capable of directly manifesting every particularity residing in its object—how can there be equality of action? And in the absence of such equality, how can the suffix *vati* (denoting likeness) be justified? True, this is so; nevertheless, because fire itself is apprehended through its mark (*liṅga*) as qualified by those specific features that bring about such a distinction [of intensity], equality of action will be established by virtue of being not far removed from it.

*Śeṣavat* means "by elimination" (*pariśeṣa*). It is the cognition of that which remains when possibilities have been excluded and there is no possibility for anything else. For example, when fire in general has been inferred in a certain place by means of smoke, and upon inquiry as to what kind of fuel this fire has, since grass, leaves, wood, and so forth are excluded, it is postulated that the fire has cow-dung for its fuel.
Or, as will be explained later, sound is inferred to be a quality because its status as a substance or an action is denied, and because it cannot belong to categories such as universals.

The *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [type of inference], however, is that in which the nature of the probandum (*liṅgin*) is not perceived even at the time of establishing the relationship, being entirely beyond the senses; it is inferred through the apprehension of a general pervasion (*vyāpti*), as for example, the auditory organ and so forth [are inferred] from the perception of sound and so forth.
Since the sense organs are themselves beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), they are never accessible to direct perception.

Nevertheless, because the pervasion of actions such as cutting with instruments such as axes has been grasped, the fact that the actions of perceiving sound and so forth are preceded by an instrument is inferred.
Regarding this explanation [of the suffix] *vati*, they raise an objection:
"In this way, only one type of inference would have been stated, not three;
for a mark (*liṅga*) whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not yet understood cannot be a means of cognition."

Furthermore, because particulars are infinite, it is difficult to ascertain their positive and negative concomitance; therefore, the apprehension of pervasion occurs everywhere only by means of the universal.
And such knowledge of pervasion is identical in all three cases as well.
Consequently, everything would be "pūrvavat" (inference based on what was previously known), since the suffix -vat is possible in every instance.
This is incorrect, because there exists a very clear internal distinction.
If it is said that inference is of one kind merely on the grounds that it is "preceded by pervasion" (*vyāpti*), that is indeed true; this type is exactly of that nature.
Nevertheless, even while that similarity exists, its threefold character is established because other distinctions are possible.

For instance, since smoke and fire were previously perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), that very same fire is now inferred from that very same smoke; thus, this inference is called "pūrvavat" (based on what was before), which is well known as being preceded by direct perception.

Now, one might ask: why is the inference of another fire from another smoke not preceded by perception? Who has said that it is not "pūrvavat" (based on what was previously perceived)? How then is it stated, "by that very same smoke"? This is stated with reference to the *jāti* (the universal class), not with reference to the *vyakti* (the individual instance).

But surely, since that [object] is determined through its generality, this would be *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* inference alone; for *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* has as its sole object that which is to be inferred and is eternally beyond the senses.

Inference by elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*) is said to be the cause for determining a specific probandum through the negation of other possibilities and so forth; as has been illustrated, for example, by the inference of fire from cow-dung fuel, or by the postulation of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) in sound.
Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), however, has already been illustrated as having an entirely imperceptible object, such as the inference of the auditory organ and so forth.
Thus, because these distinctions are possible, it is logical that inference is of three kinds.
Or, let alone the distinction between different examples; even within a single example, the threefold nature [of inference] can be stated.
For instance, in the inference "desire and so forth have a substratum because they are effects, like a jar," when the probandum is merely a substratum, it is an inference of the *pūrvavat* type.
When, by negating possible substrata such as the body and the sense organs, one postulates a specific substratum, that same [inference] is an inference of the *pariśeṣa* (residual) type.
Because the object of inference is eternally beyond the senses, that very [inference] is also "perceived through general correlation" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa).

In that case, what is the distinction between *pariśeṣānumāna* (inference by elimination) and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation)? It is said: the path for the operation of *pariśeṣānumāna* is one thing, and that of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* is another. The procedure for *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* is as follows: "The effect consisting of desire and so forth has a substratum distinct from the body and other such things, because it is an effect, provided that there exists a subverting proof against [its being located in] the body and so forth. This is the sequence for *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*.

The operation of *pariśeṣānumāna* (inference by elimination), however, proceeds as follows: the body, the sense organs, and the mind are excluded as possible substrata for desire and so forth; since there is no possibility of such [desire] residing in space, time, and the like, it follows by elimination that the Self alone is their substratum.
Furthermore, in all cases of *pariśeṣānumāna*, there is no such rule that the probandum must be entirely beyond perception, as seen in instances such as the postulation of fire from cow-dung.
On the other hand, *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* inference has as its object only that which is eternally beyond perception; thus, the threefold division is well-stated.

Others, however, cite the inference of power and action whose object is an unperceived particular characteristic (*adṛṣṭasvalakṣaṇa*) as an example of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*, because even in the case of Devadatta and others, action is imperceptible;
for in the cognition "he moves," there is no appearance of a reality of action distinct from the essential nature of Devadatta himself.
That very self of Devadatta which persists as the object of the cognition "belly," that same one appears even in the cognition "he moves. (253)
Since the cognition "it moves" has as its object a continuous series of closely succeeding conjunctions and disjunctions, that cognition does not arise at all times.

If it is asked, "How then does inference proceed regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of action, which is eternally beyond the senses?"—[the answer is: because an effect, being occasional, must be preceded by a cause; for if the visible nature of the substance itself were the cause, there would be the consequence of the effect being produced at all times, since that nature exists at all times. Yet, the effect is not produced at all times; therefore, there is an inference of an action distinct from that [substance].
The same should be understood regarding capacity (*śakti*) as well.

Since the essential nature of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is eternally beyond perception, inference is said to have as its object the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) perceived therein, but not the particular (*viśeṣa*), because it is impossible to grasp a pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to particulars.

This is untenable; for action, which consists of motion and is divided into types such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) because it manifests in the cognition "it moves" and so forth. Therefore, it cannot be eternally inferable (*nityānumeya*).

If, however, [action] were to have conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) as its objective basis, the cognition would be "it is conjoined" or "it is disjoined," rather than "it moves," since a cognition arises according to its specific object. Furthermore, the determination of an object follows the nature of the experience itself.

Otherwise, even in the cognition of a jar, there would be the status of a cloth as its objective support (*ālambana*). Furthermore, if [the cognition] were based on conjunction and disjunction (*saṃyoga-vibhāga*), the cognition of "moving" would occur even when [an object] is standing still, since conjunction and disjunction are possible there as well.
Moreover, in the case of a post (*sthāṇu*) possessing conjunction and disjunction with a hawk, there would arise the appearance that "it moves.
Even in a continuous series of their production without interval, because past and future conjunctions and disjunctions are imperceptible, it is the present ones that are apprehended.
And since those two remain even after Devadatta has moved, why is there not the cognition "he does not move" with respect to them as well?

And because a continuous series of conjunctions and disjunctions is observed [in the case of the earth], the cognition "it moves" would arise regarding the earth as well, just as it does regarding a person. //254//
Now, one might think: since conjunction and disjunction are produced by action, the cognition "it moves" and so forth occurs only with respect to that [action], and not elsewhere.
Furthermore, those two (conjunction and disjunction) are produced by Devadatta’s action, and not by the inactive earth; therefore, such a notion does not arise with respect to the latter.
If this is the case, then because it follows the presence and absence of action, this cognition has action as its object, not conjunction and disjunction.

For if those two [cognitions] had that [earth] as their objective support, then since there would be no difference in their both functioning toward two objects, a reason for the distinction must be stated—[the distinction] by which this cognition is of the person alone and not of the earth. However, the distinction cannot be based on being produced by Devadatta’s action, because when the action is imperceptible, we do not know at all whether that action resides in Devadatta or resides in the earth, since the inference from the effects of conjunction and disjunction is equal in both cases.

Furthermore, when Devadatta is walking on the ground, or even on a stone on the bank of a river characterized by incessant conjunctions and disjunctions with flowing water, the cognition "it moves" is not observed [to apply to the stone].
Therefore, the cognition "it moves" has action as its sole object; it does not have conjunction and disjunction as its objective support.
Furthermore, even when conjunction and disjunction are not perceived, the cognition "the bird moves" is observed as it traverses the supportless sky;
yet the conjunction with space is not perceptible, because it resides in that which is other than the perceptible, just like the conjunction between a wind-carrier and a tree.

If it is argued that the whole consisting of the parts of light and the space, as well as its conjunction with the bird, are perceived, this is not so; for even at midnight, when the sky is covered by a mass of clouds dark as a tamāla tree and in deep darkness, a moving firefly is seen. (255)

In that case, there exists no whole composed of light particles nor any whole composed of darkness particles; by what, then, could conjunction or disjunction be perceived? Furthermore, when an earthquake or a portent occurs, there is the cognition "the earth moves," yet neither conjunction nor disjunction is perceived therein, much less so during the deep of night.
Therefore, the cognition "it moves" does not have conjunction and the like as its objective support, but rather has action (kriyā) alone as its objective support.

Furthermore, an action that is eternally imperceptible cannot even be inferred, because according to your view, it is impossible to grasp the relationship [between cause and effect], since an effect must be preceded by a cause.
For you do not hold that the nature of the substance is the cause, but rather that it is the substance as qualified by action.

And since action is imperceptible, it is not easy to perceive the substance permeated by it; thus, due to the non-grasping of the causal nature, the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is difficult to establish even in the case of a jar or similar objects.
But this fault does not apply to the inference of the self, because the effect, such as a jar, which is dependent [upon it], is perceived through direct perception.
Therefore, action is not to be inferred from its effect.

Nor can conjunction be inferred [from action], according to the principle that "action terminates in conjunction," because it is impossible to infer a present action by means of that [conjunction]; and the doctrine of inferring action has been refuted in detail under the section on the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
By this, the inference of *śakti* (potency) should also be understood as refuted;
furthermore, the detailed rejection of supersensuous *śakti* has already been accomplished previously.
Therefore, it is appropriate that [the object] has the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of an unperceived causal capacity;
this is not "inference from general observation" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa), as was previously stated. //258//
Thus, when the suffix *matup* or the suffix *vatu* is being described, this threefold inference stated here is indeed logical.
But when this [work] exists, the definitions composed by other poets possess no splendor, just as the light of the moon has none in the presence of the sun.

The definition [of inference] has been refuted by the same direction of criticism applied to the "necessary connection" (pratibandha) taught by the Buddhists; moreover, the Śaiva system—which relies solely on positive concomitance (anvaya) established through repeated observation—is pitiable.

As for the Sāṅkhyas, how can there be any establishment of inference, since for them this universal (jāti) is distinct from its modifications (vikṛti), and thus their positive concomitance is untenable?
This is now considered:

this perception belonging to people such as ourselves, which is characterized by being produced through the contact of the sense-faculties and so forth, generally has as its object a thing qualified by the present time.
Likewise, is this inference also restricted to that same domain, or is it capable of determining other times as well?
Therefore it is said that inference has the three times as its object.
Why? Because it grasps the three times;
objects connected with the three times are apprehended by means of inference.
Past rain is inferred from the swelling of a river; likewise, future rain [is inferred] from the rising of clouds, and present fire from smoke.

Therefore, that which is stated by the Mīmāṃsakas—"For the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) alone is capable of making known an object such as what has been, what is, what will be, the subtle, the concealed, and the remote, and nothing else"—is incorrect; for it is possible for other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), like the injunction itself, to have objects of this same nature.
It has been stated that even the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of yogins has the three times as its object, and for people like us as well, [such perception] occurs in certain instances.
Regarding this, they raise the following objection:
"If time exists, then the apprehension of the three times must be considered; however, that very [time] is difficult to establish.
In its absence, for what could the distinction between present and so forth be determined? Time is not apprehended by direct perception in the manner of a jar or other such objects."
Even the cognition of "slow" or "quick" and so forth relies solely upon the effect. //257//
Nor can time be postulated on the basis of this very mark;
for no necessary connection (pratibandha) is observed here, as there is in the case of smoke and fire. //260//
However, the appearance of something more than [the mere moment] may somehow be possible by relying on some kind of accumulated succession of moments of activity. (261)
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to conceive of time as having the nature of the movement of planets and constellations; for time is nothing other than action itself. (262)

In the world, all practical transactions will be conducted by means of purely conceptual units such as moments (muhūrta), watches (yāma), days and nights (ahorātra), months, seasons (ṛtu), half-years (ayana), and years. //263//
If, however, time is considered to be a single, all-pervading, eternal substance, from what source does the conventional distinction between the past, the present, and so forth arise? (264)
When this has been raised as an objection, some maintain that time is indeed accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it appears as a qualifier in the cognition of an effect. (265)
Cognitions such as "done gradually," "done simultaneously," "done quickly," or "done after a long time" would not be possible if they were based solely on the effect itself. (266)
For indeed, without a distinction in the object, a distinction in the appearance cannot be conceived.
Surely this time is formless; how could it be perceived by the eye? Even for you, how could form itself be perceived by the eye? //267//
Or how could atoms, though possessing form, be imperceptible? Therefore, cognition must be sought; what is the use of examining the cause? //268//
Is it not the case that this rule applies to substance (*dravya*) and not to qualities such as color (*rūpa*)?

Even regarding substance, this is not a rule that "whatever possesses color is perceptible," by which the atoms (*paramāṇu*) would possess such a status; rather, it is that "whatever is perceptible possesses color."
Thus it has been said: "[The three [substances] possess perceptibility, possession of form, fluidity, and so forth]."
This statement is not divine— that is, it is not something that cannot be transgressed—
and perceptibility or imperceptibility is not established by mere verbal assertion.
For perceptibility is defined as being an object of sensory cognition.
If that [time] exists, who can prevent the perceptibility even of that which is formless? Let the possession of form belong to those substances, since they are observed to be so.
Furthermore, for one whose eyes are not opened, there is no arising of cognitions such as "quick" and so forth;
since these [cognitions] follow the presence of that [opening], time is therefore visual. (269)

If it is asked, "Why then is time not perceived independently, like a jar or other objects?"—the answer is that this is simply the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of things and is not subject to questioning. Its perception occurs when it has become a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of a material substance (*rūpidravya*), but not as something independent like a staff or similar objects. However, since space and the like are never perceived even as qualifiers of other things, they are imperceptible; this is not, however, because they lack color-form (*arūpatva*).

Now, if it should be argued that only a qualifying attribute possessing color, such as a staff, is apprehended by the eye and not [attributes] such as time, that is incorrect; for even a qualifying attribute such as a universal (*sāmānya*), though devoid of color, is apprehended by the eye.

If it is claimed that there is a restriction regarding substance (*dravya*), it has already been stated in this regard: whatever comes within the range of cognition produced by the instrument of the eye, that alone is "visual"—whether it possesses color or is colorless, whether it is a substance or a non-substance.
Thus, since there is a manifestation of "heaviness" in gold and other such substances, heaviness is also perceptible; it is not merely inferable from falling.
Therefore, let that which is accessible to visual cognition—whether as an independent entity or as a qualifier—be accepted as perception. (270)
For this very reason, time is perceptible;
likewise, by the same principle, space—which is cognized through notions such as "prior" and "posterior"—should also be understood as perceptible.

Others think that time is indeed inferable, because—just as in the cases "Devadatta has a staff" or "the lotus is blue"—no object distinct [from the other factors] is perceived, yet a specific excellence of cognition occurs; and since this excellence can be accounted for by its cause even on the view that time is imperceptible, time must be inferred.
Nor is it logical to conclude that time does not exist merely because it is imperceptible, just as the lower part of the earth or the far side of the moon [are not perceived yet exist]. (271)
Even though time does not appear [distinctly], it will—like a mental formation (*saṃskāra*) accompanied by the sense faculties—produce recognition and the cognition of "quickly" and so forth.

A great dispute has already been waged regarding the definition of perception as to whether the difference in appearance arises solely from a difference in the object, or also from a difference in the means (*upāya*).
Therefore, enough of further refuting that [position].
It has been determined that determinate perception (savikalpaka-pratyakṣa) is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa);
therefore, cognitions of "slow," "fast," and so forth are not merely conceptual constructions (kalpanāmātra). //272//

Furthermore, it is not tenable that these [differences] are produced solely by visible causes; for even when there is equality in the collection of causes—such as the threads, shuttle, loom, beam, and weaver—for a product like a cloth being made, one observes a difference in perception, such that in some cases it is made quickly and in others it is made slowly. Therefore, another causal factor must be considered.

[Objection: "But surely the distinction between actions such as movement (*parispanda*) is the cause here; for one movement is swift and another is slow, and thus there is quick cognition in some cases and delayed cognition in others. [Reply: This is not correct, because even the swiftness and slowness residing in movement are themselves produced by other causes. For even regarding movement, we observe cognitions of "slow" and "quick," such as "he goes slowly" or "he runs swiftly."

He said: "The cognitions of succession, simultaneity, and so forth are not based on the movement of Devadatta and others; rather, they are based on the movement of the planets, constellations, and so on.
And that very movement of the planets, constellations, and so on is called 'time.
It is precisely due to this that the conventional designations of watches (*yāma*), days and nights (*ahorātra*), months (*māsa*), and so forth are established."
Since that [time] is inherently distinct, there will be no need for the laborious conceptualization of distinctions based on external conditions (*aupādhika-bheda*).
In the determination of difference, the *nālikā*, the *prahara*, and so forth serve as the means; one thinks, "this much is a *nālikā*, this much is a *muhūrta*, and this much is a *prahara*.

In that regard, when many tasks are being accomplished within a single *muhūrta* or *prahara*, the cognition arises that they are "simultaneous" (*yugapat*), whereas with respect to other *muhūrtas*, the cognition is that they occur "successively" (*krameṇa*).
Therefore, time is simply the movement of the planets and so forth, whose measure is indicated by various such causes;
and those who know time—the astronomers and calculators—they alone perceive it as such.
That is incorrect, because even in the case of determining the positions of the moon and other planets, one observes the perception of their sequential order and so forth.
The sun has set after a long time, while the moon has risen quickly;
Mars and Venus appear as if they have both risen simultaneously. (273)
Thus, this appearance is observed;
yet it cannot be said that this [appearance] has the movement of planets and so forth as its cause, because that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.

Therefore, time is not the movement of planets and the like, but rather a distinct entity (vastvantara) by virtue of which this conventional usage of succession, simultaneity, and so forth is established.

Now, is this time imagined by you inherently characterized by succession and non-succession, or does it derive from another cause? If it possesses that nature inherently, then let the very effect—such as a cloth or other visible objects—possess that nature; what is the use of postulating "time"? On the other hand, if it depends on another cause, there is an infinite regress, because that cause too would require yet another cause. This is a foolish objection, for one could say the same regarding qualities such as whiteness.

If a quality were inherently white by its own nature, let that belong to the substance itself; what is the use of a quality? Furthermore, if one postulates another quality [for the first], there would be an infinite regress.
If it is argued that this objection does not apply because such [simultaneity] is observed there [in those cases], then it is the same here as well:
in the case of effects such as cloth and the like, the conventional usage of "succession" and so forth is produced by another cause; one need not seek yet another cause for that other cause.
Therefore, time exists as the cause for the conventional usage of "simultaneity" and the like.
And thus, this reversal of priority and posteriority caused by space, as observed between a youth and an elder, cannot be established without time. (274)

Devadatta and others delimited by a more distant direction appear as "distant" (*para*), whereas those delimited by a proximate direction appear as "near" (*apara*). These two—distance and proximity produced by direction (*dik*)—are seen to occur in reverse:
for a youth situated at a distance is called "near," while even an elderly man situated nearby is called "distant."
Therefore, since no cause other than time is logically possible in this case, time is inferred from this.

And this time is one and the same everywhere, like space; for just as space is one because its mark, sound, exists everywhere without distinction and because there is no mark of differentiation, so it is with time.
It is all-pervasive (*vibhu*) because it is designated as such everywhere;
it is partless (*niravayava*) and without support (*anāśrita*) because no parts or substrata are perceived.
Precisely because it is without support, it is a substance (*dravya*).
Therefore, it is eternal because the causes for its destruction, such as the disjunction of its parts, are impossible.

[Objection: But if time is thus a single entity, how can there be a division into present and so forth? In the absence of such a division, how can inference be said to have the three times as its object? [Reply: It is replied: the distinction of time into present and so forth is not real;
rather, although it does not exist, it is postulated by means of some limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the sake of establishing conventional usage.

What, then, is this limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)? We reply: it is "action" (*kriyā*). But surely, even for that [action], there is no distinction of present and so forth by its own nature; or, if such a distinction exists, let that very [action] be so [distinguished]—what is the need for time? Do not say so. Action is said to consist of a succession of various moments delimited by results associated with arising, persistence, and cessation; and it is that [succession] which possesses the distinctions of present and so forth.

For instance, the action beginning from the placing of the pot on the stove until its removal is called "present" (*pacati*) because it is delimited by the fruit known as cooked rice (*odana*). Due to that delimitation, even time itself is said to be "present" for that duration, like the space within a jar. When the continuum of motion has its fruit fully accomplished, it becomes "past" (*apākṣīt*); due to that delimitation, time also is said to be "past."

Because it is delimited by a fruit that has not yet begun, an action yet to come is expressed as "he will cook" (*pakṣyati*); likewise, time is also [so designated]. Thus, the conventional usage of the triad beginning with the present is based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*).

Therefore, the argument that is stated—that when a leaf falls from a tree, its past and future paths are perceived but not its present path, and thus present time does not exist—is irrelevant; for time is not manifested by paths. Indeed, the distinction between times is not manifested by paths.
However, according to the sequence already described, it is indeed manifested by action (*kriyā*).

Furthermore, this conventional usage of moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), *kāṣṭhā*, *kalā*, *nālikā*, *muhūrta*, watches (*yāma*), days and nights, months, seasons (*ṛtu*), half-years (*ayana*), years, *yuga*s, *manvantara*s, and *kalpa*s is based on distinctions conceptually constructed through action. Enough of this digression.

Furthermore, the determination of the distinctions of lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth is an auxiliary factor for the performance of Vedic rituals, as in: "One should sacrifice on every full moon day; and on every new moon day.

Likewise, the distinction of seasons such as spring is also an auxiliary factor for those [rituals], as in: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring, a Kṣatriya in summer, a Vaiśya in autumn, and a chariot-maker in the rainy season."

And this division of seasons, lunar days, and so forth, is perceived through action—namely, by the positions of the moon and other planets as they enter specific zodiacal signs as taught in the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra)—and by various worldly signs.
For example: "The spring is announced by the cuckoos themselves, with their sweet warbling and by clusters of copper-colored mango sprouts kissed by the tips of their beaks. (275)
The paths, where the vegetation has been scorched by the fall of the sun’s fierce rays and which bear the fragrance of jasmine, become heralds of the summer.
The mountains, thick with clouds and displaying the grand spectacle of fierce *tāṇḍava* dances commenced by circles of peacocks, proclaim the arrival of the rainy season.
The sky, variegated by clusters of stars spread out like pearls, attains the appearance of the Yamunā’s waters, heralding the autumn season. (278)
The warm bodies of young women, whose graceful movements are made fruitful by the enjoyment of long nights, welcome the winter.
The winter winds, rough with droplets of frost and jagged by the mass of blossoming *kunda* buds, proclaim the cold season. (280)
Therefore, even this single time is differentiated according to the distinction of actions;
by this same logic, space should be understood as established through a similar principle. //281//
Because the cognitions of "east," "west," and so forth are distinct from the mere cognitions of trees and other objects, one infers the existence of another cause [for these directions].
Although space (*dik*) is unitary because its defining characteristics (*liṅga*) are non-distinct, it is divided into ten types.

This distinction of east, west, and so on is postulated as being produced by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of contact with the slopes of the Golden Mountain (*Meru*), which are kissed by the mass of rays from the solar orb as it revolves in a clockwise direction. These are: the east, the southeast, the south, the southwest, the west, the northwest, the north, the northeast, the nadir, and the zenith.

Furthermore, by virtue of being presided over by deities, this very same direction is said to be tenfold: the eastern (aindrī), the south-eastern (āgneyī), the southern (yāmyā), the south-western (nairṛtī), the western (vāruṇī), the north-western (vāyavyā), the northern (kauberī), the north-eastern (aiśānī), the nāga-direction (nāgīyā), and the brahmic-direction (brāhmī).

But surely, by the very same means—whether perception or an existing inferential mark—by which space and time are apprehended, their difference is also grasped; how then can they be one, since at the very moment of that apprehension there is likewise a manifestation of difference? It has been stated [in response] that this is because the cognition of them is indistinguishable in all cases.

And because of the observation of their interchangeability, that which is the eastern direction in one place is perceived as the southern direction in another; for example, "that region which is the east of the Surāṣṭras is the south of the Mālavas."
Even with respect to time, the distinction between "long" and "quick" is seen to be entirely unstable; for that very time which manifests as the future becomes present and then past.
Likewise, even what is long becomes quick, and what is quick becomes long.
Therefore, it is established that these distinctions are merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).
In the *Samānatantre*, space and time are considered in their full extent;
that is not written here, for in this world, those who speak too much are disliked. (282)
Time is established as being either perceptible by the eye or inferential; its plurality is established as being due to adventitious conditions (*aupādika*).
Therefore, the author of the Sūtras has correctly determined that inference is "that which grasps the three times. //283//

Since comparison is mentioned immediately after inference in the aphorism on classification, its definition is stated according to that sequence: "Comparison is the means of establishing what is to be established through well-known similarity. (NS 1.1.6)

Regarding this, the elder Naiyāyikas describe the nature of comparison (*upamāna*) as follows: it is the very statement of transfer (*atideśavākya*) which establishes the similarity between two things—one well-known and the other unknown—having as its result the cognition of the relationship between a name and the object named.
For instance, a city-dweller seeking a *gavaya* but ignorant of its actual form asks a forest-dweller who knows it: "What is a *gavaya* like?
He replies to him: "As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*."

This very statement, by expressing the similarity of an unfamiliar object with a familiar cow, makes known—by means of that similarity—that the unfamiliar object is denotable by the name "gavaya"; thus it is called comparison (upamāna).

Now, since this [verbal testimony] has the nature of sound, its meaning would already be covered by the definition "verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person" (*āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ*); thus, it would not constitute a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Nor should it be declared a distinct means of valid cognition on the grounds that its result is the determination of the relationship between a name and the named object, for if the number of means of valid cognition were to increase according to the diversity of their results, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite number of such means.

For worldly and Vedic statements that convey injunctions and prohibitions, even though they have various fruits, do not transcend the nature of being verbal testimony (*śabda*). It is said: where the reality of the matter is understood—either from the cognition arising from the words themselves or from the cognition of the person who composed them—independently of any other means, that is indeed *āgama* (scriptural authority), because the comprehension of that meaning arises from that alone.
But where a person teaches another means of comprehension, there the determination of that meaning comes from that very means;
the function of the word, however, consists merely in making one aware of that means.
Just as in an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), one says: "This mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke, like a kitchen.

For here, the cognizer does not apprehend the mountain's possession of fire solely out of trust in a person's instruction, independent of other grounds; rather, he apprehends it precisely through the power of the mark (*liṅga*) called smoke, which makes that known.

Therefore, in this case, if the forest-dweller had not stated to the city-dweller seeking a *gavaya* the means of understanding it—namely, the similarity to a well-known object (*prasiddhasādharmya*)—then that instruction would have been included within scripture (*āgama*) itself.

However, since the understanding of that object arises from that very instruction, even though it possesses the nature of verbal testimony (*śabda*), this [cognition] is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
Furthermore, a city-dweller does not understand that animal to be denotable by the word "gavaya" solely from the words of a forest-dweller; rather, he perceives its similarity with a well-known cow.

Is it that there is no conviction from the words of the *Āraṇyaka*? We do not say that there is no conviction for one who has not heard them; rather, similarity (*sārūpya*) is another means for its comprehension, and since he has taught that [similarity] for the sake of understanding it, comprehension arises from that. It cannot be denied that this cognition is not verbal, but rather analogical (*aupamānikī*). Thus, even while stating this, the claim that analogy is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) is logical.
Furthermore, the very words of the *Bhāṣya* appear to bear the shadow of witness to this position.
However, those [arguments] are not set forth here for fear of making the text too voluminous; so, enough of this digression.

The contemporary [logicians], however, explain it as follows: for a cognizer who has heard the sentence of extended application (*atideśavākya*), the cognition of the similarity between a known individual and an unknown individual (*piṇḍa*)—which arises from the senses and results in the apprehension of the relationship between a name and the named—is *upamāna*.

Although this is produced by the senses, it is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) because, like the cognition of smoke, it is a means for the valid cognition of an object that does not fall within the scope of those [sensory] objects.
For a city-dweller who has heard the sentence of extended application, while wandering in the forest, perceives a living being similar to a cow.

Then, one recalls the statement told by the forest-dweller, "As is a cow, so is a gavaya"; and having recalled it, one understands, "This is what is denoted by the word *gavaya*. This knowledge of the relationship between the name and the named object, being produced by that [recollection], is called the fruit of comparison (*upamāna*).
To begin with, perception has not exerted its effort toward this object;
for its fruit is the discernment of the form of a gavaya dwelling in the forest. (1)
Furthermore, inference does not even enter into the range of suspicion here;
for where is the relationship between the mark and the marked, and where is the cognition consisting of the name and the named? (2)
Its establishment is not [possible] even from scripture, for it does not derive from the speech of forest-dwellers;
indeed, at that time, there is no perception of the gavaya by one who possesses the name. //3//
And when there is a discernment between the name and the named, their connection becomes easy to establish, but not otherwise.
For this very reason, they say that the act of naming is preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In response to this question from the city-dweller, the forest-dweller, following the inquiry, utters an analogical statement: "As is a cow, so is a gavaya. (4)
This is its meaning: "That very animal for which you perceive similarity to a cow, know that to be the *gavaya*; and this is the apprehension of the named object. (5)
And here, the establishment of a relationship with respect to particulars is not tenable due to their infinity; rather, it is established in this manner with respect to the universal. (6)
The act of naming is preceded by direct perception; it is not a Vedic injunction (codanā). Rather, what is intended here is the delimitation of that which is to be named. //7//
Whether it be through direct perception or by means of another instrument of knowledge, the formation of a convention occurs in some instances even when the object is being remembered. (8)
That living being who was seen by you there is called a *ruru*;
however, in some cases, it is pointed out by certain people through indirect indications (*upalakṣaṇa*). (9)
Those who wish to deceive a person possessing a name apply a designation to him there, such as:
"he has protruding teeth," "he is hairy," "he is dark-complexioned," "he is a dwarf," or "he has large eyes. (10)
Just as you would identify Caitra there by his flat neck,
so too here, one identifies [the object] by its resemblance to a mass of cow-essence.
It is not at all difficult to understand the relationship between the signified and the signifier;
however, if it is argued that the cognition arising from a sentence is accompanied by error, [we respond as follows].
Even when there is a connection [between the two], no such discrepancy is experienced;
however, that which exists regarding the form of the gavaya is this: "What is it like? (13)
That [doubt] also ceases once the gavaya has been perceived directly;
therefore, what is the use of another means of knowledge regarding an object established by perception and scripture? (14)
On this point, they say: a clear cognition of the relationship between a name and the named cannot arise from the speech of forest-dwellers, because at that time the named object is not perceptible.
Even if its apprehension is established as being qualified by similarity to a cow, nevertheless, at that time the cognition remains indeed afflicted by error.
At that time, a cognition free from further expectancy does not arise;
the function of the word is held to extend until the production of that [cognition]. //15//
And this [explanation] does not hold here, because it depends upon the cognition of the denoted object;
since that is not brought about by the word, its own function would not have been performed. (16)
And even if the apprehension of the relationship is held to occur in respect to the universal, that too is not correctly determined unless the individual instances have been cognized. (17)
And at that time, the mental state having the form of a gavaya is a distortion of cognition; even though the relation has two substrata, it produces a dark (uncertain) notion.
Therefore, it is taught that the act of naming is preceded by perception;
in some cases, that very perception is the cause by way of memory. //19//

Just as a relationship was demonstrated in the case of a previously seen deer and so forth, so too is there establishment through qualifiers such as "buck-toothed" regarding Caitra, as if it were a matter of direct perception. //20//

Furthermore, here at the time of the statement of extension (*atideśa*), even though the object of designation (*saṃjñin*) is taught merely as being similar to a cow, the confusion (*upaplava*) does not indeed cease, because the teaching of the form of the object of designation depends upon its being determined by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that the error will cease by means of perception itself when one perceives the similarity to a cow, we say no; for perception, which has the nature of sensory contact and so forth, is incapable of effecting the cognition of the relationship between a name and the named object.

This [cognition], however, is accepted as true because it has a perceptible result; and we maintain that this very [cognition] possesses the status of the means of valid cognition known as analogy (upamāna). //21//

Just as the perception of smoke in a mountain cave, though it is a result of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is classified as inference (*anumāna*) because it serves as the means for cognizing fire—which is not an object of the senses—likewise, the sight of a *gavaya* individual in the forest, though it is a result of direct perception, is called analogy (*upamāna*) because it effects the cognition of the relationship between a name and its bearer (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha*) which was previously unknown.

And just as in that case [of inference], the recollection of the previously apprehended invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) between smoke and fire functions as an auxiliary cause, so too here, there is the recollection of the meaning of the previously heard statement regarding the forest-dweller.

And just as in that case, at the time of pervasion, the cognition—though not yet grasping the specific [object]—now becomes fixed upon the particular by the force of the property being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), such that "here is fire," so too here, from a sentence whose specific denotable object was previously unknown, a cognition now arises free from confusion regarding the perceived specific denotable object: "this is that which is denoted by the word *gavaya*."

One should not suspect that this is merely inference on such grounds, because that cognition arises for one who does not depend upon the complete collection of factors such as the property of the subject (pakṣadharma), positive concomitance (anvaya), or negative concomitance (vyatireka).
Therefore, a cognition such as "this is that which is called a gavaya" is produced solely by analogy (upamāna) and does not arise from any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). //22//
Nor is it non-existent or doubtful, nor is it sublated, nor is it a mere conceptual construction;
thus, it is established in every respect that comparison (*upamāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this [cognition].
Regarding this, it is said: "Comparison is the means of establishing what is to be proven through similarity with what is already well-known."

The term *prasiddhasādharmyāt* is a compound that may be analyzed as a *karmadhāraya*, a *tṛtīyā-samāsa* (instrumental compound), or a *bahuvrīhi*. It means either: "that similarity which is well-known," or "the similarity of the *gavaya* with the well-known [cow]," or "that *gavaya* whose similarity is well-known. Thus, comparison (*upamāna*) is the means of establishing the object to be proven (*sādhya*) by virtue of this well-known similarity.

The object to be established (*sādhya*) is the relationship between a name and the named; its means of establishment (*sādhana*) is the act of making it known, or alternatively, the knowledge of the relationship between the name and the named is the object to be established, and its means of establishment is its production—this is the meaning. Thus, it is stated that the result of the means of knowledge called comparison (*upamāna*), which consists in the knowledge of well-known similarity, is the knowledge of the relationship between the name and the named.

By the terms "that which is to be proven" (sādhya) and "the means of proof" (sādhana), he declares that the instrument is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); and this [definition] is to be understood as applicable everywhere, being a conventional technical term (paribhāṣita). //23//
For this very reason, it was written here in the middle so that it might pervade the definitions of the means of valid cognition on both sides.

The subversion of analogy (*upamāna*), which is based on such [erroneous] conceptualizations as absolute similarity or near-total similarity, has been explicitly rejected by the author of the Sūtras. (24)
That by which a cognition of similarity is produced is "similar"; what is the use of such conceptual distinctions as "absolute similarity" and so forth?
Just as a universal is said to be the cause of a non-distinct cognition, so too is similarity said to be the cause of a similar cognition. //25//

Now, one might ask: what use is the definition of analogy (*upamāna*) in this treatise on liberation? For, first, through scripture (*āgama*), self-knowledge—the means to liberation along with its required procedures—is understood; through inference (*anumāna*), the validity of scripture is determined; and through perception (*pratyakṣa*), the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) for inference [is established]. Thus, only these three ought to be taught.
This is true;
however, analogy (*upamāna*) is also useful in certain cases for the performance of injunctions such as the immolation of a *gavaya*,
because such immolation cannot take place when the nature of the *gavaya* is not understood.
Just as a bean-stalk [is known by its shape], so too is the *mudgaparṇī* [known]; thus, even in the thorough identification of medicinal plants such as the *mudgaparṇī*, this [method] proves useful.
And with a mind moistened by compassion through the intent to benefit all, the Sage described its characteristics even though they do not serve as a means to liberation. //26//

Now, one might object: "If this were so, many other things useful for sacrifices, medicinal herbs, and the like would also have to be taught. [We reply: No, because this is a treatise on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-śāstra*); here, only the means of valid cognition—which is the instrument for determining objects—is taught.
And it has been established that this is exactly fourfold, neither less nor more.
As for the objects of cognition (*prameya*), only those that are constituent parts of liberation (*mokṣa*) are taught; so, enough of this digression.

The followers of Jaimini, however, describe the nature of analogy (*upamāna*) differently: for one who has not heard the statement of correspondence (*atideśavākya*), after seeing the body of a *gavaya* in the forest and subsequently remembering the body of a cow seen in the city, the cognition that "the cow is similar to this" is analogy. Its object is the remote (*parokṣa*) cow as qualified by the similarity to the *gavaya* currently being perceived, or the similarity to the *gavaya* residing in that [cow].

For this very reason, that cognition is not produced by perception, because its object is the remote body of the cow. Because the statement of correspondence was not heard, it is not verbal (*śābda*).
Nor is this [cognition] merely remembrance, because there is the possibility of an excess of objects of cognition;
for the similarity with the gavaya was not previously ascertained. //27//
Even if, in my view, similarity consists in the further connection with common parts, its cognition nevertheless occurs only when the counter-correlate has been apprehended. (28)
Nor is this cognition inferential, because it occurs for one who has not even considered the properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the similarity residing in the *gavaya* cannot be the logical mark (*liṅga*) there, because it is not a property of the subject;
nor can that which resides in the cow [be the mark], because it is unestablished (*asiddha*) and because it would constitute a part of the very meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*).

Even the collection of parts such as the horns and so forth, though residing in the cow, cannot serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for one currently staying in the forest, because it is not apprehended at that time; and what is unapprehended cannot function as a logical mark.
Nor can that [collection of parts] residing in the *gavaya* serve as its mark, for the same reason as before: it does not reside in the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).

Therefore, it must be admitted that for a cognizer situated in the forest, the cognition of the remote cow-individual in the city—qualified by its similarity to the *gavaya*—constitutes a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
This is indeed untenable because there is no such cognition [of it].
For the similarity of an unknown object is understood by means of a well-known one—as in the case of the body of a *gavaya* by means of a cow—but the reverse is not logical. (29)

For instance, suppose a city-dweller who has never heard of an *atideśaka* (a word for comparison) were wandering in a forest and, upon perceiving a creature resembling a cow that he had never seen before, were to think and say: "Oh, what a creature this is, somewhat similar to a cow!
However, neither the cognition nor the verbal expression "the cow is similar to this" belongs to anyone [at that moment].

Therefore, since there is no such valid cognition (*pramiti*) at all, what is the use of investigating the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? Even if this cognition "the cow is similar to this" were to arise, it is nonetheless not the fruit of a means of knowledge because it is of the nature of memory (*smṛti*).
[Objection: "Is this not merely a memory regarding the cow-individual itself?

For its being qualified by a similarity to a gavaya, which was understood only now, was previously unperceived; therefore, this [cognition] regarding it is not a memory. [Reply: Not so, because the similarity to a gavaya was also previously apprehended therein.

Is it not strange that one who has not perceived a gavaya should perceive its similarity to a cow? It is not strange, because what is grasped is the similarity as abstracted from the particular individual.
[Objection: But is this not even more extraordinary—that something is both apprehended and yet its manifestation is obscured?
For manifestation is indeed apprehension itself; and if that manifestation is obscured, it is said that there is no apprehension at all. [Response: This too is not so extraordinary.

For instance, having seen a gavaya in the forest, a city-dweller does not recall an elephant, nor a young camel, nor even a horse; rather, he recalls only that specific object with which the similarity of the currently perceived mass was previously understood. Thus, when this [gavaya] is being seen, it is only that very object which enters the path of recollection, and no other. Although the apprehension of similarity is not consciously felt, just like the recollection of an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) regarding a familiar object, it occurs by force to the villager's experience. Therefore, it is said that this apprehension of similarity is "obscured by the individuality" (*vyaktitiraskṛta*); there is nothing surprising in this.
Therefore, this is indeed memory; for the cognition is "A cow similar to this was seen by me in the city," and not the thought "Today a cow similar to this is being seen."

But surely, how can there be a perception of similarity for a common object without the perception of its counter-correlate? On this point, you yourself have stated something contrary to your own position: "And similarity, like a universal, is fully present in each individual;
therefore, it is perceived even when the counter-correlate is not seen. (30)
Furthermore, that connection with the parts of the gavaya can be grasped even by a city-dweller who has not previously perceived those parts of the gavaya.

Now, even if there is the apprehension of that [object] at that time, if there is no cognition of similarity regarding it, then similarity is not the possession of many common parts; rather, similarity is the cause of the cognition of similarity.
As it has been said: "Similarity is simply the state of being the cause of the cognition of similarity.
Furthermore, if the possession of many common parts were defined as its characteristic, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the case of variegated paintings and the like.

Furthermore, there is over-extension [of the definition] to other living beings, even those dissimilar [to cows], because the commonalities of their parts, such as hooves and so forth, exist [in them].
As for "abundance" [of these parts], we do not know how much is required;

if it is argued that it is simply "as much as gives rise to the cognition of similarity," then it is logical to maintain that similarity itself is nothing other than being the cause of the cognition of similarity.
Therefore, since it is possible that even before seeing the gavaya one did not perceive the similarity manifested as the gavaya, this [cognition] is merely memory.

Now, it might be thought that just as for the Naiyāyikas, at the time of the statement of the extended application (*atideśavākya*), the cognition of the relationship between the name and the named—which was initially accompanied by obscuration—becomes free from obscuration through analogy (*upamāna*); so too, this cognition of similarity to a *gavaya* in a cow, which previously existed but was obscured by the individual [cow], will now become manifest through analogy.
This is not the case for those who apprehend the gavaya through its bones, because its distinctness is established by perception itself.
Just as you Naiyāyikas have been told by us, "But if there is some additional quality, it must come from perception alone," so too will the Naiyāyikas say to you.

Now, one might object: how can the perception of a cow by a cognizer staying in the forest impart clarity to the cognition of similarity regarding a cow existing in the village? What can we do about this? [The answer is: because immediately after seeing that [cow], there arises a recollection of the cow-individual as qualified by a very clear similarity to it.

[Objection: Is it not for this very reason that this comparison (upamāna) is called a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), since perception (pratyakṣa) is restricted solely to the nature of the nearby gavaya, whereas the clear cognition of similarity to the gavaya regarding the remote cow cannot be established through any other [means]?
[Reply: It has been stated in this regard that this is merely memory (smṛti), because it appears as such;
and you yourselves accept that a means of valid cognition must apprehend an object not previously known.
Or, let it be granted that this cognition is distinct from memory;

nevertheless, because it is produced by inference, it does not enter the category of a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [The formal argument is as follows: The cow, as it is being remembered, is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is similar to this" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); "because it possesses the commonality of its parts" is the reason (*hetu*); "like a second gavaya-specimen present nearby" is the example (*udāharaṇa*). In the absence of such a specimen, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be shown by way of generality: "Wherever there is possession of the commonality of parts, there is similarity to that, as in the case of twins."
Because that specific connection is the cause [of the cognition], there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).

Since it has been stated that the connection with a universal is one thing and similarity is another, the reason (*hetu*) is not a mere part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). Furthermore, because such a cognition does not arise in one who is untrained, such as a resident of the Coconut Island (*nārikeladvīpa*), or in a child, it must be said that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not the cognition of that [connection] through independence.

Therefore, it is established that this necessary comprehension is the result of comparison (upamāna), because it is produced by inference, or because it is a form of recollection, or precisely because of the impossibility [of its arising from other means] as previously stated.

And what is the independent utility of this [definition], which you have taken as your standard? For thus you say: "Even under the guise of non-examination, when one states definitions, he does not speak without regard for their independent utility. But has not the utility already been stated? [In the case of] the *saurya* oblation, the details of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) are obtained from the model of the *āgneya* sacrifice due to the similarity in substance and deity; for the injunction "[One offers] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni" is complete in itself, being endowed with the entire collection of seen and unseen procedural requirements as they have been taught.

In the injunction, "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," because only the principal act (*pradhāna*) is taught at the beginning of the rule, there is no mention of the "end of the injunction" (*vidhyanta*), that is, the description of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Yet, a ritual action cannot be performed without a procedure.

Therefore, when the expectation arises as to which collection of procedures should be adopted here, it is understood through analogy (*upamāna*) that the procedure of the Āgneya sacrifice is applied to the Saurya sacrifice; this is because the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa* are similar in substance, both being prepared from grain-based materials (*auṣadha*), and because the two deities, Sūrya and Agni, are similar in nature, both being radiant.

Moreover, since a ritual action must be completed by employing a substitute when the prescribed substance or other materials are unavailable, and since it might follow that one could employ just any substitute, the employment of *nīvāra* grain—which resembles *vrīhi*—is understood through analogy (*upamāna*).
Thus it is said: "The object of analogy has been explained as distinct from inference (*anumāna*). It is not seen to be assisted by sentences such as those concerning the *saurya* sacrifice.
How, then, could it convey [the meaning] as being joined with Agni and the others? Therefore, it is useful for us."
Furthermore, even a substitute becomes such because of its connection with similarity to *vrīhi* rice when that [primary substance] is lacking, as in the case of the *nīvāra* species;

this too is the desired result of the definition of analogy. Moreover, where the primary [meaning] is sublated by other secondary [meanings], that is also accepted. But this is inconsistent; for you have abandoned the path [stated in the rule]: "The similarity of the unknown is understood through the known," and instead you have adopted the opposite.

Furthermore, just as through analogy one perceives the similarity of a cow—established by verbal testimony—to a *gavaya* that is unseen, new, and unknown, so too here, the similarity of the *saurya* sacrifice (which is unknown) to the *āgneya* sacrifice (which is known and has its procedure established) is understood; however, it is not the case that the similarity of the cow to the *gavaya* or of the *āgneya* to the *saurya* is perceived.

Thus, in this context, where there is a need for the remainder of the injunction (*vidhyanta*), there is no understanding of similarity through analogy; or where such an understanding of similarity exists, there is no need for the remainder of the injunction.

Now, it might be argued that when the *saurya* sacrifice is perceived as requiring a specific ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*), the *āgneya* sacrifice comes to mind due to the similarity of its substance and deity; therefore, the *saurya* obtains its procedure from that very source. But even so, if the required object is established through mere recollection alone, what is the use of analogy (*upamāna*)? For the procedure for the *saurya* will simply be adopted from the recollection of the *āgneya*. If it is claimed that "analogy" is merely a specific kind of recollection distinguished by the addition of a new object, this has already been refuted; so let us stop this digression.
Furthermore, an object established through analogy does not possess the character of being defined by a Vedic injunction (codanā);
therefore, it would not be logical to derive from it the acquisition of the specific details of the *āgneya* ritual procedure.
Furthermore, there is no such substitute for the species of *nīvāra* grain; for from the comparison "you resemble [a *brīhi*]," the cognition of similarity to *brīhi* does not arise.
Rather, the notion that arises is "these *nīvāras* are similar to *brīhis*," and this cognition yields no further result whatsoever. //32//

Since the sacrifice does not require the immolation of a *gavaya* anywhere, your stated definition of comparison—as being a means for the cognition of its form and for the discernment of a substitute—is not applicable to those who are proficient; therefore, it should not be accepted by the wise as that which was proclaimed by the preeminent Sage. (33)
Thus ends the section on analogy. Thus ends the second chapter.

The Third Daily Lesson: Examination of Verbal Testimony (Śabda). Since verbal testimony was mentioned immediately after comparison in the Sūtra on the classification [of the means of valid cognition], he states the following to explain its definition: "Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person" (NS 1.1.7).

If it were stated that "instruction (upadeśa) is verbal testimony (śabda)," then because this would merely be the utterance of synonyms, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even a mere word devoid of causal efficiency (akāraka) would possess the status of a means of valid cognition (prāmāṇya). To prevent this, the terms "the goal" (sādhya) and "the means" (sādhana) are drawn over from the preceding sūtra.

Nevertheless, since there is the possibility of over-extension to that which produces another word, the term *jñāna* (knowledge) is carried over from the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra* for the purpose of excluding that which produces memory; and the terms *vyavasāyātmaka* (determinate) and *avyabhicārin* (non-erroneous) are carried over for the purpose of refuting that which produces doubt and error. Thus, it is stated that verbal testimony (*śabda*) is instruction that produces the cognition of an object qualified by non-erroneousness and so forth.

Thus, some explain the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*) as a synonym for the definition of verbal testimony (*śabda*), supplying the qualifying words taken from the preceding sūtra that were required there. They state that the mention of the "reliable person" (*āpta*) is for the purpose of determining the definition;
they will explain the mention of "derived from the elements" (*bhūtebhyaḥ*) in the sūtra: "The sense organs—nose, tongue, skin, eye, and ear—are derived from the elements."
For in this way, oral tradition (aitihya) will not constitute a separate means of valid cognition, since there is no difference in its being of the nature of instruction (upadeśa).
Others, however, say: it is appropriate that the very phrase "instruction" (*upadeśa*) constitutes the definition of verbal testimony (*śabda*).
And it is appropriate that the mention of "an authoritative person" (*āpta*) is for the purpose of ascertaining that [instruction].
However, the recurrence of the qualifying terms introduced in the preceding sūtra is not useful here, because the specific definition follows immediately after the general definition.

Furthermore, since all fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) that produce memory and the like have already been excluded by means of the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), now only the exclusion of [other] perceptions and so forth belonging to the same class remains to be stated.

In that regard, a single term of instruction would suffice as a synonym, just as in the case of terms such as "intellect" (*buddhi*); so why undergo the trouble of following along with a qualification?

Another says: the definition of verbal testimony (*śabda*) is "the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta-upadeśa*), which does not involve the wretchedness of following a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) that has not been grasped, and which does not require the supply of previously unstated qualifying words.

Since nothing at all is taught by a word that is non-productive of action, or by one that produces another word, or by one that generates memory, or by one that instills doubt, the exclusion of such [words] is established simply by the inclusion of the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*), which presupposes a precise etymological definition.

However, since the over-extension to false instructions—such as the speech of a common man on the street which causes a contrary cognition—is not thereby removed, the inclusion of the term "reliable person" (*āpta*) is for the purpose of excluding those.

Regarding tradition (*aitihya*), since it is a cause for the cognition of things as they truly are, it is not a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from authoritative inference (*āptānumāna*).

Therefore, it is appropriate that the Sūtra, exactly as it was heard, serves as the definition of verbal testimony (*śabda*). [Objection: Let it be so; but what is the meaning of the phrase "it is taught" (*upadiśyate*)? [Response: It means that the act of denotation (*abhidhānakriyā*) is performed.

If it is argued that this action of denotation is simply "cognition," then since the eyes and other sense organs are also instruments for that [cognition], they would also follow as being "instruction" (upadeśa).

If it is argued that "cognition is preceded by one's own understanding," then it would follow that smoke and the like are also *upadeśas* (authoritative instructions), since the eyes and other sense organs are also instruments for producing that cognition.

If it is argued that "cognition [arises] through similarity to oneself," then even a reflection would be an *upadeśa* when its feet and so forth are inferred; furthermore, since that [similarity] is absent in the case of a word, it would follow that a word is not an *upadeśa*.

If it is argued that cognition is delimited by sound (*śabda*), then since the auditory organ (*śrotra*) produces that [cognition], it would follow that the organ is the instruction (*upadeśa*). Furthermore, since it is denied that sound produces a cognition delimited by itself, sound would not be the instruction. Nor is the cognition instrumental in its production by sound; for if one intends the act of denotation (*abhidhāna-kriyā*) or in the case of the inference of space (*ākāśa*), it would follow that [sound] is the instruction. Thus, because the nature of the act of denotation is not determined, the instrument of that act is not the instruction.

It is said that the act of denotation (*abhidhāna-kriyā*) is the cognition of an object based on a thing perceived by the auditory organ; this is because such is the conventional usage in the world. Furthermore, it is precisely that object which has become the object of such a cognition that is designated as "denoted" (*abhihita*) in common parlance.

Since it is only the collection of phonemes (*varṇa-rāśi*), which is grasped by the ear, that serves as the instrument for the cognition of meaning—and not a word consisting of *sphoṭa* which is the object of an auditory perception—the *sphoṭa* is not the word.
For the term "word" (śabda) is well-established as referring to an object apprehended by the sense of hearing. And it is only phonemes (varṇas) that are apprehended by the sense of hearing.
If it were said that "that from which the comprehension of meaning arises is a word," then even smoke and the like would be words.
Furthermore, a word whose relationship [to its meaning] has not been grasped would forfeit its status as a word, because it would fail to produce the comprehension of the object.
Now, since cognition consists of consciousness (*saṃvit*), there is no such thing as a distinct, unprecedented "act of naming" that exists apart from consciousness;

and it has been stated that if this [act] were the instrument, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). True, in every case cognition is indeed of the nature of consciousness.
