Yet, when that [consciousness] has the eye and so forth as its instrument, it is the fruit of perception (*pratyakṣa*); when it has the logical mark (*liṅga*) as its instrument, it is the fruit of inference (*anumāna*); and when it has the auditory organ as its instrument, it is the fruit of verbal testimony (*śabda*).
For "is seen," "is inferred," and "is denoted" are not synonymous terms.
Furthermore, a word is said to function as an *upadeśa* (instruction/teaching) when it generates a specific cognition of that [object].
However, in cases such as the desire to express the inference of space (*ākāśa*), it functions solely as a logical mark (*liṅga*). Enough of this digression.

The "reliable person" (āpta) has been explained by the author of the Bhāṣya: "A reliable person is indeed one who has directly perceived the dharma, who, impelled by the desire to communicate the object exactly as it was seen, is an instructor."
"Dharma" refers to some intended object that is to be taught;
its "realization" is the apprehension of it exactly as it is. (1)

However, there is no rule that [an authoritative person] must apprehend [the object] through perception alone, because their status as an authoritative person (āpta) is not lost even when they teach matters ascertained through inference and other means.
By the phrase "endowed with the desire to proclaim," freedom from passion (vītarāgatā) is expressed;
by the term "instructor" (upadeṣṭṛ), skill in exposition (pratipādanakauśalya) is expressed. //2//

Even one who is free from passion, if mute or otherwise incapable, would be unable to teach; and even one capable of speaking and having directly realized the Dharma, if not free from passion, does not speak but remains silent.
And it is required that he be free from passion regarding the subject to be established;
yet, where can a person be found who is entirely free from passion?
The common characteristics of seers, those who seek wealth, and those who seek pleasure must be stated, as well as the definition of an authoritative person (āpta);
for in this way, even in the world, the conventional usage based on the speech of an authoritative person will not perish. //4//

Even those who describe "authority" as the destruction of defects must explain that destruction of defects in relation to the very objects being communicated; otherwise, there would be a denial of the worldly linguistic practice observed in the world, which is based on the speech of an authority.

Alternatively, since this treatise is intended for the purpose of establishing the authority of the Vedas, this definition applies exactly as it was heard to its author, the authoritative Īśvara; he is indeed one who has directly perceived dharma, because dharma falls within the range of Īśvara’s direct perception.
Regarding the phrase "impelled by the desire to make known":
it will be stated that the Blessed One is indeed compassionate;
and he is the teacher of the Vedas and other scriptures, since it will be demonstrated that they were composed by him.

He said: Let this matter rest for now; rather, consider this: for what purpose is this definition of verbal testimony (śabda) taught separately? Indeed, we do not perceive any distinction between verbal testimony and inference (anumāna).
Therefore, since its definition is already implied [by that of inference], another definition need not be stated. (5)
For both [inference and verbal testimony] are indeed equal in having an imperceptible object, and both are equal in having a universal as their object due to their dependence upon a relation. (6)
Even if the relation were grasped, there would be no engagement with even a single [particular];
moreover, because particulars are infinite, the relation is exceedingly difficult to establish. (7)
Just as fire is inferred upon seeing smoke through direct perception, in the very same way, the meaning of a word is understood upon hearing the word itself. //8//
And here too, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) exist just as they do with a logical mark (liṅga):
whatever word is observed in a particular place denotes that object. (9)

The property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) is also established as residing in the word alone, since it is the word that possesses the meaning; the subject will be conceived [in the word] just as smoke is [conceived] as possessing fire. (10)

Just as the universal property of "smokiness" functions as a logical reason (*hetu*) for fire, so too will the universal property of words such as "cow-ness" be explained here in this same manner. //11//

Thus, when there is a determination of identity due to the similarity of the totality of conditions regarding the objects, mere difference in characteristics is not at all a cause for otherness. //12//

The co-operation of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) arising from the sequence of preceding phonemes, the occurrence [of speech] in dependence upon a person, and the sequence following the speaker’s intention (vivakṣā). //13//
By such specific [distinctions] as these, there would not be another means of valid cognition;
for why should there not be a distinction here too regarding cause, effect, properties, and so forth? (14)
The state of being employed according to one's will is also not a cause for [the object] being something else, because such a state is observed even in the case of signs such as hand gestures. //15//
In the case of a familiar object, both [perception and inference] are equal in their independence from examples;
however, regarding an unfamiliar object, both depend upon the recollection of a relationship.

It is also stated that [the word] is the cause for the arising of multiple representations (pratibhā), just like words such as "something" (kaścit) when applied to an object whose specific characteristic (liṅga) is indistinct. //17//
And because there is no ascertainment of the clear meaning, it is like [cognition] arising from a fallacy of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāsa).
The same applies to the indicative mark (liṅga) and likewise to the word (śabda), which causes confusion regarding multiple meanings. //18//
Moreover, even when a mere intuition arises from a word in some cases, a certain cognition is produced by means of the mark (liṅga) of its being the speech of a reliable person (āptavāda). //19//
For this very reason, the wise consider even verbal testimony to be a form of inference, on account of its commonality with the non-contradiction of the statements of a reliable person. //20//
Furthermore, a word attains its status as a means of valid cognition only with respect to the speaker's intention;

it does not [attain it] with respect to an external object because of its deviation from that object. And with respect to that intention, this [word] possesses the character of a logical mark (liṅga). //21//
To this it is replied:
Word is of two kinds, consisting of the word (*pada*) and consisting of the sentence (*vākya*).

Among these, the sentence alone is capable of making known the meaning of the sentence even when its [constituent] relations have not been previously understood; for we observe that when a newly composed verse is heard, those whose minds are refined by their knowledge of words comprehend its meaning.
Therefore, how could there be any possibility of its being equal to inference, which functions by being rooted in the comprehension of a relationship?
However, although a word depends upon the apprehension of a relation, it is distinct from inference due to a difference in its causal apparatus and a difference in its object.
To begin with, the objects of a word and of a logical mark (*liṅga*) are indeed dissimilar;
furthermore, it will be established that the meaning of a word is merely "that which possesses that" (*tadvanmātra*).
Inference, however, has the meaning of a sentence as its object, such as "there is fire here" or "the mountain possesses fire," because it is from that [sentence] that understanding arises;
and it has been stated in that regard that "the subject (dharmin) qualified by the property (dharma) is the probandum (sādhya)."

[Objection: But surely there are also words that function with respect to the meaning of a sentence, such as "gomān" (possessor of cows), "aupagavaḥ" (son of Upagu), and "kumbhakāraḥ" (pot-maker). [Reply: True; however, even in those cases, expectancy certainly exists, because a cognition free from expectancy does not arise without another word, since the expectancy—"Who is the possessor of cows?"—is not yet satisfied.

Moreover, while the cognition of a qualifier such as fire arises from a mark (liṅga) preceded by the cognition of the qualificandum such as a mountain, the cognition of the qualificandum from a word is preceded by the cognition of the qualifier; thus, there is a difference in their respective objects.

Now, it might be argued: "Just as in inference the subject (dharmin) qualified by a property (dharma) is the probandum (sādhya), so here let the word (śabda) qualified by its meaning (artha) be the probandum. This is not so, because the word functions as the logical reason (hetu);
and that which serves as the reason cannot itself be the subject (pakṣa).

Now, one might object: "Just as it is said, 'This smoke possesses fire because it is smoke, like the smoke in a kitchen'—where that [fire-possessing nature] is attributed by others to the smoke located in a specific place—in the same way, let the word 'cow' itself be established as possessing meaning on the grounds that it is the word 'cow,' and let a universal such as 'being the word 'cow'' be made the logical reason (*hetu*). To this we reply: this too is difficult to establish. For what is being proved regarding the word, which is the subject (*dharmin*)? Is it its being qualified by the object (*artha*), or its being qualified by the capacity to convey meaning, or its being qualified by the cognition of the object? It cannot first be the proof of its being qualified by the object; for there is no relationship of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) between the word and the object, any more than there is between a mountain and a fire.

Now, if it is argued that because a word has an object as its domain, it is "qualified by that object," that too is incorrect; for it is impossible for something to have an object as its domain without first producing a cognition of that object. Once cognition is established, what is the use of its being a property of that [word] by way of having that object as its domain? If, on the other hand, the cognition of the object were preceded by its being a property of that [word] based on having that object as its domain, while having that object as its domain were itself based on the cognition of the object, this would result in a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*).
Therefore, a word qualified by an object is not the probandum.
Nor is it characterized by a capacity to convey a meaning, because there is no employment of the word with the desire for that [conveying].
A word is neither spoken nor even heard for the sake of establishing a power (śakti); rather, people hear and speak it solely for the purpose of conveying a meaning. //22//
Nor can words qualified by the cognition of their meaning undergo the status of being the subject (pakṣa), because the alternatives of being established or unestablished are untenable.
How can the word possess that [quality] through a cognition of the object if that [cognition] itself is unestablished? Or, if that cognition is established, what else remains to be inferred? //23//
If it is argued that the dilemma is the same even in the case of fire and so forth, we reply: no; for in that case, fire is not produced by smoke, but rather is inferred.

However, this [case of] verbal cognition is actually produced by the word; thus, it is precisely regarding this [cognition] that there is occasion for the dilemma of whether [the word] is established or unestablished.
Therefore, in all three ways, the word does not possess the status of being the subject (pakṣa).

Moreover, since the apprehension of the reason— which consists of the universal such as *gatva*— in the subject, which is the word "cow," is followed by the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), then by the reflective cognition (*parāmarśa*), and then by the comprehension of the object, the interval of time would be so long that the subject would have vanished;
it does not remain present like a mountain, for a word perishes as soon as it is uttered.
Furthermore, people do not apprehend a word as being identical with its meaning, but rather apprehend the meaning as distinct from the word; thus, the word itself is in no way the subject (pakṣa).

Consequently, because it is impossible for the subject qualified by the property (dharma) to be the very thing to be proven (sādhya), there is a great difference between the scope of the word and that of the logical mark (liṅga).

Indeed, there is a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*): inference has been explained as being dependent upon forms such as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*), but these forms do not exist in the case of verbal testimony (*śabda*).

Thus, since the status of the word itself as the subject (*pakṣatva*) is rejected, the universal (*sāmānya*) such as "cowness" (*gatva*) cannot function as a logical mark (*liṅga*) by virtue of being a property of that subject.
Nor can the object (*artha*) be the subject, because the dilemma of whether it is already established or not yet established (*siddhi-asiddhi-vikalpa*) is untenable.
Nor can it be said that this [property] belongs to the word, because it does not reside therein.

If it were asserted that the word possesses this property by virtue of generating a cognition, there would be the same circularity as before: the cognition arises through the force of the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth, and only when the cognition exists is the status of being a property of the subject and so forth attained.

Furthermore, if the word were a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) by virtue of being a property of the object, then just as one who has not yet apprehended the relation between smoke and fire nevertheless perceives the smoke's presence on the mountain, so too one who has not yet apprehended the relation between the word and its object would perceive the word's status as a property of that object; however, since he does not so perceive it, the word lacks the status of being a property of the subject.
Positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are also difficult to establish for that [word], because there is no co-occurrence (*anugama*) of word and object in either space or time.
For it is not the case that wherever a word is, there its object is;
as the Vedic scholars have said: "We perceive the word in the mouth, but the object on the ground."
As for us, however, we perceive the auditory organ in the space of the ear; let this matter rest.
Nor is it the case that where there is the word, there is the object, because at this very moment, although the object Yudhiṣṭhira is absent, the word "Yudhiṣṭhira" exists.

If it is argued that even though there is no concomitance between the object and the word, a concomitance will be grasped between their respective cognitions—then it must be stated: is the concomitance grasped when the cognition of the object has arisen, or when it has not yet arisen? First, if it has not arisen, since it lacks its own essential existence (*svarūpa*), how can there be a grasping of concomitance? But if the cognition of the object has already arisen, what is the use of grasping concomitance? It would be futile.
But if it were preceded by that [inference], there would be the same mutual dependence as before;
by this, the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also explained.

Surely, when the relationship between word and meaning is being determined through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*), positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) are indeed useful;

as it has been said: "In whatever place a word occurs, that object which follows it must belong to that word. This is true; however, once the cognition of the object is established by the force of convention (*samaya*), positive and negative concomitance serve only to restrict that convention regarding the word. The cognition of the object does not arise from the word through positive and negative concomitance in the same way that the cognition of fire arises from smoke.
Moreover, cognition from smoke and the like is certainly not preceded by comprehension;
here, however, the understanding produced from words is indeed preceded by comprehension. (24)
For in the common usage of elders, a child, having perceived an object from some word and understanding it, understands that very object by himself as well. //25//

Even in cases where a convention (*samaya*) is established such that "this meaning is to be understood by you from this word," it should be understood that it is *pratīti* (comprehension) itself that is indicated as the cause.

Therefore, the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), known as "invariable concomitance" (*avinābhāva*), is one thing, while the relationship between word and meaning—known by the name "convention"—is another; namely, the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*), which is the factor for comprehension.

Thus, due to this difference in objects and the difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), it is established that verbal cognition (*śabda*) is distinct from inference (*anumāna*), just as it is from perception (*pratyakṣa*).

As for the objection raised and refuted regarding the difference [of the sphoṭa] from [the phonemes], such as its dependence on the sequence of preceding phonemes—what insistence can there be on that which is largely trivial?

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that "it is an inference because it shares the quality of non-contradiction with the speech of a reliable person"—that is indeed well-said, because the objects of cognition differ.

For by means of the reason "being the speech of a reliable person," the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the cognition of the word's meaning is established, but that [cognition] itself is not produced [by that reason]. As it has been said: "The truthfulness [of the cognition] is indeed something else, having 'being the speech of a reliable person' as its cause."
Moreover, in this context, the meaning of the sentence is indeed something distinct, and that has been understood long before.
If, therefore, truth is inferred from the statement of a reliable person,
how can the cognition of the meaning of that sentence itself be considered an inference?
"For the birth [of a cognition] is equal for both the words of reliable and unreliable persons when heard;
however, that which possesses the three characteristics is more useful than mere birth in the case of inference."
Nor should it be said that this [cognition] is mere intuition (pratibhā) apart from the ascertainment of its validity, because the comprehension of the word's meaning is established by experience.
By this, the status of being the object of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) is also refuted;
for that which is called "intention" is not the denotable object of a word, but rather the actual referent (*artha*) itself is so.
For in this context, it is observed that the word functions as an inferential mark (liṅga) when there is a desire to speak;
it is like [the inference of] space from the fact of being an effect, and not, moreover, by way of being a denoter (vācaka). //26//

From the uttered word, a cognition arises first with the denoted object as its content; immediately thereafter, it may indeed lead to the speaker’s intention. However, if it were devoid of the apprehension of the object, this mode of subsistence would be established by necessity; yet, if that object is unknown, this [cognition] cannot exist as qualified by its denoted object. (27)

Surely, once its status as a means of valid cognition is established, one may proceed with an investigation into its difference or non-difference; however, the validity of the word itself is not even conceivable [in this context]. (28)
It has been described that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which generates the comprehension of an object;
however, because they are rooted solely in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), these words do not touch the actual object. (29)

When the referent of a word is investigated, what indeed can be said to be its meaning? Neither the genus, nor the individual, nor anything called "the possessor of that" [genus] can be asserted. (30)

Furthermore, its connection with the object—whether it be eternal or a convention—is not possible; or even if it were possible, how could it be understood in regard to an object that transcends the senses? (31)
Even the ultimate meaning of a sentence cannot be determined as having a nature consisting of an injunction, a productive operation (bhāvanā), a distinction, a relation, and so forth. (32)

Furthermore, it is not clearly defined whether the means for attaining that [understanding] is the word-meaning (*padārtha*), the individual words (*pada*), the sentence (*vākya*), the combined meaning (*vyatipaktārtha*), or the *sphoṭa*. (33)
Even when that cognition has been established, the cause for its firmness—
whether it be eternality or the fact of being spoken by a reliable authority— is not correctly established.
Even if the Vedic compositions were eternal, they would be preceded by an author; or, even if they were created, it is difficult to determine by whom they were made. (35)
That he is the creator, that he is free from dualities, that he is one, that he is omniscient, and that he is compassionate—it is impossible to establish any of these. //36//
Furthermore, there are numerous scriptures that are mutually contradictory;
we cannot determine which of them has Īśvara as its author and which does not. (37)
In the Vedas, defects are found: contradiction, tautology, the non-perception of results, and likewise the failure of results. //38//
And of what nature is the coherent connection (samanvaya) of explanatory passages (arthavādas) that express contradictory meanings, or of mantras, or of words such as proper names? //39//

Furthermore, because the Veda contains instructions regarding accomplished effects (*siddhakārya*), people have doubts: "Does its authority apply to what is to be accomplished (*kārya*), or to what is already established (*siddha*), or to both? (40)
Therefore, the status of the Veda as a means of valid cognition stands on precarious ground;
it must be accepted either with the thought that it is a means of livelihood or out of blind faith. //41//

To this it is replied: all these objections shall be refuted in due order; therefore, enough with this lack of confidence—may your long-lived self understand that the authority of the Veda is indeed well-established.

Now, how indeed is this very lack of contact with objects (*arthāsaṃsparśitva*) to be avoided? For words do not produce cognition regarding an external object; rather, they are seen to arise solely dependent upon conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that lack contact with rarefied realities. Following their own inherent nature, they are observed to produce cognitions consisting mostly of conceptualization, which disregard any connection with external objects—as in the case of [the statement]: "A hundred herds of elephants stand on the tip of a finger. This is the very nature of words: their lack of contact with objects.

If it is argued that the eyes and other sense organs also serve as causes for the perception of false things such as floating hairs (*keśoṇḍuka*), yet they are not non-contacting with objects (*arthāsaṃsparśitva*), we say no; for in those cases, their capacity to produce such delusions arises because their nature is defiled by defects such as cataracts (*timira*), and not by their own inherent power. If it is further argued that here too this power belongs to the defects of the person and not to the words themselves, that is not so; for even a defective person, such as one who is mute, lacks the capacity to produce such a cognitive distortion when no word is uttered.

Moreover, even in the absence of any impurity in the speaker's heart, sentences such as "the tip of a finger [is a mountain]" produce confusion simply by being uttered; thus, this is the inherent nature of words themselves, not of the defects of the speaker.

Moreover, the visual faculty and the other senses do not cease their activity upon the arising of a subverting cognition, for we observe the disappearance of error—such as the perception of silver in mother-of-pearl—only when that erroneous experience is produced.

Sound, however, even when subverted a hundred times, continues to produce an equally unreal conceptual construction exactly as it was uttered, such as "a hundred elephants stand on the tip of a finger. Thus, because their production is dependent upon conceptualization, it is precisely words that possess this nature known as "non-contact with reality" (arthāsaṃsparśitva).

As it has been said: "Words have their origin in conceptual constructions (vikalpa), and conceptual constructions have their origin in words; when these are mutually connected, these words do not touch upon the actual object. (Cited by Helārāja on Vākyapadīya Samuddeśa 3.54)
To this it is replied: This would be so if words never produced a cognition that corresponds to reality, such that one could conclude that their very nature is to be non-contacting with objects.

But, from a sentence spoken by a person possessing excellence—such as "There are fruits on the riverbank"—there arises a cognition corresponding to reality that does not disregard the external object, because for one who acts upon it, that object is attained.

Furthermore, we shall explain later that this attainment of the object cannot be logically accounted for through a conceptual construction of words that is devoid of contact with the object, just as the perception of a jewel in the luster of a jewel [leads to the jewel] only by way of a causal succession.

[Objection: Is it not the case that from a statement such as "the mouth of a virtuous person is like a well," an incorrect cognition is indeed observed? [Response: Not so; for there is an absence of the fickleness of uttering such a statement by one who is truly virtuous.

As for the case where even a reliable person instructs someone, saying, "Do not utter a statement that does not correspond to reality, such as 'there are a hundred herds of elephants on the tip of a finger,'" there, because the phrase delimited by the particle *iti* is employed as an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) with reference to the word itself, it is indeed true to reality as part of a single syntactical unit with the prohibition.
For if it were intended to refer to the object, there would be no prohibitive sentence at all.
Therefore, since the words of reliable persons lack non-correspondence to reality, words do not fail to touch upon their objects by their very nature.
This distortion is caused solely by the attachment to human defects.

[Objection: But even if authoritative persons do not employ such statements, is the negative concomitance (vyatireka) not still doubtful? Is it because words lack such a nature that no non-corresponding cognition arises, or rather because of the absence of defects in the speaker?
[Reply: This is not so! Even a person who does not utter words can be a deceiver;
by means of gestures of the hand and other such methods, he certainly produces error. (42)
Nor should it be said that there is an inference of sound from hand gestures and the like, and that the resulting error is caused by those; for it is not perceived in this way.

Furthermore, when a cognition has arisen from a sentence such as "the river," and a person, following the bank of the *Raraṅgiṇī* river, fails to obtain the result and a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) arises, he reviles the man alone, thinking, "Shame! Alas! I have been deceived by that wicked soul," and not the word.
And one who has obtained the result praises the man alone, saying, "Excellent! It was well taught by that good man."
Therefore, because it conforms to the sequence of human defects, the distortion arising from words is caused solely by human defects and is not based on the intrinsic nature [of the words].
Since this [distortion] is absent when authoritative persons remain silent, there is no production of error; thus, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not doubtful.

But surely, what can human defects do in that regard? For whether a person is virtuous or defective, their function consists merely in the utterance of the word; beyond that, the resulting effect depends solely upon the word itself. Therefore, this delusion is produced by the very nature of the word.

Well then, since the word alone performs the function even in a correct cognition such as "there are fruits on the riverbank" when the speaker is virtuous—and since the person's role is fulfilled merely by uttering it—it is not the case that non-contact with the object is the absolute nature of the word.
And this alone is logical: that the very essence of the word is simply its luminosity, like a lamp, and not its being either true or false;
for even when the object is contrary [to reality], the lamp does not cease to be luminous.
However, this is the distinction: while luminosity in the case of a lamp is independent of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), in the case of a word, it is dependent on linguistic convention.
Furthermore, for a word whose nature is luminosity, its correspondence or non-correspondence with reality depends upon the qualities or defects of the speaker.

For this very reason, even when a statement such as "a hundred elephants are situated on the tip of a finger" is sublated, a delusion persists as long as it is uttered again and again, because its nature as luminosity has not departed.
But this is not a fault of the word.
But for one who prattles on without considering the connection between the meanings of words, this is merely the speaker's own error; the word itself is not at fault here. //43//

Thus it has been said: "In this case, what is sublated is the perception [obtained] through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not the verbal connection (*śābda-anvaya*) itself—namely, that 'there is a hundred herds of elephants. For a person reveals his own perception to others by means of words; therefore, if that perception is defective, the verbal cognition is defective."
If it is not defective, then it is "not defective"; thus, for a person possessing qualities, the perception is non-defective, whereas for one possessing defects, it is defective.
Even that which is taught without having seen the actual object is itself a defect of the intellect.

Therefore, because they conform to the positive and negative concomitance with the qualities and defects residing in the person, the truthfulness or untruthfulness of verbal cognition is produced by those very factors.
As it has been said: "It may be true, and it may also be false."
Therefore, this lack of correspondence [to reality] belongs to the cognition because of the speaker's own deficiency;
it is not due to words themselves having an inherent inability to touch upon their objects. (44)
As for that lack of contact with the object which was asserted on the grounds of the exclusion of the referents of words such as "birth" (jāti) and so forth, that shall be refuted later. //45//
Regarding the matter of how verbal testimony possesses the status of a means of valid cognition, the Jaiminīyas first establish this foundational framework. (46)
Whether validity or invalidity pertains to all cognitions, let it first be investigated whether it arises intrinsically or extrinsically. (47)

Now, one might object: at the occasion of investigating the validity of verbal testimony (*śabda*), what is the relevance of an investigation into the validity of all means of knowledge? [The answer is: It is not an independent examination, but rather for that very purpose, because they share a common path.
Just as the validity of other [means of knowledge] is either intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*), so too will it be for verbal testimony;
for its validity is not dissimilar to its own nature.

That is now stated: regarding the validity and invalidity of cognitions, are both of these intrinsic (*svataḥ*), or are both extrinsic (*parataḥ*), or is invalidity intrinsic while validity is extrinsic, or rather is validity intrinsic while invalidity is extrinsic?
In this regard, it is first of all untenable that both [validity and invalidity] are intrinsic (*svataḥ*), because we observe a discrepancy in what has been set in motion.

For if validity or its opposite were apprehended by the cognition itself as being intrinsic, then when the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is apprehended either as valid or otherwise, it would be contradicted once its status as valid is determined; how then could one proceed toward it if its invalidity were already grasped? //48//
By this, the third position is also refuted— that invalidity is intrinsic while validity is extrinsic—
for if invalidity were determined to be intrinsic, purposeful activity would not be possible. Furthermore, invalidity depends upon defects in the causal instruments at the time of its production.
Certainty depends upon a sublating cognition;
how, then, could that [certainty] exist by itself? Furthermore, as for what some say—that "invalidity does not arise from a defect in the cause because it is not a real entity"—that too is trivial.
Since invalidity, consisting of doubt and error, is a real entity, the invalidity inherent in it is likewise necessarily a real entity.
However, how extrinsic validity (parataḥ prāmāṇyam) is untenable will now be explained in detail.
And in this way, since both [of these] are extrinsic (*parataḥ*), the refutation of the second position will also be established.
For it has been stated that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which reveals the true nature of an object;
its validity consists in its non-deviation from its own object of cognition.
And therefore, it would be appropriate to say "from another" only if there were dependence upon another;
yet no such dependence upon another exists for this [consciousness] anywhere.

For that [validity], when it comes into being, must either arise at the time of its production, at the time of performing its own function, or at the time of the ascertainment of its validity. If it arises at the time of production, does it depend merely on the nature of the causal factors (*kāraka*), or does it depend on excellences (*guṇa*) residing in those factors beyond their mere nature? If it depends merely on the nature of the causal factors, then one is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatvam*); for since the effect—namely, cognition—cannot come into existence in the absence of causal factors, whose validity or invalidity could possibly be considered? Furthermore, dependence on excellences residing in those factors beyond their nature is difficult to maintain;
because excellences in the causes lack any basis in valid cognition, their form is like that of a sky-lotus, and thus they cannot be objects of dependence.
Perception that apprehends the qualities of a cause is not possible;
since the eyes and other sense organs are beyond direct perception, how could their qualities be perceptible? (49)
Furthermore, a mark whose relationship [to the object] has not been perceived cannot serve as an inferential indicator for them;
rather, the establishment of the cognition of the object arises solely from a faultless causal agent. (50)

For if there were some effect called "apprehension" that was devoid of the two forms—namely, being in accordance with reality and not being in accordance with reality—then, due to the threefold nature of effects, a threefold nature of causes would necessarily be determined: a cause accompanied by excellence (*guṇa*) for apprehension in accordance with reality; a cause defiled by defects (*doṣa*) for apprehension not in accordance with reality; and for that [apprehension] which is devoid of both, a cause established in its own essential nature.
But this is not the case.
This apprehension is indeed twofold, distinguished by being either in accordance with reality or not in accordance with reality.
In that regard, an apprehension that does not correspond to the object is seen to be the effect of defective causal factors alone.

Just as the production of a crooked jar and the like is seen to arise from a defective cause, so too does the cognition of two moons arise from cataracts and other defects known through other means of knowledge. //51//

Furthermore, since the apprehension of an object as it is not (ayathārtha) is established as being the effect of defective causal factors (kāraka), and since there is now no third type of effect, the apprehension of an object as it is (yathārtha) is accounted for by the causal factors themselves remaining in their natural state; thus, it does not necessitate the postulation of "excellence" (guṇa).

Furthermore, in the case of inference, it is precisely that same collection of factors—such as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—which produces the cognition that is observed to be the cause of its validity. And causes that exist in their own nature do not remain indifferent toward the production of their effect; for if they did, one would have to postulate the operation of "excellences" (*guṇa*) in them for the sake of producing a cognition that accords with reality. Therefore, there are no such causal excellences.

The designation of "purity" regarding the eyes and so forth is based solely on the removal of defects such as cataracts and jaundice, and not from the presence of any quality distinct from their own nature.
Even the application of collyrium and the like is for the purpose of eliminating defects, not for the production of a new quality.

Therefore, consciousness that arises from the cause of abiding in its own nature is non-erroneous; however, by those very same [causes], when accompanied by an excess of defects, a distorted cognition is produced. //52//
For this very reason, its lack of validity is accepted as extrinsic; it depends upon defects for its arising and upon a sublater for its own ascertainment. (53)
Therefore, with respect to its origination, a means of valid cognition does not depend upon auxiliary qualities.
Nor does it depend on anything else for the performance of its own function, because it arises from its own cause as having the very nature of illuminating an object.
And the illumination of the object alone is the function of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since activity and so forth are dependent upon the desire of the person.
Either knowledge does not arise at all, or it arises as something that illuminates; in the illumination of an object, it requires nothing else once it has arisen. //54//
And so it has been said: "In its production, a jar depends upon clay, a staff, a wheel, a string, and so forth;
but in its function of carrying water, it has no dependence on those."
Alternatively, even a jar has some degree of dependence with respect to the fetching of water; however, such [dependence] is not at all possible for a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). //55//

Furthermore, cognition does not reveal its object by depending upon the apprehension of itself; for even when that [cognition] is not cognized, the object is established, just as in the case of the eye and other sense organs. //56//
And it has been said: "For no one perceives cognition with respect to an object that is unknown; rather, once the object is known, one understands [the cognition] through inference.
Therefore, even in the performance of its own effect, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) does not depend upon the apprehension of itself.

The ascertainment of validity is not dependent on any cause other than the causal complex of its own nature; nor does it require anything else for the ascertainment of validity, because there is nothing further to be required. To explain: the ascertainment of validity would have to arise either from the cognition of the excellence of its causes, or from the cognition of the absence of sublation, or from correspondence. It cannot arise from the cognition of the excellence of its causes, because the excellences of the causes have just now been refuted.

Furthermore, the cognition of the excellence of the cause (*kāraṇaguṇajñāna*) does not have the sense organs as its instrument, because the excellences (*guṇa*), being located in a supersensible causal factor, are themselves beyond the senses.
Rather, the nature of excellence is to be apprehended through the purification of the effect known as "cognition" (*upalabdhi*).
And for a cognizer who has not yet acted, there can be no purification of the effect.

Now, would this activity (*pravṛtti*) occur only after the certainty of validity (*prāmāṇya-niścaya*) has been established? Or otherwise, if activity is accomplished from a cognition whose validity is not yet ascertained, what is the purpose of that ascertainment later on? However, if activity occurs only when validity is ascertained, there is the unavoidable fall of the saw of a vicious circle (*cakraka*): once activity has occurred, there is the apprehension of the success of the result; from the apprehension of the success of the result, there is the understanding of the excellence of the cause; from the understanding of the excellence of the cause, there is the ascertainment of validity; and from the ascertainment of validity, activity [occurs].
Nor is the ascertainment of validity [attained] through the determination of the absence of sublation;

for that [determination] might occur either at that time or at another time. A [determination] occurring at that time is not sufficient for the complete ascertainment of validity, because in the case of counterfeit coins and the like, even though no sublation has arisen for some time, its arising is observed at a later time.
But the perpetual absence of that [omniscience] is not within the scope of one who is not omniscient. //57//

[The ascertainment of validity does not arise even from corroboration. Now, if it is argued that the ascertainment of validity arises from corroboration (*saṃvāda*), then let it be stated: what is this so-called "corroboration"? Is it merely a subsequent cognition regarding that same object, or is it a cognition of another object, or rather a cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*)? In the first case, what distinction is there between the preceding and the subsequent cognitions such that, by virtue of the subsequent cognition's corroboration, each preceding cognition should attain validity? [Validity must simply be accepted as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*) in some cases or others. Moreover, if the status of being a means of valid cognition for each preceding instance were due to the corroboration of a subsequent one—
Even speaking for hundreds of eons, they would not reach the end. //58//
Even if one goes to the furthest extent, if the validity of anything whatsoever is asserted as being intrinsic, why is there such hostility toward the first [instance]? (59)
As it has been said: "If it is maintained that for some [cognition] validity exists by its very own nature, then what is the basis for hostility toward the first [cognition] being likewise?"
Thus [it is said].
Now, if it is argued that the cognition of one object is the corroboration of another, that is incorrect because it is not observed;
for the cognition of a pillar is not the corroboration of the cognition of a jar.

Now, if it is claimed that the validity of the first cognition, which prompts activity, is established through correspondence with a cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), then how can that [second cognition], whose own validity remains unascertained, cause one to understand the validity of the first? Furthermore, what is the distinction between a cognition of purposeful action and its predecessor, such that the ascertainment of the latter’s validity depends upon the former? If it is argued that the distinction lies simply in being a cognition of purposeful action, then surely the initial cognition of water—which is seen to prompt activity toward the rays of the sun even when no water is present—cannot be a ground for trust.

Furthermore, the claim that this experience of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)—which arises for one standing in the midst of water regarding objects such as drinking or bathing—and which, because its deviation is not perceived, serves to determine its validity, is incorrect; for even in dreams, deviation is observed in the case of drinking and bathing.
Furthermore, even the emission of the final element occurs in a dream without a woman; thus, this is a great deviation [from the rule].

If it is argued that there is no deviation from its own cause because the emission of semen is caused by an excess of passion (*rāga*) or by a disorder of the bodily humors (*dhātu*) such as bile (*pitta*), that is incorrect; for it is established that it is the effect of that [passion], since it follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of embracing a young woman and other such acts, which have been experienced repeatedly.
Therefore, because the deviation of the cognition of purposeful action must be ascertained, the infinite regress does not cease during the examination of its validity. //60//

Alternatively, since the fruit has already been attained, what is the use of investigating its validity? Even in the first case, since one has already engaged [in the action], what is the use of investigating its validity? //61//
Furthermore, this cognition of purposeful efficacy does not arise for a person who has not yet engaged in activity.

In that case, if activity is preceded by the ascertainment of validity, the problem remains exactly as it was: the consequence of the circular argument (cakraka) and the saw-like dilemma (kakaca-codya) regarding the investigation of validity based on the determination of the excellence of the causes.

However, it has been stated that for one whose validity is not yet ascertained, even if that ascertainment occurs after the activity has begun, it is as fruitless as examining the constellations after one has already had one's hair shaved.
Thus it may be said: activity is indeed twofold—namely, the initial and the habitual.
Of these, the initial is like the sowing of a few seeds in a shallow bowl containing smooth clay moistened with poured water, for the purpose of testing the potency of rice and other seeds.
Then, observing their unimpaired skill in producing sprouts therein, farmers sow those seeds in the fields without hesitation; this is the habitual activity.

Likewise here as well, even a wise person, acting on the basis of some cognition whose status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been initially examined, and perceiving its validity in the resulting cognition of the respective fruit, will—when a similar [subsequent] cognition arises—easily engage in activities such as purposeful action without suspecting any impurity; thus, it is not entirely useless.
It is said: This analogy is uneven; for if a seed can be known as belonging to that same class, then it is reasonable to act toward it with certainty and without hesitation. (62)

The state of being of that kind [i.e., being of the nature of cognition] in knowledge, however, is to be understood either from its effect or from its cause, and not from its own essential nature (svarūpataḥ). //63//
Because causes are imperceptible, their comprehension does not occur through verbal testimony;
rather, it has been explained that an effect cannot come into being for one who has not acted. //64//
Therefore, this is not the method for refuting the charge of futility;
and in this way, what kind of certainty regarding validity could there be from the cognition of purposeful action? (65)

Even he who asserts that the ascertainment of validity arises from the knowledge of a capable cause is like one who, having already performed the wedding ceremony, examines the auspicious moment for the marriage.

In a certain garden where swarms of bees were delighted by drinking the nectar of fully blossomed flowers, while a lute was being played, the performer—his body concealed by a dense thicket of creepers—was not visible from afar; thus, the perception of the sound of the lute was marred by the doubt that it might be the humming of a bee. A listener, moving directly toward that sound, once the performer entered his field of vision, determines the validity [of the perception] because the doubt regarding the cognition has ceased through the ascertainment of the cause consistent with the specific notes. This is the determination of validity produced by the knowledge of the efficient cause (*samarthakāraṇajñānakṛta-prāmāṇyaniścaya*).

Even in that case, there is no observation of the causal capacity for one who has not yet acted; and if action occurs in this very manner, what is the use of that [capacity] even when it is ascertained? (67)
Or, if activity occurs because of that ascertainment, there would be a mutual dependence:
activity would arise from the ascertainment of it, and the ascertainment of it would arise from the activity. (68)

Thus, since there is no determination of validity from any source whatsoever—due to the fact that it remains free from such defects as circularity, mutual dependence, infinite regress, and futility—a means of valid cognition requires nothing else even for the determination of its own validity.

Therefore, because it is independent in its origination, in its performing its own function, and in the determination of its own validity, and because it is devoid of the three types of dependence, it is established that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*).
As it has been said: "Let it be understood that the validity of all means of valid cognition is intrinsic."
For a capacity that does not exist inherently cannot be produced by another.

Invalidity, however, is extrinsic (*parataḥ*) both in its origination—because it depends on defects—and in its own ascertainment—because it depends on subverting cognitions and the like; this has already been stated.
Therefore, since the other two positions are untenable, this fourth position alone is superior: that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) and invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
But surely, at the moment of its arising, the distinction between what is a valid means of knowledge and what is otherwise is not determined; therefore, by force of circumstances, doubt arises. (69)

The function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is mere determination (*paricchitti*). And this [function] has a nature common to both the cognition of an object as it is and its opposite. Furthermore, it is a well-known principle that the apprehension of a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is a cause of doubt.

This being the case, how can there be a determination of what is valid or invalid without corroboration by another means of knowledge or its lack thereof? Therefore, both [validity and invalidity] are extrinsic (*parataḥ*). //70//
This is not tenable.
It is true that the very function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the determination of reality;
however, since that [determination], as it arises, is perceived as having its nature untainted by doubt and the like, it possesses validity as a general rule (*autsargika*).

Furthermore, when a cognizer acts upon the determination of an object, he is impelled by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) itself, and not acting out of doubt. This being the case, while validity is the general rule, its exception occurs in certain instances where invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) arises.
And when there is invalidity, a sublation (apavāda) necessarily occurs.
Sublation is of two kinds: a sublating cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya) and the knowledge of a defect in the cause (kāraṇa-doṣa-jñāna).
As stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "That alone is an incorrect cognition in which the instrument is defective or in which there is a cognition that 'this is false'; it is nothing else."

The author of the Vārttika also says: "Therefore, the validity of cognition, which is attained by virtue of its nature as consciousness, is set aside by the knowledge of a defect arising from a cause that results in the object being otherwise."

In that case, since the first cognition arises regarding that very object precisely by way of subverting the preceding cognition, it is clearly sublated because they possess the same objective domain.

However, the knowledge of a defect in the instrument (karaṇadoṣajñāna), even though it has a different object, functions as a sublater because of the identity of the effect. For example, the rule "one fetches water with a *camasa* (ladle)" makes the *camasa* a means for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), since it is an auxiliary to the New and Full Moon sacrifices; whereas the rule "one who desires cattle should fetch water with a cow’s udder" makes the cow’s udder a means for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), since it results in the desired cattle. Thus, although the *camasa* and the cow’s udder have different objects by virtue of being for the sake of the sacrifice and for the sake of the person respectively, they share the single effect called "fetching water. Consequently, when that effect is accomplished by means of the cow’s udder, the *camasa* is set aside.

Thus, in this context, the knowledge of a defect in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣajñāna*), although its object is the defect itself, subverts the validity of that [primary] cognition because defects have the nature of producing cognitions that do not correspond to reality.

As it has been said: "But when the awareness of a defective cause arises—even if it concerns a different object—it subverts [the primary cognition] by reaching, through implication, a state of having the same object, as in the case of the *godohana* vessel and so forth."
Furthermore, where even these two types of exception are not observed, there the general validity remains uncontradicted; thus, there is no ground whatsoever for a suspicion of falsity.
As it has been said: "As long as the cognition of a defect has not arisen, the absence of validity should not be suspected."
For instance, there certainly exists here a doubt that is self-evident as soon as it arises—such as "Is this a post or a person?"—who indeed could deny that? (71)
But when [the mind] is produced by force, it destroys all ritual actions;
even in the embrace of one's own wife, there would be the suspicion that she is one's mother.
"Even the son of Parāśara has declared that one of a doubting mind is subject to destruction:
'Neither this world nor the next exists for one whose soul is filled with doubt, O son of Kuntī. (73)
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, even in cases where doubt arises regarding a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), there is no infinite regress because a third cognition is required [to resolve it].
Nor is the intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) thereby lost.
Where a third cognition arises that corroborates the first cognition, the inherent validity of the first remains established as its natural state.

However, the removal of the suspicion regarding the impurity of the letter *li* superimposed by the second cognition is performed by the third [cognition], but its validity does not derive from correspondence.
If, however, the third cognition corroborates the second cognition, then the first cognition is invalid;
and that [invalidity] is indeed accepted as extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

But the validity of the second cognition is not produced by the corroboration of the third; rather, the function of the third is merely to perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) that removes the suspicion regarding the possibility of error.
And it has been said: "Thus, no higher cognition is required beyond the production of three or four cognitions;
by that much alone, a single [cognition] attains its own intrinsic validity."

Thus, when it is established that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possess intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), by the same logic, the validity of verbal testimony (*śabda*) likewise follows. Furthermore, it has been examined that it is not the inherent nature of a word to be non-conformable with its object; rather, since it generates the cognition of an object, it possesses intrinsic validity, and any occasional distortion is caused by the intrusion of human defects.
As it has been said: "It is established that the arising of defects in a word depends upon the speaker."

In that regard, when the human word possesses excellence and the speaker likewise possesses excellence, its intrinsic validity remains unrefuted because defects have been removed by those excellences.
However, that validity is not produced by excellences, for excellences are not a constituent factor in validity;
it has been stated that validity is based solely on the capacity to produce cognition.

In the case of the Veda, however, because there is no person who composed it, even the suspicion of defects does not arise, since defects depend upon a speaker. Furthermore, no subverting cognition regarding the meaning of the Veda has arisen for anyone up to the present day; thus, the authority of the Veda is beyond reproach. And it has been said: "In that case, the absence of subversion is easily established due to the non-existence of a speaker."
"By that [means], the Veda does not incur the suspicion of being invalid."
This has been stated: "That is authoritative according to Bādarāyaṇa, because it is independent."
Since defects that cause falsehood in words reside in persons, it is logical to declare that which is not of human origin (apauruṣeya) to be of true meaning. //74//
However, they consider it illogical to claim that human speech possesses true meaning because its qualities—which are the causes of truthfulness—reside in the person [who utters it]. (75)
For the truthfulness of human qualities does not constitute a means of establishing the truth of a statement; indeed, the establishment of truth arises from the very nature of the words themselves.
Those who know the qualities maintain that even a quality of human speech has its function fulfilled merely by suppressing the defects that cause distortion. //76//

The commencement of the proof for extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*) is stated here: regarding those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception whose objects are directly perceived, since worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is established even without the ascertainment of their validity, we have no need for an inquiry as to whether their validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*); in that case, non-determination is preferable. However, regarding the unseen domain (*adṛṣṭa-viṣaya*), such as Vedic rituals which are accomplished through hardships like the distribution of vast amounts of wealth, it is improper for discerning persons (*prekṣāvat*) to engage in them without first ascertaining their validity; therefore, the determination of their validity must necessarily be performed.
In this regard, we shall explain that the authority of the Veda arises solely from something external.
That which has been established here at such length regarding the intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇyam*) must now be explained.
What is the meaning of "intrinsic validity"? Does the validity of a means of knowledge arise from itself alone, or does that very means of knowledge apprehend its own validity?

First of all, the apprehension of validity by the cognition itself is not tenable, because it lacks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain: when this perception is engaged in the manifestation of blue, we certainly know that it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to that blue, insofar as it has arisen from the contact of the sense organ with its object; this much is not to be questioned here. However, regarding the determination of its validity, one must consider what the means of cognition for that is—either perception or inference, since other means of cognition are not to be suspected [in this context].
To begin with, perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for determining its own validity; for it would have to grasp either the validity of the cognition itself or that of its result.

In this regard, since according to your view cognition—which consists of the activity of the knower—is eternally imperceptible, it is impossible for perception to determine it intrinsically (*svataḥ*); how then could its validity be grasped by perception?

Furthermore, the result—consisting of the cognition itself, which is termed the "manifestation of the object"—possesses no capacity for contact with the sense organ; therefore, even the validity characterized by "correspondence to the object" (yathārthatva) residing therein could not be determined by a perception produced through the operation of the sense organ.

Nor can it be maintained that even mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) is capable of determining the correspondence with reality (*yathārthatā*) residing in the result, because at that time [the object] is not being experienced.

Indeed, immediately after the arising of the cognition of blue, no further cognition is experienced such that one would think, "This cognition of blue is in accordance with reality. Or, if such a [second] experience were admitted, then because the correspondence of the first-arisen cognition of blue would be apprehended by that second [cognition], the determination of validity could not be *svataḥ* (intrinsic).
Therefore, this is not an object of direct perception.

By means of inference as well, it must be stated as before: of what is validity determined—of the cognition or of the result? First, we do not perceive anything that could serve as a mark (*liṅga*) for the determination of that [result]. As for cognition, which consists in the activity of the knower, its own effect might indeed be a mark; however, because the apprehension of the mere pervasion of the action [of cognition] with the result is capable of inferring only the existence of the cognition's own nature, it is not capable of inferring validity characterized by "conformity with reality" (*yathārthatva*).

For that result would either, without qualification, lead to the inference of validity for its own cause—the cognitive operation—or as qualified by its correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*). In the first case, if its validity were inferred from any result whatsoever, then nothing at all would now be invalid. Nor is the latter position tenable, as it has already been stated that there is no means for determining the correspondence with reality residing in the result.
But surely, one’s own experience (*svānubhava*) alone is the means here. For that [experience], as the cognition of blue, shines forth by itself as the fruit;

and its very nature as the cognition of blue is its "conformity with reality" (*yathārthatva*), and nothing else. If this is so, then the same logic applies even to the cognition of silver in the case of mother-of-pearl;
for there is no cognition of conformity with reality other than the cognition of silver itself.
But surely, in those cases, the status of being non-correspondent to reality (*ayathārthatva*) is brought about by the occurrence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*).

Indeed, such a subverting cognition occurs in the case of false perceptions, or in the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell in another place, or in the perception of a counterfeit *kārṣāpaṇa* coin at another time, or in the perception of two moons in another person suffering from ophthalmia, or in the appearance of a yellow conch-shell in another state.
It has already been stated that when such a [subverting cognition] is absent, it is not reasonable to entertain such a doubt.
What has been said is true, but it is incorrect.
For by speaking thus, you have asserted that validity (prāmāṇya) is dependent upon the knowledge of the absence of sublation;
and it has been demonstrated that this [dependence], whether conceived as existing at that same time or at a later time, is not tenable.
Therefore, it is not logical to claim that a means of valid cognition, at the very moment it arises, determines its own validity.
If, however, we were to ascertain the validity of knowledge at the very moment of its arising, then, proceeding from it, we would never be deceived; yet we are indeed deceived.
Therefore, we consider that its validity is not ascertained, and we engage in worldly activity only out of doubt.

But surely, at that time, even doubt is not experienced at all—[in the form] "Is this silver, or is it not silver?"—but rather the cognition is simply "this is silver. For ordinary people do not act while doubting, but only when they have reached a certainty. Is it then the case that doubt, which is not being experienced, is superimposed? This cognition, although grasping only one side, necessarily falls within the scope of doubt because of the absence of any means for certain determination; it is just as beggars think, "There is water in the well," [even though they have not seen it].
Thus, even though the appearance at that time grasps a single side—namely, "this is silver"—in reality it is nothing but doubt.

For if it were grasped as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how could it ever fail to correspond with reality? But if it is grasped as an invalid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), how could it prompt a person to act? If there is no apprehension of it in either of these two forms, then this must indeed be doubt; so why are you angry with us? (77)

As for the claim that doubt is not experienced, this is true; yet even when not being experienced, that doubt is postulated through reasoning because, in the case of a familiar object, there is a recollection of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), since at that time the cause for certain determination is absent and the causal complex for generating doubt is present.
For instance, just as the common property of being of the nature of cognition—like height and so forth—is indeed manifest at that time with respect to both the actual object and its opposite.

Furthermore, at that time, no particular feature invariably concomitant with validity appears. And if that [feature] is not apprehended, then the recollection of particulars experienced in other instances associated with it—which is dependent on the latent impressions (vāsanā) awakened by the perception of common properties—is indeed possible. Since this entire causal complex for generating doubt is thus present, how could the doubt produced by it not arise? [Objection: But surely, as soon as a cognition arises that is valid, the particularity inherent in it flashes forth; so how can you say there is a non-apprehension of the particular? [Reply: O Great-souled one, let that particularity be described!
For we, being of dull intellect, do not understand that which has not been explained.
If clarity is the distinguishing feature, then even the appearance of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is indeed clear; for there is no turbidity of non-determination whatsoever present therein.
Now, as for immovability: even in the case of mother-of-pearl, the appearance of silver is indeed immovable;
for it does not arise while trembling, like the cognition produced by the statement "the tip of a finger" and so forth.
Now, even in the case of mother-of-pearl, the appearance as silver is indeed free from doubt, because there is no consideration of the two alternatives such as "what could this possibly be?"
Furthermore, regarding the claim that "sublation is not observed when this [condition] exists," since sublation is observed in every state,
no distinction can be shown even after reflecting upon it for a long time.
Furthermore, it has been stated that even if non-deviation from its own object is indeed the distinguishing feature, it does not manifest at that time.

Moreover, if such a distinguishing feature exists, then why would one act upon a cognition in which it is not perceived? Or, how could one who acts while perceiving that distinguishing feature be deceived? Thus it was said.

Just as in the case of the doubt regarding whether something is a post or a person, even when it is not being consciously perceived at that time, there nonetheless exists within the cognition a doubt as to whether its object is real or otherwise.
Even when that [self] is postulated, it does not abolish conventional discourse, because for all embodied beings, conventional discourse is established by means of that very [self]. //78//
Therefore, for worldly people who conduct their affairs based on doubt alone, one should not utter a succession of curses. //79//
Nor do we insist that doubt must be established in every respect;
rather, our position is that validity cannot be apprehended at the time of the cognition's arising.
We shall designate this very non-apprehension of validity—which is by nature a lack of ascertainment—as "doubt" here.

Furthermore, the non-apprehension of validity has been demonstrated, because it is impossible for a cognition to determine its own validity by means of either perception or inference, which are themselves existing means of valid cognition.
Therefore, this position—that validity is apprehended by itself—is untenable.
Now, if this position is adopted—that validity is intrinsic—that too is untenable.
Because effects depend upon causes for their birth, and because validity is an effect;
and since validity exists as a real entity and is not eternal, it must indeed be an effect.
And an effect, by virtue of being an effect, cannot exist of itself.

Now, as for the claim that the self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of validity consists simply in its not depending on any quality (*guṇa*) beyond its own causes at the time of its production—and not in its being unproduced at all—that too is incorrect; for a correct effect cannot be produced apart from causes possessed of qualities.
An effect is of two kinds: either correct or incorrect.
Among these, a correct effect is produced by a cause endowed with qualities, whereas an incorrect one is produced by a cause endowed with defects (*doṣa*).
A cause that is either devoid of defects or devoid of qualities does not exist at all;
for this very reason, there is no possibility of a third kind of effect.

The probandum (sādhya) property is that the producer which generates right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) requires its own inherent properties distinct from the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) in order to accomplish its effect, because it is a producer (*kārakatva*), like a producer that generates false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). Alternatively, the probandum property is that right knowledge is connected with properties distinct from the nature of the substratum and is produced by a producer, because it is an effect (*kāryatva*), like false knowledge.
We understand the qualities of the sense organs from the tradition of Ayurveda;
for when these physicians prescribe the use of medicine for one in good health, it is solely for the purpose of enhancing those qualities and not for the pacification of defects.
And indeed, an excellence of the sense organs is observed to result from the use of the medicines they have prescribed.
Moreover, in common worldly usage, the designation "purity" (nairmalya) refers precisely to that [object], and does not rest merely on the absence of defects; so enough with this further scrutiny.
Therefore, what was stated—that intrinsic validity (svataḥprāmāṇya) exists because there is no dependence on qualities (guṇa) for its production—is incorrect.
Furthermore, as for the claim that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is independent of anything else in performing its own function, that too must be explained:
is it the *pramāṇa* itself that is independent in performing its function, or the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or a particular part thereof, or the cognition produced by it?
In this regard, it is true that the causal complex possesses independence (*nairapekṣya*) in the production of its own effect;
however, valid cognition does not arise from itself (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), because the determination of that [validity] depends upon something else.
It is unavoidable that a causal factor included within a causal complex must depend upon others for its own effect, because an effect cannot be produced from a single causal factor alone.
It has been stated that knowledge is indeed the result (*phala*) and not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, for that [knowledge] which consists of the result, there is no further effect of its own upon which one might consider whether it is dependent or independent.
As for human activity and so forth, however, dependence upon the person's desire and other factors certainly exists; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
Furthermore, as for the claim that there is independence regarding the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇya*), that too is not correct.

For the ascertainment of validity follows one of two paths: either its non-existence or its dependence upon causes; it cannot be said that the ascertainment of validity both exists and is independent of causes.
In this regard, it has already been stated that at the time of the arising of the initial manifesting appearance, there is simply no ascertainment of validity.
For it is not possible for a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends blue to determine its own validity at that very time in the same way it determines the nature of the blue object.

While it is true that there is a determination of its validity at a later time, there is no independence [from external factors] in that regard, because such a determination depends upon the efficacy of successful action (pravṛtti-sāmarthya).

[Objection: But surely, because of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), at a later time the cognition itself no longer exists; of what, then, do we ascertain the validity? [Reply: This is a mere cry of the hare (*śaśa-codya*). For of what do we ascertain invalidity either, by means of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) or the like, at a later time? Since the cognition has passed away due to its momentariness. [Objection: [We ascertain it] of the cognition that is being remembered even though it has passed away, or of the present collection of causal factors (*kāraka-cakra*) that produced it. [Reply: If this is so, then this same path applies equally to the ascertainment of validity as well.

Furthermore, as for the argument previously described—that determining validity at a later time leads either to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) or to futility (*vaiyarthyam*), like searching for constellations on a shaven head—it is not the case that there is mutual dependence or circularity (*cakrakam*), because we accept that in the case of an unperceived object, purposeful activity is preceded by the ascertainment of validity.

For in the case of a perceived object, people are seen to initiate worldly activity in the form of engagement due to doubt regarding the object’s existence, and in the form of desisting due to doubt regarding its non-existence, even while the validity [of their cognition] remains undetermined.
It has been stated that this alone is logical—that activity does not precede the ascertainment of validity; for how could there be mutual dependence?

Futility is indeed accepted as true when the object is perceptible; however, in that case, while determining validity through the capacity for successful action, one understands the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason "being spoken by a reliable person" (*āptoktatva*) with validity. Thus, there is no fault in the fact that it serves indirectly in the determination of the validity of the means of knowledge such as the Vedas, which have imperceptible objects.

But what is this so-called "capacity for successful action" (*pravṛttisāmarthya*), on account of which the Naiyāyikas claim the ascertainment of validity? It is said that the nature of this was described by the former teachers as either "a subsequent cognition dependent upon a prior cognition" or "the perception of a specific feature. However, since that [definition] is not very convincing, the author of the Bhāṣya himself—by stating, "[Effort is called 'action' (*pravṛtti*); its capacity (*sāmarthya*), moreover, is its connection with the result]"—has determined that the "capacity for successful action" is simply the cognition of the result known as "purposeful activity" (*arthakriyā*).

Furthermore, as for the objection that there is no distinction between [the initial cognition] and the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), and that if the latter also requires a determination of its validity from another source, it leads to an infinite regress—that too is an incoherent statement, because it contradicts the empirical activity witnessed by the consciousness of all living beings. This is because the validity of the cognition of purposeful action does not require examination; not every cognition that prompts activity exists such that its validity must be examined for the sake of initiating action.

Regarding the cognition of the result (*phalajñāna*), however, since its purpose has already been accomplished, there is no need whatsoever for an examination of its validity; how, then, could there be an infinite regress? Or rather, due to the absence of doubt, there is no investigation into its validity. For people may have doubts regarding the initial cognition of water—such as that of the rays of the sun—even when water is not present. But the cognition of the purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) occurring for those who are actually in the midst of water is necessarily inseparable from that [initial cognition]; thus, there is no doubt in that case.
Because that [doubt] is absent, there is no investigation into its validity, since investigation is preceded by doubt.

Alternatively, the certainty regarding the validity of the knowledge of the result arises from the observation of a specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*). If it is asked, "What is this specific feature?"—it is this continuous series of various types of water-related activities: purification, sipping water, bathing, libations to gods and ancestors, washing clothes, the removal of fatigue, and recreation. Indeed, such a vast array of effects is never observed in one who has acted upon a false cognition.

If it is argued that there is even a dream-like perception of this continuum, we say no; for this is experienced as a cognition of the waking state, which is vivid and dissimilar to the state of dreaming.
