Every person, while awake, perceives directly through their non-slumbering mind that "I am awake, I am not dreaming. Furthermore, at that time, these activities are seen to proceed without water [or other external means]; thus, due to the observation of such specific characteristics, the validity of the cognition of causal efficiency (*arthakriyājñāna*) is easily understood.

Alternatively, we shall determine its validity through an examination of its causes, as you yourselves have stated: "If, while searching with diligence, we do not perceive any defect, then, due to the absence of such a cause, we shall consider it to be faultless."

For instance, the absence of defects such as instability or similarity in the object; the lack of deficiencies in causes such as turbidity in the light; the internal organ’s state of not being impaired by sleep and the like; the self’s lack of agitation from hunger, anger, and so forth; and the pair of eyes’ freedom from cataracts and other impairments—all of this is easily known both through one's own experience by way of its effects and through the instruction of others.
Therefore, we understand that the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is produced by flawless causes.

If this is so, why is this examination of the cause not performed regarding the very first impelling cognition? For what purpose [is it done] regarding the cognition of action? O Venerable One, if the examination of the cause were performed even with respect to the first cognition, what would be the error? Would intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) be established for you or me, or would extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*) be lost? Rather, the world is seen to be as diligent toward the attainment of the result following the impelling cognition as it is not toward the examination of its cause. Thus, it is the cognition of the result alone that is examined in this manner.
For the validity of the first cognition is established precisely from the resultant cognition (*phalajñāna*).
Indeed, who would neglect a proximate means and go to one that is distant?
Alternatively, by the very capacity for doubt to arise, the determination of whether [the cognition] is true or otherwise will be obtained through the resultant cognition itself.
Indeed, doubt does not arise at all without the perception of two possibilities.

For one who does not know that the property called "verticality" coexists with both a post and a person would not, upon seeing it, entertain the doubt, "Is this a post or a person? Likewise, the observation of the coexistence of the nature of consciousness with both variability and invariability must necessarily be relied upon; otherwise, no doubt regarding that object could arise.

Therefore, once it has been established that non-deviation was observed previously, whatever means of determining that [non-deviation] existed at that time will also exist later; thus, in every respect, the certainty of non-deviation is established.

Alternatively, it is logical that the validity of the impelling cognition is ascertained through the resulting cognition (*phalajñāna*), even though its validity was previously undetermined; it is not, however, intrinsic (*svataḥ*), because at the time of its production, no distinction can be perceived between a valid means of knowledge and its semblance (*pramāṇatadābhāsa*), whereas in the resulting cognition, that distinction does manifest.

As for the objection that—having proposed the alternatives of whether a specific cognition possesses ascertained validity or unascertained validity—one either incurs an infinite regress or asserts that it is defeated by non-apprehension, that is mere idle chatter because it contradicts what is observed; enough, then, with savoring the foul fragrance arising from churning the mass of conceptual constructions of such false talk.
It is established that the ascertainment of validity arises from the cognition of successful purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*).

This has been stated: "When there is comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the means of valid cognition is effective because of the efficacy of the resulting activity.
Therefore, since validity, like invalidity, is dependent on something else, this very position—that both are extrinsic (*parataḥ*)—is the most tenable one.

As for that which someone who fancies himself wise says—that there is intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) regarding a familiar object, but extrinsic validity (*parataḥ*) regarding an unfamiliar one—he speaks of "a familiar object" and yet considers its validity to be intrinsic; thus he does not realize that he is deceiving himself.
For what is called "familiarity" (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated application of an action, its recurrence, and the familiarity of an object consists in engaging with it again and again.

Therefore, it has been stated that the determination of validity occurs through the arising of a cognition of correspondence produced many times over, such as when grasping one's own body or when there is the appearance of the walls and pillars of one's own house.
Otherwise, the state of being "self-evident" (*svataḥ-abhyastatva*) would not be possible; thus, this [objection] is trivial.
Consequently, it is established that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

Furthermore, as for what is urged by some—that the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not tenable—for that examination would have to be carried out either by means of valid cognitions or by non-valid cognitions; and even if by means of valid cognitions, it would have to be by those already examined or those unexamined. In this regard, it is certainly not possible to carry out the examination of valid cognitions by means of non-valid cognitions.

If those [means of knowledge] themselves are not examined by other means of knowledge, then it is better that worldly practice be carried out using such [unexamined] instruments; what is the use of examining them? For if they were examined by others, the process of examination would be endless, leading to the fallacy of infinite regress, and so forth.
That too is refuted by the reasoning already stated:
because in the case of a perceived object, worldly transaction proceeds even without an examination by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
whereas in the case of an unperceived object, such an examination must necessarily be performed and is logically justified.

Therefore, those possessed of wisdom must necessarily examine that means of knowledge which teaches the path to the goal of human life not yet seen; as for the claim that its validity is established extrinsically, enough with these nets of false conceptualizations that agitate the mind. (81)

Those who are well-trained say this is appropriate: that these wretched Mīmāṃsakas, like heaps of kāśa flowers in autumn, are driven far away by great and wicked logicians. For how could there be any skill in those who, while indeed accepting the theory of erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*), also claim that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*)? Since they accept erroneous cognition, there is an abundance of instances of sublated cognitions; and because of the similarity to those cases, doubt is unavoidable even in a cognition where no sublation has yet arisen.
Furthermore, since the investigation of corroboration and so forth necessarily follows upon doubt, the extrinsic nature of validity (parataḥ prāmāṇya) is unavoidable.

But when there is no cognition whatsoever in the world that is sublated, then on what basis of similarity could cognizers doubt? And being free from doubt, why would they depend upon another? Not depending [on another], how could they establish validity through something else? Thus, validity remains firmly established as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

But how can it be that there is no such thing as sublation? For cognitions of silver and the like regarding mother-of-pearl and so forth are seen to be frequently sublated. You are ignorant of the nature of sublation; for those cognitions are not actually sublated by you.
Let this be considered: what indeed is the sublation (*bādha*) of a prior cognition by a subsequent cognition? We do not even know the meaning of "sublation.

If, first of all, sublation were simply destruction, that would not be the case, because for those cognitions there is no contradiction with another cognition, as [destruction] is common to all awarenesses.
Furthermore, as for the impossibility of coexistence, that too applies equally, because even for cognitions that are not sublated, coexistence is impossible.

Now, the destruction of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) is what constitutes sublation (*bādha*); yet that too is just like the other case, for we observe the destruction of even those impressions produced by a correct cognition.

Furthermore, some impression—though deposited by a cognition you consider to be sublated—does not undergo destruction even when a sublating cognition occurs, because we observe the recollection of that object caused by it at a later time.
Now, as for the removal of the object being sublation, that too is difficult to establish;
for it is impossible to remove an object from its state of having appeared,
since a subverting cognition does not arise in such a manner as to say, "That which appeared did not appear."

Now, if the apprehension of its absence is the sublation, does that occur at that same time or at another time? If the apprehension of its absence occurring at another time were the sublater, it would follow that even a cognition grasping the absence of a jar that was previously shattered by a hammer would be a sublater of that [prior cognition].

If, at that very time, there is the apprehension of its absence, then because it possesses two forms presented by two cognitions, let the object be of a dual nature; what then could be sublated by what? Or, if sublation is defined as the deprivation of the result, that too is impossible, because the cognition—which is the fruit of the means of knowledge—having already arisen, cannot be deprived.
For a sublater does not say of what has arisen that "it has not arisen."
Now, sublation (bādha) is the removal of a result such as [the cognition of] annihilation and so forth, because that [result] lacks the status of being the fruit of a means of valid cognition.
For conventional usage such as "abandonment" and so forth is based on human intention;
by that [usage], neither is the object removed, nor does a means of valid cognition become sublated. //82//
Therefore, there is no such thing as "sublation" (bādha).
Furthermore, it does not exist.

For that [simultaneous cognition] is held to occur either between two cognitions having the same object or between two having different objects; yet it does not occur between those with the same object, because it is not observed in the case of successive streams of cognition (*dhārāvāhijñāna*).
Nor does it occur between those with different objects, because it is not observed in the perception of a pillar and a jar.

Furthermore, if by a subsequent cognition an object different from the one grasped by a preceding cognition is now apprehended, why is that preceding cognition said to be sublated? Moreover, when the preceding cognition has already attained its established status, it is the incoming subsequent cognition that ought to be sublated, not the former; yet this is not observed to be the case.
Therefore, there is no such thing as a "sublatable" consciousness. In the absence of such a consciousness, doubt based on similarity to it cannot exist.
Because that [correspondence] is absent, there is no search for corroboration and so forth; thus, validity is not extrinsic.

Now, if sublation is thus refuted, one might ask: "Do these erroneous cognitions apprehending silver in mother-of-pearl and the like remain unrefuted? O you of poor intellect, let them remain so; for we perceive no cause whatsoever for the arising of such errors.
The sense faculty alone cannot be the producer of such a cognition, because it would follow that [the cognition] must arise at all times.

Nor can it be that they are erroneous due to being defiled by defects; for a defective cause, having its power blunted precisely in the performance of its own proper effect, simply fails to produce that effect. But what power does it have to produce a contrary effect? Indeed, defective rice seeds would never possess the skill to produce barley sprouts.
Therefore, due to the absence of a cause, those cognitions cannot be erroneous.

Is it then the case that the appearance of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is itself a valid cognition? O fool, this is not a single cognition such as "this is silver"; rather, these are two: a perception and a recollection.

"This" is the appearance of the substrate (*dharmin*) present before one, characterized by its shining form; "silver," however, is a recollection of silver previously apprehended through association with it, caused by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) awakened by the sight of the shining form.

Therefore, this recollection does not arise for one who has never previously perceived silver; nor does it occur for one who has known silver, unless there is a perception of similarity [to something else] on that night or at another time.
Because this [cognition] does not manifest itself as it truly is during recollection, it is called "obscured" (*pramuṣita*).

Furthermore, since the recollection does not appear in its own essential form, the distinction between experience and recollection is not apprehended; thus, this non-apprehension is called "non-manifestation" (*akhyāti*).
For indeed, because objects appear vividly even within erroneous cognitions, a fourfold disagreement has arisen among the proponents of various doctrines. (83)
These are: erroneous cognition (viparītakhyāti), the cognition of the non-existent (asatkhyāti), the cognition of the self (ātmakhyāti), and non-cognition (akhyāti).

In this regard, erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*) is first refuted simply because its cause is absent. Furthermore, regarding erroneous cognition, there are three possible alternatives: either (1) silver from another time and place is the objective support (*ālambana*) here; or (2) mother-of-pearl, having concealed its own form and assumed the form of silver, is the support; or (3) the objective support is one thing, but something else appears. Among these, if silver were the objective support, then this would be non-existent cognition (*asatkhyāti*) rather than erroneous cognition, because the silver appearing there is non-existent.
If it is argued that it exists indeed at another place and time, then what benefit is there in its existence here [in the present] when it is not present here? (84)
Furthermore, do the place and time also appear as existing or as non-existing?
If they exist, then this silver has appeared precisely at that place and time, and thus this would not be an error.
But if both are non-existent, then like the silver, they cannot serve as the objective support (ālambana).

Now, if it is said that silver mounted upon memory flashes forth in this cognition, then what is the meaning of "mounted upon memory"? Is memory itself a form of knowledge? If so, how could even that have an unreal object as its domain?

If you argue that the very nature of memory is to be produced without an [external] object, let it be so; however, we do not say that because of its similarity to that [memory], the same [unreal] application applies here as well.
For if that were the case, how could that object be made present here by a memory that is produced without an object?
For that [cognition] does not touch the object at all;
therefore, erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*), which has as its objective support silver that is not present, is not distinguished from non-existent cognition (*asatkhyāti*) at all.

Now, if it is argued that this is not called "apprehension of the non-existent" (asatkhyāti), because a mother-of-pearl shell—having assumed the form of silver while its own body was concealed—is what appears here, then this is some unprecedented drama: "In this [instance], Sītā has appeared as a magical creation (kṛtyā)."

For instance, what is the cognition here: "this is mother-of-pearl" or "this is silver"? If it is a cognition of mother-of-pearl, then in that case, only mother-of-pearl is cognized in the mother-of-pearl, not silver; so what would be the meaning of "error"? But if it is a cognition of silver, what is the proof that "this is mother-of-pearl"? If you say, "It is understood thus from the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) itself," do not say so; for it is not proper to determine the object of this cognition by means of another cognition.
By the subverting cognition, let the non-existence of the thing grasped by the previous cognition be made known; but its object is not thereby defined.
Or, if a person does not act at any time due to a lack of desire, or if no subverting cognition arises, who will establish the object of this [erroneous] cognition?
Therefore, it is proper to say that whatever appears in this [cognition] is its object, namely the silver;
to claim that "the mother-of-pearl has its own form concealed" is merely the sophistry of the conceited.
But those who claim that in this erroneous cognition there is the apprehension of the conch-shell as the objective support and the manifestation of silver, their error is all the greater. (85)
For it is not logical that the status of being an object of cognition should be based merely on proximity;
otherwise, it would follow that the very spot of ground where one stands would likewise become an object of cognition. (86)
That very object which appears within this cognition is the objective support;
there is no such statement as that "the objective support is one thing and what appears is another. (87)

Therefore, this is indeed silver, which is grasped as real but is actually non-existent; thus, the theory of misapprehension (viparyayakhyāti) does not differ from the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti). //88//
In that case, is the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) indeed the most excellent, such that we should accept it? Not so; for even that is not tenable.

What is the meaning of "manifestation of the non-existent"? Is it the appearance of an object that is absolutely non-existent, or of one existing in another place and so forth? In the latter case, this is nothing other than the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), since others do not admit the existence of silver in that [present] location, whereas you yourself have accepted its existence in another place.
The claim that there is an appearance of this [object] despite its absolute non-existence is not sound, because things such as the sprouts of a sky-lotus never appear.

If it is argued that appearances may occur even for what is non-existent due to the habituation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), we say no; for even a latent impression is untenable without an object, since a latent impression is defined as a mental trace (*saṃskāra*) arising from the experience of an object.
How could that [consciousness] be the cause for the appearance of non-existent objects?

Let there be some other latent impression (vāsanā) favored by you; yet, since non-existence is no different [in all cases], why does it produce the cognition of silver and not the perception of a sky-lotus? From where does this restriction arise? Therefore, enough with this; the capacity of an absolutely non-existent object to bear such an unimpaired burden of worldly transaction is not conceivable.

Furthermore, because it appears as an existent entity, even the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) does not transcend the theory of erroneous manifestation (*viparītakhyāti*).

Therefore, it is better that there be self-manifestation (ātmakhyāti); for indeed, this consciousness itself grasps itself by itself, since an external object of apprehension, when investigated, is untenable. (90)
And the intellect, manifesting externally in this or that form, sustains such a worldly course here, even though it is devoid of an external object. //91//
It is said that the theory of self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*) is also not logical.
For if the nature of consciousness were to appear, the cognition would have to be "I am silver," and not "this is silver.
Furthermore, since it is accepted that "that which is an internal object of knowledge appears as if it were external," this too would simply be a case of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*).
Moreover, this non-existent manifestation (*asatkhyāti*) indeed occurs, because the external object of cognition does not exist.
If it is argued that "cognition itself exists," then its externality must be examined: is it existent or non-existent? It cannot be existent, because cognition lacks externality.
But regarding what is non-existent, it has been stated that it is the appearance of the non-existent.
Therefore, among these three theories of manifestation—which are mutually interpenetrating and logically contradictory—the most excellent is indeed non-manifestation (akhyāti). 91.
Even by those who maintain the three theories of manifestation (*khyāti*), this non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) must certainly not be rejected.

For, regarding the theory of self-manifestation (*ātmakhyāti*), it has been stated that there is no manifestation of consciousness as a self, because there is the appearance of a distinction [between subject and object].

Even in the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), the non-existence of the object does not actually appear [in consciousness], because that would entail the consequence of the cessation of all worldly activity such as purposeful action.
Even in the theory of misapprehension (viparītakhyāti), it is not accepted that a nearby piece of silver is the producer of the cognition, nor that what is not a producer appears [as such].
Therefore, in that case, it is admitted that the silver presented by the recollection of silver is what generates the comprehension;
and for this reason, the recollection of silver is unavoidable.
And that recollection of silver does not manifest at that time in its own form, because there is an absence of the cognition "I remember."
Therefore, logicians maintain that this [cognition] is a case of lost memory, just like the memory of a logical mark (liṅga) and its invariable concomitance regarding a familiar object. //93//
Thus, this loss of mindfulness, which is the non-apprehension of reality, is called *akhyāti* (non-manifestation).
This being so, this theory of non-apprehension (akhyāti) is accepted by all proponents;
yet, by making it manifest in such a manner, the Prābhākaras have swallowed their own reputation. //94//

[Objection: Let it be granted that there is no mention of the [object's] own nature (*svarūpa*) in the recollection "this is silver. However, since the substrate (*dharmin*) situated in front appears here as "this," how can this be non-apprehension (*akhyāti*)?
[Reply: It is said: the substrate situated in front is not grasped clearly as "this is mother-of-pearl" (*śuktikā*); for if that were admitted, it would follow that there could be no error at all.
Rather, only the mere substrate, characterized by qualities contrary to its true nature such as brilliance (*tejasvitā*), manifests.
Furthermore, at that time, silver is remembered because it conforms to the nature of the object [perceived].

These two—perception and memory—are indeed distinct, yet they are not grasped as being distinct; thus, non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) is the non-grasping of this distinction, rather than a total lack of cognition in every respect.
And if the heterogeneity of the perception and the memory—which belong to different loci—is not grasped, what else could constitute their homogeneity (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)?
However, there is no apprehension here through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such that "this very thing" is grasped as being "silver.

For if that were the case, it would be nothing other than the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), since the cognizer's activity would proceed precisely because the lack of coreferentiality is not grasped.
Therefore, this reasoning regarding the result—that activity proceeds due to non-discrimination (*aviveka*) and the conceit of commonality—is merely a figurative way of speaking.
Some maintain that there is also a subsequent reflective awareness (parāmarśa) occurring in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya); we do not place our trust in that. //95//
For in this way, the position of non-apprehension (akhyātipakṣa) would be abandoned due to the cognition of oneness;
moreover, false apprehension (vitathākhyāti) would be described by means of crooked syllables. //96//

Now, if the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) is thus established, how will you account for the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*)—perceived in the form "this is not silver"—which brings about the negation of the previously apprehended silver? O friend of the gods, you are ignorant of what is actually perceived!
For by this [cognition], the negation of silver is not being enjoined; rather, the distinction (*viveka*) that was previously unapprehended is being made manifest:
"This is not silver" means "that which is 'this' is indeed silver," and not "this is silver."
This is what is meant: "this is other than that silver, and that is other than this"; thus, this discrimination (viveka) is made known.
Now, let it be that in cases such as "this is silver," there is a non-apprehension of the distinction between memory and direct experience; but how will this be possible in a dream?
O timid one, what has happened? In a dream, memory and direct experience are sometimes not apprehended as distinct.
However, in a dream, it is memory alone that is not apprehended for what it truly is. (97)

If it is asked, "Whence can memory arise without the perception of something similar?", we reply: since memory has various causes, even the internal organ (antahkarana) when its fatigue is relieved by sleep certainly becomes a cause of memory.

If this is so, how can there be a "loss of memory" (*smṛtipramoṣa*) in cognitions such as those of a double moon or bitter sugar? Ah, you blockhead! How is it that you do not understand even though it has been stated repeatedly? It is not accepted that there is a loss of memory in every case; rather, it is non-apprehension (*akhyāti*). And therefore, this [non-apprehension] occurs somehow, for someone, somewhere. (98)

In some cases, there is a failure to grasp the distinction between the experience and the memory; in other cases, however, there is a failure to apprehend the object being remembered as it truly is. //99//
In some cases, the function of the eye is divided in two by cataracts and other such defects;
for [the person] is not able to perceive the moon as a single unity. (100)
In some cases, when bile is in contact with the sense of taste, because of the perception of bitterness, one is unable to discern the sweetness inherent in sugar. (101)
That which is perceived as bitterness actually exists in the bile;
yet, when swallowing sugar, he does not recognize it as such. (102)
By this, the cognitions of a yellow conch-shell and so forth are also explained.
This being so, error consists everywhere in the incorrect apprehension [of an object];
there is no false cognition whatsoever that could serve as a basis for doubt. (103)
And one who has no suspicion of falsity does not require corroboration;
therefore, no one attains validity from another. //104//
Thus, when intrinsic validity is established, that same principle applies to the Veda as well;
however, the absence of the two types of exceptions must be stated here as before. (105)
To this, the following reply is given:

What was stated—that these two cognitions, "this" and "silver," which consist respectively of memory and direct experience, are not grasped as distinct—is incorrect; for they are experienced as one, just like a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

That very same substrate (*dharmi-sāmānya*), which is present before one and possesses qualities such as a bright form, is specifically established as "silver"—just as in the perception of real silver, one thinks, "What is this standing right here? That is silver."
For it is not as something previously experienced (*anubhūtatayā*) that silver appears here, but rather as something being presently experienced (*anubhūyamānatayā*).
And the apprehension of the state of having been previously experienced is what is called "recollection" (*smaraṇa*), not the apprehension of the state of being presently experienced.
Furthermore, it is your own view that consciousness is self-luminous;
yet in this case, there is a manifestation of silver as its object.
Moreover, it is impossible for there to be a consciousness of an object that is devoid of the distinction between memory and direct experience.
Nor is it appropriate to say that this is merely a lack of cognition, because there is the experience of self-luminous awareness that is dissimilar to states such as intoxication or fainting;
just as there is self-luminous awareness regarding the aspect "this," so too is there regarding "silver."

Moreover, when the cognition of two parts is identical, from what source does this distinction arise that one is obtained through perception while the other is the fruit of memory? Furthermore, let it be examined: what is it that appears in the "this" [of the judgment]?

If the piece of mother-of-pearl appears as characterized by all its own specific qualities, then, given that perception, what occasion is there for the recollection of silver? Even if such a recollection were to occur due to similarity, it would not suffice for its non-discrimination, just like the recollection of another person similar to Devadatta that arises immediately after seeing Devadatta.
Now, it is certainly accepted that in the cognition "this," what appears is merely the substrate (*dharmin*), namely the piece of mother-of-pearl.

And this very [cognition] is the knowledge which begins with a generality and culminates in a particular—starting with "this" and ending with "silver"—caused by the recollection of a contrary particularity due to the influence of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) obstructed by the perception of a general property. This is known from the reflective judgment of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form "this is that silver.
Furthermore, it is precisely through the conceit of experiencing silver that one who desires silver proceeds toward that object.

It was stated that one acts without apprehending the distinction between non-recollection and experience; this which has been heard by you here, taken from the house of Dharmakīrti, is as follows: "One acts by unifying the perceived object and the conceptual construction."
Moreover, even this theft does not in any way nourish its own purpose;

for as long as the cognition "the visible object has been grasped" has not arisen, how could there be any activity toward it on the part of one who desires that visible object? Likewise here too, as long as the cognition "silver has been grasped" has not arisen, how can there be activity on the part of those who desire it? Therefore, there is actually a grasping of silver, and it is not merely a lapse of memory regarding that [silver].

Now, it was stated that even those who maintain the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) admit the recollection of silver. True; however, what is admitted is the recollection of the specific qualities belonging to the silver.

For just as, when an object (*dharmin*) stands before one, doubt arises from the perception of common properties such as height, from the non-perception of the specific qualities belonging to either a post or a person, and from the recollection of the specific qualities of both—so too here, from the perception of general properties such as brilliance, from the non-perception of specific qualities, and from the recollection of the specific qualities belonging to silver, there arises with respect to that object a cognition of silver whose nature is erroneous.
For while in doubt the cause is the recollection of the specific features of both [alternatives], here the distinction is that there is the recollection of the specific feature of only one;
for this very reason, this cognition does not arise for one who has not perceived silver, or when there is no perception of similarity, such as at midnight and the like.

However, one should not stop at the mere conclusion that this is simply recollection, because there is also the experience of a subversive cognition (viparyaya-pratyaya) produced by that recollection. For this very reason, those who maintain that there is a subsequent reflective awareness (parāmarśa) following it are better speakers of truth; for they do not deny the appearance itself.

As for that which was proposed as the cause for the cognition of the contrary, the authorities have already stated regarding it: "If the effect is cognized, what is the use of examining the cause? If the effect is not cognized, what is the use of examining the cause?"
Furthermore, since the accidental occurrence of an effect is untenable, a cause must be postulated;

and that cause is already established as being the sense organ itself, accompanied by defects, just as it is when assisted by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Although corrupt rice-grains do not produce barley-sprouts, they certainly generate impure products such as cakes and the like, which are the effects of rice. (106)

Therefore, from a sense organ afflicted by defects—one that lacks the skill to discern specific qualities such as triangularity residing in a subject situated before it, yet is assisted by the recollection of specific qualities belonging to another object associated with a general property—an erroneous cognition arises.
And it is called "defective" only with respect to its status as a correct cognition;
however, with respect to its own effect, which is the erroneous cognition itself, that [organ] is simply the cause and not defective.
Therefore, the experience "this is silver" is indeed a direct perception, not a case of forgotten memory.
Furthermore, this sublating cognition, "This is not silver," arises by making known the negation of the silver that was the object of a previous experience;
namely, "That which I saw is not silver.
And this negation applies to that which has been presented as a possibility.

But why is gold not also negated—just as silver is—even though it has never been experienced and is not directly perceived? As for the previous explanation that sublation (*bādhakajñāna*) consists in establishing the distinction between memory and experience when they were previously unapprehended, that is mere words, because such is not experienced;
for a sublation does not arise in the form, "That which was undistinguished is now distinguished.
Therefore, this [previous argument] is trivial.
Therefore, it is not at all extraordinary to describe this as a memory, since there was never an experience of silver, nor even a memory of silver.
As for the claim that in a dream there is a recollection of things such as the cutting off of one's own head—which have never been experienced at all—that is truly embarrassing.
If it is argued that he experienced the severing of his own head in another life, this too is a most excellent statement; for it is precisely what was experienced in another life that is recalled.
And in that regard, from where does this restriction arise, such that only at certain times is something remembered, rather than everything being remembered at all times?
Now, even by you who are refuting the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (asatkhyāti), what must be said regarding such dream-cognitions? You shall hear that very thing right there:
it is said that "the non-existent appears," but not that "the unexperienced appears."

If you ask how one knows that something is existent when it has not been experienced, [we reply: "I know it because it was experienced"—do not say this, for it was not experienced by me; it will be experienced by another.
And it is possible to say that what is experienced by another is existent.
However, since recollection of what is experienced by another is impossible, our positions regarding this matter do not share the same security or vulnerability.
Moreover, in your view, since dream-memory is not apprehended as memory, it must be considered by what form it is apprehended.
If it is apprehended by another form, that would be the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*).
But if it were not apprehended in its entirety, it would follow that there is no distinction between the states of dreaming and deep sleep.

Furthermore, since the cognition of experience is actually perceived in a dream, the claim that it is merely the non-mention of memory is nothing but a stubborn misconception; thus, what is called the "justification of the loss of memory" is entirely baseless.

Regarding cognitions such as that of two moons, how can it be said that there is non-apprehension (*akhyāti*)? Has it not been stated that the visual function, being obstructed by a cataract, is unable to grasp the moon as one? O Vedic scholar! Let such a visual function fail to grasp the oneness of the moon; but where shall we hide the erroneous experience of duality?

[Objection: But surely, that duality exists in the visual function; its non-perception as being located therein is itself the error. [Reply: This is not so, because the activity of the eyes is entirely imperceptible.
Is the oneness of the visual function perceived even when there is the cognition of a single moon? For this visual function is an illuminator even while it remains unperceived itself. (107)
And while this is being said, even in the case of perceiving a single moon, since there would be no perception of its unity of existence, it would result in mere non-apprehension (akhyāti).

As for the claim that—out of a desire to justify non-apprehension regarding the conditions such as bitter sugar—the non-perception of the bitterness of bile, which is being experienced, as residing therein (in the sugar) was described, that too is merely like clutching at straws.
If it is argued that bitterness is not perceived due to delusion because [the sugar] has entered the bile, then why is the cognition of bitterness not likewise absent in the case of sugar? (108)
For through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the cognition of bitterness arises as having that [sugar] as its locus, as in the expression "bitter sugar.

However, bile located in the sense organ, even when not perceived—just like the visual disorder *timira*—produces an error, just as bile located in the body produces fever, headache, and other diseases; but enough of this digression.
Thus, in all cases, it appears that non-apprehension does not succeed;
nor is extrinsic validity (parataḥ-prāmāṇya) undermined by this [non-apprehension] either. //109//
In the case of silver, would there be a direct experience, or is it a mistaken cognition? Since both types are observed, there would likewise be doubt in that case as well. (110)
A person who is in doubt certainly seeks corroboration;
therefore, validity produced through such dependence is definitely extrinsic.
And this is not the method for countering the doctrine of emptiness;
for memory arises even toward those who have been killed, such as one's father and so forth, even though they no longer exist.
Having made that very [dream] the illustrative example, the proponent of emptiness has arisen; it cannot be refuted merely by denying the delusion. //113//

Now, if there is some argument that negates the extrinsic validity [of cognition], then that very argument belonging to the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda) should be stated; what is the use of this [present] one? (114)
Therefore, resorting to this [theory] for the sake of its consistency with reality is not prohibited, because it is not a case of non-apprehension (akhyāti);
rather, it is simply the contradiction with direct experience that has been exposed—fie on such negligence! //115//

As it has been said: "The moral discipline has been destroyed, yet one has not united with the bodiless one (Kāma); the self has been brought to insignificance, and that task has not been accomplished."

Furthermore, as for the refutation of the three positions raised regarding the theory of erroneous manifestation (*viparītakhyāti*), that too is not tenable; let us first consider this very first position: "The silver is the objective support (*ālambana*), and it alone is what appears clearly in this cognition."
Now, it might be objected: "This would be merely the appearance of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*)," but this is not correct;
for silver exists in another location and so forth.
For in the position of *asatkhyāti*, the manifestation of an object that is absolutely non-existent is admitted.
But here, in the case of [an object] existing in another place and so forth, there is a great difference.

Now, one might object: "What is the use of considering another location for an object that is non-existent there? What can we do? For we observe the manifestation of precisely such a thing [as it appears]. (116)
But that object which does not exist even in another place or at another time—its apprehension is never observed, just like a sky-lotus and the like. (117)
And this indeed is the distinction between these two non-existent things: that the apprehension of one is observed, while that of the other is not observed.

But was it not said there: "How can a non-existent object produce cognition, or how can that which does not produce [cognition] appear? To this it was replied: "What appears here is silver presented by a memory evoked by the perception of a similar object. Nor is its presentation like leading a beast before someone after tying it with a rope; rather, it is the external manifestation of an object flashing forth within the heart.

And on this account alone, one must not say that this is *ātmakhyāti* (self-manifestation) or *asatkhyāti* (manifestation of the non-existent), because there is a perception of [the object] as distinct from consciousness, and because there is no manifestation of an absolutely non-existent object.
Alternatively, let there be the second position: that what appears here is merely mother-of-pearl, whose own form is concealed and which has assumed the form of another.

[The opponent objects: "But was it not said that this was merely a performance? Why this change of dress and speech? And how can mother-of-pearl appear as silver in a cognition of silver? This is heard as a drama, but we are not here to be objects of ridicule.
We say that what is called 'mother-of-pearl' is stated here as the actual state of affairs (*vastusthiti*):

it is the mere substrate (*dharmimātra*) standing before us, which appears here accompanied by a recollection of the specific feature of silver produced by the similarity of its shining form and other qualities, because of the experience: '[Whatever this is that stands before me, that is silver]'."

In reality, however, it is merely mother-of-pearl; because there is an absence of the apprehension of its specific qualities such as triangularity, it is said to have its own form concealed, and because of the recollection of a specific piece of silver, it is said to have assumed the form of silver.

And this [theory] is accepted in the case of such errors as the appearance of silver in mother-of-pearl, the perception of water in the rays of the sun, the sight of a city of Gandharvas in the clouds, the seizing of a rope as a snake, the vision of two moons, the determination of yellowness or bitterness in a conch or sugar, and the seeing of a mass of hair;
whereas in those false cognitions based on defects of the mind which are without an external object, it is held that only a form delineated by memory is manifested.

As for the third position held by some—that the object of cognition is one thing while that which appears is another—even there, it is not claimed that what is merely present is the object of cognition, such that one might suspect the same status for the patch of ground as well.
Nor is it the case that the producer [of a cognition] is its objective support (*ālambana*), for that would lead to the absurd consequence that even the eye and other sense organs would be so.
However, there is no fault in defining the objective support as that which, being pointed out by a finger as "this," produces the cognition in the capacity of an object (*karman*).
Now, what is the objective cause (*ālambana-kāraṇa*) for the cognition of a tuft of hair? A certain kind of cataract (*timira*) exists right in the middle of the visual faculty, like a line of hairs;
by this, the visual function is split in two, and thus one perceives the moon as double.
However, another kind of cataract remains here and there within the eye, like gaps.

Therefore, the subtle rays of the eyes, spreading out through the gaps [of the hair], being struck by the rays of the sun, take on the form of a tuft of hair; that alone is the objective support, because the cognition of a "tuft of hair" does not arise when the sun has not yet risen or has already set.
In the cognition of a city of Gandharvas, the clouds, possessing a pale-white luster and assuming the forms of houses, watchtowers, and walls, serve as the objective support (ālambana). //118//
Therefore, all three positions regarding the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) are likewise faultless.

Furthermore, regarding the confusion among the various theories of manifestation (*khyāti*) that was cited, we shall refute both *ātmakhyāti* (self-manifestation) and *akhyāti* (non-manifestation) while refuting the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*) in the chapter on liberation (*apavargahnika*); therefore, what is the need for further consideration of that? As for *viparītakhyāti* (misapprehension), however, its confusion with the others has already been avoided.

As for what was further stated— that "all theorists indeed accept the loss of memory (smṛtipramoṣa), though the Prābhākaras claim that silver was drunk"— let other theorists be as they may; we, however, who assert the appearance of forms such as silver mounted upon memory, have certainly accepted the loss of memory.
However, the mind does not rest with that alone;
rather, since the experience of silver and so forth is also perceived, one must not stop at the mere theory of the loss of memory (smṛtipramoṣa).
Therefore, it is established that the position of erroneous cognition (viparītakhyāti) alone is faultless.

As for the manner of sublation previously conceptualized, the positions such as non-coexistence or the destruction of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been refuted by their very non-acceptance; thus, the Venerable One has experienced a wasting of his throat over an inappropriate matter.
Let sublation, for its part, be the removal of the object.
Now, the manifestation of the object is not denied; rather, the meaning of "removal" is that the existence of what has manifested is made known to be non-existent.

Nor is non-existence now being made known for that which has appeared, such that there would be a sublation [of the cognition] similar to the appearance of the absence of a jar broken by a hammer seen previously. Furthermore, even at that time, one should not suspect a dual nature of the object, because the sublating cognition arises by way of subverting the form previously apprehended, in the sense that "that which was apprehended by me then as silver is not silver; that object is something else entirely."

[Objection: Since cognitions are restricted to their own specific time, how can a subsequent cognition possess the capacity to grasp the absence of that object as delimited by the time of the production of the preceding cognition? [Reply: What can we do? It is because such a cognition arises. The non-existence of that object is not grasped now as if it were like a broken jar; rather, there is the realization "it was non-existent at that very time. And just as cognitions of objects do not have only the present as their locus, we shall explain this under the refutation of the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Alternatively, let sublation (*bādha*) consist in the removal of the result;

for it has been described in the definition of perception that the cognitions of rejection and so forth constitute the result of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, by the removal of that [result], the means of valid cognition is indeed sublated. If one asks, "By doing what does the sublater remove the result of the means of valid cognition?"—[it is] even while singing, dancing, muttering prayers, or offering oblations.
If that effect has already been produced by that [primary cause], what is the use of an intermediate action? //119//
Or even if that [agency] is admitted, what was accomplished by that agent, and by doing what? In this way, what will be the ultimate limit? //120//
Enough with this intermediate question;

in any case, when a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) arises, the result of the prior means of valid cognition—consisting of acceptance, rejection, and so forth—is overturned, and thus it is said to be "sublated" by that [subsequent cognition].

The conceptual distinction between objects that are similar and dissimilar is also not tenable, because it is accepted that two cognitions apprehending contradictory aspects regarding a single object stand in a relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*).

If it is asked, "How is there no sublation in the case of a cognition of a variegated [color] and so forth?"—the answer is that there is indeed a coexistence (*samāveśa*) of those things perceived by the subsequent cognition through the displacement of the preceding cognition.

This also refutes what was stated [to the effect that]: "When the preceding condition has attained stability, a subsequent adventitious cognition may sublate it. For that subsequent cognition arises precisely by means of the sublation of the preceding one, due to its assistance from the object and its being supported by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it is logical that the subsequent cognition alone is the sublater;
thus, there exists between cognitions the relationship of the sublated and the sublater.
And this conventional usage of sublation possesses unerring efficacy only on the theory of misapprehension (viparītakhyāti); therefore, that alone is superior.

A certain ignorant Mīmāṃsaka says: "This cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl is *viparītakhyāti* (misapprehension), as it is held by its proponents; however, that is not the case here, because just as in the cognition of real silver, there is likewise the existence of the silver being manifested here.
The distinction lies merely in its being worldly or non-worldly (*laukika-alaukikatva*);
for that which is called 'silver' is what is manifested by the cognition of silver, and some of that [manifested silver] initiates practical activity while other does not."
In this context, that which initiates worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is called "worldly" (*laukika*), while that which is other than that is "unworldly" (*alaukika*).
And that which you, sirs, call a "fragment of mother-of-pearl" is unworldly silver;
because it is manifested by the cognition of silver (*rajata-jñāna*), yet because the transaction of [actual] silver does not proceed, it is unworldly.
This is the description of a creator of a new creation of objects whose past experience has not been reflected upon;
for in that case, the absence of silver is made known by a subverting cognition.
Indeed, this cognition—"this is not silver"—negates the silver; it does not indicate the extraordinary nature of a silver that actually exists.

Now, if it is explained that "this is not worldly," then alas, let a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) be made, just as in the case of [the injunction] "the limbs [are to be sacrificed] with the *saṃyajatra* verses.
This learned scholar (*śrotriya*), even here, does not abandon the path of his own treatise; yet this is not the proper occasion for it.

For if another substrate called "silver" is not being apprehended, how can "worldliness" be apprehended as a property of that [substrate]? However, there is no such fault if what is being apprehended is the absence of silver.
Because there is no relationship of property and property-possessor between existence and its absence, for it is precisely the absence delimited by a remembered counter-positive that is apprehended.
Therefore, in this case, silver simply does not exist; it is not the case that some "extraordinary" (alaukika) silver exists.
Moreover, the definition of silver is not merely being manifested by a cognition of silver, but rather being cognizable by an uncontradicted cognition of silver.

Furthermore, the distinction between the mundane (*laukika*) and the supramundane (*alaukika*) must be based either on appearance or on the actual existence of conventional usage. It cannot first be based on appearance, because such a perception does not occur; for in some cases silver is perceived, while in others its absence is perceived, but one never perceives "mundanity" or "supramundaneness" itself.

Now, if it is argued that the distinction between the worldly and the non-worldly is established by the engagement or non-engagement in practical activity (*vyavahāra*), then this must be explained: what indeed is this thing called "practical activity"? For practical activity consists in the nature of cognition and verbal designation; and it is logical [to hold] that its object does not exist.

If it is argued that practical activity is the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then it would follow that a woman being embraced in a dream and a counterfeit coin would possess the status of being worldly.
If a jar were destroyed immediately after arising, it would follow that its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) ceases, and thus it would be something non-worldly (*alaukikatva*).

Moreover, he who does not employ the conventional usage of "silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl does so because he has cognized the absence of silver, and not because of the "unworldliness" (alaukikatā) of that silver which actually exists there.

If that silver is indeed non-worldly (alaukika), for what purpose does one act here toward it for the sake of its functional efficiency? If you say, "Having apprehended the non-worldly as worldly," then this very same wretched *viparītakhyāti* (misapprehension) has arrived.
Therefore, enough with this hatred for *viparītakhyāti*;
even in this case, let the cognition established by common worldly experience be followed.
Or rather, these Mīmāṃsakas, out of their thirst for intrinsic validity, do not even wish to send their own wives out of the house at night. (121)
Even so, its establishment is not achieved, because two kinds of cognition are observed;
since doubt exists, that [cognition] likewise depends upon corroboration. //122//
By this affliction of theirs as well, not the slightest self-interest is accomplished;
let that which occurs by the turn of fate proceed simply along the royal highway. //123//

It is not self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*), because the object appears as something external; nor is it the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), for that which is non-existent cannot be an object of cognition.
The path of refutation regarding non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) has already been stated; therefore, erroneous apprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) should be adopted by the wise. (124)
And while that [cognition] persists, there arises a doubt based on its similarity to a contrary cognition;
at that time, because they await confirmation as their means of approach, cognitions attain their status as valid knowledge through extrinsic means (parataḥ-prāmāṇya). //125//
Whether the validity of perception and the other means of knowledge be as it may, the validity of verbal testimony is, beyond doubt, extrinsic. (126)

For regarding perceptible objects, activity toward tasks requiring little effort occurs even without the ascertainment of validity; thus, what insistence can there be on ascertaining the validity of the means of knowledge—such as perception—which are useful for those [tasks], since such ascertainment is difficult to achieve? However, in the case of verbal testimony (*śabda*), which teaches paths to human goals that are not perceptible, prudent sacrificers would not undertake great efforts such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice without first ascertaining its validity. Therefore, its validity must necessarily be ascertained.
And we maintain that this [ascertainment] occurs only extrinsically (*parataḥ*).
The nature of a word, once assisted by a relationship understood through the linguistic usage of elders, is established as being the producer of cognition.
We shall investigate whether this occurs by virtue of the power of an innate relationship or by the force of a convention established by a person.
However, its essential form is simply that of an illuminator, just like a lamp or similar object.

For just as a lamp, while shining, illuminates an object—whether pure or impure, and whether it is situated near or far—in the same way, a word, when employed by a person and having reached the path of hearing, produces a valid cognition regarding an object that is either true or false, coherent or incoherent, fruitful or fruitless, an established fact or a task to be accomplished; such is its nature.

However, this is the distinction between a word and a lamp: the former produces a valid cognition depending upon the mastery of the relationship [between word and meaning], whereas the lamp does not depend upon that.

The truth or falsity of that cognition produced by words depends upon the perception of the person [who utters them]. When the person is one who perceives correctly and is pure, that comprehension becomes true; otherwise, it is the opposite.

In this regard, just as it has been established that the nature of a word is its inherent contact with an object (*arthasaṃsparśitva*), so too its inherent truthfulness (*satyārthatva*) is not its nature. If this were accepted, then the observation of contradiction in the speech of deceivers would not occur.
Therefore, in the case of verbal cognition, correspondence and non-correspondence depend solely upon the virtues and defects of the person.

Furthermore, unlike in the case of the sense organs and so forth, it is not difficult to describe the qualities therein: defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like, and qualities such as compassion (*karuṇā*) and the like, are indeed well-known in persons.
It is precisely the qualities of the person that constitute the qualities of the word, and not those residing in its own body, as is the case with the eyes and other [senses].

Therefore, if the status of being a cause of validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not accepted for the qualities of the person, then let there likewise be no status of being a cause of distortion (*viplava*) for the defects either.

As for the claim that human excellences (*puruṣaguṇa*)—which have fulfilled their purpose merely by neutralizing defects—are not the cause of validity, on this point the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) can only resort to an oath.

Nor can the validity of a Vedic cognition be established merely by the non-occurrence of sublation (*bādhā*); for if it were so, the validity of such passages as "One desiring the station of a *vidyādhara* should delight with eyes full of long lashes" would also follow.
And it has been said by someone: "Just as an object seen in a dream, such as another continent..."
That which is impossible to contradict cannot be believed at all.
"Likewise, some do not have faith in an object beyond the senses that is made known by an injunction, even when it is impossible for it to be contradicted."

If it is argued that dream-cognition lacks validity because its cause is defective—namely, the defect of sleep and so forth—then what will you say regarding the statement "the eyes of the fickle woman"? If you say that its source is not known, we reply: no, for according to your own view, that [source] is indeed known even in the case of the Veda; what then is the distinction? If you say that this [Vedic statement] lacks acceptance by the great people (mahājana) and others, then one must search for the cause of its validity. It is logical that validity is inherent (*autsargika*) simply because it produces a cognition.

As long as it is not certain that a word was spoken by a person who has directly perceived [the truth], its status as a valid means of knowledge cannot be established merely by the non-occurrence of sublation. (127)

As for what is stated in the Veda to eliminate defects in the cause—namely, "Or rather, because of the absence of a speaker, there would be no defects, as they would lack a locus"—that too is incorrect; for if there is no speaker, since the excellences (*guṇa*) which are the causes of validity are also absent, the validity of that [Veda] would likewise be non-existent.
Nor is it easy to maintain the absence of a speaker in the case of the Veda; for we must first investigate this very point: does a speaker exist in the Veda, or not?

[Objection: But how could a person who directly perceives its meaning be the teacher of the Veda, which teaches the relationship between means and ends regarding various ritual fruits that are untouched by other means of knowledge? [Reply: It is said: A person is certainly not just any kind of person the author of the Veda; rather, it is the Supreme Lord, skilled in the creation of the three worlds. (128)
That God is the supreme knower, eternally blissful, endowed with compassion, and entirely free from the touch of afflictions, karma, its maturation, and so forth. //129//
To this he says: "What do you say? 'The intellect is skilled in the creation of the three worlds'—oh, how simple-minded you are! For there is no proof whatsoever for the existence of such a person."
For thus, the existence of God is not established by the single means of perception;
for He does not appear in sensory consciousness in the manner that form and other such objects do. (130)
Nor is this [self] perceivable by mental consciousness, as are pleasure and the like; because it is not established for yogins, it is not within the range of their direct perception. //131//

By the refutation of perception, inference—which is preceded by it—is also set aside; for as long as that [perception] is not established, there can be no apprehension of the pervasion (vyāpti). //132//

Nor is there any mark of inference by general observation (sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa) for this [creator]; furthermore, the fact that earth and other elements are effects is unestablished for those of sound intellect. //133//
Even this arrangement of mountains and so forth does not lead to the inference of a creator, for it is distinct from the arrangement of jars and other objects which are preceded by a maker. (134)

For whatever kind of arrangement is observed to be invariably concomitant with an agent, such an arrangement does not exist in mountains and the like; thus, [the reason] is unestablished (asiddha), just as in the case of "being an effect" (kāryatva). //135//

Even if [the world] were established as an effect, it would not follow that [God] is its cause, because of the inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to things such as grass and the like, which grow without being ploughed and arise without a creator. (136)
Since their time of production is not perceived, the visibility of a creator is likewise unobtainable; thus, his non-existence follows from non-perception. (137)

Furthermore, it is not reasonable to postulate any cause for those [effects] other than the observed causes consisting primarily of earth and water, because that would lead to an over-extension of the principle. (138)

Therefore, since we observe [specific] arrangements and so forth even in the absence of a creator, the reason is inconclusive, just as "being a human" [is an inconclusive reason] for [proving] "being a Brahmin. //139//

Furthermore, an agent who is postulated in accordance with pervasion (vyāpti) is established as being like a potter; thus, there would be a contradiction of the specific [nature of the subject]. (140)
One who possesses activity, is not omniscient, possesses a body, and is beset by afflictions—such as the maker of a jar would be—exactly so would he be for the earth. (141)
Or, if [the probandum] were to consist in a specific [creator], the illustrative example would be devoid of the probandum.
But if the existence of a creator in general is established, how can there be an understanding of his specific nature? (142)

Moreover, would the Lord create the worlds while possessing a body or while being bodiless? Furthermore, would that body of his be an effect or eternal? In every respect, [the creation of the world] is untenable.
Indeed, agency is never observed in anything that is bodiless;
moreover, this [alleged] body is subject to origination because it is a body, just like the body of Caitra. (143)
Furthermore, the body of the Lord must either be produced by Himself or produced by another Lord. In that regard, to claim that He Himself creates His own body is sheer audacity;
if it were created by another creator, it would lead to an infinite regress of Lords. (144)
If it is argued that there is no fault in this, the very absence of proof is the fault.

They have reached such confusion as to attempt to prove even a single Lord; how much more so for an infinite number? Furthermore, would the Lord create effects through exertion like a potter, or by mere will? Both are untenable. How could the world be created through exertion even in hundreds of ages?
Nor do insentient atoms follow His will. (185)

Furthermore, does the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) engage in the creation of the world having some purpose in mind, or does he do so without any purpose? If his activity were indeed purposeless, he would be like a madman due to acting without foresight.

The former position is also not tenable; for we do not see what purpose there could be for one who has attained all bliss and whose self is free from passion and other such afflictions, yet who undertakes the creation of the world. (146)

If it is argued that [the Lord] acts out of compassion, let it not be so; for prior to creation, his selves—being entirely free from contact with any afflictions—are like those who are liberated and thus do not become objects of compassion. (187)

Even for those possessed of supreme compassion, as they behold living beings whose minds are being scorched by the staff of the fire of unbearable suffering, pity arises; it does not arise [toward those] who, like those in the state of final liberation, are devoid of all suffering.
Or, if he creates the world with a heart drenched in the nectar of compassion, how could he create it as something terrible, burdened by an irresistible mass of suffering? (148)

Now, if it is argued that [the Lord] does not even know how to create a world consisting primarily of the enjoyment of pleasure, or that even once created, it does not endure for long—this too is unseemly. For what indeed could be impossible for the Supreme Lord, who abides at the limit of unsurpassed sovereignty and whose existence as all objects follows His own will? If it is argued that the Creator, Prajāpati, is dependent upon the collection of auspicious and inauspicious karmas residing in various individual souls, then let the karmas themselves create the world; what is the need for Prajāpati? If it is argued that since insentient things cannot function as creators without being presided over by a conscious being, a conscious supervisor must therefore be postulated—no, for the selves (*ātman*) who are the substrates of those karmas are themselves conscious; they alone shall be the supervisors. What is the use of another supervisor in the form of a Lord (*Īśvara*)? Furthermore, what is the point of His sovereignty if His autonomy is likewise restricted by dependence on the karmas of others? Of what use is such sovereignty, which is like a kingship dependent on ministers, when one’s desired object is not fashioned by one's own will without depending on anything else?
Another has also said: "If God does not act according to his own will by virtue of his lordship, then indeed no cause need be sought for the actions of those who possess sovereign power."

Now, if it is said that the Blessed One’s engagement in the creation of the world is for the sake of sport—that the Supreme Lord sports with such a world created in the form of both the auspicious and the inauspicious—then his nature of having attained all bliss prior to creation would be lost, because of the absence of any pleasure to be accomplished through sport.
Furthermore, even play that causes distress to all living beings, and which involves such great exertion, is not fitting for a Great Being to perform. (149)
Therefore, the Lord, the protector of the worlds, is neither their creator nor their destroyer.
For while his [the Lord's] life-force remains, his desire to utterly uproot the entire triple world at once is not fulfilled by the karmas of living beings. //150//
But on the view that karma has ceased, a new creation is not tenable;
for the emergence of the diversity of creation does not occur independently of karma. (151)

Then, when a hundred years according to the measure of Brahmā have elapsed while the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) remains established [in his state], the desire to withdraw [the world] arises in Maheśvara.
Through that [desire], the karmas—whose powers to initiate their own fruits are concealed—come into being, and thus the dissolution of all worlds occurs.
Furthermore, when a period of time equal to that has passed, which is like a night, the Blessed One’s desire to emit [the world] arises.

The claim that "actions, their potencies manifested by that [Icchā], initiate their effects" is also untenable. If you argue that their manifestation and suppression occur through the will of God (Īśvara), then let that [will] alone be the cause of the creation and dissolution of the worlds. (152)
If it is argued that this is so because of [past] actions, we say no; for under the view that everything is subject to the will of God, there are three insurmountable defects.
First, there is the mercilessness of that Great Soul himself, who creates such a cruel world without any cause.

Second, the injunctions and prohibitions of the Veda would be rendered useless, since the experience of the fruits of good and evil deeds could occur solely through the will of God. Third, human effort would become fruitless. Therefore, this theory is untenable.

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of no liberation; for even those who are liberated might, like living beings at the time of cosmic dissolution, return to transmigrate again by the will of the Lord.
Therefore, the creation or destruction of the worlds is not dependent upon the Lord.
Thus, by the method just described for establishing the existence of God, inference has no capacity; what then can be said of analogy?
It is also improper for an eternal scripture to have that [liberation] as its primary purpose;
moreover, how could someone like me have confidence in what was composed by such a being? (154)
Furthermore, the authority of scripture would be caused by its being composed by him, and the proof of his [existence] would depend on that authority; thus, there would be a circular argument. (155)
However, the Lord cannot be established through the principle of "otherwise being impossible" (anyathānupapatti), for no such effect is observed that cannot be accomplished without Him. (156)
Therefore, it is established that God is indeed non-existent, because his nature is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition regarding any existing object.
Nor is it proper to postulate that [self] based on mere common renown, because it lacks any foundation; as it has been said: "Common renown is like a yakṣa in a banyan tree. (157)

Therefore, having observed the deceptive display of the world’s birth and destruction, those who know the secret of political ethics have stated that the world has never been otherwise than it is now. (158)

Regarding the establishment of the proof for God (*īśvara*), we shall state it here: first, as for the claim that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is incapable of discerning a person skilled in the creation of mountains, oceans, and so forth—that is indeed so.
Let inference (*anumāna*) based on perception also remain set aside, as it is established by that very same path.

However, regarding the mark (*liṅga*) of "inference from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) concerning the existence of God, we say this: the subject (*dharmin*) is the effect consisting of the earth and so forth; the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is that it is preceded by a creator who knows its mode of production, its purpose, and so on; because it is an effect (*kāryatvāt*); like a jar (*ghaṭādivat*).

But was it not said that "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is unestablished? Who says this? A Cārvāka, a Śākya, or a Mīmāṃsaka? As for the Cārvāka, he would have to be a person who, while accepting the "effect-status" even of the Vedic composition—which is distinct from other compositions—how could he deny the "effect-status" of the composition of the earth and so forth? Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsaka also ought not to deny its being an effect, since he himself has said: "Even for those things whose origin is not perceived, when their form is observed, it is inferred that 'this cloth is produced by the conjunction of threads; it will perish through the loosening of that conjunction or through the destruction of the threads.'"* *Note: This passage is a citation from Kumārila Bhaṭṭa’s *Ślokavārttika*, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra-vārttika, verse 102.*
In this way, the cognition of destruction is indeed possible even for things such as mountains, whose bodies are produced through the conjunction of parts.

Furthermore, the perception of destruction is observed in some cases when a portion of a mountain has been washed away by the torrential downpour of a rain-cloud, such that one says, "A fragment of the mountain has fallen.

Moreover, the co-extensiveness (*samavyāpti*) between the properties of being an effect and being destructible was stated by the author of the *Vārttika* himself: "Therefore, where both properties are accepted as the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*)," and so forth.
For he says: "In that case as well, it is only the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatā*) that would be the logical reason (*aṅga*), not the cognition of pervasiveness (*vyāpitā*).
Therefore, since the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is inferred even from perishability, the property of being an effect is not unestablished (*asiddha*) even in his view.

How could even a Śākya maintain that the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is unestablished, such that a so-called eternal entity (*nitya*) would not be tolerated even in the playful dalliances of debate?
Therefore, the fact that earth and other elements are effects is something that cannot be rejected by any disputant.

Alternatively, we state as our reason the very fact of being characterized by a specific arrangement, regarding which even those who are most prone to denial do not dare to disagree when it is perceived through direct perception;
therefore, the reason is not unestablished.

Is it not reasonable that, because a certain kind of structure is invariably concomitant with an agent—as seen in the case of bowls and the like—one infers an agent for a jar or similar object where no agent is perceived, simply by perceiving a structure of that same kind?
However, this structure of mountains and the like is entirely different from the structure of jars and the like;
ordinary people do not perceive any commonality of structure between them.
They employ the word "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*) as a common term;
however, when two things are absolutely distinct, an inference based on them is not tenable merely through the commonality of a word.
For one cannot infer fire from a heap of *kakkola* powder simply because it shares the common property of being pale, just as one might infer fire from smoke.
As it has been said: "That arrangement and so forth, which follow the presence or absence of a presiding agent in whatever manner, is rightly inferred from that very [arrangement]."

"Inference is not valid for that which is established as distinct in one instance but is claimed to be non-distinct through mere similarity of words; it would be like inferring fire from a white substance."
It is said: "We do not understand what 'of such a kind' means.
For smoke is observed in a kitchen to be of a generally thin nature, produced by a feeble flame fanned by the breath of a servant girl;

yet, if that same smoke is observed in the mountain—spreading through the entire circle of the sky, produced from the fuel of great tree trunks being consumed by a fire leaping with powerful winds—does it then fail to produce the cognition of fire?

Now, just as smoke in its mere generality, devoid of specific qualities, is understood to be pervaded by fire in its mere generality, and from that [understanding] there is an inference of it; so too here, since the mere configuration is pervaded by an agent in his mere generality, let the agent also be inferred from that.
"O Bhikṣu, is there not here some commonality of substance (vastusāmānya) that is shared merely by the word 'arrangement' (saṃniveśa)?
Even in your own view, is there any commonality of substance in smoke?"

Let it be that there is no such thing as a universal (*sāmānya*) in the form of a real entity; however, a universal in the form of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from space, time, and so forth, certainly exists as the cause of conventional usage. Well then, in the present case as well, let there be a universal in the form of the exclusion from non-arrangement, because earth and the other elements possess a nature distinct from space, time, and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, in that case, you have accepted a universal whose nature is *apoha*, which is constructed by the force of the recurring conceptualization "smoke, smoke"; here too, because of the recurrence of the conceptualization of "arrangement" (*saṃniveśa*), let a universal in the form of *apoha* as imagined by you be admitted. Furthermore, even among those structures intended to have an agent, identity is not perceived in every respect; for the arrangement of a jar is not exactly like the arrangement of a four-winged palace.
