However, a universal of arrangement certainly exists even in mountains and so forth; thus, the phrase "of whatever kind" (*yādṛg*) is entirely unexpressive [as a qualification].

Furthermore, as for the objection regarding deviation raised by means of plants and the like that grow without being sown, that too is not valid, because they have been included within the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
If one were to urge a charge of deviation against the subject itself, it would result in the undesirable consequence of the total collapse of all logical inference.

Now, one might argue that because the time of the origin of the earth and so forth is beyond the senses, no creator is perceived; and since it is impossible to ascertain their non-existence through such non-perception, let there be doubt at will. However, we ourselves observe the very time of the production of trees and the like as being present-day events. Even when searching diligently, we do not perceive a creator for these things.
Therefore, we conclude that such a creator does not exist at all due to the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*).

Moreover, if you were to make whatever specific instance we might point out as a deviation (vyabhicāra) the very subject of your own thesis, then inference would be utterly destroyed; for in that case, even those [reasons] characterized by deviation would not lose their status as valid inference.
It is said that even though the time of origin of stationary beings (*sthāvara*) is perceptible, the agent remains indeed invisible because of the certainty of his being bodiless (*aśarīra*).

If it is asked, "In that case, since one who is bodiless is not active in their production, how can there be agency?"—this will be determined further on. Furthermore, since it is impossible to determine non-existence for an invisible agent merely through non-perception, plants born from unplowed soil do not lack an agent; thus, they do not constitute a counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

[The impossibility of the production of grass and so forth by visible causes alone: As for the argument that since plants are effects produced from visible causes such as earth and water, what is the point of postulating an invisible agent?—that is weak, because proponents of the afterlife (paraloka) also accept that invisible karmas are causes.
For the followers of Bṛhaspati (the Cārvākas), however, the very justification for that [denial of an invisible cause] is their consolation.

Now, since the diversity of the world cannot be accounted for apart from karma, the causality of karmas—even though they are imperceptible—is postulated. In that case, since it is impossible for an effect to arise from insentient causal factors that are not presided over by a conscious being, a conscious agent must also be postulated as their supervisor. Therefore, because stationary beings (sthāvara) do not lack an agent, they do not constitute a counter-example (vipakṣa), and thus there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) [from the rule] by means of them.

As for what was also said—that if whatever [reason] is pointed out as being deviant is included within the subject (*pakṣa*), then what would remain as the restriction (*niyama*) of inference?—this too is not sound. For if you were to demonstrate the presence [of the reason] in a certain counter-example (*vipakṣa*), who could then include that very thing within the subject?

When the deviation of "masculinity" (*pums-tva*) from "being a Veda-reciter" (*vipra-tva*) or of "knowability" (*prameya-tva*) from "impermanence" is urged, even Brahmā himself cannot turn that counter-example into the subject, because the determination of a real entity does not depend on the speaker's whim.
However, in this case, it has been stated that there is no certainty regarding the absence of an agent in things such as stationary objects (*sthāvara*).
Even if immobile things are made the subject (*pakṣa*), the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) does not cease at all.

For there exists no such thing as a "subject" (*pakṣa*) in reality apart from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), since it is impossible for a real entity to possess two forms simultaneously.
According to the actual state of things, if trees and the like possess an agent, they are simply included among the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

If that is not the case, then they are simply the counter-examples (vipakṣa); there is no other category whatsoever. Thus it is said: in the absence of a thesis (pakṣa), what indeed is the point of the linguistic convention regarding "similar" (sapakṣa) and "counter-example" (vipakṣa)? For a "similar" instance is defined as that which is favorable to the thesis, and a "counter-example" as that which is unfavorable to it.

If this is what must be said, then what is this so-called "subject" (pakṣa)? It is that which is ascertained by both [the proponent and the opponent] as being endowed with the property to be proven (sādhyadharma). That which is similar to it is the "similar instance" (sapakṣa); that which is devoid of it is the "dissimilar instance" (vipakṣa). (159)
But where there is disagreement between the two [parties], that we declare to be the "position" (pakṣa);
however, we do not accept that a real entity possesses a triple nature. (160)
Although the establishment of a thesis follows the cognition of the proponent, nevertheless, conventional practice exists which is based on that [thesis] as a real entity. (161)

For it has been stated that reasoning (*nyāya*) operates upon what is doubtful, neither upon what is unperceived nor upon what is already determined. An object that is being doubted alone is called the "subject" (*pakṣa*). Its status as the subject lasts for some time until a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) has arisen.
But when that [property] arises, it will certainly enter into either the similar class (sapakṣa) or the dissimilar class (vipakṣa);
therefore, the pointing out of a deviation (vyabhicāra) by means of it while it is still in the state of being the subject (pakṣa) is incorrect.

Now, it might be argued that not only a reason whose presence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is certain, but even one whose presence there is doubtful, is not truly a reason. Thus, since a structured arrangement is observed in plants and the like even though an agent is merely suspected, [this arrangement] would lack the status of a reason. This is not sound, for it would lead to the absurd consequence that smoke—though present on a mountain where fire (the dissimilar instance) is suspected by virtue of being either existent or non-existent—would likewise fail to be a reason. Furthermore, since all things would become dissimilar instances simply because of doubt regarding the existence of the probandum (*sādhya*), reasons that reside in the subject (*pakṣa*) would now become those that go to the dissimilar instance, resulting in the total destruction of inference.

Now, if it is maintained that smoke and the like, though present in a subject (dharmin) that is itself the object of the thesis and whose status as possessing the probandum is doubted—either as existent or non-existent—is still accepted as a prover because its pervasion (vyāpti) has been ascertained elsewhere, then the state of being an effect (kāryatva), though present in the earth, trees, and so forth, which are doubted as to whether they possess an existent or non-existent agent, should likewise be accepted as a prover because its pervasion has been ascertained elsewhere.
Or else, some distinction must be stated.

Others say: "What is the use of searching for counter-examples such as things produced without being ploughed or stationary objects? Here, the very earth and so forth constitute the locus of deviation, because they obstruct the apprehension of this pervasion (*vyāpti*).
For when pervasion is being apprehended, it must be apprehended by encompassing all similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

And while that pervasion is being apprehended—specifically at the moment one grasps the principle: 'Whatever is characterized by a particular arrangement is the product of an intelligent agent'—mountains and the like, though possessing such arrangements, flash into the mind as being devoid of an agent."

For example, in the inference of the non-heat of fire on the basis of its being produced—where the pervasion is grasped as "whatever is produced is non-hot"—the fact that fire is both hot and produced enters the path of the mind at the very moment the pervasion is determined.
However, if the pervasion were grasped while excluding that [instance], then the inference of the probandum from that reason would be as impossible as the birth of a son from a eunuch.

This is untenable, because it has been established in the definition of inference that the desired pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be based on a mere generality (*sāmānya*) devoid of any mention of specific particulars.

For it has already been stated that the invalidity of the inference that fire is not hot does not arise from an obstruction to the apprehension of pervasion, but rather from its contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, this method of refuting the inference of a creator with respect to the earth and so forth—namely, "the perceptions of sound and so on are preceded by instruments because they are actions, like the action of cutting"—is equally applicable to the inference of instruments such as the ear.

This is because at the very time of determining the invariable concomitance (pratibandha), one perceives actions consisting of the perception of sound and so on that are devoid of instruments; thus, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) caused by those very instances.
Moreover, to urge that there is no deviation based on the subject (pakṣa), namely the earth and so on, is utterly unworldly.
But surely, according to the actual state of things, even mountains and the like are indeed counter-examples (vipakṣa), though you have merely given them the name "subject" (pakṣa);
and the actual state of things does not change according to your wish.

[Objection: But in this way, even the perceptions of sound and so forth are, according to the actual state of things, indeed counter-examples (vipakṣa); for them too, there would be nothing more than the mere application of the name "the subject" (pakṣa). [Response: It is not the case that they are counter-examples, because there is no certainty regarding the non-existence of their instruments, and because [the reason] does not arise [in them].
Furthermore, since the certainty that there is no agent is not produced even in the case of mountains and the like, they do not constitute the counter-example (vipakṣa).
If it is argued that no agent is perceived among those [faculties], then the perception of sound and so forth is likewise not perceived at all.

If it is argued that the instrument is not perceived precisely because it is invisible, and not because of its non-existence, then the agent as well is not perceived precisely because he is invisible, and not because of his non-existence.

If it is argued that the instrument is apprehended through inference because action is impossible without it, then the agent too shall be apprehended through inference, since an effect is impossible without an agent.
Therefore, because [the creator] is to be known through inference, there is no apprehension of his non-existence.
In the absence of that [cause], it is difficult to maintain that even earth and other elements possess the status of being counter-instances. //162//
However, even regarding fire, doubt prior to the perception of the mark (liṅga) cannot be precluded;
if that were the case, smoke too would lose its status as an inferential mark. (163)
Now, its status as a fallacious mark [liṅgābhāsa] arises because no agent is observed in the case of [the production of] a leaf-cutter (likṣī) and so forth;
likewise, smoke would also be a fallacious mark in that particular place where fire is not observed. (164)
Surely, having reached that place, smoke is perceived as its mark;
by this very logic, may you live for a hundred autumns! (165)
What is the use of that subsequent perception for the validity of the mark? Or, if you have not seen the fire because you had no need for it, what will you do [with the mark] then? //166//
Therefore, in every respect, this reason is not inconclusive.

Furthermore, as for the claim that this [reason] is subject to the fallacy of "contradiction by the particular" (*viśeṣaviruddha*), that too is an unexamined statement, because there is no such thing as a "fallacious reason" (hetvābhāsa) called "contradiction by the particular.
Or, if it were admitted, it would entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference.
For even in the case of the inference regarding the auditory faculty and so forth, as illustrated in the example, one could state the same [objection].
Just as the instruments such as the sickle are understood to possess properties like hardness in the act of cutting, so too must the ear and other sense organs be of that same nature.

However, if they were to be produced by instruments possessing characteristics different from those, the example would lack the property to be proven (sādhyavikala); for it is never observed that acts such as cutting are the effects of instruments beyond the reach of the senses.

Now, since it is understood that mere action is pervaded by a mere agent, it infers only that much; so too here, since mere configuration is perceived as being pervaded by a mere supervisor, let it infer only that much.
As for specific qualities, however, there is no such mark [of inference] where there is a sublation.
Even the argument "sound is impermanent because it is produced" surely sublates the collection of sound's specific qualities, such as audibility.
Even smoke excludes certain specific mountain fires that have not been observed in a kitchen fire;

therefore, a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) is precisely that which proves the opposite of the stated probandum (*sādhya*), and not merely that which brings about the exclusion of specific instances.

Furthermore, the reason under discussion does not prove the opposite of the probandum—namely, that [the world] was not preceded by a non-agent—just as [the argument] "this is a horse because it has horns" does not.
Therefore, it is not contradictory.
Nor is it "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), because no sublation by either perception or scripture is observed; on the contrary, we shall here cite scripture as a supporting factor.

Nor is this reason countered by an opposing argument (satpratipakṣa), because factors such as the non-perception of distinguishing features—which serve as seeds for doubt—are not adduced here as reasons.
Nor is this reason non-conclusive (aprayojaka), as will be stated regarding the case where corporeality (mūrtatva) is cited as a reason for the impermanence of atoms;
for in that case, impermanence is not necessitated by corporeality.
Here, however, being produced by an agent (sakartṛkatva) is observed in various instances to be necessitated precisely by the state of being an effect (kāryatva).
For this very reason, there is no occasion here for either a contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*) or for an objection that thwarts what is intended (*iṣṭavighātakṛt*),
because when a probative reason (*prayojakahetu*) has been employed, there is no room for the application of such "throwing dust" (*pāṃsuprakṣepa*).
Therefore, by the power of the inference from effects (*kāryānumāna*), which is free from all the defects alleged by opponents, God must certainly be postulated.
Furthermore, the validity of inference must be examined even as it stands witnessed by the entire world;
and since the preparation for the defense of the validity of inference was already undertaken previously, God is indeed established.
Others have stated another inference as well:
the manifest [world], such as the great elements, produces pleasure and pain while being presided over by a conscious agent, because it possesses form and other qualities, like a musical instrument.
Likewise, the elements such as earth perform actions such as supporting while being presided over by a conscious agent, like draft animals and the like.
In this case as well, the faults should be refuted in the same manner as before.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated—“If the general nature of the agent is established, from where does the cognition of its specific qualities come?”—some say that the understanding of these specific qualities arises from scripture (*āgama*), citing: “He who has eyes on all sides and faces on all sides, arms on all sides and feet on all sides;
he blows forth with his two arms and wings, creating heaven and earth, the one God.
Likewise: “Without hands or feet, swift and grasping, he sees without eyes and hears without ears.”
"He knows all, for there is no knower of him; they call him the foremost, the great Puruṣa"—thus it is recited in the Śruti.
From this, the Lord is made known as the creator of all and the omniscient one.

Nor is it appropriate to claim that the Vedas lack authority regarding matters of established fact (*siddha*)—such as the meaning of mantras and *arthavādas*—on the grounds that they are authoritative only regarding what is to be done (*kārya*), for the authority of the Veda over established facts will be demonstrated later.
Furthermore, there is no circular reasoning, because the establishment of God does not depend solely upon scripture.

Others assert the establishment of the specific [probandum] by means of the power of a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) inference, which is rooted in a reason that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatirekin).

Just as the postulation of a self distinct from the body and so forth is described through the property of being an effect residing in pleasure, pain, and so on, so too will the earth and other effects be described as having a single, omniscient creator distinct from ourselves and others, because they possess the nature of being effects—provided that there exists a sublation (bādhaka) regarding ourselves and others. "The earth and so forth have a single, omniscient creator distinct from ourselves and others, because they are effects."
Others accept that the specific [nature of the cause] is obtained solely by the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

For it is not possible for a person who lacks extraordinary powers to produce such an effect as the world and so forth—an effect that is perceived as having manifold forms, immeasurable, and consisting of the various means for the pleasure and pain of infinite living beings.

Just as, upon observing sandalwood smoke—which is dissimilar to other types of smoke—one infers that the fire itself must be sandalwood, so too, from an effect possessing distinct characteristics, an agent possessing distinct characteristics will be inferred.

Just as a skilled weaver [knows] from [the materials for] garments, and just as a potter—being one who knows the purpose, the means, and the arrangement for the production of the entire collection of effects such as jars—is the maker of that cycle of effects; in the same way, Maheśvara must be the creator who knows the purposeful and manifold arrangement for the creation and dissolution of this threefold world, which is the means for the pleasure and pain of infinite living beings.
Therefore, he is omniscient.

Moreover, just as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is the presiding controller over the sense organs such as the eye, which function within restricted domains, and is therefore omniscient in relation to them; so too, the Lord (*īśvara*), who has power over the application of the karma of all knowers of the field, is omniscient in relation to them.
And thus Vyāsa said: "There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
The perishable consists of all beings; the one who stands at the peak is called the imperishable."
But there is another, the Supreme Person, who is declared to be the Supreme Self;
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
And a mantra restating that meaning is recited: "Two birds, companions, inseparable friends, cling to the same tree.
One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating. [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1]
And for this reason, God is omniscient.
For the lack of omniscience in men is indeed due to the bondage of impurities such as passion;
and since the Blessed One is untouched by passion and the like, he is omniscient. //167//
Indeed, for embodied beings, passion and the like arise from the enjoyment of desired or undesired objects; how could they exist in Śiva, whose nature is eternal bliss? (168)

Furthermore, defects such as attachment and the like have false knowledge as their root; how could they exist in an Īśvara who possesses eternal and stainless knowledge? If it is asked, "How is that knowledge eternal?"—it is because if He were to remain ignorant for even a single moment, there would follow the cessation of the various kinds of worldly activity impelled by His will and dependent upon karma. If it is then asked, "In that case, from where does the conception of its eternity come during the time of cosmic dissolution (pralaya)?"—do not say so. Since its eternity is established until the dissolution, its eternity will be proven at that time due to the absence of any cause for its destruction, just as the eternity of this Self is established.
Furthermore, knowledge is eternal because there is no cause for its production at the time of creation.

And thus, that [cognition] which has as its object all things—past, future, subtle, concealed, and so forth—is not divided, because the conceptual alternatives of succession or simultaneity are untenable. If one were to resort to succession, there would be ignorance regarding certain things, resulting in the collapse of worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*). If, on the other hand, it possesses omniscience through simultaneity, from where could there be any division in the cognition? Furthermore, because it shares the characteristics of perception (*pratyakṣa*), that cognition is called "perceptual"; however, it does not possess the quality of being produced by the contact of a sense organ with an object, since it apprehends objects even when they are not acting as causes, just like the light of the sun.
Other qualities of the self that he possesses, like knowledge, are likewise eternal, because their production does not depend upon conjunction with the mind.
For him, suffering and aversion do not exist at all.
Furthermore, there is no need for the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), because since he perceives all objects at all times, there is an absence of memory.
For this very reason, inferential knowledge is not admitted for him;
however, merit (*dharma*) arising from the natural disposition of reality for one who benefits living beings is not prevented.
And its fruit is precisely the accomplishment of the welfare of others.
But his happiness is indeed eternal, because it is understood from scripture that he possesses eternal bliss;
furthermore, one who is not happy lacks the fitness to undertake such a task.

[Objection: But if desire (*icchā*) is also eternal like knowledge (*jñāna*) and bliss (*ānanda*), then since that desire would be present at all times for the Lord, the world would arise at all times; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the world being infinite.
Furthermore, because the desire for creation is eternal, dissolution (*saṃhāra*) would never occur.

And by admitting that the desire for dissolution is also eternal, the continuous stream of cosmic destruction would not cease day or night for the worlds. [Reply: This is not a fault. Although desire is eternal in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) because it is not produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind (*anātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga-ja*), it is nevertheless colored (*anurajyate*) from time to time by an object—sometimes by creation and sometimes by dissolution.
But during the state of the world's persistence, in the interval between creation and dissolution, the desire arises in Prajāpati: "From this karma, let this be accomplished for him."

His effort consists precisely of a specific form of volition (*saṃkalpa*). Thus says the scripture: "He whose desires are true, whose volitions are true. Here, "desire" (*kāma*) refers to longing (*icchā*), and "volition" (*saṃkalpa*) refers to effort (*prayatna*).

Thus, among the nine qualities of the self (*ātman*), five—namely knowledge, pleasure, desire, effort, and merit—exist in God (*īśvara*); however, the four—suffering, aversion, demerit, and mental formations (*saṃskāra*)—do not exist. Therefore, God is a particularity of the self (*ātmaviśeṣa*) and not a separate substance (*dravyāntara*).
And Patañjali said: "God is a particularity of the person (*puruṣaviśeṣa*) untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, and latent dispositions."
Thus it is established that the acquisition of the specific property (viśeṣa) occurs either through scripture, inference, or from the property of the subject (pakṣadharma).
Furthermore, regarding the alternative view that "the Lord creates the world either with a body or without a body," we accept that only the bodiless one possesses the status of creator.
[Objection: Surely agency is based on the engagement in action and is not merely conventional;

since that [engagement] is absent in one who is bodiless due to the absence of action, how could it exist? And where has the agency of a bodiless being ever been observed? [Reply: It is said: agency is defined as the possession of knowledge, desire-to-act, and effort. And it has already been stated that these indeed exist in God.
And in the case of impelling one's own body, the agency of the bodiless self is observed.
And because his agency consists in mere volition, even the conceptualization of the impurity of unbearable suffering incurred through the performance of manifold activities has been set aside.
Now, it has been stated: "And like a potter, if its activity is not postulated, how could an insentient entity conform to his will?"
We too have already stated that just as the insentient body follows the will of the self, so too will the atoms follow its will. (169)
As for the alternative inquiry regarding purpose—namely, "For what reason does the Blessed One create the worlds?"—that too is not sound;
for this is simply the nature of the Blessed One, that he sometimes creates and sometimes withdraws the universe.

If it is asked, "How is it that this nature of his is restricted to a fixed time? let the "Beloved of the Gods" look at the sun, which rises and sets at fixed times. If it is argued that "this form of the sun depends upon the karma of living beings," then the same reasoning applies to God as well.
Even when the creation of the world is for the sake of sport, its state of having accomplished its purpose is not diminished;
for those engaged in sports are never seen to be suffering. //170//
Alternatively, let the Lord undertake creation and destruction out of compassion alone.

Now, it may be objected here: "Beings of such a kind are not objects of compassion, or else a creation consisting solely of happiness would be created by one who possesses compassion. It is true that this objection has been raised, but it is untenable because saṃsāra is beginningless.
The selves are indeed permeated by wholesome and unwholesome formative forces (*saṃskāra*).

Since they are bound by the shackles of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), they are unable to enter the gateway to the city of liberation; how, then, could they not be objects of compassion? For there is no exhaustion of those karmas whose fruits have not yet been experienced, and without creation, the experience of those fruits is impossible. Thus, out of compassion alone, the Blessed One initiates the creation of heavens and so forth for the experience of wholesome fruits, and the creation of hells and so forth for the experience of unwholesome fruits.

For the sake of providing rest at intervals for living beings who have become exhausted by the continuous flow of experience, He even effects the dissolution of the world; thus, all of this is solely rooted in compassion.

Now, it was objected that the simultaneous destruction of the entire world is untenable because there is no possibility of obstructing the experience of the fruits of actions (*karman*) which are indestructible; however, this is not correct, because actions whose power has been stilled remain suspended by being obstructed by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*). Impelled by His will, those actions yield their fruit, while those obstructed by His will remain indifferent to it.
If it is asked why this is so, it is because non-conscious things, when not presided over by consciousness, are never observed to perform their own functions.

[Objection: But surely the selves (*ātman*), who are conscious, will be the agents and supervisors of those very actions, as Bhaṭṭa has said: "Since that [creation] is established by the actions of all living beings, you are proving what is already proven. [Reply: This is not so; these [selves] cannot be supervisors because they are numerous and because they have conflicting intentions.

For instance, how could a single particular entity, such as a mountain or a king, which is the cause for the experience of various kinds of pleasure and pain by millions of living beings, be brought about by those many beings who possess diverse and unsettled intentions? This is because there is no consensus among them on a single point.
Even in the case of a monastic assembly, unanimity occurs only regarding a task that benefits all members in common, not in every instance.
In the construction of a great palace or similar project, it is observed that many craftsmen, such as carpenters, must follow the intention of a single master architect.

Even in the case of ants building a mound of earth, some common benefit must be postulated as the motive, like that of a master architect, or else their conformity to a single intention must be assumed.
But here, this stationary body is a source of benefit for some while being a source of harm for many others; how, then, could it be created by them acting together?
Furthermore, it is simply illogical for insentient things to initiate activity without being presided over by an intelligent agent.
Therefore, one must necessarily postulate a single presiding agent over those actions; for even if actions occur, they are not capable of producing their results without his will.

For this very reason, only one Lord is accepted, not two or many; for if there were more than one, there would be the undesirable consequence of conflict due to differing intentions, leading to the ruinous interference with the grace or destruction of the worlds.
Furthermore, because of the possibility of conflicting desires, there would follow the loss of sovereignty for some through the obstruction of their resolve. Thus, the Lord is indeed one.
It is logical that creation proceeds from his will, such that karmic actions operate toward their effects.
Because their power is paralyzed by the obstruction of His will, the karmas remain inactive; thus, dissolution is logically established.

And thus, that which was stated— "Therefore, even up to the present day, the conception of creation and dissolution here is not established through universal destruction and birth, for it lacks any means of valid cognition"— this too is incorrect.

Let alone the period of cosmic creation and dissolution; even at present, since the ripening of the karma of living beings cannot occur without His will according to the aforementioned principle, God must necessarily be accepted. Otherwise, all worldly activity would fall into ruin.
As it has been said: "This ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain; impelled by God, it goes either to heaven or indeed to hell."

Now, if that is so, let the will of God alone be the creator and the destroyer; what is the use of *karman*? Do not say so, for without *karman*, the diversity of the world cannot be accounted for. Even in the position that [God] is independent of *karman*, three faults have already been shown: the mercilessness of God, the futility of the injunctions regarding *karman*, and the consequence of the impossibility of liberation.
Therefore, the independence of the Lord lies solely in the ordaining of actions, not in being independent of them.
If it is asked, "What is the purpose of such sovereignty?", [the answer is: a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be subject to a purpose.

Or rather, is it that even for the Blessed One there is no power, despite his dependence upon karma? Enough with this crushing of the chatter of atheists whose mouths are smeared with fragments of fallacious reasoning! Therefore, having warded off the mere semblances of refutations sung forth by those who prattle on like bad logicians, the Supreme Lord, skilled in the creation of the three worlds, is established. (171)

But as for those fools who do not accept the Lord, whose nature is established by firm and irreproachable means of valid cognition—even engaging in conversation with them would surely lead to sin; therefore, it is right to desist from such talk. (172)

Salutations to Śiva, who is eternally awakened and joyful, by whose mere will the worlds arise, endure, and once again go to their dissolution at the end of the age; he is the basis for the enjoyment of all fruits. 173.

The Section on Proving the Non-human Origin of the Vedas: Now, even if the Supreme Lord, who is skilled in the creation of the three worlds, were established, it would still not be possible for the Veda to have been composed by him. (174)

One might suspect his authorship regarding the relationship between words and their meanings, or regarding the compositions of the Veda; however, that [authorship] is difficult to maintain in every respect. (175)
A collection of phonemes manifested in sequence is designated as a "word" (pada).
Since phonemes are indestructible, how can they be the product of God? //176//
The relationship as well is not its effect, for it has the nature of a capacity; and the expressive capacity in the word is eternal, like the heat inherent in fire. (177)
Even these Vedic compositions were not created by a person, for they are distinct from the compositions of poetry and other works produced by poets. (178)
And thus, the independence of the Lord with respect to the Veda is not established anywhere;
however, let him at will create or shatter mountains. (179)
We maintain that the Veda possesses intrinsic validity because it is independent of an author; however, we are not universal haters of persons. (180)
Therefore, independence alone is the cause of the Veda's authority;
even if a speaker of the Veda were to exist, what could he possibly do? (181)
But how can these phonemes, which vanish as soon as they are heard, be eternal? Or what is this desire for the independence of sound? (182)
It is said: for no argument for the non-eternality of sound manifests itself;
rather, both perception and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) lead to the understanding of its eternality. (183)

For instance, these reasons for impermanence are indeed stated as follows: "Sound is a product because it is perceived immediately after an effort. Since there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between being a product and being impermanent, the establishment of one necessarily entails the establishment of the other; thus, in certain cases, a particular means of proof is expressed. It is understood that sound, which is perceived immediately after the conjunction and disjunction of the internal air impelled by effort, is indeed a product of that [effort]. Furthermore, because it is not perceived after its utterance, sound is impermanent.
For we do not perceive it even for a moment after it has been uttered;
therefore, we understand that it has perished.
Furthermore, because of the designation by the word "to make," sound is something to be produced;
speakers employ such expressions as "Make a sound" and "Do not make a sound," and they certainly understand that sound is something to be produced.
Furthermore, because sound is perceived simultaneously in various locations and because linguistic usage by means of sound occurs in those respective places, sound is perceived everywhere at once.
This is impossible for that which is a single, eternal entity.
However, if it were an effect, its connection with multiple locations would be possible, as it is produced in many different places by many agents.
Sound is impermanent because it is subject to modification into another sound.
It is understood through both similarity and traditional recollection that in the word "dadhyatra," the phoneme *i* itself becomes the phoneme *y*.
Furthermore, because it is subject to modification, its impermanence is established, just as in the case of grapes, sugarcane juice, and the like.
Furthermore, because it increases as its cause increases:

when uttered with many great efforts, the word "cow" (go-śabda) is perceived as large, whereas when uttered with few small efforts, it is perceived as small. Just as a cloth increases as the threads increase, so too the sound must be an effect, increasing as its cause increases.
All these reasons are indeed non-probative.

For instance, since permanence is established through recognition, it is understood that because perception occurs immediately after effort, the manifestation of sound is the effect of effort, not its production.
Thus, even in the case of something manifested, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as perception can occur immediately after effort.
Furthermore, because the conjunctions and disjunctions of air that manifest sound are not long-lasting, the sound is no longer perceived after a long time following its utterance.

Furthermore, the designation by the word "makes" (karoti) will apply to this [agent] with the intention of referring to the preparatory effort (*prayoga*), just as in the expressions "make cow-dung" or "make wood.
Therefore, that [reason] is also not conclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The simultaneous perception of a single, stable sound in various locations will be established just as it is for the sun.
But its status as a distinct entity (*nikāryatva*) is indeed unestablished, because it is a different word.
The vowel *e* at the end of the word *dadhi* functions in a domain other than *saṃhitā*,
whereas this *y* is entirely different, being employed in the domain of *saṃhitā* when followed by a vowel.
Furthermore, this *ikāra* is not perceived as having actually become a *yakāra*, like milk becoming curd.

Nor is it appropriate to describe it as a modification of the former merely on the basis of similarity in place of articulation—such as the rule that *i*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa* are palatals (*tālavya*)—since such a relationship between a material cause and its modification is not observed even in the case of the eye and the lotus petal, despite their similarity.
Even according to Pāṇini’s traditional rule, *iko yaṇ aci*, the meaning is not that "the *ikāra* becomes a *yakāra*, just as milk becomes curd."
However, regarding this matter, the meaning of the sūtra is that "this phoneme (varṇa) is to be employed in this [position], and this [phoneme] in this [position].
Thus, the treatise is undertaken once the word and its relationship with the meaning are already established.
Since it is said that "it pierces" when there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*),
it follows that the relationship between original form and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) among phonemes exists only in this manner.

Nor does the sound increase with the increase of its cause; even when uttered by many powerful persons, the syllables remain exactly the same in number. It is only the sounds (dhvanis) that are perceived as increased there, not the phonemes (varṇas).
Therefore, the non-eternality [of sound] is not established by such inadequate means;
rather, it is this very *arthāpatti* (presumption) that is accepted for the eternality of sound.
The utterance of a word is intended, first of all, for the purpose of conveying a meaning;
and this [word], having perished as soon as it is uttered, is not capable of conveying that meaning.
There is no disagreement among those who employ words and their meanings on this point:
that a word whose relationship [to its object] is unknown does not denote an object.
That relationship, being cognized through the linguistic conventions of elders,
could not be known without a very long period of time.

For instance, when a child standing at a distance hears the words "Bring a white cow" uttered by one elder and observes another elder acting accordingly, he first infers that the latter has a cognition of the object, because he has seen such action preceded by such a cognition in his own case. Since no other means of knowledge is present and since the action occurs immediately after the words uttered by that elder, he concludes that the latter must have understood something from those very words.
Then, in the next moment, perceiving that object being brought by the elder, he understands: "This object has been understood from this word by this person.
And that object is perceived as a conglomeration of many forms, such as qualities, actions, universals, and individuals;
likewise, the word heard consists of a collection of many words.

By means of the method of insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhāpa*), having heard many times which specific portion of meaning corresponds to which specific portion of the sentence, one determines that—whether according to our own view or yours—the denotation (*abhidheya*) of the word "cow" is the universal "cowness" (*gotvasāmānya*), excluding qualities, actions, and so forth, or simply the substrate possessing that [universal] (*tadvanmātra*).
Thus, the life of the word is established as lasting until the comprehension of its connection, which depends upon a long duration; therefore, it is not subject to instantaneous destruction.
Or, let it be granted that even for a perishable word there is the apprehension of its relation;
nevertheless, once that word whose relation has been apprehended has perished, how can there be a comprehension of meaning from another, entirely new word whose relation has not been apprehended?
If one word were expressive when its relationship [to the object] is known,
then all words would be expressive when their connection to a single [object] is known.

Furthermore, a speaker engaged in linguistic usage does not simultaneously utter the word, establish the relationship [between word and meaning], teach that [usage] to another, and cause the other to engage in usage; for these actions cannot occur at once, as such a thing is never observed.

Now, if it is argued that once the initial apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] has occurred, speakers will understand the meaning upon hearing a newly produced word that is similar to that [original] *go* word—even though that original *go* word has perished—that too is not tenable, because similarity is not perceived.
For no such cognition is observed as "This is like the word *go*," but rather [the cognition is] "This is the very word *go*.
Furthermore, a similarity consisting in the possession of many common constituent parts is not possible for phonemes (*varṇa*), which are partless.

Since the speaker himself cannot ascertain that a newly created word possesses meaning, how could he employ it while harboring the doubt, "How will this listener understand it from me? Furthermore, if he too employs only what resembles a meaningful word, rather than something truly meaningful, then the meaningfulness of that which he employs must likewise derive from its resemblance to another [word]. This would necessitate the recollection of a primordial, meaningful word created at the time of the world's creation, because linguistic usage is rooted in that.
Yet, such is not the case.
Moreover, from that time until today, such similarity does not persist, because the original similarity is destroyed when one imagines a [new] similarity;
this is especially true in the case of words.
Due to differences in speakers, locations, articulatory efforts, and organs of production,
similarity between words situated at a great distance cannot be maintained.
And if [the cognition] were produced by similarity, the apprehension of the object would be false,
like the cognition of fire produced by mist that merely resembles smoke.
Therefore, since the cognition of an object based on similarity is untenable, one must accept that the word "cow" itself is permanent.

Now, one might argue: "Just as the various activities such as grasping the relationship [between sign and signified] are accomplished by relying on the universal *dhūmatva* (smokeness) despite the difference between individual instances of smoke, so too here, despite the difference between individual phonemes such as *ga*, those activities will be accomplished based on a universal. Do not say this; for in that case, the universal *dhūmatva* certainly exists.
However, in this context, the universal *śabdatva* (soundness) is too broad (*vyabhicārin*), while the universal *gośabdatva* (the state of being the word "cow") is difficult to establish.
How can a composite whole, such as the word "go," be constructed from phonemes that are distinct, non-simultaneous, uncombined, and perishable?
And if the word "cow" has not yet been produced, where could the universal "cowness" reside? For the universal called "clothness" does not reside in the threads.

[Objection: "Let it be that 'cowness' (*gośabdatva*) is not a universal; rather, the previously mentioned effect [of linguistic usage] is accomplished by the universals such as *gatva* (the property of being the phoneme *ga*), which reside in individual instances (*vyakti*) such as the letter *ga* that possess distinct forms. [Reply: This too is not so, because universals such as *gatva* are untenable.
For the conventional distinction between individuals and universals is established upon the cognitions of difference and non-difference.
In this case, however, this cognition of non-difference is based solely on the identity of the phoneme (*varṇa*), and is not produced by a universal.

If it is argued that the appearance of difference depends on the difference among the manifestors (*vyañjaka*), and therefore how can there be a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding universals (*jāti*) and individuals (*vyakti*), and that this same method applies even to the refutation of universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*), we say no. This is because the difference between individuals is established with extreme clarity, making it impossible for it to be based on adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) such as manifestors.

Indeed, individual clusters such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and the black cow (*bāhuleya*) are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as having mutually distinct natures. Since the difference between individuals is thus established, and since the cognition "this is a cow" occurring everywhere has no other object than that [individual], the universal "cowness" is indeed accepted.

Furthermore, in this case, where have you ever seen distinct individual instances of the letter *ga*— like the various bodies of brindled cows and so forth— on account of which you would desire a universal (*jāti*) for them?
Whether it be a child, an elder, a woman, or even a parrot who recites,
people perceive a difference in the speaker, but not a difference in the manifestation of the phonemes.

And thus Garga says "Māṭhara recites," where only a difference in the reciter is perceived; it is not a difference in the sound being uttered, as in the case of "He recites this particular Vedic portion."
Even when uttered by a single speaker, there is merely a repetition of that very same [word];
in cases such as *gaṅgā*, *gagana*, and *garga*, no different form is observed.
Even the cognition of distinctions such as "fast" and so forth is based on differences in the *nāda* (articulatory sound),
not produced by differences in the individual [phonemes], because it is like the cognition of a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and other individuals.
Even if the generality *gata* (the "g-sound-ness") is admitted, its distinctness must be accepted despite the appearance of differences such as rapidity and so forth.
One must explain that the appearance of difference in that [generality] is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).

Why, then, is this not explained in the case of the individual manifestation of the letter *ga* itself? For it is precisely because that [individual *ga*] is one that there is the cognition of unity; the delusion of difference, however, is dependent upon the manifestors (*vyañjaka*).
For in this way, the conceptualization becomes simpler;
therefore, there is no such thing as a universal called "g-ness" that exists as a property residing in various individual *ga* sounds.

Furthermore, in cases such as *go*, *guru*, and *goha*, it is determined that the difference in cognition regarding the consonants is caused solely by their association with different vowels and is thus an extrinsic property (*paropādhi*).

This same [difference] must also be an extrinsic property in the case of the vowels themselves, because they are dependent upon phonemes (*varṇa*), just like the cognition of a difference in manifesters (*vyañjaka*).
Therefore, there is no universal of "a-ness" (*atvasāmānya*) corresponding to the universal of "g-ness" (*gatva*).

Furthermore, that which is called the "family of phonemes" consisting of eighteen divisions is merely conditional (*aupādhika*), because cognitions such as short, long, protracted, closed, and open conform to the distinctions among the sounds (*dhvani*).
The manifest [phoneme] is not something other than the concealed one, like the letter *va* is different from the letter *ga*;
rather, it is that very same letter *a* which appears in such a manner.

How then, in the absence of a difference in the word, can there be distinct cognitions of meaning—as in the case of *araṇya* and *āraṇya*? Those [distinctions] will be caused by the sound (*dhvani*) alone.
If it is asked how properties such as length, which are not properties of the word itself, can be a factor in the cognition of meaning, [the answer is: they will be so, like the speed of a horse.
Just as the momentum residing in the body of a horse serves a man to accomplish his purpose,
even so, although it is another's property, a long vowel and the like are beneficial to him.
For this reason as well, this commonality of the form *a* is untenable:

for the quality of being *atva* does not extend to both long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) [vowels], nor does the quality of being *ātva* extend to both short (*hrasva*) and protracted [vowels], nor does the quality of being *ātva* extend to both short and long [vowels].
Therefore, because phonemes are unitary, intermediate sub-species (*jāti*) cannot exist.
However, since the property of being a word (śabdatva) is subject to deviation regarding the comprehension of a specific meaning, the logic of smoke and so forth does not apply here.
Therefore, the cognition of meaning from a word is not otherwise possible unless there is permanence; thus, in this case, presumption (*arthāpatti*) is a means of valid cognition.
No difference from inference is observed in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*);
therefore, it is not impossible to employ this very [presumption] as an inference.

This is what is stated: "Sound is an eternal property" is the thesis to be proven, because it conveys meaning in dependence upon the apprehension of its relationship [with that meaning], like the universal of smoke and so forth.
This has been stated [in the Sūtra]: "But its eternity would follow from its being for the sake of another.
Thus, from the time of the apprehension of the relationship until the comprehension of the meaning, since there is no cause for destruction, sound is eternal, like the self and other such entities.

For this sound does not perish through the destruction of its parts, because it is partless. If it is asked how that is so, it is said: if a phoneme were produced even by a very slight effort, or if it were not perceived, then no fragment of it would be perceived.
For in a substance that possesses parts, two kinds of parts are observed: those that have begun their function and those that have not.
However, in this case, no parts whatsoever—whether having begun their function or not—are perceived in color, as they are in threads and so forth in a cloth;
nor are they inferred, due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Nor does the destruction of sound result from the destruction of its substratum, because, like the self (*ātman*) and other such entities, it is non-dependent; or, if one holds the position that it depends on space (*ākāśa*), then [space] is eternal.
Furthermore, there exists no other cause whatsoever for the destruction of sound.

The destruction of cloth and similar objects is observed through gradual consumption or by means of cutting with weapons and the like; however, such destruction is never possible for sound at any time.
Therefore, if a sound remains even while concealed for another moment,
by what could it be destroyed once it has escaped from the jaws of death?
Furthermore, sound is eternal because of the absence of number.
People say, "The word *go* has been uttered eight times," but they do not say, "There are eight *go*-words. From this, its oneness is understood.
This suffix *kṛtvasuc*, which is prescribed for counting the repetition of an action, occurs when there is no difference among the agents of the action.
Therefore, it is merely a repetition of the utterance.
As it has been said: "Since there is no difference among the agents of the actions, the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is used for the repetitions of the action;
because of its employment, the action of that word certainly recurs."
They know that the suffix *kṛtvasuc* occurs after a word denoting number when there is repetition of an action, the existence [of that action], and the non-difference of the agents of the action.
Thus, in this manner, recognition is stated to be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the eternity of sound, witnessed by all hearers.
For indeed, there exists the cognition "this very word 'cow' is that same one," which is auditory, free from defects of the sense organ, sublation, and doubt.
This cognition is auditory because it conforms to the presence and absence of the operation of the auditory faculty;
nor is any deficiency perceived in its generative instrument;
nor does this cognition arise by touching upon two alternatives in the form of "what could it be? or "is it this or that?"
Nor do we perceive any other sublating cognition (*bādhaka*) regarding this that would lead one to conclude, "This is not so.

Furthermore, because it apprehends an additional object of knowledge—the non-existence at the present time—it ought to be considered a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps an unapprehended object.
Moreover, even according to the Blessed One’s own system, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is accepted as valid despite its grasping what has already been grasped.
For it is not possible for you to assert that [the Veda] lacks authority, unlike the Śākyas, because you accept that entities are momentary.
And it is not tenable to say that its object is similarity,
nor that its object is a universal, because both [of these positions] have been refuted.
Some claim that [the Veda] lacks authority because its existence is concealed; that is incorrect, since the very perception of it precludes its concealment.
Even in your own view, this sound persists for three or four moments;
and recognition is not unestablished within such a duration of time.
But in this life, which lasts for only a single moment, such realization is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Indeed, no object that is not a producer [of cognition] is apprehended by cognition.
This will be explained in the refutation of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga*).
Moreover, just as at midnight, amidst a mass of clouds dark as bees, something is recognized by means of the flashes of lightning; [so too is the self recognized].
Likewise, sound is recognized through the winds, which, though momentary, arise in a sequence of conjunctions and disjunctions that do not cease.
To this, [the author] replies with the introductory remark "by the Maruts": "Well said!

Let the matter of recognition (pratyabhijñāna) rest for now; first of all, that restricted perception of sound which occurs at the very outset is difficult to reconcile with the theory of manifestation (abhivyakti)."
Since all sounds exist everywhere and at all times due to their eternity and omnipresence, what is the determining factor for their perception as distinct individuals?
For what are called "sounds" (dhvanis) are either air particles characterized by conjunctions and disjunctions, or the conjunctions and disjunctions themselves residing in the air;
these are held to be the manifesters of sound.
By means of them, either the instrument (the vocal organ) is refined, or the action [of articulation], or both; and in every case, there is an error [in your position].
If the auditory organ were merely refined (saṃskṛta), then there would be the hearing of all sounds;
for what reason is there this restriction that the refinement applies only to the letter *ga*?
Moreover, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sense organ is simply the withdrawal of the still air;
and this [refinement] is indeed common to all objects situated in that location.
Just as one whose vision has reached the edge of a curtain sees every object in that location upon the stage.
Likewise, when the obstructing wind is dispelled by the spreading [of sound],
the auditory organ will perceive all sounds in that location without exception.

And you maintain that the auditory organ is space (*ākāśa*), which is all-pervading and partless; yet, when that [space] is refined in one particular location, all those who possess the means for refinement would simultaneously become so, and thus everyone would hear. Consequently, the distinction between the deaf and the non-deaf would be untenable.

But if it is the object that is being refined, then because that [word-sound] is partless and all-pervading, it would be refined everywhere and thus heard everywhere; consequently, a word such as "cow" manifested in the Madra country would be heard in Kashmir.
For its refinement cannot be mediated by its substratum, since—like space—it is not dependent on a substratum.
Even on the view that it is dependent on space, this remains the case because space is one.

Nor is the word "cow" (go-śabda) refined part by part, because it is without constituent parts. For it has been said: "When a word is uttered with even the slightest effort, the intellect either does not grasp it at all, or it grasps the phoneme clearly in its entirety."
But in the view that [the manifestation] belongs to both [the organ and the object], neither of the two faults is avoided: namely, the apprehension of all [sounds] and the hearing of them everywhere.
Furthermore, it is never observed that entities occupying the same location and perceptible by the same sense organ are manifested by specific manifestors.
A lamp brought by the householder to see a pot of curd in the house illuminates the cakes in that same place as well.

Therefore, it is only in the case of the theory that sound is produced that its apprehension is conceived as being restricted to a specific location, not in the case of the theory that it is merely manifested.
Furthermore, on the view that [sound] is manifested (*abhivyakti*), the distinction between intense and weak, as well as the suppression (*abhibhava*) of one sound by another, would not be possible.
For no sound is inherently intense or weak, since there is no internal differentiation within it.
Nor can there be any intensity or weakness in the impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the cause of its manifestation, such that a corresponding cognition of the object could arise in accordance with it.

Alternatively, if the quality of wind were intense and so forth, how could it be perceived by the auditory organ? For in the case of an object possessing parts, there is the possibility of perceiving some specific qualities while others remain unperceived; thus, depending on those [parts], a difference in cognition would occur.
But here, in the case of sound, which is partless, such a thing is not possible. Therefore, the position that sound is produced (kṛtaka) alone is superior.
To this it is replied: let it be for now that the position of the refinement of the sense organ (karaṇasaṃskārapakṣa) alone holds true;
and that sense organ, having received a particular refinement from the winds, perceives only a certain sound.
Just as, in your own view, certain conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs are held to be the producers of some particular phoneme;
Likewise, for us, certain conjunctions and disjunctions with that air alone are capable of producing a refinement in the auditory organ when some [sound] is being perceived.
Just as you maintain a restriction on their capacity for production,
so too do I maintain a restriction on their capacity for manifestation.

If it is argued that no restriction regarding manifestors is observed, who says this—not even the Thousand-Eyed One? For instance, fragrance, while residing in the earth alone, occupies the same location [as the earth] and is perceptible by the same sense organ, since it is the exclusive object of the olfactory faculty;
and its being manifested by specific manifestors is indeed observed.
In some places the fragrance of the earth is manifested through contact with fire, in some by the touch of the sun's rays, and in others by the sprinkling of water.

Nor is the refinement of the sense-organ intended to be merely the removal of stagnant air, which would be common to all; rather, it is something else entirely—specific to each respective object and characterized by its connection [with that object].

As for what was further asserted—that if the auditory organ were admitted to be space (*nabhas*), there would be only one auditory organ for all living beings—that too is incorrect, because merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) act as the determinants.

Since even space can be partitioned by other limitations, just like the "space within a jar" (*ghaṭākāśa*), the distinction between those who are deaf and those who are not is based precisely upon merit and demerit.
Moreover, this fault belongs only to you who maintain the restrictive thesis that space itself is the auditory organ (*śrotra*).

For the Mīmāṃsakas, however, the auditory organ is not necessarily space alone; rather, it is some kind of instrument (*karaṇa*) established through the presumption based on the necessity of the effect (*kāryārthāpatti*), which is restricted to each individual person. Thus, there is no over-extension of the definition.
Accordingly, Bhartṛmitra considers the auditory organ to be simply the refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by the wind.

Alternatively, let the position that the sense-object is embellished (saṃskāra) be maintained; even so, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga), because the embellishment occurs only in respect to a specific location.
Nor is there an embellishment of this [ether] part by part, because it is partless (niravayava).
Nevertheless, its apprehension will be restricted, just like [the apprehension of] a universal (jāti).
And likewise, in your own position, just as a genus (*jāti*) that is omnipresent is perceived only in the location of the individual (*piṇḍa*),
yet even though it is grasped in its entirety, it is not seen elsewhere in another individual.
Likewise, sound is omnipresent; it is not perceived in places where there is no sound, yet even when perceived in its entirety in one place, it is perceived again elsewhere.
The phoneme (*piṇḍa*) is the manifester of the genus (*jāti*), while sound (*dhvani*) is the manifester of the word;
what use is there for distinctions such as being dependent or independent?

Because of the lack of distinction between being omnipresent and being partless, qualities such as intensity and dullness, although they are properties of the sound-manifestations (*dhvani*), appear as residing in the word-sound (*śabda*) itself.

This is just as properties of an individual body, such as stoutness or leanness, are sometimes perceived as residing in the universal (*jāti*), since we observe the appearance of such cognitions as "the cows are lean" even when the specific particulars like the *śābaleya* cow have not been grasped.
Or rather, since intensity, dullness, and so forth are not perceived as properties of the phoneme itself,
it is simply the cognition that arises in such a manner, conforming to its manifestor.
Those phonemes remain exactly as they are, subject to increase and decrease;
likewise, there is no mutual overpowering among them by their own nature.
Overwhelmed by the Maruts, they were like weaklings before the Maruts;
they were like the light of lamps during the day before the brilliance of the sun.
In this way, the position of both types of conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*) becomes equally consistent, as the faults of both [theories] have been removed.
Therefore, for sound, whose permanence is established by the power of the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), manifestation (*abhivyakti*) alone is the more tenable [explanation].

And let this be considered, O noble ones: between the two positions—that [the word-meaning] is produced by the action or that it is manifested by it—wherein is the assumption regarding the perception of the word more cumbersome or more concise?
For instance, sirs, the Vaiśeṣikas, the Sāṃkhyas, the Jains, and the Buddhists are proponents of the theory that sound is a product;
as for the wretched Cārvākas, whose kind would ever come to mind in such assemblies? Furthermore, for you Vaiśeṣikas, this conceptualization regarding the hearing of sound is exactly the same:
sound arises either from conjunction or from disjunction.

Once produced, it generates other sounds of the same kind in all directions—above, below, and across—in the shape of a *kadamba* flower bud, located in adjacent regions; those [sounds] likewise generate others in the same manner. Thus, through a continuous process of initiation in the form of a wave-series, the final sound produced in the space of the auditory organ (*śrotrākāśa*) is perceived by that very organ as being inherent (*samaveta*) within it.
Thus, this is first of all an exceedingly grating conceptual construction.
That one sound produces another sound is, first of all, contrary to common experience;
for a causal relationship is not observed among them in the same way as it is in the case of cognitions.
Sounds are produced in adjacent locations, and they are similar to themselves;
[they spread] sideways, upwards, and downwards—what kind of faith is this of yours?
And how do they cease producing other sounds? For their momentum cannot be conceived as subject to exhaustion, like that of the winds.
Furthermore, how could there be a non-production of sound when there is an obstruction such as a wall? For since space is all-pervading, it must certainly exist even within the wall.

Now, if it is maintained that space—which is devoid of conjunction with substances such as walls that possess the nature of obstruction—is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) in the production of sound, then the specific proof for this must be stated here.
And how could a weak sound be produced by a strong one when their effort is equal? Moreover, it is observed that a strong sound is heard from nearby, while a weak sound is heard from afar.
Furthermore, it is difficult to maintain that sounds possess a similarity to a continuous succession of waves,
for they are insubstantial in nature and devoid of physical form, motion, momentum, and the like.

As for the argument that "sound produces its own kind because it is a quality, like color and so forth," this is unproven; for one attempts to prove something with what is itself unproven, since its being a quality is not established.
Sound is never perceived as dependent [on another substance], like color and other qualities which reside in a substance; therefore, how can it have the status of a quality?
Furthermore, sound does not originate another sound because it is a quality (*guṇa*), like color;
nor does sound originate sound because it is sound (*śabdatva*), like the sound perceived by the auditory organ.

"Conjunction and disjunction are not the producers of sound, because they are conjunctions and disjunctions, like the conjunctions and disjunctions of other things"—such counter-arguments (pratihetu) are also easily available here; therefore, this [position] is trivial.

The followers of Kapila, however, assert that the functioning of the auditory organ (*śrotravṛtti*) travels to the location of the sound and is modified by the sound; in that case, since the auditory organ is all-pervading, there would be no rule as to why its function is modified only by a sound located nearby and not by one located at a distance. And due to the absence of such a rule, the word "cow" uttered in Kānyakubja would be heard even in Gauramūlaka. Furthermore, since the functioning of the auditory organ is formless (*amūrta*), it could not be obstructed by material objects such as walls as it spreads forth; consequently, even a sound situated beyond an obstruction would be audible.
Furthermore, when the wind is favorable to the sound, its hearing would not occur;
for that wind is contrary to the functioning of the auditory faculty in one who is moving [against it].

The fact that sound is heard even at a distance when carried by a following wind, and is not heard even nearby when carried against the wind—this would be the opposite of what is observed under this [current] view.
Since there is no difference between the function and that which possesses the function, [the self] would be like the sense organ;
if the function were thus all-pervasive, why is there no perception everywhere?

The Ārhatas, however, have said: "Sound, having its body composed of subtle sound-pudgalas, emerges from its own originating level and reaches the root of each person's ear. This is indeed a very eloquent statement: "There exist certain subtle pudgalas which are the parts of a phoneme; by them, that which is called the whole—the phoneme—is produced. Behold the wonder!"
While those [phonemes] are not being perceived, what kind of sequential arrangement could there be? By what configuration could which sound be produced?
These parts are minute and are not bound together by anything;
nor are they capable of making this composite of color-parts solid.
And as he travels on, being emaciated, how would he not be scattered by the winds?
Or, struck by trees and such, how would he not break into pieces?
And what was the limit of the journey for this ascetic as he traveled? Or how could that which had entered the ear of one be heard by others?
If it were held that [the sound], having emerged from one ear, enters into the interior of the other ear,
how could it be heard simultaneously by many people?
There is no possibility of multiple obstructions arising according to the number of listeners,
because the speaker's effort remains the same whether there is a plurality or unity among the listeners.
Therefore, enough with this discussion of the cleverness of the wisdom of the naked mendicant teacher, which serves as the cause for such great ridicule.

The Śākyas, however, assert that sound is perceived by the power of the ear even without reaching it; this is the utterance of one who is utterly deluded, because if non-reach were the same for all cases, there would be no reason for the non-hearing of sounds that are distant or obstructed, and because it would entail the non-occurrence of the functional property known as "acting upon contact" (*prāpyakāritā*). Nor is it proper to disregard this matter without investigation, as the Cārvākas do.
Thus have been these logical constructions regarding the position that [sound] is a product;
now hear the construction of the Vedic scholars regarding its manifestation.
It is quite clear that the air within the body, impelled by an effort preceded by the desire to speak, issues outward due to its velocity and its possession of motion.
In the view of those who maintain that the wind is directly perceptible, it is perceived at the time of blowing simply by touching with the hand placed near the mouth of the speaker.
Even in the view that the wind is inferable, it is inferred at that time by the movement of a tuft of cotton placed in the vicinity of the mouth.
Moving in all directions, it causes a movement in the still air;
and as it reaches the space of the ear, it becomes fit for audition.
And that [effort], being of the nature of intensity and continuity,
serves as the cause for the cognition of such a kind in the case of sound.
And as he goes, performing actions through the application of unrestrained speed, he ought not to travel far, for his momentum will surely be exhausted like that of an arrow.
Being corporeal, it is obstructed by other corporeal things such as walls; therefore, there is no hearing for this [sound] when its nature is concealed by an intervening object.
Because it possesses the quality of moving with velocity, from whichever direction the hearer comes,
from that very direction he perceives the sound as approaching.
But that air, impelled by its conjunction with a conch shell or other such instruments,
becomes the cause of the manifestation of sound, which is devoid of phonetic form (avarṇarūpa).
Even though sound, insofar as it consists of phonemes, is not perceived by the auditory organ,
nevertheless the quality of "sound-ness" (śabdatva) will be grasped therein by hearing.
Therefore, in this case, we have never made any excessive conceptualization, because the movement of this wind is well-known to all the world.
Only its transition through the space of the ear has been postulated as unperceived;
yet even that is not something unprecedented, since it is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on the necessity of the effect.
Impartial judges,
considering the origin of the word, have declared that the theory of manifestation is simpler than the theory of production.

Thus, since the restriction of the order of recitation is established under the theory of manifestation, one must accept its very permanence on the basis of the validity of the cognition of recognition.
But as for the statement regarding inconclusiveness based on the recognition of cognitions and actions,
when this objection is raised against perception, it demonstrates extreme stupidity.
Perception is certainly not invalidated by that defect of inference;
however, to entertain other philosophical systems would be utterly irrelevant.
If there is unimpeded recognition of cognition and action, let them also possess eternality; if not, what similarity do they have with sound?
Therefore, for those logicians who perceive it, sound is established as eternal through the power of recognition;
the presumption previously mentioned regarding its non-eternality has been refuted, and the arguments for that instability have been discarded.
Furthermore, there is a statement in the Veda which restates what is already established—that [the word] must be declared as permanent;
therefore, even from the observation of such indicative marks (liṅga), one should consider sound to be eternal.

However, those learned in the science of phonetics (śikṣāvidaḥ) declare that sound consists solely of air; this is incorrect because it is not perceived as such. Furthermore, according to the principle of the negation of the person (pudgala-paryudāsa) well-known in the Arhat’s doctrine, even the constituent parts of air must be excluded.

Even those who, on the basis of observing gross destruction, might claim that all things perish moment by moment, are unable to assert the same for sound. For while they maintain that such a misconception arises because decay is observed at the end [of objects], in the case of sound there is neither an end nor a final destruction; how then could it be broken like a jar?

Regarding the doctrine of the impermanence of sound, we reply here: indeed, these two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which you have stated are not at all capable of establishing the permanence of sound.

As for the argument based on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that was stated—namely, "because perception exists for the sake of another"—that is already exhausted, since the cognition of the object is established even otherwise.
In this regard, even similarity has been refuted precisely because it was not accepted; thus, you are laboring in an inappropriate place.
Having resorted to universals such as "cow-ness" and so forth, and having grasped their relations,
linguistic usage— extending up to the comprehension of meaning— will proceed.
Surely the nature of going has been refuted; let this very point be examined.
This discussion concludes here, for this is our vital point.
Since motion and the like have been refuted, there can be no comprehension of an object otherwise; nor is there any other basis for recognition. Thus, we are defeated.
But once the universal property of *g*-ness is established, it is that very thing which constitutes the cognition of the object;
since that alone is what is to be recognized, you are defeated.
Therefore, setting aside all other elaborate displays of dialectical positions,
we shall now strive to establish the existence of the primordial genus (*ādi-jāti*).

In this regard, let this be investigated: is this appearance of a difference in the letter *ga* produced by a difference in the manifesting agents (*vyañjaka*), or does it have as its object a difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves?

If that [notion of identity] were produced by a difference in manifesters, then since the letter *ga* is a single entity, what would be the function of the universal *gatva*? However, if it has as its object the difference between phonemes, then since that difference is established, one must seek the object of the cognition of non-difference; thus, the universal *gatva*, which is grasped by that cognition, is unavoidable.
To this it is replied: this cognition of a difference in the letter *ga* is not produced by a difference in its manifesters (*vyañjaka*).
