For if this appearance of difference were dependent upon a difference in the manifesters, then why would the cognition of the difference between the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and so forth, not also be caused by that? Consequently, one must accept—as the Grammarians do—that the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) is a single, partless entity transcending all conceptual constructions of individual letters.

Now, if you think that because the specific forms of the phonemes *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and so forth are distinguished from one another, the cognition of their difference is caused solely by the difference in their objects and is not based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then the appearance of a difference between the letter *ga* in words such as *gaṅgā*, *gagana*, and *garga* should likewise not be dependent on a difference in the manifestors (*vyañjaka*). For even there, the specific forms of mutually distinct *ga*s are perceived.

Indeed, when there is a difference among speakers—as in the case of a parrot, a maina, and a human—one might perhaps suspect that the cognition of a difference between phonemes is produced by the manifestor, due to the possibility of a plurality of manifestors. But this is not the case here.

If, however, the mouth is one and the same, how can there be a distinction [in the sounds] produced by it? [Objection: Even in that case, the winds (*marut*) themselves are indeed distinct as manifestors; let the mouth be one—what does that matter? Or perhaps even that [the mouth] is different, some say. It is replied:
In that case, since the distinction among the winds is equal even in the case of *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and so on, let there be no distinction among these either.

Now, it was argued that while there is a perception of distinction among the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*, such [a perception] does not exist in the case of the letter *ga*; rather, the difference there belongs only to the act of pronunciation (*uccāraṇa*), not to the phoneme being pronounced (*uccārya*).
This argument is not sound. Let it be granted that there is no perception of this kind of "distinction" (*viśeṣa*); nevertheless, the cognition of difference (*bhedabuddhi*) certainly exists.
Furthermore, what is called a "cognition of distinction" is one thing, and a "cognition of difference" is another.
Even when there is no appearance of distinction, in some cases there is a specific cognition of separation.
Now, it might be argued here: "A cow-individual such as Bāhuleya is seen to be distinct from other individuals such as Śābaleya; therefore, difference exists as a reality."
But a distinct cow-individual, clearly manifested and separated from other cow-individuals, is not perceived as being produced through differences such as speed and so forth.

Thus, it has not been said that in the case of a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and the like, particularities (*viśeṣa*) residing in each individual limb—such as the dewlap, hooves, and hump—are perceived;
and these [limbs] are easily discerned because of their grossness.

However, in cases such as blue rice or horse-gram (*kulattha*), where particularities do not appear in every grain (*siktha*), there nevertheless exists a perception of distinction despite the absence of the perception of particularities, because one grain appears as distinct from another grain.
In the same way here as well, although there is no appearance of it being "this specific *ga*-sound," the plurality of *ga*-sounds is established because they are perceived as distinct.

"Is it not the case that even in the case of rice grains and the like, distinctions indeed appear from one grain to another? For if those were not perceived, even their difference could not be apprehended. Do not speak thus; for when effort is applied, specific features such as being square, triangular, or circular will also appear there.
The same applies to the letter *ga*s as well.

However, even without deliberate effort, the cognition of a division arises at the very moment of the first impact of the sense organ; by that very cognition, the plurality [of sounds] is established.

[Objection: Surely, a cognition of disjunction cannot arise for one who has not apprehended a specific difference; thus, the cognition of a specific difference is itself the cognition of disjunction. [Reply: This is not so, because even when the subtle differences among the moments of an action such as revolving are not manifested, there is still a manifestation of disjunction.
But surely, even in that case, the perception of a distinction must be postulated, since otherwise the cognition of a break would be untenable.
If this is so, then let the perception of a distinction be postulated in the case of phonemes as well, since a cognition of a break is observed in the case of space and so forth.
[Objection: "Surely that [distinction] exists, but it is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), like the cognition of redness in a crystal. [Reply: This is an unequal example.
Since a pure crystal is observed, let the cognition of redness in it be caused by an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) such as lac;

however, because phonemes always appear as possessing specific qualities such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth, and because they are never perceived devoid of them, this distinction is innate (*naisargika*).

Just as cognitions— which are devoid of specific objects such as jars or cloths— are manifold according to each respective object because they are not perceived [as identical], so too are phonemes manifold according to each specific quality such as the acute accent (*udātta*).

Nor is it tenable to argue that cognition alone is eternal and its differentiation is based on the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of different objects, since you yourself have stated that "the arising of cognition is directly perceived" (*pratyakṣa*),
and because we ourselves shall later refute the eternity of cognition.

If you argue that the distinction between objects is established by the distinction between their cognitions, then from what source does the distinction between those cognitions themselves arise? If you say it arises from the distinction between further cognitions, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Therefore, these cognitions possess distinction inherently, and the distinction among objects likewise exists inherently; it is simply that this distinction among objects is known through cognition. Thus, enough of this detour into other matters.

Just as there is a plurality of the quality of white, which possesses distinctions such as brilliant, smoky, and so forth, so too there is a plurality of phonemes (varṇa) which possess distinctions such as the acute accent (udātta) and others. If it is argued that the quality of white is indeed one and its apparent difference is due only to the difference in its substrates, then oh! the Bhaṭṭa has truly become steeped in aesthetic sentiment (rasa): "Action is one, cognition is also one, and the white quality is the only one in the world;
and this [unity] is eternal"—these are the words of a lover in the house of a woman.

Moreover, the doctrine of a single self would likewise follow [from this], since the distinction between those who experience pleasure, pain, and so forth can be accounted for even by the difference of bodies;
and this path does not lead very far from non-dualism. Enough, then, with this false boasting.

Therefore, the cognition of difference is produced solely by the proximity (*upaśleṣa*) of the space of the sky [i.e., the preceding vowel], and not by a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) [of the consonants themselves]; for this has been stated: "In your own view as well, there is no difference even in the letter *a*.
And when that proximity is absent, a distinction certainly appears between *digajaḥ* and *diggajaḥ*.

Likewise, in cases such as *samadaḥ* and *sammadaḥ*, *paṭaḥ* and *paṭṭaḥ*, *āsanaṃ* and *āsannaṃ*, *malaḥ* and *mallaḥ*, *avikaḥ* and *avikkaḥ*, *patiḥ* and *pattiḥ*, *patanaṃ* and *pattanaṃ*, and so forth, there is likewise a perception of a difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*).
Even the difference in the comprehension of meaning in cases such as *digaja* and *diggaja* must be caused by a different word (*śabdāntara*), not by a double utterance.

An increase in meaning results from an increase in the textual content (*grantha*), not from a difference in utterance; for even if the word *go* is employed a hundred times, there is no cognition of a denotable object other than that which possesses a dewlap and so forth.
Thus, those learned in words declare that in the term *diggaja*, there is a designation consisting of two *ga*-sounds, rather than a single *ga*-sound being uttered twice.

[Objection: "But surely, since the cognition of the phoneme *ga* persists even when there is a difference in the vowels (*ac*)—as in *go*, *guru*, *giri*, *geha*, and so on—this *ga* must be one and the same. [Response: Do not speak thus! For it is precisely this cognition of difference that has been demonstrated by us. Furthermore, we have described the cognition of difference even in the absence of contact with a vowel, as in the case of *diggaja* and the like.

Nor do we deny the cognition of non-difference; rather, because the cognition of difference also exists without being sublated and because it is not otherwise established, we maintain that, like cows and the like, it possesses the nature of both a universal and a particular."

However, it has already been stated that it is possible to assert that even in the case of [the sounds] *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*, [their difference] is based on a difference in their manifestors (*vyañjaka*).
Moreover, since even the cognition of differences such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) is based on the difference among the manifestors, that [universal] would have to be one and the same.

But surely, what is the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) there, by whose distinction the cognition of the distinction between individual bodies (*piṇḍa*) is held to occur? And it has been said: "In this case, there is no manifesting sound (*dhvani*) distinct from the individual body;
rather, the universal such as 'cowness' (*gotva*) is always perceived as manifested by the individual body alone."
That is incorrect, because the genus *hotṛ* is now beyond dispute, just like the universal *g-ness*;
furthermore, the cognition of difference between individual bodies (*piṇḍabheda*) can be accounted for even by the difference in the operation of the visual faculty.

[Objection: Surely, even for one whose eyes have been engaged but once, there occurs the appearance of mutually distinct individual bodies. [Reply: Not so; at that time, there is merely the cognition of "cowness.

However, regarding the apprehension of specific differences—such as "this is a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow)" and "this is a *bāhuleya* (a black cow)"—a distinction in the operation of the eye is unavoidable.

And if the cognition produced by the contact of the first sense-organ attains excellence when there is a difference between two lumps of clay, then what has caused its misfortune when there is a difference between two *ga* sounds? For even in that case, at the very moment of the first operation of the auditory organ, the difference between *ga* sounds is indeed manifested, even for one who has not yet perceived the distinctions among the manifestors—as is seen in the case of the sky or the celestial Ganges. Enough of this digression.

Therefore, this is the summary of the matter: either let the conventional usage of "universal" and "particular" be disregarded everywhere, or let there be a universal of "ga-ness" (gatva) residing in the various individual *ga* sounds, just like "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth.
The property of being a vowel (*actva*) must likewise be admitted as irreducible, because short, long, and protracted *a*-sounds appear as mutually distinct entities.

Furthermore, for one who would claim that the recognition of the sound *a* persists even in the case of the letter *ā*, it would follow that the letter *a* itself would be perceived in the cognitions of *ī*, *u*, and so on, since there is no difference in their status as vowels.
Now, if a distinction between the *ivarṇa* and the *avarṇa* is admitted despite their lack of difference [in phonetic quality], then that [distinction] must not be denied for the vowel *ā*.
And this being so, the cognition of distinct meanings from the words *araṇya* and *āraṇya* will be logically established.

Even the distinctions such as acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), circumflex (svarita), closed (saṃvṛta), and open (vikṛta) are directly perceived by those who know words, just as the division of scales, groups, and modes is perceived by those who know music.
Therefore, they declare that the letter *a* has eighteen varieties; and they designate its commonality (*sāmānya*) as the "family of the *a*-sound" (*avarṇakula*).
As for the claim that even phonetic properties such as length (*dīrghatva*) serve as a factor in the comprehension of meaning—likened to the speed of a horse—that too is unconvincing;
people comprehend meaning from the word (*śabda*), not from the winds (*marut*).

Now, if it is argued that words of the Maruts also cause the cognition of meaning because they possess such conventional usage (*vyutpatti*), then conventional usage itself would be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not the word; for while conventional usage is non-deviant, the word is deviant. Let this matter rest.

Therefore, since the effect— which consists of the comprehension of meaning— is fully accomplished through universals such as "ga" and so forth, there is no need for the individual phonemes to be eternal.

Another says: let alone the higher generalities (aparasāmānya) that exist at a distance; even the highest generality (mahāsāmānya), namely "sound-ness" (śabdatva), is not possible in the case of phonemes.
Where, upon the perception of one individual, there occurs a mental connection with another individual, there a universal of a single form is postulated, and that [connection] is produced by it.
At the time of hearing the sound "ga," there is no mental apprehension of the sound "va," just as there is no apprehension of a brindled cow when perceiving a black cow.
The cognition "this is sound, this is sound" is not the determining factor;
for this [cognition] merely conforms to the limiting condition (upādhi) of being perceivable by the auditory organ.
This is merely the statement of one who lacks a coherent investigation (*anusaṃdhāna*).
For the cognition of synthesis (*anusandhāna-pratyaya*) is not a necessary factor for the establishment of a universal (*sāmānya*);
indeed, synthesis occurs even among heterogeneous things due to similarity, just as there is a synthesis of the individual cow at the time of perceiving a *gavaya*.
Therefore, the conventional usage of "universal" (sāmānya) is established solely upon a cognition that possesses a single, uncontradicted form.
Even when a universal, which is grasped by an identical cognition, is present,
there occurs in some cases a connection with another [object], while in other cases it does not occur at all.
That [cognition] exists in the case of fragments, heads, and so forth, because it is produced by the similarity of the whole;
however, since that [similarity] is absent in the case of phonemes such as 'ga', that [cognition] does not exist there.
But it is not because of the absence of a universal.
Nor is it appropriate to assert, as the Sāṅkhyas do, that similarity alone is the universal, because such [similarity] is observed even among heterogeneous things such as cows and gavayas.

If it is argued that the recurring cognition "this is sound, this is sound" is produced by the limiting condition (upādhi) of being perceivable by the auditory organ, then one must likewise, like the Buddhists, deny the existence of universals such as "cowness" (gotva), because the single cognition regarding cows and the like is based on their performing a single purposeful action, such as carrying or yielding milk.
But this is not the case; therefore, just like "cowness," "soundness" (śabdatva) also cannot be rejected.
By this, it should be understood that the universal such as "Brahmin-ness" (*brāhmaṇatva*) is also established, because it is accessible through perception aided by instruction.

Nor does its dependence on instruction imply that it is not perceptible; for even the cognition of "cowness" (*gotva*) is seen to depend on [instruction] at the time of grasping the relationship [between word and object].
And it has been said: "Indeed, that which is apprehended after climbing a mountain peak is not thereby non-perceptual."
Furthermore, the cognition of "Brāhmaṇa" in Paiṭhīnasi, Paippalādi, and others is not based on an adventitious condition (aupādhika), because no such condition is perceived;
for it would then be possible to assert that even the nature of being a cow (gotva) and so forth is merely adventitious.
Furthermore, some maintain that the eye, even without depending on instruction, perceives the Brahmin caste—which possesses a gentle appearance and is distinct from Kṣatriyas and others;
but enough of this discussion.

The subject at hand is now stated: since the comprehension of meaning is established by means of universals (jāti) such as "going" and so forth, that which was said—that "perception exists for the sake of another"—is untenable.
By this, the argument that [the universal] exists everywhere because of simultaneity is also refuted, since the restriction of the relation is established by the phonemes *ga* and so forth alone.

As for the observation that the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is employed because of the absence of a number, that too is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), since it is seen even when there is a difference [in the referent], as in: "The slender-limbed woman performed three sidelong glances at Kāñcana, four firm embraces, and eight kisses."

Now, if it is argued that there is no difference between the woman and the man in this case, and that there is only a difference in actions such as kissing and so forth, even so, we observe the common usage: "The Brahmins have eaten five times," when Brahmins who were previously [unfed] have finished eating.
In this way, even with respect to sound, the conventional usage of that same number is observed when a poet composes a display of syllables containing alliteration.
For people indeed employ the expression, "Many *ga*-sounds have been seen";
and even that recognition which has been cited is mediated by that [perceptual experience].
Once its validity is established, it would have a universal (jāti) as its objective support,
because we [perceive] the recognition of dancing, acting, gestures, and so forth.
We are not able to rescue the recognition of sound;
we do not perceive even the slightest distinction in that recognition.
In the case of recognitions such as that of a pillar, there is no cognition of non-destruction at that very moment;
therefore, those [recognitions] are unable to counteract the doctrine of momentary destruction.
At the very moment of the recognition of sound, the destruction of the sound's form is perceived; how, then, can its permanence be established?

Although we ourselves shall establish the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) even in the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), nevertheless, this is precisely the distinction between the recognition of pillars and the like and the recognition of sound: that in the latter case, there arises a cognition as if "this very sound has perished.
For this very reason, they say that recognition is invalid even when an object is concealed.
Even though our word may persist for two or three moments,
recognition is not possible within such a short duration of time.
For instance, first the sound arises;
thereafter, it produces a cognition of its own object, because that which does not produce [cognition] cannot appear [in it].
Then, by means of that cognition, the sound is apprehended.
From that, there is the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
From that, it produces a cognition of its own object, because that which does not produce [cognition] cannot appear [in it].
Then, by means of that cognition, the sound is apprehended.
From that, there arises the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*);
from that, the recollection of the word previously known;
and from that, the auditory faculty or the mental faculty, assisted by that [recollection], will produce the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the word.

If it is argued that its long life is postulated on the grounds that "the sound will be perceived then," precisely because of the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), [we reply: it is true that such a life-span is postulated, provided that the cognition of destruction does not occur at that very time.

Moreover, because of the distinct mention of those designations—such as "this is the word 'cow'" and "this is the word 'horse'"—there would necessarily follow at that very moment a manifold recollection [of them];
and due to the non-simultaneity of cognitions, the duration of time would become excessively long.
As for what was also stated— that during nights dark as towering clouds,
there is a similarity with the recognition produced by the flash of lightning— [that too is refuted].
That [entity] is unreal because its continued existence is impossible over a long period of time,
and because destruction is observed in things such as trees struck by lightning, which makes its persistence inconceivable.

Some maintain that what is called recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is a cognition produced by the senses assisted by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), which apprehends the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between that which is being remembered and that which is being experienced.

Others think that because recognition grasps an object qualified by a previously known cognition that is being remembered, and because it is impossible for that qualifying object to be grasped by the external senses, recognition—even regarding things such as a pillar—is purely mental.
However, persistence here is not [required]; let it be as it may, whether it exists or not.
But because there is a cognition of destruction regarding the sound, that [persistence] does not prove its permanence.
But in the case of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, what indeed determines the restriction between the word’s recognition and the appearance of its destruction?
It is said: recognition is possible even otherwise;
it either has the universal (jāti) such as "g-ness" as its object, or it is caused by similarity.
Surely, the cognition of destruction will also be established through the destruction of the manifestor;
therefore, let that [cognition] also be sublated, or else let there be doubt.
Do not say this: that the cognition of destruction, reinforced by the cognition of difference, and this [cognition of identity] are both established otherwise; for such a claim is improper.
Recognition is dependent [on other factors], whereas the cognition of non-existence is independent;
therefore, in such cases as these, it is recognition itself that is sublated.
Because the absence of sound is apprehended instantaneously,
whereas its recognition depends upon the recollection of what preceded it and other such factors.
Moreover, recognition is observed to be fallible in the case of actions and the like;

therefore, what confidence can there be in this [recognition] regarding sound, whose very form is struck down by the cognition of non-existence? This is not an objection raised against perception itself for being inconclusive; rather, this example is shown to demonstrate that recognition—its power thwarted by the cognition of destruction—is unable to establish permanence even in the case of sound, just as it fails in the case of actions and so forth.
Now, one might object: "What occasion is there even for a perceptible example? True; however, grasping subjects such as yourself, failing to understand by yourselves, understand in this manner.
As for the attempt to establish the eternity of even the intellect, action, and so forth through an excessive zeal, that has been described as being utterly extraordinary.
O you who are so afflicted by the thirst to prove that sound is eternal,
do you wish to drink up the entirety of all that is moving and stationary?
Therefore, enough with these discourses attempting to prove the eternity of intellect, action, and so forth, which proceed from excessive haste.

Furthermore, as for the argument that—having raised the doubt regarding the lack of a restrictive rule for the perception of sound under the theory of manifestation—it was described as being always perceived through the refinement of the auditory organ, the refinement of the object, or the refinement of both; that is mere deception, because we do not observe that things occupying the same location and perceptible by the same sense organ are manifested by specific, restricted manifestors.
Furthermore, those odors mentioned here are perceived by the same sense organ, but they do not occupy the same location.
If one were to conceive of two things as occupying the same location simply because they both depend on the same level of existence,
then the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains would also have to be considered as occupying the same location.
Although the earth is one, the earthly objects appear as distinct;
their respective odors, which are based upon that [earth], are manifested by their various specific causes.
Let it be that sounds have no substratum, or let them be dependent upon space;
in any case, it is impossible to say that they occupy different locations.

[Objection: "But surely, even though space (*nabhas*) is all-pervading, there is a distinction of the auditory organ for each person through the conceptualization of its parts; in the same way, by the conceptualization of such parts, sounds too will not occupy the same location, and thus there will be a fixed relationship between the manifestor and the manifested. [Reply: This is not tenable. For in the very same region of space that constitutes the mouth of the speaker or the ear of the hearer where the word 'cow' was perceived, the word 'horse' is now perceived; whereas a fragrance perceived in an *atimuktaka* flower is never perceived in a *bandūka* or *madhūka* flower."

Therefore, because they occupy the same location, there would be no restriction regarding the manifestation [of the universal]; however, if it is established that [the universal] arises [simultaneously], its existence becomes logically consistent.
Whether the sound is refined by the articulations, or the auditory organ, or both—there is no restriction whatsoever regarding the manifestors; such is the certainty.
If it is argued that the restriction [of manifestation] is caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa),
then even when production is being observed, what is seen is not in contradiction [with that claim].
Furthermore, there exists no refinement of the auditory organ other than the removal of the stagnant air;
and in that regard, an over-extension [of the argument] has already been stated. Moreover, to postulate a refinement distinct from this would involve the postulation of something unobserved.

And if the impression (*saṃskāra*) that apprehends sound were stable, then even a cow-sound that has been manifested again would be heard, because the impression which is the cause of its apprehension is stable.
However, if that [impression] were momentary, then the momentariness of sound itself would be established as correct, since it is perceived as such.
As for Bhṛgumin’s claim that he regards that very refinement (*saṃskāra*) as the auditory faculty (*śrotrendriya*), this is some truly unprecedented display of scholarship!
For it is the sense organ that is to be refined, not the refinement itself that is the sense organ, as that would contradict both common experience and traditional authority (*āgama*).
Furthermore, the postulation of a sense organ that is distinct for each person and lasts only as long as the sound is untenable.
But as for the claim that if [the auditory organ] were imperishable, there would follow a constant clamor of sound—this is trivial.

This position has already been refuted with derision by Bhaṭṭa himself; so what is the point of further grinding it? Furthermore, as Bhaṭṭa said: "If, however, one must necessarily state a reversal of the logician's statement, then the nature of the quarters as the auditory organ should be established in accordance with the Veda."

Thus, that too is incorrect; because the quarters entail other functions and because the scripture has another purpose, the postulation of the quarters as a substance and the ear [as being made of them] is mere vanity.
Since it will be established that the sense-faculties are material in nature,
and since the quarters (diś) are formless, they cannot be the primary cause (prakṛti) of the sense-faculties.
Alternatively, if there were no distinction in their being all-pervasive, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that time and the self (ātman) would likewise be such [causes].

If it is argued that [the sense-faculties] do not have the nature of being material elements (*indriya-prakṛti*) because they function elsewhere than in those [two], this is equally true for the substance of space (*dig-dravya*). Furthermore, scripture (*āgama*) has another purpose;
for example: "May the eye go to the sun."
It is indeed recited that "the quarters are the ear," and it is likewise recited that "the intermediate space is the vital breaths" (*asus*).
Yet, the vital breaths do not have the intermediate space as their material cause (*prakṛti*), because they consist of air (*pavana*).
Therefore, [the claim] regarding the quarters is established.

It has been stated that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is simply a portion of space delimited by the ear-canal and bound by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which bring about the experience of sound.

[Objection: "But surely, just as there is a restriction regarding the ear caused by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), the restriction regarding the manifestation of sound will likewise be caused by those very factors.

Why, then, is this lack of restriction questioned under the view that [sound] is eternal? [Reply: This is not tenable. For while the impairment of the sense organs, such as the eye, is seen in cases like darkness and so forth to be based on *adṛṣṭa* (unseen moral force), the actual state of things does not undergo alteration through the power of *adṛṣṭa*.
Indeed, if it were to overstep the properties of its manifestors (*vyañjaka*), then even coldness—such as that of snow—would overstep its own inherent property.

It has already been stated that no fixed rule is observed regarding manifestors [of sounds]. Furthermore, since the distinction between phonemes (*varṇa*) is perceived as the cause for their fixed apprehension, why is this burden placed upon the head of an unseen principle (*adṛṣṭa*)? Moreover, how can there be a distinction between intensity and dullness on the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti*)? For qualities such as intensity must belong either to the phoneme or to the sound-pulse (*dhvani*). If they were qualities of the phoneme, then a soft *g*-sound would be different from an intense *g*-sound, which would result in our own position being accepted.
But if it is held that [the quality] is a property of sound (dhvani), how can it be perceived by the auditory organ? For the velocity residing in the air is not apprehended by hearing.
As for the point shown— that individual properties such as thinness and stoutness are perceived in the universal— that may well be possible,
because the universal, the individual, and its properties are all perceptible by the same sense organ.
But here, it is a marvel that the wind, which is perceptible by touch or even beyond the senses,
is perceived through its properties in the sound heard by the ear.

As for the claim that cognition itself possesses degrees of intensity such as "sharp" or "dull," that is a very fine statement indeed; for it is logically untenable for there to be a difference in cognitions when there is no difference in their objects.
Moreover, your cognition is always imperceptible, just like the sound;
and when that [cognition] is not apprehended, there can be no apprehension of its properties such as intensity and so forth.
Alas! These [objects], though possessing intense qualities, have fallen into an intense abyss:
that which possesses a certain quality is not perceived, and that which is perceived does not possess that quality.
Furthermore, regarding this account of suppression in your own view concerning the winds:
even when the wind is suppressed, why is sound not heard?
When a lamp is overwhelmed by the sun, it is not that form is not perceived;
rather, the notion that [the lamp] is a necessary manifestor [of form] is rejected because such a thing is never observed.
As for the claim that "sound-ness" (śabdatva) must be apprehended there in order to establish that words such as "śāṅkha" are perceivable by the auditory organ— that too is incorrect.
Speak the truth: has such a thing ever been seen or heard anywhere—that when one substrate is being sprinkled, there is the perception of its universal?
Sound does not have the nature of color for you, nor is the conch-shell the source of color;
since "sound-ness" (śabdatva) does not function as a resonance (nāda), how can there be its apprehension?

Furthermore, as for the deliberation regarding whether the assumption [of a capacity] is more cumbersome or more parsimonious in the two positions—the expressed meaning (*vyaṅgya*) or the effect (*kārya*)—that too is irrelevant because it depends upon an investigation of the primary means of valid cognition (*maulapramāṇa*).
If the eternality of sound were established by a primary means of valid cognition (*maulapramāṇa*),
then the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) stated by you would be correct, whereas that stated by me would be the case in its opposite.

The claim that the internal air, as it spreads outward, causes the displacement of the still air everywhere, is itself an extraordinary and fabricated hypothesis. Furthermore, since the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal movement of wind, and the initial motion of atoms and the mind are said to be caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), and because the nature of winds is to move horizontally, there would be no perception of sound from above or below.
As long as it is not impelled by another, more forceful wind,
so long does the natural air not abandon its horizontal course.
Even a sound uttered with the face turned downward is perceived above;
and even one uttered with the face turned upward is not heard below.
For the initiation of sound in the shape of a *kadamba* bud-cluster might be possible;
however, such a movement of the winds is not observed in the world.
When a sound is heard there that issues from a mouth covered by skin stretched tight up to the neck, there is no movement of the air within the chest.
You yourself have indeed stated that the non-dispersion of air due to obstructions such as walls is because it would not spread even when confined within a seamless leather pouch.
Moreover, even for one whose every orifice is completely closed, a deep rumbling sound is heard in the stomach of a person with weak digestion.

In this case, how could there be an exit of the manifesting internal winds? Even if they were to exit through the pores of the skin, due to their subtlety, they would lack the capacity to displace the stagnant external air.

Furthermore, if even a slight breeze were to blow outside, there would be no hearing of sound. Even a weak external wind is stronger than the powerful internal breath of the body; how then could it be driven away by that [internal breath]? If it is argued that these are entirely different, subtle winds that cause the obstruction of sound, and not these visible winds that teach the dance of the *śyāmāka* plant, we say no, because there is no evidence for such a distinction. Moreover, if those same subtle winds can conceal [sound], then they would all the more reveal it when they are even stronger; thus, this argument is trivial.

Therefore, the position that a series of homogeneous sounds is initiated is alone consistent with reason. For instance, qualities such as color and so forth are indeed observed to initiate homogeneous qualities;
and even though cognition is immaterial, it is observed to initiate another cognition.

Even in another location, that very [self] initiates an effect, as is seen in the case of Devadatta and others walking on a path, because a cognition is observed to arise in one part of the self from a different part.
Furthermore, there is also a cessation of the initiation of effects, due to the non-persistence of auxiliary causes that depend upon unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Even by one who is intense, such an undertaking arises only gradually,
when his vigor is diminished and he must depend on the strength of his sinking ministers.
The analogy of the continuity of waves is cited on account of some degree of similarity;
however, sounds do not possess a capacity for momentum and the like, as water does.

As for the objection, "Why does the initiation of the sound-series cease when there is an obstruction such as a wall?", this is not a fault; for it is on the basis of observation that the unobstructed ether (*vyoman*) is postulated to be the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) for the production of sound, and not mere space (*ākāśa*) in general.

As for the claim that the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) of sound is unestablished, some assert its quality-ness on the grounds of its being dependent (*āśritatva*); that is incorrect, for dependence is not accepted as the defining cause of quality-ness, since dependence is possible even for all six categories of entities (*padārtha*).
Kaṇabhuj maintains that all six categories are dependent, being distinct from eternal substances such as space, time, and atoms.
Nor is the sound's dependence on space perceptible, because since space is imperceptible, its being dependent upon it is likewise imperceptible.
If it is asked, "How can there be perception of sound when its substratum is imperceptible?
[the answer is: Just as there is the apprehension of cognition and so forth even though the self is imperceptible.
If it is argued that this very point is unestablished, enough with wandering into another discussion,
for it will be determined later on.

What, then, is the proof for sound being a quality? We reply that it is inference by elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*). Since substance and action—which were previously applicable—are negated, and since [sound] cannot belong to universals and so forth, sound remains as a quality alone.
Furthermore, why is sound not a substance? Because it possesses a single substance.
A substance is either without substance—such as space or atoms—or it is a composite substance consisting of multiple substances—such as dyads or other effect-substances.
Sound, however, possesses a single substance because it is dependent upon a single [instance of] space.
Therefore, it is not a substance.
Nor is sound an action, because it produces another sound;
for an action does not have the property of originating that which belongs to its own class.

Furthermore, because it is connected with universals such as "existence" (sattā) and "sound-ness" (śabdatva), the three categories beginning with the universal do not apply to it; thus, by the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya), sound is indeed a quality (guṇa).

Now, it might be argued that once its status as a quality is established, sound will necessarily reside in space, because a quality is never observed to be non-dependent on a substance, and because earth and the other elements cannot logically serve as the substratum of sound.
Consequently, there would be a circularity: sound being a quality implies its dependence on a single substance (space), and its dependence on a single substance implies its being a quality.
Likewise, even the property of initiating a homogeneous effect is rooted solely in the establishment of [sound's] being a quality (*guṇatva*).

Since sound is a quality, it resides in space (*ākāśa*); therefore, it is perceived by the auditory organ, which is of the nature of that [space]. And since that perception would not be established—given that sound produced by conjunctions and disjunctions occurring in another location could not reach the site of the auditory organ without a continuous series (*santāna*)—the postulation of a series is rooted in the establishment of its being a quality. Furthermore, once action (*karman*) is excluded by virtue of the series initiating a homogeneous effect, the establishment of its being a quality follows; thus, there is indeed a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
It is said: this fault applies to neither case.
Precisely because sound is perceivable by the auditory organ, its dependence upon space (ākāśa) is postulated, as is its production from a homogeneous cause, since it is a quality (guṇa).
For it has already been established that the auditory organ is indeed a single part of space.
Furthermore, it will be stated that the sense organs function by reaching their objects.

Since sound does not reach the auditory organ unless it is supported by space (ākāśa), and since there is no perception of an object that has not been reached, its dependence upon space is postulated.

Likewise, the fact that [sound] originates from something of the same genus is also inferred solely from its audibility when a distant sound is heard; it is not inferred from its being a quality (guṇatva). Therefore, there is no circular reasoning.
Some maintain that its dependence on space is postulated because it is an effect.

Now, one might object: "Because it is an effect, it must reside in space; and given that it resides in space, its being an effect—as established by the previous method—is preceded by a restricted perception. This is not so, because its status as an effect is established solely through the appearances of difference and destruction.

For what purpose, then, is such great effort made to justify the inclusion of the term "restricted" (*niyata*)? It is to show that the inclusion of "restricted" is consistent with the position that [the universal] is an effect (*kāryapakṣa*), and not to suggest that this alone is the logical proof for its being an effect; so enough with such minute scrutiny.

Another says: since the quality of being distinct from motion (parispanda) is perceptible, the non-actional nature of sound is established, and not [established] by its being a producer of a like kind; thus, there is no touch of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) either.
Therefore, in every way, the status of sound as a quality (guṇatva) is proven through the inference of elimination (pariśeṣānumāna).
How, then, is this [sound] connected with magnitude and so forth, given that the followers of Kaṇāda maintain that "qualities are devoid of qualities"?
There is indeed the perception that "the sound is great"; however, that statement of Kaṇāda intends qualities of the same genus, and thus there is no fault.
Therefore, sound is a quality of space (ākāśa).
Moreover, just as the quality of being a property of the self is established for desire, aversion, and so forth,
by that very same reasoning, sound will likewise be a quality of space.

As for those reasons proposed by others—such as "because it is sound" (śabdatvāt) and so forth—to prohibit [sound] from being the originator of another sound of the same genus, they lack probative force because they are inconclusive (aprayojaka).
Thus, since the apprehension of sound is possible through the operation of a continuous series,
our assumption is simpler than that of those who maintain that the individual sound-entities themselves are perceived.
As for the refutation that has been proclaimed against the systems composed by the Śākyas, Kāpilas, and Nirgranthas,
that is indeed pleasing to us.
Therefore, since the apprehension of a fixed [sound] is possible if sound is an effect, whereas it is impossible under the theory of manifestation, it is established that sound is indeed an effect.

This has been stated by the author of the Sūtras: "Sound is non-eternal because it has a beginning, because it is perceptible by the senses, and because it is treated as something produced" (NS 2.2.13).
By the phrase "because it has a beginning," it is demonstrated that conjunction, disjunction, and so forth function as causes (*kāraka*) with respect to sound, not as manifestors (*vyañjaka*);
and for this reason, the property of being immediately subsequent to effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
It has been stated that because [the word] is perceptible by the senses (*aindriyakatva*), its apprehension is necessarily restricted to the view that it is an effect (*kāryapakṣa*).
Alternatively, the meaning of the reason is that there is a difference between words for each person and each utterance, because they are perceptible by the senses.
By this, the vain hope of the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) regarding recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is dispelled.

Because it is treated as something produced (*kṛtaka*), and because we do not observe such linguistic conventions as the distinction between intense and weak or the phenomenon of being overwhelmed, it has been demonstrated that sound is impermanent, just like pleasure, pain, and so forth.

Likewise, by the sūtra *prāgūrdhvam uccāraṇād anupalabdheḥ āvaraṇānupalabdheś ca* (2.2.18), it is stated that the non-perception of sound is caused solely by the absence of sound itself; for still air cannot obstruct sound, since only that which possesses form (*mūrta*) can be screened by another thing possessing form, whereas that which is formless— like space (*ākāśa*) and so forth— cannot be so obstructed.
Nor is sound by its very nature beyond the reach of the senses, as are space and so forth.
Therefore, because it is perceived momentarily, the sound exists only for that duration; thus, even the reason "because it has no abiding place" is not otherwise established [as being irrelevant].

The author of the Vārttika has set forth a proof for the non-eternality of sound: "Sound is non-eternal, because, while possessing a genus, it is perceptible by external sense organs such as those of ourselves and others, like a jar."

As for the objection raised here that the reason is inconclusive because even universals possess universality—on the grounds that "a universal possesses a universal through inherence in the same object"—that is utterly untenable, since it is well-established that "universals and the like are devoid of further universals.
For one cannot say that because potness and earthness both exist in a jar, the universal of earthness exists within the universal of potness; therefore, this reason is indeed faultless.

Therefore, who— unless they be a mere sophist— would assert that properties such as "possessing genus" or "being perceptible by the senses," which are tied solely to the existence of a real entity, serve to establish the impermanence of sound?
Thus was it spoken by one who did not understand the movement of the *tārkika* (logician).

In this case, however, there are non-conclusive reasons (*aprayojaka-hetavaḥ*): "Therefore, the word 'cow' uttered yesterday still exists today, because it is cognizable by the cognition of the word 'cow,' just like the cow spoken of today as 'this is a cow.'"
What is called "being apprehensible by consciousness" is bound to the very nature of things;
it certainly does not serve as a determinant for [proving] either permanence or being produced.
And it is said that such [reasons] as these are non-conducive;
yet, why is it that these very things are themselves employed as reasons?
Thus, the path of reasoning regarding permanence is difficult to maintain; therefore, it must be accepted that the word is indeed something produced.
As for the scriptural restatement (anuvāda) regarding the nature of speech, once its logical validity has been refuted, what purpose would its employment serve?
Even because of the absence of a state characterized by momentary destruction, one is not able to assert the momentariness of sound.

As for what was said—that it is due to the existence of gross destruction—that too is false; for the destruction of a jar or similar object, which is grossly stable, is dependent upon subtle destruction, whereas the destruction of sound, being inherently volatile, is itself indeed gross.
If you previously asserted that sound is momentary, how can it now be described as non-momentary?
If you say this is due to another line of reasoning, then that very reasoning should be examined; what is the use of clinging to the pride of bold assertions?
Enough with this overly prolix discourse; let the doctrine of eternalism be abandoned, and let it be accepted that this word is a product.
Since it is a product, its author must necessarily be the ancient Poet, the moon-crested Lord of unceasing power.

Thus ends the third chapter in the *Nyāyamañjarī* composed by the venerable Jayantabhaṭṭa. The fourth chapter is the "Examination of Sound" (*śabdaparīkṣā*). Now that the produced nature of phonemes has been established in this manner, the independence of the person is proven in all cases, starting from the word (*pada*) which consists of phonemes.
Even on the view that words are eternal, since composition occurs within a sentence consisting of such words,
and since the possibility of agency belongs to a person, how can the Veda be uncreated?
And likewise: "Vedic compositions are preceded by an author, because they are compositions, like worldly compositions.
And this five-fold reason, being a productive [reason], is indeed a means of valid cognition (*gamaka*) and not a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

First of all, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because in Vedic sentence-sequences such as "śanno devīr abhiṣṭaye," the arrangement of words—characterized by specific features such as accent and order—is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus, the reason exists within the subject (*pakṣa*).
Nor is it contradictory, because the property of being a composition exists in the similar instances (sapakṣa), such as the *Kumārasambhava*, which possess the quality of being preceded by an author.
Nor is it inconclusive, because no arrangement is observed in things such as space—which are devoid of an agent—or in things such as sky-flowers.
Nor is it "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), because there is no production of a certainty regarding the absence of a speaker for the Veda through either perception or scripture.

Nor is there a counter-balanced reason (satpratipakṣa), because the cause for the inquiry into the matter has not been stated as a reason, just like the non-perception of the specific qualities of a post or a person.

Nor is this proof non-conclusive (aprayojaka) like the argument for the impermanence of atoms based on their corporeality, because it is certain that the operations of construction are accomplished by the operation of an agent.

Just as smoke derives its existence from fire, yet the cognition of fire comes from the smoke, so too the production of constructions depends upon an agent, while the cognition of the agent comes from those constructions.
Therefore, this reason is indeed conclusive.
But surely they dispute regarding the state of being "counter-balanced" (*satpratipakṣatva*).

Thus, a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is proclaimed here by the Mīmāṃsakas: "All study of the Veda is preceded by study from a teacher, because it is denoted by the term 'Vedic study,' just like the present-day study. This is not at all correct, because arguments of this sort—whether actually employed or not—are ineffective as logical reasons (*aprayojakatva*).
For beginninglessness cannot be established on the grounds of being denotable by that word.

He said: "Why do you wander thus, deluded by the talk of carters and others who lack the discrimination between what is real and what is unreal? For even a very small ritual act, when taught by one's mother, is performed out of trust in her words. Therefore, it is a great error to perform this entire collection of Vedic rituals—which must be accomplished through such immense hardship, expenditure of wealth, and so forth—merely by recollecting the teacher as a trustworthy person."

And this being the case, since linguistic usage would be untenable through the Veda—whose author is not remembered, like a poem written in a worn-out manuscript compiled from various sources—the author therein must necessarily be remembered.
Furthermore, a cessation of linguistic usage among the gods is never conceivable, such that there might be a non-remembrance of their author, as is the case with old wells, gardens, and the like.
Therefore, the author would certainly have been remembered.
Furthermore, it is neither recollected nor can it be recollected; for memory, when it arises, must be rooted in a prior experience.

And even at the root [of memory], no experience of an agent has occurred for anyone, because there was no beginning of creation. Or, even if such an experience had occurred, the agent—being inactive—would lack the visibility required for perception.
Or, even on the view that he possesses a body,
some such person would not be seen while composing the Veda, even though he might be visible at that time.
When this [Veda] was seen being studied, people then had doubts:
"Does he compose this Veda himself, or does he recite one created by another?"
Or if one were to recite what has been composed by him, there too indeed would be doubt;
for in this way, his beginninglessness appears as if it were being revealed through a clever artifice.
And when there is no means of valid cognition such as perception, the experience of agency—
even if established through a continuous stream of memory— touches upon a blind tradition.
It is also difficult to maintain that yogis can apprehend the agent; for how could even they apprehend that agency which is so deeply ingrained in the heart?
We do not believe that she has been grasped by yogins;
and not believing this, how could we proceed confidently upon that path?
But if the agent is understood from the Veda, there is clearly a circularity:
the authority of the Veda depends on the certainty of the agent, and the certainty of the agent depends on the Veda.
Therefore, this is an error rooted in the literal interpretation of mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas), devoid of any critical examination of their preceding and succeeding contexts.
Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate truth, no one remembers anyone as the author of the Veda;
therefore, the Vedas are uncreated, because their author—who, if he existed, would necessarily be remembered—is not remembered.
Nor is the reason incongruous, for the formal argument is stated as: "because its author is not remembered."

To this it is replied: even though that proof consisting in "having been preceded by study under a teacher" was disregarded by the ritualists (yājñika), this new reason—"because its author is not remembered"—has been employed. Therefore, let it be; we do not refute these people who have put forward a different reason. This digression has become too long.

Furthermore, is this reason—"because its author is not remembered"—employed independently to establish the absence of an author, or is it intended to refute the claim that [the Veda] possesses a composition fashioned by us?

In this regard, it is not appropriate to claim that one inference can be an obstacle to another inference, because—just as with perception and scripture—it is illogical for one inference to subvert another.
Indeed, two inferences of equal strength cannot stand in a relationship of subverter and subverted precisely because they are of equal strength.

If, however, they are of unequal strength, then since the invalidity of the weaker one is established by that very fact of inequality, what is the point of claiming "subversion by inference"? If you argue that such a statement is made merely to mock it, that too is incorrect.
Because it is impossible for two reasons that establish two mutually contradictory properties to occur simultaneously in a single subject;

for things cannot possibly possess a dual nature. Therefore, one of those reasons must necessarily be non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*). Since that reason is non-conclusive and thus fails to prove the point, what is the purpose of employing another reason merely as a mockery?
We shall explain that even what is called the "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārī) is not actually any kind of fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa).

We shall demonstrate that not just any reason (*hetu*) that possesses a counter-reason (*satpratipakṣa*) is intended as such; rather, it is one that serves as a seed for doubt, where the non-perception of specific qualities in either alternative is employed as a reason through error, and is thus so described.
Therefore, a proponent who wishes to refute a reason advanced by an opponent should direct his mind toward examining properties such as its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*);
for one seeking a counter-reason should not engage in futile wandering.

Now, which of these two arguments is non-conclusive: "because of being a composition" (*racanātva*) or "because of having no remembered author" (*asmaraṇīyakartṛkatva*)? It is said that "being a composition" alone is the decisive factor; for indeed, nowhere is the arrangement of syllables admitted to exist without a person.
O venerable sages, where in the world has this been seen or heard,
that the arrangement of words within sentences occurs spontaneously?
If the composition of words in the Veda were inherent by its own nature,
then alas, why would that same inherent nature not belong to the threads in a cloth?

Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa with the verse "The divine waters for our aid," [the author states]: "There is a deity-soul in the northern direction. Since the structural arrangement is identical, to claim that in one case there is a prior agent while in another there is its opposite is a great delusion.
For in that case, one might as well say that some smoke is even without fire.

"Has this Veda now become equal to the Kumārasambhava? Oh, has the authority of the Veda been established by this Naiyāyika, the foremost of all believers! Enough with this mockery; it is only the composition that is similar to the Kumārasambhava, and nothing else.
Nor is it proper to mock on such grounds:

does this [Veda] lack the universal property of being sound (śabdatva-sāmānya) which is common to the sound of a conch, or the universal property of existence (sattā-sāmānya) which is common to everything?"
Now, is it not the case that these Vedic compositions appear entirely distinct from those works of Kālidāsa and others, which are preceded by identifiable authors?
In this context, at the time of study, the non-artificiality of the Veda is understood from its very form, through various distinctive features that do not belong to anything else.
The modes of employment for nouns, verbs, prefixes, and so forth are manifold;
likewise are the songs consisting of praise, censure, accounts of ancient events, and the deeds of others.
The description of scattered matters that depend on what is stated in other recensions (śākhās),
and so forth, are not seen in worldly compositions.
Therefore, all groups of students consider the Veda to be uncreated by human agency because of its form; thus, the Mīmāṃsakas have indeed drunk the fame in this world.
But those like you, whose intellects are dull and who have not studied the Vedas,
assert that this [world] is a product, deluded by the similarity of its structure.

It is said: let the Mīmāṃsakas drink fame, or drink milk to remove the dullness of their intellect, or drink the *brāhmī* ghee; however, there is no doubt that the Veda was indeed composed by a person.
Just as in mountains and the like, a structure is established as having an author even though it is distinct from the structure of jars and other objects, so too is the composition in the Veda.
And whatever else needs to be said on this matter has already been explained at length previously.
Moreover, since this composition is of such a distinct character, let an author of a correspondingly distinct character be inferred; it is not, however, proper to deny him.
Furthermore, in these compositions by Kālidāsa and others, whose authorship is established beyond dispute and which are full of aesthetic wonder, a mutually distinct character is indeed perceived.
The well-spoken verses of Kālidāsa are as if sprinkled with nectar, anointed with sandalwood paste, and polished by the rays of the moon.
The words of Bāṇa have enchanted the entire community of poets through their composition of formidable syllables that harmonize with manifest aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*);
moreover, those various diversities are indeed observed in every one of his poems.
To claim that the absence of an author in the Veda is understood from its very form alone merely by means of the diversity of nouns, verbs, and so forth—this is a truly novel way of speaking.

Moreover, if your mind finds solace in the form [of the Veda], then why do you not examine even its form as denoting things that have a beginning, such as: "Babara Prāvāhaṇi desired," "Kusurubinda Auddālaki desired," and "O Purūravas, do not fall"?
If it is argued that because these entities [reappear] at every creation (*pratisarga*), they possess beginninglessness, then likewise, there will be a difference in the Vedas at every creation.
As it has been said: "In each Manvantara, this Śruti is declared to be different.
Furthermore, if its form is held to be non-artificial, then that very conception is merely a mental construction.
But the cognition of an entity possessing a beginning [is produced] by means of clear, expressive syllables.
Any alternative interpretation of these [passages] is merely an interpretation;
however, since the students themselves, while reciting them, understand many things that have a beginning from them, the Veda is not beginningless.
Therefore, the nature of its composition is not a non-probative reason.
However, the mere non-remembrance of an author is not a valid reason for [denying its existence], because it is unproven.
Or, even if the non-remembrance of an author of the Veda were established, it would be accounted for otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*).

This is because the time of the Veda's composition is so remote, and because the person who composed it was distinct from all ordinary men, lacking the assumption of a fixed body; thus, there is no remembrance of him as a specific individual (*idantayā*), like Pāṇini or Piṅgala, but it does not mean that he simply does not exist.

Since that [authorship] is understood through inference and scripture, how can it be grasped as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)? As for the non-remembrance of an author: if it refers to the non-remembrance by a single person, it is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), for such non-remembrance may apply to someone who was indeed the author. If, however, it refers to the non-remembrance by all persons, it is difficult to ascertain. How do you know that "all men do not remember an author of the Veda"? For the hearts of all people are not perceptible to you, lest it follow that you are omniscient.
Nor is it logical to claim that because you do not know something, no one else knows it either, for that would lead to an over-extension of the argument (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, the fact that the author is not remembered is indeed difficult to refute.
Moreover, if the author were remembered, the performance of the Vedic meaning would become even more lax for discerning people.
For an instruction without an author is not possible;
or, even if it were possible, how could it be a ground for confidence in the absence of any cause for determining its authority?
Furthermore, it has already been stated that the ascertainment of the validity of verbal statements arises from the absence of sublation;
therefore, it is only through trust in a reliable authority (*āpta*) that the performance of the Vedic meaning can occur without doubt and with firm foundation, and not otherwise.
Consequently, the presentation of the non-remembrance of an author as an opponent to the fact of its being a composition is not tenable.
Nor can this proof for the non-existence of an agent be considered independent;
for this [proof] is said to be a non-perception (anupalabdhi) in this manner,
yet it is untenable because an agent is perceived through inference.
Even that which is apprehended by inference is indeed apprehended.

But is this inference not improper because it relies on the recollection of the non-existence of an agent, which would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence? For only when non-perception is established can the inference be refuted, and only when the inference is refuted can non-perception be established.
If it is argued that the same defect applies even to the validity of inference (*anumāna*), we say no; for its validity is established by the power of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
Indeed, its validity does not depend upon the exclusion of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
This might be the case: we do not assert that there is validity in the absence of an author;
for the Mīmāṃsakas are those who engage in the worldly transactions of all things and categories.
However, we ask for the proof from one who asserts that the Veda has a human author.
If it were argued that "since this [subject] does not exist, the determination of its non-existence is established by force of non-perception," this would be so only if inference did not exist;
yet it has been stated that there is an inference based on the property of being an arrangement (*racanātva*).

Furthermore, as for what was said—that it is impossible to apprehend a person's authorship regarding the Vedas—that too is incorrect. How is the agency of a weaver or similar craftsman, who is not directly perceived, understood in relation to an effect such as a newly made garment?
If his agency is inferred upon seeing the arrangement of the cloth and so forth, then let his authorship be understood in the case of the Veda as well, by seeing its composition.
Since it is impossible to provide instruction to living beings without assuming a body, it is postulated that the Lord might at times assume a body as well.
Furthermore, because he does not assume a fixed body, he is not remembered like Vyāsa and others;
and thus, he is inferred to be like a poet who suddenly composes a poem this very day.
Likewise, he too is conceived as the agent by the men born at that time.
Just as your suspicion that [the Veda] was composed by another disappears with respect to that poetry,
so too will your suspicion that it was composed by another disappear with respect to the Veda.
And that which we understand through inference regarding what is beyond the senses, that is also [considered] the direct perception of yogis; so it was stated in the definition of direct perception.
Thus, since perception and inference exist as the fundamental means of valid cognition for determining agency,
there is no blind tradition regarding memory.
Therefore, that [Smṛti] is not rooted in Mantras or Arthavādas,
because other means of valid cognition, such as inference as previously described, are possible.

As for the charge of mutual dependence—that the authority of the Veda spoken by a person depends on the person’s existence, while the person’s existence is established through the authority of the Veda—that too is not correct, because it has already been refuted previously.

What is intended here is the strengthening of the cognition of the author, who is already established through inference, by means of the Vedic statements; however, the understanding of the author does not rely solely on scripture.
Furthermore, it was stated earlier that the author is inferred from the effect, such as the earth and other things.
If it is asked: "Is it by the very same creator by whom the effects such as the earth were fashioned that the Vedic compositions were also fashioned?"—we say: "Yes.

If it is asked: "What is the proof for this?"—it is replied: "In that case, an omniscient being is capable of creating such a world—a diverse universe that serves as the locus for the experience of the fruits of the karma of living beings."
Since he alone knows the connection between actions and their fruits and teaches them, it is he who has realized the Vedas; thus, one does not postulate another [author].
Since the purpose is accomplished by one alone, why should we postulate a second? Indeed, there exists no seed whatsoever for postulating multiple [entities].

Regarding the creation of the world, only one Lord (īśvara) is accepted, not two or many. This is because, in the case of postulating multiple Lords with either identical or differing intentions, there would be redundancy in the first case; in the latter case, there would follow a disruption of worldly affairs, which would consequently destroy the lordship of any single one.
For indeed, the doctrine of multiple lords is not very convincing;
if they possess identical intentions, what is the purpose of having many lords?
Whatever one who possesses true resolve intends—whether auspicious or even inauspicious—that is accomplished through his power;
what then could another do in that regard?
But if there were a divergence of intention, then due to the obstruction of the task,
surely one would become powerless through the frustration of his own resolve.
It is said that one person has the intention, "Let this man be made king," while another has the intention, "Let him be killed. How can these two enter into the same [person]?
If the desire for sovereignty is to be fulfilled, the wish to kill is thwarted;
or, if that [wish to kill] is to be fulfilled, the desire for sovereignty is ruined.
Thus it has been established that there is only one Lord, the creator of the worlds, whose intention conforms to the maintenance of the manifold activities of the universe.
Thus, just as he is the sole creator of the world, he alone ought to be the author of the Vedas as well;
for there is a lack of evidence for postulating a plurality of authors, and such a hypothesis would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (kalpanā-gaurava).

Therefore, as for what is said: "But how is it understood that one person is the author of all the Vedic branches? Why were these many texts not composed by many [authors]?"—[this objection is addressed].
Thus, that [objection] is refuted.
Therefore, the Vedas have a single author, because they are seen to teach matters that are mutually connected and consistent with one another.
For indeed, a single ritual action is performed as accompanied by the various limbs taught in the four Vedas, which, though distinct, converge upon a single purpose.

In that regard, the office of the *hotṛ* is performed by means of the *Ṛgveda*, the office of the *adhvaryu* by the *Yajurveda*, the office of the *udgātṛ* by the *Sāmaveda*, and the office of the *brahman* priest by the *Atharvaveda*.
Furthermore, the various sets of subsidiary elements taught in the different branches, such as the Pauṣpala and others, are required in their respective places;
regarding this, they say that the ritual act is one and the same, based on the authority of all branches.
And this will be determined shortly hereafter.
By that, it is understood that there is a binding of a single intention in all cases;
for how could those with different inclinations come together for a single purpose?

If it is asked what the status is regarding the completion of a poetic *samasyā* (poetic puzzle), [the answer is that] even there, it belongs to the first poet alone, because he was the one who first perceived that subject matter;
whereas the other, knowing his intention, merely follows him.
Otherwise, the poem would be incoherent, like the poetry of Viśvāvastu;
but since it is indeed coherent, that must surely be the intention of the first poet alone.

Even here, if one were to postulate a second Lord who possesses knowledge of the single intention [of the first], there would be nothing but a single intention; furthermore, what would be the purpose of such a postulation?
Therefore, there is indeed only one author for all the recensional branches (*śākhās*);
as for the designations such as "Kaṭhaka" and so forth, you yourselves have stated that these will be based on distinguished study.

Moreover, just as the branches of a tree are spread out and not all its flowers, fruits, and leaves are gathered together on a single branch, but rather on this or that particular branch, so too the branches of the Veda are scattered, each teaching different constituent rituals.
And just as all those branches [arise] from a single generative seed,
so too do all [the lineages] arise from the one Supreme Person.

It is logical that the Vedas were composed by that very creator who knows the diversity resulting from the ripening of the various actions and mental dispositions of all beings; for it is he, as the soul of the universe, who has brought forth those [teachings] intended to instruct them.
Relying upon that very Blessed One, the Lord who is without beginning, the world places its trust in the words of the Vedas;
for no wise person would ever place such confidence in those [words] on the grounds that they are unauthored, as was described previously.
And thus, it has been demonstrated that the Vedas depend upon a person with respect to the composition of words, sentences, and so forth.

As for the claim that the creation of the relationship [between word and meaning] is independent of human agency—just as the burning power of fire is innate, so too is the expressive power of a word natural—and that while this power exists, its mastery (vyutpatti) is simply acquired from elders engaged in worldly communication, so what could a person possibly do in this matter? That too is untenable, because the cognition of meaning from a word is impossible apart from a convention established through human refinement.
Indeed, there is no relation whatsoever between a word and its meaning.

Of what, then, is this dependence on a person or independence being considered? For no relation—neither one of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), like that between a wall and a jar, nor one of the nature of inherence (*samavāya*), like that between a thread and a cloth—is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) between a word and its meaning.
And since other relations are rooted in these two, they too do not exist.
Thus it has been said: "We perceive the word in the mouth [and] the object on the ground."

Nor can the relationship between a word and its object be inferred, because when the words "razor" (*kṣura*) or "sweetmeat" (*modaka*) are uttered, one does not perceive the cutting or the filling of the mouth [that would result from such a relation].

Furthermore, the object cannot exist in the location of the word, nor can the word exist in the location of the object; for the vocal organs, the points of articulation, and the efforts—which are the causes of the word—are not perceived in the locations of objects such as jars.
Moreover, the all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) of the word has already been refuted.
It is said: we do not accept that the relationship between word and meaning is characterized by conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*).
Well then, are the relationships of word and meaning those of cause and effect, signifier and signified, or basis and based? No, these too are certainly not [the relationship].

In that case, it would have no connection whatsoever with its object; yet it is not the case that the word has no connection with its object, because it is the cause of the basis for cognition, just like smoke and so forth.
In that case, would verbal testimony (śabda) not simply be inference (anumāna)?
What, then, is that occasion? We shall explain.
What is this so-called "convention" (samaya)? It is called convention because it is the application of a fixed rule regarding the relationship between the signifier and the signified.

What is the point of raising an objection regarding a connection that is not even to be suspected, and of refuting it? For it is the Grammarians, who maintain the non-difference between word and meaning, who are being rejected here, since this kind of connection in the form of a fusion necessarily follows for them.
He said: If the connection described by the grammarians is not tenable, then this convention is indeed untenable;
for that is a human-made designation, and a restriction upon an objective entity cannot be established by human will, because such will possesses unimpeded range.
Why should the object not be the signifier and the word the signified?
It is not so; for even a person who does not desire fire does not perceive it from smoke, nor does he perceive water from it even if he desires it.

In that case, just as there is an innate relationship between smoke and fire known as "inseparable concomitance" (*avinābhāva*), while causes such as repeated observation are relied upon only for its cognition, so too there is an innate relationship between word and meaning consisting of a power (*śakti*), while the reliance on the established usage of elders is for the sake of its acquisition (*vyutpatti*).

If it is argued that since the relationship is intrinsic, as in the case of a lamp and so forth, what is the need for dependence upon linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), we say no; this is because a word is a signifier (*jñāpaka*).
It is the nature of a signifier, such as smoke and the like, that its capacity to signify its own object depends upon the apprehension of a relationship.
However, things such as light, being included within the causal complex of perception itself, do not depend upon linguistic convention.
Power, however, is innate; just as a lamp or similar object possesses the power to illuminate forms, so too does a word possess the power to bring about the comprehension of its meaning.
Therefore, the comprehension of meaning does not arise from convention alone.
Furthermore, convention (*samaya*), which consists in the application of the restriction between the signifier and the signified, is nothing but cognition and not something distinct from it.
And since cognition resides within itself and not within the word and the object, there would be no relationship between those two.
Furthermore, regarding the convention being established: is it made at every utterance, or for each individual person, or was it created once by the Lord at the beginning of creation?

At each utterance, is it the very same [potency] as before that is produced, or is it something new? First, how can the capacity of a newly produced [potency] to convey meaning be understood?
