If that capacity is already understood, what is the purpose of producing it again? Furthermore, since that which was previously produced has already been made, its production again is logically untenable.
The cognition of a single entity may recur many times, but its origination does not.

Furthermore, regarding the relationship [between word and meaning], is it created as distinct for each individual person or as non-distinct? If the position taken is that it is distinct, how can there be a uniform cognition of the referent of the word "cow"—that its meaning is that which possesses a dewlap and so forth—and of the word "horse," that its meaning is that which possesses a mane and so forth?

Even though there is no difference [between the relation and its cognition], since that which has already been produced cannot be produced again, it is cognition alone that is the instrument of the relation.
Even at the beginning of creation, the production of the relationship [between word and meaning] simultaneously is untenable, precisely because such a time cannot exist;
for no time whatsoever can be conceived that is devoid of the linguistic usage of words and their meanings.
Therefore, it is only an eternal relationship that is learned from worldly convention, and not one that is newly produced.

Furthermore, the defects mentioned regarding the position of [words as] instruments (karaṇapakṣa) do not touch the position of [words as] the basis of linguistic derivation (vyutpattipakṣa), because this is established by perception.
Indeed, this is perceived directly:
for children, listening to elders engaged in discourse for their own purposes, understand various objects from various words.
When those elders were themselves children, they likewise received [the teachings] from other elders;
and those [elders] likewise from others. Thus, there is no beginning to saṃsāra.

Moreover, how could a word that relies solely on convention and lacks inherent power be distinguished from a wink of the eye, a gesture of the hand, or other such signs? For at that time, the word would be nothing more than a substitute for the lash of a whip, the hook, or the goad.

Consequently, the common worldly expression "we understand the meaning from the word" (*śabdād artham pratipadyāmahe*) would be subverted; it should rather be "we understand the meaning from convention" (*samayād artham pratipadyāmahe*). Furthermore, under the view that words are based on convention, all words would become equivalent to arbitrary names (*yadṛcchāśabda*).
Consequently, words such as "cow" and "horse" would not have restricted referents.

Furthermore, as for the statement that "the relationship is conventional in form because there is no restriction regarding specific universals (*jāti*)," it is intended here that by the word "universal" (*jāti*), "place" (*deśa*) is meant.
It is said that in a certain place, a particular word, having abandoned the meaning well-known in another place, functions with a different meaning;
for example, the word *cora*, which signifies a thief, is used by Southerners (*dākṣiṇātyaiḥ*) to mean boiled rice.

And this is logical if [the relationship] is occasional; however, if the relationship were eternal, how could there be any deviation regarding its meaning? That too is incorrect, because all words possess the capacity to produce the cognition of all meanings, and it is only in certain places that usage occurs with a particular meaning.
For this very reason, when a word is heard whose relationship [to its meaning] has not been previously apprehended, doubt arises as to what object this word might have been employed to signify.
For in the absence of a capacity [for signification], and where no convention has been established, there would be no basis for the suspicion that it conveys a meaning.
Alternatively, the meaning of words is precisely that which is established in the land of the Āryas; any other meaning, however, approved by barbarian (mleccha) people, is simply to be disregarded.

Therefore, because the position of conventional agreement (samaya) is extremely weak, the relationship between word and meaning is indeed non-artificial (akṛtrima), and thus a person has no power over it.

To this, it is replied: a permanent relationship is not tenable, because like the word and like the meaning, there is no perception or other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for a third thing [namely, the relationship] itself.

Now, it was argued that the relation is of the nature of a power (*śakti*), and since power is dependent upon that [substratum], how could it be perceived as distinct like another property? This is not correct, because a subtle power distinct from both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) has already been refuted at length.
Furthermore, power is not accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for it is not apprehended in the manner of the substance's own nature.

The [existence of a] capacity is not to be inferred, because effects can be accounted for otherwise. Furthermore, having postulated a capacity, one cannot avoid the convention (*samaya*), since the comprehension of meaning is not established without a convention. And once the convention is established, the meaning is established through that alone; so what is the use of resorting to an eternal relation? As for the claim that—because a convention depends on human will and because that will has unimpeded scope—there would be a reversal of the signifier and the signified, that is not well-said; for if there were no capacity, the word itself would possess the fitness (*yogyatva*) to be the signifier.

If it is asked, "What then is this 'fitness' (yogyatā) in the absence of capacity?"—it is this connection with universals such as *gatva* (the nature of being a *ga*-sound), which is assisted by a specific sequence.
For that which possesses a connection with universals such as *gatva* and *autva* is fit for being the signifier (*vācaka*), while the other [the word] is fit for being the signified (*vācya*).

This is just as, despite the lack of distinction in their being substances (*dravyatva*) and so forth, those possessing the universal of *vīraṇa*-grass are fit for the production of a mat, and those possessing the universal of *tantu* (thread) are fit for the production of a cloth.

And it has already been stated that there is no such potency (*śakti*) in that case. Furthermore, you [Sāṅkhyas] do not maintain that the effect exists within the cause; even in the absence of such a potency, because the relationship between the universal and the particular acts as the regulator, there is no reversal of the signifier and the signified. Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning is not of the nature of a potency (*śakti*).
Nor is there between these two a relation of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) such as that between smoke and fire;
for while a relation is perceived in that case, it is perceived thus: "smoke does not exist without fire. Here, however, it is perceived that "this [is understood] from this."
The culmination of linguistic proficiency occurs by this much alone.
For this very reason, based on the inference that "here, comprehension is preceded by comprehension," the distinctness of the word [from other means of knowledge] has been stated.
The capacity of a word to illuminate its meaning is also acquired through the grace of convention (*samaya*), not inherent;

for if that nature were innate, then the comprehension of meaning would arise from a word even when it is newly uttered—just as from a lamp—even if it were produced by someone who was deluded or from any other source whatsoever.

As for the argument that, although the word possesses an innate capacity to illuminate, it must depend upon the apprehension of a relationship because it is a cognizer—just like smoke and the like—that is an unequal comparison. For the indicative power of smoke and such is not inherent; rather, its natural strength lies in its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) with fire. In that case, if this [concomitance] is not apprehended, no cognition at all arises regarding the object; thus, it is logical that its apprehension is required for the sake of cognition. However, in the case of the word, the situation is different. Even when the relationship has not been grasped, the word’s innate power to illuminate its own form is not obstructed. Therefore, the requirement for the apprehension of a relationship is not established here as it is in the case of smoke. Consequently, the claim that the word is dependent on the apprehension of a relationship is untenable. Furthermore, since the relationship between a word and its meaning is eternal, the apprehension of that relationship cannot be the cause of the word’s expressive power. Thus, the view that the word is a signifier dependent upon the apprehension of a relationship is refuted. But here, you yourself accept that the very capacity for comprehension is innate; if it is innate, what is the use of depending upon linguistic convention?
If it is argued that we understand something to be a signifier (*pratyāyaka*) only after observing its cognition (*pratyaya*), and not upon the first hearing;

and that comprehension of the meaning occurs only after hearing it so many times that one understands "this is the name" and "this is the named object"—then this is simply a description of the application of convention (*samaya*).
For the relationship between a name and the named is precisely what is called convention.
Since its capacity to convey meaning is not understood in the absence of usage, that capacity is not inherent.

As for what was asserted—that because a convention consists of cognition, its occurrence is within the self and not in the word and its object—that too is unexamined, since it is possible for cognition to have that as its object even in the absence of being supported by it.

As for what was also said—that if one relies on a convention alone, where a word is no different from the prodding of a goad or a whip, the designation "we understand the meaning from the word" would not occur—that too is trivial.
For even under the view that there is an innate power (*naisargika-śakti*), the designation would have to be "we understand the meaning from the power, not from the word.
And by virtue of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), it would have to be "we understand fire from smoke, not from smoke-as-word."

If it is argued that there is no such designation [of "inference"] because of the lack of an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) and other factors being its constituent parts, then that same point applies equally to the other case as well.
For in the case of smoke, there is the priority of pervasion (*vyāpti*), while in the case of the word, there is the priority of convention (*samaya*);
yet, their status as instruments (*karaṇa*) is not impaired by that dependence on those two.
Moreover, worldly designation bears witness precisely to the side of convention;
for people designate in this way: "Devadatta said, 'From this word, understand the object accordingly. Therefore, it is nothing but convention.
And for this reason, in another place, by virtue of convention, there is the comprehension of a different meaning from that very same word.

Now, it might be argued that since it has been stated here that all words possess the capacity to convey all meanings, a word may be used for a particular meaning in a particular context; however, this is untenable because the conceptual alternatives of the capacities being either distinct or non-distinct from one another are logically inadmissible.
The capacities cannot be distinct from the essential nature of the word, for they are not perceived as such.
And if they were non-distinct, then, because they would not differ from the single word, there would necessarily be no mutual distinction between those capacities themselves.

Nor can distinct powers be inferred from distinct effects, since the difference in effects can be accounted for otherwise. Furthermore, if it were endowed with all powers, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of all objects [simultaneously]. If it is argued that the application of convention (*samaya*) is the regulator, then let that alone suffice; what is the use of powers? As for the claim that because doubt regarding all possible objects is observed when a word-sound is heard, its power must be postulated in respect to all of them—that too is insubstantial, for the doubt is not caused by powers, but rather is based on the commonality (*sāmānya*) of phonemes such as *g* and so forth.

And thus, while it is understood that phonemes possessing universals such as "ga-ness" possess denotative power with respect to a meaning, a doubt arises: "Of which specific meaning could these phonemes, joined with those universals, be the denotators?"

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the meaning of a word is precisely that for which the noble ones (āryas) employ it, and not that which is established among the Mleccha people—how could we possibly accept this without resorting to an oath?

For even in a barbarian (mleccha) country, the cognition of that meaning does not fail to arise, nor is it sublated, nor is it doubtful; so how could it not be the word’s meaning? If it is argued that the usage established among the Āryas is the sublater [of the barbarians’ usage], then why is the usage established among the barbarians not likewise a sublater of the Āryas’ usage? Furthermore, just as in the case of words like *akṣa*, since the existence of an object is possible through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the conceptual construction will simply have a fixed domain of objects.
Furthermore, you yourselves have relied upon the determination of the meaning of words such as *pika*, *nematā*, and *marasa* based on the usage of Mlecchas;

and in the section concerning the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice (*Aveṣṭyadhikaraṇa*), you described the word *rājan* according to its meaning as established among the Āndhras. Enough, then, with this digression! Therefore, it is logical that the relationship [between word and meaning] is simply convention (*samaya*).
Thus it has been said: "And because there is no fixed rule regarding specific castes."

Now, as for what was said—that the convention (*samaya*) is established at the beginning of creation once and for all, for each person and for each utterance—that argument has already been refuted by the fact that such establishment for each utterance and each person is not even accepted [by us];
for it is not our position that the convention is established only once at the beginning of creation.

For this very reason, it is not the case that all words are equivalent to arbitrary names (*yadṛcchā*). Only certain words are called arbitrary because we and others establish conventions for them in the present day; thus, the beginning of creation has indeed been established.
Even in the proof of God, a complete inference has been set forth.

This indeed is the distinction between us two: that this linguistic usage of the relationship between word and meaning is beginningless for you, whereas for me it has proceeded from the very beginning of the creation of the world.
However, regarding the current acquisition of the relationship between word and meaning, our path is exactly the same.
Even there, this is the distinction: that for you, the acquisition extends as far as the expressive power (*śakti*) [of words], whereas for me, it excludes that.

And thus, this much proficiency is observed in the world: that "this is the denoted of this" and "this is the denoter of this," but there is no proficiency extending to the limit of [inherent] power (*śakti*).

For instance, where a relationship is established by pointing out the word and its meaning individually, we see it being made only to this extent: "this is the denoted of this" and "this is the denoter of this."

Furthermore, even when one acquires proficiency by observing elders engaged in linguistic usage, it is only this much that one understands: "This meaning was understood from this word by such-and-such a person. One does not perceive any other power [in the word] belonging to it.

Since the cognition of meaning from a word is established by this much proficiency alone, and since this [proficiency] is unavoidable, and because there is no basis for postulating anything further, the relationship between word and meaning is not eternal.
For this very reason, we do not accept what you say—that the determination of the relationship is based on three means of valid cognition (*tripramāṇaka*).
It is true that one perceives here, by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the word, the elder, and the object denoted;

however, the claim that "one knows the twofold capacity through the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*)" is not true, because it has already been stated that [the relationship] can be established even otherwise. Therefore, the determination of the relationship is based on two means of valid cognition, not three.

Thus, since there is no relationship consisting of an innate power (*naisargika-śakti*) between word and meaning, the linguistic usage of words and their referents is based on conventions established by God; it is not beginningless.

Now, even if God were to establish the relationship [between word and meaning], he must necessarily do so by means of some word; by what, then, was the relationship of that [word] established? If it were by another word, then by what was the relationship of that one established, and by what that one as well? Thus, there would be no limit.

Therefore, this person establishing the relationship must necessarily admit that certain words, already established through the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), have their relationships uncreated.

If worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) is established, what is the use of a Lord (*īśvara*), or of a convention (*samaya*) not created by Him? Thus, the position that [convention] is beginningless (*anādi*) would be superior. To this it is replied: Your Honor has understood the weapon, but you have not perceived its target. This fault applies to people such as ourselves, but it is not applicable to the Lord.
Who could doubt the skill of that [Creator] who, by mere will, is capable of creating this world as the locus for the various fruits of karma?

Since even such a vast range of effects as the earth and so forth—which does not even enter the path of our desires—is accomplished by Him through mere will, what effort could this possibly be for Him? Thus, while there are indeed great disagreements regarding the existence of God, once He is established, what room is there for such doubts? And it has been said that regarding His establishment, inference is beyond reproach.
But we are certainly not the makers of this relationship, such that we should be questioned in this manner.
Pointing with the tip of their finger toward some object standing before them,
even those like us are seen instructing children.

Therefore, it is established that a word conveys its meaning by depending upon the acquisition of proficiency in it, which is obtained through the linguistic usage of elders and serves as the means for comprehending the relationship created by God.

Furthermore, even in the absence of an eternal relationship, a word does not fail to touch upon its object, because it has already been stated that the cognition of an object through the power of convention is established as uncontradicted; therefore, enough with this elaboration.
Therefore, since it is logical that a person possesses independence with respect to words, sentences, and their relations, the Vedas must have been composed by him.
Therefore, the Vedas are authoritative solely because they were spoken by a reliable person, not because of their eternity.

Now, how is the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) understood for the reason "being spoken by a reliable person" (*āptoktatva*)? It is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as the presence of smoke on a mountain is; for when a cognition arises through the power of the pair of ears, only the collection of sounds called the Vedas appears therein.
Nor is "being spoken by a reliable person" grasped as a property of the phonemes (*varṇadharma*), like the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth.
Nor is there inference regarding this matter, because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
For the fact of being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*) is the mark for the authority of the Veda;

yet, in the inference of its being spoken by a reliable person, we do not perceive any other mark. Thus, how can there be a certainty regarding its presence as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)? It is replied: enough with this wrangling of words; the very means for ascertaining the presence of the mark in the subject has already been stated.
For thus, the impermanence of sound has already been established at length;
and it is settled that compositions possess an author because they are compositions.
It has been established that there exists an omniscient Person who is the creator of all;
and it is settled that the efficient cause must be postulated as being commensurate with its effect.
The rejection of perception and other means of knowledge will be refuted in the Veda;
furthermore, defects such as contradiction and tautology will be addressed in another passage.
The application of injunctions, explanatory passages, and mantras will also be explained;
there is not even a single syllable in the Veda that is devoid of purpose.
Furthermore, all the previously presented conceptual constructions, such as the theory of the transformation (*vivarta*) of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*),
which contradict the nature of being an effect, will be refuted.

This being the case, what else remains in the Vedas for the ascertainment of their being the word of a reliable person? This very thing—the certainty that the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) belongs to the reason—is proclaimed as the "being the word of a reliable person" (āptoktatva), provided that the entire meaning of the scripture is established.

As for the alternative view that neither perception nor inference serves as the basis for determining [the authorship], let perception stand aside; however, those [reasons] such as "being a composition" and so forth which have been stated, and those which will be mentioned in the critique of other systems—all of these are conducive to establishing the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) regarding the fact of being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatā*). Thus, enough with this elaboration.

Furthermore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this reason is ascertained from the statements of Ayurveda and similar sciences: "By using medicinal substances such as *pippalī* and the root of *paṭola* in this manner, this desired result is attained"; and "By avoiding foods incompatible with milk, curd, and so forth, this undesirable condition is pacified. Since the meaning of these statements is determined to be exactly so through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) within the treatises of Ayurveda, their validity—known as non-contradiction with the object—is established; and this [validity] is produced by the speech of a reliable person (*āpta*).
Therefore, the pervasion is grasped that wherever there is the status of being the speech of a reliable person, there is validity.

Likewise, in the application of mantras, it has been observed that one bitten by a scorpion or snake, or one who has ingested poison, becomes free of poison; that those seized by epilepsy, piśācas, or rūpikās are liberated from them; and that crops are protected when malevolent clouds are about to rise with great violence.

Therefore, since they are skilled in pacifying poison and the thunderbolt, their instructors are authoritative (āpta); thus, in this case as well, there is a pervasive certainty [of their reliability].

[Objection: Is it not the case that the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the *Āyurveda* and similar texts is established through corroboration by perception and other means, and not from the authority of a reliable person (*āpta*)?

Therefore, how can the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being spoken by a reliable person" be grasped in those cases? [Reply: This is not so. While its authority may indeed be ascertained through corroboration by perception and other means, that authority has actually arisen from being spoken by a reliable person.
Even in the case of perception and the like, the cognition of authority arises from corroboration by the knowledge of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*).
But it has been stated that production occurs through the operation of causal factors (kārakas) possessing specific qualities.
Furthermore, sentences such as those concerning rivers and the like, when spoken by deceitful persons, are seen in the world to be inconsistent.
Therefore, being composed by a reliable person (*āpta*) is the very cause of their validity, because correct cognition does not arise in the absence of purity of the cause.
While direct perception may be the means for determining this, validity is not produced by that perception itself.
Therefore, it is logical to grasp the pervasion of being spoken by a reliable person in the case of Ayurveda and similar texts.
But even so, this is not tenable, because it is impossible to determine the status of being "spoken by a reliable person" (*āptoktatva*) in that case.
The authority of the statements in Ayurveda is rooted solely in positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), not in their being produced by a reliable person.
And authority exists only for as much of an object as positive and negative concomitance are observed, such as in the case of the meaning of statements concerning *harītakī* and other [medicines].
But where those two [perception and inference] do not apply, there is a lack of authority, as in the case of the statement: "By consuming *somarājī*, one lives for a thousand years.
If one were to assume an authoritative person (*āpta*) for such a case, it would result in the fallacy of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*):
how could that person be authoritative regarding one part of the matter while being non-authoritative regarding the other?
This is untenable because it is impossible to apprehend positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

For these two must be apprehended either within the [subject] itself, or in another individual (*vyakti*); and even in another individual, they must be apprehended either everywhere, or only in some particular individual. In every way, this path is fraught with difficulties.

Because it is impossible for a single lifetime to grasp the distinctions in the power [of things]—such as diseases, their causes, their accumulation and diminution, the means for their pacification, medicines, specific combinations and separations thereof, their quantities, and their potency, taste, and post-digestive transformation—as these vary according to differences in place, time, person, and condition;
and because one does not remember entities experienced in other lifetimes.
The population here is indeed infinite, as is the multitude of diseases; the ways of substances possessing manifold qualities and tastes cannot be numbered.
Since combinations are diverse and preceded by various transformations, how could a person cross to the further shore of medical science even in tens of millions of lifetimes?
Whatever substance serves to pacify one element, that very same thing,
through a different application, leads instead to its provocation.
The potency of a substance that exists in one person does not exist in another;
even by means of the myrobalan fruit (*harītakī*), one whose wind-humor (*vāta*) has been provoked by skin disease (*kuṣṭha*) is not purged.
For one whose bile is aggravated in autumn, curd leads to fever;
yet that very same curd, when consumed during the rainy season, destroys fever after a change of condition.
Nor is there any secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇa) for the perception of that capacity,
by which [the capacity], once grasped in one instance, would be understood everywhere.

Or, if a person is capable of knowing that [object] whose capacity has an infinite range of objects, he would be omniscient; thus, no doubt should be entertained regarding him as being so designated by his own words.
Now it may be argued that this medical tradition (*cikitsakasmṛti*) is indeed beginningless, like the traditions of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and so forth;
Caraka and the others are merely authors who intended to present [the material] either in brief or in detail, but they were not all-seeing (*sarvadarśin*).
Furthermore, there is no fault of a "blind succession" (*andhaparamparā*) in the tradition, because it is rooted in a valid source (*samūlatvāt*).
Just as the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭaprayoga*) is the basis for the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*), so too here [in medicine] are positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).

When there is a conflict with the learned, just as the tradition of Pāṇini and others which contradicts that basis is not authoritative—as they say, "it does not occur here because it is not denotable"—so too the medical tradition (*vaidyasmṛti*) which contradicts positive and negative concomitance is not authoritative. This [argument] is incorrect, because since positive and negative concomitance cannot be determined according to the method already stated, it is impossible for [the medical tradition] to have them as its basis.

If it is argued that the treatises composed by Caraka and others are based on such positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) consisting in having ascertained all the potencies of substances through observation, that is not well-founded. For we are able to perceive only as much positive and negative concomitance as exists in the present; and while one might proceed toward such a work by assuming its authority based on partial agreement with those two types of concomitance, those two cannot constitute the foundation of the entire treatise, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence that everyone like ourselves could compose such a treatise.

Furthermore, the claim that the treatises (*śāstra*) are beginningless, like the Vedas, is untenable; for there is a recorded tradition of authors such as Caraka, which is as undisputed as the tradition regarding Kālidāsa and others.
Nor can this continuous succession of medical memory be beginningless; for if it were so, it would result in a "blind tradition" (*andhaparamparā*), since no original cause could be determined.
Moreover, what is stated therein cannot be the source [of the Veda], as that possibility has already been refuted.
Therefore, Āyurveda was indeed composed by an omniscient being.
Now, one might argue that since instruction is not possible for those who are ignorant, we must assume that Caraka and others were indeed knowers.

However, what proof is there for the claim that they knew everything through direct perception alone? It has been stated that this is not the domain of inference, as both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) have been ruled out.
Furthermore, it will be explained later that it is improper to assume their teachings are rooted in the Veda—unlike the Smṛtis of Manu and others—because a commonality of authorship is impossible.

If it were preceded by the instruction of another person, what wrong has Caraka committed? In this matter, analogy (*upamāna*) is simply not to be suspected [as a source]. Presumption (*arthāpatti*), however, is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Yet, there is no lack of validity here, because its correspondence with reality is observed many times over.

Therefore, by the method of elimination, it is reasonable to conclude that Caraka and others were those who had ascertained the capacities of the entire range of things—both collectively and individually—in accordance with the specific variations of place, time, person, and condition that they had directly perceived.

If this is so, how then is there deviation in statements such as "Soma is the king"? And if there is deviation, it has been said that this is like the "half-old woman" fallacy. This is not a fault; the deviation in these cases will occur due to defects in the ritual action, the agent, or the instruments.
Furthermore, for the Mīmāṃsaka, the same quality applies to Vedic rituals.
What would be your position regarding the *kārīrī* sacrifice and others, in which rain does not occur despite the performance of the rite?
If you claim it is due to a deficiency in the agent or other factors, the same could be said here as well.

If it is postulated that some other "karma pertaining to weapons" (*śastrīya-karma*), being discordant and unexhausted, is the cause for the subversion of the fruit [of another action], then that too is equal [to the previous argument].
Furthermore, if the attainment of a fruit is observed in the performance of a certain act, then here there exist those with firm bodies and long lifespans resulting from that very application.

Therefore, it is established that Āyurveda was composed by a reliable authority (āpta) and has no other source; likewise, its status as being authored by a reliable authority is evident in the case of the Vedas and other such works which have similar results.
Therefore, the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being spoken by a reliable person" (*āptoktatva*) is established in the case of Ayurveda and similar texts.
It was precisely for the purpose of demonstrating this pervasion that the author of the Sūtras stated: "That [means of knowledge] is of two kinds, because its objects are seen and unseen" (NS 1.1.8).
This means that *āptoktatva*, whose inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) has been grasped in words with visible objects, establishes validity even in the case of words with invisible objects.
For this very reason it has been stated: "And its authority is like the authority of the Mantras and Ayurveda, because of the authority of the trustworthy person" (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.69).

[Objection: But surely, even in this case of medicine, no omniscient sage is observed to have composed it; therefore, if the apprehension of its pervasion among people were [otherwise established], the citation of Āyurveda would be useless.
[Reply: True; however, the traditional recollection (smṛti) of Caraka and others regarding medicine is firm, and since that is not based on any other composition, it is cited here as an example.

Thus, in the statements of Āyurveda and other such works, the pervasion (vyāpti) spoken by a reliable authority has been clearly explained according to the previously mentioned sequence, as has its presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatva).

Since its object is not sublated by perception or scripture, nor is it overturned by another inference, this [inference] possesses the capacity to produce knowledge due to its fulfillment of the five characteristics.
Due to its independence, the incomparable status of the Vedic words as a means of valid cognition is not tenable;
for where has the cessation of verbal error ever been seen without reliance upon human authority?

Therefore, regarding Vedic rituals and ascetic practices that must be accomplished through the expenditure of vast amounts of wealth and other means, it is appropriate to engage in them provided they do not cause harm; since their accomplishment cannot otherwise be achieved, this path—which is not [universally] accepted—is of no further use.
Therefore, it is established that the Vedas are authoritative precisely because they were spoken by a reliable person.
Others, however, describe the authority of the Veda in a different manner.

For regarding its authority, an opponent—whether one who accepts the existence of another world or one who does not—may disagree. In that case, first of all, for the sake of one who does not accept another world, one must establish the existence of another world by means of reasoning based on the permanence of the self and so forth.

However, in the view of those who maintain that there is a world beyond, this diversity of the world seen through the distinctions of the happy, the suffering, and so forth, must necessarily be based on the diversity of karma.
And actions do not come into existence unless they are performed.

How could those actions, which have not attained their own nature and are thus like flowers in the sky, serve as the means for producing diverse fruits such as happiness and suffering? Therefore, their performance must be admitted.
Furthermore, the performance of rituals is not possible for those who do not know their true nature;
since an ignorant person, however ascetic he may be, does not know what to perform, it follows that actions must necessarily be performed after they have been understood.
Now, what is the means for their full comprehension? Perception is not capable of demonstrating to people like us those actions which accomplish unseen human goals such as heaven and the like.

Nor is there inference [of such a relation], because—unlike the case of satisfaction and eating—the relationship between the means and the end (sādhya-sādhana) cannot be ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) in the case of heaven and sacrifice.

Nor is there presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); for by the fact that the diversity of the world would otherwise be inexplicable, one merely infers a diverse cause. And by that much alone, the establishment of [specific] performance is not achieved.
And it has been said: "Whether in the form of merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*), when [the cause] is not distinguished with respect to its fruit..."
Of what use is the cognition that "something exists" to human beings?
But even the comparison suggested here does not appear appropriate.

Nor is it reasonable to say that worldly people, while instructing one another, could produce rituals that have results in the next world; for those who establish such things without knowing them cannot be considered authoritative (*āpta*).

Furthermore, it has been stated that it is impossible for worldly people to know [this], as there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). For if one were to postulate a succession of human instructions, it would result in the logic of a "succession of the blind."
Therefore, those who necessarily accept the existence of the next world and who perform actions that bear fruit in the next world must accept the understanding of those actions from the scripture;
and since the scripture is indeed the Vedas, their authority is established.

But surely, the actions that accomplish dharma and adharma will be known precisely from worldly convention; what is the use of a treatise? For it is well known that benefit and harm are the defining characteristics of dharma and adharma. As Vyāsa said: "Regarding these two terms—'this is merit' and 'this is sin'—for humans down to the outcaste (caṇḍāla), the purpose of the scriptures is minimal."

Thus, this is not tenable, because worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) that lacks a foundation cannot function as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). What is called "worldly consensus" is an uninterrupted tradition (*smṛti*) among worldly people; and since it arises, it must have another means of valid cognition as its basis and is not independent. Therefore, its source must necessarily be sought. And since that source cannot be perception (*pratyakṣa*) or the like, worldly consensus must certainly be rooted in scripture (*śāstra*).
And because worldly consensus is contradictory and of a single uniform nature, people do not place their trust in that [consensus] when it is independent.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to define *dharma* and *adharma* merely by the characteristics of benefit and harm, because such a definition is absent in cases such as the recitation of mantras or the drinking of *śīdhu* liquor, and because the opposite is the case for acts such as violating the teacher’s wife; therefore, one must necessarily seek [the definitions of] these two by taking refuge in the scriptures alone.

Moreover, can such matters as "this desired mantra and so forth has such a fruit," "this person is authorized for this [rite]," "this is the procedure," "this is the place," "this is the time," or "these are the officiating priests," and so on, be understood through worldly renown? Therefore, the comprehension of specific ritual acts must necessarily be sought as dependent solely upon the scripture (śāstra).
And it has been stated that the scripture is indeed the Veda;
thus, its authority is established beyond dispute.
When it is described in this way, first of all, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra would be stated;

and because the Veda is beginningless due to the beginninglessness of ritual action and knowledge, its status as a means of valid cognition (prāmāṇya) is established precisely through the path of the Mīmāṃsakas, and not from the word of a trustworthy person (āptavāda).
Therefore, the path exactly as it has been illustrated should be followed regarding the status of valid cognition.
Alternatively, we too do not deny the position of beginningless saṃsāra; however, there is a distinction in the doctrine that all creations and destructions occur simultaneously.
And it was stated by the Blessed One that this Vedic scripture was composed from the very beginning of creation as a result of [divine] design.
Even though it is governed by God as its creator, the continuous succession of creation and dissolution is indeed beginningless;
and within each distinct creation, the awakening to karma for people would be established through different Vedas.

O wise one, what proof is there for their difference? And what proof is there for their identity? At that time, the entire world would surely be destroyed, and consequently, even consciousness would necessarily perish.
However, the Lord is one and undifferentiated; whether He creates [the world] anew or remembers the past, the sovereignty of the Moon-crested One over the Veda is certain in both cases.
For when that Veda appears in the mind of that one [Ishvara], it is not distinguished from something created;
however, for Ishvara, who has all things as his direct perception, memory is not logical as a source [of knowledge]. Therefore, only [the Veda] as an instrument [of cognition] is faultless.

Therefore, because the Veda was indeed composed by a trustworthy person, the sage Akṣapāda composed this treatise (*śāstra*) in order to generate in people a firm conviction regarding its faultless meaning, having extensively eliminated the proliferation of delusion rooted in fallacious reasoning.

On this point, someone says: It is appropriate that the authority of the three Vedas is established by means of an inference of a single authorship, based on their teaching of mutually interconnected subjects;
however, since no utility for the dharma prescribed in the three [Vedas] is perceived in the Atharvaveda, it stands outside the triad and does not share the same status as them.

Even under the view that validity is characterized by independence (*anapekṣatva*), the three Vedas alone—just as they participate in the state of being the vital breath (*prāṇabhāva*)—must be so, because we observe the intermingling of the duties of the *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and other priests involved in numerous rites such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* taught in various scattered branches of scripture; the Atharvanic revelation, however, does not have such a distinct practical application.
And so it is well known in the world that these four sciences have been set forth for the benefit of living beings: Ānvīkṣikī, Trayī, Vārtā, and Daṇḍanīti.
Even the Śruti and Smṛti are seen to have meanings consistent with this.
As for the Śruti, it says: "By means of the Ṛg-verses, the God moves at dawn..."
"With the Yajurveda he stands at midday; with the Sāmaveda he sets;
the sun moves along, never devoid of the three Vedas."
In the same way, Prajāpati desired, "May I be many; may I procreate.
He performed austerity.
Having performed austerity, he...
He created these worlds: the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky. He brooded over those worlds, and from them three lights were born:
fire was born from the earth, wind from the intermediate space, and the sun from the sky.
He brooded over those lights;
from them the three Vedas were born:
from Agni, the Ṛgveda.
From the two breaths arose the Yajurveda;
from Āditya arose the Sāmaveda.
Thus, this very triple knowledge (trayī vidyā) shines forth.
The *Smṛti* of Manu is also seen to prescribe twelve years of celibacy for each Veda, stating: "The vow pertaining to the three Vedas is to be practiced under a teacher for thirty-six years."
Even in the section on ancestral rites (śrāddha), one should with effort feed at the śrāddha a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda,
or a Śākhāntaga, or an Adhvaryu, or a Chandoga who has reached the end [of his recitation].
Thus, [the scripture] indicates that only those Brahmins who have mastered the three Vedas are to be invited to the Śrāddha feast, and not those who study the Atharvaveda;
on the contrary, a prohibition is taught in some places: "Therefore, one should not employ an Atharvan priest."

When such an objection is raised, some respond: "If the Atharvan revelation has no utility here [in the three Vedas], by what is its status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to other matters obstructed? Ritual acts for the purposes of pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), which depend upon a single Brahman-priest, are validated by it; or rather, the triple Veda (*trayī*) has its own specific domain."
But all this that has been said is not correct.

For the path established by Jaimini for the apprehension of the Veda’s authority—namely, "That [Veda] is a means of valid cognition because it is independent," as well as that revealed by Akṣapāda and Kaṇāda, "The authority of the sacred tradition [Āmnāya] arises from the authority of its words," and "Its authority is like that of the Mantras and Āyurveda, due to the authority of the trustworthy person"—is identical in respect to all four Vedas.
Not even a single grain of distinction can be found there, even when sought with the greatest effort.

For indeed, it can be argued thus only from the perspective of the Mīmāṃsaka: "The Vedic revelation regarding the three [Vedas] is indeed beginningless, because it is impossible for there to be a recollection of its author."
Nor can it be said, even in the Nyāya position, that "the three Vedas were composed by a reliable authority (āpta), but the fourth was not composed by a reliable authority.
Therefore, because there is no difference in the means for establishing their validity and they share the same status of security, all four Vedas are authoritative.

For legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is well-established for all those whose minds are adept at discerning the essential from the non-essential—by means of even the four Vedas—for the four castes and the four stages of life, throughout the four quarters on this earth girdled by the four oceans. What delusion of deviation could there be here? Furthermore, the legal procedure of those dwelling in Āryāvarta is rooted in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. And those two, the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, declare all four Vedas to be of equal status.
Even within the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas, there exist numerous passages that have the *Atharvaveda* as their concluding portion.

For example, in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, beginning with the words "Now on the third day," in the section concerning the *pāriplava* recitations of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, it is heard: "This is the Atharvaṇa Veda.
And in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, it is recited: "The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaṇa as the fourth."
But is it not indeed recited there that "the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are the fifth"?

What follows from this? Does it mean that the Atharva is not a fourth Veda simply because of the use of the word "fourth"? If you argue that its mention alongside itihāsas and the like implies it is of equal status with them and not on the same level as the Vedas—what kind of reasoning is this? If being mentioned as "fourth" were grounds for non-preeminence, then in passages such as "the three Vedas were created," the three Vedas would likewise fail to attain preeminence due to the mention of the number three.
Furthermore, the claim that being enumerated together with itihāsas and so forth is a reason for non-preeminence applies equally to all the Vedas; therefore, this argument is trivial.
Likewise, in the *Śatādhyayana* as well, having begun with "The Ṛg-veda verses are indeed the vital breaths of Brahman," it is recited: "The *Atharvaṇa* is indeed the common [breath] of Brahman."

Likewise, beginning with "Those rays of his which are directed eastward are his eastern honey-cells; the Ṛg-veda verses are the flowers," it is recited: "And those rays of his which are directed northward are his northern honey-cells; the Atharva-Aṅgiras verses are the honey-makers."

Likewise, in the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], having introduced the passage, "Therefore, within this self consisting of breath (prāṇamaya), there is another inner self consisting of mind (manomaya)," it continues: "The Yajus is indeed its head;
the Ṛc is its right wing."
The Sāman is the right wing;
the Ādeśa is the self;
and the Atharvāṅgirases are the tail, the foundation—so it is recited.
Likewise, elsewhere it is said that the great eastern quarter belongs to the *ṛc*s;
they say the southern belongs to the *yajus* formulas, and the northern to the *sāman* chants.
The great western direction is said to belong to the Atharvans and the Aṅgirases.

In the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, at the beginning of the section on the rules for the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), it says: "The Ṛg-verses are indeed the milk-offerings to the Vedas," and so on, concluding with: "The Atharvāṅgirases are indeed the fat-offerings to the gods. He who, knowing this, studies the daily private recitation (*svādhyāya*) of the Atharvāṅgirases, thereby satisfies the gods with fat-offerings; they, being satisfied, satisfy him."
Furthermore, mantras are heard that are intent upon revealing that very meaning, such as "O Agni, Atharvan churned you forth from the lotus-leaf," and so on.
Nor is an interpretation of these mantras—such as that Atharvan was merely some rishi—appropriate, because that would lead to a lack of confidence in other instances as well.
Thus far, such types of Vedic utterances have been cited.
Furthermore, there are scriptural statements as well:
Manu, for instance, says, "One should perform the Atharva-Āṅgirasa Śrutis without hesitation," and thus he employs the word *śruti* here just as he does for the triple Veda (*trayī*).

Yājñavalkya, while enumerating the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), states: "The Vedas, together with the Purāṇas, Tarka, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, and Āgama, are the fourteen branches of knowledge and of dharma. In this way, he declares that there are exactly four Vedas; for otherwise, the number fourteen would not be completed.

And it has been stated quite clearly in another Smṛti: "The four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the expansion of Nyāya, the Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstra—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyās)."
It is also stated elsewhere: "The Prāṇa, the Dharmaśāstra, Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, the four Vedas, and the six Aṅgas—these are the fourteen seats of knowledge (vidyāsthāna)."

Śātātapa also said: "Whether it be the Ṛg, Sāman, or Yajur Vedas, their ancillaries, or even the Atharvāṅgirasa, he who possesses knowledge of even a single atom of this is a great man in our eyes, provided he is one who has studied the scriptures."
Likewise, elsewhere it is stated that "an assembly consists of four who have mastered the four Vedas and are knowers of the Dharma."

Śaṅkha and Likhita said that a council consisting of at least ten members consists of those who know the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas; one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga); one who knows the Dharma; one who knows the Vākya; a Naiyāyika; a lifelong celibate student (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī); and one who maintains the five sacred fires (pañcāgni).
In the work of Prācetasa, it is stated that an assembly consisting of at least five members—four who are knowers of the Vedas and one who is a knower of the Dharmaśāstra—is [sufficient].

And likewise, in the context of those who purify the company at a meal (*paṅktipāvana*), one who knows the four Vedas and the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman, and even one versed in the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda]—these are all counted among those who purify the company.
Thus, the practice of the authors of the Dharmaśāstras is predominantly based on such proficiency in the establishment of the fourfold Veda.
Other authors of treatises as well are seen to employ [the Vedas] in exactly the same manner;
for instance, the venerable Patañjali, the author of the Mahābhāṣya, cited the Atharvaveda first, namely: "śanno devīr abhiṣṭaye" (May the goddesses be for our welfare).

The author of the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya, in the section concerning the Vedas (Vedādhikaraṇa), cited the Pauṣpalādaka as one of the Atharvaveda branches—just like the Kāṭhaka, Kālāpa, and Maudgala branches of the Yajurveda and others.

Furthermore, in the section concerning all the scriptures (Sarvaśāstrādhikaraṇa), he conducted an investigation by citing the two Atharva branches known as Maudgala and Pauṣpalādaka, just as he did with other Vedas and other scriptural schools.
Moreover, at the very conclusion of that section, it is recorded: "There is no such thing as a 'first sacrifice' among the four [Vedas]."
Thus, for those who know the Śruti, Smṛti, distinguished conduct, and worldly practice, there is not even the possibility of any disagreement on this point.

He said: We do not say that the Atharvaveda is not authoritative; rather, it is said to be "outside the Trayī" (trayībāhya). Yet the Trayī itself is likewise outside the Atharvaveda. Not only is this so, but even within the Trayī there is indeed mutual exclusion: the Yajus-mantras are outside the Ṛk and Sāman, the Ṛk-mantras are outside the Yajus and Sāman, and the Sāman-mantras are outside the Ṛk and Yajus. What fault is there in this? For all entities are established through their mutual intermingling.
Indeed, those things whose nature is sound—consisting of the composition of texts—and those whose nature is the objects denoted by them, are all essentially intermixed with one another.
And even when they are mixed with another, they do not lose their own essential nature.

Now, it might be argued that such exclusion from the *trayi* (the three Vedas) is not what is intended regarding the *Atharvaveda*; rather, its status as being outside the *trayi* consists in the fact that it does not teach rituals based on the *trayi*, nor anything connected thereto. This too is not correct, because we observe therein the teaching of rituals such as the *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, *ekāha*, *ahīna*, and *satra*. According to the principle that "a single ritual is recognized across all branches (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya*"), even for a ritual taught in the *trayi*, something related to it is indeed obtained from the *Atharvaveda*.
Is it not the case that a single ritual action is authorized by all the Vedic branches (*śākhā*)?

Yet, that [single action] is authorized only by all the scriptures connected to the three Vedas, and not by the Atharva-veda branch, because in rituals such as the Soma sacrifice, the office of the *hotṛ* is performed by the Ṛg-veda, the office of the *adhvaryu* by the Yajur-veda, and the office of the *udgātṛ* by the Sāma-veda, while nothing at all is done by the Atharva-veda. This is incorrect, because the office of the *brahman* priest is performed by means of the Atharva-veda.
Thus says the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa: "Prajāpati, being about to sacrifice with Soma, spoke to the Vedas:"

"Whom shall I choose as your Hotṛ?"—having begun thus [the text continues]: "Therefore, choose one who knows the Ṛgveda as the Hotṛ, for he knows the office of the Hotṛ; choose one who knows the Yajurveda as the Adhvaryu, for he knows the office of the Adhvaryu; choose one who knows the Sāmaveda as the Udgātṛ, for he knows the office of the Udgātṛ; choose one who knows the Atharvāṅgirasas as the Brahman, for he knows the office of the Brahman. Having stated this, it further says: "But if one chooses as Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, or Brahman someone who is not such a knower, then their sacrifice is depleted beforehand. Therefore, one should appoint as Hotṛ one who knows the Ṛgveda, as Adhvaryu one who knows the Yajurveda, as Udgātṛ one who knows the Sāmaveda, and as Brahman one who knows the Atharvāṅgirasas.
"Likewise, whatever is deficient, torn, or worn out, one should restore it by means of the splendor of the Atharvans; for without the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases, Soma is not fit to be drunk."

Now, it may be argued that these Śruti passages are studied by the Atharvaṇas alone, and not by others who know the three Vedas (trayīvidas). They, however, read as follows: "When the office of the Hotṛ is performed with the Ṛgveda, the office of the Adhvaryu with the Yajurveda, and the office of the Udgātṛ with the Sāmaveda, then by what is the office of the Brahman performed? One should say: 'By the threefold knowledge' (trayyā vidyayā). And likewise: "They performed the office of the Hotṛ with the Ṛgveda, the office of the Adhvaryu with the Yajurveda, and the office of the Udgātṛ with the Sāmaveda; whatever is the pure essence (śukra) of the threefold knowledge, by that the office of the Brahman is performed. To this we reply: We too do not fail to study such sentences.
However, this is their meaning: only one who knows the Atharva-Aṅgiras is a *brahmán*.
How so? Because that which is called the "Triad" (*trayī*) is not some distinct entity, but rather the collection (*samāhāra*) of the three Vedas.
And a collection resides in those things being collected.

Furthermore, when the three Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, are brought together, they have already fulfilled their purpose by being dedicated to the duties of the Hotṛ priest and so forth; they do not, therefore, admit of further division therein.
A collection of things that have each individually fulfilled their purpose is itself already purpose-fulfilled.

For when the cognition of a collection is analyzed, it is only the constituent members that manifest, not some distinct entity as a "whole" (avayavin), since those members are already occupied elsewhere.
However, we do not say that it is an excessive burden for the *Ṛgveda* and the others to perform the function of Brahman;
rather, it is taught that the duty of being Brahman must be performed by one who possesses a threefold nature (*tryātmakatva*).
And yet, not even one of those Vedas possesses such a threefold nature.
The Atharvaveda, however, possesses a threefold nature;
for within it, there exist all three—Ṛks, Yajus, and Sāmans. Therefore, when the office of the Brahman priest is performed by means of it, it is accomplished through the three Vedas.

Now, one might object: "If the office of Brahman-priest is performed by one who has studied the three Vedas, does that not mean it is accomplished by the Triad? Indeed, we reply: even in the case of that [sacrifice], other sacrifices are prescribed for a single desire, while the Jyotiṣṭoma is for all [desires] and the Darśapūrṇamāsa for all; yet, according to the principle of the *Yogasiddhi* section, one would prescribe these by fixing upon only the most essential element in the mind, for one cannot mentally apprehend the entire collection as a whole. Thus, it is accomplished by only one [part], not by the Triad."
But surely the other Vedas are also threefold; therefore, the Atharvaveda should not be treated separately, since there is no difference in their nature.
Their individual foundations are designated by their respective [names] such as *Ṛk* and so forth; thus, they are not to be designated by a term that refers to the collection as a whole.

As for the statement in another passage, "By means of the *śukra* (essence) of the triple knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*), one performs the office of the *brahman* priest," here this dative case is employed in place of the genitive.
Since they call *śukra* the "essence" (*sāra*),
what is meant is that the office of the *brahman* priest is performed by means of the essence of the triple knowledge.
Nor is the essence of the triple Veda (trayī) merely the triple Veda itself,
nor is it something entirely different from it, such as the Atharva-veda alone.
Therefore, we consider that this very essence of the triple Veda consists precisely of the Atharva-veda.
We consider it to be "consisting of three natures.
Because it consists of three natures, they call it "the secret" (*śukra*).
Furthermore, the word *atharvan* also signifies a secret.

"The *yajña* and the *Atharvāṇa* are the *iṣṭis* of the Veda"—by this, the office of the *brahmán* priest is performed by means of the *Atharvaveda* in its form as the *Śukra*. Thus, the *Atharvaveda* is not outside the *trayi* (the three Vedas).
In this way, in the principle that "the ritual act is one and recognized across all branches," the word "all" (*sarva*) does not become restricted [to only three].
For this very reason, it is recited in the Pūrva- and Uttara-brāhmaṇas that the Atharvaveda is the Brahmaveda, as in: "The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Brahmaveda."

And likewise, it is heard in the *Brahmaudana* section of the *Brāhmaṇa* on the study of the hundred *Kāṭhaka* recensions: "The exponents of Brahman say that Purodhā Audvalaki spoke to Āruṇi: 'I offer thee, acceptable to Brahman and Prāṇa; I offer thee, acceptable to Brahman and Vyāna. Having begun thus, it continues: "The two Atharvans are indeed the same as Brahman; he offers this very one, acceptable to Atharvan. It consists of four bowls, for these Vedas are four; he thereby makes them sharers. The Vedas are indeed the root of Brahman, and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who eat [of it] are the root of the Vedas; that is why it is called *brahmaudana* (the food of Brahman)."

Likewise, regarding the singing of the *Atharvaṇa* Sāman on the fourth day of the *pṛṣṭha* section during the *ārbhava-pavamāna*, which is heard in its injunction: "The *Atharvaṇa* [Sāman] is fourfold; it serves for the continuity of the four-night sacrifice; by means of the four-footed *anuṣṭubh* meter, this makes the fourth day an *anuṣṭubh*; the *Atharvaṇa* is indeed medicine (*bhaiṣajya*), for that [Sāman] provides healing; the *Atharvaṇa* [hymns] are the medicines for the sacrifice"—this praise is based upon such grounds.

For this very reason, it was stated previously: "Whatever in the sacrifice is deficient, whatever is torn, and whatever has lost its potency, he replenishes that by means of the splendor of the Atharvans.
Therefore, the Atharvan alone is the Brahman.
This has been established at length with logical arguments by those proficient in other treatises; thus, it is not pursued here in further detail.
As for the statement, "one should perform the Pravargya with the Atharvan," that is disregarded because, being a sentence from a Kalpa-sūtra, it contradicts the Veda.
Even if this were a Śruti statement, if it were studied within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), it would be applied only to some particular rite therein.

Even under the view that it is an independent statement (*anārabhyavāda*), since its meaning is dissimilar to the previously mentioned statements, and because the Atharvaveda—being outside the Triple Veda (*trayi*)—is incapable of providing a remedy for the [ritual] defects, it will be explained as having only a restricted scope.

As for the claim that no specific rule for the *Atharva* has been handed down—just as it is said, "The *Ṛgveda* is recited loudly, the *Sāmaveda* loudly, and the *Yajurveda* in a whisper"—that too is without substance. For this is taught as the rule for *mantras*, not the rule for the Vedas;
these four Vedic texts are by nature a collection of both *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa*.
As for the *mantras*, they are in fact of only two kinds, distinguished by prose and verse.
That which is composed in prose is called the *yajus*, that which is composed in verse-padas is the *ṛc*, and the distinct variety based on melody is the *sāman*.

For this very reason, Jaimini, having introduced the division of mantras, established their threefold nature as follows: "Where there is a metrical arrangement of quarters according to the sense, it is *ṛc*; the name *sāman* applies to melodies; and for the remainder, the term *yajus* is used. Thus has their threefold character been demonstrated.
And this property of being "high" and so forth belongs to those [sacrifices] themselves, not to the texts denoted by the word "Veda," which consist of collections of Mantras and Brāhmaṇas.
Since this same threefold class of Mantras exists in the Atharvaveda as well, this collection of properties is likewise taught there.
This designation of the "threefold" (trayī) is indeed based on the division of mantras;
therefore, even such passages as "this threefold knowledge (vidyā) shines forth" will not be contradicted.
Thus, because it is composed of a collection of mantras consisting of Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman, the Atharvaveda is included within the threefold [Veda].
And because its nature consists of a collection of textual passages established as distinct [from one another], it is proven that it is diverse.
Others, however, because of the abundance of *ṛc* verses, the scarcity of *yajus* formulas, and the absence of *sāman* chants that are not sung, designate the Atharvaveda as the *Ṛgveda* itself;
let this be the view, for there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the word "Veda" denotes only three [classes] and not the fourth, this is an extreme form of prejudice;
for in this matter, the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) is the authority.
Whenever the word "Veda" is uttered in various contexts—such as "This is a Veda" or "This is a Brāhmaṇa"—all four [classes] are understood.
When someone says, "The Veda has been studied by me," those engaged in worldly discourse ask him, "Which Veda has been studied by you?
He replies, "The Atharvaveda. They do not then disparage him by saying, "That which was recited by you is not a Veda."
If it is argued that the word "Veda" is used with a prefix in the case of the *Atharvaveda*, this is equally true for the other Vedas, as they are called the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, and *Sāmaveda*.
If it is argued that the word "Veda" is also used without a prefix in their case, it has already been stated that this is the same for the other [the *Atharvaveda*] as well;
moreover, it is well known that Bharadvāja was a student of the four Vedas (*caturvedādhyāyī*).

In every respect, however, the word "Veda" in expressions such as "Āyurveda" is necessarily accompanied by a qualifying prefix; therefore, the Atharvaveda should not be led into a position of disparagement by being treated as if it were on the same level [as the other Vedas].
It has been stated that the procedure for the *brahmayajña* according to the *śruti* is the same across all four [Vedas]. The procedure according to the *smṛti* is likewise of that same nature.
As Yājñavalkya said: "One should satisfy the gods with fat while reciting the *Atharvāṅgirasas*."

"And the twice-born should daily feed the ancestors with honey and clarified butter according to his ability"—thus, the traditional practice regarding teaching, studying, and so forth is entirely the same; enough of this digression.

Therefore, regarding their status as authoritative means of knowledge, their being denoted by the term "Vedic study" (*svādhyāya*), and their inclusion in the injunctions for accomplishing the goals of man, the four Vedas are equal.
If, however, one is not satisfied without a sequential hierarchy, then the Atharvaveda alone is the first, because from it follows the manifestation of this mantra, the Brahman, the Praṇava.

And so says the Śruti, beginning with "Brahman indeed was this in the beginning," and continuing: "He exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated the Atharvaṇa Veda; from that which was calmed, heated, and intensely heated, the syllable 'Om' emerged as the upward-pointing, imperishable Mind," and so forth.
Likewise, the origin of the Mahāvyāhṛtis—both those well-known in other Vedic branches and those not so well-known, such as "Bṛhat" and others—is from that very same source.

For one who has undergone the initiation (*upanayana*) sacrament performed according to the *Atharvaveda*, the study of other Vedas is not prohibited. However, for one being initiated according to another Veda, there is no entitlement to study the *Atharvaveda* unless he has received the initiation sacrament of the *Atharvaveda*.
Thus it has been said: "One consecrated by a knower of the *Bhṛgu-Aṅgiras* may study other Vedas; one consecrated elsewhere may not study the *Bhṛgu-Aṅgiras*."

Furthermore, even those who take refuge solely in the three Vedas must necessarily resort to this [Atharvaveda] when performing the expiatory rites prescribed by the Atharvaveda for the failure of their own ritual duties; thus, the Atharvaveda alone is superior.
As for the statement from the *Mānava* that was cited regarding thirty-six years, that refers specifically to the study of the three Vedas and is optional.

For it is said: "Having studied the Vedas—whether all of them, two, or even one—in due order," implying a vow lasting twelve years for one Veda, twenty-four for two, and thirty-six for three. Furthermore, there is another Smṛti which states that he who studies the four Vedas should observe the student's life (*brahmacarya*) for forty-eight years; and this is not disregarded by the noble ones (*āryas*).

In this regard, the interpretation that those who study all three Vedas must observe the vow for sixteen years every year is inconsistent, because it contradicts the introductory statement and serves no purpose.

Therefore, this rule of optionality is based solely on the study of different Vedas and does not depend on twelve or sixteen years; thus, even the disregard shown toward this Smṛti—stemming from its contradiction with the Śruti injunction "one should establish the sacred fires while his hair is still black"—does not specifically target the exclusion of the study of the Atharvaveda, nor does it prohibit the study of other Vedas, for there is no specific reason [to distinguish] in this case either.
This vow applies to the three Vedas; there is no restrictive statement saying it applies to these three alone.

Furthermore, regarding the mention in the section on *śrāddha*—in the injunction "one should diligently feed those who have mastered the three Vedas"—the consideration of the qualifying terms "one who has gone to the end of the Veda," "one who has reached the end of a branch (*śākhā*)," and "one who has reached the completion [of a recension]" indicates that those who study only a portion of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth have no qualification for the *śrāddha*.

However, in the case of the Atharvavedins, even one who studies only a portion [of it] is qualified for it, provided he has attained the status of a "purifier of the row" (*paṅktipāvana*) merely by studying the *Atharvaśiras*.

Furthermore, it has been shown that even by the mere study of the *Atharvaśiras*, one becomes a purifier of the assembly (*piṅktipāvana*) and is not disqualified from partaking in a *śrāddha* feast; thus, [the opposing view] is contradictory.

However, the permission for those who study only specific portions of other Vedas—such as "one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman, the Trimadhu, or the Trisuparṇa"—to eat at a Śrāddha appears to be of the nature of a secondary alternative (anukalpa), since the primary rule (prathamakalpa) prescribes the study of the complete Veda.
Therefore, this statement is not intended to exclude the Atharvavedins.

This being the case, that which is stated by the author of the *Vārttika*—as if out of fear, hatred, delusion, or perhaps with compassion—as "if [the Atharvaveda] were useful for sacrifice," and so forth, is not to the point; for in the *Atharvaveda*, in the *Pūrva* and *Uttara Brāhmaṇas*, there is a clear instruction regarding *iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices, *ahīna*s, and *satra*s. If it is argued: "Since such injunctions are absent in the other Vedas, what is the purpose of their instruction in the *Atharvaveda*?"—this is well said! For one could equally say: "Since such injunctions are seen in the *Atharvaveda*, what is the purpose of their instruction in the other Vedas?"
Furthermore, I do not know to whom this questioning of the assembly is directed: is it to the eternal Veda, or rather to its author, the Lord?
It has already been stated that both of these are beyond questioning.
Moreover, rites for other purposes—such as pacification, enrichment, and malevolent magic—are also seen in other Vedas.
For the Śyena is produced from the Sāmaveda, and the Adbhuta-śānti and others are from the Yajurveda; that too is the same [in both cases].
The claim that they depend on a single officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is also not true;
for it is stated there: "There are two modes of sacrificial procedure (*yajñavṛtti*): the *vaihārikī* and the *pākayajña-vṛtti*.
Among these, the *vaihārikī* is the instruction in the Śruti regarding multiple rites performed by many officiating priests.
"The rites for pacification and so forth are recorded in the Smṛti as being dependent on a single Brahmin priest"—this is the statement of one ignorant of the subject matter.
The claim that "only the three Vedas constitute one's own domain" is itself a form of extreme indifference (*paramamādhyamsthya*).
For there is no such thing as a Vedic meaning belonging to oneself or to another; this is because a single ritual action is established by all the recensional branches (*sarvaśākhāpratyayatvāt*).

Therefore, since all Vedas share an identical status and destiny (*samānayogakṣematvāt*), the act of singling out one [Veda] from the others occurs only in the minds of those intent on inventing penances for reviling the Vedas, and not in the minds of the virtuous; thus, we shall desist.
Thus, these hymns, worthy of praise for their increasing power and prosperity equal to [the Buddha's],
are intent upon accomplishing various desired and abundant fruits.
All four Vedas also possess the splendor of authoritative validity through their firm stability in warding off the attacks of opponents, just as the arms of Hari [possess the splendor of victory].
The Veda-tree, endowed with four trunks, its body built up by branches whose distinct parts are renowned for their mutual union, shines forth;
from each trunk there manifest the fruits and flowers of the treatises, made beautiful by the excellent nectar drunk from the mouths of the twice-born.
[The opponent] asks: "Is it being argued that the authority of the Vedas alone is established in this manner?"
Or rather, this same direction applies to all other scriptures as well.

What follows from this? If the first position is held, what answer can be given when opponents speak in such a manner? But in the latter case, all [the views] would be false, as they are mutually contradictory.

Which other scriptures (āgamas), then, does the child have in mind when he asks this—whether the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Dharmaśāstras, or those such as the Śaiva, Pāśupata, Pañcarātra, Bauddha, and Ārhata? Among these, we shall first examine the Śaiva and others.

The Dharmaśāstras composed by Manu and others are indeed authoritative, just like the Vedas, for they provide instruction on specific rites that are included within their meaning. What need is there for further deliberation regarding them? However, some declare their authority to be based solely upon their having the Veda as their root.
For instance, the teachings of Manu and others cannot possibly be based on error, because there is no evidence to the contrary;
moreover, up to the present day, those learned in the Vedas have continued to practice their contents with undiminished respect.
Nor are they rooted in experience, because perception lacks the capacity to determine dharma in its form as an effect that is not delimited by the three periods of time.
Nor can they have their root in the instruction of another person, because for that other person as well, there would be no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for understanding it.

Or, if such a means did exist, what wrong has Manu done? For, in the absence of a foundational means of valid cognition, if one merely postulates a succession of human words, it is unavoidable that this becomes equivalent to a "tradition of the blind" (*andhaparamparā*).

Nor is it a reasonable assumption that Manu and others were deceivers who taught in this way, since—as has been stated—there is no subverting evidence and their teachings are accepted by virtuous people.

Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the teachings of Manu and others must necessarily have their root in a cause known as the Veda; for that [Veda] is both consistent with and capable of being the cause.

Regarding this, Bhaṭṭa said: "Whether from non-erroneous experience or even from the speech of a person who is deceptive, because of the capacity for consistency with what is observed, the *codanā* (Vedic injunction) alone is the most parsimonious [explanation]."

In this regard, some consider that [the Veda] has its basis in injunctions inferred through the force of the mantras and arthavādas that are currently observed; others hold that it has its basis in scattered branches [of the Vedic tradition];
while still others maintain that it has its basis in lost branches [of the Vedic tradition].
We have no need for this detailed elaboration.

In every respect, let the Veda itself be postulated as the source there, according to what is logically established; no other source should be assumed, as it lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, even on the view that the Veda is the source, this universally known designation "Smṛti" (Tradition) will be upheld.

For if [the Smṛti] were based on direct perception (*pratyakṣamūlatva*), what would be the meaning of the word "Smṛti" here, as it would be identical to the Veda? Furthermore, if the Smṛti is rooted in the Veda, then in the event of a contradiction with Śruti, its sublation is easily established because it is not of equal status. The source is already established in one case (Śruti), while in the other (Smṛti) it must be inferred. As soon as you resolve to infer a Śruti for the Smṛti, a directly perceived Śruti contradicting it enters the path of the heart; how then could the Smṛti be capable of inferring its own source at that time?
