Thus he spoke this well-known proverb in the world: "When something has already been carried away by a horse, by what means could a donkey possibly recover it from there?"
Another says: in this case, conceptualization alone is appropriate. For indeed, the Veda is of two kinds: that which is being heard and that which is being inferred.
And that which is being heard is called "Śruti."
And that which is being inferred is the Smṛti;
both of these [the Veda and the Smṛti] are beginningless. Therefore, what could sublate what? For this very thing is indeed the Veda, whether manifest or unmanifest.
Consequently, it is not logical to postulate that [the Smṛti] is rooted in Mantras, Arthavādas, and so forth, because the Veda, as that which is being remembered, is beginningless.

Now, if validity is thus described as being rooted in the Veda, how are those disputants to be answered who claim that even the external Smṛtis possess validity? It is said: those poor fellows have already been refuted.
For it was stated by the venerable Jaimini: "Or rather, because the agents are the same, inference [of the Smṛti's authority] should be considered valid."

What is the meaning of "because of the identity of the agent"? It means because of the understanding that they share the same qualification (*adhikāra*). Those very agents who are qualified for the performance of the Vedic rites are the same ones for the performance of the Smṛti rites;
for we observe the employment of Vedic ritual elements such as the spreading of the altar (*vedistaraṇa*) only when they are intermingled with Smṛti ritual elements such as sipping water (*ācamana*).
However, such an understanding of a common objective is not found in the external Smṛtis;
therefore, only the Smṛtis of Manu and others are authoritative, not the external Smṛtis.

Now, it may be argued that the *smṛtis* of Manu and others are also authoritative because they are rooted in the Veda, and not for any other reason. To this it is replied: you, it seems, declare that their authority is due solely to being rooted in the Veda, while refusing to accept the perception of a yogi as a grasper of *dharma*.

This, however, is not tenable. For just as the Lord Īśvara has been established as the creator of all, the ruler of all, the all-seeing, the compassionate toward all, and the author of the Vedas, so too has the perception of a yogi—which is distinct from the perception of people like us—been established as capable of grasping *dharma* within the definition of perception itself. It is indeed skilled in apprehending *dharma*.
Therefore, let the teachings of Manu and others be rooted in that very [source].

As for the objection that how could *dharma*, which is unconditioned by the three periods of time, be accessible to perception—therefore it is said that only the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is the means of valid cognition for it—that has been answered by the demonstration of the existence of God’s perception.

Just as the perception of God (*īśvarapratyakṣa*) is the apprehender of the relationship between the goal and the means (*sādhyasādhanasambandha*) pertaining to [acts such as] heaven and the *agnihotra*, so too will the perception of the mantras and other [authoritative sources] be the apprehender of that same relationship pertaining to the *aṣṭakā* and other rites. What need is there here for [the Lord] to be either unconditioned by the three times or conditioned by them, such that—because he would not perceive the *dharmatva* (status as dharma) of the *aṣṭakā* and other rituals—the Lord would be non-omniscient? Or, having known [them], if he did not teach them, he would be lacking in compassion. This is not a fault; for the Blessed One certainly knows everything.
He teaches some things himself and causes others to teach some things.
For they are indeed the objects of the Blessed One’s grace,
and their attainment of such knowledge is brought about solely by that grace; moreover,
it is recited even in the Veda that "the Dharma is perceptible through mantras and so forth."

But surely, since there is no difference in their being rooted in perception (*pratyakṣa*), when there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, an option (*vikalpa*) would result—just as in the case of the injunctions for the Bṛhat and Rathantara chants—and not a relationship of sublation and sublated; for there is indeed no distinction whatsoever regarding the validity of the perception of the Lord and the perception of a yogin. There may, however, be a distinction based on whether it is innate or acquired. What of that? It is said: let there be an option.
What is the fault? Even by those who maintain that [the Smṛti] is rooted in the Veda, some alternative interpretation has indeed been explained;
or rather, the alternative will be explained according to the distinction of subject matter.
Furthermore, those devoted to the study of the Vedas hold that there is no example whatsoever of a contradiction between Śruti and Smṛti.
Therefore, because they are rooted in the direct perception of authoritative persons, the Dharmaśāstras possess authority just like the Vedas.
By this, the authority of the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas* should also be understood as established;
for they say that the *itihāsa-purāṇa* is the fifth Veda, and it has been said:
"One should augment the Veda with the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*."
The Veda fears a person of little learning, thinking, "He will deceive me."
Alternatively, what is the use of our persistent attachment [to this view]? Since the Smṛtis are rooted in the Veda, let the Purāṇas also possess authority, just like the Smṛtis.
There is no dispute regarding their authority.
Likewise, let the authority of even uncodified virtuous conduct (*sadācāra*) arise precisely because it is rooted in the Veda.

In every respect, first of all, these six branches of knowledge—the four Vedas, the Purāṇa, and the Smṛti—are authoritative as they teach the direct means for achieving the goals of human life, according to the manner previously described.
However, the six auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), such as grammar and the rest, are useful only by virtue of being auxiliaries; they do not directly teach Dharma.
Even in the Kalpasūtras, there is merely a compilation of scattered rules regarding ritual actions, not the instruction of anything previously unknown.

Mīmāṃsā consists of the investigation of Vedic statements, and Nyāyavistara is the cause for determining the authority of the Vedas; this was stated at the very outset. Therefore, these fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) constitute the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is established that some [teachings] are direct instructions, while others are conducive to them.
Furthermore, those other scriptures that are observed are also of two kinds: some proceed in total contradiction with the Vedas, such as the Buddhist [scriptures];
others, without contradicting them, teach various invented observances, such as the Śaiva [scriptures].
In this regard, we first establish the authority of the Śaiva Āgamas because no collection of causes for doubt, sublation, or impurity is perceived within the cognition produced by them.
Furthermore, the fact that God is the author of those [Āgamas] is established therein both by tradition (smṛti) and inference;
and it is impossible to postulate any other source, such as greed or delusion.
For in that case, no such "firstness" (of composition) is remembered;
and since numerous points of agreement with the Vedas are observed, what room is there for postulating another source?
Nor do they exist as opponents to the Veda, because they do not abandon the worldly conventions of the four castes and so forth as established by the Veda.
Although the logic of the injunctions of Manu and others does not apply to the Śaiva Āgama, nevertheless, it is not the case that its lack of authoritative validity is not justified.
The meanings of all the Upaniṣads, which touch upon the state of supreme bliss,
are seen to be discerned therein at every step.
And those who are the foremost among the knowers of the Vedas, such as Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and others,
also accept the Śaiva and other systems as authoritative.
The authority of the Pañcarātra as well has been described by that very same [author];
for there is not even the slightest cause for its lack of authority therein.
And in that [system], the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is said to be the author;
and he is indeed the Lord (Īśvara) himself.
Of that one certain primordial Person of great majesty, who is the cause of the birth of the entire world without exception,
there arises the perception of him as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, due to his association with the distinct functions of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
And in the Veda, at every step, it is recited that "Rudra alone exists; there is no second," and likewise, "Viṣṇu strode across this [universe]"; thus both Rudra and Viṣṇu are mentioned.

Furthermore, their respective yogas and the means for their propitiation are indeed enjoined in the Veda itself. However, in the Śaiva and Pañcarātra systems, those very yogas are taught in a different manner.
Nor is this alone a contradiction with the Veda,
because the means [to liberation] are optional.
Therefore, because they were composed by authoritative persons and because they do not contradict the Veda, those two [the Mahābhārata and the Purāṇas] lack invalidity.

But as for those Buddhist scriptures that liberate one from cyclic existence yet teach sinful conduct—who among the noble ones would approve their authority? For in the Buddha's teaching, its exclusion from the Veda is clearly seen, due to its definitive rejection of the conduct appropriate to the duties of one's caste.

Those who claim to liberate beings from saṃsāra are wicked, devoted to the injury of living creatures, and act solely out of delusion; therefore, their scripture is not an authoritative means of knowledge.
When an action is taught that consists primarily of the performance of what is forbidden,
whose tongue would function to proclaim its authority?
Therefore, even if some kind of accomplishment should occasionally occur for someone somewhere,
it leads to hell, like the enjoyment of vulgar pleasures acquired through the murder of a Brahmin.
By what means is the evil karma acquired through the performance of forbidden acts pacified? Therefore, one will fall again into hell even after a long interval of time.

As for the objection raised here—namely, what should be done against those opponents who, following the previously stated sequence, postulate that the Buddha and others are authoritative persons (*āpta*)—it is said in response: it is only when there is conformity with the consensus of the great multitude (*mahājana*) that the status of being "spoken by an authoritative person" can be easily established, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, the great multitude of people accepts the authority of the Vedas, of the Purāṇas and Dharmaśāstras which follow the meaning of the Vedas, and of certain Āgamas that do not contradict the Vedas; they do not, however, accept the authority of the Āgamas of the Buddhists and others which contradict the Vedas. How, then, can those [latter] be considered composed by trustworthy persons (*āpta*)? For in their case, another basis—such as ignorance, greed, and so forth—is easily asserted. Having stated this, the Buddhists and others who rival the Vedas must be refuted.
He said: "Who is this so-called 'great multitude'? What is its form, what is its basis, how many are they, and what is their conduct? You should explain this."

Moreover, Buddhists and others, in order to establish the authority of their own scriptures, claim that the Buddha and others were "authoritative persons" (āpta); they also claim that there was a "great multitude" (mahājana) belonging to themselves for the sake of establishing that [authority].

To establish that, they speak of "worshippers" and so forth; yet we do not know how to calculate the characteristics of such a person—what his hands and feet are like, what his head and neck are like, or what his number is—though he is said to be a "great multitude" renowned in the noble lands (āryadeśa).
As for his appearance, we do not know how to count his features, such as whether his hands and feet are of such a kind, or whether his head and neck are of such a kind, or what his total number is.
This great body of people, consisting of the four castes and the four stages of life and following the path of the Vedas, cannot be denied by those who propound other scriptures.
Likewise, even these wicked Buddhists and others, being constrained by the authority of the Vedas, avoid contact with outcastes and the like.

For once the arrogance of the doctrine of caste has been cast aside, what fault could there be in touching a *caṇḍāla* or others? Furthermore, even those others who perform improper acts—such as the consumption of impure things or approaching women who should not be approached—under the guise of initiation (*dīkṣā*) characterized by non-conceptuality, they too perform such deeds in secret out of fear of the great community (*mahājana*) consisting of the four castes, and not openly. For if their confidence in that scripture were free from doubt, why would they practice its purpose like a thief? Therefore, it is not this "great community" of the four castes and so forth that can be roused by Vardhamāna and others; rather, it is precisely this very community of the four castes that [must be roused].
And this great multitude of people indeed avoids any scripture that contradicts the Vedas; they do not approve of it.
Upon touching a proponent of liberation from saṃsāra, the learned bathe along with their clothes;
moreover, they have no social interaction whatsoever even with Buddhists.
Almost all people follow the dharma of the Vedas;
however, whatever scripture is outside the Vedas is merely a deception.
And such is this illustrious mass of texts called the Vedas, possessing a majesty without equal, that even other proponents of external scriptures (bāhyāgamavādins) vie with it in this very way;
for, while asserting the authority of their own scriptures,
they speak in the manner of the Vedas and strive to enter into the Veda in whatever way possible.
They incorporate Vedic matters here and there within their own scriptures;
they consider themselves as if purified by contact with the Vedas;
and even in their inner hearts, the authority of the Veda truly blazes forth.
Therefore, because such widespread renown among the great masses is not seen in other scriptures, those [scriptures] were not composed by authoritative persons.

He said: "Since the authority of the Vedas is established simply through their universal acceptance by the great masses, what is the purpose of this excessive parching of the throat that has been undertaken by your honor?"
It is proclaimed that this treatise was indeed commenced for the purpose of establishing the authority of the Vedas.

Since the authority of the Vedas is established by the very consensus of great men (*mahājana*), what is the use of a treatise? Enough with such petty objections! For some even seek to subvert the consensus of great men; therefore, the mantra of this treatise is employed to protect it from such injury.
Therefore, it is established that authority belongs only to those scriptures previously mentioned, and not to those outside the Veda.
Others, however, have denied the authority of all scriptures,
because in every case there arises a cognition free from sublation and doubt.
In all cases, as in the case of the Veda, one must postulate an authoritative author.
Because, for the most part, a correspondence is observed in those parts where the objects are perceptible.

Furthermore, as for the claim that all scriptures (*āgamas*) would be invalid because they teach mutually contradictory meanings, it is replied: since they are of equal status by virtue of being composed by authoritative persons (*āpta*), and because no cause for the weakness of any one among them is perceived, no scripture sublates any other. Mere contradiction, however, is irrelevant, for mutual contradictions are observed even among Vedic statements which are accepted as valid authorities (*pramāṇa*).
In injunctions such as touching the head of a man, seizing sugarcane, or slaughtering a cow, a collection of matters contradicted by other scriptural statements has indeed been taught.

Moreover, there is no significant contradiction even among the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because there is no dispute among anyone regarding either the means of valid cognition or the human goal (puruṣārtha).
Many means are taught through various distinctions of paths and methods;
they all converge upon that single supreme good, just as the currents of the Ganges flow into the ocean.
For thus, liberation is indicated as the goal to be attained in all treatises;
its means is taught everywhere to be knowledge;
yet they disagree regarding the object of that knowledge.
Even there, for the most part, many are in agreement regarding its having the self as its object.

But according to the view that it is the knowledge of the distinction between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), it is the person alone who is to be known once primordial nature has been distinguished from him.
However, those who propound selflessness teach in such a manner for the sake of producing a sense of detachment from the self.
For the reality of consciousness, which they maintain, is like a self precisely because of its autonomy and lack of dependence.
The distinction lies in its being immutable eternity (*kūṭasthanityatva*) rather than continuity-in-flux eternity (*pravāhanityatva*).

Thus, there may indeed be a dispute regarding the primary means and the end; however, let the ritual action (*kriyā*) vary according to each scripture—whether one adopts ashes and matted hair, or takes up the staff and water-pot, or wears red robes, or remains naked—what contradiction is there in this? Even in the Veda, are not very few distinct methods for attaining heaven, adorned with their own respective sets of procedures (*itikartavyatā*), enjoined? Therefore, even if there is mutual contradiction [among the scriptures], there is no contradiction regarding their authoritative status (*prāmāṇya*).

Therefore, the following arguments are refuted: "If Kapila is omniscient, then Sugata is not; what is the proof for this? Or, if both are omniscient, how can there be a difference in their views? This is because, when the primary cause (pradhāna) exists, there is no difference [in its nature], and where such a difference occurs, it contradicts the authority [of the teaching]. Furthermore, the lack of authority in other scriptures does not follow from the instruction of actions that cause heart-rending pain, since that is irrelevant to the question of their lack of authority.
For even that doubt which exists regarding the eating of human skulls and such things is bound up with the cultivation resulting from the practice of other philosophical systems.
And thus, even regarding Vedic acts of violence, hesitation arises in those whose minds are peaceful and who possess compassion for all living beings.
Let there be a trembling of the heart even regarding Vedic violence such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*);
for that violence falls within the category of the instrument [of action], and thus one engages in it out of desire.

However, regarding that slaughter of animals in the Agniṣomīya and other sacrifices which constitutes a part of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) and is understood from scripture as being for the sake of the sacrifice—that is, ritual activity (*vaidhī pravṛtti*)—even in this case, compassionate people become hesitant. They say: "Where the killing of living beings is dharma, what kind of thing is adharma?
And yet, the Veda's lack of authority does not follow from this alone.
In this way, it will also occur in other scriptural traditions.

As for the claim that even when one achieves goals such as the power of moving through the air (*khecaratā*) from other scriptures like the *Kaula* traditions, an inevitable transgression will inevitably occur at some later time due to the performance of prohibited acts—that too is not tenable, because those specific acts are not prohibited by those very scriptures.
Even if they were prohibited in other scriptures, it is logical to consider them as optional alternatives (*vaikalpika*).

Furthermore, because that [rite] is a means for attaining a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), once it is accomplished, how could there be any transgression (*pratyavāya*)? Or, even if a transgression were to occur at a later time, nevertheless, when the fruit of the action is enjoined according to the distinction of the qualified persons (*adhikārin*), the authority of the scripture (*āgama-prāmāṇya*) is not lost here, just as in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice. In the injunction "One desiring to practice sorcery (*abhicaran*) should sacrifice with the *śyena*," the word "desiring to practice sorcery" indicates the qualified person who is prohibited from violating the [moral] law; and for such a person, the *śyena* sacrifice is enjoined.
And he who commits a killing through that performance certainly incurs sin; yet there is no lack of authority in the Veda.
For it has been said: "In this world, both the beneficial and the harmful are sought through the Vedic injunction.
And because of the distinction in the qualifications of those entitled to perform them, the injunction of various types of actions is not untenable.
The *sarvasvāra* sacrifice is prescribed for one desiring death, and the *kṛṣṇala-caru* for one desiring long life;
therefore, this too is not a ground for invalidity.

Furthermore, even that refutation of the doctrine of caste found in the Buddhist scriptures is intended to praise the excellence of compassion that is inclined toward the welfare of all beings, and it is not to be understood literally.
For it is recited therein: "One should not ordain those who are corrupted by the duties of their caste.
Therefore, it is logical that the authority of all the scriptures composed by trustworthy persons such as Kapila, Sugata, and the Arhat is established.
Others believe that the Blessed Lord Īśvara alone is the author of all the scriptures.

For he, observing the manifold ripening of the karma of all living beings, out of compassion seeks to favor them; perceiving the various paths leading to the attainment of the further shore (*apāra*), and having understood the fitness of certain individuals for specific actions according to their dispositions, he teaches those respective means.
Furthermore, by virtue of his own sovereign majesty and through the assumption of various bodies, he himself undergoes different designations.
He alone is called the Blessed One— the Arhat, Kapila, and the Sugata—
because it would entail the unnecessary burden of exertion and complexity in postulating multiple omniscient beings.

[Objection: But surely the Buddha was the offspring of King Śuddhodana; how then could he be the Lord? [Reply: This has been answered by the Blessed Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana: "Whenever there is a decline of Dharma, O Bhārata, and an upsurge of Adharma, then I manifest myself."
The body alone is the offspring of Śuddhodana, not the self;
therefore, those who know the scriptures maintain that in every age the Blessed Viṣṇu descends in the form of Dharma.

Now, one might ask: "Why is there no such great consensus among the people regarding other scriptures that have the same author as the Veda? It is not so; for by means of the path taught by the Blessed One, only a few living beings were favored, whose disposition was observed to be of such a kind. But by means of the Vedic path, countless living beings were favored; thus, while there is great respect for that [Vedic path], it is meager regarding the other scriptures.
If it is asked how there can be mutual contradiction in that which has a single author, the resolution has already been indicated here by the Vedas themselves;
for it has been stated that even within them, a great deal of mutual contradiction is observed.
Therefore, all scriptures possess authority because they were composed by God.
Others, moreover, have accepted the authority of all scriptures on the grounds that they are rooted in the Veda.

For the reasoning stated regarding the Vedic basis of the teachings of Manu and others is as follows: "Whether due to error, from personal experience, or from the deceptive speech of a human being, the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) alone is the most parsimonious [explanation], by virtue of its capacity to accord with what is observed."
Thus, this [principle] is common to all the Āgamas;
yet, no Vedic revelation (śruti) that serves as the source for the Smṛtis of Manu and others is actually perceived.
However, the postulation of such a source through inference is equally applicable to other Āgamas as well.

But has it not been said that "inference may be a means of valid knowledge because of the identity of the agent"? And since that [identity] is absent here, how can there be an inference from scripture? This is not a fault; for the understanding of a common purpose is not the determinant of validity.
Rather, let it be the cause, if desired, for the establishment of the joint performance [of the rites].

Nor does an action, even when performed separately, fail to have its root in authoritative means of knowledge, just like the actions to be performed according to the distinctions of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).
The emergence of another root [cause] due to the absence of a common agent is likewise non-existent,
because there is no subverting evidence and because errors and the like have been refuted.
If [the Smṛti] were based on direct perception, the assumption [of such a basis] would be highly burdensome;
however, since the Veda has infinite branches, it is perfectly consistent for it to be the source in that case.
Surely, if these [Smṛtis] were not rooted in the Veda, how could those who know the Veda feel such aversion? Let them be questioned themselves regarding this, if there is any malice [on their part].
How can there be hatred toward them for the slaughter of cows when the Veda is so clearly established?
Furthermore, the contradiction has been answered, and [the objection regarding] the difficulty [of determining the Veda] due to the infinity of its branches is refuted.
Is the entirety of the Veda merely that which resides in our mouths?
Or what proof is there that no contradiction could be found with other treatises?

And thus, a Vedic indicative mark is found—namely, "the one unborn, red, white, and black"—which serves to indicate the *prakṛti* consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) as well known in the Sāṃkhya treatises.
Furthermore, this corroborative statement is seen which praises the knowledge of the true nature of the "minister of austerity" as taught by the Nirgranthas: "The sages are clothed in the wind.

In this way, even those who are diligent find that the very roots of the practices of the Raktapaṭas—such as the wearing of saffron robes, the carrying of ashes, and the holding of skull-bowls—are indeed present.
Therefore, even though identity of authorship— as in the case of the Smṛtis of Manu and others— is impossible,
every traditional scripture (āgama-smṛti) must be declared authoritative because it is rooted in the Veda.
And therefore: "Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone, all that is declared in the Veda, for it consists of all knowledge."

In this context, just as the mention of Manu is intended as an illustration for the authors of the Smṛtis such as Gautama, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, and others, so too should it be explained as being intended to illustrate Arhats, Kapila, Sugata, and the rest.
But would not the same validity also apply to the scriptures of the Lokāyatas and others?
For they contain a view based on the Vedas, stating: "This mass of consciousness, having arisen from these elements, perishes along with them; after death, there is no consciousness.
Consequently, if the Lokāyata system were established as authoritative, all other scriptures would be rendered invalid.
It is said in response: nothing whatsoever to be practiced is taught in the Lokāyata;
it is merely the talk of a caviller (vaitaṇḍika) and not any traditional scripture (āgama).
But surely, it is taught there that "one should live happily as long as life lasts.

Likewise, whatever is taught such as "it is not so because it is established by intrinsic nature" (since instruction would be futile in that case), or "dharma is not to be performed," or "one should not place trust in those instructions"—all that has already been refuted, because the Lokāyata system is rooted in the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). And thus, in that regard, the subsequent Brāhmaṇa passage states: "Indeed, I do not speak out of delusion; this self, O friend, is indeed indestructible, but it comes into contact with the material elements (*mātrā*)."

Thus, since it is rooted in the statements of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the Lokāyata treatise as well is not independent; moreover, because it is refuted by subsequent statements, it is not to be cited [as authoritative]. However, it is improper to assume that other treatises are rooted in the statements of the prima facie position.
Because no statement contradicting that [Veda] is perceived immediately thereafter, all scriptures are authoritative on account of being rooted in the Veda.
Now, if it has been established in this way that all scriptures possess the status of valid authority,
then what if I were to compose some scripture today as well?
For even that [subsequent cognition] would become a means of valid knowledge after a few days;
therefore, it is not at all difficult to state the previously mentioned principle.

Whatever has been written in the books of the world, even that is now proclaimed by some rogue as "this is our great traditional scripture. In that case too, one might imagine some trustworthy person as its author and claim that such-and-such a Vedic statement is its source; but this is not so, for those scriptures which have attained undisputed renown and whose acceptance here has been made by many learned men (śiṣṭas).
And those things which proceed today are not as if they were unprecedented;
for them no root is grasped by greed, and from them no living being is agitated.
In this context, it is accepted that only those scriptures possess the status of valid authority;
however, one does not tolerate any arbitrary measure of validity, such as the "Opinion of the Procuress."

For instance, it is said that this "Blue-Garment Vow" (nīlāmbaravrata) was devised by certain libertines, characterized by many antics performed by men and women who were unrestrained and draped in a single, boundless cloth.
Having understood that this was unprecedented, King Śaṅkaravarman, who knew the true nature of the Dharma, prohibited it; however, he did not likewise prohibit the Jaina and other such doctrines.

Thus, because these Vedic scriptures have firmly attained the status of valid means of knowledge—due to the reason of being spoken by a reliable authority (āpta) and because all defects alleged by others have been removed—their truthfulness follows from that very fact. Since other treatises lack such a root, let their status be determined by the words of men; yet, even through that medium, it is certainly impossible to attribute any impurity to the words of the Veda.
Is it not the case that even now the authority of the Veda is not well-established,
being undermined by defects such as falsehood inherent in its own composition?
It is heard in scripture: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," and "One desiring a son should sacrifice with the Putreṣṭi.
Yet, the fruit consisting of a son, cattle, and so forth, is not perceived immediately after the sacrifice.
Therefore, the injunctions for the Citrā and other such rites are non-existent.
But surely, the meaning of the sentence is merely this: "He who desires cattle should perform the sacrifice.
In that case, the claim that cattle arise from the sacrifice is already difficult to establish;
and the further claim that they arise immediately after [the sacrifice] is even more difficult to establish.

Therefore, why is it not said that injunctions such as those for the *citrayāga* sacrifice possess a true meaning? Just as "living" (*jīvana*) in the injunctions "one should sacrifice as long as one lives" (*yāvaj jīvaṃ yajeta*) and "one should offer oblations as long as one lives" (*yāvaj jīvaṃ juhuyāt*) serves as a qualification for eligibility, so too the desire for cattle—which is not something to be accomplished [by the act itself]—must necessarily be a qualification for eligibility. It will be established that for one who does not understand the attainment of cattle from that ritual action, the very eligibility for it does not arise.
Even the nature of the *ānantarya* (immediate) karmas is understood precisely by examining their intrinsic character, because it is observed that such actions yield results immediately thereafter.
As it has been said: "When this [action] existed, it did not then give its fruit; when the fruit arises, it no longer exists. Being non-existent, how will it give the fruit?"
Moreover, another perceptible cause for the result at a later time is observed, such as service and the like.

When that cause is seen, what person of subtle vision would postulate an unseen [cause] such as the *citrā* sacrifice? Therefore, injunctions regarding the *citrā* and so forth are false, because—even though they teach objects capable of being determined by means of valid cognition such as direct perception—they lack corroboration by those very means, just like the deceptive words of a fraud.
Since such a deviation is observed even in the case of words concerning paintings and the like,
a lack of confidence arises regarding the injunctions for the Agnihotra and other rites as well.
The injunction for the Agnihotra is false because it is a part of the Veda, like the injunctions for the Citrā sacrifice and others;
thus, in this case, there is a lack of authority due to inconsistency.
In the same way, a lack of correspondence should be understood in such cases as "one desiring a son should sacrifice with the Putreṣṭi."
In some instances, even contradiction is observed.

When the sacrificer has died, the Veda prescribes the ritual known as the "piling of the vessels" (*pātracayana*) and instructs: "This very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudhī*), goes directly to the heavenly world. In this regard, the reference "this" (*eṣaḥ*) as the self (*ātman*) is indeed strained, because the self is imperceptible and because it lacks connection with sacrificial implements such as the wooden sword (*sphya*) and the potsherds (*kapāla*). If, however, the body is what is being referred to by "this," it does not go to the heavenly world, since its contrary state—reduction to ashes—is perceived. Thus, there is a contradiction.
And thus, due to both non-correspondence and contradiction, the Veda is not a valid means of knowledge.

Furthermore, due to internal contradiction: having prescribed all three times for the oblation—namely, "one should sacrifice after sunrise," "one should sacrifice before sunrise," and "one should sacrifice at the time of twilight"—the text then prohibits those very same times through deprecatory explanatory passages (arthavādas): "The dark one (*śyāma*) devours his oblation who sacrifices after sunrise;
the brindled one (*śavala*) devours his oblation who sacrifices before sunrise; both the dark and the brindled devour his oblation who sacrifices at the time of twilight."
And it should not be said that this is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), because an injunction is inferred through praise, and a prohibition through censure;
for the function of an injunction and its eulogy is equal, as is the case with a prohibition and its censure.

For the principle that "censure is not employed for the sake of censuring, but rather for the sake of praising something other than the censured" is also not applicable here; since there is a negation of all three times [past, present, and future] in this case, what else could be praised by means of that censure? Therefore, the Veda is not a valid authority because of its internal contradiction, characterized by the teaching of mutually opposed meanings.

Furthermore, due to redundancy, there is repetition in the injunction "He recites the first [verse] three times, [and] the last three times," since the first and last *sāmidhenī* verses are each recited thrice.
Since their purpose is fulfilled by a single recitation, this triple recitation is useless.
Therefore, because it is defiled by these faults of contradiction, inconsistency, and redundancy, the Veda is not an authoritative source of knowledge.
Thus the author of the Sūtra says:
"Its lack of authority [is due] to the faults of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology, as seen in the case of the sacrifice for one desiring a son, in oblations, and in repetitions."
Regarding this, he states the resolution: "[It is not so] because of a deficiency in the action, the agent, or the instrument."
This is the intended meaning:
non-authoritativeness has been established by others through falsity;
and the proof for falsity is the non-perception of results.
And this [argument] is inconclusive, because the non-perception of the result can be explained otherwise:
is the non-perception of the result here due to the Veda having false meaning, or rather due to a deficiency in the performer and other factors? There is no specific reason [to decide].

[Objection: "Is it not the case that the fruit is never perceived immediately following the ritual action? Therefore, the very fact that it is not seen is the reason for its non-existence, and not a deficiency in the causal factors. [Reply: That is incorrect, because when the *kārīrī* sacrifice is performed with all its parts intact, rain is observed to occur immediately. Nor is this a mere coincidence (*kākatālīya*), since its causality is established through scripture as well as through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
However, even a result pertaining to this world, such as a son and so forth, cannot come into being immediately merely by reflecting on the nature of things;
for a son does not fall from the sky at that very moment like rain, since his birth depends upon other factors, such as the union of a man and a woman.
On the other hand, the acquisition of cattle and the like is seen to occur for some even in the near future through means such as acceptance as a gift.
For instance, our own grandfather, desiring a village, performed the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice;
immediately upon the completion of that rite, he obtained the village of Gauramūlaka.

"Surely, in that case, let visible causes alone—such as the acceptance of gifts for cattle and the like, and the union of man and woman for a son—be sufficient; what is the use of postulating the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) as a cause? Do not speak thus, for even when visible causes are present, [the result] is not seen, whereas it is observed immediately following the performance of the sacrifice.
It is determined that the state of being the cause for the union of man and woman and so forth is produced by destiny (*iṣṭa*).
Furthermore, since there is a difference in results even when service, study, agriculture, and the like are equal,
it is not reasonable to say that the attainment [of those results] arises from visible causes alone.
The doctrine of the intrinsic nature of the elements (*bhūtasvabhāvavāda*) and others will be refuted later;
therefore, there must certainly be another reason for this as well.
Thus it has been said: "For that very thing is the cause therein, and so is the word."
Furthermore, when even a ritual performed without deficiency does not yield results such as sons or cattle at some later time, one must postulate some intense prior karma acting as an obstacle.
As it has been said: "If that [karma] does not bear fruit at all times, then certainly some other unexhausted scriptural karma remains."
The mention of "deficiency in action" (*karmādivaiguṇya*) was employed by the Sage as an illustration;
however, it is not correct to assume that the Veda lacks authority, because when action is performed with excellence, the fruit is seen to occur in abundance.
Moreover, the meaning of the scripture is simply this: "The sacrificial gifts become terrified.
However, there is no evidence whatsoever for immediate succession. Therefore, this contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge concerns the subject of immediate succession.

However, an injunction such as that for the Citrā sacrifice concerns a subject matter for which no specific time is prescribed; thus, due to this difference in subject matter, it is not sublated by the other [injunction].

As Bhaṭṭa says: "The contradiction regarding immediate sequence is not able to sublate an injunction that operates without such specification, because the difference in their subject matters is clear."

As for the claim that, upon examining the nature of actions, painting and the like yield immediate results—on the grounds that "at the very time of massaging, there is the pleasure of massaging"—this is the statement of one who is utterly ignorant, because it is impossible for the fruits of injunctions to be identical to the fruits of mere physical action.
In this world, some things are the fruits of injunctions (*vidhiphala*), while others are the fruits of action (*kriyāphala*).
In the case of agriculture and the like, the breaking of the soil and so forth are the fruits of action, whereas the abundance of the harvest is the fruit of the injunction.

Furthermore, what rule exists for agriculture and the like? In the science of livelihood (vārtā), there is either the instruction of the elders as a rule, or positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) will serve as the place of the rule in that case.
In common worldly usage as well, in expressions such as "he cooks desiring wages," the rice (*odana*) is the fruit of the act of cooking, whereas the wages are the fruit of the injunction (*vidhi*).
In that regard, this rule—that they must occur in the interval between the acts—applies only to the fruits of the actions;
however, for the fruits of the injunctions, such as the wages, there is no restriction regarding time.
Even in the case of an *iṣṭi* sacrifice, the fruit of the action—such as the modification of the oblation (*havirvikāra*)—indeed occurs immediately.
However, the fruit of the injunction (*vidhiphala*), such as cattle or sons, belongs to an uninterrupted period of time.
For this very reason, the pleasure of massage, being the fruit of an action, occurs immediately.
But for a man who is being oppressed, the fruit of service is of uncertain duration.
In worldly injunctions such as "one who desires a village should serve the king," there is no restriction regarding the time for the fruit.

Even regarding the medicinal prescriptions taught in Āyurveda, the manifestation of results is not immediate like the performance of the action itself; rather, it depends entirely upon time. Thus, there is no evidence whatsoever for the immediate succession of the result.

As for the claim that there is immediate fruition based on a consideration of the nature of the qualified practitioner, who is tormented by defects such as the distress caused by separation from his wife—that too is not correct; this is merely a matter of human whim and does not function according to valid means of knowledge.
Moreover, by that much alone the result will be established as pertaining to this world (aihikatva), but not as being immediate like the fruit of an action [performed on the same day].
There are indeed actions with results in this world that depend upon another time, such as:
"For a Brahmin desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa), the rite should be performed in the fifth [year]."
In that case, a young boy who has merely been initiated in the fifth year does not become endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) immediately, but rather at a later time;
the same should be understood regarding those desiring vigor and so forth.
Therefore, since there is no rule of immediate succession for the fruits of ritual injunctions, their non-occurrence at once does not constitute a fault.
It has been stated that even when a result is not observed after a lapse of time, the cause is a deficiency in the ritual action or an obstruction by another karma.
Others, who do not approve of the hypothesis of defects in the agent and so forth,
have declared that for rituals such as the Citrā sacrifice, which yield no fruit in this world, the fruit is obtained in the next life.

Since the performance of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) involves the inclusion of all its constituent parts, what occasion is there for imagining a deficiency in the ritual? It is, however, logical to imagine that the fruit of such an action will be realized in another birth.

And thus, there is the conceptualization that the threefold karma consists of some that bears fruit only in this life, some that bears fruit only in the next life, and some that bears fruit indeterminately, yielding its result either here or in the hereafter.
In this regard, rituals such as the Kārīrī sacrifice have results that pertain exclusively to this life.
For they are undertaken during a great drought that causes suffering to the entire population;
and its result, characterized by rain, is by its very nature common to all people in the world.
It must follow that it is desirable only because of its proximity;
for such statements are indeed seen there: "If it rains, one should complete the sacrifice at that very time; if it does not rain, one should offer the oblation on the following day."
But action whose fruit belongs to the next world, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, becomes transworldly by its very nature as a fruit.
Heaven is either incomparable bliss or a specific place characterized by it;
in neither case can this [bliss] be enjoyed with this present body.
But actions such as the Citrā sacrifice have an indefinite fruit, because their result—such as cattle—may occur either in this world or in another world.
And this must necessarily be understood in this way;
for indeed, animals are seen here in this very life even among those who have not performed the Citrā sacrifice.

If it were said that these [animals] have only visible causes such as service or receiving gifts, then there would be the consequence of abandoning the fact that karma is the cause [of rebirth], which would lead to an entry into the doctrine of Bṛhaspati.

If those animals are indeed caused by karma, then it must be determined what specific karma produced them; for cattle are not produced from a rite whose fruit is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and the like.
Furthermore, the *Citrā* sacrifice—which has cattle as its fruit—was certainly not performed by them in this life.

As for karma performed in a previous birth, since it is accepted that such karma yields its fruit in that very same birth, its results would be restricted to this life alone; thus, how can there be an abundance of cattle? [Objection: But surely, on the authority of Gautama’s statement, that acquisition of cattle will be caused by the remnants of rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* performed and experienced in a previous life.

As it has been said: "The castes and stages of life, established in their own duties, after dying and experiencing the fruit of their actions, fall away; then, by the remainder [of that karma], they obtain a birth endowed with a distinguished place, learning, conduct, wealth, and so forth.
It is not proper to understand this according to the literal text. For an action intended for one specific fruit cannot bestow another fruit;
indeed, the relationship between the means and the end is fixed for fruits and actions.
Therefore, the expression "by the remainder" (śeṣa) must be explained with reference to a collection [of actions]. For people of various castes and stages of life have performed many actions;
from that collection of actions, the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices is experienced after death.
Then, by means of the "remainder"—that is, by the action consisting of the piling of the funeral pyre and so forth—they attain a distinguished birth; such is the meaning.

Therefore, the acquisition of cattle in this life is based on the *citri* sacrifice performed in a previous birth; it is not caused by no action at all, nor is it caused by some other action. Thus, because the fruit of the *citri* and similar rites is not fixed [to this specific life], even if their fruit is not seen in this life, there is no falsehood in your Vedic injunctions, for those sacrifices will yield their fruit in another birth.
To this it is replied: is this threefold classification of actions scriptural, or is it dependent upon human will?

In that regard, the scriptural statement (*vacana*) does not establish a threefold division; there is merely the hearing of such texts as "One desiring rain should offer the *kārīrī*," "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma*," and "One desiring cattle should [sacrifice] with the *citrayā*. For here, nowhere is the fruit described as being of this world, of the next world, or as being indefinite.
The function of an injunction (*vidhi*) is precisely this much: namely, the instigation of action accompanied by conviction.

In that regard, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is simply this: "this must be done by one who desires such-and-such. However, since an injunction cannot fulfill its own function—characterized as being an instigator—with respect to an activity that does not constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), it merely makes known the relationship between the means and the end between the sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like (the *bhāvārtha*), which is the object of desire, on the one hand, and heaven (*svarga*) and the like, which are the desired ends and serve as qualifiers for the qualified agent (*adhikārin*), on the other; it does not imply the actual accomplishment of the desired end either immediately or at a later time.
However, upon careful consideration of the nature of the fruit, it is understood that heaven is indeed otherworldly, whereas there is no such restriction regarding cattle and the like.
Human desire, however, is merely human desire; it is not possible to establish the meaning of a treatise by means of it. Therefore, the threefold classification lacks any basis in valid cognition.

Furthermore, the reasoning that was stated regarding the uncertainty of the results of rites such as the *citrā* sacrifice—namely, that "the fruit of the *citrā* and so forth is exhausted in that very birth," and so on—can also be applied to the *kārīrī* sacrifice, which has a certain result in this life.
If the rain-god does not send rain today because the Kārīrī sacrifice has not been performed,
why is the Kārīrī sacrifice performed in a previous life not the cause [of the rain]?
Therefore, let that [action] also have an indefinite fruit.

If you think that rain—which serves as the means for the enjoyment of happiness produced by the abundance of crops—is caused by *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit) even when the *Kārīrī* sacrifice has not been performed, then the acquisition of cattle will likewise occur for those who have not performed the *Citrā* sacrifice, being caused by the karma that brings about the pleasure of consuming curds, milk, and so forth.

Let the production of cattle and rain be brought about by the *adṛṣṭa* that serves as the means for the pleasure of eating curds and rice, [whereby] rice depends on the *Kārīrī* and curds depend on the *Citrā*.

Now, if it is argued that the Citreṣṭi sacrifice is taught as specifically yielding cattle (*paśu*) by way of "pointing with the finger" (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*), and therefore the acquisition of cattle is not based on a karma that projects the general category of pleasure; then, since the Kārīrī sacrifice is likewise recited as specifically yielding rain (*vṛṣṭi*), let rain also not be based on a general unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

Now, if it is argued that its fruit belongs to this world based on an examination of such statements as, "If it does not rain, one should offer the oblation on the following day," then in cases where no such statement exists—such as, "He who desires rain should praise with the *saubhara* chant," "If he should desire that Parjanya be a bringer of rain, he should construct the *sadas* shed low," and so forth—it would follow that the fruit belongs to the next world.

By the power of the statement alone—"and if one should offer the oblation on the following day"—let there be merely the addition of immediate fruition (*sadyastva*) regarding the result; however, the fact that certain rites possess results in this very life (*aihikaphalatva*), which is clearly established even in the absence of such a statement, does not cease to exist.

Furthermore, as for the claim that rain is a result pertaining to this life (*aihika*) because it is common to many, that too applies equally to cattle and other such things; for the sacrificer is not merely one who nourishes himself, since there are instructions regarding his own eating being preceded by the feeding of those living with him, children, guests, servants, and so forth.
As for rain, however, its quality of providing greater benefit is self-evident—so enough with weighing it on a scale.

As for the claim that rain is said to pertain to this world because it is desired due to its proximity, that too is exactly the same [as the case of cattle and so forth], since cattle and other such things are likewise desired in that very way.

Just as rain is longed for there because of its proximity, being the remedy for the distress caused by drought, here too cattle are desired precisely because of their proximity, owing to the agitation caused by poverty.

Therefore, this abundance of rain, cattle, and so forth for those who have not performed the labor here [on earth] is based solely on the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—the general means of happiness taught in such scriptural statements as, "The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food obtains imperishable happiness. Thus, it is not a fruit caused by no action at all, as the doctrine of Bṛhaspati maintains;
nor does it involve a transgression of the conventional rule regarding the fixed relationship between the means and the end of karma and its fruit.

And as for the resolution offered regarding the non-deviation from the fruit of the *kārīrī* sacrifice— namely, "If not everything bears fruit, then at some time that very same [other] scriptural karma remains unexperienced"— by that [argument], even that [kārīrī] would have an indefinite fruit;
for that other karma does not remain an obstacle until the end of *saṃsāra*,
since it must necessarily be exhausted through the experience of its fruit.
And when an obstacle has been removed, the Kārīrī sacrifice must necessarily yield its own fruit;
since it too does not perish without having given its fruit, its fruit likewise occurs in another birth, and thus even that [karma] possesses an indefinite fruit.

And in this manner, we certainly accept that even the *citriṣṭi* sacrifice has an indefinite result, where it is postulated that even when the sacrifice is correctly performed, cattle are not obtained precisely because of an obstruction by another ritual act.
In every respect, except for the fact that its fruit is not immediate, the *kārīrī* sacrifice shares the same status and conditions as the *citriṣṭi*.
By this, the sacrifices for the desire of Brahmanic luster, heroic vigor, food, a village, and so forth, are also explained.
Therefore, Gautama’s rule should be understood exactly as it was heard.

As for what was further asserted—that because the performance of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) involves the gathering of all constituent parts, there is no occasion for any deficiency in the rite—that too is worthless; for even when one proceeds with the gathering of all parts, a deficiency may occur that remains unperceived due to negligence.
And that [deficiency] is manifold, as demonstrated by the Author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*).
Therefore, the path of resolution previously stated is indeed superior.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by the opponent—that since the action ceases at another time, how can there be a fruit—that too is not correct; for although the action does not persist until the production of the fruit, nevertheless, there certainly exists a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited in the person by that action.
For the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by karma is a quality (*guṇa*) of the person, like cognition and other mental states;
its persistence is accepted because it has not yet reached its fruit.
Just as the arising of cognition in the self occurs through the conjunction of the sense faculties and so forth,
so too does the arising of its latent impression (saṃskāra) result from sacrificial acts and the like.
But his intellect is transitory, whereas his latent impression (saṃskāra) lasts until the fruition [of the result];
for otherwise, the relationship of means and end between the action and its fruit could not exist.
Furthermore, it is accepted by others as well that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is the seed of memory;
in the same way, that [impression] will be his seed for the connection with the fruit.
That which is produced by sacrifice, giving, oblation, and so forth, is called "dharma" (merit);
whereas that which is produced by the killing of a Brahmin and so forth is called "adharma" (demerit).
The followers of Kapila, however, say that dharma is a particular modification (vṛtti) of the internal organ, the intellect (buddhi);
the Ārhats designate meritorious personages (puṇyapudgala) as dharma;
and the Buddhist monks describe the mental impression (cittavāsanā) as dharma.
The older Mīmāṃsakas declare that *dharma* is a distinct entity called *apūrva*, which is produced by rituals such as sacrifices; the followers of Śabara maintain that it is the ritual act itself;

and the Prābhākaras state that the meaning of the sentence, consisting of an injunction (*niyoga*), is what is denoted by the word *apūrva*, and that very same thing is expressed by the word *dharma*.

In this regard, the two positions concerning the mode of existence of a meritorious person (puṇyapudgala) as propounded by Kapila and the Arhat [Nirgrantha] are refuted precisely by the refutation of their respective doctrines.
Furthermore, since the existence of a self will be established, it is the self alone that possesses the latent impressions (vāsanā) and not the mind; thus, the Buddhist position is also untenable.
And of that which is stable and situated within the interior of all Gayās.
Since that which is baseless and unprecedented lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the claim of the ancient followers of Jaimini is also untenable.
Furthermore, the word "apūrva" refers either to some state of the fruit yet to arise or to the potency (*śakti*) of the sacrifice.
Nor is it the case that the injunction (*niyoga*) alone is the sentence-meaning denoted by the word *apūrva*, because that [position] will be refuted later on.

Nor is it reasonable to say that "one who performs a sacrifice is called righteous" (dhārmika), because such usage occurs in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the sacrifice and so forth; for it would follow that the sacrifice itself is what is denoted by the word *dharma*, yet that is untenable because, being momentary, it cannot logically bestow a fruit at a later time.
Furthermore, there is no coreferential usage based on identity between them.
It is also a worldly convention that dharma arises through sacrifice, giving, and so forth;
there are such applications, and these serve as witnesses for the position regarding purification.

Thus, even the Vedic usage, "With sacrifice the gods sacrificed to sacrifice; those were the first dharmas," must be explained as referring to that very same [apūrva], because it is established as enduring and is therefore capable of yielding fruit at a later time.
The impression (*saṃskāra*) is a human quality that persists; therefore, it is established that this is *dharma*.
And because the fruit arises from that [impression], there is no falsity in the case of paintings and the like.

As for the argument that the statement regarding the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*) is contradicted by direct perception—since the body is observed to be reduced to ashes—that too is incorrect; for here, by means of a metaphorical identification with the body (*śarīra*), it is the Self (*ātman*) itself that is being designated.
And its going to heaven certainly does occur.
Furthermore, "going" is said to be simply the experience thereof, just as birth and death are defined as the conjunction with and disjunction from the body and so forth.
However, for that which is all-pervading, connection with action consisting of physical motion is not possible;
rather, its agency will be described as the inherence of knowledge, desire to act, and effort.

Furthermore, even the connection with sacrificial implements—whether as owner and owned or otherwise—is possible through a fixed rule despite its lack of distinction in being all-pervading; thus, there is no contradiction here.
Therefore, the refutation based on falsity and other such faults has no scope whatsoever in any case.
Furthermore, even that fault of contradiction shown regarding the rule for the time of the oblation is not actually a fault at all.
In that regard, there is an injunction concerning three periods of time according to the distinction of performance:
whatever time has been prescribed for a particular [rite], it must not be transgressed by that person.
Furthermore, when one approaches another at a certain time and then abandons him, there is blame; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever here between the injunction and the prohibition.
And although repetition occurs in the case of recitation, it is not a defect because it serves a functional purpose;
for the fifteenfold number is indeed enjoined as that which is to be accomplished in relation to the *sāmidhenī* verses.
It is heard in scripture: "With this fifteen-spoked vajra, I strike down him who hates us and whom we hate.
However, only eleven *sāmidhenī* verses are recited;
since the state of having fifteen is not possible without repetition, repetition must necessarily be performed.
And although this [repetition] was obtained without a fixed rule, it is restricted by the explicit statement that "the first and the last verses are to be recited three times.
Therefore, because it serves that specific purpose, there is no fault of redundancy.
Indeed, repetition would be a defect if it were fruitless in its practice; however, in this case, it is not devoid of result.
Therefore, defects such as contradiction, falsehood, and redundancy do not undermine the authoritative status of the Veda.

And considering that this investigation into the meaning of sentences is also conducive to establishing validity, the Sage, who is consecrated here to the preservation of the authority of the Vedas, has composed it in his own treatise.
Indeed, even by you who are so skillful, not all the defects inherent in the Veda itself have yet been fully scrutinized.
For instance: "He wept; because he wept, that is the *rudratva* (the nature of Rudra) of Rudra. "Prajāpati cut out his own omentum and offered it into the fire;
from that, the hornless goat arose."

Regarding such explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as "The gods, having settled upon the sacrificial ground for the gods, did not know the directions," one must consider whether they have as their purport the entities exactly as heard, or whether they are intended to provide instructions on matters of action (*kārya*), or whether they serve as a means for the matters of action propounded by other sentences containing injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like.
In every respect, there is negligence.

First, regarding the view that [the Veda] refers to its own nature (*svarūpa*), its lack of authority follows because it teaches matters contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for there is no certainty that such things as weeping, the excision of the omentum (*vapā*), or disorientation regarding the directions actually exist in that manner.

Furthermore, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) of this kind, such as "the mind is a thief" and "speech is a liar," very clearly convey meanings that contradict other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For it is not the case that the speech of all living beings is inherently a liar, nor is the mind inherently a thief.
Furthermore, the statement that "only smoke is seen from fire, not flame;

therefore, only flame is seen from fire at night, not smoke" contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because both are perceived day and night when there is contact between the sense organ and the object.

Furthermore, because the Brahmin caste is perceivable through direct perception aided by instruction—as in the thought, "I do not know whether I am a Brahmin or not"—this explanatory passage (arthavāda) is contradictory to that fact.
There is also contradiction with the scriptures, as it says: "For who knows whether he exists or not in that other world?
Since the scriptures teach rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma which have results such as heaven, what is this lack of conviction?
Moreover, with reference to the *Gargatrirātrabrāhmaṇa*, it is heard [in scripture]: "The face of one who knows thus shines.
For it is not the case that the face of anyone who knows thus actually shines; therefore, this would contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*).

And there is a certain explanatory passage (arthavāda) that declares the futility of other rituals: "By the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one obtains all desires"; "The performer of the animal sacrifice (paśubandha) conquers all worlds"; and "He who performs the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), and he who knows it thus, crosses over death, crosses over evil, and crosses over the murder of a Brahmin."

If the attainment of all desires occurs through the *pūrṇāhuti* alone, the conquest of all worlds through the performance of the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) alone, and the acquisition of those fruits through the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) alone, then for what purpose are other rites taught? Even those rites that have been taught would become useless, since it is observed that their fruits can be obtained by this very easy means, despite their being accomplished with great effort.

Moreover, regarding the Vedic prohibition of the piling [of the fire-altar], namely, "The fire is not to be piled on the earth, nor in the intermediate space, nor in heaven," this would here be a figurative expression for the very prohibition of piling.

Since there is no practice of piling in heaven or in the intermediate space at all, what is the use of prohibiting them? Furthermore, the sentence intended to prohibit piling on the earth would necessarily be a prohibition of piling itself, because piling that does not have the earth as its locus is impossible.
Nor is it tenable to postulate a separate object in the form of an effect based on those very [words], because it is impossible.

In the case of [the passage] "He wept; because he wept, that is the Rudra-nature of Rudra," if an effect were to be postulated, it would be postulated thus: "Rudra, it is said, wept; therefore, another person should also weep. But that is impossible, for weeping is defined as the shedding of tears under the influence of the torment produced by separation from what is dear.
That cannot be performed merely through the instruction of a Vedic injunction.
"Prajāpati cut out his own omentum; therefore, another too should likewise cut out his own omentum"—this is a matter difficult to carry out.
For who indeed would cut out his own omentum, or for whom, upon the offering of the omentum, would a hornless sacrificial animal immediately emerge from the fire?
"The gods did not know the directions; therefore, no one else could know them either"—this is an impossible instruction, for confusion regarding the directions cannot be remedied by instruction.
Furthermore, since an injunction cannot be inferred from every explanatory passage (arthavāda), the middle position is also a sound thesis.

Nor is the third alternative possible; for being subservient to a purpose consisting of an action enjoined by another injunction occurs through the prescription of materials, deities, and so forth that are useful for it, as in the case of "He offers the Agnihotra," where there is the prescription for the application of materials such as "He offers with curds" or "He offers with milk," or the prescription of a deity such as "That which he offers in the evening to Agni and Prajāpati.
And this mode of operation is not possible in the case of explanatory passages (*arthavādas*).
Furthermore, no procedure—whether perceptible or imperceptible—is taught by these [mantras] in the manner of [the injunctions] "one threshes the rice" or "one sprinkles the rice.
Therefore, they do not serve that purpose.

Now, it might be argued that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) will be useful because they generate enthusiasm for action by producing an extraordinary degree of interest among discerning people. This too is not correct; for in the view of some, the enthusiasm for action is established solely from the cognition of an independent word, while in our view, it is established from the cognition of the person who composed it. Thus, what is the use of incitement? "One desiring such-and-such should do this"—this is trivial.

Thus, since the words of the *arthavāda* sections cannot be syntactically connected even in these three ways, the rejection of the whole follows from the rejection of a single part; consequently, the Veda is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).

[Objection: Let there be non-authoritativeness only to the extent that contradiction by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is perceived; but how can there be such a suspicion regarding everything? [Reply: Do not say so, for because of the similarity between those cases, there is a lack of confidence in other instances as well.

For according to the Mīmāṃsaka position, since no Vedic texts are found that are devoid of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), a state of dependence arises everywhere through their association with those passages.

In the view of the Naiyāyikas, however, if the Lord—who is the author of the Veda—is observed to be a speaker of falsehood in some instances, how could there be firm confidence in his truthfulness in other instances? Thus, [the Veda] would be entirely devoid of authority.

To this it is replied: for the most part, the words of the *arthavāda* are recited precisely as forming a single syntactical unit with an injunction, such as: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu; Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he approaches Vāyu himself with his own share; he (Vāyu) leads him to prosperity.
Their authority derives solely from their being in syntactical unity with that injunction.

Regarding the statement, "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," even though no action is understood from it, nor any object connected with such an action, nevertheless its status as a single syntactical unit with the injunctive portion is perceived; the injunctive portion extends up to the words "one who desires prosperity."
How is there the state of being a single sentence among the words? Because they possess mutual expectancy.

Now, one might object: since the injunction has been enjoined, produced, and the listener’s lack of expectancy has been fulfilled by the sentence ending with "one desiring prosperity," and since the duty of the word has been accomplished, what is the purpose of anything further such as "the most excellent"? We reply that this is indeed a praise (stuti) of that very same meaning.

Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of praise? Whether praised or not praised, the matter remains exactly the same. This is not so; for in a sentence containing words of praise, it is the injunctive word, accompanied by those words of praise, that constitutes the injunction.

Now, is it being said that a sentence containing only an optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is not injunctive? If no words of praise (*stuti*) are heard, then indeed it is injunctive. But when these [words of praise] are present, that [sentence] becomes injunctive only in conjunction with them, not alone, because it is perceived as such.

Since there must not be a split in the sentence (*bhinnavākyatā*) when there is a connection with words of praise, the meaning is enjoined by the injunctive word and the words of praise acting together, for it is understood in that way.
Otherwise, the syntactic connection of the word-meanings as they are perceived would either have to be abandoned or a split in the sentence (vākya-bheda) would have to be postulated.
Therefore, the words of praise are not meaningless.

Now, it may be asked: "Since even a purely injunctive sentence possesses sufficient power [to incite action], for what purpose are words of praise employed? It is replied: In the view of the followers of Jaimini, the Word (śabda) is not subject to questioning; and for us, the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān Īśvara) is likewise not so subject.
Once [the injunction] has been uttered, we are the recipients of the Veda, not its authors. Furthermore, the sequence [of understanding] in the process of comprehension has already been demonstrated.

And thus, although the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) do not possess utility for the ritual action in the same way as the injunctions of subsidiaries (*aṅgavidhi*), by way of enjoining the substance, the deity, and the procedure, nevertheless, their status as auxiliaries to comprehension is not precluded.
For this very reason, they declare that these [mantras] serve as means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not as means for the attainment of the object of cognition (*prameya*).
For when only the words of an injunction (*vidhi*) are heard, the sacrificers do not pay heed to them;
in such a case, the injunctive suffix falters.
The conviction regarding the excellence of the ritual action, produced by the explanatory passage (arthavāda), supports that [action] as it were when it is sinking.

From the injunction “[One should sacrifice with the Sarvajit”], there does not arise such an excess of faith as that which arises from the words of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): “By means of the Sarvajit, indeed, the gods conquered all; for the attainment of all and the conquest of all, by this very [sacrifice] one conquers all. Even in the world, buyers do not proceed to purchase a cow with the same eagerness upon hearing “This cow is to be bought,” as they do from praises such as “This one has much thick milk, is beautiful, has offspring, and her progeny is faultless.
This matter is witnessed by one’s own experience.

For this very reason, some maintain that even in an injunctive statement (*vidhi-vākya*) where no explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is heard, one may postulate such a passage, just as in some cases an injunction is postulated from an explanatory passage.
As it has been said: "The operation of two equal [statements] is always held to occur when they share the same object.
Furthermore, an injunction is inferred from an explanatory passage whose connection with the injunction is not already known, and not from one whose connection is already known.
For this very reason, the formulation of injunctions such as "one should not weep" is accepted based on passages like "He wept.
The opponent's suspicion regarding that was entirely in vain;
for here, syntactic unity with another injunction is directly taught.

This passage beginning with "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*) is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the injunction "Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi rajataṃ na deyam*). It states: "Rudra wept;
that which was shed from his tear became silver.
For he who gives silver on the sacrificial grass will experience weeping in his house before the end of a year."
Therefore, [silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass].
The passage "Prajāpati extracted his own omentum" is a supplementary statement (śeṣa) to the injunction "One should sacrifice a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati.
It is stated—"As soon as the omentum was held over the fire, a hornless goat rose up"—for the purpose of demonstrating the greatness of the offering of the omentum.

In the remainder of this injunction, "The *prāyaṇīya* oblation is for Āditya," there is the statement: "The gods, having settled upon the sacrificial ground, did not know the directions. This indicates that the *āditya-caru* is the destroyer of delusions, just as it is the destroyer of confusion regarding the directions. In this manner, it should be understood that explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) function as supplements to various injunctions.

But how can it be said that this is indeed untrue—[that silver was born from Rudra’s weeping], [that a hornless goat emerged from the fire kindled by Prajāpati’s oblation]? It is replied: this is not untrue, for that which is to be established by this sentence has a truly real meaning. Nor is its meaning to be understood according to the literal sense; rather, some matter to be enjoined or prohibited is what is intended.
In this explanatory narration (*anvākhyāna*), two things occur: the knowledge of the event itself, and either an inducement toward or an aversion toward some matter.
In that regard, knowledge of the factual account (vṛttāntajñāna) is neither a motivator nor a deterrent; thus, due to the absence of a purpose, it is useless and not to be heeded.

Since attraction (prarocanā) and aversion (dveṣa) are auxiliary factors for engagement and withdrawal, one should grasp them as having that purpose: through attraction one would engage, and through aversion one would withdraw.
In this context, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is meaningful only insofar as its expressed content is true.

As for the objection: "If Rudra did not weep, how can there be a statement about his weeping? Or, if silver does not originate from weeping, how can it be designated as such?"—this is merely a figurative statement (guṇavāda). This figurative discourse is stated to censure silver by means of its similarity to the color white and so forth, [implying] that silver originates from weeping.

In this way, the narrative account—"Prajāpati extracted the omentum from his own body"—is to be applied for the purpose of praising the offering of the omentum (*vapā-homa*) in the animal sacrifice (*paśu-yāga*).
