For the sake of praising the *āditya-caru* [it is said]: "The gods, having settled upon the place of sacrifice, did not know the directions."
Alternatively, for the Naiyāyikas, who maintain that there are various kinds of superhuman excellence in persons, even in the case of a literal sense there is no absolute impossibility.

Let such things as the birth of silver from the weeping of Rudra, the cutting out of Prajāpati’s own omentum, the emergence of hornless cattle from its offering, and the confusion of the directions among the gods when they resolved upon the place of sacrifice, also be true; what is the harm? Therefore, in every respect, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are not non-authoritative.
Thus, the statement "the mind is a thief" and "speech is a liar" is figurative; the mind is called a thief because of its concealment,
and speech is called a liar with the intention of referring to its frequent occurrence.

"The smoke of the fire is seen by day, not its flame; the flame of the fire is seen at night, not its smoke"—this is stated with the intention of referring to their greater distance [from the observer] for some purpose, namely, for the sake of praising the deities of the evening and morning oblations.
"We do not know whether we are Brāhmaṇas or non-Brāhmaṇas"—this doubt is presented for the sake of praising the recitation of the *pravara* (ancestral lineage);
it implies that even a non-Brāhmaṇa sacrificer may become a Brāhmaṇa through the recitation of the *pravara*.
"The face of one who knows thus shines"—this is a praise of knowledge; "shines" means that his face is gazed upon with admiration by his disciples.
The phrase "he obtains all desires" refers to "all-ness" in relation to what has been previously mentioned;
and the statement regarding that fruit is for the purpose of praise concerning the study of the *Aśvamedha* chapter.

The prohibition of piling the fire-altar in heaven, in the intermediate space, and on earth is for the purpose of praise—namely, that "one should pile it after having placed gold"—and not because the fire-altar is absolutely not to be piled on earth; rather, it means that the fire-altar should not be piled on earth unless gold has been placed upon it.
In the statement "The sacrificial post is the sun," once it has been anointed, the sacrificial post is described as having the form of the sun due to its brilliance, for the purpose of praise.
Furthermore, because he performs that function, the sacrificer is called the *prastara* (the grass-bundle).
For in common worldly usage, words do not operate solely by their primary meaning; they are also seen to be employed through secondary (metaphorical) application.
In the same way, such usage will occur for them in the Veda as well.
And thus, even among mantras, the worship of the Gārhapatya fire with a verse addressed to Indra is not contradictory.
Thus, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) consisting of praise and censure are authoritative by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with an injunction;
those consisting of "deeds of others" (*parakṛti*) and "ancient accounts" (*purākalpa*) are likewise to be applied in the same manner.

In some cases, however, a certain portion [of the injunction] is completed by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) alone; thus, while that [passage] serves as a factor for comprehension, it also becomes a factor for the ritual action itself. For example, in the case of the injunction for the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice, where no specific qualification (*adhikāra*) is heard—namely, "Those who perform these *rātri* sacrifices certainly attain a firm foundation"—the element of qualification is obtained from the explanatory passage alone.

As it has been stated: "Ātreya [holds that] the fruit [is known] from the mention [in the explanatory passage]. For there, the meaning of the sentence—"Those desiring a firm foundation should perform the *satra* sacrifice"—is understood through the power of the explanatory passage.

In some cases, when there is doubt regarding the meaning of an injunctive statement (*vidhi-vākya*), its determination arises from a supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) consisting of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

For example, when it is uncertain what substance serves as the ointment in the injunction "He places down the smeared pebbles" (*aktāḥ śarkarā upadadhāti*)—due to the alternatives of ghee, oil, fat, and so forth—it is understood from the explanatory praise "Ghee is indeed brilliance" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*) that the pebbles to be placed are smeared with ghee.
Thus, because they share a single status with the injunction, these explanatory passages (arthavādas) possess authority in that same manner;
for they are connected with cognition, and in some cases, their connection with an action is observed.
Alternatively, even when they touch upon the intrinsic nature [of words], these followers of the path of validity do not abandon it;
for the Naiyāyikas, asserting the excellence of the person, declare that even the description of events here is in accordance with reality.
However, in cases such as the statements regarding the Āditya pillar, it is impossible to establish the literal accuracy of the primary sense in this manner;
yet, since their interpretation was composed by resorting to figurative usage (gauṇī vṛtti), there is no room for error even in those instances.
Now, the mantras are being examined: do they serve the purpose of the injunction by way of illuminating the meaning, or merely by their utterance?

[Objection: "But since there is no difference in their authority (*prāmāṇya*) regardless of which of the two views is correct, what is the use of investigating that? For this treatise has not been composed for the purpose of investigating the meaning of the Veda like the Mīmāṃsā, but rather solely for the determination of its authority. [Reply: True, this treatise has indeed been composed for the determination of authority. However, if the mantras were intended to have no meaning to be expressed, they would possess non-authority characterized by a lack of informative capacity (*apratipādakatva*).

By analogy, this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the Vedic and Brāhmaṇa sentences would likewise lack authority; thus, the Veda's status as a means for understanding ritual action (*karmāvabodha*) would be lost.
Moreover, invalidity does not consist solely in the production of doubt or error; rather, the production of ignorance is also indeed invalidity.

To this it is replied: Mantras assist merely through their utterance; why? Because of the instruction regarding their application, as in: "With the words *uta prathā uru prathasva*, he spreads out the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

If mantras assisted by illuminating the meaning, then since this mantra is useful for spreading by its very capacity, for what purpose would they be enjoined for the act of spreading by means of a verbal injunction? It is understood that if a man with eyes is led by another, he surely does not see with his own eyes.

And when [the Adhvaryu] says, "O Agnidh, distribute the fires," that officiating priest indeed performs the distribution of the fires; what need is there for the verbal statement? For in the case of a mantra that assists merely through its utterance, some kind of unseen (adṛṣṭa) assistance is postulated simply from its recitation.
Furthermore, we understand from the fixed order of the words that the mantras do not intend to convey a meaning;
for mantras are recited with a fixed sequence of words.
If they were to assist by conveying a meaning, then recourse to a fixed order would be useless, since the comprehension of that meaning could be achieved even through a different order.
Furthermore, the mantras do not have their literal meanings intended;
for some are seen to reveal things that do not exist, such as:
"Four are his horns, three are his feet, two are his heads, and seven are his hands."

"Bound in three ways, the bull bellows; the great god has entered into mortals"—for there exists no sacrificial implement whatsoever with four horns, three feet, two heads, and seven hands that is revealed by this [verse].
And for this reason it is so:
because an instigation directed toward an insentient object is demonstrated, as in [the mantra], "O herb, protect him!
For the herb does not perceive, "I am appointed for the purpose of protection."
"Listen, O pressing-stones," is an example;
for insentient pressing-stones cannot be enjoined to listen.
Moreover, the mantras declare what is contradictory: "Aditi is heaven; Aditi is the intermediate space.
How can she herself be heaven and that same thing be the intermediate space?
Furthermore, the meaning of certain mantras cannot even be understood;
how then could they assist by illuminating their meaning? For example: "O Indra, let thy spear be sharpened" (*abhyakṣāt indra ṛṣṭiḥ*);
"Like two sickles, O Jarbhari and Turpharī" (*sṛṇy eva jarbharī tur pharītu*).
And because of [the mantra] "Indra [drinks] the dregs of the Soma," the mantras therefore have meanings that are not intended to be expressed.

Moreover, the recitation of mantras must be performed in both ways—either for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) or for the sake of conveying meaning—since words that are not uttered are not capable of conveying even their meaning.

Since this recitation is necessarily to be performed, and since the assistance to the sacrifice is thereby accomplished, what is the purpose of adopting the mediation of the communication of meaning? To this it is replied: Is there no comprehension of meaning from the mantras at all; or does it occur even though without a cause; or, even if it has a cause, is it not intended to be significant, like the comprehension of the singularity of the cup?

It is not that there is no comprehension at all; for when one hears mantras such as "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods," which have been refined by the learning of the relationship between words and their meanings, the comprehension of their meaning occurs because it is self-evident.
Nor is this [Vedic usage] without a basis, because, as in the world, words themselves are the basis here.

Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no linguistic proficiency [regarding them], for those very words that are worldly are the same as the Vedic ones, and their meanings are the same; thus, proficiency in them is possible through worldly linguistic practice.
Nor does the comprehension of meaning arise even from mantras.
The singularity [of the cup] ought to be considered unintended, just like the cognition of the oneness of the *graha* itself, because there is no basis for such non-intentionality anywhere else.

This is because the number is already known from other statements regarding the cups; because the act of cleansing (*sammārga*), which is the purpose of pouring out the Soma, is common to all the cups; and because the case-ending in the word "cup" (*graham*) is justified even by merely imparting the status of the object (*karman*). Therefore, it is correct to say that the singularity is unintended.

In this case, however, because the manifestation of substances and other elements required for the sacrifice being performed—such as in the sentence "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods"—is required by the injunction, one performs the ritual action as remembered through the mantra.
Since the action thus performed becomes a cause of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), the manifestation of the sacrificial accessory (*yajñāṅga*) is not unintended;
therefore, mantras do not merely assist by their utterance alone.

In cases such as "one should mutter the *pāvamānī*" or "one should mutter the *vaiṣṇavī*," since the injunction itself implies that much alone, there is no need for the meaning to be revealed by the sense; therefore, what is done there? But in a case where the injunction "one should mutter" is not heard, it is not proper to disregard its meaning, which is both perceived and required.

Now, one might object: "If the injunction 'one should mutter' (japeta) is not intended to convey a meaning for the Vaiṣṇavī and other such mantras, then, because the injunction 'the Veda is to be studied' (svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ) prescribes merely the grasping of syllables, it would follow that the entire Veda has no intended meaning. This is not so. For the visible purpose of the injunction to study one's own Veda is the comprehension of ritual action (karma); thus, since it serves a visible purpose, its meaning is indeed intended. This has been determined in detail in another treatise. However, were it to be elaborated here, it would reveal our preoccupation with minor secondary discussions; therefore, we do not expand upon it.

As for the claim that the mantra lacks a literal meaning because its application to that purpose is taught by an injunction—since the application of the mantra to the act of spreading is already established by the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the words "O wide one, spread wide" (*uru prathā uru prathasva*), let the injunctive statement prescribing it be redundant at will, as it merely restates what is already obtained; however, it is not proper to discard the meaning perceived from the mantra itself. Is that statement then entirely useless? No, it is not useless; rather, it has as its object a meaning already understood.
Or that statement is for the purpose of an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda): "By that, he extends the lord of the sacrifice.
This means that when one spreads out the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) with this mantra, one thereby extends the lord of the sacrifice—the sacrificer himself—with offspring and cattle.

In some cases, however, there is an injunction for the sake of a quality (*guṇa*), as in: "He takes it up with four [verses]. The same should be understood in such instances as: "O Agnīdh, distribute the fires! and so forth.

As for the claim that mantras are useful merely for their utterance because their word-order is fixed, that too is incorrect; for the Mīmāṃsakas hold that the Veda is beginningless, and thus it is impossible for its sequence to be transgressed.
As it has been said: "And if there were a change in this [sequence], there would be a prevention of it by many."

For us as well, since the order [of the Veda] was ordained by God, what independence do students have in altering it? Therefore, the sequence of the mantras does not serve to express a specific intended meaning, just like the sequence of sentences in the Brāhmaṇas.

Furthermore, as for that statement regarding non-existent things—"He has four horns"—which was raised without suspicion, that too is due to ignorance; this is merely a praise of the sacrifice through figurative description (*guṇavāda*).

"Four are his horns"—the Vedas are thus declared; "three are his feet"—the *savanas* (pressings); "two are his heads"—the husband and wife as the sacrificers; "seven are his hands"—the meters (*chandāṃsi*); "bound in three ways"—bound by the *mantras*, *brāhmaṇas*, and *kalpas*; "the bull"—he rains down desires; "he bellows loudly"—because of the abundance of the application of *stotras* and *śastras*, he is making a great sound; "the great god has entered mortals"—meaning he is performed by human agents.

In this way, this sacrifice is praised, just as a river is praised as having breasts in the form of pairs of *cakravāka* birds, teeth and hair in the form of *haṃsas*, and garments in the form of *kāśa* grass.
The injunction addressed to the plant in the words "O herb, protect him! is for the purpose of praising it, as if it were sentient.
"Listen, O pressing-stones"—this is the praise of the Prātaranuvāka.
Indeed, this Prātaranuvāka is so praiseworthy that even the insentient pressing-stones might listen to it.
Because it is a figurative statement (guṇavāda) in the passage, "Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space," there is no contradiction;
just as in common worldly usage one might say, "You alone are my mother, you alone are my father, you alone are my sister, and you alone are my brother."
As for the claim that the meaning of certain mantras is not understood, that is a human failing and not a fault of the mantra.

Even though there are many means for comprehending the meaning, a person who is indolent in seeking them does not understand it; yet the mantra is not at fault here, because its meaning is seen to be understood through appropriate means, just as in the case of the sentences of the Brāhmaṇas.
And the primary means is indeed the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), since the words and their meanings are the same in both worldly and Vedic contexts.
Those very words which are worldly are the same as those which are Vedic, and their meanings are the same as well.

And although they read the word *agni* with the nasalization (*ṇatva*) as in the Vedic passage "May Agni destroy the obstacles" (*agnir vṛtrāṇi jaṅkṣanat*), and although a difference between worldly and Vedic words and their meanings might be suspected— as in the cases of "The divine cows indeed carry [the offerings] lying on their backs" (*uttānā vai devagavā vahanti*) and "O Lord of the Forest, golden-leaved, from of old your purpose"— nevertheless, having determined through recognition that it is those very same words that appear in the Veda with slight modification, the derivation of meaning remains purely worldly.
However, when there is a conflict with what is commonly established in the world, the consensus of those learned in the scriptures is taken as authoritative.

For example, in the injunctions "an oblation of barley," "boar-skin sandals," and "he collects the Prājāpatya offerings on a mat of vetasa reeds," the words *yava*, *varāha*, and *vetasa* are restricted by the consensus of the learned to mean long-awned grain (*dīrghaśūka*), boar (*sūkara*), and the *vañjula* reed, rather than *priyaṅgu* (panic seed), black bird (*kṛṣṇaśakuni*), and rose-apple tree (*jambū*).
But where there is no established usage among the *śiṣṭas*, even the usage of the *mlecchas* is relied upon for the derivation of that meaning,
as in the case of the words *pika*, *nema*, and *tāmarasa*.
Even in the absence of usage among the Mlecchas, the meaning must be determined from the verbal root by means of the Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyākaraṇa.

Thus, because of the context of the Āśvina hymn, it is understood that these two synonymous words ending in the dual number, *jarbharī* and *turpharītū*, which signify the acts of devouring and supporting, are designators of the Aśvins.
In this same manner, one should exercise creative interpretation in other cases as well.
Therefore, for this reason as well, one should not claim that the meaning of mantras is unintended.

Therefore, these mantras possess the status of being for the sake of action (*kriyārthatva*) solely by way of manifesting their meaning, and not merely through recitation like a *japa*. Consequently, this authority of the Veda—which is a treasure-trove of the nectar of all human goals—cannot be undermined even by that [charge of futility].
This is now examined:

it is heard in scripture, "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā*," "One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*," "One practicing sorcery should sacrifice with the *śyena*," and "One desiring sovereignty over one's own kingdom should sacrifice with the *vājapeya*.
In this regard, are these—namely, *udbhid*, *citrayā*, *agnihotra*, *śyena*, and *vājapeya*—injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*), or are they the names of those respective rites?
What is the purpose of this investigation? It is for this very reason that it is investigated: namely, that validity is not tenable in either case.

If, first of all, some accessory (*guṇa*) were enjoined by words such as *udbhid*—as in "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*) or "he offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*)—in the sense that "the sacrifice is to be performed with this particular substance," then the cognition of the verbal root's meaning (*bhāvārtha*), such as *yaj*, would have to be sought from another source; for it is impossible to enjoin an accessory when the meaning of the verbal root has not been previously understood. This is because the verbal root's meaning is enjoined there [in the injunctions] by other injunctions, such as "there is the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālo bhavati*) and "he performs the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*).

[Objection: But surely, by this very sentence, "One desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with the Vājapeya," the meaning consisting of the action called "sacrifice" will be enjoined, and the accessory called "Vājapeya" will be prescribed for that [action]. What is the fault? [Response: How is there no fault? Because there is the consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to the prescription of two meanings. One meaning would be: "One should effect self-sovereignty by means of the Vājapeya"; the second meaning would be: "One should effect the sacrifice by means of the accessory Vājapeya. And a sentence uttered only once is not capable of prescribing two meanings.

[Objection: Is it not the case that because of the formal similarity of the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice), it is connected to both [the result and the accessory], such that "[one desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice] by means of the Vājapeya"? For its form is identical in both cases. [Response: This is not so, because the formal similarity is unestablished. With respect to self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), the sacrifice (*yaji*) is enjoined because it has not been previously established; however, with respect to the accessory (*guṇa*), it is restated (*anūdyate*) because it is already established. Furthermore, since the injunction of an accessory is impossible when the action (*karman*) is not yet understood, in the view that this is an injunction of an accessory, the sacrifice—being already established with respect to the accessory—must necessarily be the object of reference (*uddeśya*) and the primary element (*pradhāna*).

Since that very [sacrifice] would have to be both subordinate to self-sovereignty (*svārājya*)—and thus something to be adopted—as a quality (*guṇa*), it would incur a contradiction of form; therefore, the sacrifice (*yajati*) cannot be connected to both simultaneously.
"One who desires to achieve self-sovereignty should sacrifice" is one form [of the injunction], while "that which one sacrifices, that should be with the Vājapeya" is another form.

Therefore, because the attainment of the meaning of the verbal root depends on another means of knowledge (the syntactical connection) under the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), that statement would lack authoritative force.
Now, if the position that these are names is adopted so that this fault may not arise, then the pointlessness of these words such as "udbhid" and the like becomes perfectly evident.
For exactly what is expressed by "one should sacrifice" is precisely the same as what is expressed by "one should sacrifice with the vājapeya.
Thus, because of this pointlessness, there can be no confidence in other instances either.
To this it is replied: regarding the position that [the term] is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), it is exactly as you have stated.
However, the position that it is a name (*nāmadheya*) is accepted as superior.

For, since the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the result, the instrumental case is employed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it.

In that context, since the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), while being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), undergoes the state of being an instrument (*karaṇa*)—namely, by means of the *vājapeya* sacrifice—the accusative case is also occasionally employed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it in view of its status as the object to be accomplished, as in the expression: "He performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*).

[Objection: Surely even a name based on a quality must indeed be prescribed, because it cannot be understood if it is not explicitly stated; and consequently, the defects such as syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) that touch upon the position of a prescription of a quality remain just as they were. [Reply: This is not so, for the Veda does not prescribe a relationship between a name and its bearer in the form "the name of this ritual action is to be known as this.
Rather, a name is understood precisely by means of some etymological derivation (*yoga*).
This is called the *udbhid* because by means of it, the breaking open (*udbheda*) of sacrificial animals is performed.
"Curd, honey, milk, ghee, rice grains, and water—these mixed together constitute the *prājāpatya* offering. It is called *citrā* because it is accomplished through various and diverse substances.
The *agnihotra* is so called because the oblation (*hotra*) is offered to Agni in this [rite].

"Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes its prey, so by this [sacrifice] one seizes one's hateful rival"—from such an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the sacrifice is called "hawk" (*śyena*) because it is like a hawk;
therefore, these are names of rituals.

As for the objection raised regarding the pointlessness [of the name] in the view that it is a name (*nāmadheya*), that too is not sound, because learned authorities have refuted it by stating that even a name is purposeful since it yields knowledge of qualities and results;
thus, it is understood that "this ritual has such-and-such a name.
In this context, the "quality" (*guṇa*) consists of the substance, deity, and so forth.
And its fruit is heaven, which is understood subsequently;
therefore, there is no contradiction in the syntactical connection of the words denoting names.

In some cases, however, when the meaning of the action has not yet been established, that action is enjoined precisely with its qualities (guṇas), such as: "The cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni is unerring on the new moon and the full moon days"; or, for example: "Having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman for this very [rite] during the Recatī verses, one desiring cattle should sacrifice with this. Enough, then, with this extensive discourse that is as dense as the belching forth of other weapons; thus, there is no challenge to its authority even by way of a name.
Thus, the status of the gods as authoritative is established in every respect.
These discussions have been conducted in this manner for the purpose of establishing the authority of the Vedas;
they are not based on the false assertions of the Mīmāṃsakas, the Cārvākas, or the Mādhyamikas.

But surely, since injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), mantras, and names are seen to be useful for action (kārya), it would follow that the Veda is authoritative only with respect to what is to be done. What follows from this? Its authority regarding established facts (siddha-artha) would be lost; and what of that? A vast mass of textual material expressing existing realities (bhūtārtha) would be disregarded. Furthermore, this treatise was undertaken precisely to establish the authority of the entire Veda.

On this point, some say that the entire Veda has authority only with respect to matters that are to be performed (*kārya*). For a word conveys its meaning only when its relationship [to that meaning] has been grasped, and the grasping of this relationship occurs through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).

Furthermore, the usage of elders proceeds only by means of words that communicate something to be done, such as "Bring water," "Tie up the cow," or "Go to the village. Thus, children acquire their linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) precisely in those cases.
For elders employ sentences with a specific purpose in mind;
and since that which brings about an already established object does not serve such a purpose, it lacks fitness for employment.
And for that which is not employed, there can be no apprehension of its relationship [to a meaning].
And that which has not had its relationship [with the object] grasped cannot be a communicator;
nor can that which is not a communicator [be so].
There is no validity.
Moreover, since a cognition free from expectancy does not arise without the utterance of a verb, a sentence must necessarily be employed as being joined with a verb.
And by the verbal element, an object in the form of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is expressed; whereas by the nominal element, an accomplished object (*siddha*) is expressed.

In the case of the utterance of both an accomplished fact (*bhūta*) and a thing to be accomplished (*bhavya*), the principle that "the accomplished is taught for the sake of the thing to be accomplished" means that the sentence culminates in the object to be established; thus, it possesses authority (*prāmāṇya*) regarding the object to be accomplished (*kārya*).

Consequently, the word has authority regarding a task to be done, because an object in the form of a task is the unique domain of the word, and therein the word attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). An already established object (*siddha-artha*), however, lacks such authority precisely because it is already well-known.

If [an object] were suitable for determination by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then in the communication of that [object], the word would be dependent upon that other means of valid cognition; consequently, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) in that case would belong only to that other means of valid cognition which grasps it, and not to the word.
And the word would be restricted merely to the presentation of that [object].
Therefore, one who desires the authority of words must accept that their authority pertains only to an object that is to be accomplished (*kārya*).
To this it is replied: what you say—that the linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) of a sentence pertains only to an object that is to be accomplished (*kārya*)—is incorrect.
For how could you state, "This is its meaning as an established entity (*siddharūpa*)"?
Indeed, the comprehension of a meaning from a word for which linguistic competency has not been acquired is not tenable.
It is indeed strange that while the apprehension of the object is observed from [such words], there is no linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) regarding them;

yet, worldly transaction does not proceed solely by means of words directed toward an effect, for transaction proceeds even from sentences describing the present, such as "The river [is here]," and proficiency certainly arises even in those cases.

Moreover, when someone points to an object situated in front with a finger or the like and says, "This has this name," then linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) indeed occurs even without an instruction regarding an action (*kāryopadeśa*).

If it is argued that this is in fact an instruction regarding an action—namely, "From this word, this meaning is to be understood"—we say no, because such syllables are not heard. For what is heard is "This has this name," and not "This is to be understood from this."

If it is argued that "this is the name of this" means that these very syllables have this meaning, it is not so; for it is impossible for the meaning of a sentence to be the meaning of word-meanings alone.

Nor can such a thing even be imagined, because the comprehension of that [meaning] is already established by the mere statement "this is the name of this," and thus the further expression of the necessity of performing that comprehension would be purposeless.

Even when linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) arises from words used in a functional context, it does not terminate merely in the sentence-meaning; rather, it extends as far as the word-meanings through the process of introducing and removing individual words.

Furthermore, for one whose mind is refined by proficiency in word-meanings, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is indeed observed even upon hearing a verse containing contemporary instruction composed by a modern poet; thus, there is no lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) caused by a failure to understand.

Nor is this cognition sublated or rendered doubtful by a class of words that expresses the actual state of affairs, such that it would have to be considered merely the fruit of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇaphala), like a cognition produced by other means of valid cognition such as direct perception.

Furthermore, as for what was stated— that a word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object that is to be accomplished (*kārya*) because it is independent of other means of valid cognition, but not so regarding an already existent object (*bhūtārtha*)— that is incorrect, because the dependence of a word upon other means of valid cognition does not cease. For we have already stated, and shall state again in the investigation of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), that a word is indeed unable to function unless the object is first understood through another means of valid cognition.
On the contrary, its dependence upon other means of valid cognition brings about its own validity rather than undermining it.
Furthermore, it must be stated what this "dependence" (sāpekṣatva) consists of:

does it mean that a word expressing an established fact is dependent on another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at the very moment of its own production, or does it mean that its object is capable of being determined by another means of knowledge? In either case, there is an over-extension of the argument (*atiprasaṅga*). If invalidity is attributed because of dependence on another means of knowledge at the time of its production, then alas, inference (*anumāna*) is destroyed, since it too is dependent on perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means at the time of its production.
And it has been stated that "inference is threefold and preceded by that" (perception).

However, if that [inference] were invalid because its object is incapable of being grasped by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it would follow that all [means], such as perception and the rest, are invalid, since the convergence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃplava*) was established previously.

Moreover, even in the case of Vedic or worldly sentences enjoined by an injunction—such as "Study!", "Bind the cow!", or "Go to the village"—since the accomplishment of activity is achieved through the understanding of the capacity of the means for attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful via positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the injunction rests solely upon the application (*viniyoga*).

Since an injunction would fail to establish the dependence on an action—due to the absence of its own independent operation characterized by instigating what has not yet occurred—it would be a mere restatement; thus, for those who maintain that the authority of scripture lies solely in its prescriptive meaning, every worldly sentence would be devoid of authority.

But those who postulate injunctions and prohibitions even in worldly statements that speak of existing facts and bring about engagement or withdrawal are exceedingly simple-minded. For where an injunction, though explicitly heard, becomes a mere restatement, they postulate one that was not even heard—what could be more naive than this? Furthermore, in such cases, an injunction is certainly not the motivator for engagement, because engagement among people in the world is established either through the understanding of the capacity to achieve a human goal via positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), or through personal conviction.
In this regard, it might be argued that because worldly sentences are intent upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), they do not have action as their purpose;
as it has been said: "Furthermore, from a human statement, there arises the cognition: 'This person knows it to be thus,' but not the cognition: 'The object is thus.
Vedic sentences, however, being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), are exclusively intent upon action. This too is not sound, because the notion of an authorless speech has already been refuted.
For even in the Veda, the existence of God as the creator has been established.
Furthermore, it has been shown that even human speech does not have the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) as its primary meaning.

For instance, intention is not the meaning of a sentence; in the collection of words "Devadatta, drive the cow, the black one, with a stick," the word for intention is not heard, and it is impossible for that which is not the meaning of a word to be the meaning of a sentence.

Moreover, unlike the case of a statement about eating poison, the power of *tātparya* (implicatory force) regarding the speaker’s intention cannot prevail in the case of human speech when it serves to preclude eating at another's house.
For the power of intentionality (tātparya-śakti) does not operate by entirely disregarding the denotative power (abhidhātrī śakti); thus, it does not have the speaker’s intention as its sole object.
If it is asked, "How then is the intention (vivakṣā) understood from the utterance of human speech? we reply: "By means of inference.
Because the arrangement of words is an effect, its being preceded by human intention is inferred.
And the inference of the speaker's intention from human speech is preceded by the comprehension of the meaning, in the form: "He knows this" and "He intends to say this."
For the mere intention of speaking, devoid of any coloring by an object, is established by its very nature among living beings.
However, an intention that is colored by an object—such as "this meaning is intended by him"—cannot be understood unless the object itself has been understood.
If the object is first understood from the sentence, then that [intention] cannot have the speaker's intention as its primary referent; rather, it must have the object itself as its primary referent.

If worldly sentences were intended solely for the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), then because it would be impossible to grasp the relationship [between word and object] with respect to an external referent, the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence could not arise even from the Veda; therefore, enough of this digression.
Therefore, the authority of a word does not consist solely in its being directed toward an action to be accomplished.
Furthermore, it was stated that a sentence lacking a verb is not fit for usage,
because without it, the absence of expectancy (nairākāṅkṣya) cannot be established;
and the meaning of a verb is of a future (bhavya) nature, unlike that of a noun, which is of a past (bhūta) nature.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "when there is the mention of both an accomplished entity (*bhūta*) and a thing to be accomplished (*bhavya*), the accomplished is taught for the sake of the thing to be accomplished," and thus everything everywhere has action as its ultimate purpose—that too is not tenable. For in common worldly usage, sentences that cause pleasure or pain, which do not enjoin activity or cessation, and which are not verbal roots (i.e., not *ākhyāta*), are employed with great frequency, such as: "A son is born to you" and "Your daughter is pregnant."

Furthermore, if one explains that the intent there is directed toward an action by saying, "Be happy" or "Be miserable," that too is not tenable; for such syllables are not heard [in the Veda], and any such assumption would be fruitless.

Indeed, one does not become happy merely from the instruction "Be happy," nor does one ever set out to become happy on that basis alone, because one has already previously engaged in the means [for achieving happiness].
Furthermore, activity toward the goal would be impossible;
rather, he becomes happy simply by hearing of the birth of a son.

Likewise, when someone is sleeping somewhere with his body covered by an upper garment, and someone playfully winds a rope around his body so that at the time of waking he suddenly thinks himself encircled by a serpent and does not open his eyes out of fear, the words "You are bound by a rope" uttered by someone else reach his ears; even though they inform him of what is already established, they constitute a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, there is no purpose for the conceptualization of the application "do not be afraid" in that case, because the cessation of fear is already established by the very cognition that it is a rope coiled up.
Likewise, one observes statements that convey a factual reality, such as "this path is infested with venomous serpents" or "this region of the earth contains a treasure"; yet these are not invalid.

Nor is it appropriate to claim that these words have the purpose of enjoining or prohibiting—such as "do not go by this path" or "take the treasure"—because such injunctive or prohibitive phrases are not heard in them.
Is it not the case that, because a speaker acts with deliberation and does not utter words devoid of purpose, the imperative syllables "Do not go" or "Take" must necessarily flash in his mind?

It is not correct to say that these were somehow not uttered due to laziness or the like; for precisely because the speaker acts with deliberation, it is only logical that he utters words that merely describe the nature of things as they exist, since activity and cessation are established through the force of the circumstances (*arthāt*), and because an instruction directed toward a specific [action] is untenable given that the intentions of others are unstable.
For one who lives by all manner of bonds, a path containing even serpents appears as something to be embraced;

yet for one who has transcended desire and knows Brahman, such as Lord Govinda—who has risen above the quest for wealth—even a treasure appears as something to be abandoned. Thus, what could possibly be taught to whom? When the true nature of reality is stated, let someone engage with it or withdraw from it according to the passion or aversion residing in their own heart. A wise person merely states the facts as they are; he ought not to employ injunctions or prohibitions.

Even those who assert that at the very beginning there must be an injunction regarding the necessity of comprehension—on the grounds that a sentence lacking an injunction is unfit for use—they too do not understand correctly; for when a person who knows the relationship between words and their meanings hears a word, comprehension is established by itself and thus cannot be an object of instruction. Or, if comprehension were not already established, from what source could even the necessity of comprehension be understood?

Now, one might argue that without a word expressing an action (*kārya*), other words do not even enter into a relationship with one another, because their connection is dependent upon the requirement for an action; therefore, it is said that in all cases, words have action as their primary purpose. This is not a fixed rule—that every relationship must be grounded in the requirement for an action—because we observe that sentences containing descriptions of the present (*vartamānāpadeśaka*) uttered by prudent persons generate an understanding of mutually related meanings. Indeed, sentences describing the present are not like the nonsensical utterance "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*).
For if the relation were based on the effect, there would be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) even for those things devoid of that [effect];
yet such a positive concomitance has been shown in the case of the sentences cited previously.
Moreover, even in a sentence joined with a word containing a verbal suffix (liṅ), the mutual connection between the meanings of the other words is indeed observed;
how will that be accounted for?

For one who asserts that all words are connected to the action (*kārya*)—on the basis of which the action is required—and not to each other, would have to say: "Once the connection with the action is first understood in every case, the mutual syntactic connection (*vākyīya parasparānvaya*) will subsequently be established, according to the principle of the red, one-year-old cow (*aruṇaikahāyanīnyāya*). Alas, in that case, the requirement for the action (*kāryākāṅkṣā*) is the cause of the mutual connection; therefore, in the sentence "He buys Soma with a red, tawny-eyed, one-year-old cow," since the substance and the quality are both joined to the purchase of Soma by virtue of their case-endings (*vibhakti*), it is understood that their primary connection is indeed with the purchase.

Furthermore, regarding that subsequent mutual coreferentiality (*parasparānvaya*), the case ending (*vibhakti*) which brings about dependence on the effect is not the cause; for even in its absence, coreferential usage—as in "a white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*)—establishes the connection.

Therefore, the rule that states that coreferentiality is based solely on the identity of the effect is born of mere conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*) and is not accessible through the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛttigamya*).

As for the claim that when there is a mention of both an accomplished entity (*bhūta*) and a thing to be accomplished (*bhavya*), the accomplished is taught for the sake of the thing to be accomplished—this too is not a universal rule, since the reverse is also observed in cases such as "one sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*).

Enough with this wretched example of the sprinkling of rice grains (*vrīhiprokṣaṇa*), which, by being situated within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), depends helplessly on the primary purpose of those rites. However, the injunction "the Self is to be known" (*ātmā jñātavyaḥ*) is indeed an instruction regarding an end already established;
for here no action to be accomplished as a primary goal is taught, since there is no mention of a specific qualification (*adhikāra*).
Nor is it possible to assume a qualification here, as one might do in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others.
And we shall explain that the knowledge of the self is not the cause for the engagement in action.
The explanatory passage (arthavāda), however, is merely an arthavāda; it is not capable of establishing a qualification for ritual action.

Therefore, in that context, the focus remains solely on abiding in the essential nature of the Self, which is endowed with qualities such as being free from evil (apahatapāpman). Once that is realized, since the wretchedness of seeking other persons is no longer possible, that alone constitutes the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha).
And that [liberation] is already established, not something to be accomplished;
however, they explain that the effort made by those of perfected intellect is solely for the sake of the cessation of ignorance.

If it is argued that this injunction is intended for the necessity of performing the practice, we say no; for practice is a form of valid cognition (*pramiti*), and valid cognition is necessarily directed toward its object (*prameya*). Furthermore, the suffix *kṛtya* in the word "to be known" (*jñātavya*) is prescribed in the sense of the object (*karman*).

And because the object of action (*karman*) is that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*), it is understood that the person is intent upon that very thing. Even if an injunction (*vidhi*) were to extend there, where could it exert its force? For the fruit (*phala*) is not at all the domain of the injunction.
As Bhaṭṭa has said: "Regarding the factor of the fruit, the suffix is not injunctive of the productive energy (*bhāvanā*)."
But the means is indeed knowledge;
and it has been stated that knowledge is grounded in the object of knowledge.

Furthermore, that instruction regarding the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*)—consisting of the observances (*yama*), restraints (*niyama*), and so forth—is also established as proven, for it is employed therein for the sake of attaining the nature of the Self by means of dissolving the manifold expansion (*prapañca*) of names and forms, which are of both real and unreal natures.

Or let it be granted that the injunctions regarding the procedures for self-knowledge—such as the observances (*niyama*), restraints (*aniyama*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*)—as well as other injunctions like those for the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, are all ultimately directed toward that [Self]. This is the position of the Vedāntins:

because everything to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is perishable and thus not worth pursuing, whereas the already established Brahman alone—which is beyond beginningless ignorance and imperishable—is the true human goal; and because, by means of gradually dissolving the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), these injunctions render one fit for the highest qualification, they are indeed the means for attaining Brahman.

And so Manu says: "By the study of one's own Veda, by vows, by oblations, by the knowledge of the three Vedas, by sacrifices, by sons, and by the great sacrifices and other rites, this body is made fit for Brahman."
Thus [it is said].
Thus, they say that the Veda possesses the status of a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) precisely with respect to an already established goal;
for all injunctions culminate in the attainment of Brahman.

Let this subject rest, for much could be said; however, the status of speech as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is indeed equal [to that of inference] when the object is something to be accomplished (kārya), because the resulting cognition (pramiti) is identical in both cases.

What kind of dependence exists between these two? This debate is of no great use to us for a long time, for we have undertaken our efforts solely to establish the authority of the Veda by adopting a stance of contentment.
Whatever was necessary to be said here regarding the application of the means for establishing validity has been stated according to its utility.
We shall now state something else that ought to be said; let it be heard, provided that your minds are not weary.
Salutation to Him who has taken refuge [in the Lord], who brings relief to those who have lost their way, and whose very nature is bliss for those who suffer.
Salutations to the kinsman of the cause, who fulfills the firm hopes of those who possess them.
Now, as for the claim that words do not touch upon their objects because a real referent corresponding to the word does not exist—that is being refuted.
Sound is of two kinds: the word (*pada*) and the sentence (*vākya*).
Since the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the meaning of its constituent words, the meaning of the word is first indicated and then examined.
A word (*pada*) is said to be of two kinds: noun (*nāman*) and verb (*ākhyāta*).
It is taught that prepositions (*upasarga*), particles (*nipāta*), and adverbial prefixes (*karmapravacanīya*) are also included within nouns themselves.
Thus it has been stated: "A word is that which ends in a nominal suffix (*su*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*)."
In this context as well, the author of the Sūtras says: "Those [elements] ending in an inflection (*vibhakti*) are a word (*pada*).

Among these, the investigation into the meaning of words ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) will be undertaken precisely at the occasion of the analysis of the meaning of sentences (*vākyārtha*), because it is useful for that purpose.
However, the meaning of those ending in nominal suffixes (*subanta*) is now being stated.

And these words, which consist of nominal stems ending in case-terminations, are of four kinds: genus-words (jātiśabda), action-words (kriyāśabda), quality-words (guṇaśabda), and substance-words (dravyaśabda).

In this regard, the meaning of genus-words such as "cow" and so forth is merely the individual (vyakti) as delimited by the genus such as "cowness" (gotva), which is proclaimed in the house of the Naiyāyikas as "that which possesses it."

Now, one might object: since a substance (*dravya*) is the substratum of qualities such as whiteness and the locus of action, while an individual (*vyakti*) consists of the configuration of parts such as the dewlap, and a class (*jāti*) is the form common to all cow-individuals such as Śābaleya, how can this word "cow" (*go*), when uttered in the presence of these three—individual, configuration, and class—set aside the others and take on the status of denoting only that which possesses them? To this he says: "Indeed, this extensive discussion shall be examined first."

But let this be considered: since the universal (*jāti*) itself transcends the means of valid cognition and is therefore non-existent—like the horn of a hare—how can there be a thing that possesses it? As it has been said: "First of all, sensory cognition cannot be capable of apprehending a universal, because its function is exhausted solely in the determination of the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is not connected with what precedes or follows."
The very nature of a universal is its uniform occurrence;
how can sense-born cognition, which is independent, touch that which is dependent [on other factors]?

When similar things have been perceived, the universal is grasped by attending to the common form of their mode of being; thus, the apprehension of its own nature is dependent [on prior perception]. Now, how could this cognition—which arises from the initial contact of the sense organ with the object and is devoid of any synthesis between preceding and succeeding moments—be independent and capable of grasping that [universal]? Furthermore, the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that follow upon it are by their very nature devoid of skill in touching the actual reality. Therefore, even though the universal is made an object by them, it cannot possess ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*).

Furthermore, neither inference nor verbal testimony possesses the capacity to establish the reality of the nature of the universal (*sāmānya*), because words and logical marks (*liṅga*) have conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as their object and thus cannot grasp real entities.
However, the conventional usage regarding the attainment of such [universals] will be demonstrated by another method.
And for this reason, the universal is not perceived as distinct from the individual;

for instance, when a water-lily, an *āmalaka* fruit, a *bilva* fruit, and so forth, are held in the palm of the hand, they are observed separately, but the genus and the individual are not [so observed]; therefore, there is no distinction between the two.
Furthermore, because their spatial distinction is not perceived:

for indeed, when one thing is distinct from another, it is determined to occupy a location separate from the location occupied by that other, as a cloth is distinct from a jar; but such is not the case with the universal and the individual, and thus there is no difference between them.
And for this reason, when that [particular] is not apprehended, there is an absence of the cognition of it;
for whatever is distinct from something else is apprehended even when that [other thing] is not apprehended, as a cloth is [apprehended] from a jar.
And yet, when the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) is not perceived, the universal (*jāti*) is not perceived.
Therefore, it is not distinct from that.
If it is argued that because the universal resides in those [individuals], it is not perceived when they are not perceived, we say no, because its mode of subsistence is untenable.
Does the genus subsist in each individual in its entirety, or by way of parts?
Both alternatives are untenable.
If a universal were to reside entirely within a single individual,
then because it would be fully exhausted therein, it could not be apprehended in another individual.

If, however, it were to exist only partially, the universal "cowness" would not be present in its entirety anywhere; how then could the cognition of a "cow" arise with respect to every individual object?
Furthermore, because a genus (*jāti*) is partless, there are no parts by which it could reside in each individual (*piṇḍa*).

Nor can it, having been fully present in one individual, reside again in another individual by way of being fully present; for a thing that has already reached its full extent cannot have another instance of full presence without a new production.
Moreover, such a mode of subsistence is never observed anywhere.

Furthermore, we do not understand that mode of existence of the universal (*sāmānya*) within individuals (*piṇḍa*) which is described by the followers of Ulūka (the Vaiśeṣikas) as being of the nature of inherence (*samavāya*).

As for what they say—"Inherence is that relation between inseparable entities (*ayutasiddha*) standing in the relationship of the supported and the supporter which is the cause of the cognition 'it is here'"—that is a contradiction.
How could "inseparability" and "relation" be compatible? For two things established separately, such as a bowl and a jujube fruit, or a man and a woman, are related to one another.
But if they were not established as separate, then because of their identity, what could be related to what? For I am not related to myself.

If it is argued that a relation indeed exists even between substance and quality despite their being inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*), this is merely the description of a madman by another madman; for even the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) is not perceived as distinct from the qualities themselves.
It is truly strange that [the opponent] does not demonstrate the self of the possessor of qualities as something other than color and so forth, yet still desires its distinction from them.

Furthermore, as for the technical definition (*paribhāṣaṇa*) made in your own treatise regarding "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*) through the distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal: [it states that] for eternal atoms, separate establishment is the possession of distinct motion; for non-eternal things, however, it is the state of being inherent in a common substratum (*yutāśrayasamavāyitva*). [And it claims that] for all-pervading entities such as space (*ākāśa*), there is no mutual relationship at all. But even that is merely a conventional procedure (*prakriyāmātra*); for "separate establishment" is said to mean establishment as distinct entities (*nānātvena siddhiḥ*), or its accomplishment (*niṣpatti*), or its cognition (*jñapti*).
From the opposite of that, there is inseparability (*ayutasiddhi*), which is established as being one;
and such being the case, a relationship is difficult to explain.
2.08a.07 The relation consisting of inherence (*samavāya*) between a part and a whole must also be refuted in exactly this same manner.
2.08a.08 As Bhaṭṭa has said: 2.08a.09 "There is no relation for that which is not yet produced; when it is produced, there is the state of being established separately (*yutasiddhatā*). //

A relationship between an atom and space, or between an atom and time, is accepted, but not a mutual relationship between space and time; thus, this is merely a conventional procedure, so enough with this intermediate deliberation.
Therefore, no mode of subsistence whatsoever is logically possible between a universal and an individual.

2.08a.13 However, those who are well-trained explain that "form" (rūpa) is the characteristic of both the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), as well as their relationship. 2.08a.14 That too is not tenable.

Is the word "form" (*rūpa-śabda*) a term for white and so forth, or a term for shape (*ākāra*), 2.08a.15 or a term for intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? 2.08b.01 If it were a term like "white" and so forth, then substances such as wind and mind, which are devoid of form, as well as qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), 2.08b.02 would be devoid of generality (*sāmānya*).
Even if they are said to possess form, those very qualities and so forth, being devoid of any arrangement of parts, do not attain the state of possessing a universal (sāmānyavattā).
But if it were a statement of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there would be no distinction at all between the genus (*jāti*) and that which possesses the genus (*jātimat*).
For the nature of a thing does not appear as distinct from that which possesses that nature;
this [distinction] is merely verbal, not ontological.

2.08b.08 Furthermore, what is this so-called "form"? Is it a property of a real entity by virtue of being a real entity itself, or is it a distinct entity? 2.08b.09 It has already been stated that, for now, it does not appear as a distinct entity.
Even if it were a property of the thing itself, it would not manifest as existing apart from that [thing];
and it has already been stated that if there is no such separation, the linguistic expression of a "relation" is untenable.

2.08b.12 Nor is there any relation characterized by "form" and "the state of being formed" that is distinct from conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*). 2.08b.13 It cannot be analyzed and explained as "being such-and-such" by those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). Therefore, the logical argument (*yukti*) must be stated.
2.08b.14 Only something new has been presented here; no actual meaning is being imagined. Thus, enough of this digression.
Furthermore, this "universal" (jāti) must either be omnipresent in all things or omnipresent only in its own substratum.
If it were omnipresent in all things, then the cognition "this is a cow" would arise even with respect to a white horse and the like.
The cognition of "horse" would apply to a brindled cow and the like, while the cognition of "camel" would apply to a goat and the like;
in this way, a total confusion of categories would result.
2.08c.03 Furthermore, even if it is argued that this confusion does not occur because of the restriction of the capacity of the individual instances (*vyakti*),
2.08c.04 for individual instances such as a white horse (*karka*) do not possess the skill to manifest [the universal] "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth.
2.08c.05–06: Let it not be so; for even though the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is manifested through individual cows such as Khaṇḍā, it remains partless.
[If it were otherwise], it would either be perceived only in those specific locations, or it would not be omnipresent.
In the case of censuring that location, there is indeed nothing that restricts it;
for the body is a manifestor like a lamp, but it does not reside within that body.
And what logic is there in saying that it exists everywhere even though it is not perceived anywhere? Therefore, it is not tenable for "cowness" to be omnipresent in everything.
2.08c.11 But if [the universal] were present in its entirety in each individual, this might indeed not be a fault;
2.08c.12 however, there would be no cognition of "cow" in a cow born today.
Birth does not exist when the body has not yet arisen, nor does it exist once it has arisen;
it does not migrate from one body to another, for it is devoid of action.
Even as it arrives, it does not cast off its former mass;
nor does it exist there by means of parts—such is the miserable succession of calamities.
The followers of Bhaṭṭa, however, assert that a single entity is both different and non-different, and is both inclusive and exclusive.
That form of it which is inclusive is the universal (*sāmānya*), and that which is exclusive is the particular (*viśeṣa*).
For thus [it is said]: "In all things, cognition consists of both exclusion and inclusion."
It arises as having a dual nature, and without that, it is not established.

2.08d.06. On the view that the category [of substance] consists solely of particulars (*viśeṣa*), the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) would be without an objective basis (*anālambana*). 2.08d.07. Furthermore, on the doctrine of the universal alone (*sāmānyamātra-vāda*), the cognition of a particular (*viśeṣa-buddhi*) would be untenable.
2.08d.08 [Nor is it accepted that one or the other is an error by way of metaphorical designation;
2.08d.09 for those who maintain that there is error, because cognition is always firm, it would have to be an error.]

For, unlike the non-perception of water when there is a mass of rays from the sun, the cognition of the particular does not arise by subverting the cognition of the universal, nor does the cognition of the universal arise by subverting the cognition of the particular; rather, both appear simultaneously without contradiction.
For this very reason, it is accepted that even by means of non-conceptual cognition, an entity is grasped as possessing a dual nature.
This very point, as it is being stated, does not appear at all pleasing:
by yourself asserting that multiplicity of forms is not contradictory for a single entity,
you have merely exposed our own fault while attempting to refute us.

"That very thing is the universal, that very thing is the particular; that very thing is one, that very thing is manifold; that very thing is eternal, that very thing is non-eternal; that very thing exists, that very thing does not exist"—this which is called the "remnant of the Jainas" (jainocchiṣṭa), even when stated, is not elegant. If it is argued that there is no contradiction because it is observed [in experience], that is not so, because it is not perceived as such. For it has been said: "Visual cognition does not apprehend an object that persists [through change]."
Those whose intellects are utterly deluded by the continuity of various conceptual constructions think thus:
"Let it be so";
however, a single entity cannot possibly possess multiple forms.
For one form belongs to the actual object, while the other is a mental construction; it is not fitting for the wise to place trust in conceptualizations that follow after recurring appearances.

For the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is perceived immediately through contact with other [objects] without dependence; therefore, the distinction is real, while the universal concomitance (anugama) is false.
The firmness or lack of firmness of cognitions remains unimpaired even without investigation;
to accept a duality merely because of the appearance of two things is an error.
The falsity of cognitions does not arise from the mere notion that "it is not so" alone;
rather, those who perceive with subtlety must also conduct an investigation through reasoning.
Nor is a single variegated object the domain of non-conceptual cognition;
for without the synthesis of other individuals, how could there be a cognition of a universal?
For when those [particulars] in which [a universal] inheres are not being synthesized by the intellect, it is impossible to grasp the commonality residing therein;
nor does the intellect possess the capacity for such synthesis.
For this very reason, they do not correctly understand knowledge born of direct perception;
out of a desire for non-duality, they have asserted that perception functions as non-distinction.
Therefore, since perception does not have difference as its object, the universal is not cognizable by it.
But if the universal is thus denied, how will this recurring cognition, "cow, cow," with respect to the *śābaleya* and other individuals be accounted for? To this it has been said:
this cognition is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and conceptual constructions do not arise dependent upon external objects.
And so, even regarding universals such as "existence" (*sattā*) imagined by others, recurring conceptual constructions such as "universal" certainly do occur.
Furthermore, other universals cannot exist within universals, because it is accepted that universals are themselves devoid of further universals.

If it is argued that this recurring conceptual construction regarding universals is merely conditional (*aupādhika*), then, O long-lived one, even in the case of cows and the like, there will be a continuous conceptual construction such as "cow, cow" based on some specific condition (*upādhi*).
If it is asked, "What, then, is this limiting condition (upādhi)? we reply: it is the capacity to perform a single purposeful action (ekārthakriyākāritva).
Whatever function, such as carrying or milking, is produced by one individual cow, that same function is produced by others; thus, there arises a continuous, recurring cognition with respect to them.
Is it not the case that the effect is indeed distinct for each individual instance? True; however, because there is no cognition of difference, it is metaphorically treated as one.

For just as the difference of this [whole] from the effects of its parts, such as the hoof and so forth, is perceived, the difference of the effect of a broken pot from the effect of a shaven head is not seen in that same way.
But let it not be so;
however, the effect of the two halves is certainly not non-different.
Quite right.
In that case, their perception will be one and the same, and that [perception] will be non-differentiated.
But surely even perception is different for each individual object? True; however, it is called "one" because of its effect, namely the subsequent reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).

Just as when there is the perception of an individual such as a brindled cow (*śābaleya*), there immediately follows the reflective awareness "cow," and likewise when there is the perception of an individual such as a black cow (*bāhuleya*), there is the very same reflective awareness "cow"—it is on this basis that their unity is asserted.
Thus it has been said: "Because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness, cognition is non-different;
and by virtue of being the cause of that single cognition, individual manifestations are also non-different."

Therefore, because the recurring cognition is conditional (*aupādhika*), there is no such thing as a real universal (*sāmānya*). To this, he replies: "If a universal is not admitted, how then can there be the operation of words and inference, which arise dependent upon the grasping of a relation?"
For it is not possible here to grasp the relationship within individual instances; for that [relationship] would have to be grasped either in all individuals or in some single one.
It is not [applicable] to all [instances], because due to differences in place, time, and so forth, it would be impossible [to apply it] owing to their infinity;
nor is it [applicable] to a single [instance], because of deviation. Therefore, that word is seen to function even elsewhere.
Furthermore, when the relationship [between word and object] has not been apprehended, neither the word nor the logical mark (liṅga) is capable of producing cognition.
It is replied: this would indeed be so if the operation of the word and the logical mark were directed toward every single moment within the objective domain of perception.

[Objection: "But if their operation upon an object of perception is not admitted, then due to the affliction of defects such as infinite regress, there would be no operation at all. [Reply: Do not speak thus! How is it that you do not understand, even though it has been stated repeatedly, that the operation of verbal testimony and inference is held to be upon conceptual constructions (vikalpa)?
And it has been described that these conceptual constructions have non-entities as their objects."

[Objection: But if no recurring object is admitted even for conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), then verbal testimony and inference would surely perish. [Reply: Certainly, there is an underlying object for conceptual constructions, but it is not real.

If one asks what this is, it is said: "Conceptual certainties take as their objective support a universal that is by nature the exclusion of what is other than itself (*atadrūpaparāvṛtti*), which is not external but appears as if it were external."
And that which is the domain of conceptual constructions is precisely the domain of words;
for this very reason, they declare the meaning of a word to be the exclusion of others (anyāpoha).
For indeed, conceptual constructions do not touch the real object.

Why? [Since the single nature of the object exists as something directly perceived by itself, what other unperceived part could there be that would need to be examined by means of valid cognitions? Therefore, their activity is for the purpose of negating other forms superimposed by the causes of error.

Just as another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates upon mother-of-pearl to remove the form of silver superimposed due to its similarity in appearance—saying "there is no silver here"—so too in this case, when the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) such as a brindled cow has been apprehended in its entirety by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), conceptual cognitions (*vikalpāḥ*) exclude a form other than that of a cow which has been superimposed for some reason, saying "this is not a non-cow. However, their operation does not concern the particular of the cow itself, because it has already been grasped previously.

Now, if it should be argued that some previously ungrasped qualifier of that object—whose form is variegated by a multitude of various qualifiers—is grasped by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), that too is untenable. For even in the case of an entity adorned by a multitude of various qualifiers, no nature is perceived apart from the capacity of those qualifiers to assist the object. Since there is no difference [between the entity and its qualifiers], at the very moment the nature of the object assisted by those qualifiers is grasped, the grasping of them as inlaid within it is established; thus, other conceptual constructions would be entirely purposeless.
As it has been said: "Even for one who holds that the cognition grasps an object possessing various distinct attributes..."
Even for that [cognition], the capacity assumed through various limiting conditions does not indeed exceed [the nature of cognition itself].
"When the self, which is non-different from the capacities that are the constituent parts of the assistance provided by various limiting adjuncts,
is perceived, what distinction could there be regarding the assisted object that remains undetermined in its entirety?"
Therefore, words and conceptual constructions have exclusion (apoha) as their object.
Now, it may be objected that the Bhaṭṭa has unleashed a great shower of refutations against the doctrine of Apoha;
for indeed, what is called Apoha is intended as an exclusion, which is a non-entity (abhāva).
And a non-entity is not apprehended as something independent in the manner of a jar.
Therefore, it must be stated that this [non-existence] depends on something else;
and what its substratum is must be considered.
First of all, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the cow is not the substratum, because it does not belong to the domain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Nor is the intermediate generality (*avāntarasāmānya*), such as "being a *śābaleya*," the substratum; for that too, by virtue of its nature as a generality, has exclusion (*apoha*) as its essence, and it is impossible for a non-existence to have a non-existence as its substratum.

Furthermore, the universal "Śābaleya" is not the locus of the exclusion of non-cows; rather, it serves as the locus for the exclusion of non-Śābaleyas. For it is not tenable to say, "A cow is not a non-Śābaleya," but rather, "A Śābaleya is not a non-Śābaleya.
Indeed, the exclusion of non-Śābaleyas exists even in cows such as the Bāhuleya and others.

Now, if they were to say that the collection (*samudāya*) of individual particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*), such as the brindled cow and others, is the locus of the exclusion of non-cows (*agovyāvṛtti*), that too is untenable, because that collection is not perceived apart from its constituent members.

Furthermore, since the individual particulars that constitute the collection are infinite due to differences in space, time, and so forth, it would be impossible to group them together even in a hundred lifetimes; thus, the collection also cannot be their locus.
Therefore, some entirely new entity must be asserted as the substratum for the exclusion of non-cows, which is common to all [cows] and fully present in each individual object.

And that [exclusion] is simply "cowness" itself; once that is accepted, what is the use of the laborious effort of postulating an exclusion of non-cows? Furthermore, it is not only because of the absence of a substratum that such an exclusion cannot be apprehended; rather, even if those various things to be excluded—the horse and so forth which constitute the form of the non-cow—were themselves apprehended, their exclusion would still be difficult to grasp.
Nor is their apprehension possible because they are infinite in number.
Furthermore, there exists no common characteristic among them that could serve as a basis for their classification.

Furthermore, in your view, horses and the like are not apprehended as positive entities, but rather solely through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). Thus, since their apprehension would likewise involve the grasping of an exclusion, the same situation persists; consequently, it is impossible for conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) to ever take *apoha* as their object.
And since no worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is possible without conceptual cognition, there follows the undesirable consequence that all practical activity would be utterly destroyed.
Furthermore, all these words such as "Śābaleya" and so forth would be synonyms, since they are indistinguishable in their denotation of an exclusion (apoha).
If it is argued that this fault does not apply because the excluded objects (apohya) are different, we say no; for there is no difference among exclusions themselves.
Or, if they were indeed differentiated, it would follow that they are real entities (vastu), just like particular characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).

If it is argued that even in your position there is the same fault of synonymy, since there is no difference in the fact that they denote only universals (*sāmānya*), we reply: no, because universals are positive in nature and are understood to be manifold due to their essential nature of being mutually exclusive;
however, exclusion (*apoha*) does not differ from one another, as it is indistinguishable in its nature as mere negation (*abhāvamātra*).

If it is argued that the exclusion (*apoha*) differs according to the difference in its substrata, such as the white cow (*śābaleya*) and others like the black cow (*karka*), we say no; for their status as substrata has already been refuted.
Alternatively, if one accepts that the exclusion differs due to the difference in its substrata, it would follow that there is a distinct exclusion for every particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Consequently, its nature as a universal (*sāmānya*) would be lost.
