Now, if it is argued that synonymy is refuted by determining the difference between the objects to be excluded (*apohya*), that too is worthless; for even then, the difference [of the words] due to the difference of the objects excluded does not remove their synonymy, since that [difference] is merely figurative and not primary.

Nor can a distinction in the exclusion (*apoha*) itself be conceived on the basis of a distinction among the things to be excluded (*apohya*). For how can that which cannot be differentiated even by its substrates—despite their potential for contact—be divided by external things to be excluded that are far removed and lack any connection? Even granting this for the sake of argument, we say: if the difference of the exclusion follows from the difference of the things to be excluded, then it must also follow from their unity.

Consequently, when a cow and a horse are established through the exclusion of others, the things to be excluded—non-cows and non-horses, such as elephants and so forth—are equal and numerous in both cases.
However, the unique [exclusion] is one: a cow is distinguished from a non-cow, and a horse from a non-horse.

In this regard, one might consider whether there should be a difference between cow and horse due to the difference in their respective excluded objects (*apohya*), or whether there should be no difference because of the non-difference among the many excluded objects; in such an inquiry, according to the principle that "when there is a concurrence of contradictory properties, the majority shall possess the common character," non-difference alone would be the logical conclusion.

Now, if it is maintained that the exclusion of the non-cow (*go-apoha*) is nothing other than the exclusion of the horse (*aśva-apoha*) due to their non-commonality, then since that [exclusion] also exists in lions and so forth, a lion would now also have to be a cow.

Now, if that which is to be excluded—the non-cow-form—is said to be devoid of any specific designation such as "horse" and so forth, it is impossible to apprehend each instance individually because of their infinity.
Furthermore, there is no basis whatsoever for their categorization;
for indeed, all non-cows, such as horses and the like, do not possess a common location or a common time.

Now, if the negation of the non-cow (*agopratibedha*) alone is intended as the basis for the classification [of cows], then, alas, the cow must be accepted as already established prior [to that negation], since it is by the negation of which the non-cows would be understood. But once the cow is already established, what is the purpose of non-cows or of their exclusion (*apoha*)? If it is argued that the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the cow is indeed already established, we say no, because there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) based upon that. However, if the universal cow (*gosāmānya*) is already established, then the effort toward exclusion is futile; this has already been stated.

Now, if the universal "cow" is established through the negation of the non-cow, then there arises an insurmountable circularity: the establishment of the cow depends on the negation of the non-cow, and the establishment of the negation of the non-cow depends on the establishment of the cow.
Therefore, since the object to be excluded (apohya) itself cannot be defined, the differentiation of the exclusion (apoha) based on the differentiation of that object is not established.

Furthermore, would horses and so forth be excluded by way of their universal form or by way of their specific individual natures? Not by way of their specific natures, because those are infinite and because they are not denotable by words.
But since even those [particulars], by virtue of their universal nature, consist of exclusion (*apoha*), they are of the nature of non-existence.

And how can there be the negation of non-existence itself? Or, if such a negation were made, because of the application of a double negation, an affirmation would result; thus, the meaning of a word would be of the nature of a positive entity (*vidhi*).

Furthermore, regarding a horse or the like, which consists of exclusion (*apoha*), its exclusion must either be distinct from it or not; if it were distinct, it would follow that it has the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*).
If, however, it were not distinct, then the exclusion would be exactly the same as that which is excluded (*apohya*); consequently, even a cow would be a non-cow.

Furthermore, on the view that the meaning of a word is *apoha*, linguistic conventions such as the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—as in the expression "blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*)—would be lost.
For it is not possible for two *apohas* to reside in a single object;
nor is there any object whatsoever in which they could reside, because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the referent of a word, and no other [real] object exists.
Nor is there even any mode of existence whatsoever.
Because it is impossible to determine what is to be excluded (*apohya*) for words such as "existent" (*sat*) and "knowable" (*jñeya*), they do not have exclusion (*apoha*) as their denotation.
For nothing that is non-existent (*asat*) or unknowable (*ajñeya*) is apprehended such that it could be excluded;
if it is apprehended, then it is existent, and if it is known, then it is knowable.
Therefore, how could the word "existent" exclude only the existent, and the word "knowable" exclude only the knowable?
That which is unknown is certainly not to be excluded;
moreover, that which is imagined cannot be spoken of [in this way], because it exists and is knowable only through imagination.
It must be considered what is denoted by the word *apoha*.
[The etymology is: it is an *apoha* because it is not a non-*apoha* (*anapoha*).
But what is this non-*apoha*, or how does it not exist? Or, if it does not exist, what remains? Thus, everything [in this definition] is non-denotative.

And what is the status of words such as *nañ* and others which express negation? In this context, what is the meaning of "it is not" or "no"? Furthermore, how could prefixes (*upasarga*) and particles (*nipāta*) have exclusion (*apoha*) as their object? Moreover, it is difficult to establish the exclusion of verbal expressions (*ākhyāta-śabda*) such as "he cooks" (*pacati*).

If you say that it is only those class-words (*jātiśabda*) whose status as denoters of a class or as denoters of a possessor of a class you accept that are intended to have exclusion (*apoha*) as their object, then what is the status of other words? If they denote external objects, why this hatred toward class-words? If [all words] lack an objective basis and instead rely on a portion of cognition, let that be the case for class-words as well; why this delusion regarding the doctrine of exclusion? Just as the meaning of a sentence is postulated to be mere mental intuition (*pratibhā*), let it be the same for the word-meaning; why do you persist in grasping at exclusion?
Such extensive refutations of apoha have been demonstrated at length;
therefore, how could the Buddhists claim that this [apoha] is the meaning of words?
It is said that this is the statement of those who have not understood the Buddhist tenets.
If exclusion (*apoha*) were accepted as having the nature of a real entity (*bhāva*) existing externally, then your web of arguments regarding entities would apply; however, it is not so.
But indeed, this internal essence of cognition, which is the *apoha* accepted by the followers of Sugata, is what is meant.

And if this were accepted, it would be appropriate to say only this much: that this verbal formulation regarding exclusion (apoha) concerns the objects of knowledge of things within their own respective parts.
This too does not exist; this exclusion (apoha) is neither internal nor external, but rather something entirely distinct from both cognition and the object.
But surely, how can that which does not exist either internally or externally from the perspective of ultimate reality be said to be the referent of a word, since it simply does not exist?
Thirsting to establish the meaning of words from the ultimate standpoint,
we have come here so that we may be questioned by you.
Precisely because it exists neither internally nor externally, it is proclaimed to be "false" and "conceptual.
What, then, is that which is superimposed? It is merely some form that colors conceptual thought.

Now, one might ask: apart from an external object, what is this form said to be that colors internal cognition? Is it not the case that for conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), it is the shadow of the perceptible that acts as the colorer, and not the perceptible object itself? For an object excluded [from others] is the domain of perceptions, and it has been stated that conceptual constructions are incapable of touching that [object].
Now, conceptual constructions (vikalpa), which rely upon that reflection, are said to have exclusion as their object because they do not apprehend what has been excluded.

[Objection: But surely, since there is no difference between the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and that which possesses the exclusion (*vyāvṛttimat*), whatever is the exclusion and whatever is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) characterized by that exclusion are one and the same. Thus, by means of conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) apprehending the exclusion, the excluded object itself would be apprehended; consequently, those conceptual cognitions would be exactly like direct perception (*darśana*). [Response: This is not so. By means of conceptual cognitions, the excluded real entity (*vastu*) is not apprehended. Nor is the exclusion ultimately real (*pāramārthikī*); rather, it is some kind of superimposed form (*āropita ākāra*). For if the exclusion were real, these faults—which consist in the [concepts] touching the actual entity—would manifest.
But it has not been stated that this [consciousness] belongs to her.

For this very reason, the objection raised by some—namely, that if one accepts the apprehension of the excluded (*vyāvṛtta*), then a triad must be apprehended: that which is excluded, the cause by which it is excluded, and that from which it is excluded—and since there is no such apprehension of a triad, how can there be an apprehension of the excluded—is thereby refuted. For if the users of language had the mental impression "we apprehend that which is excluded," then they would indeed be subject to such an inquiry; but since this is not the case, the objection is untenable.
Surely, in this way, conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) have been shown to have only superimposed forms as their objects;

thus, the statement that they have "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) as their object is inconsistent. To this it is replied: this has already been addressed. Conceptual cognitions such as "cow," which arise subsequent to perception, delineate forms that are excluded from what does not produce that effect.
For conceptual cognitions of a cow do not delineate horses and the like—which do not produce that effect—and they do not touch upon the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, a real universal does not exist;

therefore, by this reasoning, it is established that conceptual cognitions have as their object only the exclusion (*parāvṛtti*) of what does not produce that effect. Thus, their status as having *apoha* as their object is stated on logical grounds, not through direct perception.
Now, it may be argued that just as the perceptible nature of an object is indeed excluded from what does not produce its effect, it is likewise excluded from its own class;
therefore, they might represent an aspect that is excluded from both its own class and other classes.
For the exclusions from similar and dissimilar classes are not distinct from the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
And we do not perceive any cause for the restriction to the delineation of only one of these two aspects.
O wise one, do not think thus:
[if] cognitions were of the nature of certainty and free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*),

then because they would ascertain their object in its entirety through the delineation of an aspect excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes, there would be no occurrence of further conceptual constructions or other words.

And likewise, the conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) arising from the word "cow" is experienced as delineating an aspect excluded from those of a different class, and not as delineating an exclusion from those of the same class.
Since words have the same objects as these conceptual cognitions, they are said to have "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as their object.
This superimposed form is not external, precisely because it is superimposed;
nor is it internal, because it lacks the nature of consciousness.
Therefore, it is nothing at all.
Since nothing at all exists as an exclusion (*apoha*), it is merely figuratively designated as such by way of its result;

therefore, the "Beloved of the Gods" (the opponent), experiencing a parching of his throat while laboriously offering refutations based upon an external exclusion, is distressed in an inappropriate place.

Furthermore, an object that is the domain of conceptual construction is perceived as having a determinate form, as being similar to an external thing, and as implying existence or non-existence brought forth by other conceptual constructions.
Yet these three characteristics are not tenable in an external entity.
For when an external entity is cognized in its own nature, a connection with existence brought forth by another conceptual construction is not possible, because it would be redundant.
Nor is it connected with non-existence (*abhāva*), because that would involve a contradiction.

Furthermore, the restricted nature of the object of conceptual construction—comprehended as "this is indeed a cow, not a horse"—is not possible without the exclusion of other things; thus, by necessity, its object is exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
Otherwise, a definitive determination (*niyamapariccheda*) would be impossible.
And an object that is doubtful is not apprehended.

Thus, when the external object as the referent of conceptual constructions has been refuted, their non-external nature must be established according to the principle that "there is only a single nature of the object," for otherwise there would be redundancy.
This non-external [referent] is a superimposed form, and it appears as if it were external.
Since there is no similarity between the external and the superimposed other than the shadow of exclusion (vyāvṛtti), conceptual constructions are in effect directed toward exclusion alone.

Even though their activity proceeds in a positive form, such as "cow" or "horse," nevertheless those who know the principles of logic establish them as having only the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) as their object.
As it has been said: "Indeed, it is the commentators who analyze in this way, not the users [of language].

This very thing—which is neither internal nor external, but some other superimposed form—because it possesses the shadow of exclusion, is called the meaning of the word "exclusion" (apoha); this is the path containing within it the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (asatkhyāti).

Alternatively, the reflection of conceptual construction—which is merely the form of cognition and not external—though its diversity of forms is imposed by the distinctions among various latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), appears as if it were external and sustains the course of worldly life.

And because it possesses the shadow of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it is conventionally designated as "exclusion" (*apoha*). This is the path that contains within it the theory of self-cognition (*ātmakhyāti*).

Now, if conceptual constructions lack an objective reality as their domain in both ways, how can practical activity regarding real entities proceed? For even when a real entity such as a blade of grass is perceived, activity does not necessarily occur; rather, it is the desire for an object that is the cause of activity.
[Objection: Surely even the perception [of the object] is a cause, just like the desire for it;

for even one who desires [something] does not act toward it if he does not see it. Furthermore, in the case of the theory of exclusion (*apoha*), it must be explained how one who has acted attains the real entity (*vastu*). [Response: It is said that action, first of all, is based on the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized.

When a conceptual construction arises immediately after the perception of the object, the cognizer does not apprehend it as being a conceptual construction. Deceived by the immediate succession of the perception, however, he thinks that the object itself has been grasped,
and he acts on the basis of that conceit.

This is what they call "unification": that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not apprehended as distinct from the perceived object (*dṛśya*). It is not, however, intended as an unification consisting in the determination of non-difference between two things that are actually different;
for it is impossible to point out silver as something distinct from the mother-of-pearl that is perceived, and because there is no means for determining non-difference [between them].
In the determination of non-difference, perception is not the means, because it is not an object of conceptual construction;
nor is conceptual construction [the means], because its object is the perceived [particular].
Therefore, activity proceeds precisely from the non-determination of difference.

Even attainment (*prāpti*) belongs only to a perceptible object, that is, to a thing capable of causal efficacy (*arthakriyākārin*), because the continuity of effects is ultimately rooted in that [perceptible object].
The process is as follows: from the perceptible comes perception, from that comes conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and from that comes purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).
For one who acts after having apprehended an object existing at its root attains it.
When there is light emanating from a jewel placed inside a room, as if issuing from the aperture of a keyhole, one proceeds with the cognition that it is a jewel;

however, where there is no object even at its source, one who proceeds there out of delusion is indeed frustrated, just like one who proceeds toward the light of a lamp with the cognition that it is a jewel.

Thus, even when conceptual constructions that are devoid of contact with external objects arise, worldly people harbor the conceit: "An external object has been apprehended by me," "I have engaged with it," and "It has been attained by me.
However, this is not rooted in a determination of an actual object. As it has been said: "Because it is not as it is determined, and because it is not determined as it truly is."

In this passage from the treatise, "Because there is activity due to the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object within what is not an object—namely, one's own internal appearance"—the "determination of an object" must be explained as precisely the non-determination of difference (*bhedānadhyavasāya*).
Thus, having unified the perceived object and the conceptualized object, one engages with and attains the object.
In this very way, the worldly transaction of the world is made possible; even by one who discerns reality, the course of worldly life must be carried out as it is done by the world.
Therefore, they say that the object of a word is the conceptual reflection known as *apoha*;
however, when its mode of apprehension is not analyzed, it produces in people the delusion of a universal (*jāti*).

Whatever variety of restrictive rules operates regarding the occurrence or non-occurrence of [linguistic] functions among classes of entities, that same variety applies equally to exclusions (*apoha*s) as well; the only difference between them is that [exclusions] are produced by their lack of substantial reality.
Just as certain medicinal herbs are capable of pacifying a fever despite being equal in their difference [from one another],
so too individual entities (vyakti), though devoid of a commonality (sāmānya), may possess the capacity for specific effects.
For us, the establishment of linguistic usage such as qualifiers and so forth is not untenable even in the case of a non-entity (*tuccha*) such as *apoha*;
therefore, you should cease this deliberation regarding whether the referent of a word is a genus (*jāti*), a configuration (*ākṛti*), or an individual (*vyakti*).

To this it is replied: Is the partiality for the theory of apoha due to the non-existence of external objects such as universals and so forth, or rather, is it simply on the strength of [our] cognition?
Since you yourselves have not accepted that cognition has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object, what is the use of this quarrel?

Nor is there non-existence of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, because they are cognizable through a cognition produced by the contact of sense-faculty and object that is free from sublation and doubt, just like a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
For it is only the very first visual consciousness that comes into contact with the object, not those that arise subsequently; what kind of royal decree is this?

Let that very [non-conceptual cognition] be the means of valid cognition; however, by it too, the nature of the object is understood as being excluded [from others], and not as something pervasive—what proof is there for this? For, because the duration of non-conceptual cognition is extremely subtle, how can this dispute between us be settled as to what appears and what does not appear? You say that only the excluded [part] appears;
I say that the pervasive [part] also appears.
When two people are thus disputing, what is the means of determination? Indeed, neither an oath nor the falling of a cry for help falls within its scope.
Therefore, its determination must be made by reflecting upon the effects produced over gross durations of time immediately following the state of non-conceptualization.
And in that case, if non-conceptual cognition were to have only the particular as its object,
how could this determination of a universal arise all of a sudden?

If it is argued that this conceptual construction is verbal, do not say so; for one perceives a recurring form even when the word is unknown, just as a person from the South suddenly sees a succession of camels.
Even one who has not yet understood the relationship between word and meaning, when in the proximity of the meanings of individual words, perceives indeed their form as both inclusive and exclusive.
Moreover, at the very first contact of the eye, four fingers being observed are understood through a form that moves from one to another;

how then can visual cognition be based solely on particulars? Furthermore, for one who has previously seen a cow of the Śābaleya breed and later sees a cow of the Bāhuleya breed, a memory regarding the previously seen Śābaleya cow is experienced as arising.
Therefore, it is not tenable that there is no apprehension of a universal.
When one unique particular (svalakṣaṇa) is perceived, what role does the recollection of another play? Yet it does occur; therefore, we conclude that there is a perceived form common to both.
Furthermore, even when another individual is perceived, there arises the recognition "this is that very same cow.
Its validity has already been demonstrated and will be shown in detail in the refutation of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga*).
Therefore, that recognition has as its object a recurring form, since the difference between individuals is clearly established.

Furthermore, where a sesame seed of extremely small dimension is situated in proximity to a mass of rice and other grains, its specific individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not perceived as distinct; rather, it is only the recurring form (*anuvṛtta-rūpa*) that is apprehended by the sense organ.

Therefore, since a recurring form appears even in the purely non-conceptual [perception] just as much as the excluded form (*vyāvṛtta*), there is no denial of the universal (*sāmānya*); both differences are real.
How could there be no apprehension of "this is a universal" in that case? Or why would there not be a cognition of "this is excluded [from others]" regarding the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)?
Furthermore, the cognition of a universal does not depend upon a common occurrence [of multiple instances].
But because it is present there, there is no failure to grasp it, just as in the case of the individual instance.
Since a universal is not apprehended because it depends upon a common mode of functioning,
the particular should likewise not be apprehended, for it too depends upon exclusion.
For what means is there for the apprehension of those things in which this [word] conforms? And what means is there for the apprehension of those things from which it is excluded?
Now, if it is claimed that the object itself is apprehended independently of both its similarities and its differences, then let it be told: what kind of thing is that?
At the time of non-conceptualization, that [object] cannot be pointed out;
however, the certainties arising from it provide testimony in both cases.
The wise accept that an entity possesses both natures;
therefore, those two who assert that it has only a single form are both ignorant.
As for what was also stated—that the coexistence of mutually contradictory forms in a single entity is not tenable—that too is not correct.
Nor is there mutual contradiction here, because that [contradiction] is not experienced;
for when one [of two things] is sublated, there is no cognition of the other, as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

For where there is contradiction, one form is perceived through the sublation of another form; but in the present case, this is not so—what, then, is the meaning of "contradiction"? Even if shade and heat were seen in the same place, what could be said to be contradicted by what? It is because they are not seen [together] that they are called contradictory. But since such non-perception does not occur here, there is no contradiction.
For this very reason, neither of the two cognitions here can be false;
for it is impossible for two cognitions to arise by mutually subverting one another.

And thus it has been said: "Just as in the case of a multicolored object, the determination of its color is according to one's wish, so too, because an entity is manifold, there is the ascertainment of both difference and non-difference."
Thus, since difference and non-difference are determined without contradiction,
let things possess a dual nature, just as in the position of Bhaṭṭa.

But let this matter rest for now, as your honor has desisted from it as if out of fear of the various difficulties regarding its subsistence and so forth; we shall simply state that the universal exists in the individuals, being indeed distinct from the individuals themselves.
And whatever refutation was described there regarding the alternatives concerning its mode of existence and so forth—
all that would be countered by the very power of direct perception itself.
As for what was stated—that there is no appearance of difference [between them] like that of a blue lotus and an amalaka fruit—the difference in their cognition has indeed already been demonstrated.

As for the argument that [the universal] is not perceived because it is not perceived when its locus is not perceived—due to the difference in location—the reason for this is that the universal is dependent upon that [locus], and not because it is non-existent.

Since the universal resides in the individual, it is not perceived as having a separate location; or rather, it is not perceived when the individual is not perceived, but this is not because the universal is absent as something distinct from it.

As for what was said—that the occurrence [of the universal] is untenable—it is replied to this as well: "The universal exists in its entirety within each individual. If it is argued that there would be no perception of it in another individual, what can we do? To whom shall we appeal? For there is indeed perception of it even in another individual. And how could we deny this to you? There simply are no parts of a universal by which we might speak of its partial occurrence.
If you say, "Where else have I seen this?"—oh, what skill you possess, you who demand an illustrative example even for that which is directly perceived, as if it were a matter of inference!
If it is asked what the name of this category is, we do not know its name; we simply declare that it is the genus inherent in the individual.

Now, it may be argued that inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation between two things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*). But since that [inherence] has already been refuted by the very same contradiction, how can it not be refuted? [We reply: There is indeed a distinction [between the two] due to a difference in cognition; however, a difference in location is not admitted. Therefore, the mode of existence (*vṛtti*) postulated in this case is called inherence.
This same mode of subsistence applies to the part and the whole, as well as to the quality and the qualified.
Their being distinct entities will be demonstrated later;
moreover, it has already been shown by this very path that there is no difference in location between them, and thus their inseparability (*ayutasiddhatva*) is evident.

As for the claim that "there is no relation for that which is not yet produced, and once it is produced, there is separate existence" (*yutasiddhatā*), this too has been refuted by the Teachers who state, "The universal (*jāti*) and its relation exist at one and the same time.
All of this is postulated on the strength of uncontradicted experience, and not by means of technical definitions within one's own school.
Even for all-pervading entities (*vibhu*), a mutual relationship is not accepted precisely because it is impossible, and not merely due to the technical definitions of one's own school.
There is no conjunction (*saṃyoga*) among them, because there is an absence of non-attainment (*aprāpti*);
for conjunction is indeed attainment preceded by non-attainment.

There is no inherence [of universals], because that which would reside in it is not perceived; enough of this digression. Furthermore, the modes of existence found here in cases such as a garland, a thread, or a necklace—which are like those of a string—are distinct from those two [inherence and conjunction] because universals and the like are partless.
Therefore, the argument "because the functioning [of the mind] is untenable" is not a valid refutation.
As for that which was refuted by conceptualizing [the self] as being either omnipresent or localized in a single body—that too is trivial;
we accept it exactly as the venerable Blessed One’s cognition indicates.
It is first accepted that the universal (jāti) is omnipresent;
its non-perception everywhere is due to the absence of a manifesting individual (vyañjaka-vyakti).
The individual instance attains the state of being a manifester of the universal only through its own perception, and not otherwise;
wherever and whenever there is the perception of the individual instance, at that very place and time occurs the cognition of that universal.
Birth exists everywhere, yet it is not perceived everywhere;
it is perceived only where there is a manifesting individual that brings it to manifestation.
What is the proof for its existence elsewhere than in the individual? To this it is said: even here, when another cow is brought in, there is the perception of "cowness."

There is no possibility of its arrival together with the body of the cowherd girl, just as there is none of the self [arriving] with the body; therefore, its existence here [in this world] must also be admitted.
Manifestation, however, occurs at that same time as the perception of the manifest object;
therefore, once manifested, it is not perceived at any other time.
And because it is manifested in whatever location its manifestation is perceived,
it is therefore manifested in that very place and is not seen in any other location.
Even if some of our own school maintain that the universal is omnipresent in every individual, [the objection remains]:
when a cow is born today, there will be a cognition of "cow" [with respect to it] because of the apprehension of [that universal] in such a manner.
For the word is born as something that has a counter-correlate even while it is being born;
indeed, the time for its birth and the arising of its relation is one and the same.
In this case, there is no prior existence of the genus, nor is there any transference from another;
rather, that individual arises from its own cause as being exactly of such a nature.
And as for those who inquire, "How is this so?",
well then, let this other matter also be inquired about by them.

The bull is hornless and the cow is black, and she eats blue grass; how can the calf produced from them be white? Just as that individual is perceived as connected with its form and other qualities, so too is it joined with its universal (jāti)—what is this endless series of grievances to you? Or, if [the universal] consists merely in the exclusion of what is not a cow (agovyāvṛtti), this question does not cease.
Why is it that this particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), which is excluded from non-cows, has arisen today?
Therefore, setting aside the habit of fault-finding regarding the fact that the nature of a thing cannot be questioned because it is a positive reality,
let the correct understanding of it be investigated.
Furthermore, practice regarding universals has been shown to be just as faultless as that regarding particulars;
therefore, like a particular, a universal cannot be denied.

In this regard, it might be argued: "Since the particular entity itself possesses the capacity to generate the cognition of a universal, what is the use of postulating a universal? That is incorrect; because the universal is as perceptible as the particular, what is the point of postulating it? For if we were to postulate a universal that is to be inferred from its effect, then indeed we could be questioned thus: "Since the effect can be established otherwise, why postulate that [universal]?"

But as for the universal being directly perceived, what is this inquiry, and what is this capacity that produces the cognition of recurrence—is it non-different from the particulars or different, eternal or non-eternal? Since these alternatives, when analyzed, merely state the "universal" (jāti) under another verbal formulation or amount to nothing at all, this [objection] is trivial.

Now, it might be argued that just as the universal "cowness" and so forth subsists only in specific individuals and not indiscriminately, so too a certain cognition of a cow or the like is produced by only certain individuals; but this is not so, because a distinction in cognition cannot be accounted for except through a distinction in its object. If, however, you maintain that a distinction in the means [of cognition] produces the distinction in cognition, then why such hostility toward a distinction in the object? And once a distinction in the object is established, the existence of a universal (sāmānya) is impossible to deny.

[Objection: But surely, a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttibuddhi*) is indeed observed even among various universals (*sāmānya*) without another universal; what confidence can there be in this [claim]? [Reply: It is said: it cannot be the case that [the universal] exists in its entirety in all fifty [substances].

For if cognitions such as "army" or "forest," which arise without depending on an object distinct from elephants, horses, dhava, khadira, and so forth, are false, does it follow for that reason that cognitions such as "pot" must also be false?
Indeed, the status of cognitions as being either false or not false is based solely on the presence or absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).

In that regard, since there is an absence of any other universal (*sāmānyāntara*) in [the category of] existence (*sattā*) and so forth, erroneous cognitions (*mithyā-pratyaya*) proceed by means of some limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); however, this is not the case for cows and the like. Therefore, this [objection] is trivial.

As it has been said: "Therefore, the application of a universal term (*sāmānya-śabda*) to diverse things—whether based on that [application] to a single entity, or by way of producing a single cognition—is [found] in the case of existence and so forth."

"Is it not said that here too, the cognition of a single form will be established based on the condition of performing a single purposeful action? True, this has been said; however, it is incorrect, because the very fact of performing a single purposeful action remains unproven."

As for what was stated—that "cognition is non-different because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness" (ekapratyavamarśa)—that too is incorrect, because the oneness of reflective awareness itself is untenable.

For a single conceptual construction (vikalpa) is not produced by multiple perceptions acting together; rather, following various perceptions, conceptual constructions arise with distinctness, their birth being secured by the respective capacities of those perceptions.
Furthermore, there is no other effect belonging to them by virtue of which they might attain unity.
And by what means is the unity of conceptual constructions apprehended? It is not by perception, because that has only the perceived object as its domain.

Nor is it by another conceptual construction, because all conceptual constructions—since they terminate in superimposed objects or have their own internal forms as their domain—lack the capacity to determine mutual difference or non-difference.
One might say that the unity of conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) results from the non-apprehension of any difference in the forms delineated by them.

For the very same form—namely, "cow"—that is delineated by a conceptual cognition arising immediately after the perception of one particular individual, such as a brindled cow (*śābaleya*), is likewise delineated by a conceptual cognition born immediately after the perception of another cow-individual; thus, their unity is asserted on account of the non-difference of their objects.

For when that object is being delineated, no difference appears; therefore, this conceptual construction (vikalpa) blends even distinct perceptions together because it fails to grasp the difference as it has ascended upon the perception. This statement, too, is not convincing. For conceptual constructions, being by their very nature moments of consciousness, are indeed mutually distinct.

As for that form delineated by conceptual construction, whose internal differentiation is not perceived, it must be either distinct from those [particulars] or non-distinct from them. If it is distinct, then this is merely the universal (sāmānya) stated under another name.
If you argue that the distinction lies in its being unreal (avāstava), we say no; for there is no logical justification for its unreality.

If that form (*ākāra*) is not distinct from the cognitions, then it must indeed be differentiated just like the nature of the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); so how can there be their identity, or how can the blending of even distinct perceptions be possible through that identity? Furthermore, O fool, when you are questioned as to where the production of a single-form conceptual construction comes from in the absence of an admitted universal (*sāmānya*), if you reply "because of the identity of the conceptual construction," this results in circular reasoning (*itaretarāśraya*): the identity of the conceptual construction [is derived] from the identity of the effect, and the identity of the effect [is derived] from the identity of the conceptual construction.

As for the claim that "the identity of the effect follows from the identity of the conceptual construction," it is stated even more clearly immediately after that the identity of the conceptual construction arises precisely from the identity of the conceptual construction itself.

How could anyone who is not insane say such a thing? Therefore, the statement—“Cognition is non-different because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness”—is the utterance of one who is utterly deluded.

As for that which was prattled on to establish that conceptual constructions and words have "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as their object—beginning with the phrase "[of a single nature of an object]" and so forth—that too is trivial; for an object perceived in its entirety is certainly not perceived again, since it has been demonstrated that even those cognitions which grasp what has already been grasped possess validity.
And once momentary destruction has been refuted on the grounds of differences in place, time, and so forth,
it is not the case that the apprehension of an entity already apprehended is untenable.
Furthermore, in our view, of a substratum endowed with distinct properties,
some property of it will be apprehended by some particular cognition.

Furthermore, how could there be a difference in the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) due to a variety of causal powers such as those of the *sahakārin* (auxiliary factors), given that its essence is already differentiated by the capacity for the assistance of various adjuncts (*upādhi*)? Moreover, if a thing has indeed been determined in its entirety by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), and subsequent conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) were to determine it again, they would merely incur futility. Can this fact alone justify the assumption that these [subsequent cognitions] grasp an object not previously apprehended? For one who has ceased from thirst cannot, on the grounds that the moonlight is fruitless, be made to imagine that very [moonlight] to be silver.
Therefore, this is merely a vain hope.

And thus, when the object of conceptual cognitions and words is asserted to be an external thing consisting of the negation of others (anyāpoha), we do not perceive any means whatsoever to ward off the force of the insurmountable refutations set forth by Bhaṭṭa Kumārila.

Furthermore, even that conceptual reflection—which is imagined as something colored by the shadow of exclusion (vyāvṛtti) consisting merely of a superimposed form, intended to remove those very objections—is not capable of entering the path of conventional discourse.
That which is called conceptual construction has awakening as its essence, and it is clear by nature;
it does not become turbid except through contact with something else.
Surely, some coloring factor must be admitted for this [consciousness],
whether it be internal in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) or external in the nature of an object.
Furthermore, that which exists neither internally nor externally—by means of that one is attached;
this so-called "consciousness" is a great illusion created by a master deceiver.
Only objects directly color the cognitions;
latent impressions (vāsanās) are not said to do so in that way, because they are produced by the cognition of objects.

Therefore, let cognitions be colored by some object existing in another place or time; however, coloring them by something that is absolutely non-existent and merely superimposed is impossible and amounts to mere idle talk.
Furthermore, it is not even possible to superimpose an aspect that is absolutely non-existent.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) which arise subsequent to perception perform the same function [as perception] by apprehending only the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), since the perceived object is excluded from both its own class and other classes, there exists an exclusion of both. How then could these conceptualizations, while touching upon that [exclusion], touch only the exclusion from heterogeneous instances? If it is argued that because they involve a simultaneous consideration of both, they would be redundant and thus purposeless—[we reply: they are not purposeless. Let them be purposeless or let them take another object altogether if they fall within the category of valid cognition; however, we do not believe that those which apprehend exclusion can fail to do so even partially.
Furthermore, there is no difference between the exclusion of the similar and the exclusion of the dissimilar,
because contact with either one is not possible within a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

If, however, conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) were to apprehend the exclusion of similar and dissimilar instances just like perception, they would likewise apprehend only the unique particular (*asādhāraṇa*); consequently, due to the absence of the conventional operations such as grasping the relationship based on a universal (*sāmānya*), verbal communication and inference would meet their end.

If exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) were also external, then the thunderbolt of Kumārila’s refutation would remain as it was. If, however, it were internal, then conceptual construction could not be colored by it.
To say that it is neither internal nor external is merely a clever turn of phrase.

Is that [object] something of such a nature, or is it nothing at all? If it is nothing at all, then conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) cannot be produced by it, because it is impossible to bring about a coloring [of the mind] by means of that which is nothing.

Furthermore, since utterly non-existent things like a donkey’s horn lack the status of being objects of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), we shall provide the answer here by following the very method used to refute the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*).
If it exists at all, it must necessarily exist either internally or externally.
Therefore, this new path devised with the desire to avoid the refutations offered by Kumārila and others is likewise fraught with difficulties.
Consequently, it is logical that reality is precisely as it is determined through conceptual ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*).
Furthermore, even the connection with existence, non-existence, and so forth, which is brought about by other words regarding an external object, is not untenable;
for every cognition produced by words such as "cow" has as its object the universal alone, independent of [qualities like] existence and so on.
Another word, such as "is" or "is not," is employed to satisfy the expectancy [of the initial cognition] and is thus connected [to it].

The state of having a fixed form is indeed established in an object whose own nature is determined, based on the exclusion of other objects, as in "a jar is a jar and not a cloth. However, this does not mean that *apoha* (exclusion) itself is what is being communicated; enough with this excessive scrutiny. Since linguistic usage regarding external objects is thus possible, why does a person act by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object?

And what kind of unification [of the object and its cognition] could there be? If it is distinct [from the cognition], then there would be a similarity to states such as fainting; how then could there be activity toward it? Or, if some form of the object flashes forth—[is that] visible? If so, the linguistic usage of *apoha* (exclusion) is fruitless. Or, if a second [aspect] shines forth by its own form, then when that [object] is firmly established, what person of sound mind would exert effort [toward it]? If the conceptualizable [object] flashes forth in a visible form, let it be; it may well be a mistaken cognition, but it is not a lack of discernment (*aviveka*).
In this world, there exists nothing that is not a seed of consciousness, nor is there any subverting cognition, such as the conceptualization of a lotus in the rays of the sun.

Therefore, the attainment of the object arises directly from the continuous stream of cognition whose domain is the real object; why then is it said, by way of an extreme analogy, that this is like [attaining] a jewel through its luster?

Since the validity of conceptual cognition has been established, the existence of external objects is secured; we shall now proceed to examine the theories regarding the denotation of individuals, forms, and universals.

Thus, when the external object has been established and those who would subvert it—the Tathāgata’s [Mādhyamika] arguments—have been refuted, we now consider whether the word "cow" denotes the form (ākṛti), the individual (vyakti), or the universal (jāti).
In this context, by the term "form" (ākṛti), the configuration (saṃsthāna) is intended;
it is not the universal (jāti) as held by the followers of Jaimini, because [configuration] is mentioned separately in the Sūtra.
For Jaimini teaches that the universal (*ākṛti*) is the genus (*jāti*) in the sūtra: "But the universal [is the meaning], because [the word] is for the sake of action.
The author of the Bhāṣya also employs the same convention when he says: "We say that the universal is that which is characterized by the dewlap and so forth.
And the author of the Vārttika has likewise explained: "They call the genus itself the universal; it is that by which the individual is formed (*ākriyate*)."
And that universal is the basis for the single cognition of individual objects.

But here, since the author of the Sūtras stated that "the individual, the configuration (ākṛti), and the genus (jāti) are the meanings of a word," and thus spoke of the configuration as distinct from the genus, he considers the configuration to be nothing other than the shape (saṃsthāna).
The world also designates the configuration as consisting of the arrangement of parts, as in the saying: "Where there is configuration, there qualities reside.
Therefore, it is the very arrangement of parts that is called the configuration.
And whether its status as the meaning of a word is tenable or not is indeed worthy of investigation; it has not been neglected, as by the followers of Jaimini, on the grounds that "it is correct.
Therefore, since the word "cow" (go-śabda) is employed when the individual, the configuration, and the genus are all present together, it is investigated: "What is its meaning?"
Regarding this, first the proponents of the universal (ākṛtivādins) say: "The determination of the meaning of a word occurs through usage and comprehension.
When learned people employ a word for its own object, and when hearers comprehend that object from it, that is its meaning."

In this regard, if the word "cow" is not applied to that which possesses a mane and so forth, but is applied to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, then it is understood to have as its object only that specific configuration (sanniveśa).
A term such as "cow" is applied to an object of perception,
and perception has the form (ākṛti) as its object.
For the configuration of a cow's body is perceived by the sense organ as distinct from the configuration of a horse's body;
indeed, the mutual distinction between things is produced solely by that [configuration].
Therefore, a word applied to an object within the domain of perception ought to apply only to the *ākṛti* (form).

As for the claim that the connection with actions such as sending and so forth will belong to the generic form (ākṛti) by way of the individual (vyakti), that is incorrect; for one observes different configurations in each individual, and because of [the faults of] infinity and deviation, it is impossible to know the relationship [between the word and the individual].
The word "cow" is not the designator of the specific configuration of a brindled cow (śābaleya), because that configuration is not seen in a black cow (bāhuleya) even in the absence of the former;
nor can it be understood as denoting the configurations residing in all individual cows contained within the three worlds, due to their infinity.
Consequently, the generic form (ākṛti) is not the meaning of a word, because action is impossible with respect to it.
For it is not the configuration that is the means for accomplishing actions such as sending and so forth, but rather the individual instance.
And when told, "Bring a cow," a wise person does not bring some painted hill, even though its form may be present.

[Objection: But even on the view that the genus (*jāti*) is the denotable object, since the genus "cowness" (*gotva*) is omnipresent, why is a clay cow not brought? [Reply: It is said: in that case, why is an elephant not brought, since the genus is omnipresent? [Objection: Even if it exists everywhere, it is excluded by the restriction of the manifesting individual (*vyakti*). [Reply: Ah, then the living being possessing a dewlap and so forth is the manifester of the genus "cowness," and not a clay cow; thus there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, those who maintain that the configuration (*saṃniveśa*) is the denotable object do not escape this over-extension, because that configuration is present in that [clay cow] as well.
Furthermore, if the word "cow" (go) denoted a class-form (ākṛti), it could not achieve grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with other words expressing qualities such as "white.
For qualities like whiteness do not reside in the class-form, but rather reside in the individual (vyakti).
Since the force of that coreferentiality and so forth is superior, it is better to accept that the individual is the meaning of the word.
In the case of an individual (*vyakti*), there is a connection with action; in the case of a universal (*jāti*), there is excellence of relation.

This twofold [requirement] does not exist in the case of a form (*ākṛti*); therefore, how could it be denotable? Consequently, a deliberation must be made regarding whether the universal or the individual is the denotable object.
Regarding this, first those who maintain that the individual is the denotable object say:
The individual (vyakti) is the meaning of the word, because the injunctions regarding ritual application are otherwise inconsistent.
Injunctions such as "seizing," "slaughtering," and "sprinkling" would not be applicable to a universal (jāti);
for a universal cannot be seized, slaughtered, or sprinkled.

Furthermore, in such expressions as "six should be given," "twelve should be given," or "twenty-four should be given," it is not the genus (*jāti*) that is connected with numbers like six and so forth, but rather the individual (*vyakti*).
Therefore, that [individual] alone is the meaning of the word.

Furthermore, [if an animal that has been dedicated should escape, one should sacrifice another of the same color and age]. If the word-referent were the genus (*jāti*), the substitution of another would not be possible; for the genus is the very same in the other sacrificial substance being brought forward.
In that case, the relation of "otherness" is possible only with respect to the individual (*vyakti*), not with respect to the genus. For this reason as well, the individual is the word-referent.

Conceptual constructions such as increase, decrease, aggregation, and the relationship between property and its owner find immediate coherence under the view that the individual is the denotable object.
Individual manifestation is not the means for the definition [of a universal], nor is such an effect appropriate;
one should not take a circuitous path when the way lies straight ahead.
By relying on a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), the cognition of the connection with the genus (*jāti*) will be established;
thus, there will be no fever caused by infinity (*anantya*) or deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Furthermore, even by others, the operation of a word is accepted as having the perceptible object as its domain;
moreover, an abstract universal alone is not within the range of perception.
Therefore, let it be accepted that the individual (vyakti) alone is the meaning of a word;
for it is only with respect to that [individual] that the cognition arises for one who has heard the word.
This is not accepted by the followers of Jaimini.

For they hold that the meaning of a word is either the individual (*vyakti*) alone or a qualified individual; it cannot be the individual alone, because speakers do not employ the word "cow" with respect to just any individual, nor do hearers understand just any individual from the word "cow."

Now, if it is argued that the meaning of a word is an individual qualified by "cowness" (*gotva*), then in fact "cowness" alone is the meaning of the word "cow," not the individual. Listen to how this is so: if the individual were the meaning of the word, the word would not be applied to other individuals.
Yet, if it is applied to other individuals as well, then its meaning must be that which is common to all individuals, and not the individual itself.
But surely, another individual is also just an individual;

thus, this word "cow" (go-śabda) is applied to an individual and not to a universal. Not so. If the word "cow" is applied to an individual, it would have to be applied even to an individual such as a white horse (karka). If you argue that it is applied only where its application has been observed, then one should not apply it to a cow born today, for its application has not been observed there.
Therefore, perception is not the cause [of the cognition], because it is impossible for it to occur with respect to each individual instance.
If the individual were the meaning of the word, the cognition would be "This is a cow" or "That is a cow," but not "This too is a cow.
Yet such a cognition does indeed occur.
Furthermore, this application of words by chance cannot proceed without a governing principle; therefore, its regulator must be investigated.
If it is argued that "cowness" (*gotva*) alone is the restrictor, then, O long-lived one, you understand well;
however, you ought to state whether that cowness is cognized or not cognized. It cannot be uncognized, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is already understood, from what do we understand it—from the word or from something else? Not from anything else, because other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are not present.

If it is from the word, then the word must first of all apply to the universal "cowness" (gotva), according to the logical principle that "there is no cognition of a qualified object without the qualifier having been apprehended."

Now, it might be argued that the word "cow" intends to express the genus as the qualifier and the individual as the qualified; however, it cannot do so, for that would entail an excessive burden on the word.
Nor is there any other way to apprehend the individual such that we would impose such a heavy burden upon the word. Indeed, we do not deny your position regarding the cognition of the individual.
Nor do we deny that there is the cognition of the universal (jāti) and the individual (vyakti), since both are perceived through their being cognizable by self-awareness (*pratyātmavedanīya*).

Furthermore, it would be an excessive burden for a word to possess expressive power (*abhidhātrī śakti*) with respect to both; for the cognition of one is established through the cognition of the other.

Thus, in the investigation as to whether a word denoting a universal implies the individual, or a word denoting an individual implies the universal, the universal must be the meaning of the word, because it is apprehended earlier due to its status as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*).

And once that [universal] has been understood from the word, the understanding of the individual will be established from that very same source; thus, the word does not exert its function in both cases.

[Objection: But surely, just as from the word *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer), we shall understand both the qualifier—the genus (*jāti*)—and the qualified—the individual (*vyakti*)—from the word *go* alone; what is too much for it? [Reply: This example is flawed. For in that case, the cognition of both is possible through the distinction between stem and suffix.
The word *daṇḍa* denotes the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) as its base form (*prakṛti*),
and the possessive suffix denotes the qualified (*viśeṣya*).
However, this principle does not apply in the case of the word *go*.
In that case, the word *daṇḍin* does not apply to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), nor does the word *daṇḍa* apply to the qualified (*viśeṣya*).

Here, however, the single word *go* applies to either the qualifier or the qualified. When it applies to the qualified, it requires another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) for the qualifier.
But when [a word] functions as a qualifier, it conveys that [qualifier] and thereby implies the qualified object as well; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
This is directly perceived by oneself: that when a word is uttered, an individual entity (vyakti) is understood.
However, the discrimination as to whether that [understanding] arises from the word itself or from the universal (jāti) is not perceptual;
it is understood through reasoning.

Because it would involve excessive effort for a word to denote two things simultaneously, because no such successive operation is perceived, and because the cognition of the individual is observed even without the word when the universal is understood, it is determined that this cognition of the individual arises from the universal itself, while the cognition of the universal arises from the word.

Furthermore, you yourselves have indeed admitted that the apprehension of the qualified object is preceded by the knowledge of the qualifier, as Kaṇāda said: "From the whiteness inherent [in the object] and from the cognition of whiteness, there arises the cognition of the white [object]; these two stand in a cause-and-effect relationship."

Furthermore, as for the claim that the individual (vyakti) is the meaning of a word because of its connection with actions such as seizing, slaughtering, and sprinkling—that too is inconclusive, since even in the case of a genus (jāti), a connection with action is observed in some instances, as in the injunction: "One should pile the *śyenacit* fire-altar."

"Is it not the case that here too, it is only the individual (vyakti) that constitutes a constituent part of the ritual action, and not the formless genus (jāti)? No, it is not so; for here the hawk (śyena) is not indicated as the means of accomplishment, as in the injunction *yajeta paśunā* ('one should sacrifice with an animal').

Rather, based on the traditional teaching of the learned (*abhiyukta-smaraṇa*)—namely, *karmaṇy agnyākhyāyām* ('when the name of a fire-altar is to be designated')—the meaning of the word is understood to be a hawk-shaped structure produced by the act of piling (cayana).
And it is impossible to produce an individual hawk through the act of piling."
For it is recorded in the Smṛti: "[In the rite called 'fire' (agnyākhyā)].
Indeed, a bird is not produced by the piling of bricks;
rather, fire is produced in that shape. Therefore, in this case, it is the genus (*jāti*) that serves as a constituent part of the ritual action, not the individual (*vyakti*).
Now, it might be argued that similarity will be established by means of an individual; however, this cannot be established, because dissimilarity with other individuals is also possible.
For that which is similar to one individual is also dissimilar to others.
As for the objection that an immaterial genus cannot be a constituent part of an action, this is not a fault;

for even immaterial qualities and actions can function as means of accomplishment, as seen in such injunctions as "he buys with a red cow" (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*) and "he offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāmaṃ juhoti*).

Furthermore, through the mediation of the implication of the individual, the genus will be established as a means of accomplishment in the injunctions regarding practical applications such as touching, slaughtering, and sprinkling.
But that effect which is to be accomplished by a manifested individual (vyakti) is held to be accomplished by that [individual];
just as that which is produced by the elements and the senses is said to have the self as its agent.
The self, being authorized in all ritual acts and being their agent,

becomes the agent in those acts by accomplishing tasks such as the wiping of the *audumbarī* post and the gazing at the clarified butter (*ājya*) through the medium of the body and the senses— since it is incorporeal. In the same way, a genus (*jāti*), by means of the individual (*vyakti*), accomplishes those tasks and thereby attains the status of a causal instrument (*sādhana*).
Therefore, the Mīmāṃsakas have declared that the genus (*jāti*) alone is the constituent part (*aṅga*);
and its status as a constituent of the ritual action is mediated by something else, just like the Self (*ātman*).
In this way, the statements "six should be given" and "one should sacrifice another of that same color" are to be applied as having that very [principle] as their basis.
By this, the accumulation, depletion, and combination [of atoms] and so forth are also explained.

Furthermore, tasks such as the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] are easily established only on the view that universals (jāti) exist, because there is no room for objections such as infinite regress or deviation.
Furthermore, as for what was asserted— that a word operates within the domain of perception,
and that the universal alone (*sāmānyamātra*) is not the object of perception— that has been refuted by the author of the *Vārttika*:
for the object of perception is a manifold entity (*citrātmakaṃ vastu*).
"And no word is able to express that [reality] in such a way;
every word functions only after having extracted the general components."
Indeed, no single word is found to be capable of imparting a complex object characterized by a variegated form composed of a multitude of diverse properties;
nor is it easy to grasp the relationship [between a word and its referent] in such a case. Therefore, it is logical that the word must be based solely on the generic aspect (*sāmānyāṃśa*).
Consequently, the universal (*jāti*) alone is the meaning of a word.
To this it is replied: a universal (jāti) cannot be the meaning of a word.
For a word is a collection of phonemes ending in an inflectional suffix (vibhakti), not merely the nominal stem (prātipadika).
And in that regard, it is established that the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) express their meanings as mutually related to one another.

Furthermore, when a case-ending (vibhakti) such as the second [accusative] and so forth is uttered following a nominal stem (prātipadika), it expresses its own meaning as being inherent in the meaning of that nominal stem.
Moreover, the threefold meaning of the case-ending—namely, the grammatical relation (kāraka), gender (liṅga), and number (saṅkhyā)—is expressed simultaneously.
Yet, these three do not cohere with the meaning of the nominal stem, which is the universal (jāti).
Birth is not the agent;
nor is there a division of birth into female, male, and neuter;
nor does it possess duality and so forth.

Now, it was argued that everything will be explained through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the individual (*vyakti*); however, what was said is not tenable. A word employed once does not express some meaning in one part, indicate another meaning from that, and then further denote gender, number, and so forth as belonging to that [indicated object]. This sequence is not one that is experienced in cognition.
But to state that [the agent] is directly endowed with that [action] would be incoherent;
it would be like an injunction such as "one should sprinkle with fire."
But surely, just as in the case of a person (pums), agency will exist in the universal;
thus, this syntactic connection expressed by the case-ending is appropriate as being mediated by an intermediate stage.

The case ending expresses its own meaning precisely as something residing in the general sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and not by way of residing in an individual (*vyakti*) that is merely indicated; for if it were so, there would be an inconsistency in the mode of expression. As for that meaning of the case ending, since it cannot apply directly to the universal (*jāti*), it will be mediated by an intermediate stage. This [objection] is not valid, because the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is possible for the self through its connection with cognition, effort, and so forth. However, since the universal does not have even the slightest touch of activity directly, its status as a *kāraka* is inherently unattainable.
Therefore, how can there be an application of the meaning of the case-ending there [in the universal], when that which is conjoined with number and so forth is not described as residing therein?
And that which is described as residing in something else is not conjoined with it.
Furthermore, people do not consider the cognition of a discrete individual to be mediated by an interval;
nor is there ever a sequential perception [of letters] even on the grounds of their inexplicability otherwise.

And we perceive the individual as being colored by the universal, as well as being associated with number and other qualities; it is indeed this [individual] that possesses the status of a "thing" (padārtha).

As for what was stated regarding the connection of the genus with the ritual action in the case of "the altar built in the shape of a hawk," since that refers to a specific configuration, the genus has no status as a constituent part of the rite.

If it is argued that there is no similarity between the brick-pile and a specific individual hawk because of deviation from other individuals—and certainly not with an immaterial universal (jāti), which, like space, cannot be conceived as having similarity—then this is merely a frivolous example.

But in other applications, such as "Give a cow" and so forth, because the performance of purposeful action belongs to that which possesses [the universal], they say that very thing is the referent of the word.
The word directly expresses its meaning as possessing that [quality],
and there is neither a remote cognition nor any heaviness of burden.

Even linguistic usage such as grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and so forth, being established through the primary mode of signification (mukhyayā vṛttyā), shall not be construed otherwise.
Therefore, the meaning of a word is precisely that which possesses those [universals].

Now, who indeed is this so-called "possessor of that" (tadvān)? Since it is said that "one who has that is a possessor of that," it is the particular itself that is called the "possessor of the universal."
Furthermore, if the particular were what is expressed by the word, the faults of infinite regress and deviation would remain as they were.
Moreover, a universal cannot be indicated unless it is itself expressed by the word.

And it has been stated that expressing both [the universal and the particular] would be an excessive burden for the word. Therefore, it is said: the particular, such as a *śābaleya* cow, which is pointed out by its "this-ness" (*idantā*), is the possessor of that [universal].
Nor is every individual entity existing within the three worlds the possessor of that [universal];
rather, some substratum of the universal, in which particulars such as the *śābaleya* cow are not specifically delineated, is called its possessor.
And because it is a substratum of the universal, there is no occasion for the fallacies of infinite regress (*anantya*) or deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in this case.
Nor do we accept that a word expresses the qualified object without expressing the qualifier, such that we might burden it with an excessive weight.

Since the apprehension of the convention occurs merely with respect to the substratum of the universal, what excessive burden is there for a word that expresses only that much? In this way, the refutation beginning with "because the possessor of the [universal] is not independent" is avoided.
Furthermore, perception does not indeed grasp an isolated portion consisting of a universal;

and how could a word, which functions within the domain of that [perception], express such [an isolated entity]? Therefore, a word functioning with respect to an object of perception ought to have precisely that same object as its domain, and it cannot be restricted to the universal alone.
Is it not the case that the simultaneous cognition of the qualifier and the qualified is never observed even in perception, nor is it accepted by you?
For, according to your view, the relation of cause and effect exists between those two cognitions;
therefore, regarding the qualifier—the universal—there must first be a cognition produced by the sense organ.

Even from a word that requires the cognition of a relation dependent upon that [universal], the understanding occurs with respect to that very [universal] alone; thus, even the individual is not the denotatum.
It is said: first, in the case of perception, both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) are objects of the sense faculty.

Even in the case of a universal (*sāmānya*), the sense faculty, operating through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), apprehends the qualified object just as it does the qualifier.
Indeed, there is no such conventional usage as "the universal is perceived while the particular is to be inferred."
If the sense faculty were to grasp only the quality in this manner, then the possessor of the quality would be the object of inference;
but such is not the case.
Therefore, perception extends as far as the qualified substratum itself.
Likewise, it is logical that a word also has an object corresponding to that [particular], and does not reside in the universal alone.

As for the claim that "every word functions by extracting the universal components," this is said out of fear of infinity (*ānantya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*) when the word is held to denote the individual alone;
however, since these fears do not exist when the word denotes that which possesses the universal (*tadvat*), the word should not be restricted to denoting the pure universal alone.

Now, it might be argued that verbal cognition does not have an object identical in every respect to that of perception, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the two cognitions being identical.
Furthermore, the cognitions arising from verbal testimony and from the senses are not the same.

As it has been said: "One who has been burned perceives the burning quite differently depending on its connection with fire," and so forth. To this it is replied: this has already been refuted previously.
Because the distinction between cognitions is established by the apprehension or non-apprehension of all particularities,
and because the convergence [of means of knowledge] was stated with reference to the substratum (dharmin),
a word does not terminate in the universal alone on this account.

Moreover, if it is maintained that a word expresses an abstracted portion of a universal (sāmānyāṃśa), then the cognitions arising from the word "cow" (go) and the word "cowness" (gotva) would be identical.
Consequently, just as one has the cognition "[the cow] is white," one would likewise have the cognition "cowness is white.

Furthermore, just as in the case of words like "cāturvarṇya," the suffixes denoting abstract state (bhāvapratyaya), such as *tva* and *tal*, would be applied to the word "cow" in its own primary sense.
Now, if you should think that the word "cow" expresses the universal (jāti) as one that implies an individual (vyakti),

whereas a word ending in an abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya) rests solely upon the isolated essential nature [of the universal], that is untenable, because a universal that does not imply an individual is never observed.

Now, if it is argued that at the time of hearing the word "cow," the universal (jāti) is understood as being in contact with the individual (vyakti), whereas when the word "cow" is heard ending in an abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya), it is cognized as being devoid of that [individual]—if this is so, you have come upon my own path. For if the universal is said by the word to possess a substratum (āśrayavatī), then the substratum of the universal has necessarily been expressed;
otherwise, it could not be said to possess a substratum.
When there is a desire to express the mere generality of the dependent (the quality) by excluding its substratum, suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* are employed.
Thus they have said: "For when a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a certain quality, the suffixes *tva*, *tal*, and so forth, are used to denote that [quality].
The words "for when a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a quality" are the very letters that bear witness to the position that the quality is the denotable object (*vācya*).

And it has already been stated that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is possible only in that case. Therefore, just as the operation of the sentence is held to extend up to the completion of the injunction, so too should the operation of the word be held to extend up to the individual (vyakti).
Because that [object] is understood while the operation of the word has not ceased.
Furthermore, by one who accepts that words denote [their meanings] as already endowed with [the universal],
it must be stated all the more clearly that the cognition arising from a word culminates in the individual.
For there is no mutual concomitance among universals that are independent of individuals, nor is there any denotation of those that do not so concur; such is the established rule.
Just as in expressions such as "the cowherd settlement on the Gaṅgā," there is indication (lakṣaṇā) based on proximity,
so too in expressions such as "the white cow," indication of the individual (vyakti) is not understood.
Through both application and practice, this is determined from the elders;
therefore, it is established that the referent of words such as "cow" is the possessor of that [genus].

This has been stated by the author of the Sūtras: "The individual, the form, and the genus are the meaning of a word. The word "but" (*tu*) serves to provide a qualification. What is being qualified? It is the fact that the status of being the primary or secondary element in the meaning of a word is not fixed. Even though the possessor of those [attributes] (the individual) is the denotable object, in certain usages the genus is primary and the individual is subordinate; for example, in the statement "A cow must not be touched with the foot," a prohibition regarding all cows is understood.

In some cases, there is predominance of the individual (*vyakti*) and subordination of the genus (*jāti*), as in the commands "Release the cow! (*gāṃ muñca*) or "Bind the cow!
