Now, if it is either desire or aversion [that constitutes the sentence-meaning], then this is merely the position of Akṣapāda—namely, that the meaning of a sentence is either the desire for pleasure or the wish to avoid pain—and nothing new at all.
Furthermore, even the "activity" (vyāpāra) consisting of the vibration of the self (ātmaspanda) postulated by the Bhāṭṭas is nothing other than *bhāvanā* itself; it is not a different entity.

If it is argued that "exertion" (udyoga) is some object to be accomplished that impels one toward the goal, then that is simply a *niyoga* (an injunction); this is merely a difference in prefix, not a difference in the underlying reality.
Therefore, because it has been composed by one who had never heard it before, this Udyoga Parva is within the range of the people of the Bharata lineage, but not of those like me.
Others, however, maintain that *pratibhā* (intuition) is the meaning of a sentence;
but that position has already been rejected by the refutation of the theory that cognition manifests as a relation [between word-meanings].
Intuition is indeed consciousness, and that arises from sound;
yet it is not the object of the sound, just as the cognition of color is not the object of the eye.
If it is argued that because an external object does not exist, consciousness itself is the object, we say no, because that [existence of an external object] has already been established.

Furthermore, when it is said, "A tiger has arrived," various types of actions arise depending on whether the persons concerned are brave or cowardly; since this occurs upon the apprehension of an external object such as the arrival of a tiger, following from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), it does not have mere mental intuition (*pratibhā*) as its sole cause.
For in that case, the object being known is the instrument (*karaṇa*), not the mere cognition itself.
If it is argued that the object does not exist at that time, then this must be a deceptive statement that lacks a real referent, but it does not mean that the object is non-external.

Just as when an external object exists in its actual state, various intuitions (*pratibhā*) arise—such as "a corpse," "a beloved woman," or "food"—according to one's latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), so too, when the arrival of a tiger is understood from a word, effects such as courage in the brave or fear in the timid occur.
However, on this account alone, intuition ought not to be considered the meaning of a word.

Therefore, even if intuition is said to be the sentence-meaning by virtue of being the purpose of the sentence, let it be so called; nevertheless, it is not the denoted object (*abhidheya*) of the word.

If it is argued that even though it is inexpressible, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is like a relation (*saṃsarga*), that too is incorrect. The sentence-meaning is the related things, not the relation itself; likewise here as well, the sentence-meaning consists of the objects as they appear in intuition (*pratibhā*), not the intuition itself.

Furthermore, since a word—unlike perception—does not have as its object only that which is present, the claim that words denoting future objects and the like are "devoted to intuition" (*pratibhā*) because they lack the presence of their referents is also untenable; for it has already been established that even when referring to the future and so forth, such words still have real objects as their domain. Thus, enough of this elaboration.

The meaning of the sentence is indeed the ultimate reality; thus, this [sentence-meaning] is not constructed by conceptualization. Furthermore, that which possesses such a meaning is declared to be the object of the word. Therefore, the charge of invalidity leveled against the word on the grounds of the absence of an external object is refuted; its validity remains stainless.
Indeed, the validity of the word has not yet been established;
for the seed of the cognition of the meaning of words and the meaning of sentences has not been determined.
It is said: what is there to be determined in this matter?
For that which arises immediately after something else has that as its cause.
Since the comprehension of the meaning of words and sentences occurs when words and sentences are heard, those [words and sentences] alone are the cause therein.
Furthermore, what is this that is called a "word" (pada), and what is a "sentence" (vākya)?
It has been stated in this regard that a collection of phonemes (varṇa) is a word, and a collection of words is a sentence.
But surely they cannot tolerate this very point:
for there is no such thing as a collection of phonemes that exists in reality; therefore, how could a word be a collection of those?
And because of that absence, it is not at all possible for a collection of words to constitute a sentence.
Furthermore, it is not tenable for phonemes to possess expressive power, as they are undermined by the dilemma of being either taken individually or collectively.
Therefore, they maintain that the word which conveys meaning is something entirely distinct, consisting of the nature of *sphoṭa*.
Let it be so;
let the *sphoṭa* itself be the distinct entity that conveys the meaning.
What loss is there for the Naiyāyikas? How could there be no loss? For they have stated that the authority of a word consists in its being composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*).
Furthermore, because the *sphoṭa* is eternal, it cannot be something produced by a reliable authority (*āpta*).

Consequently, that word consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*), whose impermanence has been established, is not the cause of the cognition of meaning; therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As for the word consisting of the *sphoṭa*, which is the cause of the cognition of meaning, it is neither impermanent nor produced by a reliable authority. Thus, the Naiyāyikas would be needlessly distressed in an inappropriate place.
Therefore, it must be established that only impermanent phonemes possess the capacity to signify meaning,
and the *sphoṭa* must be rejected.

To this it is said: since there is no comprehension of meaning when the phonemes such as *ga* and so forth are not apprehended, and since there is [comprehension] when they are present, the capacity to convey meaning belongs to those [phonemes] alone.

And it is these very [phonemes], by virtue of being the objects of cognition through the instrument of hearing, that receive the designation "word" (*śabda*). Therefore, one must postulate some entity called *sphoṭa*, which is not established by experience and transcends both perception and inference.
[The opponent] asks: "How can this be so?"
These mental constructs are far-fetched.

How could phonemes possess the capacity to convey meaning? For those phonemes, such as the letter *ga* and so forth, in conveying an object, would they convey it collectively or individually? First, they cannot do so individually, because even when each phoneme is heard one by one, the cognition of the object does not arise.
There is no such thing as the simultaneous existence of phonemes at all.
For that [simultaneity] would have to exist either by virtue of their mere being or by virtue of their being perceived.
In the view of the Naiyāyikas, simultaneity by way of existence is non-existent, since it has been shown that sound is subject to rapid destruction.

Furthermore, even if it is maintained that sound is eternal according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, since simultaneity in terms of existence is common to all phonemes, it cannot be determined which meaning would be conveyed by which collection of phonemes.

Now it is said: unlike the eyes and other sense organs, phonemes do not possess the nature of a producer (*kāraka*), such that their mere simultaneity while remaining unperceived could be a factor in the communication of meaning.
Because they are indicators (*jñāpaka*), they convey meaning only when they have been perceived, like smoke and the like; thus, their totality is required only at the time of cognition.
This too is untenable.
For regarding the totality of cognition, does it pertain to phonemes uttered by a single speaker, or to those spoken by various persons?

In that regard, since phonemes spoken by many persons at once consist of a confused din (*kolāhala*), their distinct individual forms are difficult to discern; thus, for what could one consider "totality" or "non-totality"?
Or, even if such a totality were present, there would simply be no comprehension of the meaning.
However, in the case of sounds uttered by a single speaker, because they do not abandon the sequence of effort, place, and articulatory organ (*sthāna-karaṇa*), a sequence necessarily occurs.
And since that sequence exists, it follows that the cognition of meaning would be produced by each individual phoneme taken separately;
yet this is not observed. Thus, because the alternatives of [the letters] being denotative either individually or collectively are untenable, the phonemes are not the denoters.
The cognitions of the phonemes as objects should likewise be analyzed in this same way;
they too do not occur simultaneously.
And if they were to occur in succession, it would follow that the comprehension of the meaning would arise from the cognition of each individual phoneme.
As for the claim that the final phoneme, accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, is the conveyor of meaning—that too is untenable.
For a so-called "impression" is something produced by an experience, and it generates a memory directed toward that very same object, but not a cognition directed toward a different object.
If it is argued that the phoneme will then convey the meaning by way of memory, this is also not the case, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of a simultaneity of cognitions.
For immediately after the cognition of the final phoneme, the recollection of the convention occurs just as the recollection of the preceding phonemes does;
and consequently, there would be a simultaneity of cognitions.
Furthermore, we do not perceive any reason for their arising in succession.
Even if they were to exist in that sequence, at that time the cognition of the final phoneme would have ceased; so whose assistance would the memory of the preceding phonemes provide?

And this has been stated by assuming a single memory whose object is many preceding phonemes; however, there is no single memory that has all phonemes as its domain. Why? Because [memories] have as their cause the diversity of latent impressions (vāsanā) produced by distinct perceptions.
Memories would be distinct [in each case], but a single [cognition] does not have multiple objects.
Now, it might be argued that there will be a single synthetic cognition (*saṃkalanājñāna*) whose object is both existent and non-existent phonemes,
and that the phonemes, mounted upon that [cognition], will convey the meaning; but that too is a mere vain hope,
because there is no cause for the arising of such a cognition.
Furthermore, the sense organ is not capable of apprehending a past color, nor does the mental impression (saṃskāra) grasp what is present.

Nor do the sense organ and the mental impression produce this cognition simultaneously; for since the mental impression has its capacity for producing mere recollection already ascertained through the awakening of impressions deposited by the observation of concomitance, it lacks any further operation together with the sense organ.
Therefore, individual phonemes are not the expressive units.
And for this reason, if these [phonemes] were the expressers [of meaning], they would convey the meaning even when employed in a reversed order.

If, however, a sequence is required, it must be considered whether it is distinct from or non-distinct from the phonemes themselves. If it is non-distinct, those very same phonemes are present; so why do they not cause cognition? But if it is distinct, you have effectively accepted some additional entity as the expresser, and thus you are coming over to my own position.
But surely, a word functions as a conveyor of meaning by virtue of its linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).

And in that convention, however many phonemes, in whatever order, are observed to denote a particular object, those same phonemes, in that same order, will denote that object; so what is the use of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?
As it has been said: "However many, of whatever nature, and whichsoever [phonemes] are employed in the communication of a certain object..."
The phonemes possess the capacity for both manifesting and non-manifesting cognition; they are likewise the means of awakening [to that].
To this it is said: this very process of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) is what must be investigated.
For one’s own comprehension from a word is preceded by the comprehension of another;

and regarding that comprehension of another, who [used] how many [words], in what manner, and for what purpose were they seen employing them, such that one might understand that same meaning from them in that very way? Indeed, the path of phonemes (*varṇavartanī*) is difficult to master.
"You speak thus regarding how many, what kind, and who they are;
yet you have not been asked how many, what kind, and who they are."
Therefore, in every respect, individual phonemes are non-expressive.
Yet, this comprehension of their meaning occurs once the sound has been uttered;
nor can it be that this [comprehension] is devoid of a cause.
Therefore, let this [sphoṭa] be its instrument; let this be an inference from an effect, or a residue-inference (pariśeṣānumāna), or a presumption (arthāpatti).
In any case, that instrument which is postulated by virtue of the effect characterized as the cognition of meaning is called the sphoṭa.
And since it is partless, eternal, unitary, and without cause, it does not fall into the category of being subject to the refutations that are effective against the position of the phonemes (varṇas).
And for this reason, the *sphoṭa* is that which conveys the meaning, because of the common linguistic usage: "We understand the meaning from the word" (*śabdād arthaṃ pratipadyāmahe*).
For you, it is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the phonemes (*varṇa*) that conveys the meaning;
in that case, the meaning of the nominal stem in the expression "[from] the word" (*śabdāt*) would be untenable.

Now, if it is argued that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are what are denoted by the word "word" (*śabda*), and that these [phonemes] convey the meaning, this is established otherwise; nevertheless, the singular number in the case-ending of "[from] the word" (*śabdāt*) is not consistent.
There would instead be the common usage: "we understand [the meaning] from the words" (*śabdebhyaḥ*)."

But if it is maintained that the word which conveys the meaning is the *sphoṭa* itself, then both the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) and the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) in the expression "from the word" (*śabdāt*) are justified.

Now, it might be argued that the word "sound" (*śabda*) does not denote the *sphoṭa*, but rather only the phonemes (*varṇa*), for the term "sound" is well-established as referring to an object perceived by the ear; and these [phonemes] alone are perceived by the ear. This is not so, because the property of soundness (*śabdatva*) also has the nature of being perceived by the ear.
Furthermore, although things such as the gurgling sound of a waterfall are apprehended by the sense of hearing, they cannot logically fulfill the function of "sound" (śabda).
Therefore, that from which the comprehension of meaning arises is "sound.
And since the comprehension of meaning arises solely from the *sphoṭa* and not from the phonemes (*varṇa*), the *sphoṭa* alone is "sound."

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then since smoke and other such things are also causes for the cognition of objects, they too would attain the status of being *śabda* (words). Do not speak thus. When it is stated—beginning with the question, "In the auditory manifestation of the word 'cow' (*gaur*), many objects appear; among these, which is the *śabda*? and concluding with the answer, "That from which the comprehension of the object arises is the *śabda*"—where is there any room for the suspicion that smoke and the like possess the nature of *śabda*?

But surely, this comprehension of meaning—which occurs when the phonemes are present and does not occur when they are absent—how could it be considered the effect of the *sphoṭa*, while setting aside those phonemes?
It is said in reply:

the fact that something exists only when another exists (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*) establishes that it is the effect of that other only when it is not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*), not when it is otherwise established.
What, then, is this "establishment through another means" (anyathāsiddhi)?
Because the phonemes (varṇas) are the manifestors of the sphoṭa, their immediate succession [of the phonemes] appears as the cause of the comprehension of meaning;
it is the sphoṭa, manifested by the phonemes, that brings about the comprehension of meaning.
People wander, thinking that this comprehension of meaning is produced by the phonemes.
Now, one might object: "In the manifestation of the *sphoṭa*, where have those alternatives regarding the phonemes (*varṇa*)—whether taken individually or collectively—gone?
To this, Bhaṭṭa says:
"For whom the partless *sphoṭa* is manifested by the cognitions of the phonemes..."
Even he is not liberated by this [argument], for it is subject to further questioning.

The author of the Bhāṣya also raised the objection, "But surely, if one postulates a *saṃskāra*, there is the postulation of something unperceived," and provided the following rebuttal: "[In the case of postulating a word (*śabda*), there would be both that [postulation of a *saṃskāra*] and the postulation of the word itself]. This is not a fault;
for conceptual constructions (*vikalpāḥ*) have no power over the manifestation of the *sphoṭa*.
Why [is this so]? First, some maintain that at the very moment of hearing the first phoneme, the *sphoṭa* becomes manifested;
nor is there any futility in the second and subsequent phonemes, because they produce an intensification of its comprehension.

Just as for jewel-examiners, although the form of the jewel does not appear clearly upon the first glance, yet as they examine it again and again, the flawless essence of the jewel shines forth in their mind; so too here, even though the *sphoṭa* is manifested by the hearing of the first phoneme, other phonemes will be employed for the sake of a clearer perception.
Others, however, maintain that it is the sounds (*dhvani*) alone that manifest the *sphoṭa*.

By these winds, this partless *sphoṭa*, while being manifested, appears as if associated with various parts such as the letter *ga* and so forth—these appearing through the influence of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) consisting of the conjunctions of the places of articulation (*sthāna*) and the vocal organs (*karaṇa*).
And because the winds are flickering, they perish as soon as they are uttered; thus, they cause that [unitary *sphoṭa*] to appear in an imagined form.
Moreover, it is observed that even a form which is unreal may appear due to the influence of limiting conditions (*upādhi*),

just as the face appears dark, long, and so forth, depending on the differences among manifesting media such as a sword, a jewel, or a mirror. Indeed, sound— which is not essentially identical [to its medium]— is seen to assume a variety of forms according to the differences among manifesting media such as the lute, the flute, the drum, and the kettle-drum.
Therefore, those phonemes are not ultimately real, nor are they manifesters of the sphoṭa; so where could the alternatives of being taken collectively or individually possibly arise?

Appearing through the differentiation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), those cognitions of objects, though possessing unreal forms, are observed to follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the objects.
Therefore, as for the claim that "in the conceptualization of a word there is a doubling of conceptualization," in that case, even a single conceptualization does not exist;
what then to say of a doubling?
Consequently, the cognition of meaning arises from the word itself, which consists of *sphoṭa*.
It is established, however, that its conformity to color is proved by another means.
Moreover, because logicians are fond of inference, this inference was stated for their satisfaction and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
From the perspective of ultimate reality, however, the *sphoṭa* is indeed directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), appearing as it does in auditory cognition.
He said: "What is this unprecedented conduct of a thief?

Even though the phonemes (*varṇas*) are directly perceived, the unfortunate one [the opponent] claims they are not perceptible; yet the *sphoṭa*, though never appearing, is fortunate enough to be called perceptible.
It is replied:

We do not say that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are not perceptible; rather, although they are non-existent [as discrete entities], they appear by virtue of limiting conditions (*upādhi*), like the lengthening of a sound when speaking. Sound (*śabda*), however, is perceived as a single, partless entity.
And thus, there exists a single uniform cognition in the form "this is a word" or "this is a sentence"; yet the distinct phonemes do not become the objective support (*ālambana*) for that cognition.
For a cognition of a universal does not have an individual instance as its objective support, nor does a cognition of a whole have its parts as its objective support.
Furthermore, the cognition of words and sentences is not unreal—like the cognition of an army, a forest, and so forth—because there is no subverting evidence.

If it is argued that this uniform cognition is produced by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of having a single object-cognition, then from what source does the cognition of that single object now arise?

For the cognition of word-meanings and sentence-meanings is preceded by the cognition of words and sentences; and because of the identity of the effect called the cognition of word-meanings and sentence-meanings, the claim that the cognitions of words and sentences are uniform in form leads to an unavoidable circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
And it is equally easy to claim that the cognition of a universal or a composite whole is also merely conditional (*aupādhikatva*).
If it is argued that the objection is avoided in those cases because of the firmness of a cognition free from sublation or doubt, that is the same for the other case as well.

Therefore, since the object of the cognition of a word is the word-sphoṭa and the object of the cognition of a sentence is the sentence-sphoṭa, the sphoṭa is indeed perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In that regard, the comprehension of the meaning of a word arises from the word-sphoṭa, and the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence arises from the sentence-sphoṭa.
He said: If the word, being of the nature of *sphoṭa*, is partless, then the sentence too is simply the word;
let it not have parts consisting of words.
But if it does have parts consisting of words, then let the word also have parts consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*).
It is said:
"My heart has, as it were, breathed a sigh of relief;
I believe that the light of solitude will arise for you, long-lived one."
Being thus instructed, you may come to understand something.

This indivisible *padasphoṭa* has been demonstrated by us for the sake of enlightening someone like you, whose intellect is deceived by the appearance of distinct phonemes (*varṇa*) arising through the differentiation of limiting adjuncts (*dhvanyupādhi*).
However, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no such thing as a *padasphoṭa* that exists as a constituent part of a sentence.
The sentence is indeed partless, and it is the conveyor of a sentence-meaning that is likewise partless.
As they have said: "Because words do not exist within a sentence, the meanings of those words [do not exist] within its meaning; thus, both the sentence and the sentence-meaning are partless."

For if one were to postulate constituent parts, just as sentences have parts which are words, and words have parts which are phonemes, so too must phonemes have parts, and those parts must have further parts; thus, due to this infinite regress, what final determination could there be? If one is to desist from postulating parts upon reaching the phonemes, then one should desist at the sentence itself.

For the cognition of the sentence-meaning, which takes the form of a single unified event, deserves to arise from a sentence of precisely that kind. Indeed, users of language acquire proficiency regarding word-meanings through the linguistic usage of elders. In that context, a word is never observed to be used in isolation, because it does not constitute a factor of communication; rather, since a sentence is fit for use, proficiency arises with respect to the sentence alone.
From that alone arises the comprehension of the meaning;
however, the appearance of constituent parts is merely an illusion.
Furthermore, the meaning of a sentence is indeed one, having the form of Narasiṃha.
For Narasiṃha is indeed a different category of being;
therein, there is neither the meaning of "man" nor the meaning of "lion."
Thus, the meaning of a sentence is indeed distinct from the meanings of the individual words, like a beverage and so forth.

Just as a beverage is something other than its ingredients such as sugar, nāgakeśara, and black pepper; and just as a painting is something other than its colors such as vermilion, yellow arsenic, and lac; or just as a musical mode (*grāmarāga*) is something other than its constituent notes such as *ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, and *dhaivata*—in the same way, a sentence is distinct from its words, and the meaning of a sentence is distinct from the meanings of the words.

If it is asked, "How then is there an understanding of its parts?", [we reply: that is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*); it is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). If it is argued that the parts possess ultimate reality because one observes the following of their respective meanings when the word is followed, [we say] no;
for even though the single phoneme *u* is common to the words *kūpa*, *sūpa*, and *yūpa*, there is no corresponding following of their meanings.

Nor can its status as a cause be asserted merely by its following after [the words], for that would lead to the absurd consequence that a line of ants, being seen following a cloud of dust like elephants and horses, would also be the cause of it.

Therefore, just like the division into base and suffix, the postulation of non-existent entities is resorted to as a means for understanding the meaning of a sentence; however, no such objective reality is perceived there, just as in the case of the word "aśvakarṇa" (horse-ear).
Even that which is unreal is seen to function as a means to the real:
for instance, the bite of a false snake becomes a cause of actual death,
and written letters, though themselves unreal, bring about the comprehension of real objects.
If it is argued that those [letters] are real in their own nature, we say no; for in the form of mere lines, they do not convey meaning.
It is only when the lines are perceived as "this is the letter *ga*" that they become the cause of the cognition of meaning.
In that form by which they are true, they do not convey meaning; and in that form by which they convey meaning, they are not true.
[Objection: But surely even the parts such as stems and suffixes are ultimately real, because they appear [in cognition] and because they are causes for the comprehension of meaning.
[Reply: This is not so;
for it is impossible to determine their essential nature and extent through various grammatical analyses (*anvākhyāna*).
Regarding the word *bhavati*, the root *bhū* is explained in some instances, while in others it is the word *bhava*.
Since there are discrepancies in the explanations concerning suffixes, substitutes, augments, guṇa, vṛddhi, and the elision of phonemes, what is the ultimate division between root and suffix?
This notion that "this is the root" and "this is the suffix" is merely a mental construction.
In this same way, the extraction (*apoddhāra*) of word-meanings (*padārtha*) occurs only through the conceptual construction of sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
As it has been said: "Some divide the word into two, four, or even five parts; having extracted them from sentences, just like bases (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and so forth."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, if words possessed ultimate reality, their nature would necessarily be non-contradictory; however, they are indeed contradictory.
Since we observe that the arrangement of phonemes is common to both nouns and verbs, their nature is not fixed.
Therefore, that is merely conceptual and not real;
nor can it even be ascertained.
Regarding the phrase "kālānadantināgāḥ," what kind of word division (*padavibhāga*) is there? Or rather, because both [interpretations] are possible.

And since the phonemes are identical in both cases, one must determine whether these words are arranged as "Did you go (agāḥ) by means of a black (kālena) tusked (kṛṣṇena) elephant (dantinā hastinā)? or rather, "At the time (kāle), at the moment (samaye), the elephants (nāgāḥ), the tuskers (kariṇaḥ), or the hooded serpents (phaṇinaḥ) roar (nadanti) and make a sound.
Therefore, because there is no fixed rule, the distinction between a word and its meaning is not ultimately real.

Now, if the distinction between words and their respective meanings is established in accordance with the meaning of the sentence as it is first understood, then what is the use of establishing that distinction at that time, since the meaning of the sentence has already been apprehended?

Furthermore, in the expression "there is curd here" (*dadhy atra*) and "there is honey here" (*madhv atra*), even though the phonemes *i* and *u* are not perceived in the words *dadhi* and *madhu*, the comprehension of their respective meanings is observed.
Therefore, it is established that the division of words and phonemes is not ultimately real;
rather, the sentence, being devoid of parts, is the signifier of a sentence-meaning of that very same nature.
Now, one might object: just as there are no phonemes within words and no words within sentences, so too there would be no intermediate sentences within great sentences (*mahāvākya*).
What follows from this? It would follow that even great sentences are not ultimately real (*tāttvika*) in relation to the context (*prakaraṇa*).
And what follows from that? It would follow that even contexts are not [ultimately real] in relation to the entire treatise (*śāstra*).
Does it follow from that as well that this reality of the treatise is indeed one alone, undivided, and non-dual?

It is said: if you ask about reality or understand it, then it is exactly so, O virtuous one. This non-dual Śabdabrahman alone, appearing as if afflicted by the impressions of beginningless ignorance, manifests through the mode of objects (*arthabhāvena*). However, there is no such thing as a denoted object that exists as distinct from the denotative word.
Therefore, this division between the denoted and the denotative is merely conceptual; thus, ignorance itself is resorted to as the means to knowledge.
The nature of speech (*vāgrūpatā*) is the reality (*tattva*) present in every cognition, because it never departs from it.

As it has been said: "If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness, the manifestation would not be manifest, for it is that which performs reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśinī*)."
And this speech appears established in a threefold manner as *vaikharī*, *madhyamā*, and *paśyantī*.

Among these, that speech which consists of a collection of phonemes such as the letter *ga* and so forth, manifested through the sequence of articulatory locations (*sthāna*), producing organs (*karaṇa*), and efforts (*prayatna*), is called *vaikharī*.
The term *vikhara* refers to the aggregate of the body and the sense organs.
Among those, the *vaikharī* is the manifest speech.

As it has been said: "The *vaikharī* speech, which assumes the form of articulated phonemes when the air is expanded within the [articulatory] locations, is dependent upon the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of speakers."

Furthermore, that speech which consists of a sequence being mentally conceptualized, yet is devoid of the manifestation of the forms of phonemes perceivable by the ear, is called the *madhyamā* (intermediate).

As it has been said: "The *madhyamā* speech proceeds, relying solely upon the intellect (*buddhi*), following the form of a sequence, and transcending the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*)."
But that speech which is devoid of the distinctions of objects to be grasped, sequence, and so forth, and whose nature is self-luminous consciousness, is called *paśyantī*.
As it has been said: "But *paśyantī*, because it is undivided, has its sequence entirely withdrawn;
it is the light of its own nature within, the subtle, imperishable speech."
Therefore, enough with this excessive digression; since this very long discussion would cause an interruption to the subject at hand, it shall not be further elaborated.
In this context, however, the purpose is simply this: that linguistic usage does not consist of individual phonemes and words.

Since in the world usage occurs by means of sentences, and since the distinction between part and whole is untenable in that case, the sentence alone is the indivisible signifier, and its indivisible meaning is the signified object. Furthermore, it is not denied that even a subordinate sentence (*avāntaravākya*), being fit for use, is a cause of linguistic usage.
This state of ignorance persists;
therein, let this course of worldly convention remain exactly as it is perceived.
In the state of knowledge, however, all of this is indeed devoid of essence.

Since there is no linguistic usage based on a single phoneme (*varṇa*) or a single word (*pada*), and because such a unit is never employed in isolation, its intrinsic nature is not accepted as real even in this state [of analysis].
Therefore, the sentence-sphoṭa—devoid of sequential order and consisting of imagined, unreal divisions—produces a cognition of its own denoted object of such a kind.
These phonemes, however, being naturally light and established solely in imagination, do not produce a cognition of that meaning; thus, enough with talk of them.
To this it is replied: Is this acceptance of the *sphoṭa* based on the power of inference, or by virtue of the strength of perceptual cognition?

First of all, the nature of the *sphoṭa* cannot be established through inference, because the comprehension of meaning is successfully accomplished by means of a collection of phonemes possessing a specific, perceived sequential order (*anupūrvī*).

Now, it may be argued that the capacity of phonemes to denote meaning has been destroyed by such conceptual alternatives as being "separate" or "combined. This is not so; those are merely ill-conceived alternatives. To begin with, we do not at all accept that phonemes are denotative when they are separate.
They are denotative only when combined.
As for the claim that "there is no such totality because [the causes] arise sequentially," that is incorrect;
for we frequently observe that even things arising sequentially can produce an effect when they are present together.
For example, three stones seen existing simultaneously are observed to hold up a beam when they are all together.
Likewise, it is observed that all morsels, though occurring sequentially, produce a single state of satisfaction;
for if even a single morsel is missing, such satisfaction does not arise.
Therefore, it is only the totality of those morsels that is the cause of satisfaction.
Moreover, even all those morsels cannot be consumed simultaneously.
Similarly, when a single section (anuvāka) is being learned, there is efficacy in the totality of the ritual terminuses (saṃsthās), even though they occur sequentially,
because it is impossible to bring them all to mind through a single terminus alone.
Thus, in the world, the totality of things occurring in sequence is observed.

Even in the Veda, it is observed that the sacrificial procedures beginning with the Āgneya—which possess a collective unity conveyed by the copulative compound *darśapūrṇamāsābhyām* indicating mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), which must necessarily occur in a sequence because they are to be performed on two separate occasions, and which together accomplish a single entitlement (*adhikāra*)—function as a single unit.

Likewise, it is observed that the various repetitions of Soma-drawings, such as "he draws the Aindravāyava" and "he draws the Āśvina," though occurring in a sequence, effect a single primary rite when taken as a whole.
Therefore, this contradiction exists between totality and sequential occurrence.
In this way, even though they occur in succession, the phonemes themselves will be the expressers of meaning.
Now, it may be argued that for things such as morsels of food and the like, it is appropriate that they exist in a sequence,
since their effects— such as satisfaction— are also seen to be accomplished sequentially.
However, from letters being heard in succession, no such measure of comprehension of meaning is seen to be produced.

If this is so, then what effect produced in succession from the Āgneya and other rites is perceived? We reply: it is the intermediate apūrva (intermediate transcendental result), because of the authority of the verbal testimony (*śabda-prāmāṇya*). As for the production of the supreme apūrva, it is said that it will be accomplished when those [intermediate apūrvas] exist in their totality. Now, regarding the production of the intermediate apūrva, what intermediate effect or what production of that effect is perceived in the case of the momentary actions (*kriyā-kṣaṇa*) that constitute parts of the Āgneya and occur in succession?
Moreover, activity proceeds with the intention toward whatever effect is desired;
that [effect] is not perceived anywhere prior to its totality.
For no portion of heaven whatsoever is brought about by an intermediate apūrva, because at that time the purpose of the scripture has not yet been accomplished.
Therefore, what is the use of an intermediate apūrva, even if it were produced?
For whatever effect is generally associated with an intermediate apūrva can also be shown to exist in the case of phonemes as well.
If one asks what that effect is, it will be either the apprehension of their own form or a refinement (saṃskāra).
If it is argued that these two do not possess the status of being parts (*avayava*) of the primary effect, let there be no such status; however, their utility toward it certainly exists.
Furthermore, the conventional usage of "part" and "whole" is difficult to establish even for intermediate and ultimate *apūrvas*.

But in the case of words, it is extremely clear that they indeed possess the capacity to produce the effect known as the knowledge of word-meanings—which constitutes a part of the primary effect characterized by the comprehension of the sentence-meaning—and thus this defect does not manifest in their case.

Even in the case of phonemes, although there is no manifestation of their effect as a whole accumulated through a sequence—just as there is none for the moments of the action of going toward the attainment of a village, or for morsels of food toward satiety, or for constituent parts toward the act of bringing something before one's face—nevertheless, because they perform the effects conducive to that [final result], such as perception and mental impression (*saṃskāra*), a portion of that effect is indeed accomplished; thus, the fact that they operate sequentially is not lost.

In that case, the preceding phonemes, though past, will provide assistance, while the final phoneme is present; thus, this collection of phonemes—just like an imagined aggregate of moments of action—is what conveys the meaning.

Alternatively, even though the phonemes are perceived sequentially, there arises a mental synthetic cognition (*saṃkalanājñāna*) in the form of a retrospective judgment (*anuvyavasāya*) that has all the phonemes as its object; this will serve as the means for conveying the meaning.
Furthermore, a simultaneous mental retrospective judgment is observed even regarding other perishable objects experienced in succession, such as the cognition: "Devadatta has eaten a hundred mangoes.
Nor is this cognition non-existent, doubtful, or sublated.
If such a synthetic cognition were not admitted, many worldly transactions based upon it would perish.

And this synthetic cognition (saṃkalanāpratyaya) is accepted as being variegated in form, having both existent and non-existent phonemes as its object, because it has as its domain both previously experienced and currently being remembered final phonemes. Alternatively, since it occurs when the final phoneme has vanished, it has only non-existent phonemes as its object; yet, being a single entity, it is the cause for the comprehension of meaning. Thus, the dilemmas regarding whether [the phonemes] are taken individually or collectively find no footing.

Now, even in the case of the cognition of synthesis (*saṃkalanā-pratyaya*), if those phonemes appear sequentially, then that [cognition] would be no different from the individual cognitions of the previously arisen phonemes; thus, the phonemes mounted upon it would not be the cause for the comprehension of meaning.

However, if that cognition possesses a form like a single cluster of flowers, then since no sequence is perceived therein, those phonemes—even if their order were reversed—would bring about the comprehension of meaning.
It is replied:

For it is the synthetic cognition (*saṃkalana-pratyaya*), which arises immediately after the experience of a series of phonemes (*varṇamālā*) in a specific sequence, that is the cause of the comprehension of meaning; it is not merely the perception of a cluster-like form.
Furthermore, at that time, from where could there be any suspicion of a reversed order?
In the appearance of a cluster, there is no sequence whatsoever.

Whose reversal or non-reversal would there be, given that this collective cognition arises immediately after those preceding cognitions of the phonemes, which appear only in a specific sequence? Since those preceding cognitions of the phonemes appear in a fixed order, how could there be a conceptualization of reversal?

Therefore, there is no fault: those phonemes, possessing a sequence determined by their initial recitation, produce the comprehension of meaning when they are mounted upon a synthesizing cognition that appears simultaneously immediately following them.

Or rather, let the letters themselves be the conveyors of meaning, just as it has been described by the venerable author of the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya: that the final letter, accompanied by the impressions (saṃskāra) produced by the preceding letters [is what conveys the meaning].

Now, has it not been stated here that the capacity of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) to produce the cognition of an object has never been observed before, since its function pertains only to memory?
Is this some kind of royal decree—
that memory alone must be produced by the latent impression?
This is not a royal decree, but rather a logical injunction;
for that which is called a "latent impression" (*saṃskāra*) is not some independent entity.
Rather, it is that cause of memory within oneself with respect to objects grasped through impressions of intense practice, reverence, or repeated cognition.

And that capacity, being postulated solely on the basis of its effect, which is memory, cannot possess another capacity for the production of the cognition of an object; for what other effect could it produce apart from that very effect for which it was postulated? Furthermore, the experience of the object is the cause for the production of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the cause of remembrance.
However, we do not perceive any cause for the birth of this latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—which has its basis in experience and consists of a novel occurrence;
therefore, it does not become a cause for the cognition of an object.
This is not the core point: for a person whose mind is conditioned by the experience of phonemes, the cognition of meaning is observed;
indeed, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is not the power of memory, but rather a quality of the self (*ātman*) called *vāsanā*.
And that [cognition] is capable of producing not only memory but also the comprehension of an object; for us, perception is the authority in all cases,
and its capacity to generate recollection is likewise understood from such observation.
Thus, this production of experience is indeed observed to arise from that [word];
yet we shall explain that the phonemes and their experiences have passed away, and no other essence of sound (śabdatattva) is experienced.
Nevertheless, the comprehension of meaning does occur.
It cannot be without a cause;
for, since it does not arise apart from a cause, it implies a cause.
That which is its cause is the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Thus, just like memory, the cognition of an object—being its effect—is indeed an inferential indicator of that [impression].
As for the question, "From where does such an impression (saṃskāra) arise?", this is a query of the dull-witted, because it is well-known that it has experience as its cause.
And so they say: "For this is the nature of things (vastudharma): that a vivid experience deposits the seed of memory."
Now, as for what is called the "seed of memory," how could that be the seed of experience?
This is not a fixed rule that it is the seed of memory alone;
rather, experience first deposits such a quality (dharma) within the self.
Even that difference in effects does not seek another cause for its production;
and it has been stated that this difference in its effects is understood from such observation.
Alternatively, what is the use of this insistence? The linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*) does not produce the comprehension of meaning directly;
it will do so by means of memory (*smṛti*).

Due to the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) left by the preceding phonemes, there is recollection (*smaraṇa*), while with the final phoneme, there is direct experience (*anubhava*) via the auditory faculty; thus, the cognition of the meaning would be produced by phonemes that are both being recollected and being experienced.
What is the fault in this?
[The opponent objects: "Surely, following the power of the impressions deposited through the sequence of experiences, the recollections themselves ought to arise sequentially and not simultaneously."
And thus, the same previous fault remains because of the absence of totality.
This is not a fault.

Through successive experiences directed toward various phonemes, a single refinement (*saṃskāra*) of such a nature is imparted to the self—like the repeated heating of gold—that by means of it, the self remembers all previously perceived phonemes simultaneously.

If it is argued that the production of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) from a [preceding] impression is something extraordinary (*alaukika*), it is not so; for this is established through the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana*).

Since the act of utterance is momentary, if one does not admit an impression produced by it which itself generates further impressions, then the final utterance would not differ from the first utterance.
What follows from this?
Even in a full human lifetime, one would not even master a single section of the Veda.

Now, is this kind of process to be postulated for the sake of establishing a single recollection, or is it rather the capacity of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) to be the cause of the cognition of the meaning that must be postulated? In either case, this is a postulation of the unseen (*adṛṣṭakalpanā*). Therefore, we do not see what partiality there is toward the latent impression, nor what animosity toward the *sphoṭa*, such that the former is postulated while the latter is not.

On this point, it has been stated by that very commentator of auspicious name: "In the case of the conceptualization of a word, there is both that [conceptualization] and the conceptualization of the word."
Is it not the case that there is no contradiction with conceptual construction?
For a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra) remains exactly as it is conventionally established;
what conceptual construction could there be in that regard?
For we have not overstepped the nature of *saṃskāra* as having memory as its sole cause, as you have done.
How is it that you have not overstepped [the bounds of logic]?
For even by you, the fact that all phonemes (varṇa) produce a single recollection regarding their object has been postulated as a matter of course;
indeed, the very same path that leads to the comprehension of meaning from the phonemes is also the path for the manifestation of the sphoṭa.
And having postulated that [the cognition], the word is likewise postulated as something else.
Therefore, while bypassing the fact that the *saṃskāra*—which is known by both parties—is the cause of recollection, we have merely asserted that it is the cause of the comprehension of meaning.
You, however, starting from the very root, have produced an entirely novel universe.

First, the existence of a word that is unprecedented, then its distinctness from the phonemes, and furthermore its lack of constituent parts—all these are postulated; how then is there not a burden of conceptual construction (*kalpanāgurutva*)?
As it has been said: "The existence and the distinction, as well as the exclusion of parts—these would be additional for you; therefore, this effort [is directed] toward the cognitions of meaning."

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that at the very moment of the cognition of the first phoneme, the reality of the *sphoṭa* is manifested and is led by each subsequent cognition to become the object of an increasingly superior apprehension, like the reality of a jewel—this is an unequal analogy.
For since a jewel possesses parts, there is room for subsequent cognitions that grasp subtler specific parts not yet made objects of the first cognition.
But the *sphoṭa*, being partless like the nature of a phoneme itself, has its entire essence manifested by the very first phoneme.
What, then, will other phonemes do? Furthermore, the manifestation of a single part is impossible for a phoneme that is partless, as it has been said:
"Even when a sound is uttered with the slightest effort, the cognition..."
Or else, it does not apprehend the color at all, or [it apprehends it] clearly and in its entirety.

As for the second example cited—that just as a *śloka* or an *anuvāka*, though initially grasped through one arrangement, becomes more clearly distinguished through the practice of other arrangements, so too the *sphoṭa* will undergo an intensified manifestation through the subsequent letters—this too is not a fitting example, because it is impossible for a *śloka* or an *anuvāka* to be partless (*anaṃśa*).

Certain parts, whether consisting of phonemes or words, which do not manifest in the first cognition, will become manifest in that [subsequent] cognition when it has acquired excellence through repeated practice.
But since the *sphoṭa* is partless, like a single phoneme, what connection with excellence could there be for the cognition in that case? Therefore, this example as well is not consistent.
Furthermore, those who think that because the sphoṭa is manifested by sound (dhvani), there is no occasion for the conceptualization of phonemes (varṇa) with respect to it—
they too do not see correctly;
for the cognition of the word-sound (śabda) does not arise from sounds unless the cognition of the phonemes has preceded them.
Furthermore, because the distinctions between phonemes are not perceived when they are uttered too rapidly, there is no comprehension of meaning from such a word.

Now, if it is argued that sounds, while bringing about the manifestation of the word, display an unreal differentiation of phonemes (varṇa) in accordance with the places of articulation and the organs of production— just as a sword [reflects] a dark complexion and so forth on a face—
that too is incorrect, because there is no cause for such unreality;
for the phonemes are indeed perceived by an unimpeded cognition.
But no word is perceived beyond that [phoneme].
If it were said that what is not perceived exists, while what is perceived does not exist, it would follow that the rabbit does not exist but its horn does.
Therefore, this path also is not capable of avoiding the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
Therefore, it has been well said: "[In the conceptualization of a word, there is both that [conceptualization] and the conceptualization of the word]."
Therefore, since the sequence that must be relied upon for the apprehension of the sphoṭa can be relied upon for the cognition of the meaning itself, what is the use of that sphoṭa?

Others, however, maintain that phonemes convey meaning by possessing existence immediately following their perception; this is not accepted here because, due to the momentariness of phonemes, existence after perception is impossible.
In every respect, the conveyance of meaning by phonemes follows established linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*); it is accepted exactly as it was previously observed.
Thus it has been said: "As many as there are, and of whatever kind."
As for that which was stated here in opposition—namely, "how many and of what kind?"—the cognitions themselves must be questioned therein; thus, "we are not ascetics" is a mere trifle.
Furthermore, as for what was further asserted— that phonemes might convey meaning even when employed in a reversed order,
or that the sequence itself might be the *sphoṭa*— that too is not sound.
For a "sequence" (krama) is indeed nothing other than a distinction of time.
Nor can time itself be the sphoṭa.
Furthermore, sequence is not an independent signifier, nor does it reside in some other category of entity; rather, it is dependent solely upon the phonemes.
Regarding this, it has been said: "Even though both [phonemes and sequence] exist, one must understand which among them is the signifier of the meaning here:
are the phonemes signifiers when endowed with sequence, or is it the sequence residing in the phonemes?"

As for the claim that "sequence is a constituent part of those things possessing sequence," what need is there for it to be established by reasoning? It is merely an attribute of them; it is not accepted as a separate entity.

Therefore, since those phonemes which are observed to convey a certain meaning when they appear in a specific sequence will convey that same meaning when they appear in that same sequence, the comprehension of meaning does not arise from a *sphoṭa*.
Thus, it is established that neither inference based on an effect (*kāryānumāna*) nor presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is capable of proving the existence of the *sphoṭa*.
As for the claim that the common usage "we understand the meaning from the word" supports the position of the *sphoṭa*, that too is without substance;
for once it has been established by the aforementioned reasoning that phonemes (*varṇa*) possess the capacity to denote meaning, such usage is equally possible even on that [phonemic] view.
Now, how is this possible? First of all, the term "saṃskāra" is not expressed by the word "sound," for there is no such conventional usage in the world.
Furthermore, it is difficult to establish the linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) regarding a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) that serves as the expressive word;
for one's own comprehension from a word is preceded by the comprehension of another.
Moreover, a mental impression residing in another person cannot be apprehended while producing comprehension in that other person, because it is imperceptible (*parokṣatvāt*).

Furthermore, regarding the word "word" (*śabda*) as it applies to phonemes (*varṇa*), does it apply to each individual phoneme or to the collection of phonemes? If the word "word" were to apply to each individual phoneme, there would be no comprehension of meaning from the word, because it is impossible for a single phoneme to be expressive.
On the other hand, the word "word" cannot apply to a collection [of phonemes], because it is a generic term (*jātiśabda*).

For when individual instances are expressed by words ending in dual or plural suffixes, a generic term ending in the singular suffix is not used in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with them.

For it is not the case that one says, "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are a person," nor that "the dhava, khadira, and palāśa trees are a tree"; likewise, it is also not the case that "the phonemes *ga*, *au*, and the visarga are a sound.

If it is argued that the word "sound" (*śabda*) must denote a collection—just as the word "forest" (*vana*) denotes a collection of trees—and not a genus-term, we say no. For in the case of the forest, we observe designations that distinguish it from the collection, such as "the forest of mangoes" (*āmraṇāṃ vanam*) and "the forest of wood-apples" (*kapitthānāṃ vanam*). But here there is no such designation of distinction, because we do not see expressions such as "the sound of the *ga*-phoneme and so forth."
Now, if one should say: "The word 'forest' is also employed even without distinction, as in 'the mango trees and so forth are the forest';
likewise, here too, one will employ [the expression] 'the phonemes *ga* and so forth are the word,'" this also is not the case.

In the case of a forest and the like, since the designation of difference is established through the application [of the term] to each individual tree, and since it is a collective term, it is appropriate to use the expression "the mango trees and so forth are the forest" by means of the metaphorical identification of the whole with its parts. However, in this case, the expression "the word consisting of the phonemes *ga* and so forth" is never seen as a designation of distinction; therefore, its status as a collective term is untenable. Consequently, for those who maintain that words consist of phonemes (*varṇa*), this designation—"we understand the meaning from the word"—is in every respect unaccountable.
It is said:
what is the use of this being either logical or illogical?
If this is logical, then what of it?
Even if it is not tenable, what follows from that?
For the status of a thing does not depend upon worldly designations.
But do not the authors of the treatises themselves employ such usage, as in the statement: "one expresses a state of being by means of a verb"?
No;
for even from the usage of the authors of treatises, it is not possible to accept a meaning that lacks authoritative basis.
And what is this so-called "worldly designation" as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
Inference (*anumāna*) has already been rejected,
and perception (*pratyakṣa*) will also be rejected.
And no other means of valid cognition applies to the proof of the sphoṭa; therefore, this grandiosity regarding the sphoṭa based on an investigation of worldly designations is misplaced.
Nor is this worldly designation entirely inconsistent with the view that the word consists of phonemes;

for when the final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions produced by the preceding phonemes, is the expressive agent, this designation is perfectly consistent, because it is a single entity and possesses the nature of speech (śabda).
Even in the view that phonemes (*varṇa*) possess denotative power when mounted upon a synthetic cognition (*saṃkalanāpratyaya*), there is no fault.
For this word *śabda* is not employed in conjunction with a word for distinction [such as *bheda*], as in the expression: "We understand the meaning from the word consisting of the phoneme *ga*, etc.
However, the generic term (*jātiśabda*) *śabda* in the singular number is not contradictory even when referring to many phonemes.
Furthermore, on the theory of *sphoṭa*, this designation "from sound" (*śabdāt*) is even more untenable, because the meaning of the nominal stem is absent;
for people in common usage are not seen to employ the word "sound" (*śabda*) with respect to the *sphoṭa* as they do with respect to the phonemes (*varṇa*).

The definition of sound (*śabda*) as "that which is the cause of the comprehension of meaning" is incorrect, because it is over-extended (*vyabhicāra*) to smoke and other such things. Even if, by considering the context, the definition of sound is stated as "being the cause of the comprehension of meaning, qualified by being perceptible by the auditory organ," this is not established with respect to the *sphoṭa*, because the *sphoṭa* lacks the status of being an object of auditory cognition.
And since the very quality of being apprehended by the auditory organ is sufficient to exclude everything else, that alone is appropriate; what is the use of mentioning both?
Furthermore, since the quality of being apprehended by the auditory organ belongs only to phonemes (*varṇa*) and not to any other entity, it follows that phonemes alone are words (*śabda*).
As it has been said: "And [phonemes], independent of one another, are perceived by the auditory cognition in their own form."
"Only the phonemes are determined, not two things consisting of a preceding and a succeeding element."

If it is argued that being perceptible by the ear is the definition of sound because it also exists in [the universal] existence (*sattā*) and so forth, we say no; for what is intended is the restriction that it is perceptible by the ear *alone*.
If it is argued that the restriction [of the definition] is unestablished because [the object] is apprehended by both the ear and the mind, we say no;
for the purpose of the restriction is to exclude those of the same class, and by it only the eye and so forth are excluded, not the mind.
If it is argued that [the reason] nevertheless deviates with respect to "sound-ness" (śabdatva), we say no;
for this is because a qualification—namely, "provided that it possesses a genus"—is required as understood from the context.
Nor is there deviation even with respect to the sound of thunder and the like, since those too are admitted to possess "sound-ness."
Thus it was said by the author of the Bhāṣya: "And this sound is of two kinds: consisting of phonemes (varṇa) and mere resonance (dhvani)."

However, it has been stated that "the capacity to convey meaning" is not a defining characteristic [of a word], because even in the case of a sound consisting of phonemes whose relationship [to a meaning] has not been grasped, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of it not being a word due to the absence of that capacity.
Furthermore, since that very same sound would become a word once the cognition of its relationship [to a meaning] occurs at a later time, this definition is unstable.

Furthermore, we do not understand what the intention was behind the suspicion that the universals, qualities, actions, and so forth—which are the denotata of words—might themselves be of the nature of sound, along with the subsequent refutation of that suspicion in the context of defining the nature of sound; for these [denotata] are perceived as having forms that are entirely distinct [from sound].

Therefore, since sound is what is apprehended by the auditory organ and the sphoṭa lacks the property of being apprehended by the auditory organ, it is established that the common worldly expression, "We understand the meaning from the word," is favorable only to the proponents of phonemes (varṇavādins) and not to the proponents of the sphoṭa.

But how is it that the audibility of the sphoṭa is not accepted, given that there exists a single-formed cognition produced by the auditory organ—cognized by each person individually—as "a word" or "a sentence"? And it has already been stated that the phonemes cannot be its objective support.
This statement is not tenable.

For here, in the case of a brindled cow and others, the cognition "this is a cow" arising with respect to each individual animal takes as its object a form common to all those individuals; that is accepted as the universal "cowness.

Likewise, if for every letter the cognition "this is a word" or "this is a sentence" were to arise—just as in the case of a genus—then we would perceive some single form residing in all the letters as the word or the sentence; however, such a cognition does not exist.

Just as at the very first moment of visual perception, a cognition of an effect such as a cloth arises regarding its parts like threads without the apprehension of their difference, so too, if there were a cognition of a "word" or a "sentence" independent of the grasping of the individual forms of each letter as they arise in succession, then we might accept that the word or sentence is a single entity like a composite whole; but this is not the case.
For a word is not produced by letters in the way a cloth is produced by threads or a mat by *vīraṇa* grass.
As for the fact that the cognition "cow, cow" is observed to grasp [the object] as non-different, that is due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of being a single [phoneme].
However, when there is contact with distinct [phonemes], as in the case of "Devadatta" and so forth, one experiences only the gradual apprehension of multiple syllables.
And this is not the case in cognitions such as "cloth," where its constituent parts ever appear as separated.
Therefore, a sentence does not appear as an undivided unity, like a composite whole, nor like a universal, nor like a single word.
But is it not the case that this very cognition which arises from the word "word" is itself the cognition of the sphoṭa?
"What now?
Is it that the very universal of 'sound-ness' (śabdatva-sāmānya) is itself the sphoṭa? Not so; this is the sphoṭa itself, not that universal of sound-ness.

For that which is called a "universal" (sāmānya) is that wherein, upon the perception of one individual, there is a mental synthesis (anusandhāna) of another individual, as when the apprehension of a *śābaleya* cow involves the [recollection of] a *bāhuleya*.
But here, upon the apprehension of the sound *ga*, there is no synthesis of the sound *va*; thus, this is not a universal.
Rather, this appearance of a single form has as its object the very reality of the word (*śabdatattva*).
And the reality of sound is called *sphoṭa*.
It is understood.
For it was out of that very fear that some, suspecting a *sphoṭa*, denied the universal of "soundness" (*śabdatva*);
yet this alarm is misplaced.
For *śabdatva* (the universal "sound-ness") is not the *sphoṭa*.
For with respect to each individual phoneme (*varṇa*), there is the cognition "this is sound, this is sound," yet there is no *varṇasphoṭa*.
Thus, it is precisely this universal *śabdatva* that is the objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition of "sound," not the *sphoṭa*.
However, it has already been determined that when a universal is established, the recollection of other individual instances is not a cause;
therefore, even in the cognition of non-words, the sphoṭa does not appear, just as it does not appear in the cognitions of words and sentences.

And one person has spoken the truth: that this cognition of words and sentences is of the same status as the cognitions of forests, armies, and so forth—which are based on their performing a single function.
Nor is there a lack of confidence regarding the cognitions of universals and the like, since their distinctness has already been demonstrated.

Furthermore, as for the objection regarding mutual dependence raised concerning the cognition of non-difference—which is based on the performance of a single function—namely, that "the cognition of words and sentences is preceded by the comprehension of a single meaning, and the comprehension of a single meaning is preceded by the cognition of words and sentences," that too is not correct.

We have already stated that this comprehension of meaning is produced solely by the phonemes (*varṇa*) being remembered and experienced, and not preceded by the discernment of indivisible words (*pada*); how, then, could there be mutual dependence? To argue that "without the oneness of word and sentence, how could the comprehension of the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning be of a single form? is an exceedingly foolish objection.
For the distinction or non-distinction of cognitions follows the distinction or non-distinction of their objects, not the distinction or non-distinction of the means [by which they are apprehended].
Even though the means—such as the eyes, light, the internal organ (manas), and so forth—are distinct, a cognition that grasps a single, undivided object is indeed produced.
Therefore, in this case, since the cognition of the word-meaning is unitary, let the word-meaning which is its object be one;
but the word itself is not one, for it is merely the cause [of that cognition].

Since the cognition of the sentence-meaning is also unitary, let there be a single sentence-meaning, but not a single sentence. This—namely, the capacity to convey a single meaning—is the cause for grouping together the many phonemes that occur in succession; it does not, however, imply the non-difference of the word and the sentence.

Furthermore, the grammarians are indeed deceived; they believe that there is no difference between the word and the sentence, and they maintain that the meaning of a word is non-different from the word itself. However, this is merely their delusion, because the difference between them is established by firm means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Moreover, the superimposition of the word [upon its meaning] is not accepted because it contradicts actual experience; so enough of that discussion.
Therefore, it is established that the *sphoṭa* is not even accessible through perception.

Now, one might object: since the cognition of the sentence-meaning is unitary, and because the unity or diversity of cognitions follows from the unity or diversity of their objects, the sentence-meaning must be unitary.
To this we reply: certainly it is unitary, but it is not partless; for even things like a jar, though unitary, possess parts.
As for that which is called "partlessness," it is an utter statement devoid of skill in reflecting upon consciousness; the inquiry as to whether parts exist or do not exist is entirely irrelevant.
It is only proper for the wise to consider whether that which is partless exists or does not exist.
This is because the distinction between words and their respective meanings appears clearly in every sentence, whereas neither the sentence nor its meaning ever appears as having undivided parts.
If it is argued that there is indeed the cognition of the parts, but that [cognition] is erroneous, we say no;
because there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka).
Furthermore, some cause for error must be stated.
If you say it is "similarity," we do not know to what it belongs or with what.

For if primary constituent parts were established somewhere, then one might understand that there is an illusion elsewhere due to similarity to them, even in the absence of those parts; but this is not the case, because all sentences are partless.
Even in the case of Narasiṃha, the human parts and the lion parts are recognized separately.
In the same way, here too, if [the truth of the whole] is accepted, then certainly the truth of the individual members must be admitted in some sentence.

Even in a variegated painting, the forms of yellow orpiment, vermilion, and so forth; in a beverage, the flavors of cinnamon, cardamom, and so forth; and in a musical mode (*grāmarāga*), the collection of notes such as *ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, and *gāndhāra*—are all perceived separately. Therefore, these are not examples of partless [wholes].

If it is argued that the cognitions of the painting and so forth are the examples, we say: certainly. We maintain that even the cognition of the meaning of a sentence is indeed partless, because all cognitions, being impartite, are devoid of constituent parts.
However, the object made the content of a cognition is possessed of parts in both the case of the example and the thing illustrated.
Therefore, it is not logical to claim that the sentence and its meaning are without parts.

As for what was further asserted—that the cognition of the relationship arises from the linguistic usage of elders only with respect to the sentence and its meaning, and not with respect to the word and its meaning because there is no usage involving individual words—that too is incorrect;
for even when learning occurs through a sentence, it extends down to the level of the individual words.
For in this way, the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence will be possible even from a sentence newly composed by one whose mind is refined through knowledge of words and their meanings.

Since sentences are infinite due to the variety of the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*), it is impossible to acquire proficiency (*vyutpatti*) with respect to every individual sentence; furthermore, such proficiency will not even be required.
For otherwise, it would necessarily have to be depended upon.
As for the claim that a word is never used in isolation, that is false;
and the further claim that a subordinate sentence is never used in place of a major sentence would likewise be false.
If you argue that a word is used in its own primary sense, we reply that a word is indeed used in its own primary sense in certain instances.
Where the meaning of other words is obtained through the force of the context and so forth, there they utter only that word which has not yet been reached.
Furthermore, even during the occasion of learning the text, the determination of the phonemes' own form (*svarūpa*) is fruitful.

Or, even if phonemes and words were not to possess such fruitfulness, nevertheless, their existence as distinct entities is unavoidable—just as, for example, the parts of a chariot must exist even if they lack the individual capacity to perform the functions of the chariot.
If it is argued that the parts of a chariot exist for the sake of another effect [the chariot], then words and phonemes will likewise exist for the sake of another effect.
If it is said that the parts of a chariot produce some mere portion of the chariot's function, then words also certainly produce some mere portion of the function of a sentence.
Furthermore, certain phonemes are indeed meaningful.
Therefore, words and phonemes are not non-existent.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that just as a sentence has words, words have phonemes, so too phonemes must have further constituent parts—this is a novel kind of scholarship!
For it does not follow that because pots have parts, atoms must also have parts;
nor does it follow that because atoms are partless, pots must also be partless.
For the apprehension and non-apprehension of things are what establish their reality:
whatever is apprehended in a certain way exists in that way;
whatever is not apprehended in a certain way does not exist in that way.
Furthermore, parts are perceived in sentences and words, but not in phonemes;
for it has been said:
"Even when a word is uttered with the slightest effort, the cognition..."
Or else, it does not grasp the color at all clearly and in its entirety.
Therefore, this objection raised by the ignorant—that there should be parts even for a phoneme, or that there should be none for words and sentences—is [unfounded].

For this reason as well, both the sentence and its meaning possess parts, because one observes the arising and passing away of their respective meanings through the arising and passing away of the words.
By this very logic, it should be understood that even the constituent parts of words—such as roots and suffixes—are real and not established merely through conceptual construction.
For instance, in the cases of *vṛkṣam* and *vṛkṣeṇa*, while the meaning of the root remains constant, the meaning of the suffix differs.
In the cognitions "tree" and "jar," while the meaning of the suffix follows along, the meaning of the base changes.
In that case, it is determined that whatever meaning follows a particular word is its meaning.
How then can the parts [of words] be unreal? Furthermore, in cases such as *kūpa*, *sūpa*, and *yūpa*, even though there is a continuity of phonemes, no continuity of meaning is observed.
Furthermore, the claim that there is a sequence of phonemes because the cognition of meaning occurs without [any other] cause is incorrect;

for a cognition that has not yet arisen is not produced by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), such that one might suspect its production in cases like [the perception of] a well. Rather, once the cognition is established, the function of these two [concomitances] lies in determining the restriction regarding the extent of the expressive portion.

Furthermore, since the apprehension of meaning is not observed to follow from the apprehension of phonemes in one instance, it is not reasonable to forcibly impose it elsewhere even when it is not seen.
The objection raised regarding the deviation [of the inference] based on the case of a line of ants following a cloud of dust is not well-founded;
for by observing a line of ants devoid of a mass of dust, one ascertains that such a line does not produce the cognition [of an elephant].

However, although there is deviation in the case of individual elephants, young elephants, horses, and so forth, the cloud of dust is understood to be caused by them precisely because the commonality of the form of many living beings is never absent.

As for the claim that because the individual word-meanings are lost in terms like *aśvakarṇa* (horse-ear), the same must apply elsewhere as well—that too is not tenable. For in certain cases, by the force of context or meaning, the power of the individual components becomes subordinate; thus, while the manifestation of another entity occurs with the individual word-meanings set aside, there is no total absence of those component meanings. This is because we observe the comprehension of those very meanings in other uses, whether in isolation or in combination, such as the separate usages:
*aśvam āroha* ("Mount the horse") and *karṇe kuṇḍalam* ("An earring in the ear").

However, when it is intended to convey the meaning "the ear of a horse," the compound usage *aśvakarṇaḥ* is observed not to abandon that meaning; thus, the constituent parts are not entirely devoid of meaning.
