Furthermore, the claim that the rule for the division of base and suffix cannot be established because it contradicts subsequent explanations is also not tenable, due to the authority of the words of the most reliable teachers.
For we shall accept the division of base and suffix as unerring precisely in the system of Pāṇini, known as the *Trimunivyākaraṇa*.
Moreover, there is generally no dispute among all commentators regarding a significant portion [of the system].
However, mere disagreement regarding suffixes and the like is of no consequence;
therefore, because the portions consisting of stem and suffix possess ultimate reality, they cannot be separated by mere conceptual construction.

As for the objection that the knowledge of word-division is difficult to achieve because of the commonality of phonemes—as in the case of *kālena dantinā gāḥ*—that too is without merit, because there exist means for discerning the distinction between words, such as the recollection of accents and so forth.
For instance, the form of the verb *sarāmaḥ* is different from that of the noun;
even if it were a noun, *saḥ* and *rāmaḥ* would still be two distinct words.
The form of one of these two is different;

even in a single word such as *saharāmeṇa* ("together with Rāma"), the form is different. For those possessing specialized application, everything is auspicious; thus, the determination of the division of words is not impossible.

As for the argument that even when such word-forms as *dadhy atra* and *madhv atra* are not observed, there is still comprehension of their meaning, that too is not a fault; for some say that these very same words are merely slightly modified, and thus they are recognized as such.

Alternatively, just as the words *dadhi* and *madhu* ending in *ik* vowels are used, so too words ending in *yaṇ* vowels are correct in other contexts because they are derived from those very forms; thus, even words ending in *yaṇ* will convey meaning. Enough, then, with such vain utterances born of false hopes!

Furthermore, for what purpose do the elders exert such great effort in the acquisition of words if they themselves are unreal? If it is argued that even the unreal serves as a means to the real, we say no, because this has never been observed. As for the examples cited here—such as a false snake-bite causing actual fainting—they are not truly so, because even the *fear* of poison can be the cause of that effect.
For fear is indeed a cognition (*buddhi*), and a cognition is certainly not without a cause.
Nor is it the case that cognition is non-existent.
Furthermore, as for the claim that even unreal written characters convey a real meaning, that too is the speech of one who is ignorant;
for the lines themselves are real in their own nature.
And these [lines] serve as indicators of the phonemes for one whose mind has been refined by the instructions of Khaṇḍika and Uṣadhyāya;

thus, because the relationship [between them] has been grasped, the comprehension of meaning arises from the phonemes inferred from the lines. Therefore, they are not unreal, even though they are means to the real.

The notion that "this is the letter *ga*" is an error of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), arising from the metaphorical treatment of the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*) as non-different.
Just as barley-meal measured by a *prastha* is called a "prastha," so too, because the letter *ga* is inferred from the line, the line itself is said to be the letter *ga*.
If this were not accepted, even one ignorant of the script would understand the meaning from it, since the lines—which are not the actual phonemes—would still be present.
But this is not the case;
therefore, the comprehension of meaning from written marks is preceded by the inference of the phonemes.
Because the object is familiar and because time is subtle, the sequence is not perceived, but it is not otherwise that the comprehension arises from them.
Therefore, since words and their meanings possess ultimate reality, it is established that neither the sentence nor the sentence-meaning is partless.

Furthermore, as for the attempt to demonstrate that the non-dual Śabdabrahman alone exists by means of the path of negating sentences, word-parts, words, and phonemes—we shall explain the meditative absorption (samādhi) regarding this in detail further on.
Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding the threefold nature of speech, that too is not accepted;
for it is well known that there is only one speech, namely *vaikharī*, which is designated as "speech."
Internal discourse is described as the middle speech; this is essentially of the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), not a division of vocal speech.
Scratching out both the signified and the signifier, it does not abandon its own form, which is the state of pure awareness.
The expression "they see" is merely an alternative name devised for non-conceptual cognition.
For consciousness, whose nature is luminosity, does not possess the form of speech eternally.

Once this [consciousness] has arisen as the manifestation of an object, there may or may not subsequently follow a verbal reflective awareness (*avamarśa*); yet, consciousness never touched by speech would ever become insentient.
Let this discussion of the Word-Brahman rest; let us follow the subject at hand.
Thus, these phonemes, made objects of a cognition expanded [by reflection], possess the status of being words or sentences; and they alone are the expressive agents.
There is no *sphoṭa* other than that which appears to the auditory sense, nor is such a thing capable of producing a cognition of the meaning when its manifestation is obstructed.
When the sphoṭa has thus been refuted and it is established that phonemes (varṇas) are the expressive units, someone says: "Granted that the cognition of word-meanings arises from the phonemes;
however, they lack the capacity for the cognition of sentence-meaning."
From what, then, does the comprehension of the sentence-meaning arise? He says: from the word-meanings.
And thus, since the phonemes have fulfilled their purpose in the comprehension of word-meanings, they possess no capacity regarding the sentence-meaning; rather,
it is the word-meanings that remain with their capacities unimpaired,
and they are the producers of the cognition of the sentence-meaning.
For the capacities of phonemes in their functions are postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
In that regard, since the cognition of word-meanings cannot be accounted for otherwise, the capacity of phonemes to convey them is understood according to the principle already stated.
However, the comprehension of sentence-meaning can be accounted for in other ways as well; therefore, it does not require one to postulate a capacity for them in that respect.

Furthermore, do the phonemes (varṇas), by producing a single mental impression (saṃskāra), cause one to understand both the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning, or do they produce distinct impressions? In that regard, how could two effects arise from a single mental impression?
Nor is it perceived that there is any impression for these [phonemes] other than the preceding one.
Since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs even otherwise, there is no basis for postulating multiple latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Moreover, in the case of words, when the preceding phonemes have not passed away too long ago, it is possible for the intellect to bring them together so that a synthesis occurs at the moment of the final phoneme; however, in the case of sentences, the synthesis of a succession of syllables that have been obscured for a much longer time is extremely difficult, unprecedented, and thus impossible.
Yet, when words are uttered with an interval between them, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is indeed observed, even where there is not even a trace of a synthesis of the preceding phonemes.
Therefore, the phonemes are not the causes of the cognition of the sentence-meaning.
Furthermore, do the phonemes, while conveying both the meaning of individual words and the meaning of the sentence, convey them simultaneously or sequentially?
In that regard, it is impossible for those uttered only once to effect both [meanings] simultaneously, because it is incapable of being done.

Even in the view that there is a sequence, if the presentation of the sentence-meaning occurs first, that is incorrect, because one does not observe the cognition of a sentence-meaning in someone who has not understood the word-meanings.

If, on the other hand, the presentation of the word-meanings occurs first and only then the communication of the sentence-meaning, then—alas! since the cognition of the sentence-meaning is already established through the cognition of the word-meanings—why resort to the labor of another operation?
Therefore, words have their capacity exhausted in the presentation of the word-meanings.
Thus it is established that the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises from the word-meanings.
Moreover, it is understood through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the meanings of its constituent words.
For one who, due to a mental lapse, does not comprehend the word-meanings even when the words have been heard, certainly does not comprehend the sentence-meaning;
whereas one who knows the word-meanings from other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), even when the words have not been heard, indeed comprehends the sentence-meaning.
"For one who sees a white form, hears the sound of neighing, and hears the sound of the stamping of hooves, there arises the cognition: 'A white horse is running.'"
"Or [a sentence] seen as devoid of words is nowhere found without word-meanings."
Therefore, this cognition of the sentence-meaning does not deviate from the apprehension of word-meanings;
however, since it does deviate from the apprehension of individual words, it cannot be the effect of those [words] alone.
As for the claim that word-meanings cannot be the cause of the comprehension of sentence-meaning because they are individually deviant and collectively uncommon, that too is incorrect.
To begin with, we do not even accept that they possess the capacity to convey meaning individually;
as for their being uncommon when combined, even if that were the case, it would do no harm to our position.

For these [words] are not indicators that depend upon the apprehension of a relation in the manner of a logical mark (*liṅga*), such that they would be impossible due to their uniqueness (*asādhāraṇya*).

Rather, even when the relation has not been previously grasped, they mutually coalesce through the consideration of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and intention (*tātparya*).
That very collection of word-meanings thus coalesced, or one distinguished by the others, is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
Nor should it be suspected that the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is non-verbal (*aśābda*) in this way, because it is verbal insofar as it is rooted in the comprehension of words;
for when the word-meanings are understood from the words, the sentence-meaning is understood—thus everything is faultless.
As it has been said: "For words, having denoted their respective meanings, cease their operation."
Now, it is held that the word-meanings themselves, once understood, bring about the understanding of the sentence-meaning.
To this it is replied: the comprehension of the sentence-meaning does not arise from the word-meanings, but rather from the sentence itself.
Thus, there is the common consensus that "this is the sentence-meaning," and not "this is the word-meaning.

For just as a word—consisting of an imagined collection of phonemes—produces the cognition of a word-meaning, so too a sentence—consisting of an imagined collection of words—will produce the cognition of a sentence-meaning.

Now, it might be argued: "There is no sentence other than a collection of words; rather, the words themselves are the sentence. And since words have their purpose fulfilled in their own individual meanings, they lack the capacity for the meaning of the sentence. This is not correct, because word-meanings also have their purpose fulfilled. Where, then, do they have their purpose fulfilled?
In one's own practice.
But surely, words, having fulfilled their purpose in their own individual cognition, bring about the cognition of word-meanings;
how then can those same words again bring about the cognition of the sentence-meaning?
However, word-meanings, after their own comprehension, do not have their purpose fulfilled anywhere else; therefore, let them be the producers of the cognition of the sentence-meaning.
This is not so, because the final term has no other purpose elsewhere.
Some maintain that the final word itself, aided by the recollection of the preceding words, is called the "sentence" (vākya),
and that the meaning of that sentence is the meaning of the sentence as qualified by the meanings of the preceding words;
therefore, the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises from the sentence alone.

However, does the word produce two effects through a single latent impression (*saṃskāra*), or through distinct latent impressions? In this regard, the well-established path is that a difference in causes is inferred from a difference in effects.

Even though a single latent impression is beyond the senses and is postulated on the basis of its effect, many such impressions will likewise be postulated for that very same reason, because the effects are distinct.
As for the claim that it is difficult to connect a sequence of phonemes that have long since disappeared, that too is not sound;
for by means of a certain mental construction (kalpanā), just as phonemes [are connected] in the cognition of a word, so too words can arise in the cognition of a sentence.
This will be demonstrated immediately hereafter.
As for the further hypothesis that phonemes might operate either simultaneously or sequentially in the cognition of the meaning of a word or a sentence, it is replied to this as follows:
first, simultaneity is refuted simply because it is not admitted;
as for their sequence, it is of such a nature that they first cause the understanding of the word-meaning and subsequently [the understanding] of the sentence-meaning.
If it is argued that, in that case, the meaning of a sentence is thus said to be preceded by the meanings of the words, it is not so;
for what is called the "meaning of a word" is indeed an object of cognition (*prameya*),
and they do not fall within the category of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Nor is there an absolute difference between the meaning of a word and the meaning of a sentence, such that there could exist between them a relationship of signifier and signified—whether dependent on the apprehension of a connection like smoke and fire, or independent of it like a lamp and its form. Indeed, the linguistic convention of "the signified and the signifier" does not apply to the very same entity. How is it that you have become like a disciple of a Buddhist who maintains the doctrine of essential identity (*svabhāva-hetu*)?
But surely, a word functions with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*), while a sentence functions with respect to the particular (*viśeṣa*);
moreover, the universal is one thing and the particulars are another.

As it has been said: "For universals, being established otherwise, lead to the understanding of the particular. Thus, there is indeed a distinction between that which conveys and that which is conveyed.
It is said:
Certainly, there is this much distinction;

however, just as when the eye has ceased its activity, there is no cognition of fire from smoke and so forth, nor from the object of knowledge (prameya), so too there is no cognition of the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) from the word-meaning (padārtha).
For word-meanings, having become objects of cognition (*prameya*), cannot themselves become means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) like smoke;
rather, it is the words themselves that culminate in the comprehension of the sentence-meaning by way of conveying those [word-meanings].
How is it that you do not understand your own very treatise?
In the cognition of the sentence-meaning, the presentation of word-meanings is an inseparable concomitant of their activity, just as the burning of wood is inseparable from its cooking.
For an intermediate operation does not preclude the status of being a *kāraka* (a causal factor) in relation to the primary operation of that *kāraka*.
For words possess a twofold power: the denotative power (*abhidhātrī śakti*) and the purposive power (*tātparyaśakti*).
Among these, their denotative power is employed with respect to the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*).
And the power of intention culminates in the meaning of the sentence.

The author of the *Bhāṣya* as well, by stating that "words, having denoted their respective individual meanings, cease their operation," speaks only of the cessation of the power of denotation (*abhidhā*), not of the power of intention (*tātparya*). Words cease their operation after having denoted [their meanings], yet they do not cease their operation with respect to that toward which they are directed; for in this way, the verbal nature of the cognition of the sentence-meaning is not lost. However, if the word were to cease its operation in every respect, that [verbal nature] would necessarily be lost.

If verbal cognition were considered verbal simply because it is rooted in the apprehension of sound, then it would also have to be auditory, since the ear is its indirect source. Furthermore, once the operation regarding the word has ceased, we do not know what that means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) could be whose fruit is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.
It is not perception, because the meaning of a sentence transcends the senses;
nor is it inference, since that has already been refuted by the author himself in an extensive passage beginning with "Nor is this cognition an inference" (na cānumānam eṣā dhīḥ);
nor is it verbal testimony, because the operation of words has ceased.

For according to the principle that "generals, being established otherwise, do indeed lead to the understanding of the particular," if you say it is *arthāpatti* (presumption), then what now is this *dharma* that is to be understood through *arthāpatti*?
And this is neither logical nor acceptable.
Thus, this seventh means of valid cognition, called "being for the sake of another" (pārārthya), would have to be admitted;
yet even this is not accepted.
Therefore, the cognition of the meaning of a sentence is not caused by the meanings of individual words.

As for what was said—that through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) has the meanings of the words (*padārtha*) as its cause—it is true that since the meaning of a sentence consists essentially in the connection of word-meanings, the understanding of the sentence-meaning is indeed admitted to be preceded by them; however, it is not produced by them, because the operation of the word (*śabda*) has not ceased. Furthermore, when there is a mental lapse, there is no perception of even the words themselves; for at a later moment, with his mind composed, he says: "I did not hear this; my mind was elsewhere; say it again."
For otherwise, having remembered the words, one would understand their meaning directly and would not ask again;
therefore, the apprehension of the words themselves is the cause for understanding the meaning of the sentence in that case.
As for the statement, "one sees a white form," that too is of no consequence.
Is it not the case that by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) one sees a white cow walking?
It is not the case that the meaning of the sentence "a white cow walks" does not exist.
However, because it appears as a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is said that this is indeed the object of perception itself and not the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*).
Thus, this cognition—such as "a white horse is running"—is inferential (*ānumānika*), like the cognition "there is fire on the mountain.
But without hearing a sentence, there can be no sentence-meaning; so, enough of this digression.

Therefore, it is logical that the cognition of word-meanings and sentence-meanings arises from the phonemes themselves, which have attained the status of words and sentences through a certain conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Consequently, it is established that the understanding of the sentence-meaning is not produced by the word-meanings;
rather, this [understanding] arises from the sentence itself, whose operation has not ceased.
He asks: "By what conceptualization, moreover, do phonemes, having attained the status of words and sentences, bring about the cognition of word-meanings and sentence-meanings?"
In this regard, the teachers have presented the following conceptual model:
first is the cognition of the initial phoneme; from that, a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) arises;

then follows the cognition of the second phoneme; and by means of that [second cognition] together with the impression produced by the cognition of the first phoneme, a more potent impression is formed.
Then, from that [cognition], there arises a cognition of the third phoneme, which produces a more intense latent impression (*saṃskāra*) than the preceding one;
and so on, up to the cognition of the final phoneme.
Immediately after the final phoneme, however, from that latent impression, there arises a single recollection whose object is all the preceding phonemes.
Therefore, while the cognition of the final phoneme is in the state of perishing,
it is understood that a word (*pada*) is a collection of phonemes that has been made the object of both the perception occurring in its state of perishing and of recollection.
From that, from the cognition of the first word, a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) arises.
From that, in the same manner and by the sequence of phonemes, there occurs the cognition of the second word.
By that [second-word-cognition] and by the mental impression produced by the cognition of the first word, an even more potent mental impression is generated.
Again, by that same sequence, there arises the cognition of the third word;
and by that, together with the preceding mental impression (*saṃskāra*), an even more robust impression is produced.
In this manner, until the cognition of the final word, a single recollection encompassing all the words is generated by means of a very powerful impression.
Since a *saṃskāra* is indeed a single entity, that very collection of phonemes, which has been made the object of both memory and direct experience, is called a "word" (*pada*).
A collection of words is called a "sentence" (*vākya*).
From that, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) arises.
Furthermore, one must necessarily admit that there is a skill in the formation of one mental impression (saṃskāra) for producing another mental impression;
otherwise, the practice of action in all cases would be purposeless.
Regarding this, they say: "This process is not valid, because it would entail the simultaneous occurrence of cognitions.

For instance, immediately after the appearance of the final word, just as there must be a recollection of the preceding words, so too must there be a recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) at that very same time.
Indeed, for one who has not grasped the relationship between the word and its meaning, there can be no comprehension of the sentence-meaning."

Furthermore, there is no cognition of the meaning of a word for one who does not remember the convention (*saṃketa*). Even in cases where the remembrance of the convention is not consciously perceived regarding a familiar object, it is necessarily inferred that there is indeed a remembrance of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), because—as in the case of an inhabitant of the Coconut Island (*nārikeladvīpa*)—there is an absence of the comprehension of meaning for one who has not understood the relationship between the word and its referent. Moreover, since the experience of the relationship occurred previously, it is now of service by way of being remembered.

Therefore, immediately after the cognition of the final word, because the remembrances of the conventions for the preceding words arise simultaneously, there is a simultaneity of cognitions (*jñānayaugapadya*).

Now, even if it is maintained that the recollection of the preceding word occurs immediately after the recollection of the convention (*samaya*), there would still be a simultaneity of cognitions, because the cognition of the word-meaning arises at the very time of that recollection.

Nor can it be said that the cognition of the word-meaning does not arise at that time, for the causal complex for its production is present in its entirety and there is no opposing factor (*pratināyaka*) at that moment. If it is argued that the recollection of the preceding word should instead occur after the cognition of the word-meaning, then, in that case, the final word-cognition would have ceased, and the sentence would be devoid of its last word.
For at the time of recollecting the convention, the cognition of the final word is in the state of perishing, and at the time of cognizing the word-meaning, it has already perished.
If one were to say that even though it is not being experienced at that time, the final term nevertheless exists, then all hail to the Nyāyavistara!

Furthermore, even if it exists at that time while being unperceived, what is accomplished by the final phoneme? If you argue that there will be a subsequent cognition of it, from where would that arise?

It cannot arise from the auditory organ, because no such operation of the auditory organ after it has ceased is perceived; nor can it arise from the mind, because the mind lacks independent capacity regarding external objects.
Furthermore, even if that [object] were understood, there would still be no avoidance of the simultaneity of cognitions.

Moreover, what benefit is there in the recollection of preceding words—which, being devoid of meaning, are dry, tasteless, and insubstantial—even if they are remembered immediately after the experience of the final word?
For the recollection of such words is not a factor in the communication of meaning.

If, on the other hand, the meaningful prior words are remembered, then there would result a simultaneity of cognitions for every word across many branches, caused by the confusion of effects such as the recollection of convention and the cognition of the word-meanings; therefore, this hypothesis is untenable.
The commentators, however, have explained another process: first, the cognition of the initial word arises in the form of a sequential apprehension of the phonemes;
from that, there is the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).
[Objection: Since it has already been obtained even as it perishes, what is the use of that recollection?

And because that [simultaneity] is absent, there is no occasion here for objections such as the simultaneity of cognitions; moreover, since the cognition of the final word as previously demonstrated is itself the cognition of the sentence-meaning, its purpose is not fulfilled elsewhere. Thus, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning will be established from the sentence alone, and not from the word-meanings.
Others maintain that this conception is also not faultless, because it is impossible for the cognition of the second word to arise preceded by the coloring (impregnation) of the first word;
for the recollection of the relationship occurs immediately after the cognition of the first word,
and by that very [recollection], the former [cognition] is in the process of perishing.
Furthermore, at the time of the comprehension of the object-meaning, the cognition of the word has already perished;
for it is heard as a general rule that "a cognition in its state of perishing is opposed by another cognition."
One might say that the cognition which is the cause is contradicted by the cognition which is the effect, but not cognition in general by cognition in general;
this is incorrect, because there is no evidence for such a distinction.

Even granting this, we say: let the relationship of destroyer and destroyed exist only between two cognitions that possess the status of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the specific [object].

Nevertheless, the cognition of the word is indeed the cause of the recollection of the convention (*samaya*), just like a latent impression (*saṃskāra*); for, just as in the case of a latent impression, that [recollection] does not arise without it.
If it is argued that its function lies in the awakening of the latent impression, even so, that which is the cause by way of that medium is simply a cause.

Thus, in this case, the cognition of the word, the recollection of the convention, and the cognition of the word-meaning—these three cognitions would have to exist simultaneously; this is a great absurdity.
Furthermore, the cognition of a word arises through the sequence of its phonemes, not all at once, since the theory that a word is a partless whole has already been refuted.
And therein, two or three, three or four, or five or six phonemes will be apprehended in succession.
For the cognitions directed toward those [words], occurring in succession and characterized by arising and passing away, would perish at this interval;
it is a mere vain hope to think that the cognition of the first word will persist in a state of decay so that the cognition of the second word may arise colored by it.
Furthermore, the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is observed even from words uttered with an interval between them.
There, with his heart distracted by the consideration of various tasks, the master says "Kandalaka! and after attending to another matter, he says "the horse.
Again, having occupied himself with yet another purpose, he says "saddled," and so forth;
and again, having done something else entirely, he says "bring it."

In that case, there arises an understanding of the sentence-meaning: "O Rekaṇḍalaka, bring the horse equipped with a saddle. Yet, according to your view, this is difficult to establish, because the coloring by individual words (padānurāga) is impossible therein.
And because the recollection of the preceding member [of the compound] is not admitted.

Furthermore, unlike those who follow the *Pravaramata*, for you [the Yogācāras], in the cognitions of qualified objects (*viśeṣya*), the objective support (*ālambana*) is not two entities—the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified—rather it is the qualified object alone; the excellence of cognition arises solely from a difference in the means (*upāya*).

Consequently, even if there is a residual impression (*anurāga*) from the preceding word, since that [impression] does not appear [in the cognition], the cognition of the second word has become purely [of its own object]; so what is the use of that residual impression?
Therefore, this conceptualization is untenable, because the apprehension of the convention (*saṅketagrahaṇa*) for the second word occurred as something purely [denotative] of its own referent.

When a word was used for the first time somewhere, it was now [claimed] to have become colored by other words; since such a word would not have its relationship [to its meaning] grasped, it could not be the cause of the comprehension of meaning—let alone this unprecedented scholarship of Śaṅkarasvāmin!

He said: "If all these conceptual constructions fashioned by the Tantrikas are indeed faulty and not superior, then let some faultless and excellent conceptual construction of your own be presented. It is replied: "We are not capable of producing any new conceptual construction of our own."
For this poor intellect of mine is not capable of perceiving even a blade of grass, which was not unseen by the ancient poets who possessed subtle vision.
What then is this desire of yours to compose a work that must be scrutinized by the intellects of the learned?
Such a desire is not a fit subject for questioning; nor can it be stilled by the instruction of others.
But I, O King, have been cast into this soundless, deep dungeon;
indeed, here my days have been passed in the diversion of composing literary works.
Nevertheless, it must be explained how the meaning of a sentence is understood from the phonemes.
It is said in reply: whether they have long since passed away or have not yet long since passed away is not the cause of recollection;
for recollection is produced by means of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

And that [impression] makes no difference whether it perishes immediately or after a long time; thus, through mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), there will be recollection of all words—even those long since vanished or uttered with an interval.

Furthermore, if one admits that the final word is being directly experienced, there would follow the fallacy of the simultaneity of cognitions and so forth; therefore, it is better that even the final word be something remembered.
All words, once ascended upon memory, will bring about the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.
In this regard, the following is the conceptual construction:
first, there is the cognition of the initial word through the sequence of phonemes;
then, the recollection of the linguistic convention and the mental impression (saṃskāra) arise simultaneously.
For the simultaneity of two cognitions is prohibited in the treatise, but not that of two mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
From that [cognition] arises the cognition of the word-meaning;
from that also arises a mental impression.
Furthermore, through the sequence of phonemes, there arises the cognition of the second word;
from that, the recollection of the linguistic convention occurs;
and by means of that [recollection], together with the previous mental impression (*saṃskāra*), a more intense mental impression is produced.

Again, by means of the sequence of preceding phonemes, there arises the cognition of the third word, which produces a stronger latent impression (*saṃskāra*) based on the preceding impressions; thus, when a robust impression produced by the cognition of the words and a similar impression produced by the cognition of the word-meanings are established, immediately after the cognition of the final word-meaning, two recollections arise sequentially from the three impressions: a recollection having all the words as its object from the word-impressions, and a recollection having the word-meanings as its object from the word-meaning impressions.
In that regard, the collection of words mounted upon one memory is the sentence (*vākya*), while the collection of word-meanings mounted upon the other is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

[Objection: "But since memory is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), the understanding of the sentence-meaning must now also be invalid. [Reply: Not so; for the connection [between word and meaning] is grasped in that very way. For this defect occurs only where the connection is grasped in one way and the comprehension is in another, as when fire is inferred from mist after the connection has been grasped in relation to smoke.

In this case, however, since it is impossible for phonemes that occur in a sequence to be apprehended otherwise [than in their actual order], the cognition occurs exactly as the linguistic convention (vyutpatti) dictates; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Furthermore, a memory that arises immediately after an experience that has just ceased is treated as if it were the experience itself.
Alternatively, enough with this hypothesis of recollection (*smaraṇakalpanā*).

Immediately after the cognition of the final word-meaning, there will arise a mental after-cognition (*mānaso 'nuvyavasāya*) whose object is all the words and word-meanings, standing in the same position as the cognition of "one hundred" and so forth.
The sentence consists of the words mounted upon that [after-cognition], and the sentence-meaning consists of the word-meanings mounted upon it.
And such a mental after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) cannot be denied, as it is witnessed by all people.
Now, one might ask: after the cognition of the final word-meaning, what is the use of a recollection or an after-cognition regarding the preceding words and their meanings?
If the final word-meaning has been cognized, the task is finished; what else remains that must be accomplished by means of a primary cognition (*vyavasāya*), a recollection, or an after-cognition?
How could this not be established? For the cognition of a sentence and its meaning is of a single form; being personally experienced within oneself, it cannot be denied.
Moreover, this [cognition] does not come about without recollection or subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*); thus, these are necessary.

In this way, this collection of words, having ascended to recollection and being made the object of a synthetic cognition (*saṃkalanājñāna*), constitutes the sentence, and such is the meaning of that sentence.
Granted, let there be no word-sphoṭa nor sentence-sphoṭa as the expressive agent;
and let it not be that these two—the sentence and the sentence-meaning—are devoid of parts.
Let these phonemes alone be the denoters; why should it be needlessly claimed that a word is a collection of phonemes and a sentence is a collection of words?
Let the conceptual constructions of words, sentences, and so forth, as explained by you, be as they may; however, let it be told: what is the path regarding the connection between word-meanings?
For word-meanings such as "cow," "horse," "man," and "elephant" are indeed unconnected; they do not ascend to the status of a sentence-meaning.

Indeed, when they are made objects by recollection or by a subsequent cognitive awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) occurring immediately after the cognition of the final word-meaning, they are made objects exactly as they were previously understood.
However, it must be considered from where the comprehension of their connection arises.
It is said: there is a dispute on this point.
Some maintain that word-meanings are denoted by words only as already mutually connected, for otherwise it would be impossible for those words to constitute a sentence.

Others, however, maintain that words denote only pure word-meanings; these meanings, having been thus denoted, bring about their mutual relation through a consideration of expectancy, proximity, and semantic competency.
In this regard, the following must be considered: linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) is more powerful, for a word does not convey its meaning independently of linguistic usage.
And as for that linguistic usage, does it belong to a sentence with respect to the sentence-meaning, or to a word with respect to the word-meaning?

If the understanding of a sentence occurs with respect to the sentence-meaning, then there is "expression of the related" (anvitābhidhāna); if the understanding of a word occurs with respect to the word-meaning, then there is "connection of the expressed" (abhihitānvaya).
What, then, is established? That there is "connection after expression" (abhihitānvaya), because the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is preceded by the comprehension of the word-meanings.

For it is never observed that one who has not understood the meanings of the individual words can comprehend the meaning of the sentence; moreover, the distinction between word-meanings is clearly perceived: "the meaning of this word is a genus," "this is a substance," "this is a quality," and "this is an action. And this [distinction] is possible only if that meaning is expressed by the words themselves. But if that [sentence-meaning] is expressed while being colored by the meanings of other words, then the precise extent of that meaning cannot be determined, because the cognition of the meaning arises in the form of a confused cluster (kadamba).

If it is argued that the determination [of word-meanings] occurs through insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*), this is not so; for even at the time of examining insertion and deletion, the cognition of the cluster [of words] (*kadambaka-pratīti*) does not disappear.

Indeed, it is not the case that one particular sentence alone is composed of words expressing related meanings, whereas elsewhere the meaning of the words is merely isolated; rather, in every instance, the resultant cognition in the form of a cluster is understood from the means in the form of a cluster. Thus, the distinction between individual word-meanings is difficult to discern.

Furthermore, if the meanings of the words were not taken into account, from the sentence "Bring the cow" (gām ānaya), there would be understood an injunction to bring a horse; and from the sentence "Bind the cow" (gāṃ badhāna), there would be understood an injunction to bind a horse.
However, the meaning of the words is indeed required;
and that required meaning must be determined as being of such a specific extent.
That determination [of the relationship] is possible only in the case of words whose denotations are pure;
therefore, an innate relationship between the word and its meaning is accepted.

Furthermore, even in the linguistic usage of elders, the acquisition of proficiency (*vyutpatti*) arising from a sentence extends down to the individual word; otherwise, one would have to rely on the acquisition of proficiency for every single sentence. Since that would be impossible to achieve due to the infinity [of sentences], the practice of verbal communication would come to an end.

Moreover, it is observed that those who understand the meaning of words derive the cognition of the sentence-meaning even from the verse of a newly emerged poet; this is possible through their proficiency in words and their individual meanings.
However, if proficiency in sentences and sentence-meanings were required, such cognition would simply not occur.
Therefore, it is not the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna).

And for this reason, since it would otherwise follow that the utterance of other words is futile, the comprehension of the second word-meaning—which serves as a qualifier—is already established by the first word alone. Furthermore, by the very same logic—that each word expresses its own meaning as colored by others—a single word alone becomes expressive of the meanings denoted by all words; therefore, let linguistic usage proceed by means of that [single word] alone.
And this [comprehension] does not come to pass;
for when "cow" is uttered, because all qualities and actions are understood, it is not known what should be taken up.
Indeed, a comprehension of everything is no different from non-comprehension, since practical activity (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible.
For even the full ocean does not surpass Mount Meru for those who know its taste, because the function of water remains unfulfilled;
however, we perceive no reason for the word "cow" (go) to convey its own referent when it is colored by restricted qualities and actions.

If it is argued that the proximity of other words is the cause of restriction, is this by way of their mere form or by way of their conveying meaning? If it were by way of their mere form, then even if there were proximity—as in the case of words in a muttered mantra—it would not differ from non-proximity; for no benefit produced by such [mere] proximity is observed in the absence of a connection with a word that possesses a subordinate status (*anu*).
If, however, another word serves as the cause for restriction by means of conveying its own meaning, then this is what is called the "connection" (*anvaya*) of the meanings already expressed.

Therefore, that alone is superior: the meanings, having been conveyed and extracted from the words, become mutually connected by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatva*).
Whatever is expected by whatever else, whatever is proximate, and whatever is capable of being connected, that is connected with it—and nothing else.
For this very reason, there is no connection in the statement "a hundred herds of elephants reside on the tip of a finger," because of the absence of semantic fitness (*yogyatva*).

For those who maintain the theory that words express meaning through mutual connection (*anvitābhidhāna*), however, since they hold that what is not connected cannot be expressed, it would follow that even in such a case there must be a connection;
yet such a connection does not exist.
Therefore, it is logical that the syntactic relation belongs only to the word-meanings as they have been denoted.
As it has been said: "For words, having denoted their respective meanings, cease their operation;
then, the meanings, now understood, bring about the sentence-meaning."

This being the case, it is replied: a word does not convey its meaning independently of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), like a lamp [which illuminates objects]. And linguistic convention arises from the usage of elders (*vṛddha*).
Furthermore, the usage of elders occurs through sentences, not through isolated words, because an isolated word is never employed.
When a word is employed for the sake of cognizing another object that is obtained through the context and the sense,
it is indeed said to constitute a sentence.
The speaker employs a sentence with the intention of expressing a composite meaning;
likewise, the listener understands it, and so too does a bystander.
This is the mastery of a sentence with respect to the meaning of that sentence.
And what is called a "sentence"? Those who know of sentences maintain that a sentence is a collection of words that expresses a meaning through their combination.
In that case, this very collection of words constitutes the meaning.
Thus, the words would not express a meaning through their combination if each individual word were operative in every instance.

Just as all external causal factors such as wood and so forth are operative in the act of cooking, and just as all those who carry a palanquin together lift the palanquin, and just as even three stones together support a pot, so too do all words convey the meaning of the sentence. This is what is called *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of the related). For if words were to terminate in their own isolated meanings unrelated to others, there would be no operation of all [words] toward the sentence-meaning.

Now, it might be argued that if each individual [word] performs the entire function, then since the whole is accomplished by just one, the utterance of other words is useless. This is not so, because without the other words, the complete accomplishment of the function does not occur from a single one alone. If it is then asked, "In that case, a single word does not perform the whole," do not say so; for each one is involved in an operation that extends to the final result of the whole. When each one is present, the operation extending to the final result of the whole is brought about; without each one, it is not brought about. Thus, each one individually performs the whole.

[Objection: "In that case, let the aggregate alone be the agent; what is the use of the constituents? And thus it follows that the sentence and the sentence-meaning are partless. [Reply: This is not correct, because, like the effect of the collection as a whole, its own individual effects are also observed.

What is the function of the aggregate (*saṅghātakārya*), and what is its own function (*svakārya*)? The comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthapratipatti*) is the function of the aggregate; however, the comprehension of the word-meanings (*padārthapratipatti*) is its own function.
Just as cooking is the function of the aggregate.
Their own function consists of burning, containing, and so forth, as in the case of wood, a pot, and other such things.

Now, if the communication of word-meanings is the own-function (*svakārya*) of words, then the meaning of a word in isolation would not be the "pure" word-meaning; for pure words that do not perform the function of a composite (*saṅghāta*) are never observed. Indeed, there is no separate employment of these words for their own function apart from the function of a composite, since they are employed exclusively for the function of a composite in every respect.
Even for those who are engaged in that [activity], their own specific function is not unperceived;
for this very reason, a sentence is not held to be partless, because its own function is recognized.

Those [words] are seen to perform the function of a sentence when they are combined; indeed, the sentence itself does not exist apart from its components. Even when the components are combined, their own individual functions are perceived separately. For example, regarding the parts of a chariot, one cannot say "this part was made by this person" and "that part by that person," for the chariot-parts, when employed individually, do not perform even the slightest function of a chariot. Thus, it is logical that a word is not merely a word in isolation, nor is it a word when used alone without being a factor in its own function; rather, a word is truly a word only when it performs its function as integrated with the meaning through its operation together with another word.
Thus it has been said: "Words express a meaning by combining together; or, a sentence is a collection of words having a single unified meaning."

Thus, because we perceive the effects of the constituent parts, we do not deny the causal factors as the Grammarians do; and because we determine the operation to extend until the complete accomplishment of the result, we do not accept the denotation of isolated word-meanings as the Mīmāṃsakas do.

As for what was further asserted—that for every sentence, linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) must be required, otherwise the meaning of a verse by a new poet would not be understood even by one who knows word-meanings—this is an objection raised by someone ignorant of proficiency. For proficiency does not consist in the notion that "the meaning of the word *go* (cow) is that which is connected with white," since that is subject to deviation, as it is seen to be connected with black [cows].
Nor is its meaning that which is connected with everything, because that would be impossible to comprehend due to infinity.
Rather, its meaning is colored by an object that is desired, capable, and proximate.
And through the process of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*), sentences produce various forms of linguistic expression that give rise to this proficiency (*vyutpatti*).

Although proficiency may extend as far as the meaning of individual word-meanings (*padārtha*), it is observed to be of such a nature [in the context of sentences] and not restricted solely to the domain of isolated word-meanings, as it was stated that there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) based on a single word alone.

Nevertheless, it is not the case that the extent of a word’s meaning is unknown; for, like the parts of a cart, the distinction in their respective functions is demonstrated through insertion and deletion.

Thus, in this way, a linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) need not be required for every individual sentence. For when a relationship has been grasped in one instance through the denotation of its own meaning as qualified by an object that is proximate, capable, and expected, that relationship is effectively grasped in all instances.
Consequently, the comprehension of meaning from even a verse by a new poet becomes logically possible.
However, it has been stated that there is no linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) regarding the word and its referent, because of the absence of a means [to establish it].

As for the claim that the utterance of words is fruitless, that too has been refuted, because it has been stated that when other words are in proximity, all words become fully effective. If it is argued that [the effect] is produced by the proximity of other words, this same inquiry applies equally to all causal factors (*kāraka*s). Rather, it is said that all causal factors act by combining together.

Likewise, even though words assist by denoting their respective meanings, there is no such thing as "connection of the denoted" (abhihitānvaya), because there is no linguistic acquisition (vyutpatti) regarding a meaning that has not been connected. Alternatively, if one does not accept this [position], the connection of word-meanings is difficult to establish, due to the absence of any means [to ascertain it].

Now, it was said that expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatva*) constitute the means [of comprehension]; however, that which was said is not correct. Whose is this expectancy? Is it of the word, of the meaning, or of the cognizer? First of all, since both the word and the meaning are insentient, they cannot possess expectancy.
In fact, the expressions used here and there—such as "the word expects another word" or "the meaning expects another meaning"—are merely figurative.

Furthermore, the desire of the independent knower is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the state of things cannot be brought about by the will of a person. However, when a person's desire arises following upon the means of valid cognition known as verbal testimony (*śabda*), it becomes the cause for the connection of meanings; thus, this is the extremely long-reaching function of the word, like that of an arrow. But once the function of the word has ceased, the mere desire of the person is not the cause of the relation.
Furthermore, in this way, the cognition of the sentence-meaning would result in being non-verbal;
moreover, such an imposition is improper when the status of being verbal is directly possible.
Therefore, it is established that words denote [their meanings] as already connected.
For this indeed is the path for the cognition of relation: it is through the cognition of interrelated objects that the relation itself is understood;
there is no other cause for the cognition of relation.
Indeed, it is not said that "bring the white cow" is an expression of relation; rather, in certain worldly transactions, the word "relation" (saṃsarga) is used by the learned as a synonym for it.
For even if this [work] were composed by some fool,
it would surely be devoid of coherent meaning, like the sentence "ten pomegranates."
Therefore, it is logical that only those [words] which are already connected [to a meaning] are denotative.

He said: "In sentences such as 'the tip of the finger' and so forth, how is there coherence for you? It is replied: And in the case of the connection of the things already mentioned, how is there coherence for you?"
He said: "Is it not the case that here non-connection is accepted due to the absence of semantic competency (*yogyatā*)?
For I maintain that connection depends upon the triad beginning with expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)."

I too have stated that words possess the capacity to express their own meanings as combined with those [meanings] such as "the fit" (yogya) and "the proximate" (āsanna); yet, since that [capacity] does not exist in those [words of yours], there is a lack of syntactic connection (ananvaya).
He said: "For you are indeed a proponent of the theory that words denote meanings as already connected (anvitābhidhānavādin);
consequently, for you, there would be non-denotation here because of the impossibility of connection."

I, however, am a proponent of the theory that the syntactical connection is expressed (*abhihitānvaya-vādin*); therefore, for me, even though [the object] is not explicitly expressed, this does not contradict its denotation.
It is said: Alas! Even you, a Mīmāṃsaka who perceives with subtle vision, have still not determined the ultimate reality of the operation of words.
For the function of a word is inherently that of illumination;
however, its status as having either a true or false meaning depends upon the virtues or defects of the person [who utters it].
In this case as well, the cognition of the connection between action and its factors arises from words;
it is of that very same nature, yet it is incorrect due to the fallibility of human intellect.
Thus it has been said: "In this case, the perception of another means of valid cognition is sublated."
For this very reason, the validity of the word is incomparable and intrinsic; for even with respect to the action denoted by the word, no subverting factor (bādhaka) ever approaches it.
Therefore, even in the statement regarding the tip of a finger, there is indeed a verbal coherence (*śābda samanvaya*),
because the designation of the locus, the located, the action, and so forth is perceived therein.
In reality, however, that which is an impossibility is exactly the same for both of us,
because it destroys the purpose of cognizing a relation due to its unfitness [to enter into such a relation].

If, however, there were no semantic connection (*anvaya*), this would be a mere enumeration of phonemes such as *ka-ca-ta-pa*, or it would be equivalent to the incoherent prattle of "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*) and so forth.
Because it expresses what is unconnected, it would not even possess the status of a sentence (*vākyatva*).
Yet, the status of being a sentence does exist.
Therefore, we consider that there is a verbal concomitance (*śābdo 'nvaya*); thus, even here, the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) is not contradictory.
It has been stated that any sublation (*bādhaka*) pertains only to other objects, and not to the domain of verbal connection itself.

For this very reason, regarding the word—which possesses the function of causing cognition through its own inherent capacity and without external dependence—he will explain the unimpeded authority of the Veda as being intrinsic, because, due to its non-human origin, no distortion is possible.
And since its own activity is pure by its very nature, enough with this excessive prolixity.
Thus, since the cognition of the sentence-meaning is possible through the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*),
the theory of the relation of the expressed (*abhihitānvaya*)— which lacks [explanatory] consistency— should be rejected by the wise.
Even this [objection] is not accepted: that which was said—that linguistic proficiency arises from the usage of elders—is true;
that usage occurs by means of the sentence is also true;
and that all words function together toward the goal (kārya), like men carrying a palanquin, is indeed true as well.

Let the nature of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) be considered: does it consist solely in the mastery of the effects produced by the combination of the forms of individual syntactic actions, or does it extend as far as the meanings of the word-constituents (*padārtha*) themselves?
In the former case, acquisition would have to be undertaken for every single sentence;
and it has already been stated that this [latter view] involves many errors.
However, when linguistic proficiency extends to the ultimate meaning of words (*padārtha*), one must certainly determine that "the meaning of this word is precisely this much.
Even you yourselves have admitted the determination of a word's function by describing the analogy of the parts of a cart.
Otherwise, if there were no regard for the restriction of word-meanings, a speaker intending to say "bring the cow" might even employ the word "horse" as a substitute.
For your comprehension of the sentence-meaning does not consist of a word-meaning that is entirely disregarded, as is the case for the Grammarians.

Therefore, whatever meaning of the word *go* is determined through the consideration of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*), that very same meaning belongs to it even when it is functioning within the operation of a composite whole (*saṅghāta*).

[Objection: "But was it not said that its [the word's] object is that which is colored by a meaning that is required, capable, and proximate? [Reply: This is not correct; this is a delusion of yours who perceive this word as always functioning in conjunction [with others]. Its object is only as much as its denotative power extends."

To what extent does it have the power to denote, and to what extent does it have the power not to denote? It is to the extent that it does not abandon that meaning as long as it is connected with other words that are mutually expectant and proximate.

And how much does it not abandon? Only the state of being a cow (gotva), or only that much; therefore, by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatireka), its denotative power is determined to extend only to that extent.

Beyond this, because a single word is never employed in isolation, its capacity for *tātparya* (implicatory power) operates toward the primary meaning—since it is always impossible to ascertain the proficiency of its own form when devoid of the function of a syntactical aggregate—and not its denotative power (*abhidhātrī*).
By failing to distinguish that [denotative power] separately, you have accepted the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related);
and that is incorrect, because the denotative power remains indistinguishable in all cases.
Because defects such as the failure to determine the restriction of word-meanings and the futility of uttering other words would not be eliminated.

If a word such as "cow" (*go*) denotes an object as connected with something else, then in the absence of denoting that [other thing], there would be no comprehension of the object as so connected; for it would be a contradiction to hold that while that with which the relation exists is not grasped, the object related to it is nevertheless grasped.
Alternatively, if it were to denote that [related thing] as well, then by the same principle, it would have to denote everything, and thus the single word "cow" would come to signify all things.

Therefore, it is not tenable that a word possesses a denotative power (*abhidhātrī śakti*) with respect to everything; hence, the theory of the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) is untenable.

Furthermore, under the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of related meanings), how could there be no relation (*anvaya*) even in the sentence "the tip of a finger"? If you argue that verbal relation certainly exists [there], it follows that the word would not touch upon the actual object, since there is no external relation. If you claim that its function is merely to manifest [the meaning], we grant that; however, it is proper to understand that this function pertains to both related and unrelated objects, rather than being restricted solely to related objects. For we observe that sentences such as "ten pomegranates" do indeed convey meanings that are [formally] related.
If it is argued that this is not a sentence, then the statement "the tip of a finger" is likewise not a sentence at all;
however, the cognition of a relation between locus, located, and action is merely an error.
Therefore, the claim that words denote meanings as already syntactically connected is incorrect.
Now, one might ask: "Are objects expressed by words as mere iron rods, entirely unconnected to one another?

This too is not the case, because such linguistic usage does not exist, because the subsequent synthesis (anvaya) is difficult to perceive, and because no awareness of a [word's] operation occurring after [the initial utterance] is experienced.
Therefore, neither of the two positions is tenable.
As it has been said: "But we do not favor either of these two views at all;
for how can there be the expression of what is already connected, or how can there be the connection of what has already been expressed?"

However, another formulation of the argument made by some— that there is a word whose connection [to its meaning] is already established, and a meaning whose connection [to a word] is being expressed—
that too does not satisfy the heart.
For these two actions are not experienced as existing separately;
the action of denotation is one thing, and the action of connection residing in the signified object is another.

For these two [actions] would either occur sequentially or simultaneously. In the case of sequence, if the act of relating (*anvaya-kriyā*) occurs first, then this is precisely the theory of "expression of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*), not the "expression of that which is being related" (*anvīyamānābhidhāna*). If, however, the act of expression (*abhidhāna-kriyā*) occurs first, then this is precisely the theory of "relation of the expressed" (*abhihitānvaya*), not the "relation of that which is being expressed" (*abhidhīyamānānvaya*).
But there is no perception of the two actions occurring simultaneously.
Because an action directed toward an object is not perceived at the time of the employment of the word.
Only the act of denotation itself is examined by those who understand it;
for how could there be a sequential following of objects without denotation?
In the case of "the cow is white," how could we understand the connection between the genus and the quality—even though they both inhere in the same substance—without the word?
It must be understood that it is only the *ukti* (the expression) that is new, and not the object (*vastu*) itself;
furthermore, even here, the defects that touch both sides of the argument do not cease to exist.
Others think that there is "expression of the related" (anvitābhidhāna) in a general sense, and "expression of the related through what has been expressed" (abhihitānvaya) in a specific sense.

For the word *go* (cow) expresses its own referent as already associated with universals (*sāmānya*) such as qualities and actions whose particulars are not yet known; this much constitutes "expression of the related.
However, the connection with specific qualities such as "white" is understood from another word.
This specific distinction called "abhihitānvaya" (the connection of what has been expressed) is likewise just like that.

Whatever fault is found in the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), that same fault applies to the theory of the expression of the general (*sāmānya*); and whatever fault has been stated regarding the theory of the expression of the already-expressed (*abhihitānvaya*), that same fault applies equally to the theory of the particular (*viśeṣa*).
Nor has this unprecedented matter been described.
Proponents of the theory of "connection of the expressed" (*abhihitānvayavāda*) maintain that connection occurs only among particulars;
for while a word functions with respect to a universal (*sāmānya*), a sentence functions with respect to a particular (*viśeṣa*).

And since the theory of the connection of already-expressed words (abhihitānvaya) is resorted to for the sake of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, it should be understood that the previously mentioned path alone is the one intended.
How then is linguistic usage possible, since we perceive this [process] as if it were confused because faults arise everywhere? It is said in reply: there is never any confusion here.
For it has been stated that words function through cooperation;
by means of words combined together, a single sentence-meaning is conveyed.

And since that is simply some entity (padārtha) itself, conjoined with other categories (padārtha) that have become its qualities (guṇa) and possessors of qualities (guṇin), what confusion is there in this?

Now, is it not the case that this doctrine of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) is intended to be revived once again? Do not say so; this is not the doctrine of the expression of the related.
How then is the cooperative functioning (*saṃhatyakāritā*) of words stated? Cooperative functioning indeed exists, yet there is no expression of the related.
Words, acting together, bring about a related meaning, but they do not express a related [meaning].
Do words now produce the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) in the same way that clay and other materials produce a jar? This too is not the case, because they are merely indicators (jñāpaka).
What, then, is this mode of expression: "Words act in combination, yet they do not denote the related [meaning]"? This is the explanation:
words cause the related meaning to be understood (pratyāyanti), but they do not denote the related meaning.

The denotative power (*abhidhātrī śakti*) does not have the related meaning as its object; rather, it has as its object only the isolated individual meanings (*niṣkṛṣṭasvārtha*) followed by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

However, their *tātparya* (intentional) power extends up to the comprehension of the related meaning, because they function together, and because this specific function of theirs culminates in the production of a cognition free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*).
For indeed, cognitions arising from perception and other means of knowledge proceed in exactly this way.
Displaying before them an object that is either complete or incomplete.
The verbal cognition unfolds with respect to its objects in a quite different manner;
it is a process that produces for the cognizer a cognition free from further expectancy.
For this very reason, a word is not employed in the world in isolation;
for by means of it alone, the listener's mind is not rendered free from expectancy.

Now, is there not some other operation of the word, distinct from denotation and consisting of comprehension extending to the complete result, which cannot be denied by any proponents of relational connection (*saṃsarga*)?
For it is not the case that the relation is denoted, yet it is indeed perceived from the sentence.

[Objection: Surely, when there is the expression of a conjoined [relation], the conjunction would be cognized, and not otherwise. [Reply: This is not so; for the cognition of conjunction is established precisely because [the words] act in combination.
Indeed, nowhere is a combined operation seen to be without a conjoined effect.

Moreover, the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) denote their meaning in mutual dependence. The meaning of the suffix is not denoted by the base, because the mandate (niyoga) is not expressed by a verbal root (dhātu). Nor is the meaning of the base denoted by the suffix, because it is untenable for the mandate and so forth to be expressed by the optative suffix (liṅ).
And those two do not perform their respective functions separately;
likewise, words also, being mutually dependent, will perform their function by acting in combination.
Nor will they express their meanings to one another; and sentences occurring within a specific context are exactly like this as well.
Thus it has been said: "Just as a root and a suffix depend upon one another, so too do a word depend on another word, and likewise a sentence on another sentence."
This very position is superior: that words function through mutual cooperation and possess non-overlapping meanings.

If the application were independent [of the meaning], it would be like a mere tally-stick of iron; but if there were the expression of what is already associated with that [meaning], then another word would be purposeless.
But in the case of acting in combination, not even a single fault exists;
therefore, this path, free from thorns, should be adopted.
The expressive power (*abhidhātrī śakti*) of words is considered to reside in their own individual meanings;
however, their power of intentionality (*tātparyaśakti*) is the means for the comprehension of the relation [between those meanings].
For we do not here tolerate the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna); however, the comprehension of the related is certainly accepted by us.

Furthermore, because words function through collective action (*saṃhatyakāraka*), they are not uttered solely with the intention of denoting their own individual meanings; rather, it is for the sake of accomplishing the primary task.

As it has been said: "In their activity toward the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, the presentation of word-meanings is an inseparable concomitant, just as the flame is to wood in the process of cooking."

This vast creeper of wisdom—its beauty of sprouts emerging from the multitude of words rooted in etymological derivation, its noble leaves being the mental impressions (saṃskāra), and possessing clusters of flowers in the form of radiant word-meanings—bears this sweet fruit, the reality of the sentence-meaning. Yet, when that [fruit] has entered the dense heart, men reach a state of desirelessness.
And it has been said: "This wisdom which unfolds for the knower from the very beginning with the word—having blossomed upon the meanings of words, it will bear fruit upon the meanings of sentences."
Therefore, by another principle, the cognition of relation (*saṃsarga*) arises as correct; and it was previously stated that related word-meanings constitute the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

And this very means for determining the meaning of a sentence, which has been demonstrated as established by worldly convention, must also be understood to apply to the Veda; for there too, the words are the same and their meanings are the same.

He said: In the world, because the meaning of a sentence is determinable by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is possible to establish that words serve as the means for its comprehension.
However, the meaning of the Veda is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
Furthermore, people like us, whose minds are defiled by defects such as passion and the like, possess no skill in perceiving objects that transcend the senses.
And since that [Veda] is not perceived, it is simply impossible to acquire proficiency in it through the linguistic usage of elders.
Thus, desiring today to understand the meaning of the Veda, I would have to approach some teacher who knows the Veda;
yet, since he too does not perceive supersensuous objects, he likewise lacks such proficiency and would have to approach someone else.
Thus, one would fall into a succession of blind men, each depending on another.

Furthermore, the Veda itself does not teach—unlike Pāṇini who stated *vṛddhir ādaic*, or Piṅgala who said *mastriguruḥ*, or the author of the Abhidhānamālā who explained *hastaḥ karaḥ pāṇiḥ*—that "this is the meaning of this word of mine.

Therefore, the meaning of the Veda is in every way difficult to comprehend; as it has been said: "If he who possesses passion and other defects does not know the meaning himself, he cannot know it from anyone else."
"Even the Veda does not perceive [it]; how then can there be an understanding of the meaning of the Veda?"

Now, if the conceptualization of word-meanings is performed by means of grammar (*nigama*), etymology (*nirukta*), and philology (*vyākaraṇa*), then—because teachers possess diverse opinions and because verbal roots, nouns, prefixes, and particles have multiple meanings—it is impossible to establish any fixed meaning for them, since such conceptualizations could otherwise be possible in various ways.
And it has been said: "Therefore, regarding the Vedic revelation that 'one who desires heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice'..."
"If one were to say, 'One should eat dog-meat,' what would be the authority for the claim that this is not the meaning?"
Thus has this Rāmāyaṇa been described by us for the deaf—those who, even having heard this, still seek a means to comprehend the meaning of the Vedas.
For by this exposition clarifying the means of comprehending the meaning of sentences, everything is resolved.
For it has been said that there are no Vedic words whatsoever that are new.
In the Veda, only the arrangement differs, but not the words;

and this practice of those who know the Veda has been in operation since the beginning of creation. It is precisely because it has proceeded as a long-standing tradition that we acquire proficiency in it even at our present age.
And as we become proficient, we shall explain each respective meaning.

Furthermore, where have the sciences such as grammar and Mīmāṃsā—which are the means for the thorough comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas—gone, that the meaning of the Vedas is not determined by those who claim to be living-liberated?

Moreover, O fool, one who is himself possessed of passion and the like does not understand the meaning of the Veda; for what purpose would there be a person possessed of passion? Let it be granted that the perception of one possessed of passion does not operate upon an object beyond the senses; however, such a person would still fail to understand from the sentence "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra" that the ritual act called Agnihotra is a means to attain heaven.

If it is asked, "How can there be a fixed linguistic convention regarding an object that transcends the senses? it has been stated in this regard that, like the Veda, its usage—the means for comprehending that object—is firmly rooted from time immemorial.
The meaning of the Veda, the comprehension thereof, the means thereof, and its performance have not come into being only at the present time;
according to some, these are indeed beginningless.
In our view, however, these [scriptures] have been operative from the very beginning of the creation of the world;

what opportunity for questioning them exists today? This denigration of the Veda—uttered by this dull-witted evildoer through such abusive speech as "he might eat dog-meat"—serves only to make the master of the field at Avīci [Hell] feel gratified; no new point of refutation has been conceived here.

Then another said: "Why is this poor fellow being driven away? What offense has he committed? What contradictory thing has he asserted? For it is not possible to acquire an understanding of the meaning of the Veda from the world."
Who is this person called "the world"? Is it anyone who is merely common, or is it one who has mastered Sanskrit as a grammarian?

In this regard, carters—whose minds are unacquainted with the employment of correct words, who by their very nature have uninjured throats, and who are wretched—conduct their affairs using only such words as *gāvī* and the like, which are devoid of grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*).

And how could those who transact business with such words ever acquire proficiency in Vedic terms? Even though some correct words—such as *eṣi* and *emi* among the Kaśmīris, *gaccha* among the Darvābhisāras, and *karomi* among the Madras—are employed even by common folk, nevertheless, because that usage is extremely rare in practice, it is entirely unsuitable for the purpose of acquiring proficiency in Vedic words.
