For this very reason, fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) are enumerated together with the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*): "The auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the expansion of Nyāya, the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge."
Even those conceptual constructions regarding the refinement of sounds and so forth that have been made are merely produced by the epilepsy of excessive talkativeness; they do not touch upon reality.
In this matter, the learned alone should be questioned;
they alone know which words are refined (*saṃskṛta*) and which are the opposite.
And what is their refinement?

We do not, however, claim that grammar has its root solely in the usage of the learned (śiṣṭa), since its beginninglessness has already been demonstrated like that of the Veda. Rather, it is stated that its root lies in the usage of the learned only with the desire to avoid the fault of falling into a blind tradition.

This is because, like medical tradition (*vaidyakasmṛti*), grammar is rooted in positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). For those words which are taught as correct in the grammatical tradition are seen to be used in that very way by the learned (*śiṣṭas*), just as health results from eating *harītakī* and the like.
It is not, however, the case that Pāṇini composed his work after having acquired a collection of words from the learned.
Nor did he compose the Caraka-saṃhitā after ascertaining the potencies of substances through positive and negative concomitance, because it is stated that the sciences are beginningless.
By this, the objection of mutual dependence is also refuted, for grammar does not originate from the learned.

As for the description of even the learned being prone to negligence—namely, that many ancient sages indeed employed ungrammatical words (*apaśabda*)—the path for removing such errors has already been demonstrated by those who are highly proficient in the field;
however, it is not elaborated upon here for fear of making the book too voluminous.

Furthermore, as for the inconsistencies in the Pāṇinian system regarding the instruction on verbal roots, nominal stems, case-roles, and so forth—which have been proclaimed to be manifold-branched—these too have indeed been rectified by those of subtle intellect.

Nor does this lead to an infinite regress, because it is impossible for caviling scholars who seek to cause disruption to find any opening along the path clearly shown by those of subtle insight, since it is possible for them to perceive flaws even in those [earlier commentators].

By this, those defects imagined by some—such as the non-inclusion of words like *śobhā*, *cīrṇa*, *varṇa*, *vareṇya*, *gaṇeya*, *bhrājiṣṇu*, *kāndiśīka*, and *ādiśabda*, as well as the issues of non-recollection, doubt, and error—are also to be understood as refuted; and they have been resolved by those very same [authorities].

The Bārhaspatya Sūtra is likewise merely a set of aphorisms; therefore, enough of this distressing investigation into the nature of things—a discourse whose faltering speech is caused by the seizing of the throat of false pride in scholarship, inflated by the grandiosity of numerous ill-conceived fancies devised by one’s own imagination.
It is established that the sky of grammar, which is inherently pure and exceedingly noble, cannot be stained in the slightest by such showers of dust from slanderous accusations.

Therefore, one should study grammar in order to make oneself more pure than all other purifiers, highly esteemed by noble people, possessed of the four aims of human life, and refined beyond vulgarity.
And it is said: "Water is the first purifier on earth; indeed, the mantras are the supreme purifiers of water.
And the great seers have declared that among those [mantras] of the Sāma, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas, grammar is the purifier."
It has also been said here: "Those men whose mouths are purified by the refinement of grammar dwell upon the surface of the earth as gods in another form."
Moreover, it would indeed be better to be born as mute crocodiles in a deep,
muddy pool than to be humans whose speech is devoid of the refined cultivation awakened by the application to grammar.

And Manu has recorded in his own *Smṛti* that both the grammarian and the Mīmāṃsaka are purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*), stating: "He who explains speech and he who investigates the sacrifice.

Puṣpadanta also said: "If, unfortunate as I am, I have fallen from my residence in the city of Śiva due to the curse of the Goddess, or if I must be born in the sorrowful world of mortals turbid with impurity;
may I quickly fill my ears with the utterances of grammarians, which are as pleasing as streams of milk and distill drops of pure, sweet nectar, so that I may thoroughly conquer [all others]."
Thus, through the mature expressions easily attained by scholars who apply themselves to grammar, the derivation of various Vedic words is acquired without effort.
Furthermore, when the Veda expands its own meaning—strengthened by other auxiliary sciences such as Nirukta and the rest—how could there be any subversion of its authority?
Since our cognition regarding the subject matter of Vedic matters is established here by the science of grammar independently of the [grammatical] components themselves,
how could there be this mutual dependence?
How could this grammar— which is honored by noble ones who possess learning and whose linguistic practice is unerring, and which follows the tradition of the Bhagins—
be beginningless, given its similarity to the characteristics of Prakrit?

Thus, whatever false arguments were raised by ignoble persons who, like imagined demons, sought out every possible flaw, all of those have been completely removed; therefore, the authority of the scriptures remains unassailable.
Thus have these four means of valid cognition been examined according to the instruction;
for those who employ them in practical discourse, all the multitudes of human goals are accomplished.

Thus, when the category of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been examined, [the author] now states the following in order to demonstrate that which is the object of that examination—namely, the object of valid cognition (*prameya*): "The self, the body, the sense organs, the objects, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation are the objects of valid cognition" (NS 1.1.9).
In this case as well, the wise have explained this sūtra as being like the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*,
thus establishing the general definition of its divisions.
The term "object of cognition" (prameya), which extends as far as the words "self" (ātman) and so forth,
restricts the status of being an object of cognition to those alone and to nothing else.

Just as in the case of the expression "Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra should be fed," even without hearing a particle such as *eva*, it is understood through the inherent power of the words that these very individuals are connected to the act of eating and no others; so too here, when it is said that "the self and so forth are the objects of cognition" (*prameya*), the exclusion of objects of cognition other than those is likewise determined.

Now, how is it determined that the objects of cognition (*prameya*) are exactly twelvefold, when in the *Samānatantre* (the Vaiśeṣika-sūtra), after enumerating six categories—namely, the nine substances beginning with earth, the twenty-four qualities beginning with form, the five actions beginning with upward throwing, generality which is twofold by way of the division into higher and lower, ultimate particularities residing in eternal substances, and one inherence—it is described that the objects of cognition are infinite due to their intermediate subdivisions?
It is asked: what, then, is intended here by the term "object of cognition" (prameya)? First, let its general definition be examined.

He said: "This is well said: 'When asked in the ear of someone, he wags his tail. You have raised the objection regarding the twelvefold nature [of the means of knowledge] but do not provide a rebuttal;
instead, you examine the general definition of the object of cognition."
It is said: enough with this play; this alone constitutes the response here.

For it is not merely the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is intended here as the cognizable (*prameya*), because such a thing, being already well-known, is unworthy of definition.
Once the means of valid cognition is thus known, its object—the cognizable—is indeed understood by itself.
What is the use of defining that? Therefore, it is the specific object of cognition (prameya) that is defined here.

Whether correctly or incorrectly known, that which leads to either liberation or worldly existence is intended here as the object of cognition (*prameya*), and not merely the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And that [dependent origination] consists of exactly twelve types, neither fewer nor more; thus, being established in this way, there is an implication for its classification.
Furthermore, from where is this specific object of cognition (prameya-viśeṣa) obtained? It is because the treatise has the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) as its purpose.

For it is asserted that the knowledge of the object of cognition, like the knowledge of the means of valid cognition, is itself—without depending on the utility of another knowledge—the cause of liberation through the sequence beginning with the cessation of false knowledge.
And such a state of being a means to liberation exists only in respect to the self and so forth.

Let it be so; but how does the Sūtra possess the capacity to establish such a specific object of cognition? It is because of the specification of the particular and because of the power inherent in the employment of the word "tu" (but).
It is true that space, time, direction, and so forth, being objects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), are indeed objects of knowledge (*prameya*); however, they do not serve a purpose.

The intended meaning is that the self, body, senses, objects, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation alone constitute the object of knowledge, because these alone are the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

Thus, this word "prameya" indicates here a specific object of knowledge, such as the self and so forth, by means of excluding other objects of knowledge that do not contribute to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).

Although it is of twelve kinds, it is described as twofold for those seeking liberation, according to the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, for the very purpose of accomplishing meditation.
In this regard, everything from the body to suffering is established as solely to be abandoned;
liberation, however, is that which is to be accepted, for the self exists in two states.

That which has the nature of being an experiencer of pleasure, pain, and so forth, is indeed to be abandoned; however, that which is turned away from worldly activities such as enjoyment is to be accepted.
For the body is the locus of experience for the self;
the sense organs are the instruments of experience;
and the objects of the senses are that which is to be experienced.
The mind is the cause of experience;
activity consists of merit and demerit;
and the defects such as passion and the like are the causes for the birth of the body and so forth.
And the repeated conjunction with and disjunction from a body and so forth, caused by this [ignorance], is rebirth (pretyabhāva).
And the fruit in the form of pleasure and pain within saṃsāra is caused by this very same [ignorance];
moreover, it is indeed manifold.
For one possessed of discernment (*viveka*), everything is indeed suffering.
Thus, everything from the body up to suffering itself should be cultivated as something solely to be abandoned;
and even the self (*ātman*), when it is not employed [for liberation], is likewise [to be abandoned].
But the self (ātman) when dissociated from these [afflictions] is called liberation (apavarga).

And since that is to be cultivated as something to be attained, for this very reason there is a further mention of it, even though it was already included by the word "self," because it is the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha).

Thus, by meditating through the knowledge of reality upon these twelve kinds of objects of cognition as things to be abandoned or adopted, one destroys false knowledge—which consists of a contrary apprehension regarding those objects—through repeated practice.
When false knowledge has been sublated by the arising of the knowledge of reality,
defects such as attachment and aversion reach their destruction, since they are rooted in that [false knowledge].
For one whose defects have been exhausted, no activity pertaining to merit or demerit arises;
in the absence of that [activity], its effect—the body and so forth—is not produced.
And the self, being bodiless, is not touched by the manifestations of suffering;
the cessation of all suffering is designated as liberation (apavarga).

Thus, it is established that this twelvefold object of knowledge (prameya) alone serves as a great lake for quenching the terrifying torments arising from the exceedingly deep wilderness of saṃsāra; therefore, it alone is worthy of instruction.
Enough with these discourses on dispassion uttered by ascetics for the wicked;
rather, why is it not thoroughly investigated whether the self itself exists or does not exist?
And likewise, the Lokāyatikas, who deny the existence of another world,
maintain that there is no self other than the body permeated by consciousness.

Furthermore, the self is not apprehended through direct perception by an external sense organ like a jar or the like, nor can it be determined by the mind like pleasure and so forth, because it is impossible to delimit it in such ways. Moreover, for the Cārvākas, inference is not even a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa),
and there exists no inferential mark (liṅga) whatsoever for the establishment of the self.

However, the conjunction with knowledge and so forth will belong only to the elements (*bhūta*) themselves, which have acquired a preeminent power through a specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*).

Just as molasses, flour, and other ingredients, upon undergoing a transformation into the form of liquor, acquire an intoxicating power that was previously non-existent, so too the insentient elements, even while in the state of clay and so forth, will come into contact with consciousness (*caitanya*) when transformed into the form of a body;
and at another time, [they will lose it] due to disease and the like.
Those very [elements], having abandoned their specific transformation, will fall into a state devoid of consciousness;

and because their possession of consciousness does not depart, they themselves will continue for that duration of time to experience proficiency in carrying out activities such as memory and the synthesis of experiences. Thus, what need would there be for an inferred self? As for the scriptures, whose authority is merely mounted upon one's imagination, how could they possibly make the self known?
Furthermore, there is indeed this scriptural passage: "Having arisen from these very elements as a mere mass of consciousness, it perishes along with them; after death, there is no consciousness.
Therefore, since there is no eternal self that transmigrates to another world, what is the use of these fruitless and laborious discourses on the next world?
In this regard, the followers of Upavarṣa have accepted the self to be perceptible; so too have some of our own school, on the grounds that it is cognizable through the notion of "I."
There exists this notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya), some of which is coreferential with the body— as in "I am fat" or "I am thin"—
and some of which is coreferential with the knower— as in "I know" or "I remember. Among these,
let us first consider the notion of "I" that is coreferential with [attributes such as] being fat and so forth.
As for that cognition "I" which possesses co-referentiality with knowledge, desire, pleasure, pain, and so forth,
nothing other than the self is manifested therein.
For there is no connection of cognition, pleasure, desire, and so forth with the body, the sense organs, and the like;
nor do cognitions such as "I know" arise with respect to an object that is devoid of cognition and the rest.
Even the appearance of mere cognition is refuted by recognition:
"I myself knew [it] at first, and I myself know it today."
Neither the subsequent nor the preceding [moment], nor both moments of cognition,
nor the continuum appears within this [present] condition.
One who possesses superior knowledge did not know it previously, nor does he know it now;
the two do not possess both [knowledges] together, yet the continuum is not real.
And because it is not a real entity, that [consciousness] did not know anything previously, nor does it know anything today.
Therefore, it is understood that in the cognition "I indeed knew yesterday" and "I indeed know today," the knower appears as the one persisting through both yesterday and today.

Furthermore, this body is not [the self] because it is manifold due to the differences between states such as childhood and so forth, and because it is insentient. Thus, when the cognizer—who is grasped by the recognition and the "I"-notion—is established, one might then suppose that this "I"-notion, which is co-referential with "stout" and other qualities, exists in the body through a metaphorical attribution of non-difference [between the body and the self], and is therefore false. However, it is not logical to assume the falsity of the "I"-notion—which is co-referential with cognition and other mental factors—merely on account of that [body-based notion], because it is uncontradicted.
Indeed, the cognition "I" cannot be rendered turbid by any minor cause of defect;
therefore, the self alone is its primary object, while any entity other than that is secondary.
Thus, because it is accessible through the cognition "I," the self is perceptible.
Regarding this, they say: these are merely the utterances of words, such as "I know," "I desire," "I am happy," and "I am suffering.
However, no substratum (āśraya) distinct from the very nature of cognition and so forth appears in these cognitions.
How could the self be both the agent and the object within a single consciousness?
The state of being both the apprehended object and the apprehending subject in a single cognition will be refuted;
since this is not accepted by you either, that [duality] does not exist for the self (ātman) as well.

Furthermore, the attempt to establish the relationship of apprehended object (*grāhya*) and apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) for a single self by relying on a distinction based on its states—namely, that the substance-form and so forth of the self is the apprehended object while its cognizer-form is the apprehending subject—is untenable. For if the substance-form and so forth were the apprehended object, then "apprehendedness" would not be established for the cognizer;
this is because the substance-form and so forth residing in the self are equivalent to [external objects] such as a jar.
Even if it is argued by those who consider themselves clever that the knowerhood (*jñātṛtā*) itself must be the grasper,
nevertheless, there is indeed a distinction produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the object:
for knowerhood delimited by a jar is the grasped, whereas pure knowerhood alone is the grasper.

What is the meaning of "I know the jar"? How can it be conceived that one knows the self while knowing [the object], based on the blending of the use of the first-person pronoun (*asmat*)? In other cases, there is simply the apprehension of the pure object, as in "this is a jar. But this too is merely a simple deception; for just as in the cognition "this is a jar," the consciousness is directed solely toward the jar, so too in the case of the blending of the first-person pronoun in "I know the jar," the intellect is directed solely toward the jar.
However, this is the distinction: previously there was merely the apprehension of the jar, whereas now there is the reflective awareness of the jar as qualified by cognition.
Now, when cognition is being analyzed, let it be granted that “this is a jar” is the apprehension of the object (*viṣaya*), while “I know” is indeed the apprehension of the cognition (*jñāna*).

But what is the apprehension of “I”? Furthermore, it is not reasonable to claim that within a single cognition there is both validity and invalidity based on a division of parts—such that “the jar” and “I know” are valid, while “I” is not valid.
Therefore, in this case, the manifestation of the knower must be admitted.
It has been stated in this regard that within a single cognition, the self cannot simultaneously possess both the status of agent and the status of object.
However, this adjunct (*upādhi*) which you attempted to infer is untenable, because it is inclined toward the jar.
Even when the cognition "I know the jar" is analyzed, it results in two parts—"the jar" and "I know"—both of which reside solely in the object.
But as for this part "I," if it is held to have the self as its object, then that very self remains as the pure residue, being both the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
The distinction between them based on their states would not be established.

Furthermore, by asserting that a single entity possesses the nature of both the apprehended and the apprehender without any limiting conditions (*upādhi*) due to the absence of such a distinction, one would be following the path of the Vijñānavāda.
Therefore, one who wishes to describe the object of the "I-notion" as an apprehended object distinct from the apprehending subject must admit that the body itself is the apprehended object.
Furthermore, since its co-referentiality with knowledge is untenable, it would be better to admit that this [notion] is false rather than having the self as its objective support.
Therefore, the cognition of the coreferentiality of "thin" and "dark-complexioned" will not contradict the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), which has the body as its objective support.

[Objection: But surely, because of the appearance of difference in the cognition "this body is mine," how could the notion of "I" have the body as its objective support? [Reply: O good sir, one should not trust such [arguments], for we also observe the cognition of difference in the form "my self."

Now, if an argument is maintained in whatever way possible through distinctions such as different states (*avasthābheda*) and so forth, then that same path shall be followed here even regarding the body as the objective support (*ālambana*).

Therefore, the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) has the body alone as its objective support; and while it is false when it is co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with cognition (*jñāna*) and the like, it is correct when it is co-referential with grossness (*sthūla*) and the like.

However, those two cognitions—“my body” and “my self”—are both false, because the notion of "mine," like the notion of "I," lacks a real self as its objective support, and because a distinction [between the self and the body] is logically untenable with respect to the body.
The notions "my hand" or "my arm" are tenable because they are distinct [from the self];
however, the conceptualization "my body" is like the notion of Rāhu’s head [which is not distinct from him].
Therefore, since both "I-making" (ahaṃkāra) and "mine-making" (mamakāra) lack an object, it is established that the self is imperceptible.

Others, however, say: we do not maintain that a single self simultaneously possesses both the state of being an object and the state of being an agent through the conjunction of both the grasped and the grasper; rather, we accept the reality of the self as being of the nature of pure consciousness (*citiśakti*), independent of other means, and directly manifest.

For the self is not illuminated by knowledge produced by something else, like a jar or similar objects, but is illuminated by itself alone. Furthermore, its sentience is innate, not dependent upon a connection with consciousness brought about by an instrument.
For if consciousness were due to conjunction with consciousness, then that consequence would apply even to jars and the like.
Nor is there any restrictive cause such that consciousness—though its body is composed of a multitude of various causal factors—makes only itself the knower and not any other causal factor.
Therefore, it is better to maintain that its nature as consciousness is simply intrinsic.
This self-manifestation is to be understood as being like consciousness (saṃvit).
As they say: "Consciousness is known by consciousness itself, not by way of being an object of knowledge";
the meaning is that no state of being an object of action (karmabhāva) exists for it.
Thus, since the self is manifested solely as the grasper and not as the grasped, the objection regarding its dissimilarity is untenable.

This too is not tenable, for what is the meaning of "not requiring another means of proof"? That the reality of the self exists as manifesting independently of any other means is incorrect, because a cognition devoid of an instrument (karana) has never been observed.
Furthermore, that would be some unprecedented thing, a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) exceeding those [means] accepted according to established doctrine.
Nor do we see any cause for a restriction here, such that when manifesting in this way, only one's own self manifests and not the self of another.
Since the self is manifest, its state of being experienced must certainly be asserted;
and being experienced consists in being the object of experience, for otherwise its very perceptibility would not be possible.
Now, if it is argued that "the self is not perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), but rather immediate (*aparokṣa*)," this is merely a statement of synonyms;
only the ignorant are thus deceived, not those who rely on valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).
It is truly strange to claim that something is not perceptible and yet is immediate.
If it is argued that this [Self] does not possess the status of being an object of perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*), then let it likewise lack immediacy (*aparokṣatva*).

If it is argued that it possesses immediacy because it is luminous (*prakāśatva*), we say no; for even in the case of light such as a lamp, it is impossible for it to be manifest when it is not perceived by those who are blind and so forth.
Therefore, if the Self is luminous, it must necessarily be experienced; thus, its status as an object (*karmatva*) is unavoidable.
And therefore, the objection regarding its having two forms remains exactly as it was.
And we shall refute the position that cognition is self-luminous;

for that same logical principle applies equally to the self as well. Furthermore, there is a discrepancy in your conceptualization: you hold that the self is self-luminous and that consciousness is self-luminous.

And even one of subtle intellect is not able to demonstrate such a distinction as: "this is consciousness, self-luminous and consisting of the fruit; this is the self, self-luminous and consisting of the knower.
And it is remarkable that between these two luminaries, their operation—known as cognition—has become something hidden (parokṣa).
Now, in the cognition "I know the jar," there is a manifestation of a triad: the object "the jar" appears, the self "I" appears, and the consciousness "I know" appears.
It has been stated in this regard that in the cognition "I know the jar," there is the manifestation of an object as a qualifier of the cognition;
however, the notion "I" is an error consisting in the attribution of knowerhood to the body, because it is impossible for a single self to possess the status of both the grasped and the grasper.
Furthermore, even that which is imagined—the self's inherent nature of being conscious—is likewise devoid of logical justification.
It is conscious through its association with consciousness; without that association, it is inert.
For we do not consider "consciousness" to be anything other than the manifestation of objects.

If the self possesses the capacity for the manifestation of objects by its very nature, then what is the purpose of the sense organs? Furthermore, if one holds the position that the self has the power to discern objects independently of the senses, it would follow that everyone is omniscient.
Therefore, the self's status as a cognizer must necessarily be based solely on its association with cognition.
Nor should one fear the over-extension [of this principle] to jars and the like,
because the diversity of actions arising from the very nature of things is well-known to all the world; furthermore,
actions such as consciousness do not inhere in karma.
However, actions such as going are inherent in the agent;
therefore, this action of cognition is likewise inherent in the agent alone.
Furthermore, the power of a real entity cannot be subject to questioning.
Consciousness does not inhere in action and the like, even though there is no difference in their insentience;
nor does odor touch fire, even though there is no difference in their being substances.
Therefore, it is established that the self is not perceived through direct perception, nor is it an independent cognizer.

However, some of our own school argue as follows: "If the self is held to be imperceptible on the grounds that it is impossible for a single entity to possess both agency and objecthood simultaneously, then how will this self be apprehended even by means of inference? For it is the self alone that infers the self through a logical mark (liṅga).
Therefore, in that case, its status as both agent and object must certainly be admitted."
In that case, just as the self becomes the object of inferential knowledge,
so too let this [self] become the object of the direct perception of the "I-notion."
And just as that which is distinct from the body and so forth is understood through an inferential mark,
so too should it be understood through the notion of "I" as being characterized differently from those [corporeal elements].
Now, what is the nature of the self that is directly realized through perception? If this is so, then what is the nature of pleasure and the like that is held to be apprehended by mental perception?

Now, it is well known that pleasure and so forth have bliss and other such qualities as their very nature; therefore, you should understand that the self also has the nature of being the substratum of those qualities.
For pleasure and the like, when being cognized, are indeed experienced as independent;
however, the apprehension of the self is established through the permeation of the possessive suffix (*matup*).
The cognition "this is pleasure" is observed, but not like a jar or other external objects;
rather, the awareness "I am happy" illuminates the self as well.
Moreover, the author of the Bhāṣya himself indeed demonstrated that the apprehension of an object is qualified by both the knower and the cognition; how could that possibly be ignored?
They maintain that one cannot have a cognition of a qualified object without having grasped its qualifier;
furthermore, the recollection of something previously unexperienced is not possible.
Nor could there be a cognition of an object qualified by that [self] after first knowing the self as a qualifier through inference, because no such sequence can be determined.
Therefore, the self is perceptible.
Furthermore, how could that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) which is observed when being synthesized in memory, direct experience, and so forth, be possible?
First, there is the cognition of an identical object: "Previously I experienced that object, and today I experience it again.
In that case, the identity of the agent also manifests; otherwise, the self could not even be inferred.
Knowledge, desire, pleasure, pain, and so forth are indeed the marks of the self;
known as having a single locus, they provide the cognition of a unifying subject.
And that knowledge of it as such is preceded by the knowledge of its substratum;
for if that [substratum] is already known, the logical mark (liṅga) is fruitless, and if it is unknown, it lacks the status of being a logical mark.
Therefore, it is better to accept that the self is indeed directly perceived,
in accordance with the traditions of the elders and through the observation of consciousness itself.
Alternatively, what is the purpose of this insistence?
Let the self simply be inferable by means of the mark consisting of desire and so forth.
Regarding this, the author of the Sūtras says: "Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks of the self" (NS 1.1.10).

Desire, first of all, arises in this manner: a person who has previously experienced happiness by employing a certain kind of object, upon later encountering an object of that same kind, recollects its quality as a means to happiness and desires to acquire it.
This desire, arising through such a sequence, leads one to infer a substratum capable of synthesizing the preceding and succeeding moments, because an effect cannot logically exist without a support.
And when the mere substratum is to be cognized, this very reason—characterized by positive and negative concomitance—is what establishes it.

Desire is the subject (dharmin); "is dependent" is the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma). The reason (hetu) should be stated as either "because it is an effect," like a jar and so forth, or "because it is a quality (guṇa)," like color and so forth.

And that desire and the other [mental states] possess the nature of qualities has been demonstrated by the Teachers through their being perceptible by non-visual perception, just like taste and so forth.

Thus, when by this reason—possessing both positive and negative concomitance—the mere existence of a controller (adhiṣṭhāna) has been inferred, and when that controllership might be attributed to the body, senses, and so forth, an examination of the production [of the effect] as dependent upon the recollection of its being a means to pleasure experienced previously leads to the realization that it must have the same agent as its effect. Once the body and such are thereby excluded, that very reason, functioning as a purely negative inference (kevalavyatirekin), leads to the inference of a specific substratum: "The desire has a substratum distinct from the body and so forth, because, while there is a sublation [of its presence] in the body and such, it is an effect."
And since a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is not possible here, a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is demonstrated.
And that is indeed the jar itself.
That very jar which served as the similar instance when "being an effect" was stated without qualification, serves as the dissimilar instance when it is stated with a qualification.
It cannot be said that where there is no dependence on something dissimilar, there is also no "effectness" (kāryatva) accompanied by its qualification, as in the case of a jar and so forth.

For even though mere effectness is present there, because effectness accompanied by its qualification is absent, dependence on something dissimilar is also absent; this is because it is perceived through direct perception as depending on the primary elements (bhūta).

Now, it may be argued that a mere negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), perceived without the observation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), becomes doubtful; for one might wonder whether the exclusion of the reason from the locus of the probandum is caused solely by the absence of that probandum, or rather caused by some other factor. Logicians maintain that a reason with a doubtful negative concomitance is non-probative, just like a reason whose deviation is certain. To this it is replied: this would indeed be so if a reason were employed that first lacks any known positive concomitance and relies solely upon negative concomitance.

However, where a reason that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) assumes the status of a purely negative reason (*kevalavyatirekin*) by relying upon a certain specific qualification (*viśeṣa*), there the possibility of "doubtful negative concomitance" finds no room.

For a jar is perceived through direct perception as being supported by the ground; thus, its lack of the qualified reason arises precisely from the absence of a substrate distinct [from the subject], since its connection with that [reason] was observed in the unqualified state. Therefore, the negative concomitance is not doubtful.
Alternatively, "being a body" (śarīratva) may here be employed as a counter-example based on dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta);
for in that case, there is not even a suspicion of its being an effect in every respect,
nor does it reside in something of a different nature, since its residing in a body is perceived through direct observation.

Thus, it is established that this desire, being understood as having the same agent as its effects—such as the first perception of an object—is made known to have a substratum distinct from the body and other such things, by virtue of its being an effect characterized by specific qualifications;
and as for that distinct substratum, the designation "Self" (ātman) applies to it on the basis of scripture.
In the same way, it must be stated that hatred and so forth are signs of a self.

When a person has experienced suffering due to the proximity of a certain kind of object, upon perceiving another object of that same kind, he recognizes it as a means to suffering and feels aversion toward it;
this process of recognition would not be possible without a single, continuous cognizer.
Immediately following these two—desire and aversion—effort arises;
that too, according to the aforementioned sequence, is preceded by deliberation.
For one who exerts effort, pleasure and pain come into being.
Those two also are to be viewed in exactly the same way.

Although cognition may indeed occur initially even without depending on synthesis (*anusandhāna*), and that too can certainly be stated to have the self as its mark (*liṅga*), nevertheless, because it occurs within a context of effects such as desire preceded by synthesis, only cognition consisting of a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*) should be cited as an example.
For in that case, it is observed to be preceded by the desire to know (*bubhutsā*), deliberation (*vimarśa*), and so forth; thus, its having a single agent is inferred.
Thus, it is established that desire and the rest are the marks of the self.
In a treatise, the statement of multiple reasons is not a fault as it is in formal debates;
for a certain student might state something by recollecting it from somewhere or other.
Thus, the compassionate Sage has indeed taught many paths of reasoning here in this world.
Now, it may be objected: "How is it known that this effect, such as desire and so forth, is not possible without a synthesizing subject (*anusandhātṛ*)?

As for the claim that 'it is because this is observed in a single cognizer (*pramātṛ*),' by thus mentioning a single cognizer, you would be admitting the perceptibility of the Self (*ātman-pratyakṣatva*), and therefore inference would be useless."

However, if there were no apprehension of a single cognizer, it would be impossible to infer desire and so forth because their necessary connection [with that cognizer] could not be apprehended; this objection has already been answered by us, who have described desire and the rest as being indicative marks (*liṅga*) precisely by virtue of being effects, and not by virtue of having a common substratum with memory and so forth.

What, then, is the purpose of introducing the argument of "reconnection" (pratisandhāna) regarding the body and so forth? It is for the purpose of refuting their status as the substratum [of desire and other mental states].
However, we have not explained it in this way—as an inference of a single substratum based on observing that the effects such as desire belong to a single cognizer.
Therefore, there is no fault.

But how is there no fault? For even when proving the negation of having the body and so forth as a locus, it is impossible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason (*hetu*). As long as the entire collection of effects—such as seeing, hearing, and desiring—is not determined to be restricted to a single cognizer, how can those in our situation establish the negation of having the body and so forth as a locus, nor the dependence on a single self (*ekātmāśritatva*) which is preceded by that [negation]?

Who says this? [If you say] "it is not apprehended that desire and so forth have a single agent," then if it has been apprehended, it must be stated where it was apprehended or by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) it was apprehended.
If you say "within oneself," then this self would have to be perceptible (*pratyakṣa*). Or, if this is not admitted, there is no apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
It is said: the self is not perceived, yet there is no non-apprehension of pervasion;
nor is pervasion apprehended in another locus (*dharmin*), but rather only within one's own continuum (*svasantāna*).

Nevertheless, the inference regarding the restriction to a specific cognizer is not established; how could it possibly be established? For it is observed that the act of synthesis occurs among different mental continua by virtue of being preceded by a single cognizer.
Now, what here is the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*)? For, as in the case of perception and inference, there ought to be a distinction between them.
What follows from that?
How could the pervasion be grasped within one's own mental continuum alone, or how could the restriction of the cognizer (*pramātṛniyama*) be inferred therein?
This is like a rope with nooses at both ends:
either the self is directly perceived,
or its pervasiveness is difficult to comprehend.
This is not so; for just as in the Śākya school there is the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the inference of momentariness from existence (*sattva*), so too shall it be here.

For in that case, the very exclusion of existence from permanent things by way of the exclusion of succession and simultaneity is itself the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with momentary things; thus, without depending on any other factual substrate (*dharmyantara*), both the apprehension of the necessary connection and the inference are demonstrated even regarding the subject (*dharmin*) to be proven.

Likewise, here too, although there is no apprehension of the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) in another factual substrate by way of its being preceded by a single cognizer, [the pervasion is nonetheless established].

Nevertheless, regarding the difference between distinct mental continua (*santānāntara*), the very fact that there is no perception [of another's cognition] is itself the perception of a single agent; so what is the distinction between these two in their status as logical reasons (*hetu*)? Surely, in that case [the proof of momentariness], the exclusion from succession and simultaneity can be grasped through the exclusion [of the cause] from eternal things; but here, however, the exclusion of the synthesis [of cognitions] due to a difference in cognizers is difficult to ascertain, for even within one’s own continuum, the cognizers are nothing other than the moments of cognition themselves.
And yet, the linking of rebirth is not excluded from them.
Let alone positive concomitance; even by way of negative concomitance, this inference is difficult to establish:
because within one's own continuum, there is no perception of a difference between cognizers, as there is between distinct continua.
For if that difference were perceived, there would be no distinction between one's own and another's continuum.
If this is so, then since there is no apprehension of a distinction between cognizers, the self has once again become perceptible.
It is not so; the self is not perceived by direct perception.
For it has been stated that a difference between cognizers within one's own continuum is not apprehended, yet their identity is likewise not apprehended.
Furthermore, the non-apprehension of difference is one thing, and the apprehension of their identity is another;
since the pervasion (vyāpti) is established through the mere non-apprehension of difference, there is no difficulty in inference.

But is it not the case that even within one's own continuum, the non-perception of a distinction between cognizers is not determined as to whether it arises from the unity of the cognizer or from the causal relation between cognitions?

Consequently, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) remains doubtful. We shall explain immediately and in detail how there is no causal relation between cognitions, and how this worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is not produced by such a relation.
Therefore, the inference of a single cognizer based on effects such as desire and so forth is indeed valid.
But surely desire and the like will reside in the body itself;
Bṛhaspati has declared that consciousness belongs to the elements alone.

And it has been said that "one's own knowledge is like the power of intoxication. It is stated that the body, for its part, is not the substratum of desire and so forth, because it is distinct according to the different stages of childhood, youth, old age, and so on.
For indeed, an object seen by one person cannot be remembered by another;
nor does a desire arise in one person for an object that has been remembered by another.
Therefore, because the cognition of objects arises from that [mind] and because desire originates from its very nature,
some substratum must be asserted for this single wheel of effects.
Furthermore, the body is distinct according to the differences in its states, such as childhood and so forth;
therefore, it cannot be the substratum [of memory], just like one separate continuum.
For just as there is no recollection by Yajñadatta of an object seen by Devadatta, likewise there would be no [recollection] by the adult body of what was experienced by the infant body.

Surely, it is understood through the authority of the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that only the states are different, while the essential nature of the substratum—the body—is indeed non-different.
Nor is this recognition established otherwise (as being fallacious), like the recognition of hair or nails that have been cut off and grown back again, because no destruction is perceived.
For the refutation of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitva*) regarding pillars and the like will be accomplished by recognition itself.
And if that [recognition] here too were exactly like that [recognition of a pillar], it would be incorrect; for in the case of a pillar and the like, no cause for their being different is perceived.
But here, because a difference in the transformation of form, configuration, and so forth is observed, this recognition is merely an error based on similarity.
Indeed, an identical measurement and so forth are not perceived in the body of an infant, the body of a youth, and the body of an old man.
Furthermore, the transformation of the body is understood to result from the transformation of food;
otherwise, food would not undergo decay through the process of digestion.
For there would be no nourishment from consuming curd, milk, and the like;
nor would its redness be observed upon the use of fermented gruel and similar substances.
With some parts diminished and others newly arisen,
how can the whole (avayavin) remain undivided?

And thus, some have postulated the destruction and arising even of a pot or similar object while being baked, on the grounds that it possesses a form and other qualities dissimilar to its prior state, by considering solely the conjunction with the substance of fire possessing velocity, which is the cause of the baking.
Even though jars and other objects placed in a pit, their forms covered by grass, leaves, and the like, are perceived without being destroyed by the visual ray extending through the gaps therein;

even though they are seen with their same number, size, configuration, and location despite having been baked; even though they are not perceived as falling; and even though, because the collection of causal factors such as an agent is impossible at that time, their reassembly appears as if it were impossible—nevertheless, their destruction is postulated through inference.
Because qualities distinct from the original form and so forth are perceived both internally and externally across all parts due to heating, the entry of fire is inferred.

Indeed, through the impulse or impact of that swift substance, fire, action arises in the constituent parts that originate the jar and other objects; from action comes disjunction; from disjunction comes the destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance; and from the destruction of that [conjunction] comes the destruction of the substance.

Even in the case of penetration, because one must necessarily assume the existence of subtle fissures, there is a disjunction of the conjunctions of the parts of the jar and so forth; thus, there is indeed destruction.
Moreover, after cooking, when jars and other vessels are being removed from the fire, some are seen to have burst, some have become crooked, and others have assumed entirely different shapes;
therefore, we see from this as well that they perish.
The argument "because they possess that number" is entirely inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to cases such as pots and the like whose necks have been pierced by the tips of needles.

Therefore, according to the previously stated principle, when the effect-substances such as pots have perished, it is only the atoms that undergo baking (*pāka*). Having been baked, while not abandoning their previous qualities such as blackness, they experience the acquisition of other qualities such as redness; impelled by *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), which serves as the means for sentient beings to experience pleasure and pain, they conjoin with one another and, through the process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), originate an effect-substance such as a pot of precisely that same kind.

In this regard, the process—namely, that at such-and-such a moment there is the production of such-and-such an effect and the dissolution of such-and-such another—is not described here, for fear of excessive prolixity and because it serves no purpose.
The same principle applies to mangoes and other fruits being ripened by heat and sunlight.

Likewise, when food, drink, and so forth are being digested by the internal heat within the body, they undergo transformation into the states of nutrient-essence (*rasa*), waste (*mala*), and bodily constituents (*dhātu*); since production and destruction generally occur at every moment, there is an absence of stability. Therefore, how could that [self] be connected to activities such as recognition?
Others, however, on account of the force of direct perception, maintain that the destruction of the jar and so forth occurs while it is being baked;
and because the substance is composed of porous matter, baking can take place both internally and externally.
Furthermore, even when the pot is baked, the cold touch of water poured into it is perceived on the outside.

Consequently, just as there would be destruction caused by the entry of a mass of blazing fire-flames at the time of cooking, so too would there be the undesirable consequence of destruction caused by the entry of a multitude of extremely cold water-drops at that same time;
yet no such observation is made through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, since a product-substance such as a jar is produced precisely because of its inherent porosity, and the occurrence of cooking is possible due to the intermittent entry of particles of fire, there is no need for the postulation of [the object's] destruction.
The position that it is cooked in a pot is indeed the most elegant.
For just as a jar placed upon a furnace for baking is seen to be exactly the same when it is removed from there after the baking has been completed.
In some cases, however, the observation of a different configuration will be explained as being caused by the impact of wood or other materials;
if it were caused by contact with fire, such a state would occur everywhere.
Therefore, jars and other objects are cooked while remaining entirely undestroyed.
But this principle of the pot and so forth is not accepted in the case of the body.

For the digestion of food does not occur there even when stability is present, as is the case with the baking of jars and the like; indeed, the body is observed to be subject to increase and decrease.
Therefore, since differences in size and other attributes are observed, it is established that the body is not a single entity; thus, the recognition of it is like the recognition of a flame.

As for the claim that there is indeed a plurality of states while the substratum of those states—designated as the "body"—is one and the same, that too is untenable because the conceptual alternatives of identity and difference are logically inconsistent.
If those states were entirely distinct from the body, then, due to their plurality, it would follow that the body itself is multiple.
Conversely, if the states were not different from the single body, then there could be no mutual distinction between the states themselves.
Now, if the states were distinct from the body, then their apprehension as distinct entities would have to be demonstrated;
yet such [apprehension] does not exist.
In the case of "cowness" and so forth, the recurring cognition—which, being established otherwise, brings about the distinction between the universal and its possessor—is not refuted by anyone.
Furthermore, in this case, the cognition that grasps the identity of the abider is erroneous because it is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) according to the previous reasoning.

Therefore, since the body is distinct [in each instance], just like one separate continuum (*santāna*), its connection with effects such as memory and recollection is difficult to establish; thus, the body cannot be the substratum for effects such as desire.

Furthermore, the body cannot possess knowledge and other such qualities because it is subject to transformation, like milk; because it possesses form and other sensible qualities, just like that [milk]; because its nature consists of a collection of many parts, like a triple-staff (tridaṇḍa) and similar objects; and because it is composed of the primary elements arranged in a specific configuration, like external material objects.
The body is devoid of consciousness because it is a body, like the body of the elements (*bhūta*).
Consciousness is not a property of the body, because it does not persist as long as the substance [the body] exists.

Nor is there any deviation [from this rule] due to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, since it is observed that the arising and passing away of those [qualities] are produced by other causes, whereas here [in the case of consciousness], such [other causes] are absent.
Alternatively, by including the qualification "provided it is a specific quality" (viśeṣaguṇatve sati), there is no deviation [from the rule].
For if consciousness were a specific quality of that [self], it would follow that it is indestructible, since—like color and other such qualities—it would persist as long as the substrate remains.

As for what was said regarding the analogy with the power of intoxication (*mada-śakti*), there the acceptance [of the analogy] is due to the perceptibility of the power of intoxication, but there is no perception of cognition (*jñāna*) therein.

[Objection: But is not cognition also generally seen to follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [intoxicant]? For when the elements are nourished by the consumption of food, drink, and so forth, consciousness (*cetanā*) becomes acute; and when that is reversed, the opposite occurs.
And when the body of the prince has been refined by the consumption of *brāhmī* ghee and other such substances, sharpness of intelligence arises.

Furthermore, during the rainy season, due to perspiration and other factors, after a relatively short period of time, the very components of curd and similar substances are perceived as moving in the form of worms such as *pūtana*.

Moreover, even the conventional usage of "heaviness" and "lightness" regarding consciousness will be determined by the presence or absence of a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) in the elements. Thus, it appears that the position that consciousness belongs to the elements (*bhūtacaitanyapakṣa*) alone is consistent with reason.
This is not correct; for the body is observed to be the locus of the sense organs and their objects.

When there is nourishment of the sense organs through the nourishment of that [body], because the instruments [of perception] become sharp, the apprehension of objects also becomes, as it were, more acute.
And there is no such thing as consciousness other than the apprehension of objects.
By this, the use of *brāhmī* ghee is also explained.
Since the self (*ātman*) is all-pervading and thus present everywhere, it sometimes takes up the constituent parts of the elements as the locus of experience;
therefore, just like semen and blood, it will take up modified constituents of curd.
And thus, the claim that the creation of beings proceeds with many divisions—such as those born from sweat and so forth—in dependence upon the ripening of diverse karmas, is trivial.
Therefore, it is established that sentience does not belong to the elements in any way whatsoever.
Nor do the sense organs serve as the substratum for the aforementioned effects such as cognition, because a single object is apprehended through both seeing and touching. (3.1.1)

"I now touch with my sense of touch that very object which I previously saw with my eye; I now see with my eye that which I previously touched with my sense of touch"—which sense organ could thus perform this synthesis? Neither the eye, because it does not have touch as its object, nor the tactile sense, because it does not have visible form as its object.
Therefore, there exists some synthesizer capable of grasping the objects of both senses; thus, he is understood to be distinct from the sense organs.
In this very context, the existence of a substratum possessing qualities (guṇin) as distinct from form and the rest must be established; its proof is based upon this cognition.
For this cognition would not occur if form and the other [objects] were independent;
neither form is its object, nor is touch, nor is both of them.

Therefore, the reason stated by the opponent—that "the possessor of qualities (guṇin) is not distinct from the qualities because it is not perceived separately"—is unestablished, since we have already demonstrated that they are indeed perceived as distinct.

As for the refutations of the dilemmas regarding subsistence (vṛtti-vikalpa) and so forth, these were discussed during the establishment of the universal (sāmānya), and will be explained in the section on the establishment of the parts; so, enough with this digression.
Furthermore, the sense organs do not possess consciousness because they are instruments, like an axe or similar tools;
moreover, we shall describe the sense organs as being composed of material elements (bhautika).
Therefore, the same reasoning that was set forth for the refutation of consciousness in the primary elements (bhūta-caitanya) should also be applied to those [senses].
And for this very reason, [the soul exists] because of the transformation of another sense organ. 3.1.12.
For when an object is seen with the eye as beautiful with the flow of its flavor,
there may be a transformation of the tongue, but not a flooding of saliva from the teeth.
Furthermore, there would be a diversity of intentions among the many sense faculties;
consequently, there would be multiple consciousnesses within a single continuum.
And this position that the senses possess consciousness is utterly trivial; so why write much on this matter?
[Objection: "In that case, the mind (*manas*) will be the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for desire and the rest;

for it is eternal, unitary, all-pervading, and non-material, and thus it is not touched by the aforementioned defects. [Reply: It is said: "The status of being the substratum of that [desire] is also untenable for the mind.
Why? Because the knower possesses the instruments of knowledge; it is merely a difference in terminology. (3.1.17)

For if the mind were the locus of desire and the like, it would possess agency with respect to cognition and so forth; consequently, since it would be impossible for that [mind] alone to simultaneously produce cognitions of external objects such as odors, there must exist some internal instrument (karaṇa) capable of perceiving objects such as pleasure and pain, performing functions such as memory, and being efficient in presiding over the instruments of smell and the rest. Thus, the designation "Self" (ātman) would apply to that [instrument], and the designation "mind" (manas) would apply to the agent, which is the Self.
Furthermore, all his activities are not accomplished by means of external instruments;
nor are the eyes and other senses the means for memory, pleasure, desire, and so forth.
Therefore, neither the mind nor the sense organs is the support for desire, volition, pleasure, pain, and sensation;
even the body does not attain the status of being their substratum. Consequently, we postulate a Person (puruṣa) distinct from these.

This is merely an indication of the direction, stating that desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition serve as marks for the self; however, in that regard, there exists a vast multitude of other reasons.
Indeed, the state of being employed by an agent is observed in the case of the collection of instruments such as the sickle;
likewise, the skin, the ear, and other organs must also be employed by an agent.
Furthermore, purposeful activity directed toward the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful is observed as being invariably present in the body;
we therefore infer that it is presided over by a conscious agent, just as a moving chariot or similar vehicle is.
Regarding the vital breaths and other winds that move within, possessing both stable and unstable motions,
some cause for their innate transformation through their own karma is inferred.
And observing that this process of growth, wounding, breaking, and healing— which is difficult to find elsewhere than in the body—
is constant, a person, like the movement of a planet, directs his course toward the security of his own refuge.
And it is logical that the sense faculties, being unpresided over by the mind, would lack the skill to produce valid cognitions of their respective objects.
There might be some effort conducive to a desired object, impelled by which the mind presides over them.

Now, as for the probans consisting of the instrument and so forth, what could possibly serve as an example for that which possesses knowledge, effort, and the like? This objection does not apply to us regarding the effect [as a probans], because even for you, a mere generality (sāmānyamātra) is established.

The worldly transaction that occurs through means of valid cognition such as direct perception and the rest cannot exist without an eternal [self]; therefore, for this reason as well, there is the conceptualization of this [self].
Since that cognition which is perceptual and of the nature of recognition does not acquire its own existence if there were a difference in the knower,
just as the identity of the object to be grasped is established, so too is the identity of the person who is the grasper established.

The apprehension of the inseparable relation, the cognition of the mark (liṅga), the recollection of its concomitance, and the resulting cognition of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin)— this [process] would not constitute a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) for one who differs from the cognizer.

When the analogical statement has been learned from the mouth of a forest-dweller, and a deer resembling a cow is seen roaming in the forest, one obtains the result [of the cognition] "this is what that name denotes. This is not established as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) distinct from the other types of knowledge.

The hearing of the phonemes in their sequence, the grasping of word-meanings through the recollection of convention (*samaya*), the reflection upon them at the time of perceiving the final phoneme arising from those mental impressions, and the synthesis of the sentence-meaning produced by the connection [of words] based on expectancy and so forth—this would be extremely difficult to accomplish without a single cognizer; therefore, the existence of an eternal Self is established with certainty.
Thinking, "This was performed by me yesterday; this other thing must be performed tomorrow," people engage in activities such as learning, agriculture, and trade.
Since they act in this way after careful investigation, they certainly perceive that Person who persists through all states of existence.
Thus has been stated the definition of the self: that it is the substratum of desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and pain.
A seeker of liberation should determine that which is associated with these [qualities] as something to be abandoned here, and that which is dissociated from them as something to be realized.
Furthermore, the Tathāgatas have said: "What use have you for a postulated person?
Through mere cognition alone, the aforementioned worldly transaction is established."
Is knowledge accepted by the followers of the Sugata as being eternal like the Self,
and capable of such activities as the desire for recollection and the synthesis previously demonstrated?
How could knowledge possibly be eternal within the house of a Buddha?
Let it be understood that all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as well are momentary.
If the effect is held to be momentary, it does not depend on anything whatsoever;
therefore, cognition alone is independent, and nothing else is inferred by means of it.
Furthermore, this differentiation of cognition—consisting of desire, aversion, pleasure, and so forth—is not a distinct entity; thus, there is no postulation of anything other than that.
Even the state of being a quality does not exist for this [entity], which is why one postulates a substratum;
moreover, there is no such thing as a "possessor of qualities" that exists apart from the qualities themselves.
In the aggregates of consciousness, which are momentary and without a substratum,
how can there be effects such as memory, or even how can there be a future world?

Even if there is a future world, how are the faults of "attaining what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was done" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) refuted? For, since the cognition by which the act of worshipping a shrine (*caityavandanā*) and so forth was performed has perished, one would not experience its fruit;
and as for the one who experiences the fruit, he did not perform that act. This is not a fault, because the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is the regulating factor.
Indeed, there is a continuous stream of the causal relationship between cognitions, proceeding as an beginningless succession.
This very [series] is called the "continuum" (saṃtāna),
and it is by this that the restriction of effects such as recollection and so forth is established.
Because the continuum is beginningless and because it is uninterrupted, the existence of another world is not a burdensome conceptual construction.

Although it is observed that a cognition in one continuum can be produced by a cognition belonging to another continuum, nevertheless, the designation of a "continuum" (santāna) or the fulfillment of effects such as recognition does not occur through such a causal relationship; rather, this restriction is established solely on the basis of a specific [causal] nature consisting of the material cause (upādāna).
Only when that is the case is the distinction between the continuum of its own nature (svarūpa-santāna) logically possible.
The loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done are to be avoided, just as in the case of memory,
by means of the transition of its continuum, like the color of a seed in a flower.
And it is said: "For in whichever very continuum the impression of karma is deposited, there alone does it bear fruit, just as redness [appears] in cotton."

Just as the color called redness, once produced in a specific cotton seed, results in a flower of that same red color and not of another, so too, whatever kind of karmic impression exists within a particular stream of consciousness, such a fruit arises in that very stream and not in another consciousness; this is the meaning.
And thus, the faults of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) are dispelled.
If the self, which is accepted as eternal, undergoes modification through the arising of pleasure and so forth, then it would be declared to be non-eternal, like leather and such things.
But if it is devoid of change, then what difference does the fruit of karma—whether existent or non-existent pleasure, pain, and so on—make to it? Thus, karma would indeed be rendered fruitless.
As it has been said: "What effect do rain and sun have upon the sky? Their effect is upon the leather."
"If it is like a hide, it is impermanent; if it is like space, it yields no fruit."

Therefore, let this first delusion of the consecrated—the grasping at a self—be abandoned. With its cessation, the grasping at "mine" will also cease [with the realization: "I myself do not exist; what is mine?"]. Thus, by severing the knots of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and possessiveness (*mamakāra*), one should rely upon the very vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*), which is the gateway to Nirvana.
And its path is the determination of momentary entities;
for when all things are momentary and without support, since even cognition lacks a support, how could there be any conception of a self?
But how can this doctrine of momentary entities, which transcends all means of valid cognition, be accepted by the Śākyas?
Indeed, if things were momentary, sense-born cognition would not be a valid means of knowledge,
because it is impossible for such a cognition to arise with the conceptual construction of a momentary form.
Alternatively, because the cognition of a reason that is invariably concomitant is impossible,
there is no ground for inference, since it is restricted to conceptual construction.
Since recollection and recognition are established as proving stability,
the teachings on the rapid perishability [of things] are merely deceptive.
It is said: whether momentariness is accessible through perception or not—this will be investigated later.
However, inference is now being stated: "entities are momentary because they exist.
Existence, for its part, is defined as the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
As it has been said: "That which is capable of causal efficiency is alone ultimately real."

For if existence were defined by being cognizable through valid means of knowledge (*sat-pramāṇa-gamyatva*), it would follow that even a mass of floating hairs (*keśoṇḍraka*) and the like would possess existence.
If, however, existence were defined by being related to the universal *sattā*, then universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth would be non-existent because they do not relate to that [universal].
Furthermore, worldly convention follows existence as the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*).
Even when a son exists, worldly people designate themselves as "childless" because his functions are not being performed;
conversely, even when there is someone other than a son who performs those functions, they say, "We have a son.
Therefore, existence consists precisely in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).

Let it be so; however, as for your question, "Where and how is the pervasion (vyāpti) grasped by means of momentariness?"—O Illustrious One, let that pervasion be grasped wherever it pleases you, whether in a jar or in a cloth.

O wise one, why should it be thought that the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) is possible only with respect to the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin)? What error is there here? For there is no such thing as a "subject of the thesis" created by fate;
if pervasion can be apprehended, let it be apprehended wherever it may be.
As for the question of how this [non-existence] is apprehended, it is said in reply: for the existence of entities is pervaded by either succession or simultaneity.
And since a pervader is not perceived among eternal entities,
existence— which is pervaded by that [non-eternality]— is necessarily excluded from them.
And since there is no third aggregate, because of the exhaustion of other states of existence,
the notion of a "sentient being" relies solely upon those momentary phenomena.
And that [object] is cognized without doubt through the cognition that apprehends it,
since the incapacity of its cause has been refuted by the very arising of the cognition.
Indeed, the arising of anything from that which is incapable is never observed;
whether it is produced by the capable or the incapable, there is no doubt regarding its cognition.
For this very reason, they have always declared that knowledge to be a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa);
for regarding its own nature and its capacity to produce an effect, doubt and the like are impossible.

Let cognizers indeed entertain doubt regarding the specific aspect—whether "this is silver" or "this is mother-of-pearl"—but no oscillation whatsoever is possible regarding its capacity, such as: "Is this cognition produced by something capable, or by something other than that?

For it is logically impossible for what is incapable to be a producer. Furthermore, even in the case of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) which grasps pervasion, its validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), because doubt and error are likewise absent therein.

Furthermore, how is it stated that succession and simultaneity—two properties that pervade all existing things—are not perceived in eternal entities? For an eternal entity would have to produce its effect either successively or simultaneously, since a third mode is logically impossible for things whose natures are established through mutual exclusion.
It cannot be that [the cause] acts successively, for it must either be capable or incapable [of acting].

If it is capable, why would it act successively? For it is impossible for that which is capable to delay. But if it is incapable, it does nothing at all simply because of its incapacity; so what is the point of its acting successively? If you argue that it acts by depending on auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), we say no, because it is impossible for an auxiliary cause to bestow capability upon that which is inherently incapable.
Because if that which is capable possesses its own capacity inherently, auxiliary factors would be useless.

Furthermore, even when auxiliaries are present, its agency would have to be either by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*) or by way of another nature (*pararūpa*). If it were by way of its own nature, since that nature exists even prior [to the presence of auxiliaries] and is thus already a causal factor (*kāraka*), what would be the use of an auxiliary? If agency were by way of another nature, then because it would involve the abandonment of the previous nature and the acquisition of that other nature, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) would necessarily follow.
In this way, even an auxiliary cause must be analyzed in terms of its being either capable or incapable.

If it possesses capability by its own nature, what need is there for the wretchedness of seeking assistance from another? But if it is incapable, what can that poor minister do, even after having arrived?

Furthermore, does the auxiliary (sahakārī) perform some function or not? If it performs no function, then everything would assist everyone everywhere in every effect. If it performs a function, it must be stated what that function is.
If it is argued that there is a benefit [conferred], is that which is benefited distinct from or non-distinct from the benefactor? If it is non-distinct, then that very thing would be produced.
If there is distinction, what has happened to that [beneficiary] such that it does not remain as it was before?
The assistance [rendered] by the effect must also be considered in terms of both difference and non-difference.
It is not different from the effect, because it is not perceived as such,
and because there is no production of a duality.

But if the assistance being rendered by the auxiliary cause is not distinct from the effect itself, then the effect would be produced by that auxiliary alone, and thus the primary cause would be rendered useless.

But is it not the case that a single entity alone is the causal factor (*kāraka*), for it is that which is capable? And since the proximity of other things is brought about by the force of their own causes, it does not deserve censure. This is not tenable, because a single thing is never observed to be a causal factor, and its capacity is therefore difficult to establish.
For it is in this way that he is called "capable": if he were ever seen producing an effect alone, but he is not seen even in one's memory.

Now, if it is argued that this is the very nature of the effect—that it does not arise from a single cause—while the cause is indeed capable, that too is incorrect. For if the effect were dependent on the nature [of the cause], it would follow that the cause lacks causal capacity. Indeed, a cause could be said to be "capable" only if, disregarding the nature of the effect, it could forcibly produce the effect independently by itself.
Since this is not observed, such an argument is trivial.
Now, suppose the cause is indeed capable;
however, its nature is such that it does not produce the effect immediately, but rather produces the effect after an interval of several moments.
If this were so, the production of the effect would never occur.

Even at the time of producing an effect, since its nature of generating that effect after being separated by several moments has not departed, there would be the requirement of waiting for those several moments again.
When those several moments have passed, that very same nature of his remains as it was; thus, this [process] would occur yet again. So when, indeed, would it ever produce the effect?
