Therefore, because they are afflicted by such defects, entities do not possess the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) through a gradual succession.
Nor can they exist simultaneously, because such usage is not observed in the world.
Furthermore, for a permanent entity that has already performed its function, there would be no cause for it to act again;
and even if it were to act again, the entity could not produce that very same effect, because it is impossible to perform what has already been performed.

But if it were to perform another action, that very same position of succession would recur; thus, succession and simultaneity are excluded from eternal entities. Since these two are pervaders of existence (*sattva*), when they are excluded, existence itself is excluded from them at the outset. Deprived of existence, and lacking any other alternative state, existence must reside only in momentary things.

Therefore, although in the case of a causal reason (*kāryahetu*), as with smoke and fire, or even in some cases of an essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), as with "being a tree" and "being a *śiṃśapā*," there was previously no apprehension of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) in a different locus (*dharmāntara*), nevertheless, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) will be established in the very subject (*dharmin*) where the probandum is to be proven, because the exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*) is well-ascertained. And that very exclusion from the dissimilar instances is itself the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of this reason with its own probandum.

For it is not possible that existence (sattva) is excluded from eternal things yet not distinct from momentary things, because there is no third category and because it would be impossible for it to lack a substratum.

Thus, if that very same subject (*dharmin*) in which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) was grasped is at some point used as an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for another person, let it be so; what fault is there in this?
Is it not the case that non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is itself an inference?
And if the apprehension of pervasion by means of one inference were to depend upon another inference, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
There is no infinite regress, because the process terminates at that very point;
for the determination of pervasion does not arise from another inference based on the non-perception of the pervader, but rather from perceptual conceptualization itself.
Thus, through this determination of pervasion, it is established that whatever exists is momentary.
Others, however, explain the ascertainment of pervasion in a different manner:

when two contradictory things are determined as one, the exclusion of the other necessarily follows precisely because they are contradictory; and existence and permanence are contradictory according to the very principle previously stated.

Furthermore, the existence (*sattva*) of entities is clearly perceived; therefore, from that perception, their permanence is excluded. The exclusion of permanence itself is the ascertainment of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), because there is no other alternative possibility.
[Objection: Since cold and heat are perceived separately, it is logical that upon the ascertainment of their opposition, the exclusion of the second occurs when the first is apprehended.

But here, only existence (*sattva*) is perceived, not permanence (*nityatva*); how then can there be the exclusion of the other due to opposition with it? [Response: This is not a fault, because even though both are not perceived separately, the very establishment of existence results in the establishment of the negation of permanence.

How can a cognition directed toward one thing reject another? It is said: just as the cognition of a single lunar orb, though its object is not that [second moon], is the cause of the falsity of the perception of two moons.
Likewise, the cognition that grasps capacity,
though it does not have stability as its object, nevertheless performs the function of excluding its absence by being permeated with stability.
Multiplicity is the state of having diverse intrinsic natures, while stability is the state of having a single intrinsic nature;
indeed, it is not impossible to demonstrate through reasoning that these two are contradictory.
Therefore, the very perception of existence is the negation of permanence, and that itself is the pervasion by momentariness; thus, it is established that momentariness follows from existence.
Moreover, since an effect is never produced at all times, one must necessarily admit that the causal state (*kārakāvasthā*) of entities lasts for only a single moment—

whether this be through the influence of engaging in an operation (*vyāpārāveśa*), as in the view of the *Śrotriya*s and others, or by attaining the proximity of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), as in the view of the Naiyāyikas.
For the nature of a thing called "causality" exists only in a single moment, since it is postulated solely on the basis of the production of an effect.

Therefore, whether prior to or subsequent to [an action], because of its connection with being an agent (*kārakatva*), it is precisely this agency that is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*); for that which is not an agent lacks the capacity to produce cognition, and thus even its existence is difficult to maintain.
Consequently, almost all proponents of philosophical systems have accepted this momentariness; thus, the Buddhists have drunk nothing but their own fame.
Therefore, it is established that whatever is a causal factor and whatever exists is momentary.

And therefore, entities are momentary, because they do not depend on external causes for their destruction. For an entity must either be inherently perishable by its own nature or the opposite; if it has a perishable nature, what is the use of causes of destruction? And if it has a non-perishable nature, what indeed could causes of destruction accomplish?
Where, then, does the operation of the hammer and so forth lie? We say: in the production of a heterogeneous continuum.
However, a non-existence produced by that [cause] is simply not possible, because it contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For while an entity (*bhāva*) does not exist by way of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), it is not the case that non-existence also occurs for it. If its own nature were of the nature of coming into being, it would necessarily exist at all times and could never not exist.
But that very [destruction] cannot be of the nature of non-existence, because there would be no dependence on anything else;

for the destruction of a jar or similar object cannot depend on other causes such as a hammer, since the entire array of conceptual alternatives—such as whether the auxiliary cause produces a distinct or non-distinct assistance, and whether it is capable or incapable—is equally unavoidable in the case of destruction as it is in the case of production.
Now, if it is maintained that an entity has as its very nature destruction occurring after a few moments have elapsed, then, according to the previous reasoning, it would never perish at all;
for even at the time of destruction, since that nature has not departed, there would follow the consequence of requiring yet more few moments.
Moreover, even when it is to perish, no cause of destruction whatsoever occurs that is distinct from its own nature;
and since that very nature is exactly the same for it in the first moment as it is thereafter, it would either perish at that very moment or never at all.
If its first moment has escaped untimely death,
then— given that its nature is indestructible— let it remain for even hundreds of eons.
And this is not accepted [by you].
Therefore, since destruction is inseparable from the acquisition of its own nature (*ātmalābha*), momentary disintegration (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the cognition of recognition—which apprehends the stability of things—is a sublater of the inference proving momentary destruction, that too is not sound; for when the reason possesses an unshakable logical connection (*pratibandha*), there is no room for a sublation.
As it has been said: "Because sublation and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) are contradictory, they cannot coexist in one and the same place."

In the case of the argument "fire is not hot because it is produced," it is precisely the absence of an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) that obstructs the establishment of the probandum, not sublation by perception (*adhyakṣabādhyatva*).

Alternatively, what is the point of this insistence? In cases such as the inference of fire from smoke, it is logical for perception to subvert [the inference], because that [perception] is established as not being otherwise possible; however, this is not appropriate here.

Even under the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), recognition is possible for those whose minds are deceived by the production of a series of successive moments that are similar [to one another].

This being the case, if the weakness of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, what is the use of recognition? On the other hand, if the weakness of the pervasion is not established, what is the use of recognition?
Nor is recognition itself the cause of the failure of pervasion (*vyāpti*), because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

When inference is set aside due to the failure of pervasion, recognition becomes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and when that [recognition] has become a valid means of knowledge, inference lacks authority due to its deficiency in pervasion.
If it is argued that the same defect applies even to the validity of inference (*anumāna*), we say no; for its validity is established solely by the power of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
Indeed, its validity is not based on the weakness of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Furthermore, your honors ought to investigate with precision what this so-called "recognition" (pratyabhijñā) actually is.

Is it a single cognition, such as "this is that very same pillar," or are these two distinct cognitions—a memory and a perceptual experience? If it is a single cognition, its cause must be stated, for that from which it arises.
It cannot be the sense faculty, because the faculty lacks the capacity for that specific aspect [of the object].
And there is no mental formation [regarding] that [object], because of the absence of skill in the aspect [of thinking] "this belongs to him."
Nor is that cognition produced by both acting together;
for their skill has been ascertained to be effective when each acts separately.
The effect of the mental formation (*saṃskāra*) is memory alone, while that of the sense faculty is experience alone;
however, a single effect is not produced by the two acting together.
For indeed, a single effect in the form of either a jar or a cloth is never observed to be produced from both a lump of clay and a thread.
Nor is the sense faculty alone capable of such a task;
for it is a marvel that the sense faculty, which has as its object only the aspect of the thing present before it, should produce recognition.
Therefore, these are two distinct cognitions: "that" is memory, and "this" is direct experience.
Memory has as its object that which is to be remembered, and perception has as its range that which is to be perceived;
no other cognition is observed that reflects upon them as being one.
Just as the cognition of a jar and the memory of a cloth, though arising in immediate succession,
do not have the same object, so too will these two be.
Or let it be called by whatever name; for sensation is indeed one.
Nevertheless, let it be examined: what kind of object does it touch?
If it is argued that [the cognition] is connected with the past, it does not differ from memory;
if it is distinguished by the future, it is essentially nothing more than conceptual construction.
If stability is restricted solely to the present, then it is well-established;
however, if it were to encompass all three times, that would be difficult to maintain due to contradiction.
For things that are established as having their own natures through mutual exclusion,
a coexistence in a single locus is not possible in any way whatsoever.
For just as blue becomes ascertained by the cognition of blue when it excludes red and other colors that are inseparable from the absence of blue; so too [is the case here].

Similarly here as well, the cognition of a present object, by effecting the exclusion (apohana) of past time and so forth— which are invariably concomitant with the absence of that [present object]— would attain the status of grasping that [present object].
By this, the claim that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) apprehends an object qualified by a prior cognition is refuted;
for since the prior cognition no longer exists at the present time, it cannot function as a qualifier,
and there can be no cognition of a qualified object when its qualifier has not been apprehended.

Now, if it is argued that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is that which grasps the true nature of an object as being devoid of appearance and disappearance, that too is incorrect; for it has already been demonstrated that [recognition] is restricted solely to the present.
Furthermore, it has been stated that regarding the destruction and birth of entities, whether it be the present time or another, nothing other than those two can be apprehended.

If, however, the present time—the very moment of their arising and perishing—is what is being discussed, then by the apprehension of that [time], the arising and perishing of entities, which are inseparable from it, would also be apprehended.
This ascetic woman has come to establish her steadfastness;
having refuted the doctrine of impermanence through recognition, she will depart.

Furthermore, the recognition observed in cases such as hair and nails that have been cut and grown back again would, by virtue of their similarity, likewise fail to establish stability even in the case of pillars and the like.

If it is argued that this is because there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) in those cases, we reply that a subverting factor has already been stated here as well: namely, that it is impossible for mutually contradictory states, such as different times, to coexist in a single entity.
Therefore, since there is no subverting factor for the cognition of recognition, the momentariness of entities established through inference is proven.
Others, however, declare that momentariness is indeed accessible through direct perception alone.
The eye does not examine past or future times;
since the present consists of only a single moment, visual perception is restricted to that alone.

Furthermore, if it is maintained that perception apprehends something distinct from presentness, then it must be stated: is the preceding cognition capable of grasping an object delimited by a future time, or is the subsequent cognition skilled in discerning an entity embraced by a past time?

In that regard, at the moment when the initial consciousness arises, because a time subsequent to that instant is not present, there can be no apprehension of it by that [consciousness]; or if there were apprehension of the future, how could there be apprehension of a future birth? Likewise, at the moment of the production of the succeeding consciousness, because past time has already passed, it is not present; or if there were apprehension of a non-present past time, it would follow that there is apprehension of a previous birth.

If you think that the past and future times are apprehended by way of entering into the present, then, because of that entry into the present, that time would be apprehended as only the present, and not as the past or the future.

Now, if it is argued that no time whatsoever is apprehended anywhere, and that only the object itself appears, that is incorrect; for you do not admit, even in your own system, the apprehension of an entity that is not delimited by [time].
Now, what indeed is this so-called "time"? For the Śākyas, it is nothing real, but rather its conventional usage is purely conceptual.
In every respect, cognition born of the sense faculties has only the present as its object;
it does not rely upon the skill [of discerning] contact with prior or subsequent states.
And how long is the present time? It is but a single moment;
the preceding moment touches upon the state of the past, while the succeeding one touches upon the state of the future.

But surely, even in expressions such as "he cooks" or "he reads," an extended time is perceived even while [the action] is present. This is not sound; for there exists no composite whole of time consisting of a collection of various moments.
To say that "the present moment is long" is the talk of a fool.

If it were composed of a collection of moments, it would necessarily possess a manifold nature due to the inclusion of past and future moments. Therefore, the present consists of a single moment, and that is exceedingly brief; thus, visual perception, which perceives an object as encompassed by a single moment, does not grasp the existence of an entity prior to or subsequent to that moment. Consequently, all things are indeed momentary.
But surely, since its non-existence prior to or after the present moment has also been apprehended just as its existence was, how can there be momentariness?
Who says this? [We do not say that] non-existence is not apprehended, because the conventional expression of non-existence arises precisely from non-perception.
For the existence of entities is perception, and their non-existence is non-perception; seeing and not seeing are indeed the defining characteristics of existence and non-existence.
Therefore, since it is not perceived at another moment, its non-existence is established; thus, it is settled that direct perception grasps momentariness.
But surely, the determination of long duration arises from recognition;
why even now are you not free from your craving for its validity?
For its true nature, effect, and cause have been thoroughly examined;
it is simply impossible for that [nature] to establish stability with certainty.
Neither prior nor subsequent cognition can grasp [an object], because it persists through a duration of time;
though you understand this, you do not perceive it, being blinded by passion.
For the preceding cognition grasps the object at its own time, and the subsequent one likewise grasps it at its own time; there is no grasping whatsoever in the interval.
Indeed, they say that the interval is precisely non-grasping.
Indeed, for those whose vision is uninterrupted, a pillar or the like does not appear as something existing in a fragmented state; so how can it be said that this [object] is momentary?

This is not so, because even there, cognition exists for only a single moment; in the subsequent moment, that very cognition no longer exists. Therefore, whose existence is uninterrupted, whose existence is severed, or what could be the sublater? If it is argued, "Surely consciousness does exist in the subsequent moment because the perception is uninterrupted," do not say so; since cognition does not endure for a long time, let your honor determine that this is merely the arising of another cognition.
Therefore, just as the arising of moments of cognition occurs through the functioning of a continuum,
so too let this succession of pillar-moments be produced in that same way.
Thus, this conceit of grasping the existence of objects as uninterrupted and unbroken has arisen for those whose vision is unceasing.
Even by means of a stable cognition, there is no apprehension of long-duration persistence;
for it has been explained that perception does not apprehend what is not present.
At that time, there is no coexistence of the two moments— the past and the future—
and the single present moment does not attain length.
Therefore, even if cognition were stable, the stability of the object would be difficult to maintain;
however, by the principle of immediate succession, even that [cognition] does not persist for long.
For that [consciousness] too, because it is self-cognized, manifests as being confined to a single moment;
therefore, it is established that perception grasps what is momentary.
But surely the stability of objects is understood through inference;
for, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one perceives that the mallet and other such instruments are the destroyers [of those objects].
Therefore, based on that scripture, it is first ascertained that jars and other such things are devoid of destruction;
thus, their continued existence is established.
This is because destruction, which possesses a cause, is not perceived as something distinct from non-perception;
for the existence of entities consists precisely in their perception, while their non-existence consists in their non-perception.
Furthermore, the non-perception of a jar is not the effect of a mallet or similar instruments, since it exists even prior to them.

[Objection: Surely, the certainty of non-existence arises from the non-perception of what is perceptible, and that [certainty] is possible for a jar only at the time it is a potsherd; however, since non-observation during the intermediate period could be due to other causes, non-existence is not established by mere non-observation alone. [Reply: Not so. For even in the intermediate period, according to your own view, there is the non-apprehension of the very same jar which is perceptible; therefore, its non-existence remains a fact even then.
Furthermore, even if there is no non-perception of the jar by everyone in the interim,
what proof is there that this is likewise true for everyone at the time [the jar has become] shards?

If you think that what I do not know, another does not know either, then no one at all would see a jar in the middle [of its destruction]; thus it would not exist at all, like a jar that has become shards.
Furthermore, if you believe that what you do not perceive, another does not conceive of either, then let this man not experience the pleasure of touching his own wife’s hips!
Or if you understand that which you have attained, let another also attain it;
let him too attain the pleasure of touching the hips of your wife.
Therefore, enough of your concern with the affairs of others' houses.

Know that what you perceive exists, and understand that what you do not perceive does not exist. Thus, the very non-perception of things is their destruction; it is not the effect of hammers or other such instruments. Consequently, even inference does not establish permanence.
Therefore, it is established that, according to the sequence described, perception alone is the determiner of momentary entities.

Recollection, recognition, and the state of being the experiencer of the fruits of one's own actions are explained as possible even under the doctrine of momentariness, by virtue of the causal relationship between preceding and succeeding moments.
Therefore, let this momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅgitā), which has been thus established, be accepted;
and let go of the grasping at permanence, which is the cause of long-lasting cyclic existence (saṃsāra).
To this it is replied: neither of these two means of valid cognition is capable of establishing the momentary destruction of entities.
As for the claim that existence consists in the capacity for causal efficiency,
that is refuted by the ascertainment of its deviation in the case of non-existent things such as counterfeit gold.
Rather, existence is defined as being cognizable by a non-sublated, positive cognition;
whereas the designation "existent" or "non-existent" regarding a son and so forth is merely figurative.
And thus, a cognition that apprehends existence and is intent upon seeking the absence of sublation cannot possess intrinsic validity.
Furthermore, there is even doubt regarding the existence of a sentient being, as witnessed by all living creatures;
this will be explained through the lack of a fixed rule for perception.
Let it be that "existence" as you have defined it—namely, the capacity for causal efficiency—is indeed [the nature of existence];
nevertheless, because it lacks pervasion, it is not a valid logical reason, just like the property of possessing odor.
Even for an entity that is momentary, existence does not exist at all;
for such an entity, whether sequentially or simultaneously, is incapable of performing an action.
What kind of succession could there be for that which is momentary? Furthermore, if it were to act upon [an object], even a single moment of a thing would entail a differentiation of its form.
How could it produce diverse effects through a single form?
For if there were a contradiction in the diversity of forms, the non-existence of the entity would follow.
Momentariness is examined only when the existence of a thing is established;
but if that thing does not exist, such an inquiry is like the act of chewing a cud in the sky.
If you argue that there is a consideration of momentariness regarding cognition itself, what is the point of refuting that [cognition] as well?
These treatises proceed on this basis; and if the object of knowledge does not exist, how could that [cognition] exist?
Moreover, regarding the position of momentariness, it must be examined whether one arises from one, or one arises from many, or many are produced from one, or many arise from many.
First of all, there is no production of a single effect from a single cause, because that is contrary to worldly experience;
for we observe that even from a single fire, a multitude of diverse effects—such as ash, smoke, and the transformation of the fuel—are produced.

Furthermore, it contradicts the statement in the treatises that "nothing whatsoever is a producer by itself alone," since in every case we see effort being made to bring together auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) in order to accomplish an effect.
By this, the third position—that multiple things arise from a single cause—is refuted.

Furthermore, a single [cause] producing multiple [effects] could not do so either sequentially or simultaneously; it could not do so sequentially, because that would entail the consequence of [the cause] being non-momentary (sthairyaprasaṅga).
It is not simultaneous because it is not observed as such;
furthermore, since a single entity possesses the capacity to produce multiple effects, its differentiation would entail the consequence of manifoldness.
If unity is admitted even when there is a conjunction of contradictory properties,
then let an entity be accepted as one even when it is conjoined with multiple moments.
Now, if the position that "one [effect] arises from many" is adopted, then it must be stated: what is that single effect, and by which many is it produced?

For, unlike us, you do not hold that the effect has the nature of a composite whole (*avayavin*) constructed from a multitude of various means; rather, you maintain that only aggregates (*saṃcita*) are produced by aggregates.

Furthermore, if a single effect is said to have multiple causes, its very oneness is contradicted by the fact that it would possess a plurality of natures brought about by the difference of those causes.
For if there were otherwise, the nature of entities would not be dependent upon causes, which would lead to the absurd consequence of their being accidental.
Moreover, if even that which possesses a plurality produced by the difference of causes were to be one, then a single entity—even one existing at different times—would likewise be one.
Alternatively, it should be stated, as before, that there is a non-existence of a thing whose intrinsic nature is differentiated.

If it is argued that cognition is of a single form despite the difference in causes—such as the eye, light, and attention—it is not so; for according to your own position, it possesses distinctions consisting in its grasping of the form of the object and its nature as self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).

For a Buddhist who maintains the theory of formless cognition (*nirākārajñānavādin*), the systematic determination of objects (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) is not established, because if the object were to appear [in the cognition], it would follow that the object is permanent, and because the position that [cognition] depends on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is impossible. Even if it were possible, there would be no cause for the restriction of what is to be grasped.
Now, it is said: what is the point of crushing a position that has not even been accepted?
Our position is simply this: "from many, there is the arising of many.
A preceding causal complex (*sāmagrī*), proceeding by way of a continuous stream (*saṃtāna*), produces a subsequent causal complex that is similar to itself.
But when heterogeneous causes intervene, it becomes dissimilar.
Now, what is this so-called "causal totality" (*sāmagrī*)? It is not distinct from the individual factors, because it is not perceived separately from them.
If, however, it were not distinct [from its parts], then the totality would simply be the complete collection [of those parts].

In that case, when a subsequent collection is produced by a preceding collection, either the individual members contained within that collection would each produce one [result] individually, or all of them together would produce a single [result].
In that case, regarding the first position, this would be said to be the production of one from one;
and that has been refuted.

Now, regarding the production of each individual constituent of a composite whole, there must be an operation by all the constituents; and this [operation] occurs either successively or simultaneously. In that regard, if the position of succession is taken, there is a loss of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). For those moments which exist as the five or six constituents therein would, after producing one [constituent], begin another, and then yet another; thus, because of waiting for such a duration of time, there is a lack of momentariness.

Now, if all [causes] were to operate simultaneously toward the production of everything, then the effect would arise from a cause that is itself a mere aggregate (*nikurumba*), and because there would be no rule of causal distinction (*kāraṇavivekaniyama*), there could be no differentiation between form, taste, and so forth. How could it be determined that "this is form" and "this is taste"? Since a variegated [effect] would be produced by a variegated [cause], everything would be form, or else everything would be taste.
Or rather, it would be some other entirely different entity, neither form nor taste.

Now, if it is argued that although the totality of form, taste, and so forth is the producer of that very totality, nevertheless, in some cases one thing is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and the other is the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*);

and that because form is the material cause in the production of a moment of form while the others are auxiliary causes, there is no confusion of categories—this is incorrect, because the status of being a cause does not depart in any way whatsoever.

Moreover, if that very nature by which form (*rūpa*) is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) with respect to another form were also its cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) with respect to taste (*rasa*), then once again there would be no distinction between form and taste. If, on the other hand, form has the nature of being a material cause of form through one nature, and is a cooperative cause of taste through another, then due to this difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*), there is a plurality [of entities]. And if there is plurality, it has already been stated that there is either instability or non-existence. Now, if there is no contradiction whatsoever between these two intrinsic natures, how can you, born in the house of the Buddhists, speak in such a manner?
Since entities are established by way of mutual exclusion, there certainly exists between them a contradiction based on their defining characteristics (*lākṣaṇika-virodha*).

Moreover, if all things were momentary, even the distinction that "this is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of this" and "this is the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*)" would be difficult to discern.

For instance, what is this so-called "material cause"? Is it that which produces an effect by perishing along with its own continuum, like a seed, or is it that which produces [an effect] by imparting its own specific qualities?
If the former position were true, then the discussion of the next world (*paraloka*) would have to be disregarded, just as by the Cārvākas.
Because it would entail the consequence that, upon the destruction of one continuum of cognition, another cognition would have to begin.

Even on the view that [the indeterminate cognition] imparts its own specific qualities [to the determinate one], there would have to be either the imparting of all specific qualities or the imparting of only some specific qualities; if it were the imparting of all specific qualities, then non-conceptual cognition could not be the material cause of conceptual cognition.
And how can there be a recollection of the invariable concomitance produced by the observation of a logical mark?
Or how can there be the cognition of taste immediately following the cognition of color?

If it is argued that [the recognition] will occur because of the multiplicity of the continuum (*santāna*), we say no; for this would entail the collapse of linguistic convention, which is based on the synthesis dependent upon a single cognizer.

Without a permanent, unitary self, such a convention is not even possible when there is unity of the continuum itself—how much less so when there is a multiplicity within the very same continuum of Devadatta?

If, however, [something] were to be the material cause by virtue of imparting only a few specific qualities, then even color-form (*rūpa*) would attain the status of being the material cause of cognition.
Therefore, there is no such thing as a "material cause.
And by the refutation of that, one should understand that the "cooperative cause" (*sahakārin*), whose nature is defined by its distinction from that [material cause], is also excluded.
Moreover, O monk, you reject the auxiliary cause in every respect within my position, yet you yourself accept it; thus, you appear like one possessed by passion.
Where have those conceptual constructions of yours— such as "distinct" or "non-distinct" assistance—
which were devised to reject the existence of auxiliary causes, gone now?
It is understood that this fault was devised by you through the power of logic; it does not afflict you, like a snake raised up by a mantra.

Alternatively, let alone the distinction between the material cause (*upādāna*) and the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), this very relationship of cause and effect is difficult to establish according to the venerable Bhadanta’s doctrine.
For if something is called a "cause" even while it is not at all operative toward the arising of another, then everything would be the cause of everything.
And for that [entity] which has not yet acquired its own nature, there can be no activity in a subsequent birth;
however, if it has acquired its own nature, its persistence in activity during another moment is established.

Now, if one should say that "depending on this, that arises," and thus the causal relationship is merely "conditionality upon this" (idampratyayatāmātra), even so, since there is the cognition of a moment that has already attained its own-being, the persistence of that moment into a second instant remains unavoidable.
Nor can the relation of cause and effect be grasped by mere contiguity alone,
because such contiguity is observed even in cases where there is no causal relationship between the antecedent and the consequent.
Furthermore, for that which is subject to momentary destruction, there is no activity whatsoever toward the production of another;
neither of what is present, nor of what has passed, nor of what is yet to come.

Now, if you should think that just as there is a simultaneous lowering and raising of the two ends of a scale, so too there is destruction and arising of the preceding and succeeding moments—such that, because the subsequent moment arises through the destruction of the preceding moment, they may thus attain the status of cause and effect—this too is not satisfactory, for you, long-lived one, have not correctly grasped the analogy of the scale.
In that case, gold and other such things are indeed the cause of both lowering and raising;
however, raising is not established by means of lowering, nor is it established by means of that [gold].
For here, the subsequent moment does not arise either from the preceding moment nor from its destruction;
and since there is nothing else here that could serve as the locus for gold, only non-arising remains.
In every respect, that which is devoid of activity cannot be a cause for the production of another;
yet if agency belongs only to that which possesses activity, then momentariness becomes difficult to establish.
And thus, existence being excluded from momentary things specifically,
it would become a cause for doubt by virtue of that very uncommonness.

Alternatively, since an entity that has already acquired its own nature is determined to be a causal factor (*kāraka*) by virtue of being active toward the production of another thing, it must necessarily abide for two or three moments according to the logic just stated; thus, rather than proving momentariness, this reason actually proves non-momentariness through its existence, and is therefore contradictory (*viruddha*).

And thus, since it is established that only eternal things possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*)—which is threefold, consisting of the inherent (*samavāyin*), non-inherent (*asamavāyin*), and instrumental (*nimitta*) causes—having come into mutual contact, produces the effect according to its proximity. Therefore, enough with your alternatives regarding succession and simultaneity; whenever the causal complex exists in its complete conjunction, at that very moment the effect arises.
For this very reason, effects do not arise simultaneously;
nor is the cause eternal, for the causal complex does not exist at all times.
The ripening of the karma of living beings is also included within our [concept of] causal totality (*sāmagrī*),
because it is established as the cause for all pleasure, pain, and so forth.

Furthermore, the dilemma regarding whether the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is distinct from or non-distinct from its constituent parts does not undermine our position, because the causal complex possesses the properties of its constituents.

Moreover, it has been explained in the general definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that, in relation to the complete set of factors, the causal complex itself is the instrument (*karaṇa*) due to its connection with the excellence of the specific result.
The conceptual distinction between capacity and incapacity is also not tenable;
for capacity belongs to the causal complex itself, since it is from that alone that the effect is observed.

However, the capacity of the collection of causal factors contained within that [sāmagrī], such as the parts of a cart and so forth, is indeed admitted to the full extent [of its function], because the status of the sāmagrī as the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) is established in dependence upon them;
for it is not the case that one can say "whiter than black."

However, the capacity of the causal complex itself is indeed complete, such that the production of the effect occurs immediately thereafter; this is understood precisely from the observation of the production of the effect.
As for the claim proclaimed by others that the agent must exist for only a single moment, that too is incorrect, because its duration extends until the completion of the effect;

furthermore, it is impossible for the effect to be completed in a single moment. After the completion of the effect, however, the causal complex (sāmagrī) dissolves, yet the individual members of that complex do not [dissolve], since the wheel, the string, the staff, and so forth are perceived here and there individually.
Thus, since the capacity for causal efficiency belongs only to stable entities, momentary destruction is not established on that basis.

Thus, what was prattled regarding the exclusion of the "other" through the very perception of existence—on the grounds that existence and permanence are contradictory, just as the cognition of a single moon excludes its opposite—is thereby refuted.

As for what was also said—that things are momentary because they do not depend on anything else for their destruction—that too is trivial; for it has been established in detail during the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that the non-existence (*abhāva*) of a jar or similar object, which is the effect of that [destruction], follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the operation of causes such as a staff.
Furthermore, it is precisely this "non-existence through destruction" (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) that is called "destruction."
Conceptual constructions such as "perishable" or "imperishable" are not tenable;
for the destruction of entities depends upon a causal complex, just like their own acquisition of self-nature.

What is produced for the jar by the causal complex of the hammer and so forth? And what is produced for it by the causal complex of the lump of clay and so forth? If you say that its self-acquisition [is produced], then by this [latter complex] its self-destruction will also be brought about.
Is it not the case that this same sophistry applies even to production? For if the cause is perishable, its effect would be fruitless; if it is imperishable, it is incapable [of producing].

If the pot has the nature of coming into being, it comes into being by itself—what is the use of the collection of causal factors such as the staff? But that which does not have the nature of coming into being cannot be produced, just like a donkey’s horn.

If it is argued that this objection is unfounded because we observe that destruction is the effect of the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*), then the same resolution applies to non-existence as well; for, like arising, destruction also conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of causal factors.
Therefore, for an entity that has just arisen, there is no destruction;
its persistence is its "stability" (sthiti), which lasts as long as the presence of the cause of destruction.

Now, if it be argued that for things dependent on other factors, their occurrence is not necessarily certain—and thus a jar might perhaps never encounter the cause of its destruction—then why should it not be eternal? Oh, what a great oversight! The subjects are ruined; a great thunderbolt has fallen! This fault, so difficult to avoid, has arisen:
if the jar were eternal, it would reduce even the three worlds to ashes, like Kālāgnirudra at the end of time.

Moreover, O fool, for that which possesses parts, which is dependent, and which is an effect, destruction must necessarily occur at some time or other—either through the disjunction of its parts or the destruction of its substratum. What occasion, then, is there for suspecting its eternity? For instance, the world does not see the consecration jar of Rāma persisting even to this day in the palace of the Lord; therefore, a cause for its destruction must inevitably exist. Consequently, since destruction has a cause, entities do not perish by their own nature alone.

Moreover, recognition—whose continuous succession of established conclusions has dispelled the darkness of the Buddhist tenets by the power of its own brilliance, which incessantly displays an unbroken multitude of entities, and which blazes forth on all sides like the thousandfold radiance of the sun—is such that who could truly assert that entities are momentary?
And whatever has been poorly stated regarding it, all of that is inconsistent.

Regarding this which has been conceptualized—whether "this is that very same thing" constitutes one cognition or two—it is said in response: because of the experience of a single cognition directed toward the illumination of a single object through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), what room is there for the suspicion of duality? Indeed, this [cognition] "that which is this is that," or "that which is that is this," is a single [act] characterized by the apprehension of unity.

As for the multiple cognitions experienced intrinsically, such as "this is a jar," they do not constitute two distinct cognitions with different objects, like the case of a cognition of a jar arising immediately followed by the recollection of a cloth. Rather, it is a single cognition.
As for the question, "What is the instrument in the production of a single cognition?": if the effect is already understood, what is the use of investigating the cause?
And if the effect is not understood, what is the use of investigating the cause?
Furthermore, an effect cannot exist without a cause, for it would be impossible for it to possess the very nature of being an effect; thus, there must necessarily be a cause for it.
And indeed, the sense organ accompanied by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) exists as the distinct cause of this cognition.
Moreover, the fact that these two are effects is understood precisely from their being perceived.
Therefore, since both [the clay and the threads] are present here and function toward the production of a single effect, why is that [single effect] not accepted?
A single effect consisting of clay and thread is not admitted precisely because it is not observed;
however, this [effect in question] is difficult to deny because it is actually perceived.

However, since an effect is not observed even when there is the operation of the sense-faculties alone in some cases, it is not the case that such a [cause] produces an effect everywhere; for it generates other effects by depending on auxiliary factors (sahakārin).

As for what was asked—namely, "What kind of object appears in recognition?"—we are deeply distressed that these disputants, despite having been answered a hundred times, persist in questioning us again.
It has already been stated in this regard that it is the cognitions (*pramiti*) that should be questioned, not the disputants.
In this [recognition], the object appears as qualified by a past time and delimited by the present time.
Surely, the prior and posterior times are mutually contradictory; they do not both enter into a single [locus]. Therefore, due to that difference in time, the entity itself is divided.
This is not so, because Devadatta remains the same despite the differences in his armlets, crown, bracelets, earrings, and so forth.
To investigate whether the whole (avayavin) exists or does not exist is to enter into another debate;
furthermore, the whole will be established in detail in the chapter on liberation (apavargāhnika), so let this matter rest.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction between the earring and the others, we say no; for you yourselves admit a contradiction based on their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇika-virodha*).
Indeed, by asserting that "all entities are established through mutual exclusion," you accept this contradiction among them.
Now, one might argue that even though bracelets and such [ornaments] are mutually exclusive, their coexistence at one time makes it possible for them to belong to the same Devadatta;

however, since the past and the present cannot exist simultaneously, how can a pillar or the like be said to be qualified by both? It is indeed strange that both times are perceived, yet neither is present!
If it is asked whether past time exists even now, do not say so; it is not said that "it exists," but rather that "it was.
If it were said to "exist," it would be only the present, not the past.
Well then, if it has already become past simply by virtue of being past, how is it that it appears as existing now? We reply: it appears precisely as something past.

A past time is apprehended as pastness alone, and even the present is apprehended as presentness alone; however, the object itself is one and the same, persisting through both states, because it is so apprehended.

Now, one might object that since the past time does not exist at present, a cognition having that as its object would be produced from a non-entity. This is not so, because the substratum (dharmin) delimited by that [past time], which is the producer of the cognition, does exist. If it is asked how the past can be a delimiter, it is because it appears as such; consider the recognition: "This is that very same thing."
"That which existed previously exists even now"—
it is this very object, qualified by past time, that appears in this cognition.

[Objection: How can a cognition produced by the sense organs take as its objective support an object qualified by a past time that is non-existent? [Reply: It is said: at the time of the cognition of the final number, those [units] previously observed produce cognitions such as "a hundred" and so forth, just as individual soldiers [produce the cognition of a "hundred soldiers"].
The past time, while being a qualification of the creation,
serves as the cause for the recognition of pillars and other such objects.

If it is argued that while there are countable foot-soldiers, past time does not exist, then what will the "Beloved of the Gods" say when eating wood-apples (*kapittha*)? For we observe the cognition: "The Vāhīka has eaten a hundred wood-apples.
Moreover, when ninety-nine wood-apples have been consumed and one remains unutilized, there is no thought such as, "I have eaten a hundred in this very place."

Therefore, just as in that case the ninety-nine mangoes, though already passed away, serve as the cause for the cognition of "a hundred" because they have ascended to the level of appearance, so too the connection with past time, appearing [in consciousness], will bring about recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
If you say that "a hundred cognitions" is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*), O Great-souled One, why is yours not also merely a conceptual construction?
For these proponents of the validity of conceptual cognition (*savikalpakaprāmāṇyavādinaḥ*) are indeed living beings.
And that very method which was previously demonstrated for the establishment of universals should be applied for the sake of establishing the existence of numbers such as duality and so forth.

Enough with this diversion into other topics! Indeed, our curiosity lies in this: how can recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—which grasps what has already passed—be born from the contact of a sense organ with its object?
What is the nature of this curiosity? For there certainly exists before it an object that serves as its cause, such as a pillar or the like.

Now, it is true that this [cognition] occurs only at the present time; however, it is not only by means of an object conjoined with the present time that the cognition is produced. For, just as the present time, so too the past time functions as a delimiting factor (avacchedakatā) for it. And that object, delimited by that [time], and this cognition, produce [the effect]; thus, while this [cognition] is born from the object, it is also born from the sense faculty, since it conforms to the presence and absence of that [faculty].
Now, one might ask: "How does a sense organ operate with respect to an object that has passed away? To whom is this question directed? Not to the sense organ, because it is insentient.
As for the person (puruṣa), he perceives even when his eyes are not opened; thus, he too is not to be questioned.

Now, one might argue that it is reasonable to assume this cognition lacks validity because it apprehends what is past, since the capacity of the sense organ has never been observed to function with respect to the past; but this is not so. Invalidity is indeed postulated on the basis of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), and such a cognition does not exist in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Furthermore, inference (*anumāna*) as a subverting factor has already been rejected.
But surely, non-validity is indeed postulated on account of defects in the cause as well?
"Venerable one, let him also be summoned."
It has already been stated that the sense faculty lacks the capacity to apprehend an object that is past.
My child, you have not spoken correctly;
this is not a defect of the sense faculty, such as cataracts or other maladies.
In the past time, the capacity of the self-instrument [the sense organ] does not belong to it when it has become a qualifier of the present object to be grasped;
rather, it has been stated that its capacity belongs to it only when accompanied by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

Therefore, it is established that this cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which has as its object a present thing such as a pillar standing before one and qualified by a past time, arises precisely from the contact of the sense organ with the object.
Alternatively, let it be accepted that mental recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) apprehends an object distinguished by a prior cognition,
just like the perception of a jasmine flower when its fragrance is present.

For just as even when a jasmine flower (*kundakusuma*) is within the range of the eye, its apprehension through the external sense-faculties is impossible if it is qualified by a fragrance that is not an object of those faculties—such that the cognition "the flower is fragrant" is purely mental—in the same way, when a pillar or the like is qualified by a previous cognition, its qualifier is an object of a past moment; thus, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is mental.

Furthermore, it has been stated many times that if one accepts that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) grasps an external object as qualified by a cognition produced by previously engaged external sense-faculties, there is no consequence of the non-existence of the blind and others.
[Objection: But surely there exists a present qualifier, such as fragrance, for a lotus and the like;

however, in this case, the prior cognition is past—so how can it be called a qualifier here? [Reply: What will you do with that which exists [only potentially]? For even in cognitions of "hundred" and so forth, we observe that a wood-apple (*kapittha*) and the like, though already passed away, serve as the cause.
Thus, even by means of recognition arising from the internal organ, the stability of entities is indeed established.
As for the claim that the recognition of Śiva and other deities is similar to the recognition of a shaven head and so forth, that too is inconsistent.
In that case, the sight of a shaven head in the interval would indeed be a subverting factor;
but here, there is nothing of the sort.

For this very reason, it has been stated that recognition, being brought into a state of impairment by the cognition of destruction flashing forth at that very moment, is incapable of establishing stability for the sound.

Even in the case of a flame and the like, recognition is erroneous because it is sublated by the inference of the exhaustion of the oil and the wick; however, in the case of a pillar and the like, there is no such inferential sublation.
As for the inference based on existence (*sattva*), that has already been refuted.

Although this is not an absolute rule—that in a conflict between perception and inference, perception is stronger—since we observe that even the perception of a whirling firebrand, which is perceived as a circle due to its extremely rapid rotation, is sublated by inference; nevertheless, in the present case, the inference of momentariness is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*), whereas perception is not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*). Thus, perception alone is the sublater of the inference of momentariness.

Nor is there the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), because we do not accept that the validity of the perceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa*)—which is the basis for the falsity of inference—is dependent on that [inference].
Perceptual recognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) solely by virtue of the strength of its own causes;
it does not suffer from such wretchedness as to require becoming a valid means of knowledge only when inference is proven false.

Or rather, the recognition that arises from this [second perception], which is the cognition of a pillar and so forth produced by the first moment of sensory contact— that too sublates the doctrine of momentary destruction.

Since dependence upon an identical causal complex (*sāmagrī*) has been refuted, and since the absence of form (*nirākāratva*) will be refuted later, and since it is certain that an object is what is manifested because its status as a producer is ascertained by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) aided by positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), it follows by necessity that the object must persist for two or three moments—first, because the object, having arisen, produces cognition, and second, because it is grasped by that cognition once it has arisen. Therefore, how can there be momentariness? If, having acquired its own nature, it has not perished in the first moment, then its destruction must be due to another cause and cannot be inherent to its own nature.
And here, a manifold cognition of objects is observed:
some is a long-standing mental impression, while some is a great [cognition] born at that very moment.
The understanding that the pitcher has been carried away by a pole is one way;
likewise, the understanding that the pitcher has been pulled out by its base is another.
By this, even Ravigupta was made to have a withered face—
he who prided himself on being an expert at postulating a perception capable of tolerating momentariness.

For instance, it has been stated that a cognition grasping the form of a present object, by manifesting its own generative object according to the method just described, leads one to understand that the object persists for two moments.
Furthermore, some initial cognition touches upon the future time;
as Bhaṭṭa said: "Indeed, silver, when being perceived, is perceived as persisting for a long duration."
It has also been shown that subsequent recognition illuminates an object as delimited by past time.
Nor should one suspect the apprehension of past and future births, because the capacity of a cause is restricted to this extent;
for it is not the case that the apprehension of past and future births is impossible to perform, and thus even the apprehension of what is currently being perceived ought to be denied.

Nor, by this much—namely, by the mere apprehension of a present object delimited by past and future time through *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference]—should an unperceived knowledge of the past and future be postulated.
For objects are established according to how they are perceived; one does not, upon seeing something, postulate another thing that was never seen, nor does one deny what has been perceived.
Moreover, perception that apprehends objects such as pillars and so forth—which possess uninterrupted series of moments—is established through unblinking vision;
how then can it be said to apprehend only the momentary?

And as for what has been conceptualized there—namely, that because the past and future moments are not present, they cannot be grasped by perception, and because the present moment is extremely subtle, it is the momentariness itself that is grasped by the perception apprehending that time—that is established. Let it be granted that there is no grasping of past and future times; however, let it be considered how much time elapses even during an uninterrupted visual perception of the present, since there is no opportunity for even a blink of the eye to interrupt the vision.
For as long as perception is not interrupted, for that long time is present; by grasping that [perception], stability is grasped, not momentariness.
But surely that duration is a collection of moments, not a single moment;
and a single moment exists only as the present.
Therefore, the preceding and succeeding moments are respectively the past and the future.
And it has been stated that there is no apprehension of those two.

O Great-souled One, this can indeed be said when momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) has already been established, but not at the time of proving it; for in the *Anumānaparīkṣā*, it was proven that time is one, eternal, and all-pervading,
and not that time consists of an aggregate of moments.

Furthermore, it has been examined in that very same context that the divisions of time are merely postulated based on limiting conditions (*upādhi*), such as the production and destruction of actions.

Thus, for one who observes a blink of an eye, because the interruption of the visual perception cannot be grasped, that duration is a single unit of time; it is not a collection of various moments (*kṣaṇa*).
Or, even if time were composed of a collection of moments, since the interruptions of the visual perception cannot be determined, let the collection of moments itself be what constitutes the present.

Now, is it not the case that so-called "time" is no ultimate entity at all, but rather the very objects being perceived that serve as the basis for the conventional usage of "present" and so forth? And since these are not experienced for long, they are called "momentary. O monk, enough with this digression! Let there be no such thing as time.
Because the uninterrupted gaze of the observer upon the existent object does not cease, the object is seen as not perishing; therefore, perception does not grasp [things] as momentary.
But surely even you do not accept that cognition is stable.

And when cognition has perished, by what would that object be grasped in the second moment? As for the claim that it is grasped by another cognition, what certainty is there that it is indeed the same [object]? Some maintain that for one whose vision is unblinking, cognition never perishes at all.
Alternatively, what is the use of this?
For it has been stated more than once, and will be stated again, that cognition does not manifest at the time the object manifests;
therefore, how could we know what its nature is?
The object, however, is apprehended as having an uninterrupted existence;
knowledge, moreover, though belonging to the present time, can grasp objects of the past and future, just like the recollection of what has occurred or the inference of past and future perceptions.

[Objection: But surely the operation of the sense faculty does not persist for another moment; therefore, when that [operation] is absent, how can there be a perception of the object’s extension over time? [Reply: O Venerable One, you are weary! Be ashamed to speak thus.
There is not even a separation of this [perception] caused by the blinking of an eye.
Moreover, since the operation of the sense organ is not stable, it is merely the state of being a grasper;
and its operation in the apprehension of the object is contact (*sannikarṣa*),
and that [contact] is indeed stable.
Therefore, it is established that there is perception of an object at the time it is extended [in space].

This being the case, the destruction of entities is not based solely on their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), but rather is dependent upon another cause. Consequently, entities persist as long as a cause of destruction does not intervene; and it is thus established that those things for which no cause of destruction exists—such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth—are indeed eternal.
Furthermore, the claim that the very perception and non-perception of things constitutes their existence and non-existence is the speech of one who is utterly deluded.
It is through perception and non-perception that existence and non-existence are determined; however, perception and non-perception themselves are not existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, non-existence has been established at length previously;
and since that [non-existence] is caused, entities do not perish by themselves alone.

If, however, this [position] were not accepted—that is, if one maintains the view that objects are stable—then the worldly transaction consisting of "the perception of a determinate object which produces cognition," "activity directed toward that object once it has been made the content of perception," and "attainment of that which was made the content of activity" would not be possible, because of the multiplicity of momentary objects.
Furthermore, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (bādhyabādhakabhāva) is observed in certain cases among cognitions;

yet that would not be possible [on your view], because a cognition apprehending the non-existence of an object such as silver previously perceived cannot function as a sublator, just like a cognition of the absence of a jar that has already been smashed by a hammer-stroke. This is because it is illogical for such a cognition to be a sublator.

Furthermore, such worldly transactions as the recollection of what was previously seen, the recognition of something already recollected, and the completion of a house or similar object that was only half-finished after it had been recognized, would all be lost.
Now, if that [causality] is established by relying upon a continuum (*santāna*), it is not so;
for the conceptual alternatives of its being either different or non-different are untenable.
If they are non-different, conventional practice cannot be established, just as it is not with a single moment;
if, however, they are distinct, this [relationship] must be considered whether it is real or unreal.
If it is unreal, then the previously mentioned effect is once again undermined;
if it is real, consider whether it must be permanent or momentary.
The continuum would be devoid of its constituent moments, as the continuum itself is momentary;
thus, the aforementioned conventional usage would once again fail to be established.

Moreover, if you maintain that there exists an entity called a "continuum" which is eternal and ultimately real, then stand up, O monk! Your hopes have borne fruit; this doctrine of momentary destruction is now finished.
This being so, since the deceptive disguise of a "continuum" has been refuted,
let the course of worldly affairs be established by means of stable entities alone.
Thus, with its range destroyed by the multitude of refutations just described,
neither perception nor inference would be a valid means of knowledge regarding momentariness.
And once momentary destruction has been refuted, the effect must necessarily have a substratum;
therefore, it is logical to postulate a locus on the basis of effects such as cognition.

The distinctness of effects such as pleasure from cognition was stated previously; therefore, that too is something other [than cognition] and serves as its inferential mark. Furthermore, you do not accept a self that belongs to the next world.
You are departing for the next world, and the multitude of cranes is known to you.
The worship of a shrine performed by one person within the continuum of karma is now experienced as its fruit by another who did not perform that action.
Nor does its completion occur through the act of worshipping a shrine;
not even by a single moment of cognition is any action brought to an end.
Furthermore, that causal relationship which was asserted has been refuted;
for even if a causal relationship exists, distinctness does not cease to exist.
Furthermore, this [reason] is inconclusive due to the cognitions belonging to other mental continua;
moreover, the specific qualification consisting in the nature of being the material cause has already been refuted.
Furthermore, the analogy of the transfer of dye from cotton that was described is also untenable, because it is observed there that [the color] exists in its own nature.
That very redness which was produced in the cotton seed is seen in the flower; however, no other quality arises from it.
In this way, there would be a continuation of karma, but the experience of its fruit would be difficult to establish.
This persistence of karma does not belong to any single entity,
because of the distinction between cause and effect, as in the case of the cotton flower and so forth.
For the action would be in one place and its fruit in another;
moreover, no one performs an action for the sake of their own mental continuum's enjoyment.
"May the fruit belong to me alone"—with this thought everyone engages in action;
in every respect, for the Śākya monks, the world beyond is in a state of collapse.
Nor is there any way for them to proceed toward establishing that [position].
The reason— "the first cognition at birth and so forth is preceded by another cognition,
because it is a cognition"— is held to be inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).
Furthermore, let it be shown that [the reason] is inconclusive by means of cognitions arising immediately after fainting and so forth;
as for the claim that "even one who has fainted possesses consciousness," that is merely a deception.
For there is no other form of cognition whatsoever apart from the comprehension of an object;
how then could it exist in states such as fainting, or in the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*?
Or if consciousness is asserted to exist during the stage of the *kalala* and so forth,
then let it also exist in the semen and blood residing within the mother and father.
Consequently, two volitions would occur within a single continuum,
or there would be a multiplicity of volitions— as in the case of a husband and wife who have many children.
Nor is there this rule in the world that like arises only from like;
for the production of scorpions and other such creatures is seen even from cow dung.
And how could there be the skill of the cognitions in migrating to another body? They possess neither corporeality like a flame, nor pervasiveness like the self.
If they are led to another existence by means of a subtle body (ātivāhika-deha),
then how indeed is their movement possible even within that subtle body?
Let it be that this [self] might indeed live even when the body is traveling on a road;
but how could there be, for you who maintain [the self to be] cognitions, a movement from one location to another?
For these [faculties] do not lack the nature of being real entities, nor do they lack the power of movement by themselves;
their functioning is not like that of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, nor are they all-pervasive like the self (*ātman*).
Thus it was when you emerged from the interior of the monastery cell.
Then the body becomes like wood, because the transmission of knowledge is impossible.

Thus, this is the summary of the meaning: either one must abandon the *kaurukucī* [pedantic quibbling] and reject it, or else one must accept an eternal self, just like the Teacher of the Gods (Bṛhaspati), regarding the next world as real.

2.345.17 As for the claim that this [self] is subject to destruction because it is conceptualized as being like the sky or a hide, or else that it is merely fruitless—that is not at all correct; for even while engaged in the experience of the states of pleasure and pain, this self does not undergo destruction.
And its transformation, produced by the arising of pleasure or pain, does not indeed cause such [a state] to be lost;
rather, it arises through the power of auxiliary causes, and that [transformation] necessarily attains the status of being an experiencer.

Alternatively, some maintain that when a person's various states of existence arise and pass away according to the distinctions of their own periods (daśā), there is no actual difference [in the person], just as there is no difference in a serpent that assumes successive conditions such as being coiled (kuṇḍala) and so forth.
These states alone are distressed by the terror of violent dissolution, whereas the single substratum shines forth with an unassailable and stable form.
If this [substratum] did not exist, there would be no accomplishment of effects belonging to the realm of memory regarding objects previously perceived; thus has this been skillfully demonstrated.

But surely even one who is eternal does not reflect upon action while experiencing its fruit; for no one submerged in hell thinks, "Indeed, that sinful karma which I committed in a previous existence is now bearing fruit, and it is being experienced by me."
At the time of experiencing the result, what function does this [inference] have? Its activity is neither now nor is there cessation from it.
That reflective awareness which is the cause for generating its own activity necessarily arises from the scripture for those who know the scripture.

"Let this deliberation come later; for whatever—be it good or bad—I, as a youth, performed when the object was perceived by me, I, now grown old, experience the fruit of that today. Thus, there exists this person who is stable and capable of experiencing the fruits of well-performed deeds and so forth.

There is no self, yet there is merely the enjoyment of fruits; there is the worship of shrines for the sake of heaven, yet these conditioned formations are momentary; these monasteries have been built to endure for an eon;
all this is empty, yet one is commanded, "Give your wealth to the Guru. What else is this but the conduct of Buddhists? This is the ultimate pinnacle of hypocrisy.

Here, the well-trained Cārvāka says: "Let it be granted that as long as the body remains, there is a single reality of the cognizer (*pramātṛtattva*) capable of the practical activities of synthesis and so forth; who would dispute that?
But as for its existence after the body, what is the proof for this? Moreover, the cognizer does not transfer from one body to another after abandoning the previous body."
For if this were the case, then just as one remembers objects experienced during the state of childhood within this very body, one would also remember objects experienced in past lives.

Indeed, since there is no difference in its permanence and no difference in the distinctness of bodies, we perceive no specific cause for the distinction in memory such that one remembers only what was experienced in this life and not what was experienced in those other lives.

Therefore, having discarded the loathing toward talk of the next world—which is rooted in the doctrine of a permanent self—one should cast it aside and live according to one's pleasure, [thinking] that after the body there is simply no cognizer.
As it has been said: "One should live happily as long as life lasts; there is no escaping death.
Once the body has been reduced to ashes, how can there be a return?"
Thus it is said.
To this it is replied: You have certainly not displayed the refined skill of a well-trained Cārvāka teacher.

You ought not to forget what you yourself have stated—that there exists a single, persisting reality of the cognizer (*pramātṛtattva*) as long as the body lasts. Furthermore, you have recently engaged in an excessive dispute with the Buddhists to establish this point: that the destruction of entities is not an inherent property inseparable from their existence, but rather is caused by some other external factor.
Furthermore, no cause for the destruction [of cognition] is found anywhere, even when investigated by the knower for a very long time;
nor can such a cause be postulated simply because it is not perceived.
For the self is not perceived as having parts like a cloth or similar objects, such that it could be understood to perish through the disintegration of its parts.
Nor is the arising of the self observed, from which its destruction might be inferred—as in the case of action and other partless things—by its necessary concomitance with that arising.

Furthermore, this [self] is not a quality belonging to anything else, such that it would undergo destruction either through the destruction of its substrate or through the emergence of a contradictory quality.
Nor can it be said that its destruction is perceived through direct perception itself, independent of an inference for a cause of destruction;
for unlike the body, this [self] is never observed being burned or torn apart by birds.
Therefore, since destruction is not observed and an inference for a cause of destruction is impossible, it must be concluded that if the self exists, it is indeed eternal.

Therefore, like the ancient Cārvāka teachers, it would be better to rely on the doctrine that consciousness is merely a property of the material elements (*bhūtacaitanya*), taking satisfaction in the denial of the next world as one's refuge, with a heart capable of finding ease in the easily obtained pleasures of some degree of worldly activity.
However, as long as the reality of the cognizer (*pramātṛtattva*) persists even after the body has perished, these desires to deny the next world bear no fruit.
Furthermore, the position that consciousness belongs to the material elements has already been refuted previously.
Therefore, there exists an eternal cognizer who transmigrates to the next world.
If it is eternal, its connection with a previous body and its connection with a future other body are not difficult to establish.
As for what was said—that there is no movement of this [self] from one body to another—that is indeed correct.

For what purpose would there be movement for a self that is all-pervading and exists everywhere? If it is asked what the proof for its all-pervasiveness is, the answer is: the perception of effects everywhere is the proof.
Even when I have gone from here to Vārāṇasī, my connection with effects such as memory and desire certainly occurs.
And that [consciousness] has the self alone as its source;
yet, unlike the body, there is no movement of the self into it because it is formless,
nor is it like a quality of the body because it does not depend upon it.
It is not like the vital breaths and so forth, because it lacks the quality of functioning within the body.

If it is asked what the proof is for the absence of its functioning within the body, it is said: if it were to function within the body, there would be only two possibilities: either functioning in one part [of the body] or filling the entire body.

In that regard, if [the self] fills the entire body, it would follow the dimensions of the body; consequently, as in the case of the bodies of a child, a youth, and an old man, there would be a difference in dimension according to the previous reasoning, and thus—due to its being different [from its former state]—there would again arise the undesirable consequence of the failure of functions such as reconnection [to a new birth].
