Furthermore, regarding the connection with the bodies of an elephant and a gnat, contraction and expansion would have to occur due to the transformation of karma;
yet these two are incompatible with something eternal.

But if [the self] were to reside in only one part, then those parts not presided over by it would lack the nature of a self; consequently, like the limbs of a dead body, they would become like wood, incapable of being employed according to one's will.

If it is argued that the self, though existing in only one part like a lamp, can still govern the entire body, then—just as a mass of light is intensified in the area of the wick—there would be a perception of consciousness with greater intensity in one specific part of the body.
If it is argued that there is indeed an excellence [of consciousness] in the region of the heart, we say no, because it is not perceived.
Upon contact with fire, snow, a sword, or the like, we do not observe any particular sensation in the heart or in any other part of the body.
Therefore, the self does not reside within the lotus of the heart like a lamp.
Therefore, the statement of Vyāsa, "Yama forcibly dragged out the person the size of a thumb," must be understood as not having such a [literal] meaning.

If, however, it is argued that the self is the controller of the body because it is atomic in dimension, residing in a single part of the mind, and moving rapidly [throughout the body], even so, this contradicts the observation of perspiration, horripilation, and other sensations pervading the entire body that arise suddenly upon seeing a beloved who has returned after a long absence.
Furthermore, the functional relationship between agent and instrument cannot be established between two things that are both atomic, namely the self and the mind.
Therefore, the self is neither atomic nor is it merely the size of the body; thus, it remains as something all-pervasive.
Thus, since this self exists even in Vārāṇasī, the observation of its effects there is logically accounted for; it cannot be explained by any other means, such as the act of traveling.

Is it not the case that because the effects of pleasure, pain, cognition, and so forth are observed everywhere, there should be only one self for all living beings? No, because the distinct distribution of pleasure and pain is observed, and because the distinction between the self will be demonstrated through the established rules governing bondage and liberation.

If it is argued that agency likewise belongs to the omnipresent [Self], it has been established that its agency consists solely in the inherence of knowledge, desire-to-act, and effort, and not in connection with physical activity.

Now, one might object: since the self is all-pervasive, why is its effect not perceived even outside the body? For the production of its effects is dependent upon the presence of auxiliary factors such as the body and the sense organs, which are drawn along [by the self];
how then could that effect exist outside of them?
Therefore, it has been established by the manner just described that the self possesses a state of existence in another world, because of its permanence and its omnipresence.
The author of the Sūtras, however, has set forth other reasons to establish the existence of the next world.
A newborn infant possesses joy, sorrow, and so forth, as inferred from facial expressions such as smiling and crying.
Furthermore, in the case of a young body and the like, crying and other such behaviors are understood to have sorrow and the like as their causes.
The expansion of the face and so forth is caused by joy;

likewise, in the case of an infant as well, its arising is based on that [joy]. Furthermore, those two—joy and sorrow—must have as their causes either the attainment of the means of pleasure or pain, or the recollection thereof, because it is observed to be so.
And since, in this state, he has no experience of objects that are the means to pleasure or pain at that time, only the recollection of them could be the cause of joy or sorrow.

Even the recollection of those [objects] arises from the experience of them; and since no such experience exists for one newly born in this life, the arising of joy and sorrow in this infant must be caused by the recollection of the means of pleasure and pain experienced in another birth. Thus, because of the persistence [of consciousness] into another birth, the self is eternal.

[Objection: Surely this expansion of his face is caused solely by the joy of beholding the new world of living beings, and likewise, his crying is due to being tormented by the pain of the unceasing [suffering] arising from the exit through the birth canal; therefore, it is not reasonable to postulate a recollection of experiences from a previous life, for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). [Reply: Not so, because joy and grief are observed to occur quite spontaneously even in one who has never experienced such causes of pleasure and pain.

Now, one might object: "Could not the effect, such as the opening of a child's mouth, be merely natural, just like the blooming of a lotus bud? What is meant by 'natural'? Does it mean causeless, having an unknown cause, or having an indefinite cause? It cannot be causeless, for that would entail the loss of its status as an effect."
Nor is it logical that this effect should exist without a known cause, for an effect is indeed perceived;

therefore, let your honor strive to fully understand its cause rather than remaining indifferent, since it is impossible to know [the cause] while ignoring the effect itself, as the effect alone serves as the indicator of its existence therein.
Nor is there any effect that has an indefinite cause,
because the restriction of the cause is established precisely by the restriction of the production of the effect.
For this very reason, worldly people, desiring to bring about a particular effect, employ only its specific, restricted cause.
Even in cases where the cause is uncertain, such as cow dung and the like being the source of a scorpion,
those who are skilled do not fail to perceive the distinction therein.

Thus, even the restriction of causes is difficult to establish because of the observation of specific effects; for it is understood that joy alone is the cause of a smile, since this is observed to be so a thousand times.
However, since the cause of the expansion of insentient things such as lotuses and the like is observed to be their contact with the mass of sunbeams and so forth, that too is not inherent.
Therefore, joy is the cause of the expansion of the face, memory is the cause of joy, and experience is the cause of memory; and that [experience] belongs to the infant in another birth.

[Objection: But surely, if an infant remembers experiences from previous lives, it would follow that they must remember everything at all times. [Reply: No, because a cause is postulated only for as far as there is an effect;
for the recollection of everything at all times is not experienced, nor is any cause found for such a postulation.

Furthermore, it has been stated more than once that this is the proper path for investigators: that one should not postulate everything based on a single observation, nor should one deny even what has been observed.

Moreover, recollecting that milk is the cause of satisfaction, an infant fixes its gaze upon the slope of the mother’s breast out of a desire for breast-milk; yet it cannot be said that the child has understood its status as a means to that end in this life. Therefore, we conclude that the apprehension of the relationship between them must have occurred in a previous birth.

Nor is it appropriate to claim, on the basis of the analogy of the magnet, that the infant's approaching the vicinity of the jar-like breasts is indeed natural, for that has been refuted immediately thereafter.

Now, if it is argued that even for one lying in the womb, since nourishment is observed, the cause of that [nourishment] must be understood through the very recollection of its acquisition—if such an effect is thus understood, what fault is there in understanding its cause in that case as well? However, those learned in Āyurveda state that the nourishment there occurs through the transfer of the digestion of food and drink fallen into the mother’s belly; how then can there be a postulation of recollection and so forth in that instance?

Or, if it were a mere mental construction (*kalpanā*), then since the transformations of semen and blood such as the *kalala* stage arise immediately after conception, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that memory and mental construction must also exist during those stages.
And we have no objection even to that assumption.

However, this eagerness of the infant to look toward and approach the jar of breast milk out of a desire for milk is produced solely by the recollection of that [previous experience]; thus, because of the inference of a connection with another birth, this self (*ātman*) is eternal.
And for this reason, because the birth of one who is free from passion is not observed [in this world]. (3.1.25)

Because they are not abandoned by the habitual practice of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion and so forth—which has become firmly rooted and has proceeded as an uninterrupted stream from beginningless time—sentient beings are born with passion indeed. Indeed, no such creature is seen in the world who is born free from passion.
Thus, this one being born with passion follows after the latent impressions of passion and so forth accumulated in previous lives; therefore, the connection with another birth is established.
And likewise, some are born solely devoted to greed,
such as mice and other creatures whose minds are one-pointedly intent on the accumulation of material goods.
There are some, such as pigeons and others,
who consist of the very essence of love, their minds intent on kissing the beaks of their beloveds as they coo.
And some, such as serpents and others, are characterized by a predominance of anger.
Their faces are overspread with a network of flames from the blazing fire of poison;
and as for that diversity of the world, consisting of the distinctions of pleasure, pain, and so forth—

Even when agriculture, service, and so forth are equal, there arises a distinct variety of results; for some, there is the sudden discovery of a treasure, while for others, there is a stroke of lightning.
In some cases there is fruit even without effort, while in other cases there is no fruit despite effort;
thus, this is seen to be difficult to reconcile because [the result] deviates from its supposed cause.
Therefore, some unseen cause must be admitted for this;
for the invisible property of the elements is the cause of the diversity of the world.
If someone were to accept [this], what fault would there be in the conceptualization of karma?
And if it were merely a matter of terminology, then there would likewise be a dispute between us regarding the truth.
Just as with a living being, it is impossible for the nature of a living being to be invisible;
yet this is seen in the case of a virtuous woman and her twin sons, who were born from the same womb.
The inherent nature of excellence in vigor, knowledge, fortune,
and the perfection of health in all effects has just now been refuted.
Therefore, this emergence of the diverse world arises from actions alone.
If the diversity of actions were indeed produced by other actions,
then that [diversity] which is established by itself in the world must simply be accepted as such.
The capacity of actions to produce various fruits is known from the scriptures;
and that [capacity] is also seen through direct perception in the case of statements concerning perceptible objects.
Therefore, it is reasonable to postulate a cause for an effect that is perceived;
however, since the cause itself is unperceived, what is the point of considering another cause?
But what is the point of merely saying that there is no other cause for that [effect]?
Is it even logical to deny a cause for this effect which is actually perceived?
Even if one postulates a variety of karma caused by other causes,
there is no danger of an infinite regress, because saṃsāra is beginningless.
And so it is recited in the treatises on Dharma: "A living being is born virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action."
Therefore, such [objections] have been made by means of an objection that is rooted in fallacious reasoning, which merely follows upon observed effects,
and which is contrary to the consensus of all the world.
Therefore, actions must be postulated for the sake of accounting for the occurrence of observed effects.
And because these [factors] are subject to momentary destruction, their duration occurs by way of a formative force (*saṃskāra*).
That karma-produced formative force is what is designated by the terms "dharma" and "adharma."
And without a permanent self, there can be no abiding of merit and demerit.
Therefore, the person is eternal, experiencing the enjoyment of bliss and suffering as they evolve through the sequence of merit and demerit produced by his own [past] actions.
Furthermore, the authority of the scriptures has already been clearly established; from them, too, the self is proven to be a reality that transcends birth and death.

As for the Vedic statement beginning with "a mass of consciousness" (*vijñānaghana*), that was established as a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by those whose hearts were devoid of reflection upon the preceding and following context; such was the meaning grasped [by them].

But when the venerable Yājñavalkya, being questioned by Maitreyī, said, "The self (*ātman*) does not perish at all," this is the speech that constitutes the essence of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Therefore, by this establishment of the permanence of the self, the path to the next world is very clearly proven;
for those who know that [reality] declare that very conjunction with another body to be the next world.

Thus, the rogue found great delight in devouring meat-stew, in seizing the property of others, in the company of gambling dens, and in kissing the lotus-face of courtesans, thinking that there was no future life; yet now, alas, he suffers because of the realization of its attainment.

Therefore, this self is eternal and does not possess the fruit of defilement; this connection with passion, hatred, and so forth is not its innate nature, but rather its true form is entirely devoid of all qualities.

Consequently, one should strive to attain the supreme good—which transcends all fear—by completely abandoning suffering brought about by the ripening of karma accumulated through an beginningless continuity of transformation.

The Eighth Daily Lesson: Examination of the Objects of Cognition. Immediately following the self (*ātman*), the body (*śarīra*) was mentioned in the Sūtra on Classification; therefore, in order to determine its essential nature as it has not yet been described, [the author] says: "The body is the substratum of the remaining sense organs and their objects" (2.2.32).
Both the definition of the body and the manner in which it, when clearly discerned, serves as a means to liberation are here set forth.
In this regard, first of all, being a body (*śarīratva*) itself is the primary definition of a body;
for by means of that, it is distinguished from both homogeneous and heterogeneous classes.

Even though that [being a body] exists, its definition is stated as "the substratum of effort, sense-faculties, and objects," in order to indicate that the body is the locus of experience for the self (*ātman*) in that form.
For the body becomes the means for the self's experience by being the locus of activity, the sense organs, and their objects.

And since the seeker of liberation—one whose mind is fixed on the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), which consists in the true nature of the self that is devoid of the experience of pleasure and pain—should regard the body as the substratum of such experience, he must exert effort toward its abandonment; thus the Teacher has stated that "being the locus of activity, the sense organs, and their objects" is its definition.
[Objection: But surely "activity" (*ceṣṭā*) is "action" (*kriyā*).

Even though trees and the like possess a substratum of action, they do not have the nature of a body; thus, the definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*). [Reply: No, because it is understood from the context of defining a specific object of knowledge that the definition refers to being the substratum of a *specific* activity.
For a body is said to be the locus of an operation capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, not merely the locus of any movement whatsoever.

Nor is there over-extension [of the definition] to chariots and the like, because the specific qualification—“in the absence of being impelled by another”—is obtained precisely through the force of the aforementioned context.

The meaning is that the body is the substratum of a particular kind of activity characterized by the adoption of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful, which is independent of any impeller other than one's own effort.

[Objection: But surely there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*), because the body of a frog inside a stone is not observed to have that [action] as its substrate; for even in that case, the capacity [for action] exists. [Reply:
Even though the capacity for action is present, that wretched frog is unable to move because the space is obstructed on all sides by a solid, seamless mass of stone.

Furthermore, when that stone cracks open, it is seen to move at that very moment; thus, although no movement is observed at that time—just like one whose body is confined within a dense enclosure—there is no over-narrow definition.

Some maintain that the body of one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) alone is the defining characteristic (*lakṣya*). They argue that there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) by the bodies of frogs and the like, because those are not intended to be defined. This is incorrect, because there is no fixed or determinate body of one desiring liberation; moreover, the bodies of frogs and such are extremely conducive to world-weariness (*nirveda*).
Even one desiring liberation, perceiving the manifold ripening of karma, cannot fail to suspect even for himself the possibility of becoming a frog.

Since for one who is about to enter the city of liberation, whose intellect is most refined, and who is in his final birth—a seeker of liberation—what use would there be for instruction on the definition and so forth? Therefore, the previously stated avoidance of the fallacy of under-extension (*avyāpti*) alone is superior.

Let it be so that being the locus of activity is the definition of the body. But how is it the locus of the sense-faculties? For the sense-faculties are material; the olfactory, gustatory, visual, and tactile faculties are supported by their own constituent parts.

As for the auditory faculty and the mind, since they are eternal substances, they are indeed without a physical locus. How, then, can the body be said to be the locus of the sense-faculties? It is replied: here the meaning of "locus" (*āśraya*) does not consist in the relationship of container and contained; rather, because they are sustained by it, the sense-faculties are said to be "supported" by the body.

For the sense organs of a person whose body has been nourished by wholesome food appropriate to the place, time, and condition, as well as by physical exercise, massage, and other such treatments, become highly efficient in grasping their respective objects.

However, for a person whose body is afflicted by such things as traversing long distances, eating unwholesome food, or the use of worn-out sandals, the sense organs possess dull power; thus, because they support them, the body is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the sense organs.
As for certain objects such as color, taste, smell, and so forth, the body indeed serves as their substratum because they are inherent in it;
however, by that much alone, no characteristic has been stated that is conducive to its being a locus of experience.
That definition is also over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), because the inherence (*samavāya*) of color, taste, and so forth exists even in trees and the like.

Therefore, what is intended here by "being the locus of those objects" is as follows: those objects—such as the bodies of other women and so forth, and external objects like blossoming *mucukunda*, *kunda*, *kandala*, and *kumuda* buds—which, existing in the body of the experiencing self (*bhoktr-ātman*), bestow loveliness and become causes for the increase of passion, do not exist when the body is absent. Thus, the body is the locus because it serves as the instrument for the enjoyment of objects.
Therefore, it has been well said that the body is the substratum of purposeful activity, the sense organs, and their objects.
Thus, the meaning is that [the body] is to be abandoned because it is a cause of bondage by virtue of being the locus of experience.
Now, this body of ours and others is examined: is it composed of earth alone, or is it constructed from various elements?

Now, what is the purpose of this investigation? For that utility for the highest good which has been shown to belong to the body does not differ from it even if it possesses multiple constituent natures.

Do not speak thus; for one who has already attained its true nature, its utility for action may be considered. However, even for one who desires to accomplish a task, effort must first be directed toward determining that nature.
And thus, the sense organs will be examined by distinguishing whether they are elemental or derived from the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra).
How many objects are there, and what are their qualities?

One should apply this same principle to all cases: is *buddhi* the first transformation of *pradhāna*, denoted by the term "the Great" (*mahat*), or is it simply a momentary attribute of the self known as knowledge? Thus it should be understood everywhere.
Regarding this, some maintain that our own bodies and those of others consist of earth alone,
for the specific quality of earth, namely odor, is perceived therein.
Others say that earth and water are the cause [of cohesion],
because moisture is observed even in that [earth];
for in the absence of contact with water, the particles of earth do not undergo moistening.
Others say that [the smell] is produced by earth, water, and fire, because it is perceived there even in the presence of heat, just like the smell of moisture.

Others [hold] that the water on the earth is produced by the wind moving through one another's channels, because they determine that there, a specific arrangement—which is an effect of the wind—is present.

Others, however, maintain that [the body] is produced from earth, water, fire, air, and space; for, just like smell and the other [sensory objects], space—which is an effect of ether—is observed there as well.
Indeed, the body is perceived as having cavities.
Furthermore, even though space is merely a portion of ether, it is designated as its effect figuratively—just as the ear is—by intending to refer to it as a delimited portion within that space.
Therefore, what is the truth here? [The body] is indeed composed of earth alone, because a composite whole (*avayavin*) that is an effect of a different genus is impossible.

Furthermore, since there is no possibility of sublation for the cognition of non-difference—which apprehends the body as a whole inherent in its earthly parts—that cognition is like the cognition of non-difference regarding grass, leaves, stones, roots, and so forth.
We do not, however, intend here to deny the causal status of the other elements.
Even though it is undisputed that [an object] such as a jar is composed solely of earth, water and the other elements do not cease to be its causes;
for without them, it would be impossible to bring a jar or the like into existence.

However, we maintain that even in the case of the body, as in the case of a jar and so forth, the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) consists solely of the parts of earth, because its being composed of that [earth] is apprehended through direct perception. The notions of moisture, heat, motion, and space perceived therein are, however, due to the connection with other elements that have entered as auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*). For example, in the case of bodies produced solely from water and so forth in the world of Varuṇa and elsewhere—as described in scripture—the observation of stability and other qualities occurs by virtue of the support provided by the parts of earth that have entered as auxiliary causes.
Therefore, the body of those such as ourselves is composed of earth.
And likewise, such usage is observed in the Veda:

at the time of the dissolution of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, or during the rite of piling the sacrificial vessels for a deceased sacrificer, after beginning with "May your eye go to the sun," it is recited, "The earth is your body.
And that is a statement regarding the return to the primordial source (*prakṛti*).
The meaning is that whatever has arisen from this primordial nature (prakṛti) must dissolve back into that very same nature.
In this regard, just as the movement of the fiery eye is taught to be into the fire known as the sun, so too is the movement of the body into the earth.
Therefore, there is no dispute among the wise regarding the fact that this body of ours and others is bound together by the constituent parts of the earth;
yet, since this very thing is a harsh pillar for the sense-organ within the abode of suffering, it must be abandoned with diligent effort.
The sense organs—the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and ears—arise from the elements. (1.1.12)
In this context, the general definition of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) as the cause of the apprehension of objects is well-established.
Their classification as "the five external sense-faculties" has also been set forth in the aphorism (*sūtra*).
This will be demonstrated immediately thereafter by refuting the sense-faculties of action (*karmendriya*) propounded by other schools.
The specific characteristics of the five, however, are to be understood—just as in the case of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—through the power of their respective names and etymologies.
It is called the nose (*ghrāṇa*) because one smells by means of it; the nose is the uncommon cause for the apprehension of odor, as it perceives odor.
The tongue (rasana) is that by which one tastes; it is the specific cause for the apprehension of taste, as it grasps taste.

It is called the eye (*cakṣus*) because one sees (*caṣṭe*) by means of it; since it perceives form (*rūpa*), the eye is the uncommon cause for the apprehension of form, and thus it is termed "the seer" (*īkṣaṇa*) or "the beholder" (*locana*).
It is called "touching" (*sparśana*) because one touches by means of it; it is the specific cause for the perception of touch, as it grasps touch.

Although one should have said "touching" (*sparśana*), the term "skin" (*tvak*) is used by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*)—as in the expression "the beds cry out"—in order to demonstrate that [the sense-faculty] has that as its locus.

Just as the olfactory faculty has the nostrils as its locus, the gustatory faculty has the tongue as its locus, and the visual faculty has the eyeball as its locus, so too the tactile faculty has the skin as its locus, because touch is perceived from the head down to the big toe of the foot.

Furthermore, by "skin" (*tvak*) one does not mean merely the external hide; rather, it refers to that which pervades the entire body, since at the time of drinking water as cold as frost-drops, a sensation of cold is perceived even within the heart.

Furthermore, although the sense organs are inherent in their own constituent parts, their being the substratum (āśrayatva) of the triadic contact and so forth is stated merely with respect to their being a locus (āśrayatvamātra), not because they are the inherent substratum (samavāyitva).

The ear is that by which one hears; it is the ear because it grasps sound. It is the uncommon cause for the apprehension of sound. Although it is not supported [by anything else] because it is a portion of space, it is said to have its locus in the ear-cavity.
Thus, the five specific characteristics of the five [senses] have been stated.

These very sense organs, characterized by the apprehension of their respective objects, are to be contemplated as things to be abandoned because they are the instruments of the self's experience and thus causes of saṃsāra. When contemplated in this manner, they will lead to liberation through the means of world-weariness, dispassion, and so forth.
Why was it said, "from the elements" (*bhūtebhyaḥ*)? For the definition of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) is indeed the grasping of their own respective objects.
In this context, the mention of the elements is not for the sake of a definition, but rather for the sake of determining that [definition].
Just as in the statement "verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person" (*āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ*), the mention of "reliable person" (*āpta*) is for the sake of determining the definition.
For the characteristic of the sense organs being the apprehension of their respective objects is established only if they have the elements as their material cause (prakṛti), and not otherwise.
Furthermore, the causes of these sense-faculties are the primary elements (bhūta), namely earth, water, fire, air, and space.
From these five, respectively, the five sense-faculties—the olfactory, gustatory, visual, tactile, and auditory—arise.

When "having the primary elements as their nature" (bhūtaprakṛtitva) is explained as "having the primary elements as their intrinsic nature" (bhūtasvabhāvatva), it applies to all five [faculties] alike.
However, the state of having the elements as their cause (*bhūtakāraṇakatva*) applies exactly in the same way to the other four [senses] as well.
As for the ear, it must be established through conventional usage by intending the portion of space delimited by the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*).
This being the case, since the sense organs, being composed of the elements (*bhautika*), are capable of apprehending their respective objects, their definition as such is proven.
Therefore, it is said: "[From the primary elements]."
Now, this must be examined:
is it the case that the sense organs, being composed of material elements, function as the instruments for grasping their respective objects, or is it otherwise?

For thus the Sāṅkhyas proclaim: "The sense faculties, being derived from the ego (ahaṅkāra), are capable of accomplishing their object, and not otherwise. For an agent, precisely because it is an agent, must act by reaching its object. How could the sense faculties, if they were composed of the elements (bhautika), reach objects situated at a distance?"

But for those who maintain that [the sense organs] consist of *āhaṃkāra*, since they are all-pervasive, it is easy to explain that their functioning—which consists of a transformation into the form of the object—is indeed possible as being non-different from the possessor of that function; thus, the theory of reaching the object (*prāpyakāritva*) is well-established.
Moreover, the apprehension of both the large and the minute is possible only if those [senses] are derived from the *ahaṅkāra*, not if they are elemental (*bhautika*).

For if they were elemental, an apprehension would grasp an object only of that same dimension as itself; yet there is the apprehension of objects like cloth or jars, which are larger than the physical globes of the senses, as well as the apprehension of objects like the seeds of a banyan tree, which are smaller in dimension.
For this reason also, the sense organs are not elemental.
Even among material things such as lamps and the like, which illuminate other objects, it is observed that they also illuminate their own nature.
In the same way, the sense organs also illuminate the nature of cloth and other objects; they should likewise illuminate their own nature.
Since they do not so illuminate [themselves], for this reason also they are not material.

To this it is replied: as for what you have asserted—that reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*) is not possible if [the eye] is composed of material elements (*bhautika*)—it appears certain that you have conceived in your mind that the eyeball itself is the eye; otherwise, how could you have said such a thing?
This is a great error on the part of your long-lived self.
Indeed, the black pupil (*kṛṣṇasāra*) is not the eye; rather, the light residing therein is the eye.
And since that [sound] possesses velocity and is a substance, it extends even to a great distance; so what cause for doubt could there be regarding its functioning by reaching [its object]?

Now, since medical treatments such as emetics are applied to the eyeball (golaka), and since the perception of objects follows the qualities and defects of the eyeball, the eyeball itself must be the eye.
Furthermore, how can light, which is not perceived, be called a sense organ?

Furthermore, even if the eye were struck by a forceful flash of light, how could one suddenly perceive the moon, the sun, and the stars situated at a distance of hundreds of thousands of yojanas? Or else, how could that small and wretched ocular faculty have its movement obstructed by the immense radiance of the sun, whose power is renowned throughout the entire world as it spreads in all directions? Thus, the perception of the sun would not be possible. Moreover, if the eye were composed of light, how could the perception of objects hidden behind glass, mica, clouds, or crystal be explained?
Therefore, O virtuous one, it is better to accept that the eye is simply the eyeball (golaka) endowed with a specific power (śaktiviśeṣa).
It is said in reply: We certainly do not accept a matter that contradicts reason by virtue of your instruction alone.

For an instrument is observed to function by reaching its object (*prāpyakārin*). Now, in the case of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇasāra*), how could there be such functioning by contact? Furthermore, even if a power (*śakti*) were to be postulated, it should not be postulated as being without a substratum; thus, in considering its substratum, the eyeball alone cannot be the substratum, because that would entail the consequence of [the eye] functioning without contact. Therefore, light itself must be the locus and the substratum of that power.
But surely, it is precisely the nature of reaching the object (*prāpyakāritva*) that must be examined;
for that is observed in the world only in the case of the tongue and the sense of touch.
As for the eye and the ear, however, since they grasp objects situated at a distance, how could they be of the nature of reaching the object?

The olfactory organ, however, perceives the fragrance of an object placed near its three-fold cavity, and it also apprehends the scent of blossoming jasmine and other flowers wafted by the force of a moving wind from afar. Since there is no contact with that organ even when a substance is brought close to the vicinity of the three-fold cavity, that [organ] too must indeed be one whose action is without reaching the object (*aprāpyakārin*). Therefore, let it be accepted that the sense organ is simply the substratum characterized by a specific power;
let the position that it acts by reaching the object (*prāpyakāritva*) be abandoned.
It has already been stated that the eye, which perceives the moon, sun, planets, and so forth, possesses the quality of reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*) to an extreme degree.
To this it is replied: we cannot abandon the principle that [the senses] act by reaching their objects;
for if that were so, we would have to abandon their very status as causal factors (*kāraka*).
And it is a marvel to claim that something is both a causal factor and yet acts without reaching its object!
Even an unseen cause, because the self is all-pervasive, would not fail to reach its object—being no less so than the qualities residing therein—let alone a visible causal instrument such as the eye.

Furthermore, if the sense organ functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*), there would be no distinction in its capacity; consequently, even an object obstructed by a wall or similar barrier would be visible to the eye.

If it is argued that the capacity is not postulated because the effect is not perceived there, then one must consider what it is that should be postulated: is it "capacity" or "light" (*tejas*)? Upon such deliberation, since light is a substance (*dravya*), obstruction and the like are compatible with it; however, for an immaterial capacity (*śakti*), obstruction would not be a hindrance. Therefore, it is light itself that should be postulated as the sense organ, and neither the capacity nor the substratum of that capacity.

Furthermore, the fact that the auditory organ functions by reaching its object was demonstrated in the *Śabdādhikaraṇa* through the means of initiating a succession of sounds similar to a series of waves.

The sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) also functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritā*), because it perceives the odor residing in a mass of pollen scattered from *kunda* flowers and the like, which are shaken by the wind.
Nor should one suspect a depletion of the substance due to the movement of atoms, for atoms are exceedingly numerous.

For this very reason, they prescribe expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) for smelling impure substances in order to remove the taint caused by contact with those substances through the medium of the odor.
The eye functions by reaching its object because its light radiates outward.
If it is argued that this light is not perceived, [we reply: is the far side of the moon or the lower part of the earth ever perceived? Indeed, objects do not have perception as their sole refuge;
their apprehension is certainly possible through inference and other means as well.
And inference has been stated:
by the effect, which is the perception of form, the eye is inferred to be composed of light alone;
for it is observed that a substance of light, such as a lamp, is the illuminator of form.

If it is asked why the ocular light (*nāyana-tejas*) is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is said in reply: for the movements of substances and their qualities vary according to the predominance or suppression (*udbhavābhibhava*) of their powers.

For example, the seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira occur when one is pervaded by a substance that spreads in all directions, possesses a thick and intense cold touch, and serves as the substratum [for that quality];
for a quality of cold touch is never perceived without a substratum.
Now, even though the substance of water is present there, only its quality—the sensation of cold—is perceived, and not its white color.
Furthermore, summer occurs when the substance of fire expands unrestrainedly to a great degree;
in that case, even though the substance of fire is present, only its quality of hot touch is perceived, and not its luminous form.
And in luminous substances such as gold, a color is perceived as well as a hot touch.
Furthermore, when fire is within water that has been heated by its flames, the quality of fire—the sensation of heat—is experienced, but its luminous form is not.
Thus, since neither color nor touch is perceived here in the substance of light—the rays of the eye—whom shall we blame?

And it has been said: "The injunction and prohibition of things seen and inferred would be untenable, because a means of valid cognition has reality as its object. Furthermore, there is not a non-perception of the ocular ray in all cases;

for in certain instances, such as among nocturnal animals like cats moving at night in a house smeared with a thick layer of the mire of dense darkness, their ocular light—which possesses a brilliant form—is indeed perceived even as it spreads to a distance.
In other cases, however, the ocular ray of people like us is not apprehended, just like the light of a meteor at midday.

However, this is the distinction: the meteor-form is not perceived because it is overwhelmed by the power of the sun's rays, whereas the form of the ocular ray is not perceived precisely because it is non-manifest.

As for the perception of objects screened by glass, layers of water, or crystal, since some of these—such as glass—are extremely transparent and others are porous, they lack the capacity to obstruct the outward diffusion of the visual light; thus, the eye’s non-reach-based operation (*aprāpyakāritva*) is not thereby established.

As for the objection: "From what cause does the visual ray have such a movement—that it traverses the sky, touches the sun garlanded with rays, and is not obstructed by the powerful solar energy?"—it has been stated here that "the prescription or prohibition of things perceived through inference is untenable.
For such a cause is postulated on the basis of the existence of its effect as one which spreads even to a distance and, while spreading, is not blocked by another.
And the non-obstruction of fire is observed in cases such as a frying pan, since the cooking of the substance being heated is thereby accomplished.
Furthermore, because the cold touch of water poured into a jar is perceived externally, there is no obstruction;
the same will apply to the visual ray as well.

It should not be said that it is simpler to assume the coldness belongs only to the fire-brand (holaka), for that would entail the abandonment of the essential nature of the instrument as something that acts by reaching its object (*prāpyakārin*).
The eye and the ear function by reaching their objects, just like the sense of touch and the others.

For this very reason, the experts in the scriptures, observing that all sense organs function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*), have explained the contact between the sense organ and its object as being of six kinds. Furthermore, such reaching cannot belong to the physical eyeball (*golaka*), because mountains and the like which are not reached are perceived, whereas things that are actually reached—such as collyrium or a firebrand—are not.
Therefore, the eyeball is not the eye.

The application of medical treatment and the like which is carried out upon the eyeball (golaka) is this "refinement of the substratum" (ādhārasaṃskāra), which benefits that which is supported (ādheya).

For this very reason, it is also logical that the perception of objects conforms to the qualities and defects of the physical orb (golaka), since those qualities and defects belong to the contained [the visual organ] by way of its substrate [the orb].

Therefore, because the apprehension of an object not in contact [with the sense-organ] is untenable, the position of the "eye as the physical orb" imagined by the mendicant (Buddhist) finds no rest in the hearts of the discerning. Thus, it is established that the eye is indeed light that acts by reaching [the object].

Thus, even in the theory that the sense organs are composed of material elements (*bhautika*), their functioning through contact (*prāpyakāritva*) is established; therefore, the claim by the followers of Kapila (*Kāpila*) that the sense organs are derived from the ego-principle (*ahaṅkārika*) is untenable.

Now, since the theory of reaching the object (*prāpyakāritva*) is established in both positions, why is this excessive attachment of yours toward their being composed of the elements (*bhautikatva*)? It is said in reply: if the sense organs were of a single material nature (*ekaprakṛtika*), there would be either only one organ capable of illuminating all objects, or all organs would grasp all objects, because there would be no distinction in their cause.
For the determination of the effect depends upon the determination of the cause.
And the cause called *ahaṅkāra* (the ego-principle) is endowed with the power to illuminate all objects.
The sense-faculties would likewise be so.

Since that [body] is endowed with the power to manifest a single object, how could other sense-faculties grasp different objects? However, if they are material, then because the primary elements (bhūta) are distinct and possess an excellence of specific qualities, the sense-faculties have as their nature the grasping of specific objects.
And likewise, although many objects such as color, taste, and so forth are present near a light source like a lamp, it is observed that the light illuminates only color.
Therefore, the visual faculty, which has light as its nature, must also be an illuminator of color alone.
The same should be stated for the other sense faculties as well.
Thus, this restriction of the objects of the sense organs is caused by the restriction of their material nature; therefore, the sense organs are composed of the elements.

If this is so, how is it that by means of the ocular organ, which is of the nature of fire (*taijasa*), there is the apprehension of color-form (*rūpa*) belonging to earth, or by the gustatory organ, which belongs to water, the apprehension of taste belonging to earth, or by the tactile organ, which belongs to air, the apprehension of touch belonging to earth and the other elements? Even if there is such a restriction regarding their essential natures (*prakṛti*), why is there this confusion of objects (*viṣayasaṃkara*)? This is not a fault; for their restriction concerns the objects such as color-form themselves, not the substrata (*āśraya*) in which those objects reside.
Indeed, a substance such as a lamp, though composed of fire, is seen to illuminate only color-form, and not necessarily only the color-form inherent in fire itself.
Even water, as a substance, manifests only taste and not [taste] residing exclusively in water;
however, there is no fault regarding the sense of smell, because its object, odor, resides solely in earth.
Thus, even if [the sense organs] are material, it is not contradictory for a substance to be apprehended by both sight and touch.

As for what was stated—that because they grasp both the large and the small, the sense organs are not composed of the gross elements—that has been refuted by demonstrating that the sense organ is something distinct from its physical seat, such as the eyeball;
and since that [organ] is itself pervasive, it is indeed capable of grasping what is pervasive.
Furthermore, even by means of a pervasive light, such as that of a lamp, a minute substance like rice and so forth is seen to be illuminated.
For this reason as well, there is no identity between the ego-sense and the self.

Furthermore, as for the claim that if the sense organ were material (bhautika), it would illuminate its own quality just as it illuminates the qualities of others—that is incorrect. This is because the sense organ possesses its status as a sense organ precisely by virtue of possessing its own quality; for it is only when the sense organ exists [as such] that an object is discerned by it.
If this [organ] possessed its own quality, its status as a sense organ would not exist at all without that quality; thus, devoid of its own quality, it would not be a sense organ at all.

And how could that which is not a sense organ (*anindriya*) be a grasper? Because the qualities of the sense organs are included within the limits of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it [the non-organ] does not possess the status of being a means of valid cognition.
Therefore, it is established that the sense organs, being composed of the primary elements (*bhautika*), perceive their respective objects.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the olfactory organ belongs to the earth, because, while being a substance, it manifests only odor among [the qualities] beginning with color-form, just like a substance possessing fragrance.
In this regard, "merely manifesting" is inconclusive; therefore, it is specified as "manifesting only odor.

This reason would otherwise be unestablished (*asiddha*), since the property of odor-ness (*gandhatva*) is also manifested by the olfactory organ; thus, the phrase "among [the qualities] beginning with color-form" was stated.
Nevertheless, because there is deviation [from the rule] due to proximity (*sannikarṣa*), the qualification "provided it is visible" (*dṛśyatve sati*) is added in order to exclude that.
In this same manner, the formal arguments should be constructed for the sense of taste and the others as well.
However, that the ear is a portion of space has been determined in the section on sound (*śabdādhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, the status of the senses as "senses" belongs to those things which are bound by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which serve as the cause for the experience of pleasure and pain based on the perception of objects such as odor; thus, they are postulated in whatever way their capacity to grasp specific objects is appropriately established, and so everything is beyond reproach.
He said: "Let it be that the sense-faculties are material; however, it is not correct to say there are five.
For the skin alone ought to be the single sense-faculty, since it is present everywhere without exception."

If it is argued that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving color even by means of the tactile sense-organ located in the palms of the hands, the cheeks, or the throat, we say no; for there is a restriction of specific capacities to specific parts [of the body].
Indeed, it is not possible for a living being to perform the function of the genitals with its foot.
And there exists a diversity of specific natures (svabhāva) in specific parts [of the body].
In the northern Mānasa lake, filled with water as pure as frost and camphor,
the testicles of one who bathes swell, but not so the buttocks.
Just as a sharp pain arises in the head or eyes due to ground consisting of damp, moist grass, wood, and so forth, it does not arise in other parts of the body in that same way.
Therefore, the skin alone is the single sense organ, variegated by various powers established in its specific parts.

It is said: From where has this unprecedented, highly wise disputant come, seeking to deceive us of simple intellect? For even while relying on a specific capacity within a specific component, he considers [all] to be a single sense-faculty (*indriya*).
Given the difference in capacities and the difference in substrates, it is only logical that these sense-faculties are manifold; enough of quarreling with those of great soul!
Indeed, conversation with humans does not become fitting for those who are emaciated;
these speakers, however, are gods appearing in human form.
But even on the view that they are distinct, how is there a restriction to five?
Since there are two ears, two eyes, and [two nostrils], how are these considered a single sense-faculty?
And it is said: "Because there is recognition [of the eye] by means of the other.

If it is argued that this is because the genus *cakṣustva* (eye-ness) is one, then, since the genus *indriyatva* (faculty-ness) is also one, there would have to be only one faculty. It is stated [in response]: the eye is determined to be light (*tejas*). And that is indeed one; its locus is also one, though it is perceived as if multiple because it is divided by the bridge of the nose.
Or let it be divided;

nevertheless, because its effects are identical, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) must be understood as being one and the same even though its substratum is distinct. It is essentially a single portion of space (*nabhodeśa*) pervading both ear-cavities, since the identity of its effect exists there as well.
Therefore, because a single effect is observed despite the difference in their physical bases,
and because that commonality is one, the ear and the eye are [considered] as one.

Nor, because the genus of the sense-organ (*indriyajāti*) is one, is it postulated that there is only one sense-organ; for there are five kinds [of sense-organs] due to the fivefold nature of: (1) the effect characterized as perception; (2) the cause, such as odor and so forth; (3) the locus, such as the nasal cavity and so forth; (4) the movement, consisting of outward diffusion; (5) the shape, whose nature is dimension; (6) the genus, such as "olfactoriness" (*ghrāṇatva*) and so forth, which is denoted by the word "genus"; or (7) the source (*yoni*), such as earth and so forth.

Just as, despite the lack of distinction in the generality of "atom-ness" (*paramāṇutva-sāmānya*), four kinds of atoms are postulated because their effects—earth and so forth—are seen to be of four kinds.
But even so, there are not just five faculties;
for, just like the faculties of cognition, the five faculties of action must also be enumerated.
As it has been said: "Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals are called the faculties of action."

And their status as sense faculties (*indriyatva*) arises from accomplishing the fivefold functions consisting of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing pleasure; for those functions cannot be accomplished by one another.

To this, he says: "It is said that there are only five organs of action; however, there are indeed other organs of action as well. For instance, why is the throat not called an organ because it performs the function of swallowing food, the chest because it performs the embracing of the jar-like breasts, and the two shoulders because they perform the carrying of burdens? If you argue that these are not called organs because such functions are seen in other parts of the body as well, [we reply]: Do animals not swallow food and drink with their hands or feet, or do they not perform grasping with their mouths and so forth? Even humans sometimes do so."
Moreover, even in the absence of the organs of action as conceived by you, their respective effects are seen to occur in other ways;
however, this is not the case for those [organs] which are the instruments of cognition.
In one whose eyes have been plucked out, there is not even the slightest notion of form;
yet, a slight movement, taking up [objects], and so forth, are seen in those whose feet and hands have been severed.

Moreover, even walking is not accomplished by the pair of feet alone, but is also produced by the feet together with the knees, thighs, shanks, and so forth; likewise, even taking up an object is performed by the hands together with the arms, and not by the hands alone.
The vocal organ (*vāgindriya*), however, must be entirely above the navel.
For thus they say: "The vital air (*vāyu*), having risen from the navel, expands in the chest, turns at the throat, strikes the head, and returning, moving within the mouth, manifests various sounds.
Such an experience exists for those who chatter, and especially for those singing an uninterrupted song.
And thus, since the entire universe consists solely of the organs of action, the body could not possibly exist as something distinct from those organs.

If, on the other hand, the designation "organ of action" were applied merely to the various parts of the body that perform distinct functions, then—as has already been stated—there would be the over-extension [of the term] to the throat and so forth.
And how is the faculty of the genitals counted as one? Because, like pleasure, it is the means for the discharge of urine as well.
The vocal organ, however, is even more heart-captivating.
External sound, which is produced by conjunction and disjunction, is perceived;
and it varies according to its specific differences.

For the sound produced by the contact of a drumstick and a drum is not the same as that produced by the contact of a tortoise-shell and a plectrum; likewise, from the contact of various places of articulation (*sthāna*) and instruments (*karaṇa*), a diverse sound consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) arises. Thus, there is no such thing as a "speech-organ" (*vāgindriya*).
Furthermore, the world designates by the word "speech" (vāk-śabda) only that sound whose nature consists of articulated phonemes (varṇa).
And sound is an object of the sense organ, not the sense organ itself.

Therefore, this body—fashioned by the transformation of karma capable of casting one into the experience of a particular kind of suffering—brings about for the self the experience of various fruits of karma through its various constituent parts. Thus, enough with such a simplistic conception of the sense organs.
The threefold division of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is also untenable, since a single mind (*manas*) alone is sufficient.
Furthermore, the intellect (*buddhi*), because its nature is that of apprehension (*upalabdhi*), is the effect of an instrument rather than an instrument itself.
Likewise, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is also merely an object of cognition and not an instrument.
And we shall explain this in detail in the section on the definition of the intellect (*buddhi*).
Therefore, it is established that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is not of thirteen kinds.
Because it balances deficiency and excess, there are exactly five sense faculties capable of apprehending external objects;
however, the author of the Sūtra will later describe the sixth, the mind (manas), as that which is employed in the apprehension of internal objects such as pleasure and the like.
Therefore, one must act in such a way that these senses— which are as fickle as thieves and greedy for the forceful enjoyment of sense-objects—
do not steal the jewel of discernment, which bestows bliss, from a person fallen into the ocean of existence.
Smell, taste, visible form, touch, and sound are the qualities of earth and the other elements; these are the objects [of the senses].

Regarding the phrase "having that as their object" (*tadarthāḥ*), one must show the term to be defined (*lakṣyapada*) as "objects" (*arthāḥ*), either by extracting it from that very phrase or from the context of the introduction.
"Having that as their object" (*tadarthāḥ*) is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). The word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the sense-faculties (*indriya*) previously introduced.
Their objects are the sense-objects; that is to say, they are the objects of the sense-faculties. This is their general definition.
Their classification is as follows: odor, taste, visible form, tangibility, and sound.

Furthermore, the specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) should be construed as "their objects" (*tadarthāḥ*). The word "their" (*tat*) refers back to the nose and so forth, which were designated by their specific names.
In this way, the specific definition is stated: "the object of the nose is odor," "the object of the tongue is taste," and so forth.

However, because smell-ness (*gandhatva*) and the like are also perceivable by the nose and other senses, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*); therefore, the qualification "qualities of earth and so forth" is employed.

Furthermore, these aforementioned smells and other objects of the senses, being objects of enjoyment, are causes of attachment and bring about the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*); thus, they should be contemplated as things to be abandoned.
But in that case, would not the first cause of passion—the composite whole (*avayavin*) which is the substratum of qualities such as odor—be excluded?
And yet, he will state: "[The conceit of a composite whole is caused by that].
Indeed, other qualities such as number, dimension, and so forth, also possess the status of being causes of passion.

For just as the form of a playful woman’s mass of hair—variegated by a cluster of crushed flower petals that imitate a bundle of *barhi* grass—steals the hearts of youths, so too does the number "many" residing therein [steal them].
And just as the form of her orb-like hips, resembling a slab of molten gold, [steals them], so too does their dimension.
And it also impetuously steals away even the conjunctions and disjunctions of her limbs.
Likewise, in games such as with a ball and the like, there is the entire range of activities, such as graceful circling, which is sweetened by the burgeoning essence of playful charm.

Likewise, by excluding those of the lowest castes and so forth, even the possession of a caste corresponding to oneself and all other such causes of attachment—such as substance, quality, action, and so on—would remain unstated.
In this regard, some explain it as a *dvandva* compound, namely "the earth and so forth, and the qualities" (*pṛthivyādīni ca guṇāśca*).
By the term "earth and so forth," the composite substance (*avayavidravya*) which is the locus of the qualities is expressed;
and by the two qualifiers [beginning with] "residing in," all the qualities are indicated.
By the mention of "qualities" (guṇa), everything including action-universals (karma-sāmānya) and so forth is also stated, just like number (saṃkhyā), dimension (parimāṇa), and the rest;
therefore, there is no failure of inclusion.

This, however, is untenable; for at that time, the mention of the apprehension of odor and so forth would be purposeless, as its meaning is already established by the very statement "and the qualities.
If it is argued that those are included for the sake of specifying a distinction, then why resort to describing them as a *dvandva* compound? Let this very [other] solution suffice.

Although substances, actions, universals, and other qualities such as number and dimension certainly possess the quality of being causes of attachment, it is nevertheless observed that this [causality] belongs primarily to odors and the like.

For there is no capacity for substances, numbers, or universals—when independent of form and the rest—to serve as causes of attachment; thus, form and the others alone are the primary causes of passion, because the intellect proceeds toward them with immediate speed.
And it has been said: "Nevertheless, for men, forms and the other [objects of the senses] lead to an extreme increase of passion;
those very things have been sung by poets as the five arrows of the five-arrowed god."
Therefore, the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) "the qualities of earth and so forth" is indeed superior;
moreover, the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) as distinct from the qualities has already been established on the basis of the validity of the cognition: "I touch that which I previously saw."

Regarding what was stated—that these are the qualities of earth and the other elements—they are now described in detail, specifying how many qualities belong to each. Among them, the four beginning with odor are to be assigned as the qualities of earth; from water, fire, and air, however, one is excluded at each successive stage, starting from the preceding element.
Excluding odor, water possesses taste, color, and touch; fire possesses color and touch, excluding taste; wind possesses touch alone, excluding color;
and the quality of space is sound.
Is it not the case that this assignment of qualities is not sound? If earth possessed four qualities,
then all four of those qualities would be perceived by the olfactory sense organ, which is composed of earth.
The same should be stated for the subsequent [qualities] as well.

Therefore, let it be said that the qualities of the dhātus are indeed each single; this is not so, for qualities are not obtained by one's own will, but rather they are designated according to how they are perceived.
For we take empirical experience as our authority.
In that regard, since all four qualities are perceived in the substance earth, how can we say that earth possesses only one quality?
Furthermore, if fire possessed only the single quality of color, then earth and water—being devoid of color like wind—would be imperceptible.
Therefore, there are three material elements.
If this were so, since all [qualities] are perceived everywhere, let all elements possess all qualities:
let the earth crackle (*paṭapaṭāyate*), the water quiver (*calacalāyante*), the fire hiss (*dhagadhagāyate*), and the wind roar (*kathakathāyate*); thus, sound would be the quality of all [elements].
It is said in reply: not all qualities are perceived everywhere, because water is observed everywhere to be devoid of odor.
However, in moist substances and the like, odor is perceived in the water due to the transfer of earth particles.
Thus, in the case of gold, which is a fiery substance, the perception of taste and other qualities occurs through inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*).
Sound, however, is always perceived as residing exclusively in space (*ākāśa*);
since it arises from the conjunction and disjunction of the parts of earth and other elements, it creates the illusion of being dependent upon them, yet its apprehension cannot occur without space.
It has already been established previously that sound is indeed a quality of space;
therefore, it is not the case that all things possess all qualities.

As for the argument that if earth possesses four qualities, then all four of those qualities should be perceptible by the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇendriya*)—that is not so, because the predominance of a specific quality is the determining factor. The olfactory organ is composed of particles of earth alone, which serve as the substratum for the quality of odor in its most excellent form, are devoid of even a trace of contact with parts of heterogeneous substances, and are assisted by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); thus, it is the perceiver of odor alone.
And this very point they call "abundance" (*bhūyastva*).
As Kaṇavrata said: "Due to its abundance and its possession of odor, earth is the material cause (*prakṛti*) in the cognition of odor.
Here too it has been stated: "But the determination of that [object] is due to abundance."
Moreover, powers that determine specific effects are observed even in objects composed solely of earthy constituents;
for example, although there is no difference in their being earthy substances, poison is a cause of death,
whereas another medicinal substance serves for the sake of life.
Therefore, this [objection] cannot be pursued by the king: "Just as odor is perceived by the sense of smell, why are taste and the other [objects] not also perceived?"

It has been determined in the investigation of the sense organs (*indriyacintā*) that even when endowed with their own specific natural qualities (*sātiśayaprakṛtiguṇa*), the senses lack the skill to perceive those very qualities of their own. However, the fact that sound—their own quality—is perceived by the auditory organ is a matter established by the means of knowledge known as inference by elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*); this point was examined precisely in the *Śabdaparīkṣā*. Therefore, enough of this digression.
Thus, this conception that [the self] possesses the sole quality of being the substratum of all qualities is not accepted by those of subtle intellect.
Therefore, let this stainless rule for the application of qualities be accepted exactly as it has been stated.
These objects of the senses are to be known as such: they display a form that is sweet only when contrived, yet they emit a bitter scent and result in calamity at their conclusion.
When these are abandoned by a person who has cleared away the mire of great delusion, he has crossed this ocean of existence, so fierce with its waves of afflictions.
Intellect, apprehension, and knowledge are synonymous. 1.1.15.
Is this not merely the utterance of synonyms, rather than a definition of cognition? No, for it is precisely the employment of synonyms that is capable of serving as a definition.
Indeed, a definition is said to be that by which the object to be defined is distinguished from both similar and dissimilar classes.

And cognition is indeed distinguished from those [other things] by its very state of being expressible through synonyms such as "cognition" (*buddhi*) and so forth; therefore, this is not a mere string of names.

[Objection: Since the cognition of the meaning of a word is conventional, and since convention follows the will of persons, how could this definition be established? [Reply: Not so; for it is impossible to subvert a convention that is universal among all people, and because that which is qualified by such a convention is the definition of its denotatum.
If it is asked, "Why has its definition not been stated by means of another method?", this is the same objection as regarding the *śiṃśapā* tree;
for even when that has been stated, one might still inquire, "Why has it not been stated in such-and-such a way? by you.

Furthermore, there is a purpose for describing the definition by means of synonyms: namely, the removal of the delusion of the Sāṃkhyas. For the Sāṃkhyas assert that "intellect (buddhi) is one thing, knowledge (jñāna) is another, and apprehension (upalabdhi) is yet another. To dispel this misconception, it is said: "Intellect, apprehension, and knowledge are not different in meaning; they have but a single referent. This is the sense.

Thus, when the intellect (*buddhi*) is known in its true nature, it is regarded as something to be abandoned because, being of the nature of experience (*bhoga*) and being the means thereto, it is the cause of *saṃsāra*. The cognition of pleasure and so forth is "experience," while the cognition of the means thereto is the "means of experience. But how is it that the followers of the Great Sage (the Sāṅkhyas) declare that the intellect is one thing, knowledge another, and apprehension yet another? For they consider the intellect to be eternal.
Thus, as long as these two, primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), do not perceive each other through discrimination, there is saṃsāra;
from the knowledge of the discrimination between primordial nature and the person comes liberation.
What, then, is *prakṛti*? It is the state of equilibrium of the three qualities (*guṇas*)—namely, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
That which consists of the three qualities in a state of equilibrium is called *pradhāna* and the *avyakta* (the unmanifest).
Now, as to the question of what proof there is for its existence, he says: "Inference.
For this reason, this entire universe, consisting of the moving and the non-moving, is perceived as being invariably concomitant with pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Indeed, within the world extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, not a single entity is found that is devoid of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

In this regard, *sattva* has the nature of pleasure, *rajas* has the nature of pain, and *tamas* has the nature of delusion. Since joy, sorrow, and despondency are observed everywhere, and since illumination, activity, and restraint are likewise perceived, the entire world consists of the three *guṇas*.
Furthermore, whatever effect possesses a form that is mutually interconnected is seen to arise from a cause that possesses a single uniform nature.
For objects such as jars, bowls, and water-pots, which are permeated by clay, arise from a single cause consisting of clay;
likewise, this entire universe is permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion, and therefore it must be the effect of a cause whose nature consists of those same qualities.
That cause whose nature consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion is *prakṛti*, composed of the constituents *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
In this way, reasons such as dimension (*parimāṇa*) and so forth should also be refuted by means of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

For it is observed that effects possessing a certain dimension—whether in terms of magnitude or shape such as squareness and the like—possess a single primordial material cause (*ekaprakṛti*). Furthermore, these qualities (*guṇas*) are seen to exist in their effects in unequal proportions.

In some cases, goodness (sattva) is predominant while passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas) are deficient; in some cases, passion is preeminent while goodness and darkness are slight; and in some cases, darkness is increased while goodness and passion are negligible.
Therefore, for these effects—which possess a universal form manifested through various states of imbalance—there must exist at some point a state of equilibrium;
that is called *prakṛti*.
This *prakṛti* is insentient and is the object of experience.
But its enjoyer is the conscious Puruṣa.

Now, by what means is the *puruṣa* inferred? It has already been stated that the enjoyer is inferred from the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). For the status of being an object of enjoyment cannot logically belong to that which is insentient (*acetana*) without an enjoyer.
Since that status is observed, an enjoyer is postulated.
And that [Self] is indeed of the nature of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*), its essential form being excluded from the entire range of worldly transactions such as agency and the like.
They say that the very state of being a witness (*draṣṭṛtva*) is the essential nature of the Person (*puruṣa*).
It cannot be as you conceive this Self to be—possessing attributes such as determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth—because determination and the rest are properties of the intellect (*buddhi*).
A person is not able to bend even a blade of grass;
he merely perceives the object as it is presented by another.
Nature itself unites this [Puruṣa] with both enjoyment and liberation;
and since Nature, being changeless, would not be capable of effecting enjoyment, it undergoes transformations such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest.
Through the analogy of the lame man and the blind man, Nature and Puruṣa become conjoined.
Nature (prakṛti) is insentient, visible, and an object of experience; it requires the Puruṣa as its seer and enjoyer.
The Puruṣa also is a seer and an enjoyer; he requires the visible world as his object of experience.
Thus, their union occurs like that of the lame man and the blind man.
Through the union of the power of vision in the lame man and the power of locomotion in the blind man, the accomplishment of the task occurs.

In the same way, through the conjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, creation proceeds. As it has been said: "The purpose of the *puruṣa* is for the sake of seeing, and likewise the purpose of *pradhāna* is for the sake of isolation (*kaivalya*). The conjunction of both is like that of the lame and the blind; from that, creation is produced."

That which arises from Pradhāna in this manner as the principle of Mahat is the intellect (buddhi); it consists of the nature of ascertainment and is said to be the principle of Mahat when conjoined with the modifications (vṛtti) consisting of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, power, and their opposites.
From the intellect (buddhi), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) arises;
and its essential nature is self-conceit (abhimāna).

From the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), however, there arises the group of sixteen: the five sense organs of cognition beginning with the nose, the five organs of action beginning with speech, the eleventh organ which is the mind (manas) characterized by volition, and the five subtle elements (tanmātras) of smell and so forth.
From that group of five subtle elements (tanmātra), beginning with smell, the five gross elements (mahābhūta), beginning with earth, are born.
And it is said: "From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the I-maker (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen;
and from five among that group of sixteen, the five gross elements arise."
These are declared to be the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*). Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), which is Nature (*prakṛti*) itself, is not a modification (*vikṛti*).

The seven—the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—are modifications with respect to their respective preceding causes, yet they are natures with respect to their respective succeeding effects.
The eleven faculties and the five elements are indeed modifications (*vikṛti*).
But the pure *puruṣa* is neither primordial nature (*prakṛti*) nor modification.
Thus it is said: "Root primordial nature is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), are both primordial natures and modifications."
The group of sixteen, however, is a transformation; the Puruṣa is neither a primal nature nor a transformation.

Thus, nature (*prakṛti*), possessing great transformations, accomplishes the experience (*bhoga*) of the self (*ātman*). And what is this experience? It is the state of conforming to the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*).
The person (*puruṣa*) perceives the modification of the intellect—which consists of cognition—as colored by the modifications of the sense organs that have transformed into the forms of objects.
Even in the act of perception, there is no difference whatsoever in that [consciousness];
it is that very perception which constitutes the reflection therein.

Thus, when there is a conjunction of these two—the intellect and the person—the attribute of the person, characterized by the state of being a cognizer, although non-existent in the intellect, appears as if it were existent.

Furthermore, the attributes of the intellect (buddhi), such as agency and so forth, although non-existent in the Self which stands in the position of a witness, are nevertheless perceived as if they were existent.

As it has been said: "Therefore, through its conjunction with that [Self], the insentient linga appears as if it were sentient; likewise, although the gunas are the agents, the indifferent [Self] appears as if it were the agent."

Now, as for how *prakṛti* conduces to the liberation (*apavarga*) of the self, they explain that it does so by manifesting its own true nature (*svarūpa*). A person whose true nature is not yet determined, while remaining established in his own nature, imagines everything produced by *prakṛti* to be produced by himself and thus enjoys what has been acquired by her.

But when he perceives her as distinct, then, realizing "let this [prakṛti] be merely a cause of exertion for me," he does not enjoy what is produced by her and remains established solely in his own nature.

Even Prakṛti does not venture to appear before him, thinking, "I have been seen by him; he now regards me as something separate. Thus it is said: "It is my conviction that there is nothing more delicate than Prakṛti, who, once seen, returns to invisibility for the Puruṣa."

Furthermore, because the primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa) have their respective capacities frustrated with respect to one another, even though their conjunction exists due to their omnipresence, creation does not proceed at all; thus he says: "One [the Spirit] becomes indifferent, thinking 'I have seen [her]'; the other [Nature] ceases, thinking 'I have been seen.
Even when their conjunction exists, there is no further purpose for creation."

For a man whose curiosity has not yet faded cannot be deceived once he has perceived the truth; thinking this, Nature desists even though her capacity to act remains.
