Thus it is said: "Just as a dancer, having displayed herself upon the stage, withdraws from the dance, so too does Nature, having manifested herself to the Puruṣa, withdraws."

Thus, it is nature alone that proceeds in saṃsāra, and nature alone that experiences liberation; therefore, he says: "Therefore, truly, no one is bound, nor is anyone liberated, nor does anyone transmigrate;
it is nature, resting upon various supports, that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated."

If it is asked, "For what purpose does this Prakṛti act in this way?"—what can be done? This is simply the inherent nature of that cruel Destiny: by various means, she serves the man who does not return her favor;
though she herself possesses qualities, she acts fruitlessly for the sake of him who is devoid of qualities.

If it is asked, "Since this [Prakṛti] is insentient, how can it have such causal activity?", it has been said in this regard: "Just as the activity of insentient milk proceeds for the sake of the growth of the calf, so does the activity of Pradhāna proceed for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa."

[Objection: But surely, when true knowledge has arisen in a person, since *prakṛti* turns away from initiating effects such as the *mahat* that are conducive to experience, then once one knower of reality is liberated, all would become liberated. [Reply: This is not a fault, because *prakṛti* remains indifferent only toward that specific person who knows reality; since it is common to others, its activity does not cease for them.

And thus Patañjali says: "Though it has perished for one who has achieved his purpose, it has not perished, because it is common to others. Now, [an objection]: if this is so, then at the very moment that the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) arises, the fall of the body would occur for the person who has ceased the experience of the fruits of karma acquired by primordial nature (prakṛti). To this he replies: "He remains, holding the body due to the force of residual impressions (saṃskāra), like the whirling of a potter's wheel."
Then, when the latent dispositions have ceased and the dissolution of the body has occurred, because its purpose has been fulfilled and primordial matter (pradhāna) has withdrawn,
one attains both the certain and the absolute isolation (kaivalya).
Alas! Indeed, our hearts being captivated by the flavor of the tales of the poet Kāpilaka, we have written far too much through excessive digression upon digression.

Therefore, this primary transformation—the first [evolute] denoted by the term "mahat"—is that intellect (*buddhi*). Although it has perished for one who knows the reality (*tattva*), it is nonetheless not destroyed for others because it is common to all; thus, it is eternal.
And because of its eternity, the intellect is capable of sustaining the continuity of worldly transactions such as recognition, memory, and connection.
However, knowledge is its function (vṛtti), whereas apprehension (upalabdhi) is the Puruṣa’s perception of the intellect (buddhi) as possessing that function; thus, these are not synonymous terms.

To this, it is replied: This very thing called "intellect" (*buddhi*), which the Sāṃkhyas have postulated as being insentient (*asaṃjñā*), actually exists in the Self alone—which is eternal, all-pervading, the cognizer, the knower, the determiner, that which is joined with merit, demerit, and so forth, and the agent of effects such as recognition.
As for the fact that sentience is not admitted [by them] even though it belongs to that which is joined with knowledge and the rest, that is an extreme delusion of the most ignorant.
For he alone who perceives, knows, and determines, also sees and is conscious.
Indeed, we do not perceive any difference in the essential nature of the entity here.
In that regard, it is said—either out of delusion or for the sake of deception—that "the intellect perceives, knows, and determines," whereas "the person sees and is conscious."
As for this statement, "The Puruṣa perceives the object determined by the intellect (buddhi)," that must be explained: what is this nature of being a seer?

If it is said to be "reflection," does the intellect, possessing its modifications, transfer into the Puruṣa which is transparent, or does the Puruṣa transfer into the intellect which possesses its modifications?
In that regard, since the power of consciousness is immutable and non-transferring, there is no transfer of the Puruṣa into the intellect.
But even when the cognition has been transferred to the person, what has occurred for the person by virtue of which he becomes a seer?
If it is argued that being a seer is its very nature, then what is the purpose of its reflection in the intellect?

If it is said that it serves to delimit specific objects, then since prior to that [reflection] the state of being a seer would be impossible without an object, the person could not possess an innate nature as a seer.
If it is argued that the power of vision is innate [to the self], that is not so, because it is impossible to determine whether that power is distinct from or non-distinct [from the self].

Furthermore, in the case of the theory of reflection (*pratibimba*), since mutual coloring (*anurāga*) is equal for both and they are inseparable, how can it be determined which of these are the properties of the intellect (*buddhi*) and which are the properties of the person (*puruṣa*);
for never has their individual nature been ascertained through their separateness.
Furthermore, because their distinct functions have not been determined, even their difference is difficult to state.

If it is argued that their difference is evident due to their being conscious and unconscious, respectively, and their being the enjoyer and the enjoyed, then it is a marvel that the intellect (buddhi) is characterized by consciousness, knowledge, and so forth, yet is also unconscious!

Moreover, even if one were to postulate a distinction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*), the attributes of the intellect would have to be superimposed upon the person, and the attributes of the person upon the intellect; for what purpose, then, is this distinction? And if there were a distinction, since the intellect is endowed with cognition and other such qualities, it would follow that it possesses consciousness; thus, within a single aggregate of cause and effect, the undesirable consequence of two conscious entities would ensue.

If it is argued that the conception of the intellect (buddhi) as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is necessary because perception by the person (pums) could not occur without one, then the mind (manas) alone is eternally the internal organ.
By means of that instrument, the activity of perceiving objects is accomplished by the agent, the self (ātman);
and that very [activity] is designated as "intellect" (buddhi), for there is no other eternal intellect.

Furthermore, for what reason should one abandon the agency of knowledge and so forth that is directly perceived as belonging to the self, and instead accept that same agency in the intellect, which is not so perceived?

What excellence is there in this? [Objection: Surely, if the person possesses agency consisting of independence, there would be no liberation because of the endlessness of experiencing the fruits of one's own actions;
for the exhaustion of karmas cannot be accomplished even in hundreds of millions of births.
But when Nature binds the non-agent who is thus indifferent, then that very same [Nature], having become the knower, liberates him; thus, the path to liberation will not be far off.

"Alas! It seems that all folly resides only within the hearts of the Sāṃkhyas; for how could people now be considered fools? For if the unconscious *pradhāna* were the unrestrained binder, liberation would be utterly impossible. If it is argued that *prakṛti* does not bind even a man who knows the truth, then what is its restrainer? Even then, the conjunction remains the same, according to the maxim of the blind man and the lame man.
If it is said that the man has ceased his curiosity, *prakṛti* remains with unabated eagerness, like a newlywed bride."

Moreover, O fool, what was done by that ascetic man previously, such that he became bound? For his nature is essentially the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*), which is inseparable from him; thus, even in the state of liberation (*kaivalya*), that nature does not perish at all. Therefore, why would *prakṛti*—which is boundless—not proceed toward his bondage even then? If you argue that she desists because she has "seen him," that is not so; for she is not gripped by the obsession of a vow of fidelity to a single husband.
Let this matter rest: like a courtesan who possesses the fortune of being enjoyed by men without hesitation, she ought not to be dealt with according to fixed rules.

Furthermore, this entire web of theoretical constructions—such as the claim that from *prakṛti*, which is designated by the term "pradhāna" because it exists in a state of equilibrium among the three qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, there arises that which is called "the Great One" (*mahat*), namely, the intellect (*buddhi*)—is merely handed down through a succession of teachers following the maxim of a "blind tradition," and is not rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For a cause is observed to be smaller in dimension than its effect, but never the reverse;
this is seen in the case of jars, cloths, and the like, which are perceived as resting upon their own constituent parts.
Because its parts are small in comparison to that [other clay],
the large magnitude of another piece of clay is irrelevant [as a reason].
Moreover, what is called "intellect" (*buddhi*) is the apprehension of objects;
"egoity" (*ahaṅkāra*) is also a specific state of intellect (*buddhiviśeṣa*), consisting of the conceit of "I.

To claim that by means of this [egoity] the external sense organs are produced, and from those [organs] the qualities such as odor, and from those qualities the elements such as earth, is a great delusion.
And this is strange: for it is well known that pleasure and the like are produced by objects;
yet now, objects have become produced by pleasure and the like—this is a creation of the sage Sāṃkhya, as it were, like that of Viśvāmitra!
Nor does the existence of Pradhāna possess valid proof, because reasons such as "concomitance" (anvaya) and so forth are non-conclusive;
for while it may well be that sentient beings are endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion,
it is a truly eloquent statement to claim that insentient elements (bhūta) possess pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Who could maintain that pleasure, pain, and delusion exist in a pot, a cloth, or a cart? Furthermore, since illumination, activity, and restraint are observed only in conscious beings and not in unconscious things, the reason [you provide] is unestablished; therefore, the Pradhāna is not proven.

Moreover, this delusion of the ascetics—that "everything exists everywhere"—is rooted in the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). Consequently, perceiving [the effect] as already established in the cause, they are intent upon establishing the Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*).

Yet, when the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect is examined, it does not exist at all; so how can there be the establishment of a logical reason? Surely, in the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect, the relationship of cause and effect between entities occurs, and not otherwise.
For instance, there would be four possible positions here:

an effect such as a jar, being produced by a cause such as a lump of clay, is either (1) produced as non-existent, or (2) produced as existent, or (3) produced as both existent and non-existent, or (4) produced as having the nature of neither.
In that case, there would be the production even of things such as a donkey’s horn from a cause, since they are non-existent.

For if a jar is non-existent, what difference is there between it and a donkey’s horn? Since there is no distinction in their non-existence during the states of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), there would have to be production in the state of destruction just as there is in the state of prior non-existence.
Furthermore, if production were from what does not exist, the necessity of employing specific material causes would not obtain;
one seeking oil would take up sesame seeds and mustard seeds, but not sand.
And if oil were non-existent [in both], what distinction would there be between mustard seeds and sand?

And if the effect does not exist, the operation of the agent would be without an objective basis; for that operation cannot have the lump of clay and so forth as its object, since the effect is non-existent.

Furthermore, if the effect to be produced were non-existent and distinct from its cause, why is the essential nature of that cause—such as a lump of clay—no longer perceived once it has produced the effect, such as a jar?
Alternatively, if it is maintained that the cause produces the effect through its own destruction, then this would mean that existence arises from non-existence.
And in that case, what is the rule by which the non-existence of the lump of clay brings about the jar immediately after it occurs, rather than after a long time has passed?
And for this reason, when the preceding lump of clay has perished, there would be the production of this jar.

Now, if the effect is produced by the cause as something non-different from itself, then, because the cause exists, the effect—which is not distinct from it—must also exist; thus, there is no production of that which is non-existent.
It is not logical to say that an effect is both existent and non-existent, because existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive and cannot coexist in one and the same thing.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction due to a difference in form (*rūpa-bheda*), we reply: no, because the effect, when analyzed, is a single unity.
If that effect exists in its own nature as an effect, it could not be non-existent.
If it is non-existent, it is not existent; however, the non-existence of all entities indeed exists by way of their other-nature (pararūpa).
Since an entity that is neither [existent nor non-existent] does not exist at all, by the principle of exhaustion, the effect must indeed be existent.

If it is asked why that [effect] is not perceived at that time, we reply: even by inference, that which is perceived as existing—how could it be unperceived? However, its non-perception at that moment through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is due to its lack of manifestation.
And the efficacy of the exertion of causal factors lies precisely in bringing about this manifestation.
As for the effect itself, it is indeed existent.

To this, it is replied: In what form do you consider the effect to be existent at that time? If you hold that the jar exists on the wheel in the form of having a broad base, a belly, and a specific shape, which is capable of purposeful action such as carrying water and is produced by the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*), then because it already exists in its manifested form, the operation of the causal factors would be utterly futile.
Furthermore, if the causal factors were to proceed in this manner, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of their operations never ceasing;
for, having perceived the effect [already] prior [to their action], why would the causal factors ever desist?
Now, if it is said that the pot exists at that time in the form of a lump of clay, then it does not exist as a pot at that time; rather, it exists only as a lump of clay.
For it is impossible to say that one thing exists in the form of another;
otherwise, even a camel would exist in the form of a lump of clay.

Furthermore, the form of a camel is not produced even at a later time, whereas a jar is produced from that [clay]; if this is so, then it exists only at the very moment it is produced and not prior to that.

Furthermore, the claim that its existence was previously [established] by way of its potentiality (*śakti*) and is now produced by way of manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is also untenable; for manifestation, when analyzed—whether it be different or non-different from its own nature, and whether it be existent or non-existent—does not escape the aforementioned fault.
And what is this manifestation? Is it existence in the form of an effect, or a specific configuration, or rather cognition?
If its existence as an effect did not previously exist but has now come into being, then the effect was non-existent [previously].
Or, if it existed even previously, then the causal agents would again be rendered futile.

Shape (*saṃsthāna*) is also a particular arrangement of parts; and that [shape], being non-existent, is produced. But as for the parts themselves, who would dispute their existence? For we do not deny the existence of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

However, the cognition of a jar depends upon the collection of causal factors such as the eye and so forth, and is not produced by the cycle of causal factors such as the lump of clay, the staff, and the wheel; therefore, that [cognition] does not exist at all on the top of the wheel, and thus the jar is non-existent [there].
For the existence and non-existence of a thing depend respectively upon its being perceived and not being perceived;
since the jar, though visible, was not perceived, its non-existence was established by that [non-perception].
Just as with the top of a wheel, because a jar is not perceived even in its state of destruction, it follows that it simply does not exist;

therefore, the claim that "the existent does not deviate from non-existence, nor does non-existence exist for the existent" lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), since the essential nature of an entity is not observed at either the prior or the subsequent limit.
Regarding the claim that this [effect] exists even in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), it must be considered here: what is this so-called "potentiality"?

If it were distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the jar, then the jar would exist in the form of another entity and not exist in its own form; thus, the effect would be declared to be non-existent.

However, if the potentiality were non-different from the jar, then the statement "the jar exists in the form of potentiality" would amount to saying that the jar exists only in its own essential form.
And that [position] is refuted by contradiction with direct perception.

Furthermore, as for the objection raised against the position that what is non-existent is produced—that even things like a rabbit's horn would be produced—that arises from a failure to understand the grammatical formulation.
The formulation is not "that which is non-existent is produced," but rather "that which is produced is non-existent."
Whatever causes—such as intrinsic nature, auxiliary conditions, and so forth—are observed to bring something into being, that very thing is produced; for a sky-flower or the like is never produced.
Furthermore, the operation of a cause is observed during the state of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), but not at the time of destruction (pradhvaṃsa); therefore, whom shall we question?
However, that which is not seen everywhere despite the presence of all the conditions for perception does not exist there;
rather, it is due to such an observation.
Even in contemporary practice, no linguistic usage proceeds that is not previously established;
it is followed exactly as it was observed from the elders.
No one seeking oil is seen gathering sand;
and having not seen such a person, no other seeker of that [oil] runs toward it today.
And positive and negative concomitance are apprehended through conventional usage;
since this cycle of existence is beginningless, to whom can a challenge be directed?
Alternatively, the restriction of the material cause will be established simply from the restriction of capacity.
However, no eternal and subtle power (śakti) is accepted here;
for if such a thing were admitted, it would follow that the effect would be produced eternally.
Rather, power (*śakti*) is simply the presence of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as delimited by its capacity (*yogyatā*), together with its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
This very power is said to be twofold: inherent (*avasthitā*) and adventitious (*āgantukī*).
The essential nature delimited by [properties such as] "earth-ness" (*mṛttva*) is the inherent power.

Furthermore, the production of an effect brought about by two potencies—such as that which takes the form of a conflict between an incoming [potency] and a staff, wheel, or the like—is repeatedly observed; therefore, those who seek that effect undertake the acquisition of those [causes].

Furthermore, capacity (*yogyatā*) is not some separate entity, but rather a specific property of the thing itself; thus, since the restriction of the material cause is established by this very restriction of the specific property of the thing, the effect is not pre-existent.
Nor should it be said that the capacity itself is the effect;
for the nature of the effect is established through its perception as something distinct from that [capacity].
Furthermore, if the capacity were the effect, it would amount to accepting the production of an effect from an effect itself.
Furthermore, a pot cannot arise from a [previously existing] pot;
rather, it is accepted that an effect arises from a capacity.
Therefore, the effect is one thing and the capacity is another.

Now, it may be argued that since a power residing in both [entities] is observed between the signified and the signifier (the word and its meaning), as well as between the manifested and the manifester (the lamp and the jar), this same power ought to reside in both the cause and the effect.
For if the second entity called the "effect" were non-existent, how could this power be said to reside in both?
This is because power (*śakti*) is accepted exactly as it is observed.
Furthermore, a form seen in one place is not to be sought elsewhere;

since both the denoted and the denoter, as well as the manifested and the manifester, are observed to be distinct, power is admitted to reside in both. Thus, due to the non-perception of these two reasons, power exists solely within the cause.
And it is thus established that the restriction of appropriation is caused by that [volition].
It is only within the framework of the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*) that an investigation into the restriction of material causes (*upādānaniyama*) is appropriate.
Indeed, the consideration of appropriation (upādāna) applies to that which has arisen and is established;
but for that which exists [inherently], it simply does not exist—so what is the use of considering appropriation?

Furthermore, in the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), the restriction of material causes (*upādānaniyama*) is even more difficult to establish, because everything would exist everywhere.

For if one considers the nature of the oil in sesame seeds—just as sprouts and other effects arise in a restricted sequence from seeds sown in sand, sesame stalks, riverbanks, or fields—it follows that oil must also be possible in sand, since it exists in sesame seeds.
And if everything existed everywhere, the entire practical activity (*vyavahāra*) based on specific objects, such as avoidance and acquisition, would collapse.
Moreover, great compassion has arisen in my mind, thinking, "How will this poor fellow perform such an extremely difficult penance as the *taptakṛcchra*?

Furthermore, he eats food; and since there is feces in food, he is indeed being purified by the consumption of excrement. Enough with this negligence regarding the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).

Furthermore, the claim that the arising of an entity from non-existence might occur because an effect does not arise when its cause—defined as non-existence—is not destroyed, and that in such a case there would be no rule for the immediate succession of arising, is also untenable. This is because it is contradictory for corporeal things to occupy the same location; thus, the identity of place between cause and effect is not accepted.
Nevertheless, the arising of an entity cannot logically proceed from non-existence merely on that account, since we observe that its production is dependent upon a cause.
For this very reason, the restriction regarding immediate succession is also established.
Furthermore, one should not say that the effect exists [prior to its production] because of the non-difference between cause and effect;
for their distinct natures are established by direct perception.

As for the objection that the activity of causal factors (*kāraka*) is without an objective basis, that has been refuted by the Commentator with the statement: "But that is non-existent, established only by the intellect" (*buddhisiddhaṃ tu tad asat*). Having understood the relationship between cause and effect through the linguistic usage of elders, and having determined within the intellect that "from such a cause, this kind of effect arises," the agent employs the causal factors; thus, the operation of the causal factors is not without an object.

Thus, since the theory of its being an effect lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because the reasons such as positive concomitance (*anvaya*) based upon that [theory] cannot be established, the existence of Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) is not proven.
And in its absence, there can be no eternal, non-intelligent transformation of it; rather, it is precisely of the nature of the apprehension of cognition (*jñāna*).
Thus it has been correctly aphorized: "Intellect (*buddhi*), apprehension (*upalabdhi*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) are not different in meaning."

For this reason as well, cognition is impermanent: because it manifests throughout the three times—such as "I know," "I shall know," and "I knew"—possessing the nature of arising and passing away like the cooking of food, and because no cognition is perceived apart from the act of knowing.
However, this is the distinction:
for actions such as cooking, there is an extension of time mediated by the delimitation of results such as softening;
but for perception, whose purpose is fulfilled solely by the manifestation of the essential nature of the object, there is no extension of time at all.
For this very reason, even though it is impermanent, they declare cognition to perish immediately upon arising, like a sound, and not to persist for a duration of time like a jar or similar objects.

And this cognition, although it is the product of a multitude of causal factors such as the self, the internal organ, words, lamps, sense organs, and objects, does not inhere in the external object or the external action;
nor does it inhere in the external instruments such as the eyes,
nor in the internal organ, the mind.
However, [the agent] is indeed the agent alone;

and that agent is the eternal, omnipresent self (ātman), not something whose nature is a mere aggregate of elements (bhūta-saṅghāta) or a produced effect (kārya), as was determined in the *Ātmaparīkṣā*.
Furthermore, its status as a quality (*guṇatva*) has also been demonstrated in that very same work.
But if this is so, then there can be no impermanence of cognition (*buddhi*), because of the absence of a cause for its destruction.
For the cause of the destruction of qualities (*guṇa*) is twofold: either the destruction of the substratum (*āśraya*) or the manifestation of a contrary quality.
In this case, there is no destruction of the substratum, because the self (*ātman*) is eternal.
Nor do we perceive any quality of this [cognition] that would contradict [its permanence], because it perishes quickly, like sound.

Just as sound—even though it is a quality of the eternal ether—perishes after having produced another sound, so too cognition perishes after having produced another cognition; this is postulated because such is observed.

And whatever reasoning has been stated regarding the impermanence of sound—such as the observation of its destruction or the perception of its diversity—all of that should likewise be applied to cognition.
For this very reason, there is no simultaneity among cognitions occurring in a single knower, just as there is none among phonemes uttered by a single speaker.

However, although two cognitions—one in a state of perishing and one not yet perishing—are both rapidly perishable, their simultaneity is accepted on the basis of experience; enough of this excessive detail.
Furthermore, there is generally no dispute among all theorists regarding the impermanence of cognition (*buddhi*).
Thus Jaimini said: "When there is contact of a person's sense organs with an existing object, the arising of cognition is perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
Therefore, like a flash of lightning, the intellect is by nature perishable; its progenitor is its own self, which alone is its support.

That intellect, which unites one with the very moment of birth in the sufferings arising from the desert of existence, should be abandoned by the knower of ultimate reality as the mother of calamities.
Thus concludes the examination of the intellect (buddhi). "The non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark of the mind (manas). (NS 1.1.16)

Whatever is the means of valid cognition for the existence of the mind, that very thing constitutes its characteristic of being inaccessible [to direct perception], because it functions to exclude both homogeneous and heterogeneous classes.
Objection: Since the mind (manas) is a sense-faculty (indriya), its inclusion in that very category would be appropriate;
what is the purpose of this separate mention? [Reply: It is not because of a difference in nature (dharmabheda). The material sense-faculties have restricted objects.
Furthermore, these [other senses] possess qualities and function as sense organs;
however, the mind (*manas*) is not composed of the elements, does not have a restricted object,
and it does not function as a sense organ while possessing qualities.
And that [consciousness] is not composed of the primary elements because it is not an effect; for this very reason, it does not possess those qualities,
nor is its object restricted.
Its possession of all objects, however, is due to its being the presiding controller over all the external sense-faculties,
and because it grasps objects such as pleasure that are not accessible to them.
For the external sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth, are capable of functioning toward their respective objects only when presided over by the mind, and not otherwise.

If it is asked why this is so, it is because cognitions do not arise simultaneously. Furthermore, since there is a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of those objects even at a later time when the external senses are no longer active, the non-simultaneity of cognitions regarding certain universals, qualities, and so forth— which are accessible through a single sense-organ— is not a proof for the existence of the mind (*manas*).
In that case, because it is impossible to apprehend the genus and so forth simultaneously due to defects of the object and the like, such as distance;

Since simultaneous perceptions do not occur even when objects such as odor, taste, color, and so forth—which are perceivable by the senses—are present together, and even when their respective apprehensions exist with all their causes intact—those causes whose presence being inferred from their own effects—it is therefore concluded that these [perceptions] necessarily require another cause;
and that is designated as the "mind" (*manas*).
But surely there are Kapila Brahmins who, while eating long, fragrant, and cool dry cakes, simultaneously possess the five purities.

Moreover, when this teacher studies, walks, holds his water-pot, sees the path, hears the sounds produced in the forest, and—being afraid—desires to discern the signs of wild beasts, these cognitions do not arise for him simultaneously because their sequence cannot be perceived. This is not due to simultaneity, but because of rapid production; since time is exceedingly subtle, like the moment it takes for a needle-point to pierce a cluster of lotus petals, the sequence therein is not distinguished.
Nevertheless, there must indeed be such a sequence.

If the perceptions of objects such as form were accomplished solely by the instruments such as the eye, independent of any other cause, then how could there be a subsequent reflective awareness—such as memory and so forth—even for those whose instruments have been impaired? Therefore, it is certain that there exists another unimpaired instrument, like the eye, which grasps that [object].
Furthermore, that [cognition] is not all-pervasive;
for if cognitions were all-pervasive, their simultaneity would not be excluded.
Yet this worldly convention exists: even when someone has spoken something, another says, "I did not hear this; my mind was elsewhere."
Therefore, the mind is not all-pervasive.
And it is one for each body; furthermore, if it were manifold, the simultaneity of cognitions would still not be avoided.
And that [body] must possess activity, because it is impossible for the sense organs to function without an active presiding agent.
And that [action] is corporeal, because action is impossible for that which is incorporeal.
Being corporeal while being eternal—that [is established] because it is partless and because it is non-dependent; we shall explain later that corporeality is not a probans for impermanence.
And it is partless, because there is no means of valid cognition for the conceptualization of parts in it.
And it is "possessed of speed" because of its rapid movement;
for without rapid movement, the swiftness of perception that is observed would be impossible.
And that [substance] is connected with the sense faculties because it possesses fluidity.
And it is a substance because it possesses qualities such as velocity, because it possesses action, and because it is non-dependent.
That [mind] is insentient because it is an instrument; for otherwise, due to the coexistence of two sentient entities within a single body, there would be a lack of coherent functioning.
Therefore, the mind is of such a nature.
Furthermore, that its nature is as described by the Sāṅkhya is untenable; this has already been explained through the refutation of their system itself.

There are indeed other signs of the mind, such as cognitions of memory, inference, scripture, doubt, intuition, dreams, and recollection, as well as cognitions grasping internal objects like pleasure, pain, desire, and aversion;
for it is impossible for these to be accomplished by the operation of the external sense organs, and because no action is observed to be produced without an instrument.
Recollection (*smṛti*) is produced by the mind alone.
However, inferential and scriptural knowledge, because they have objects that are beyond the senses, are mental [perceptions].
Furthermore, it will be stated that some doubt (*saṃśaya*), although mental, is also [of this nature].
Intuition has already been shown to be mental, as in the thought, "My brother will come tomorrow.
How then could dream-cognition—which occurs when the entire collection of sense-faculties has ceased—be anything other than mental?
Even reasoning (*tarka*), like doubt, certainly has a mental object in some cases.
Furthermore, just as the cognition of pleasure and so forth depends on the mind, their production (*utpatti*) also depends solely on the mind.

For, regarding the production of the effects that are qualities of the self (*ātmaguṇa*), even though other proximate causes might be possible, the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanas-saṃyoga*)—whose efficacy is already established—is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
And for this reason, even in the case of pleasure and the like produced by the experience of an object, contact with the mind (*manas*) is the cause.
Furthermore, the view that pleasure and the like possess the nature of consciousness and are self-cognized has been refuted;
therefore, the mind alone is the cause for their apprehension.
Thus, this self (ātman), possessing the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previously performed good and evil karma, attains conjunction with the body in a particular location solely by its own power;
and it is precisely therein that the worldly activity of living occurs.
For they say that "living" is the conjunction of the self and the mind accompanied by the latent dispositions (*āśaya*) of maturing karma.
The mind, conjoined with the self, becomes the cause of saṃsāra by serving as the means for various enjoyments in those various places of rebirth.
Since both the self and the mind are eternal and saṃsāra is beginningless, one should not raise the objection: "How is it that the conjunction of the self and the mind occurs for the very first time?
For there is no such thing as a "first" moment in time, since even the initial creation depends upon a prior creation.
For it has been established that even Īśvara is indeed dependent upon karma as the creator of the diverse world; therefore, enough with further elaboration.

The mind, which provides the enjoyment of pleasure and the like, and which acts as the charioteer for the horses of the flickering senses, is the cause of bondage; therefore, it must be abandoned with effort by the wise.
Thus concludes the examination of cognition; activity (pravṛtti) is the undertaking of speech, cognition, and the body. (1.2.27)
It has been explained that "speech" refers to the conjunctions and so forth which are the causes of sound consisting of phonemes, and not the sense organ.
Here, "intellect" refers to the mind (*manas*) and not to apprehension (*upalabdhi*).
"Body" is well known.
Their "undertaking" (ārambha) is their activity, or the undertaking by them; in any case, it is said to be the engagement in their respective actions.
And that [action] is of two kinds: meritorious and sinful.
Among these, sinful action is tenfold: fourfold by way of speech, threefold by way of mind, and likewise threefold by way of body.
Therein, the engagement of speech is fourfold, consisting of the forms of false, harsh, malicious, and incoherent speech.
The threefold activity of the mind consists of coveting the wealth of others, longing for what belongs to others, and dwelling upon nihilistic thoughts.
The activity of the body is threefold, consisting of violence, theft, and the practice of prohibited sexual intercourse;
the mention of "sexual intercourse" is intended to include by implication such acts as the drinking of intoxicants and the like.
This tenfold activity serves as the fuel for the fire of hell, which blazes incessantly and bestows unsurpassed sensations of suffering.
Meritorious activity of speech is also fourfold, consisting of words that are truthful, pleasant, beneficial, and the recitation or study of sacred texts;
for in the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), it is indeed the reading of the sacred texts performed either in a whisper or as internal muttering.
The threefold mental activity consists of non-attachment, compassion, and faith in the next world.
The threefold activity of the body—consisting of giving, protection, and service—is likewise tenfold.
And this [practice] is like a staircase for the gateway to the abode of heaven.

This aforementioned activity (*pravṛtti*), which consists of twenty varieties in its two aspects, is in brief of only two kinds, due to the distinction between the means of understanding it as consisting of injunction and prohibition.
For the comprehension of what is existent and non-existent karma depends solely upon the comprehension of injunction and prohibition.

In this regard, the performance of enjoined acts leads to heaven, while the practice of prohibited acts leads to hell; thus, this activity—which serves as the cause for connection with the bodies, sense organs, and other factors that are the locus for the experience of pleasure and pain—becomes the supreme cause of *saṃsāra*.

Indeed, this conjunction of the body with the divine, human, and animal wombs; this conjunction of the intellect with each respective sense-object; and this conjunction of the mind with the self—all these are merely the expansion of the transformations of *pravṛtti* (active manifestation).

And although every *vṛtti* (mental modification) is momentary due to its nature as an action (*kriyā*), there nevertheless exists a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the self—denoted by the terms *dharma* and *adharma*—which follows upon that [action] and persists until the experience of the fruit of karma is completed.
Furthermore, *dharma* and *adharma* do not perish without having yielded their fruit.
For they declare that dharma and adharma are the opposers of the final experience of pleasure and pain;
and there is no effect or entity whatsoever in the world whose occurrence is not projected by dharma and adharma. Therefore, one who desires liberation must apply effort toward their eradication.
Thus, dharma and adharma—which arise from the activity of merit and demerit—act like shackles to cause suffering within the bondage of existence.
If you desire to bring an end to this boundless suffering, you must by all means abandon the unrestrained activity of mind, speech, and body.
Defects have the characteristic of being present in all systems. //2.2.27//
*Pravartanā* is the state of being an instigator toward activity (*pravṛtti*). Those whose characteristic is this are "defects characterized by instigation" (*pravartanā-lakṣaṇā doṣāḥ*).
For it is one impelled by defects that engages in either meritorious or sinful action.
Is it not the case that the nature of the defects (*doṣas*) is indeed directly perceived, since they are to be individually experienced?

Why, then, is their form defined by means of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)? True; even though they are individually experienced, the fact that their characteristic is "instigation" (*pravartanā*) is taught in order to make known that they are the cause of *saṃsāra* in this specific capacity.
For the connection with the locus of suffering, such as the body and so forth, is produced by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
And since the defects of the cause of that seed-like action impel the person toward the action, they are said to have the characteristic of "impelling" (pravartanā).

The claim that the definition [of scripture] as "having the characteristic of inciting to action" is stated for the sake of cognizing the defects residing in the mental continua of others—because those defects are not directly perceptible—is a misinterpretation, as it serves a trivial purpose.
These faults consist of three groups: attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*).
Among these, attachment is characterized by longing for agreeable objects; aversion is characterized by intolerance toward disagreeable objects;
and delusion is characterized by false resolve due to a failure to discern the ultimate reality of things.

But surely, since other defects such as envy (*īrṣyā*), malice (*asūyā*), greed (*lobha*), pride (*māna*), arrogance (*mada*), and avarice (*matsara*) are possible, how can it be said that the defects are only those [already mentioned]? [The answer is: because envy and the others are included within exactly those [defects] as they have been specified.
Desire (*kāma*), envy (*matsara*), longing (*spṛhā*), thirst (*tṛṣṇā*), and greed (*lobha*) constitute the fivefold category of attachment.
Desire is the wish for union with a woman. Envy is the desire not to relinquish an object that does not diminish even when shared with others, as if it were one's own wealth.
Craving (*spṛhā*) is the desire to acquire things that do not belong to oneself. Thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) is the desire that serves as the cause for the reconnection with renewed existence (*punarbhava*).
Greed (*lobha*) is the desire to take hold of prohibited objects. Thus, due to these different types of longing, this [greed] belongs to the category of attachment (*rāga*) alone.
The category of hatred (*dveṣa*) is also fivefold: anger (*krodha*), envy (*īrṣyā*), malice (*asūyā*), harmfulness (*droha*), and resentment (*pradāśa*).
Anger is of the nature of a blazing fire, the cause of distortions in the eyes, brows, and so forth.
Envy is the inability to endure another's seeing or enjoying even a common object.
Envy (*asūyā*) is intolerance toward the virtues of others;
malice (*droha*) is the intent to harm others;

resentment (*amarṣa*) is indignation directed toward another without manifesting facial expressions or other outward signs. Thus, this category of slight hatred consists of various forms of intolerance.
The side of delusion (*moha*), however, is fourfold: false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), pride (*māna*), and negligence (*pramāda*).
False knowledge is the cognition of something as being what it is not.
Doubt is the inquiry, "What could this possibly be?"

Pride (*māna*) is the notion of self-excellence through the superimposition of non-existent qualities. Negligence (*pramāda*) is the failure to perform what ought to be done due to contempt, thinking "this can be done later"; that very state is designated as intoxication (*mada*).
Thus, this category of delusion consists of the various modes of not fully understanding reality.
Thus, there are only these three faults. Sorrow and joy, however, are said to be pleasure and pain, not distinct faults;
for among them, delusion is the most evil, since the other two derive their very existence from it.
For in one who is deluded, passion and hatred arise, as is experienced from their production through false conceptualization (*mithyā-saṃkalpa*).
And false conceptualization has false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) as its source.
Thus, this entire manifold burden of the suffering of saṃsāra is the play of the Blessed One, False Cognition itself.
If this is so, then delusion (*moha*) does not lose its status as a fault (*doṣa*), because its definition has not been sublated by the argument that it is merely a cause of other faults.

Even though it is a cause for other faults, delusion does not forfeit its status as a fault—just like attachment (*rāga*)—because it itself possesses the characteristic of being a motivator for human activity.
These faults are the causes of saṃsāra; therefore, they must be pacified with effort.

But how can these [defilements] be pacified? It has been stated in this regard: "They are not accidental, nor are they eternal; their means of pacification are not unknown, nor are they impossible to remedy.
This will be examined in detail in the *Apavargaparīkṣā*.
Indeed, these defects have false knowledge as their cause.
Since they have been destroyed by the power of right knowledge, they simply do not arise due to the absence of their cause.

[Objection: But if, in this way, the causes of production and destruction are one and the same, would there not be only a single fault, whereby the triad [of faults] would be lost? [Reply: No, because their distinction is established by experience (*anubhava*).
For the essential natures (*svarūpa*) of passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*) are experienced as mutually distinct.

However, the oneness of the cause is not a determining factor (*prayojaka*), since we observe a diversity among the odors, tastes, colors, and tangibles residing in earthy objects, even though they are produced and destroyed by the very same contact with fire.
Therefore, it is rightly said that faults are of three kinds.
These three defects alone are the paths leading into the prison-house of saṃsāra;
by applying oneself to the effort of abandoning them, one does not undergo birth and death again.
Rebirth is re-arising after death. 1.1.17.

Furthermore, of what is this "re-arising" (punar-utpatti) said to be? Is it of the self (ātman) or of the body (śarīra)? In that regard, since the self is eternal, there is no arising at all; what talk can there be of the meaning of the word "again" (punar)? As for the body, however, while there is arising, it is not by way of repetition. For a dead body does not arise again as that very same one.

Therefore, the aphorism stating that "re-arising is rebirth" (pretyabhāva) is said to be non-expressive, because it is impossible to avoid the meaning of the word "again," which has been intentionally taught [in the definition].
Because this very [self] possesses instruction suitable for application toward liberation by means of generating world-weariness (*nirveda*),
and because, due to the self's permanence, the repetition of actions is possible, we speak of its repeated arising;
death, moreover, is like birth.
Thus, this very self, having died, undergoes rebirth; this is what is called "existence after death" (pretyabhāva).

Now, it has been stated that both birth and death do not exist for the self because of its eternity; this is true. However, there is no fault, because those terms are used with reference to the conjunction with and separation from the body and so forth.
"Death" is said to be the self's dissociation from the body, senses, and other instruments of experience, while "birth" is the association with them.

These very processes of abandoning and assuming bodies and senses, occurring through the repetition of actions in accordance with the ripening of the latent impressions (*karmāśaya*), constitute death and birth; this is called *pretyabhāva* (post-mortem existence), and it is precisely this that is *saṃsāra*.
For one who reflects in this manner, what conscious person would not experience world-weariness?
Thus it has been said: "Let alone old age, separation, death, and disease;
why does even birth not repeatedly cause shame to the wise man?"

Now, as for those bodies, sense organs, and so forth, by whose arising there is a connection with the self, how does their production occur? To this, the author of the Sūtras has stated: "The production of manifest things from the manifest, because of the authority of direct perception. By the phrase "from the manifest," he asserts that atoms are the causes of effects such as the body, thereby negating the cause consisting of the unmanifest (avyakta) composed of the three guṇas as accepted by the followers of Kapila.
For instance, this fourfold effect—consisting of the earthy, the watery, the fiery, and the airy—is perceived as resting upon its own parts.

In this regard, just as a jar, which possesses parts, rests upon its potsherds, so too the potsherds, being themselves possessed of parts, rest upon their own constituent parts; and those parts likewise rest upon further constituent parts, and so on until one reaches the partless atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Wherever there is the perception of a collection of effects resting upon their own parts, that very [perception] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein.
After that, inference.
For even that effect must reside in its own parts because it possesses parts, just like any other observed effect;
however, if it were partless, it would simply be an atom.
Furthermore, since the reason—that it possesses parts—is unestablished in the case of atoms, there is no need to postulate further constituent parts.
For if those [composite objects] were to possess parts, their parts would have to be atoms (*paramāṇu*).
However, atoms are not inferred by way of a process of destruction in the same manner as the process of production;

rather, when a clod of earth is being divided, there are its constituent parts, and further, the parts of those parts, and so on, until one reaches that which cannot be broken down and is beyond the range of perception.
Therefore, those beyond which no further division of parts is possible are called atoms (*paramāṇu*).

For even if those [atoms] were further divided, their parts would simply become other atoms; thus, because such a sequence of destruction is observed—just like the sequence of production—atoms do indeed exist.
For in this regard, there are three possible courses:

either this effect, such as a jar, must be partless, or it must possess an infinity of parts, or it must terminate in atoms. Among these, partlessness is untenable, because the parts—the threads in a cloth and the potsherds in a jar—are perceived by direct observation.

Nor is the possession of an infinite number of parts logical, because if Mount Meru and a mustard seed were equally endowed with an infinite number of parts, they would necessarily follow as being equal in magnitude.
Therefore, it is logical that the ultimate limit is indeed the atom.

If it is argued that these atoms, lacking the impulse of volition and desire, would be unable to achieve their effect because they fail to attain a specific sequential mutual conjunction due to their insentience, then a conscious Lord is accepted as their supervisor, possessing an intellect skilled in the creation of the entire universe.
And for the sake of establishing this, a faultless inference has already been presented, preceded by the dispelling of the darkness of all fallacious reasoning.

It has also been demonstrated that even the Lord (Īśvara), if he were not in accordance with the diversity of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) ready to ripen within the various selves, would not be capable of creating the diverse birth of living beings.

Furthermore, atoms do not begin an effect by joining together all at once in a number corresponding to the magnitude of the effect being produced; rather, they proceed through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth.

For if the production were simultaneous, then when a jar is broken, it would immediately reach the state of ultimate atoms, bypassing the sequence of shards, gravel, fragments, and powder, because every conjunction would be destroyed instantaneously by a simultaneous disjunction of all its parts.
Consequently, this would contradict the observed sequence of shards and the like.

Furthermore, how could it be maintained that even when a cloth or the like has not yet perished, its dependence upon constituent parts such as threads is perceived? For, since atoms are imperceptible, their being the substratum [of the cloth] cannot be apprehended; moreover, no other effect is produced between the atoms and the jar.
Therefore, atoms initiate an effect through a process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*).

Now, what is the reasoning stated for the claim that exactly two atoms first combine? It is because we observe that the number "many" is the cause of large magnitude (*mahat-parimāṇa*). If three atoms were to meet first, then in their effect, the number "many" would initiate large magnitude, and consequently, that effect would have to be perceptible. Yet, it is not perceptible due to its extreme subtlety. Therefore, a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is produced first from two atoms.

And that [dyad] would likewise be imperceptible, like an atom, because of the non-production of magnitude (*mahattva*). However, if the commencement of an effect by two dyads were desired, it would follow that there is no distinction between that [triad] and a dyad, since there is no cause for the production of magnitude even in that case, as there is in a dyad.
Therefore, a triad (*tryaṇuka*) is commenced by three dyads.
And in that case, by virtue of the number of its many parts, its magnitude will also be initiated and it will become perceptible.
Beyond that, however, while there is evidence for the general sequence— namely, the observation of the fragments of its own parts upon the breaking of a clod of earth and so forth—
there is no evidence for the specific sequence that "the initiation occurs in this particular manner."
Or rather, wherever perception exists, let that be the means of valid cognition for the specific sequence.
The relationship of being the originator (*ārambhakatva*) is accepted for those corporeal things because of the contradiction in their occupying the same location.

For atoms do not first originate an effect and then, subsequently, those very same atoms originate further effects at later times. Rather, the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), which is the effect produced by the atoms, is the originator of another effect; that [dyad] too [is the originator] of the subsequent effects, and so on until the completion of the whole consisting of parts (*paripūrṇāvayavin*).

And thus, a cloth is produced from threads, not from the filaments which are the parts of the threads; for otherwise, even as each successive effect is initiated, the preceding causes would not disappear, and there would result a spatial co-location of material entities.
Since this is not observed, the aforementioned sequence alone is superior.

Thus, it is established that the production of composite wholes such as bodies occurs through a sequence of effects beginning with dyads, which are brought about by the successive actions of atoms impelled by the will of the Lord, as this will proceeds in accordance with the ripening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) inherent in multiple selves.
However, other doctrines contrary to this are contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For instance, the claim that the body and so forth are eternal and characterized by non-origination is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, since earth and the other elements possess a specific arrangement of parts, their status as effects has been established in the proof of God (*īśvara*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for an effect such as the body to be spontaneous, because we observe a fixed regularity of causes, and because the arising of an entity without a cause is impossible.
The arising of an entity from non-existence is likewise exactly the same.

Furthermore, the fact that effects such as earth and so forth have as their cause the mahat, ahaṃkāra, and the rest—which are transformations of the pradhāna consisting of the three guṇas—has already been refuted previously.

The claim that these atoms alone—possessing no produced effects in the form of composite wholes (avayavin)—sustain the course of worldly affairs while being characterized by aggregation, is also not tenable; for aggregation cannot be established through the dilemmas of identity or difference, and because atoms, due to their extreme subtlety, are imperceptible.
Even on the view that the effect belongs to the individual (paudgalika), the description of atoms by means of another synonym, or their lack of authoritative proof, [remains].
The theory that [the world] is a transformation (*vivarta*) of sound is untenable, because the persistence of that [sound] is not perceived.
Nor is it possible for the Supreme Self to be the material cause, precisely because that [Supreme Self] itself lacks any means of valid cognition.
Nor is it appropriate to resort to the lazy argument that "the world has never been otherwise," because the continuous succession of creation and dissolution has already been established.
And thus, because other positions are weak, the creation of the elements is established as it has been described.
Homage to that crest-jewel of scholars who, even while seeing it, would deny it!

Alas! In this beginningless saṃsāra, for beings of deluded mind, there has occurred birth followed by death, and even after dying, there is birth again. Reflecting that "this is the path of sufferings," the wise person should fix their mind upon the state that cuts off birth and death.
The object produced by activity and defects is the result. 1.1.20.
The defects of activity have already been explained.
The object produced by those [defects] is called the "result" (phala).
The inclusion of the word "object" (artha) is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between the secondary and the primary [result].
Pleasure and pain are the primary fruit;
however, the body, the sense organs, the objects, and so forth, which are the means to those, are secondary.
For it has been stated that all this is a fruit projected by activity and defects.

This very fruit, proceeding through a beginningless continuum and being enjoyed again and again, is the cause of great weariness; thus, when contemplated as such, it serves as a means for liberation by leading to the path of world-weariness, dispassion, and so forth.
For a person who discards what has been grasped and seizes what has been discarded,
alas, what a miserable toil is this water-wheel of worldly results!

Furthermore, is that fruit produced immediately by the action, or after an interval of time? It is said: action is ordained as being of two kinds—prescribed and prohibited. Among these, there is no fixed rule regarding the timing for the fruits of prescribed actions;
for the fruit of an action such as "he milks" or "he cooks" is seen to arise immediately thereafter.

However, that there is no fixed rule regarding the fruits of ritual injunctions has been established in the *Śabdaparīkṣā* during the occasion of refuting the objection concerning the *Citrā* sacrifice.

Furthermore, by examining the statements of the injunctions (*codanā*), it is determined that some results of ritual action (*vidhiphala*) occur immediately, such as rain resulting from the *Kārīrī* sacrifice. On the other hand, certain actions whose fruits are to be experienced in this life, such as the *Putreṣṭi*, depend on a later time due to the nature of things;

for the acquisition of a son does not occur instantaneously like the discovery of a treasure, as it depends on a sequence beginning with the embrace of a wife who is the cause for the birth of offspring.

However, rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which have heaven as their fruit, result in rewards pertaining to the next world solely by virtue of the greatness inherent in the nature of the fruit of action.
For heaven is unsurpassed bliss, or else—by way of postulating what is otherwise inexplicable—it is a place of enjoyment such as the peak of Mount Meru;
in either case, it does not attain a state suitable for enjoyment by this present body.
Some have stated that painting and the like yield indeterminate results;
whether that is correct or incorrect has been examined in that very same context.
However, for almost every prohibited action, the result occurs primarily in the next world.
For instance, in cases such as violating another's wife, the immediate fruit of the act—such as the pleasure of sexual union—is the result in this life;
whereas the result of the prohibitive injunction, namely falling into hell, belongs to the next world.

Just as with heaven, so too with hell—which consists of unsurpassed suffering and whose nature as a location is postulated because it could not otherwise exist—there is an unsuitability for the enjoyment of this [present] body.

Those who know the scriptures maintain that action performed with intense urgency, whether prescribed or otherwise, results in a ripening of its fruit in this very life, as in the cases of Nandīśvara and Nahuṣa.
Furthermore, certain individuals such as thieves and killers of Brahmins are frequently seen to experience immediate retribution; thus, the ripening of these karmas is manifold.
Furthermore, as for the claim that "at the time of the action the fruit does not exist, and at the time of the fruit the action no longer exists;
moreover, at another time, another perceptible cause of the fruit is observed, such as service and so forth"—this too has already been refuted.
For even though actions perish, there exists the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by them, which is designated by the terms *dharma* and *adharma*.
Furthermore, because there is deviation in visible causes such as service and the like, the postulation of an unseen force (adṛṣṭa) is necessarily required.

Nor can it be objected that there is a difference in locus between the action and its fruit—since dharma and so forth inhere in the self, while the fruit, such as a son or cattle, inheres elsewhere—for it is impossible for the primary fruit, which consists of pleasure and pain, to have a different substratum;
for pleasure and pain reside in the self, and dharma and adharma likewise abide therein.

Since what is seen is certainly not the cause of happiness, why then, through attachment to its cause, would one feel aversion toward that which is also not the basis of suffering? Therefore, reflecting that "the fruit has action as its cause," a wise person should not form an attachment to action by which they fall into this saṃsāra, which is difficult to cross.
Suffering is characterized by affliction. 1.1.21.
Affliction (*bādhanā*) means oppression and torment.
That which has this as its characteristic is "suffering characterized by affliction" (*bādhanā-lakṣaṇa*).
In that context, regarding suffering as the primary object of characterization (*lakṣya*), the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is used in its literal sense.
For it is precisely by way of affliction (*bādhana*) that the nature of suffering (*duḥkha*) is characterized; [the root *duh*] means "it afflicts" or "it causes pain.

However, when the body and so forth—which are secondary forms of suffering—are the objects of characterization, it should be explained as "that which has the characteristic of affliction" or "that which is connected with affliction."

If it is argued: "Since suffering has already been taught by the very mention of 'fruit' (*phala*) as explained in the previous sūtra, for what purpose is this instruction given again? It is for the sake of rejecting pleasure (*sukha*)," [we reply: no, because that would contradict what precedes and follows, and because pleasure cannot be rejected since it is attested by the experience of all living beings. Furthermore, if its rejection were intended, for what purpose was the word "fruit" included in the sūtra on the objects of knowledge (*prameya-sūtra*)? For it was indeed explained there that "the fruits are pleasure and pain."

And thus, when pleasure is rejected, only suffering remains; and since that has already been indicated by this very word "suffering," what is the purpose of mentioning the "result" (phala)? It is said: the mention of "suffering" is not for the sake of rejecting even a mere fragment of pleasure experienced here and there by living beings in saṃsāra;
rather, it is for the purpose of teaching the cultivation of the realization of its suchness (tathātva) everywhere.
For even that fragment of pleasure should be contemplated as being indeed suffering; one should consider its means of accomplishment to be nothing but suffering.
There is no resolve of men, no action, no word,
and no object of enjoyment here in this world that does not result in suffering.
Thus, those who know the scriptures maintain that suffering is most intense among animals, moderate among humans, slight among the gods, and even more slight among those free from passion.
The attenuation of suffering for those free from passion is understood through reasoning as well, because suffering has passion as its basis.
For when everything is reflected upon from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is all suffering to the discerning person;
like honey mixed with poison, this so-called pleasure turns into suffering.
Indeed, a person striving out of greed for the attainment of pleasure [finds only pain].
One encounters suffering indeed, which has a thousand branches, in the very acquisition thereof.
Thus, for one who constantly contemplates that "all this is suffering," a sense of world-weariness arises toward all places of rebirth.

For the embodied being who has become disillusioned, there arises dispassion; and for one who is dispassionate, the emergence of the supreme good occurs through the gateway of abandoning the afflictions and karma.

[Objection: "In that case, then, the mention of 'fruit' (*phala*) need not be made, since its meaning is already covered by the word 'suffering' (*duḥkha*). [Reply: It is not so; for it has another purpose.
Namely, that pleasure and pain should be contemplated as being produced by activity and defects (*pravṛtti-doṣa*), and that one should abide in them through practice.
For when one reflects upon the fruit as being produced by karma and defects, may attachment and aversion not arise in him toward their two causes—the favorable and the unfavorable.

And by means of repeated practice, one is carried along by the stream of the abandonment and acquisition of the result together with its means; thus, "one should become utterly weary of that"—this is the inclusion of the term "result.
Therefore, in this way, the result is useful for the supreme good in one manner, whereas in another manner, even though it possesses the nature of a result, it is [useful] for the sake of suffering.

All pleasure, being the cause of long-lasting suffering, is itself of the nature of suffering; this entire range of objects of knowledge, beginning with the body and ending with suffering, must be contemplated as something to be abandoned by one who seeks liberation.
Thus, one of subtle intellect who avoids everything as being nothing but suffering— the web of afflictions, karma, and the like within the body—
contemplating the reality of the self as unborn, undecaying, and infinite, attains that which is fearless, immutable, and eternal.

Thus, having determined the objects of knowledge to be abandoned—beginning with the body and ending with suffering—for the sake of which this instruction is given, [the author] speaks in order to define that supreme object of knowledge to be attained, for the sake of which the treatise was commenced: "Liberation (apavarga) is the absolute release from that [suffering]. (1.1.22)
The word "that" (tad) refers back to the suffering under discussion.

Furthermore, it is not only suffering in its primary sense—that which has the nature of affliction—which is referred to; rather, everything that serves as a means to it and everything associated with it is included.
Liberation (apavarga) is the dissociation from that suffering.
Even at the time of dissolution (pralaya), there is for the self a separation from suffering;

however, that is not liberation (apavarga), because at the time of creation, since there is again a connection with a body and so forth corresponding to the unabated latent impressions of karma (karmāśaya), suffering arises.
Therefore, in order to exclude that [temporary state], the term "absolute" (atyanta) is employed.
Apavarga is the absolute cessation of suffering; it is not limited by time.

Since the pronoun "all" (sarva), which refers to the two kinds of suffering, implies all the qualities of the self just as it does suffering, and since the inclusion of the word "absolute" (atyanta) denotes a separation from them in every respect, it is stated that apavarga is the uprooted destruction of the nine qualities of the self: cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impressions.
As long as all the qualities of the self, such as latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth, have not been completely severed,
an absolute cessation of suffering cannot be conceived.
For the arising of pleasure and pain is caused by merit and demerit;
these two alone are the foundational pillars of the house of saṃsāra.
But upon its cessation, since there is no longer the affliction of the body and so forth which are its effects, pleasure and pain do not exist for the self; thus, it is called "liberated."
Desire, aversion, effort, and so forth are bound to the locus of experience;
for one whose locus of experience has been severed, the self is no longer joined even with those.
Hunger and thirst belong to the vital breath (prāṇa), greed and delusion to the mind (cetas), and cold and heat to the body; Śiva is free from these six waves.

Thus, when it is asserted that liberation (*apavarga*) is the root-and-branch eradication of these nine specific qualities of the self (*ātma-viśeṣaguṇa*), this very point is what is expressed by the statement: "Liberation is the absolute release from that."
Indeed, in that state, what kind of self remains—one established solely in its own essential nature and abandoned by all qualities?
The wise declare that his form transcends the six waves;
it is untainted by the suffering, afflictions, and other defects subject to the bonds of saṃsāra.
On this point, the Vedāntins say: "This kind of liberation ought not to be an object of effort for those who possess discernment.

For who indeed would strive to produce a self that is like a fragment of stone, devoid of all contact with the experience of happiness? Wise men declare the fourth human goal to be beautiful with an infinite, unsurpassed, and natural bliss—superior even to heaven, which yields only limited, conditioned, and finite joy—and possessing the capacity for its experience that never fades."

If, however, the self were in that state entirely insentient and indistinguishable from a stone, then what is the use of liberation? Better would be cyclic existence itself, wherein at least here and there, even if it be defiled by suffering, a modicum of pleasure is enjoyed.
Consider this: is the experience of slight pleasure better, or is it simply the total eradication of all pleasure?
Therefore, one should accept on the authority of scripture that eternal bliss exists for the self, just as its greatness does;
and that [bliss] is not experienced during the state of saṃsāra because of the influence of the veil of ignorance.
However, when the continuous veil of ignorance has been overcome by the cultivation of the practice of the knowledge of reality, the self experiences it in that state.
This is untenable because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of eternal happiness in the self.

To begin with, perception (*pratyakṣa*)—whether ours or that of others—cannot prevail regarding this matter; what talk can there be of it? Nor is inference (*anumāna*) possible, since not even a trace of a logical mark (*liṅga*) is observed.
But has it not already been stated that inference is for the sake of liberation, wherein the effort of the discerning is directed?
For the wise do not exert themselves for the attainment of pleasure, lest they make themselves as inert as a stone.

Therefore, this effort of one desiring liberation is for the sake of attaining a desired goal, because it is an effort preceded by discernment, like the effort involved in agriculture and similar pursuits.
For the wise, afflicted by disease, are seen striving for the cessation of even that which is undesirable, because it does not have the ultimate as its object.

Furthermore, since this burden of the suffering of saṃsāra is exceedingly difficult to bear, the virtuous, striving for its cessation, do not exert themselves without purpose; therefore, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive.
Now, it might be understood from scripture that one's own self is inseparable from eternal bliss by virtue of its omnipresence.
And thus it is recited: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss. This would indeed be so if this scriptural statement alone were heard;
however, another statement is also heard: "For one who possesses a body, there is no cessation of pleasure and pain."
"Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless."
Surely the scriptural statement cited by you can be explained in another way:

since the context begins with "of one who possesses a body," the meaning is that when worldly pleasure and pain—which arise from the perception of agreeable and disagreeable objects—are possible, the self does not touch that which is bodiless at that time.

Well then, even the Vedic statement studied by you, "Brahman is bliss" (ānandaṃ brahma), will be explained as referring to the cessation of suffering precisely because it occurs in a context concerning the avoidance of the miseries of saṃsāra;
for indeed, there is no subject beyond the Blessed One’s capacity for explanation.
Moreover, the use of the word "happiness" (sukha) is observed in reference to the cessation of suffering.
Those who are afflicted by the suffering of diseases such as chronic fever and headaches, upon their recovery, apply [the term "happiness"] thinking, "We are happy today."

If, moreover, on the basis of the statement "bliss" (*ānanda*), eternal happiness is accepted for the self, then—just as omnipresence follows from the statement "Brahman" and knowledge from the statement "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)—knowledge must also be admitted to be eternal for it.
Consequently, since knowledge, like happiness, is eternal, there would be the perception of eternal happiness even in *saṃsāra*.
And thus, this eternal happiness would be experienced in conjunction with pleasure and pain, which are the fruits of merit and demerit.
Moreover, just as his pleasure and knowledge, let his body, sense organs, and so forth also be conceived as eternal; in this way, liberation would become even more delightful.
Now, the effect is the cognition of pleasure; its cause must be investigated—that from which it arises.
If you say it arises from *dharma*, then it must be stated what that *dharma* itself originates from.

If you say it is born from the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of yoga, then because that [absorption] is its own effect and terminates in the experience of the pleasure that is its own effect, it could not be eternal.
Furthermore, the non-destruction of the Dharma is without inferential proof;
for there is no inference whatsoever to establish that the Dharma born of yoga and meditative concentration does not perish.
On the contrary, there is well-known inference to the contrary, since one observes that everything which is produced is impermanent.
And when the dharma has perished, because there is no knowledge of its effects, even though happiness exists, it is not perceived and thus does not differ from non-existence.
If it is argued that this bliss is self-luminous, [we reply] no, because it would follow that it would be perceived even in saṃsāra.
If it is argued that the connection with the body and so forth is the cause of obstruction, [we reply] no, because the body and so forth exist for the sake of experience;
since the body and so forth serve the purpose of experience, the notion that they effect an obstruction to experience is not a sound hypothesis.

If it is argued that due to the veil of ignorance (*avidyāvaraṇa*), one's own self-luminous bliss is not perceived in *saṃsāra*, [we reply] that it is impossible for the self-luminous to be veiled by something insubstantial (*tuccha*). Nor can this ignorance, which is of a nature contrary to and insubstantial compared to the bliss of the Self that is of the nature of light, be capable of veiling it; for we observe the veiling of the sun’s rays by clouds and the like.

Though the day was darkened by a mass of clouds as black as a dense herd of cows, and the orb of the sun was obscured, it was not like night; yet such was the power of delusion that it seemed so at once.
Even clouds, being distinct from the sun, are real by their very nature;
