however, ignorance—which is inconceivable as being either identical to or different from [the self]—is not capable of acting as an obscuration.
Therefore, it is not easy to maintain that the self possesses eternal bliss.
Moreover, if liberation were of the nature of eternal bliss, one seeking liberation who strives with attachment to it would not attain liberation;
for those who know liberation maintain that there is no liberation for those possessed by passion.

If it is argued that the same fault applies to one who exerts effort toward liberation—even though liberation consists in the cessation of suffering—because of an aversion to suffering, we say no; for the seeker of liberation lacks aversion.
Since the seeker of liberation knows that passion and aversion are the causes of saṃsāra, how could it be consistent for him both to seek liberation and to hate suffering?

If it is argued that he has no attachment even toward pleasure, we reply: no, because it is possible for attachment to arise toward liberation (apavarga), just as it does toward heaven, since liberation is not distinct from heaven [in being a state of bliss].
However, detachment arises in one who desires liberation because they are weary of suffering, not because of hatred directed at suffering itself.
Furthermore, for one who is detached, effort is directed toward liberation, not toward hating suffering; thus, the logic is not the same.

As for the claim that such liberation is not an object of effort for discerning people, that too is incorrect; for the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not occur in accordance with a purpose.
Indeed, a means of valid cognition cannot be subservient to a purpose.

If liberation were devoid of bliss, it would not be pleasing to those who possess discernment; let it be so if you wish, but we cannot imagine that there is no bliss there for which there is no authoritative basis.
Nor is such liberation entirely undesirable to the virtuous,
nor do they fail to strive for its attainment;
for they discern in this way:

Because there is no possibility of enjoying a happiness that is empty of contact with suffering and eternal, and because suffering must necessarily be abandoned, yet its abandonment is impossible—just as when poison and honey fall into a single vessel, both pleasure and pain should be renounced.

Therefore, liberation from this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is superior, wherein this immense and most difficult-to-endure succession of suffering is torn asunder; it is better that such a momentary fragment of pleasure be abandoned than that such a burden of suffering be borne for its sake.
Consequently, liberation does not consist in the enjoyment of pleasure.

But let liberation aside for a moment; even in cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), there is no such thing as happiness. This entire conventional usage of the term "happiness" is merely the absence of suffering.
For instance: when the mouth is parched with thirst, one drinks sweet and fragrant water; when afflicted by hunger, one devours grains of rice seasoned with meat-broth;
when the fire of passion is ablaze, one embraces a wife tightly; thus people mistakenly perceive what is actually a remedy for disease as being happiness.

It is said in reply: this is merely a display of the "Kaurukucī" artifice—a pretense of artificial dispassion—because it is impossible to conceal the bliss that is of the nature of *ānanda* and is experienced by every living being.
Furthermore, since one experiences pleasure even when suffering has not ceased, pleasure is not simply the absence of suffering;
for we observe the experience of pleasure occurring even in one who is free from desire, upon contact with an object that serves as a means to pleasure and which presents itself unexpectedly.
The claim that pleasure is simply the absence of suffering characterized by longing is also not pleasing.

As for the designation "pleasure" applied to the absence of suffering—which was previously shown to be like the case of those whose diseases have been pacified—that is a figurative expression (*bhakti*); however, on that basis, it is not proper to deny the pleasure witnessed by one's own direct experience (*svasaṃvedana*).
Yet, eternal pleasure in liberation (*mokṣa*) is not accepted because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish its possibility.
Furthermore, this inquiry as to whether or not there is happiness in liberation is not appropriate for authoritative persons.
Those who know liberation maintain that liberation is the self’s abiding in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
In that case, one should reflect upon what the very nature of the self is, rather than upon the nature of liberation as something distinct from it.

It has been determined in the definition of the self that pleasure, pain, cognition, and so forth are adventitious qualities of the self and are not innate like its magnitude, because the self is inferred from its effects such as pleasure and the rest.
For this very reason, it is also not tenable that the self has the nature of the power of consciousness as described by the followers of Kapila.
It is conscious through its connection with consciousness; without that connection, it is insentient.
What is called "thinking" is the cognition of an object, and for it, that [cognition] occurs only occasionally.
There exists no so-called consciousness other than the perception of objects;
and since that [consciousness] is dependent upon a causal complex, how could it exist in liberation?
Knowledge arises for the self whether it be waking, dreaming, or even in deep sleep; however, there is no fourth state such as that.
In the waking state as well as in dream, the nature of pleasure is cognizable by the intellect, because of the subsequent reflective awareness: "I slept happily" and so forth.
At that time, although not being perceived, the intellect (buddhi) is nevertheless postulated as existing in deep sleep;
however, the fourth state (turya) is the abiding of the self devoid of consciousness.
As for that form of the Self which some describe as transcending the fourth state (turya),
since it lies beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition, it is merely a mental construction.
Even if this self possesses the capacity to produce consciousness due to the proximity of the causal complex, it does not thereby possess the nature of consciousness itself.

If, however, the consciousness of the person (*puruṣa*) is said to be merely the capacity for the power of seeing, then such a state of isolation (*kaivalya*) would be identical to our own notion of liberation.

This is because, even though the mere capacity for the production of true cognition exists, the self’s status as a seer is impossible in the state of isolation due to the deficiency of the causal complex— such as the contact between the object and the sense organs—
and because any other form of consciousness devoid of seeing has already been refuted.

The followers of the Sugata, however, maintain that liberation (apavarga), which is designated by terms such as "nirvāṇa," is either the cessation of the continuum or a pure continuum of consciousness.
Both of these two views have already been refuted previously; for the continuity of consciousness has been shown to be destroyed, and the eternal self has been established.
But the position that maintains the total annihilation of the continuum is even more lamentable than the view of the Naiyāyikas; for in it, not even a trace remains, like a stone in the desert.
Even in the case of the Arhat, that form which depends on another does not belong to the self alone; thus, our position is identical.
However, the susceptibility to transformation in living beings is utterly inconsistent;
like sound or matter (pudgala), this must be rejected because it is impossible.
Therefore, neither the knowers of the Vedānta, nor the Sāṅkhyas, nor the Buddhists and others, speak of liberation;
thus, the final release described by Akṣapāda is the most excellent, for it is indeed the absolute liberation from that [suffering].
[The opponent] says: "Let this liberation (apavarga) be such as you describe;
however, let it be explained how it is attained.

[The author] replies: It has already been stated by the Blessed One, the author of the Sūtras: "Upon the successive disappearance of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the disappearance of each preceding one, resulting in liberation" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.2).
It has been stated that liberation (apavarga) is the total eradication of suffering.
Since suffering is an effect, its eradication results from the eradication of its cause;
and its cause is birth.
For when there is birth, suffering comes to be.
Indeed, "birth" (*janman*) is the soul's connection with the body, the sense organs, and so forth;
that too must be eliminated only by the elimination of its cause, which is birth.
Therefore, its cause—activity—is to be eradicated;
since that too is eradicated through the eradication of its cause, its causes—the defects—are to be eradicated.
But the cause of those is false knowledge.
Therefore, since faults are destroyed when that [ignorance] is destroyed, false knowledge is what must be eradicated.
And the means for its eradication is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
For this matter is well-known and has already been established at length previously: that the knowledge of reality is the sublater of false knowledge.
Therefore, from the absence of knowledge of reality, through the sequence of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, there is liberation.
Even though false knowledge is an effect of birth, it is nonetheless impossible for a disembodied self, because false knowledge cannot arise in such a state.

The states beginning with false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), which proceed as an beginningless continuum through a mutual relationship of cause and effect—like that of a seed and a sprout—are designated as "saṃsāra. Nevertheless, when considering the eradication of its cause, if one were to investigate from what point the eradication should begin, the conclusion would be reached that it could start from any point whatsoever, due to the absence of a specific restriction. However, since the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is found to be the specific cause for the eradication of false knowledge, and because there is no evidence for any other distinction, the eradication of that [false knowledge] is what is undertaken.

For this very reason, it is said that saṃsāra has its root in false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). When that [false knowledge] is eradicated, because its own eradication becomes possible, it can be determined even by those of subtle intellect that from that point onward saṃsāra no longer proceeds; for its beginninglessness is thus overcome.

Thus, when false knowledge is removed through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), there follows the removal of the defects (*doṣa*) which are its effects; with the removal of the defects, there is the removal of activity (*pravṛtti*); with the removal of activity, there is the removal of birth (*janman*); and with the removal of birth, there is the removal of suffering (*duḥkha*). This very state is liberation (*apavarga*). This is what was stated [in the Sūtra]: "Upon the removal of each subsequent member, the one immediately preceding it is removed."
This meaning of the sūtra is not understood; rather, it is merely a mockery of unattainable desires or a manifestation of false faith. Indeed, the narrow path to liberation is difficult to master.
This very triad—characterized by dharma, artha, and kāma—is what is to be accomplished;
however, the fourth aim of human life shines forth only in stories.
When separation from loved ones and the like become causes for agitation,
then let discourses on liberation be freely delivered for the sake of pacifying that grief.
However, at the time of exertion, we do not perceive a path capable of attaining that [liberation], because the continuity of the flow of debts and afflictions is difficult to cross.

First, regarding the bond of debt: "A Brahmin, being born, is indeed burdened with three debts—to the sages by means of the life of a student (*brahmacarya*), to the gods by means of sacrifice, and to the ancestors by means of offspring. Thus it is recited in the Veda.
In this regard, one first practices the life of a student with the thought, "May I be free from debt to the sages."

Thereafter, thinking "May I be free from debt to the ancestors," he takes a wife and engages in activity for the sake of procreating offspring. While remaining a householder, he is authorized to perform rituals beginning with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and ending with those lasting a thousand years, thinking "May I be free from debt to the gods. What opportunity does he have for the resolve toward liberation? Is it not the case that such an opportunity exists, based on the traditional law (*smṛti*) of Manu and others which states, "Having discharged the three debts, one should apply the mind to liberation"? No; because this contradicts the statements of the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

For it is thus heard in scripture: "This sacrificial session, namely the Agnihotra and the New and Full Moon sacrifices, lasts until old age and death; for by old age one is indeed released from this, or by death.
And it is not possible to desist from rituals due to an incapacity to perform them, because for one who is personally incapable, there is the instruction regarding external agency:
"Or a pupil may offer the oblation, for he has been purchased by means of the Veda."
Or one who has been purchased [as a servant] should offer oblations, for by this he is hired out.

And how can there be power even for one incapable of practicing the means of liberation? Due to the persistence of the afflictions (*kleśa*), there is an absence of final release (*apavarga*). For those defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which have been accumulated in the self for a long time—why would one be able to pacify them, they which are of the nature of returning again?
Even after having conquered desire, anger, or greed for a long time,
people are generally seen falling back under their sway once again.

For it is heard that even Viśvāmitra—though his mind had long been restrained by asceticism and though he had not yet conquered the transformations wrought by the uneven-arrowed god (Kāma)—fell under the power of the Flower-Bowed One merely upon seeing the breasts and hips of a passionate woman whose garment was blown away by a light breeze.
Enough with this narrative;
even today such things are seen by the hundreds, so these faults are difficult to eradicate.
Furthermore, it has been examined in the *Ātmaparīkṣā* that "the birth of one free from passion is not observed."

A living being is born indeed not separated from the defilements; and since objects such as forms are the causes for the increase of those defilements, how could they possibly remain indifferent toward their own effect?
To whom do betel-rolls, breezes fragrant with flowers, the moonlight reflected in palaces,
and the words of messengers moist with the nectar-fluid of fresh affection not bring an increase of passion?
Moreover, whose mind is not captivated by the faces of those with long-lashed eyes, which possess sweet speech washed pure by innocent smiles?
Thus, because the underlying cause is not pacified, the continuity of the afflictions remains firmly established.

Furthermore, there is the continuity of active involvement: impelled indeed by passion and the like, a person undertakes actions through which the latencies of merit and demerit extend out for a very long time.
And that causal momentum which is the continuity of activity leading to another birth,
by means of that other birth, another latent impression of karma is produced.
Sometimes, a single such action occurs that must be performed,
the fruit of which is not experienced even in a hundred thousand lifetimes.

This chain of birth, suffering, and so forth, which arises from the continuous succession of afflictions and karma, revolves again and again; by what means can it be broken? There is no destruction of karmas without the experience of their fruits.
To claim that they are consumed by the fire of knowledge is merely a display of blind faith.
For the relationship of cause and effect between actions and their fruits is indeed determined solely through the scriptures; how then could that relationship ever cease?
Furthermore, karma is not held to be a cause of bondage that depends upon ignorance;
for if it were so, it would remain indifferent toward those who possess self-knowledge.
This is the very nature of actions, independent of ignorance, that they are invariably concomitant with their results.
Therefore, because of this continuous succession of debts, afflictions, karmic activity, and so forth, there can be no attainment of liberation; thus, the exertion for that purpose is fruitless.
Considering that effort toward an impossible object is in vain, the wise should abandon discussions of liberation and sit at ease in their own homes.

To this, it is replied: First, as for what was stated—that [it is because of the connection with debt]—that is incorrect, because no word expressing an injunction (*vidhi*) is heard. By employing the figurative term "debt" (*ṛṇa*) and the term "being born" (*jāyamāna*), this is merely a praise of ritual action (*karmastuti*), as in the passage: "A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, when being born...
It does not enjoin a prohibition against effort directed toward human goals that are not distinct from that [ritual action].

For this term *ṛṇa* (debt) is well-known in another context as its primary meaning: that wherein a creditor gives wealth to a debtor with the thought, "I shall receive this back from him along with interest," and the debtor likewise accepts it with the thought, "I shall give this back to him along with interest. This is the primary scope of the word *ṛṇa*, and it does not exist at all here.
Even "being born" (*jāyamāna*) refers primarily to one who is currently being produced—that is, one emerging from the interior of the mother's womb.

And that poor wretch, the infant, is not bound by *karmans*. Therefore, this is a praise of ritual action (*karman*), understood through the employment of figurative language: "the procreation of offspring, the performance of the sacrifice, and [the study of] the Veda—this triad is like a debt, a duty that must necessarily be performed."
Nor should it be suspected that, on this account alone, there is an absence of opportunity for the resolve toward liberation, since another stage of life (āśrama) conducive to that end is observed.

But surely, since there are instructions regarding the duties of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices within the procedure for death, how can there be the undertaking of another stage of life (*āśrama*)? This is because the statement that one "should live until old age or death" is intended as a praise of ritual action (*karman*), in order to demonstrate that it should not be abandoned.
For there are many scriptural passages (*mantra* and *arthavāda*), such as "The four paths leading to the gods," which are in praise of the fourth stage of life.

The Smṛti texts of Manu and others are seen to be composed as systematic treatises that provide instruction on the fourth stage of life (the *caturthāśrama*) and are dedicated to prescribing the full range of duties, such as the rules of purity and conduct appropriate for that stage. For instance, having begun with the verse: "A twice-born graduate (*snātaka*), having duly remained in the householder stage, should dwell in the forest, well-restrained, subsisting on alms and with his senses conquered," Manu has devoted the entire sixth chapter to the instruction on the practice of the means to liberation (*mokṣa*) appropriate for the fourth stage of life.

And in the Jābāla-śruti, the four stages of life are taught step by step by an injunctive Brāhmaṇa passage itself: "Having been a student, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce."

And how can the instruction on the procedure for the internalizing of the fires (agnisamāropaṇa), which is directly heard in scripture— as in "Having internalized the fires within himself, a Brahmin may go forth from his home"— be denied?
Moreover, the study of the Upaniṣads would become entirely purposeless if the fourth stage of life (caturthāśrama), which is capable of implementing the means to liberation, did not exist.
For if the Veda were restricted solely to the performance of ritual acts (kriyākāṇḍa), what purpose would the instruction of the knowledge-section (jñānakāṇḍa) serve?

Therefore, since this teaching regarding "until old age" (*jarāmaryavāda*) is established as a direct injunction even for all four stages of life (*āśrama*), and because for those in the fourth stage there exists the opportunity for the practice of cultivating the knowledge of reality—the means for attaining liberation—it stands that this statement is intended merely as a praise.

Furthermore, from the scriptural statement, "By old age, indeed, he is released from this [debt], or by death," it is understood that the very occasion for the fourth stage of life is when one is permitted to renounce ritual action (*karman*) due to old age. Thus it has been said: "But when a householder perceives wrinkles and grey hair upon himself..."
When he has [only] the offspring of his offspring, then he should resort to the forest.
Thus [it is said].
For otherwise, he would have said, "one is liberated from that very death," yet he spoke thus;
therefore, they recognize the fourth stage of life as appropriate for the state of old age.
Or let alone the stage of old age;

even for a youth whose faculties are fully matured, it is declared that he has the qualification for liberation without depending on the sequence of the four stages of life (*āśrama*), as it is said: "One should renounce the world directly from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*)."
For this very reason, the religious student (brahmacārin) is of two kinds: the *upakurvaṇa* and the *naiṣṭhika*.
Among them, the *upakurvaṇa* is one who, having completed his period of studentship, enters the stage of the householder;
he is one whose passions (*kaṣāya*) are not yet matured and whose attachment is not fully stilled.

With reference to this very point, it is said: "A twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, without having procreated offspring, and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downwards."
However, he whose impurities (*kaṣāya*) have ripened becomes a lifelong celibate student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*) and does not enter the state of a householder.
Even a householder whose impurities have ripened is qualified for the life of an ascetic (*yati*), having transcended the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*).
As it has been said: "One may go forth from the home or from the forest."

However, some declare that liberation belongs even to a householder who knows the Self and whose passion has been extinguished, provided he performs action as a duty, free from attachment to the fruits of action;

as Yājñavalkya says: "One who has acquired wealth by righteous means, is devoted to the knowledge of reality, is exceedingly dear to his preceptor, performs ancestral rites, and is learned in the Vedas—even such a householder is liberated."
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that there is an absence of liberation due to this connection with debt.
As for the claim that [liberation is impossible] because of the persistence of the afflictions (*kleśa*), that too is merely a lack of conviction;
for it is easy to pacify the afflictions through the cultivation of their antidotes and other means.
For if the defects were eternal, or even if they were impermanent yet accidental, or even if they had a cause, that cause would have to be eternal.

Furthermore, if this [affliction] were not to be known as something to be remedied, or if the means for its pacification were not known once it was known, or even if known, it were impossible to carry out—that being the case, who indeed would seek to eliminate it?
However, these afflictions are not accidental, nor are they eternal; they do not have causes that are eternally unknown, nor are their means of pacification unknown, nor are they beyond remedy.

For defects are not eternal like the nature of the self, since they are perceived as having the properties of arising and passing away; moreover, false cognition is determined to be their productive cause, so they are neither accidental, nor caused by something indestructible, nor caused by something unknown.

Furthermore, the defects of innate ignorance can be uprooted along with their very foundations through the cultivation of the practice of their antidote, which is right knowledge; thus, they are not without a remedy. And it has been said by someone: "Because all [defilements] have counteragents, because they depend on diminution and increase, and because of the habituation to those [counteragents], the outflows (āsravas) may be abandoned somewhere through that becoming one's own nature."
Thus, for by perceiving the defects of sense objects, passion characterized by attachment toward them is stilled.
For when this discerning person reflects: "That woman with tremulous pupils and full, high, firm breasts..."
Today she is seen being plundered by birds in the wilderness.
Her body appears from the outside alone like the fragrance of a lotus,
yet within it is crowded with marrow, bones, feces, urine, fat, and swarms of worms.
Bones, bile, excrement, moist intestines, and blood— this,
bound together by skin, is called a "woman" (kāminī).
How can those two lumps of flesh called breasts be golden jars?
And as for the buttocks, which are merely excrement and urine, what is this delusion of them being golden slabs?
The opening for urine and blood is impure, a moist and loathsome cavity;
yet it is precisely this that becomes the seat of pleasure—oh, what a mockery of men!
Just as a dog feels pleasure while licking the blood flowing from its own mouth onto a dry bone, so does a man feel pleasure toward a woman who exudes his own bodily fluids.
With her mouth agape, her eyes rolled back, her complexion pale, and gasping with a rattling sound—
how is it that this poor woman does not feel passion even as she dies today?
"Alas! This poor snake, thirsty at an untimely hour, has come with its mouth wide open to drink our blood."
What offense has this committed against us? When fire burns by its very nature upon being touched, with whom should one be angry?
Favorability is not the cause of what is pleasant, nor is unfavorability the cause of what is unpleasant;
I experience the fruit of my own actions—so who is my friend, and who is my enemy?
Thus, for one who contemplates day and night with an utterly tranquil mind, equanimity arises toward all things, and the knots of the afflictions dissolve.
For this very reason, in the treatises on liberation,
various counteractive meditations are taught many times for the purpose of subduing each respective obstacle.

But is it not the case that even through the cultivation of the antidote, the side of the defects does not undergo destruction in its entirety—just as the phlegm constituent (*kaphadhātu*) does not vanish while the use of *nimba* is being practiced? This is not so; for in that case, unlike the use of *nimba*, one observes the use of food and drink that is concordant with it.
Furthermore, out of fear of the total disappearance of the substratum (*dharmin*), complete destruction is not desired there.
An excess of phlegm (kapha), however, must be eliminated for the sake of achieving equilibrium among the bodily constituents (dhātus).
In this context, all afflictions that cause cyclic existence must be eradicated in their entirety;
and their eradication occurs through the cultivation of their antidotes in a continuous and one-pointed manner.
And no other means for its pacification proceeds, having set aside the single weapon that is the repeated cultivation of the antidote.
For desire for sense objects does not cease through their enjoyment.

As it has been said: "Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired things; like a fire fed with sacrificial butter, it only increases all the more. It is also stated elsewhere: "Passions increase in accordance with the practice of enjoyment, as do the skillfulness of the senses."
The son of Parāśara also said: "This pit for digging up straw is bottomless and difficult to fill; by whom can it be filled?
For even when filled by the great, it is merely dug out again by that very act of filling."

Therefore, it is the cultivation of the antidote alone—the Blessed One of terrifying beauty—which, blazing incessantly within the wilderness of the internal organ like the radiance of a forest fire, burns away the thickets of defects.
Thus, since there exists a means for the destruction of the continuity of defects, one must not assert that the path to liberation is blocked by them.

For this very reason, some maintain that because the conscious principle (*cetanā*) is pure by nature, because impurities are adventitious, and because the aforementioned means for removing those impurities are possible, the attainment of omniscience is not far off; for when those impurities are removed through the practice of those means, the mind remains in its own state as consciousness whose inherent nature is the capacity to perceive all objects.

As for what was said—that the emptiness of afflictions (*kleśa-śūnyatva*) of the self is never perceived because afflictions function as a continuous stream—that too is untrue, because the self is perceived every day in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) untouched by defects. Even for one who is awake, such a state is indeed observed in which the self remains in its very own nature, stainless.
As it has been said: "Day after day they go to the world of Brahman."
Therefore, enough with this persistent attachment to a discourse on the succession of faults.

As for the argument that was put forward—that activity persists because of its continuity—that too has been refuted by the author of the Sūtras: "Activity does not lead to rebirth for one whose afflictions have been destroyed.
When the defects, which are the causes of bondage, have dissolved, even activity is no longer capable of producing the body, sense-faculties, and so forth.
Granted that, due to the destruction of the defects, there may be no further accumulation of karma;
but how can past karma be extinguished without having yielded its fruit?

On this point, some say: "Karmas indeed give their results; they do not cease without having given them. Nevertheless, for the yogin, the latent impressions (saṃskāras) of bondage do not arise. This is because, having produced the bliss of the yogin born from tranquility, contentment, and so forth, merit (dharma) will perish; and demerit (adharma), having delivered suffering through the afflictions of cold, heat, and the like, will likewise perish."

Now, since there is a fixed rule of cause and effect regarding actions and their fruits—namely, that "from such an action, this fruit arises"—how could the experience of those fruits occur through this [intermediate state] alone? Therefore, others describe the experience of those fruits in a different manner.

For the yogin, through the perfection of yogic power (*yogardhi-siddhi*), having fashioned all his own past actions—both dharma and adharma—and having assumed, in various places of rebirth, those various bodies along with their sense organs and internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that are suitable for experiencing those [fruits], as well as the abandoned bodies left by liberated selves, he—having attained sovereignty—experiences the fruit of all his karma at once; thus, there is the exhaustion of karma through such experience.

Others, however, say: "What is the use of this exertion for the sake of experience? The karmas will perish even without their fruits being experienced; such is the power of the Blessed One’s knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) that when it arises, even long-accumulated karmas go to destruction all at once.
Furthermore, their destruction through experience is also understood solely from the authority of the scriptures."
Likewise, precisely because of its authority, we shall understand from that very knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) the destruction of those [karmas].
And thus it has been said: "Just as a well-kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes."

Nor is this merely a matter of faith, for it has been stated by the sage Vyāsa himself, the foremost among those who know the Vedas; indeed, he would not have spoken what is not the meaning of the Vedas.

Others do not think so; they hold that there is no burning away of all karma by means of [the fire of knowledge]. Rather, even though [karmas] exist in their own nature, due to the deficiency of auxiliary causes, they become indifferent toward performing their own effects; thus, like spoiled seeds, they suffer a loss of the capacity to produce sprouts.
Since it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces an effect, and not the individual factor alone,
therefore actions (*karma*) by themselves do not become the cause for the birth of the body, sense organs, and so forth, which are fit for the experience of results; rather,
they do so only when accompanied by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) and the defects (*doṣa*).
Thus it has been said: "Ignorance, craving, and merit and demerit are the causes of birth."
And for one who knows reality, precisely because of that knowledge of reality, ignorance—which consists of false cognition—does not exist.
As for the defects, their sequence has already been shown in the first [chapter].
In the absence of those, even if merit and demerit exist, they are not capable of causing bondage.
For seeds remaining within a granary are not capable of producing their own effects, such as sprouts and the like.
Just as even for seeds that have fallen [from the granary], their inherent power has merely become diminished,
so too let it not be that the inherent power of karmas becomes slackened;
nevertheless, like a seed situated within a granary, there is a non-commencement of the effect due to the absence of auxiliary conditions.
Thus it has been said: "There is no further engagement for one whose afflictions have been diminished."

Now, one might object: "If dharma and adharma exist in their own right (as intrinsic entities), how can it be said that liberation is the absolute eradication of the nine qualities of the self? This is not a fault. For even the mere persistence of these two—which, like the conjunction with the mind, produce no further effects—is no different from their eradication. Furthermore, because the liberated self is omnipresent, conjunction with the mind is unavoidable; yet at that time, although it exists, it does not function toward the production of pleasure, pain, cognition, or the like.
In this way, even though merit and demerit exist, if they do not project a fruit, what will they do? Thus, in effect, they become utterly destroyed.
Therefore, liberation is the destruction of the nine qualities of the self; this is not contradictory.
Thus, because there is also an absence of the cause of bondage—the persistence of active engagement—liberation is not difficult to attain.

Others, however, say: since the necessity of the causal relationship between actions and their fruits is understood through the treatises (*śāstra*), the exhaustion of karma cannot occur merely by producing pleasure and pain through means such as tranquility, contentment, cold, or heat; nor can it occur because, even through yogic power (*yogarddhi*), it is impossible to experience the results of pleasure and pain spanning a long duration all at once. Furthermore, if [karma] were consumed by the fire of knowledge (*jñānāgni*), it would follow that the Vedic injunctions teaching those very actions would become either purposeful or useless. Since karma whose fruit has not yet been given does not cease, in the case of its mere persistence, there is the consequence that—even after remaining for a long time like a seed stored in a granary—it would project its fruit again at a later time. Therefore, the exhaustion of karma must necessarily be stated to occur only through the door of experiencing its own fruit.
Nor should one fear a lack of liberation, because its attainment is possible even after a long time.

Thus, the seeker of liberation must necessarily perform obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites; for if he fails to perform them, he would incur sin (*pratyavāya*). How then could there be bondage for him? Desirable (*kāmya*) and prohibited (*niṣiddha*) actions, which produce heaven and hell, are clearly the means to bondage; therefore, he should certainly avoid them. In this way, first of all, no further accumulation of karma proceeds.

Thus it is said: "One who desires liberation should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with the wish to avoid transgression; one should not engage in those rites that are performed for specific desires or those that are prohibited."
The exhaustion of previously accumulated karma occurs only through its experience;
and this sequence of practice belongs to the seeker of liberation who knows the Self, not to anyone else—it is he alone who is thus liberated from bondage.
As it has been said: "This [liberation] exists for the knower of the Self; therefore, that knowledge is put to use."
In that state, for those who have realized the true nature of the self, when previous karma is exhausted through experience, [liberation occurs].

Because there is no further accumulation [of karma], the body is not produced again. Now, one might object: "In the view that obligatory (*nitya*) rites must be performed, liberation simply does not exist. For those very rites that are taught as obligatory—such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, which are enjoined by such injunctions as 'One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives'—are heard in scripture to possess results; thus they ought to be considered optional (*kāmya*) rites as well, since they are not performed without being preceded by an intention for a result, as seen in [injunctions] such as 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*' and 'One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*.'"
Thus it has been said: "The desired fruit, once known, will not come to pass for one who lacks the desire for it.
This is the distinction regarding engagement;
there is also a distinction regarding the application [of the means].

Since optional (kāmya) action, when performed with the inclusion of all its constituent parts, is the means for attaining a result, it should not be performed according to one's capacity in such a fragmented manner. However, because non-performance of obligatory (nitya) action leads to demerit (pratyavāya), it must be performed even according to one's capacity; for even a performance that is deficient in some way is better than non-performance, as it serves to avoid the demerit incurred by failing to act.
But in the case of an optional rite (kāmya), even if one is unable to perform all the auxiliary parts (aṅga), let him not undertake it; for by not undertaking it, he would incur no transgression.

And thus, that very same ritual action, such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, which is taught by the injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*) and is therefore obligatory (*nitya*), does not lead to bondage when it is performed without aiming for its fruit. If it is asked, "Where has its power to produce heaven gone?"—we do not perceive the power or lack of power of actions through direct perception;
rather, we, as Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), have the scripture alone as our refuge.

That "injunction alone is the authority regarding dharma" is our family tradition. And that injunction proceeds by depending upon a person who possesses desire and is capable of action; since its qualification [as an authority] would not exist without the accomplishment of a result, it establishes itself as culminating in a result.

In other cases, however, an injunction that proceeds by means of obtaining an eligible person (adhikārin) defined by the meaning of the word "life" as long as it lasts, does not lead to a [specific] fruit; rather, when the purpose of the scripture is not performed, there is sin because the one who is eligible has abandoned the purpose of the scripture. In the case of a rite for a desired object (kāmya), however, one who has not yet produced the desire is not even eligible; thus, since the one who is eligible has not abandoned the injunction, he does not incur sin.
Once one has begun, however, one is simply not permitted to abandon it midway.

Whether the desire for the fruit has vanished or the fruit has been attained, that [action] must necessarily be completed, just like the completion of the ritual acts themselves; therefore, enough with this extensive discourse containing the core of other treatises.
In every respect, it has been well said: "One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites."

"Is it not the case that, according to the view that past karma is exhausted through experience, liberation appears as if remote because it requires a long period of time? Have you realized this only now?
[Thinking] 'By merely uttering "Hum," one would attain liberation without delay'—this human goal is certainly not easily obtained."
Have you not heard this word of Vyāsa, O venerable one: "Having attained perfection through many births, he then goes to the supreme goal"?
The statement regarding the burning by the fire of knowledge is intended solely as a praise of knowledge;
thus, it is said that liberation results from the combination of knowledge and action.

To this it is replied: Indeed, the exhaustion of karmas by means of experiencing their fruits cannot be accomplished even in hundreds of millions of births. For it has been said: "In some cases, a single karma of such a nature arises that its fruit is not experienced even in a hundred thousand births."
"By means of bodies intended for the experience of those very actions, no other karma will be performed;
this notion that 'the body is a bondage' is merely a vain hope of ascetics. Thus, by those ritualists who teach such a path to liberation, the neglect of liberation is taught implicitly.
Therefore, the fact that actions are the cause of bondage must be refuted precisely according to the method previously stated.
Is it not the case that a fault has been stated for all four positions? No, because the fourth position is irreproachable.
Since actions do not initiate their effects due to a deficiency in auxiliary conditions—just like seeds remaining in a granary—there is no fault whatsoever.
And this very non-initiation of an effect is precisely what constitutes their "burning" (destruction).
But surely, since their essential nature is not destroyed, they will eventually begin to produce an effect—just like seeds in a granary;
therefore, it would be better that they simply be annihilated.
Why then do we now strive to annihilate even the eternal self?
For since he was previously an enjoyer, even though liberated he might again attain the state of being an enjoyer; therefore, it would be better if they were simply annihilated.

If it is asked, "In the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), how could he again attain the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*)," [we reply: "How, too, would the karmas initiate an effect in the absence of auxiliary causes? Furthermore, it cannot be said that passion and the like are not auxiliary causes for the binding function of karmas, because it has been stated more than once that 'one who is free from passion is not seen to be born'.
Therefore, this very path taught by the author of the Sūtras is the elegant one: "There is no engagement [in rebirth] for one whose afflictions have been eliminated."
Regarding this statement that liberation results from the combination of knowledge and action, the following must be said:

in what way do actions serve as an auxiliary factor toward liberation? For liberation cannot be something to be accomplished by action, since that would entail the consequence of its being impermanent, like heaven and other such rewards.

Moreover, liberation is said to be the self itself abiding in its own true nature; and the nature of the self is not to be accomplished by action, because it is established as being without beginning or end.

[Objection: But surely, since one would incur sin by failing to perform obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), action (*karman*) itself might be a limb of liberation (*mokṣāṅga*) because it serves as a means for avoiding bondage through that very performance. [Reply: No, because it has already been stated that this is due to the direct scriptural injunction (*pratyakṣopadeśa*) for the rule of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

However, we certainly accept that for those whose mental impurities (*kaṣāya*) are not yet ripened, the performance of action is a means to liberation through a traditional succession (*pāramparya*), as it serves to gradually bring about that ripening.
As Manu says: "By the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) and by the [Vedic] sacrifices, this body is made fit for Brahman (*brāhmī kriyate tanuḥ*)."
Furthermore, those who know the inner self consider the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa) to be merely instrumental to the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa).

For if liberation were directly achievable through action, it would follow that it is transitory, like heaven; since everything produced is impermanent, it has been stated that the knowledge of reality alone is the means to liberation.

Furthermore, even that collection of ritual acts consisting of the minor and major restraints (*yama* and *niyama*) and so forth, which are to be accomplished and serve as constituent parts (*aṅga*), is not prevented from becoming such a part;

yet, because liberation (*mokṣa*)—even while being an effect of those acts—is by nature the non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of all qualities, it does not possess perishability like heaven (*svarga*).
It has been stated, however, that anything else is not liberation.
In that process for attaining liberation previously described, the knowledge of reality alone is the means;
ritual action, however, is a subsidiary element therein, consisting of various acts such as purification and the like, which must be preceded by the refinement of the self.

Now, let the knowledge of reality as it has been explained be considered: what is its object that makes it conducive to liberation, or from where is its status as a means to the supreme good understood?

But has it not already been stated many times that knowledge of the self is the cause of liberation? What is the point of this question? It is because there is no consensus; for disputants indeed contradict one another on this matter.
This distinction between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) is one and the same, being merely imagined through ignorance (avidyā).
According to the proponents of Brahman (brahmavādins), liberation occurs when ignorance is dispelled by the knowledge of the reality of the supreme self.
The grammarians [hold that it arises] from the ascertainment of the non-duality of sound.
"Because of the vision of the non-duality of consciousness," so say the Buddhist monks.
"From the discriminative knowledge of the distinction between primordial nature and the spirit," so say the followers of the Great Sage.
And others say that it arises from devotion to the Lord.
Therefore, it must be stated: for what purpose, then, would those seeking liberation long for the knowledge of reality?
It is said: first, let it be accepted that selves are indeed distinct; for the knowledge of the self alone is the means to the supreme good.

As for the question, "From where is it understood that this [knowledge of the self] is a means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)?", we reply: "From the word of Akṣapāda. Akṣapāda has indeed taught thus: "[The attainment of the supreme good results from the knowledge of the self]. Now, this seer would not have taught a matter devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, there must be a means of valid cognition in this regard. That [means] is the Vedic injunctive statement: "The self is to be known."

Thus, this injunction is not devoid of a qualification (*adhikāra*), for an injunction lacking a qualification cannot be fit for performance. Therefore, the search for its qualification must be undertaken.

Furthermore, because it is not recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of another, it does not belong under the heading of a primary act (*pradhāna*), like the injunction regarding the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*).

Therefore, according to the principle of the Viśvajit section, as long as the person desiring heaven (svargakāma) appears to the mind of the performer as the qualified agent here, we accept that very [attainment], like "establishment" (pratiṣṭhā) in the case of the Rātrisattra, as its fruit.
And this very [liberation], even while being realized, shines forth as eternal by virtue of its very nature;
it is a state from which there is no returning, unlike heaven, which is subject to decay.
Is it not the case that when a visible purpose is not obtained, there is occasion for the postulation of an invisible purpose?
And here, a visible purpose for the knowledge of the self is indeed perceived: its being the cause for engaging in ritual action.

For who would perform rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma—which require the expenditure of much wealth and effort—upon perishable, insentient beings alone that end with the cremation ground? Therefore, the eternal self, which goes to the next world, must be known.
For in this way, one may proceed with actions free from doubt.
This [objection] is untenable because it is already established through other means.

For the followers of Jaimini, the self is ascertained to be eternal by means of the perceptual cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and for the Naiyāyikas and others, it is so ascertained by the power of inference (*anumāna*).

What, then, could an injunction (*vidhi*) accomplish here? Furthermore, the instruction on the entire collection of ritual procedures (*itikartavyatākalāpa*) would, at that time, be utterly purposeless.
And since these Vedic texts, though so very vast, terminate at this very point, it follows that this is like a small sparrow being pulled out from a great bamboo thicket.
Therefore, some maintain that the injunction for the knowledge of the Self relies solely on the fruit consisting of non-return, which is presented by the explanatory passages (arthavāda).

But those of subtle vision say: even this is a great difficulty, namely that it has been stated that this injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) consists in merely looking for the pleasure found in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
In the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice or the Rātrisatra, what else could be done?

For since no qualified person (*adhikārī*) can be obtained by examining the nature of the Viśvajit itself, one must either postulate someone such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) by force, or rely on the one provided by the explanatory passage.

But where that [result] is apprehended through the very power of the nature of the injunction itself, what is the use of such a conceptualization, or of this wretchedness of not looking at it, as if it were merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)?

And here, because of the indication of the state of being most desired (*īpsitatamatva*) by means of either the gerundive suffix (*kṛtya*) or the accusative case—as in "One should study one's own Veda" (*svādhyāyo ’dhyetavyaḥ*) or "One should establish the sacred fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*)—it is established that the action has that [result] as its ultimate end.

In this regard, just as the injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*)—being understood as being for the sake of the fires—is satisfied by the mere acquisition of those fires because they are useful for the multitude of rites that serve various injunctions and human goals, and thus does not require any further fruit; or just as the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*)—because its purpose is the grasping of the syllables, and because it is determined that the grasping of syllables is a means to the supreme human goal by way of the comprehension of fruitful rituals—does not require any other fruit such as streams of honey and ghee beyond that.

Nor does it function as a subordinate element (aṅga) to the injunction for teaching, because it attains its own qualification through the very power of its own nature by means of purifying that which is most desired; likewise here too, the thorough knowledge of the true nature of the Self—characterized by being free from evil and so forth—makes known its status as the supreme human goal, thereby precluding the possibility that this injunction has any other purpose.

It is said that some rule of consecration (*saṃskāravidhi*), although residing in the object being consecrated, looks toward another [purpose] in consideration of the purpose of that which is being consecrated, as in the case of "he sprinkles the rice grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*).

On the other hand, some [rule], failing to find a purpose for the object being consecrated and thus unable to fulfill its status as the most desired object (*īpsitatama*), abandons its very nature as a rule of consecration, as in the case of "he offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*). As it has been stated: "A substance is held to be fit for consecration only when it is of use either as something already existing or as something yet to be produced."
"The roasted flour-grains will not be consumed, nor have they ever been consumed anywhere."

But for one for whom there exists a person to be consecrated—like a priceless jewel, like unfaded nectar, like the lunar orb that has not set, or like a lotus that has not withered—what desire, then, could there be for a postulation of a result by looking toward an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) or by depending on its recitation in the context (*prakaraṇa-pāṭha*)? For this very reason, the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is not prompted by a scriptural injunction regarding desire (*kāma-śruti*), nor is the study of the Veda prompted by the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*).

Therefore, because the injunction for the knowledge of the self shares the same status as the injunctions for Vedic study and the establishment of the sacred fires, it is understood that the knowledge of the self produced by that injunction is for the sake of liberation (*apavarga*).
Liberation is said to be the very nature of the self when it is devoid of those attributes produced by external limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Since this knowledge of the self alone is thus the means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) and cannot be obtained through any other means, the teacher Akṣapāda taught precisely that.
However, that view which regards consciousness, existence, the self, sound, and so forth as non-dual is merely false knowledge; therefore, it is not a means to the supreme good.

Now, how can it be said that the Advaita view is false? On the contrary, it is logical that the perception of duality—whether termed ignorance (*avidyā*), illusion (*māyā*), or even false knowledge—is what is false.
To demonstrate this, let Your Honor first examine perception itself with care.

For in that context, it is understood that whatever appears instantaneously as the very nature of an object by way of independence from anything else is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), while everything else is conceptual (*kālpānika*).
Furthermore, it is the very form of existence (*sadrūpa*) that shines forth there as undifferentiated and independent of anything else;
whereas difference (*bheda*), being dependent on other things, does not become an object of sensory cognition (*akṣajavijñāna*).

In this regard, just as from the state of clay up until the stage of the jar, within this interval, the forms of effects—such as the pot, shards, fragments, gravel, and particles—which appear and disappear, enter the path of conventional usage while being non-ultimately real;
yet in ultimate reality, it is only the clay.
As they say: "Clay alone is true."
Thus, even that form of clay is not ultimately real when considered in relation to *sattā* (Being); therefore, *sattā* alone is the ultimate reality everywhere.
They say that this very characteristic of Being is Brahman.

Furthermore, scripture—beginning with "One alone, without a second," and so forth—demonstrates non-difference alone, as in: "There is not the slightest diversity here," and "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity.
Nor can it be said that scripture, which proclaims non-difference, contradicts perception.
For perception is not capable of negating anything else, because its function is exhausted in the apprehension of its own specific form (*svarūpa*) alone.

And since difference is difficult to establish without the negation of another form, perception is indeed blunt regarding difference; how then could it contradict scripture which apprehends non-difference? As it has been said: "The wise say that perception is a producer [of knowledge], not a negator."

Therefore, the scriptural teaching of non-duality is not contradicted by that perception. Now, one might object: "If Brahman is indeed one and there is nothing else, then since that Brahman is by nature eternally pure and enlightened, it must remain liberated.
By whom, then, is it bound? For what purpose, then, is this effort of those seeking liberation?
And from where does this manifestation of the diverse world arise? We reply: the effort of those seeking liberation is for the purpose of destroying ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, this manifestation of the diverse world is indeed abandoned.
If this ignorance were distinct from Brahman, there would be no non-duality;

if it were not distinct, then it is Brahman itself and nothing other than that, so how could it be destroyed? Do not say such a thing; for against such a reality, the objections of bad logicians do not apply.
This ignorance, however, is said to be of the nature of a non-entity—a *māyā* whose very essence is false appearance.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the non-apprehension of reality (*tattva*).

But how can that which is called "non-apprehension" be conceptualized as having the attributes of a real entity? Furthermore, to whom does this ignorance belong, even though it consists in the non-apprehension of reality?
For ignorance cannot belong to Brahman, since its nature is eternally awakened.
But there is no other substratum for it; nor can false knowledge exist without a locus. It is said that ignorance belongs to the individual selves (jīvātman), not to Brahman.
"Are not those individual souls (jīvātman) also to be considered in terms of being either different or non-different from Brahman? Ah, you petty logician! You are ignorant of everything.
The individual souls are indeed Brahman itself; they are not other than it.
For sparks, even though they appear as distinct from a mass of fire, do not fail to be of the nature of fire."
Is it then that ignorance belongs to Brahman alone, yet is not [inherently] of Brahman?

For just as the single ether appears as if divided by the distinctions imposed by the concealment of jars and the like—appearing as "the space within a cloth" or "the space within a jar"—and just as it becomes turbid with dust, smoke, and so forth solely due to those concealments, yet upon the cessation of those concealments, its turbidity vanishes and it is recognized as that very same supreme ether; in exactly the same way, the individual selves (*jīvātman*), though their distinctions are imagined by ignorance, experience the various kinds of turbidity produced by that [ignorance].
And upon the cessation of that [activity], they dissolve into the supreme Brahman.
But even if this were so, this distinction between Brahman and the individual self (*jīvātman*) is imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*), and that ignorance is said to belong to the individual selves.
Thus, a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*) results: the individual selves exist when there is the imagination of ignorance, and ignorance exists when the individual selves exist. Let this circularity be.
This entire manifold of ignorance is without exception.

To whom does this fault belong? If its beginninglessness is the defense, it will be like the case of the seed and the sprout. Furthermore, you yourselves also accept that this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is indeed beginningless.
And it is said that cyclic existence exists solely through ignorance.
Now, how can there be the eradication of beginningless ignorance? Does it not happen that what is beginningless cannot be eradicated, as in the case of the earth or form?
Or rather, how do you yourselves eradicate the beginningless cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)? Indeed, when the means exists, even that which is beginningless is eradicated.
What, then, is the means for its eradication according to the Advaitins? We reply: it is ignorance itself.
Even hearing, reflection, and meditative contemplation are themselves forms of ignorance;
yet, when practiced, they destroy other forms of ignorance while they themselves also perish,
just as milk digests milk and itself becomes digested.
Just as one poison neutralizes another poison and itself subsides,
or as dust thrown into water turbid with dust settles that dust and makes the water clear by withdrawing itself,
so too this very ignorance, while cutting through another instance of ignorance, becomes a means to knowledge (*vidyā*).
[Objection: But how can this ignorance, which is unreal by its very nature, produce a real effect? [Reply: It is said: the accomplishment of a real purpose from that which is unreal is possible;
for illusions such as a snake and the like are seen to be causes of real fear.
Lines, the letter *ga*, and so forth are seen to be unreal, yet they serve as means for the cognition of real objects.
If it is argued that they are real in their own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), what is accomplished by that? For it is precisely as the letter *ga* and so forth that they convey [the meaning].
And that [nature] of theirs is unreal.

Now, since Brahman is eternally pure and the individual souls (jīvas) are non-different from it, how can ignorance find any scope among them? This has already been resolved by the description of the analogy of the space within a jar.

Moreover, just as the reflection of a face, though perfectly pure, displays non-ultimate forms such as dark, long, or thick due to the influence of limiting conditions (upādhi) like water, a gem, a sword, or a mirror—even in the absence of those qualities in the face itself—so too does Brahman appear within individual souls (jīvas), despite its own lack of such attributes.

Surely, because the Supreme Self is eternal, the individual souls (*jīvas*) are also non-different from one another; thus, when one is awakened or liberated, all would be either bound or liberated. O you whose mind is defiled by fallacious reasoning, how is it that you do not understand this, even though it is evident? For when the space within a jar becomes established in the supreme space upon the destruction of the jar, the space within a cloth does not likewise become so.

Even for a single individual soul (*jīvātman*), a difference in the experience of pleasure and pain is observed due to the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); as in the cases, "There is a pain in my foot" and "There is a pain in my head. Furthermore, for one who has undergone slight exhaustion from the intense heat of the sun, wherever on the body's limb the attendant applies a cool patch of sandalwood paste, there alone is the experience of the cessation of that suffering, and not elsewhere. Thus, even though the individual souls are established merely through conceptual construction within the one Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the distinction between the bound and the liberated is indeed established. Therefore, it is proper to accept this doctrine of the unity of the self (*ekātmavāda*) in accordance with the scriptures, rather than the plurality of selves.

To this it is replied: while you may possess supreme skill in composing a tangled web of secret techniques for a drama of deception and in establishing a succession of corresponding examples, you are truly wretched when it comes to defining the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For instance, since difference is sublated by valid cognition, is this acceptance of non-difference on your part due to the fact that non-difference itself is established by valid cognition?
Neither of these two cases is the case.
For all means of valid cognition, such as direct perception and the rest, are indeed established upon difference.

As for the claim that difference cannot be apprehended by sensory cognition because it is dependent upon something else—that is incorrect; for non-difference is even more dependent upon something else.

For instance, when one discerns the entire series of effects starting from a lump of clay up to the jar, the potsherd, and the powder, and perceives the nature of clay that persists through them, only then can the identity of the clay with those [effects] be ascertained, and not otherwise.

But the Bhikṣus say that visual perception grasps the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) as it has been excluded [from others], and does not have non-difference as its object, because non-difference is dependent upon something else.
If it is argued that the cognition "this is other than that" is a cognition dependent on another, then the cognition "this is inherent in that" is likewise dependent on another.
Therefore, in this matter, both you and the monks are equally afflicted by a misconception;
for it has been examined in detail during the *Sāmānyacintā* that sensory perception is incapable of grasping either difference or non-difference.
Indeed, it was stated that even when four fingers appear, they manifest as having both mutually distinct forms and a common form.
Whether there be exclusion or inclusion among things depending on something else,
entities nevertheless appear in sensory cognitions with unmixed intrinsic natures.

As for what was said—that "perception is an affirmer, not a negator"—that too is incorrect. What is the meaning of "affirmer"? Does it mean that this [perception] grasps the intrinsic nature of an object and does not negate other forms?
If you say it is perception, do not say so; for in that case, it would not be knowledge.
For without the negation of other forms, even the determination of its own nature is not accomplished.
Indeed, blue is apprehended as "blue" only when it is excluded from yellow and so forth, and not otherwise.
Thus it has been said: "It determines that [object] and excludes the other."
Furthermore, we have already established that perception is capable of apprehending non-existence just as it apprehends existence;
therefore, because perception grasps the specific nature of entities as mutually distinct, it does not have non-difference as its object.

Since the operations of both verbal testimony and inference regarding their respective objects depend upon the apprehension of a relation, their very nature would not be possible without a distinction [between those objects]; thus, both of them have difference as their object.
Even though there is an absence of a particular object, inference has difference as its object because it determines a general mark (liṅgasāmānya) that is distinct from everything else.

However, regarding the word as consisting of a *pada*, whose denotable content takes the form of distinctions such as "tadvat" (possessing that) and so forth, it has already been established that its object—the meaning of the sentence—is either a collection of word-meanings mutually colored by one another, or the form of one particular word-meaning qualified by the other word-meanings.
Therefore, in every respect, difference (*bheda*) is not sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is there any means of valid cognition that apprehends non-difference, according to the very reasoning already stated.

Scriptures such as "It is one only, without a second" and "There is no diversity whatsoever here," though recited, should not have their meaning accepted exactly as heard, because they are *arthavāda* (explanatory or eulogistic passages).

[Objection: But surely you have already accepted the authority of the Veda even with respect to established matters. [Response: Certainly we have accepted it. However, in the case of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that express meanings contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge—such as "only smoke was seen from fire during the day, not its flame"—one has resorted to an interpretation based on a figurative sense (*gauṇī vṛtti*), setting aside the primary sense.
In this same way, this statement also, while expressing a meaning contradicted by other means of knowledge, is explained otherwise.

However, those explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) which do not state matters contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) may possess authority with respect to their own literal form, such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" and so forth.

Therefore, even though there is a difference between the states of pleasure and pain, there is no difference in the self that remains constant; likewise, despite the multiplicity of the body, senses, and so forth, there is no multiplicity in that [self]. In this manner, this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) must be interpreted somehow or other. However, there is simply no scriptural statement here in the form of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) that is intent upon teaching non-duality. Thus, non-duality is not established even by the authority of scripture (*āgama*).

Furthermore, regarding the objection concerning the distinctions of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth—which was raised and then refuted by repeatedly raising the doubt—the doubt itself is well-founded, but the resolution is not elegant. What is the meaning of this statement that "this ignorance is indefinable in terms of being either identical to or different from reality"? It means that it proceeds as a beginningless continuum and is capable of acting as an obscuration.
If this ignorance is to be eradicated through effort, how can it be said to be non-existent?
If it is argued, "Who could destroy this [ignorance] if it exists?", this is merely the terror of the faint-hearted.
For it is observed that only existing things, such as trees and the like, are subject to destruction, whereas non-existent things, such as a rabbit's horn, are not.
Therefore, because it is something that can be destroyed, ignorance should not be considered eternal; rather, being existent, it certainly does exist.
That which is eternal cannot be destroyed, whereas that which is impermanent can be destroyed;
non-existence is one thing, and the impermanence of entities is another.
Moreover, ignorance is not merely the non-apprehension of reality; doubt and error are also indeed ignorance.

Since these two possess the nature of positive entities (*bhāva-svabhāva*), how could they be non-existent? Furthermore, it cannot be said that the prior absence of apprehension is non-existent, because even non-existence (*abhāva*) has been established as having existence. Thus, in every respect, ignorance is not non-existent.
And if its non-existence is refuted, its existence would necessarily follow by force;
for a category distinct from both existence and non-existence is utterly impossible to find.
And because the second ignorance exists within sentient beings, there is no duality.

As for the claim that because Brahman is eternally awakened, it cannot be the locus of ignorance, and that it is therefore the individual souls (jīvas) who are the locus of ignorance—and that upon the cessation of ignorance, those very souls dissolve into the supreme Brahman like the space within a jar—that too is not tenable. This is because the jar and so forth, which cause the limitation of space, are actually present;
whereas since ignorance is non-existent, the idea that it causes a limitation of the Supreme Self is an unequal analogy.
Furthermore, due to the absence of any limiting factor, even the conceptualization of the division of the jīvas is rendered impossible.

Furthermore, as for the beginninglessness of ignorance that was asserted in order to avoid the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), in that case, its reality would necessarily follow—just like the seed and the sprout, or like the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) accepted by other schools. And if it exists as a process set in motion from time immemorial, it is only logical that its removal should be effected by the application of a contrary cause; however, for those who maintain the doctrine of a single self (*ekātmavāda*), this is extremely difficult to accomplish, and thus there would be no liberation at all.
As Bhaṭṭa has said: "No one is able to eradicate innate ignorance;
for an innate state can only perish somewhere when there occurs the emergence of something of a different nature."
"But there is no single, distinct cause for the various means [of knowledge]."

Furthermore, as for the revelation of a succession of examples regarding the claim that ignorance itself is the means to knowledge (*vidyopāya*), that too leads only to exhaustion and not to the establishment of the intended point;
for in every case, the means exists by its own nature,
whereas that which is non-existent, such as a sky-flower, lacks the status of being a means.
Although lines, syllables, and so forth do not exist as having the nature of phonemes (*varṇa*), nevertheless, they certainly do exist by way of their own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

[Objection: But surely this arrangement of lines, when perceived as "this is the letter *ga*," becomes the conveyor of meaning; yet it does not exist in that form [of the letter *ga*]. [Reply: Do not say so. For an object that exists in its own nature (*svarūpa*) is seen to be a cause for worldly transaction even when perceived through another form, just like a counterfeit coin (*kūṭakārṣāpaṇa*), and this is logical.
However, that which does not exist even in its own nature cannot serve as a factor in worldly transaction either by its own self or through another.
And since the arrangement of lines exists in its own nature, even though it does not exist as the essence of the phoneme (*varṇātmatva*), it is capable of performing its function.
But this principle does not apply to ignorance, because it lacks intrinsic existence.
In the case of a snake and so forth, however, just as the nature of the snake itself is perceived, the fact that the cognition of it is also its effect is likewise understood.
For this very reason, they teach the medical treatment for the poison of doubt within their own scriptures.

Thus, even when an untrue statement is made—such as "This lion has emerged from the depths of the forest cave and is advancing right here in a rage"—the effects observed, such as the flight of cowards and the spirited raising of weapons by heroes, are real actions. Since the cognition of the lion is the cause of those actions, it is not the case that what is unreal can serve as a means (*upāya*).
By this, the analogy of the reflection is also refuted, because in the case of a sword and so forth, there exists therein the cause for the conceptualization of impurities such as those of the face;
however, in this case [of consciousness], that is absent.
Furthermore, even that example of pain in the foot cited to establish the aforementioned system has been thus refuted, because the delimiting factors such as the foot are ultimately real there.
However, it has been demonstrated many times that for the proponents of non-duality (advaitavādins), the seed for the conceptualization of difference is difficult to establish in this case.

In this regard, the summary of the matter is as follows: if ignorance (*avidyā*) were non-existent, then this entire manner of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) as it has been illustrated would not persist, for it is produced by that [ignorance]. But when it exists, there is no non-duality.

For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras stated: "The absolute establishment of [either] plurality or unity is not proven, because of the [respective] applicability or inapplicability of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
If there is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the establishment of non-duality (*advaita*), then that itself constitutes a second entity, and thus there is no non-duality.

On the other hand, if there is no means of valid cognition, then non-duality is all the more impossible, because there is an absence of establishment when there is no authoritative means of knowledge.
Therefore, having abandoned the doctrine of non-duality— which is rooted in conceptual constructions arising from the literal interpretation of mantras and explanatory passages—
one should accept this distinction between categories of objects as it is cognized through perception, inference, and scripture.
By this, the doctrine of the non-duality of sound (*śabdādvaitavāda*) is also refuted, as in: "Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the imperishable essence of sound;
it manifests in the form of objects, from which the process of the world proceeds."

It is said in response: therein, both that which is proclaimed as "eternity"—the existence of a reality devoid of beginning and end and lacking prior or posterior limits—and that which is established by the term "Brahman," namely "pervasiveness," have already been refuted with respect to sound (*śabda*). Furthermore, the partless *sphoṭa*-nature of sound has indeed been rejected.
As for that which is said to be eternal and all-pervading, what is the reasoning for calling it the "essence of sound" (*śabdatattva*)?
He says: it is the essence of sound because it is apprehended by sound.
For indeed, every cognition arising does not arise without delineating a word;
for a cognition that lacks such delineation has not attained the nature of illumination, and thus it would be no different from what has not arisen at all.
In this way, if the essence of awareness were robbed by the failure to grasp [the object] as "it is like this" and so forth, it would not even possess the nature of being a cognition.
