Even those cognizers who, due to their lack of utility in the linguistic conventions of the elders, have not acquired a specific proficiency in the relationship between words and meanings—those who are like young children—even they certainly do not perceive any object of cognition without mentally representing (ullikhantaḥ) that collection of words such as "this" or "that.

Therefore, since all cognitions possess a nature of illumination attained through the power of the extraction of words, let it be determined that the essence of all words is this: that the capacity to make [an object] known is permeated by words.
As it has been said: "There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words."
"All knowledge is understood as if it were permeated by sound."
If this were not admitted, however, because consciousness would be devoid of luminosity, the entire world would be like one who is blind and mute, with no objects ever apprehended.
And it has been said: "If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from cognition, there would be no manifestation; for manifestation is that which possesses reflective awareness."

Therefore, you should be instructed in this manner step by step: because there is no distinction caused by the interpenetration of the qualification known as "word," every cognition—whether sensory and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) or conceptual (*savikalpaka*)—illuminates an object as qualified by a word. Understand that in a cognition where the object appears as delimited by a genus, a quality, or an action—such as "the white cow is walking"—it is precisely the object as qualified by the word that flashes forth.

If you have thus entered into the understanding [of this], then when asked about the true nature of that particular object colored by the qualifier called "word," you demonstrate it by means of the word itself; or rather, you experience it through experience as having a nature whose manifestation is obtained without abandoning the word. Therefore, know that even that qualified object is of the very form of the word.
Thus, it is established that the word alone, mounted upon the object, appears.

Thus, even if you have reached this far, you ought to understand that since it is now impossible to demonstrate or experience that which the word has ascended to as something separate from itself, this object is merely a transformation (*vivarta*) of the word appearing in such and such a way; it is nothing other than that.

Just as this is the procedure regarding the appearances born of the sense faculties, so too it should be understood that in the case of verbal cognitions, either the object appears as qualified by the word, or the word is mounted upon the object, or the word itself manifests in the form of the object.

Therefore, it is logical that this single Śabdabrahman, which displays various distinctions through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of ignorance (avidyā), manifests its true nature as it actually exists once ignorance has ceased.

To this it is replied: indeed, even these three modes are not tenable. For we observe that even in those who lack the knowledge of the relationship between words and their referents, there arises a cognition produced by the senses—which is inclined toward the apprehension of a pure object and is established solely in its own nature—characterized by the absence of association with untrustworthy words.

Furthermore, even for those whose intellects are refined by having mastered the relationship between words and objects through familiarity with the linguistic usage of elders, the initial manifestation of the pure object, which serves as the cause for awakening the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of word-recollection, cannot be avoided.

For when a word is applied to a particular object, that which has been determined by one skilled in words during linguistic usage comes to the path of memory upon seeing that object, due to the awakening of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*); it does not happen otherwise.
Even in the case of general terms such as "what is that? and so forth, the same principle applies as it does for particular terms;
for even they cannot be the cause of the comprehension of meaning in the absence of etymological derivation and utility, just like the warbling of various birds wandering in the forest.

Even in the state of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), people do not perceive a lotus as being qualified by its denotative word or as inlaid with variegated qualities; this has been examined in detail under the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And it has been said: "Cognition of objects does not arise in a form identical to the word;
for the cognition that exists prior to the word is exactly the same as the cognition [that follows] from the word."
Now, it is merely the state of being named (*saṃjñitva*) that ascends to the intellect upon the proximity of the sound, not the object qualified by that [name].
For its apprehension is not possible through the eye, nor through the ear, nor through both, nor by the mind alone, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Indeed, a word serves as the means for determining one particular attribute within a substratum (*dharmin*) that possesses many attributes.
One does not superimpose oneself upon that [object].
For means of cognition, such as lamps and the sense faculties, do not superimpose themselves upon their respective objects, such as visible form;
therefore, the doctrine of non-difference between them, produced by the delusion that they are identical because they are means to that [object], is also untenable.
For it is not logical that the means should be non-different from its goal;
for there is no non-difference between form and either the lamp or the eye.
Furthermore, if the object appears as non-different from the word, what is the purpose of superimposition (*adhyāsa*)?

Even if there is non-difference, since this [word] alone is the universe, what is the purpose of superimposition even in that case? The error of superimposition among the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), however, is produced by the fault of designating [the object] with a single form.
As it has been said: "The designation is indeed *gauḥ* (cow); it is the denotable, the cognition thereof, and the word for it."

When asked, "What object was seen by you? one says, "A cow"; when asked, "What kind of cognition arose in you? one says, "A cow"; and when asked, "What kind of word did you employ? one says, "A cow. From this, the delusion arises.
In reality, however, these objects of words and cognitions are indeed distinct.

As it has been said: "In the case of a cow, when there is a cognition of the form 'cow' which expresses the real nature of the dewlap and so forth, the ultimate consciousness consists of both [the object and the cognition] being devoid of [intrinsic] forms."
Thus, it is logical that the nature of the word itself is not superimposed upon verbal cognitions, just as it is not so in the case of sense-produced cognitions.

Furthermore, if a word were to convey its meaning by means of its own form (*svarūpa*), then because the word "akṣa" is one and the same, there would be an identical cognition regarding a die, a vibhītaka tree, and the axle of a chariot.
Nor can it be argued that the words "akṣa" are different, for the recognition of their identical form remains unimpaired.
Because, upon its utterance, a doubt is observed regarding three possible meanings.
Furthermore, because the words *bhavati* and [the verb forms] ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and nominal suffixes (*sup*) are identical in form,

under the view of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), they would result in the cognition of an identical meaning. Consequently, even though one is experiencing the cognition of something already established as being what is to be proven, that very experience would be denied.
In this same way, it should also be understood in cases such as "a horse has come," "goats and sheep [have come]," and so forth.

Since a word is established as an accomplished entity (*siddha-rūpa*), if one were to maintain that the cognition of an object occurs through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of that [word] upon it, then in cases such as "one should sacrifice," "one should give," or "one should offer oblations," no cognition of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) would ever arise;
for a cognition of something to be accomplished is incompatible with the superimposition of an accomplished entity.
We do not understand by what cause words denoting genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*)—such as "cow," "white," and "goes"—invariably conform to superimposition (*adhyāsa*).
This is because there is no basis for postulating an inherent multiformity (*vaiśvarūpya*) in a word that is established independently of its objects;
nor is any defining characteristic observed that would restrict the application of a specific word.

Furthermore, for the proponent of the theory of verbal superimposition (*śabdādhyāsa*), the distinction between the words *vṛkṣa* (tree) and *plakṣa* (fig), as well as between the words *ghaṭa* (pot) and *paṭa* (cloth)—based on their difference in intrinsic form (*svarūpabheda*) and their independence from external objects—would not constitute the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) or grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
For these two words do not apply to a single underlying entity (*vastu*) as their denotable object (*vācya*).
By this, the blue lotus as well is refuted.

In this regard, it might be argued: "There is no such thing as a qualified object called 'blue lotus' (*nīlotpala*) characterized by the quality of blueness; rather, this is a distinct entity whose constituent parts have been discarded, like the word *aśvakarṇa* (horse-ear), while the description of qualifier and qualified is merely a mode of etymological derivation. This is incorrect, because there is no perceived reason to deny the cognition of the meanings of the constituent parts as they are actually experienced. In the case of *aśvakarṇa* and similar words, it is appropriate that they denote a distinct entity, for in those cases neither the meaning of "horse" nor the meaning of "ear" is present.
Furthermore, the doctrine that the meaning of a sentence is partless has already been refuted at length; therefore, enough with this repetitive discourse.

If it is argued that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the tree is a *plakṣa*" is based solely on the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of two words, that too is not tenable; for in that case, coreferentiality would result even for synonyms such as "tree" (*vṛkṣaḥ*) and "arboreal being" (*taruḥ*), since such a [superimposition] is possible there as well.

Furthermore, in the case of synonyms such as *hastaḥ*, *karaḥ*, and *pāṇiḥ*, if one adopts the position that there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of differences in the forms of the words, it would follow that there is a difference in the cognition of the object;
yet such a difference does not exist, so there is no superimposition.

Moreover, even a word that is independent of the apprehension of a relationship [with its object] would, by conforming to its own inherent capacity, produce a cognition through the superimposition of itself [upon the object].

Or, if there is dependence upon that [relation], we do not understand what the connection could be between which two things, since in your view it is difficult to establish the existence of a word and its meaning as distinct entities.
Or, if you admit an object separate from the word, then why this vain effort to justify the superimposition of the word? Let us desist from this pursuit of a mirage.
Furthermore, superimposition occurs in some cases due to similarity, as silver [is superimposed] upon mother-of-pearl;
in other cases it occurs due to coloring, as lac [colors] crystal.
However, in the case of word and meaning, whose natures are extremely distinct due to being corporeal and incorporeal respectively, similarity is first of all untenable.
Furthermore, passion (*anurāga*) is likewise impossible for that very reason,

because of their being in different locations and because they are perceivable by different sense organs. Even the description of a reflection is not tenable, since there is no contact between the word and its meaning due to their being situated at a distance.

And when the two [the moon and the lotuses] have not yet met, their reflections would be seen like the beautiful women of Vāsudeva dwelling in the city-gates and gardens; their unblown lotus-faces, with locks of hair darkened by curls stirred by the wind from the ocean waves, would be reflected in mirrors of camphor and ice-stones located in the caves of the Snowy Mountain, which are as clear and bright as moonlight.

Now, if it is asserted that words reach the location of their objects because they are omnipresent, then, due to the commonality of all words with all objects, an extreme confusion of superimpositions would result, for which no restrictive cause for distinguishing them could be determined. Enough of this over-extension;
in every respect, the theory of the superimposition of words is untenable.
The theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*) is also not tenable.

For what is the meaning of the statement that "it manifests as the nature of objects"? It cannot be that the word undergoes a transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the form of an object, like milk transforming into the form of curd; for if it were subject to such transformation or modification, it would follow that it is impermanent, just like milk and the like.

Even if such were the case, non-duality would not be established; for the object, which is a modification of the word, is distinct from it—just as curd is a modification of milk—and because of this distinctness, there exists a difference established by cognition free from the disturbances of sublation, causal factors, or impurities.
Now, the claim that "the word manifests an object-appearance which, though unreal, appears like a net of sensory faculties"—this is the meaning of *vivarta*—is also not tenable.

This is because an external entity denoted by a word, such as a genus (*jāti*) or an individual (*vyakti*), has already been established; and because the relationship between the expression and the expressed, such as mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, has also been previously proven. Furthermore, the analysis of the parts [of words] will be demonstrated shortly thereafter.
Furthermore, we do not perceive any reason here why the network of the sense faculties should be non-correspondent with reality, as is the case with dreams and the like.

Now, the argument for the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) is that the word appears in the form of the object, just as mother-of-pearl appears in the form of silver; yet even this is not more convincing. For it can be said that the mother-of-pearl shines like silver because such an appearance is possible through a similarity of form between the mother-of-pearl and silver.

But in this case, since the word and its object have entirely dissimilar natures, and no cause for the superimposition of one’s form upon the other can be determined, how can one thing appear in the form of another?
Furthermore, in cases such as mother-of-pearl and silver, that [illusory nature] is understood due to the force of sublation (*bādhaka*).
But in this case, it has been explained that there is no sublation, nor will there be any.

Now, the claim that the transformation of the word (*śabda-vivarta*) consists in its imparting a cognition of an object—whether real or unreal—while not abandoning its own penetration (*anuvedha*), has also been refuted just now;
for it has been demonstrated that there are numerous cognitions which are largely devoid of the penetration of the word.

Furthermore, no wise person perceives any other mode of transformation (*vivarta-prakāra*) such that one could say "it transforms into the form of an object" (*arthabhāvena vivartate*); thus, this statement is inexpressible.

Now, the claim that the Word-Brahman alone creates the world is stated as a theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*); yet even this is not correct, because, being insentient, the Word cannot function as a creator in the same way as the Lord (*īśvara*).
Nor can it be its cause in the manner of atoms (*paramāṇu*), since the effects such as earth and so forth are perceived as being composed of constituent parts through inherence.

If, following the scriptural statement "Consciousness, bliss, Brahman," the state of being conscious is described as belonging to the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman) just as its omnipresence is, then the name "Word-Brahman" would simply have been applied to the Lord (Īśvara) himself.

As for what is said—"Two Brahmans are to be known: the Brahman of sound and that which is the supreme Brahman; one who is proficient in the Brahman of sound attains the supreme Brahman"—even in that case, Brahman is not truly abundant or entirely transcendent, because one of the two Brahmans is merely conceptual.
Or, if it were not the case that [the world] is merely a mental construction (*ākārapratibhāsa*), how could there be the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*)?
Therefore, enough with this *śabdabrahman*;
may there be well-being for the Supreme Brahman.

Furthermore, the notion that the manifestation of various distinctions is produced by the illusion of ignorance (*avidyāmāyā*) has already been refuted on the occasion of critiquing the non-duality of existence (*sattādvaita*); thus, it is established that the non-duality of sound (*śabdādvaita*) is likewise untenable for the same reason.
By this, the doctrine that the Supreme Self is the material cause is also refuted;
for it is logically impossible that the Supreme Self, which is by nature immaculate, should be the cause of such impure transformations.
The claim that the entire collection of transformations appears within the Supreme Self due to ignorance, despite being unreal, has also been refuted;
therefore, in every respect, no position of non-duality (advaita) is faultless.

Now, as for the claim that there is only one single Self for all living beings and not multiple Selves—that too is without proof. For we observe a fixed distinction: when one person is happy, not everyone is happy; when one person is suffering, not everyone is suffering. Furthermore, the conventional usage of "self" and "other," which is established by the common consensus of all people, is impossible to deny. Moreover, when an object that is a cause of pleasure or pain has been perceived by one [person], the entire range of effects such as desire, aversion, and so forth—which are preceded by memory and mental synthesis—is not observed in another.
And because, when one person who is free from passion has attained liberation, others see that the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) remains infinite.
Because the notion of "I," which functions with respect to the inner self, cannot possibly apply to anything else;
because the diversity of the world, which is based on attributes restricted to distinct individuals, would otherwise be inexplicable;
and because the distinction between selves is clearly established.

Furthermore, since the refutation of the collection of examples—such as the sparks of heated iron, the space within a jar, and the sensation of pain in the feet—has already been established, the doctrine of a single self (ekātmavāda) is likewise not tenable; enough of this elaboration.

How could this entire manifold of objects, which flashes forth as a manifestation (*vivarta*) of sound and appears with forms distinct from it, be a transformation (*vikṛti*) of Brahman? Therefore, the creation of the elements arises from atoms set in motion by the will of the Lord, which manifests in accordance with the ripening of the various good and evil deeds accumulated by individual souls.
While all the proponents of non-duality remained thus silent,
the learned proponent of non-duality, however, spoke up once more.
It is indeed logical not to accept that Brahman—which is real, without origination, without cessation, immeasurable, and non-dual—is endowed with reasoning;

for we perceive that it is consciousness alone that is momentary, characterized by arising and passing away, proceeding as a beginningless stream of continuity, which appears in such and such ways, and that there is no such thing as a second, objective form distinct from it.

But surely, since it has been shown by means of valid cognitions such as direct perception that there is a cognition of the essential natures of mutually dissimilar objects, how can this appearance belong to consciousness? For, in the absence of an object, the nature of consciousness would be untenable;
indeed, consciousness consists in the grasping of an object to be grasped, not in the grasping of a grasping.
It is said: first, let this be examined.
Regarding this perceptual cognition which arises as "this is blue" or "this is yellow," does a single form manifest therein, or a pair?
If these two appear—the object as "this is blue" and its cognition—then what is there to be deliberated upon? You have already won;
let whatever follows for the victor be assigned to us.

Now, if this single form alone manifests, then there is occasion for investigation: to whom does this form belong—is it of the object or of the cognition? And when that form is thus investigated, if it belongs to the object, then you, sirs, will be victorious.
"But on the side of Jñānākara, we shall go," they said.
What, then, is reasonable here? That this is the aspect (ākāra) of cognition.
Why? Because, for now, the conceptual construction (kalpanā) involved here is the simpler one.

For in the view that objects are external, since an object whose nature is insentient cannot be self-luminous, it could not otherwise function as an apprehended object; thus, the postulation of another apprehending subject necessarily follows, resulting in a redundancy of assumptions.

Now, if it is argued that the object itself, which is of the nature of the apprehended (*grāhya*), is what is called the apprehender (*grāhaka*), then since that [apprehender] is indeed luminosity (*prakāśa*), the dispute would be merely over terminology.
If it is claimed that there is a distinction based on being external or internal, then alas, the "beloved of the gods" (the fool) is a connoisseur of distinctions!
For the externality of the apprehended consists precisely in its being severed from the apprehender.
External status does not belong to that which depends upon the body.

And when the apprehending subject is held to be non-different from the apprehended object, then it is not separated from it; thus, because it is not external, it is simply cognition itself—so how can there be no dispute over the name?
Since cognition is established for both [parties], it is logical that this form belongs to it;
for there is no dispute whatsoever regarding cognition.
Therefore, it is correct to say that this form belongs to that [cognition] alone, because the postulation of a single object is superior to the postulation of multiple things.
And for this reason, this is the form of cognition;
for you maintain that cognition is the illuminator of an object that is itself non-illuminating.
Consequently, it must be apprehended prior to the object.
For it is observed that light, such as a lamp, does not function as an illuminator when it is not itself apprehended.
Furthermore, even when objects such as jars have arisen, their non-apprehension occurs either due to a deficiency in illumination or due to the presence of an obstruction;
however, for knowledge that has already arisen, there is no obstacle whatsoever to its being apprehended.
Nor does it depend on another illuminator, because, like a lamp, its very nature is illumination by itself.
Therefore, at the very moment of its arising, its apprehension must necessarily occur;
otherwise, it would not occur even at a later time.
For what will there be for it at another time, or what was not present then, by virtue of which it would be grasped at another time but is not grasped then?
If it is argued that it will be grasped at another time by another cognition, then by what will that [second cognition] be grasped? If you say by yet another, then what is the limit?

If you say, "It is due to fatigue," then indeed one might cease meditating out of weariness; however, one would simply not have grasped the object at all, because if the illumination [of the cognition] is not apprehended, it is impossible to discern that which is illuminated by it. Thus, there would never be a grasping of the object.
Therefore, even for one who maintains that the object is grasped, the prior apprehension of the cognition must necessarily be admitted.
As it has been said: "For one whose perception is not itself perceived, the seeing of the object is not established."

Therefore, it is thus: because of the observation of a subsequent reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) following upon cognition—namely, the reflective awareness, "This object has been known by me"—cognizers infer the prior apprehension of the cognition itself from that reflective awareness. For there can be no cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) without the apprehension of its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it is established that the apprehension of cognition must also precede it.
Furthermore, since knowledge being apprehended cannot be grasped as devoid of an aspect (ākāra), it must necessarily be accepted as possessing an aspect itself.
When knowledge is apprehended as having an aspect, and given the absence of a second cause [for the appearance of that aspect], how could there be an external object distinct from knowledge?

For this reason as well, knowledge possesses an aspect; otherwise, its systematic determination according to specific objects (pratikarmavyavasthā) would be untenable in the absence of such an aspect.
Even if one were to postulate an external object, the possession of a form by consciousness must necessarily be asserted in order to establish the restriction of its objects.
For how is it that this cognition of blue, arising when many things are present, takes as its objective support exclusively the blue alone, while excluding all other entities?
This is because its nature as pure awareness is indistinguishable with respect to all things.
Furthermore, how could the activity of those who act with foresight be directed toward that single object alone?

Nor is it appropriate to say that this restriction to the apprehension of that [object] is caused by its being produced from blue, because since it is also produced by other causal factors such as light and the eyes, it would follow that it must have them as its objects as well.
Therefore, the very fact of having the form of blue (*nīlākāratā*) is the cause for establishing that blue is the object, and not any other factor.

And it has been said: "In that regard, because cognition—which is essentially similar [to its object]—is manifested by means of that which is non-self (the external object), it is differentiated according to each respective object. For this very reason, when the object is established by relying on the excellence consisting precisely in the grasping of the form (*ākāra*), cognition itself will be the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) and thus the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Otherwise, in the absence of the observation of such an excellence in the causal factor (*kāraka*), it would be difficult to establish its status as the most effective instrument for that [cognition].
Furthermore, even in worldly convention, there is seen a practice that bears witness to knowledge possessing an aspect (*sākāra*).
Thus do worldly people speak: "This object is blue, because a cognition with its form has arisen here.
Therefore, since the restriction of each specific action would otherwise be inexplicable, cognition must necessarily possess an aspect.
Even if an external object exists in this way, the postulation of a form for cognition might still occur; therefore, it would be better to remain satisfied with that alone.

However, those who maintain that because cognition is by nature inherently clear (*svaccha-svabhāva*), the appearance of blue, yellow, and so forth must necessarily be due to an external adjunct (*paropādhi*), just as a crystal takes on redness through contact with lacquer and the like;

and therefore, although an external object is not experienced separately, it is inferred from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the appearance of the image within cognition—as it has been said: "The existence of the external would be established through [the cognition's] singularity."
This is untenable because no positive concomitance is observed.
For when an object exists, cognition is with-form; in its absence, it is without-form.
Where has a proponent of the doctrine that external objects are always inferable ever seen such cognition?

In the case of lac, crystal, and the like, such [coloring] is indeed possible, because one observes fragments of crystal colored by them. But here, on the other hand, we certainly do not perceive cognition— which is by nature formless— being colored by an object, as a crystal is [colored] by lac.
For it has been stated that there is no manifestation of two forms. Or, if such a position were accepted, the fault of an insurmountable infinite regress would be difficult to avoid.

Furthermore, if it is asserted that the form of the object is perceived and the form of the cognition produced by it is also perceived, then first of all, the form of the object must be grasped by a cognition that possesses a form.
Now, even this cognition possessing a form would become another cognition with a form because it is an object of apprehension;
and that other cognition possessing a form would likewise have to be apprehended by yet another cognition of the same nature—this is an undesirable consequence.

Now, if that cognition is held to be self-luminous and endowed with a form (*sākāra*), then because it does not depend on another cognition, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Indeed, since no form of an object distinct from the self-luminous, formal cognition appears, let that [cognition alone] be the case.
Whence, then, could there now be a second—the form of the object? Nor is the postulation of such a thing justified even by the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*).
For this is not a royal decree that cognition must possess a form corresponding to the object;
what fault would there be if cognition itself were to possess the form of blue and so forth?
If it is argued that [the fault is] that the object would [then] come to possess the form of blue and so forth due to its connection with that form, [we reply:]...

It has been stated that there is dispute regarding cognition (*saṃjñā*). If it is argued that, because a second [cognition] is absent and because cognition is inherently clear, it is logical that its turbidity is caused by something else, [we reply: that will be produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Although cognition is clear by its own nature, it appears as if its form were stained by the turbidity of manifold aspects, brought about by the manifestation of the beginningless latent impressions of ignorance.

Furthermore, because the distinction between the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the continuum of cognition is beginningless—just like the relationship between a seed and a sprout—there is no occasion for the objection: "From where did these impressions arise?

Therefore, since the variety of cognitions is established by the variety of beginningless impressions, there is no need for an external object as something to be inferred; thus it is proven that this form belongs to cognition alone.
Therefore, this form belongs to cognition alone; for apart from cognition, the form of an object is never perceived anywhere.

Cognition, however, is clearly perceived even when devoid of an object, as in the case of a city of Gandharvas, illusions, and the like. Thus, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), we understand that [the object] has the nature of being a form of cognition. Furthermore, if the object were to exist as a self-subsistent entity separate from cognition, it would be perceived even in the absence of cognition; but such is not the case.
Therefore, there is indeed no difference between cognition and its object; as it has been said: "Because they are invariably perceived together, blue and the cognition thereof are non-different."
Furthermore, the form (ākāra) cannot be a property arising from the conjunction of cognition and the object.

For if we were to perceive the object separately as being without form, and the cognition separately as being without form, and then perceive that the two conjoined cognitions possess form, only then could we conclude that this form is a property of their conjunction.
But such a sequence does not exist.
Furthermore, it has been stated that even though memories and cognitions such as those of dreams lack an external object, they nevertheless possess a formal aspect (ākāra).

Therefore, how can the formal aspect be a property resulting from a relation [between an object and a cognition]? Moreover, in the case of the single object "star," how could there be the coexistence of mutually contradictory grammatical genders, as in *nakṣatram*, *tārakā*, and *tiṣya*?

And how could a single object in the form of a woman experience the state of being the domain of three distinct appearances—as a corpse for a wandering ascetic, as a mistress for a lustful man, and as food for a dog?
Regarding the word *dārāḥ*, how could a single individual woman come to be the object of a masculine plural expression?
And as for the term "ṣaṇṇagarī" (the six cities), how could there be both the unification and the feminine gender of many things that possess different genders?
Furthermore, since short and long [vowels] are perceived only in mutual dependence upon one another, how could either one of these forms be ultimately real?

However, because cognitions are distinct, there is no contradiction whatsoever in their arising in accordance with the forms of various auxiliary conditions, such as the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Therefore, it is cognition alone that appears in various ways everywhere; there is no such thing as an object distinct from it. Thus, this entire conventional usage of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the act of knowing (*pramiti*) is fully contained within cognition itself. For its state of possessing the form of the object is the *prameya*, its state of possessing the apprehending form is the *pramāṇa*, and self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is the result (*phala*).
As it has been said: "That which appears [in cognition] is the *prameya*; the states of being the *pramāṇa* and the *phala* [belong to cognition] in turn."
Therefore, the triad consisting of the grasped, the grasper, and the self-awareness has not been made separate from this [consciousness].

Thus, because the vision of reality has been distorted by the play of the habitual tendencies of beginningless ignorance, knowledge itself appears as if it possessed the distinction between the grasped object and the grasping subject within the mind;
however, upon the cessation of ignorance, it becomes purely transparent, such that "nothing at all" is perceived.

Thus it has been said: "There is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there another experience of it; because it is devoid of the distinction between grasped object and grasping subject, it manifests itself by its own nature. (PVin 1.38) Manorathanandin: [The intellect] does not manifest as something other than its own form, due to the absence of the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender; it shines forth by itself.

In that way, although the nature of cognition is undivided, it appears as if possessed of the distinctions of the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness to those whose vision is distorted.
Thus, seeing that this is indeed mere consciousness, devoid of both object and form,
one abandons the succession of suffering and attains the fearless state of nirvāṇa.

To this it is replied: Indeed, a single conscious self cannot possess the dual nature of being both the apprehended object and the apprehending subject, because it is impossible for two forms such as the apprehended and the apprehender—which are mutually dissimilar—to coexist within a single entity. For instance, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is determined that the nature of consciousness is distinct from blue and other objects; even when the arising or ceasing of blue, yellow, white, and so forth occurs, the form of consciousness persists as the cognition "this is the knowledge of blue," "this is the knowledge of yellow," and "this is the knowledge of white. Thus, it is established by these means to be different from blue and the like.
Moreover, you have accepted that cognition has the ego as its locus, possesses a nature consisting of bliss and so forth, and appears as if it were active in its own operation;
the object, however, does not have such a nature. How, then, can there be non-difference between these two?

Even though there is no appearance of two distinct forms such as "this is cognition" and "this is the object," nevertheless, when this single form appears, it appears only as that which is illumined (*prakāśya*), not as the illuminator (*prakāśaka*). The form of the apprehended (*grāhya*) appears as entirely separate from the apprehender (*grāhaka*), as in "this is blue"; there is no appearance of their identity as in "I am blue. Thus, [the object] does not appear as one with [the subject].
Moreover, it is reasonable that the apprehension of an object of illumination, such as blue, is dependent upon the illuminating cognition;
however, it must be considered what causes the apprehension of that very cognition which performs the grasping.
It cannot be based on another cognition, for that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.
Nor is cognition self-luminous, because there is no such manifestation as "I am blue."
Is it not the case that there is indeed no difference between the apprehended and the apprehender?
That which you have accepted as the appearance of the apprehended is itself the appearance of the apprehender;
for if the apprehended were other than the apprehender, it would necessarily be insentient by nature.
The subject, however, has the nature of luminosity precisely because it is the subject.
And it has already been stated that there is no manifestation of duality.

In that regard, when one or the other appears, upon considering which of the two—the insentient or the luminous—is logically fit to manifest, by necessity it is luminosity alone that manifests, not the insentient.

Furthermore, that which is formless cannot manifest as manifestation; therefore, when that [cognition] possessing form is being manifested, how could there be an insentient object existing apart from it?
This is improper, because the concealment of that which is to be reached by means of the means itself cannot be accomplished;
for the eye is the illuminator of form—
it is not possible to deny the existence of form simply by saying, "Let the eye alone be the illumination."

Therefore, this cognition—which possesses a nature contrary to that of the object, whose self is characterized by specific attributes such as form, fluidity, and solidity—is the illuminator; it is not that very object itself which can manifest [the cognition], just as the eye cannot manifest [itself].
[Objection: But surely cognition possesses the status of an instrument (upāyatva) like the eye, because its intrinsic nature is illumination (*prakāśasvabhāvatva*).

For that which is called "illumination" produced by the eye is designated as cognition; and it is a well-known principle that an unapprehended illumination does not illuminate the object to be illuminated. [Response: True, the illumination produced by the eye is accepted as cognition. However, that illumination is the illumination of objects such as color-form (*rūpa*), not the illumination of illumination itself.
For light is not illuminated by the eye; rather, form (rūpa) is illuminated.
In this context, that which is called "form" is the object, the apprehended; that which is said to "illuminate" is the illumination, namely the cognition, the apprehender.
And since form becomes illuminated merely through the arising of that [cognition], illumination does not depend upon being apprehended.

But has it not been stated here that "an object does not manifest when cognition is unperceived; for one whose perception is not itself perceived, the seeing of the object is not established"? That is incorrect; on the contrary, for one whose perception is not itself perceived, the seeing of the object is indeed established.
The very arising of the perception is the seeing of the object, and not the seeing of the perception itself.

[Objection: But surely, if there is no apprehension of the cognition itself, then because there would be no distinction between its production and non-production, even an object whose perception has not arisen would be perceptible; thus, the consequence follows that everyone would be omniscient. [Reply: This is a very clever argument! For perception is indeed of the nature of the manifestation of the object. How then could that which has not arisen not be distinguished from that which has arisen?

Therefore, since knowledge consists in the direct perception of the object, it is precisely its production that constitutes the perceptibility of the object, not its apprehension. Thus, it is logical that cognition makes the object manifest even while it remains unapprehended.
As for the claim that knowledge is mentioned first because it serves as a means (upāya), it has been stated that this is inconclusive (anaikāntika) with respect to the eyes and other sense organs.
If cognition, once apprehended, were to illuminate its object—like smoke or like a lamp—it must be stated which it is; if it is like smoke, [then...]
There would be the consequence that [the cognition] is inferable from its object, but that has been refuted by you yourself;
moreover, it is not like a lamp, because there is no perception of two distinct forms.

In the cognition "I see the jar by means of a lamp," there is the perception of two things; however, there is no apprehension of a duality in the form "I know the object of knowledge by means of knowledge."

As for the claim that cognition must be apprehended prior [to its object] because it is luminous (*prakāśatva*), like a lamp—that too must be explained: what is the meaning of "because it is luminous"?

If "luminous" (*prakāśa*) means "that which illuminates," then its state is "luminosity" (*prakāśatva*); this has already been stated to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the eyes and other [senses].
If, on the other hand, "manifestation" (prakāśa) means "the act of manifesting" (prakāśana), then the reason "because of being manifest" (prakāśatvāt) is unestablished (asiddha);
for at the time of apprehending an object, there is no manifestation of the cognition itself.
Now, if the word "illumination" (*prakāśa*) is indeed a synonym for "cognition" (*bodha*),
meaning that because of its luminosity it has the nature of cognition,
then the example is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*), since a lamp lacks the nature of cognition.
Therefore, the position of self-awareness is not logically tenable, because nothing whatsoever has ever been observed to possess self-luminosity.

Now, as for the claim that cognition, words, and lamps are illuminators of both themselves and others—that is incorrect. For both words and lamps depend upon other causal complexes for their own apprehension and for the illumination of objects.
A word depends upon the apprehension of convention (*samaya*) for the illumination of an object, but upon the sense of hearing for its own illumination.
A lamp, too, is itself apprehended only by depending on the eye and so forth, and it causes the object to be apprehended in the same way.
However, there is this distinction: in the perception of objects such as a jar, the eye functions in dependence upon light; but in the perception of light itself, it functions independently.
Yet, by this much alone, the lamp would not possess self-illumination.
And in this way, in relation to the eyes of nocturnal animals such as cats, all things including jars would be self-luminous.

It is observed that cognition possesses only the property of illuminating other things, not self-illumination, because it has been shown that at the time of illuminating an object, it itself is not illuminated.

In vain have these three—lamp, cognition, and sound—been declared by you to be illuminators of both self and other; for they are designated as lamp, cognition, and sound because they are objects of knowledge and knowers produced by distinct causal complexes.

But for those who maintain that the self is directly perceived, a distinction between the apprehended and the apprehending aspects certainly exists due to the difference in their states; therefore, cognition is not self-luminous in any way whatsoever.

As for what was also asserted—that cognition, at the very moment it arises, is apprehended precisely then because it is independent and unimpeded, and not otherwise at any other time—that too is incorrect, because at that time the causal complex for its apprehension is absent.
Nor is cognition possible through mere non-obstruction; for even in the absence of a means [of apprehension], there would then be no grasping of that knowledge.
Furthermore, unlike the followers of Jaimini, we do not declare knowledge to be eternally imperceptible;
for we observe that at a later time, there is the apprehension of an object qualified by that [knowledge], as in the cognition: "This object has been known by me."
Just as in the cognition "this is a white cloth," that [cloth] appears as possessing that quality,
so too in the case of the cognition "the object is known," the object appears as a qualifier of the cognition.
Nor is there cognition of the qualified object when its qualifier has not been apprehended;
nor do you perceive a subsequent cognition [of the whole] in this manner, because no sequence [of cognitions] is apprehended.
Furthermore, it has already been examined that cognition which is eternally beyond the senses cannot even be inferred.
Enough, then, with this talk;
why should we now pursue Śrītriyā, having already abandoned her?

And therefore, as for what was said—that because one observes the reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) following the cognition, the apprehension of the object is preceded by the apprehension of the cognition—that is not universal; rather, it is accepted only in certain cases due to the experience of an object qualified by a cognition.

Consequently, since the cognition does not manifest prior to the apprehension of the object and since there is an absence of a determination (*avasāya*) of a form [belonging to the cognition], this claim that "this form belongs to the cognition itself" is a mere vain prattle of those whose garments are dyed red with the dawn of ignorance.

Furthermore, as for what was further asserted—that on the position that cognition possesses a form (jñānākāra), conceptual construction (kalpanā) is minimal—in that case, according to the reasoning already stated, when the external object is the apprehended thing accessible to perception, what kind of conceptual construction could there be?
Or of what nature would that "minimality" or "magnitude" be?

As for what was said regarding the fact that cognition is established for both parties: if the status of an entity depends upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the object too is indeed established for both.
But if the status of an entity were dependent on desire or aversion, how could even the cognition itself be established for both? Thus, this [objection] is trivial.

Furthermore, as for this which was stated— that even while admitting an external object, the connection of form (*ākāra*) must be accepted in cognition in order to establish the determination of each respective object (*pratikarmavyavasthā*)— that too is not correct, because the determination of each respective object is possible through another means.
Even if a cognition of blue arises when many things are present,

and even though the nature of consciousness (*bodhasvarūpatva*) is common to all [objects], nevertheless, since it is produced by the objective factor (*karmakāraka*) of blue alone, it remains fixed as residing in blue alone.

If it is argued that [the cognition] is also produced by the eye and so forth, that is true—it is indeed produced—but not by the eye as an existing action (*karman*). Rather, it arises through blue which has become the object (*karman*); therefore, it has precisely that [blue] as its single object.
If it is asked, "From what does this restriction arise? it is simply brought about by the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things.
This same objection applies equally even in the case of the aspect (ākāra).

As for what is asked—why it is that blue alone is the objective factor (karmakāraka), or why it is that cognition has blue alone as its object—the answer must be stated in terms of the intrinsic natures (vastusvabhāva) of things.

Furthermore, regarding how cognition takes on a form as its material cause—why does it take on the form of the very agent of the action and not that of another agent? In this matter as well, the inherent nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*) alone is the refuge.
Furthermore, that an object generates knowledge is understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
For when someone seeking Devadatta goes to his house,
if he is not present there, he does not see him even after having gone.
In another moment, he perceives Devadatta approaching;
therein, the nature of that cognition consists in the existence or non-existence of that [object].

When Devadatta was in the future, the cognition of his divinity did not arise; when he arrived, that cognition arose. Since [the cognition] exists only when he exists, it is determined to be produced by him. And since the restriction [of the cognition to its object] is thus established solely through being produced by that [object], enough with the postulation of a mental form (ākāra).
By this, the activity of a person directed toward a specific object is also explained.
Furthermore, the status of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) has already been determined in the general definition of the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, even the worldly designation that was cited is inconsistent;

for ordinary people do not designate it by saying, "This object is blue because a cognition having that as its object has arisen. Therefore, what was stated—that even though an object exists, cognition must be admitted to possess a form—is untenable.

As for the claim that there is no difference between the blue object and the cognition thereof because they are necessarily perceived together, that too appears to us like the talk of a child, since the meaning of "together" (saha) is untenable if there is no difference.

Now, if the intended meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is "because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension" (*ekopalambhaniyamāt*), then this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). This is because at the time of perceiving the object to be grasped (*grāhya*), such as blue and so forth, its grasper (*grāhaka*) is not perceived.

Indeed, what is demonstrated in such instances as "this is blue" is merely the appearance of an external object to be grasped, which is distinct from that [subject] and devoid of any permeation by the form of a grasper.
And in some cases, there is observed even a mere reflection upon the subject unattached to the form of the object, as in: "I do not remember that any object was grasped by me at that time.
Thus, since there is a perception of the forms of both knowledge and the object as mutually distinct, how [can they be identical]?
It is said that "there is no difference between the blue and the cognition thereof because of the rule of their being perceived together.
By saying "between the blue and the cognition thereof," you yourself are actually pointing out this very difference.

If it is argued that this is merely a restatement of the opponent's view, we say no; for if there were no difference [between the cognition and its form], even a separate designation of them would be impossible.
Therefore, for this reason as well, this is not the form of the cognition.

As for the claim that even in the absence of an external object, the cognition itself possesses a form—as seen in dreams, gandharva-cities, illusions, and the like, and therefore it is logical that this form belongs to that very cognition—that too is mere wishful thinking, because in all cases there appears a form of its own apprehended object distinct from the cognition.

For in erroneous cognitions, there are four possible theories: self-manifestation (ātmakhyāti), manifestation of the non-existent (asatkhyāti), non-apprehension (akhyāti), or misapprehension (viparītakhyāti).

In that case, because there is the appearance of a single object through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form "this is silver," and because according to that [Yogācāra] view consciousness is immediate (*aparokṣa*), one who desires that object acts toward it under the conceit of having apprehended silver; furthermore, since the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) arises as being intent upon negating such a cognition, it is not the case that this is non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), as has already been established previously.
Even the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) does not hold, because that which is absolutely non-existent, such as a sky-flower, cannot possibly appear in consciousness.
Even an erroneous cognition in living beings has as its object only a thing previously experienced but separated by space and time; it does not have an absolutely non-existent object.
For error is of two kinds: that born of the external senses and that which is mental.

Among these, in the case of erroneous cognition arising from the external senses—whether produced by a defect in the object or a defect in the sense organ—no instance is observed where there is a lack of an objective basis (*nirālambanatā*).
Indeed, due to a defect in the object, such as its resemblance to a shining form, mother-of-pearl appears as silver.
The solar radiance fallen upon a desert expanse shines as water due to its resemblance to shimmering waves;
likewise, due to a defect of the sense organ, sugar appears bitter to one whose sense of taste is afflicted by bile;
and for one whose visual faculty is partitioned by cataracts, even the single orb of the moon appears as two.

Furthermore, the very rays of the eyes, having issued forth through the apertures of the mass of specks in the cataract and being mingled with the sun's rays, appear in their subtle state as having the form of a tuft of hair.

However, that delusion which arises through a defect of the internal organ occurs even in the absence of a woman and so forth, for those whose selves have been captivated by the flower-arrowed god [Kāma].
That too is sometimes accompanied by the defects of the object, and that [defect] resides precisely in the objective support.

Just as the cognition "this is her hand" might arise in some instances with respect to a young sprout trembling in the waves of pure breezes; [so too does the cognition of self arise with respect to the aggregates].
Furthermore, the thought of a proud woman whose mind—due to the power of the intoxication of love—is filled with longing for a man who does not even look at her; |||

In that [recollection] as well, there is a mental representation of the form and other qualities of a woman perceived in the past, brought forth by memory which is overwhelmed by the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as passion; however, it is not like the [representation] of something absolutely non-existent, such as a donkey’s horn.
Even in a dream, which arises from mental afflictions such as flashes of inspiration or sleep, there is only the recollection of that very form previously perceived.

When one perceives substances melting due to fire ignited by a lattice-work, the question arises whether the form resides elsewhere or in another place; however, it is not that such a form is non-existent.
Thus, in erroneous cognitions, there is no manifestation of things that are absolutely non-existent;
rather, it is only the alteration of the object's place and time that appears.
Now, if an object that is non-existent appears there, what use is its existence in another location and so forth?
For whether it exists or does not exist in another location, that object is simply not present there [at the time of appearance].
And there is no distinction whatsoever between two types of non-existence.

If one considers whether the place and time also appear as existing or non-existing, the same fault applies to them as well. Do not say this; for you too, who maintain the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), is that non-existence of the object accepted everywhere, or only in that specific place? In the first case, what is your own position gained by mere non-proximity? But if it manifests as non-existent everywhere, how does this restriction arise—that despite the lack of distinction in their non-existence, only non-existent silver and the like manifest, and not things such as a donkey’s horn?

However, this is the distinction between the two types of non-existence: it is logical that an object which is non-existent in another location and so forth may appear through the mediation of memory and the like, but this is not possible for that which is absolutely non-existent.
In this same way, the objection regarding the conceptualization of existence and non-existence concerning space and time should also be refuted.

And since there is no cognition whatsoever that grasps an absolutely non-existent object, why should one postulate the voidness of all objects everywhere on the strength of an illustrative example? Therefore, non-apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti) is not [the case].
But as for the theory of self-manifestation (*ātmakhyāti*), this is a great calamity indeed, since it is formless.

And regarding that, it has been stated many times: the object of cognition appears as strictly distinct from the subject, such that one perceives "this is blue," rather than "this is blue" as something separate from that [subject].
In cases of erroneous cognition, let there be error because the object is not present; it is not, however, the grasping of the true nature of the self.
And as for what is said—that the form which is an internal object of cognition appears as if it were external—this would amount to an admission of *viparītakhyāti* (misapprehension).
Therefore, it is better that this very [theory], though wretched, be accepted as the more sound one.

Now it is said: "The object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is truly distinct from the act of apprehension (*grahaka*"; however, that [object] is of the very nature of cognition (*jñāna*). In this regard, the claim that it is "distinct" has been stated agreeably; but what is the reasoning for its being cognition? Furthermore, the relationship of apprehended and apprehender (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) is not tenable between two cognitions, whether they arise simultaneously or sequentially.
For if they were simultaneous, there would be no fixed rule of apprehended and apprehender, just as in the case of the left and right horns of a cow.

Even in the case of succession, if the former [moment] were the grasper of the latter, it would abandon its momentariness because of the observation of its production and its grasping at the same time.
If the latter were the grasper of the former, the same argument applies;
for without persisting for that duration of time, it is impossible for it to be grasped by that [former].

Furthermore, no universal called "cognitiveness" (jñānatva) appears as something inherent in both the apprehended and the apprehender, like "cowness" (gotva) in a brindled cow and other individual cows.
Therefore, if the apprehended portion were distinct from the apprehender, it would be the object itself; thus, this cannot be a form belonging to cognition.

As for what was stated—that the nature of a relation (*saṃsarga*) cannot be the form (*ākāra*)—that is indeed correct; for there is no relation whatsoever between the object and the cognition, like that between a vessel and its contents, nor can there be possession of a form produced by such a relation in those two which were previously devoid of form.

Thus, because the arguments stated by Śakyamati are weak, because there is a manifestation of interruption everywhere, and because the diversity of cognition as it actually exists is untenable, it is established that this form belongs to the object itself.

As for the objection raised against the theory that the object possesses its own form—namely, that it is not logical for mutually contradictory forms such as "nakṣatra," "tārakā," and "tiṣya" to coexist in a single object—it is replied: our conviction is that nothing is impossible where it is not contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). We understand even what is contradictory provided we do not perceive it as being resident in a single locus.
Therefore, if these three distinct forms are clearly apprehended in one place by an uncontradicted cognition, how could this not be possible, or how could it be contradictory?

If it is understood that one [form] has a nature definitively established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while the other is conceptual (*kālpnika*), let it be so; what is the fault? Furthermore, the coexistence of multiple colors is observed in things such as a variegated painting.
Nor is it appropriate to assume a contradiction or non-contradiction everywhere simply because it was observed in one instance.
For the actual states of things are based on uncontradicted cognition, not upon constructions of the imagination.
Alternatively, the grammatical correctness of the employment of words might be explained solely by disregarding whether the actual nature of the object exists or does not exist.
The word *dārāḥ* does not possess either masculinity or plurality with respect to a single individual woman;
rather, this word is grammatically correct when employed in that sense.
Its lack of contact with the object does not, however, remain established merely by that much;
rather, it is able to express the thing exactly as it is in its essential nature.
Furthermore, the cognitions of corpses and so forth produced by wandering mendicants and others do not entail the emptiness of objects, because an object possesses multiple capacities.
Is that woman not capable of being devoured by a dog?
Or does she not quench the fever of passion in those who desire her?
Or in what form would she be distinguished from a corpse for the yogin?
For the threefold cognition does not belong to all [beings], due to the absence of auxiliary causes.

For the acquisition of each specific cognition depends upon the cooperation of various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) determined for each individual; thus, there is no cognition characterized by total similarity for all [beings].
If that is so, O virtuous one, if the diversity of latent impressions alone is the cause for the arising of various appearances, what is the use of postulating external objects?
Why do you still not abandon this long-practiced verbal artifice of conceptual construction?
For an object is not merely postulated; rather, it simply appears.

However, regarding that [cognition] which possesses many forms, some cause such as a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is postulated in certain cases to determine the delimitation of one particular form among them;
but to that extent, there is no occasion for the denial of the object.

As for what was said—that the diversity of cognitions is caused solely by the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and that the beginningless succession of mutual causality between cognition and latent impression is like that of a seed and a sprout—that too is untenable. What is this so-called "latent impression"? If it is non-different from cognition, then because it too is of a transparent nature, it could not be the cause of the particularity of cognition. If the latent impression is different from cognition, then that which is the cause of its diversity would simply be the object itself, expressed by another name.
Moreover, what is known in the world as "latent impression" (*vāsanā*) is a mental formation (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the experience of an object.
And a mental formation, being constituted by a particular experience, produces a recollection of that very same thing on some occasion;
it does not, however, bring about such a variety [of effects] as this.

Furthermore, in the case of the Buddhist position, just as the relationship of grasped and grasper (*grāhya-grāhakabhāva*) among cognitions must be rejected due to their momentariness, so too must the relationship of perfumed and perfume (*vāsya-vāsanābhāva*) be rejected.
For it is enduring entities, such as sesame seeds, that are perfumed by enduring things, such as *campaka* flowers;
it is not the case that cognitions—which perish immediately upon arising—can perfume other cognitions of the same nature.
And because there is destruction without any continuity,
no part of that [preceding cognition] persists by which the subsequent cognition might somehow be impressed by the preceding one.
Moreover, within a single continuum such as that of Devadatta, there might arise thousands of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that produce a variety of cognitions;
for indeed, the cognition of an elephant does not arise from the latent impression of a cow.
Even though these [causes] are indeed infinite, from what source comes the restriction at the time of their commencement?
If they were to act without order, there would be a collapse of worldly convention.
When the cognition of smoke has been produced by the latent impression of smoke,
why would the latent impression of water not then produce a cognition of water?
Furthermore, the latent impressions (vāsanās) would only serve as causes for the initiation of a series of latent impressions, and would not strive to deposit a cognition of prior experience;
for your view is that "from the similar, the similar arises."

Moreover, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) do not exist without a substratum, and on your view, no such substratum is possible; for since cognition is momentary (*bhaṅguratva*), it cannot logically serve as their locus. If all habitual tendencies were based upon a single cognition, they would all perish when that cognition perishes.
If there were no difference in the substratum for each latent impression, then due to their infinity, there would be an indetermination with a hundred branches.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as the so-called *ālayavijñāna*.

Even if it existed as the substratum for thousands of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) without exception, because it is momentary, the destruction of the knowledge residing in the womb of such impressions would occur all at once.
And even if it were to arise again, how could that very same kind of knowledge be produced?
But there would be no fixed order for the cognition of cows, horses, and so forth; therefore, this path is entirely one of convention.
Thus, this is a mere mirage for ascetics, since the course of worldly life is established through mental impressions (*vāsanā*) alone—what need is there for an external object?
Enough with this excessive prolixity; for when examined by the wise over a long time, it is established that the form such as "blue" belongs to the object itself, and not to the cognition.
Furthermore, how can a single cognition bear the forms of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the resulting knowledge (*pramiti*)?
Moreover, it was stated previously, during the investigation of perception (*pratyakṣacintā*), that the result is distinct from the means of knowledge.

However, those who say, "Let the path of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) be set aside," and while conceptualizing the object of cognition (prameya) itself, do not admit any external object whatsoever as being beyond dispute;
for instance, this so-called "whole" (avayavin), such as a jar and so forth, is not at all conceivable, because no whole is perceived apart from its parts.
For whatever is distinct from something else is perceived in a location distinct from the location occupied by that thing, just as a cloth is perceived in a location distinct from that of a jar.
Furthermore, the whole (avayavin) is not perceived as occupying a location separate from its parts;
for when those [parts] are not apprehended, there is no cognition of that [whole].
Just as a cloth is perceived even when a jar is not, but a whole is not perceived when its parts are unperceived, how can it be distinct from them?
Furthermore, the perception of its parts is impossible;
for it is not possible to perceive all its parts, since only those situated on the near side would be perceived, while those located in the middle or further parts would not.
And because it is not perceived when analyzed by the intellect:

for when one places a cloth in the hand and analyzes it with the intellect, thinking "this is a thread, this is a thread," then, while analyzing from the eastern edge to the western edge, one perceives only the continuous series of threads and no composite whole (avayavin) distinct from them.
And because the mode of subsistence is untenable:
the whole does not subsist entirely in one part, for that would entail its non-existence in the other parts;
nor does it subsist by way of occupying a portion [of each], for there exists no location distinct from its own constituent parts.
Or, if it were admitted [that the whole exists in its parts], there would be the consequence of an infinite regress:
by what parts does that [whole] exist in those parts? By other parts; and in those [latter parts], by yet others—thus there would be no end.
Furthermore, if the whole were unconnected with its parts, how could it be connected even with its own constituent causes through the mediation of those parts?
Therefore, even though it is not devoid of fear, its function does not reside in the parts.

However, [powers such as] holding and attracting are observed even in wood, roots, cotton, and so forth, when their effects have not yet begun; thus, [the argument for a whole as a distinct entity] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

As for the cognition of a single form, that is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*). Based on causes such as occupying a single location, just as one has the notion of an "army" with respect to elephants, horses, foot-soldiers, and so forth, or a "forest" with respect to *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees, the cognition of a "jar" and so forth will likewise occur with respect to the accumulated parts themselves. Thus, through the thorough investigation of parts and sub-parts, nothing remains but a mere collection of atoms (*aṇu-saṃcaya-mātra*), and nothing else.
Furthermore, even an accumulation (*saṃcaya*), when analyzed as being either distinct or non-distinct [from its parts], does not exist at all; thus, only atoms (*aṇu*) remain.
Yet even atoms, through their simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms], result in each atom having six parts; thus, when subjected to such analysis, they too collapse.
Moreover, this worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) cannot be accomplished by those things which are so exceedingly subtle.
Therefore, since an external object of cognition cannot be established when subjected to analysis, one must accept that this is merely consciousness alone.
Even they, speaking in this manner, appear more pitiable than the monks of old;
for unprecedented is this path of reasoning, wherein, having abandoned established conviction, the determination of things is made by the snapping of fingers.
If the whole (avayavin) has indeed been apprehended by a firm means of valid cognition whose nature is free from sublation and the like, what is the use of these childish prattle?
Now, if there is no apprehension of that [object] by any means of valid cognition, let this very point be stated; what is the purpose of these alternatives regarding its mode of existence?
And we were not able, at every step, to engage in excessive quarreling with those wretched Śākyas, who, seeing nothing new or even slight, asked about the very same things again and again.
It has been established that determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It has also been shown that even by indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), an object is apprehended precisely as it is grasped by determinate perception, though devoid of the mere verbal expression (*śabdollekha*).

Furthermore, it has been described that apart from the single form of the object, nothing can be asserted regarding the basis for the unity of that cognition—such as its having a single effect or occupying a single location—other than [the fact that] it is otherwise established.

Nor is it correct to argue that because a sublation occurs in certain cases—such as when encountering an army or a forest—the cognition of a single entity is false, and therefore it is not logical to assume falsity in all instances;
for what is there that has not already been stated during the occasion of establishing the universal?
Therefore, by that very same principle, the composite (avayavin) is indeed established, since the perception grasping it is free from any exception.

As for the argument that [the whole] is not perceived because it is not perceived in distinct locations, and that there is no cognition of it when those [locations] are not perceived—the cause for this is simply its dependence upon its parts, not its non-existence.
For how could cognition belong to that location when there is a difference in location?
Indeed, it is not independent; rather, it rests upon its constituent parts.
In this case, it depends upon as many [factors] as there are for which the cognition of apprehension arises; it does not depend upon the apprehension of all [of them]. This is the established rule.
When the constituent parts are being analyzed, it is logical that the whole is not apprehended; for at that time, the destruction of the composite object indeed manifests in the mind.
For the separation of the parts is indeed the cause of the destruction of the whole (*avayavin*).
When that [separation] is delineated by the mind, the destruction of the whole would likewise not fail to be delineated; so how could the whole be perceived at that time?
Furthermore, its subsistence (*vṛtti*) in the parts is understood to be only as a collective whole (*vyāsajya*).
Its completion does not occur in each individual part, as is the case with a genus and its individual instances.
For that which exists as a distributed whole certainly does not exist [separately] through other parts, because it is not perceived [as such];
nevertheless, it indeed exists.
And thus they have said: "We say that it exists, because that which is without support is not perceived."
As for the claim that such a mode of operation has never been observed elsewhere:
what is the use of searching for an illustrative example regarding an object already perceived through direct perception?

Therefore, since the whole (avayavin) is perceived precisely through direct perception (pratyakṣa) by virtue of its existence in its parts, there is no occasion for alternative views regarding its subsistence therein.

Even the occurrence [of a whole] in its parts, such as in a garland or a thread, is accepted because it is observed to be so; therefore, why is this occurrence of a whole in its parts—which is of such a nature and accessible to perception—denied?
Furthermore, there is no argument whatsoever against the perception that apprehends a whole.
How can a cognition that arises from an unseen cause, for which no sublation has appeared, and which is free from doubt, be said to be false?

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to assert that the perception of a whole (*avayavin*) is like [the perception of] an army or a forest, because while that [assertion] is uncontradicted in the case of the army and so forth, there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) in their case.

Moreover, since the observation of elephants, horses, foot-soldiers, Pilu trees, Palāśa trees, Śiṃśapā trees, and so on is possible therein, the cognition of an "army" or "forest" as inherent in them might still be justified.
But here, one must consider whether the cognition of a "cloth" has the collection [of threads] as its object.

If it is argued that [the cognition of a cloth] has the collection of threads as its object, then what is the object of the cognition of the thread now? That too must have its own parts as its object; and if one continues to analyze part after part in this way, atoms must be stated to occupy the position of the "horse-ear" (*aśvaśama*), the *śimśapā* tree, and so forth. However, their apprehension in that manner is untenable because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*). Therefore, the cognition of a composite whole (*avayavin*) does not have those [atoms] as its object. Consequently, it is established that the composite whole exists as something perceivable by direct perception (*pratyakṣagrāhya*).
It has already been established that even atoms possess a nature that is eternal and partless, as determined through inference from their effects;
therefore, it is impossible to prove that they possess parts by means of their conjunction with six [other atoms] and so forth.
Furthermore, it will be shown that corporeality (mūrtatva) is not a probans for impermanence.
Therefore, even by way of an investigation into the objects of cognition (*prameya*), it is not easy to establish the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*).
For even in the examination of the object of cognition, it is precisely the functioning of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is scrutinized.

Consequently, that very same terrifying face of the discourse on the means of valid cognition has been encountered even upon that path of the discussion of objects of cognition which the Tathāgatas adopted after fleeing in fear from the debate concerning the means of valid cognition.
One is prepared to point out the path for every kind of calamity;
