yet when an obstacle arises in the course of action, where can one flee?
Therefore, whether a matter is possible or impossible according to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it must be determined as a reality.
Thus, this resorting to the blades of kuśa and kāśa grass is improper for you, resembling a mere act of suicide.
Thus, having abandoned this fruitless heron-like vow of the proponents of emptiness,
let worldly transaction proceed by means of external objects alone.

Now, if it is taught that "everything is empty," "everything is momentary," and "everything is without support" in order to produce a loosening of attachment, then what is the purpose of this false speech? For even while a self exists and while real entities exist, detachment certainly arises for those possessed of discernment through the perception of the defects in sense objects; thus, the description of doctrines such as Nihilism (*śūnyavāda*) for the sake of producing that [detachment] is a circuitous path.

On the contrary, the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), perceiving that the discourse on momentariness, selflessness, emptiness, and so forth is subverted by reason, suspects that this teaching is like a deception.
This adoption of the doctrine of emptiness belongs either to those devoid of intelligence or to those intent on deception; it does not belong to those who perceive the true nature of reality.
Therefore, when subjected to critical examination, this doctrine of the non-duality of consciousness, like the doctrine of the non-duality of sound and so forth,
turns out to be nothing more than a city of Gandharvas.
Thus, from the perspective of non-duality (advaita), the attainment of the supreme good for living beings is not perceived;
therefore, a person of action should strive for the realization of liberation through reflection on the true nature of the Self as it has been described.

As for that means for the method of achieving liberation which the Sāṅkhyas have stated—namely, the realization of the difference between primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the self—that has already been refuted.

Furthermore, who is capable of restraining primordial matter, which is ignorant, powerful, full of transformations, and binds the person (*puruṣa*), yet does nothing for him? Or rather, [who can restrain it] so that it binds no more?
A man has never performed even the slightest action that could serve as a cause for bondage;
it is nature alone that churns him, unrestrained like an intoxicated female elephant trampling lotus groves again and again.

These Kṣapaṇakas desire liberation by means of plucking out their hair, wearing rags from dust heaps, and performing the ritual of treading upon mountains; may those who know the ultimate truth indeed surpass them.
Because body hair grows constantly, bald men would attain liberation in an instant; by being naked, the cessation of saṃsāra would immediately occur even for animals;
and those dwelling on mountain peaks would be liberated forever simply by climbing them. By whom has such a path to the apavarga of living beings been shown?
Therefore, the wise declare that knowledge of the Self is the cause for attaining liberation;
and this has been taught by various teachers in every spiritual tradition under different designations.

Furthermore, although some here claim that meditation upon Īśvara as a form of conceptualization is the means for achieving liberation, they too have declared this to be the vision of the Self; for Īśvara is renowned as a particular kind of Puruṣa.

Having observed that the scope of other philosophical systems is limited to this extent and is incapable of touching upon or even perceiving the path to liberation, they wander for a long time here in this very abyss.

Therefore, those who have fallen into the desert of worldly existence should quickly take hold of this path taught by Akṣapāda; it is near at hand, conducive to well-being, and perfectly suited for the attainment of liberation.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Nyāyamañjarī composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Jayanta.

The Tenth Daily Lesson: Examination of Doubt. Since it has already been established that the group of categories beginning with doubt—though included within the categories of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*)—must be explained separately because they serve as the purpose for the operation of reasoning (*nyāya*), and since doubt was mentioned immediately after the objects of valid cognition in the first aphorism, [the author] speaks in order to set forth its definition according to the sequence of that mention: "Doubt is a deliberation requiring a specific distinction, arising from the perception of common or multiple properties, from conflicting testimony, and from the non-settlement of perception and non-perception. (NS 1.1.23)

1-1-23 Objection: Since doubt is of five kinds due to the difference in its causes—such as the perception of common characteristics (*samāna-dharma*) and so forth—it is necessary to state its general definition, its classification, and its specific definitions.

In that regard, two sūtras would be appropriate for the general definition and the classification, and five sūtras for the purpose of the specific definitions of those five varieties; thus, seven sūtras ought to have been composed.
Yet, only this one sūtra is heard.
How then will this be? It is said: You have spoken the truth;
however, this very same single sūtra will be construed in seven ways by resorting to the method of repetition.

In this regard, the teachers first explain as follows: "Doubt is a deliberation dependent upon a desire for specific distinction, arising from the occurrence of common properties, from the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception"—this much of the sūtra establishes the general definition.
"From the occurrence of common and multiple properties, from conflicting testimony, and from the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception"—this is the sūtra of classification.

Furthermore, because of the occurrence of common properties, and because of the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception, doubt is a deliberation that depends on specific characteristics; thus, this very sūtra is the one that sets forth the specific definition of the first type of doubt.

Now, one might object: "If this very sūtra is intended for the definition of doubt in its general sense, and if this much alone constitutes the complete definition—neither deficient nor redundant—then how can it be said that 'doubt arises from the apprehension of a common property which is the cause for recollecting the particulars, from the non-apprehension of the particulars, and from the non-recollection of the particulars'? This is indeed something to be personally experienced.
However, in the sūtra, the phrase *viśeṣāpekṣaḥ* (requiring the particulars) teaches the recollection of the particulars."

Furthermore, by the phrase "the non-establishment of perception and non-perception," the non-apprehension of specific qualities is indicated; thus, this much is common to both definitions of the general and the particular.

However, the word *samāna* (common), when understood as implying the general, expresses the definition of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), whereas when it expresses the general that is pervasive [of particulars], it expresses the definition of the particular characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).

But how is it that this very [definition] implies a commonality by implication, and how is it that it expresses a commonality through concomitance? It is said: by the very arising of doubt, a mere common property is implied, because when that [property] is perceived, it serves as the cause for awakening the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) which are the seeds for the recollection of particulars; for doubt does not arise in the absence of that [common property].
For indeed, doubt has as its nature the mental apprehension (*avamarśa*) of contradictory particulars.

Now, there can be no apprehension of contradictory particulars that are present in a subject (*dharmin*) standing before one, because they cannot coexist in a single place precisely due to their being contradictory.
Therefore, it must be an apprehension of those [particulars] mounted upon memory.

Since memory does not arise without a cause, one must necessarily rely upon that which served as the cause for its recollection—namely, the previous successive apprehension of those specific features associated with it, occurring by way of the awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by that perception.

Now, whether that [cause] be inclusive, exclusive, of a contradictory nature, internal, or of the form of a non-determination between perception and non-perception—it is precisely because of this that the word *samāna* (similar), which expresses a universal (*sāmānya*), conveys the meaning of a "common characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), since the five [objects] share a common form.

When a word with a common application (*samānaśabda*) expresses a property (*dharma*) that is already understood—namely, the essential nature consisting of height, girth, and so forth—it serves the purpose of defining a specific characteristic (*aviśeṣalakṣaṇārtha*).

In this regard, the application of the Sūtra is as follows: "Commonality" (*sāmānya*) refers to a property such as circumference and the like; although it is distinct in each substance by virtue of being a quality, its status as "common" is established because it is the object of a cognition that apprehends an identical form.
Its "establishment" (*upapatti*) means its perception (*upalabdhi*).
Alternatively, the word "establishment" (*upapatti*) may also denote existence (*sattā*).
Since that [perception] also exists only as dependent upon perception, it follows that doubt arises from the perception of a common property in every respect; this is what has been stated.

Now, one might object: "The common property is a different entity from the subject (dharmin), and when a different entity is perceived, doubt cannot arise regarding another. This is not so, because it is a specific property of that very entity.

However, the "particularity of another object" (arthāntaraviśeṣa) is said to be the locus itself (dharmin), insofar as it is qualified by another object such as its circumference and so forth. Thus, when that very locus—which is the object upon which common properties have been superimposed—is present before the path of vision, a doubt arises precisely therein, consisting of the mental apprehension of the particularities residing within it:
"Is this thing seen, characterized by height, a post or a person? Therefore, the fact that [the particularity] is another object is not a flaw.

Nevertheless, for one who perceives specific features such as the curvature of the corners [of the eyes], the skin, the hands, and the feet, doubt is not observed; therefore, another cause is stated: "due to the non-determination of perception and non-perception.
This means "due to the non-apprehension of specific features.

But how is the non-apprehension of specific features expressed by the phrase "due to the non-determination of perception and non-perception"? It is expressed in this way: in that case, neither perception—whether as "this" (*idantayā*) or as "not-this" (*anidantayā*)—nor non-perception is determinately established.

For when specific features are perceived, the determination of that [object] becomes possible: "This is a post, not a person," upon perceiving specific features such as curvature, hollows, and so forth;
whereas, through the discernment of the head, hands, and other [limbs], one concludes, "This is a person, not a post."
Thus, by this term, the non-apprehension of a specific feature (*viśeṣa*) has been stated.

Nevertheless, since doubt is not observed even in one who has mounted a swing, perceives common characteristics (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and does not apprehend a specific feature, another cause is stated: "dependent on the specific" (*viśeṣāpekṣa*).
The meaning is "dependent on the recollection of the specific" (*viśeṣasmṛtyapekṣa*).
Now, it might be argued that there is a requirement for particulars only when doubt arises; for when they are being experienced, it is the removal of doubt that occurs, not the doubt itself.
Or rather, memory is obtained precisely from the determination of the meaning of the word *apekṣā*.

*Apekṣā* means expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); and those particulars, though not currently perceived, being previously experienced, are what is expected. This is the memory of them, because expectancy toward things that are either presently perceived or exclusively unexperienced is impossible.

Now, one might object: let there be only two causes—the occurrence of common characteristics and the recollection of specific features—so what is the use of including the non-apprehension of specific features? Furthermore, since the non-apprehension is already implied by the very recollection of specific features, how could apprehension and recollection occur simultaneously?

This is true; however, for a lover who is deeply attached to his own beloved woman who is not very far away, even when there is perception of common characteristics, non-perception of her specific qualities, and recollection of her, no doubt arises at all.

Therefore, since the production of doubt is not invariably concomitant [with the mere non-perception of specific qualities], another term is employed to establish the non-apprehension of specific qualities that are obstructed by space and time: the non-apprehension now of specific qualities that were previously perceived in another place or at another time is the cause of doubt, not merely the non-apprehension of specific qualities in general.
Thus, by these three words, this definition of doubt has been stated.

But surely, according to the principle that "an effect is commenced by causal factors acting in combination," a doubt—which is produced by three causes characterized as the perception of common properties, the non-perception of specific properties, and the recollection of those [properties]—would entail the simultaneity of cognitions;
for if cognitions occur sequentially, there can be no simultaneous operation toward the production of a single effect.

Furthermore, since many particulars (*viśeṣa*) can also exist, there would likewise have to be numerous simultaneous recollections of them; but this is not so. Immediately following the perception of common characteristics (*sāmānyadharma*), there will arise a single recollection directed toward that [object], mediated by the robust latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) accumulated through a succession of previous experiences of various particulars—just as was described regarding the cognition of meaning from phonemes.

Furthermore, the non-apprehension of specific features (viśeṣānupalabdhi), which is indicated by the lack of a settled state regarding apprehension and non-apprehension, is indeed non-apprehension itself; it is not of the nature of cognition, but rather the non-arising of cognition. Thus, even as a third cause, it is not of the nature of cognition. Therefore, there are only two causes that are of the nature of cognition: the perception of common characteristics (samānadharmagrahaṇa) and the recollection of specific features (viśeṣasmaraṇa).

Of these two, the first—the perception of common characteristics—is in a state of perishing, while the second—the recollection of specific features—is in a non-perishing state; together, they produce doubt.
And it is established in the treatise that the simultaneity of these two types of knowledge is not contradictory.

Thus, by means of these three factors—the apprehension of common properties, the non-apprehension of specific differences, and the non-recollection of specific differences—this faultless definition of doubt is stated.
Not approving of this explanation by the Teacher, others explain it otherwise: first of all, the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is presented by the word "deliberation" (*vimarśa*) itself.
For this is not merely a synonym, as in "deliberation means doubt";
rather, "doubt" is the term to be defined (*lakṣya*), while "deliberation" is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
And like the term *pramāṇa*, this term is capable of conveying its definition only when dependent upon an etymological explanation.
"Vimarśa" (doubt) is the apprehension of contradictory objects, such as "Is it a post or a person?

By this much, the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) has been stated, which is distinguished from heterogeneous categories such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the like, and which is accompanied by the fivefold doubt belonging to its own class.

Furthermore, the enumeration of causes that produce doubt is not useful here, just as it was not in the case of the phrase "produced by the contact of a sense organ with its object," because other causes such as the contact between the self and the mind are likewise unavoidable.

Now, if it is intended to point out the uncommon causes of other [cognitions], what is the purpose of that? For the general definition is what is intended to be established, and that is already established from the very term "investigation" (vimarśa).

Furthermore, the description of the non-apprehension of a particularity being presented by a term that is itself undetermined as either apprehended or unapprehended is extremely strained; thus, to require that it be explained exactly as it was heard when the definition of a particularity is under discussion would be an excessive burden.

Thus, when the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—which effects the exclusion of heterogeneous objects—is described by the word "investigation" (*vimarśa*), the single word "because of the occurrence of a common property" (*samānadharmopapatteḥ*) is capable of effecting the exclusion of other internal doubts regarding similar classes and is sufficient for the specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*); therefore, even in that case, the employment of three words is not appropriate.
Regarding these two explanations, those who know the matter are the authority as to which one is superior.
Regarding the phrase "due to the occurrence of multiple properties" (*anekadharmopapatti*), the Teacher also describes this definition by taking three terms:

"due to the occurrence of multiple properties," "due to the lack of determination between perception and non-perception," and "due to the requirement for a specific [differentiator]. The meaning is that doubt arises from the apprehension of a non-common property, from the apprehension of a specific [differentiator], and from the recollection of that specific [differentiator]. Furthermore, the purpose of including each individual term here should be demonstrated in the same manner as previously shown.
Nor is it appropriate to urge an enumeration of other causes, such as the contact between the sense organ and the mind, because those are equally present in the arising of all cognitions;
for here, the context is the instruction regarding the specific cause of doubtful cognition.

Others, however, have described—as before—that very locus of the occurrence of multiple properties, which is skilled in establishing a definition characterized solely by the exclusion of similar things once the exclusion of dissimilar things has been accomplished through the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Now, one might ask: how can the term "multiple properties" (*anekadharma*) denote a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*)? It is explained as follows: "multiple" refers to both those of the same class and those of different classes; therefore, a property that is excluded from those [others] is called a "multiple property."
Or rather, what is the use of this strained interpretation? There is this word *eka*, which is a synonym for "the same" (*samāna*).

In that case, it is quite clear that by means of a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*), "non-identical property" (*asamānadharmā*) is expressed as "multiple properties" (*anekadharma*), that is, as "common property" (*sādhāraṇadharma*). Thus it is said.
Let it be so; however, it must be considered how a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) can be a cause of doubt.
For they say that doubt has its cause in the recollection of contradictory particulars (*viruddhaviśeṣa*).
And the cause for the recollection of particulars is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), whose activator is that with which these [particulars] were previously perceived in alternation.
However, because a unique property (asādhāraṇadharma) is indeed unique, it has never previously been perceived in association with anything else;
if such association were to exist, its very status as a unique property would be lost. Therefore, how could it be the cause for the recollection of that [object]?

If it were the cause of recollection merely by way of being excluded [from others], then it would follow that it is the cause for the recollection of the entire three worlds, since it is likewise excluded from those as well.
This is not a fault, because it serves as a cause for recollection by way of another method.
For here, in certain cases, uncommon properties existing in certain subjects are accompanied by other common properties residing in those same subjects.

For example, properties such as earthness and odor, while being uncommon to earth, are likewise seen in water along with properties such as viscidity, both being concomitant with substantiality (*dravyatva*).

In the case of color and so forth, the properties such as "colorness" are concomitant with "quality-ness"; in the case of upward throwing and so forth, the properties such as "upward-thrownness" are concomitant with "action-ness.

Likewise, in the present case as well, when some uncommon property is perceived in a subject, it must be concomitant with some common property; thus, by means of the recollection of that specific [uncommon] property, it becomes a cause for doubt.

[Objection: "In that case, since it is precisely due to their being excluded [from others], doubt arises regarding things possessing common properties (*samānadharmādi*) and not from multiple properties (*anekadharma*). [Reply: Do not say so; for that very *anekadharma*, by way of that path, serves to produce doubt by calling to mind the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*). For if that were absent, what would be the objective basis (*ālambana*) for the state of being excluded? Enough of this overly subtle scrutiny.
The author of the Bhāṣya has shown an illustration of this: "the state of being produced by disjunction in sound.

For just as in the case of earth and other substances, a specific property such as "earth-ness" is seen to coexist with inclusive properties such as "substance-ness," so too, one might suspect that the property of being produced by disjunction in sound must coexist with one or another of the inclusive properties such as "substance-ness"; thus arises the doubt.

But is it not the case that being produced by disjunction (*vibhāgajatva*) is not at all an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of sound, since it also exists in the case of a disjunction produced by disjunction? And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*) would be: "Sound is a quality (*guṇa*), because it is produced by disjunction, like a disjunction produced by disjunction. To this, some say: "It is true that being produced by disjunction exists even in the case of [that] disjunction;
however, a specific distinction regarding sound is intended [in the definition]."
For disjunction produced by disjunction is of two kinds: that preceded by the disjunction of causes, and that preceded by the disjunction of a cause and a non-cause.
Here, "cause" is intended to mean the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
First, regarding that which is preceded by the disjunction of causes: from the disjunction of the threads [from each other] arises the disjunction of the thread from space.

But the disjunction between the hand and space is preceded by the disjunction between the finger and space; and from the disjunction between the hand and space follows the disjunction between the body and space.

Sound, however, invariably arises from a disjunction preceded by a disjunction of its causes; for instance, from the disjunction of the bamboo segments there arises the disjunction of the segment from space, and from that disjunction of the segment from space—which serves as the non-inherent cause—sound is produced. By this specific characteristic, the unique status of sound as a property arising from such a disjunction is stated.

Others, however, unable to tolerate the notion of a disjunction produced by disjunction, maintain that the quality of being produced by disjunction belongs exclusively to sound, exactly as it is stated in the scriptures.

Now, why do you not accept a disjunction produced by a disjunction? For there is indeed this logical principle for establishing it: when an action has arisen in a part and produces a disjunction from another part, it does not at that time produce a disjunction from a location such as space; but when it produces a disjunction from a location such as space, it does not at that time produce a disjunction from another part—this is the established rule.

If it is asked what causes this state [of stability] to exist, it is replied: for that action which produces the disjunction of a part from a portion of space is not observed to initiate a disjunction that is the opposite of the conjunction that originates the substance, as is the case with the action that causes the opening of a lotus petal produced by the touch of the sun’s rays. If it is asked how that is so, it is because the lotus is determined to be non-perishing due to its being recognized in both the states of bud and full bloom.

However, this action of splitting a bamboo stalk is observed to originate a disjunction that is the opposite of the conjunction initiating the substance [the stalk], while itself not originating a substance; it is also observed to produce a disjunction that is the opposite of the conjunction [that initiates the parts]. Therefore, since it cannot originate a disjunction in space (nabhas), this established principle exists, and thus the hypothesis of a "disjunction-born disjunction" is formulated.
It is established that action terminates in conjunction (*saṃyogānta*).
For otherwise, it would follow that it persists for a duration of time, and being inherent in eternal substances, it would itself be eternal.
Therefore, because action is short-lived, there must be a conjunction that serves as its destroyer.
Subsequent conjunction, however, arises only when the preceding conjunction has ceased, and not otherwise;
furthermore, there exists no destroyer of conjunction other than disjunction.
But action (karma), which produces skill born from a subsequent conjunction,
is not capable of bringing about the destruction of a prior conjunction.
Therefore, disjunction must necessarily be the opposite of conjunction.

Since a disjunction residing in a particular substratum can only terminate a conjunction residing in that very same substratum—and not, for example, can the disjunction of the fingers suffice to destroy the conjunction between the bowl and the jujube fruit—it follows that the disjunction occurring in the bamboo splinters is not capable of destroying the conjunction between the splinter and space; therefore, there must certainly be a disjunction between the splinter and space that acts as the adversary to the conjunction between the splinter and space.

Therefore, when now considering the cause of its production, since the action has fulfilled its purpose by merely producing the disjunction of the bamboo segments, and because no further operation is perceived after it has ceased once that [initial] disjunction has been produced while producing another disjunction, one must necessarily admit that the very disjunction of the bamboo segments, due to its proximity, is the producer of the disjunction with space within the segment.
For if this were not admitted, it would follow that the action is eternal.
Regarding this, they say:

even if the permanence of action is not accepted, there will still be a disjunction produced by disjunction, because the subsequent conjunction—which is the cause for the destruction of the action—exists.
If it is asked, "How can that [subsequent disjunction] arise if the prior conjunction has not ceased? [the answer is: certainly, the prior conjunction has indeed ceased.

If it is asked, "What is the cause of its cessation?", [the answer is: for that very action which is accepted as the cause of the subsequent conjunction will itself bring about the destruction of the prior conjunction.
The cause that is conjunction with fire is incapable of producing [a quality] and incapable of destroying it;
[yet it is the cause] for both the production and destruction of qualities born of baking (pākaja).

Just as there is a restriction regarding the locus in the case of disjunction—namely, that disjunction, having a certain substratum, destroys only the conjunction that has that same substratum—so too is there a restriction regarding action. Action also, by virtue of its own substratum, destroys that conjunction which is based on a conjunction with another direction, because it exists in a direction opposed to that [conjunction]. Thus, there is no over-extension [of the definition]; for the observation of a subsequent conjunction in that which is permeated by action is not a fault, since the conjunction with the intervening space is destroyed by it.
Furthermore, that very action which is said to cause the disjunction of the petals from one another will also be the cause of the disjunction of the petals from space;

what fault is there? [Objection: It has been stated that an action causing disjunction from space does not originate a disjunction that is the opposite of the conjunction initiating a substance, as in the case of the action of a lotus. [Reply: True, this has been stated, but it is incorrect, because even the action of the petals of a hundred-petaled lotus (*śatapatra*) originates a disjunction that is contrary to the conjunction initiating a substance.
And that action is determined by the certainty of the difference between the bud-like lotus and the blossomed lotus.

But surely, since we observe the recognition of a lotus as "this is that very same lotus," free from doubt or error, how can there be any difference between them merely due to the distinction between the states of contraction and expansion? Enough with this misguided hope! For even in the case of the body, we observe recognition despite its nature being clearly perceived as divided by the distinct states of childhood, youth, old age, and so forth. Furthermore, we do not perceive even the slightest trace of a difference between the body and the lotus; how then can they be one and the same?

Or, let it be that the *puṇḍarīka* does not perish; however, this has been described as a mere illustration, and it was stated that there is no fixed causal connection by which the action of splitting a bamboo stalk could be assumed to be identical to the action of a red lotus sprout.
Furthermore, the property of being an "action" (*kriyātva*) is simply irrelevant, because those actions serve as causes for diverse effects.
Alternatively, the disjunction from the bamboo split is not one thing and the disjunction from the space within that split another;
rather, this is a single disjunction, appearing as distinct only due to the difference in its substrates,
because both the space and the bamboo split occupy the same location.
For it is contradictory for corporeal things to exist in the same location;
however, because space is omnipresent, its presence there is possible.

But if [the disjunction] resides in a single location, that which produces disjunction from one thing is the very same that acts upon the other; thus, there is no such thing as a disjunction born of disjunction.
Others, however, with an impetuosity mounted upon the refutation of disjunction produced by disjunction, declare: "Let alone disjunction produced by disjunction, which remains far off;
there is no such thing as even a disjunction produced by action.
If one were to admit such a thing—which must be the opposite of conjunction—it would necessarily have to be pre-established, like a mallet or similar object."
Furthermore, if a pre-existing disjunction were to uproot conjunction—as in the case of a jar and a mallet—then one would perceive conjunction and disjunction simultaneously in the same place.
But this is not the case.
Therefore, the cognition of "separated" has as its object merely the absence of conjunction; it does not establish itself as having disjunction as its objective support.

Even though that disjunction exists, because conjunction has not yet been destroyed at that moment, there is no appearance of being separated. However, in a subsequent moment, when conjunction is destroyed, it does occur; thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is determined that [the cognition] has as its object merely the absence of conjunction. Therefore, disjunction is not accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, it was established previously that the very act of conceptualizing it by means of the mark (*liṅga*) of the destruction of conjunction is what destroys it.

How then is it that the Commentator cited the fact of sound being produced by disjunction? It is said in reply: he explains that the production of an effect depends upon three kinds of causes—the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Among these, the inherent cause is that in which the effect is perceived as inhering, such as the threads are for a cloth.

The non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), however, is of two kinds: that which is proximate by way of the relation of inherence in the same object as the effect (kāryaikārthasamavāya), or that which is connected by way of the relation of inherence in the same object as the cause (kāraṇaikārthasamavāya).
Among these, an example of proximity through the relation of inherence in the same object as the effect is the conjunction of the threads [in the case] of a cloth.
An example of proximity through the relation of inherence in the same object as the cause, however, is the color of the threads [in the case] of the color of the cloth.

Furthermore, that which is determined to be the cause must be accepted as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Therefore, although other mental qualities such as desire (*icchā*) exist at the time of the arising of cognition, they do not possess the status of being the non-inherent cause when there is a conjunction with a single object; rather, it is only the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*), whose causal efficacy has been established, that serves as the non-inherent cause.

However, that cause which is distinct from both inherence and the inherent substratum, and whose capacity for the production of an effect is well-established, is called the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa).
This being the case, since the permanence of sound has been refuted and its non-universality established, regarding its production: space is, first of all, the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*);
as for the instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*), they certainly exist in great number;
however, the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) remains to be considered.
And that [sound] must necessarily be supported by space (*ākāśa*);
otherwise, there would be no proximity.

Furthermore, because other qualities such as all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) have their capacities undetermined, and because we observe the production of sound immediately after the splitting of a bamboo stalk, we think thus.
At the very moment that an action destroys the conjunction resting upon the bamboo split,
at that same moment it certainly produces some specific excellence in the ether.
That excellence of space which is produced by action and is the cause of sound is called "disjunction"; it is said that sound is produced from that.
Thus, we have set forth this view of the Teacher in accordance with the scriptures.

And this should be investigated by the wise: is there some specific excellence of space that serves as the non-inherent cause? Or is it rather that, just as the conjunction of the drum and the sky is the non-inherent cause for sound which is the effect of the conjunction of the mallet and the stick, so too is the disjunction of the bamboo-splinter and the sky the [non-inherent cause] for that [sound] which is the effect of the disjunction of the bamboo-splinters?
Furthermore, regarding the disjunction of the bamboo-splinter and space, does it arise from the disjunction of the splinters, or does it arise solely from action?
In every respect, there is no need for the mere statement that some uncommon property must be cited as a cause of doubt.
Contrary cognition is *vipratipatti*.
Some say "the self exists," while others say "the self does not exist.
This *vipratipatti*, being perceived, brings about doubt by way of recollecting the specific characteristics [of each position].
And here, no property that is either concomitant or excluded is the cause of doubt; rather, it is simply the disagreement [of authorities].
Therefore, regarding this case as well, one should follow the views of the two teachers as before: whether the definition is described by employing three terms or by a single term alone.
Because perception is not determinative, doubt arises even regarding that which exists;
for water is perceived in lakes and the like where it actually exists, yet it is also perceived in certain desert plains where it does not exist, due to the shimmering reflections of the sun's rays.
Thus, because perception is not established [as definitive], when something is being perceived, a doubt arises: "Is this being perceived as existent, or is it being perceived as non-existent?"
Furthermore, doubt arises from the lack of a fixed rule regarding non-perception:

some things that are simply non-existent are not perceived, such as the sky-flower and the like; while other things, though existent, are not perceived, such as the base of a stake hidden by soil or water.
When that [object] is not perceived elsewhere, a person doubts: "Is this simply non-existent that it is not perceived, or is it existent?"

By the term "indeterminacy" (*avyavasthā*), it was previously indicated by way of synonym that there is a non-perception of the specific qualities inherent in existence and non-existence as they have occurred in prior succession; now, however, it is described that doubt arises for those whose minds are devoid of the perception of specific qualities such as causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamarthatā*) and the like, because only perception and non-perception are established.

Nor should it be suspected that, this being the case, there would be a lack of confidence in all matters, for doubt is admitted only according to experience, and because in all cases the presence of the causes for its production—such as the non-apprehension of specific qualities and the recollection thereof—is impossible.
Here too, the establishment of the definition by means of either three words or a single word should be understood as being the same as before.

But is it not the case that perception and non-perception are equally properties of both the existent and the non-existent, and thus this has already been covered by the previous [section]? This is not so; for the previously mentioned property, such as "verticality" and so forth, resides in the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), whereas perception and non-perception reside in the knower (*jñātṛ*).

For this very reason, they declare this doubt to be mental (*mānasa*), and not born of the external sense organs (*bāhyendriyajam*) like a doubt dependent on the apprehension of common properties such as upwardness associated with an external subject (*bāhyadharmisambaddhasādhāraṇordhvatādidharmādhigamādhīna*).

But surely, it is the state of being perceived (*upalabdhitva*) or the state of not being perceived (*anupalabdhitva*) that is the cause of doubt here; for that does not reside in the knower (*jñātṛ*), but rather in the cognition (*buddhi*). How then is this a distinguishing feature? True, it is so; nevertheless, even a non-common property such as "being perceived" and so forth is said to be distinct [from the common property] because of the specific basis upon which it rests—that is, it resides in the cognizer. Therefore, it is mentioned separately from the [common] distinguishing feature.
For just as it is based on the state of being unique, so too, by relying on a distinction of this very kind, a fivefold nature is analyzed in certain cases.
In ultimate reality, however, a pervasive relationship [of doubt] with respect to all things is difficult to avoid, because doubt is produced by the recollection of specific features. Furthermore,
since it is impossible to recollect those specific features with which one previously had a perception if they are not currently perceived,
its similarity [to other types of cognition] cannot be avoided, as it follows after many specific features.

For this very reason, the teachers explained that the word *samāna* (common), which denotes a general property (*sāmānya*) that is implied [by the context], refers to the "characteristic of generality" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); enough with this elaboration.
Thus has this fivefold doubt been explained and shown by the Sage— that which,
as a constituent of inference, sustains its status as a cause for fruitful worldly activity.

Indeed, it has been previously deliberated by the wise that it is precisely through inference regarding an object already perceived that doubt about the matter carries one along the path of worldly activity.
Thus ends the examination of doubt. That object with reference to which one proceeds is the purpose (prayojana). 1.1.24.

In the word *yam*, a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is to be understood in order to encompass the various specific purposes that differ according to distinctions of place, time, person, and circumstance.
"Object" (*artha*) refers to that which is sought after; it is not spoken of merely as a thing-in-itself, since even non-existence can function as a purpose.
"Engagement" (*adhikāra*) is the determination regarding the object.

Whatever object, whether to be attained or to be abandoned, with reference to which an effort proceeds, and for the sake of whose attainment or avoidance a person exerts himself—that is the purpose (prayojana).
And that [purpose] is twofold, distinguished as primary and secondary.
The primary consists in the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering; the means to achieve these, however, is the secondary.

Even when sandalwood, wealth, the essence of jewels, necklaces, and beautiful women—which are means to happiness—are intended to be expressed as the primary goal because they are what is to be attained, their status as secondary should be understood in relation to the means for obtaining them.
And that purpose becomes unsettled due to the lack of distinction regarding place, time, and person.

For example, when the sun scatters what resembles a mass of sharp, polished embers under the guise of its rays upon a desert plain in summer, water bristling with clusters of ice particles is the supreme means of happiness for one afflicted by thirst; yet that very same water, in the winter which causes the whole world to shiver, results in distress for the fire of the stomach whose numbness is produced by the accumulation of phlegm, while the waters in Kashmir have been rendered thin by the harsh winds.
Therefore, this status of things as the means for pleasure or pain is indeed indefinite.

And although an object that was once known as a means to pleasure, having been used and passed away, no longer exists, nevertheless, those who desire it still proceed toward another entity of the same kind, whose status as a means to pleasure is determined by the mark of belonging to that same class.

Now, it may be argued that it is not logical for a purpose (*prayojana*) to be the motivator (*pravartaka*), because it cannot be established through the alternatives of being either existent or non-existent.
If it were existent, activity directed toward it would be unnecessary, like [the effort to produce] ears or a nose;

if it were non-existent, it would be even more so, like a sky-flower. This is not a fault, however, because that which has been made the object of desire to obtain (*īpsā*) or desire to avoid (*jihāsā*) serves as the motivator.
For that [object] is not unachievable like a sky-flower and the like,

nor is it already established like the head, hands, and so forth; rather, it is this very fact— attained by the intellect as something to be accomplished— that is the motivator, as witnessed by all the world.
Therefore, it is logical that it is that which has been made the object of desire which is the motivator.
Thus, when the Sage has established that the purpose is the motivator,
all the alternative positions regarding an external impeller asserted by others are shattered.
Therefore, a purpose is indicated by all prescriptive injunctions; indeed, all the actions of embodied beings are bound to a purpose.
Even for a worm, as it maintains its life in whatever manner possible, its activity is certainly never seen to be devoid of purpose.
The caviller (vaitaṇḍika) strives for the establishment of his own position, and he knows that this [establishment] has the negation of the opponent's position as its objective.
Therefore, even though this vitanda is devoid of a proof for one's own view, it is logical that it should be purposeful.
Thus concludes the examination of purpose. An example is that object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding among ordinary people and experts. 1.1.25.
The proponent and the opponent should be understood as those who are worldly and investigative, given the context of the definition of an example;
they are not the fool and the scholar, for that would be irrelevant to the subject at hand,
and because there is no connection between them [and the topic].

And between those two [the similar and dissimilar instances], that object—whether it be an existent intrinsic nature (*bhāvasvabhāva*) or one consisting of non-existence (*abhāvamātra*)—in which there is a consensus of cognition (*buddhisāmya*), whether regarding its status as the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) established through the relationship of the prompted and the prompter, or regarding the exclusion of the proving property preceded by the exclusion of the property to be proven; that is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Its being a substratum for such properties, or its being devoid of them, is to be understood from the definition of the "illustration" (*udāharaṇa*) to be stated later.

Just as in the definition of inference (*anumāna*), the phrase "based on that" (*tatpūrvaka*) was established merely as the means for grasping the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), whereas its actual nature was determined in the definition of the members of the syllogism (*avayava*)—namely, that "the reason (*hetu*) is the means of proving the probandum through similarity to the example, or likewise through dissimilarity"—in this way, only the mere consensus of the proponent and opponent regarding the example has been shown.

However, its two-fold nature will be explained right there: "The example is an illustration (*udāharaṇa*) which, by virtue of its similarity to the probandum, possesses the property of that [probandum]; or, conversely, it is the opposite by virtue of its dissimilarity."

"Sound is impermanent because it is produced; whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, as for example a jar"—this is an example by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). "On the other hand, that which is not impermanent is certainly not produced, as for example space"—this is an example by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
However, due to a deficiency in the characteristics as previously stated, there occurs the status of a fallacious example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).

The manifestation of the various types of fallacious appearances (ābhāsa) will be explained by you in the context of discussing examples and definitions; since some of these fallacious appearances are produced by defects in speech, they must be stated precisely within the definition of the members of a syllogism.
Those of sound vision must exert effort to understand both kinds of example;
for it is the immovable trunk of the great tree of inference, which is a treasure-trove of fruits.
Thus ends the examination of examples. A tenet (*siddhānta*) is the established position resulting from the acceptance of a system within a treatise (*tantra*). (NS 1.1.26)
That by which the status of things is established is called *tantra*, meaning a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
An *adhikaraṇa* is a substratum or support.
That whose *tantra* is its *adhikaraṇa* is *tantrādhikaraṇa*; the meaning is that it is rooted in a means of valid cognition.

Acceptance (*abhyupagama*) means taking something as one's own; its establishment (*saṃsthiti*) is the determination of its state of being, which is the restriction of properties (*dharmaniyama*). "This" is a general indication, while "in this way" is a specific indication.

Thus, the general definition of a tenet (*siddhānta*) is stated as follows: a tenet is an object possessing both general and specific characteristics, which is made the subject of an acceptance based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and which consists in the established formulation of that acceptance within a system (*tantra*) or a particular context (*adhikaraṇa*).
Others, however, explain it thus: a *tantra* is a treatise (*śāstra*) that is an instruction on a collection of topics mutually related;
a *adhikaraṇa* is called a "position" (*pakṣa*) because it is the subject under discussion;
and *abhyupagama* is exactly as previously described.
The word *saṃsthiti* (establishment) is connected with each [term].

By the phrase "the establishment of a system (*tantra-saṃsthiti*), the establishment of a topic (*adhikaraṇa-saṃsthiti*), and the establishment of an admission (*abhyupagama-saṃsthiti*)," there is an indication of the *sarvatantra-siddhānta* (universally accepted tenet) and the *pratitantra-siddhānta* (tenet specific to a particular system), due to the similarity in their designation as systems.
By the other two terms, the latter two—the *adhikaraṇa-siddhānta* (tenet established by a topic) and the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (tenet established by admission)—are indicated.
But this is a misinterpretation; for in this way, no general definition consistent with the four established doctrines (siddhānta) has been stated.
Nor is this sūtra intended for the purpose of classification or for the purpose of a specific definition, since the exposition of those [topics] will be carried out by subsequent sūtras.
Furthermore, since there would be no purpose in restating what has already been said,
it is better to describe the general definition of the established tenet (siddhānta) according to the previous method alone.

He states its own classification by way of his own words: "It is fourfold because of the existence of different meanings: [the thesis] common to all treatises (*sarvatantra*), [the thesis] specific to a particular treatise (*pratitantra*), the admission of a premise (*adhikaraṇābhyupagama*), and the established tenet (*saṃsthitārtha*). (1.1.26)

For the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is of four kinds: the universally accepted conclusion (*sarvatantrasiddhānta*), the conclusion specific to a particular treatise (*pratitantrasiddhānta*), the conclusion by implication (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*), and the provisional acceptance (*abhyupagamasiddhānta*).
Among these, a tenet that is not contradicted by any other systems and is intended within its own system is a tenet established by all systems (*sarvatantrasiddhānta*).

In this context, by the word *tantra* (system), a treatise (*śāstra*) is meant; that object which is taught in one's own treatise and is not contradicted by any other treatise is a *sarvatantrasiddhānta* (tenet established for all systems).
For example: "Perception is a means of valid cognition."
But surely, they [the Vedāntins] also object here:
"For the proponents of Brahman, all of this is indeed ignorance (*avidyā*);

and how can ignorance be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? This is not so, because even they accept its validity within the context of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*). Let there be disagreements regarding number, definition, and object for each respective treatise.
That there is such a thing as visual perception as a means of valid cognition is a point on which all disputants are in agreement.
The term *artha* (object) is used here in the sense of "that which is under discussion in a treatise" (*tantra*).

For example, according to our own system, atoms impelled by the will of God are established as the cause [of the world] in the *Kaṇāda-vrata-mata*, which is a *samāna-tantra* (a concordant treatise); however, they are not accepted in that same way in the *paratantra* (an opposing treatise), namely the Sāṃkhya philosophy.

Or again, the production of the elements from *prakṛti*—which consists of the three *guṇas*—in the form of the *mahat*, *ahaṃkāra*, and so forth, is an object established independently for the Sāṃkhyas; it is indeed established even in the *Pātañjala-yoga-śāstra*, which is a *samāna-tantra*, but it is not established in the *paratantra*, such as the Vaiśeṣika system.

"Now, how can this have its basis in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇamūlatā*)? This is a pertinent question; it is true that in our own system of tenets established by each specific treatise (*pratitantrasiddhānta*), the state of being based on valid means of knowledge is indeed factual.
However, although the Sāṃkhya system lacks a basis in valid means of knowledge, it was cited here to demonstrate its dependence [on other systems].
Or rather, its status as being based on valid means of knowledge should be stated with reference to that [other] intention.
When, upon the establishment of one thing, another matter is established as a consequence, that is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*. (1.1.30)
That which is "being processed" (*prakriyate*) is called a "topic" (*prakaraṇa*), which refers to a thesis (*pakṣa*).

When the establishment of a certain matter results in the establishment of other matters, that is an "established conclusion based on a topic" (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*), because it follows from the establishment of those other matters contained within that topic.

Furthermore, what is it that is referred to by the pronoun "that" in the phrase "upon whose establishment"? Is it the thesis (*pakṣa*) or the reason (*hetu*)? If it is the thesis, how can one thesis serve for the establishment of another thesis? For it is by means of the reason that the establishment of the thesis is effected, not by the thesis of the reason. But if the reason itself were an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*, how could the operation of logic proceed by relying on a *siddhānta*? Thus, the purpose for the enumeration of that [category] has been described.
For *nyāya* is simply the reason (*hetu*),
and that very thing is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.
Moreover, a reason does not perish along with its substratum.
It is said: there is no fault in either case.
For in some instances the reason (*hetu*) itself becomes the thesis (*pakṣa*), and the thesis likewise becomes the reason.
In that context, since the establishment of the thesis depends directly upon the reason, it is the reason alone that is referred to by the pronoun.
Since the establishment of other matters follows from the establishment of that [one], that alone is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.

How, then, is it said that the operation of reasoning (nyāya) has that as its basis? Even the reason (hetu), being itself one of those [factors] and being established as if it were the probandum (sādhya), becomes the subject (pakṣa) and will thus serve as the basis for another reasoning.
Alternatively, let the very thesis (*pakṣa*), when referred to by a pronoun, be the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.
And that is clearly the basis of the reasoning (*nyāya*).
Since it is established only by necessarily implying other alternative positions (*pakṣāntara*), it possesses the character of an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.
An example of this is: "The knower is distinct from the sense organs, because there is the apprehension of a single object through both seeing and touching.

Here, while it is established that the knower is distinct from the sense organs, other related propositions are also established, such as: the sense organs are manifold, they have restricted objects, substance is distinct from qualities, and so forth.

Because one accepts [a general principle] without prior examination, the subsequent examination of its specific details is the *abhyupagamasiddhānta* (the tenet based on what has been accepted). 1.1.31.

In this context, following the ablative case-ending (*pañcamī*) as it is heard in the phrase "because of the acceptance of what has not been examined" (*aparīkṣitābhyupagamāt*), and adhering to the general definition that "a tenet (*siddhānta*) is an object made the subject of acceptance based on a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*"), some explain it as follows: in the investigation and discussion regarding the permanence or impermanence of a subject (*dharmin*) such as sound, one must proceed with an acceptance of that very subject while it remains unexamined—that is, devoid of an examination of attributes such as being a specific quality of space (*ākāśaviśeṣaguṇatva*). Then, from this "acceptance of what has not been examined," what is established? It is said: "the examination of its specific [attributes]."

For the investigation into the permanence or impermanence residing in that [sound] is possible only when the subject (*dharmin*) is presented in a general sense, devoid of an investigation into properties such as being a specific quality of space (*ākāśa-viśeṣaguṇatva*).
If, however, sound were presented as the subject specifically qualified by being a specific quality of space, the thesis would have a qualifier unestablished (*asiddha-viśeṣaṇa*) for the opponent.

Even when this has been done, if he should further conceptualize the subject (*dharmin*) by asking, "Of what kind of existing thing is the eternity being proved by you— of a substance (*dravya*) or of a quality (*guṇa*)?", then by thus conceptualizing, he is already defeated because he has strayed into a different matter (*arthāntara*). Nevertheless, wishing to display the superiority of his own intellect and out of contempt for the opponent's intellect, the proponent says to him who has already been defeated, "Let sound be a substance."
We do not understand this explanation.
For those who explain it in this way, what exactly is determined to be the *abhyupagamasiddhānta* (the tenet based on personal acceptance)?

If, first of all, the statement "sound is impermanent" is the *abhyupagamasiddhānta*, then that very designation of the subject (*dharmin*) called "sound"—which was initially presented as being devoid of distinctions such as substance, quality, and so forth—is itself the tenet based on personal acceptance.
In this regard, what is the meaning of "acceptance" (abhyupagama), and what is its distinction from the tenets established within one's own system (pratitantrasiddhānta)?

Now, if it is argued that the statement "sound is a substance" is an *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (a tenet based on provisional acceptance) because it is subsequently accepted through the conceit of one's own superior intellect—thereby designating sound as qualified by the property of substantiality (*dravyatva*)—then the sūtra [NS 1.1.31], "because of the acceptance of what has not been examined," would not apply; for they have interpreted the meaning of that sūtra in a completely different way.

Therefore, it is explained as follows: an *abhyupagamasiddhānta* (a tenet based on mere acceptance) is precisely that which is formulated through one's own ingenuity without prior critical examination—such as "let sound be a substance.

However, the inclusion of the phrase "making an acceptance rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)" within the general definition should be applied specifically with the intention of [addressing] the views of the Pāṭavādin and others:
"Let the quality of being a substance (*dravyatva*) in sound also be rooted in valid means of knowledge; nevertheless, its impermanence remains [to be established]."
It is said that while a partless substance is not at all impermanent, I shall nevertheless prove the impermanence of sound, even though it is of such [partless] nature.
How then is the fifth [member] to be understood? What indeed is the nature of the fifth member such that it has been explained by us in this manner?

The fifth [type of] is also to be applied in this manner. To the question, "For what purpose, then, is this acceptance of the substantiality of sound—already examined—being made? the answer is stated by means of the ablative case (*pañcamī*): because the examination of its specific qualities, such as impermanence, is only possible through an unexamined acceptance; therefore, even an unexamined acceptance constitutes an *abhyupagama-siddhānta*.

However, it should not be thought that the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* is the examination of those very specific qualities themselves, because of the use of a coreferential (genitive) designation; for examination is dependent upon a [previously established] tenet (*siddhānta*).

Therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is that the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (acknowledged tenet) is that which is formulated by a master debater for the purpose of examining its specific details, based on what has been accepted without prior investigation;
and it is precisely in this manner that the practice of disputants is conducted in various contexts.
These four divisions of philosophical tenets are the primary cause for the commencement of reasoning;
indeed, a discourse on reasoning never proceeds among investigators if it is not based upon them.

Thus concludes the examination of the purpose. For here, one who seeks to demonstrate to another an object already understood by oneself through inference must employ as much of a collection of words as is necessary to complete the proof of that object to be established.
And those learned in logic call that very [collection of words] *parārthānumāna* (inference for the sake of others).
But is it not the case that there is no such thing as inference for others (parārthānumāna) at all, whether with respect to the speaker or the listener, because such [an inference] is untenable?
For that object was inferred from the speaker; it is not being inferred now.
That is the listener’s inference for oneself, which has the comprehension of the sentence as its cause.
Just as one understands fire upon seeing smoke through direct perception, so too does one understand it from his words; in what sense, then, is [the inference] "for the sake of another"?
However, this scripture would be divided: one part teaches the meaning, while another part teaches the method and the path of reasoning for realizing that [meaning].
Thus [it is said].
It is true that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is not logically tenable;
however, there are two kinds of cognizers:
one who has personally understood the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the mark (*liṅga*) as it actually exists, and one who is the opposite of that.

In that regard, inference is not taught at all to one who has personally ascertained the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), because for such a person, the cognition [of the object] arises from their own side alone. However, for one who has not ascertained the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the pervasion itself must be demonstrated; therefore, for such a person, inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is explained as being nothing other than the statement that teaches it.
For indeed, a speaker does not employ this statement based on their own conviction alone.
"May Patañjali understand that matter from my words alone."
However, he thinks, "I shall awaken him by means of inference."
However, one does not perceive that [object] oneself through the mark (liṅga) which possesses pervasion;
because this [inference] is the means for the cognition of that [object], it is called "for the sake of others" (parārtha).
Therefore, this is indeed an inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) on the part of the listener;
however, when a speaker communicates in such a manner to another, it is said that they employ an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*).
Nor is it tenable that this [utterance] is a mere restatement for the speaker,
since he exerts himself correctly for the sake of another's comprehension.
Therefore, because it teaches a meaning not previously established, it is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

However, if it were considered a restatement with respect to one's own understanding, then no statement of a trustworthy person (*āptavacana*) would ever be of a non-repetitive nature, since everything is preceded by one's own prior perception.
Therefore, since the formulation of a statement of inference for others is possible, its constituent parts—the members—are logically established and thus defined.
The members [of a syllogism] are the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion.

1-1-32 This single sūtra expresses both the general definition of the members (*avayava*) and their classification, just as [the same sūtra] does for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely: "Perception, inference, comparison, and word are the means of valid cognition.

In this context, the terms *avayava*, *bhāga*, *aṃśa*, and *ekadeśa* are synonymous; thus, the word *avayava* declares the general definition of the members as being a portion of the collection of statements that culminates in the comprehension of the object to be established.

And although there exists no ultimate collection (*samūha*) of phonemes—just as there is none of trees—which emerge from single utterances, are by nature fragile, short-lived, and subject to an unavoidable sequential birth, nevertheless, a conceptual aggregate (*kalāpa*) of them has already been established previously on the occasion of defining the sentence, based on their utility for a single purpose consisting in the communication of the intended meaning; thus, their parts (*bhāga*) are indeed possible.

Furthermore, it is not merely individual words that constitute an inferential statement (*anumānavākya*), but rather complete sentences; for it is impossible to express the proposition (*pratijñā*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), and so forth by means of a single word alone.
However, the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*) may sometimes consist of even a single word, such as "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*).

Or, when employed with a qualification, even that word conveys its meaning through its collective force, as in: "because of being produced while possessing substantiality" (*vastutve sati kṛtakatvāt*).
Even the statement of the example, such as "like a jar," is employed out of mere laziness;
for that [example] must be stated thus in order to demonstrate pervasion: "Whatever is produced is observed to be impermanent, just like a jar."
Therefore, the defining characteristic of the members [of a syllogism] is precisely their status as members, not their status as words.

The specific enumeration as well—namely, that there are five members beginning with the proposition (pratijñā), neither fewer nor more—is understood precisely from the mention of the "members" (avayava) in proximity to the words "proposition" and so forth.
Surely, some here dispute this, asserting a deficiency in the members [of the syllogism],
by claiming that the statement of proof consists of either three or two members.

Others, however, state that there are ten members, including the five beginning with the proposition (pratijñā), together with the desire to know (jijñāsā), doubt (saṃśaya), feasibility (śakyaprāpti), purpose (prayojana), and the removal of doubt (saṃśayavyudāsa).
It is said that the deficiency will be rectified as the occasion arises;
furthermore, excess is also untenable, because since desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and the rest do not have the nature of words, they cannot logically constitute members of a syllogism (*vākya*).
For instance, when an object is not yet cognized, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is what prompts the activity whose purpose is cognition.
Since this desire is by its very nature an immediate attribute of the cognizer, it is not a constituent part of the sentence.
Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a deliberation regarding an object that accomplishes a purposeful action, such as "Is this thus, or is it otherwise?
Since that too consists in the nature of cognition, it is not a member of a syllogism.
The "possibility of attainment" (*śakyaprāpti*) is the conviction that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when operating, are capable of delivering the object of cognition (*prameya*);
this too, being of the same nature [as the preceding], is not a constituent part of the sentence.
How could the purpose, which consists in the determination of that which is doubted, partake in being a member of the syllogism?
The removal of doubt, however, is a direct perception;
and even though it has the nature of speech, it does not attain the status of being a member (*avayava*) of the proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*).

Therefore, it is well said that doubt and the rest are causes for the commencement of a discussion, but they are not members of a syllogism; rather, the members [of a syllogism] are the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion.
"Among these, the statement of that which is to be proven (sādhya) is the proposition (pratijñā). (NS 1.1.33) "Proposition" is the indication of the definiendum;
"the statement of that which is to be proven" is the definition.

Since it is impossible for a mere locus (*dharmin*), a mere property (*dharma*), two independent [entities], or a property qualified by a locus to be the object of proof, it has been established in the definition of inference that the locus qualified by the property is the object of proof (*sādhya*).
Its definition is: a thesis is a statement of acceptance.

Now, since sentences possess a restrictive force (*avadhāraṇa*), is the restriction that "the statement of the probandum alone is the proposition" (i.e., *pratijñā*), or rather, that "only the proposition is the statement of the probandum"?

If it is determined that the thesis (*pratijñā*) is exclusively the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*), then—according to the principle that "the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) applies to what is other than that from which the particle *eva* is employed"—the thesis would be restricted by the rule "do not abandon the statement of the probandum. However, since the statement of the probandum itself is not so restricted, it could exist even while abandoning the status of a thesis; thus, the definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*).

Now, if it is determined that "the thesis (*pratijñā*) is indeed the statement of the probandum (*sādhyānirdeśa*)," then the statement of the probandum is restricted so that it may not abandon the status of being a thesis. However, since the thesis itself would remain unrestricted and could exist even apart from the statement of the probandum, the definition [of the thesis as the statement of the probandum] is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), because the thesis is not fully encompassed by the statement of the probandum.
This is incorrect;
for not every sentence is restrictive (sāvadhāraṇa), as in the example: "This path goes to Sṛdhna."
For in that case, it is not possible to restrict [the movement] by saying "it goes only here," or "only to Śrudhna," or "it goes only thus."
Furthermore, even if a restrictive rule must necessarily be adopted, let it be that "the statement of the probandum alone is the thesis" (*pratijñā*).

Nor is there the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because apart from the thesis, no other instance of the statement of the probandum is observed; for although this [definition] is unrestricted, it is not seen anywhere else.
Therefore, it is established that the statement of the probandum alone is the thesis.
For example, [in the proposition] "sound is impermanent.
Now, in this case as well, is the restriction (avadhāraṇa) "sound is indeed impermanent," or "only sound is impermanent"?

If one says "sound is indeed impermanent," then by the exclusion of other properties belonging to it, even its being produced (kṛtakatva) would not exist there; thus, the reason (hetu) would be unestablished (asiddha).

If, however, one were to restrict [the statement] to "sound alone is impermanent," there would be a lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) for the reason because impermanence would be excluded from the pot; yet this is not a fault, since we have already shown that a verbal formulation can be employed even without such restriction. Alternatively, in the restriction "sound is indeed impermanent," there is no negation of all other remaining properties—such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which are neither different from nor incompatible with impermanence.
Rather, there is only the negation of its opposite, permanence; the meaning is: "Sound is indeed impermanent, not permanent."
As it has been said: "A restrictive rule is postulated from that which is contradictory to it, not from that which is non-contradictory. Therefore, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Now, is it not the case that the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is irrelevant within a proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*), because it is a statement of a non-constituent part of the proof?
For the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) occurs through the statements of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); therefore, only those two should be stated.
Furthermore, not everything perceived during one's own realization must necessarily be communicated to another.
Alternatively, let only the subject (*dharmin*) be stated in the formal statement;

for in one's own cognition, there is first the apprehension of the pure subject, such as a mountain, prior to its being colored by the specific property (*dharma*)—such as fire—that one intends to prove. If it were otherwise accepted, it would follow that inference is rendered useless.
Therefore, how can there be, at the very outset, the presentation of a subject (dharmin) whose nature is already superimposed with the property to be proven (sādhyadharma)?
Moreover, since the meaning of the thesis is obtained from the very dispute itself, what is the purpose of stating it explicitly by one's own throat?

It is said that by one who follows their own realization, the realization of another must be produced; therefore, the subject (*dharmin*) first perceived in one's own realization must indeed be stated.
For if the subject were not stated, where would the reason (*hetu*), being without a locus, establish the probandum (*sādhya*)?

Furthermore, if the subject is not delimited, an inference regarding a mere property (*dharmamātra*) is useless, because it is already established without dispute that "impermanence exists somewhere."
Furthermore, without the specification of a subject (dharmin), the reason (hetu) would be unestablished in its locus (āśrayāsiddha); therefore, the property (dharma) must necessarily be specified.

Even though the initial perception was merely of the locus (*dharmin*), nevertheless, for the sake of quelling objections as to what this reason (*hetu*) might be intended to prove, the statement of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) must also be made.
For if one were to employ [the argument] simply as "sound, because of being produced" (*śabdaḥ kṛtakatvāt*), this would be like the speech of a blind man, failing to constitute a proof.

Now, if one were to desist by means of the statement of the example—“Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent”—which is intent on demonstrating pervasion, or by the statement of the conclusion—“Therefore, it is impermanent”—that would be a flaw; nevertheless, in a proof-statement whose fruit is the cessation of the listener’s desire to know, the probandum must be indicated in order to generate the expectation for the understanding of the proof.

For when only the word "sound" is stated, no one requires a proof for it; therefore, in order to create the occasion for stating the proof and to ensure the efficacy of its employment, the statement of the thesis, "Sound is impermanent," must certainly be put forward.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā) is already obtained through the very fact of dispute (vivāda), this is merely an acceptance of the proposition under another name.
For "dispute" (vivāda) means contradictory discourse:
one says, "Sound is eternal," while the other says, "It is non-eternal."

Thus, this adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis is nothing other than a dispute, which is simply a proposition (*pratijñā*). Whether that adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis occurs on that very day or on another day—what does this distinction matter?
The statement of a proposition is unavoidable.

The thesis itself is called the "position" (*pakṣa*). When such a definition of the position has been demonstrated, fallacious positions (*pakṣābhāsa*) are necessarily excluded. For example, "fire is not hot" is a position contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣaviruddha*).
"The eye does not grasp form" is contradicted by inference.
Contradiction with scripture (*śabdaviruddha*) has many branches; for example, "Brāhmaṇas should drink liquor" is a contradiction with traditional authority (*āgama*).

"My mother is barren" and "My father is a celibate student" are contradictions with one's own words (*svavacanaviruddha*), because there is a mutual opposition between the subject (*dharmin*) and its attributes (*dharma*).
"The moon is not the hare-marked one" (*na candraḥ śaśī*) is a contradiction with worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhiviruddha*).
However, "This object similar to a cow is not denoted by the word *gavaya*," is a contradiction of the standard of comparison (*upamānaviruddha*).
"Caitra has a crest made of sky-flowers" is an instance where the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*).
"The lotus of the sky is fragrant" is an instance where the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is unestablished.
