An example where both [the subject and the predicate] are unestablished is: "The son of a barren woman has a crest made of sky-flowers.

Even in cases where the essential natures of both qualifiers are already ascertained through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such a statement is also merely a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*), as in "snow is cold" or "fire is hot"; because there is an absence of anything to be proven (*sādhyatva*), there is no occasion for the application of inference (*anumāna*).
This very state is what is called "the unestablished nature of the probandum" (*siddhyasādhyatā*).

Those faults of the thesis (pakṣadoṣa), such as contradiction with direct perception, and those faults of the example (dṛṣṭāntadoṣa), such as the deficiency of the means of proof (sādhanavikalatva) which will be mentioned later—all of these, according to the actual state of things, are indeed faults of the reason (hetudoṣa).
The description of the faults of the thesis and the example is merely an elaboration.
Thus, it has been stated that "not being sublated" (abādhitatva) is itself a characteristic of the reason.

Furthermore, by relying on the observation of examples, the very definition of the reason (hetu) loses its distinctness from positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka); thus, all those [criticisms] are indeed merely defects of the reason.
For this very reason, in this treatise, the Sage who perceives reality did not mention fallacious positions and the like, but rather demonstrated the fallacious reasons.

Someone might have an understanding that, though independent of a logical reason, is established by mere assertion alone— such as that produced by one's own statement and so forth, which conforms to inference.

Since the reason (*hetu*) has such a characteristic, once its essential nature has been determined, the statement expressing it is itself identified as the "mouth" [of the proof]. Therefore, first the definition of the reason as an objective entity is stated: "The reason is that which establishes the probandum through similarity with the example" (NS 1.1.34).
Thus it is said.

Now, is it not the case that inference is a reason consisting of an object (*arthātmaka*), and that it has already been defined previously by the statement, "Inference, which is preceded by that [perception], is of three kinds"? True; in that context, by describing the fact that it is rooted in perception through the pronoun "preceded by that" (*tatpūrvakam*), only the means for determining the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) was set forth.
Here, however, the very nature of that necessary connection is also being explained.

For instance, when the reason (*hetu*) is understood as having the nature of an actual object (*arthātman*), they omit the ablative case and recite the aphorism: "The reason is the means of proving the probandum through similarity with the example" (*udāharaṇasādharmye sādhyasādhanaṃ hetuḥ*). They explain that if it were simply stated that "similarity is the reason," then the uncommon reason (*asādhāraṇahetu*), such as "possessing odor," would result in being a valid reason because it possesses the form of similarity by virtue of occurring in individual instances of the subject (*sādhyadharmin*). Furthermore, a contradictory reason (*viruddha*), which occurs in both the subject and its opposite, would also result in being a reason because it has the nature of similarity to that [subject]. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "example" (*udāharaṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding those cases.

An example (*udāharaṇa*) is a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) because in it the relationship of the "employed" (*prayojya*) and the "employer" (*prayojaka*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*) is illustrated.
As for the question "with what is there similarity by means of that [example]?", it is understood—due to the context and proximity—that it is with the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*).

Thus, when there is similarity with the example, the reason (*hetu*) is a property common to both the subject of the probandum and the corroborative instance; therefore, there is no possibility of such a definition applying to the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) and other such fallacious reasons.

Even so, since [faults such as] being a non-conclusive reason (*anaikāntika*), or being unestablished in one part (*ekadeśāsiddha*)—as in the case of "possessing smell" (*gandhavattva*) and the like when the four types of atoms are taken as the subject (*pakṣa*) for the sake of proving impermanence—and also because of the cases of the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) and the "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), these could potentially function as reasons (*hetu*) due to the possibility of their sharing a common property with the example; therefore, the terms "probandum" (*sādhya*) and "probans" (*sādhana*) are included [in the definition] to exclude them. Furthermore, since the probandum (such as impermanence) is indeed a common property shared by both the subject of the probandum and the subject of the example, it too might inadvertently be considered a reason; thus, the inclusion of the terms "probandum" and "probans" is made to prevent that consequence.

The reason (*hetu*) is that similarity with the example (*udāharaṇasādharmya*), which serves as the means of proof (*sādhana*) for the sake of obtaining the commonality of the mark (*liṅgasāmānyalābha*) regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
Furthermore, the term "probandum" (sādhya) and "probans" (sādhana) indicates the necessary connection (pratibandha).
Since that connection does not exist in cases such as the "inconclusive" (savyabhicāra), these are not valid reasons (*hetu*).

And because the necessary connection possesses five characteristics, the Teacher has already indicated the five types of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) simply by describing the loss of each individual characteristic.

[Objection: "In that case, let the definition of a reason (*hetu*) simply be the apprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*); since that alone is capable of excluding all fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), what is the purpose of including the phrase 'similarity with the example' (*udāharaṇasādharmya*)? [Response: It is not so, because it serves to exclude those of a different class (*asamānajātīya*). For non-reasons (*ahetu*) are indeed of a different class."
The exclusion of that [other type] follows from the mention of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).
The mention of similarity with the example (*udāharaṇasādharmya*) is for the purpose of excluding the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) inference, which belongs to the same class [of arguments].

Is it, then, that a purely positive (kevalānvayin) reason is intended as the subject of definition? No, because such a reason does not exist; rather, only that which possesses both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is the subject of definition. In that case, since the possibility of similarity and dissimilarity with the example exists, similarity is indeed present.

Nor should this mention of "similarity with the example" (udāharaṇasādharmya) be described as a definition of the purely positive inference (kevalānvayin) as a restrictive rule in the form of a specific injunction alone.

[Objection: If it is maintained that there are two kinds of logical reasons (*hetu*), then the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) should be stated first, and thereafter the specific definitions (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*). [Reply: It is said in response: the very mention of "the probandum" (*sādhya*) and "the probans" (*sādhana*) will constitute the general definition as an indicator of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). However, the mention of "similarity with the example" (*udāharaṇasādharmya*) is the definition of the reason that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*); and the subsequent sūtra [will provide] the definition of the purely negative reason (*kevalavyatirekin*).
Disregarding the fifth [type of reason], they declared that there is no purely positive (kevalānvayin) reason at all, and thus explained the definition of a reason as consisting of its actual object.

Alternatively, let it be granted that even there the reading of the fifth [member] has the result of eliminating doubt. Someone might say: "The statement 'the proof of what is to be proven' (sādhyasādhana) is merely a recitation of synonyms; it is not the definition of a reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore, let this [reason], being perceived again in that very same subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) where the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) was determined to be necessitated by the property of the reason (*hetudharma*), bring that [subject] to mind."

But in the case of another subject (*dharmin*), since that [reason] is perceived there, let there be doubt as to whether the presence of the reason here is inseparable from the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhūta*) or otherwise.
To this, the following reply is stated: "Because of similarity with the example" (*udāharaṇasādharmyāt*).

The meaning is this: because specific places, times, and individuals are subject to deviation, the determination of an invariable concomitance (pratibandha) does not occur with respect to them, but rather only between two general properties (sāmānyadharma).
For if [the reason] were based on a distinction between individual instances, there could be no apprehension of pervasion at all;
how then could you grant even this much concession regarding the example?
However, by virtue of the recognition of that [invariable concomitance], the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) in a general sense is indeed accepted.

And when that exists, the establishment of the probandum occurs precisely through the similarity with the example; there is no doubt, because doubt arises from the non-apprehension of specific characteristics.
In this case, since the specific characteristic—the universal mark (liṅgasāmānya)—is apprehended as included within the term "similarity with the example," how could there be any doubt?

The term "probandum-probans" (*sādhyasādhana*) is not merely a synonym; rather, by indicating the five-fold characteristic (*pañcalakṣaṇaka*) of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), it serves specifically to establish the status of the reason (*hetu*) as a valid reason. Why? Because a reason is a reason precisely because it is a probans—that is, because it is a means of cognition (*gamaka*). Furthermore, this quality of being a probans cannot be established without the five-fold characteristic necessary connection; therefore, that [connection] is indicated by the term "probandum-probans."

And since that [instrumentality] also attains the status of being a constituent part of the means of accomplishment by containing the relationship between the instigator and the instigated, it is indicated as being of precisely that nature.
For this very reason, it will be stated that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, only the non-probative (aprayojaka) is a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa).

As for the question, "From what does this relationship of being the probandum and the probans (sādhyasādhanatva) of the reason arise?", it is stated by means of the ablative case ending (*pañcamī*)—which serves to exclude doubt—as being "due to similarity with the example" (*udāharaṇasādharmyāt*).

Therefore, as for what is said by others—that if similarity (*sādharmya*) were the reason (*hetu*), there would be neither a constituent of the sentence nor the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*)—this is untenable. For if the fifth case-ending has the meaning [of the reason] as its essence, it is useless with respect to the reason; or else, even in that case, [the reason] is established by it. Furthermore, a different definition is provided for the constituent of the sentence.
And this is now stated: "The reason (hetu) is the means of proving the probandum through similarity with the example.
That speech which proceeds from the aforementioned similarity with the example by way of the intended [conclusion] and so forth is the reason.

And although the production of knowledge also occurs—whether from that which is the object of action or from that which is the instrument—by virtue of its similarity to the example, nevertheless, it is determined to be "speech" (vacana) by the power of its being an instrument for the constituent parts of a sentence.
If this is merely the formulation of a component of a sentence, for what purpose then was the exposition of meaning stated here? It is because that [exposition] is useful for it.

What is the purpose of including the mention of the "probandum" (*sādhya*) and the "probans" (*sādhana*) in the definition of a statement? For the exclusion of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) is already established simply by the exclusion of reasons that are not real entities; thus, that [mention] is not for the sake of excluding the utterance of a fallacious reason.
Rather, it is for the sake of understanding the specific nature of the statement of a valid reason.

A statement that indicates only the essential form—such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth—should not be employed; rather, it must be expressed with a case-ending denoting a reason, such as "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*), "by means of being produced" (*kṛtakatvena*), or "this is produced from this" (*kṛtako 'yam asmāt*).
For in this way, that becomes the proof of what is to be proven.
Likewise, [the reason is not established] due to dissimilarity (vaidharmya). //1-1-35//
The mention of "example" (*udāharaṇa*) and "proving the probandum" (*sādhyasādhana*) continues [from the previous rule].
And this is understood from the force of the inclusion of the word *tathā*: "the reason (*hetu*) is that which proves the probandum through dissimilarity to the example.

Here too, because the verbal expression of the reason is preceded by the actual reason as an entity (*arthātmaka*), it is the actual reason as an entity that is employed first. Therefore, they explain the sūtra for its definition as being devoid of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), just as in the previous case.

When it is stated as "the reason characterized by dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyahetu*), there would arise the undesirable consequence that even a property dissimilar to the subject (*pakṣa*) which occurs in the counter-subject (*vipakṣa*)—such as the argument "these horses are horned because they are horses," where all individual horses are taken as the subject—would constitute a valid reason; therefore, the term "example" (*udāharaṇa*) is included [in the definition].

Nevertheless, since it would follow that even the uncommon [reason] and so forth—which lack similarity to the example—would possess the status of a reason, the terms "probandum" (sādhya) and "probans" (sādhana) must be supplied here as before; these indicate the necessary connection (pratibandha) and serve to exclude all fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).

Therefore, since the exclusion of all fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) is established by that alone, the inclusion of the term "dissimilarity to the example" (udāharaṇavaidharmya) must be explained as serving to exclude those reasons that possess both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with similar instances.

Now, it might be objected: the word "dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya*) is indeed capable of excluding a purely positive reason (*kevalānvayin*)—which lacks negative concomitance (*avyatireka*)—because such a reason is devoid of any dissimilar instance. But how can it be said that this word excludes a reason possessing both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*), since such a reason possesses dissimilarity just as it possesses similarity with the example? [The author replies: Just as the exclusion of the purely positive reason is understood from the employment of the word "dissimilarity," so too is the exclusion of the reason possessing both positive and negative concomitance understood.
For the terms "probandum" and "probans" indicate a necessary connection;
and that necessary connection has been explained as consisting of negative and positive concomitance.
Even in this case of establishing through dissimilarity (vaidharmya), if that same [fault] is described,
then because it has already been stated previously, the inclusion of dissimilarity would be useless.
Therefore, the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) stands as fruitful, intended to express the logical connection known as pure negative concomitance (kevalavyatireka).
Alternatively, let the word "only" (eva) be supplied [from elsewhere] to exclude that;
or let the explanation be provided by way of a specific injunction.
Furthermore, no purely positive reason (kevalānvayihetu) is ever observed;
therefore, its object of exclusion will be exactly as previously stated.

[Objection: "In that case, by this very logic, the previous sūtra would be for the purpose of defining the purely positive (kevalānvayin) reason; just as here the mention of 'dissimilarity' (vaidharmya) serves to exclude similarity (sādharmya), so there the mention of 'similarity' would serve to exclude dissimilarity. [Response: It has been stated in this regard that a reason called "purely positive" is not possible, and thus it is simply not to be defined. Therefore, it is established that the previous sūtra is for the definition of the reason possessing both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), whereas this [present] sūtra is for the definition of the purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason.

Even in the view that the definition of a reason (*hetu*) consists of its objective referent (*arthātmaka*), the reading of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) should be explained, as before, as having the result of dispelling doubt.
The Sūtra should likewise be applied to the view that the definition of a reason consists of its verbal expression (*vacanātmaka*):
"A statement proceeding from the aforementioned dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), which establishes the probandum, should be employed ending in a case-ending denoting a reason."
They object as follows: "A definition can only be stated when there is an object to be defined (lakṣya).
However, since a so-called 'purely negative' (kevalavyatirekin) reason does not exist at all, for what is this definition being stated?
For it has been stated that the capacity of a reason to produce cognition depends upon an invariable concomitance (pratibandha)."
And the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been explained as having five characteristics.
There will be five fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) based on the absence of each one of these characteristics respectively.

Therefore, just like an unestablished reason (*asiddha*) that lacks the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), it is not logical for a reason that is devoid of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) to function as a valid reason.

If a probandum were established by a reason that relies solely on negative concomitance (*kevalavyatireka*), then since such a means of proof would be so easily available, anyone could prove whatever they pleased.
Or else, why would even an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason—despite possessing negative concomitance—not be accepted as a valid reason?
Moreover, because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not definitively ascertained, there is doubt regarding negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as well:
does the exclusion [of the reason] from the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) occur, or otherwise?

For when a positive concomitance (anvaya) has been apprehended in some instance, the exclusion of the reason (hetu-vyāvṛtti) understood elsewhere is determined to be caused precisely by the exclusion of the probandum (sādhya-vyāvṛtti), and not otherwise.
It is only in this way that one avoids the fallacy of "doubtful negative concomitance" (sandigdhavyatireka), and not otherwise.
And if the negative concomitance is doubtful, how can there be the relationship of the probandum and the probans?
Since the object to be defined is thus absent, this definition of it is stated.

Therefore, one should not describe the general definition of the two types of reasons by first mentioning the apprehension of the probandum and the probans, and then describing the positive-negative (anvayavyatirekin) reason by mentioning the similarity with the example, and the purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason by mentioning the dissimilarity with the example.
Rather, the definition of a single type of reason—one possessing both positive and negative concomitance—should be explained by means of the two sūtras.
Since both positive and negative concomitance are constituent parts of the means of proof, the first sūtra defines positive concomitance, while the other sūtra elucidates negative concomitance.

For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya did not ask, "Is the definition of the probans (hetu) merely this much? nor did he say "no"; rather, he explained [the sūtra] as a single syntactical unit with the words "likewise by dissimilarity" (tathā vaidharmyāt).

Furthermore, in both sūtras, he stated the same example for the probans that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatirekin), namely: "because of having the property of being subject to origination" (utpattidharmakatvāt).

Regarding this, they say: if we were to accept some purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) reason as being exclusively dry [i.e., lacking positive concomitance], then we would indeed be subject to such an objection. However, we maintain that this reason possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), and that in certain specific cases of the probandum (*sādhya*), it assumes the status of a purely negative reason by virtue of its qualification.
For example, the quality of being an effect (*kāryatva*) residing in desire and so forth, in the proof of the Self (*ātman*).

For in that case, the mere state of being an effect is observed to be pervaded by the mere state of being dependent, as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), since it is seen that effects such as a jar are dependent [on a substratum].
Furthermore, where there is no dependence, there is also no state of being an effect, as in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.

This very reason, possessing both positive and negative concomitance, becomes a "purely negative" (*kevala-vyatirekin*) when it is employed with a qualification—namely, *kāryatvāt* (because of being an effect)—in order to prove that [the self] resides in a substratum distinct from the visible body and other such supports, provided that subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) apply to the body and so forth.
Because the self (*ātman*), which is the substratum distinct from the body and so forth, is eternally imperceptible, its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) cannot be observed.

Since that which is perceptible, which is rooted in positive concomitance (*anvaya*), attains the status of a purely negative reason (*kevalavyatirekin*) in that state and is thereby accepted as a logical mark (*hetu*), there is no occasion for the previously mentioned fault.
For no one is able to prove everything by means of such a reason;
nor, this being the case, does it follow that an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason would function as a valid probans.
Its possession of five characteristics will also be in relation to its previous substratum.

As for the suspicion that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) might be doubtful, that too finds no place in the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*), which is rooted in both positive and negative concomitance; for an effect is observed to be dependent, and one observes the exclusion of "being an effect" from space (*vyoman*) and the like through the exclusion of "dependence.
Now, the specific exclusion observed in the case of a jar or a body is understood to be caused precisely by the exclusion of a particular substratum; thus, the negative concomitance is not doubtful.

And since this has been determined in the context of the *Ātmasiddhi*, there exists indeed an irreproachable purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) reason for the definition of the "definable" (*lakṣya*); therefore, the subsequent sūtra is intended for that definition.
The preceding sūtra is intended for the definition of the positive-negative (*anvayavyatirekin*) reason.
A purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) reason does not exist at all.
Regarding the general definition, however, it should be understood either from the words "probandum" and "probans," just as in the definition of inference.
We shall certainly follow the commentators, or we shall explain it in some way or another;

however, we cannot disregard such a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*), which is the supreme weapon for establishing the self (*ātman*) and other principles. Therefore, even an explanation that does not strictly follow the commentary is preferable.
An example (udāharaṇa) is an instance which, by virtue of its similarity to the subject to be proven (sādhya), possesses the property of that [subject]. 1.1.36.
In the passage "inference preceded by that," only the means for grasping the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) was set forth;
here, however, the nature of that connection and its similarity to the example (*udāharaṇasādharmya*) are stated.

Likewise, regarding the statement "an example is that object upon which ordinary people and investigators have a consensus of understanding," the general definition of both types of examples—being accepted by both the proponent and the opponent—is stated.

In this case, however, it is appropriate that the definition consists of one being the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the property that proves (*sādhana*), established through the relationship of the instigator and the instigated (*prayojya-prayojaka-bhāva*), while the second is devoid of those properties.

In that context, "possessing the property of that [subject] by virtue of similarity with the probandum" is the definition of a similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Although we are currently dealing with words, the investigation of the example as an objective entity must be carried out just like the investigation of the reason (*hetu*), because it is instrumental to that purpose.

The subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is [the minor term]. "Similarity with that" (*tena sādharmyam*) means a common property (*samāno dharmaḥ*), which is the general mark (*liṅgasāmānyam*). That very similarity with the example (*udāharaṇasādharmyam*) mentioned previously is designated by both terms because it resides in both; thus, it is expressed here by the phrase "similarity with the object to be proven" (*sādhyasādharmya*). Therefore, "that which possesses the state of having that property" (*taddharmabhāvī*) refers to that in which there occurs a property of the object to be proven—such as permanence (*nityatva*) and so forth—which exists due to that similarity with the object to be proven. By the use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), the sense of being the cause or motive (*prayojakatva*) is expressed.

The meaning is that a *sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta* (an example by similarity) is that wherein the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) exists along with the property that serves as the reason (*hetudharma*).

And since that very [example], when functioning as the object of speech, becomes the *udāharaṇa* (the illustrative instance), there is no contradiction in the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words *dṛṣṭānta* and *udāharaṇa*, which respectively denote the "object" and the "statement of the object."

When the example itself, being expressed by a statement that demonstrates the positive concomitance (anvaya), is called the "illustration" (udāharaṇa), then the statement expressing that [example] indeed becomes the illustration:
"Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, just like a pot."

[Objection: "In that case, an example would have to be taught only where the possession of common properties (*sādharmyavattā*) is produced by the reason (*hetu*), as in the rising of clouds and rain; it would not be taught where the existence of the reason is produced by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), as in the inference from smoke. [Reply: The 'Beloved of the Gods' (the fool) does not understand what is being shown here. Here, the relationship of producer and produced (*prayojyaprayojakabhāva*) is not intended with respect to *origination* (*utpatti*), but rather with respect to *cognition* (*jñapti*). And in the context of cognition, smoke itself functions as the producer of the knowledge of fire.
For the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) between smoke and fire is not based on a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)."
However, it has been stated more than once that this is by means of a relationship called "restriction" (niyama), which consists precisely in constant concomitance (nitya-sāhacarya).
Let smoke indeed arise from fire by its own nature;
however, fire does not imply this [smoke], for it is smoke itself that implies fire.
If the status of being an instigator were expressed by the fifth case-ending [the ablative],
then the instruction would have to be stated as "wherever there is fire," and so forth.
For that whose status as an instigator (prayojakatva) one wishes to express,
that indeed requires mention by means of the word "yat" in the preceding [verse].
And in that case, fire would indeed be the cause with respect to smoke;
yet it is not proper to say so, because of the fault of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika).
Therefore, they maintain that [the reason] functions as a motivator (*prayojaka*), not with respect to origination;
rather, it is intended with respect to cognition (*jñapti*), and that is indeed appropriate for a logical reason (*hetu*).
Therefore, that in which the property to be proved (sādhyadharma) is shown as being connected with the property of the reason (hetudharma) is the example based on similarity (sādharmyadṛṣṭānta).
It is thus established that the statement of such an example is the "illustration" (udāharaṇa).
Or, by the reversal of that, the opposite [is established]. (3-2-37)
The term "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is understood here as "illustration" (*udāharaṇa*). The word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the similarity with the probandum (*sādhyasādharmya*).

Although that was explained in the previous sūtra as the generality of the mark (*liṅgasāmānya*), nevertheless, because both are possible here, it should be understood as the generality of the object to be inferred (*anumeyasāmānya*) which possesses similarity with the probandum.

By contrast with that, the example which possesses the opposite properties—that is, which lacks the probandum and is devoid of the means of proof—is the example by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). When this becomes the object of speech as before, it constitutes the "illustration by dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya-udāharaṇa*).
The use of the neuter gender in the word *viparītam* is in reference to the illustration (*udāharaṇa*).

But for what purpose is the absence of the probans described through the absence of the probandum in the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), rather than—by way of the established rule of the example of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*)—the absence of the probandum from the absence of the probans itself? To this it has been said: "The relationship of pervaded and pervader that exists between the properties of the probandum and the probans must be understood as being reversed in the case of their absences."

What is the reason? For when the property to be established (sādhyadharma), fire, pervades the property that establishes it (sādhanadharma), smoke, non-fire—finding no place there—must reside in smoke alone, as there is no other possibility.

Likewise, when the absence of the property to be established, non-fire, is pervaded by the absence of the property that establishes it, non-smoke, smoke finds no place there; having no other resort, it resides in fire alone.

If, however, just as in the case of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is demonstrated by the statement "in the absence of the probans, the probandum does not exist," then non-fire, being pervaded by the absence of smoke, would have no place to reside other than in fire itself; thus, it would necessarily depend upon smoke alone.

But this does not hold, because fire is observed even in the absence of smoke. Therefore, the status of being a logical reason (*hetu*) for that which exists only in a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣaikadeśavṛtti*) is well-established, provided that the pervasion is established through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Moreover, when it is stated that the absence of fire is pervaded by the absence of smoke, then "non-smoke" is restricted [by the rule]: "let it not be non-fire.
However, since fire is not necessarily [pervaded by] smoke, it might—due to its independence—touch upon smoke; thus, because of this deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the logical connection would collapse.
As it has been said: "But when the absence of the probandum contradicts the fallacious reason..."
Then the object to be proven, having been perceived from that [reason], would abide within the means of proof.
In this way, when the probandum is restricted, it becomes manifested within the proof;
however, because the proof is independent, it could occur even in the absence of the probandum.

Therefore, even in a case where the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) have equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*), and where it might be suspected that the [probans] is not a valid reason because it occurs only in a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), one must still demonstrate the absence of the probans in the absence of the property to be proven—intending to show the exclusion of the probans from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
For example: "Wherever there is no impermanence, there is also no 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*)," as in the case of space (*ākāśa*).

Even a reason for which the counter-positive (vipakṣa) does not exist is all the more excluded from that [counter-positive], because it does not occur there due to the absence of that [counter-positive].

Therefore, even one who asserts the impermanence of all things is not prevented from demonstrating a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) in this way: "Wherever there is no permanence, there also is no producedness, as in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like."

Both these examples—by way of similarity and dissimilarity—are possible when the reason possesses both positive and negative concomitance; they should be employed alternatively, since the pervasion is demonstrated by either one alone—what need is there for the other?
Some, however, desire the formulation of both [the positive and negative concomitances] in order to demonstrate the excellence of the pervasion (vyāpti);
whether this be so or not,
it is not a matter for great dispute.

Now, one might object: "Is this not declared to be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called 'excess of reason and example' (*hetūdāharaṇādhika*)? That [point of defeat] will apply here, but with the intention of referring only to cases of the same kind;
that is, it is a point of defeat when there is a multiplicity of examples based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or a multiplicity of examples based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Let this matter rest."

Thus, having explained the nature of the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), those instances that lack its defining characteristics become fallacious instances (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*). Among these, there are three fallacious similar instances caused by defects in the factual basis: being deficient in the probandum (*sādhya-vikala*), deficient in the probans (*sādhana-vikala*), and deficient in both (*ubhaya-vikala*).
There are two caused by defects in the verbal expression: the lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) and the inverted positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*).
For example, in the argument "sound is eternal because it is incorporeal," the instance "like cognition" (*buddhi*) is deficient in the probandum;

"like an atom" (*paramāṇu*) is deficient in the probans; and "like a jar" (*ghaṭa*) is deficient in both. Furthermore, the claim that "in space (*vyoman*), incorporeality exists because of its eternity" is an instance of lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*).
When it should have been stated that "whatever is formless is eternal," stating instead that "whatever is eternal is formless" constitutes a reversed positive concomitance (viparītānvaya).

There are also exactly five fallacies of the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*): three based on the object—the one from which the probandum is excluded, the one from which the probans is excluded, and the one from which both are excluded;
and two based on the verbal expression—lack of negative concomitance (*avyatireka*) and inverted negative concomitance (*viparītavyatireka*).

For example, regarding that same reason [“immateriality”], the statement “wherever there is no permanence, there is also no immateriality, as in the case of atoms” is an instance where the probandum is not excluded (*sādhyāvyāvṛtta*).
For example, "as in the case of a Buddha" is an instance where the probans is absent from the dissimilar instances (sādhanāvyāvṛtta);
"as in the case of space" is an instance where [the probans] is absent from neither (ubhayāvyāvṛtta).
Since permanence and incorporeality do not exist in a jar, this constitutes a lack of negative concomitance (avyatireka).

When it ought to be stated that "where there is no permanence, there is also no incorporeality," stating instead that "where there is no incorporeality, there is also no permanence" constitutes a reversed negative concomitance (viparītavyatireka).
And these, in accordance with the actual state of things, are indeed defects of the reason (*hetudoṣa*), because they follow upon it;
for this very reason, they were not taught by the author of the Sūtra, just like the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
However, we have demonstrated them in this way for the benefit of our students.
The application (upanaya) is the connection of the probandum with the example, by means of the phrase "so it is" or "not so it is," depending on the illustration. (NS 1.1.39)
The application (*upanaya*) is the subsumption of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), which depends upon the example (*udāharaṇa*) for its own attainment.
It is of two kinds—either "so it is" or "not so it is"—due to the twofold nature of the example.
Among these, the application "so it is" depends upon an example based on similarity (*sādharmya*).

"That which is produced is seen to be impermanent, like a jar; yet sound is not produced in that way"—this is the application (upanaya) based on an example by dissimilarity (vaidharmya). "That which is permanent is seen to be unproduced, like space; yet sound is not produced in that way.
Here too, due to the conjunction of two negations, an affirmation is indeed understood.
[Objection: Is not the phrase "of the probandum" (sādhyasya) unexpressive [in this context]?
For the application (upanaya) is the application of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma), not the application of the probandum (sādhya).

For the probandum would have to be either the property (dharma) or the locus (dharmin); yet this application belongs to neither of those two. [Reply: It is said that here, by "probandum," only the locus (dharmin) is intended, not the property (dharma).

In this context, the application of the reason is as follows: "and likewise, sound is produced. This genitive case in the word *sādhyasya* (of the probandum) should be understood as having the sense of the locative;
thus, the application of the reason to the subject (*dharmin*) which is the probandum is called the *upanaya* (application).
Surely, if the locus (*ādhāra*) is intended to be expressed here, the locative case would apply;
or, if only a mere relation (*saṃbandhamātra*) is to be expressed, how can it be called a locus?

This [connection] does not occur even when a general relation has been stated; rather, there is a conjunction with the substratum (dharmin), though it may serve as the locus (ādhāra) when a specific consideration is made.
When a specific relation is hidden within [the meaning], the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is generally employed;
the established rule is that the so-called "residual" (*śeṣa*) is simply the non-intention of expressing the specific grammatical relations (*kāraka*).
And likewise, in cases such as "the king's man," "the Brahmin's water-pot," and "the tree's branch," the distinction is always established internally.
And therefore, "inquiry into dharma" (*dharmajijñāsā*) means inquiry for the sake of dharma;

for just as in the expression "the desire to know that," this genitive case, although conveying a mere relationship, will result in signifying a specific [qualificative] relation. Thus, it is well said that there is a restatement of what is to be established.
Is it not the case that the statement of application (*upanaya*) is purposeless?
What is not already sufficient by the statements of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), for the sake of which the statement of application is uttered?
If it is for the purpose of establishing the presence of the reason in the subject (*dharmī*), then this [application] is in vain; it is indeed a useless exertion.
Because [the property] is already established by the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) itself, such as "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*), and so forth.

Now, as for the utterance [of the example] in order to establish a similarity between the subject (*sādhya*) and the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), that too is not clever; for its purpose is already served by the very statement "because of similarity with the example" (*udāharaṇasādharmyāt*).
Indeed, the statement of similarity with the example would be nothing other than the statement of the reason (*hetu*).

Now, regarding one's own realization, because that object is seen therein, there is the communication of it to another; yet even with respect to that reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*), they dispute.
Moreover, if after one has personally consumed the curd, some inference should occasionally arise in one's mind, why should that be taught to another?

Even this sequence of application consisting of the proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*) is based solely on an attachment to one's own system and does not proceed by the force of reality.
For indeed, from the mere statement, "Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, and sound is produced," who indeed would not understand the impermanence of sound?
In this matter, you alone, whose wealth consists of your vow of truth, are the authority.
Abandoning this *ḍiṇḍika*-like passion and closing your eyes for a moment, consider this: do you understand the meaning by this much, or not?
Therefore, casting aside partiality for your own system and disregarding such a five-membered syllogism, employ the statement exactly as it has been described.

To this it is replied: first, let your honor explain when asked—do we construct verbal formulations for the purpose of instructing others by following our own personal experience, or by conforming to the minds of others?

In this regard, because the intention of another is diverse and imperceptible, and thus difficult to comprehend, we do not know whether we should speak, what we should say, whether we should raise our arms, whether we should cause pain to the other with our elbow, whether we should communicate by hand gestures, whether we should employ merely a reason alone, whether we should utter a three-membered syllogism, or whether we should provide an even longer narrative than a five-membered syllogism—since the intention of another is thus unsettled, the other person is to be informed only by following one's own understanding.

In that regard, regarding one's own cognition, the subject (dharmin) such as a mountain is first perceived; thus, it is stated by means of the proposition (*pratijñā*). Thereafter, the mark (*liṅga*) such as smoke is apprehended; this is made known by the statement of the reason (*hetu*).
Then, the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, "wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen"—occurs; this is expressed by the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Then, the reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*)—"and thus, there is smoke here"—arises, which is communicated by the statement of application (*upanaya*).
Thereafter, the inferential cognition—"therefore, there is fire here"—is produced, which is expressed by the conclusion (*nigamana*).
Since the process culminates in the understanding of another, what else remains to be taught?
Nor can it be anything other than similar to the momentary state of curd, because it serves as a means for the comprehension of the object to be inferred.

Even for those who maintain that there is no such thing as "subsumptive cognition" (*parāmarśajñāna*), the statement of the application (*upanaya*) must necessarily be admitted; for, in order to achieve the comprehension of the object of inference, only a reason whose power has been demonstrated in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is effective, and not otherwise.

Therefore, although by the statement of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) only the mere connection between the reason and the subject has been established, nevertheless, since it remains uncertain whether that reason—whose capacity has been demonstrated in the example—actually exists in that same manner within that very subject, the doubt regarding its non-establishment cannot be dispelled without the statement of the application (upanaya). Thus, it must necessarily be employed. Furthermore, because the construction of a formal argument follows one's own internal realization, the sequence [of the members] is also useful exactly as stated.

For this very reason, the statement "whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent" is untenable; because when the subject (*dharmin*) and the reason (*hetu*) residing therein have not yet been understood, it is impossible to recall the pervasion (*vyāpti*) at the very outset, and thus such a statement is improper.
We shall explain that this is an instance of the defeat-condition (*nigrahasthāna*) called "speaking out of order" (*aprāptakāla*), which is a reversal of the members of the syllogism.

Furthermore, by asserting that one should employ only this much—"Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, and sound is produced"—you have admitted the statement "and sound is produced" as the application (*upanaya*), yet you have concealed the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) as "because of being produced. If you argue that the statement of the reason consists only of "and sound is produced," that is trivial, because a probans ought to be indicated by the ablative case or similar grammatical markers. Thus, this [position of yours] is nonsensical.
As for the statement that "for the wise, only the reason (*hetu*) alone is to be stated," that too is not correct, because the wise understand the reason precisely by virtue of their knowledge.

These "wise" ones are unprecedented indeed, who claim to know the meaning of the four members of the syllogism beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*), yet do not find the meaning of the statement of the reason itself.

Therefore, since the intention of another is entirely difficult to discern, one should convince the other by constructing a formal argument (*vākyaracanā*) according to the previously mentioned sequence, which is based on the witness of one's own experience.
The conclusion (nigamana) is the restatement of the proposition (pratijñā) following the presentation of the reason (hetu). //1.1//

The *upanaya* (application) is the statement of the reason (*hetvapadeśa*), by which the reason—whose capacity has been ascertained in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*)—is applied to the subject to be proven (*sādhyadharmī*).
The *nigamana* (conclusion) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following from that statement of the reason.
It is called *nigamana* because by means of it the previously stated members [of the syllogism] are brought together (*nigamyante*) and directed toward a single object to be proven.

Therefore, "sound is impermanent because it is produced"—this is the conclusion (*nigamana*). Whether the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are distinguished by similarity or dissimilarity, and whether the application (*upanaya*)—which depends upon them—is of two kinds, namely "in that manner" (*tathā*) or "not in that manner" (*na tathā*), it remains exactly the same as the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

Now, is it not the case that the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) itself is useless, because it is a statement of something that is not a member of the proof? Furthermore, how can this talk of the conclusion (*nigamana*) being fruitful as a restatement of that very same proposition be maintained? For the text is not expressive [of that], since the proposition is the indication of what is to be proven (*sādhya*), whereas the conclusion is the indication of what has been proven (*siddha*).
In the case of the speaker or the written text, the conclusion (nigamana) is redundant precisely because it involves repetition;
furthermore, in one's own realization, it is observed that the comprehension of the probandum occurs immediately after the knowledge of the consideration (parāmarśa).
Since that same comprehension arises for another person immediately upon hearing the statement of the application (upanaya), what is the purpose of stating the conclusion?
It is said: first of all, the fruitfulness of the thesis has indeed been established.

And this restatement of it is made because, despite the difference between the proven and the yet-to-be-proven, there is a similarity consisting merely in the indication of the property-possessor (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*).
Furthermore, precisely because of the distinction between the proven and the yet-to-be-proven, there is no fruitlessness caused by tautology.

Furthermore, for one's own realization, once the cognition of the probandum has arisen following the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it does not become purposeless when it is communicated to another.
Just as I have understood this probandum from this reason, so too should you understand it; let there be no obstacle for you in this matter.
When this has been stated, the doubt of one who is doubtful is dispelled, and the error of one with a perverted mind is corrected;
and for that purpose lies this labor of presenting an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
Therefore, they call this the conclusion (*nigamana*), which serves to negate the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the opposite.

However, those who—out of a desire to justify the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) which consists of the formulation of the probandum exactly as it was heard—still fail to understand the establishment of the proposition even now, [should be corrected as follows]: the suspicion of the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason has already been dispelled by the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For the suspicion of being uncommon would arise only if there were a possibility that a specific property might serve as the reason.
But when the statement of the example, "whatever is produced is impermanent," declares that the general property is the reason, how could one raise the objection of its being uncommon?

If, however, it should be suspected that the reason is "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) because it is applied to the subject of the thesis by means of the statement of application (upanaya), then its occurrence in the instance-subject (dṛṣṭāntadharmin) must be demonstrated.
Once that has been demonstrated, one might again suspect that it is "unestablished" (asiddha) with respect to the [thesis] subject because of its occurrence there.

Furthermore, to exclude that [fault], one must apply the reason to the subject (*dharmin*); thus, one would proceed under the suspicion of being either "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) or "unestablished" (*asiddha*), and consequently, there would never be a cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore, the application of that [reason] is not for the purpose of removing the suspicion of being uncommon, but rather according to the previous method alone.

Therefore, in order to unify the constituent members— which have been arranged in the aforementioned sequence— within the intended meaning, the statement of conclusion (*nigamana*) should be employed.

These five members, beginning with the proposition and ending with the conclusion, when supported by the means of valid cognition such as scripture as appropriate, and being mutually connected, establish their own object.
In that regard, in the primary sense, all the members are supported by inference alone, which is the means of comprehension;
however, for the sake of elaboration, it is stated that they are supported by other means of valid cognition.
First of all, scripture is accepted as supporting the thesis because it has the nature of instruction; however,
regarding such a subject as "sound is impermanent," the speaker, like a seer (*ṛṣi*), teaches through inference due to his independence.
The statement of the thesis (pratijñā), however, follows its shadow [i.e., the inference] because it conforms to its form;

or rather, for the sake of establishing the authority of verbal testimony (śabda-prāmāṇya) within this treatise, the thesis is said to be supported by scripture (āgama), since that thesis has sound as its object.
The statement of the reason is supported by inference.
The example, however, is based on perception, because the determination of pervasion (vyāpti) is rooted in that [perception].

Just as in the case of "as is a cow, so is a gavaya," by the analogy "as is a jar, so is sound"—because it resembles the statement of a forest-dweller or similar person which serves as the cause for comparison—the comparison (upamāna) is said to be that which supports the application (upanaya).

As for the conclusion (*nigamana*), however, because its purpose is to join all the members [of the syllogism] together in one place, it is indeed supported by all the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Because they are mutually dependent, the reason (*hetu*) would be without a basis in the absence of the proposition (*pratijñā*); therefore, that [proposition] must be stated first: "Sound is impermanent.
Then, since the opponent desires to know the reason, the statement of the reason is uttered: "Because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*).

Once the reason has been heard, the example (*udāharaṇa*) is stated to demonstrate where its pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been ascertained: "Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar."

When this has been stated, the *upanaya* (application) is introduced to dispel the doubt as to whether such a reason—whose power has thus been ascertained—actually exists in the subject (*dharmin*) to be proven or not, which would constitute the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddha*).

Following that sequence, the *nigamana* (conclusion) is articulated to demonstrate that the realization of the probandum (*sādhya*) occurs for you as well, thereby establishing all the members [of the syllogism] toward a single object to be proven.
Since this entire connected discourse would be incomplete without at least one of these members, a five-membered statement must be employed according to the prescribed order.

Thus, having begun its assistance, this collection of members—mutually dependent and established through means of valid cognition such as scripture (āgama) by means of results conducive to that [purpose]—necessarily establishes the range of objects to be proven.

And regarding that which is skillful concerning these objects of knowledge, the author of the *Vṛtti* declared: "A thesis cannot be defeated by those who primarily employ fallacious arguments (*jāti-prayoga*)."
Thus ends the examination of the members [of a syllogism].
Thus ends the tenth chapter of the Nyāyamañjarī, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Jayanta.

Since *tarka* (reasoning) was mentioned immediately after the members of the syllogism in the first aphorism, its definition is stated in accordance with that order of mention: "Reasoning (*tarka*) is the deliberation (*ūha*) for the sake of knowing the truth regarding an object whose true nature is unknown, based on the application of logical grounds" (NS 1.1.40). Regarding the phrase "[an object whose true nature is unknown]," because it is expressed in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the referent of the compound is the object (*artha*) itself, not the person. Indeed, the person would have been indicated by the genitive case, as in "one whose true nature is unknown.
By the inclusion of the word "true nature" (*tattva*), it is indicated that the subject (*dharmin*) is known merely in its general characteristics, while its specific nature remains unascertained.

Regarding the phrase “by way of the occurrence of a cause,” he states that the observation of a cause conducive to establishing one of the two sides being delineated by a state of doubt is what gives rise to *tarka*.
For this very reason, although the desire to know (*bubhutsā*) and deliberation (*vimarśa*) occur when the true nature of an object is unknown, they do not attain the status of *tarka*.
By the phrase “for the sake of the knowledge of reality,” he directly excludes its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
However, by assisting the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) through the purification of its object, it (reasoning) conduces to the knowledge of reality.
We shall explain the purpose for employing these synonymous terms, such as "reasoning" (tarka) and "investigation" (ūha).

Therefore, this is the meaning of the sūtra: when the true nature [of an object] is unknown but the subject (*dharmin*) is known in a general way, the cognition of probability (*saṃbhāvanā-pratyaya*), which is an appearance of necessity (*bhavitavyatāvabhāsa*), arises from the observation of a reason favorable to one side; by weakening the other side, it assists the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends that [truth], and proceeding easily toward the knowledge of reality, it is *ūha*, namely *tarka* (reasoning).
For example, upon seeing a subject characterized by height in a place such as a pleasure garden, there arises the cognition: "This must be a person."

Now, one might object: since "for the sake of the knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñānārtham*) has been stated, the state of having an unknown reality (*avijñātatattvatā*) is already obtained by implication; why then is it restated explicitly? True. However, in some cases, even when the reality of an object is already known, if it has been previously discarded through reasoning, it may later be grasped as being qualified by that very reasoning, as in the recollection: "This matter was reasoned out by me. In such a case, the reasoning serving as a qualifier would become an end in itself for the sake of knowing reality. To exclude this possibility, the term "having an unknown reality" is mentioned once again.
What is intended here is that reasoning serves the purpose of attaining knowledge of reality by way of purifying the path;
and this is possible only when the object whose reality is not yet known.
Is it not the case that there is no such thing as a conceptual cognition (*tarka-pratyaya*) existing in an interval between doubt and certainty?
For instance, if this cognition occurs for one who has not yet apprehended the specific distinction, then it would simply be doubt;
if it occurs for one who has apprehended the specific distinction, it would touch upon certainty itself.
Even a cognition that lacks the manifestation of the meaning of the restrictive particle "eva" in the phrase "it is the person alone" cannot fail to be a definitive ascertainment (*niścaya*).

If one considers even the sight of a place associated with the galloping of a horse to be capable of setting aside the possibility of it being a post (*sthāṇu*), then that very sight would indeed be a cause for its ascertainment, just like the sight of specific features such as hands and feet.

Furthermore, if you suspect that someone might be burying a post in that very same horse-riding ground at night, then by resorting to the position of the "post," there would again be doubt; thus, a third position does not exist. Since there is no object to be defined (*lakṣya*), for what, then, would this definition (*lakṣaṇa*) be?
It is said: Indeed, cognitions that are to be personally realized cannot be removed by the expansion of conceptual constructions imagined by one's own mind.
For instance, there is one cognition, "Is it a post or a person?"; another is, "This is certainly a person";
and yet another is the intermediate, third cognition of probability, "This must be a person," which is witnessed by one's own heart.
For in a case of doubt, there is an equal mention of both sides;
however, in a definitive conclusion, the other side is not touched upon even in the slightest.
But reasoning, as if raising up one side or another,
shines forth upon seeing the sight of the horse that serves as the seed for the expectation of a man.

For the sight of a particular place suitable for riding produces in a man merely a possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), but it is not capable of determining him as a man by completely excluding the alternative of a post, as is the case with the perception of specific features such as a head or hands.

Therefore, this cognition belongs to one who has not yet grasped the specific characteristics; yet it is not a doubt (*saṃśaya*), because it arises through the occurrence of reasons favorable to one of the two alternatives.

But how could a specific place for riding on horses, like a particular man distinguished by his hands, feet, and so forth, fail to produce a specific effect? Or, if it were to do so, since the position of the opponent has been refuted, this would simply be a definitive conclusion; who then is there to question this? For just as the determination of a "man" occurs upon seeing a head, hands, and so on, it does not occur in the same way upon seeing a horse-riding place.
Furthermore, entities are not subject to such questioning as "let them be thus" or "let them not be thus."
And whereas in another place the faction of the post remains as if in competition, it does not do so on the grounds for the sport of riding; rather, it becomes slackened.
Furthermore, because of the possibility of negligence, it does not cease entirely.
"Now, if it does not cease, then let it contend;
or rather, let it not contend.
For the position of the post remains as it was, so this is merely a doubt"—do not say such a thing.

The aspect of the post does not cease in its entirety, nor does it remain [as such]; rather, just like Triśaṅku, it hangs suspended, serving to exclude other possible conditions. It is only through the experience of such a cognition that this is conceptually constructed. For when one sees a place suitable for a man’s amorous play, specific men come to mind, whereas specific posts do not.
And since doubt arises from the recollection of two specific features, this particular place for riding and playing weakens the "post" alternative but does not sever it entirely.
From seeing that, there arises another cognition of a deliberative nature: "This must be a man. Enough with excessive detail.

As for the example of reasoning (*tarka*) provided by the Commentator—namely, that because one observes the cessation of birth, there is the conviction that [birth] is produced and has a cause—that does not strike the heart.
For, according to that sequence, this is indeed a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*); it is the true nature of its cause, not reasoning (*tarka*).
Alternatively, since this is an illustration of the effect (*kārya*), even in that case, the cognition of reasoning (*tarka-pratyaya*) occurring between doubt and certainty should be understood;
it will serve as the illustrative example.
What is the purpose of stating "ūha" as a synonymous designation?
It is precisely to establish the definition of *tarka* (reasoning), namely its nature as *ūha*.
As for the other [synonym], it is a mention of the result in the sūtra for the sake of specifying the particular cause.
"By way of the occurrence of a cause" is the indication of the cause; "regarding an object whose true nature is unknown" is the indication of the object;
"for the sake of the knowledge of that true nature" is the indication of the result.
Moreover, some employ the word *tarka* (reasoning) in the sense of inference (*anumāna*),

as the authors of the legal codes (*smṛtikāra*) recite: "He who investigates the instruction on Dharma given by the seers through reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures— he, and no other, knows Dharma."
Thus,
here too, the term "ūha" (speculative deliberation) is employed so that *tarka* (reasoning) might not be understood as *anumāna* (inference).
In this context, *ūha* refers to *tarka*, not to *anumāna*.
Its purpose of leading to the knowledge of reality is also not direct, but rather through its being an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
and it is employed in debate precisely for that reason, in order to establish the object [of inquiry] and to manifest the purity of one's own heart.
The followers of Kapila, however, assert that inference (*ūha*) is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*).

That [view] has already been refuted by the path of rejecting the worldly conventions of the creation of the universe and so forth, which originate from *prakṛti*—as established in their own tenets and consisting of the forms of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
The followers of Jaimini, however, maintain by reasoning that *ūha* (adaptation) is the determination of the application [of ritual elements].
For in this system, a ritual action consists of a complete collection of causes and duties to be performed, whose nature—both seen and unseen—is taught;
as for example, the passage "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" recited in the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
In some cases, however, only the primary action is taught while no specific procedure is mentioned by name, as in: "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a sacrificial pap to Sūrya."

In this regard, it is deliberated: is the application of the meaning of the scripture completed there by merely accomplishing the primary act exactly as heard, devoid of its procedure (*itikartavyatā*), or must that primary act also be performed together with its procedure?

In that case, since the distinction between the performances of the ritual acts is established by their being prompted by a unique (apūrva) result, and because a principal act cannot be performed without its constituent parts, it follows—by the established principle of the section on the extension of injunctions (vidhyanta)—that the modified (vaikṛta) rite must be performed just like the archetypal (prākṛta) one; thus, it is performed together with its entire procedure (itikartavyatā).

Thus, once the principle of the extension of general rules (*sāmānyātideśa*) has been established, the inquiry arises as to which modified (*vaikṛta*) rite should acquire its ritual properties (*dharma*) from which original (*prakṛti*) rite. When it is settled that the properties in question must belong specifically to that original rite whose proximity is brought about by the consideration of similarity in the injunction regarding the substance, deity, and so forth, then—given the acquisition of a continuous stream of properties obtainable through the entire section on the concluding rites (*vidhyanta*) brought in by the unrestricted operation of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) occurring simultaneously—the determination of the performance (*prayoga*) through reasoning is called "adaptation" (*ūha*). By means of this, the properties are determined as to how they are to be employed in this specific manner.
And that is threefold, having as its objects mantra, sāman, and ritual refinement (saṃskāra).

Regarding the subject matter of *mantras*: first, consider the case here in this very context of the *saurya* oblation. When the question arises as to how the *nirvāpa-mantra*—which, by virtue of the principle of "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*), is extended from the *āgneya* sacrifice as "I offer you, acceptable to Agni" (*agnaye tvā juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*)—is to be employed, it is determined that since *mantras* are not useful through mere recitation, their utility is established by way of illuminating the substances, deities, and so forth that are integrated into the performance. In this instance, if this very archetypal mantra were used as "acceptable to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭam*), it would be inapplicable because it fails to illuminate the object actually present in the performance.

Since the mantra is being relinquished in its entirety, the ritual action revealed by that mantra would not be performed; therefore, it is understood that the mantra must be employed by extracting the word "Agni" and substituting the word "Sūrya," as in: "We offer you, acceptable to Sūrya."

Now, one might object: since the *ūha*, *pravara*, and the mention of names are not themselves mantras, would the ritual act not thus fail to be performed with a mantra? This is not so, by virtue of the principle that "that which is modified in a single part is not different from the original."

Since it is established that "the Sāmans are songs (*gīti*) whose subject matter is the *Sāma*," there are scriptural injunctions regarding certain ritual acts such as, "One sings the *Rathantara* upon the two *uttara* verses" and "One sings the *Bṛhat* upon the two *uttara* verses. That song (*gīti*)—whether the *Bṛhat* or the *Rathantara*—which arose in its original source-verse (*yonibhūtā ṛc*), is also employed upon another verse. Even when the syllables of that specific verse are altered, that same song is recognized even in the syllables of a different verse, as seen in common usage such as, "The *Rathantara* was sung by him using this *śloka* verse."

Furthermore, regarding *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite): in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the rite of purification is enjoined by the rule, "One threshes with the mortar and pestle that have been sprinkled"; and in some modification (*vikṛti*), it is heard: "The sacrificial porridge (*caru*) is one split by the nails.

In that case, since the mortar and pestle in the archetype serve a purpose by way of producing rice grains after first removing the husks and chaff required for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), in the modification as well, the purificatory rite called "sprinkling" is performed upon the nails which have taken over that function.
This is the threefold *ūha* (adaptation).

Some, however, describe *ūha* as being fivefold, following the sūtra: "[Since dharma is produced by purpose]" and "[When sequence is denied as distinct from substance, quality, and refinement, there is a connection with the injunction because of its concomitance]. But this, when elaborated, leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

"Furthermore, the ritualists accept that *ūha* is of only three kinds. On this point they say: "This word *ūha* is employed by the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) in the sense of inference (*anumāna*), just as the word *tarka* is used by the authors of the *Smṛtis* [in the passage]: 'he who investigates by means of *tarka*.'"

For instance, the modified (vaikṛta) rite is that which is accomplished through the employment of mantras that illuminate the substance inherent in that rite; this is the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma), because it is a ritual action (karma), like a primary (prākṛta) ritual action.
Since the pervasion (vyāpti) is grasped in such a manner regarding primary rituals, this entire path is indeed one of inference.
For example: "The fingernails are to be sprinkled with water for purification (prokṣaṇīya), because they bring about the rice grains used in the performance [of the sacrifice]."
In the case of the Sāmans, however, there is an explicit statement: "He sings the Rathantara on the two following verses.
Even in its absence, it shares the same status as the preparatory refinement (saṃskāra) of the mantra.

Moreover, in the Mīmāṃsā system—which consists of the elucidation of thousands of logical principles (nyāya) following upon the words [of the Veda]—it has been established that the object obtained through those principles is precisely the meaning of the *codanā* (Vedic injunction).
Therefore, lest the status of being the meaning of the *codanā* be lost to the object obtained through such reasoning (*ūha*) as described, this *ūha* must be included within the word itself;
otherwise, *dharma* would fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Modification (*ūha*), which consists of a specific application of logic, would not be something distinct from inference.
The substitution of the word "to Sūrya" in place of "to Agni" is the result of modification, not modification itself.
Therefore, the ritualists have not stated that modification is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) distinct from inference.

But here, according to the principle stated previously, *ūha* has been established as distinct from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, the Vedic scholars (*śrotriyas*), being ignorant of that, have applied the term *ūha* metaphorically to the system of logic (*nyāya*) and its fruit. Enough, then, with these discourses as dense as the expositions of other treatises.
Thus, this *ūha* (modification) postulated by the Mīmāṃsakas does not fall outside the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
however, what is described here in this treatise as *tarka* (reasoning) is that which exists in the interval between the states of doubt regarding the means of valid cognition.

Since determination occurs after deliberation, as it has been taught, it is defined: "Determination is the ascertainment of the object through the examination of the thesis and the counter-thesis. (NS 1.1.41)
When it is said that "ascertainment" (avadhāraṇa) means "determination" (nirṇaya), the inclusion of the word "object" (artha) is intended to prevent the inclusion of false ascertainment.
For there certainly exists an ascertainment of reality produced by the sense organs and other such means;

however, since the determination arising from the cessation of reasoning (nyāya) was the subject under discussion, it is specified here that only that which is produced by inference is to be defined. Thus, it is stated: "by means of the thesis and the counter-thesis."
Two properties residing in the same substratum, existing at the same time, and being contradictory,
when each is separately grasped, are declared to be the thesis and the counter-thesis.

"In that case, there is no determination by those two, for a determination has one of the two as its object, and not necessarily that which is produced by them. This is true; however, here, by the words *pakṣa* (proposition) and *pratipakṣa* (counter-proposition), the proof (*sādhana*) and its refutation (*tadupālambha*)—which have those two as their objects—are indicated.
And these two are indeed the instruments (*karaṇa*) with respect to that [determination].

But why is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) resorted to? Why was it not simply stated in the aphorism "[by] proof and refutation"? If it were stated thus, then the objects of those two would still have to be sought.
But when there is the employment of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), that [secondary meaning] would also be understood;
for having denoted the primary [meaning], the other is indicated.

It is indeed so; however, how can there be a determination by means of two? For it is only a single proof (*sādhana*) that is fit for determination. This is true; we do not say that a second proof is also a cause of determination. Rather, there is the proof of that [position] and the refutation of the proof (*sādhanopālambha*); these two are "proof and refutation," and by means of them, determination occurs.
This is what is meant: by finding a proof for his own position and conceiving a refutation of the proof for the opposing position, the cognizer determines his own position.
It is certainly not that I do not know this;
however, what role does the objection (*upālambha*) play in the production of a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*)?

For it is true that it would indeed destroy the proof of the opponent's position; yet, by means of that destruction, one who manifests the conviction in proving one's own position is indeed capable of bringing about the conclusion. Thus, it is logical that both [the proof and the objection] function as causes.
Now, is not the inclusion of the word "object" (artha) seemingly redundant?
For a semblance of a conclusion (nirṇayābhāsa) cannot possibly arise depending upon such a means of proof (sādhana).

It has already been stated that even the words "proposition" (pakṣa) and "counter-proposition" (pratipakṣa), whose meanings are characterized by proof and refutation, are unable to denote the object [of the debate]; so what is the purpose of including the word "object"? It is said: regarding the two, the proposition and the counter-proposition, there is a determination of the meaning of one or the other, but not of both.
And the inclusion of the word "object" (artha) is for the purpose of demonstrating that this alone is the object in the ultimate sense, whereas the other is constructed by delusion.

However, some maintain that the word "object" (*artha*) is for the purpose of indicating the scope of the terms "proposition" (*pakṣa*) and "counter-proposition" (*pratipakṣa*), because these two terms are restricted to the demonstration of the proof and the refutation of the object being characterized.
[Reflecting: For what purpose? It is solely for the sake of stating the nature of the object (*vastu*).
For it has been stated that here, a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*) based on inference (*anumāna*) is being characterized;
and since inference operates upon an object of doubt, it follows immediately after deliberation (*tarka*).
It is for this very reason that it is included [among the pramāṇas].
For it is observed that deliberation (*tarka*) proceeds immediately after doubt, and determination (*nirṇaya*) proceeds after deliberation;
therefore, it is accepted as being preceded by those two.
