But when certainty has arisen, the desire to know ceases;
for this very reason, they consider that the investigation of logic ends with that.

Let it be so; however, this must be considered: where does restriction apply—is it in the deliberation (*vimarśa*), in the proponent and opponent (*pakṣapratipakṣa*), or in the final determination (*nirṇaya*)?
It is not tenable in any of these three.
Determination does not follow only from deliberation, because it occurs even without deliberation.
It is not [the case that tarka is] merely the thesis and counter-thesis, because it arises even from the sense organs and so forth;

nor is it merely a definitive conclusion (nirṇaya), because in some cases tarka does not cease. Regarding this, it has been stated in the *uddeśasūtra* that since the term "knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñāna*) is employed and the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) implies its fruit, there is no purpose in mentioning mere definitive conclusion. Rather, a specific kind of definitive conclusion is intended as the object of definition (*lakṣya*).
For that determination which is produced by reasoning and constitutes the object of investigation— in that case, these three rules are indeed not inappropriate.
For he indeed acts only after deliberation, since investigation is preceded by deliberation;
and since inference operates upon a doubtful object, such is generally its conventional usage.

Although it is observed that inference sometimes functions even regarding an object that is not doubtful—such as when one who desires fire infers its presence upon seeing smoke issuing from a mountain slope unexpectedly encountered—nevertheless, experts in logic maintain that inference must concern a doubtful object due to the inherent nature of things. Furthermore, the present determination (nirṇaya) cannot be restricted to occurring only through the presentation of a thesis and a counter-thesis, for otherwise the process of reasoning would never cease;
however, in the context of a formal treatise (śāstra), determination occurs even without doubt.

And although the author of the Sūtras has stated there too, through both direct instruction and extended application, that all investigations are preceded by doubt, nevertheless, this is not a definitive conclusion established by the treatise itself, because it is merely the preliminary task of investigation.
Any determination of an object that arises from scripture alone occurs without deliberation (*vimarśa*). Even in debate (*vāda*), the determination is devoid of deliberation;
for both parties engage in debate only when they are certain, since one who is in doubt lacks the qualification [to participate].

How, then, is this common saying—"the fruit of debate is the cutting off of doubt"—to be understood? At first, when both parties are certain of their positions, debate proceeds; however, in the interim, a doubt arises by force due to the encounter of two conflicting arguments. Since debate culminates in the determination of the true state of affairs, they declare that its fruit is the cutting off of doubt.
Even if one of unsteady mind does not engage in debate after hearing the application of another's system,
he will surely establish his own position by resolving his doubt through an internal consideration of the relative strength and weakness of the two views.
Discussions among proponents that are capable of investigating reality by means of the examination of logic consist of *vāda* (formal debate), *jalpa* (wrangling), and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).

Among these, *vāda* is first defined: "Vāda is the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis, employing means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*) for proof and refutation, not contradicting established tenets (*siddhānta*), and endowed with the five members [of a syllogism]. (NS 1.2.1)
The proponent's position (*pakṣa*) and the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) have been explained. Their "adoption" (*parigraha*) is the commitment (*abhyupagama-niyama*) [to them].
One person says: "Sound is eternal."
But another says, "Sound is impermanent.
This taking up of a thesis and a counter-thesis is *vāda* (debate).

Since this form is common to all three types of discourse (*kathā*), he states the distinction: "it consists of the establishment and refutation by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*)."

Because proof and refutation are carried out in this [debate] by means of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), it is called "proof and refutation by means of the instruments of valid cognition and reasoning. However, such is not the case with *vaitaṇḍika* (cavil), because its nature is devoid of the presentation of a proof for the counter-position.

Now, one might object: since the instruments of valid cognition, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), are not a means for producing understanding in another person, proof and refutation cannot be effectively performed through them in a debate.

However, even the capacity of reasoning (*tarka*) to establish cognition is not possible, because its nature consists of the mental state of probability; how much less could it be a constituent part for communicating [a conclusion] to another? Therefore, it is all the more impossible for it to be a cause for establishing [an argument] or for refuting [an opponent's position]. This is true; however, in this context, the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) does not denote perception and the other [means], but rather refers to the members of the syllogism which have their root in the means of valid cognition.
And by means of those [reasons], proof and refutation are accomplished.

Thus, although reasoning (*tarka*) itself is devoid of skill in producing proofs or refutations, it is nevertheless included because it assists the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); its inclusion is for the purpose of demonstrating, through a traditional lineage, that it is a cause of that [proof].

If this is so, then since the members (*avayava*) rooted in those [means of valid cognition] are already indicated by the term "means of valid cognition" alone, the inclusion of the phrase "endowed with five members" is redundant.

Regarding this, some explain that because the definition of *vāda* (debate) is stated as "establishment and refutation by means of valid cognition and reasoning," while the definition of *jalpa* (wrangling) is stated as "establishment and refutation by means of quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat," it follows that in *vāda* there must be a total prohibition of quibbles and the like; therefore, the inclusion of the phrase "endowed with the five members" is intended to permit the pointing out of certain points of defeat.

By this, the pointing out of "deficiency" (*nyūna*)—when a statement is lacking even one of its members—and "excess" (*adhika*)—when it contains more than the necessary reason (*hetu*) and example (*udāharaṇa*)—is permitted.

Furthermore, by the inclusion of the phrase "not contradicting the established tenet" (*siddhāntāviruddha*), the pointing out of the fallacious reason called "contradiction" (*viruddha*)—defined as "having accepted a tenet, then acting in contradiction to it"—is also permitted. Thus, in formal debate (*vāda*), these three points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are to be pointed out.
Others say that only the contradictory (*viruddha*) fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is to be urged in debate, and not the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and others.

How is this tenable? Because of the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "The fallacies of the reason, which are taught separately from the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), shall be urged in debate"; and because, by the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), there is an implication of its constituent members (*avayava*), and thus, when the refutation of that which is rooted in a fallacious means of valid cognition occurs, the exposure of all fallacies of the reason is thereby established therein.

By the inclusion of "not contradicting the tenet" (*siddhāntāviruddhagrahaṇa*), there is the admission of the point of defeat called *apasiddhānta*—defined as "the occurrence of a debate due to lack of restriction after having accepted a tenet. Thus, it is claimed that eight points of defeat are to be raised in a formal debate (*vāda*). This is untenable; for there is no Vedic injunction or royal decree stating that either three or eight points of defeat must be urged in a debate. Rather, everything that serves as a means for establishing the purity of the subject matter (*vastupariśuddhi*) is fit for use therein.
However, this is the distinction: in *jalpa*, at certain stages, the employment of quibbles (*chala*) and other such fallacies may even be performed intentionally;
in *vāda*, however, their employment is not like that.
Yet, if they are somehow employed through error, they must necessarily be pointed out, because if they are not pointed out, there can be no purification of the subject matter.
How, then, are these two phrases—"not contradicting the established tenets" and "endowed with five members"—consistent?

The learned maintain that they are intended solely for the purpose of permitting those points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) that are conducive to the purification of the subject matter in such a manner, by demonstrating the correct direction of refutation regarding "departure from the tenets" (*apasiddhānta*) and other such faults.

For lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), evasion (*vikṣepa*), and the like are not causes of defeat in a formal debate (*vāda*); even if one fails at first, having returned at another moment and recollected [the argument], one is not defeated if one then proceeds to state the proof or the refutation therein.
However, all the grounds for a proper defeat, such as the abandonment of one's thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) and so forth, are permitted here by these two terms.

Now, one might object: "Is the separate mention of 'means of valid cognition' (*pramāṇa*) and 'reasoning' (*tarka*) not redundant? For, by the very phrase 'endowed with the five members,' the instruction on members rooted in the means of valid cognition is already given, and the permission for points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) conducive to the purification of the subject matter is also granted; so why has this not been stated? [The answer is: No, because it is intended to demonstrate the distinction between *vāda* (disputation) and *jalpa* (wrangling) by way of revealing the purity of intention.
Even the means of proof such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) used for one's own realization are appropriate to employ in *vāda* in order to manifest the purity of one's underlying motive.

In this matter, one must also state such things as: "First, my reasoning proceeded in this way regarding this subject; thereafter, this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) was applied. For this very reason, debate (*vāda*) concludes precisely with the determination of one of the two positions. It does not, like frivolous talk (*jalpa*), end in the humiliation of the opponent through a display of false refutations; thus, because there is no deliberate employment of fallacies, it is said to be a discourse free from envy. Therefore, the terms *pramāṇa* and *tarka* are used for the purpose of speaking with a pure and guileless intention.
Moreover, its purpose is also to demonstrate the interconnection between the proof (*sādhana*) and the refutation (*upālambha*).

For it is only when both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) are examined by the two disputants in mutual succession that they bring about the state of formal debate (*vāda*); this does not occur when they are being analyzed in private or within a treatise.

Furthermore, the inclusion of that term serves to dispel the doubt regarding the restrictive rule that "in debate one must proceed solely with means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas in wrangling (*jalpa*) one may proceed solely with quibbles (*chala*) and so forth. Others have already stated this, so let us refrain from further prolixity.
In every respect, the definition of debate is well-established.

However, one should engage in debate only with disciples, fellow students, and teachers who are free from passion and seek the fruit of a definitive conclusion; one should not undertake it with those whose minds are corrupted by the persistence of rivalry, which increases through the impetuosity for fame and gain.

Debate (*jalpa*) is the employment of means for establishing one's own position and refuting that of the opponent, characterized by the use of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), as previously described. 1.2.2.

Some, fearing that if the entire [definition] were extended by the inclusion of the phrase "as previously stated and established" (*yathoktopapanna*), there would be no distinction between *vāda* (formal debate) and *jalpa* (wrangling), explain that this extension applies only to the adoption of a thesis and a counter-thesis.

However, since this much is already established by the recurrence of the previous sūtra, the statement "*yathoktopapanna*" would yield little result; therefore, it is better to extend the entire definition. Moreover, even in that case, there is no equality between *vāda* and *jalpa*, because the implied meaning is not extended.
Only the explicitly stated meaning (śrauta) is extended by analogy, not the implied meaning (gamyamāna);
and the distinction between those two is based precisely on that.
And likewise, in the phrase "by means of proof and refutation through valid cognition and reasoning" (*pramāṇatarkasādhanopālambha*), the implied meaning is the restriction of intention;
that [restriction] is not explicitly extended [to the subsequent rules].

Furthermore, in the phrase "not contradicting the established tenets and endowed with the five members," there too is an implied meaning consisting of the restriction regarding the prohibition of the intentional employment of futile rejoinders (*jāti*) and the like, as well as the requirement to point them out when they occur.
Since that [deceit] also is not extended [to the other two], how could there be no distinction between them?

For this very reason, it is said that "quibbling, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat constitute the means of proof and refutation for the sake of permitting the employment of intentional [speech]."
Let it be so; however, since *chala* (quibble) and the others are fallacious rejoinders (*asaduttara*), how can they possibly serve as causes for the refutation of a proof?

If you argue that they do so by means of rejecting the opponent's position, we say no; for even if they effect a rejection, they lack the capacity to do so because they are fallacious rejoinders. Furthermore, it would truly be the case that the mention of "proof" (*sādhana*) would be entirely useless. Nevertheless, this is indeed true: in certain circumstances, these [fallacies] are also employed for the sake of protecting the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) produced by one's own proof of understanding.

When one, although knowing the weakness of the opponent's position and the strength of one's own position, at some point on an occasion when the opponent has employed a proof, suddenly does not perceive a refutation or does not immediately recall the proof for one's own position, then even by employing *chala* (equivocation) and other such means, one overcomes the opponent and protects oneself.

Now, one might object: "If the opponent also understands the quibbles (*chala*) and so forth, and were to offer the appropriate rejoinder (*uttara*) to them, how could he be defeated? On the contrary, he would surely win. This is true; nevertheless, it is entirely reasonable to employ these [quibbles] as a means of manifesting a grand display, for it is better to have a doubtful outcome than a certain defeat.
[Objection: Surely such purposes as these belong to a person desiring victory in an assembly of common folk;
even for him, they are not appropriate in a highly learned assembly.

For one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), however, this subject is far removed; so how can there be an instruction on wrangling (*jalpa*) and the like in this treatise on liberation? [Response: This is not so, because even for one who desires liberation, it is useful in certain circumstances.
Thus it has been said: "Sophistry and cavil are for the purpose of protecting the determination of reality, just as a fence of thorny branches is for the purpose of protecting the growth of seeds."

For suppose some ignoble person, though supposedly wise, were to approach a teacher who was sitting comfortably in a certain hermitage, attended by a multitude of disciples, teaching the secret truth with a tranquil mind; and with a voice faltering from the heavy pride born of having mastered only a few poorly acquired syllables, he were to say: "O ascetic, what is being explained? Hm! This science of *ānvīkṣikī* is simple and very easy."

"Where are the Vedas? Where is the authority of the Vedas? Where is the knowledge of the Self? Where is liberation?"—laughing very softly at such words, he suddenly raises a clamor like a wicked cloud manifesting a sudden, unseasonable thunderstorm that terrifies the herds of deer in the hermitage; thus he agitates the web of the world. Although the Teacher knows this to be the play of a master illusionist, if he neglects him or treats him with contempt, and if, even when the correct means of proof is not apparent, he does not immediately silence him through quibbles and the like, then once that person has departed, the assembly of disciples will rise up and say: "Alas! We have been troubled in vain."
This teacher of ours, who was renowned as the greatest knower of logic,
has now been defeated by another scholar after he arrived here.

Hearing this, let no other person also suddenly follow him out of a laxity in standing upon the path of the righteous; for that wretched chatterer must surely be led away from the assembly to a place of humiliation by those who are not base.
The Sage taught the weapon of unrestrained speech for the purpose of composing that work;
its incidental benefit among passionate people has also been described.
That which is devoid of the establishment of a counter-position is vitanda (cavil). 1.2.3.
That very *jalpa* (disputation), characterized as previously described, becomes *vaitaṇḍikā* (cavil).
If one asks what the distinction is, he says: "it is devoid of the establishment of a counter-position.
The proponent of the latter position is the *vaitaṇḍika*.

With respect to the first thesis being established, that thesis is called the "counter-thesis" (pratipakṣa) according to the analogy of an elephant and its rival. The proponent indeed accepts this [counter-thesis], yet he does not provide a formal proof for it; rather, he proceeds by merely refuting the opponent's position.
In that case, since there is no means of proof, that subject (pakṣa) of his does not exist at all.

Let it be said that *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is merely the absence of a counter-position; what is the use of including the term "establishment" (*sthāpanā*), since its existence [as cavil] follows from mere non-acceptance?
For who would listen to one who prattles without accepting that [position]?
Or rather, its position consists solely in the form of refuting the opponent's view, used in a figurative sense.

For if that [thesis] exists, his own position would indeed be established; and because his activity is directed toward the refutation of another's view, by virtue of this, the proponent of the second position is indeed a *vaitaṇḍika*. Thus, it has been correctly formulated in the Sūtra: "That which lacks the establishment of a counter-position is *vitaṇḍā*," meaning that while he holds that "the position exists," he has no proof for it.
Thus have these three narratives been cited, each possessing mutually distinct characteristics;
yet, even though they are grossly different, they are described as "one single doctrine" by the disciples of the Śākya.

The five characteristics of the reason (*hetu*) have been stated as being its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Since there are five fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) resulting from the omission of each one of these [characteristics], he says the following to demonstrate them: "The fallacious reasons are the deviating (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the equal to the point at issue (*prakaraṇasama*), the identical with the probandum (*sādhyasama*), and the mistimed (*atītakāla*). (2.2.4)

In this context, the very mention of the term *hetvābhāsa* (fallacious reason), accompanied by its etymological definition, conveys the general definition: "Those which appear as reasons (*hetu*) though they are not reasons (*ahetu*) are called *hetvābhāsas*.
Furthermore, because of the application of even a single part of the definition, the appearance as a reason is possible even for that which is not a reason.
Some maintain that even when all the defining characteristics are absent, the use of the ablative case ending (*pañcamī*) and so forth serves as a cause for error.

However, it has been stated that the very same scriptural text, extending as far as the terms *savyabhicāra* (inconclusive) and so forth, conveys the classification [of fallacies], just like the scriptural text concerning the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, because there is no fixed order among the definitions such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*) and the rest, the reading "the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are the inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the similar-to-the-probandum (*sādhyasama*), the mistimed (*atītakāla*), and the counter-balanced (*prakaraṇasama*)" was not adopted.
Is it not the case that there are only three fallacious reasons? This is not possible, because a reason sublated by perception and scripture was already demonstrated previously.

Now, one might object: since a single reason lacks two of the required forms, why should there not be six or more types of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) based on its divisions? For instance, in the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is visible," should this be called "unestablished" (*asiddha*) due to its absence from the subject (*pakṣa*), or "inconclusive" (*savyabhicāra*) because it does not exclude itself from the general class of counter-examples (*vipakṣa*), or is it simply a different category altogether from those two? This is not so; for when the fivefold distinction is established by means of the loss of each individual form, no new category arises from the loss of two or three forms, but rather there would be a mere combination of those very same categories.

Moreover, since this [reason] has already been established as a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) by the deficiency of whichever one form was first grasped, what is the use of examining the other forms? Let this matter rest.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that there exists a sixth fallacy of the reason called 'the non-probative' (aprayojaka), so that the number [of fallacies] is not five? We reply: No; since that [non-probative] is established by another way (anyathāsiddha), we shall state that its inclusion occurs within the 'unestablished' (asiddha) itself.
However, when there is a desire to express the internal subdivisions, it is established that there are exactly five fallacies of the reason.
Among these, the "deviating" (savyabhicāra) is first stated: the deviating [reason] is the inconclusive (anaikāntika). (NS 1.2.5)

*Vyabhicāra* means the absence of restriction to a single [locus]. That which exists together with that is *savyabhicāra*, meaning it does not exclude the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). That which exists at one end is *aikāntika*;

by its opposite, it is *anaikāntika*, which has the same meaning. Thus, in this context, the relationship between the term to be defined (*lakṣya*) and the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is accepted according to preference, rather than being fixed as in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth.

In the word *savyabhicāra*, which denotes the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), the term *anaikāntika* expresses the definition (*lakṣaṇa*); whereas in the word *anaikāntika*, which denotes the object to be defined, the term *savyabhicāra* conveys the definition. This should be understood as being like the words "pika" and "kokila," depending on whether the referent is well-known or not. When it is said, "The pika is the kokila," one for whom the meaning of the word "pika" is already established will understand the meaning of the word "kokila" from it; whereas one for whom the meaning of the word "kokila" is already established will understand the meaning of the word "pika."
He said: "Let it be so; however, this must be considered:

is this [term] *anaikāntika* (inconclusive) a *paryudāsa* (presuppositional negation) or a *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation)? In the case of the *paryudāsa* view, that which is other than the inconclusive reason restricted to one's own side would itself be the inconclusive; thus, there would be only a single fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). But in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha*, the status of being a fallacious reason would belong to the mere absence of the conclusive reason—which is of the nature of a negation—and not to another reason such as 'knowability' (*prameyatva*) that is intended as the subject of definition and which occurs in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). It is replied: this very question is untenable."
For one who is in doubt asks another;
and doubt arises from seeing two possibilities.

Furthermore, the negative particle *nañ* does not connect with the noun (*nāman*) that it is syntactically linked to—as in "the faithful man does not eat" (*śrāddho na bhuṅkte*)—but rather with the quality expressed by the noun, such as "faithfulness" (*śrāddhatva*).

Even when connected with a verb, in certain instances—due to the force of the context—it abandons the connection with the meaning of the suffix and, embracing the meaning of the verbal root alone, functions as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), as in "One should not look at the rising sun.
However, a word joined with a noun is never seen to transcend the function of *paryudāsa* and rely solely on the status of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation);
for in all cases such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), we observe the understanding of something other than that [the Brahmin]. So whence can this doubt arise?
Alternatively, what is the use of this intermediate deliberation? The answer is given exactly as it was asked:

that which is restricted (*niyata*), absolute (*aikāntika*), and occurring in only one side—whether the side of impermanence or the side of permanence—is called "conclusive" (*ekapakṣavṛtti*). That which is other than this, occurring in both sides, is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).

Thus, it is not the case that all fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) occur within both categories; therefore, there is no loss of numerical count. Consequently, there is no fault in the position of exclusion by negation (paryudāsa).

Even in the case of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), that which is not invariably [present] is itself the "non-reason" (*ahetu*); thus, it does not have as its sole purpose the mere cessation [of a property].

Just as one says of a person, "one who eats at non-śrāddha ceremonies," referring to the person and not merely to the absence of eating at śrāddha ceremonies, so too here, by means of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), it is the reason itself—qualified by the negation of invariable necessity—that is expressed, and not mere absence. Thus, in either case, there is no fault.
An example of this is: "Sound is eternal, because it is knowable.
For this [reason] is not restricted to either of the two sides—eternal or non-eternal—and thus, by virtue of occurring in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it is called inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

But surely, opponents maintain that the inconclusive (anaikāntika) reason is of six types: the four common (sādhāraṇa) types—namely, that which occurs in one part of the similar instances (sapakṣa) while pervading the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa); that which occurs in the dissimilar instances while pervading the similar instances; that which occurs in one part of both the similar and dissimilar instances; and that which pervades both the similar and dissimilar instances—as well as the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) and the non-erroneous contradictory (viruddhāvyabhicārī).

Why is this not specified here? It is said in reply: first, demonstrating distinctions such as the pervasion of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and so forth is both useless and impossible, because the sub-varieties of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are infinite.

Here, what is intended as the definition of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is simply the absence of even one of the essential features of a valid reason—namely, that which lacks exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is "deviant" (*vyabhicāra*).
And that has already been stated.
What is the use of enumerating the intermediate subdivisions?

As for the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) and the non-erroneous contradictory (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), however, they do not exist [in the context of inference], as they are themselves fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*); therefore, they are not explained here.

[Objection: But surely, since even an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇa*) such as "possessing odor" is observed to be a cause of doubt—just like a common property (*sādhāraṇa*)—how can it be impossible? Furthermore, you yourselves have explained that doubt arises from the occurrence of multiple properties (*anekadharmopapatti*). [Reply: This is not so. For the perception of a property concomitant with both specific features (*ubhayaviśeṣa*) produces doubt when accompanied by the recollection of those two. An uncommon property, however, because it is uncommon, has never been perceived as concomitant with either; how then could it be a cause of doubt? [Objection: How then is it described as arising from "the occurrence of multiple properties"? [Reply: This has already been explained.

For a certain specific property of an object is observed to be non-common and invariably concomitant with some other property; this property of the [sound] in question, called "being produced by disjunction," might be concomitant with some other property such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) or quality-ness (*guṇatva*). Thus, because multiple properties are possible, doubt is described.

Therefore, even here, if the possession of odor (*gandhavattva*) is described as a cause for doubt precisely because it is an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇa*), then the doubt would arise from its being a property of a real entity (*vastudharmatva*)—which is common [to both alternatives]—and not from the uncommon possession of odor itself.
For that [possession of odor] has never been observed to coexist with either of the two, the eternal or the non-eternal.
However, since a property of a real entity is seen to follow after other properties, it is the status of being a property of a real entity alone that is the cause of that doubt.
Therefore, one should not state that "the earth is eternal because it possesses odor" constitutes an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*).

Even the "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) need not be mentioned at all, because it is impossible for two reasons that establish two mutually contradictory [conclusions] to occur with respect to a single locus (dharmin).

[Objection: Is there not a conjunction of two reasons, namely, "Air is perceptible because it possesses touch, like a jar," and "Air is imperceptible because it lacks color, like space"? And these very two are called a "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) reason. To this, it must first be said: what kind of unprecedented scholarly convention is this, that perceptibility or imperceptibility is established by means of inference?
For an object is "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) for you only when it is the object of a cognition produced by the sense faculties.
This very wind is indeed manifest in the cognition born of the sense-faculty; what then is the use of inference?
Or, if it is not manifest there, even so, what is the use of inference?
Furthermore, one of these two reasons must necessarily be inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), because it is impossible for a single entity to possess two natures.
Once a reason has been put forward, let the opponent simply examine its merits and defects; what occasion is there for the presentation of a counter-reason?
If it is argued that this presentation is for the sake of mockery, we say no, because a mockery constitutes a type of futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*).
In this context, only those pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) that are real defects of inference are [to be considered];
for it has already been stated that, in a single case, there is an impossibility of the coexistence of two reasons, just as there is no coexistence of two [valid] purposes.
If it is asked, "How then is *prakaraṇasama* [to be classified]? we shall explain its specific distinction in that very same place.

Now, if it is claimed that the nature of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) consists merely in the presentation of a thesis and its counter-thesis accepted by both disputants while being devoid of the application of a logical reason (*hetu*), then this results in doubt arising from conflicting opinions (*vipratipatti*), and not from this [fallacy] being a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

Furthermore, if the definition of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) were stated as "the production of doubt," then one might as well attribute the status of being a cause of doubt to either the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) or the non-erroneous contradictory (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) reason and thereby call it inconclusive; however, the production of doubt is not its defining characteristic, because that would entail the same status for the sense organs and so forth, since they too produce doubt. Rather, the definition of the inconclusive is "occurring in both sides of the thesis" (*pakṣadvayavṛttitva*).
It is simply the nature of things that such a reason, by virtue of occurring in both sides, also produces doubt.

Therefore, although the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) and the non-erroneous contradictory (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) reasons may in some way cause doubt, they are not included within the category of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because they do not subsist in both sides of the thesis (*pakṣadvaya*). Where, then, will those two be included? We shall state that they are included among "futile rejoinders" (*jātyuttara*), since those are infinite in number.

Therefore, those who do not consider the presence of a reason termed "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) or a "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) declare it to be inconclusive (anaikāntika); they are ignorant of that [matter].
The contradictory [reason] is that which, having accepted a tenet, contradicts it. (1.2.6)
The definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) consists in its presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and its absence in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

When these two are seen to be reversed—that is, when a reason does not occur in the similar instances but occurs in the dissimilar instances—it becomes "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite of what is to be proven (*sādhya*). This is what is called [the fallacy] "having accepted a tenet" (*abhyupetya-siddhānta*).

Although the term *siddhānta* has been explained as the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by a property (*dharma*), such that "an object made the focus of an acceptance [in the form] 'this is thus' is a *siddhānta*," nevertheless, here it is characterized as referring specifically to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), which is a single part of that [subject].
The meaning is: that which, having accepted that *siddhānta*—the property to be proven—contradicts it, strikes it down, and establishes its opposite, is "contradictory" (*viruddha*).
Now, it is traditionally taught that the suffix *ktvā* is used when there are two actions with the same agent (*samānakartṛka*).
In this case, since a cause is admitted to be insentient, an agent is impossible; therefore, the Person (*puruṣa*) would have to be its agent.

[And thus the reason contradicts the established doctrine. To avoid this charge of having different agents, it will be explained that agency is attributed to the cause itself only figuratively (*upacāra*), so as to establish the identity of the agent.
When the acceptance of a person is made by means of the power of a reason, it is in fact accomplished by that very reason;
and thus, since the one who accepts is the same as the one who contradicts, there is no difference in the agent.

Now, if the adoption of a metaphorical usage is indeed intended, then three things must be stated here: the sublation of the primary meaning by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the ground (*nimitta*), and the purpose (*prayojana*).

As for the sublation of the primary meaning by a means of valid cognition, it has already been stated that the cause (*hetu*) is insentient. As for the ground, it exists as well, since the acceptance [of the doctrine] is established by means of that cause.
The purpose, however, is to exclude those [reasons] that are contradictory due to their specific [qualifications] from being fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).
Even regarding the term *siddhānta*, which denotes a whole [system], its restriction to a single part has as its sole result the exclusion of what is contradictory to that specific [part].

For if one were to accept that those [reasons] which contradict specific qualities (*viśeṣaviruddha*) are indeed fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), it would follow that all inference (*anumāna*) would be abolished. Indeed, no such reason can be found here in this world which, when stated for the sake of establishing a probandum (*sādhya*), does not somehow subvert either a specific quality of the property (*dharma*) or a specific quality of the locus (*dharmin*). To illustrate: the reason "because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*)—which is well-known in every house of the logicians—is established as proving impermanence; yet, while proving impermanence, it is countered by the fact that "whatever is produced is observed to be inaudible."
Whatever is produced is not a specific quality of space; thus, [the reason] would indeed contradict a qualification of the subject (*dharmin*), and so it would be a non-reason (*ahetu*).

Since this is not tenable, one should not accept a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) called "contradictory to a qualification" (*viśeṣaviruddha*); rather, it is simply that which establishes the opposite of the very nature of the probandum (*sādhyasvarūpaviparyayasādhana*).

For this very reason, as described in other schools, the contradictory (*viruddha*) is of four kinds: that which establishes the opposite of the nature of the property (*dharmasvarūpaviparītasādhana*), that which establishes the opposite of the nature of the subject (*dharmisvarūpaviparītasādhana*), that which establishes the opposite of a qualification of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparītasādhana*), and that which establishes the opposite of a qualification of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparītasādhana*).
Likewise, this is not accepted here because an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) has been demonstrated;
an example of this is: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced," and so forth.
But has it not been stated that there are five fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) because of the absence of each individual characteristic?
And for this reason, both characteristics are absent:
for just as it does not subsist in the similar instances (sapakṣa), so too is it excluded from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).

If this [reason] were indeed excluded from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) just as it is from the similar instances (sapakṣa), it would be "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa), like the property of possessing odor; this is true. Thus, non-exclusion from the dissimilar instances functions as a cause for deviation (vyabhicāra). For that which goes to the opposite side is said to be "deviant. However, the cessation of its occurrence in the similar instances is not a cause for establishing the contrary; rather, even when there is occurrence in the dissimilar instances, its status as a "contradictory" (viruddha) reason is said to be based solely on the cessation of its occurrence in the similar instances.

One that has not fallen away from the counter-example (vipakṣa) would not establish its own probandum; however, since this [reason], by not occurring in the similar example (sapakṣa), establishes the opposite as well, they declare its contradictory nature to be caused precisely by the loss of its defining characteristics. Enough with such subtle scrutiny!
Thus it has been said: "Having accepted a tenet, that which contradicts it is the contradictory (viruddha)."

Others, however, explain it otherwise: they claim that just as [the fallacy] that proves the opposite of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma-viparyaya-sādhaka) is included, other instances contradicting a tenet (siddhānta-virodhin)—such as those resulting from a contradiction with one's own tenets (apasiddhānta) or a contradiction with the thesis (pratijñā-virodha)—should indeed be included.
Yet, if explained in that manner, those [other cases] would not be included;
furthermore, the suffix -ktvā and the word *siddhānta* would not be properly construed.

Therefore, when the meaning of the sutra has been explained as "contradictory to an accepted tenet" (*abhyupagatasiddhāntavirodhī*), it will encompass both that which contradicts an accepted tenet at the time it is formulated, and that which contradicts one established at a later occasion; furthermore,
the term *siddhānta* (tenet) will not be restricted in its scope.

The suffix *ktvā*, however, is simply disregarded because it is inconsistent, because there is a difference in agents, and because the immediate succession that would be implied is of no practical use.

And thus, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated an example that contradicts his own previously accepted tenet without qualification: "This modification departs from its manifestation because of the negation of permanence; yet even when departed, it exists because of the negation of destruction.

For here, the reason—"because its nature as permanent has been negated"—contradicts the tenet that "even though the modification has departed from its manifestation, it still exists," or rather, it is itself contradicted by that very tenet.
However, this explanation seems unconvincing.

Since the *nigrahasthāna* sūtra teaches points of defeat such as "contradiction with one's own tenet" (*apasiddhānta*) and "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodha*) separately from fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), what is the point of including them here?
On the contrary, their inclusion is itself a fault.

For if one who has accepted "I am a Mīmāṃsaka" were to say, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot," this reason would not be contradictory (*viruddha*) even if it were abundant; rather, he would be defeated solely on account of his own failed tenet (*apasiddhānta*).

Therefore, only that which proves the opposite of what is to be proven is called "contradictory," and not that which contradicts one's previously accepted own tenet. Nor was the use of the gerund (*ktvā*) by the author of the Sūtras made without intention; rather, it was employed while also taking into account the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) understood from it.

For that which, having accepted and asserted a tenet, is employed for the sake of establishing it, yet contradicts that very [tenet], is the "contradictory" (viruddha) fallacious reason; thus, the previous explanation alone is faultless.
Therefore, because it proves the opposite of the thesis, the reason becomes contradictory; otherwise, it would not.
Furthermore, its manifold nature—based on the sublation of specific [qualifications] and so forth—is not accepted as a fault in this case.
Because it is a deliberation regarding a category [of reasons] that is presented for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion, it is called "the counter-balanced" (prakaraṇasama). 1.2.7.

It is said that the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) called *prakaraṇasama* (the "neutralized" or "equally balanced") must be mentioned because it is defined by the deficiency of having no counter-position (*asat-pratipakṣatva*), due to the assertion of five types of fallacious reasons characterized by the removal of each individual characteristic.
However, that [fallacy] is not possible, because there is no such thing as a reason that possesses a counter-position.

For it has been stated more than once that since entities do not possess a dual nature, there can be no coexistence of two reasons that would establish two mutually contradictory properties in a single locus.
For this very reason, the "non-deviant contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārī) has been rejected;
moreover, an inference that contradicts another inference is simply not accepted.

Since a pseudo-reason (hetvābhāsa) characterized by having a counter-argument is thus excluded, and because there is no such object to be defined, [the author] says "because... and so forth to address the question: "Of what, then, is this the definition?"
The "treatise" (*prakaraṇa*) consists of the thesis and the counter-thesis, which possess the characteristics previously described;
although the investigation (*cintā*) of these occurs from the point of doubt until the final determination, here it is understood specifically as consisting of inquiry (*vimarśa*).
That [inquiry] arises from this [which follows].
And why is that [fallacy] yours? Because of the non-perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣānupalambha*).

If that very non-perception of a distinguishing feature is taught for the sake of a definitive conclusion, it becomes "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) because it transcends the specific context of the argument.
For example: "Sound is eternal, because no property of the impermanent is perceived, like space."
"Sound is impermanent because its permanent properties are not perceived, like a jar.
This very reason, which possesses a counter-argument, is found here as something to be characterized.
Nor is it the case that things possess a dual nature, and that the cognizer, being unable to determine their fixed form, merely wanders in error in this way.

For instance, one person, perceiving the presence of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), might understand the probandum (*sādhya*) as such because of the non-perception of its specific qualities; likewise, he would communicate it to another.

The other, too, having understood the means of proof due to the non-perception of the specific qualities of the second [alternative], offers a counter-objection. Thus, this "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacy of the reason is witnessed solely by one's own cognition.

And thus, this is not first of all a valid reason (*samyag-hetu*), because its capacity to establish its own probandum is void due to being impaired by its counter-position. Even if it were a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), it is not "unestablished" (*asiddha*), because the reason—the state of possessing non-perceived eternal properties—is present in the subject (*dharmin*) of the probandum, namely sound. Nor is it "contradictory" (*viruddha*), because it is impossible for it to be inseparably connected with presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), which would be the cause for proving the opposite of the probandum.
Nor is it inconclusive (anaikāntika), because there is no determination of its being common to both the [proponent's] position and its opposite;
furthermore, as has already been stated, the capacity to produce doubt is not its defining characteristic.
Is it not the case that what is restricted to one side is *aikāntika* (conclusive), while its opposite is *anaikāntika* (inconclusive)?
Since this [reason] is not restricted to either of the two sides—eternal or non-eternal—it would indeed be *anaikāntika*.
Furthermore, they say: "Invalidity is divided into three types: falsity, non-cognition, and doubt."

In this regard, just as the status of non-validity is attributed to the sense organs and so forth either because they do not produce cognition or because of their inherent defectiveness in generating appearances characterized by doubt or error, so too does inference assume the state of being a fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) by that very same path.

In that regard, first of all, the unestablished [reason], not obtaining its presence in the subject (dharmin), is incapable of producing a cognition of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) therein; thus, because its result is ignorance, it experiences the result of invalidity.
But you yourselves have admitted that a contradictory [reason] is one that proves the opposite.
Rather, it is that which generates doubt which ought to be the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason;
however, it is not appropriate for its definition to be merely "occurring in a conventional counter-example" (*vipakṣa*).

Since both [the uncertain and the contradictory] have a body consisting in the absence of restriction to either side, why would they not cause you to reflect upon them as being inconclusive? Thus, there are only three fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
It is said: a restriction on the characteristics cannot be established by means of a restriction on the results.

Even though a result may be of two or three kinds, such as the result of a non-authoritative cognition (*apramāṇa*), nevertheless, the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is not fully realized in a mark possessing only three characteristics; rather, it is established that [the mark] must possess five characteristics.
And due to the deficiency of these [characteristics], there are likewise exactly five types of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
Let the result be twofold or threefold;

for we do not perceive any logical mark (*liṅga*) that does not produce comprehension, nor is non-comprehension produced by effort, since its prior absence is established by nature. Enough, then, with this intermediate deliberation.
The projection of a result is not a restriction defined by a logical mark (*liṅga*).

In that regard, just as being devoid of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is the definition of the unestablished (*asiddha*), so too the deficiency of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the definition of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). And since this reason is not deficient in even one of the forms—namely, the property of the subject, positive concomitance (*anvaya*), or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—how could it incur inconclusiveness? For if they were separated, all these definitions would indeed exist [individually].
However, the "entirety" (samasta) has not been put forward as a reason at all, on account of the non-perception of properties that are both eternal and non-eternal.

Now, if this [reason] possesses the property of being present in the subject (pakṣadharma), as well as positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), without exception, why then is it not indeed a valid reason?

If you say, "In that case, since the other [reason] also lacks the property of being present in the subject and positive and negative concomitance without exception, why should that one not also be a valid reason?", we reply: no, because it is impossible for a real entity to possess two contradictory forms simultaneously.

Thus, these two reasons, while producing a cognition in both positions, bring about doubt; they are not like the "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) reason, which causes doubt by occurring in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa). Therefore, they constitute a distinct type of fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa).
And if this kind of *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized reason) is given the name *viruddhāvyabhicārī* (the non-erroneous contradictory), let it be so;
nevertheless, it does not fall under the category of the *anaikāntika* (inconclusive), because it does not touch upon its defining characteristics.
For these two reasons produce the cognition of both [sides], yet they do not subsist in both positions.
Nor is this [reason] "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because no sublater of either perception or scripture is perceived.
Furthermore, it has been stated that one inference is not capable of subverting another inference.

Nor should their lack of establishment (*asiddhatva*) be asserted on the basis of mutual dependence; for while the production of doubt is established by experience, the non-perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣa*) cannot be dismissed.
Now, since one is entitled to employ a proof only when [the subject] is certain, one might somehow employ a proof;

yet, if there were certainty, the mutual non-establishment of those two properties—the property [of the subject] and the non-perception—would indeed be established. This is not so. For, by perceiving the presence of the property in the subject (pakṣadharmatva) and the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) through the non-perception of the property of only one [of the two], he attains certainty; he does not do so while cognizing the non-establishment of the second property’s non-perception.
Therefore, this fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) is rooted in error.
However, if there is a certainty that the non-apprehension of the second property (*dharmin*) is established, then it would indeed be a valid reason (*samyag-hetu*).

Even if its non-establishment is not definitively determined, one who employs a proof after having become certain of mind through observing the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) of his own reason, will nevertheless fall into doubt upon perceiving the three characteristics of the opponent's counter-proof when the latter—likewise certain of mind—has formulated it. Enough of this digression.

Thus, because it is the opposite of the characteristics of the unestablished (*asiddha*) and so forth, the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) named "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) is unestablished insofar as it conforms to [the opponent's] understanding.
Others, however, state another example for this: "Sound is eternal, because it is one or the other of the subject and the similar instance (sapakṣa), like space. And:
"Sound is non-eternal, precisely because it is one or the other of the subject and the similar instance, like a jar."

Now, it might be argued that "one of the two" (anyatara) ought to be the moon, either among the subject (*pakṣa*) or the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). In that case, if the subject were denoted by the word "one of the two," there would be no co-referential connection (*ananvaya*);
for the subject, which is called "word," being a property-bearer (*dharmin*), does not reside in another property-bearer.
However, when any one of these [reasons] is stated as being present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there is no "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*);
for space and so forth, which constitute the similar class, do not exist within the subject (*dharmin*) called "sound."

It is said: the reason is not employed as "because it is the subject" (*pakṣatvāt*) or "because it is a similar instance" (*sapakṣatvāt*), such that one could say [the reason is] "because it is either the subject or a similar instance.
And that is some common characteristic shared by both.
For the cognition regarding "Varuṇa is to be sacrificed to" is exactly the same as the cognition regarding "either Mitra or Varuṇa is to be sacrificed to."
However, if one were to insist—by force—that it must reside in a specific [individual], the result would be the total destruction of all inference.

Nor is it appropriate to say that "one-or-the-other-ness" (anyataratva) is a non-real form superimposed by mere words, because the claim that [inference] does not touch upon the actual object has already been refuted.

If it is argued that the reason "because of being one or the other" (*anyataratvāt*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), on the grounds that this [subject] is not "one or the other of the subject and the similar instance" (*pakṣasapakṣayoḥ*), that is incorrect; for precisely because this is the subject (*pakṣa*), it is therefore one or the other of the subject and the similar instance.
Indeed, that which is not the subject could not be one or the other of the subject and the similar instance;
for it has already been stated that Varuṇa is not one or the other of Mitra and Varuṇa.
Moreover, although this is a thesis, it is not employed as a reason in the form "because it is a thesis," but rather as "because it is one or the other.
And when it is employed as a reason in this manner, not even a single fault arises.

Another example is: "The omniscient one exists, because he is devoid of everything other than that, like a jar," and "The omniscient one does not exist, because he is devoid of everything other than that, like a donkey's horn. Here too, the manner of raising and resolving the objection should be followed as before.
And [the fallacies] such as being unestablished in accordance with the property (dharmyasiddhatā) must be carefully considered with effort.
The wise do not approve of examples of this kind;

for when a cognizer, having correctly or incorrectly inferred a certain matter by means of a reason, employs that very same reason to communicate it to another, that reason—by virtue of proceeding from the power of the actual state of things (vastubalapravṛtta)—becomes either a valid reason (hetu) or a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa).

For instance, when a substratum possessing height and breadth stands before one, because the specific features belonging to a post are not perceived, there arises for one person the cognition "this is a man," whereas for another, because the specific features belonging to a man are not perceived, the thought occurs "this is a post."

And thus, when one person, in order to establish that something is a post (*sthāṇu*), might state to another the "non-perception of the properties of a post" as a reason, and the other person should counter-argue by establishing its being a post through the "non-perception of the properties of a human," then—because the statement of the proof is preceded by following one's own cognition and because error is possible—it is appropriate to cite such an example.

In the same way, [the arguments] "Sound is eternal, because no non-eternal property is perceived, like space" and "Sound is non-eternal, because no eternal property is perceived, like a jar" should also be understood.

As for that [reason] which is not rooted in reality but relies solely on mere imagination—never before seen even in one's own cognitions—what is the point of adducing it? By this, the arguments involving a "counter-correlate" (*sadvitīya*) are also refuted. For example, when a certain proof has been formulated, an opponent might object as follows: "The pot is accompanied by something else (is *sadvitīya*), because it is either the subject-pot or a pot that is devoid of being the locus of the property to be proven under discussion, since it is unproduced, like a wall."

Just as [in the previous example], this subject called "pot" is accompanied by either of the two—the subject under discussion or the property (dharma) intended to be proven, namely, being empty of that [property]—and the reason (*hetu*) therein is "unproducedness," which is pervaded (*vyāpti*) in such things as walls.

Speak the truth: if such a sequence of cognition exists anywhere, then in the case of the statement "the subject (dharmin) 'pot' is accompanied by one of the two [the pot or its property]," the word "one of the two" (*anyatara*), although denoting a generality, must be explained as referring to the subject.
For the pot itself cannot possibly be accompanied by the pot; therefore, enough with this skill in fabricating false conceptualizations!
Those reasons which are observed to produce cognition within one's own self—whether correctly or otherwise—are certainly fit to be employed for the sake of informing others.

But as for those [reasons] that are incapable of producing even their own realization in such a manner—being fabrications arising from the power of imagination and devoid of any real entity—what fruit is there in employing them?

But those who, scorched by the pride of an excellence of wisdom capable of subtle investigation, employ such [arguments] merely to display their cleverness in artificial composition—they demonstrate nothing but themselves; no purity whatsoever has been brought about regarding the direction of the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Only on rare occasions might such things, which cause confusion for others, attain fruitfulness, as was previously stated in the case of *jalpa* (wrangling).

In that case, however, he speaks these words out of supreme pride in his own wisdom; or rather, when his concentration (samādhi) is to be explained by one of subtle intellect according to the previous method, enough of this excessively long assembly of those who consider themselves logicians—this is merely a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa), specifically a "neutralized" reason (prakaraṇasama), as has already been determined.
That which is not distinct from the probandum, because it is itself yet to be proven, is the "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama) [fallacy]. //1.2.8//
That which is accepted by one of the two disputants and is employed to prove something else is the "probandum" (sādhya).
A reason that is not distinct from that [probandum] is "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama).
If it is asked how the reason (hetu) is equal to the probandum (sādhya), he says: "Because it is itself to be proven" (sādhyatvāt).

Just as the probandum is to be proven because it is unestablished (asiddhatvāt), so too the reason employed for the sake of establishing that [probandum] is itself to be proven because it is unestablished; since it is not distinct from the probandum, it is called "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama).

And this is the definition of the *anyatarāsiddha* (unestablished for one of the two parties) alone, as in the case [of the argument] against a Mīmāṃsaka: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for something unestablished for both parties, such as *cakṣuṣatva* (visibility), to function as a probandum (*sādhya*), the definition of the unestablished (*asiddha*) should be described simply as "that which is not distinct from the probandum" (*sādhyāviśiṣṭaḥ*), without the phrase "because it is a probandum" (*sādhyatvāt*), in order to include all varieties of the unestablished.
The probandum (sādhya) has two aspects: its state of being unestablished (asiddhatva) and its state of being a probandum (sādhyatva).

In this context, it is precisely the state of being unestablished that is relied upon as the cause for its non-distinction [from the reason], because it is common to all varieties of the unestablished; it is not the state of being a probandum, which is restricted to only one of the two types of unestablished reasons.
Thus, it is the state of being unestablished alone that is stated to be the definition of the unestablished (asiddha).

That which lacks the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—that is, a reason (*hetu*) which does not reside in the subject (*dharmī*) whose property is to be proven (*sādhya*)—is called "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
Its divisions are numerous. First, regarding the nature of the reason itself, there is the non-cognition, doubt, or error of one or both of the two disputants.
Likewise, regarding its locus, the subject, there is similarly the non-cognition, doubt, or error of one or both [of the disputants].
Furthermore, when a matter has been largely established as a thesis, there may be the application [of a reason] to one part of it and its non-application to another;

even in the case of such partial application, there are likewise ignorance, doubt, and error regarding either both or one of the two [pakṣa and vipakṣa]. Thus, a detailed description of examples for these various types is of little utility and is therefore not undertaken here.
Regarding that which is unestablished for one of the two parties, however, they do not dispute it, because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is impartial.

If, first of all, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is ascertained with respect to sound by means of valid cognition, then it is established for the Mīmāṃsaka just as much as it is for the logician (*tārkika*). On the other hand, if there is no valid cognition whatsoever capable of ascertaining "being produced" in that case, then let the logician remain silent as well.
This reason is unestablished for both parties, just like [the property of] being visual and so forth;
however, it is improper to declare it unestablished by mere word alone, because that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
True, we do not maintain that a reason which is unestablished for one of the two parties is always a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa).
However, regarding the phrase "for some time":
when one disputant has employed a reason (*hetu*) and the second disputant says, "This reason is not established for me," then the employer of the reason must state its proof (*sādhana*).
Since it is established by the mere fact of its not being stated, no formal proof was presented; thus, for that duration, it remains unestablished for one of the two parties.
Immediately thereafter, however, it will become either a valid reason or unestablished for both.
As for unestablishedness due to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*), it is indeed included within the aforementioned varieties.
For example: "Sound is eternal because a crow is black."
Furthermore, some maintain that even a reason with a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*) can sometimes be a prover.

For example, a dense mass of smoke, dark-bodied like a moving rain-cloud, pervading the expanse of the sky, is capable of proving the presence of fire there, even if its status as a property of the mountain, the cave, or other specific locations has not been determined.

Or, when one employs the argument, "This place possesses fire, because smoke is perceived," then the perception—being a property of the self (*ātman*)—serves as a prover despite the difference in locus.
Others, however, cite "being established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhatva*) as a distinct type [of fallacious reason].
That reason for which, although its presence in the subject (*dharmin*) occurs, it does not lead to the occurrence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), is "established otherwise.
For example: "The atoms of the mind are impermanent because they are corporeal, like a pot."

Now, how is it that this is called "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*), rather than being a valid reason (*sadhetu*)? Does corporeality (*mūrtatva*) not exist in atoms (*paramāṇu*)? Is impermanence (*anityatā*) not seen to pervade jars and the like? Does it not exclude [the probandum] from the heterologues (*vipakṣa*), such as space (*ākāśa*) or a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*)? Is it sublated by perception (*pratyakṣa*) or scripture (*āgama*)? Or is it overpowered by a counter-reason (*pratipakṣa*), such that it incurs the status of a fallacy (*ābhāsa*)? It is not so, because there is no absence of a logical connection (*pratibandha*).

[Objection: "Is it not the case that among the five characteristics of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), one of them has become lax? [Response: We do not say that there is laxity in any one of them. [Objection: Then is the necessary connection not complete in all five characteristics? [Response: It is not that it is not complete; they indeed exist in him [the subject]. Yet, to say "this is not a necessary connection" is a mere pretense. For the necessary connection between the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) is determined—just like smoke and fire—by way of the relationship between the prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*)."
And since this relationship of the prompted (prayojya) and the prompter (prayojaka) does not exist here,
it is for this very reason called "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha) and "non-probative" (aprayojaka).

How, then, is its lack of probative force (aprayojakatva) understood? It is said: corporeality (*mūrtatva*) is indeed a property consisting of the specific dimension of substances that are either all-pervading or otherwise; it is dependent solely upon the intrinsic nature of the thing itself. Unlike "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, it is not capable of proving impermanence. For instance, if atoms were established as existing, then corporeality residing therein might prove impermanence; otherwise, it would fall into the fallacy of the unestablished substratum (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).

Furthermore, atoms are established as partless either by way of the inference from effects possessing parts, or through the process of conceptualizing a succession of parts appearing upon the disintegration of a clod of earth.
For if they possessed parts, those parts would themselves have to be atoms, and not [the original object];
and if one were to further conceptualize parts for those [parts] as well, there would be no distinction due to the infinity of parts, resulting in the equality of a mustard seed and Mount Meru.
And that [destruction] does not exist.
Thus, in partless atoms, non-dependence is established by their very nature.

Consequently, since there is an absence of causes for destruction—such as the destruction of a substratum or the disjunction of parts—and because the doctrine of intrinsic destruction has been refuted, how could permanence not touch the atoms?

However, although corporeality exists because it is a property of real entities, it is not the determining factor [for being an object of cognition], since it is itself subsumed under cognizability (*prameyatva*).
However, this is the distinction: while "knowability" (*prameyatva*), by touching upon both sides [of the debate], is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and thus non-probative;
this "corporeality" (*mūrtatva*), on the other hand, even though it lacks familiarity with anything distinct from the impermanent, is not probative.
But is it not the case that corporeality (*mūrtatva*) also occurs in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), just like knowability (*prameyatva*)?

In what does it reside? Only in atoms (*paramāṇu*). But since they have been made the subject (*pakṣa*), how can they be the counter-example? No; a thing does not change its nature according to human whim. For that which is established by firm means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being possessed of a property contrary to the property one intends to prove is called the "counter-example."
Furthermore, these atoms, whose permanence has been established by the method of reasoning just explained, are in reality the very counter-examples (vipakṣa) for those who advocate impermanence.

Even if, due to a heart defiled by passion and hatred, such a person were to state them as being the subject of the thesis (pakṣa), let him indeed say so; however, the status of being a counter-example does not cease for those things which are clearly established as permanent.
This is untenable, because by this same reasoning, there would follow the consequence that even the inference from smoke would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For smoke indeed exists on a mountain (*mahībhṛt*) which is a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) devoid of fire;
if it is argued that the absence of fire is not ascertained there, has its presence then been apprehended? If so, what is the use of inference?
If, on the mountain, neither the presence nor the absence of smoke is ascertained, then its status as a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful.

Just like a [reason] that definitely occurs in a counter-example, one that occurs in a counter-example only doubtfully does not escape being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, it would be as if a funeral offering were made to all inferences.
Nor is it the case that there is no such thing as a "thesis" (pakṣa) even when its status is established only as a conceptual construction within the mind of the proponent.
If that were absent, with respect to what would the conventional distinction between similar instances (sapakṣa) and dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) be made?
Furthermore, even in the view that [the thesis] is mounted upon the intellect, neither the similar nor the dissimilar instances possess the status of being the thesis.

Furthermore, things cannot possess a dual nature; rather, for a time, when an object has fallen into a path of dispute, it is treated as the subject of the debate (*pakṣa*), much like when one of two possibilities is not yet established. However, once a definitive determination arises and the dispute ceases, that object will certainly fall into one of the two categories. Therefore, in no way is it appropriate at that stage to point out its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).

Now, if the subject (*pakṣa*) were separated from both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) by this path, then neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) could be apprehended therein;
for positive concomitance is apprehended in the similar instances, and negative concomitance in the dissimilar instances.

Since this [subject] is a distinct entity from those two, the reason—its nature being one in which neither positive nor negative concomitance has been apprehended—would be as incapable of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*) as a eunuch is in the procreation of a son.
Enough with this childish intimidation!
For it has already been determined that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not precede the mental representation of every single instance of the similar and dissimilar classes;
nor does the apprehension of pervasion occur by excluding those instances, such that there would be occasion for the charge of its being like the son of a eunuch.
For when pervasion is apprehended in a general sense, it is indeed apprehended there [in the subject] as well.
And by that [subject], too, one must necessarily enter into either the class of similar instances (sapakṣa) or the class of dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) at another time.
However, since that [subject] is distinct from those two during the state of doubt, a reason operating therein does not become inconclusive (anaikāntika).

By this, it should be understood that the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the inferences for God and so forth is also refuted; therefore, corporeality (*mūrtatva*) is not non-conclusive and thus non-probative, but rather [non-probative] precisely because of its being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhatva*).

[Objection: Even so, because the power of the inference that establishes the atom is so great, corporeality (mūrtatva) becomes incapable of proving impermanence; consequently, due to being "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), it would not incur the status of being "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha). [Reply: This is not so. For a "mistimed" reason is said to be one whose subject matter has been preempted by perception or scripture, as in cases such as "fire is not hot" or "wine should be drunk by the twice-born. As it has been shown: "Furthermore, an inference that contradicts perception or scripture is a fallacy of reasoning (nyāyābhāsa)."

Furthermore, since atoms are by their very nature as atoms perpetually beyond the reach of perception, it is impossible for a perception that apprehends the opposite of impermanence to operate [regarding them].
And since there is no scripture [to the contrary], how can there be the fallacy of "mistiming" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa)?
Now, is this merely the word of a king, or is it a Vedic injunction, that only perception and scripture can sublate an inference, and not another inference?
For if the inference establishing the atom—which is firm—were to subvert that weak inference of impermanence based on such [reasons] as corporeality, what fault would there be?

Now, if you think that this is a fixed rule—that when there is a conflict between perception and inference, perception alone is stronger and thus it is proper for that [perception] to sublate the inference, and not some other inference—then that is incorrect; for even perception, such as that of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) and the like, is indeed sublated by an inference that is otherwise unestablished (*ananyathāsiddha*).

Is it not the case that, upon the cessation of the whirling, the very perception grasping the firebrand of limited size serves as the sublater of that [previous] perception, rather than inference? It is not so; for at the very moment the appearance of a circle arises from the incessant whirling, its erroneous nature is ascertained by means of inference.

If it is argued that the perception which has previously occurred—delimiting the object as not having the form of a wheel—is the sublater [of the erroneous cognition], we say no; for it has already passed away precisely by virtue of its having occurred previously.
Therefore, inference alone is the sublater of the cognition of a wheel.

And since it is thus established as the fundamental pillar and the foundation of all inference by virtue of being non-otherwise-established (*ananyathāsiddha*), it sublates even perception. How then could it not be the sublater of poor wretched inference? Consequently, because the mention of perception and scripture is intended as an illustration, that which is sublated by inference is indeed designated as "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
This is incorrect, because the relationship of sublated and sublator is untenable in the case of inference and the like.
For in all cases, it is that which has the form of a fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) that is sublated; indeed, what is called a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) cannot be sublated.
Even in the case of the fire-brand circle (*alātacakra*) and similar phenomena, it is inference that sublates the fallacious perception, not [valid] perception itself.
Thus, here too, it is the fallacious inference that is sublated, not the valid inference.
Now, consider this: by what is its status as a fallacy of inference (anumānābhāsa) produced?
