If you say it is due to its lack of the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), then what need is there for another subverting inference (bādhaka)? If you argue that it is called a fallacy because it is subverted [by such an inference], then the same would apply to the other case as well.

If it is argued that the inference based on atoms as the primary cause is not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*), whereas corporeality (*mūrtatva*) here is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*), you have come to my own path. Since its lack of authority is already established by the very fact of its being otherwise established, what is the point of refuting it?

If it is asked, "How is it that [the property] is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhatva*)?", we reply: No; in the case of a jar and the like, impermanence is not caused by corporeality (*mūrtatva*), but rather by being an effect (*kāryatva*). For since the destruction of an effect occurs either through the disjunction from its cause or through the destruction of that [cause], it is logical that being an effect alone is the determinant of impermanence, not corporeality.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that if corporeality were the factor implying impermanence, then the very nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*) would be lost.
Therefore, corporeality is neither a producer nor an indicator of impermanence; thus, it is "established otherwise" (anyathāsiddha).

If this is so, how can this [reason] be counted among the unestablished (*asiddha*) group? If you argue that its occurrence in the subject (*dharmin*) endowed with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) does not exist, then, because all five [types of reasons] lack such occurrence, the unestablished would be the only fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

Now, even though the status of being a "prompter" (*prayojaka*) exists, these fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are held to possess a pentad of designations based on the distinctions of their subordinate forms, such as occurrence in the counter-example (*vipakṣavṛtti*) and so forth—namely, the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and the rest.

Well then, regarding this present reason, "because of having form" (*mūrtatvāt*), should it be called inconclusive, or rather, is it "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), or perhaps "contradictory" (*viruddha*), or else "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*)?

If it is argued that not even one of these can be stated because its definition is untenable, then let it be; even if it is unestablished, do not say so, for its definition is untenable precisely because it exists in the subject (pakṣa).

Let it be, then, that this is indeed a sixth fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). For it certainly does not possess the status of a valid reason (*samyagdhetu*) according to the method already described, nor is it included within the [other] categories; thus, by necessity, it remains as a sixth one.
If it is asked, "What is the Vibhāgasūtra? [we reply: we would be transgressing this sūtra.
While transgressing it, we might deny this fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) which is clearly seen even by those who do not accept its utility; yet that is not proper.
Therefore, it is better to transgress the sūtra than to transgress reality (*vastu*).
Alternatively, it is better not to transgress the rule of the author of the Sūtras;
for one like me, who has limited vision, might speak otherwise through negligence,
but the Blessed Akṣapāda is one who has seen the further shore of the great ocean of logic.
Therefore, we shall subsume this fallacious reason within the very category of the unestablished (*asiddha*).

Now, one might object: how can that which exists in the subject (*pakṣa*) be classified there [as unestablished], given that just as it is proper for it to exist in the subject by virtue of being the motivator of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), this [reason] simply does not exist there? To this we reply: by not being too far removed [from the definition], this indeed becomes unestablished (*asiddha*).
For this very reason, it is called "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddha*).

According to this principle—that what is unestablished becomes established, yet is not established in that way, but is established otherwise—even when one merely attains a superficial occurrence, this remains unestablished.
Thus, it has been stated that [the fallacy of the unestablished] is not included even by way of figurative interpretation among the other pseudo-reasons (hetvābhāsa).
Alternatively, since this form called "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhatva*) follows upon all fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), it is not a sixth distinct fallacious reason; rather,
it is sometimes seen in isolation,
while at other times it coexists with other fallacies such as inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*).

Therefore, since the Sage taught the number five precisely with reference to such forms as deviation (vyabhicāra) and so forth, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra on the divisions; enough of this excessive detail.
Therefore, this fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) named "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha) is a single offspring;
it is that whose occurrence in the subject (pakṣa), though present, is not governed by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).
This is the common form of the entire collection of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): although there are distinctions made by other definitions, they do not arise from anything else.

A universal devoid of the nature of particulars does not exist as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Just as it should not be so in this case, such is the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*), and thus this objection has no object.
The "mistimed" (kālātīta) is that which is pointed out as having passed its proper time. //1.2.9//
When a reason is stated after the proper time for its application has passed, that reason is called "mistimed" (kālātīta), meaning it is stated when the time [for its application] has elapsed.
In this regard, some say:
"It is proper to employ the reason immediately after the thesis;

therefore, that which is employed either before the thesis or even after the statement of the example and so forth is called 'mistimed' (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa). This is untenable, because [such a reason] possesses an unimpaired logical connection and brings about the comprehension of the probandum.
The status of being a fallacious reason does not arise merely from the transposition of the sequence.
And how great is this fault, namely, the utterance being separated by other words?

For even when separated, that which is authorized to connect with its appropriate counterpart excludes everything else—even what is read in immediate proximity—and enters into a relationship with that very counterpart, however distant it may be.
As in the example: "On the path, [he saw] a long-eyed herb walking along with iron... (ayasā pathi gacchantīm auṣadhīm dīrghalocanām).
"You have seen her in the field, she whom you are cutting down—my beloved! he said.

Moreover, this which has been stated as a distinct point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is untimely; and being repeated, it does not serve any purpose for its own meaning. Therefore, this is a misinterpretation.

Another says: when a reason is employed with a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), that which does not persist until the time the effect occurs—because its qualification has passed its time—is called "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
For example: "Sound is permanent because it is manifested by conjunction (*saṃyoga-vyaṅgyatva*), like color.
Here, it is not mere manifestability (*vyaṅgyatvamātra*) that is intended as the reason, but rather manifestability qualified by conjunction (*saṃyoga-vyaṅgyatva*).

Furthermore, this conjunction, which acts as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), is observed in the case of the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*)—such as color—to persist until that [color] is perceived, as in the case of the conjunction with a lamp or similar object.

However, in the case of sound, which is the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), it does not remain in such a manner; for even when the axe has been separated from the wood by the conjunction of the woodman’s axe, the sound is heard while the axe is being raised again by the woodcutter. Since the sound is perceived at a time when that [conjunction] has already ceased, this reason is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
This too is not consistent, because it cannot be established as a distinct fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) on the grounds that its nature is unproven (*asiddha*).
Therefore, the meaning is this: the time for the employment of a reason is precisely the occasion of adopting a thesis (*pakṣa*) that is not sublated by perception or scripture.
If one employs it after that time has passed, it becomes "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), as it operates upon an object already sublated by perception or scripture.
An example of this has already been demonstrated previously.
Heat is not a composite substance (avayavin), because it is produced, like a jar and so forth.
Wine may be drunk by a Brahmin, because it is a substance, like milk or water.
Whatever was to be stated here has all been said in the definition of inference;
furthermore, since something was mentioned in the investigation of the "insufficient reason" (aprayojaka), we shall now desist from that.

These fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), having their forms determined by the cognition [of the true reason] as being distinct from others, have been ascertained; when practiced, they produce great purity regarding the fivefold object. Since the validity of those [reasons] is not established anywhere without the heavy labor involved in discerning the various modes of occurrence in the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth, they are therefore not accepted by those who know them.

It has been stated that the purpose of debate (jalpa) and destructive criticism (vitaṇḍā) is the protection of the determination of reality. Sophistry (chala), futile rejoinders (jāti), and points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) are their constituent parts. Furthermore, although there is permission for some of these in formal discussion (vāda), [others are not].

Nevertheless, since cavil (*jalpa*) and wrangling (*vitaṇḍā*) are their primary domain, it is appropriate to define their nature for that purpose; thus, following the order of enumeration, he first states the definition of quibble (*chala*): "Quibble is the subversion of a statement by means of a fabricated alternative meaning" (NS 1.2.10).
Since the *chalas* possess internal divisions, their general definition, classification, and specific definitions must be stated.

Regarding all of these, the author of the Sūtras—considering that his skill in composing aphorisms had reached its pinnacle through the definition of inference (*anumāna*) in the phrase "inference is preceded by that" (*tatpūrvakam anumānam*), which, though conveyed in only three or four syllables, encompasses an immeasurable range of topics—and thinking, "What is the use now of a desire for overly concise expression that would cause distress to the minds of my students? spoke as follows.
In this context, the sūtra "defeat of speech" (*vacanavighāta*) establishes the general definition.

"Defeat of speech" refers to the obstruction of another's speaking, that is, the cessation of their expression; it is quibble (*chala*). One might ask: is it by means of covering the mouth and so forth? No, he says: "by means of the application of a different interpretation of the meaning" (*arthavikalpopapattyā*).
The proponent of quibble (chalavādī), having superimposed upon the speaker’s statement—by implication—an unintended meaning, proceeds to negate that [superimposed] meaning.

If it is asked how there is a superimposition of another meaning, the answer is: by means of the application of an alternative interpretation of the meaning; that is to say, by construing the meaning in a different way.

"What example shall we give regarding the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*)? Why is it not stated right here? We say: because it is impossible; for a universal (*sāmānya*) without a particular (*viśeṣa*) is not logically tenable."
When that [general term] is being employed as an illustration, it necessarily remains restricted to a specific instance.

In other general injunctions as well, such as "A cow must not be touched with the foot," it is not possible for the application of touch—or its prohibition—to pertain to the universal (*jāti*), which is formless and whose nature is indistinguishable from space; rather, it pertains only to individuals. Therefore, since the connection with action occurs everywhere only within the domain of particulars, it is appropriate to provide examples only in that regard.

How then is it that the general definition of the entire class of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), namely "irrelevancy" (*aprayojakatva*)—which does not depend on specific types such as the inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*) or the contradictory (*viruddha*)—is demonstrated by way of an example, as in: "Atoms are non-eternal because they possess form, like a jar"? It might be argued: "In that case, why is the general nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) not illustrated independently of its specific types, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Let this further fault be granted. But that too is improperly maintained here; it is said in response: it was not illustrated because it is impossible to do so, not out of laziness or negligence.
The form common to the entire collection of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), however, is "irrelevance" (*aprayojakatva*); it is cited as such because it is possible [for it to apply] in that way.
Nor should it be said that because of that generality, the same should apply here as well;
for it is not possible for fifty [reasons] to be visual.
Therefore, it is not possible to speak in this manner.

Just as in the case of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), "irrelevancy" (*aprayojakatva*) is observed as a general form devoid of specific forms such as "contradiction" (*viruddha*) and so forth, so too should it be observed in the case of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as being devoid of specific forms such as "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth.

Or, just as that [irrelevancy] is not observed among the valid means of knowledge, let it likewise not be seen among the fallacious reasons; for it is untenable to subject the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of real entities to such questioning.

Furthermore, the general property of being "irrelevant" (*aprayojakatva*) is observed to occur even in those specific instances that lack the nature of contradictory reasons (*viruddha*) and so forth, just as it does in the specific types of contradictory reasons themselves.
For this very reason, it too has been illustrated as residing specifically within its own particulars, as in: "Atoms are impermanent because they possess form" (*mūrtatvāt*).
Nor is there any such thing as a general irrelevance that is entirely without a basis, like space (*ākāśa*).
Therefore, it has been well said: "It is not possible to provide an illustration by means of a general characteristic."

Having thus stated the general definition, he states the classification of *chala*: "It is threefold: quibble regarding words (*vākchala*), quibble regarding a generality (*sāmānyacchala*), and quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāracchala*). (1.2.11)

The sūtra has been explained by its very utterance. Furthermore, it was stated previously that there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence of instruction for the divisions and the general characteristics.
Now, he states the definitions according to their order of division:
"Among these, verbal quibble (*vākchala*) is the imagining of another meaning based on the speaker's intention when a thing has been stated without qualification" (NS 1.2.12).

When a word endowed with the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia)—which possesses the skill of conveying meanings that are common to multiple possibilities even when a distinction is possible—is employed, the denial of the meaning intended by the speaker after having imagined another meaning from it, while speech serves as the instrumental cause, is *vākchala* (verbal quibble).

In the case of the compound *navakambalaḥ* (nine blankets), although there is a distinction visible at the stage of analysis—namely, whether it means "this young man has a new blanket" (*navaḥ kambalo 'sya*) or "he has nine blankets" (*nava kambalā asya*)—this compound term remains indistinguishable in both meanings.

In this context, the opponent objects by concealing the speaker’s intended meaning—which is the connection with a brand-new blanket and which is supported by valid evidence—and instead superimposing a connection with the number nine; he then opposes him by denying that: "Where does he have nine blankets? This is *vākchala* (verbal quibble), occurring when a common word is spoken.

Just as it is appropriate to employ quibbles (*chala*) and other such devices in certain circumstances during a debate, and thus they are explained; likewise, since one must state a rebuttal even when faced with what has been employed by an opponent, that too is explained.

[The opponent asks: "How did you understand that my intended meaning was 'I wish to say that he has nine blankets' (*nava-kambala* as a *bahuvrīhi*)? Is this *bahuvrīhi* compound not perhaps intended simply to convey the connection with new blankets (*abhinava-kambala*)?
[The author replies: It is possible for both alternatives to occur.

If you are indeed one who understands the usage of words whose specific denotations are determined by a careful consideration of the power of the context, the subject matter, and so forth, then, having understood the meaning established by those factors—namely, the very connection with a "new blanket"—remain silent.

But if, like the domestic slave of a family of dry logicians, you are simply ignorant of the function of words, then, being in doubt due to the possibility of both alternatives, ask me myself: "What is it that you wish to say? It is as a negator that you have begun to speak.

But surely you too are engaged in the employment of words that culminate in results such as the attainment of an object; why then do you employ this common speech which is like the "blindman's leap"? O fool, it is your own speech here that is like the blindman's leap!
He who does not understand that the specific meanings of words are restricted by their dependence on context and purpose speaks in this way [incorrectly].
In this regard, these words would first be common to two meanings;
furthermore, class-words (jātiśabda) project thousands of individual instances (vyakti).
Even those [words] that necessarily require interpretation are understood through context and other factors;
for instance, in the case of "feed the Brahmins," that meaning was not learned by a child.
Therefore, when there is doubt regarding the meaning of a word, either the speaker is questioned, or else—
without superimposing another meaning upon it— the negation of that [other] meaning is enjoined.

Quibble regarding the general (*sāmānyacchala*) is the postulation of a non-existent meaning based on the application of an overly general sense to a statement that has a possible meaning. (NS 1.2.13)

An "over-general" (atisāmānya) is a universal that is too broad. Because of its connection with that—that is, because of the possibility of it occurring—there arises the conceptualization of an unreal object regarding some manifest meaning that is being produced or whose production is being anticipated by a speaker. This conceptualization consists in imagining a cause that is an over-general one which the speaker did not intend. An opposition based on such a conceptualization, having that over-general universal as its motive, is "quibble regarding the general" (sāmānyacchala).

For example, in a royal court where the noble Brahmin families—who are honored by appropriate services and speech—are highly esteemed and where talk of them is abundant, a certain well-born man praises a certain elder Brahmin, saying: "Oh, how truly this Brahmin is perfected in both learning and conduct!
In that context, another person of similar character, encouraging him, says: "Perfection in learning and conduct is possible in a Brahmin."

In this regard, Piśuna, the speaker of deceit, says: "If the perfection of knowledge and conduct (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpat*) is possible in a Brāhmaṇa, then it should also exist in a Vrātya, because his Brāhmaṇa caste (*brāhmaṇatvajāti*) has not been lost."

In this regard, the universal "Brāhmaṇahood" is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), because it transcends the perfection of knowledge and conduct while still touching upon individual instances of a Brāhmaṇa through association with them.

Since the meaning consisting of the perfection of knowledge and conduct—which was intended by the speaker—is possible [in those instances], the quibbler (*chala-vādī*) opposes it by superimposing the status of a cause that is merely an over-generalized universal (*atisāmānya-hetutā*) onto that which was not actually intended by the speaker.

To this, the reply is: by whom was it stated here that the status of being a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇatva*) is the cause [of omniscience], such that you have countered [the argument] by making it inconclusive?
This statement regarding "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*) has been presented for the sake of praise;
for a Brahmin is indeed a worthy recipient of the perfection of knowledge and conduct.
When one possesses the status of a brahmin, the perfection of knowledge and conduct arises through the ripening of merit accumulated in previous births;
yet that [status] alone is not its cause.

Just as when a statement intended for the praise of a field is uttered—such as, "Rice grows in this field"—it does not follow that one must say, "If the field alone is the cause for the production of rice, then rice would grow in this place even without the equipment of plows, oxen, and so forth, and even during a great drought.
Let this speech of yours, which shows ignorance of the manner in which such explanatory passages (arthavāda) function, rest here.
However, I ask you this, O Great-souled One: [Is it] naturally pure, touching upon the definitively certain reality, and obtainable through thousands of merits?
By whom was such a virtuous speech of yours, so well-disposed toward all people, composed?
In the exposition of the conceptualization of dharmas, the negation of the existence of an object is a quibble regarding metaphorical designation (*upacāra-chala*). 1.2.14.

The property of a designation (*abhidhāna*) is manifold: whether by primary function (*mukhyā vṛtti*), secondary function (*gauṇī*), or indicative function (*lākṣaṇikā*), it is that which conveys a meaning. When a statement is made using such a variable property—whether secondary or indicative—and there occurs a denial of the actual existence of the meaning, namely a denial of the primary meaning, that is a "quibble based on metaphorical usage" (*upacāracchala*), which has metaphorical usage as its cause.

For example, when it is said, "The benches are shouting," a caviller says: "How can inanimate wooden structures, which are the benches themselves, be shouting? It is these people sitting on the benches who are shouting, not the benches."
In this regard, the understanding of word-meanings arises from the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).

And in that context, words are seen to function by means of the primary mode of operation (*mukhya-vṛtti*) alone; yet, since the employment of other modes of operation is also well-established, it is not the case that we have applied a word for another [object] without any basis whatsoever, because this usage is preceded by one or another of the sets of bases (grounds) announced in the sūtras beginning with "sahacāraṇa."
This figurative usage [of the term "self"] is based on its location;
you who object in this manner are entirely outside the comprehension of the application of words that are secondary (gauṇa), indicative (lākṣaṇika), and so forth.

If it is asked, "What is the distinction between the secondary (gauṇa) and the indicative (lākṣaṇika) [functions]? it is said: True, the indicative function is indeed present in the secondary as well.

This being so, the word *go* (cow), having denoted its own primary meaning—the animal possessing a dewlap and so forth—indicates its qualities such as dullness, stupidity, and standing still, as well as its actions such as urinating;
yet it does not cease there alone.

But that term also applies to the Vāhīka by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); when it is employed in the form "The Vāhīka is a cow" (*gauḥ vāhīkaḥ*), it becomes figurative (*gauṇa*).

However, that word which, immediately after denoting its own primary meaning, indicates another object—whether it be a quality (*guṇa*) or a non-quality (*aguṇa*)—and is not employed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with respect to that other object, is *lākṣaṇika* (indicative), as in the example: "A hamlet dwells in the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ prativasati*). Thus it has been said: "For usage [involves] the secondary sense (*gauṇa*), not indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Enough, then, with these discourses thick with the expositions of other treatises.
Having conveyed its primary meaning, or its indicative, or even its secondary sense,
the word maintains the linguistic usage prescribed by both the world and the Veda for those whose minds are conversant with it.

If someone should raise an objection by considering the primary meaning in a figurative usage, there is no fault on the part of the speaker; rather, it would merely reveal his own ignorance of the operation of words. In this matter, the elders are the authority.

Having thus stated the specific definitions of quibble (*chala*), he raises an objection for the purpose of its examination: "Quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*) is indeed the same as quibble regarding figurative usage (*upacāracchala*), because there is no distinction between them. (NS 1.2.15)

Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever between verbal quibble (*vāk-chala*) and figurative quibble (*upacāra-chala*). When multiple meanings are possible for a word, the conceptualization of a meaning other than that intended by the speaker and the subsequent negation thereof are identical in both cases.
Furthermore, if one were to accept a diversity based on internal sub-distinctions, it would result in an infinite regress.
Regarding this, he states the [correct] position: "No, because that does not exist as a separate entity" (1.2.16).
This is not so; quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*) is not the same as quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāracchala*), because they are distinct matters.

For in the case of *vākchala*, such as "new blanket" (*navakambalaḥ*), the word retains its primary meaning whether it refers to nine blankets or to a new blanket, just as in the case of "with Rāma" (*sarāmaḥ*).
However, the proponent of the quibble superimposes upon the speaker one of these two meanings—which was not intended by the speaker—and then refutes it.
In the case of a figurative deception (*upacāracchala*), however, the word "bench" (*mañca*)—which primarily denotes a wooden structure—is applied by metaphorical attribution (*bhakti*) to a person;
and a secondary meaning is understood only after the primary meaning has been expressed.
But this sequence does not apply to words that are common [to both meanings], and thus there is a great difference.
In the case of a verbal quibble (*vākchala*), it is the very existence of the object that is denied— as in "How can he have nine blankets?"—
whereas here, however, the capacity of an existing bed (*mañca*) to cry out is what is denied.

In the case of *samādhi* as well, when one demonstrates another's ignorance of common words, it should be stated as a quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*); however, in the case of a quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāracchala*), it concerns ignorance of the figurative function of words—thus there is a great distinction.
Or, if there were no distinction [between the types of quibble], it would follow that there are many kinds of quibble based on any slight similarity. (1.2.17)

Having permitted the duality of *chala*, you now prohibit its triplicity; for, having set aside *sāmānyacchala* at your side, you have asserted that there is no difference between *vākchala* and *upacāracchala*.

Just as this prohibition of triplicity is based on the argument "because of the non-distinction from that," so too [the prohibition] of duality [would apply], since some commonality (*sādharmya*) exists even in *sāmānyacchala*.

For instance, if you consider that this "equivocation" (*chala*) and that [other type] both proceed when speech is the instrumental cause, and thus regard them as non-distinct, then do not speak of "general equivocation" (*sāmānyacchala*) as something separate.

For that too does not proceed in the body, the mind, or the intellect, but rather in speech alone; therefore, there would be only one kind of equivocation, namely "equivocation regarding speech" (*vākchala*).

Now, even if this is so, the specific distinction that is observed is not set aside; nor is the meaning of the word altered in the case of "quibble regarding the general" (*sāmānyacchala*), but rather the fact that the general [property] serves as the reason (*hetutva*)—though unstated—is superimposed, and thus it is held to be distinct. If that is the case, then it has been shown that there is indeed a distinction between the quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*) and the quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāracchala*). Therefore, the threefold nature of the quibbles (*chala*) is logically established.
Nor is there an infinity [of universals], because the three causes that determine their finite extent have already been shown;
rather, an infinity consisting of internal subdivisions is indeed accepted, just as in the case of genera—so enough of this digression.
Therefore, this triad of fallacies, each having its own distinct essential nature, has been taught here;
their application is sometimes made by oneself, and likewise, the resolution of them when stated by others must be explained.

Immediately following the enumeration of *jāti*, he first states its general definition: "A *jāti* is an opposition [to an argument] by means of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). (NS 1.2.18)

In this context, they state that the term *pratyavasthāna* (counter-position), independent of terms such as *sādharmya* (similarity) or *vaidharmya* (dissimilarity), serves to define the general characteristic of a *jāti* (futile rejoinder), thereby encompassing all its specific varieties, including those occurring across the three periods of time.
"Pratyavasthāna" means standing in opposition.

It is incorrect to designate as a "jāti" (futile rejoinder) merely that which arises as some kind of reply to a reason adduced by another, simply because it is a mere counter-position independent of similarity (*sādharmya*) and so forth; for if mere counter-position were a *jāti*, then even the pointing out of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) would incur the status of a *jāti*.

Now, if it is argued that because [the opponent's response] is a correct rejoinder (*samyaguttara*), and because here only a mere objection (*pratyavasthāna*) without qualification has been established, what is intended by "futile rejoinder" (*asaduttara*) is merely a triviality (*phalguprāya*) classified as a "point of defeat" (*jāti*); even so, the consequence that a quibble (*chala*) would also be a "point of defeat" remains unavoidable.

If, however, something such as "provided that it is other than that" (*tadanyatve sati*) is supplied to exclude those [other fallacies], then what fault is there in this heard mention of the apprehension of similarity and dissimilarity? Is it not a fault that the *traikālyasama* (balancing the three times) and so forth are not included? No, this is not a fault; for by not forming a compound in the phrase "by means of similarity and dissimilarity" (*sādharmyavaidharmyābhyām*), there is an indication that this is merely pointing out the general direction. This is because in the cases of *traikālyasama* and the rest, there is no counter-positioning (*pratyavasthāna*) by way of either similarity or dissimilarity.

Whether by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), when an objection is raised in such a manner—asking "How does this reason become a reason? or "What is accomplished by this?"—along the path of counterfeiting the reason (*hetupratibimbavartmanā*), that is called a *jāti* (futile rejoinder). In this way, there will be an inclusion of all its specific varieties; for even in cases such as the "equalization by the three times" (*traikālyasama*), one can apply some form of similarity or dissimilarity, however slight. For what is intended here is not the similarity to the example as the means of proving the probandum, nor its dissimilarity, but rather the mere presence of similarity and so forth.

In that regard as well, since it is not ultimately difficult to understand, it is logical that the general definition of a *jāti* (fallacious rejoinder) is simply its establishment through similarity and dissimilarity exactly as it was heard.

Now, because it possesses divisions, he states the twenty-fourfold classification of *jāti*: "The *sādharmya-sama*, *vaidharmya-sama*, *utkarṣa-sama*, *apakarṣa-sama*, *varṇya-sama*, *vikalpa-sama*, *sādhyasama*, *prāptisama*, *aprāptisama*, *prasanga-sama*, *pratidṛṣṭāntasama*, *anutpattisama*, *saṃśayasama*, *prakaraṇasama*, *hetusama*, *arthāpattisama*, *aviśeṣasama*, *upapattisama*, *upalabdhisama*, *anupalabdhisama*, *nityasama*, *anityasama*, and *kāryasama*. (NS 5.1.1)

In this context, since the designation "equal" (*samā*) is identical for both feminine and masculine, it should be explained as either a feminine designation with respect to the genus (*jāti*) or a masculine designation with respect to the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*).
Furthermore, in the sūtras defining specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), a masculine designation is generally observed;
however, that [masculine form] must be interpreted in those instances with respect to the prohibition, which we shall explain at the very occasion of its commentary.
Now, let the description of the specific definitions be set aside for a moment;
rather, this alone should be considered first:
for what purpose is such a collection of fallacious rejoinders (asaduttara) expounded in the treatise?

Furthermore, since such fallacious rejoinders—which are like the scattering of dust, which are capable of being disregarded by the discerning who are able to examine what is essential from what is not, and which are infinite in number—how is it that they are numbered at twenty-four? This is a source of great wonder to us.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the purpose [of debate] is the preservation of the determination of reality, that too is not convincing, because it is impossible to preserve the determination of reality by means of presenting fallacious rejoinders.

If, on the other hand, its protection is sought by means of deluding others through the skill of manifesting hideous contortions, then let the spitting, laughing, threatening, crushing of the shoulders, tearing of the loincloth, and the slapping of the feet also be taught here in this science of liberation.

Furthermore, let this be considered: where should one employ *jāti*-objections when a correct proof (*samyaksādhana*) has been adduced by an opponent, or when a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) has been adduced? It cannot be in response to a fallacious proof; for in that case, it is appropriate to employ those very reasons—such as "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and so forth—by which that [proof] acquired its status as a fallacious proof, namely the *jātis*.
And by those very reasons, the opponent is defeated.
Nor can they be employed against a correct proof, because even if those *jātis* are employed there, they are utterly ineffective.
For even a correct means of proof (samyaksādhana), though defiled by the employment of a futile rejoinder (jāti), cannot fail to be a valid means of proof.

Thinking that uncertainty is better than certain defeat, they proceed in this manner; yet even there, one who proceeds in such a way—who would he convince? Certainly not those who know the principles of logic (*nītividaḥ*), for those who know logic surely recognize: "This person, being unable to speak as is appropriate, has begun to utter some web of nonsense.

However, convincing carters and the like might occasionally be useful for someone desiring profit and so forth in the village assemblies of remote borderlands; but in a treatise on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*), such an instruction is not elegant.

To this it is replied: this has already been settled by the Blessed One, the author of the Sūtra himself, who stated that "these are for the purpose of protecting the determination of reality, like the encircling of thorny branches.

For quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are constituent parts of disputation (*jalpa*) and wrangling (*vitaṇḍā*). Thus it was said: "The separate teaching of quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat is for the sake of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*)."

"For those [fallacies] that have been identified, there is avoidance in one's own statement and a formal challenge (*paryanuyoga*) regarding the statement of another; however, when a *jāti* (futile rejoinder) is employed by an opponent, the resolution is easy to state and its application is easy to perform oneself."

For when a seeker of liberation has acquired knowledge of reality through either scripture or reasoning, yet has not yet attained the excellence of its firmness through the grace of the practice of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), if at that stage he were to be confounded by someone stating something resembling an inference, then—even though he possesses respect for both reasoning and scripture—he might suddenly experience a slight trace of doubt regarding the knowledge of reality produced therein.
Or, even if his own conviction remains firm, the disciples standing near him might become lax in their resolve.

Therefore, not seeing a refutation [of his own position], he would certainly suppress the opponent even with the employment of futile rejoinders (*jāti*); he would not remain indifferent—this was stated in the definition of *jalpa*.
Or, having recognized through inference those classes that have been refuted by others, one should abandon them at that very moment; thus, the exposition of the categories (jāti) is fruitful.

Just as in a field where the crop has recently been sown and the boundary is bristling with a multitude of tender sprouts now emerging, one suspects that it might be damaged by some quadruped or biped moving very swiftly from anywhere; and to prevent this, a continuous hedge of thorny branches is placed all around it—so too here, one must provide protection for the ascertainment of reality through the application of [the categories of] birth and so forth, and through their refutation.

As for the objection raised—that the application of a *jāti* (futile rejoinder) occurs only when there is a semblance of a valid proof (*samyaksādhana*)—it is said in response that, according to those who claim a *jāti* and the like must be employed by one who fails to perceive a valid refutation (*samyagdūṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, let that perception of a "refutation" (saddūṣaṇā) occur either because of the absence of a valid proof (*samyaksādhana*) or, in the case of a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), due to negligence and the like; what difference does it make here? However, for one seeking liberation who has known the truth and is challenged by someone propounding something contrary to it, there arises an occasion for the employment of a futile rejoinder (*jāti*) when that person—driven by the force of rejecting the truth—fails to perceive a genuine refutation directed at the fallacious proof itself.

Even having recognized the fallacious nature of the arguments (*sādhana*), it is entirely appropriate for one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*) to immediately rebuke this person of evil conduct—thinking, "Let him be censured"—in order to generate enthusiasm among the delicate students standing nearby by composing a display of sophistry (*jāti*) and so forth.

Furthermore, since the treatise begins with reference to the seeker of liberation, the employment of a *jāti* (futile rejoinder) regarding fallacious arguments is directly relevant to that perspective.
For this very reason, the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) first presented examples of *jāti* as illustrations of fallacious arguments.
However, even when one is engaged in the correct accomplishment of gains and so forth, an attack on [the opponent's] birth and other such factors is indeed appropriate;
for otherwise, defeat would be certain. And this is said to be a secondary purpose.
Furthermore, as for the claim that one should employ slaps or the like when speaking a false rejoinder—that too is incorrect, because such a thing is utterly unconventional.
For the world would think at that time: "Surely this person does not know how to give a fitting reply;
otherwise, why would he abandon speech and strike with his hand?"
But he who tires the opponent with the fidgeting of his hands, feet, and so forth,
is called by the wise in the assembly merely a buffoon, not a solid debater.
But one who is attacked on account of his birth is not ridiculed in such a manner;
for the appearance of corruption is not entirely out of place in that case.
Therefore, there is no parity between these [fallacious rejoinders] and such things as the removal of one's loincloth. Thus ends the discussion on futile rejoinders (*jātyuttara*).
As for the claim that someone must be made to understand by those [means], that is not so; for not everyone is like an omniscient being, nor is everyone like a common cart-driver.
There are indeed people who occupy an intermediate position, and they will be made to ascend [to understanding]. Enough of this digression.

Furthermore, as for the objection that because fallacious rejoinders (*asaduttara*) are infinite, how can they be numbered at twenty-four—it is said in response: although the types [of fallacies] are indeed infinite, their twenty-fourfold classification was described with the intention of providing unmixed examples; however, no restrictive limit to their number was established.

Thus, an objection raised here on the basis of similarity (*sādharmya*) that is not distinct from the reason for the original position is the "balancing the similarity" (*sādharmya-sama*) fallacy. And that same [fallacy] is employed with a reason of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) as well; likewise, an objection proceeding by way of dissimilarity is the "balancing the dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya-sama*) fallacy. Objections raised through the means of augmentation (*utkarṣa*) and diminution (*apakarṣa*) are the "balancing the augmentation" (*utkarṣa-sama*) and "balancing the diminution" (*apakarṣa-sama*) fallacies; in this manner, it should be applied in all cases.

The fact that [the opponent's argument] cannot be distinguished from the original by way of its being established as a reason (sthāpanāhetu) should be understood with reference to the intention of the proponent of the *jāti* (futile rejoinder).
For the proponent of the *jāti* speaks thus: "Just as your proof (sādhana) has been employed, why should this [rejoinder] not be likewise?
It is for this very reason that it is said that the presentation of a *jāti* occurs solely through the medium of reflecting the original reason.
Now he states the specific definitions:

"In that context, when a conclusion is drawn through similarity or dissimilarity, the two fallacies known as *sādharmya-sama* (balancing the similarity) and *vaidharmya-sama* (balancing the dissimilarity) arise from the possibility of the opposite of that property. (5.1.2)
It should be observed in each instance that the use of the masculine gender is dependent upon the negation [of the probans].

In that context, after the proponent has stated a proof—either by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—and has concluded with the thesis he intends to prove, the opponent’s counter-argument (*pratyavasthāna*) which, being indistinguishable from the original reason for establishing the position, seeks to establish the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) by means of similarity, is the "balancing of similarity" (*sādharmyasama*) negation.

The example, however, is as follows: when the reason is employed through similarity—namely, "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort; for whatever follows immediately upon effort is seen to be impermanent, like a jar"—the proponent of a futile rejoinder (jātivādī) opposes it by means of similarity alone: "Sound is permanent because it is partless; for a substance that is partless, such as space and so forth, is seen to be permanent.

And here there is no specific reason [to prefer one over the other]: that sound is impermanent due to its similarity to a jar in terms of following immediately upon effort, rather than being permanent due to its similarity to space in terms of being partless.

Likewise, in this very context, there is an opposition based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): "Sound is eternal because it is partless; for whatever is impermanent is observed to have parts, such as a jar or other substances.

And there is no specific reason [to prefer one over the other] such that sound is impermanent due to its similarity to a jar—namely, its being produced immediately after an effort—and not eternal due to its dissimilarity to a jar, namely, its being partless.

Even when a reason based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-hetu*) is employed through the formulation of the proof and so forth—such as: "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort; for that which is not impermanent does not follow immediately upon effort, like space and so forth"—in this case, one should cite these very two previously mentioned forms of counter-argument based on similarity and dissimilarity (*sādharmya-vaidharmya-pratyavasthāna*).

Just as the nature of universals (*jāti*) was introduced for the purpose of explaining how their own application is sometimes utilized, so too must an answer be stated regarding them when they are applied by another.
Therefore, for the sake of explaining that, he says: "Their establishment is like the establishment of 'cowness' (*gotva*). (5.1.3)
This is the response regarding the positions based on similarity and dissimilarity:
if it were claimed that mere similarity or mere dissimilarity constitutes the proof of the probandum, this infinite regress would occur;
furthermore, there would be no distinction between such [fallacious] reasons employed by you and the reason for the formal establishment [of a thesis].
However, when a specific similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is stated as the probans (*prayojaka*), it is not undermined by such objections.

For example, although a cow possesses a connection with generalities such as "existence" (*sattā*), a connection with qualities such as "whiteness," and a conjunction with actions such as "movement," it is established as being a cow—not because of its similarity to those things, nor because of its dissimilarity to horses and the like—but rather solely through its non-deviant connection with "cowness" (*gotva*).
Likewise here too, it is an unerring rule of similarity or dissimilarity that is the basis for establishing the probandum, not mere similarity and so forth alone.

The sophistries known as *utkarṣasama*, *apakarṣasama*, *varṇyasama*, *avarṇyasama*, *vikalpasama*, and *sādhyasama* arise from the variation of properties in the subject (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and because both [the property and the subject] are yet to be proven. //5.1.4//

The "balancing by addition" (utkarṣasama) refutation is that which, while applying a property of the example to the subject of the thesis—thereby superimposing what is non-existent—performs an opposition through exaggeration. For example, when it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar," another person says: "If sound is impermanent like a jar because it follows immediately upon effort, then like a jar, it must also be corporeal; if it is not corporeal, then let it not be impermanent either. Thus, the introduction of another property, such as corporeality, is the balancing by addition.

*Apakarṣasama* (the equalization by subtraction) is the counter-argument consisting in the subtraction of a property from the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), even though that property has already been established, by means of the very same conceptualization of the property in the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharma*).
In the aforementioned argument: "Since a jar, being produced immediately after an effort, is seen to be non-audible, let sound also be non-audible because it is produced immediately after an effort;
if it is not non-audible, then let it not be impermanent either, like a jar"—this removal of the existing property of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is *apakarṣasama*.
The property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is that which is to be made known, praised, and intended to be communicated;
by contrast, the property of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharma*) is "not to be praised" (*avarṇya*), meaning it is already established.

When one creates an opposition by reversing these two—the "to be praised" and the "not to be praised"—and thereby equates one with the other, those two refutations are respectively called *varṇyasama* (balancing the to-be-praised) and *avarṇyasama* (balancing the not-to-be-praised).
If sound is described as being eternal and thus established, then a jar should also be so described; this is *varṇyasama* (the "equal-to-the-thing-to-be-proven").
If a jar is not so described, then sound should likewise not be so described; this is *avarṇyasama* (the "not-equal-to-the-thing-to-be-proven").
*Vikalpasama* (the refutation by means of alternative conceptualization) is an opposition based on the conceptual differentiation of other properties (*dharmāntara*).

Regarding that very same formal argument (*prayoga*), one observes that some things produced immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyaka*) are soft, such as *dukūla* silk, *rāṅkava* woolen blankets, or beds, while others are hard, such as potsherds or axes.
Likewise, among those things produced immediately after effort, some may be impermanent, such as jars, while others may be permanent, such as sound and so forth.
The "equal-to-the-probandum" (sādhyasama) refutation is an objection that arises by reducing both the probandum and the example to the status of being themselves probanda.
If it is the case that as the jar is, so is the sound, then it follows that as the sound is, so is the jar.
Since the sound is to be proven as impermanent, the jar must likewise be something yet to be proven.
For otherwise, it would not be equal to that.

In this regard, the answer to the five [objections] is: "There is no refutation on the basis of dissimilarity, because the establishment of the conclusion is achieved through some degree of similarity. (NS 5.1.5)
An application [of analogy] is established through some commonality, as in: "As is a cow, so is this gavaya.

However, it is not possible to establish an absolute identity of form between the two, because it is impossible to effect a confusion of the mutual forms of entities whose distinct natures have been cognized through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

And thus, when the similarity based on its own necessary connection (*svapratibandhasādharmya*) is well-established, it brings about its own probandum (*sādhyam*) within the establishing reason (*sthāpanāhetu*); therefore, a refutation cannot be achieved by one who attempts to introduce a variation of properties between the probandum and the example or who asserts some dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Now, the answer to the sixth [objection] follows from the statement of the probandum and the illustration being established. 5.1.6.

As for the claim that "the pot, like sound, should also be something to be proven," that is not so; for a *dṛṣṭānta* (example) is that object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding between ordinary people and investigators.
By means of that [consensus], the property is extended to sound without error:
just as a pot, being produced immediately after an effort, is impermanent, so too is sound.
Thus, since the example is established through the extension of the property to be proven, it is not tenable to designate that very example as the property to be proven.

The "equivalence based on reaching" (prāptisama) and the "equivalence based on not reaching" (aprāptisama) [are fallacies] because a reason is indistinguishable whether it reaches the probandum or does not reach it, and because it cannot establish [the probandum] if it does not reach it. //5.1.7//

The refutations known as *prāptisama* (balancing by attainment) and *aprāptisama* (balancing by non-attainment) consist in demonstrating faults in both cases, preceded by the conceptualization of attainment and non-attainment. When a reason (*hetu*) has been employed by the proponent of the proof (*sādhana-vādin*), the opponent says: "Does this reason establish the probandum (*sādhya*) by attaining it or without attaining it? If by attaining it, then since attainment occurs only between two things that have already acquired their own nature (*labdhasvarūpa*), there is no distinction: what is the probandum and what is the means of proof?
If, on the other hand, it establishes without attaining it, its status as a prover (*sādhakatva*) is untenable, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."
For a lamp does not illuminate what is to be illuminated without reaching it.

The answer to these two is: there is no prohibition [against the use of mantras], because [the mantra] brings about the production of a jar and so forth, and because it effects the subjugation [of an enemy] through ritual affliction. //5.1.8//
This negation is not tenable, because the causal nature [of things] is observed in both ways:
it is seen that the causal factors such as the staff, the wheel, and the string, having reached the clay, produce effects such as a jar;
and by means of malevolent rites such as the Śyena sacrifice, the tearing apart of even a distant enemy is accomplished.

The [two fallacies] *prasaṅgasama* and *pratidṛṣṭāntasama* consist respectively in an objection based on the failure to state the reason for the example and an objection by means of a counter-example. (5.1.9)

The refutation that consists in an objection by way of establishing an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is the "balancing the consequence" (*prasaṅgasama*) refutation. Regarding the very reason previously cited—namely, that "being produced immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is the proof for impermanence—one might now ask: what is the proof for "being produced immediately after an effort"? And what is the proof for that? For no cause whatsoever is pointed out for the impermanence of the jar and other such things used as examples.
Because that leads to an over-extension in the search for its cause, this refutation is a "balancing the consequence" (prasaṅgasama) fallacy.
The refutation by means of a counter-example is the "counter-example-equivalent" (pratidṛṣṭāntasama) objection.

For example: "Just as a jar, being produced immediately after an effort, is seen to be impermanent, so too space, though not produced immediately after an effort, is seen to be permanent; likewise, sound should also be permanent.
But who indeed would assert that space is produced immediately after an effort? Only someone who considers space to be created by such acts as digging a well might say so.

[Objection: "But even so, this pointing out of an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) is a correct reply; it is not an application of a futile rejoinder (*jāti*), which is a type of 'non-existent' reply. [Response: This is not so. For this proponent of the *jāti* does not oppose [the opponent] like a virtuous person by pointing out the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason (*hetu*).
Rather, he has arisen [in debate] seeking to establish permanence itself by means of a counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*); thus, this is indeed an application of a *jāti*.
Even fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), when presented by way of the reflection of another reason while concealing their own true nature, certainly attain the status of a *jāti*.

Regarding this, he first states the reply to the *prasaṅgasama* (balancing the consequence): "Just as there is the cessation of the consequence regarding the acquisition of a lamp, so too is there the cessation of that [consequence]. (5.1.10)
For that which is unestablished (asiddha) is indeed what is to be established, not that which is already established, because effort would be fruitless in that case.
Indeed, people in the world bring a lamp into a dark house to see objects such as a cooking pot, but they do not bring another lamp for the purpose of seeing the [first] lamp;
for the lamp is seen even without other lamps.
Thus, since for worldly investigators the state of being produced immediately after an effort is established in the case of a jar and the like, the citation of a cause in that regard is purposeless.
Therefore, this is not the proper subject for the charge of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Now, the reply to the "balancing by a counter-example" (pratidṛṣṭāntasama) fallacy: When a counter-example functions as a reason, the original example is not a non-reason. //5.1.11//

If you have presented the counter-example itself with the intention that it be the proof, then a specific reason must be stated by which this counter-example alone is the proof and not the [original] example.
Yet no such specific reason is stated.
Therefore, the counter-example is not the cause of proof; rather, the example alone is the proof.
Even if the status of a counter-example as a reason were established, an example that lacks a reason would not be a proof;
yet it has been stated that such a thing does not exist.
Therefore, an example cannot be devoid of a reason.

Now, if one objects on the grounds that just as the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) is not a proof, so too the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) should not be a proof, then [the response is]: "Well then, you have yourself stated with your own lips that the counter-example lacks probative force; therefore, since that [counter-example] is not a proof, the example itself is indeed the proof."
The "balancing the non-arising" (anutpattisama) fallacy occurs because there is no cause prior to the arising [of the effect]. //5.1.12//

The "balancing by non-arising" (anutpattisama) refutation is an opposition based on non-arising. Regarding the very same previous argument, the proponent of the futile rejoinder says: "That which is impermanent is said to have the property of arising.
And that which has the property of arising must, prior to its arising, exist in a state of non-arising."

Furthermore, while the subject (*dharmin*) called "sound" has not yet arisen, where could the property (*dharma*) of "being produced immediately after effort" reside? And how could that which has not yet established its presence in the subject prove impermanence?
If impermanence is not established for sound, then by default, permanence itself follows due to the absence of a cause;
that is to say, because of the absence of the cause for establishing impermanence, namely, the property of being produced immediately after effort.
Alternatively, because the causes that produce sound are absent, sound has not arisen; thus, the logical reason (hetu) would be without a substratum (nirāśraya).
The answer to this is: because that which has arisen exists in such a manner, and because a cause is logically established for it, there is no negation of the cause. //5.1.13//
The permanence or impermanence of the subject known as "sound" is investigated only when it exists as an established entity;
for if that [subject] were unestablished, of what would you assert permanence? Furthermore, such a state occurs for that which has arisen, not for that which has not arisen;
indeed, this sound is said to be "arisen," not "unarisen."

Since [the entity] has not yet acquired its own nature prior to arising, what could be said of it? Furthermore, because the state of being produced immediately after an effort—which is the cause of impermanence—is already present once its own nature has been acquired, this negation is indeed untenable.
Doubt arises because of the commonality of being both eternal and non-eternal. //5.1.14//
The refutation known as *saṃśayasama* (the equalizing by doubt) is an opposition characterized by the induction of doubt through the presentation of both permanent and impermanent commonalities.

Regarding this very reason—"Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort"—there exists in sound the commonality with the impermanent, namely, following immediately upon effort; and there also exists a commonality with the permanent, namely, being perceptible by the senses (*aindriyakatva*), as in the case of the universal (*sāmānya*).

Therefore, the opponent objects as follows: "Is sound impermanent because of its similarity to the impermanent—namely, its being produced immediately after an effort—or is it permanent because of its similarity to the permanent—namely, its being perceptible by the senses? This constitutes a doubt.
Furthermore, this should not be suspected as being merely a *sādharmyasama* (balancing the similarity) fallacy, because its function is specifically to induce doubt.

The answer to this is: doubt arises from similarity, or from dissimilarity, or from both; yet, even if there is doubt, there is no absolute doubt [regarding the existence of the universal], because the eternity of the universal is not admitted, and thus it is not refuted. //5.1.15//

Regarding the doubt, "Is it a post or a person?", the uncertainty arises from the similarity (*sādharmya*) between the post and the person—such as their common property of being upright—and not from the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) of having a head, hands, and so forth;
on the contrary, one turns away from that [dissimilarity].
If, however, doubt were to arise from dissimilarity just as it does from similarity, then an absolute and perpetual doubt would result.

Furthermore, in this case, there exists in sound the property of being produced immediately after an effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), which serves as the means for establishing impermanence—a factor that outweighs the perception of similarity. Therefore, it is not accepted that permanence residing in the universal (*sāmānya*) is the cause of doubt.
Consequently, this objection—which consists in attempting to induce doubt based on the commonality with the universal of permanence—is not a valid refutation.
The "neutralized" (prakaraṇasama) [pseudo-reason] occurs because the process of proof is established through the commonality of both sides. //5.1.16//
The proponent's position (*pakṣa*) and the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) have been explained in the definition of determination (*nirṇaya*).
These two together constitute a "treatise" (*prakaraṇa*).
A refutation that does not go beyond this treatise is the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) refutation.

In the very same original argument, the proponent of the *jāti* (futile rejoinder) sets forth a counter-argument of this kind—such as "Sound is eternal because it is partless, like space"—and thereby establishes his own position.
Furthermore, the mention of "similarity" (*sādharmya*) is illustrative;
even when a counter-argument is presented on the basis of "dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya*), the refutation remains precisely the same as that of the *prakaraṇasama*.
"Because the process of proof is established through the dissimilarity of both [the subject and the example], it is called 'neutralizing' (*prakaraṇasama*).
This pair of applications is to be understood as applicable to the original reason (*mūlahetu*) as well, whether it is employed by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

But surely these two—similarity and dissimilarity—are already included within the fourfold classification of the "balancing" (sādharmya-vaidharmya-sama) fallacies, since they are employed as either a reason based on similarity or a reason based on dissimilarity; thus, this application of a fallacy is not new. Furthermore, it is said that the claim that there are four such fallacies is inconsistent with their being unified. In that context, the counter-argument was illustrated as being inclined toward the refutation of the opponent's position, whereas here it is presented under the guise of establishing one's own position.
For this very reason, this fallacy is called *prakaraṇasama* ("the equal-to-the-issue").
"The position of the eternal is also refuted by us in the same manner as the position of the non-eternal.
Furthermore, the diversity of *jāti*s arises from the different modes of their manifestation;
and the enumeration of twenty-four types is intended to provide distinct, unmixed examples.
In reality, however, it has been stated that they are infinite.

To this, the reply is: since the subject matter is established by means of a counter-argument, the refutation [of that counter-argument] is untenable, because the counter-argument itself is valid. (5.1.17)
A discussion (*prakaraṇa*) comes to an end through the arising of a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*); prior to that conclusion, it remains exactly as it was.

Therefore, by you who have raised this discussion here, you have stated that "similarity to both" (*ubhayasādharmya*) is the cause for its initiation, saying, "because the discussion is established through similarity to both.

And indeed, the similarity to both that I have mentioned is also present; otherwise, what would be the meaning of the word "both"? Furthermore, in this way, that which you have accepted as the cause of the discussion is established.
And nothing has been stated for the sake of producing a definitive conclusion or for the cessation of the discussion, because both [positions] have been expressed as having common characteristics.
The "equal to the non-reason" (ahetusama) occurs because the reason is untenable in all three periods of time. //5.1.18//
A refutation that proceeds by challenging the reason on the grounds that it is untenable across the three periods of time constitutes the "equivalence of the non-reason" (*ahetusama*).
A reason is a means of proof (*sādhana*).

And a means of proof must exist either prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously with that which is to be proven (*sādhya*). If it exists prior, then since the *sādhya* does not yet exist, for what would it be a means of proof? If it exists subsequently, then the *sādhya* is prior; in that case, since the means of proof does not yet exist, of what would this be the *sādhya*?

If the probandum is already established, what is the use of a proof? Or, if the probandum and the proof arise simultaneously, then there could be no relationship of probandum and proof between them, just as there is none between the left and right horns of a cow; thus, this reason is no different from a non-reason.
The response to this is: "There is no non-establishment [of the reason] across the three times, because the establishment of the probandum follows from the nature of being a reason. (5.1.19)
There is no failure to establish [the effect] across the three times.
Why? Because the probandum is established by means of the reason (*hetu*).

First, regarding origination, this objection is addressed: it has already been stated that the establishment of a future, non-existent effect, such as a cloth, occurs by means of a previously established cause, such as the threads.
"But that which is established by cognition is non-existent.

This fault has already been refuted even with respect to cognition, because there is no fixed rule regarding the priority, posteriority, or simultaneity of the object that is the cause of its apprehension and the object that is the content of that apprehension;
for it was stated in the *Pramāṇaparīkṣā* that "the establishment [of things] is according to how they are perceived."

Moreover, it is observed that the production of what is to be produced occurs by means of a cause of production, and the apprehension of what is to be apprehended occurs by means of a cause of apprehension.

Since an object is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what kind of objection is this? Furthermore, this same challenge applies equally to the negation itself; thus he says: "And because negation is untenable, there is no negation of that which is to be negated" (5.1.20).
When it is considered whether the negation must occur before, after, or simultaneously with that which is to be negated, it is found that it is not capable of negating the object of negation.
Arthāpattisama (the equal by implication) occurs because the counter-position is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). //5.1.21//
The establishment of the counter-position follows by implication; thus, a negation formulated in this manner becomes "equal to implication" (*arthāpattisama*).

In the very same argument, if it is claimed that sound is impermanent because it shares the property of being produced immediately after effort—just like a jar—it follows by implication that it must be permanent because it shares the property of being a substance without parts, just like space.
And indeed, it possesses this commonality with eternal substances such as space: namely, its partlessness.
And how can it be said that there is a distinction between types of futile rejoinders (*jāti*) based on the difference in the modes of their presentation?
The answer to this is: because the unspoken [consequence] follows by implication, there is the establishment of the defeat of one's own position. //5.1.22//

For one who asserts that a proof which has not been explicitly stated is nonetheless established by implication when it is uncontradicted, the loss of one's own position (*pakṣahāni*) also follows as a consequence. For when my own position—that [sound] is impermanent—is established, the loss of your position—that it is permanent—is established by implication.
He states another defect: "And because presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) is inconclusive" (5.1.23).
This *arthāpatti* (presumption) is equal for both sides, because it can be employed even in the opposite manner.

Even when it is stated thus—"Sound is eternal, because it is partless"—it is possible to argue that if sound is eternal by virtue of its partlessness, which is a property shared with the eternal ether (*ākāśa*), then by implication it must be non-eternal because of its being produced immediately after effort, which is a property shared with non-eternal things such as jars. And even in this case, no objective conclusion is established.
Indeed, when it is said that "there is no falling of a solid stone," it does not follow by implication that there is an absence of falling for liquid water.
Because a single property is established in some cases and not established in others, there is no negation [of the possibility of the property]. //5.1.25//
The refutation that establishes a lack of distinction is the "balancing of non-distinction" (*aviśeṣasama*) counter-argument.

If it is argued that because sound and a jar share the single property of being produced immediately after an effort, they are indistinguishable in their impermanence, then it follows that all entities would be indistinguishable.
How so? Because they are established as existing; that is to say, because they are connected with existence (*sattā*).
This is the refutation known as "balancing the non-distinction" (aviśeṣasama).
The answer to this is: "In some cases there is no negation because that property is possible; in other cases it is because it is impossible. (5.1.25)
In some cases a property that serves as a cause for establishing non-distinction is possible, while in other cases it is not; thus, this is not a valid refutation.
Sound and a pot share a single property—namely, being produced immediately after an effort—by which another property, impermanence, is established as a form of non-distinction between them.
However, there is no such collection of properties existing among all entities that could serve as a cause for such non-distinction.

As for the argument "because existence is established," what is being proven by that? Is it some other property (*dharmāntara*) of an undifferentiated nature, or is it impermanence itself? If it is impermanence, then the thesis (*pratijñārtha*) would be established as: "All entities are impermanent because they exist.
But this is untenable, because no example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is possible; for all entities have been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*) of the proposition.

Not a single example remains [unexamined]. Furthermore, it is impossible to take even a part of the thesis itself as the example, because of the distinction between what is established and what is to be proven;
for the object stated in the thesis is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), whereas the example is that which is already established (*siddha*).
Furthermore, a reason devoid of an illustrative example does not possess the capacity to establish its own probandum.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that existence, having been excluded from eternal things by the non-perception of a pervader according to the Buddhist doctrine, finds its footing only in impermanent things;
nor can it be said that the very exclusion from the heterologous (vipakṣa) is itself the concomitance with the probandum (sādhya), because that doctrine has already been refuted.
Indeed, the proof for momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) has already been explained in detail.
For some collection of entities endowed with existence is impermanent while others are permanent; thus, it is not an absolute rule that all existing things are impermanent simply because they exist.
Moreover, when the impermanence of all entities is being proven, since sound is included among them, its impermanence would also necessarily be admitted; thus, this [objection] remains unrefuted.
The "balancing by the possibility" (upapattisama) occurs because both [the probans and its contradictory] can be established. //5.1.26//
The refutation known as "balancing the justification" (upapattisama) consists in describing the establishment of both sides by means of the occurrence of the same grounds for both.

If the reason for impermanence—being produced immediately after an effort—is applicable to sound, then sound is impermanent; yet if the reason for permanence—being partless—is also applicable to it, then it would be permanent.
For the reason is applicable in both cases.

Is it not the case that this very [fallacy] is either *sādharmyasama* (balancing the homogeneity) or *prakaraṇasama* (balancing the doubt), and not a different variety? No, it is not so; for there is a distinction based on the manner of its presentation.
*Sādharmyasama* and the other [balancings] result from the intent to crush the opponent's position, whereas *prakaraṇasama* results from the desire to establish an alternative position.
This is a proof based on logical consistency, intended with the purpose of leading to the ultimate non-apprehension [of intrinsic nature].

To this, the following reply is given: there is no refutation because the validity of the reasons has been admitted. By asserting a refutation through the establishment of both sets of reasons, you have admitted the establishment of the reasons for both positions.
If that [establishment] is admitted, how can there be a refutation of one side?
And if there is a refutation of one side, how can there be the establishment of the reasons for both?
It is a contradiction to claim both the establishment of reasons for both sides and the refutation of one side;
for if you argue that the refutation is possible precisely because of this contradiction, then the contradiction is equal,
since by that very [reasoning] one's own position is as much struck down as the opponent's position.
For a contradiction does not establish one position while subverting another.

*Upalabdhisama* (the "equal to apprehension" fallacy) is an objection based on the apprehension [of the property] even in the absence of the stated reason. It is a refutation consisting in an opposition based on the perception of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), despite the absence of the stated cause for establishing that property.

For example, although the "immediacy following effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) has been taught as the reason for the impermanence of sound, impermanence is indeed observed in sound even in the absence of that reason—as in the case of a sound produced by the falling of an old tree being shattered by the force of a powerful wind.
Furthermore, even in the case of lightning and other such phenomena, impermanence is indeed perceived even in the absence of being produced immediately after an effort.
The answer to this is: "There is no refutation [of our position], because that property can arise even from another cause" (NS 5.1.29).
In this regard, first of all, it must be said that what has been pointed out here regarding this reason is its subsistence in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
And a reason that subsists in only a portion of the similar instances is not non-probative;
for being produced immediately after an effort is tied to impermanence, but impermanence is not tied to being produced immediately after an effort.
For the pervasion is "whatever is produced immediately after an effort is impermanent," and not "whatever is impermanent is produced immediately after an effort.
It is not like saying, "where there is effort there is fire," but rather "where there is smoke there is fire."

Thus, the perception of impermanence in sounds such as those produced by trees being felled by the force of the wind, or in lightning and the like—even in the absence of being produced immediately after human effort—does not undermine its status as a logical reason.
Furthermore, the expression "being immediately subsequent to effort" (prayatnānantarīyakatva) denotes this arising from a cause; it does not, however, restrict the cause to effort alone.
In that case, just like the sound of a tree produced by the impact of the wind, there may exist another cause for its production even in the absence of effort.
