And it is not contradictory for sound—whether produced by another cause or like lightning and so forth—to possess impermanence.

But how is it understood that sound is produced as something non-existent by means of effort and so forth, rather than being manifested as something already existent? Because there is no cause for the non-perception of an existent thing. If it is argued that the cause is an obscuration, we say no; since sound is not like water in a well or similar things [which can be obscured], it follows that sound, being non-existent, is simply brought into being by effort and the like.

When the non-existence [of a thing] is established through the non-apprehension of its apprehension, the proof of the opposite of that [non-existence] constitutes the "balancing of non-apprehension" (anupalabdhisama). //5.1.30//

The "balancing by non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhisama*) refutation consists in opposing an argument by means of the presentation of a further non-apprehension. As for what was said—that because an obstruction is not apprehended, and because sound is not perceived prior to its utterance when no obstruction exists, sound must be non-existent and is merely produced through effort—that is incorrect; for there is also a non-apprehension of that very non-apprehension of the obstruction. And from the non-apprehension of that [non-apprehension], there follows existence, because through a double negation, an affirmation is indeed understood. Thus, due to the non-apprehension of the non-apprehension [of the obstruction], the obstruction exists; and due to the non-apprehension of the obstruction, the sound exists. Therefore, the claim that sound is non-existent is untenable.

Furthermore, since an obscuration is perceived, the existence of that obscuration is established; therefore, the non-perception of sound is caused precisely by that [obscuration] and not by its non-existence. Thus, effort and the like are merely the causes of its manifestation.
The answer to this is: because non-apprehension consists in the nature of non-perception, it is not a valid reason. //5.1.31//
The reason stated as "there is no non-perception of obstructions because there is no perception" is not a valid reason.
Why? Because non-perception has the nature of non-perception; the meaning is that its essence consists in the negation of perception.

For the existence and non-existence of entities are established through perception and non-perception: that which is perceived exists, like a rabbit; that which is not perceived does not exist, like a hare's horn.
Furthermore, no obstruction of sound is perceived, such as earth [obstructing] roots or water; because it is not perceived, it is understood that it does not exist.
It is the non-perception that makes [the absence] known, not the non-existence of perception itself; therefore, due to the presence of non-perception, the very existence of an obstruction is absent.
And because of the internal awareness of the existence and non-existence of conceptual cognitions. //5.1.32//
Cognitive constructions (*jñāna-vikalpa*) are the modes of apprehension.
Their existence and non-existence are experienced by every living being.

Thus, everyone experiences the results of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*), such as direct perception, inference, and knowledge based on scripture—as in the thought "I have knowledge"—as well as the results of other cognitions such as memory, doubt, and so forth.
And this non-perception of an obstruction is experienced internally, just like perception itself—as in the thought, "there is no obstruction of the sound, such as earth, roots, water, and so forth.

Thus, just as there is direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) regarding the existence or non-existence of external objects, there is likewise direct perception regarding the existence or non-existence of internal cognition; therefore, the objection—"because the non-perception [of an obstruction] is not perceived, an obstruction must exist for the sound"—is untenable.
Consequently, it is established that the sound is indeed non-existent prior to its utterance.
The "balancing by non-eternality" (anityasama) occurs because, since a property similar to that of the probandum is found [in other things], it would follow that everything is non-eternal. //5.1.33//
The refutation known as "balancing the impermanent" (*anityasama*) is an objection based on the consequence that all things would be impermanent.

If it is argued that because sound shares a similarity with an impermanent object such as a jar, it must therefore be impermanent, then since all things share some kind of similarity with a jar, it would follow that everything is impermanent.

If it is argued that this is merely the fallacy of "balancing the non-distinction" (*aviśeṣasama*), we say no; for in that case, the lack of distinction among all entities is brought about by applying the property of existence (*sattā*) to them all, whereas here, impermanence is established solely on the basis of similarity with a jar.
Furthermore, it has been stated more than once that the diversity of *jāti*s arises from the difference in the modes of their presentation.
To this, the reply is: because [the reason] is unestablished even by virtue of similarity, the negation is unestablished, since it possesses similarity with that which is to be negated. (5.1.34)
For one who commits this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the following is intended: that the establishment of impermanence through its similarity to a jar and so forth [is not proven].

And if the establishment of impermanence through its similarity to a jar and so forth is not proven, then this very sentence of yours which constitutes the negation is also unestablished, because it shares a similarity with the sentence being negated.
For there is indeed a similarity between the sentence of negation and the sentence being negated, namely, the possession of members such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth.

Furthermore, because the property (dharma) asserted as the probandum-probans relationship in the example serves as the logical reason (hetu), and because that [reason] exists in both ways, there is no distinction [between the two cases]. //5.1.35//

For mere similarity (*sādharmya*) alone does not constitute a proof; rather, it is either similarity or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) whose capacity has been ascertained in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*). If such [similarity] exists among all things, let them also be impermanent—what is the objection? If it does not exist, what is this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? For similarity whose capacity is known in the subject of the example does not occur in both ways [universally and non-universally]; it does not touch upon another alternative.

Because the cause is a specific similarity and because that [specificity] is impossible in all cases, not everything is impermanent. Furthermore, whatever solution was stated regarding the objection concerning non-distinct universals (jāti) should also be stated here.
The "balancing of the eternal" (nityasama) occurs because, due to the existence of the non-eternal in the eternal, the eternity [of the non-eternal] is established. //5.1.36//
The "balancing the permanent" (nityasama) refutation consists in establishing the permanence of sound by means of conceptualizing the nature of the probandum-property called impermanence.
For when it is proposed as a thesis that "sound is impermanent," the proponent of the futile rejoinder (*jāti*) conceptualizes: "Is this impermanence of sound permanent or impermanent?
If, first of all, it is impermanent, then it might at some point cease.
Because it does not perish, sound is eternal.

Now, if non-eternality were itself eternal, then, since a property (*dharma*) is eternal and because it is impossible for it to exist without a substratum, its substratum—namely, sound—must also be eternal.
For if sound were non-eternal and perished, where would that property, which has sound as its substratum, abide?
The answer to this is: because the property of impermanence always exists in that which is to be negated, its impermanence is established; therefore, there is no negation [of it]. (5.1.37)
If it is asserted that impermanence exists eternally in the sound that is to be negated, then that sound is effectively said to be impermanent.
Furthermore, since impermanence is established, its negation is not tenable.
To say "the sound has eternal impermanence" and yet attempt to establish its permanence is a great delusion on the part of your venerable self.

Now, as to how a property (*dharma*) could exist without a substratum (*an-adhikaraṇa*), that is explained as follows: "impermanence" (*anityatva*), "cessation" (*nirodha*), "destruction" (*pradhvaṃsa*), and "non-existence" (*abhāva*) are not different in meaning.
However, the expression "non-existence due to impermanence" is merely a matter of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-mātra*).
Furthermore, this impermanence is delimited by the word (*śabdāvacchinna*), but it does not have the word as its substratum (*na śabdādhikaraṇā*).
The absence of a jar cannot have the jar as its locus;
for phenomena (dharmas) that possess the nature of existence (bhāva-svabhāva) are dependent upon a locus, whereas non-existence (abhāva) is not.

Even though it depends on the state of non-existence, it does not depend on its counter-positive (pratiyogin), but rather exists in a different location, such as the ground-portion where the jar is absent.
Furthermore, because of the contradiction between permanence and impermanence, since impermanence exists, sound is not permanent.
The "balancing of the effect" (kāryasama) occurs because the effects of effort are manifold. //5.1.38//
The counter-argument based on the presentation of the diversity of effects produced by effort is the refutation known as *kāryasama*.

When it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort," another person says: "Indeed, two kinds of effects of effort are observed: some thing that was previously non-existent is brought into being by effort, such as a jar and the like;
while some thing that already exists is manifested by effort through the removal of obstructions and so forth, such as water hidden beneath the earth."

Thus, because there is a diversity of effects produced by effort, there arises this doubt: is a non-existent sound brought into being by effort, like a jar; or is it merely manifested while already existing, like water hidden beneath the earth?
Nor is this the fallacy of "balancing the doubt" (*saṃśayasama*), because here the opposition is raised by means of an alternative interpretation of the meaning of the reason (*hetu*).

For in that case, doubt was induced by the presentation of properties of space such as partlessness; here, however, it is by means of an examination of the meaning of the reason—namely, "being produced immediately after effort"—as stated by the proponent of the proof.
And it has already been stated that the diversity of the modes of pointing out [the opponent's flaws] is the cause of the variety of these fallacies (*jāti*).

To this, the following reply is given: [The argument that] effort is not the cause [of sound] because it is a different effect [from other things produced by effort] is untenable, since no reason for its non-perception is established. (NS 5.1.39)
Even though a difference between effort and its effect is perceived, nevertheless, in the case of sound under discussion, effort is not the cause for its manifestation.
Effort does not manifest sound; rather, it brings about the very appearance of what was previously non-existent.
Why? Because no cause for its non-perception is possible.

For in those cases where effort is the cause for manifesting an existing entity, there exists a cause for its non-perception—such as water and the like—namely, an obstruction by clay or similar substances; thus, its manifestation is accomplished by an effort that removes that obstruction. But it has been explained that for sound, no such basis for non-perception, such as an obstruction, is possible.

Therefore, the effort involved in pronunciation and so forth is for the sake of bringing about the acquisition of its own nature (*ātmalābha*) for that which is non-existent, not for the sake of manifesting that which already exists.
Consequently, it is established that sound is impermanent.

Thus, by this path of instruction consisting of the rebuttals to twenty-four types of examples regarding birth, the entire collection of objections raised by others against the proof of the non-eternality of sound has been refuted by the venerable author of the Sūtras, according to the maxim of watering a mango tree and thereby satisfying one's ancestors.

Now, this further point is taught: even when the twenty-four types of futile rejoinders (*jāti*) have been employed by an opponent, the proponent of the original proof (*mūlasādhanavādī*), having first examined the clear characteristics of the inference, should state the reply exactly as it has been taught; he should not, however, engage in a "six-sided debate" (*ṣaṭpakṣī*) through the capricious speech of a futile rejoinder that merely mimics the opponent's application.
For if that debate is undertaken, there is a failure for both the proponent and the respondent alike, because they are speaking of what is non-existent.
To show how the "sixfold cycle" (ṣaṭpakṣī) proceeds, he says: "For the same fault applies to the negation. (5.1.40)

The proponent of the probans for establishment (sthāpanāhetu), being the first party, has employed a probans for establishment as follows: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced immediately after an effort."

Then the proponent of the theory of birth (jātivādī), standing on the second position, states that the reason—"because there is a multiplicity of things produced by effort"—is inconclusive (anaikāntika), since "the state of being immediately following effort exists even in the case of sound that is merely manifested."

Therefore, if now the proponent of the probans residing in the third position, following the aforementioned sequence of the non-perception of an obstruction and pointing out a distinction, removes the inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā), then the discussion concludes at that very point; since there is no room for a fourth or subsequent positions, the "six-winged debate" (ṣaṭpakṣī) does not descend at all.

But if, bypassing that sequence, one who stands in the third position says: "If he points out the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason, then because of that inconclusiveness, it would not be a proof"—well then, is not this very negation of yours also inconclusive, such that it negates one thing and not another? It negates the reason's capacity to prove (*sādhanatva*), but not its own nature.

Precisely for this reason, since the negation is thus inconclusive, it too would not establish only the position of manifestation (*abhivyakti*); for even in the case of the position of production (*utpatti*), the efficacy of effort is established.

And since no specific reason has been stated for either case, when the proponent of the proof has thus asserted the inconclusiveness [of the argument], it becomes the turn of the opponent who offers the refutation; thus, the "six-winged debate" (ṣaṭpakṣī) commences.
For he, standing in the fourth position, says: "In the counter-refutation of a refutation, there is a fault just like the fault in that original refutation. (5.1.41)
A variety of refutations is stated here, but not a contradiction (*vyāghāta*), because there is no connection with the subject at hand.

This fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*) which is alleged even against the refutation is equally applicable to your own proposed refutation of that refutation; for that too, as before, is indeed inconclusive. Therefore, by resorting to the fifth position, the proponent of the original proof (*mūlasādhana*) brings forward the charge of "admission of the opponent's view" (*matānujñā*).
And having accepted that the negation is faulty, to incur an equal fault in the negation of the negation is "admission of the opponent's position" (matānujñā). 5.1.42.

Since you have failed to remove the fault already raised—that the same fault applies even to the refutation—and instead, having accepted that refutation as faulty, you attempt to impose the consequence of an equal fault upon my counter-refutation of that refutation, you fall into the point of defeat known as *matānujñā* (admission of the opponent's position).
For when it is said, "You are a thief," the accused must refute his own theft; he should not, however, accept the other's claim by saying, "You too are a thief."

When the proponent of the fundamental proof (*mūlasādhana*) has thus stated his fifth position, the opponent resorts to the sixth position and speaks again: "If I am to be designated as one who has fallen into the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called 'admission of the opponent's position' (*matānujñā*), which arises from failing to remove the faults of one's own position while attributing faults to the opponent's position, then alas, that very same point of defeat descends upon you as well; for you too have acted in this same way.

For instance, by me, standing in the second position, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) was raised on the grounds that '[the reason] is not unique because it is produced by effort' (*prayatnakāryānekatvāt*)."
"Since the same fault applies even when [the reason] is not extracted [from the opponent's position], you have directed a counter-accusation against me alone.

Having learned this very thing from you, I too, standing in the fourth position, have attributed the fault to you in that same manner; thus, if there is an admission of my own position (*matānujñā*) on my part, it would belong to you first and foremost."

This is what he says: "In the statement of the reason for the application of proof based on the characteristics of one's own position, the fault is equal because of the acceptance of the faults of the opponent's position. (NS 5.1.43)

One's own position (*svapakṣa*) is that stated by the proponent of the fundamental proof: "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort. A refutation (*pratiṣedha*) characterized by that, originating from that, and having that as its object is: "Because there is a multiplicity of effects produced by effort. Proceeding while taking that refutation into account—without having removed or acknowledged it—the conclusion that the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*) applies to the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*) is established by the statement: "The same fault applies even to the refutation."

And since this "indication of the reason" for that [objection] constitutes an inconclusive (anaikāntika) refutation, one thereby accepts the fault of inconclusiveness stated by the opponent; because one fails to extricate oneself from that and instead merely points out a contrary fault against him, there is the equal fault of "admitting the opponent's position" (matānujñā). This is the sixth position.
This is the sixfold set of positions (*ṣaṭpakṣī*). Among them, the first, third, and fifth are the positions of the proponent who asserts the establishment [of the thesis].

The second, fourth, and sixth [arguments] are proponents of negation; and when these are examined as means of proving the thesis (*sādhya*), they do not serve to establish the thesis for either disputant, because they are afflicted by defects such as tautology (*paunaruktya*) and admission of the opponent's position (*matānujñā*).
For indeed, since there is no difference in meaning between the fourth and sixth positions, they entail the fault of redundancy (*punarukta*).
In the fourth position, it is stated that the opponent shares the same fault;
in the sixth as well, it is exactly the same.

In the third and fifth [turns], in the third case, a commonality of fault (*samānadoṣatva*) is admitted indirectly; in the fifth as well, by one who brings forward the "admission of the opponent's position" (*matānujñā*), that very fault is accepted. Furthermore, because the faults stated by the opponent have not been removed in the third and fourth [turns], it is indeed "admission of the opponent's position. Thus, in the six-turn debate (*ṣaṭpakṣī*), there is a lack of proof for both sides.
Therefore, the treatment of faults is most effective only through valid rejoinders, not through invalid ones, because of the consequence of the "six-winged" [fallacy].

If it is asked: "Even when presenting a false rejoinder, does the process not stop at the sixfold set (*ṣaṭpakṣī*)? Why does a hundredfold or thousandfold set not proceed? What is the rule here?"—it is said in reply: The scope for speech ceases at this point alone; therefore, an infinite number of positions (*anantapakṣatā*) is impossible.

For instance, there are simply two parties—the proponent of the prior position and the proponent of the subsequent position—who respectively advance the proof and the refutation; what further deliberation is there on this matter?

In that regard, concerning the proponent of the reason for establishment (*sthāpanāhetuvādin*), while he is still in the process of speaking and beginning his argument with correct logic, the decision as to whether or not he is able to extricate the refutation of his position depends at that very moment upon the presiding judge.

But when the opponent has presented a false rejoinder with his third statement, the proponent of the refutation (dūṣaṇavādī), having found an opportunity, learns from that very instance and, standing at the fourth statement, applies a counter-argument.

Thereupon, the proponent of the original reason (sthāpanāhetuvādī), finding his counter-application fruitless, difficult to answer, resulting in an equal expenditure of effort, and impossible to execute, desists from further exertion; instead, having conceived some novel refutation, he stands at the fifth statement and asserts "concession of the opponent's position" (matānujñā).

Then, seeing that even this [sixth statement] does not transcend the position of the opponent, the proponent of the negation stands upon the sixth statement and applies it to that very side. Since no further refutation is possible when things have proceeded in this manner, and since any attempt at a counter-application would be devoid of substance, it is proper to remain silent; thus, the cessation of speech occurs at that point alone, and there is no occasion for a proliferation of a hundred or a thousand positions. For this reason, the Teacher has demonstrated only the "sixfold cycle" (*ṣaṭpakṣī*).
And he, in order to instruct his pupil, taught him thus: "May you proceed by this path; do not proceed by another.

Therefore, those who know [the truth] should offer a faultless reply even to one who employs fallacious arguments (jāti). One should not, however, engage in a debate consisting of a fabrication of six positions with words that are base and fallacious replies.

If one should speak with impurity in mind, thinking "as was the sacrifice, so too is the offering," then even a pure cause becomes fruitless for him; his splendor withered by the spreading of the six positions and other fallacies, he is unable to produce conviction regarding his own thesis before the judges.
Thus has been clearly explained here the twenty-fourfold nature of the castes, free from confusion with its own proper course;
a man who knows their true essence will not be bewildered in an assembly when refuting those [theories] composed by others or when presenting his own.

Since the "points of defeat" (nigrahasthāna) are enumerated immediately after the "categories" (jāti), he says the following for the purpose of explaining their definitions: "Misapprehension and non-apprehension are points of defeat" (NS 1.2.60).
"Defeat" (nigraha) means loss; its "basis" (sthāna) refers to its support or cause. Furthermore, the causes of defeat are misconception (vipratipatti) and non-apprehension (apratipatti).
Misconception is a distorted, contemptible cognition that functions as a fault-finding.
Non-apprehension (*apratipatti*), however, is the failure to initiate action regarding an object that requires initiation.
The object of initiation consists of refuting [an argument] when it is being established, and rescuing [an argument] when it is being refuted.
The failure to perform either of these two is non-apprehension.
For a proponent is defeated in two ways: by failing to undertake what ought to be done, or by establishing the opposite.

For this very reason, they do not prescribe defeat for the action (*karman*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*), because no fault is committed by those two when they are employed within their own respective domains, as their capacity remains unimpaired.
But the speaker, being negligent—either by employing what should not be employed or failing to employ what should be employed—deserves defeat;
for generally, those who speak what is not true are subject to defeat.

Even a proponent of reality (tattvavādī), when engaged in debate or cavil (vitaṇḍā), may present a correct proof; yet, if he fails to perceive the appropriate method for refuting the fallacious refutations (dūṣaṇābhāsa) put forward by the opponent, he is indeed defeated.
For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "Points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) overwhelm both the proponent of reality and the non-proponent of reality.
The use of the non-compounded form [in the sūtra] is intended to include the various distinct types of points of defeat.
For this very reason, he has stated immediately thereafter: "From the differentiation of those [cases], there arises a multiplicity of *jāti*s and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). (NS 1.2.61)

The word "tat" (that) refers to the counter-objection (*pratyavasthāna*) by means of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), as well as to error (*vipratipatti*) and non-comprehension (*apratipatti*).
"Vikalpa" means manifoldness, which signifies a diversity of modes;
because there are many modes of counter-objection through similarity and dissimilarity, there is a multiplicity of *jāti*s (futile rejoinders).
That has been explained.
Because there are many varieties of misconception and non-comprehension, there are many points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

He demonstrates that by dividing it into twenty-two types: loss of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*), shifting the proposition (*pratijñāntara*), contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*), abandoning the proposition (*pratijñāsannyāsa*), shifting the reason (*hetvantara*), the irrelevant (*arthāntara*), the meaningless (*nirarthaka*), the unintelligible (*avijñātārthaka*), the incoherent (*apārthaka*), the mistimed (*aprāptakāla*), the deficient (*nyūna*), the redundant (*adhika*), the repetitive (*punarukta*), failure to restate (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), lack of understanding (*ajñāna*), lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), evasion (*vikṣepa*), admission of the opponent's position (*matānujñā*), neglecting to censure when one should (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*), censuring when one should not (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), deviating from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*), and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). These are the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). (NS 5.2.1)

In this context, non-reiteration (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), evasion (*vikṣepa*), and overlooking what is worthy of censure (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) are subsumed under non-comprehension (*apratipatti*); the remaining two—repetition (*punarukta*) and redundancy (*adhika*)—are subsumed under misconception (*vipratipatti*). Alternatively, by the use of the non-compound form, it is intended that they are indeed comprised within misconception alone; so why resort to the cumbersome assumption of a non-compound?
For that too is indeed a contemptible practice, namely, the employment of what is redundant or superfluous.
And the enumeration of twenty-two varieties is intended to provide unmixed examples;
for if one considers their internal subdivisions, they are infinite, just like a genus (*jāti*).
Regarding this, Kīrti says: "We do not accept that the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are divided into twenty-two types, and that their specific definitions are now being described word by word.
Why? Because [the two categories] 'stating what is not a member of the proof' (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) and 'failing to point out a fault' (*adoṣodbhāvana*) [already encompass them]."
However, another point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) is not accepted, as it is not logical.

The proponent must state the proof (*sādhana*) in order to establish the thesis (*pakṣa*) he intends to prove; if he should state something that is not a member of the proof, he shall be defeated. Likewise, the opponent (*prativādin*) must also point out a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) regarding the proof stated by the proponent.
If one were to point out what is actually not a fault as being a fault, he would be defeated;
these two alone constitute the points of defeat for the proponent and the opponent.
To effect a defeat otherwise is simply unjust.
In each instance, the irrationality of the thesis and its various subdivisions will be demonstrated.
Furthermore, certain points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) have been specified that consist mostly of the prattle of young students;
to imagine such things in a treatise is the height of instability.

To this it is replied: with the intention of speaking concisely, there are indeed only two points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). For have we not also stated: "Misapprehension (*vipratipatti*) and non-apprehension (*apratipatti*) are the points of defeat"?
And this is a general definition capable of encompassing all its specific varieties, whereas that which was stated by you is not.

For instance, when one of two disputants is defeated due to a lack of ready wit (*uttarāpratibhāna*), it is said that he is either defeated or not defeated; why then is it asked, "Let him go having won at the very root"?
If he is indeed defeated, what has he done wrong? Has he not failed to bring forth a fault [in his opponent]?

If, then, the non-utterance [of a fault] is explained by way of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), it would follow that the utterance of a fallacious refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*) is thereby permitted.

Alternatively, if one first explains the non-utterance of faults and then, by repeating the phrase, describes it through relative negation (*paryudāsa*) as the "utterance of what is not a fault," then, alas, these two would simply be described as "non-comprehension" (*apratipatti*) and "miscomprehension" (*vipratipatti*).
For the non-utterance of faults is non-comprehension, while the utterance of contrary faults is miscomprehension.
In this way, the statement that lacks a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) is also to be analyzed:
if it is the non-statement of a member of the proof by way of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), this is non-comprehension (*apratipatti*);
if it is a statement other than a member of the proof by way of relative negation (*paryudāsa*), this is misconception (*vipratipatti*).

Therefore, having learned precisely that same pair of points of defeat from the venerable Akṣapāda himself through different terminology, this has been composed by him in these two verses; nothing new, even in the slightest degree, has been imagined here.

Furthermore, it should not be described that two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) apply to each of the two [parties] according to a fixed numerical correspondence; rather, whichever point of defeat is applicable for either party should be assigned as the occasion arises.
It has already been stated that the enumeration of twenty-two varieties of points of defeat is mentioned with the intention of providing unmixed examples, and not as a restrictive rule.
Moreover, their mutually distinct definitions are now being taught.
And in that very context, their irrationality or their status as the mere prattle of fools is indeed refuted; so, enough of this excessive digression.

Having thus stated the general definition and the classification, he states the specific definitions: "The admission of a property belonging to the counter-example within one's own example is the abandonment of the thesis. (5.2.2)

When the proponent has stated a proof for the sake of establishing his thesis, and the opponent has raised a refutation therein, if the proponent, while engaged in his third speech, admits a property of the counter-example into his own example, then his thesis is lost; this constitutes the point of defeat known as "loss of the thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*).

For example, when it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a pot," the opponent says, "The universal (sāmānya), though perceptible by the senses, is seen to be eternal; therefore, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika)."
In this regard, the proponent of the proof says: "If the universal (*sāmānya*) is perceptible by the senses and yet eternal, then likewise the jar (*ghaṭa*) must also be eternal.
The error of one who speaks thus is as follows: he thinks that his reason (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it occurs in both the eternal and non-eternal categories;
however, if the jar were eternal, the reason would occur in only one category—the eternal—and thus he would abandon its inconclusiveness.
Thus, for one who speaks in this manner, there is an abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*).
For if the jar were eternal, then by the very force of that example, sound too would have to be eternal.

Regarding this, Kīrti says: "The thesis itself is merely the statement of a non-constituent of the proof; therefore, its utterance ought to be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), not an abandonment of it."

Nor is there even a loss [of position]; for even if he were to accept the property of the counter-example—namely, permanence—with respect to the jar used as the example, would he thereby abandon his thesis that sound is impermanent? Just because of this much, he does not relinquish his proposition.
Furthermore, fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are indeed included within the category of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

Since one is defeated precisely through the employment of a fallacious reason such as the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), it is not by way of "abandoning the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*); therefore, a different scope for the latter must be stated.

To this it is replied: first of all, it has been established in the definition of the members [of a syllogism] that the thesis (*pratijñā*) is not a statement of a non-member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*).
Indeed, the effort of all disputants is directed solely toward the establishment of the thesis;
and since it is impossible to prove it if it is not stated, its statement is not a statement of a non-member of the proof.
Even in worldly legal disputes concerning matters such as the non-payment of debts, they say that the failure of the plaint (*pratijñāhāni*) alone is the primary cause of defeat.
As Nārada says: "The plaint is declared to be the very essence of legal proceedings; upon its failure, the plaintiff loses, while he who upholds it becomes the winner."
By accepting the property of the counter-example within his own example, he indeed abandons his proposition.
For he admits that even a jar possesses permanence, like a universal;

by the force of that example, he wishes to establish permanence in sound as well. Surely, in this case, the very property of permanence belonging to the jar would be established in sound; how then is his proposition of its impermanence not lost?

As for what was said—that the employment of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) alone is the cause of defeat, and not the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*)—this would be so if the proponent, having been countered by the respondent who maintains the second position through the raising of an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), were to desist right there. However, being at the third stage of speech, he utters such a statement with the intention of rescuing that [position], whereby he abandons his thesis.

Therefore, since this defeat is based on the loss of one's own proposition (*pratijñāhāni*)—which arises from the statement that concedes the property of the counter-example out of a desire to avoid the fallacy of deviation—it is proper that his defeat be attributed solely to that, and not to the employment of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). This alone is the primary scope of the loss of one's proposition.
When the meaning of the proposition has been refuted, the indication of another meaning by means of a qualification regarding the property is "shifting the proposition" (pratijñāntara). //5.2.3//

When the opponent has refuted the matter asserted by the proponent, and the proponent then states another property regarding that very same subject (*dharmin*) as a means of proof, this constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "shifting the ground" (*pratijñāntara*).

When it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," the opponent, having raised an objection as before by pointing out a deviation on the basis of universals (*sāmānya*), says: "It is logical that a universal which is perceptible by the senses is eternal;
for that [universal] is all-pervading (*sarvagata*), whereas our view is that sound is not all-pervading."
Thus, one who initially proposes the thesis "sound is impermanent" and then makes another thesis, "sound is non-omnipresent," becomes defeated by means of a change of thesis (*pratijñāntara*).

To this, he says: "This is not the introduction of an irrelevant new proposition, but rather the production of a specific qualification for the purpose of refuting the deviation (vyabhicāra) pointed out by the opponent."
This is what is meant: "Sound is impermanent because, while being non-pervasive, it is perceptible by the senses.
How can this, which is employed for the purpose of establishing the proposition that sound is non-pervasive, be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)?

For when one who has said to a Mīmāṃsaka, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced," is reproached by the opponent on the grounds that "producedness" is unestablished (*asiddha*), and he then strives to establish that producedness—would he be defeated simply because he makes another proposition regarding producedness?

But he who, disregarding his previous proposition, should suddenly begin another, irrelevant proposition, would at that time be nothing but a madman. And it is not appropriate to provide a formal definition in a treatise for the ravings of a madman. Furthermore, since the grounds for defeat are already evident in the statement of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), why should "shifting the proposition" (*pratijñāntara*) be mentioned as a separate point of defeat?

To this it is replied: the established rule is that for the sake of establishing one's proposition (*pratijñā*), one should employ a reason (*hetu*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), but one must not formulate another proposition.
In this case, when the reason adduced by him has been rendered inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by his opponent, he has not adopted a suitable method for its refutation;
rather, he has merely mounted upon another proposition, namely, that [the self] is not omnipresent (*asarvagata*).

Now, it might be argued that this qualification is intended to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) and is not a restatement of the thesis (*pratijñāntara*). This is not so, because it is unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*). A qualification is indeed established;
however, for one who maintains the eternity [of sound], the non-omnipresence of sound is unestablished.

If it is argued that [the subject] is being proved, then this is merely another proposition (*pratijñāntara*), because it differs from the other members such as the reason (*hetu*) and because the definition of a proposition—as the statement of what is to be proved—is applicable here.

For, in order to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), a qualification of the reason must be stated as something already established, but not a qualification of the subject (*dharmin*) which is yet to be proved.

In the case of a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) that is unestablished for one of the two parties, however, providing a justification for it is entirely consistent with the course of the argument; thus, it does not constitute the defeat-ground (nigrahasthāna) known as "shifting the proposition" (pratijñāntara).
Here, however, one is defeated because, while striving to avoid the inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) [of the reason], one falters by failing to see a suitable path.
Furthermore, even for one whose intellect is skilled in the application of reasons, examples, and so forth, such a statement is possible through mere error.
And he does not speak thus merely out of a desire for victory through a mere thesis, but rather because he wishes to avoid fallacious deviation.

Nor is this merely the ravings of a madman, for it is employed with the intention of conforming to the subject at hand. Furthermore, you yourselves have indeed defined in your treatise a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) called "unestablished for both parties" (*ubhayāsiddha*), such as: "Sound is impermanent, because it is visible. This is not the ravings of a madman. Thus, to claim that "that which has been cited as an example is a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*) and is the ravings of a madman" is a novel kind of attachment to one's own view and aversion toward the views of others on the part of this monk!
For who indeed, even a child, would claim that sound possesses visibility?
This designation, however, is certainly possible;

yet, although the qualification of the reason (*hetu*) was already established and ought to have been stated, this person, through delusion, stated instead the qualification of the subject (*dharmin*) and the probandum (*sādhya*), and is therefore defeated.

And it has been stated that he speaks thus while remaining at the third statement; this is another ground for determining his defeat. However, it was already stated in the discussion on the "abandonment of the thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*) that one would incur defeat precisely upon the employment of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) at the conclusion of the second statement itself.
Contradiction between the proposition and the reason is "contradiction of the proposition" (pratijñāvirodha). //5.2.4//

Where a proposition (*pratijñā*) is contradicted by a reason (*hetu*), or a reason is contradicted by a proposition, that constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodha*). For example: the proposition is "substance is distinct from its qualities," and the reason is "because no object other than color and the rest is perceived. This is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason: if substance is distinct from its qualities, then it is not the case that no object other than color and the rest is perceived.
Now, if there is no perception of an entity distinct from color and the other [sensory qualities], then substance is not separate from its qualities.
Furthermore, it is a contradiction to claim that substance is distinct from its qualities while simultaneously asserting that nothing distinct from color and the rest is perceived.
To this, it is said: this cannot be an example of a contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), because the reason is impossible [in this case].
For only a possible reason can either contradict the proposition or be contradicted by it.

In this case, however, there is simply no non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility; for it is impossible for an entity distinct from color and so forth to be fit for perception as a separate thing.
Furthermore, even if such a reason were possible regarding this subject, it would not escape two classes of faults: either being contradictory (*viruddha*) or being unestablished (*asiddha*).
For one who maintains that substance is distinct from its qualities, the reason—“because it is not apprehended separately”—is unestablished.
Or, if it were established, it would be a "contradictory" (viruddha) reason because it proves the opposite of what is to be proven;
therefore, since its meaning is already covered by the inclusion of "fallacious reasons" (hetvābhāsa), this point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) need not be stated separately.

As for that other example cited by others—“Sound is eternal because everything is impermanent”—that too is incorrect, because it is stated in this manner by those poorly trained in the method of the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
[They state: “Sound is eternal because it is partless.

In that regard, one who demonstrates the absence of the reason in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāve hetor abhāva*) must state: “Sound is eternal because it is not-all-impermanent, because it possesses parts.”

Thus, by means of this method of demonstrating an unlearned dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) through inversion, it is actually a dissimilar example itself that has been stated [in the form] "because everything is impermanent.

As it has been said: "For that is indeed stated as an example by those well-trained in terms of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Therefore, even this is not an illustration of a contradiction between the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*).

To this it is replied: as for the claim that this is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because of the impossibility of a reason (*hetu*), that is not tenable, since a reason expressed in the ablative case has indeed been demonstrated.

However, if its impossibility is asserted due to the absence of a faultless reason, then the classification of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) would likewise have to be abandoned. Nevertheless, the employment of a reason based on the error of human intellect can certainly result in such a statement.

Furthermore, regarding what was further asserted—that even if this reason (*hetu*) were possible, it would be either unestablished (*asiddha*) or contradictory (*viruddha*), and not a separate fallacy—we reply: This is true; however, at the time of examining the essential nature of the reason, if its contradictoriness is stated because one perceives no fault in that [reason] despite the presence of a fault within it—just as when you describe a contradictory reason such as "Sound is eternal, because it is produced," and although other faults such as proving what is already established (*siddhasādhya*) or the loss of the example (*dṛṣṭāntahāni*) might be possible, they are disregarded and only its contradictoriness is demonstrated.

Or, as we have stated in the definition of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): although the argument "sound is impermanent because it is visible" possesses the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the fact that it is unestablished (*asiddha*) first enters the path of the mind; therefore, it is called "unestablished" and not "inconclusive.

Likewise here, when an investigation is conducted into the merits and defects of the reason, its status as a fallacious reason—such as being contradictory (*viruddha*) and so forth—is what is described.

However, when the meaning of the sentence—the meaning of the five-membered or, according to the opinion of others, the three-membered inference for others (*parārthānumāna*)—is considered as a collection of word-meanings mutually connected, then because there is no syntactic connection (*asaṃsarga*) between the words of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), which express mutually contradictory meanings, that very contradiction immediately revolves in the mind; thus, that alone ought to be the cause of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). For even in a sentence, if one expresses a meaning that is mutually contradictory, there occurs either a misconception (*vipratipatti*) or a lack of comprehension (*apratipatti*); this alone is the ground for defeat.
Furthermore, a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) is said to be that which proves the opposite of what is to be proven (*sādhya-viparyaya*) and thereby subverts the very thesis (*pratijñā*).
In this case, however, it must be considered whether the reason is subverted by the thesis or the thesis by the reason;
therefore, this is indeed a separate point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Since this very example is thus established, the investigation of another example is merely a fruitless wandering.

The Bhāṭṭas, however, have described your proof for the lack of an objective basis (*nirālambana*) as an example of a contradiction with one's own thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*), namely: "All cognitions are without an objective basis, because they are cognitions. For if the cognition grasping the reason (*hetu*)—namely, "being a cognition"—possesses an objective basis, then by that very fact the thesis is contradicted.
On the other hand, if that [grasping cognition] were itself without an objective basis, there would be a total absence of the reason.
Thus it has been said: "The contradiction between the reason and the probandum stated by Akṣapāda is quite clear; failing to see this, others have claimed that this is indeed not a valid refutation."
Therefore, it is established that this point of defeat, known as the contradiction between the proposition and the reason, is in every respect an easily understood example.
Withdrawal of the proposition (pratijñāsannyāsa) is the abandonment of the matter proposed when one's own position has been refuted. //5.2.5//

When the opponent has refuted the proof of the thesis, the proponent's failure to rescue it and instead withdrawing the very thesis constitutes the point of defeat known as "renunciation of the thesis" (pratijñā-saṃnyāsa).

When it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and the inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) regarding the universal (sāmānya) has been exposed in that very same manner, if he replies, "Who says that sound is impermanent?", he, speaking thus, is defeated due to the abandonment of his proposition (pratijñāsannyāsa).
To this he replies: "This is indeed a gross negligence!

For what opponent, having made a proposition in the presence of judges, would—while his mind is unafflicted by epilepsy or similar disorders—right then and there, in front of those very same persons whose mental impressions remain intact, deny that very proposition?"

Moreover, like a deceitful gambler who remains indifferent after having lost his stake in a game of dice, why is this person not defeated even though he does not abandon his thesis, given that his reason is inconclusive?
For the abandonment or non-abandonment of a thesis is not the cause of one's defeat or non-defeat; rather, it is solely the merits or defects of the reason.
Since this proponent is already defeated because his proof is erratic regarding the impermanent position, enough with this [pretext of] renouncing the debate.

To this it is replied: For one whose mind is agitated by the anxiety of removing the refutation of the "inconclusiveness" (anaikāntikatva) of the reason advanced by the opponent, it might indeed be so; for one who says, "Since I have made 'not being manifested by conjunction and disjunction' the subject of my proposition, there will be no deviation (vyabhicāra) on account of generality (sāmānya)," even that is exactly like that. For [generality] is likewise [unmanifested], because it is manifested by its own substratum. Thus, for one who is deluded and has fallen into such a gross error, there is certainly a ground for defeat (nigrahasthāna). But for one who is not negligent, there is truly no such thing as defeat either in this world or in the next.

As for the claim that he is defeated solely because of the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of his [opponent's] abandonment or non-abandonment of the proposition—this might be so if, immediately after the pointing out of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*), he were to remain silent. However, by speaking in such a manner, he is defeated by that very reason for defeat which is now proximate, and not by the employment of the inconclusive reason itself.
When a reason has been stated without qualification and that reason has been refuted, the proponent’s desire for a qualification constitutes "shifting the reason" (hetvantara). //5.2.6//
When a reason has been stated without qualification and is then refuted, stating a specific qualification for it constitutes the point of defeat called "another reason" (*hetvantara*).
For example, when a Sāṃkhya speaks thus: "This manifest world has a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*), because it possesses finite magnitude (*parimāṇa*), like a jar and so forth.

[The opponent objects: "A characteristic of finite magnitude is observed in two ways among transformations: first, in things such as sprouts up to fruits; and second, in things such as jars preceded by clay, which possess a square shape and so on."
Since this limited collection of effects is observed to have a single nature, therefore all of this must necessarily have a single nature;
and that which is this single nature is the Pradhāna.

The reason for this [proposition] is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because transformation is observed even among things of diverse natures; wishing to avoid this [objection], he states the qualification "because of homogeneity" (*samanvayāt*).
For it is observed that everything manifest and finite is permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Because that [proposition] lacks the connection with the nature of another primordial substance, it follows that there is only a single primordial substance.

This is a "different reason" (*hetvantara*), which is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), because the proponent himself does not accept the status of being a valid reason for the previously stated unqualified reason.
To this it is said: "Is this one being burned who has already been burned, or is this one being killed who is already dead?

By the very presentation of an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*), this poor fellow is indeed defeated for stating what is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga-vacana*); therefore, enough with invoking another point of defeat called 'shifting the reason' (*hetvantara*). To this we reply: That which was stated applies to the second statement when the debate is concluded, just as you yourself have said.

However, when one proceeds to state another additional qualification now in order to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*), one is defeated by that very act of adopting it; this is currently regarded as "grinding what is already ground" (*piṣṭapeṣaṇa*). And in *jalpa*, which consists in testing the capacity of the person, this is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

But in *vāda*, where the reality is being examined with a pure intention, even if another qualification is adopted, the investigation of that [qualification] should be undertaken, and a defeat should not be declared—so say the learned.
An irrelevant digression (arthāntara) is a different matter that is not connected to the subject at hand. //5.2.7//
When one states something irrelevant—that is, a different matter than the subject under discussion—it constitutes the point of defeat known as "irrelevance" (*arthāntara*).

For example, suppose a certain rogue grammarian, having fixed in his mind the word as being of the nature of *sphoṭa*, intends to assert its eternity by stating, "Sound is eternal because it is partless," yet, fearing that this reason might be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the existence of past actions (*durita-karma*) and so forth, and wishing to fall into the point of defeat called "shifting the subject" (*arthāntara*), he rises up at that very moment under the guise of a supplementary statement: "We, the followers of Pāṇini, maintain that sound is eternal because it is partless—namely, those who are the disciples of the venerable Pāṇini."
Who indeed was the Blessed Pāṇini? He is that teacher Pāṇini by whom, having received the traditional enumeration of phonemes from Maheśvara, the entire science of grammar was proclaimed to us.

Who, indeed, is Maheśvara, from whom Pāṇini learned the traditional collection of phonemes? Maheśvara is the one who has the moon knotted within the tip of his most formidable mass of matted hair; he is the sole cause of the maintenance and destruction of the universe.

Moreover, Indra, with palms joined in reverence, bears upon his head the dust from the feet of Him whose dress and ornaments are inconceivable in reality, and who performs the wild dance (tāṇḍava) at will during the nights.
Furthermore, in what manner does the wielder of the axe (Śiva) perform his *tāṇḍava*? It is such that in it there is this sequence of *cārīs*, and such movements of the hands;
wherein there are such cuts of the hips (*kaṭiccheda*) and likewise such staff-like foot-strikes (*daṇḍapāda*).
Thus, teaching each [point] one by one, he rises and dances;
this is the "irrelevant digression" (arthāntara) point of defeat, as it is not a constituent part of a proof.
This is also approved by Kīrti as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for both the proponent and the opponent when they state something irrelevant to the subject at hand;
specifically, for one who does not perceive a faultless proof and for the second who offers a refutation [of that which is not a proof], respectively.
It is "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*), like the mere recitation of a sequence of phonemes. (5.2.8)

A mere employment of the sequence of phonemes devoid of a subject matter (*abhidheya*) constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as the "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*). For example: "Sound is impermanent because *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa* are *ga-ja-ḍa-da-ba*s, just like *gha-jha-ḍha-dha-bha-v*. Such is a point of defeat.

Furthermore, when both parties do not know how to state the proof (*sādhana*) and the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) in their proper order as is appropriate, there is a point of defeat for both, as previously described.
To this he replies: "This person has begun to characterize the treatise as nothing but the ravings of a madman;
for such syllables do not issue from the mouths of those who are not mad.
And if such things were to be taught in a treatise, then by all means let cheek-beating, slapping the cheeks, and striking the flanks also be taught therein."

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "like the instruction on the sequence of phonemes" (*varṇakramanirdeśavad*), if it is taken as a possessive compound (*matup*)—that is, *varṇakramanirdeśavat*—then every point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) associated with the instruction on the sequence of phonemes would become a point of defeat; consequently, even hand gestures and the like would now be introduced as formal debates (*udgrāhiṇikā*). Alternatively, if the suffix *-vat* is used, it means "just as in the case of the instruction on the sequence of phonemes. In the case of the possessive suffix (*matup*), everything connected to the instruction on the sequence of phonemes would constitute a point of defeat, whereby even hand signals and so forth would now be presented as formal debates.
Even if it is explained that [the statement] is joined with a description of a sequence devoid of meaning, even so, the restriction remains untenable;
for the mere utterance of phonemes lacking meaning is not itself meaningless, as it is not useless in the present context.
Furthermore, the description of the sequence of phonemes is indeed seen to be purposeful in certain treatises, just like the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated notation).
In the view of the opponent, however, this is indeed a demonstration of the day; nevertheless, because its meaning is already understood through another sense, it need not be stated separately.
To this it is replied: by means of either the suffix *matup* or the suffix *vati*, what is intended here is merely the state of being devoid of a denotable object (*abhidheyaśūnyatva*).
Thus it is said that "speech devoid of a denotable object is meaningless" (*nirarthaka*);
and this alone is its distinction from [the category of] "another meaning" (*arthāntara*).
In that case, even though there is a referent, it is irrelevant to the subject at hand;

however, here there is no referent at all. Therefore, instances where even the specification of a sequence of letters serves a purpose due to the context of a particular treatise do not constitute examples here.
If you ask for a clear example and do not grow angry, then every word of yours here is itself an example;
for in the Buddhist system, words do not touch upon actual objects, as they do not apply to the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*),
and since even "exclusion" (*apoha*) is utterly insignificant, all that naming is devoid of meaning.

For this very reason, even the Śākya monks—who speak like those demented, yet whose conduct is entirely pure, who perceive the reality of the next world, and who are not outsiders in matters of cleanliness, ritual practice, and social intercourse, being great and learned men—do not deserve to be considered insane, even though they may speak that which is devoid of [external] objects.
Likewise, another person who utters sounds such as *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa* due to a lapse of wisdom does not become insane.

As for what was said—that there is no final limit to the enumeration of such [types]—that has been refuted more than once; it is simply that the state of having twenty-two varieties was adopted with the intention of providing unmixed examples.
Furthermore, things such as cheek-music (kapolavādana) are truly inconceivable because they do not possess the nature of discourse.

If, in the course of this discussion on discourse, something like cheek-instruments were to flash across one's mind, even something else that is extremely base would enter one's heart; therefore, enough with such depraved conversation!
That which is not understood even after being stated three times by both the assembly and the opponent is the "unintelligible" (avijñātārtha). //5.2.9//

When a statement of proof or a statement of refutation has been stated three times and is not understood by the assembly or the opponent—due to the use of obscure words, the use of unfamiliar terminology, or being uttered too rapidly—this constitutes the point of defeat known as "the unintelligible" (*avijñātārtha*).
Furthermore, this is resorted to by the crafty in order to conceal their own lack of competence.
Here it is asked: since the lack of comprehension of the meaning is the same, what is the difference between this [nirarthaka] and the "meaningless" (nirarthaka)?

If he speaks a meaning that is suitable for application to the subject at hand, then while the dullness of the assembly and the opponent may indeed be great, defeat cannot rightly belong to the learned speaker who is debating.
And we do not know by what this rule of triple recitation was established—whether by royal decree or by its own inherent authority.

To this it is replied: In the case of the meaningless, there is a total absence of meaning in every respect; however, here, even though a meaning exists, it is not apprehended due to factors such as excessively rapid pronunciation. Thus, how can there be no distinction? Furthermore, one must surely assume that [the opponent], wishing to conceal his own incapacity, speaks in this manner, for a learned person who is capable does not fail to speak clearly.
Even the rule regarding the number three is not based on Vedic injunctions or the commands of a sovereign; rather, it arises simply from the nature of things.
For it is possible that what was stated once or even twice might not be grasped due to inattention or other causes;
however, if what has been spoken three times is not understood, that is solely the dullness of the speaker himself.
When something is stated in an assembly of many judges and others, it is necessarily understood by someone;
however, if it is not understood by anyone at all, the speaker alone is defeated.

If one were to desire that the statement be made four or five times, it would result in the consequence of there being no limit to the speaking. Therefore, the rule of stating [the proposition] three times is logical.
That which lacks a connected meaning due to the inversion of the prior and subsequent [parts] and so forth is "meaningless" (apārthaka). //5.2.10//

The point of defeat known as "the meaningless" (apārthaka) occurs when a collection of words is uttered that lacks logical connection between what precedes and what follows, such that the meaning of the sentence remains unestablished.
For example: "Ten pomegranates, six cakes, a bowl, a goat-skin, a lump of meat, and Caitra’s father has died of a chill."

Here it is asked: Why are "incoherent speech" (*asaṃbaddhavākya*) and "incoherent context" (*asaṃbaddhaprakaraṇa*), which are like disconnected [speech], not stated as separate points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? If it is argued that they are already included by this [present category] alone, then for the same reason—namely, that their meaning is already covered—one should not mention "the meaningless" (*anarthaka*) separately from "the irrelevant" (*apārthaka*). To this it is replied: In the case of the meaningless, there is neither the meaning of a word nor the meaning of a sentence; only dry phonemes are uttered.
In the case of the irrelevant, although the meanings of the words are connected, something is stated that does not assist in establishing the intended meaning of the sentence.
But here, even when the individual word-meanings are understood, the meaning of the sentence cannot be determined because their mutual connection is impossible; thus, the distinction is clear.

If it is asked, "What is the distinction regarding the subject matter that constitutes the current dispute? it has been stated here that when one intends to speak in brief, there are only two points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). However, when one intends to provide unmixed examples, there are twenty-two varieties.
Yet, the establishment of the subject matter under discussion remains exactly the same even in the case of these twenty-two.

As for the claim that "incoherent sentences" (*asaṃbaddhavākya*) and "incoherent contexts" (*asaṃbaddhaprakaraṇa*) must be enumerated separately, that is not so; for they are already included by the very term "incoherent word-meaning" (*apratisaṃbaddhapadārtha*). However, if it is necessary to mention incoherent sentences and incoherent contexts separately, then your own treatise is indeed consistent with that. For instance, according to the Vaibhāṣikas, there exists an external object, and that is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).

For the Sautrāntikas, although this [external object] exists, it is merely inferable; for the Yogācāras, it is only cognition with its own mental aspect (*sākāra-jñāna*) and not an external object, and that [cognition] is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*);

for the Mādhyamikas, it is only pure consciousness devoid of mental aspects (*ākāraśūnya-svaccha-jñānamātra*). Thus, this entire Śākya scripture consists of a series of statements that are mutually inconsistent.
And it is said: "Who could find authority for such a statement as 'Ten Pomegranates,' for a Buddhist scripture, or for any other incoherent work?"
A statement in which the members [of the syllogism] are inverted is "untimely" (aprāptakāla). //5.2.11//

An inferential statement that is employed by transposing its members, thereby overstepping the proper sequence of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*), constitutes the point of defeat known as "untimeliness" (*aprāptakāla*).
To this, he says: Indeed, there is no fixed order for words within sentences.
For it is logical that phonemes attain the status of words only when they possess a fixed order, because without that [order], their meaning cannot be understood.
For instance, if one says "ṭagha," the understanding of "ghaṭa" (pot) does not occur.

In sentences such as "Devadatta, drive the white cow with a stick" (*devadatta gām śuklām ābhyāja daṇḍena*) and "With a stick, drive the white cow for Devadatta" (*daṇḍena śuklāṃ gām abhyāja devadattena*), since the meaning is understood in exactly the same way despite a different order, what is the use of sequence?

However, regarding an inferential statement, the claim that "it consists of five members" is first of all improper, because the members beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*) are not statements of the means of proof (*sādhana*).

Furthermore, the employment of those five members, the intended order in their employment, and the violation of that order constitute points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); thus, this is a great feat of folly.
To this it is replied: In other sentences, let there be an intention regarding sequence or let there not; we have no need for that here.

However, in an inferential statement, the sequence arises by force of the facts (*ārtha*), because the production of another's understanding follows one's own understanding. And since in one's own understanding, the perception of the locus (*dharmin*), the ascertainment of the property of the reason (*hetudharma*) residing therein, the recollection of the connection (*pratibandha*), the reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*), and the certainty of the probandum (*sādhyaniścaya*) are observed to occur in sequence, it must be stated to another in exactly that same way. This has been determined in detail in the definition of the members of the syllogism (*avayava*).

The claim that the statement of the members [of a syllogism], such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, lacks the character of being a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacanatva*), has already been refuted in that very same context.
Therefore, since the sequence [of these members] is here logically justified, its transgression indeed constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
That which is deficient by even a single member [of the syllogism] is "deficient" (hīna). //5.2.12//

When it is established that a statement consisting of five members must be employed, for one who employs it lacking even one of those members, there occurs the point of defeat called "deficiency" (nyūna).

Here it is argued: "Since the collection of members beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the statement of non-essential parts of the proof, there is no defeat for one who does not state them; on the contrary, defeat is logically appropriate for one who does state them. To this it is replied: This has already been refuted immediately above, and in detail within the definition of the members (*avayava*). For an inference-statement is employed to satisfy the expectation of the listener; thus, first, the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), which is the object of that expectation, is presented. Then, when there is an expectation for the cause, the statement of the reason (*hetu*) is uttered.

When there is a desire to know where its invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) has been observed, the example (*udāharaṇa*) is established. When there is a doubt as to whether this reason, whose concomitance is thus established, exists in the subject (*dharmī*), the statement of application (*upanaya*) is uttered.

Immediately thereafter, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is employed for the purpose of synthesizing all the constituent parts into one; since the non-employment of any one of these [five members] constitutes a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), there is no point in initiating a dispute at every single step regarding this very matter.
That which has an excess of reasons and examples is "excessive" (adhika). //5.2.13//

When an object has already been established by means of a single reason or example, for one who employs an additional reason or another example, there occurs the point of defeat known as "redundancy" (*adhika*).
This is certainly not accepted in the case of *vāda*, which consists of dispassionate discourse and results in the determination of the true state of things;
however, even in *jalpa*, this constitutes a point of defeat for a proponent who speaks while having previously accepted a specific rule.
For indeed, only he who, having been restricted by the rule that "neither I nor we two shall state an additional proof or example," yet proceeds to state one, is thus defeated, and no other.
And this was stated in exactly the same way by Kīrti as well: "But there is no fault in discursive talk."

Another says: "Even if a restriction (*niyama*) is accepted, this fault does not arise, because that [second reason] is stated for the sake of strengthening the understanding. This is incorrect; by abandoning the restriction he had accepted, he would be subject to defeat (*nigraha*). Furthermore, what is this "strengthening of understanding"? For a reason (*hetu*) employed for the first time that produces only a weak understanding would not even qualify as a valid reason. It is logical to produce again a cognition (*pratyaya*) that has already arisen.
In that case, the former reason does not lead to firmness, nor does the latter lead to firmness;
therefore, when a restriction is accepted, stating anything further is indeed a fault.
Another opinion holds that it is indeed a fault even for one who has not made a formal restriction;
for even in a discussion of elaboration (*prapañca*), once a conclusion has been reached by means of a single reason or example, a second reason is unfit for application.
The repetition of both word and meaning is called "redundant statement" (*punarvacana*), except in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*). (5.2.14)

The restatement of what has already been established by implication, or the repeated utterance of a word or a meaning that has already been expressed—excluding mere repetition for the sake of recitation—is the point of defeat known as *punarukta* (repetition).
First, verbal tautology (*śabdapunarukta*) occurs where the very same word that was previously uttered is uttered again, as in: "Sound is eternal; sound is eternal."

Redundancy of meaning (*arthapunarukta*), however, occurs where that same meaning which was previously stated by one word is stated again by another synonym; for example: "Sound is impermanent; sound has the nature of cessation."

And although there is indeed a repetition of meaning even when there is a repetition of words, nevertheless, because the recognition of meaning is preceded by the word, it is the repetition of the word itself that is designated as such due to its being recognized first.

Furthermore, the conventional usage of "repetition of words" depends upon the genus (*jāti*) and not upon the individual instance (*vyakti*), because phonemes (*varṇa*) are momentary and thus cannot be employed again.
However, repetition in the case of restatement (*anuvāda*) is not a fault;
for example: "The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the statement of the reason (*hetvapadeśāt*)."
Even that which is already established by implication is indeed a tautology if it is stated again using its own words.
For example, when it is said, "When clouds are absent, there is no rain," it follows by implication that "when they are present, there is rain.
Why, then, is this stated again explicitly?
For the employment of words is for the purpose of conveying meaning;
once the meaning is understood, what is the use of them?
And this should be understood as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) when one has undertaken a formal restriction;
however, for one who has not made such a restriction, this is not a very serious fault.

To this, it is said: repetition does not apply to the meaning; rather, repetition applies to the word, because even when there is identity of sound, a difference in meaning is observed—as in the verse:
"Remember Giriśa! Who, like Giriśa, would not remember with great joy that city which belongs to him who hates unequal enemies, he whose arrows are not uneven?
Therefore, repetition occurs only through the meaning, not through the word.

Moreover, in extensive discourses, if there is a doubt that something was not properly heard, how much negligence would it be to state it again? And if the restatement, by its own words, of what has already been established through the force of the meaning is called a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), then the initial statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) itself would be the first point of defeat.
It must be stated what the distinction between "redundancy" (*adhika*) and "repetition" (*punarukta*) is;
for if they were designated as separate based on some such slight difference, it would be impossible to enumerate the distinct points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

If it is said that the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) because of the indication of the reason (*hetvapadeśāt*), then first of all the proposition itself is not valid;
how can there be any talk of its restatement being valid?
To this it is replied: as for what was stated—that there is no such thing as verbal repetition distinct from the repetition of meaning—that is indeed so.

However, the separate mention of it is intended to show that one who, desiring to demonstrate an excellence of skill, initiates a debate after making the vow, "A word used once by me must not be used again," is defeated by verbal repetition; for defeat occurs only for the proponent who is bound by that rule.
Consequently, for another person who speaks again out of a suspicion that the opponent has not heard correctly, there is no fault.
Even the statement of what is implied by the sense is a fault only for one who has made a formal restriction, not for anyone else.

For this very reason, this is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in formal debate (*vāda*), but rather only in the two types of discourse—disputation (*jalpa*) and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*)—which are intended for those seeking victory.
And that these two possess a specific purpose and constitute distinct forms of discourse has already been established previously.

As for the claim that the statement of the proposition and its restatement [in the conclusion] are fruitless because they are already implied by the meaning, this has been thoroughly settled in detail within the definition of the members of the syllogism.
However, this distinction between the "superfluous" (adhika) and the "redundant" (punarukta) is indeed quite clear:

one who states another reason or another example for that very same probandum becomes a speaker of the superfluous; whereas one who states that same reason or example again becomes a speaker of the redundant.
