As for the objection that an enumeration is untenable when such specific distinctions are adopted, that is indeed so when one intends to express intermediate distinctions;
however, it was stated that there is a mention of twenty-two varieties in order to demonstrate unmixed examples.
Non-reproduction (ananubhāṣaṇa) is the failure to repeat what has been understood by the assembly, even after it has been stated three times. //5.2.17//

When a proponent has been understood by the assembly and has stated his argument three times, the failure to repeat it constitutes the point of defeat called "non-reproduction" (*ananubhāṣaṇa*). Without repeating it, on what basis could one state a refutation?
Now, one might object: if someone were to offer a reply even without restating the opponent's argument, why should he be defeated?

Furthermore, it is not the case that whoever is incapable of restating the argument is necessarily incapable of providing a reply, because human capacities vary so widely. To this we say: this is not so; for if one does not restate the argument, one lacks knowledge of the subject matter of the reply, so where could the reply be applied?
Or, even if it were applied, how could it be recognized as such?
Nor do we say that whatever is stated by the proponent at length, all of that—without omission, without addition, and without losing the sequence—the opponent must repeat in that very same way.
Even if one were to perform such a complete repetition, it would merely demonstrate one's own skill or intelligence;
however, one does not incur a fault simply by not doing so.
By repeating [the opponent's argument] little by little and likewise refuting it step by step, one would not incur defeat.
Here it is asked: if the proponent should introduce a great deal of irrelevant and unproduced matter by way of explaining the proof of his own position, must all of that be repeated by the opponent?
It is not right to declare a defeat for one who, having restated merely the reason (*hetu*), brings forward a refutation.

However, he who is unskilled even in restating the mere reason—which is the very object of the refutation—is indeed incapable of formulating a rejoinder because he does not understand the subject matter of the reply; thus, let him be defeated on account of "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*).
What is the use of failing to repeat [the opponent's statement]?

Furthermore, what is this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "it must be stated three times"? Thus, a proponent might employ a statement either for the sake of making another understand or for the sake of harassing another. In a statement intended for making another understand, the very act of making them understand is the rule for the expression; there is no restriction of twice or thrice.
As many times as it takes for understanding to arise in the other when the statement is employed, that many times should it be employed.

However, the utterance of speech for the sake of harming another is certainly not dharma; for even by communicating with the judges through some such convention, or by creating a display consisting of the use of ill-fitting and difficult words, one might cause blindness and obstruct others—this is a great moral corruption.
Nor is this worthy of being taught in the treatise.
Therefore, the opponent must be made to understand even after being addressed many times.
But one who has spoken twice should not be defeated if he does not repeat it.
To this it is replied: Indeed, we have not instructed that one must repeat the entire composition of the words written by others at once, without any delay;
rather, one need only repeat those portions which are the proper objects of refutation.

As for the claim that one who is not bold enough to repeat even a small portion [of the opponent's argument] lacks the capacity for a rejoinder (*uttara-pratibhāna*), that is incorrect; for non-repetition (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) is one thing, and lack of capacity for a rejoinder is another. This is because we observe that someone, even after having repeated [the argument] in its entirety, may still fail to produce a rejoinder. Therefore, this failure to articulate a response regarding a subject where no rejoinder exists is called a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), but it is not "lack of capacity for a rejoinder."
The lack of a rejoinder will be explained immediately hereafter.

As for the objection raised regarding the source of the rule concerning the threefold utterance (*trir uccāraṇa*), that has been answered under the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "the naming of something whose meaning is not understood.

While in a formal debate (*vāda*) consisting of a discussion between those free from passion, conducted with learned persons and others, it may well be that the utterance of sentences extends until the opponent's understanding is achieved;

however, in the case of a disputation (*jalpa*), which is a debate between those seeking victory, a restriction on utterance must necessarily be adopted because of the examination of a person's skill.
In that regard, the failure to grasp what has been stated once or twice—even if it occurs due to lack of attention or similar causes—does not constitute a point of defeat (*nigraha*).
However, if there is a failure to grasp what has been stated three times by everyone, the fault lies solely with the speaker.
But if others have grasped it while the opponent (*prativādin*) has not, then the opponent is defeated.
If, however, one were to continue speaking even beyond three turns, there would be no conclusion to the debate at all;
for it would become a mere schoolroom for students rather than a ground for formal dialectical inquiry (*udgrāhaṇikā*).
Or, non-consciousness is ignorance. //5.2.18//
Even when the statement of the proponent has been understood by the assembly, the opponent's failure to understand it constitutes the point of defeat called "non-understanding" (*avijñāna*).
For how could one who does not know the subject matter of the reply provide a reply?
"We do not perceive any distinction between these two: 'ignorance' (*ajñāna*) and 'lack of ingenuity' (*apratibhā*). To this it is replied: "There is no fault, because their objects are different.
Ignorance is the non-comprehension of the subject matter of the response; lack of ingenuity, however, is the failure to produce a response."

[Objection: "Surely, he who does not know the subject matter of the reply does not know the reply itself either. [Response: Not so; it is observed in the world that even one who knows the subject matter of the reply may not know some particular reply. If that is the case, then "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is already covered by "non-reproduction" (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), for when the meaning of another's statement is unknown, one is seen to lack the capacity to reproduce it. Indeed, there are some who, being unable to reproduce it orally, report it by means of writing on a leaf or similar materials. Thus, the failure to restate any of these three [points] constitutes non-reproduction.
Inability to provide an answer even when a statement has been repeated is *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity).

Now, if it is argued that even when ignorance (*ajñāna*) is equal, a plurality of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is thus stated by relying on the difference of objects, then other distinctions must also be mentioned due to the variety of modes of ignorance. To this it is replied: with the intention of summarizing the essence, only two points of defeat have been stated—namely, misconception (*vipratipatti*) and non-apprehension (*apratipatti*). However, the state of having twenty-two divisions is mentioned in order to indicate the direction of mutually dissimilar examples; as for their internal subdivisions, their infinity is indeed admitted.
And likewise, it is recited in the *Dvāviṃśatiprakaraṇa* [as "and the fallacious reasons"]:

"The fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are, by their very nature, fivefold—namely, the inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the equal to the point at issue (*prakaraṇasama*), the unproven (*sādhyasama*), and the mistimed (*atītakāla*).
And indeed, their internal subdivisions are exceedingly numerous."
In this context, however, only one point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) has been specified, namely: "and the fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) as previously described.
Therefore, since the description has been given both in brief and in detail, enough with questioning at every single step.
Non-reproduction of the opponent's argument is *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity). //5.2.19//
Even when the opponent's position has been grasped, the failure to produce a reply constitutes the defeat condition (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*) for the respondent.
Its distinction from ignorance and other such factors has already been demonstrated.
Kīrti also indeed accepts this as a defeat condition.
Surely, how could an opponent remain in the assembly without offering a reply, merely boasting at random?
For instance: "Where is a person such as myself, whose face is brightened by all the stainless sciences blooming within the lotus of his heart;
and where is this mere boy, whose tongue is smeared with only a few fragments of syllables? How can we debate with him?"
Where is the lion, whose terrifying tips of claws flash as he splits the broad temples of scent-elephants moistened by rut?
Where are these deer, their eyes darting with fear at the falling of old leaves stirred up by the wind?
Thus he remains, prattling on about this or that.
Distraction (*vikṣepa*) is the interruption of the discussion due to preoccupation with other business. //5.2.20//

Having initiated a formal debate, or having promised, "I shall grasp that [point]," when the opponent is face-to-face and the audience is present, he excuses himself from his duty by saying, "This task of mine is being neglected; I must go," and thus interrupts the discussion. He who does so is defeated by way of evasion (*vikṣepa*).
For a discussion must end with the defeat of one of the two parties;
and by conducting the discussion in this manner, he defeats himself by his own hand.
"I have developed a throat obstruction due to a cold; it is not even possible for me to speak a single word.
My mother has passed away; having brought her to the cremation ground, I shall consign her to the flames."

To this he replies: "If, first of all, the task of his mother’s death and so forth has actually occurred from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), then why does this poor fellow lose? Let him not be defeated in debate! Why did he not even cremate his deceased mother? This is a truly great saying!"
Or how could one whose vocal organs and articulations are obstructed by a cold (*pīnasa*) utter speech?
If, in order to conceal this incapacity, he describes such an engagement with business that is even false, then he is truly defeated;
but not by way of distraction, rather by way of something else entirely.

First, the proponent is defeated by resorting to a pretext of having urgent business to attend to, or by shifting to another subject (arthāntara), and so forth; whereas the opponent is defeated solely by lack of ingenuity (apratibhā).
Furthermore, such a manner of instruction would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of the categories.

To this it is replied: that which is called *arthāntara* (an irrelevant digression) occurs when, having commenced a discussion, or having stated a proposition (*pratijñā*) or a reason (*hetu*), one resorts to the pretext of explaining that very point but introduces some other matter—this is what was illustrated at the outset.

But here, in the prelude to the discussion or during the discussion itself, after stating something that merely resembles a task to be performed, one departs from the assembly in fear; how then can there be any similarity between this and *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity)? For in the case of *apratibhā*, one who has heard the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is defeated; whereas here, one either does not hear the prima facie argument at all, or does not even attempt to formulate it.
The significant distinction is that [the opponent] flees at the very outset;
moreover, the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) has been refuted more than once.

As for Kīrti’s claim that this [fallacy of] "procrastination" (*kāryavyāsaṅga*) is included within the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), that is indeed very well said; for where is the fallacy of the reason, and where is procrastination? This is a most delightful deliberation!
Fallacies of the reason are those which appear like reasons while being non-reasons. Our curiosity is great: was it seen by Kīrti that this procrastination, being a non-reason, appears like a reason?
Matānujñā (conceding the opponent's position) is the attribution of a fault to the opponent's position by admitting a similar fault in one's own position. //5.2.22//

When one does not remove a fault imputed to one's own position by the opponent, but instead accepts that very same fault and applies it perversely to the opponent's position, there occurs the point of defeat called *matānujñā* (admission of the opponent's view), because of the acceptance of the other's opinion.
For example, when it is said, "You are a thief, because you are a human being, like a well-known thief," the respondent says, "You too are a thief, because you are a human being.
By speaking in this manner, he has accepted the fault imputed to himself by the opponent; thus, he is defeated through *matānujñā*.

To this it is said: when an opponent has stated a non-conclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*), why is the respondent (*prativādin*) who points that out in this manner defeated? It is the proponent (*vādin*) alone who is defeated for employing a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
To this it is replied: It was stated at the very outset that "the reason is shown to exist even in one who is not a thief, because of the presence of humanity.
For in this way, that fault is removed.
However, by failing to state this and instead saying, "You too are a thief because you possess humanity," you are indeed conceding the opponent's position.

Therefore, when the inconclusiveness [of a reason] ought to be stated, one who disregards the proper order of its presentation and instead incurs an over-extension of the argument certainly becomes subject to defeat.
Furthermore, even when an inconclusive reason has been employed by the proponent, he does not suffer defeat if that inconclusiveness is not pointed out;
for this point of defeat belongs primarily to the opponent alone.
Overlooking the point of defeat when it has been reached is called "neglecting the censurable" (paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa). //5.2.22//

"One who is to be censured" (paryanuyojya) means one who is to be urged by the occurrence of a ground for defeat, such that one should say: "This ground for defeat has come upon you; therefore, you are defeated.
He who overlooks such a person and does not censure them is himself defeated due to "overlooking the censurable" (paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa).

Regarding this, one asks: who brings about this point of defeat for whom—is it the one who should be questioned (*paryanuyojya*), or the one who neglects him? First of all, the one who neglects him does not even know that the other is subject to being questioned; or if he knows, how could he neglect him?

Or, having neglected him, why would he speak thus while manifesting a point of defeat for himself alone, saying: "Although this person was subject to being questioned, I neglected him; therefore, I am defeated"?
"Even though you are subject to censure, why do you not reveal your own fault, saying: 'This is my defect, yet it was not pointed out by you;
therefore, you have been defeated'?"
Indeed, by speaking thus, placing impurity upon his own hand while desiring to defame another, he experiences his own defilement even as he defames the other.

Furthermore, this is not designated as a separate ground for defeat (nigrahasthāna), but rather as simply a lack of ingenuity (apratibhā). For if the proponent of the reply (uttarapākṣika), while explaining the opponent's (pūrvapākṣika) fallacious proof, were to remain indifferent and fail to bring forth a refutation, he would not be defeated by his failure to understand that reply; nor is there defeat through indifference toward what ought to be questioned.

In reality, however, the determination of victory and defeat for both parties in that case is untenable, because one has stated a fallacious proof while the other lacks the presence of mind (apratibhā) to provide a reply to it.

Now, if the proponent (pūrvapakṣika) does not defeat the respondent (uttarapakṣika)— who has fallen into error by propounding a fallacious refutation— nevertheless, the latter's lack of ingenuity (apratibhā) remains a failure to respond. Furthermore, neither victory nor defeat can be determined for either party,
because one is propounding a fallacious refutation while the other fails to point out that fallacy.
To this it is replied: No, because non-ingenuity (*apratibhā*) has as its object a correct proof (*samyaksādhana*).
When a correct proof has been employed, the failure to perceive a response to it constitutes non-ingenuity.
However, when a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) has been employed, the failure to point out its fallacious nature constitutes "overlooking what is to be censured" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*).
In this case, however, the proponent of a fallacious proof (sādhanābhāsavādī) is subject to censure;
he has been disregarded.
But the proponent of a valid proof (samyaksādhanavādī) is indeed not subject to censure—this is the distinction.

As for the fact that, according to the actual state of things, there is neither victory nor defeat for anyone at all—that is indeed so; however, this is called a "point of defeat" (nigrahasthāna) in the context of debate (jalpa), which is an examination of human capacity.

Regarding that which is even imagined by the proponent [of the fallacy], it is said: when a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) has been employed by the proponent (*pūrvapākṣika*) and the opponent (*uttarapākṣika*) has not pointed out its status as such, there is no occasion for the judges (*prāśnika*)—who have not been asked—to speak. At that time, how could that very proponent of the fallacious proof not be defeated if, out of sheer audacity, he should say: "I employed this fallacious proof desiring to test his [opponent's] capacity, but this fool does not recognize it"? By this, the one who employs a fallacious refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*) is also explained.
Alternatively, the assessors— whether requested by both parties or appointed by the presiding judge— who speak in such a manner, certainly censure the one who neglects to raise an objection.
For the statement of a fallacious proof may arise either from deceit on the part of the proponent,
or from ignorance of the correct proof, or from doubt regarding the matter.
But since the proponent of the rejoinder fails to point that out only through delusion, he alone is defeated.
The charging of a ground for defeat where there is no ground for defeat is *niranuyojyānuyoga* (objection against one who is not to be censured). //5.2.23//

If one should say "you are defeated" to someone who has spoken appropriately, without abandoning the proper sequence, who speaks what is relevant, and who is not negligent—even if that person is not deserving of defeat—then it is that very speaker who is defeated by the exposure of a non-existent fault.

Here it is asked: if the proponent of the reply (*uttarapākṣika*) charges the proponent of the prima facie case (*pūrvapākṣika*), who has stated a faultless proof, with faults that are entirely non-existent, then since he fails to provide a reply that points out actual faults, he should be defeated by the very ground of defeat known as "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*); why then is he defeated by the new ground of defeat called "charging what is not to be charged" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*)? On the other hand, in the case where he charges with actual faults, the proponent of the prima facie case is indeed one against whom a charge could be made due to his employment of fallacious proofs; thus, he ought not to be the object of the charge of "charging what is not to be charged."
Regarding this, it is said:
"Alas! This poor fellow, failing to perceive the distinction between a relative negation (*paryudāsa*) and an absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), is utterly deluded.
The non-appearance of an actual fault is one thing, and the appearance of a non-existent fault is another."
In one case there is non-comprehension, and in the other, a distorted comprehension.

Among these, non-comprehension regarding an actual fault constitutes *apratibhā* (inability to respond); the attribution of a fault that has not occurred constitutes *ananuyojyānuyoga* (objection against what is not to be objected to).
Furthermore, regarding that which you have declared to be points of defeat— namely, the statement of non-essential members of a proof and the failure to point out a fault— it is now being discussed.

In that case, if one were to rely solely on absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), even fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) would not constitute points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); rather, only the failure to state a member of the proof (*sādhana-aṅga*)—that is, mere silence—would be a point of defeat.
Therefore, the statement of what is not a member of the proof and the failure to point out a fault (*adoṣodbhāvana*) must indeed be explained through relative negation (*paryudāsa*).

Consequently, the failure to point out an actual fault is *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity), and the pointing out of a non-existent fault is *niranuyojyānuyoga* (reproaching one who should not be reproached).

If it is argued that even when one points out a non-existent fault, the inability to respond regarding an actual fault certainly exists, and therefore that alone should be the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), then silence alone would be the only point of defeat; for it has already been stated that the same could be said regarding the failure to state a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*).
An apasiddhānta (departure from a tenet) occurs when, having accepted a tenet, one proceeds with the discussion without restriction. //5.2.24//
Whoever initiates a debate after first accepting a certain tenet,

yet while so engaged, asserts something contrary to that tenet— either out of haste in supporting the point they wish to prove or out of a desire to refute an objection— is defeated by the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

For example, a Sāṃkhya, in the presence of an opponent, first propounds his own established tenet: "The non-existent has no coming into being; the existent has no ceasing to exist. Then, in order to establish the Pradhāna (the primordial cause), he employs a formal argument for proof: "The manifest world of transformations must have a single primordial cause, because it is observed to be permeated by a common nature. For the various products of clay, such as jars, bowls, and basins, are seen to have a single primordial cause when they are permeated by clay. Likewise, since this manifest world of transformations—cows, horses, and so forth—is observed to be permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion, it must necessarily originate from a single primordial cause whose essence consists of those [three qualities]."
When he had spoken thus, he was questioned by the Naiyāyika: "Now, what is called *prakṛti* (primordial nature), and what is *vikṛti* (modification)?
For how could one who does not know the true nature of *prakṛti* and *vikṛti* understand that modifications have a single *prakṛti* as their source, or that they are of one essence?

Being thus questioned, the follower of Kapila replied: "That which, while remaining constant, undergoes the cessation of one attribute (*dharma*) and the emergence of another attribute, is *prakṛti*."
"That other property which arises is the modification"—

by speaking thus, he is defeated by the fallacy of *apasiddhānta* (deviation from a tenet), because he asserts something that contradicts his previously accepted doctrine that there is no arising or ceasing of what is existent or non-existent.

If there is the manifestation of another dharma upon the cessation of a previous dharma, then your own established tenet—that "the existence of the non-existent does not occur, nor does the non-existence of the existent"—is abandoned.

Alternatively, if that tenet is not abandoned, then because the distinction between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*) would be uncertain, the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished, which results in the non-existence of the probandum (*sādhya*).

To this, [the opponent] says: "When Kapila has formulated his logical argument, the Naiyāyika stands in opposition by pointing out its unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*). What occasion is there for a question regarding the essential nature of the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modifications (*vikṛti*)? This would be a case of the Naiyāyika shifting to a different subject matter (*arthāntara*)."

For one who asks in this manner, "shifting to another matter" (*arthāntara*) is declared in one's own treatise to be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); yet now, you employ that very same thing—what kind of logic is this? If the Sāṃkhya doctrine is what you wish to refute, then the reason should have been exposed as being simply unestablished (*asiddha*), on the grounds that the continuity of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is impossible in its transformations (*vikāra*).
For a transformation is characterized by the properties of arising and ceasing.

Furthermore, if the unmanifest were of such a nature [as you claim], then because it would follow the properties of the unmanifest, the very essence of modifications—consisting of their emergence and cessation—would be lost. Thus, since the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), the Sāṃkhya is defeated precisely by the employment of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*); therefore, "contradiction of one's own tenet" (*apasiddhānta*) is not a separate ground for defeat.
To this it is replied: It is true that this reason (hetu) devised by the followers of Kapila is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Indeed, its lack of establishment can be determined even through the sequence of questions regarding what is a primary cause (*prakṛti*) and what is a modification (*vikṛti*). However, once the form of the reason has been determined, its refutation must be stated; for it is impossible to refute that which has not been determined. Thus, the inquiry into that [nature of the reason] does not constitute a departure from the subject matter (*arthāntara*).

Speaking only in terms of question and answer, one has entered the domain of another ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)—namely, the statement of an "unestablished conclusion" (*apasiddhānta*) that flashes forth in close proximity during the process of reflection; thus, one does not travel far on the path of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
When even a single cause for the subjugation of another has first entered the path of the heart, no other reason need be considered; for what indeed is the fruit of grinding what is already ground?
And fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are as previously described. //5.2.25//

"But fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), being characterized by the very definitions previously stated, become points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) when they occur as described; for this reason, he [the author] spoke thus."
The state of being an object of cognition for the means of cognition, and the state of being a means of cognition for the object of cognition—
just as these are seen to be distinct by way of their defining characteristics, so it is not observed in these [cases].

For what purpose have these been stated separately? The reasoning for this has already been explained here previously: indeed, those skilled in the method of logic should employ these in debate to effect the purification of reality.
Furthermore, even Dharmakīrti had no disagreement regarding these distinctions of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Thus, following the tradition of the Sūtra-author without neglecting the scope of the Bhāṣya, refuting the opinions of others at various points through my incomparable skill,
and composing even some reflections on the meaning of sentences, I have here, in due order, precisely determined these sixteen categories within my own treatise.

Victorious is the sage Akṣapāda, whose feet rest upon the bowing heads of many great ṛṣis who are prostrate in their longing for the nectar of his knowledge; he by whom the Lord of Gaurī was gratified through debate with his profound and pure speech issuing from logic—just as the god [Śiva] in the form of a Kirāta was gratified in battle by Kirīṭin—and who thus obtained noble boons.
He who was renowned as Jayanta, having achieved victory in debates and being the leader of the virtuous; whom the wise praise by the meaningful name of the author of the *Navavṛtti*;
the son of that moon whose fame pervaded the quarters of the earth with its lunar luster—he, a meditator on the feet of Him whose crest is the crescent moon, has composed this blessed work.
Homage to Śambhu, whose beauty of the crescent sprout is comparable to ten million digits of the moon,
and who is a wish-fulfilling tree for the intentions of those who have sought refuge in him.
